https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Pochettino: I’d tell Guardiola to ‘take it’ if he’s offered US coaching job
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer in Cincinnati and Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Outgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.
So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.
“You know what I noticed?” Pochettino asked, smiling as he recounted the story during a meeting with reporters on Monday. “[Guardiola had a] good relationship with JT.”
Back then, Pochettino didn’t seem to be going anywhere. Only a month earlier, he’d signed a four-year contract to guide the US through the 2030 World Cup. Guardiola was, and still is, in the middle of a year-long sabbatical from coaching. He remains the federation’s white whale, often mentioned in the same breath as the US job over the past decade-plus but just as quickly dismissed as a pipe dream.
Just three months after taking in that game at Yankee Stadium, Pochettino is on his way to Manchester United and Guardiola has once again found himself at the center of the rumor mill, with reports suggesting that he and US Soccer are set for exploratory talks.
On Monday, Pochettino was asked what he’d tell the Barcelona and Manchester City legend if he was asked for his opinion on the US job.
“Take it,” Pochettino said, flatly. “Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation. Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style.”
Guardiola was one of many topics the Argentinian manager covered during the roundtable, which lasted about an hour. At times defiant, at times emotional and cycling through Spanish and English, Pochettino spoke of his potential legacy at US Soccer, what lies ahead for him at United and how he views soccer in America as a whole.
Quotes have been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
On assessing players regardless of league level
However you assess his results, one of the inarguable successes of the Pochettino era are the relatively unheralded players whose status has risen over his tenure. The Argentine cited defender Alex Freeman and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter as two such examples, both of whom were playing in MLS when making their national team debuts under Pochettino and both now playing in Europe. Asked how he assesses players to add to the national team, and how he compares players across different leagues and playing styles, Pochettino insisted that the level of competition matters less than individual form.
“You need to project the individual player,” Pochettino said. “Because he’s playing well, the level is no issue. That player can be good, like Freeman, like Sebastian. That is the example, and I think that is so important. There is talent everywhere … This one is one of the things that we learn – all [of us], we were young and then we start to be a coach, no? That we cannot make a mistake [and] measure the level of the player because of the level of the league.”
On managing a club v managing a national team
With the US being his first international job, there were some doubts going in about how Pochettino would adapt to coaching without daily contact with his players and staff.
“I am ready [to return]. This is what I miss a little bit. I miss to be, every day, with something here,” Pochettino said. “Guardiola asked me when I was at the game, he said, ‘Oh, you don’t want to come back to the Premier League?’ I said, ‘No, I’m happy here.’ [He said] ‘Yeah, but you don’t miss, every day, to…’ I say, ‘A little bit, yes, because you think now today, and then we have December camp against Jamaica for the MLS [players in the pool]. But after, you need to wait [until] March. What do you do? You need to watch games, you need to travel – administrative things. That is nice, it’s good. But every day, to be involved: press conference, training, everything … this type of possibility, like with United, you say yes. I want that. I want to prove myself again.”
But what did Pochettino think of his maiden international job?
“I like and not like,” he said. “I like because it provides you the possibility to manage your time, to be busy, but at the same time, be free and to have some time with your family. Now, I have a grandchild, and [number] two is coming. You can share the life with your people. But now, ciao, because now is [gestures] tra-tra-tra-tra-tra. It’s impossible to spend time with the people you want.”
On the perceived status of the US coaching gig
In the grand scheme of international football, the US national team coaching job has never been close to the top of the list of most desirable destinations. Pochettino’s hire was seen as a possible sign that could be changing. Now, after nearly two years in the position, Pochettino believes it has.
“The vision from Europe, I promise it is completely different after the World Cup,” Pochettino said. “Now, being head coach of the USA is more prestigious. If Manchester United, or Real Madrid, or Barcelona is coming for the US coach, if you start to think about that, if you are another coach – maybe [Antonio] Conte, someone else, you say ‘oh, this is a great opportunity.’ [In my case], ‘Oh, Pochettino, from Chelsea he goes to the US? And now to Manchester United.’
On one thing he’d change about soccer in the United States
Pochettino has coached some of the most famous players and clubs in the world, giving him a unique perspective on how soccer has developed in the US. Pochettino stopped short of prescribing neat solutions to improve the sport, though.
“I think that business [and] the sport, is [done] in a holistic way. Everything is important, and you cannot pick one. You cannot change one [thing], and that can change everything,” he said. “I think it’s a little bit of everything that you need to change. If you adjust this, you need to adjust this. The balance of the thing changes if you touch here, that will force you to touch all the areas in soccer here, or in the world To find the good balance, no? A process of little by little, is all that we made in these last two years. I think it’s the beginning of [a process]. If that has continuity, it’s the beginning of the new soccer in the USA that can be.
“I think that is, for me, the beginning of the change for the future: that idea that the American player can be very good, can be very competitive. The talent is here; it’s so powerful in this country. I think that is why I feel proud. Maybe that was our job, because I don’t believe in coincidence. That has happened because something needed to happen. Now the tough job is done. Maybe now [the United job] is my reward because of this tough job.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.title: After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.text:
In one of Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s prison drawings, swans skim a swimming pool inside a cell. In another, a clownish figure peers over the prison wall, perched with apparent ease on barbed wire. The Cuban artist and leader of the San Isidro Movement made thousands of such works in Guanajay, a maximum-security prison outside Havana, where he served time after his arrest on July 11, 2021, amid anti-government protests across the island. His release this year, after international outcry over creative freedom, was contingent on exile to the United States. A small selection of those works makes up “Tocar el cielo,” their first public showing, now at the New York gallery Foreign & Domestic (curated by Alexander Meurice, and on view through December 13).
Art that emerges from incarceration tends to speak first in material, with scarcity making resourcefulness something like a protagonist. Otero Alcántara recounted drawing on drink cartons and cigarette packs, and smuggling in colored ink that ended up on other prisoners’ skin, when bodies were canvas enough. Who gets to make art inside, and who can get supplies to them, comes with its own politics. But he describes his five years in prison as one long performance, an “involuntary artistic gesture,” and the show reflects rather than transcribes the specifics of injustice. It’s an oblique testimony to how, bereft of sky or savior, the mind can slip its confines.
ARTnews spoke with Otero Alcántara via email about his experience making art in prison, and settling into his second life in Miami. The following conversation has been translated from Spanish and condensed for publication.
ARTnews: How is your spirit these days? What has surprised you most about settling into life here?
Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara: I think it’s been a shock. It’s unsettling, and it scares me a little.
People outside Cuba could connect with my work, but it grew out of life in the neighborhood, out of my connection with the people there. Above all, it came from knowing that neighborhood called Cuba, that neighborhood called Havana, where I was like a fish in water.
In New York, I’m getting to know other ways of thinking, other ways of doing things. I’m learning how art relates to people here and how people relate to art. There’s the language barrier, too. In my own practice, I want art to disappear into the social fabric, into people’s lives. I want it to have a real effect on the person walking down the street.
I feel like an embryo, like I’m learning from scratch how art and people relate to one another. So yes, it scares me. I’d call it a difficult process, but it’s a living process.
Can you tell me about making art in prison? How did you get supplies, and when did you work? What did materials typically cost you?
I started making art the moment I set foot in prison. They put me in a punishment cell, and I spent about two or three months there. Before prison, I was detained more than 50 times in three years. Even if they only held me for two or three days, I always made something in the cell. At first, I didn’t have the materials I had later. When I finished a drink my family had brought me, I’d keep the carton and draw on it. I used cigarette packs too. I’d stitch them together to make a surface I could draw on.
Once the materials from home ran out, my friends sent me more. When I called, all those friends of mine—Yanelys Núñez, Claudia Genlui, Coco Fusco, Camila Lobón, Anamely Ramos—picked up the phone. That was an act of resistance and an act of friendship. They took money they could have spent on food or on things they needed and used it to send me good art supplies, really good ones, all the way to Cuba, into the prison where I was being held.
That’s what I mean by cultural resistance. For my friends, it meant keeping the art alive and keeping the artist alive. They taught me how good it is to have a friend, and how good it is to be one.
Can you tell me about the recurring figure in the prison cell works? You’ve depicted him as a clown. Who does he represent? Who, or what, is the joke?
The clown keeps coming back in my work. When I look back at everything I made in prison, from beginning to end, I can see that the figures in those first drawings and paintings really were clowns. Over time, all that was left of the clown was the nose and traces of this strange makeup that gradually broke down. The colors started to bleed into one another. I feel that had something to do with how I was changing, how I was growing older in prison. At one point, even the paper tears. I tear it. I don’t know if it was hatred, if I was channeling hatred through my hands, or frustration. I don’t know why it was a clown.
As for the question about the joke, I remember being on hunger strike once, in a group of prisoners that included several men who’d protested on July 11. We’d become friends in there. They were getting sentences of ten years, eight years, five years. It literally seemed like a joke.
	To me, the whole thing felt like a circus, like watching a show, only this show had real consequences for people’s lives. So if there’s a joke in it, if there’s an irony, that’s where I see it. They put up this whole circus tent. What happens under it affects so many people’s lives, and none of it makes any sense.
What was it like to go years without seeing your whole reflection?
In prison, there was a tiny mirror. Mirrors are prized possessions in there. You hold yours out and someone in another cell, maybe three or six feet away, holds his out too. And there, in that little piece of mirror, you can see the other man’s face. You can see when a guard is coming.
If your mirror is only four inches across, all you ever see of yourself is a piece of your face. You never see your whole body. You go into prison looking one way and come out looking another. The first time I stood in front of a full-length mirror again, it was like coming back to see someone and finding myself face to face with a new person.
I think that found its way into my work. I have a series of self-portraits where my features start to disappear. They’re smudges, scratches, moods. Most of the work I made in prison was like that. I painted states of mind.
	The only portraits that came close to being realistic were the ones I made of my friends. It was all about memory. I wanted to keep existing in my friends’ minds, and I wanted to remember them, too.
Two of your works involve faith: a cross, and beside it a pile of idols sinking into an abyss. What is the relationship between your art and faith?
My art has a lot to do with faith and religion. For me, those are two different things. Both are tied to being Cuban. And for as long as I can remember, people have had faith that the system would fall, that the dictatorship would come to an end, that life would get better.
In Cuba, you have very little power to change the reality you live in. There’s no democracy, and the system makes you feel like you can’t fend for yourself. On the island, you’re always waiting for somebody on the outside to save you. And by “save you,” I mean a cousin or a brother sending you money. It’s like having faith in a god who lives somewhere out there, some kind of extraterrestrial being who’s going to keep you going on the island. You put your faith in finding a girlfriend or a boyfriend who has money, or in a foreigner coming along, marrying you and taking you away. The system is so rigid that you have very little room to change your own circumstances.
Before prison, I made performances that drew on images of the Virgin Mary and the saints. What interests me is how these objects change the way people behave, how they shape a culture, and how those in power use them to manipulate people.
Prison is maybe one of the last places where you lose whatever say you still had over your own life. Your future is in the hands of a prosecutor or whoever else gets to decide. It’s like living in a jungle where a lion decides which animal it wants to eat that day, and you pray it won’t be you.
Confinement also brings you face-to-face with yourself. You get in touch with something more visceral in yourself, something more animal. And all you’re left with is the faith that tomorrow might be better.
That reminds me of a story about a friend of mine in prison. He’d been waiting a year or so for his trial, and he was getting desperate. Nothing had been proven against him.
One day he used the five minutes a week they gave him on the phone to call his lawyer. He said, “Hey, tell me something. Any news?”
His lawyer said, “Don’t worry. Last night I dreamed they were going to let you go.”
In another work, a maze fills the cell. Is it a way out or another kind of trap?
I think the labyrinth has to do with how you feel in prison. When you’re in prison, you really have no way out. But there’s also the question of what you can do with that one small space. You have to turn it into your own amusement park. For me, the labyrinth is about the thousand ways you have to reinvent one space to survive in it.
There’s also something about getting lost so you can find yourself again, and finding yourself only to get lost again. As time goes by, you get tangled up in nostalgia, in sadness, in forgetting. You feel whole places in your mind starting to disappear, and you find yourself holding on to the memory of them.
Your practice is so community-driven. How did you keep that part of yourself alive in solitary?
The place where I lived was called Pasillo 20, Corridor 20. It was in the maximum-security section at Guanajay, cut off from most of the other prisoners. For five years, I lived among about 20 men.
Some of the men painted or drew. I started what I called the San Isidro Grants. For two or three months, as long as my money lasted, I gave some money to men who painted and bought them materials so they could keep painting. I brought in art history books and gave them away.
I also made work outside the prison while I was still inside. One piece that mattered a lot to me was Momento Cero, which I made with Coco Fusco. People counted down the days I had left in prison. There was also Fe de vida. During the Havana Biennial, we invited curators and artists to come to visit me in prison. Reaching out to people outside was connected to what I was doing with the men I lived with, finding ways to make room for community, kindness and love in a place that was so violent.
You arrived in the United States at a moment when artists here are facing censorship and funding cuts on a scale I haven’t seen in my lifetime. What has it been like to land in this context?
First of all, I feel like I haven’t quite landed here yet. I mean that physically, in my body, but also in my thinking and how I see things as an artist. What I can say is that the little I’ve seen and heard here doesn’t come close to the lack of freedom in Cuba.
Now I’ve come to a country I hope will be a place of passage for me. When you speak from New York, your words carry more legitimacy than if you’re speaking from, say, Havana or Haiti. I don’t know why the world gives that so much weight. Well, yes, I do know why.
Coming here, I can see that this country is going through a transition, a crisis. There’s conflict in the relationships between institutions, art, and artists. I think this is a moment when artists have to take responsibility. We can use art to resist, to change things, and to put forward a vision of a better world.
Do you see any parallels between what you experienced in Cuba and what’s happening here, or do you see them as fundamentally different?
The danger in drawing a parallel is that someone can always say, “Look what happens to people in Cuba. That doesn’t happen to you here. You’ve got me to thank for that, so you have to do what I say.” That’s where populism comes in. If you understand which freedoms an American artist enjoys and what artists elsewhere have to live without, you have a starting point. You can defend the ground you’ve gained and recognize when someone is using those freedoms to blackmail you.
We need to keep those differences in view. That’s how we recognize what we’ve already won as a nation and keep fighting for the freedoms we still need.
How have Cubans on the island and in the diaspora responded to the politics of your release and to your ability to keep making art in prison?
I think my art and the art of my generation, the work of the San Isidro Movement and others, have had an impact on Cuba, both on the island and in the diaspora. It’s only been five years since July 11, 2021, and people already recognize the part that my work, and the art we made together in San Isidro, played in the spirit of rebellion that emerged in 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021.
For me, those five years in prison are one big work of art, one long performance. I call it “an involuntary artistic gesture.” The dictatorship acts on my body against my will, and what it does to me provokes an aesthetic response in other people.
The other thing that matters is social media and everything that played out there when I arrived in the United States. What struck me was how it exposed some bad habits that have taken hold in the way Cubans use social media. I’m talking about people acting irresponsibly. Some influencers have learned how to make money on YouTube, Facebook and Instagram. Controversy brings in viewers, and viewers bring in money.
What matters most to me is what I’ve experienced walking the streets of Miami. From 99 percent of the people I’ve met, if not 100 percent, what I’ve felt is affection. I’ve felt love.
When you think about what art is for and what an artist owes the world, has your view changed since prison?
I think art is one of the tools we have as human beings to transform society and culture. And when I say culture, I mean it in the broadest sense, right down to the way we behave. Those in power know what art can do. They use it when it serves their interests. When it doesn’t, they go after it. They try to put art itself in prison.
Art is one of the teeth on the gear that keeps society moving. And the artist is the one who thinks, who proposes something, who puts their own body on the line. So, I think the artist bears the greatest responsibility.
An artist’s responsibility extends to humanity as a whole. There’s a commitment to humanism there: understanding that you have power and, more than that, a responsibility. Because if you don’t use your art to help people, someone else will use it for purposes that don’t help them.
When you picture your studio, or your next show, a year from now, what do you see?
A year from now, I’d love the work I brought out of Guanajay to have found homes in archives, museums and private collections. I want someone standing there to get a sense of what one human being lived through in confinement. I was a Cuban in prison. I was also a human being locked up. Someone in a prison anywhere in the world could go through what I went through, you know? For my studio, what I want is room to work and room to try things. There are sculptures I want to propose, ideas I couldn’t develop in Cuba because of the repression.
I also hope I’ll have helped more Americans understand something about Cuba. Our two peoples are so close, yet there’s still a romantic view of Cuba here, and that has consequences for us Cubans. Fidel Castro was a dictator. We’ve lived under a dictatorship for more than 60 years.
	More than anything, I’d like people in the arts here to understand our work and make room for it in the stories and images that are part of everyday American life. What happens on that island finds echoes in so many other places.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Big wave surfers line up to ride ‘raw power of the Pacific’ during Super El-Niño swells
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lois Beckett
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
While this year’s Super El Niño storms are battering the California coast and destroying homes and infrastructure, surfers are finding a silver lining: waves so epic that pro athletes from around the world are making last-minute journeys to experience them.
Big wave surfers converged on northern California this Saturday to ride massive, storm-driven swells at the famously dangerous Mavericks Beach, an event some surf fans called “Monster Day.”
Kai Lenny, an American pro surfer, Clément Roseyro, a French big wave surfer, Jamie Mitchell, an Australian big wave surfer, Lucas “Chumbo” Chianca, a Brazilian pro surfer, and Luca Padua, a local star surfer who is from Half Moon Bay, were among those who risked the waves this weekend.
Lai wrote on Instagram that he “nearly didn’t make it” to Mavericks over the weekend after “all flights were grounded nationwide”, but that he was one of the lucky few to make it to San Francisco, which is just 20 miles north of Mavericks, near Half Moon Bay, California. Justine Dupont, a French pro surfer, wrote on social media that she had been heading to Mavericks, but was “locked in the Boston airport”, the Washington Post reported.
The conditions on Saturday were so rough that even some experienced big wave surfers decided not to risk it: “If the waves are 60ft and you’re not feeling 100%, the stakes are just way too high,” Bianca Valenti, an American pro surfer who has surfed Mavericks many times, said in a social media post.
Surfer Ridge Lenny, Kai’s brother, called the day “very wild” and “frankly terrifying”, in an Instagram post.
Others described the Mavericks El Niño surf as “no joke” and “survival mode”.
Mitchell, the Australian big wave surfer, found himself crushed by one of the waves on Saturday, and though he triggered his inflatable safety vest, the power of the ocean was so strong that the vest “ripped off”, photographer Fred Pompermayer wrote on Instagram. “This is the raw power of the Pacific.”
“The waves were breaking in areas that they almost never break in … You’re talking six, seven stories-plus,” Grant Washburn, a longtime local surfer, who watched the action at Mavericks, told the San Francisco Chronicle.
It “took all my years of experience to survive that”, Mitchell wrote on Instagram.
But some of those who risked the six-story waves, such as Lenny, produced jaw-dropping footage of their exploits.
“Well hello El Niño ... it’s good to see you,” surf filmmaker Tucker Wooding wrote.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there had been ‘no change in Russia’s position’ as Russia and Ukraine strike major infrastructure.
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.
“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.
Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.
US envoy reports progress, warns of difficult choices
Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.
He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.
The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.
Europe prepares to join, Moscow withholds agreement
Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.
Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.
European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”
Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.
“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.
Russia rules out a temporary respite
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.
He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.
Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.
“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”
The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

Cadre territorial en Seine-Saint-Denis, infirmière en oncologie à Rouen et professeur des écoles en région parisienne, Thibaut, Mathilde et Basile ont tous trois fait des études supérieures et exercent, par choix, un métier à forte utilité sociale dans le secteur public. À mesure que leur pouvoir d’achat s’érode, ces agents peinent à se construire la vie à laquelle leur statut leur permettait d’aspirer.
Leur choix professionnel ne doit rien au hasard. Il s’agit avant tout d’un engagement au service du bien commun pour Basile, Thibaut et Mathilde 1. « Je voulais un métier où il y avait du travail, qui soit utile et qui puisse me plaire. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Freeman Johnson, oldest survivor of Pearl Harbor attack, dies aged 106
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Auzzy Byrdsell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The oldest known survivor of the Pearl Harbor attack died Saturday aged 106 years old. Freeman Johnson, a fireman below the deck during the attack, died in his home in Massachusetts, according to the Boston Globe.
Only 11 known Pearl Harbor survivors are still living, all of whom are centenarians.
At 21 years old, Johnson said, he never saw the attacks from the Japanese fighters that Sunday morning in Hawaii on 7 December 1941.
He worked on the USS St Louis, which was his first deployment after basic training. It was the only major ship that left the attack “unscathed”, according to the Pentagon. The ship graced the nickname “Lucky Lou”.
“While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” Johnson told the Associated Press in May.
Johnson heard machine guns and felt vibrations while he was reading that morning.
“That was the first sign we knew something was wrong,” he told the Boston Globe in 2018.
He was tasked with fixing parts of the ship’s boilers as another member of the crew passed the boiler’s pieces to Johnson.
Johnson said, however, that his work during Pearl Harbor didn’t make him heroic, nor was it a source of his pride.
“I wasn’t brave, I was there,” he said last year in a Pacific Historic Parks interview. “I just did what I was told. I did my job.”
His pride, instead, came when he married his late wife Ruth Hills in 1950. They went on to have three daughters, served as foster parents to several others and eventually had two grandchildren.
After leaving the navy, he worked several jobs including at a machine shop for 40 years, a convenience store and delivering meals to seniors. He formally retired at 90 and eventually lived with his daughter Diane Johnson until he died.
“It’s going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving,” Diane Johnson told the Associated Press. “He’s going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.
During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.
“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.
Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.
The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.
The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.
Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.
Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.
“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”
Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.
Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/lycees/u.title: Un observateur de la LDH blessé par des CRS : que s’est-il vraiment passé au lycée Pierre-Gilles-de-Gennes à Paris ?
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/lycees/u.author: Tania Meller
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/lycees/u.text:
Les CRS ont brutalement chargé des élèves pour lever un blocus pacifique, lundi 16 novembre devant le lycée Pierre-Gilles-de-Gennes à Paris (13e). Un observateur de la LDH a été blessé. Les professeurs du lycée dénoncent une intervention « disproportionnée », et un recours aux forces de sécurité « contre-productif et source de tensions ».
Du calme au chaos. Les élèves du lycée Pierre-Gilles-de-Gennes (13e) avaient organisé un blocage filtrant devant les grilles lundi 16 novembre. Une action réalisée dans le calme, jusqu’à l’arrivée des CRS pour dégager les entrées du lycée par la force.
L’établissement figurait sur la liste des lycées où tout rassemblement ou manifestation non déclarés étaient prohibés « dans un rayon de 100 mètres ». Un arrêté pris dimanche 15 novembre, contesté en référé par l’Unef devant le tribunal administratif de Paris ce lundi.
Présent sur les lieux dès 8 heures du matin, Pierre (le prénom a été modifié), un observateur de la LDH a pu constater la brutalité des CRS. « Ils sont arrivés à 8 h 30, avec neuf camions. Les jeunes ont commencé à bloquer les rues dans lesquelles ils avaient garé les camions avec des poubelles et des vélos. Le commandant des CRS est venu à leur rencontre pour discuter. » Le dialogue s’engage, et les manifestants lèvent leurs barricades et mettent les poubelles le long du trottoir.
« Puis, sans aucune sommation, les CRS ont chargé, raconte Pierre. Ils sont allés au contact des élèves avec leur bouclier. Moi j’ai été pris en sandwich entre deux lignes de CRS. Ils m’ont bloqué contre les poubelles, j’étais coincé. J’ai pris des coups au niveau des côtes et un coup de poing dans la tête. J’ai vraiment eu peur, c’était ignoble. » Son médecin a constaté ses blessures et fixé un jour d’ITT. Des parents d’élèves présents sur les lieux ont aussi été menacés de verbalisation.
Les personnels du lycée dénoncent l’intervention des CRS
Face à ce déchaînement de violences policières « disproportionné », les professeurs et personnels du lycée font part de leur « inquiétude » face à « la présence massive de CRS devant le lycée ». Ils rappellent « qu’il n’y a eu ni dégradations, ni tirs de mortiers, ni menaces à l’égard des personnels depuis le début du mouvement. »
Dans un communiqué envoyé par voie hiérarchique à la rectrice de Paris, Julie Benetti, ils rappellent « qu’un tel déploiement est contre-productif et source de tensions. Il génère de l’anxiété chez les élèves, y compris celles et ceux qui ne participent pas au mouvement. »
Les personnels trouvent par ailleurs « choquant que l’intervention des CRS pour lever le blocus se soit faite sur le mode de la charge et que les CRS menacent même de verbaliser les collègues et les parents d’élèves présents, alors qu’ils tentaient d’apaiser la situation. »
Face à la stratégie du pourrissement adoptée par le gouvernement et le recours systématique à la police pour lever les blocages, le personnel éducatif du lycée redoute que de « telles interventions ne permettent pas de sortie de crise et (…) aggravent la situation. » Comment leur donner tort ?
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Third US aircraft carrier brings thousands more troops to Middle East
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.
The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.
The George HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.
In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.
The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.
The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.
Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.
Last week, Trump warned Iran that the US military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.
Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.
Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.
In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.
Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.
Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.
Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.
Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.
US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade.
Independent assessments from Lloyd’s List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/mamda.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/mamda.text:
Mamdani to disband special NYPD unit deployed during pro-Palestinian protests
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday that he will keep his campaign promise to disband the New York Police Department's Strategic Response Group (SRG) and replace it with “de-escalation groups”.
The armour-clad SRG is made up of 500 highly trained NYPD officers who have become infamous for their “crowd control tactics” and mass arrests during protests in New York City, where they use batons, tear gas, pepper spray and other “de-escalation” weapons on disruptive protesters.
The group came under particular scrutiny during pro-Palestine protests during the height of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and campus protests led by the student movement that started at Columbia University.
New York Civil Liberties Union executive director Donna Lieberman applauded the move and said, “These important changes will make protests safer and allow more New Yorkers to raise their voices”.
Police commissioner Jessica Tisch told ABC7 that despite the disbandment of the SRG, “New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to" and that "nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions”.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
But a press release from the NYC mayor's office says there will be significant change in how police interact with protesters.
“This overhaul will transform how the City prepares for and responds to protests, placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest,” the statement said.
Civilian-led unit
The SRG will be replaced with a “civilian-led” unit called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division from the mayor's Office of Safety and Community, and will look to improve the NYPD’s protest response through a “specialized dialogue team” called the First Amendment Support Team. The team will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation.
In this SRG overhaul, the mayor's office also announced the Patrol Support Division, a group of vetted officers who will receive specialised training to arrest protesters in “rare instances”.
The act outlaws many things that Mamdani announced his administration was attempting to do away with, including certain crowd-control methods during protests like kettling, tear gas, and pepper spray for mass crowd control. The use of long guns will be prohibited, and long-range acoustic devices will be limited to 90 decibels.
It also imposes a public reporting mandate requiring the NYPD to report every three months on how and where it was deployed.
In Mamdani’s SRG disbandment announcement video, he also endorsed the CURB Act, which was introduced and authored by Assemblyman Chi Osse. The CURB Act stands for Communities United to Reject Police Brutality, which is meant to strengthen First Amendment protections by curtailing aggressive tactics that the NYPD can use on protesters.
In Monday's press release, Mayor Mamdani said: “New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation. These reforms accomplish the key changes called for by Councilmember Chi Ossé’s CURB Act - a bill I am proud to support. Protecting New Yorkers’ rights and keeping our communities safe go hand in hand.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
Ethiopia’s unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands.
Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement.
The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume.
The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services.
A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations.
The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal.
A territorial dispute reignites violence
According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), the latest escalation began on October 18, when Somali regional police clashed with ethnic Oromo militia members following the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed locality of Moyale.
The conflict monitor’s East Africa senior analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru, reported that a 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed during the confrontation. However, accounts of how she died differ: some people said she was caught in crossfire, while others claimed she was killed after trying to remove the flag.
Members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened and stopped the initial fighting, according to ACLED. The following day, Oromo residents staged a demonstration against the office opening and the girl’s death, blocking the main road and forcing businesses to close.
Elders and security officials from both sides later agreed to remove the Somali regional flag and suspend the office’s opening. However, the agreement did not prevent further confrontations. ACLED reported that Somali residents also demonstrated against the arrangement on October 20, closing the main road and disrupting transport services.
Fighting escalated again on October 22, when Somali regional police clashed with Oromia regional police and Oromo militia members in several locations in Moyale. ACLED also reported clashes involving Oromo and Somali militias in parts of Arero and Wachile districts.
The violence is rooted in longstanding disagreements over administrative boundaries, political representation and access to land and natural resources. These disputes have repeatedly fuelled tensions between Borana Oromo and Somali communities along the regional border.
Federal government under pressure to intervene
A security official familiar with the situation in Moyale told Al Jazeera that clashes were continuing and that attempts to broker an agreement between representatives of the Oromia and Somali regional administrations had failed. He said resolving the crisis required direct and immediate involvement by the federal government.
The federal government’s role has consequently become a central question in efforts to contain the violence. Although members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened during the initial October 18 confrontation, ACLED documented further clashes involving regional police and militia members from October 22 onwards.
The crisis has also drawn attention beyond Ethiopia’s borders. On November 9, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said he had spoken with his Ethiopian counterpart and urged the government in Addis Ababa to help restore stability so that people who had fled into Kenya could return home.
Reporting by Kenya’s The Star newspaper said Mudavadi put the number of Ethiopians who had crossed into Kenya at approximately 40,000 at the time. He said the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it would work towards restoring normality.
Unresolved boundaries and political tensions
Cameron Hudson, a political and security analyst and former director for African affairs at the US National Security Council, said the crisis reflected wider challenges facing Ethiopia’s federal system and its management of regional disputes.
Hudson said federal forces were already preoccupied with security challenges elsewhere in the country. He also pointed to a perception among Somali communities that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party favour the Oromo, Abiy’s ethnic group.
Hudson said previous mediation efforts had largely failed because the territorial dispute along the regional border remained unresolved.
The historical background includes a referendum organised on October 24, 2004, to determine the administration of 463 small communities along the Oromia-Somali regional border, according to Ethiopia’s National Election Board.
However, research by Boku Tache, published in a doctoral thesis at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences in 2008, found that the referendum was conducted in Liban and parts of Arero, while the Moyale case remained unresolved.
The research also examined how displacement, competing claims over grazing land and access to traditional resources contributed to tensions between Borana and Somali communities. These historical disputes continue to provide important context for the current confrontation.
Hudson added that successive Ethiopian governments had failed to engage local communities to address the underlying causes of territorial tensions, instead responding after violence had erupted.
The humanitarian consequences have extended beyond Ethiopia. On October 28, the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) said local authorities estimated that up to 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya since October 22 to escape the fighting. The agency said registration and verification were continuing, meaning the figure remained provisional.
Many of those arriving in Kenya were women and children, according to the UNHCR, which identified food, drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and healthcare as urgent needs.
For residents in the affected areas, immediate priorities remain the restoration of security and the resumption of livelihoods. With the territorial dispute unresolved and the two regional administrations yet to reach a lasting agreement, uncertainty continues over when affected communities will be able to return to normal life.
“The federal government is ultimately responsible for addressing violence, even along regional borders,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.

https://taz.de/Deutsche-Abschiebezentren.title: Deutsche Abschiebezentren in Ruanda: Ein obszöner Deal
https://taz.de/Deutsche-Abschiebezentren.author: Frederik Eikmanns
https://taz.de/Deutsche-Abschiebezentren.text:
Deutsche Abschiebezentren in Ruanda : Ein obszöner Deal
Deutschland will Menschen nach Ruanda ausfliegen, die dort noch nie waren. Es droht eine moralische Katastrophe.
D eutschland steht vor einem Dammbruch. Wohl schon ab nächstem Jahr will die Bundesregierung ausreisepflichtige Menschen nach Ruanda ausfliegen, wenn sie sich nicht in ihr Herkunftsland abschieben lassen. Viele Details sind noch unklar, und doch weiß man gar nicht, wo man anfangen soll.
Damit, dass Ruanda eine Diktatur mit zweifelhafter Menschenrechtsbilanz ist und nur sehr schwer überprüfbar sein wird, wie dort mit den Abgeschobenen umgegangen wird? Bei der Arroganz, mit der Deutschland und seine Partnerstaaten meinen, Afrika als Deponie für diejenigen verwenden zu können, die man im Westen nicht haben will? Oder damit, dass sich die Europäer von einem Regime abhängig machen, das sie zuvor diplomatisch isoliert hatten, weil es im benachbarten Kongo die Rebellenmiliz M23 unterstützt?
Man kann einwenden, dass es womöglich erstmal um Kriminelle gehen dürfte, die nach Ruanda abgeschoben werden sollen. Und auch bei denen um nur so wenige, dass man eher von Symbolpolitik sprechen muss statt von ernsthaften Maßnahmen. Das mag stimmen, doch es ändert nichts.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Es ist ein bekanntes Muster deutscher Asylpolitik, dass Verschärfungen erst an denen ausprobiert werden, für die sich niemand so richtig interessiert, etwa weil sie Straftäter sind. Wenn die öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit dann weiterwandert, geraten aber schnell auch andere ins Visier. Man kann das bei den Abschiebungen nach Afghanistan beobachten, die bei verurteilten Kriminellen begannen und zuletzt heimlich auch auf Menschen ausgeweitet wurden, die keine Vorstrafen haben. Und Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt hat schon angedeutet, dass Verhandlungen mit anderen afrikanischen Staaten laufen. Es dürfte also bald weitere Deals geben, die Zahl der Betroffenen wird wachsen.
Menschen sind keine Dinge
Wichtiger aber ist die grundsätzliche Dimension. Hinter dem Ruanda-Deal steht die Vorstellung, man könne Menschen hin und her schieben wie Dinge. Und der Glaube, man könne die Krisen der Welt von sich fernhalten, indem man Diktatoren im Globalen Süden ein paar Millionen Euro überweist.
Noch vor zwei oder drei Jahren schien dieses Konzept am Ende. Großbritannien war da gerade mit einem ähnlichen Versuch gescheitert, der Hunderte Millionen Pfund verschlungen hatte, ohne das eine einzige Person nach Ruanda gebracht wurde.
Seitdem aber hat die Idee, Ausländer in Länder abzuschieben, in denen sie noch nie waren, eine Renaissance erlebt. Italien zwingt sie in Haftlager auf albanischem Boden. Die USA fliegen sie in riesige Gefängniskomplexe in El-Salvador aus oder nach Libyen, Uganda und Ruanda.
Dass die Bundesregierung sich nun in eine Reihe stellt mit Trump und Meloni, ist bezeichnend für die Radikalisierung der deutschen Migrationspolitik in den letzten Jahren. Vor allem aber ist es moralisch eine Katastrophe.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.humanite.fr/medias/france-in.title: Rebecca Manzoni accusée de censure dans « le Masque et la Plume » : « Arnaud Viviant savait très bien qu’il allait déclencher une tempête »
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/france-in.author: Caroline Constant
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/france-in.text:
Le chroniqueur du Masque et la Plume a démissionné avec fracas de son poste de chroniqueur, vendredi 13 novembre, sur le réseau social X. Il accuse Rebecca Manzoni, la présentatrice de l’émission, de censure. Ce qui tient difficilement, compte tenu du travail de la productrice, y compris sur la question palestinienne, depuis des années mais qui jette le doute sur les positionnements de France Inter.
Vendredi 13 novembre, Arnaud Viviant, critique littéraire, journaliste indépendant, chroniqueur du Masque et la Plume depuis 26 ans, a lâché une bombe via un post sur le réseau social X (le réseau d’Elon Musk, au passage) : il y dénonçait l’interdiction qui lui aurait été faite par la présentatrice de l’émission depuis 2024, Rebecca Manzoni, de parler du livre de la députée européenne LFI Rima Hassan, Palestine Errante (éditions la Fabrique).
Deux heures avant le début du Masque et la Plume, dimanche 15 novembre, il a publié une tribune plus étoffée sur le site du mensuel Regards. Depuis, il est partout, à accuser Rebecca Manzoni et France Inter de censure. Or, le travail de Rebecca Manzoni, sur la durée, ne supporte pas cette insulte, rendue possible en revanche par les errements coupables de France Inter comme de France Télévisions sur la question palestinienne, sur Gaza, et Rima Hassan.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: I spent months testing pillows to find six top picks for every kind of sleeper
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Jon Chan
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
It’s pretty common advice that you should invest in anything that connects you to the ground. Most people think of shoes, tires and mattresses. However, I think people overlook things such as socks and pillows. The humble pillow can spell the difference between a fantastic night’s sleep and tossing and turning until dawn.
Goldilocks and I are on the same page. You need a pillow that isn’t too soft, hard, cold or hot. It needs to be just right.
Why you should trust me
I have been testing and reviewing products for more than 13 years, including for the Guardian’s Filter US since October 2025, with items such as bath towels, dryer balls and space heaters. I got my start at a product-testing lab where I tested household products under a combination of established and bespoke standards, and I specialized in washing machines and fabric care, and helped develop sleep lab protocols. I’m all about making sure products live up to what is advertised on the tin and provide good value. Plus, I love naps.
How I tested pillows
A good pillow should be able to provide support without feeling hard and be soft without completely enveloping you. To test this, I placed a 20lb weight on each pillow’s center and measured the amount of compression.
Whether you’re a hot or cold sleeper, your pillow is a big factor in whether you get a comfortable night’s rest. To test each pillow’s temperature regulation, I placed heating pads in the microwave for 15 seconds in order to bring them up to around 100F (roughly body temperature). The heating pad went between each pillow and a folded towel for 20 minutes, then I used a thermal camera to measure heat dissipation.
For any pillows with specific claims, I spent time measuring each pillow and researching what each brand claimed their pillows could do, and did extra tests to see if they lived up to the hype.
Best pillow overall: 
Coop Original Adjustable Pillow
Why we love it: The Coop Original Adjustable Pillow checks all the main boxes. It’s an adjustable model, meaning it comes with a bag of memory foam cubes that you place into the pillow to customize its height to help align your head, neck and body. The medium firmness of the foam feels supportive without being hard. Also, the cubed, cross-cut nature of the filling requires less fluffing and fuss than a down pillow.
(If you’re interested in latex, copper or cooling gel, the brand offers different types of filling to buy separately.)
Having slept on this Coop for years on my own and three days for testing, I forgot that it was there after a time since the support for my neck and shoulders felt so seamless. It essentially feels like an extension of the mattress, letting me sleep oblivious to the fact there is a pillow there at all. That is why I think the Coop is the best option. Most people just want a good night’s sleep and not have to think about their pillow. The adjustable nature means you can make sure the pillow contours to your body and the fill material is robust enough to resist compressing throughout the night.
It’s a shame that: When you first take the Coop out of its box, it will smell terrible. The off-gassing period will take a few days. Also, if you’re the kind of person whose ideal pillow makes you feel like sleeping on a cloud, the Coop isn’t for you.
Fill type: Memory foam and microfiber
Case type: 60% polyester, 40% bamboo-derived viscose
Best down alternative pillow:
Quince Premium Down Alternative Pillow
Why we love it: If I had to describe the Quince Premium Down Alternative Pillow in one word, it would be “elevated”, quite literally. It’s about 7.5in thick, stuffed with a very dense microgel and ultra-fine polyester fibers. Back sleepers take note: the loft will lift your head quite high up. I personally felt my head was out of alignment with the rest of my body, but your mileage may vary. However, I think bed readers will enjoy how well the Quince pillow props you up when leaning against your headboard.
The exterior is made from sateen, a cotton fabric that resists wrinkling and feels smooth, with a double-stitched hem. When you combine that with a dense filling, you get a pillow that doesn’t require a lot of fluffing and fussing. Also, this pillow’s sheer mass translates to higher heat dissipation – there’s so much space, you’ll find a cool spot.
If you’re interested in a big pillow that elevates your head and shoulders or an additional pillow to grasp for side sleeping, the Quince Premium Down Alternative Pillow is worth checking out.
It’s a shame that: This pillow is not easily adjustable. One of its greatest strengths is that it’s stuffed it to the rafters with filling, but that also means if you’re someone who likes to shift their pillow around, the Quince Premium Down Alternative Pillow will not oblige.
Fill type: 100% polyester
Case type: 100% cotton sateen
Best down pillow: 
Brooklinen Down Pillow
Why we love it: Duck feathers are a classic pillow filling, and the Brooklinen Down Pillow is a prime example of why. It’s soft, cozy and filled with premium, high-grade Canadian duck down and down feather fibers (incomplete and broken feathers). The exterior is made from sateen cotton, which enhances the soft feel – and the feathers are Downmark certified, which means the down is gathered sustainably and humanely.
Sleeping on this pillow is a cozy experience. After about a minute, my head sank immediately into the surface, molding to the shape of my skull. I’d describe the feeling as cloud-like.
However, being enveloped by a pillow did make my head warm. Heat retention is one of the main reasons to buy a product with real down. It is why jackets made for the Arctic are filled with goose down. The second reason is weight – light as a feather is quite literal in this case. A light and fluffy pillow works well with anyone who likes to readjust their pillow throughout the night, such as someone who switches between stomach and side sleeping. As a back sleeper, I felt like this pillow cupped my ears too much, as if it was squeezing my head.
Overall, the Brooklinen Down Pillow 2.0 is perfect for someone who wants hygge – the Danish word describing a sense of warm, cozy contentment – while they sleep.
It’s a shame that: Since real down is a luxury, it comes with a high-end price tag. If you’re used to paying less than $50 a pillow, the Brooklinen Down Pillow might be too rich for your blood.
Fill type: 100% down feathers and feather fibers
Case type: 100% cotton
Best pillow for hot sleepers: 
Nest Easy Breather Pillow
Why we love it: Unlike the other options on this list, the Nest Easy Breather Pillow feels different right out of the box – it’s cold to the touch. A lot of that comes from the pillow’s unique (and removable) fill of cut foam and breathable fibers. Thermal imaging showed that the pillow’s surface is about 2F cooler than the ambient temperature. During testing, the Easy Breather proved to be one of the best for hot sleepers, wicking away 1.2F per minute during our heat test.
Like the Coop, you can also remove the fill to adjust the loft height. If you decide to try this one out as is, fresh out of the box, it stands about 8.5in tall, which will probably lift your head a hair too high, but your mileage may vary – and it’s always better to have too much removable filling than not enough. I would suggest following Nest’s recommendations to remove about 25% of the fill for back sleepers and 33% for stomach sleepers.
I enjoyed sleeping on the Nest Easy Breather Pillow. After adjusting to the desired loft height, it’s supportive without being hard and never made me feel sweaty.
It’s a shame that: It is very similar to the Coop Adjustable Pillow, but slightly more expensive.
Fill type: 80% memory foam, 20% polyester fiber
Case type: 49% polyester, 49% icecore fabric , 2% spandex
Best budget pillow:
Beckham Hotel Collection Pillow
Why we love it: The Beckham Hotel Collection Gel Pillows would not be out of place atop a bed in a five-star hotel suite – fluffy, like one of those Japanese pancakes. While you might think that a luxury experience would be pricey, Beckham’s pillows are surprisingly affordable – more so than the majority of pillows in this guide.
What’s nice about this pillow is its versatility. It’s firm enough that it provides neck support, but soft enough that your head sinks into the surface, a Goldilocks solution that results in a pillow that I can only describe as huggable. In terms of cooling, I found it to be relatively cool when side sleeping, but if you’re sleeping on your back, the gel pillow will mold around you, trapping heat.
It’s a shame that: I found that the Beckham Hotel Collection Gel Pillow requires a lot of readjusting. The filling is very squishy and not very dense, so it tends to shift around a lot during the night.
Fill type: 100% polyester
Case type: 100% cotton
Best latex: 
Saatva Latex Pillow
Why we love it: Latex pillows offer excellent support and good temperature regulation, and they are known to be super durable. The Saatva Latex Pillow is a prime example. It’s a good blend of soft yet supportive. Also, since the interior is a mix of latex and polyester, it’s not too dense. This is a pillow you can fluff and readjust throughout the night.
Overall, I found the Saatva checks all the right boxes. I never felt too hot while sleeping on it. During our heating test, it wicked away about 1F per minute, putting it near the top of the heap. The standard-size model I tested was comfortable while on my back and acceptable on my side.
It’s a shame that: I have a sensitive nose, and even after a week, I could still smell the latex odor through my pillowcase.
Fill type: 59% polyester, 41% latex foam
Case type: 100% cotton
Everything else we tested
Purple Harmony Pillow
Why we love it: The Purple Harmony is the most feature-filled pillow I tested. It comes with a nylon and spandex outer cover, fantastic for wicking away moisture. Purple’s proprietary honeycomb gel surrounds an inner core of talalay latex for support and structure. The gel essentially gives you the lightness of down with the support of foam that helps the pillow contour around your head without enveloping it and creates space between you and the pillow.
The Harmony did very well in our heat retention test, wicking away 1.2F per minute. I also liked that my head felt bouncy while sleeping on it. It reminds me of the rubber mulch they put in playgrounds to prevent injuries – squishy to a point, then firm.
It’s a shame that: It’s by far the most expensive pillow on this list that I tested, with an average price that hovers at about $200, even when considering sale prices. Yes, the latex core means this is very durable and can be seen as an investment, but you can get very similar performance for less.
Supa Modern Cooling Pillow 
The Supa Modern Cooling Pillow is a bit of a niche product, with a “cooling side” and a “soft side”. The cooling does feel cool to the touch. Our heat retention test showed it was about average for wicking away heat. While this option is quite affordable, I found it to be rather thin compared with the competition.
Amazon Basics Firm Pillow
The best way to describe the Amazon Basics Firm Pillow is that it lives up to its name – it’s the most basic expression of a pillow. Its exterior and fill are made from polyester, a material that isn’t known for its breathability. During the compression test, the Basics Firm Pillow didn’t prove to be that firm, compressing down 80% of its loft height. But given the price tag, it’s hard to complain – for a guest bedroom, or when you need something for a dorm room, the Amazon Basics Firm Pillow delivers.
What else you need to know about pillows
What should you look for based on your sleep position?
Typically, side sleepers should look for higher-loft pillows that are softer, while back sleepers are best served by medium-loft pillows that are firmer, and stomach sleepers will be most comfortable with low-loft pillows.
What are the differences between the different types of pillow fillings?
Pillows are generally stuffed with three types of filling, all with specific properties for specific needs. Foam provides high amounts of support and breathability, while latex and gel make for a durable pillow with a nice balance of support and softness. And down and its alternatives are soft, warm and generally shapable, but will not give you the support of the other two.
How do you wash pillows?
As a rule of thumb, most outer casings can be thrown in the washing machine on a gentle cycle with warm water and a small amount of detergent. Foam and latex pillow cores can only be spot-cleaned.
Down and down alternative pillows can often be machine-washed in their entirety.
However, always check the care tags and follow the instructions.
What pillows are best for hot sleepers?
Foam and latex tend to be better for heat dissipation. Real down tends to trap warmth. You should also pick a breathable and moisture-wicking pillowcase material such as cotton or linen.
What is an adjustable pillow?
If you see a pillow advertised as adjustable, it usually means you can remove or add filling to adjust the height of the pillow to align with your body.
Other pieces you might enjoy from the Filter, the Guardian’s guide to buying fewer, better things:
- The best sleep masks and best Bluetooth sleep masks in the US
- The perfect pillow for my neck and back is filled with buckwheat hulls
- My wife swears by weighted blankets to sleep – and now I understand why

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Iran still retains up to 2,500 ballistic missiles: Report
The US believes Iran has between 1,500 and 2,500 ballistic missiles in its arsenal, a substantial number that contradicts the Trump administration’s claims that Iran has been militarily decimated.
The US intelligence community ranked the assessment “low confidence”, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, but the American estimate generally aligns with Israel’s, which says Iran has more than 1,500 missiles.
President Donald Trump has regularly characterised Iran as a defeated and broken nation. Full-scale war between the US and Iran has subsided, but the two are still exchanging strikes.
Iran attacked US military assets in Bahrain twice in the last week in response to US strikes on its own military infrastructure. Iran also said on Monday that it struck two vessels in the Strait of Hormuz with mines, sinking one Very Large Crude Carrier, known as a VLCC.
The fact that Iran retains a vast arsenal of ballistic missiles may be why the US has refrained from relaunching strikes on Iran, despite Trump boasting that the US had “won” the war and achieved a “93 percent victory” over the Islamic Republic.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/presid.title: Présidentielle 2027 : remplacer les fonctionnaires par l’IA, la dernière idée de génie des candidats de droite
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/presid.author: Aurélien Soucheyre
