https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120390.title: S-Bahn | 14 Monate Ringbahn-Sperrung für Brückentausch in Berlin-Friedrichshain
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120390.author: Nicolas Šustr
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120390.text:
- Berlin
- S-Bahn
14 Monate Ringbahn-Sperrung für Brückentausch in Berlin-Friedrichshain
Die 1910 gebaute Bahnbrücke über die Gürtelstraße muss durch einen Neubau ersetzt werden. Die Deutsche Bahn plant einen Baubeginn im Jahr 2030.
Da kommt etwas auf die Fahrgäste der Ringbahn zu – und auch die Anwohner werden ihr Päckchen zu tragen haben. Denn die Deutsche Bahn plant den Abriss und Neubau der Brücke über die Gürtelstraße in Berlin-Friedrichshain unmittelbar südlich der Frankfurter Allee. Außerdem müssen zwei weitere Brücken der dort vom Ring abzweigenden Gleise Richtung Rummelsburg ebenfalls erneuert werden. Es sind die bereits in Lichtenberg liegenden Querungen der Wartenbergstraße und der Tasdorfer Straße.
Der Befund in den Unterlagen des Planfeststellungsverfahrens ist eindeutig. Die 1910 erbaute Brücke über die Gürtelstraße »weist erhebliche Schäden auf, sodass die Verfügbarkeit auf Dauer nicht mehr gewährleistet ist«, heißt es. Auch bei den beiden anderen Brücken aus dem Jahr 1927 sei »die Nutzungsdauer erreicht und ein Ersatzneubau erforderlich«.
Der größte Brocken ist die Brücke über die Gürtelstraße. Im Auftrag des Eisenbahn-Infrastrukturbetreibers DB Infrago sind diverse Varianten durchgespielt worden, sowohl was den Brückentyp als auch den Bauablauf angeht. Im Ergebnis sollen zwei über 65 Meter lange Stabbogenbrücken gebaut werden, je eine für die Gleispaare von S-Bahn und Fernbahn. Ein hoher Bogen sorgt bei solchen Stahlbrücken für Stabilität.
Ergebnis der Abwägungen ist auch, dass die Brücken für Fernbahn und S-Bahn zeitgleich abgerissen und neu gebaut werden sollen. Das ergibt mit 20 Monaten die kürzeste Gesamtbauzeit. Und die 14-monatige Totalsperrung der beiden Ringbahn-Gleispaare wäre nur einen halben Monat länger als Varianten, bei denen die S-Bahn-Gleise bauzeitlich auf die Fernbahntrasse verschwenkt werden würden. Beginnen soll die Sperrung im dritten Quartal 2030 und im dritten Quartal 2031 beendet sein. Die Gesamtbauzeit bei anderen Varianten wäre deutlich länger und es kämen monatelange weitere Erschwernisse wie eingleisige Sperrungen dazu.
Bis auf die Phasen des Abrisses und des Einhubs der neuen Brücken kann so auch der Verkehr auf der Gürtelstraße weitgehend laufen. Das sei auch wichtig für den Bus-Ersatzverkehr zwischen den Bahnhöfen Frankfurter Allee und Ostkreuz, der ansonsten große Umwege nehmen müsse, heißt es in den Unterlagen. »Die meiste Zeit soll mindestens ein einspuriger Autoverkehr in beide Richtungen aufrechterhalten bleiben.« Mit der BVG werde fortlaufend abgestimmt, inwiefern der Straßenbahnverkehr während der Bauzeit gewährleistet werden muss.
Bei der Umweltprüfung schneidet diese Variante allerdings am schlechtesten ab. Vor allem, weil 120 Bäume dafür gefällt werden müssen – die höchste Zahl aller Varianten. Allerdings müssten selbst für die baumschonendste Variante 80 Exemplare weichen.
Die neue Gürtelstraßenbrücke wird rund 20 Meter länger als das etwa 47 Meter lange Bestandsbauwerk. Das hat der Senat bestellt, damit auf einem längeren Abschnitt der Straße als bisher die Straßenbahn und die zwei Autospuren pro Richtung voneinander getrennt werden können. Rund 73,5 Millionen Euro soll der Ersatzneubau dieser Brücke kosten.
Die beiden Stabbogenbrücken sollen auf einer Fläche östlich der Gleise und der Gürtelstraße gleichzeitig vormontiert und an einem Wochenende eingehoben werden. »Die Bogenbrücken müssen aufgrund der großen Abmessungen im direkten Umfeld des Einbauortes montiert werden«, heißt es in den Unterlagen. Für diesen rund 140 Meter langen und 20 Meter breiten Montageplatz müssen viele Bäume fallen.
Deutlich prosaischer sind die Neubauten der Brücken über Wartenbergstraße und Tasdorfer Straße. Sie sollen als Stahlbeton-Rahmenbrücken neu entstehen. Erwartete Kosten hierfür werden nicht genannt. Am Bahndamm werden auch Vorkehrungen für eine mögliche Führung der Verlängerung der Stadtautobahn A100 getroffen, deren mögliche genaue Lage bisher nicht bekannt ist.
Nicht nur die Brücken werden die Optik im Gebiet verändern, sondern auch der geplante Lärmschutz. Östlich der Gleise sollen auf 454 Metern durchgehend sechs Meter hohe Lärmschutzwände entstehen. Westlich der Gleise sollen es sogar 513 Meter werden, mit drei bis sechs Metern Höhe.
Besonders für die S-Bahn wird die 14-monatige Sperrung einen großen Einschnitt darstellen. 630 Züge passieren mit den Linien S41, S42, S8 und S85 täglich den Abschnitt.
Damit möglichst viel Verkehr auch während der Bauzeit aufrechterhalten werden kann, soll nördlich des S-Bahnhofs Frankfurter Allee ein doppelter Gleiswechsel eingebaut werden. Nördlich vom Ostkreuz soll eine provisorische Wendeanlage entstehen. Es ist aber trotzdem davon auszugehen, dass nicht alle Züge diese beiden Bahnhöfe erreichen werden. Im Berufsverkehr sind derzeit in zehn Minuten drei Bahnen pro Richtung unterwegs – zu viel für einen stabilen Betrieb.
Die betroffenen Fernbahngleise werden planmäßig nur für Betriebsfahrten von Fernzügen und wenigen Güterzügen pro Tag genutzt. Die Strecke bindet den Tunnelteil des Hauptbahnhofs auf kürzestem Wege an das ICE-Betriebswerk Rummelsburg an. Allerdings werden die Ringbahngleise immer wieder für Umleitungen von Regionalzügen bei der Sperrung anderer Strecken genutzt. Derzeit fahren hier wegen der Sperrung der Stadtbahn die Züge der Linie RE2. Bis zur Eröffnung der Dresdner Bahn Ende 2025 nutzte der Flughafenexpress FEX die Srecke.
Für die Betriebsabwicklung der Deutschen Bahn kann die 14-monatige Sperrung durchaus eine Herausforderung werden. Ein- und aussetzende ICE werden große Umwege über teils hochausgelastete Strecken fahren müssen. Entlastung könnte der von der DB geplante »ICE-Boxenstopp« in Berlin-Schönholz bieten. Doch der Stand des Projekts ist unklar. Der letzte Eintrag auf der Internetseite zum Vorhaben stammt von Juli 2024. Die 2021 angekündigte Inbetriebnahme 2026 ist jedenfalls obsolet.
Einwendungen zum Projekt können im Rahmen der Öffentlichkeitsbeteiligung noch bis 21. Dezember 2026 erhoben werden.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.title: Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out.
https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.author: Katie Nixdorf, Debbie Cenziper, Megan Rose, Brandon Roberts
https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.text:
These days, we know where almost everything comes from. Everyday items like food, clothes and pens all carry labels listing where things are grown, manufactured or even designed.
So why is it so hard to find where prescription drugs are made?
That question set off a 14-month investigation into where our medications are made, how the FDA polices drug manufacturers and what happens when inspectors report issues inside factories.
The vast majority of prescriptions filled in the United States are for generic drugs, which are often far cheaper than brand-name alternatives. 
For years, Congress, doctors and watchdog groups have questioned the quality of generic drugs made overseas. India produces about half of all generics used in the U.S., but the labels on pill bottles often don’t list where a drug is manufactured. Inspection reports describe unsafe manufacturing conditions at generic drug factories, but the Food and Drug Administration redacts the names of the medications made in those factories. That means if drugs made in errant factories wind up in your medicine cabinet, you’d have no way of knowing.
To better understand how the FDA regulates the generic drug industry, Debbie Cenziper and Megan Rose interviewed current and former factory inspectors, tested medications in a lab and sued the federal government for critical documents.
Here’s what they found:
- Birds defecated on boxes of sterile equipment. Inspectors reported finding dirty labs, mold and foul water at factories. Records referenced vials of medication that were “blackish” from contamination. Inspectors found what appeared to be metal shavings on equipment.
- Drug manufacturers manipulated and destroyed drug-testing records. At one factory, an analyst poured acid on records stuffed in a trash bin. At another, inspectors said in a report that records were “routinely manipulated” to cover up the presence of particulate matter —  which could include glass, fiber or other contaminants — in generic drugs.
- A lifesaving generic drug contained a lower amount of a key ingredient. We worked with an independent lab to test generic versions of tacrolimus, used to prevent organ rejection. We found some pills contained a lower amount of the key ingredient in the drug. Doctors and experts said that underdosing can leave patients vulnerable to organ rejection.
- The FDA allowed generic drug imports from banned factories — and didn’t inform the public. The agency gave some manufacturers a special pass to continue to ship drugs made in factories whose manufacturing practices were so bad they had been banned from the U.S. Over a dozen years, the FDA exempted at least 150 drugs or their ingredients from banned factories.
- A transplant patient’s lungs failed after she took generic versions of tacrolimus. Hannah Goetz had a double-lung transplant as a teenager and had to take tacrolimus twice a day. Her lungs failed in 2023, and she died at 21 years old, after years of relying on the generic drug made by two manufacturers with documented problems. Lawyers told Goetz’s mother that it was impossible to draw a straight line from Hannah’s death to a generic manufacturer, but her mother said she wonders if her daughter would still be alive if she took a different brand of tacrolimus.
In a response to ProPublica, a spokesperson for the FDA said in a statement that the exemptions given to banned factories are “thoroughly evaluated through a multi-disciplinary approach” but declined to say exactly what those evaluations entailed. The agency also said it requires manufacturers to conduct additional quality checks with third-party oversight before sending drugs to the U.S. The agency did not respond to questions about how it can know that generics are safe without a more robust testing program.
In statements to ProPublica, drug companies said that they take patient safety seriously, adhere to quality standards and are committed to working with the FDA on any regulatory issues.
ProPublica’s investigation, which went on to be a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting, published in 2025. 
Use our tool to find where your prescription drugs were made.
ProPublica’s Brandon Roberts and a team of data journalists made a tool called Rx Inspector that will show you the facility that manufactured your generic prescription drugs and any inspection reports, warning letters and import bans we have from the FDA. 
The data isn’t perfect; it’s possible the FDA hasn’t published everything it knows about a given facility, for example. Also, one company may have acquired another or moved the factory somewhere else. This tool also isn’t meant to provide you with medical advice: If you find something troubling, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your drug is compromised. Doctors and pharmacists advise that you not stop taking your medications. Instead, you should talk to your healthcare provider about any concerns.
Step 1: Enter the name of your prescription drug, as well as the company name found on your pill bottle or drug label.
Step 2: If there are multiple matches in our database, you can narrow your search using the markings found on a pill, for example.
Step 3: When you click on a drug, we’ll show you any manufacturing facilities we’ve been able to connect to it. Click on a facility to see any information we have from the FDA.
FDA inspections come with compliance outcomes, such as import alerts or warning letters. The best possible outcome of an inspection is “acceptable state,” which means the FDA took no compliance action and ProPublica found no issues documented by inspectors. Search your prescription here.
ProPublica described Rx Inspector and the methodology used to build it to the FDA, which did not comment. The agency previously told ProPublica that it doesn’t reveal where drugs are made on inspection reports to protect what it deemed to be confidential commercial information.
Read more of Cenziper, Rose and Roberts’ reporting from their series Rx Roulette or watch their video explainer.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.title: Debunking Pete Hegseth’s Bullshit Impeachment Defense
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.text:
On the eve of a House impeachment vote, self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth made a rare appearance before the Pentagon press corps. Over half an hour, he declared every military operation he has overseen “lawful” and claims of civilian harm “slander.” He said the Iran war was a great victory and only 18 Americans have died in the conflict. He also claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.”
None of it is true.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday afternoon, charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Democrats are overwhelmingly expected to join Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide. “I am a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the presumed next House speaker.
Massie wrote on X that if his impeachment resolution advances Tuesday evening, he will request a separate vote on each of the eight articles. “I’ve heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them,” Massie wrote. “If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I’ll request a vote on each of the Articles separately.”
As Hegseth steels himself for a vote that could see him put on trial in the Senate and sink his chances of serving for the rest of Trump’s term, The Intercept is dissecting his self-defense and examining Hegseth’s false claims about his disastrous war-making.
Everything Was “Lawful” and “Notified to Congress”
“Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen — every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress, and executed by American warriors who did their jobs.”
Experts in the laws of war, a Pentagon official, and members of Congress from both parties say Hegseth’s boat strikes against “cartels,” which have now killed upward of 240 people, are illegal extrajudicial killings. The military is not permitted to deliberately target civilians — even suspected criminals — who do not pose an imminent threat of violence.
Sarah Harrison, who previously advised Pentagon policymakers on issues related to human rights and the law of war, said that the attack on Venezuela was also a clear violation of international law and that the administration’s justifications for the raid were baseless.
Of the Iran war, Air Force Lt. Col. Rachel VanLandingham, a former chief of international law at U.S. Central Command, said the opening strike “clearly violates the U.S. Constitution and the War Powers Resolution,” which requires the president to seek congressional approval to start a war in most cases. Harrison Mann, a former U.S. Army officer and intelligence official and now the associate director for campaigns and policy at Win Without War, drew specific attention to the attacks on the bridges and water reservoirs in Iran. It is “quite dangerous to be conditioning the U.S. military to carry out orders that are clearly war crimes,” he warned.
Hegseth’s claims about notifications are also spurious. Congress never authorized the Iran war, and a call to the congressional “Gang of Eight” the night before is not the formal report experts say the law requires. Following the January attack on Venezuela, Republicans privately complained they were not told in advance.
“The Terrorists That We Hunt”
“As to the claim that the American military targets civilians, well, that is a lie and that is a slander against every professional who flew, sailed, and fought on these missions. The only people who target civilians are the terrorists that we hunt.”
The U.S. boat strike campaign has only targeted civilians. The summary executions of more than 240 people are a significant departure from standard practice in the long-running U.S. war on drugs, in which law enforcement agencies detained suspected drug smugglers and brought them to trial on criminal charges.
A U.S. military investigation also found U.S. forces attacked an elementary school in Minab, Iran, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. One official called it “colossal negligence.”
For months, Central Command has failed to answer questions about additional civilian casualties, including eight members of a family — the youngest, a 20-day-old infant — killed in an attack documented in an Intercept investigation.
These attacks came after Hegseth conducted a comprehensive campaign to undermine efforts to prevent and mitigate civilian harm. The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, for example, slashed its staff from 40 personnel in January 2025 to just nine by the end of the year, according to the report.
“Dead Where They Should Be”
“More than 70 narco vessels sunk. 218 narco-terrorists dead where they should be. Maritime smuggling down at least 65 percent and dropping even further.”
Hegseth misstates the toll of his own boat strike campaign. The Intercept’s tracker counts 72 strikes and at least 243 dead. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., after reviewing classified material, wrote that the evidence suggests the military killed people not involved in drug trafficking. A top Pentagon Joint Staff official told lawmakers in a classified briefing that victims of human trafficking could be among the dead of the first strike.
The drug claims fare no better. Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Americas Security Affairs Joseph Humire, for example, offered completely different numbers to Congress, telling the House Armed Services Committee in March that there “has been a 20 percent reduction of movements of drug vessels in the Caribbean and an additional 25 percent reduction in the Eastern Pacific.”
The Pentagon’s latest civilian casualty report, meanwhile, claims no civilians were killed in the boat strikes. One U.S. official said it had “absolutely no credibility.”
Iran Was a “Historic Military Victory”
“By every measure, we achieved a historic military victory. Under 40 days of sustained combat…”
The Iran war, by all objective measures, is an abject failure. The conflict undermined the decades-old U.S. security framework, as well as America’s archipelago of bases, in the Middle East. Iran determined how to overwhelm U.S. air defenses, offering up a playbook for U.S. adversaries around the world. This, in turn, damaged U.S. military security across the globe. From Jordan to Kuwait to the United Kingdom, U.S. outposts are now increasingly vulnerable to attack. As a result, the Iran war has left the military on the brink of a “breakdown.”
The Trump administration’s attempt to rebrand its faltering forever war hasn’t slowed the mounting toll of U.S. casualties, either. While Hegseth focused on the conflict’s first 40 days, the U.S. has suffered more casualties as a result of the conflict since the war formally ended and, in July, underwent a name change to “Overseas Operations.”
Voters did not see a victory either: About 6 in 10 told The Associated Press the war was the wrong decision, and Vice President JD Vance agreed, writing of the GOP’s crushing defeat in last week’s midterms: “The reason we lost is the war.”
18 Americans
“Eighteen Americans have given their lives in Operation Epic Fury.”
Hegseth spent his rare press conference using the troops under his leadership as a shield, claiming that indictments of him were actually indictments of them. When not using them for cover, Hegseth praised them. “They are the best of our nation. Like the president, I will defend them with every fiber of my being every single day,” he crowed.
What he didn’t care enough to do was offer an accurate count of the war’s toll. The official Pentagon count of deaths during Epic Fury is 15, not 18 — but that’s misdirection at best and a lie at worst. At least 23 military personnel have died in Operation Epic Fury and “Overseas Operations,” the new moniker for the war introduced in July, according to the Pentagon’s official count. (This includes 11 killed by hostile fire.) The actual number of troop deaths in the region since the war began is higher.
“One Disgruntled Congressman”
“This is one disgruntled guy who drew up some really flimsy articles.”
In Hegseth’s telling, Massie is pursuing his impeachment out of resentment over the loss of his Kentucky congressional seat to Trump-backed far-right candidate Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL. But Massie’s impeachment effort has strong bipartisan support. The entire House Democratic caucus is widely expected to vote in favor of the impeachment effort. While no House Republicans aside from Massie have openly committed to voting yes, the outgoing congressman said Monday that he believes “several” Republicans will vote for the measure.
Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz agreed. So did Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment. “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” she told The Intercept of Massie’s effort. In April, Ansari filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight.
Discontent with Hegseth is widespread within the military establishment as well. The Intercept recently spoke with six current and former defense officials who said Hegseth had undermined the rule of law; irreparably harmed the U.S. military through purges of top commanders; spurred religious extremism; and diminished the department he leads due to an almost endless raft of scandals and culture-war clownishness. In fact, 64 percent of active-duty service members, veterans, and military families disapprove of Hegseth, according to a recent poll conducted by Common Defense, a grassroots veterans organization.
The American people, writ large, appear to agree with Ansari, Massie, the U.S. officials, and those in the military’s orbit. Just 32 percent of voters approve of the way Hegseth is handling his job, while 57 percent disapprove, according to a Quinnipiac University poll in September.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Bringing Billionaires to Account at the Ballot Box
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Futrelle
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Bringing Billionaires to Account at the Ballot Box
Last week’s midterms were a powerful repudiation of MAGA, but the fight against oligarchy will be a longer struggle.
The midterms were more than just a victory for Democrats—they were also a critical blow for democracy, as well as a powerful repudiation of President Donald Trump’s crass authoritarianism and of the Republicans who have enabled his worst impulses. But if we want to enable our still-fragile democracy to thrive again, we need not only to purge it of the baleful influence of MAGA but also to confront directly another dire, and continuing, threat to self-rule: that of the billionaires who are increasingly using their wealth and power to try to override the will of the people. In some cases, our moneyed oligarchy quietly (or not so quietly) bankrolls the worst among the Republicans; in others, it puts considerable rightward pressure on the Democrats it supports.
Do we the people have a chance against billionaire money? We just might, as two case studies from the midterms make clear: James Talarico’s successful Senate candidacy in Texas, and the failed campaign for a billionaire wealth tax in California.
On the surface, the two campaigns seem to offer radically different lessons. In Texas, Talarico was able to overcome some $200 million in spending from Elon Musk and deliver a decisive victory, one that Talarico touted as proof “that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”
But it was more than simply people power that enabled Talarico to win; he also responded to Musk’s intervention in the race with a certain shrewdness, ultimately recognizing that in many ways Musk and his money were more formidable opponents than the corrupt and uncharismatic Ken Paxton. (Even Trump, Paxton’s key political supporter, jokingly referred to him as a “pain in the ass” who didn’t know how to dress, or talk, properly.) Given that Talarico was essentially running against a tag team of Paxton and Musk, he made the world’s richest man one of his primary foils in the campaign—thereby turning the millions that Musk directed into the coffers of the Paxton campaign into a political liability. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon,” Talarico said on the campaign trail. “If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too.” Musk, Talarico said, clearly “wants his very own personal United States senator,” one who would do Musk’s bidding in the state where he lives in exchange for purchasing his office.
All in all, Musk spent close to half a billion dollars in the midterms and got close to zero return. Six of his seven Senate picks went down in defeat (with one race still too close to call), and only a small handful of the 43 House candidates he supported prevailed. But it was the Texas race that marked his most significant defeat. Talarico, not surprisingly, sees his victory as a major blow in the battle against billionaires in politics. “We’ve just sent a message to every millionaire mega donor, to every trillionaire mega donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system,” he declared in his victory speech.
In California, the lesson seemed to be of a rather different sort. The backers of Proposition 40—the voter initiative to ratify a billionaire wealth tax—were unable to fend off a “no” campaign backed by billionaire money. One top staffer of the SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the ballot initiative, blamed the campaign’s likely defeat on “billionaire-funded propaganda” that misled voters.
There was indeed a torrent of such propaganda coursing through California’s airwaves. After the billionaire tax was first put forward by Dave Regan of the SEIU-UHW, a number of the state’s wealthiest residents began strategizing how to defeat it in a secret Signal group chat. Google cofounder Sergey Brin, worth a cool $219 billion even after the dip in Big Tech stock values last week, led the charge, cofounding an innocuously named group called Building a Better California. Brin’s outfit quickly amassed a $333 million war chest, plumped up considerably by a $102 million donation from Brin himself. The group quickly realized that its biggest backers could ill afford becoming the face of the campaign; its own polling showed that “billionaires are seen as having a net negative impact across issues,” as internal documents seen by The New York Times put it. (Ya think?) And so their “billionaire-funded propaganda” starred not Brin himself but an assortment of non-billionaire opponents of the measure, Anti-Prop 40 ads thus featured doctors, carpenters, firefighters, and teachers, and even the Democratic governor of California, Gavin Newsom.
As the casting decisions for these ads suggest, the story of Prop 40’s defeat was far more complicated than a simple blame-the-billionaires narrative would suggest. Regan is a divisive figure, to put it mildly—a publicity-hungry activist who’s considered something of an asshole not only by tech billionaires but also by some Democratic politicians; he has also, more significantly, been credibly accused of bullying and worse by union officials. He pushed the referendum largely on his own, without first making much of an attempt to build a coalition. He also sidestepped (some would say stepped on) an already existing campaign by the California Teachers Association (CTA) for another ballot proposition calling to make permanent an increased income tax on the wealthy (happily, despite all the confusion, this measure has passed). Prop 40 would have directed almost all of the proceeds of the wealth tax toward healthcare—a provision that alienated some union leaders who felt that at least some of the money should have gone to support their members as well. As a result, several leading unions, including CTA and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, came out against the tax.
In the end, the SEIU-UHW spent most of the $34 million it raised on gathering signatures, according to The New York Times, leaving only a small fraction of money on hand to counter the massive ad spending from Brin’s group. That enabled the “no” voices to define the terms of the debate. Weirdly, the union spent some of its paltry ad money on perplexing campaigns directed at Planned Parenthood, which had come out against the bill, and Newsom himself. (The anti-Newsom message was featured in ads that didn’t even run in California.) Why they went this way instead of pulling a Talarico and going directly after Brin I don’t know. When you’re fighting billionaires, you need to fight billionaires—not just in general but with great specificity, by name.
It didn’t help that Regan was not himself the best face for the Prop 40 campaign. The controversial and often volatile activist has long had a reputation as a bully. The issue came to a head in September when the press got hold of two investigative reports on his behavior sponsored by SEIU’s national union and its California council that substantiated accusations of threats and bullying of union officials by Regan—and a 2009 physical assault on a woman who was then SEIU California’s executive director. One of the reports concluded that Regan has a “propensity for bullying women and women of color.” (Regan dismisses the allegations as “politically motivated,” ginned up by opponents of Prop 40. A union hearing is set for December.)
And then in the final week of the campaign, as a sort of dysfunctional cherry on top, some 230 of SEIU-UHW’s own staffers went on strike, saying that the union wasn’t negotiating with them in good faith over a raise, derailing the union’s attempts to seal the deal with voters.
In the end, Prop 40 was defeated by more than all this internal dysfunction and a well-funded pro-billionaire agitprop offensive. Voters also appear likely to have passed a poison-pill measure bankrolled by the billionaire’s coalition, Prop 42, that bars future wealth taxes in California. Prop 42’s passage would leave proponents of a California wealth tax in worse shape than if the initiative had never been put forward in the first place. “What a waste of resources and what a squandering of an opportunity,” one prominent supporter of Prop 40 told Politico. “There was no coalition, they pissed off everyone, and so many of those natural allies that would’ve supported it refused.” Billionaires, in California and elsewhere, emerged from the fight not only with their wealth intact but feeling empowered. The apparent lesson for them was that they can win any future battles over wealth taxes by simply sacrificing a small sliver of that wealth to political donations.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But the ongoing struggle to contain the damage wrought by the superrich is hardly as hopeless as Prop 40’s defeat might make it seem. Talarico’s win shows that even the world’s richest man can lose to a charismatic politician who knows how to mobilize the disgust most Americans feel toward the excessive power of money in politics. In Talarico’s case, it certainly didn’t hurt that Musk himself is an odious, cringey edgelord who has almost completely squandered whatever goodwill he once had as a supposed tech wunderkind; his favorability rating, as measured by recent polls, is in the 30s, right alongside Donald Trump’s. But the thing is, most Americans seem to have grown profoundly tired of our billionaire class as a whole; they’re not just sick of Musk. If you start looking at our other billionaires, particularly of the tech variety, you’ll find that some are as widely despised as Musk, if not more so. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from last year, Amazon’s bald, newly buff Jeff Bezos had a 29 percent favorability rating; Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg garnered a pathetic 26 percent.
In other words, the people, if not the billionaires, are on our side here. According to the most recent Harris Poll Americans and Billionaires survey, more than half of all Americans think billionaires are a threat to democracy. And they want something done about it: 69 percent say the ultra-wealthy should have less influence in politics, 71 percent think wealth taxes should be imposed on the rich and 53 percent that there should be actual caps on wealth. They’re right on all counts, of course. We just need to do a better job of convincing them to vote as if these opinions matter.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.title: Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.author: Matt Sledge, Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.text:
Self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment Tuesday night, as solidarity from House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Though Democrats overwhelmingly joined Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide, the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the charges to a committee, allowing Republicans to slow the process. With 11 Democrats absent, they lacked the numbers. Massie, however, dismissed the impact of Democratic absences to The Intercept. “No, there were enough Republicans to rally to get here,” he said.
The procedural vote spared Republicans a more difficult vote on whether to impeach Hegseth on Massie’s eight charges, including waging wars without Congressional authorization and undercutting measures to prevent civilian casualties. It followed a week of increasingly desperate efforts by the Pentagon chief to shore up Congressional and White House support, including a campaign-style video intended to influence Trump, a social media campaign by underlings, and a rare appearance by Hegseth himself before the Pentagon press corps.
Over half an hour on Tuesday morning, Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight charges. He claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.” That, too, turned out to be false as 203 members of Congress voted with Massie.
On Tuesday, a coalition of more than 40 civil society organizations – including Oxfam America, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Common Defense, Demand Progress, MoveOn, and the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft – sent a letter calling on all House members to vote for every article of impeachment filed against Hegseth.
“Pete Hegseth’s time at the Pentagon has done grievous harm to the nation and to the Constitution,” said Demand Progress Senior Policy Advisor Cavan Kharrazian. “This is a man who ignored the will of Congress to execute an illegal war in Iran, kidnapped a foreign leader for oil, restarted war on Yemen, sent missiles to kill suspected drug traffickers and weaponized the Pentagon against a political enemy.”
The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In neither case did the Senate vote to convict.
After the vote, Massie called out the display of inaction from his Republican colleagues.
“They diagnosed why they lost the election,” Massie said of fellow Republicans following the vote on Tuesday night. “But tonight they were paralyzed to do anything about it. And that’s the story of Congress.”
Absent from the vote were Democratic Reps. Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi, of California, Laura Gillen of New York, Steven Horsford of Nevada, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Brittany Pettersen of Colorado, Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico, Haley Stevens of Michigan, Marilyn Strickland of Washington, and Frederica Wilson of Florida. The absent Republicans were Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Neal Dunn of Florida, Russell Fry of South Carolina, Julia Letlow of Louisiana, Tom Tiffany and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin, and Rudy Yakym of Indiana.
A senior Congressional staffer predicted that Hegseth would face a very rough road if he survived impeachment. “Oversight is going to come crashing down on his head,” that staffer said. “Will Hegseth continue to obstruct? Yes. But wait until the subpoenas start.”
Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who will head the House Armed Services Committee in the next Congress, said Hegseth and Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg would be first on the list to testify.
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, told The Intercept there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., told The Intercept that the incoming Democrats have Hegseth in their sights. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached. I want him prosecuted, They murdered people in the Caribbean. And we killed 163 little girls in Iran,” he said. “Everybody in my class is ready for him to go. We tried it, It didn’t work. Well do it again.”
In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump celebrated the outcome while expressing confusion over the vote. Trump called it the “Democrats’ attempt to impeach” Hegseth, despite the fact the effort was introduced by Massie, a Republican, who he called “a major LOSER.” He claimed it was an “EXONERATION” of Hegseth and added: “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.title: Nuevo grupo de demócratas latinos busca ampliar su influencia política en los cinco condados de Nueva York
https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.text:
Share This Article
La organización busca aumentar la representación latina en la política local, formar futuros líderes y fortalecer la participación comunitaria en toda la ciudad de Nueva York, según su fundadora, Jamey Battle.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 4 de noviembre. Traducido por Jacob Velez. Read the English version here.
Después de años de participar en clubes demócratas, organizaciones de mujeres y redes profesionales, Jamey Battle dijo que se hacía constantemente la misma pregunta.
“Pensaba: ¿dónde están los demás latinos?”, dijo Battle, quien antes trabajó en la Asamblea Estatal de Nueva York y en una compañía haciendo lobby. “¿Cómo puedo incorporarlos a este espacio? ¿Cómo podemos involucrarnos en este movimiento político?”.
En lugar de seguir buscando representación latina dentro de las organizaciones políticas existentes, Battle decidió ayudar a crear un espacio propio, centrado en las voces y experiencias de la comunidad latina.
El mes pasado, Latino Democrats of New York City (LDNYC por sus siglas en inglés) celebró su lanzamiento oficial como organización 501(c)(4). Fundada en octubre de 2025 como un grupo de organización voluntaria, LDNYC cuenta actualmente con casi 200 miembros, según un comunicado de prensa.
La organización busca aumentar la representación latina en la política local, formar futuros líderes y fortalecer la participación comunitaria en los cinco condados de la ciudad de Nueva York.
“Se me ocurrió la idea de Latino Democrats hace aproximadamente un año. Le envié un mensaje de texto a mi vicepresidenta, Evelin Vazquez, y nos comunicamos con personas de nuestra red que compartían dos valores: la integridad y el compromiso de poner a la comunidad en el centro”, dijo Battle, presidenta de la organización.
“Finalmente me di cuenta de algo: ¿por qué estoy dedicando tanto tiempo a intentar que los latinos encajen en un espacio que nunca fue creado para nosotros, que no está dirigido por nosotros ni para nosotros y que tampoco responde a nuestras necesidades?”.
El grupo celebró su reconocimiento como organización sin fines de lucro el 21 de octubre con una recepción inaugural llamada “Primera Noche”, realizada en Lighthouse Rooftop, en Long Island City, Queens.
La velada reunió a funcionarios electos, líderes comunitarios, organizadores y simpatizantes en una celebración que incluyó discursos, entregas de reconocimientos y conversaciones sobre la participación política latina.
Entre los asistentes estuvieron Claire Valdez, quien asumirá su cargo en el Congreso en enero para representar al Distrito 7 de Brooklyn y Queens; Brian Romero, recientemente elegido para representar a Woodside y Jackson Heights en la Asamblea estatal; además de los asambleístas de Queens Catalina Cruz y Steven Raga, entre otros.
Durante la recepción, los oradores compartieron historias personales sobre sus familias, sus trayectorias profesionales y las experiencias que los llevaron a involucrarse en el servicio público.
Uno de los participantes recordó haber crecido con una madre salvadoreña que llegó a los Estados Unidos sin documentos migratorios a los 12 años. También relató las historias familiares que escuchaba sobre explotación laboral, robo de salarios, prácticas policiales y operativos de las autoridades migratorias, experiencias que, según explicó, continúan influyendo en su manera de defender a la comunidad.
En el estado de Nueva York, los latinos representan 2.2 millones de votantes elegibles, lo que los convierte en el grupo racial o étnico más numeroso después de los votantes blancos, según el Pew Research Center.
Para Battle, el lanzamiento de la organización representa una oportunidad para incorporar a más neoyorquinos latinos a los espacios políticos y desarrollar una red más sólida de líderes comunitarios.
El lanzamiento ocurre mientras los demócratas celebran amplias victorias en todo el país en las elecciones de mitad de mandato del martes, incluidos los triunfos de varios candidatos respaldados por Latino Democrats NYC.
“Estoy muy emocionada por los próximos años, por la oportunidad de movilizar y entusiasmar a la comunidad latina de Nueva York y de construir poder político para todas las comunidades latinas de la ciudad”, dijo Battle.

https://hellgatenyc.com/nikki-lucas-not-.title: SHOCKER: BK Dems Stealthy 10 p.m. Online Leadership Election Was Illegitimate, Judge Says
https://hellgatenyc.com/nikki-lucas-not-.author: Jessy Edwards
https://hellgatenyc.com/nikki-lucas-not-.text:
Despite state Assemblymember Nikki Lucas claiming for over a month that she is the new boss of the Brooklyn Democratic Party—elected in a late-night Sunday Zoom call where participants were repeatedly warned that they were in contempt of court—a judge has ruled that no, she is not.
The ruling is the latest swerve in a nearly indecipherable sequence of events that began in June, when a reformist faction of the party won enough district leader seats to take over the party leadership. That prompted former Party Chair Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn to take a series of extraordinary measures to retain power, culminating with the October 4 10 p.m. Zoom meeting to "elect" Lucas, Bichotte Hermelyn's close ally, as her successor. The reformist faction of the party almost immediately filed a lawsuit to nullify the meeting after it happened. 
On Tuesday, Brooklyn Supreme Court Judge Peter Sweeney ordered that that meeting was not legal and that "no chair or any other officers of the Executive Committee were elected at such meeting."
For the past month, Lucas has been plastering her new title up and down marketing and fundraising fliers, right up to the day Sweeney's decision came down.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Charlotte Jansen
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad.
 
In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, completely took over my life. It took the air out of every room – I couldn’t talk about anything else. People stopped commissioning me because they assumed I was busy going to space; every conversation I had was about it. This was going to be the rest of my life.
That day in April was pivotal. We were there to watch SpaceX’s Integrated Flight Test 1. After four minutes, following a relatively successful liftoff, the vehicle experienced what they call in space terms an “RUD” – Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly – and broke apart in the air. We put on a brave face but secretly I was thinking: “Wow, the risks are no longer theoretical. I could have been on that.”
 
The dust cloud in the image emerged from the concrete launchpad and tower – obliterated by the power of the raptor engines. The debris ended up all over the local houses and SpaceX closed the launch facility for reconstruction for four months while they conducted a huge clean-up operation. Going to space feels futuristic and grandiose but there are still the practical problems – like people wiping dust off their windows.
Unbeknown to me, this photograph marked the beginning of the end of dearMoon. We didn’t know at that time there was trouble in paradise and a loss of faith in the project and its viability. Maezawa had gone back to Japan after the first launch attempt had been scrubbed the day before, and so missed this launch. Eventually, in mid-2024, we all received an email invite to a Zoom call. We were told that they were not continuing the project, but it was made to sound like the disappointment should be only equal to finding out your favourite TV show was cancelled. But it was completely flooring. This wasn’t just a project – it had become my whole identity. I still dreamed about it every night. It was a poisoned chalice and it obliterated my career as I knew it.
This photograph is now part of my Rhi-Entry project, which is my version of a modern-day tragic cycle. I am Icarus, who flew too close to the sun and my wings melted. It is both tongue-in-cheek and deadly serious, moving through bathos, pathos and hamartia. The exhibition combines the visual tropes of the space museum, brings together facts and fiction, a reflection on the past and my fears for the future, with my personal story as its spine. The irony is, all of my work is about calling out structural abuses of power, and I was blinded by the wild promise of an almost impossible dream.
 
I wanted to change how we collectively feel about who is selected to go to space. I’m a 5ft 2in, gobby, messy queer who grew up on a sailing boat. Living in a tin can floating with blackness above and below, surviving with what you have – it was the closest thing on Earth to going to space, and uniquely prepared me for potentially leaving our planet. We still think of people who go to space as untouchable superheroes. The chiselled-jaw GI Joe lookalike with a wife at home. I wanted to break that mould. It was also about exploring ideas and debates around the colonisation and ownership of space, and who has the right to explore it – and to craft our collective future.
 Rhi-Entry is at the International Centre for the Image, Dublin, until 23 December. Rhiannon Adam’s work is also part of Space @ Fotografiska Tallinn until 17 January. Her book Polaroid: The Missing Manual is published by Thames and Hudson. See more @rhiannon_adam
 
Rhiannon Adam’s CV
Born: Cork, Ireland, 1985
 
High point: Being selected for dearMoon. Strangers coming up to me to tell me that my book Big Fence changed the way that they move through the world
 
Top tip: It never gets easier, so don’t expect it to! Remember that we’re all in the same boat; you can win the biggest award at 20 or at 85, and whichever way it happens, don’t count your chickens. Be nice to everyone, be generous with your time, treat others as you want to be treated – being a diva isn’t a good look. No matter how much success you have, remember half of it was luck and being in the right place at the right time. Listen to Baz Luhrmann’s Everybody’s Free to Wear Sunscreen at least once a year

The rendering of a verdict, the setting of bail, the dragging away of a person to a metal cage, all occur in contrast with court officers, judges, social workers, and lawyers joking around, making small talk, trying to pass the time, and tapping their shoes on the floor waiting for the next one to drop.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Pope Leo Goes to War—Against the Department of War
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Victor Gaetan
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Pope Leo Goes to War—Against the Department of War
The growing divide between Rome and Washington.
Over the last year, a divide has widened between Rome and Washington. It is one based on radically different views of diplomacy and war. It has compelled leading American bishops, encouraged by the Chicago-born Pope Leo, to take public positions at odds with the administration’s bellicose worldview.
Pope Leo XIV’s recent declaration, for example, that military spending enriches a few while diverting billions from peoples’ authentic needs, is in sync with the message of so many candidates who were swept to office in the blue tsunami, especially in Texas, where the arrest by ICE of a nun on her way to Mass galvanized the faithful.
What deserves more attention though, is Vatican suspicion of the US Department of War’s casual normalization of “tactical” nuclear weapons, when there are few codified international restraints.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth recently announced a new decision-making structure linking robotic, drone, and AI capabilities known as Autonomous Warfare Command or AutoWarCom. Leo’s major focus on artificial intelligence includes the conviction that AI-enabled weapons of war, deployed with devastating effect in Gaza and Iran, pose an unacceptable global risk.
Longtime Critic
Since 1945, the Vatican has been a consistent critic of nuclear arms, especially considering that the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki obliterated much of Japan’s Catholic community.
Pope Francis ratcheted up Vatican engagement in the anti-nuke movement, first by negating the ethics of deterrence, then by outright condemning these arms. To an audience in Hiroshima, he declared, “Possessing nuclear weapons is immoral,” a statement crystallizing Vatican support for the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear States (TPNW), which bans developing, testing, producing, acquiring, possessing, or using nuclear weapons.
The TPNW went into force in 2021, once 50 countries had ratified it. To date, 75 countries have affirmed the treaty, excluding all nine nuclear powers, namely, China, France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. But without their support, the treaty can’t have any meaningful effect, which is why the Trump administration’s entertainment of new forms of nuclear weaponry is so dangerous, in the Vatican’s view.
Unilateralism
According to the Vatican’s former nuncio (ambassador) to the United States, Cardinal Christophe Pierre, the pope’s advisers saw “disturbing things” in the Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy, especially an emphasis on military solutions and a dismissal of multilateral consultation.
Then, while the Vatican was negotiating for their removal to a third country, President Nicolás Maduro and his wife were abducted by US forces from their Caracas residence and thrown into a Brooklyn jail. Regardless of offenses committed by the Venezuelan strongman—and local Catholic bishops largely opposed him for violating human rights—the US military had no right to trample Venezuela’s sovereignty, as Pope Leo swiftly pointed out.
American bishops were also increasingly agitated at evidence of illegality by US officials: ICE agents attacking people born abroad, many of them faithful Catholics, and speedboats being bombed in the Caribbean, supposedly for transporting drugs. The first practice violates domestic due process and the second international law.
When Pope Leo spoke to diplomats accredited to the Holy See, an annual New Year tradition, he lamented, “War is back in vogue and a zeal for war is spreading.’”
The Department of War took offense and summoned Pierre before Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defense for policy—an unusual scenario. If Colby, a Catholic, thought he could silence the Vatican by delivering a “might makes right” lecture to a priest-diplomat of 50 years, he was wrong. The encounter seemed to trigger a more combative Catholic clergy.
On Easter Day, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who serves a global diocese of Catholics in the US military (comprising 1.8 million service members and their families), told Face the Nation that the war against Iran can’t be called “just,” a theological category requiring wars to be defensive. The following Sunday, three American cardinals appeared on 60 Minutes reiterating criticism of the Trump administration’s “war of choice” and protesting “indiscriminate mass deportation.”
The Iran War inspired a public feud between Leo and Trump, who called the pope “terrible for foreign policy.” The next day, Leo pledged to “continue speaking out loudly against war,” including the use of AI targeting, blamed for obliterating an elementary school in southern Iran on the first day of bombing. Around 175 people were killed, most of them girls ages 7 to 12. Parents asked Pope Leo be a voice for the tragedy; he emphasized that international law requires belligerents to protect innocent lives.
Pierre told me, “The real history of America is that it built institutions for dialogue. But now you say no to dialogue? You destroy people then offer to engage in dialogue after that? It will never happen. Trump wants to isolate America and make America great against the others. Before, America became great with the others.”
Pope Leo’s geopolitical critique was formalized with the May 25 release of Magnificat Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence. It describes a “culture of power” ignoring dialogue and diplomacy, promoting war as an instrument of international politics, and advancing a false realism that conflict is inevitable. Though he never mentions a specific country, the narrative reads like an indictment of American foreign policy.
The document became the basis for an assembly of Nobel laureates in July at the pope’s summer residence, Castel Gandolfo, then at City Hall in Rome where laureates signed the Rome Declaration on AI and Nuclear Weapons. The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists called it the first gathering of experts and activists tackling dangers of the “AI-nuke nexus.”
Former president of Colombia Juan Manuel Santos, a Nobel Prize winner, helped organize the event. Echoing the pope, he declared, “We are seeing the erosion of ethical restraints in favor of the pursuit of raw power. The development of increasingly advanced artificial intelligence adds additional unpredictability.”
At Castel Gandolfo, Dr. Ira Helfand, a cofounder and past president of Physicians for Social Responsibility who helped win two Nobel Peace Prizes related to nuclear arms, confirmed the Vatican as a longtime ally, adding, “Unfortunately, many people, including many practicing Catholics, are unaware of the Vatican’s clear and uncompromising position that nuclear weapons must be abolished. It has been clearly stated in diplomatic settings, but not in most parish churches.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Vatican Deployment
A major reason for Pope Leo’s visit to the city of Metz, France in late September was to highlight a historic picture of goodwill reversing hatred: The European Coal and Steel Community, which evolved into the European Union, was founded there. Flying back to Rome, he again challenged Trump, this time insisting that safety concerns about AI are not “fake news.”
While Leo was in France, his secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, used a UN speech to reiterate: “The control of these powerful tools must not remain in the hands of a select few; they must serve humanity, not the other way around. In particular, the development of lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) raises profound moral questions.” Last month, the Vatican’s new representative to the UN, Lebanese-born Archbishop Christophe-Zakhia El-Kassis, spoke of “additional risks” caused by the integration of AI into nuclear systems.
A major motivation for Rome’s thematic repetition is the evidence that the Trump administration intends to expand its arsenal, including “tactical” nuclear options. Colby revealed this in a speech to military brass, as reported by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The Vatican sees an upcoming opportunity to flag US irresponsibility at the first UN review of the TPNW, to be held in New York, November 30–December 4.
Meanwhile, advisers close to the American pope say he is encouraging a new movement against the AI-fueled, nihilistic nuclear arms race.

https://citylimits.org/more-than-138000-.title: More Than 138,000 NYC Students Experienced Homelessness Last School Year, New Data Shows
https://citylimits.org/more-than-138000-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/more-than-138000-.text:
Share This Article
Though student homelessness declined by 10 percent from the previous school year, advocates warn that tens of thousands of children continue to face housing instability, transportation barriers and educational challenges.
More than 138,000 New York City public school students experienced homelessness during the 2025-26 school year, roughly one in every eight students, according to data released Tuesday by Advocates for Children of New York (AFC).
The figure represents a 10 percent decline from the previous school year, when student homelessness surpassed 150,000 for the first time. Still, it marks the 11th consecutive year that more than 100,000 city students lacked permanent housing.
Of those students, more than 50,700, or 37 percent, spent time in shelters, while approximately 81,100, or 58 percent, were “doubled up”—temporarily sharing housing with relatives, friends or others because of housing loss or economic hardship, according to the report.
The decline was largely driven by a 22 percent decrease in the number of students living in shelters, though that population remained 41 percent higher than a decade ago.
“While it’s encouraging to see that student homelessness is declining after reaching historic highs in 2024-25, today’s data is no cause for celebration,” said Maria Odom, executive director of AFC, in a statement Tuesday.
The Bronx recorded the highest student homelessness rate among the five boroughs at 16.4 percent, followed by Manhattan at 14.1 percent, Queens at 11.9 percent, Brooklyn at 11.6 percent and Staten Island at 5 percent.
Rates varied significantly across the city’s 32 school districts. More than one in five students attending schools in District 9, covering Highbridge and Grand Concourse in the Bronx, District 23 in Brownsville, and District 32 in Bushwick experienced homelessness.
In Brownsville, more than one in eight students spent time in shelters, approximately three times the citywide rate.
Housing instability also creates challenges for students trying to attend school regularly and succeed academically.
According to AFC, nearly half of students living in temporary housing and 63 percent of those in shelters were chronically absent during the 2024–25 school year, accounting for at least 1.1 million missed days of instruction.
In 2025, only 27 percent of third through eighth grade students living in shelters demonstrated reading proficiency on state tests, less than half the rate of their permanently housed peers. Just 59 percent of students in shelters graduated high school on time, while 14 percent dropped out.
Transportation remains another obstacle. During the 2025-26 school year, 37 percent of families were initially placed in shelters in a different borough from their youngest child’s school. Additionally, 1,775 students living in shelters ended the school year waiting for bus service.
Jennifer Pringle, director of AFC’s Learners in Temporary Housing Project, called for improvements to school transportation and greater coordination among city agencies to address shelter placements far from students’ schools.
Nearly 40 percent of homeless families with children are placed in shelters outside the borough of their child’s school, forcing long commutes, early mornings, and strained community ties, as City Limits previously reported.
Christine C. Quinn, president and CEO of Win, a nonprofit providing shelter and supportive housing to homeless families, also urged city officials to address the crisis.
“Students experiencing homelessness are fighting an uphill battle, battling chronic absenteeism while routinely struggling to reach the benchmarks achieved by their housed peers,” Quinn said in a statement Tuesday. “In the wealthiest city in the world, we cannot accept this as normal.”
Quinn called for expanding affordable housing, strengthening rental assistance programs such as CityFHEPS and improving educational support for students experiencing homelessness.
“It’s time for our leaders to be bold and bring forward innovative solutions that put families in permanent homes and bring this crisis to an end,” Quinn said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Botticelli painting saved from leaving UK goes on view in Oxford
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.
The Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which announced plans in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.
The UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport said that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).
The painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, says an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.
The Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.
Founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: German museum returns Slevogt painting to heirs of Nazi-persecuted collector
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Anzhela Khachaturova
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A painting by the German Impressionist painter Max Slevogt, which has been restituted to the heirs of Eduard Fuchs—a collector, Communist and writer who fled Nazi Germany with his Jewish wife—will be auctioned next month. Slevogt's Paradiesvögel (Birds of Paradise, 1900), was acquired by the Von der Heydt-Museum in Wuppertal, western Germany, in 2006 and following an investigation that began in 2020 was approved for restitution by the Wuppertal city council on 13 July 2026. Paradiesvögel will be offered at Ketterer Kunst's 5 December Day Sale with an estimate of €40,000–€60,000.
Given the large number of heirs a sale was the only option, Ketterer Kunst's head of communications Anja Häse tells The Art Newspaper. The heirs consigned the painting once the restitution was completed, she adds. Another work by Slevogt from Fuchs’s collection, Don Quichotte und die Schafherde (Don Quixote and the Flock of Sheep, 1907) is also included in the auction with an estimate of €20,000–€30,000. According to Ketterer Kunst's provenance information, a settlement was reached between the current private owners and Fuchs's heirs in 2026, allowing the work to be offered at auction free of restitution claims. The terms of the “amicable restitution” have not been disclosed.
Fuchs's collection was confiscated by the Nazis but later released. In 1937, he was forced to sell works from the collection to pay a punitive emigration tax imposed by the Nazi authorities. Paradiesvögel was auctioned in Berlin in June 1937 and acquired by the art dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, passing to Fritz Slevogt in 1939.
Paradiesvögel was included in a sale at Kunsthaus Lempertz in December 2004, estimated at €100,000-€120,000, but went unsold. According to Meyer, the work remained in the auction house’s custody afterwards and was subsequently exhibited at the Von der Heydt-Museum in 2005. The museum then purchased the painting through the auction house in 2006 for €120,000. Meyer says that while the painting's provenance was documented in the 2004 auction catalogue, the museum can no longer establish whether a provenance check was carried out before the acquisition or how thoroughly it was assessed. She also confirmed that the museum is not considering any legal action against Kunsthaus Lempertz regarding due diligence on the painting.
The provenance investigation began after Fuchs's heirs contacted the institution in 2020, the museum's press officer Marion Meyer tells The Art Newspaper. The research drew on a wider project, supported by the German Lost Art Foundation, to reconstruct Eduard and Margarete Fuchs's collection.
“Restituting Max Slevogt's Paradiesvögel means losing a painting, but we gain something far more important: the certainty that we have acted responsibly towards history,” the Von der Heydt-Museum's director Roland Mönig says in a press statement. He describes provenance research as “an essential part of our work”.
In 2024, the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart restituted Slevogt's Der verlorene Sohn (The Prodigal Son, 1899) to Fuchs's heirs. The triptych was sold at Ketterer Kunst later that year.

The National Gallery of Art has announced part two of its Across the Nation lending program, which will bring masterworks from its collection across the United States. The initiative began last year to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary. The new cycle follows a $116 million gift from the Mitchell P. Rales Family Foundation.
In its first year, Across the Nation traveled to ten states. In its second iteration, it will expand to Alabama, California, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, and Wisconsin. Its goal is to lend work to museums in all fifty states within the first decade of the program. Partner museums for this cycle are the Crocker Art Museum (Sacramento, CA), Dayton Art Institute (Dayton, OH), El Paso Museum of Art (El Paso, TX), Gilcrease Museum (Tulsa, OK), Madison Museum of Contemporary Art (Madison, WI), Mobile Museum of Art (Mobile, AL), South Dakota Art Museum (South Dakota State University, Brookings, SD), and the Westmoreland Museum of American Art (Greensburg, PA).
Each institution will receive important works from the National Gallery collection, including historical and contemporary pieces spanning painting, sculpture, video, and installation. The loans will include works by artists such as Claude Monet, Mark Rothko, Donald Judd, Georgia O’Keeffe, Sol LeWitt, Henri Matisse, Rembrandt, and Susie J. Lee. Works will go on display as early as summer 2027 and will be on view through 2029.
“Everyone deserves to experience the awe-inspiring power of art. Through Across the Nation, we are proud to extend the reach of the nation’s art collection by bringing incredible works of art from throughout history directly into American communities together with our partner museums. It is an honor for the National Gallery to partner with our valued colleagues from museums located in communities across America,” said Kaywin Feldman, director of the National Gallery of Art, in a press release. “This would not be possible without the generosity of Mitchell P. Rales, whose historic gift will allow the program to continue expanding access to defining works of art for generations to come.”
