The One Issue to Rule Them All
To win in 2028, Democrats must commit to doing a full Supreme-Court Press—and breaking the power of the court for good.
The 2028 Democratic presidential primary season has officially begun. With the midterms officially in the rearview mirror, but with the Democrats’ strong showing buoying the party from Georgia to Texas and beyond, we can expect an energetic primary full of people eager to ride the blue wave straight to the White House.
The last time there was an open primary for the Democratic nomination, in 2020, 29 candidates tried to convince voters they could defeat Donald Trump by defeating inequality, student debt, and climate change (though I think one guy was just trying to sell us coffee). Then Covid arrived, followed by the mass marches for Black lives, and the focus shifted to the once-in-a-generation deadly virus and the daily reality of deadly racism.
It is impossible to predict which combination of policy proposals, violent assaults, and global crises will prove dispositive to voters this time around. Will it be data centers, gas prices, and ICE? Healthcare, democracy, and the Iran War? Smoky eyeliner, American-flag cuff links, and GLP-1s? It’s hard to say. But no matter which combination dominates, there is one issue that must be championed by any Democrat serious about rescuing the country from the depths of Trumpism: Supreme Court reform.
Reforming the court is, in many ways, the skeleton key that unlocks the entire Democratic agenda. It’s the issue upon which all other issues depend. That’s because without reforming the Supreme Court, no other Democratic policy matters. Without reform, a Democratic president will hold power in name only. Without reform, the Democratic legislative agenda will never be implemented. The current Supreme Court has been designed by Republicans to make winning elections irrelevant, to give them ultimate control over federal law and policy regardless of who happens to win the White House. A Democrat who is unwilling to break the power of the Supreme Court is a Democrat who is wasting all of our time.
I know that for many politicians, and the political consultants they trust with our lives, “the Supreme Court” and “issues that matter to regular people” can sound like two vastly different things. But in practice, they’re the same. You cannot, for instance, have Medicare for All if the Supreme Court is going to strike it down. You cannot have a Green New Deal if the court will immediately declare it unconstitutional. You cannot implement meaningful restrictions on AI if the court is unwilling to enforce those restrictions the moment the tech-bro mafia unleashes a barrage of lawsuits to try to stop them. And this is true of nearly every issue Americans talk about at their kitchen tables. There is simply nothing the current Supreme Court will allow Democrats to do—unless the court itself is reformed first.
Think about it this way: Trump will be gone in 2029, unless the Supreme Court rules that he, or his chosen successor, can stay. That is its real power—not to be a king, but to make one out of thin air. If Democrats do not address the court, they will address none of the damage Trump has done to this country.
Unfortunately, the current assumed front-runners for the Democratic nomination have yet to get the memo. They’re still treating Supreme Court reform as a niche issue to be sidestepped, instead of the key to the return of liberal self-government. California Governor Gavin Newsom is perhaps the saddest example of this failure. Newsom likes to talk tough—at least to defenseless trans kids. He’s got all kinds of smoke for trans girls who want to play sports, but when it comes time to deal with John Roberts and the cabal of Republicans who took away the rights of women and girls to control their own bodies, Newsom becomes cautious. In September, he told Don Lemon that he was “evolving” on court reform, but he was still unwilling to commit to the biggest reform of all: Supreme Court expansion. “I normally have very clear conviction on things. I’ve been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this,” Newsom said. But while he considered two potential reforms—term limits and ethics reform—to be “a no-brainer,” he still felt “caution” (but also “an openness”) about expanding the court.
Right, so Newsom has very clear convictions about things like who should be allowed to play girls’ field hockey, but he still needs more evidence as to whether the right-wing Supreme Court can play with our lives? Good to know.
Newsom isn’t the only one, of course. J.B. Pritzker, the tough-talking Illinois governor and billionaire, also needs the Supreme Court to bash us over the head for a few more years before he finds enough “evidence” to act. “I think I want to see, you know, a little more out of this Supreme Court before I would make a judgment [about expanding the court],” he told Politico in May. “But I will say that if that is what is necessary in order to restore our Republic to what it was, you know, which is standing up for individual rights the way it was before Donald Trump, then that may be what we need to do.”
Since 2020, the Supreme Court has overturned abortion rights, affirmative action, and most of the Voting Rights Act. It has adopted a pro-gun-rights view so extreme that it’s even struck down Republican-backed gun restrictions. It’s allowed the GOP to gerrymander at will and given wealthy Republican donors the nearly unfettered ability to buy victories for their preferred politicians. Pritzker’s insistence that he needs to see more from this Supreme Court before advocating for reform is like Abraham Lincoln saying, “We should let this Confederacy thing play out a little longer before I make a judgment on restoring the Union.”
The progressive wing of the Democratic Party has been a little bolder about court reform. Potential presidential contenders like Ro Khanna and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have come out in favor of both court expansion and ethics reform. Pete Buttigieg had the most aggressive Supreme Court–reform plan during the 2020 cycle, so we know he takes the issue seriously. The entire party seems to be behind 18-year term limits, which is a reform that polls well but fundamentally fixes nothing in the short term. But even when Democrats support court reform, they frame it as a secondary issue, something to be addressed separate and apart from the affordability crisis or healthcare or whatever else.
This is the critical mistake. Democrats treat the Supreme Court as an issue for nerds, policy wonks, and elites. Republicans, by contrast, use the Supreme Court to mobilize voters and win elections. The Supreme Court is the reason that so-called “Christians” had no problem supporting a godless, thrice-married sexual predator. They knew that, despite his many “sins,” Trump would provide them with the justices they needed to achieve victory over the secular state and allow them to practice public bigotry under the guise of private religion. And he has.
Democrats are losing on issue after issue because they have not focused on the Supreme Court, and because they have not told their voters to focus on the Supreme Court. The rise of the white wing over the past 20 years tracks neatly with 20 years of Democratic malpractice when it comes to the courts. This generation of Democratic failure was captured most famously by Rahm Emanuel, Barack Obama’s first chief of staff, who, when asked if Obama would prioritize nominating and confirming judges, responded: “I don’t give a fuck about judicial appointments.” Since then, presidents and presidential contenders—from Obama to Hillary Clinton to Joe Biden to Kamala Harris—have consistently failed to pay more attention to the court than the Republicans pay to Greenland.
This decades-long political and moral malfeasance must end. Now. The 2028 primary cycle should not be a question of whether a Democratic candidate has a plan for the Supreme Court. It should be a knock-down, drag-out fight over whose plan is best.
The first step for Democratic presidential hopefuls who want to be taken seriously on Supreme Court reform is simply to talk about the court at every opportunity. You can’t lead on an issue if you’re afraid to mention it. Talking about the court should happen organically whenever these candidates talk about literally anything else on their legislative agenda, because there is no legislation that can or will survive a Republican Supreme Court.
Take abortion rights. Every single Democrat on the presidential-debate stage will say they want to “restore Roe.” But Trump didn’t overturn Roe, nor did the Republican Congress. The Supreme Court did that. When you are talking about restoring Roe, you are literally talking about overruling a Supreme Court decision.
So how do candidates intend to do that, exactly? Democrats should be expected to answer that question, which means not only laying out their plan but telling voters how they intend to get it past the six robed theocrats who think the fallopian tubes are stairways to heaven.
There are four potential ways to do that, four elements of any Supreme Court–reform plan, and 2028 candidates should have proposals for all of them. These elements target the court’s corruption, its excessive power, its immutability, and its conservatism, and they do that through a combination of methods: creating a code of ethics, stripping the court of its right to rule on certain cases, imposing term limits on justices, and, most important of all, adding justices to the court.
Let’s start with the code of ethics, because that’s the lowest-hanging fruit. The Supreme Court is corrupt. Everybody has seen it. Everybody feels it. Even if wealthy Republican interests aren’t directly buying votes, they’re most certainly buying access and the influence that access provides. And yet the Supreme Court is the only court in the land that operates without an ethics code that is enforced by a separate body.
Politicians and policymakers have discussed at length the idea of passing a Supreme Court ethics code through Congress. Those efforts have failed in part because the court claims that only it can police itself. Letting any other branch do so violates the separation of powers, according to the court.
I happen to think the court’s constitutional interpretation is wrong, but I’m not on the Supreme Court, so I can’t make the justices listen to me, or to Congress. But Congress could potentially get the court to abide by a legislative ethics bill by pulling on the lever that is unquestionably within its constitutional powers: the budget. The Supreme Court’s budget, like every other budget in the federal government, is controlled by Congress. Democrats running for office should promise to cut that budget—“defund the court,” if you will—unless the court agrees to be bound by an ethics code administered by some other body. The Constitution says there will be a Supreme Court; it doesn’t dictate how Congress must fund it. It doesn’t say that Congress has to give the justices a fancy courthouse to hold their hearings in. It doesn’t say that Congress has to give the justices clerks and assistants to do all of their research. It doesn’t say that Congress has to provide the justices with security. The Supreme Court can do its work from Clarence Thomas’s RV parked outside a Walmart, for all the Constitution cares.
If you cut the court’s funding to change its decisions, it looks like a form of bribery. But if you cut its funding until the justices agree to stop taking bribes, it just looks like a win.
The next reform Democratic candidates should promise to pursue is “jurisdiction stripping,” although Democrats shouldn’t call it that on the campaign trail unless they want to put their audiences to sleep. I’d call it “reclaiming the Constitution from the Supreme Court.” The basic idea here is that Congress has the power to limit the Supreme Court’s ability to overturn laws, to deem them unconstitutional, and this reform would allow Congress to do just that.
To understand how, it helps to remember that the word unconstitutional appears nowhere in the Constitution, which means the power to declare laws unconstitutional was given to no specific branch of government. Instead, the Supreme Court took that power for itself and dubbed it “judicial review” in the landmark 1803 case Marbury v. Madison. But Congress can take that power back, because Article III of the Constitution gives it the authority to restrict which kinds of cases the courts can review and thus limit the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction.
Congress can’t tell the courts how to rule, but it sure as hell can tell the courts what they’re allowed to rule on. Democrats could say, for instance, that the Supreme Court is not allowed to rule on political-redistricting cases and then pass a national anti-gerrymandering law. They could say the court is not allowed to rule on campaign-finance laws, and then pass a law negating Citizens United and restoring meaningful restrictions on campaign contributions. Taking power away from unelected elites and giving it back to the people is always a winning electoral issue.
Getting rid of Citizens United, courtesy of jurisdiction stripping, would be popular. So would forcing Clarence Thomas to pay for his own vacations by imposing a code of ethics. Still, the most popular Supreme Court reform is term limits. Nearly all Democrats already support imposing 18-year term limits on Supreme Court justices.
The question I have for Democrats promising term limits is: How? I have explained the political and constitutional levers Democrats can pull to get other Supreme Court reforms over the line, but on term limits, the Constitution is pretty clear that federal judges serve “during good behavior,” which has consistently been interpreted to mean “for life, unless impeached.” Many legal scholars have made arguments for how term limits can be imposed without a constitutional amendment, and I think those arguments are brilliant. But the people who get to decide whether those arguments are correct are the very justices whom we are trying to kick off the court.
As of this writing, the justices who have served for more than 18 years are Thomas, John Roberts, and Samuel Alito. How, Democrats, are you going to convince them that it’s time to leave? My response to Democrats promising term limits is to cite my forever president Josiah Bartlett’s “next ten words” speech, in which he effectively argues that a sound bite of support for a policy is useless without an explanation of how that policy can be accomplished. Or as he says: “How are we going to do it?” If Democrats have a compelling case for how term limits can be implemented over the objection of the justices who would be required to leave, I’d love to hear it.
This brings us to the reform that is the most essential—and also, somehow, the most controversial. All three of the reforms mentioned so far do a lot of important work. But at the end of the day, none of them—not term limits, jurisdiction stripping, or ethics rules—will change how the Supreme Court’s conservative supermajority rules. These reforms put up important guardrails, limiting the justices’ power and the time they have to abuse that power, but they don’t prevent the court from scuttling the liberal agenda. If you want different decisions to come out of the Supreme Court—decisions that allow the Democrats to enact their programs and policies—then you’re going to have to increase the number of justices who believe that liberal priorities are constitutional.
That means we’re going to have to add members to the Supreme Court. There’s no other way. We need a majority of justices who believe in liberal, multiethnic, multi-faith democracy. We need a majority of justices who believe that women are people who deserve equal-people rights. We need a majority of justices who believe guns are not people and do not have an inalienable right to kill us all. We don’t just need more justices, we need liberal justices committed to undoing, overturning, and reversing the precedents laid down over the past 50-plus years. The last time a majority of the Supreme Court’s justices had been appointed by Democratic presidents was… 1969. That stat alone should tell you why we’re now at the point where court expansion is the only reasonable solution.
And expanding the court is reasonable. It is also easy, constitutionally speaking. Court expansion can be accomplished through simple legislation passed in the House, passed in the Senate with 51 votes (or 60, if Democrats lack the courage to abolish the filibuster), and signed by the president. That is literally all it takes to add justices—no complicated constitutional hocus-pocus required. If you want national single-payer healthcare or abortion rights or gun-safety laws, then you simply have to have a majority of justices who are willing to uphold those laws as constitutional.
If I were running for president, I would tie Supreme Court expansion directly to gun reform. That’s because the Republicans currently on the court are even bigger gun extremists than mainline Republican voters. There is no way to keep our children and our society safe from gun violence without expanding the Supreme Court to include more members who want the rest of us to live. There is no way to get real background checks, to close the gun-show loophole, to ban bump stocks and ammunition drums, and to enhance licensing and safety requirements without expanding the Supreme Court.
That has to be the message from all Democratic Party candidates. Moderates who are squeamish about court expansion should be asked if they are perhaps more squeamish about wiping the blood off the blackboard after the next school shooting. Show the people that the court is getting us killed and must be stopped.
A line I have often heard from people who think of themselves as “pragmatists” is that Democrats should focus on winning the election first, and worry about fixing the Supreme Court only after they’ve secured power. The theory, as I understand it, is that Democrats should campaign on broadly popular kitchen-table issues, like affordability, instead of focusing their campaigns on something as esoteric as the Supreme Court.
I agree with half of that. Obviously, winning is paramount. There can be no Supreme Court reform unless Democrats actually win. If Democrats can win by promising to lower the price of eggs, they should do that. If Democrats can win by promising to fight data centers with water guns, they should do that. If Democrats can win by promising every single voter in the country a universal basic income and a new puppy, they should do that. If Democrats can win by doing all of the above while walking backwards and chewing gum, in heels, they should do that.
My argument is that Supreme Court reform must be put front and center while the Democratic candidates are promising all the other things. Because if they don’t do that, everything from regulations on price gouging to free puppies will be overruled by the Supreme Court. Democrats must build the conditions under which Supreme Court reform doesn’t just become preferred but inevitable. The Democrats running and winning on the presidential nominee’s coattails must similarly know that court reform is inevitable. Again, that’s because court reform is the first step, not the last, in unlocking the rest of their agenda. Democrats can do nothing unless they win, but that victory will be meaningless without court reform.
If you will forgive the classical reference, I would handle the balance between so-called kitchen-table issues and the overwhelming need to reform the court the way Cato the Elder pressed for his signature obsession in ancient Rome. Famously, Cato ended every single speech he made in the Senate, regardless of the topic, with the line Ceterum censeo Carthago delenda est: “Furthermore, I think Carthage must be destroyed.” That is the bare minimum we should demand of Democratic candidates in the 2028 cycle. “We’re going to have Medicare for All. We’re going to keep AI data centers out of your communities. We’re going to get guns off our streets and out of our schools. Furthermore, the Supreme Court must be destroyed.”
Cato, it must be said, got his way, and I’m confident that Democrats could mimic his success. Today’s voters, and particularly Democratic-primary voters, are hungry for candidates who will take back our power from the Supreme Court. The court is extremely unpopular—just 34 percent of adults (and only 23 percent of Democrats!) approve of what the institution is doing. But voters like the idea of Supreme Court reform. According to a September poll by Marquette Law School, 89 percent of adults approve of enforcing an ethics code for justices; 79 percent favor term limits; and 53 percent like the idea of increasing the number of justices. Or as Josh Orton, the CEO of Demand Justice (disclosure: I’m a board member), told me, “In 2028, a Democratic presidential candidate won’t be taken seriously unless they have a clear plan to break up the Roberts majority within two years of taking office.”
This isn’t hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen Democrats go from “marriage is between one man and one woman” to Gene Hackman in The Birdcage in one election cycle. Democrats must be leaders here, whether they get there through rational self-interest or idealistic good government. The people are ready for candidates who take the fight for our rights and democracy all the way to the Supreme Court.
I want Democrats to win. I want to win the campaign season and the governing season. I want to win the battle and the war.
Supreme Court reform is how Democrats win. It’s an unpopular institution, staffed and protected by elites, that has made itself the enemy of the popular will. If Democrats want to fight for individual rights, market regulations, environmental justice, healthcare, and fair taxes on the impossibly wealthy, then they have to fight the Supreme Court.
If they don’t, we’re looking at another cycle of failure, regardless of who happens to win.

The Fugitive From Brazil
The implications of Trump’s red-carpet rollout for Flávio Bolsonaro.
As millions of Brazilians celebrated President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s come-from-behind reelection, the defeated candidate was secretly preparing to flee the country. On October 27, two days after the runoff vote, Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami aboard a private jet, having slipped out of Brazil in a furtive journey involving multiple countries and, as would later emerge, assistance from officials close to Donald Trump. Within hours he declared himself “president-elect,” then “leader,” then head of the Brazilian opposition-in-exile, insisting that Lula’s victory was illegitimate. Flávio’s apparent hope was that Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaro family who has aggressively criticized Lula’s government, would support his efforts to challenge the legitimacy of Lula’s win.
“I want to make it clear: I did not flee Brazil. I left for the sake of Brazil,” Bolsonaro proclaimed in a slapdash statement that had to be rescinded and reissued several times. If his intention were to dictate the course of the resistance to Lula’s unprecedented fourth term, Flávio obviously would have stayed in Brazil. But his electoral defeat meant losing the parliamentary immunity that came with his Senate seat, leaving him more exposed to police questioning and possible prosecution on various counts.
It is now clear that for Flávio the 2026 campaign was a high-stakes, last-chance gambit. There was no Plan B. What compelled him to run away was the fear of being arrested in connection with a host of illicit activities. And by coming to the United States there was always the possibility that his patron, Donald Trump, might aid and abet the Bolsonaro family’s quest to return to power.
The Banco Master Scandal
Credible accusations of criminal wrongdoing have swirled around Flávio for years. But his immediate legal exposure centers on three investigations currently before Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court.
The most serious concerns the financing of a planned film about his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overthrow the election he lost to Lula in 2022. Flávio negotiated a $24 million investment from Daniel Vorcaro, then the owner of Banco Master, a Brazilian bank that collapsed amid revelations of massive alleged financial fraud. Vorcaro, who has been arrested in connection with the scheme, is suspected of orchestrating fraudulent financial operations involving billions of dollars and bribing political figures across the ideological spectrum. Unlike Lula, Flávio is directly implicated in the scandal.
According to the Federal Police, approximately $12.3 million of the promised $24 million was routed to an account in the United States linked to associates of Flávio’s brother Eduardo, a former congressman who relocated to the United States last year. Investigators suspect that some of the money may have been diverted for other purposes, including possibly funding Eduardo’s lavish lifestyle in the United States. The production company has yet to provide a detailed accounting of how the funds were spent. Flávio was formally placed under investigation in July 2026 for suspected money laundering, corruption, and illegal transfers of funds abroad.
A second inquiry concerns Flávio’s relationship with lawyer and businessman Willer Tomaz, whom police suspect of helping him conceal a financial interest in an online betting business. Investigators found e-mails suggesting Flávio had been registered as a privileged user on a bank account belonging to Alcazar Holdings, a company controlled by Tomaz, which is linked to the holding company behind the online betting platform Rede Loto. Police also found that companies linked to Tomaz paid for private flights taken by Flávio and his family. A third investigation concerns Flávio’s social-media accusation that Lula was involved in drug trafficking and money laundering—statements of slander that have prompted a criminal defamation inquiry.
So far, none of these investigations have resulted in any prosecutions. But they presented Flávio with the prospect of prolonged police scrutiny and potentially serious legal proceedings. “You already know where they are going with this, right?’” the former president reportedly told his son during a meeting the day after the election, to which Flávio responded: “Dad, I already know. And I am prepared, I know what I have to do.” The next day, he ran.
Trump and Bolsonaro
The Trump administration has offered Bolsonaro a warm welcome. After Lula’s victory, Trump baselessly questioned the legitimacy of the election, alleging that it had a “very bad look.” The president subsequently said he had approved Flávio’s arrival in the United States and that the defeated candidate could stay “as long as he wants.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio recommended that Flávio and his family be admitted under humanitarian parole, a temporary immigration arrangement that Trump immediately approved.
Indeed, Trump’s administration has spent much of the preceding year attempting to boost the Bolsonaro family to power, beginning with efforts to shield Jair Bolsonaro from the legal consequences of his 2022 coup attempt. Flávio’s brother Eduardo spoke openly about his sustained effort to push Trump to punish Brazil for daring to prosecute his father. In July 2025, Trump levied a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian imports as an explicit demand that Jair Bolsonaro be set free, despite his being charged with coup plotting that included a plan to assassinate Lula. “The way Brazil has treated former President Bolsonaro, a Highly Respected Leader throughout the world during his Term, including by the United States, is an international disgrace,” Trump wrote in a letter to Lula, posted on his Truth Social platform. “The trial should not be taking place. It is a Witch Hunt that should end IMMEDIATELY!”
Washington’s overt interference in Brazil’s judicial proceedings not only failed—the former Brazilian president was sentenced and duly incarcerated—but also gave Lula a potent rhetorical weapon to wield against the opposition in the form of a defense of national sovereignty.
Flávio campaigned as a MAGA acolyte, criticizing Lula’s independent streak on the world stage and promising to join the Shield of the Americas, Trump’s haphazard effort to create a militarized law enforcement coalition among like-minded hemispheric leaders. If elected, Bolsonaro insisted, pardoning his father would be among his first acts.
For its part, the Trump administration harbored no doubts that Flávio would be much more amenable to US dominance of Brazilian rare earth minerals and other resources than Lula, who insists on conditions for foreign involvement in key areas. Flávio visited the United States six times in 2026, meeting with conservative activists, attending the Conservative Political Action Conference in Texas, and making repeated trips to Washington.
On May 26, Trump received him in the Oval Office, where he also met Secretary Rubio, Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau, and presidential adviser Jason Miller, who reportedly assisted Bolsonaro’s escape to the United States. The White House offered no official account of the meeting. But by posing in the Oval Office with the presidential hopeful Trump signaled a personal bond that Bolsonaro implied would translate to policy wins for Brazil if he won.
Implications for US-Brazil Relations
So far, the Trump administration has been unwilling to back Flávio’s absurd claims that he is the legitimate president of Brazil; but Washington evidently wants to show the world that it takes care of those who offer their allegiance.
Using the United States as a base, Flávio can continue lobbying American officials, cultivating conservative media, and portraying the Brazilian judiciary as an instrument of political persecution. There is always a grift to be had for a reactionary Latin American politician in Miami.

Moreover, Flávio’s presence serves the Trump administration’s apparent goal of keeping the Lula government on its heels. The energized far-right opposition is already preparing to challenge the Supreme Court, particularly Alexandre de Moraes, whose prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro and supporters involved in the January 8, 2023, insurrection in the Brazilian capital remains a central grievance of the movement. This agenda offers the opposition a way to keep the country in a state of political confrontation independently of Flávio. While his congressional allies can obstruct and confront Lula at home, Flávio and Eduardo can cheerlead from abroad and cultivate support for their cause in Washington.
Unsure of what exactly Washington might do next, Lula’s government has, so far, simply ignored the pronouncements of the defeated candidate-in-exile. The strategy is clearly to avoid turning Flávio’s departure into a diplomatic crisis with Trump, particularly while the two governments are negotiating on trade and tariffs. The Foreign Ministry did summon Argentina’s diplomatic representative to explain the circumstances of Flávio’s passage through that country, but has left the question of his departure and possible legal consequences to Brazil’s courts and the Federal Police. To date, no formal extradition request to Washington has yet been reported.
For his part, Lula has mocked Flávio’s escape, drawing a connection between his arrival in the United States and Trump’s historic midterm defeat days later. Lula also delivered a pointed prediction: “You’ll have to come back to Brazil to face the cases against you.” After losing the 2022 race, Jair Bolsonaro also came to Florida with the hope of returning to power by hook or by crook. The former president ultimately went back to Brazil, where he ended up on trial and in prison instead. Flávio insists that he will not repeat the mistake of returning.
The shifting political landscape in the United States adds to the uncertainty of Flávio’s presence. Overwhelming Democratic victories in the midterm elections last week delivered a stunning rebuke to Trump. The president is likely to face congressional investigations, including challenges to the “Donroe Doctrine” of maximum US control in the region that Trump’s interventionist efforts in Brazil have sought to advance.
“Trump is convinced that Brazil is no longer a full democracy,” Flávio told The Washington Post last week, implying that further aggressive action from Washington was still possible. Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff—Millier is a rabid defender of the “might makes right” principle of US power in Latin America and an extremist with ties to several Bolsonaro allies—has offered a rare bit of good news for Flávio’s future.
Still, the dramatic change in Trump’s political fortunes has forced Flávio to change his tune on the US assistance in his fleeing Brazil. When Bolsonaro arrived in the US, he thanked Trump for his support. But, perhaps in anticipation of increased scrutiny, he now claims that his presence in the US owes very little to Trump. His escape was entirely his own doing, he told The New York Times: “It was all me. There was help from absolutely no one, from no government.” When it came to “how I got here,” he would “take that to the grave with me.” In the same interview, Flávio praised Trump for staying out of Brazil’s election, claiming that the president had done the right thing by not taking sides—presumably notwithstanding that campaign photo op in the Oval Office.
So far, Trump officials have been publicly noncommittal on Bolsonaro’s efforts to overturn Brazil’s election. Members of the administration may have their own reasons to keep some distance. After all, a White House operation to extract a defeated foreign presidential candidate facing criminal investigations and supporting his aspirations to overturn a free and fair election in Latin America’s largest nation are precisely the sort of scandals a newly empowered Democratic Congress might decide to investigate. It also threatens to complicate relations with Lula at a moment when Washington has considerable economic and strategic interests in Brazil.
Trump has consistently favored the Bolsonaro family. But his willingness to protect them will be tested if doing so begins to carry a political price at home.
Flávio, meanwhile, has little choice but to tie himself to the mast of a MAGA ship taking on water. As Lula plans his fourth administration, he may well find that the most consequential postelection development is not Flávio’s flight to Miami but the diminishing political prospects of his American host.

France’s Left, Divided at the Worst Possible Time
Years of progressive infighting weigh on Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s presidential ambitions.
A lot should be playing in the French left’s favor this autumn. With the country engulfed by one of the most intense cycles of social protest in years, public attention has turned to the needs of high school students and financially stressed households—and away from the culture-war issues that have made the fortunes of far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen. But it most of all adds up to a rebuke for outgoing centrist President Emmanuel Macron, whose erstwhile allies are being forced to run against a legacy that counts fewer and fewer defenders by the day.
“Everyone hates the Macronist regime,” left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon told supporters at a campaign rally this Saturday, six months from presidential elections that could well sign the death certificate for the country’s traditional political class. On November 9, Macronist Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu conceded to an accelerated rise in the minimum wage, the latest bid to calm the anger.
So where does it all leave the left? In many respects, this fall’s crisis is the dreamed-of preelection scenario for Mélenchon’s party La France Insoumise (LFI). Having long billed itself as the party-political companion to French social movements, LFI hopes to emerge as the natural electoral outlet for the pent-up frustration that has spilled onto the streets since September.
“The France of rebellions and revolutions—our dear country, we’re all well at home here,” Mélenchon boasted to the packed audience gathered in Le Bourget, a suburb just north of Paris. “France has reached a boiling point. In demonstrations and then elections, our people are looking for and will find a solution to its problems.”
For LFI, which currently leads the pack of progressive contenders for next spring’s vote, this Saturday’s rally was a showcase for its sprawling policy platform. The party is calling for a radical social-democratic program, including a jump in the minimum wage to €1,700 per month, or just over $1,900. Among the over 1,000 measures in the platform are a massive injection of funds for public services, a lowering of the pension age, price freezes on gasoline and food, and a program of reindustrialization through “ecological planning.”
With France’s budget deficit hitting well over 5 percent of GDP, a platform like this is predicated on confronting the European Union over the bloc’s stringent fiscal rules—something the left-wing force does not shy away from. The party also wants broad wealth redistribution, namely a cap on inheritances at €12 million, or nearly $13.5 million, and the creation of a so-called “Zucman tax,” a 2 percent annual charge on the country’s largest fortunes. Named for the French-born Berkeley economist Gabriel Zucman, it’s France’s version of the wealth tax that California voters defeated in a referendum last Tuesday.
“I only have one thing to propose, something that is ultimately quite reasonable: We must change everything,” Mélenchon summed up on Saturday, arguing that the country needed a politics adapted to what he called a “global crisis of human civilization.”
For the more than 10,000 people in attendance, the November 7 rally was also a reminder that the party knows how to put on a show. Beyond the candidate’s undeniable rhetorical talents, the convention featured a genre-bending display of political communication. Preceding Mélenchon’s headline speech was a video montage of scripted vignettes highlighting the party’s main proposals, scenes that drifted into onstage dramatizations featuring leading party MPs. As far as pedagogical political theater goes, Bertolt Brecht could hardly have done better.
And yet, the palpable enthusiasm among the left-wing base for Mélenchon’s candidacy, his fourth since 2012, is difficult to square with the many roadblocks on the way to power next spring. French progressives are marginalized and divided in a country tilting dramatically to the hard right, as Le Pen’s grip over a wide swath of the electorate shows few signs of giving way.
For the April 18 first-round vote, well over 30 percent are estimated to back the far-right front-runner. That’s a double-digit lead over Mélenchon, who currently finds himself in a distant second place, benefiting from the dispersal of candidates to his right—something that’s likely to change before Election Day. For now, however, the veteran left-winger is ahead of both the weak field of other progressive contenders and even Macron’s centrist and conservative allies, who are caught in their own factional fights and reeling from the outgoing president’s stark unpopularity. The runoff looks similarly dire. Polling has been proven wrong before, but the most drastic predictions have Le Pen leading Mélenchon in a hypothetical second-round vote by over 30 points, a wider gap than Le Pen’s lead over other potential runoff opponents.
The story of how France got here is a long one, and there’s plenty of blame to go around. Most goes to Macron, who has devoted much of his presidency to catering to hard-right priorities on subjects like immigration and public order. Propelled by drastic shifts in France’s media landscape, in particular the sudden rise of a television and news pole owned by hard-right billionaire Vincent Bolloré, the culture of French politics has undergone nothing short of a counterrevolution in the last 10 years.

But the left has also inflicted far too many wounds on itself. Its current weakness is downstream of the various failed attempts at cross-party coalition building in recent years, starting with the Nouvelle Union populaire écologique et sociale (NUPES) formed after Macron’s 2022 reelection as president. Long gone, too, are the days of the Nouveau Front populaire (NFP), the revamped left-wing alliance that delivered a surprise first-place finish in the snap parliamentary elections called by Macron in June 2024.
Stemming the tectonic shifts dragging France rightward was the best argument for progressive unity. But powerful forces opposed just that very strategy. Mélenchon’s sworn enemy since he bolted from the party in the late 2000s, the centrist Parti socialiste (PS) has lent its institutional stamp to the reckless pillorying of the radical left. This October, the party selected the anti-LFI media personality turned politician Raphaël Glucksmann as its candidate, confirming the center left’s definitive break with the Mélenchonists. Glucksmann and the various center-right figures now battling over the remnants of Macron’s coalition disagree on many things, but they seem to see eye to eye on the spurious idea that “Mélenchonism” represents as grave a danger to the country as Le Pen.
LFI has also painstakingly worked to undermine left-wing unity. Since the crack-up of the NFP and the NUPES before it, the open secret on the left is that the other main adversary of coalition politics was Mélenchon himself, who feared that a durable alliance would evolve into the institutional framework for a multiparty primary that might jeopardize his presidential candidacy. “My aim is not to unify the left,” the candidate told journalists shortly before taking to the podium this past Saturday.
Instead, LFI’s defining strategy has been to maintain hegemony over a left-wing electorate, itself reduced to a shrunken third of the political space amid the tripartite division of the French party system since 2017. There’s plenty of racist dog-whistling in the attempt to discredit Mélenchon’s appeal to what he calls the “new France” represented by the country’s diverse urban areas. But beyond these electoral strongholds, LFI has struggled to build out support in rural parts of the country and in smaller towns, a share of the electorate potentially requiring other types of candidates, messaging, and campaigning than those perfected by Mélenchon and his allies.
On international politics, possible allies have also long accused Mélenchon of foot-dragging when it comes to condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine since 2014. After Saturday’s rally, progressive and moderate critics were again up in arms at Mélenchon’s call for a referendum in the Donbas to decide control over the territory, currently largely occupied by the Russian military. Add on top of that the party’s often loose standards for fiery communication, which have landed it in a now-lengthy series of antisemitism scandals. They have had the combined effect of distracting from LFI’s otherwise principled—and often courageously solitary—defense of the Palestinian cause.
“Clarity” is the response from many France Insoumise supporters when they’re pressed on the infighting that has derailed the various attempts at left-wing coalition building. With their standard-bearer now positioned as the left’s lead contender for 2027, they also argue that it’s not too late to make up for lost time. Nonaligned factions in a progressive camp divided between Mélenchon and Glucksmann will have little choice, they claim, but to take sides as Election Day approaches. Then there are the abstentionists. And given Mélenchon’s undeniable knack for debating, many confidently assume that their candidate can trounce Le Pen in a head-to-head debate before the May 2 runoff.
For that matter, Mélenchon has long argued that the breakdown of France’s party system would lead to a decisive battle royale between what LFI calls the “left of rupture” and Le Pen. But if the cards fall hard next spring, one wonders just how much virtue there’ll really be in clarity.

A Sprawling CIA Plot
Forty years ago, on the evening of October 5, 1986, I sat conferring with members of my local Nicaragua solidarity organization. We were trying to understand the implications of the day’s events in San Carlos, a small town in southern Nicaragua. A young Sandinista soldier had fired a shoulder-launched missile, bringing down a plane in a wreck survived by one Eugene H. Hasenfus. The plane contained U.S.-supplied weapons destined for the Contras, the counter-revolutionary force illegally supported by the CIA to overthrow the Nicaraguan government.
Hasenfus was captured, tried, and convicted of terrorism, and then, in a clever PR move by the Sandinista government, pardoned and released in time to spend Christmas at home with his family in Wisconsin.
Hasenfus’s capture — along with his planeload of AK-47s, 50,000 rifle cartridges, some shoulder-mounted missiles, and grenades — provided concrete evidence of something we’d known for a while: The Reagan administration was actively defying Congress by illegally funding and supplying the Contras. In those years, the Boland amendments (addenda to laws funding U.S. intelligence agencies) prohibited the CIA from using appropriated monies to support the Contras. Hasenfus’s capture not only demonstrated that those amendments were being violated, but also eventually led to the unraveling of a much bigger plot, known today as the Iran–Contra affair.
Oliver North, Iran, and “The Enterprise”
The trail from Hasenfus led to a military aide at the National Security Council, Oliver North, who was running a project to fund the Contras — with money from congressionally outlawed missile sales to Iran. Iran needed the military hardware for a brutal war of attrition with neighboring Iraq. The Reagan administration wanted to free U.S. hostages held in Iran and by Iran’s ally Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. So the arms-for-hostages deal was cooked up. Ollie North saw a way to use that one illegal deal to enable a second one. He would funnel unappropriated funds for the Contras by charging Iran a steep markup on the weapons and stashing the difference in Swiss bank accounts, outside U.S. government control.
At the suggestion of CIA Director William Casey, North had recruited Richard V. Secord, a retired Air Force major general, to establish what they called “the Enterprise.” North would later describe the Enterprise as an “off-the-shelf, self-sustaining, stand-alone entity that could perform certain activities,” i.e., covert overseas operations. The congressional committee that eventually investigated the Iran–Contra affair reported:
The Enterprise, functioning largely at North’s direction, had its own airplanes, pilots, airfield, operatives, ship, secure communications devices, and secret Swiss bank accounts. For 16 months, it served as the secret arm of the N.S.C. staff, carrying out with private and non-appropriated money, and without the accountability or restrictions imposed by law on the CIA, a covert Contra aid program that Congress thought it had prohibited.
North became something of a comic figure in U.S. history, especially after the escapade in which he choked a government office shredder during a late-night document “shredding party.” He and the coterie of implicated officials both above and below him all received pardons from incoming President George H. W. Bush, who’d served as Reagan’s vice president.
There is no way of knowing just how large North’s Enterprise might have grown had Hasenfus’s plane not been shot down, or what other sorts of dirty money-making businesses it might have spawned. Perhaps today we’d be living in a country with a largely self-funding, and therefore (even more) unaccountable, national security apparatus.
Big, “Dirty” Business in Venezuela
I thought about the Iran–Contra affair and North’s Enterprise for the first time in years when I read that Pete Hegseth’s Defense Department is getting into the oil business in Venezuela. Under the new arrangement, the Department of Defense would receive “penny warrants” for an ownership stake in at least one company developing Venezuelan oil fields. These warrants, according to the New York Times, “would give the Pentagon the option to take up to a 35 percent stake in the parent company” of North American Blue Energy Partners.
The company, which is legally registered in Barbados, is run by Alejandro Betancourt López, a Nicolás Maduro crony, around whom corruption rumors have swirled for at least a decade. The deal would also provide the Defense Department with the right to purchase up to 20 percent of the company’s oil output “at production cost” and first refusal on the remaining 80 percent, presumably at market rates.
There are a number of issues to consider here: The U.S. invasion’s legality, the logistical difficulties of extracting and using Venezuela’s “dirty” crude, and, of course, the human folly of pouring even more oil on the climate fire. But what especially caught my attention in the Times story is that the Pentagon taking an equity stake in a private oil company looks a lot like a new edition of North’s off-the-shelf operation from the 1980s.
The Pentagon isn’t alone among federal agencies acquiring ownership stakes in a variety of companies. Perhaps most notable is the Commerce Department’s purchase of an almost 10 percent interest in the chip manufacturer Intel for $8.9 billion, a stake that’s now reportedly worth $42 billion. As the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported in February, “the Trump administration is acquiring a strategic portfolio of investments in companies directly related to national security, spanning minerals, nuclear energy, and semiconductors, among other sectors.”
The CSIS report lists several smaller — though still enormous — Defense Department equity investments, among them:
- Vulcan Elements, a manufacturer of rare earth magnets: warrants to purchase equity at an undisclosed fixed price; $620 million loan against a $50 million equity stake
- MP Materials, a rare earth magnet manufacturer: 15 percent stake for $400 million
- Korea Zinc, a joint venture with Commerce and private investors in a Tennessee smelting installation; Defense Department to take 40 percent ownership, total cost $1.9 billion
- ReElement Technologies, a rare earth magnet recycler: warrants for future stock purchase; $80 million from Defense “matched by private capital”
- Trilogy Metals, a Canada-based company with Alaskan mining rights: 10 percent stake purchased for $35.6 million, with warrants to purchase another 7.5 percent
Since that report was published, DoD has continued to expand its portfolio with other equity purchases, which seem to be aimed at least in part on restocking American weapons reserves depleted by the Iran war:
- L3Harris Missile Solutions: $1 billion direct equity investment for solid rocket motor and missile production
- The Elmet Group: $450 million preferred equity investment in the only U.S.-based tungsten producer. Tungsten is crucial in the production of Patriot missiles, an essential defense against incoming missiles and drones, and a much-depleted armament in U.S. stores because of the Iran war.
- Hertha Metals: an apparent $65 million investment — for an undisclosed number of shares — in a steel manufacturer. The libertarian Cato Institute, which generally opposes federal ownership stakes in corporations, called the investment with Hertha an “apparent” deal, as only the company, not the DoD, has announced it publicly.
Beyond taking direct ownership shares in corporations, DoD continues to diversify its loan portfolio beyond traditional military materials. For example, President Donald Trump recently promised a $100 million Pentagon investment to rebuild a pharmaceutical factory in Winchester, Kentucky — but only if Republicans won the midterms in that state.
How Does Government Ownership of Corporations Work?
The federal government has taken temporary partial ownership of U.S. corporations before Trump’s current string of acquisitions. What makes this round of purchases different is that it seems the Pentagon intends to make them permanent. In the past, when the federal government acquired warrants or corporate shares, the move was part of a program to shore up failing institutions in the midst of a more general financial disaster.
This was the case with the Troubled Assets Relief Program, which formed part of the Obama administration’s response to the 2008 fiscal crisis, and more recently when airlines faced bankruptcy during the 2020-21 Covid pandemic. In neither case did the government retain permanent ownership of the entities it bailed out.
The evidence is that this time around, the Trump administration envisions permanent ownership stakes in companies it deems essential to military preparedness and national security. In the case of the Pentagon, two related offices are responsible for overseeing DoD’s equity investments.
The Office of Strategic Capital was established in 2022 during Joe Biden’s administration and funded under the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2024. The OSC’s initial purpose was to facilitate Pentagon loans to industries it deems crucial to national security. Other parts of DoD use grants or purchases to get money to defense industries. Only OSC can lend those corporations money. Still, neither the NDAA for 2024 nor subsequent NDAAs permits the OSC to buy shares in companies.
The OSC received a huge funding boost under Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. While simultaneously meting out drastic cuts to programs that support Americans’ actual everyday security — such as Medicaid, nutritional assistance, housing, and student loans — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act awarded OSC $1.5 billion in additional funds.
The other entity tasked with overseeing Defense equity investments is the Economic Defense Unit. Established this year through an internal DoD memo, the EDU offers a hint that the Pentagon isn’t ready to give up on capital. Like the Office of Strategic Capital, the EDU is overseen by Defense Department Undersecretary Stephen Feinberg, a billionaire, major Trump donor, and co-founder of the private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management.
EDU’s ostensible purpose is to coordinate U.S. economic competition with adversaries such as China, Iran, Russia, and North Korea. But reporting suggests another reason Feinberg established the unit. Quoting a knowledgeable inside source, The American Prospect says that the EDU “operates as a ‘venture capital firm-type entity that looks at deals, what the government’s going to do and evaluates them,’” determining what the government’s ownership stake should be.
The Cato Institute says of the EDU:
Available information points to an investment apparatus being created within the Pentagon, staffed by financiers connected to the same private-equity world that stands to benefit from it.
It sounds like another attempt by the administration to construct a pseudo-sovereign wealth fund controlled by the executive branch.
In other words, the Economic Defense Unit looks like the beginning of a Defense Department investment bank.
As of today, no law explicitly permits the Pentagon to own pieces of corporations or to develop its own pseudo-investment bank, but the 2027 NDAA may change that.
In the meantime, what happens to any revenue derived from DoD’s investments? Such income could include interest on loans, share dividends, or proceeds from the sale of equities. Legally, any such income should be deposited to the U.S. Treasury within three days, according to the U.S. legal code section § 3302(b), perhaps in the Pentagon’s Industrial Base Fund at Treasury.
History tells us North sent the Iran–Contra money to Swiss banks, not the U.S. Treasury. Can we trust Hegseth — who just this week survived an impeachment vote — and his boss not to do something similar with the Pentagon’s earnings today? How would we even know if that trust were violated?
Just Like Egypt and Iran?
The prospect of a metastasizing U.S. Defense Department may seem far-fetched, but it’s already happened in a number of other countries. In Egypt, popular demonstrations brought down President Hosni Mubarak, the country’s effective dictator, during the 2011 Arab Spring. After a brief period under an increasingly unpopular elected president, the Egyptian military staged a coup and has ruled the country directly ever since.
But Egypt’s army is more than a military force. It’s the most powerful economic entity in the country as well. As the Carnegie Middle East Center describes the situation, the Egyptian military has its tentacles in every aspect of Egypt’s economy. Members of the military:
… deliver massive infrastructure projects, produce consumer goods ranging from food to household appliances, manufacture industrial chemicals and transport equipment, and import basic commodities for civilian markets. They have expanded into new sectors as diverse as steel production, pharmaceuticals, gold prospecting, and managing religious endowments and pilgrimage.
At the same time, “thousands of retired senior officers have benefited from the powerful political influence of the military to occupy senior positions throughout the state’s civilian apparatus and public sector companies, securing extra postretirement incomes for themselves while complementing the formal military economy in return.”
(This sounds a lot like the egregious post-service opportunities promised to the investment bankers being recruited to work in the Pentagon’s EDU. After serving on the Pentagon’s new 30-person investment team, where they would have “unmatched access to top-level government officials and privileged information flow,” the recruitment pitch goes, “if you ever want to raise your own fund, you will gain access to fund-raising channels that include royal families and foreign sovereign contacts,” according to the New York Times.)
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has emerged as Iran’s most powerful economic force, plays a similar role, according to CSIS:
The IRGC now owns businesses in the oil and gas sectors, as well as land, marine, and air transportation. The IRGC-owned company, Khatam al-Anbiya, established as the IRGC’s arm in the construction sector, currently controls 812 officially registered Iranian companies which have a total of some 1,700 governmental contracts. Another IRGC-owned company has also recently bought a 51 percent stake in the Iranian Telecommunications company that was privatized at a value of $5 billion.
Can It Happen Here?
Could the Pentagon really emerge as an economic power in its own right, one that operates in tandem with, but parallel to, the federal government? Not tomorrow, certainly, but now is the time to step on the brakes to prevent that scenario.
The prospect of an economically independent U.S. military would be frightening under any circumstances. But it becomes both more frightening and more likely with a Pentagon that Hegseth is reshaping in his own white Christian nationalist and misogynist image. He’s already removed many of the potential human guardrails by purging long-serving top military leadership. As long as DoD doesn’t threaten any of the enterprises of the Trump family and friends — including those of Don Jr. and Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, and Steve Witkoff — we can expect little resistance from the demented relic in the White House.
Fortunately, Hegseth is not the sharpest bayonet in the armory. As with many aspects of this nightmare administration, we may yet be saved from a metastasizing Pentagon by the ineptitude of its leader. Let us work to make it so.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘I railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian’: the cheeky, feminist photography of Jill Posener
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Philippa Kelly
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
If it were a lady it would get its bottom pinched. If this lady was a car she’d run you down.” These are the words that Jill Posener immortalised in November 1979, when she picked her way through traffic on London’s Farringdon Road to photograph something most would have overlooked: a graffitied billboard. The first sentence was there by design – a sexist attempt at wit intended to promote a new Fiat. The second she has since been repeatedly accused of adding herself.
In reality, the image-maker, playwright and nonprofit founder explains from her home in California, the now infamous phrase had been daubed by two women working at the nearby offices of the socialist newspaper Morning Star. “They had seen the billboard go up and were so incensed that they came up with this solution,” Posener recalls. “They didn’t think anything of it until they saw the postcard. I sent them a whole bunch and we all had a good laugh.”
It was in a small West End print shop that Posener first produced about 100 postcards featuring her image of the defaced – or, to use her preferred term, refaced – Fiat advertisement. In the years since, she estimates that more than 1m have been sold. Although, she hastens to add, she has never made much money from them.
Not that profit was ever Posener’s goal: the postcards were simply a way to disseminate what would become her signature brand of political satire. They were created at a time when the women’s liberation and gay rights movements were at odds with Margaret Thatcher’s socially conservative vision for Britain, and explicitly railed against the stereotype of what Posener describes as “the humourless lesbian or humourless feminist”. As with much of the photographer’s work, they also carried another message: “a big fuck you to the establishment”.
More than 40 years after it was taken, in 2023 the Fiat image enjoyed a somewhat unexpected revival when it featured in Tate Britain’s landmark exhibition Women in Revolt. For Posener, who had shifted her professional focus to animal welfare more than a decade earlier, the experience was cathartic. “I had absolutely walked away from photography,” she recalls. “So I do credit the Tate show with – and I don’t mean to sound dramatic – giving me my old life back.”
The show also sparked renewed institutional interest in her work, and eventually led to a new Glasgow School of Art retrospective, Jill Posener: Stage and Street. The exhibition looks far beyond that one well-timed photograph, traversing the image-maker’s years as a member of Britain’s first professional gay theatre troupe, Gay Sweatshop, exploring her time photographing party conferences for the Daily Mirror, and re-examining her influential 1987 series, Dirty Girls Guide to London. It also features several less famous – though equally deserving – examples of wry billboard graffiti.
Together, these works make Stage and Street Posener’s most significant UK solo show to date, and the first to recognise, in its entirety, a 50-year career dedicated to cultural production and social justice. Now 73, she is stoic about the overdue nature of the honour. “I think part of it is that I’m not a particularly gifted photographer,” she says, “and I’m not being self-deprecating. But I am somebody that sees things, and it’s possible that I can see things others don’t.”
This was certainly the case in November 1979, when Posener first caught sight of the graffitied Fiat billboard. Does she worry that, even now, this remains the defining moment of her photographic career? “I think, if you have one image that so encapsulates a moment, a movement, then embrace it,” she says. “I have no problem being a one-hit wonder.”
Casts, creches and kisses: Posener’s political pictures
Join Lesbians United, London, 1981 (main picture)
  
“I’m not sure how I came upon this one, but I think it was in north London. You can’t help but laugh when you see it. Maybe because I’ve lived with a lot of anger in my life, I loved that we could respond to these things with humour, and that other people could then recognise and take pleasure from that.”
Promotional photo for Posener’s play Any Woman Can, performed by the Gay Sweatshop theatre company, 1976
  
“At the time, there was a lot about it that resonated with people,” says Posener. “The last line was: ‘You’re looking at a screaming lesbian, and I’m looking right back at you.’ For me, as a young woman, this was both a reflection of my own coming out and my confrontational nature toward the world.”
Margaret Thatcher at the Conservative Women’s Conference, London, 1987
  
“I took some photographs at the Tory party women’s conference that really made fun of that audience, and sometimes I feel embarrassed that I did that. On the other hand, they were showing who they were, and I was identifying that and photographing it. Thatcher in the creche was just the most hilarious thing I could possibly imagine.”
From A Dirty Girls Guide to London, 1987
  
“It’s called A Dirty Girls Guide to London because it was like a tourist brochure. But instead of just icons of British culture, there’s two women kissing, basically saying: ‘We can do this right here, in front of everybody.’ It’s about not hiding, and it’s about saying: ‘You cannot control our lives and you cannot control our bodies.’”
Drew Griffiths performs in Jingleball, a Gay Sweatshop production, eight years before his murder, which remains unsolved, 1976
  
“When Sweatshop had its first press conference, Drew actually couldn’t face the press. He was too ashamed to face the media, so he had his back to them, even though he’d started the group. And I think that’s what we all felt: this terrible fear, and yet this hope and possibility of something new.”
Jill Posener: Stage and Street is at Reid Gallery, The Glasgow School of Art to 9 January

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Eileen Kinsella
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in New Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.
The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.
“What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.
According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.
“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke says. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”
According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker says. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”
Things moved quickly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director says.
After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.
“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree says, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.
Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.
“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Women finally start to get pride of place with central London sculptures
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Louisa Buck
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
London bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It says something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical new works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.
In Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.
“She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is important to add more images and visual representation,” she said.
Meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, New York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is currently having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.
Eisenman’s column
At its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.
Barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s New York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.
Eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.
In strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.
