https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: From the Ground Up: Here’s What It Takes to Build, Build, Build Affordable Housing
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Facing down New York’s housing crisis, city leaders of all stripes are pushing three words: build, build, build. But building affordable housing is a complex and time-consuming process.
But it takes years of work, millions of dollars and countless hours traversing red tape before new apartments are ready for tenants.
As part of The City Reporter’s series on the New York City affordable housing lottery, we took a look at a fairly typical 100% affordable housing project in The Bronx to show exactly what goes into making a new building like this one real — even before it’s listed on Housing Connect.
New York City severely needs to build more affordable housing, and those in power feel the crunch. On his first day in office, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he’d quicken the pace. The day he took office, he convened a Streamlining Procedures to Expedite Equitable Development (SPEED) Task Force, whose recommendations promised to slash eight months from the time it takes to build affordable housing by focusing on interagency communication, financing, permitting, construction and lease-ups. On the state level, Gov. Kathy Hochul and the Legislature also reformed the environmental permitting process to accelerate housing development.
At Twin Parks Terrace, a 182-unit complex in The Bronx’s Fordham Heights, here’s what it took to transform a parking lot into the 14-story affordable apartment building: navigating multiple agencies, $81 million and almost a decade of work.
The project went, by all accounts, as smoothly as anyone could hope.
“There are no easy sites in New York. Things go from difficult to nightmare, and this was not a nightmare of a project,” said Eli Weiss, principal at Joy Construction, which oversaw the project with Settlement Housing Fund.
The process by which Twin Parks Terrace came to fruition is not representative of all affordable housing projects, and if it was built now, it would benefit from some of the changes happening at the local and state levels. But it is a good example of a subsidized, fully affordable housing project built on city land and relying on common financing options.
“The journey for any project is many years,” said Emily Lehman, Settlement’s vice president of real estate, who formerly worked at the city housing department for more than a decade. “The timelines we saw for this particular project might look different for a project that was awarded today.
2017: The proposed idea
The city Department of Housing Preservation and Development and NYCHA formally asked developers to come up with ideas for building 100% affordable housing on a NYCHA-owned parking lot in The Bronx. Settlement Housing Fund and Joy Construction were among the development teams that submitted a proposal with their affordable housing concept. The submission included the team’s vision for the site, proposed financing, designs, plans for property management and more details.
The team met with the agencies to answer questions and talk through the idea.
2018: The concept gets a green light
HPD and NYCHA decided to move forward with Settlement’s proposal. The development team celebrated, and then they got to work.
So began what is called the “predevelopment timeline,” where several processes happen simultaneously so that everything is ready to put shovels in the ground as soon as the team locks down financing.
Danois Architects started advancing the project’s designs, which needed approvals from HPD and the Department of Buildings.
Meanwhile, environmental review took place, which analyzed impacts on air quality and noise, among other conditions. There was a mountain of paperwork to fill out and submit to various entities, including reviews for compliance and integrity.
At the same time, the team figured out how to finance the project with dollars from multiple sources. The general contractor priced out the project’s construction, a process that influenced both the financing side and the designs, too.
The financing included tax-exempt bond financing from the city Housing Development Corporation and subsidies from HPD. The team also used a federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit and a bank letter of credit, and they received $1.5 million in capital subsidies from local officials.
Each financing partner had a checklist with hundreds of requirements for the team to complete.
“I remember at the time saying that my checklists were having baby checklists,” said Judy Herbstman, president at Settlement.
2020: Money locked in, shovels in the ground
The development team closed on construction financing — which meant building could begin.
This marked the end of the predevelopment timeline, which took two years — “pretty fast by today’s standards,” Lehman said. “Two years is roughly the minimum the project spends in predevelopment, but it could take longer depending on the specifics of the project and subsidy availability.”
When the team closed, they signed a 99-year lease with NYCHA for the land, a process that included coordination with the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. In the development world, leases set for 99 years are very common.
The construction team started construction on closing day, in late December 2020.
2021: Construction continues
The Covid-19 pandemic meant the construction team faced some challenges, but they ultimately finished on time despite unforeseen delays.
Weiss, of Joy Construction, said starting in late 2020 meant the “initial craziness” of the Covid-19 pandemic had ebbed a bit. Though supply chains were snarled and shipping delays were common, the team had planned its supplies in advance and they were ready to arrive by the time the building’s foundation had been poured. And labor restrictions had eased up, too.
“There were two sides to Covid,” Weiss said. “There was everything you read about labor shortages, but there also wasn’t a lot of construction going on in the city. There was less traffic in the city. I don’t want to say Covid was helpful, but I think it netted out.”
Digging the foundation took about eight months, which was fairly typical for a project, Weiss said — even though challenges crept up during the excavation on The Bronx’s rocky ground. The team had to redesign the foundation because the soil was different than expected. The team also had to pay for a generator to power most of the construction work after Con Ed was unable to provide temporary power for many months. The generator’s gas was costly, Weiss said.
After the foundation, the team constructed the building itself, topping off at 14 stories five or six months later.
Another three to four months after that, the team enclosed the building, making sure it was weathertight, Weiss said. That allowed work to start on the interiors, including kitchens, bathrooms and floors.
2022: Marketing preparation
As construction continued, Settlement began to prepare for marketing the apartments in the building as part of the housing lottery on Housing Connect. The team worked with HPD to prepare advertisements for how the building would be shown to potential tenants.
2023: Construction is substantially completed, and the housing lottery opens
By February, applicants could apply to live in Twin Parks Terrace through the housing lottery on Housing Connect. There were 135 apartments priced for households making between $22,700 for one or two people, and up to $160,720 for a family of seven.
In addition, 46 apartments were set aside for formerly homeless New Yorkers, who were referred to Settlement by HPD.
“You get the list of people and start qualifying them so that people are ready to sign leases as soon as the building’s ready to open,” Herbstman said. “Then you continue qualifying households and signing leases after you get your temporary certificate of occupancy.”
Meanwhile, as construction neared an end, the team began closing out permits with various agencies and other entities. For instance, it needed Con Ed to turn the utilities on and to get a certificate of occupancy inspection with the Buildings Department, a key step for a building to be tenant-ready.
The development team in April received a temporary certificate of occupancy, which allowed residents to start moving into the building. DOB had to make sure the plumbing was up to snuff and elevators were safe, among other items.
That same month, the lottery closed. By the fall, the first tenants started moving in.
2024: Tenants fill up the apartments.
Residents continued moving in.
2025: The building reaches full occupancy
After most of the tenants moved in and the building was operating for about three months, the team converted to permanent financing, which allowed them to pay down the construction loans and borrow with a lower interest rate while also unlocking more money for the project.
The DOB issued the final certificate of occupancy in March. The process of moving from a temporary certificate of occupancy to the final version was all about paperwork, Weiss said: “It’s closing out the jobs.”
Today
Now, Twin Parks Terrace stands tall, wedged up a slope on a busy avenue. The building has play areas for children, laundry machines and bike storage. There’s a discount store on the ground floor, which also features another retail space for lease.
On a weekday afternoon, individuals and families streamed in and out of the building.
One of them was a tenant named Veronica Lopez. The sexagenarian moved into her one-bedroom apartment about three years ago, after seven years of applying to the housing lottery.
“The apartments are beautiful. When I came in, I was the first one in my apartment,” Lopez said. “It was clean, new. Everything was perfect.”
With a laugh she added, “It still is perfect because I have OCD.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/h.title: Highway or the Highway: Brooklynites Slam BQE Bypass Proposal
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/h.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/h.text:
Mayor Mamdani should not simply rebuild the ailing Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, and saddle future generations with its inevitable and costly upkeep, but instead explore options to transition away from the roadway’s truck-first approach, Brooklynites said at a public meeting on Thursday night.
The Department of Transportation has begun gathering feedback for a required environmental review of its $4 billion proposal to rehab what it calls BQE Central, a deteriorating section of the highway between Atlantic Avenue and Sands Street, over the next decade. The agency wants to construct a temporary bypass that involves a dramatic flyover above the Brooklyn Bridge’s approach in Dumbo.
Residents and advocates called on the Mamdani administration to broaden its scope, not double down on the Robert Moses infrastructure. “You are asking New Yorkers to spend $4 billion to end up in 2040 with the same 1954, racist highway that Robert Moses built,” said Red Hook resident Victoria Hagman Alexander at the virtual feedback session with the agency. “Your scope studies two options: build it or don’t. And that’s not a choice for communities. And it’s a choice that we’ve rejected multiple times.”
According to DOT’s Oct. 2 draft scope of work for the environmental review, the agency will study the impacts of building a bypass versus not rebuilding the BQE — an approach the leader of the influential Brooklyn Heights Association described as “far too narrowly defined.” 
“The purpose and scope have to include the goal of moving people and freight much more efficiently and much more sustainably throughout our borough, and preferably not in thousands of cars carrying one person at a time, as we see now on the BQE,” said the BHA’s executive director, Lara Birnback. In 2018, the BHA successfully rallied against former mayor Bill de Blasio’s proposal to erect a six-lane temporary highway atop the Brooklyn Heights promenade.
Construction is set to begin in 2030 and last 10 years, and the rebuild will extend the BQE’s lifespan until 2080. Mamdani’s DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn has argued that the city needs to renovate the BQE to facilitate the movement of its daily 130,000 motorists, including 13,000 trucks, and that the agency has run out of time to consider larger overhauls to reduce the city’s dependence on the highway.
New York City maintains an unusually heavy reliance on trucks: Nearly 90 percent of all goods move through the city on big rigs, compared to a national average of 70 percent. The city could instead spend its finite time on pivoting to alternative methods of moving freight, such as Blue Highways, good-old-fashioned rail or smaller vehicles like cargo bikes.
“This draft scope of work asks us in the community and beyond — all of us adjacent to the BQE — to endure at least a decade and likely more of highly disruptive construction, just to end up with the exact same loathed and discredited infrastructure that we’ve already endured for 70 years. We have to do better,” Birnback said.
The mayor’s proposed bypass highway will run next to the triple-cantilever level with the upper roadway, and sit within feet of adjacent residential buildings like 360 Furman Street, said a representative for the building’s roughly 1,200 residents. 
“The proposed bypass highway would come within four feet of our façade,” said Diane Genova. “A decade is not temporary for the people who have to live next to it.”
The city should look at construction approaches that don’t create an entirely new highway, such as a lane-by-lane rebuild with a traffic reduction plan, Genova said. In 2021, following recommendations by an expert panel, de Blasio reduced the triple-cantilever’s six lanes to just four. The intervention cut cut the number of daily vehicles on the bridge by 15 percent.
Transportation officials must also finally fix the chaotic Atlantic Avenue interchange by closing the Queens-bound on-ramp and removing the dangerous pedestrians crossings to and from the waterfront, said a representative for an area business group. De Blasio’s expert panel emphasized the same recommendation in its six-year-old report, to avoid creating exactly the kind of spillover traffic that now plagues adjacent neighborhoods. But neither subsequent mayor followed through and DOT now plans to rebuild it.
“The ramp truly just should be closed. For years, this has invited and incentivized cut-through traffic into our neighborhoods,” said Layla Passman, director of special projects at the Atlantic Ave BID. 
DOT has shied away from decommissioning the structure, saying that its retirement would dump car and truck traffic onto residential streets — but that has already happened amid the agency’s inaction.
Agency officials have said closing a ramp would trigger federal reviews, which could delay the project, but former commissioner Hank Gutman recently countered that the city could temporarily shutter it without an intervention by Uncle Sam, as he did under de Blasio with an off-ramp at Cadman Plaza to shore up the triple cantilever’s retaining wall.
But the winds in Washington, D.C., have shifted with the flipping of both houses of Congress to Democratic control in the election last week, and the city should use that political leverage to think bolder, said another resident.
“When this project was conceived… there was no expectation that the extent of the blue wave that we experienced last week,” said Bill Stein of the Fulton Ferry Landing Association. “So there’s going to be fresh air, let’s say, in Washington come January, and hopefully even fresher air by November ’28.”
Preserving the Atlantic Avenue interchange has encouraged motorists to cut through residential streets between Hamilton Avenue and the Atlantic on-ramp to avoid traffic on the trench section slicing through Cobble Hill and Carroll Gardens. This led some frustrated residents to ask DOT to re-widen the cantilever to three lanes, even though doing so would encourage even more traffic.
“Having the pinch at the cantilever of two lanes has been disastrous on Columbia Street, Hicks Street. The traffic has been increased. The pedestrian safety has been decreased,” said Michelle Ocampo at the hearing. “The BQE has to be expanded to three lanes, supporting all structure implementation to make that happen.”
Another public speaker argued for the exact opposite: the city should simply shut down the highway and commerce would survive. “I think there’s a way for businesses to thrive and and take cars off the cantilever,” said Wendy Hoopes. “I personally don’t drive on it, it’s not safe. I think it should be left for pedestrians and bicyclists alone, and I don’t see how building temporary highways makes any sense when they’re four feet from where people are living.”
“We’re talking about [a] long construction period for a 40-year end frame,” Hoopes added. “You want to break up a lot of people’s lives and neighborhood to have a 40-year fix. That is not sensible, and there’s got to be a better way.”
DOT will draft an environmental impact statement over the next year, before preparing a final EIS in 2028. The city also plans to commence the city’s uniform land use review procedure, or ULURP, the same year. That will require sign-off from the City Council along with separate state approval to alienate several pieces of parkland along the project to make way for construction.
An agency spokesperson reiterated that the city has run out of time and that the deadline to repair the triple cantilever was “more immediate.”
“For too long, the BQE debate has been governed by politics. Today, it is governed by physics,” said Will Livingston in a statement. “While the triple cantilever is safe today, our latest engineering work tells us something we cannot ignore: the window to act is more immediate, and we are running out of time.”
The rep added that shoring up the triple-cantilever “does not preclude future work” to rethink the larger BQE, the majority of which is controlled by New York State. “We are out of options and must pivot towards the shortest-term rehabilitation plan needed to keep the structure safe and stable,” he said.
DOT is accepting public comment through Jan. 11 via this contact form, by emailing BQECentral@dot.nyc.gov, or sending snail mail to:
NYC Department of Transportation
Division of Bridges – BQE Central Project Team
Attention: Albert Silvestri
55 Water Street, 5th Floor
New York, NY 10041

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: How To Apply for the NYC Housing Lottery
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Want to secure an affordable, rent-stabilized apartment through New York City’s housing lottery? Step right up and try your luck!
As The City Reporter has shown, your chances of winning a subsidized apartment through the affordable lottery are a long shot, but not unheard of. In recent years, there has been one apartment available through the lottery for every 510 applications.
Those lucky New Yorkers have a fabled, enviable opportunity: Moving into (typically) brand-new buildings with stabilized rent that’s likely cheaper than the market.
But even when your number comes up in the lottery, there are a lot of hoops to jump through before you secure a lease. We spoke to leasing agents, city officials and some winners to find out the inside scoop on the lottery.
Here’s our guide for locals on how to access those opportunities, tips to navigate the process and how you can prepare — with insight from people who won the lottery and professionals who screen applicants for lottery apartments.
I’m Ready to Apply! Where Do I Start?
You can sign up for and apply to housing lotteries on Housing Connect, a web-based system run through the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development that lists and manages all available subsidized apartments.
Think of Housing Connect as the portal through which you enter lotteries for individual buildings.
First, create a profile.
You’ll include details about all sources of income, including from jobs, government assistance, investments or workers’ compensation, as well as the value of your assets in bank and investment accounts. You must include this income information for the people you’d live with.
You’ll also indicate your current residence, whether it’s a rental, NYCHA building or a homeless shelter, and whether anyone you’re applying with receives rental assistance.
The information must be provided on the profile for each member of your household — that is, the people you’ll live with in that lottery apartment, not necessarily your current household.
Make sure this information is complete, or else you won’t be able to submit an application.
You can also include details about your preferences, such as interest in a ramp or elevator, number of bedrooms and a pet-friendly policy.
One thing to keep in mind: “Anything you put on your profile, you will have to prove that it’s true,” said Wout Stienaers, a founder of Homey, a paid service that helps people apply to the housing lottery. “Don’t lie about anything.”
For instance, Stienaers said applicants might be tempted to say they have a disability because there are apartments set aside for those who do (more on that later). But you’d be asked to provide proof of that disability, like a letter from a doctor.
You can get free help to apply for the housing lottery through HPD’s Housing Ambassador Program.
I Made a Profile on Housing Connect. Now What?
Once you’ve made a profile, check buildings for which you’re eligible and click “Apply Now.” You’ll know if you’re eligible if your household income falls within a range based on the number of people you’ll be living with. (How is that income range determined? Read our guide on that here.)
Keep the information about your household and income updated as you go along. For example: If you or your partner get a raise or lose a job, make sure to log that information. If you become a parent, add your child as a member of your household!
One caveat: don’t change your household size after you apply to a lottery.
“If a household is a single mom and a teenager, and then they find out they only qualify for a studio, they can’t then add the grandmother with Social Security income to see if they qualify for another unit,” said Christine Wendell, CEO of Pront Housing, an affordable housing leasing company. “If they try to do that, they will be rejected, so they should just pick their household size, and stick with it.”
MORE: What Is ‘Affordable Housing’ in New York, and What Are My Options?
Make sure to check back on Housing Connect frequently, as new opportunities come online often.
Application periods for each building are open for two months. It doesn’t matter when you submit your application within that period, as long as you apply before the lottery closes.
“No matter at what point in time you submit your application, you have the same chance to win as everybody else,” Stienaers said.
Don’t be shy about throwing your hat in the ring! You can apply to as many lotteries as you’re eligible for.
“You can apply to an unlimited number of buildings,” Wendell said. “Just statistically speaking, you will have a greater chance of getting an affordable housing unit if you apply to a lot of buildings, which everyone is completely allowed to do.”
How Can I know if I’m Eligible?
To be eligible for affordable housing through Housing Connect, your household income must fall within a specific band. Your household’s assets must also fall under a certain amount.
The asset limits vary based on building and requirements. That means if you have a lot of savings or holdings in a stock portfolio, you may not be eligible for the lottery, even if your income falls within the bands.
Can I Apply With a Voucher or Rental Subsidy?
Yes! If you get rental assistance through programs including Section 8, CityFHEPS or Medicaid Waiver, you’re good, and then you’re not subject to minimum income requirements. But the amount of rent of the apartment you’re applying to must be within the limits of what your voucher covers.
“If you have a voucher, you should apply for everything because your income isn’t your limiting factor anymore,” said Michelle de la Uz, executive director at the nonprofit Fifth Avenue Committee. “It’s basically whatever your voucher is approved for.”
That means as a voucher-holder, you may be eligible to apply for more housing lotteries than you think. Even if you don’t make enough money, you can apply for apartments based on the amount of rent — as long as it’s no more than what your voucher is worth.
Can People Apply to the Lottery if They Don’t Live in New York City?
Yes, they technically can, but applicants who are New York City residents get priority.
“While any and everybody can apply for Housing Connect lotteries, it first focuses on folks that reside within the five boroughs of New York City before it can move someone that does not reside in New York City into one of its apartments,” said Shaheem Taylor, a marketing outreach coordinator at HPD, in a webinar.
It’s very rare for outside applicants to secure an apartment through a lottery. A New York City resident who applies to the lottery is over 10 times more likely to sign a lease for an affordable apartment than someone who lives outside the city, according to an analysis of HPD data by The City Reporter.
MORE: What Are Your Odds of Winning NYC’s Affordable Housing Lottery?
Having set his sights on someday moving back to his birthplace of New York City, Grayson Sparrow applied to housing lotteries from his home in Virginia. He lucked out when he moved back to the city in April 2024 and was asked to submit his documents for a housing lottery building in East New York just three months later.
“I’d been applying just in the event if I move back someday and maybe it lines up with something,” Sparrow, 30, said. “My info went in and by the time they pulled it, I had New York residency.”
Can I Apply to the Lottery for a Rental Apartment if I Own Property?
If you or a member of your household own property within 100 miles of New York City, then you can’t apply through the lottery. (And you can’t try for an affordable homeownership lottery if you own, or ever owned, property anywhere.)
Can I Apply for One Lottery Multiple Times?
No! One entry per household.
Your household means all the people who will live in the apartment you’ll be applying to. Only one member of the household should apply for the lottery. And you can’t apply for the same lottery twice, even if, for example, you’re applying with a roommate and then on your own.
If more than one member of a household applies to the lottery, the application is automatically disqualified.
Christina Harsch, director of leasing and compliance at Wavecrest Management, recommends keeping track of what you’re applying to and the information you’re sending in, if you get your number called.
“Keep a journal of what you’re applying to and when you apply, keep copies of the [Housing Connect] ad if you can and even copies of applications so you remember what you’re doing,” she said.
That way, you know your household only applies to one lottery and you can follow up with the agents if need be.
Need more help? Connect with a housing ambassador to get assistance preparing for and applying to the housing lottery.
What Else Might Improve My Chances of Being Selected?
If you work for the city government, are a military veteran or live in the same neighborhood as the building you’re applying for, you might get a boost in the lottery. That’s because a percentage of the available apartments are set aside for people who fall under specific categories. In all new buildings, 5% of apartments are for households where a member has a mobility disability and 2% for households where a member has a hearing or vision disability.
In addition, 10% of apartments are set aside for city employees and military veterans, and 20% for residents of the community district where the building is located. Some projects offer preferences for seniors or formerly homeless individuals, as well.
OK I Entered a Lottery! How Long Will It Take Before I Hear Back?
Once you apply, you get assigned a random number called a log number. The lower it is, the better chance you have of being contacted for the development.
And then it could be weeks, months or years before you hear back if your number has been selected. Some people never hear back, even if they are eligible! Others don’t hear anything for a long time, but all of a sudden, will be notified their number was chosen for multiple buildings.
Pro tip: Make sure to stay on top of your Housing Connect account so you don’t miss any notifications. Taylor, of HPD, recommends applicants check their Housing Connect account three times a week.
Jumelia Abrahamson, director of programs at University Neighborhood Housing Program, said she tells people to log into Housing Connect “as often as you’re logging into your social media.”
She also tells applicants to check their email on a daily basis.
“Leasing agents are not calling, they’re not texting, and if these communications are going into the junk mail or if people don’t check their emails on a daily basis, they’re missing a lot of communication,” she said.
(If you applied on paper, you can choose whether to get notifications via email or in your actual mailbox — but ideally, you’ve applied through Housing Connect! Otherwise, it can be a slower process.)
What’s the Status of My Lottery Application?
Housing Connect will indicate where your application is in the process. Here’s what those statuses mean, according to experts:
- Pending just means you submitted your application. Nothing else!
- Action required means there is a request for documentation, indicating you moved to the next stage in the process — your log number was pulled — and you need to respond to a request from the lottery administrators. (If you happen to be rejected, that will also appear under “action required.”)
- In process could mean one of two things: either that you submitted your documents and they are under review, or you missed the window to submit the documents.
- Completed indicates the end stage of the application process. It can mean that you signed a lease and received your keys. Or it could mean there are no more apartments available in a development. Or it could mean you were rejected in the process and did not appeal the rejection within the required timeline.
My Number Got Picked! Now What?
Once you’re notified your number was called in a lottery, get ready for a long road. This is where the process can get tricky, as you must provide a pile of paperwork to verify your eligibility, including identifications and proof of income. You have 10 business days to submit those documents.
And if the leasing agent requests more documents beyond what was in your original application, an applicant has five business days to respond.
“Five days is really not a long time if you’re not checking, and once that five days is gone, your place in line has been passed by,” said Charmaine Marizan, the affordable housing marketing and leasing manager at Fifth Avenue Committee. “If you don’t get back quickly, there’s a bunch of people who need it.”
It’s good to get as many of your documents in order as you can before you’re selected, experts say. Keep a digital file of PDFs of important information so you can send it off quickly if your number is called. Here is a list of the documents you may need to provide.
In sum, you must provide IDs — such as IDNYC, drivers’ license, or state ID card — for all members of the household, plus birth certificates for minors.
You’ll need to show all sources of income so the agent can verify you qualify within the income bands. That includes interest from assets, student loans, child support payments and even regular checks or Venmo payments from family members or others. Applicants employed by jobs must submit a month of pay stubs, and self-employed applicants must provide tax returns.
If you get benefits through SNAP, TANF or Social Security, you can simply submit the income determination you got through those programs.
You’ll also have to show your assets, if you have more than $51,600 saved and in investment accounts. That means providing bank account and retirement account statements, among other records. If you have less than that $51,600 in assets, you can just self-certify that that’s the case — no need to prove it.
Once it’s confirmed that you’re eligible for an apartment — and there’s a vacancy available — you can either show you’ve paid rent for the past year, or you can opt for a credit check.
There’s no application fee, but you might be charged $20 for a background or credit check.
You might have a back-and-forth with the listing agent who represents the development. They may ask for more information or clarification. You can also ask them questions.
Amira Willingham, 25, who won her Chelsea studio through the lottery, said the agent asked her about specific transactions on her bank account.
“I had to explain to them every transaction,” she said. “I bought a lot online so I had lots of receipts to show.”
On one occasion, Willingham had to get a copy of a friend’s bank statement with everything blacked out except a transaction showing Willingham sending the friend money for a dinner.
“There’s no privacy in the process,” Willingham said. “I wish I had known to have a folder of everything I’d ever done put together and up to date.”
When she wasn’t sure about how to move forward, Willingham turned to an online forum she found helpful to chat with others navigating the process.
Dan B., a musician who lives in a Greenpoint apartment he won through the lottery, advised following up with the agent to get clarity on requirements and to check in for updates: “You really have to advocate for yourself because no one’s going to care more about you getting it than yourself.”
And when you advocate for yourself, it’s good to stick to email when contacting agents in order to maintain a record, said Mildred Flores, director of affordable housing marketing and compliance at Settlement Housing Fund.
“Everybody’s going to do things differently. There are some marketing agents that terminate applications as quickly as they can, and then there are others that you know will work with applicants,” Flores said.
She said she typically tells applicants to wait to contact agents for a status update until 30 days have passed since the start of tenant selection. Have patience, she cautioned, as agents often are working to lease up multiple buildings at a time and handling hundreds of applications.
For those who inquire, Flores said she will give applicants a sense of their chances and the timeline based on their log numbers — again, the random number assigned to you when you enter a lottery.
I Got Turned Down. What Can I Do?
You can appeal the decision. Within five days of the decision, write to the agent to say why you think you should not have been rejected, or why you think you should still be moving forward, and send in supporting documents.
“An applicant can appeal at any part in the process, except during the initial qualification period,” Flores said. If an applicant successfully appeals, they will not lose their place in the queue.
HPD is not involved in this process — it’s the agents associated with the building who handle the appeals.
Often, applicants face rejection because they don’t meet income or household eligibility requirements, because a single household submitted more than one application for a building or because there was insufficient information provided to the leasing agent.
Willingham said she appealed at least three times during the process when agents disqualified her based on insufficient information or not providing the right documentations.
“I had to kind of be a Karen about it,” she said. “This is one of the only paths to affordable housing in the city. Doing anything you can to fight to get it is really important.”
I Got Approved. What’s Next?
You’ll likely take a tour of the apartment — or multiple open apartments in one new complex — and if you like what you see, you can decide to move forward. You’ll have 30 days to accept a lease offer or complete a purchase, if it’s a lottery homeownership opportunity.
You’ll have to pay the first month’s rent and a security deposit (equal to a month’s rent) upfront, so make sure you have savings!
You’ll also have to figure out how to get out of your current lease, sometimes with limited notice. That requires negotiating with your landlord.
How Long Will This Whole Process Take?
It can vary a ton! The answer has to do with how fast you as the applicant are able to mobilize, and what kind of obstacles may pop up in the screening process.
Between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026, the median time it took for an applicant to get approved for an apartment after the lottery ended was 136 days (about 4.5 months).
For Sparrow, who had applied to the housing lottery from outside New York, a year passed between when he applied for the building and when leasing agents reached out to ask for documents. Three months after that, he signed the lease for his affordable apartment.
“It is a little surprising how my process was seamless,” he said. “I’ve seen other people where they get asked for documents and it takes months for them to move into the apartment.”
WIllingham, on the other hand, applied for her building’s lottery in February of one year, received a request for documents by November, and moved in the following March.
What Happens if My Life Changes Between When I Get a Call for the Lottery?
That can happen — and it’s why you should keep your Housing Connect profile updated.
If your life changes between when you apply for a lottery and your number gets picked, you get screened for your current situation. Maybe you got married and had a family, or maybe you got promoted. Either way, you may or may not qualify for the apartment any more. The agent will work with you to figure it out.
But be careful! You don’t want your situation to change during the screening process. Marizan, for instance, cautions against earning too much overtime, which can alter your income.
“If you’re currently in the screening process and you’re due a promotion, hold back on it,” she said. “You cannot be over-income by a penny.”
Any Other Way to Secure Affordable Housing?
Yup: look for apartments that people won through the lottery but are now vacant.They’re called re-rentals (or re-sales, for homeownership). These kinds of apartments don’t go through the lottery — at least until April 30, 2027. That means you can apply for these affordable apartments almost like any other apartment — essentially, first-come, first-served. You can find listings here and here, or on the sites of individual property management companies. StreetEasy, Zillow and other listings sites may also feature vacant affordable housing re-rentals.
Harsch, of Wavecrest Management, suggested reaching out to affordable management companies by cold-calling or emailing to ask about their re-rental stock. (She mentioned even if there’s nothing to offer, she may add people who get in touch to a mailing list and send them info about new housing opportunities.)
If you apply for a re-rental opportunity, you still must be eligible for the apartment based on your income and household size — details that the leasing agent will need to verify. So it takes time! And they may add you to a wait list that they’ll pull from if another applicant doesn’t work out.

https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists.title: Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists.author: Arlene Dávila
https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists.text:
Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
Without guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.
Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry: Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.
Over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic. Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins. They are using culture to reclaim heritage and reframe the narrative. This marks a distinct departure from older paradigms, where artists were taught — or forced — to believe that conforming to mainstream, assimilationist models was the only path to success. While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.
Sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires. We see this in contemporary fashion with designers like Willy Chavarria and Raul Lopez (Luar), who draw from working-class aesthetics, immigrant youth, and urban street culture. Most importantly, these designers openly credit their sources of inspiration, making clear that Mexican-American communities and neighborhoods and Black and Brown queer nightlife are fashion-forward in and of themselves. They frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.
In other cases, artists reassess their communities' histories to directly challenge historical marginalization, as seen in the work of Gina Gwen Palacios in Brownsville, Texas. As SpaceX expands across the region, treating the land as empty of people and culture and ripe for corporate speculation, Palacios centers the rich legacy of Mexican-American communities and their direct links to the present. Through paintings that highlight her family’s legacy as fieldworkers alongside the underrepresented landscape of South Texas, Palacios elevates everyday elements such as nopales and mesquite trees to tell stories of migration, hard labor, and policing.
Against the settler-colonial myths propagated by SpaceX pundits, artist-led projects in the area, such as Boca Chica, Corazón Grande, have focused on crowdsourcing archival materials from residents to uplift their deep roots in the region. This effort reaffirms Boca Chica Beach’s identity as "the people’s beach," directly challenging claims that Brownsville and Rio Grande Valley communities are devoid of people and value, and merely sites for space launches, by centering residents' memories and their continued symbolic and living ties to the land.
The political significance of these types of projects cannot be overstated. While Guadalupe Rosales's landmark archival initiative Veteranas and Rucas has garnered considerable recognition in art circles, similar crowdsourced, post-custodial digital archives are emerging across Latinx communities nationwide. Examples include Nuevayorkinos, Documenting the Nameplate, Rhizomes: Mexican American Art Since 1848, and, of course, Boca Chica, Corazón Grande. By inviting community contributions, these platforms deliver the empowering message that everyone's history is inherently worthy of analysis and documentation.
This spirit is also evident in New York City’s public art, where artists are Latinizing the cityscape through projects that draw on marginalized elements of history, such as Afro-Indigenous heritage and the city’s Latinx and multicultural history, challenging the erasure of their presence across the city’s memorial and monument landscape. Melissa Calderón, the first Latina to create a permanent public monument in the city, paid homage to Roberto Clemente with “Para Roberto” (2019), the first monument of its kind in the Bronx. Maria Magdalena Campos Pons’s “Procession of Angels for Radical Love and Unity” (2024) reframed New York City’s history from the perspective of its Black and brown residents in a performance filled with Orisha Santeria references. That same year, Edra Soto’s “Graft” (2024–25) took over the Doris C. Freedman Plaza in Central Park, inaugurating a sculptural installation drawing on Caribbean and Puerto Rican vernacular architecture. Think also of David Rios’s “Get Carried Away, You have the Right” (2023), drawing on Afro-Taino futuristic images in his installation at Amtrak, and Shellyne Rodriguez’s “Phoenix Ladder: Monument to the People of the Bronx” (2025), a reproduction of a Bronx building evoking the borough’s strength and rebuilding after the 1970s fires.
It is true that many of these artists remain marginalized, navigating a chronic lack of opportunities and resources. Consider the last time you saw a film by award-winning independent Latinx directors like Cecilia Aldarondo or Diana Peralta on a mainstream streaming home screen or in a theater. Yet when we look at the work itself — its courage, its artistry, and its local impact — the movement is undeniably transformative. It demonstrates that Latinx communities are resilient and that art and culture are powerful tools of empowerment and continuity.
This realization is vital not just for us, but for society at large. Appreciating Latinx art offers a clear path beyond the polarized, distorted representations that have dominated public discourse for so long. The narratives Latinx artists uplift are the very ones everyone must champion as we navigate the rapid rise of AI technology and the growth of violent capitalism. Artists in the Rio Grande Valley, for example, are fiercely defending the intrinsic value of their environment and history, reminding us that community and culture are ultimately priceless. Others are also confronting traditional histories and value hierarchies within creative industries while redefining what is considered fashionable, memorable, and significant.
Most importantly, artists’ visions have the potential to generate change in all of us. This work actively transforms the lives of future generations: raised with powerful models of resistance against dehumanization and persecution, their imaginations will remain free.
Arlene Dávila's new book, Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond (2026), is now out through Duke University Press.

https://taz.de/FC-St-Pauli-sucht-neue-St.title: Hamburg sucht eine Hymne: Neues Lied
https://taz.de/FC-St-Pauli-sucht-neue-St.author: Klaus Irler
https://taz.de/FC-St-Pauli-sucht-neue-St.text:
Hamburg sucht eine Hymne: Neues Lied
Der FC St. Pauli sucht gerade eine neue Stadionhymne und setzt dabei auf die Fans. Dieser Songcontest lässt tief in die Seelen der Beteiligten blicken.
Es sind die letzten Minuten vor dem Anstoß. Die Ränge im Stadion sind bereits voll, es liegt diese freudige Anspannung in der Luft, die Lust auf das Spiel, das die Menschen anzieht, weil man vorher nicht weiß, wie es nachher ausgeht. Aus den Stadionboxen kommen die ersten Takte, die Fans halten ihre Schals hoch und dann singen viele Tausende Leute zusammen ihre Hymne. Die TV-Kommentatoren nutzen das Wort „Gänsehaut“ und halten den Mund. Letzteres ist eine unter TV-Kommentatoren durchaus unterentwickelte Fähigkeit. Ihr Schweigen zeigt, wie hoch das Thema hängt.
Nun ist ausgerechnet den gesanglich so engagierten FC-St- Pauli-Fans die Stadionhymne abhandengekommen. Lange wurde im Millerntorstadion der 50er-Jahre-Schlager „Das Herz von St. Pauli“ gesungen – ein Stück voll schlichter Seefahrerromantik mit der zentralen Erkenntnis: „Das Herz von St. Pauli, das ruft dich zurück / denn dort an der Elbe, da wartet dein Glück.“
Der Text beschränkt sich auf Hamburger Hafenfolklore, geschrieben hat ihn allerdings ein Nazikarrierist namens Josef Ollig. Das fand das FC St. Pauli-Museum heraus und die Fans entschieden mit großer Mehrheit: Den Text eines Nazidichters wollen wir nicht singen – auch wenn er noch so harmlos ist.
Anders als die anderen Vereine dieser Welt entschied der FC St. Pauli, die Suche nach einer neuen Stadionhymne zur Sache der Vereinsmitglieder und der Saisonkartenbesitzer*innen zu machen. Mehr noch: Alle, die wollten, konnten nicht nur bereits existierende Songs vorschlagen, sondern auch selbst kompositorisch tätig werden.
Eine Menge an Vorschlägen
Die Menge an eingereichten Vorschlägen war verblüffend: Ende Oktober wurden 75 bereits veröffentlichte und 296 eigens komponierte Songs zur Abstimmung gestellt. Die Songs wurden auf der FC-St- Pauli-Website veröffentlicht oder verlinkt. Mittlerweile ist die Seite leider offline.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Nun haben alle gut zu tun. Die Mitglieder und Saisonkartenbesitzer*innen sollen über insgesamt 371 Stücke abstimmen, und zwar in einem dreistufigen Verfahren – aus den 371 Stücken werden zunächst 25, aus den 25 werden 5 und aus den letzten 5 Stücken wird eines. Ende November soll der Gewinnersong feststehen.
Im Laufe des Verfahrens sind bei Coverversionen die Rechte zu klären und KI-generierte Songs herauszufiltern. Und obendrein gibt es am 14. November noch eine Mitgliederversammlung, bei der eine Gruppe „Herz von St. Pauli“-Apologeten beantragen will, die alte Hymne zu rehabilitieren – und damit den Songcontest abzuwürgen.
Dass dieser Antrag durchkommt, ist nicht zu erwarten, dass die Songcontest-Abstimmung auf solider Kenntnis der Kandidaten basiert, aber auch nicht: 371 Songs zu überblicken und zu bewerten ist selbst für Menschen mit viel Freizeit nicht zu wuppen. Das könnte man monieren.
Einblick in die Seelen der Fans
Andererseits ist durch den Wettbewerb eine Schatzgrube entstanden, in der umzuschauen sich lohnt: 296 selbst geschriebene Stadionhymnen ermöglichen einen Einblick in die Seelen der Fans, den kein Meinungsforschungsinstitut je zustande bringen könnte. In Sachen Fußballkultur ist der FC St. Pauli damit Weltklasse. In Sachen Fußball gab es zuletzt in der Zweiten Bundesliga auswärts eine 1:4-Klatsche gegen Magdeburg.
Zur Fußballkulturweltklasse gehört auch, dass die Beiträge der Menschen oft weit über die Begrenzungen des Formats „Stadionhymne“ hinausgehen. Der Damenlikörchor zum Beispiel hat mit dem Song „Haut sie weg“ eine ergreifende Bedürfnis- und Liebeserklärung abgegeben, die die herkömmlichen Fans im Millerntorstadion allerdings in Ermangelung sängerischer Fähigkeiten nicht reproduzieren könnten. Ähnlich ist das Problem gelagert bei dem zum Kunstlied tendierenden, zweistimmig zum Klavier vorgetragenen „Für Dich St. Pauli“ von Bianka Kilwinski und Carsten Zundorf. Oder bei dem vertonten kapitalismuskritischen Gedicht „Rennpferd“ von This is The Artist’s Job. Ebenso fern von Gut und Böse ist aus Stadionhymnensicht die „Millerntor Anthem“ von Psykator – hierbei handelt es sich um elektronische Clubmusik ohne Text.
Es ist aber auch viel Hymnentaugliches dabei. Das „Monster mit der Ukulele“ zum Beispiel singt mit dunkler, weiblich gehörter Stimme zur sanft melancholischen Klampfe: „Kein Platz für Nazis / kein Platz für deren Hass. Auf uns als Fans / ist immer Verlass. / Gegen Faschismus, gemeinsam Hand in Hand / wir bleiben stabil, wir bleiben in Stand.“ Als Kommentar zum eigenen Song schrieb das „Monster mit der Ukulele“: „Leider war ich bei der Aufnahme erkältet und bin stimmlich sonst besser und ich hatte keine Gelegenheit mehr, den Song in einem Tonstudio aufzunehmen.“
Ähnliches ist häufiger zu hören und lesen: Zum einen das Antifaschismusbekenntnis, zum anderen der Hinweis auf das Spontane, Unvollendete, per Smartphone Produzierte. Beim Songcontest zeigt sich, was alles möglich ist an Homerecording in Zeiten von digitaler Musikproduktion und KI.
Wobei der Umgang mit KI ein veritables Problem darstellt für den Wettbewerb: Ausschließlich von einer KI komponierte und gedichtete Songs waren von der Teilnahme ausgeschlossen, da bei einem reinen KI-Song keine Urheberschaft zu bestimmen ist – im schlimmsten Fall, schreibt der Verein, „liegen Nutzungsrechte sogar beim KI-Anbieter“. Lediglich unterstützend durfte KI eingesetzt werden, etwa bei der Ergänzung von Instrumenten.
Nur, wie lässt sich überprüfen, wer was komponiert und getextet hat? Der Verein vertraut hier auf die Angaben der Teilnehmenden. Auch ein KI-Detektor soll zum Einsatz kommen. Genaueres ist nicht zu erfahren.
Von Schlager bis Punk alles dabei
Im Hinblick auf Genres sind die Einsendungen so vielfältig wie die St.-Pauli-Fans. Eine Künstlerin namens Nike Neandertal macht Disco-Pop, Boerney macht Hardrock, George Blue macht Schlager im Freddy-Quinn-Stil, Dr. Huhu eine Cover-Version von Beethovens „Freude schöner Gotterfunken“. Häufig vertreten ist Punkrock, klar, schon die geschasste Hymne „Herz von St. Pauli“ wurde im Stadion in einer Punkversion gespielt.
Textlich finden sich immer wieder Perlen: Bei Wasted Hours etwa reimt sich „Fairness“ auf „Awareness“, Joanna Bars dichtet „Wenn dein Tag mal wieder grau war / lass den Flutlichtmast dein Leuchtturm sein“, Asphalt Adel singt: „Wir stehen auch hier in Sturm und Regen / es riecht nach Rasen, stinkt nach Leben.“ Die Aufzählung ließe sich lange fortsetzen.
Die wirklich spannende Frage ist nun: Wofür entscheiden sich die Fans? Wird es ein Underdog? Oder doch ein Song aus dem Bereich „bereits veröffentlicht“ – denn den gibt es ja auch noch. Vorgeschlagen wurde zum Beispiel der nasale Funk-und-Soul-Charakterkopf Jan Delay mit „Auf St. Pauli brennt noch Licht“ oder der Indie-Pop-Sympath Thees Uhlmann mit „Das hier ist Fußball“.
Einer der erfrischendsten Vorschläge ist überraschenderweise ein Stück von Udo Lindenberg: Der beklagte sich 1978 im Song „Reeperbahn“ darüber, wie scheiße es ebenda geworden ist im Vergleich zu den 60ern. Der Song wäre ein schöner Kontrapunkt zum gemeinsamen Nenner des Genres Stadionhymne, der darin besteht, die eigene Stadt zu loben – oder im Fall des FC St. Pauli den eigenen Stadtteil.
Diese mitunter schwülstige Heimatverbundenheit ist etwas, um das auch die Fans des FC St. Pauli nicht herumkommen. Neben der Hafenromantik ist es vor allem das Nachtleben, genauer die Toleranz und Offenheit der einzelnen Soziotope und Subkulturen, die St. Paulianer sentimental werden lässt. Wobei sich aus den Texten schließen lässt: Offenbar sind viele St. Paulianer zugezogene Kleinstadtflüchtlinge. Jedenfalls ist der Tenor: Hier bin ich Mensch, hier kann ich sein – endlich.
Seit dem 13. November befindet sich der Songcontest in der zweiten Auswahlrunde. 25 Songs sind übrig geblieben, bis zum 18. November kann abgestimmt werden, welche 5 Songs in die Finalrunde kommen. Die finale Abstimmungsrunde findet dann vom 20. bis zum 25. November statt. Wann und in welcher Form die neue Stadionhymne präsentiert wird, stand zum Redaktionsschluss noch nicht fest.
Danach wird der nächste spannende Moment sein, ob die so gewählte Hymne im Stadion akzeptiert wird. Werden die Fans mitsingen? Oder wird es Kritik am Verfahren und Boykott geben? In St. Paulis Fußballhochkultur ist beides möglich.
Transparenzhinweis: Der Autor ist Mitglied in der Tischfußball-Abteilung des FC St. Pauli. Am Songcontest war er in keiner Form beteiligt.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. Leipzigs neue Flaniermeile: Assimilation, Digga
Der Parkbogen Ost soll für Leipzig sein, was die High Line für New York ist: ein hipper Ort, wo einmal Gleise waren. Nicht alle fühlen sich da wohl.
W o früher eine verlassene Bahntrasse lag und man Kleeblätter zwischen Schienen sammelte, rollen jetzt Kinderwagen und Gravelbikes über asphaltierten Boden. Neben in Kästen eingepflanzten Birken und hellen Holzbänken überall traut man sich kaum, sein Sterni mit einem Feuerzeug zu öffnen. Um es mit den Worten meiner Mutter zu sagen: Scheiße, ist der glatt, scheiße, sieht das gemacht aus. Scheiße, warum hat nichts hier Persönlichkeit?
Diese kluge Frau kommt mich an dem Wochenende besuchen, an dem der Parkbogen Ost gerade eröffnet worden ist, so nennt sich die aufgemöbelte Trasse. An der Haltestelle Annenstraße gehen wir die Treppe hoch. Oben angekommen, keucht sie, dann zieht sie an ihrer Vape. Begeistert ist sie von dem Projekt nicht und das sagt sie auch: Dieser Ort ist zum Kotzen! Ich, als Queen of Assimilation, schäme mich für ihre laute Stimme, denke: Uff, Mama, das ist peinlich. Red leiser, bitte.
Den Parkbogen entlang kommen uns vor allem Jack-Wolfskin-Jacken entgegen, oder Rentner. Rentnerlifestyle finden viele meiner Freund:innen gerade richtig geil, zu Hause sitzen und stricken. Blöd nur, dass zu diesem Lifestyle auch Einsamkeit gehört.
Das merkt man, weil meine Mutter innerhalb von zwei Minuten eine ganze Lebensgeschichte erzählt bekommt, es geht um den besten Bäcker und die tote Frau. Meine Mutter wird zugelabert, wahrscheinlich, weil sie sich in ihr wieder erkennen: Sie steckt in einem Körper, der gezeichnet ist durch drei Jobs, Erschöpfung, chronische Krankheit. Ein Körper, der unangepasst ist und so zeigt, dass hier gar nichts okay ist.
Der Verschleiß des Körpers durch Arbeit und Einsamkeit, man erkennt sich irgendwie. Oder man startet den ausweglosen Versuch der Anpassung, gibt sein weniges Geld für teure Kleidung aus und senkt die Stimme. Bloß nicht auffallen. Ich schlucke, schaue mich um. Glaube, Blicke zu spüren. Mama, bitte rede leiser.
Dabei komme ich von: Kaffeepulver, aufgelöst in heißem Wasser, Schinken-Käse-Croissants jeden Freitag, Wandtattoos, auf denen „Lebe, Liebe, Lache“ steht. Ich komme von: Mama pennt im Wohnzimmer, damit ich und meine Schwester ein eigenes Zimmer haben können. Ich komme von: Antifa-Punksongs auf maximaler Lautstärke auf dem Nachhauseweg hören, damit jeder weiß, wie scheiße ich Deutschland finde. Ich war mal lauter und jetzt:
Jack-Wolfskin-Jacken schauen genervt
Lebe. Liebe. Lache. Leipzig Ost. Die Leute um mich herum tragen Sprüche-T-Shirts nur ironisch, würden aber jeden Mann peinlich finden, der „Es läuft. Zwar bergab und rückwärts, aber es läuft“ trägt. Digga. Ich würde niemals mehr laut Musik über eine Musikbox hören – freue mich aber, dass es hier passiert. Jack-Wolfskin-Jacken schauen genervt, ich rieche frischen Lack.
Menschen, die die Codes sprengen, machen die Machtverhältnisse eines Raumes sichtbar. Wer darf den öffentlichen Raum mitgestalten und für wen? Wer hat diesen Ort vorher viel benutzt und wofür? Das ist ja auch unser Raum, der muss nicht aussehen wie von Ikea.
Etwas entfernt von uns steht das Team von Sachsenfernsehen und versucht, Passant:innen abzugreifen. Vorzugsweise Patagonia-Fleecejacken, aber ganz sicher nicht meine Mutter. Wir sitzen da und vapen.
Es ist Mittag und es ist November und es ist Sachsen, und als wäre das nicht schlimm genug, schauen wir einem jungen Mann dabei zu, wie er in die Kamera was von Neoliberalismus und Viertelaufwertung schwafelt. Ich stupse meine Mutter von der Seite an: Du solltest lauter reden, sonst checkt der da hinten nicht, was Verdrängung bedeutet.

https://taz.de/Umfrage-und-Studie-zu-Dis.title: Umfrage und Studie zu Diskriminierung: Viele psychisch Kranke sehen sich im Job benachteiligt
https://taz.de/Umfrage-und-Studie-zu-Dis.text:
Umfrage und Studie zu Diskriminierung: Viele psychisch Kranke sehen sich im Job benachteiligt
Mobbing statt Beförderung? Wer eine psychische Erkrankung hat, ist auf der Arbeit oft mit besonderen Schwierigkeiten konfrontiert.
epd | Viele Menschen mit psychischen Erkrankungen sehen sich im Arbeitsleben benachteiligt. Rund 40 Prozent der Betroffenen gaben an, dass sie bereits eine solche Diskriminierung erlebt hätten, heißt es in einer am Dienstag vorgestellten Umfrage im Auftrag der Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes. Konkret wurden unter anderem eine schlechtere Leistungsbewertung als bei anderen Mitarbeitenden und ein respektloser Umgang beklagt.
Von den rund 8.000 Befragten berichteten den Angaben zufolge gut 27 Prozent von einer aktuellen oder früheren psychischen Erkrankung. Unter den Betroffenen mit einer Angst- oder Zwangsstörung sprachen demnach 45 Prozent von Diskriminierungserfahrungen, bei Menschen mit Depressionen waren es 42 Prozent und bei Menschen mit einer Suchterkrankung 37 Prozent.
Verunsicherung und Rückzug als Folgen
Bei der Frage, wie die Diskriminierung aussah, wurde am häufigsten (47 Prozent) eine schlechtere Bewertung der Leistung als bei anderen genannt. 45 Prozent gaben an, sie seien respektlos oder unangemessen behandelt worden. Berichtet wurde beispielsweise auch von Mobbing oder davon, bei einer Beförderung, Gehaltssteigerung oder Entfristung übergangen worden zu sein. Als Folge der Diskriminierung erklärten 52 Prozent der Betroffenen, sie seien verunsichert gewesen und hätten sich zurückgezogen.
„Wir brauchen mehr Wissen über psychische Erkrankungen, eine klare Haltung gegen Diskriminierung und eine Unternehmenskultur, in der niemand seine Erkrankung verstecken muss, um beruflich bestehen zu können“, folgerte die Antidiskriminierungsbeauftragte des Bundes, Ferda Ataman. Niemand solle Angst haben müssen, im Job über eine psychische Erkrankung zu sprechen.
Online-Umfrage und qualitative Studie
Für die Erhebung wurden im Frühjahr 8.004 Menschen zwischen 18 und 66 Jahren online befragt, die erwerbstätig sind oder waren. Die Umfrage wurde den Angaben zufolge durch eine qualitative Studie mit Einzelinterviews und Gesprächen in Fokusgruppen ergänzt.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: ‘Come stay all day’: US libraries see rise in visitors as patrons seek affordable resources
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Public libraries have experienced a surge in demand in the last few years, a welcome development in the US amid concerns about federal funding cuts and a decline in literacy rates.
For example, public libraries in Union county, North Carolina received 433,517 visitors during fiscal year 2026, a 20% increase from just two years earlier, according to a county report.
Brooklyn public library received more than 150,000 registrations this year through August. That was 20,000 more than the same period in 2024, the library reported.
In Haverford, Pennsylvania, physical visits to the public library increased from 106,383 in all of 2022 to 123,205 during the first nine months of this year, according to the library.
Librarians offer a range of reasons for why they are busier – inflation, an increase in services, more people wanting social connection, greater interest in books – but the outcome is the same: libraries appear to be playing a bigger role in American life.
“Everybody has their individual reasons for coming, but our goal is to appeal to the masses,” Nina Chaffin, Union county public library director, said.
While libraries are, of course, best known for their books, they serve other roles in society and have continually evolved. They often provide sanctuary for homeless people during the day. They offer job training services. They offer ebooks, audiobooks and DVDs. And in recent decades, more of the institutions have become “libraries of things”, offering instruments, camping gear and gardening tools, among other items.
Despite the important services libraries provide, early in his second term, Donald Trump signed an executive order to eliminate the Institute of Museum and Library Services, which provided $160m in federal funding to state library agencies.
Attorneys general of 21 states sued, and a US district judge blocked the executive order. The Trump administration reinstated the institute’s grants.
Meanwhile, academics have also raised concerns about how many people actually still want books. In July, the Atlantic published a cover story titled, The End of Reading is Here.
The New Yorker recently published a story, The New Age of Reading, which downplayed the concern, arguing that people have always panicked about a loss of interest in books.
Plenty of people still do seem to be reading. Sunderland, a town of 3,600 in western Massachusetts, has one library with one full-time leader and five part-time staff members.
“We are located right at one of the bridges that crosses the Connecticut River and at the junction of two main routes, so a lot of commuters come past,” said Katherine Umstot, library director. “We serve a lot more than just the Sunderland residents.”
In addition to books, the library offers free kayak rentals for people who want to set out from the nearby launch. The library saw a 10% increase in book circulation between 2024 and 2025, Umstot said. Much of that came from adult books.
The library has also seen a 10% increase in visitorship. The staff offers help to people applying for jobs. They lend out DVD players too.
“We also see a lot of families coming in, never having visited the library before and realizing: ‘Oh my goodness, we can borrow DVDs, now that we can’t afford our streaming services,’” Umstot said.
Libraries are “finally doing a better job” of communicating what they offer, said Tamika Barnes, president-elect of the American Library Association. She pointed to Billy Allen, a librarian in Wilmington, Delaware, who has more than 36,000 followers on Instagram and posts about his weekly event, Hip Hop Storytime.
This weekend, the library will also offer free winter coats to children who need them.
“Everything is increasing – groceries, gas, entertainment – and so at the library, we are able to offer some resources for people to help alleviate some of the pressures of today’s economy,” said Barnes.
Still, inflation is not the only reason libraries are seeing more foot traffic.
“When there is a recession, you see more people coming in looking for the basics,” said Chaffin, the North Carolina director, who has worked in libraries since 2003. During the Covid-19 pandemic, “we were more focused on helping people get jobs, so everything we did was really job-focused, and now if we try to do those things, those are not well attended.”
Instead, people are interested in the library’s educational and recreational offerings, like its book clubs. In Steps and Stories, people gather to take a walk and listen to an audiobook. Afterwards, they go to a coffee shop to discuss the book.
“People are definitely looking for ways to connect with one another,” said Chaffin.
In September, the Brooklyn library started to offer supplies for crafting. They were all checked out almost instantly, and there is now a waiting list, according to Fritzi Bodenheimer, spokesperson for Brooklyn public library.
She isn’t sure why the library has seen such an uptick in membership.
“We really don’t like to speculate,” Bodenheimer said. “One of the promises of the library is that we don’t ask. Come stay all day; take out what you like. We don’t question it.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Polly Klaas’s murder is routinely used to justify the death penalty. As her sisters, we oppose it | Annie Nichol and Jess Nichol
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Annie Nichol and Jess Nichol
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
For more than three decades, our sister Polly Klaas’s murder has been used to justify California’s death penalty.
When people debate the merit of punitive policies passed in Polly’s name, politicians, advocates, even strangers have asked: “What about Polly?” As if our loss were an argument that speaks for itself.
After so many years of hearing our family’s tragedy invoked in support of capital punishment, we wanted to make clear where we actually stand.
A few weeks ago, we met with the California governor, Gavin Newsom, on the former death row at San Quentin to explain why we do not support the death penalty. He has since said that conversation helped shape his decision to commute California’s death sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
We wholeheartedly embrace that decision as a critical step toward a more just system.
We are writing to share what we have learned over more than 30 years of living alongside a system that promises justice, but has given California an expensive, error-prone process that prolongs trauma rather than preventing harm.
In our case, Polly’s killer was convicted and sentenced to death. More than 30 years later, he is still on death row.
If you’ve ever wondered what the death penalty “does” for victims’ families, that fact is a good place to start. A death sentence does not bring closure. It binds families to decades of hearings, legal filings, and headlines – keeping us tethered to the person who harmed us when what we want is to be able to move on with our lives and learn how to heal.
To be clear: we admire survivors who have done the courageous work of finding forgiveness for the people who harmed them or their loved ones. In our case, we have not forgiven the man who killed our sister. We still feel moments of intense grief and anger, as is natural after a loss like ours, and we still feel the persistent pain of Polly’s absence.
Even so, the feelings of vengeance so many survivors experience – however understandable – should not be the basis for public policy.
Survivors’ anger is real, and it deserves a response. The state can honor survivors’ anger without turning to an irreversible punishment. Yet while the death penalty is often justified in the name of victims, survivors’ needs are as varied as the harms we have lived through.
For many of us, the long arc of healing creates the space to ask deeper questions about what justice would actually require: what might help us recover, what could prevent another person from experiencing the same harm, and what forms of accountability might be possible.
Instead, the criminal legal system appropriates those questions and offers punishment as a one-size-fits-all substitute for the far more complicated work of healing, accountability and prevention.
Capital punishment exploits survivors’ most vulnerable moments of rage and pain. Our criminal legal system isn’t built to support the slow, human process of recovering from trauma – even though, for survivors, our grief changes shape over time, and the meaning we make of our loss changes with it.
Most survivors, however, are given no resources to help them heal or recover from their trauma.
In California, fewer than one in five survivors receive counseling, medical assistance or financial support after surviving a violent crime. This means many people remain in that pit of anger and trauma for their entire lives. They are told that punishment is the only justice they are allowed to ask for or expect, and far too often, the only “help” the system offers to survivors is the promise that someone else will suffer, too.
Survivors deserve more than this. They deserve healing, safety and counseling, the ability to pay for medical bills and housing and take care of their children – not an execution carried out decades later as a substitution for care.
Nonpartisan analysts have estimated that ending the death penalty in practice and converting death sentences to life without parole could save California taxpayers up to $150m annually, largely by reducing the extraordinary costs unique to capital cases. Imagine what $150m a year could mean if we invested it in the programs that actually prevent harm: mental health treatment, substance use intervention, gun violence prevention, trauma recovery centers, and support for survivors navigating the long aftermath of violence. Imagine what it will mean for solving cases, preventing future victimization, and stabilizing families before people fall through the cracks.
Nothing will undo our loss, and we don’t ask anyone to pretend otherwise. What we are asking is that California stop treating survivors’ pain as permission for state killing – and start choosing a public safety approach that supports healing and prevents harm.
To this day, people still invoke Polly’s name as if it settles the debate. It doesn’t. Execution isn’t a system responding to victims’ needs. It’s a system borrowing our pain to justify what it already intended to do.
We are grateful that Newsom has made these commutations a part of his legacy. Families like ours shouldn’t be trapped in an endless loop of promised violence. Instead, we should be building a public safety strategy that is bigger than vengeance – one that treats survivors as whole human beings, not as instruments of punishment.
We loved Polly. We miss her. We carry her with us. We deserve better than the death penalty. And so do all survivors.
- Annie and Jess Nichol are survivor advocates working to replace punitive responses to harm with healing, accountability and care

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iraq-.title: Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iraq-.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iraq-.text:
Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline
Iraq has resumed the pumping of crude oil for export through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan Pipeline to Turkey, as it looks to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Iraq plans to pump up to 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil through the 960km-long pipeline that runs from the Iraqi city to Turkey’s Mediterranean port, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said in a statement reported by the state-owned Iraqi News Agency on Tuesday.
He said the flow could reach 500,000 bpd after “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests” on the pipeline, which has been shuttered for more than a decade.
Iraq is one of the countries hardest hit by the US and Iran’s competing blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly all of Iraq’s oil exports exited the waterway before the US-Israeli war on Iran, and revenue from sales contributed to 90 percent of Iraq’s budget.
Restarting oil flows from Kirkuk to Ceyhan is the first step in Iraq’s efforts to reduce its dependence on Hormuz. Baghdad wants to connect Basra, its energy hub in southern Iraq, to the Mediterranean via the Syrian port of Baniyas and Turkey’s port of Ceyhan.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Middle East Eye was the first to report US efforts to revive a pipeline connection between Kirkuk and Baniyas. US ambassador to Iraq Tom Barrack hailed the reopening of the Kirkuk-Ceyhan line on Tuesday in a post on social media.
“Go Iraq, Go,” Barrack wrote.
Iraq began reexporting oil to Turkey in September 2025 from the semiautonomous Kurdistan region after a two-year dispute.
That agreement saw the Kurdistan regional government (KRG) and foreign oil producers operating in the region agreeing to allow 180,000 to 190,000 bpd of crude to flow to Turkiye’s Ceyhan port.
But Tuesday’s announcement will allow for oil from Iraq’s federal government to flow directly to Ceyhan.
Turkey has been pushing for a direct connection between Basra and Ceyhan. The Kirkuk pipeline has a capacity of more than 1.5 million bpd.
Energy industry experts tell MEE that tens of billions of dollars will be spent on new infrastructure in the coming years to get around Hormuz. The UAE is leading the way in building pipelines around the chokepoint.
But recent attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline attributed to the Houthis and militias in Iraq underscore how those workarounds remain vulnerable.
