https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump’s dealings with Venezuela after winning control of Congress.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump is facing criticism over how it has handled billions of dollars in oil revenue collected from Venezuela.
Since January 3, Trump’s government has controlled Venezuela’s oil exports, gathering the revenue in an account overseen exclusively by the US Treasury.
Last week, the Department of State released a 53-page report aimed at shedding light on the account’s activities. It revealed that at least $12.11bn have passed through the account since the start of the year.
But critics say the report lacks key details about where the money came from and who it is going to.
“There’s been zero transparency on all of the financial engineering associated with how $12bn of Venezuelan oil was changing hands and being utilised,” said Tyson Slocum, the director of the energy programme at Public Citizen, a US-based consumer advocacy nonprofit.
“All we have now is a very barebones narrative of how the funds were used, but not details on what entities were involved.”
Questions of sovereignty
Concerns about Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil sector began late last year, when his government began seizing oil tankers leaving the South American country.
Any oil on board, Trump said, would be kept or sold by the US. He and members of his administration framed the confiscated fuel as compensation for the losses incurred when Venezuela nationalised its oil industry decades ago.
“American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the time. “Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property.”
Tensions between the US and Venezuela reached a tipping point on January 3, when Trump authorised a military operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
In a speech that morning, Trump highlighted the role oil had played in his decision. “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Trump said.
He proceeded to explain that some of the Venezuelan oil proceeds would go “to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country”.
Days later, Trump revealed he had spoken to oil companies “before and after” the operation. He also held a meeting with oil industry executives at the White House to discuss plans for Venezuela.
Legal experts have raised concerns that the January 3 operation was an attack on Venezuela’s sovereignty, in violation of international law.
They have also questioned the legality of seizing another country’s natural resources, given that a 1962 United Nations resolution grants nations “permanent sovereignty” over their own natural resources.
But supporters of Trump’s actions have pointed to Maduro’s history of violent repression and anti-democratic actions in Venezuela as justification for the operation.
Maduro has since been replaced by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has largely cooperated with Trump’s demands.
But the focus on Venezuela’s oil revenue has left some critics questioning whether Trump plans to address the human rights issues in the South American country.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed the importance of democratic elections in Venezuela, said John Feeley, a former US ambassador and senior diplomat in Latin America.
“Trump has made patently clear that he has no interest in the democratic future of Venezuela,” said Feeley, calling the US-Venezuela relationship “protectorate neocolonialism”.
‘The biggest oil deal in history’
More recent manoeuvres have also raised speculation about the Trump administration’s commitment to transparency in its management of Venezuelan oil.
In late August, for instance, Trump announced his government would have a direct stake in extracting nearly a fifth of Venezuela’s oil.
Under the terms of the agreement, the US gained “majority control” in a 100-year deal for 17 Venezuelan oilfields, with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels.
North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, was given the rights to operate the fields.
The Pentagon, meanwhile, took a 35 percent stake in the company, and the US was guaranteed 20 percent of the oil output at cost. Trump called it “the biggest oil deal in history”.
But Betancourt has faced investigations in the US, Spain and Switzerland over accusations of money laundering.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado also said the contract with NABEP “evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants”.
Venezuela has long struggled to export its oil, so the fact that it will now be sold on the open market is beneficial to the country’s economy, said Luis A Pacheco, a former executive with Venezuela’s state oil company and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute Center for Energy Studies at Rice University.
But Pacheco is sceptical of Trump’s deal with NABEP.
“This is an obscure outfit with no known financial sources, with very little tech wherewithal,” he said. “This so-called mega-deal, without doubt, will certainly yield very little of what’s expected of it.”
Little transparency over billions of dollars
The shroud of secrecy surrounding the Venezuelan oil deals has spurred some Democrats in the US Congress to press for greater accountability.
In September, Democrats in the House of Representatives (PDF) and Senate asked the administration to disclose what had been uncovered by KPMG, an outside accounting firm hired to audit transactions involving Venezuelan oil exports.
The State Department did issue its report last week. But key portions were redacted, including who deposited money into the accounts and who the final recipients of the funds were.
Feeley, the diplomat, said there are also questions about the total sum of the proceeds. Only $12bn is accounted for in the report.
“We have no idea how that money was used, and we have no idea what percent of the total amount of money deposited in the US Treasury that $12bn represents,” said Feeley. “But most experts allege that it is only a fraction.”
In a statement to Al Jazeera, a State Department spokesperson said its report “provides a comprehensive account, down to the cent, of the Venezuelan natural resource revenues deposited in, held by, and disbursed” from the account.
Venezuela’s requests for disbursement are checked against a “list of approved and prohibited expenditure categories”, the spokesperson added.
The funds are then used for “essential public services, macroeconomic stability, and the rebuilding of key sectors such as energy, healthcare and infrastructure”.
But who receives those funds remains unclear. Pacheco said there is no reason the US could not disclose details of the monetary flow.
“Even though this report gives you some information, it still doesn’t give you light into the most important thing, which is what is the Venezuelan regime is doing with the money,” Pacheco said.
“You can affirm with very good certainty, when you talk about billions of dollars, something is draining away.”
Pacheco also questioned the supervisory role the Trump administration has claimed over the Venezuelan government. At one point, Trump even claimed he would “run” the South American country.
“The discourse of the White House is that they exert some sort of tutelage over the Venezuelan regime,” Pacheco said. “But apparently that tutelage doesn’t go as far as to tell the Venezuelans where is the money going to.”
New Congress, new oversight?
But this year’s midterm elections could usher in a wave of oversight into the Venezuelan oil money.
Democrats won majority control in both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, and lawmakers have already floated the possibility of opening investigations, once the new Congress arrives in January.
“The admin is sending billions to Delcy Rodriguez’s corrupt government where the list of who benefits is kept murky,” Representative Joaquin Castro wrote on social media after the election.
“I will continue to demand answers, and use every tool we will have with the incoming Democratic majority, including congressional hearings, to uncover what the United States is doing in Venezuela.”
One area of exploration might be the role private oil trading companies play in the Trump administration’s deal. Firms like Vitol, a Dutch multinational energy company, could be put under the microscope.
A week before Trump sent troops into Caracas to abduct Maduro, John Addison, a senior trader with Vitol, held a secret meeting with Vice President JD Vance on a tarmac in Montana, according to the news agency Reuters.
Vitol was later able to buy oil from the state-owned Venezuelan oil company at a steep discount. Addison and his wife donated $6m to Trump’s election campaign in 2024.
Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have long been eager to investigate the dealings of firms like Vitol in Venezuela.
“Oversight Democrats will not stop until we know exactly what companies are profiting from these foreign policy decisions, especially in Venezuela,” Representative Robert Garcia said in January.
Garcia is expected to chair the oversight committee next year.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down.
In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events.
The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored.
The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily.
The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said.
Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff.
A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong.
The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights, a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services. None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible.
Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.”
He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe.
Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions.
While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly.
“Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week (Outlook, the FAA, the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like.
“What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”
Shrai Popat contributed reporting

https://www.middleeasteye.net/trending/m.text:
Mamdani's moustache sparks meltdown as critics see Saddam Hussein, terrorism and NYC's demise
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has sparked a fresh wave of outrage over what may be his most controversial political statement yet: his moustache.
Facial hair took centre stage on Monday after Mamdani posted a video announcing the disbandment of the New York Police Department's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a controversial police unit responsible for both counterterrorism operations and policing protests.
But while Mamdani was busy explaining the overhaul, some online appeared far more concerned with what was happening directly above his upper lip.
For certain critics, the moustache was apparently all it took to transform New York City's first Muslim mayor into the deceased former Iraqi dictator, Saddam Hussein.
For a moment I thought I saw Saddam.
— Abhijit Chavda (@AbhijitChavda) November 16, 2026
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Conservative commentator Will Chamberlain offered an even more elaborate interpretation of the mayor's facial hair.
"Trying to beat the allegations of being an Islamist by adopting the aesthetics of the secular Ba’athists," he wrote on X.
Apparently, the moustache had not only become a political statement but an ideological rebranding exercise, with Mamdani allegedly swapping Islamist imagery for the look associated with the secular Arab nationalist movement that once ruled Iraq under Hussein.
All this from a few millimetres of facial hair.
It looks like Saddam Hussein is running NYC.
— Spencer Pratt (@spencerpratt) November 16, 2026
The timing of Mamdani's announcement only added fuel to the outrage.
Some critics interpreted the disbandment of the SRG as evidence that the Muslim mayor was weakening New York's counterterrorism capabilities, with the moustache seemingly providing all the visual confirmation they needed.
One user took the alarm a step further, writing: "Terrorists have realised it's easier to get elected by Democrats than to fly planes into buildings."
The implication was hardly subtle: New York's first Muslim mayor was not merely dismantling a counterterrorism unit but somehow represented the very threat it was supposed to combat.
By then, the moustache had graduated from a questionable fashion choice to a full-blown national security emergency.
But the NYPD is not abandoning counterterrorism.
Under the restructuring announced by Mamdani and police commissioner Jessica Tisch, the SRG's counterterrorism responsibilities will be transferred to the department's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau, while protest policing will be handled separately.
The changes follow years of criticism over the SRG's aggressive tactics against demonstrators.
Still, the combination of a Muslim mayor, a disbanded police unit and a newly prominent moustache proved irresistible to those inclined to see a national security threat in a grooming decision.
Far-right activist Laura Loomer, who has repeatedly promoted anti-Muslim rhetoric, was quick to offer her own interpretation, once again framing a Muslim politician's actions as evidence of an impending Islamist threat.
Muslim Mayor gets elected in NYC and immediately moves to eradicate the counter terrorism program in NYC. Gee, I wonder why? 🤔 As I said, jihad is coming. Soon Americans will experience their very own October 7th style events in American neighborhoods . The Islamic takeover of America is rapidly accelerating.
— Laura Loomer (@LauraLoomer) November 16, 2026
Apparently, reorganising a police unit was now proof of an imminent terrorist takeover.
And the explanation behind the supposedly ominous new look makes the controversy even more remarkable.
Mamdani had already announced in early November that he was participating in Movember, an annual campaign encouraging men to grow moustaches to raise awareness about prostate cancer, testicular cancer and men's mental health.
He also announced a $4m investment in a new prostate cancer centre at Kings County Hospital in the borough of Brooklyn.
In other words, the moustache that some interpreted as a tribute to Middle Eastern authoritarianism was actually intended to promote cancer awareness.
The reactions also illustrate how quickly familiar anti-Muslim stereotypes can enter the conversation, with a Muslim politician's appearance and decisions on policing being interpreted through the lens of terrorism.
If you’re a brown guy participating in Movember people will immediately start accusing you of becoming a totalitarian dictator.
— Murtaza Hussain (@MazMHussain) November 17, 2026
For now, Mamdani's moustache remains the subject of online debate, while New York's counterterrorism responsibilities remain within the NYPD.
Whether the internet can survive another two weeks of Movember is another question entirely.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ce.title: Celebrating the Inaugural Art Week NYC, Organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ce.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ce.text:
ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum just wrapped up the inaugural edition of Art Week NYC, a citywide event celebrating all the New York art world’s ecosystem has to offer, from museums and galleries to artists, collectors, and cultural tastemakers from the Lower East Side and Tribeca to Chelsea and the Upper East Side.
Art Week NYC kicked off with an opening party at the Mallory in Chelsea, a 19th-century warehouse building that used to be home to the Tunnel nightclub. Programming took place over four jampacked days, from November 11–14. A launch event at the Metropolitan Museum of Art had in attendance New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, City Council Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal; New York State Senator Jose Serrano, and City Council member Virginia Maloney. David Breslin, the Met’s curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, referred to Art Week NYC as “a defining tradition in our city’s cultural landscape—and that’s saying a lot.”
On November 13 and 14, ARTnews hosted a slate of programming at PMC’s ground-floor studio across the street from the New York Public Library. The two-day event was presented by Amazon, in partnership with Louis Roederer Champagne, Piaget, and Flying Whale Wines.
Friday featured in-depth conversations with art world insiders, such as dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky on what separates collectors from speculators; Tina Vaz, the MTA’s director of arts and design, speaking about several newly announced public art commissions; and photographer Stephen Shore detailing his new book, The Mental Image, a mix of memoir, pictures, and art history. Top 200 Collectors Larry and Allison Berg discussed the increasing crossover between sports and the art world, while art adviser Sophia Cohen gave insights on how a new generation of collectors is reshaping the market.
On Saturday, ARTnews welcomed two of our sponsors to the PMC Studio: Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, talked about Andy Warhol’s love of timepieces and how the watchmaker came to collaborate with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, while Frédéric Rouzaud, president of Maison Louis Roederer, discussed lasting ways for private patrons, like the Louis Roederer Foundation, to support contemporary art.
The day also looked back on what has happened to art in the 2020s (so far), synthesizing the impact of the pandemic, the NFT boom and bust, the rise of AI, and social and political upheaval; featured a spirited chat with New York Magazine’s Jerry Saltz on the current state of art criticism and the art world; and explored the importance of art collecting as both a personal passion and a creative practice from the point of view of two fashion executives, Carolina Herrera global creative director Wes Gordon and Oribe cofounder Daniel Kaner.
Before bidding farewell to our very first Art Week NYC, ARTnews revealed the winners of the third annual ARTnews Awards. This year’s jury included top curators from across the United States, and you can read more about the categories and the winners here.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Nvidia shoots down calls for Jensen Huang’s return amid strong earnings
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Nvidia shoots down calls for Jensen Huang’s return amid strong earnings
Nvidia board chair says chip giant ‘does not intend’ to reinstate Huang as it projects revenues of $130bn in Q4.
Nvidia has shot down the prospect of Jensen Huang returning as CEO amid the chip giant’s latest blockbuster earnings results.
Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday during an earnings call that the company had no plans to reinstate Huang following his “voluntary resignation” for “personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms”.
“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said.
Jones, appointed Nvidia’s first-ever board chair after Huang’s resignation last week, made his comments as Nvidia continued its run of stellar earnings in the third quarter.
Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8bn in the quarter that ended October 25, up 103 percent year-on-year. Net profit came in at $64.9bn, up 109 percent year-on-year.
Interim CEO
Nvidia, currently led by interim CEO Colette Kress while its board seeks a permanent replacement, said it expected next quarter revenue to reach $130bn, plus or minus 3 percent.
“Earnings were very strong, and were just what the market needed to shake off some AI-related jitters experienced over the last couple of weeks,” Will Rhind, chief executive officer at GraniteShares Advisors, told Al Jazeera.
“The earnings call, of course without Jensen, was a signal for the bulls that life carries on without him and the foundation the company has built is as robust as ever,” Rhind said.
Huang resigned amid scrutiny of his relationship with a tech executive accused of being a Chinese intelligence operative or asset. He said earlier on Tuesday he would be “honoured” to return if the board deemed it in the best interests of shareholders and the company.
Nearly 200,000 people have added their names to an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.
Shares of Nvidia, which have fallen more than 30 percent over the past month, closed down 0.4 percent on Tuesday, before rising 4.8 percent in after-hours trading.
Megaspeed probe
Nvidia has been under intense scrutiny over its relationship with the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls.
On Monday, the US Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice confirmed that prosecutors had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
President Donald Trump’s administration also moved on Monday to close a legal loophole that had allowed Chinese AI developers to access advanced chips remotely at data centres in third countries.
The rule issued by the Bureau of Industry and Security designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as export destinations with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those countries to obtain an export licence.
Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, said investors will closely watch how the clampdown on China’s access to high-end chips affects Nvidia’s business.
“I think they had a good quarter and guidance, in particular, raising their revenue forecast for next year,” Goldberg told Al Jazeera.
“But not sure how much of that matters until we get more clarity on who the next CEO will be and just how much exposure they really have to PRC AI companies,” Goldberg said, using the acronym for the People’s Republic of China, the country’s official name.
“As for their comments about Jensen returning, I think they said what they had to say. The board has to navigate a lot of legal guardrails. I think it is still possible for Jensen to return. Unlikely but possible.”
Megaspeed, whose former executive Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with Jensen Huang and has been accused of working with China’s Ministry of State Security, has denied wrongdoing, saying media reports about its operations were “not supported by verifiable evidence”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims of espionage, which have been circulated in the media by unnamed US officials.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/crs/lo.title: L’opération de communication de Laurent Nuñez sur les blessures des policiers… pour éclipser celles des manifestants
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/crs/lo.author: Arthur Dumas
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/crs/lo.text:
Pour éclipser les blessures et mutilations dont sont victimes les manifestants, le ministre de l’Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, convoque la presse pour livrer le bilan des blessures chez les policiers et gendarmes. Un chiffre livré sans aucune précision concernant la nature de ces souffrances.
Après chaque journée de mobilisation, c’est le même refrain. Pour éclipser les blessures et mutilations dont sont victimes les manifestants, le ministre de l’Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, convoque la presse pour livrer le bilan des blessures chez les policiers et gendarmes. Une manœuvre qui sert surtout à appuyer la thèse que la réponse policière ne serait que le miroir d’une montée en puissance de la violence des cortèges.
Si l’on additionne tous les chiffres distillés au compte-goutte par le locataire de la place Beauvau et le premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu, on dépasse largement les 2 000 blessés chez les agents depuis les premiers blocus lycéens. Mais lorsque ses chiffres sont livrés aux journalistes ou aux parlementaires, aucun détail n’est donné quant à la nature ou la gravité de ces blessures.
Selon les informations de Mediapart, une très grande partie des blessures des fonctionnaires sont en réalité légères. Et certaines d’entre elles n’ont strictement rien à voir avec la violence des manifestants. À partir d’un fichier interne recensant les 1 233 blessés des CRS sur le mois d’octobre, le média d’investigation révèle que 94,6 % d’entre eux sont classés comme « blessés légers » en interne.
Dans certains cas, il n’est question que de contusions ou de douleurs, sans plus de précisions. Et d’autres sont directement liées à l’utilisation de l’arsenal des policiers et gendarmes. Dans ce fichier, Mediapart recense ainsi 123 cas d’acouphènes, que l’on peut aisément relier à l’usage des grenades assourdissantes ou de désencerclement.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
Illegal activities in the Amazon pose grave risks to uncontacted Indigenous groups like Brazil’s Awa, advocates stress.
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
Pressure on the forest
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups, mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: A 2-0 win over Haiti ends Pochettino’s USMNT tenure with confident hope
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The US men’s national team is through to the semi-final of the Concacaf Nations League, following Saturday’s 6-0 romp with a workmanlike 2-0 win over Haiti in the Cincinnati-hosted second leg. Christian Pulisic opened the scoring with an acrobatic overhead goal, while 18-year-old Julian Hall scored his fifth goal in six caps since debuting in September. Towering 19-year-old center back Neil Pierre was cap-tied to the US with an appearance, eliminating the potential for him to represent Haiti in future windows.
In keeping a clean sheet, the United States has now played over 400 minutes without conceding a goal, last allowing a goal against Chile on 29 September.
The real impact of the match, though, is on the sideline; the win marks the end of the USMNT’s Mauricio Pochettino era, with the manager trading his summer safari duds for an all-black outfit including a puffer vest to mark his final match in the role. The Argentinian will now follow his assistants across the Atlantic to try turning things around at Manchester United. That undertaking will be even more daunting than the project he inherited from Gregg Berhalter two years ago, due to the scale of the work to be done and the relative expectations around United and the United States.
Much has been written, here and elsewhere, about the short-lived and abruptly ended Pochettino tenure. With his time in the role having firmly drifted into the rear-view, what can we make from his two-plus years in charge?
Pochettino and his staff launched a deep and wide-ranging survey of the US player pool in their first year, giving 77 different players run-outs over 25 months. That work didn’t just pull together a credible 26-man roster for the World Cup, but gave the group a crucial lens into the considerable rising talent this program boasts. By the time this international window rolled around, it wasn’t a surprise to see Hall, Diego Kochen, Cavan Sullivan, and other young emerging talents in the squad. The culture, in this game and across both of Pochettino’s final two windows, felt invigorated.
Indeed, while Pulisic’s acrobatic opener stunned, Julian Hall’s cool finish under pressure to double the lead in the 43rd minute might be the most promising sign of the US’s direction. The New York Red Bulls striker has exceptional ability to find space in the final third and a natural finishing touch, and after Saturday’s appearance is now cap-tied to the US after interest from Poland.
The US are now a near-blemishless 6-0-0 since getting bounced by Belgium in the last-16. The rout of Haiti will have hardly surprised, but the previous window saw the US completely outplay Mexico and withstand a physical test from Canada, as well as multi-goal wins over Chile and Peru.
“The way we played, that is what we dream[ed] when we arrived,” Pochettino told reporters afterward. “When you talk about these games, it looks like it was easy. But Haiti is a World Cup team. The players make the job easier.”
Then again, Pochettino’s tenure hasn’t seen players pushed beyond their comfort zones terribly often. Tuesday’s win in Cincinnati was the 35th of Pochettino’s 37 matches in charge to be played within the United States. The other two came nearby in Mexico and Jamaica.
International coaches seldom book their team’s friendlies, of course, and the global Nations League era makes booking cross-confederation dates a tough task. Still, it’s one that the federation would be wise to incorporate between now and a 2030 World Cup played across three continents. Haiti, for as heroic as their World Cup appearance was, were simply not on the same level as the US tonight or in Miami on Saturday, where the same US lineup played through them with ease.
At this stage, the US is largely composed of two bands of talent. The relative old guard is the wave ushered in by Pulisic at the tail-end of 2018 qualifying, with Tyler Adams, Weston McKennie, Antonee Robinson, and Chris Richards alongside, all between ages 26 and 29. Sullivan heads up the next generation, a group teeming with potential who grew up aspiring to follow in Pulisic’s footsteps. A few others, like Sebastian Berhalter, Folarin Balogun, Gio Reyna, Malik Tillman, and Alex Freeman bridge the gap. While there are still untapped options to test – with Santiago Castañeda and Reed Baker-Whiting becoming the 31st and 32nd national team debutants of Pochettino’s tenure on Tuesday – the skeleton is there upon which to flesh out a dark horse challenger for a deep World Cup run.
“I am sure that this group of players will achieve big things in the future. I have no doubt,” Pochettino said. “Experienced players, with the mix of younger talent that is coming, it’s the perfect combination.”
Pochettino also made clear that this player pool isn’t one to relish playing as relative underdogs. This is a generation of aspiring entertainers, players who want to dictate the proceedings by carrying a majority of possession and fashioning dangerous chances whenever on offer. How to sustain that ethos in the testy arenas of World Cup qualifying is now somebody else’s problem.
Along the way, Pochettino had a knack for heightening the national team’s relevance. Even on Tuesday afternoon, American sports programs like Pardon the Interruption that treat discussing soccer like a taboo that would demand censorship threw the US’s second leg against Haiti into the rundown.
The US men’s national team felt more important, because Pochettino decided it was important enough to lead it. Time will tell whether his successor can demand a similar focus.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/w.title: Wednesday’s Headlines: A Tale Of Two Ribbon-Cuttings Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/w.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/w.text:
Noooooo! Photo: Ed Reed / Mayoral Photography Office
Two visions for New York City were in stark relief on Tuesday — and Mayor Mamdani’s gaze was filled with the wrong one.
At 10 a.m., the mayor was a no-show at the symbolic opening of his administration’s signature transportation project: turning Flatbush Avenue from a sclerotic artery into a free-flowing transitway for buses. He should have been there — and maybe he would have except Hizzoner likely didn’t want to face questions about how he and the governor recently stiffed the MTA for $200 million in mandated contributions … to the agency’s bus operations, as Streetsblog reported.
Two hours later, Mamdani was right next to Gov. Hochul in Queens to cut the ribbon on another transformative project: the $1.4-billion widening of the Van Wyck Expressway. As pols rued the highway’s epic “gridlock” and recalled a famous “Seinfeld” episode from more than 35 years ago, Mamdani hailed the repairs as a victory for drivers.
My god, where to begin?
First of all, you can pretty much dismiss Hochul’s promotional video for the Van Wyck expansion (however slickly it was produced); within a year, max, the law of induced demand will kick in and the gridlock will be back. Everyone knows this, but people like Mamdani were just too polite to ruin the governor’s celebration yesterday: When you build for cars, you get … more cars.
Worse, if we learned anything from the election earlier this month, it’s that voters want better transit, not more highways. Hochul herself won re-election in no small part because she ran as a champion of public transportation.
Our own incoming Editor in Chief David Meyer had the take of the day, linking the ribbon-cuttings to the larger political climate:
The good news, of course, is the good news: As Streetsblog and Gothamist reported, the Flatbush Avenue busway is working great. Here’s hoping Mamdani will take the “W” — and give us lots more bus lanes.
In other news:
Speaking of buses, we think the Post editorial board blamed Mamdani too much — and the governor not nearly enough — for the $200-million raid of the MTA coffers that we reported on earlier this week. Also, the Post’s editors need to read their own paper — they say that Mamdani isn’t doing enough to make buses faster, but the paper’s own news pages are filledwithNIMBYcomplaints about how he’s trying to speed up the buses too much!
And speaking of Mamdani, is he really considering bringing cars back to Central Park?! (Streetsblog, NY Post)
The Brooklyn Eagle is providing wall-to-wall coverage of the shortcomings of the Mamdani plan for the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, but it doesn’t seem like anyone is offering anything better.
The Times covered the marathon reading of “The Power Broker” from over the weekend.
This driver with the vanity plate SIMBAH is a jerk twice over: first for harassing the staff at a popular Williamsburg bar (as Resident Advisor reported) and also for driving recklessly, according to city data.
NY1 confirmed that Gov. Hochul will raise the congestion pricing toll to $12 on schedule in 2028 …
… and the same station had a nice video of the governor talking about the coming renovations to the Chambers Street subway station, which fans of Dave Colon know as the worst station in town.
Will the robo-car take the keys away from itself? (Fast Company)
A pedestrian was killed by a driver in Harlem. (Patch)
Tabloid legend Gersh Kuntzman has been with New York newspapers since 1989, including stints at the New York Daily News, the Post, the Brooklyn Paper and even a cup of coffee with the Times. He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop," which was a hit at the NYC Fringe Festival in 2016, and “SUV: The Musical” in 2007. He also writes the Cycle of Rage column, which is archived here.

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: Les lycéens décernent leur prix Renaudot à Abdellah Taïa pour « Debout dans tes rêves »
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Muriel Steinmetz
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
L’écrivain marocain a été distingué pour « Debout dans tes rêves » (Julliard), un roman sur l’exil, les dominations de toutes sortes et la possibilité de l’amour.
L’écrivain marocain Abdellah Taïa a remporté, ce mardi 17 novembre, le prix Renaudot des lycéens, pour Debout dans tes rêves (Julliard, 224 pages, 21 euros). Plus de 400 élèves ont participé à cette 35e édition, dont le verdict a été rendu à Loudun (Vienne). La distinction va à un roman qui fait de la rencontre entre un jeune immigré marocain et un enfant français un fragile espace de résistance aux humiliations et aux rapports de domination.
Majid, gay, arabe, précaire, a quitté le Maroc pour étudier Jean-Honoré Fragonard en France. Mais son directeur de thèse lui dénie la légitimité de s’intéresser à ce peintre du XVIIIe siècle. En quête d’un titre de séjour à renouveler sans cesse, il devient le baby-sitter de Gabriel, deux ans et demi, fils de la grande bourgeoisie française. « Gabriel offre à Majid ce lieu d’utopie où il devient possible de renégocier avec le monde et avec la vie », nous confiait Abdellah Taïa lors d’un entretien accordé à l’Humanité.
L’enfance traverse l’œuvre de l’écrivain, de même que l’exil, les blessures sociales et le désir. Dans Debout dans tes rêves, le regard du gamin échappe encore aux préjugés des adultes. Majid, lui, s’engage à ne pas lui transmettre ses propres blessures : « Je ferai tout pour que ce qui ne va pas en moi ne passe pas en toi. » Pour Abdellah Taïa, Gabriel « incarne presque l’innocence perdue de la France ».
Une critique subtile des rapports de domination
Néanmoins, le roman refuse l’idéalisation. Il dénonce le racisme, qui s’exerce jusque dans l’université et parfois même, aussi, au cœur de l’intime dans les relations amoureuses. Grégoire, l’amant français du héros ne voudrait-il pas que Majid renonce à une part de sa langue et de son imaginaire marocains. « Faut-il s’annihiler pour être accepté ? », interroge l’écrivain. Le roman déploie ainsi une critique subtile des rapports de domination qui traversent les frontières, les classes sociales et la vie privée.
Abdellah Taïa, né à Rabat en 1973, revendique une littérature née d’une expérience charnelle du monde. Évoquant les jeunes Marocains contraints de risquer leur vie aux frontières, il se souvient de sa mère qui priait pour les pauvres et les mendiants de Salé : « J’ai l’impression que j’écris pour continuer ses prières à tous les démunis. », nous confiait-il. Et de résumer ce qui anime son œuvre : « L’écriture ne doit pas être située dans un territoire théorique et intellectuel. Elle commence d’abord quand le cœur saigne avec les autres cœurs qui saignent. »
Rappelons que le romancier, couronné en 2024 par le prix Décembre pour Le Bastion des larmes (Julliard), roman d’un retour sans merci au pays natal, est l’un des premiers Marocains à avoir publiquement révélé son homosexualité, qui y reste considéré comme un crime passible de six mois à trois ans de prison. Abdellah Taïa, qui vit aujourd’hui en France, a aussi écrit sur les années de plomb du règne d’Hassan II (Le Jour du roi, Seuil, 2010).
Au plus près de celles et ceux qui créent
L’Humanité a toujours revendiqué l’idée que la culture n’est pas une marchandise, qu’elle est une condition de la vie politique et de l’émancipation humaine.
Face à des politiques culturelles libérales, qui fragilisent le service public de la culture, le journal rend compte de la résistance des créateurs et de tous les personnels de la culture, mais aussi des solidarités du public.
Les partis pris insolites, audacieux, singuliers sont la marque de fabrique des pages culture du journal. Nos journalistes explorent les coulisses du monde de la culture et la genèse des œuvres qui font et bousculent l’actualité.
Aidez-nous à défendre une idée ambitieuse de la culture !
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Shaken and stirred: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in picking new James Bond
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Maanvi Singh and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Amazon’s founder and billionaire chairman Jeff Bezos has said he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.
Amazon paid more than $1bn for “creative control” of the Bond franchise last year, striking a deal with the longtime heirs and stewards of the films, shocking fans who worried that Bezos’ takeover would signal an end to the franchise as they knew it.
Bezos said he felt there was “something special” about Pattinson, revealing during an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event that he reviewed several rounds of auditions.
“There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists,” he said. “We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”
He added that he and the film’s director, Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, were initially biased against Pattinson, seeking an unknown talent. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond,” he said.
Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005 and has gone on to star in films including The Twilight Saga, The Lost City of Z and Tenet.
Bezos’ Amazon acquired the MGM studio in an $8.5bn purchase in 2022. Bond fans and film critics have speculated over where Amazon will take the Bond franchise, with industry experts speculating the company may seek to expand the films into a Marvel-style universe of spinoffs.
Amazon has grown into a massive conglomerate in recent years, which includes not only an entertainment arm, but also computing and the company’s original business of online sales. Bezos also separately founded the space exploration company Blue Origin.
Amazon’s surveillance technology has come under criticism as a Guardian investigation this week unveiled that Israel was using its facial recognition tool to surveil Palestinians as part of a larger project to move its data on to Amazon servers.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea, stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017, after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
What is Trump hoping to achieve at APEC meeting in China?
US president expected to meet with Chinese leader for third time this year; possible trilateral summit with Putin.
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.
The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.
Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.
The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.
“Trump will work to strengthen his rapport with Xi, but the meeting is unlikely to produce any substantive breakthroughs,” Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at Crisis Group, said.
As for Russia, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters on Monday that “the significance and symbolism” of the meetings between the three superpower leaders “are hard to overestimate”.
Progress on AI?
Neither side has yet released a formal agenda for an expected Trump-Xi meeting, although the White House announced plans for the two countries to support each other at APEC and at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
“The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” according to a White House statement.
As in previous meetings, AI regulation is set to loom large. Both the US and China, as industry leaders, have faced pressure to jointly agree to safeguards on the transformative technology.
In September, both sides pledged to set up a mechanism to quickly communicate AI-related incidents and to hold a dialogue on emerging risks.
Still, the Trump administration has repeatedly downplayed the need to integrate developmental guardrails. Following the White House meeting, Trump said the US would “not be putting on brakes” on the AI industry.
Speaking at a National Committee on US-China Relations event last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both sides “expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology”.
“As we do so, we should harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China,” he said. “And our approach to every challenge, likewise, will not always converge.”
The Nvidia scandal
The recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, will also loom large over any Trump-Xi meeting, even if it is not directly addressed.
Huang’s close relationship with Trump, including accompanying the US president to Beijing during his May visit, and his ties to alleged spy Alice Huang have renewed questions about the influence he exerted over the US government as he pushed to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to Beijing.
Trump administration Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced particular scrutiny, including from prominent members of the Republican Party, over his reportedly lax enforcement of export controls related to China.
“Trump will be under enormous pressure from Congress and members of his own administration to raise the scandal and warn Xi that their relationship could suffer if Trump concludes that Xi has been deploying Huang and other prominent business executives to sabotage US artificial intelligence efforts,” according to Crisis Group’s Wyne.
Still, some experts expect it to have little bearing on his interaction with his Chinese counterpart.
Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera last week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.
The Reuters news agency reported on Friday that US officials said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of Alice Huang with Xi.
China has denied Alice Huang was working as a spy on its behalf.
Taiwan
Trump has already bucked longstanding US policy on Taiwan during his recent meeting with Xi.
Following the Beijing summit in May, Trump told reporters he had discussed US arms sales to the self-governing island, which Beijing claims as its own, “in great detail” with the Chinese president.
The US has provided arms to Taiwan since 1979 as mandated under the Taiwan Relations Act. But under the 1982 Six Assurances document, Washington has not consulted with China on such sales.
In a subsequent Fox News interview, Trump also referred to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China. He has since held up approval of a $14bn arms package earmarked for the island.
The language “invites Beijing to expect something in return for each future approval”, Bonnie Glaser and Noah Munk of The German Marshall Fund of the United States (GMF) wrote in a recent analysis.
“The more successful that bargaining appears, the more Beijing will press it, and the more it will treat the next notification as a concession from Washington rather than a routine measure under the Taiwan Relations Act,” they wrote.
For its part, the White House has defended the delay, citing limited production capacity, particularly amid the US-Israel war with Iran, as well as the delicate nature of the US-China trade truce.
Democratic control of Congress, and general bipartisan support for Taiwan, could see pressure increase on the issue in Trump’s final two years in office.
“Today, the results of the midterm elections are on balance favourable for Taiwan,” Robert Sutter, a professor of international affairs at George Washington University, wrote recently for the ThinkChina publication.
Taiwan, a member of APEC, will be represented at the summit by Acer Group founder Stan Shih.
Trade breakthroughs?
US-China trade relations took a nosedive at the start of Trump’s second term, with the US president initially launching 10 percent tariffs on China for allegedly failing to crack down on the trade of fentanyl precursors.
By April, additional US tariffs on Chinese goods had reached 145 percent, while China’s retaliatory tariffs on US goods reached 125 percent.
Agreements to bring down the temperature faltered until Trump and Xi agreed to a yearlong truce in Busan, South Korea, in October of last year. The deal was extended through January 10, 2027, following Xi’s White House visit in September.
A particular issue has been US access to China’s rare earth minerals, which was severely restricted. Still, a recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US imports of China’s rare earth minerals during the first 11 months of the agreement remained 75 percent lower than prior to the escalation.
“The recurring challenge is the persistent gap between China’s diplomatic commitments and actual export volumes,” the analysts wrote. “Despite successive agreements in Switzerland, London, and South Korea intended to restore supplies, shipments of controlled rare earth materials to the United States remain approximately 75 percent below pre-restriction levels.”
US agricultural exports were also hard hit during the trade war, an issue for farmers that resonated during the midterm elections. In recent meetings, China has agreed to buy 25 million metric tonnes of US soya beans, as well as what the White House has described as $17bn per year in US agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028.
Those purchases have also lagged behind the commitments.
A Putin-Xi-Trump meeting
The most significant outcome of this year’s APEC summit may be the three-way meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin.
Such a meeting would likely be seen as a massive boon for Putin.
“By sitting down with the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries in a trilateral format, Putin will be recognised as a major player on the world stage rather than a pariah,” Ryan Hass, a China expert at the Brookings Institution, wrote in a recent analysis.
Xi, in turn, would “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter for how China, Russia, and the United States will relate to each other”.
The benefit for Trump, who the White House says will focus on denuclearisation efforts, remains less clear, according to experts.
“A trilateral meeting would showcase the extent to which both Trump and Putin seek to curry favour with Xi,” Crisis Group’s Wyne said.
“It would also further unnerve US allies and partners that fear Trump’s openness to an informal ‘G2’ or ‘G3’ arrangement,” he said, referring to a global realignment that bypasses other world powers.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/houth.title: Houthis are 'occupying' part of Saudi Arabia, Tucker Carlson says
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/houth.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/houth.text:
Houthis are 'occupying' part of Saudi Arabia, Tucker Carlson says
Conservative US podcaster Tucker Carlson said that Yemen’s Houthis are “occupying” parts of Saudi Arabia, and that the American media is not covering the wartime development.
“The Houthis are legitimately threatening the Saudi kingdom right now,” Carlson said in a podcast, released on Monday, where he interviewed American geopolitical analyst Brandon J Weichert.
“They are occupying part of Saudi right now… I don’t know if this is even covered in the American media, but it’s a fact. It’s a really big thing,” he said.
“Are there Houthi forces on Saudi soil right now? There are,” he added.
Carlson did not say where he obtained the information about a Houthi “occupation” of Saudi territory, but the media personality often speaks with senior Arabian Gulf leaders.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The Financial Times reported in October that Carlson visited “certain Arab Gulf royals on their Mediterranean yachts”. Carlson claimed in his interview that he spoke to leaders in the Gulf “this week”.
Carlson has criticised the US defence and intelligence establishment, but he counts Vice President JD Vance as a friend.
Although he has blasted President Donald Trump over the war on Iran and Israel, he told Weichert that he recently had a long conversation with the US president.
'Houthi incursion'
Carlson’s claim follows an exclusive report from Middle East Eye on 2 November, citing western and Arab officials, that the Houthis were launching raids into Saudi Arabia. The sources said that the raids took place in October, but did not confirm that the Houthis were still holding Saudi territory.
Saudi Arabia’s rugged border with Yemen is effectively off limits to journalists. The terrain is a mix of mountains and vast desert. Whole villages there were uprooted after the last round of fighting in Yemen, which saw the Houthis launch cross-border incursions into Saudi Arabia.
Fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government is focused inside Yemen’s borders. The Houthis are moving towards the port city of Aden, the government’s provisional capital.
But the Houthis have openly spoken about their territorial ambitions in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis lay claim to the kingdom’s three southern provinces of Asir, Jazan and Najran, which Yemen ceded to Saudi Arabia in the 1934 Treaty of Taif.
The Houthis originated in Yemen’s Saada governorate, the mountainous region south of the border with Saudi Arabia.
The movement takes its name from its founder, Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi and follows the Zaydi sect of Shia Islam. The Houthis recruit across Yemeni society, but their senior leadership claims Hashemite descent, which would link them to the Prophet Muhammad.
Carlson also said that he believes the Houthis are being aided in their war effort by backers other than Iran, who hope to see the kingdom of Saudi Arabia weakened.
“You do wonder who is controlling the Houthis,” he said.
“I think Iran has had a huge effect on the Houthis, but is that the only power that is behind this?” he said.
Carlson did not say who he believes is supporting the Houthis, but Dropsite News reported in October that Yemeni factions backed by the UAE were quietly assisting the Houthis in targeting advice.

Prosecutors allege man ‘destroyed’ US military plane at Irish airport
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, has been charged with damaging a US military C-130 aircraft while it was parked overnight.
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.
Smashed every gauge in the cockpit
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.
According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft.
He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit.
O’Corrain also inflicted damage on the exterior of the aircraft with an axe, prosecutors said, and poured ball bearings into the transport plane’s fuel tanks.
“As a result of O’Corrain’s attack, the aircraft was effectively destroyed,” the office of the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York said in a statement.
“The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the aircraft – worth approximately $60 million – will not return to active flight status.”
Shannon Airport, which was used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a US military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a US military jet was parked.

Israeli lawmakers on Tuesday elected Matan Kahana, a parliament speaker from the camp opposed to caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
