Rideshare driver Mohamed Yusuf is in a critical condition after he was allegedly assaulted by a passenger.
A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”.
Mohamed Yusuf, 51, suffered broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car in the city of Hopkins early on Saturday, according to court documents. His family said he was in a coma.
“It was an incredibly brutal attack,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on Tuesday.
She said her office had charged Samit Apurva Patel with one count of second-degree attempted murder and one count of first-degree carjacking for the assault on Yusuf on November 14. Patel was taken into custody on Saturday.
Yusuf’s family claimed the attack was driven by hate, while civil rights advocates demanded a hate crime investigation.
Prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behaviour was motivated by bias, though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now”, Moriarty said.
The court filing said Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger just before 1am on Saturday. His brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like the name Mohamed.
“He was apparently pulled out of the car and was standing there when Patel drove over him and might have circled back and driven over him again,” Moriarty said.
Uber ‘horrified’
Patel’s parents called police for a wellness check after he arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior”, according to the court filing.
When the officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged. The phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was”, the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, that it has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
Rights advocates have raised concerns about rhetoric against Somali Americans by US President Donald Trump and his allies, and condemned his immigration crackdown in Minnesota.
US rights advocates have also noted rising Islamophobia over the past two-plus decades following the September 11, 2001, attacks, and more recently due to anti-immigration policies, rising white supremacy movements and the fallout from Israel’s war on Gaza.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster.
Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees.
Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown.
In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day.
Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday.
Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter.
“We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.”
When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”.
When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”.
Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy.
Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions.
Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”.
Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.”
Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.
Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”.
“While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.”
Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. The company is also facing an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China in the wake of Huang’s resignation, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.

https://taz.de/Ungleichheit-in-Deutschla.title: Ungleichheit in Deutschland: Schere geht laut Wirtschaftsinstitut nicht mehr auseinander
https://taz.de/Ungleichheit-in-Deutschla.author: Hannes Koch
https://taz.de/Ungleichheit-in-Deutschla.text:
Ungleichheit in Deutschland: Schere geht laut Wirtschaftsinstitut nicht mehr auseinander
Laut einer neuen Studie des DIW ist die Ungleichheit zwischen niedrigen und hohen Einkommen zuletzt nicht mehr gewachsen. Die Hans-Böckler-Stiftung sieht es anders.
Ein vergleichsweise positives Bild von der Entwicklung der Einkommen in Deutschland zeichnet das Deutsche Institut für Wirtschaftsforschung (DIW). Der Abstand zwischen hohen und niedrigen Einkommen „hat sich seit 2020 kaum verändert“, schreibt DIW-Wissenschaftler Markus Grabka in seiner neuen Studie. Die Ungleichheit zwischen Arm und Reich habe in dieser Hinsicht nicht zugenommen.
Der Bericht, der am Mittwoch offiziell erscheint, lag der taz vorab vor. Die neuesten verfügbaren Daten reichen nun bis 2024 und 2025. Sie sind ein Beitrag zu der politischen Debatte über die Frage: Wird Deutschland ungerechter? Auch die aktuelle Diskussion über die Bezahlbarkeit des Lebens – laufen die Preise den Einkommen davon? – spielt eine Rolle.
Unbestritten ist, dass die Ungleichheit der Einkommen seit Mitte der 1990er Jahre stark zunahm – unter anderem durch Steuersenkungen für hohe Einkommen und die kärgliche Sozialleistung Hartz IV. Seit einigen Jahren sei dieser Prozess aber mehr oder weniger zum Halten gekommen, argumentiert Grabka. Das sei an den Haushaltsnettoeinkommen zu sehen. Diese Größe umfasst die Einkünfte, die die hiesigen Privathaushalte etwa aus Lohnarbeit und staatlichen Leistungen beziehen. Die Spreizung zwischen hohen und niedrigen Bezügen der Top- und Geringverdiener habe zwischen 2020 und 2024 mehr oder weniger stagniert, heißt es im DIW-Bericht.
Denselben Befund leitet Markus Grabka aus der Armutsquote ab. Diese beschreibt den Anteil derjenigen Personen, die weniger als 60 Prozent des mittleren Einkommens aller Haushalte zur Verfügung haben. „In den letzten sechs Jahren bis 2024 stagniert die Niedrigeinkommensquote bei etwa 17 Prozent“, schreibt der DIW-Verteilungsforscher. Während sie Mitte der 1990er Jahre unter 11 Prozent lag, stieg sie bis 2019 auf 17 Prozent, bis 2021 auf 17,4 Prozent. Seitdem ist sie leicht gesunken. Diese Schwankungen in den vergangenen Jahren interpretiert Grabka als Stagnation, auch wegen statistischer Unschärfen.
Böckler-Stiftung eher kritisch
Einen anderen Akzent setzt die gewerkschaftliche Hans-Böckler-Stiftung. In ihrem neuen Verteilungsbericht heißt es: „Die Ungleichheit der verfügbaren Einkommen in Deutschland befindet sich nach den aktuellsten Daten auf dem zweithöchsten Niveau seit 1992.“ Auch „die Quote der Haushalte, die in Armut leben, liegt ganz nah beim Höchststand über die letzten gut drei Jahrzehnte“. Böckler-Forscherin Dorothee Spannagel betont, dass die Werte in den vergangenen Jahren höher waren als 2019. „Streiten kann man sich darüber, ob dieser Anstieg 'nennenswert’ ist – das ist natürlich eine normative Frage der Bewertung“, schreibt Spannagel.
DIW-Wissenschaftler Grabka untermauert seine positive Sicht der Entwicklung mit weiteren Daten. 2025 äußerten sich 86 Prozent der im Rahmen der Langzeituntersuchung Sozio-oekonomisches Panel befragten Bürger:innen einigermaßen bis sehr zufrieden mit ihrem Haushaltseinkommen (siehe Interview). Um 2005 herum waren das erst 76 Prozent – für Grabka ein deutliches Zeichen der insgesamt besseren finanziellen Situation der großen Bevölkerungsmehrheit.
Darauf deute auch hin, dass mittlerweile viel mehr Leute Geld zurücklegen könnten. Während vor 20 Jahren 57 Prozent der Haushalte sparten, waren es vergangenes Jahr 72 Prozent. Grabka: „Mehr Menschen können sich einen höheren Konsum leisten oder alternativ sparen.“ Für solche Verbesserungen macht der DIW-Forscher auch politische Entscheidungen wie die Einführung und die regelmäßige Erhöhung des gesetzlichen Mindestlohns verantwortlich.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Former world boxing champion Jorge Linares faces deportation after ICE arrest
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Former world boxing champion Jorge Linares has been detained by US immigration authorities in Texas, despite his lawyers insisting the retired Venezuelan fighter is legally in the country.
Linares is being held at the El Paso Processing Center, according to federal detention records reviewed by the San Antonio Express-News. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said he was arrested at El Paso International Airport on Sunday after overstaying the period he was authorized to remain in the country.
The 41-year-old boxing great, who captured titles across three weight classes from featherweight to lightweight, first disclosed his detention in a post on X on Sunday.
“ICE has me at the Texas border crossing. This is crazy,” Linares wrote in Spanish. He has not posted publicly since.
ICE spokeswoman Leticia Zamarripa said Linares was arrested by US Border Patrol agents and ICE officers on 15 November after entering the United States on 26 October 2023 with permission to remain for a temporary period.
“In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome,” Zamarripa said in a statement to the Guardian. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”
Zamarripa did not specify when Linares’ authorized period of stay expired. She added that a pending immigration application or work authorization did not confer legal status in the United States.
The immigration law firm Wilner & O’Reilly, which is representing Linares, confirmed his detention on Monday and said he was legally present in the United States.
“Mr Linares is legally present in the United States and has cooperated fully with the authorities,” the firm said in a statement. “We are working closely with ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to resolve this matter as quickly as possible.”
Linares’s lawyers said they were confident in their client’s legal position and expected the matter to be resolved once the immigration process had concluded. They also asked supporters and the media for patience.
The conflicting accounts leave unresolved the question of Linares’ immigration status. His lawyers have maintained that he is legally present in the country, while ICE has said he overstayed his authorized period of admission.
Gilberto Mendoza, president of the World Boxing Association (WBA), one of the sport’s four major sanctioning bodies, confirmed Linares’ detention and said he was in regular contact with the fighter’s family.
“His case is in the hands of immigration lawyers, and I am in constant contact with his family,” Mendoza wrote on X. “As WBA president, I will always support our champions, inside and outside the ring. Stay strong, Jorge.”
Linares, who fought out of Las Vegas and later Miami under the nickname El Niño de Oro (the Golden Boy), was regarded as one of boxing’s finest technicians during his 21-year professional career.
Born in Barinas, Venezuela, he moved to Japan in 2002 to turn professional at 17, a year before he would have been eligible to do so in his home country, and fought 18 of his first 23 bouts there before winning his first world championship at 126lb on his US debut in 2007.
After becoming a two-weight champion at 130lb, Linares’ most successful period came at lightweight, where he held versions of the WBA and WBC titles between 2014 and 2018.
His reign at 135lb ended in a memorable showdown with Vasiliy Lomachenko at Madison Square Garden in May 2018. Linares knocked down the heavily favored Ukrainian with a right hand in the sixth round and pushed him to the limit before being stopped by a body shot in the 10th.
Linares announced his retirement in October 2023 after losing to Britain’s Jack Catterall in Liverpool, just five days before the date ICE says he last entered the United States. He ended his career with a record of 47 wins and nine defeats with 29 knockouts, including notable victories over Oscar Larios, Rocky Juarez, Jesús Chávez, Anthony Crolla (twice) and Luke Campbell.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
The US-led board has decried continued fighting in Gaza and delays in implementing the terms of a 2025 ceasefire deal.
The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza.
In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board cautioned that, without immediate steps to implement the 2025 ceasefire deal, the truce between Israel and Hamas may be on the brink of collapse.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, which The Associated Press obtained.
The Board of Peace was created in 2025, at US President Donald Trump’s behest, to oversee the ceasefire deal and reconstruction in Gaza.
Since October 2023, the narrow coastal territory has been the target of a genocidal war carried out by Israel, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
‘Cannot be sustained indefinitely’
In recent weeks, Israel has continued to carry out deadly air strikes, and its ongoing restrictions have prevented the delivery of life-saving aid into Gaza ahead of the winter season.
“Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” the board said in its report.
According to the board, the widespread devastation in Gaza has left Palestinians facing “another winter in tents and rubble”.
Trump first proposed the Board of Peace in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.
The board’s mission was laid out in a 20-point Gaza peace plan, as well as the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire formally began on October 10, 2025, though attacks have continued since.
The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
But in Tuesday’s report, the board said Israel and Hamas have fallen far short of their commitments in the ceasefire deal.
“A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely,” the report said. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.”
The board also noted that Israel has blocked the technocratic civil administration body created to run Gaza on an interim basis.
“The absence of decisions by the government of Israel on the necessary conditions and arrangements for the training, deployment and return of civilian police to Gaza continues to impede full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan,” the report said.
“The Board of Peace calls on the government of Israel to take these decisions without delay.”
To break the deadlock, the board called on the UN Security Council to press both sides to fulfil their agreements.
“Neither party may treat the other’s delay as license for its own inaction, and together these obligations are the only route to Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction at scale,” the report said.
It also added that the outcome must establish a credible path towards Palestinian statehood and self-determination, warning that no unilateral actions should be permitted to derail that ultimate goal.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Israeli parliament elects new speaker backed by Netanyahu’s opponents
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Associated Press in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.
The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.
They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.
Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike
Crew says their boat was attacked by drones launched from US-operated vessel as part of ‘manifestly unlawful’ campaign.
A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March.
The lawsuit, filed on Monday in a Pennsylvania federal court, seeks financial restitution and any additional relief the court considers just.
It also petitions the court to issue an order ending the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
The complaint centres on the March 17 sinking of the fishing boat La Negra Francisca Duarte II, based in Ecuador.
“We filed the lawsuit because the boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us,” the ship’s captain, Hernan Flores, told the Reuters news agency. “They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we’re alive.”
The government has not claimed responsibility for the strikes on La Negra Francisca Duarte II and two other Ecuadorian vessels that were attacked and sunk in recent months.
A report from the Washington Post in August, however, suggested that the vessels were targeted by the CIA as part of a secret overseas mission.
Other reports have raised the possibility of the attacks being conducted by a US government contractor or a regional ally.
The attacks appear to be similar to an ongoing campaign the US military has claimed credit for.
Since September 2025, the US government has publicly undertaken a series of boat strikes, with the aim of killing alleged “narcoterrorists”.
At least 244 people have been killed as part of that campaign, which experts have described as extrajudicial killing, in violation of international law.
The lawsuit filed on Monday alleges that two drones were launched from a vessel operated by the US in March and proceeded to attack La Negra Francisca Duarte II.
The boat was set ablaze, resulting in “serious burns” for two of the 16 crew members.
“All of the Plaintiffs ended up jumping off the ship and into the sea. They then found their way onto small emergency boats,” the filing said, calling the strike part of an “unprecedented and manifestly unlawful US military campaign”.
After the strike, the crew members say they made their way towards what they believed was a tuna fishing boat nearby but were met by armed men speaking English dressed in military uniforms.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he has launched a hardline campaign to combat drug trafficking into the US.
That push has coincided with a policy of expanding US military operations across Latin America, often in collaboration with right-wing political allies in the region.
But critics have raised concerns over transparency and potential rights abuses during such operations.
No suspects have been identified in the boat strike campaign undertaken by the US military, for instance, nor has any evidence been presented to the public.
Families, however, have stepped forward to claim the dead as their loved ones. Many have argued that the people killed in the boat strike campaign were not drug traffickers but fishermen and informal workers.
In December 2025, the family of the missing Colombian fisherman Alejandro Carranza filed a complaint about the boat strikes through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, claiming his right to life had been violated.
A few weeks later, in January, the families of two workers from Trinidad and Tobago – Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo – filed a wrongful death lawsuit in a US federal court in Massachusetts. The men had reportedly been travelling home from Venezuela after taking work abroad.
But experts say that efforts to hold the US government to account will be difficult, given the lack of transparency surrounding the boat strikes.
The lethal boat strike campaign has continued in recent weeks, with a recent attack taking place on October 27.
The US government has also been involved in non-lethal interception efforts, stopping suspected drug-trafficking boats.
The watchdog group Human Rights Watch said that the US and Ecuador intercepted at least eight vessels between late August and mid-September, on the basis that they were being used to supply drug trafficking groups.
Of the 160 crew members on board those vessels, Human Rights Watch says that 56 were released without charge by court order, 40 were acquitted for lack of evidence, 50 are awaiting trial, and 14 were not formally charged.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Portugal’s new No 7 Forbs channels Ronaldo for winner as Wales are denied
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Ben Fisher at Cardiff City Stadium
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
One way or another, Portugal’s No 7 shirt has caused quite the commotion in recent weeks and months, if not years. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that the first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era would come courtesy of the player wearing the updated jersey, one with a cross through the number to preserve Ronaldo’s eternal legacy, as the Portuguese Football Federation put it. A sumptuous finish by Carlos Forbs, a second-half substitute, was ultimately enough to clinch victory on a topsy-turvy night with Portugal surviving Pedro Neto’s sending-off for two yellow cards.
For Wales, a Nations League relegation playoff double-header awaits in March, with Slovenia, Hungary, Republic of Ireland or Bosnia and Herzegovina – who knocked them out of World Cup qualifying this year – all potential opponents in Friday’s draw in Switzerland. Afterwards Craig Bellamy stressed the importance of keeping elite company to accelerate improvement but reiterated that he will not be in the job beyond Euro 2028, after which his contract expires.
“If we want to develop as a football nation and continue to move forward, we have to be playing against the best teams,” Bellamy said. “It’s only going to improve us. I was the best manager going in [Group] B, finished top … how good am I? Now I’m in [Group] A, we’ve played quite well, but I’m crap. It’s about playing the best teams, that’s how we’re going to get better. I won’t be here for the next Nations League, I won’t be the manager then, so I’m doing it for the next one.”
This was a welcome victory for Portugal, who advanced to the quarter-finals as group winners after a bruising 4-1 home defeat by Denmark in Braga. Turn a new page and all that. There were plenty of positive takeaways for Wales too. David Brooks cancelled out Bruno Fernandes’s opener and Wales seized the lead through Sorba Thomas, who applied the finish after a slick team move. But Neto, who picked up two bookings inside two minutes, the second for a foul on Brennan Johnson, levelled before half-time. Bellamy’s side were fun and, at times, freewheeling but Forbs had the final say with a neat run and finish.
Bellamy stressed the importance of locking down Vitinha and João Neves, two of his favourite players, but Wales did not allow the Paris Saint-Germain pair to have things all their own way. It was a ludicrously open game and, approaching the half-time interval at 2-2, a stray Renato Veiga pass supplied the all-action Harry Wilson with a speculative opportunity from halfway. Wilson intercepted the ball and, after taking a touch to roll it into the opposition half, the Leeds midfielder launched a marvellous left-foot lobbed effort towards goal, his 45-yard shot skimming the roof of Diogo Costa’s goal net.
Portugal may have levelled a few moments earlier, Neto easily beating Jay Dasilva in the six-yard box to prod in Francisco Trincão’s brilliant cross, but Wilson’s attempt at the audacious was another gentle reminder of Portugal’s precarious state. After suffering their heaviest competitive home defeat against Denmark on Saturday, Portugal were again susceptible defensively. Before Thomas capped a scintillating team move to seize the lead on 40 minutes, Wilson twice went close, Diogo Dalot making a desperate block for the first.
This was an entertaining contest for which it was worth braving the winter conditions. When Fernandes picked his spot on 11 minutes, sending an unerring strike into the top corner, Portugal appeared in the groove. But Wales responded two minutes later when Brooks, who scored with a superb dinked finish in Norway, dug out another clever effort. Wilson saw a shot repelled by Costa but when the ball squirted free Rubin Colwill had the presence of mind to calmly square for Brooks, who squeezed a left-foot shot into the far corner. Colwill, a fan favourite here for Cardiff, thoroughly enjoyed his first Wales start under Bellamy.
Colwill impressed in a deep midfield role alongside Josh Sheehan of Bolton, whose former clubmate Aaron Collins, now of MK Dons, arrived from the bench midway through the second half for his debut. Portugal, meanwhile, introduced João Félix and the Club Brugge winger Forbs, the latter wearing the tweaked No 7 shirt that will always be synonymous with Ronaldo. An unmarked Ben Cabango, who replaced Joe Rodon as a precaution at half-time, went close to earning Wales the lead with a header. The weary look on Costa’s face as he pawed Cabango’s header away from goal for a corner said it all.
The moment Forbs surged on to a loose Cabango header and then at Davies before applying a low finish provided light relief on an uncomfortable night. For Wales, a challenging campaign ended as it began, with a heartening defeat by Portugal.
“Look, it’s a £1.2bn squad against a £170m squad,” Bellamy said. “I live in the real world. I’m beyond happy. I couldn’t ask for more. Against a top team, if you make a couple of mistakes as we did, you will get punished. We’ve offered a really good version of ourselves, we’ve been a massive part of this group. It’s just about those fine margins.”

https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.title: Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Der Kampf um die Klimawahrheit
https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.author: Nanja Boenisch
https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.text:
Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Der Kampf um die Klimawahrheit
Fossile Staaten blockieren den Weltklimarat IPCC, der die wissenschaftliche Basis für Klimapolitik liefert. Wer sich auf welcher Seite positioniert.
Mary Robinson sagt, es habe auch früher schon Angriffe auf die Klimawissenschaft gegeben. „Aber ich habe noch nie eine solche Bedrohung wie jetzt erlebt.“ Robinson, 82 Jahre alt, war in den 1990ern Irlands erste weibliche Staatspräsidentin, dann UN-Kommissarin für Menschenrechte. Bei der Weltklimakonferenz COP31, die vor gut einer Woche im türkischen Antalya begonnen hat, macht sie sich nun für die Arbeit des UN-Klimarates IPCC stark.
„Der IPCC hat die Grundlage für die Klimadiplomatie der Vergangenheit geliefert“, sagt Robinson am Dienstagmittag in einem der Gebäude auf dem Konferenzgelände vor Journalist:innen. „Er ist weiterhin entscheidend für die Verhandlungen und sollte seinen nächsten Bericht in dem Zeitrahmen fertigstellen, auf den sich die internationale Gemeinschaft schon einmal geeinigt hat.“
Der Hintergrund: Kurz vor der COP31 war ein Streit im weltweit größten wissenschaftlichen Klimagremium hochgekocht. Eigentlich soll der IPCC bis 2028 seinen nächsten Sachstandsbericht vorlegen, in dem er den Stand der Klimaforschung für politische Machthaber:innen zusammenträgt. 2028 steht die nächste globale Bestandsaufnahme zur Umsetzung der Pariser Klimaziele an. Eine Gruppe von Staaten, zu denen Saudi-Arabien, China, Indien und Russland gehören, blockiert den Prozess – sie will die Veröffentlichung auf 2029 schieben.
Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya
Vom 9. November an treffen sich Regierungen aus aller Welt, um über Klimakrise sowie Klimaschutz zu verhandeln – und darüber, wer zahlt. Die taz berichtet von vor Ort.
Diese Staaten hängen noch stark an fossilen Energien; viele haben sich schon in der Vergangenheit einen Namen als Bremser gemacht, die den Beschluss ehrgeiziger und verbindlicher Ziele bei Klimakonferenzen zu verhindern wussten. Bei der Weltklimakonferenz in der Türkei wollen dem IPCC nun andere Verhandlungsparteien den Rücken stärken und die Einhaltung des ursprünglichen Zeitplans explizit in die Abschlusserklärung reinverhandeln.
Deutschland will den Weltklimarat verteidigen
Die Delegation aus Saudi-Arabien, dem größten Erdölexporteur der Welt, versuchte sich am Dienstag zu rechtfertigen. Sie wolle die Klimawissenschaft nicht verzögern, sondern „die wissenschaftliche Integrität und Inklusivität der IPCC-Bewertungen durch angemessene Veröffentlichtungsfristen“ wahren. Verhandler:innen aus Indien argumentieren wiederum, der IPCC solle sich mehr Zeit lassen, um wissenschaftliche Expertise aus „Entwicklungsländern“ in den neuen Bericht einfließen zu lassen.
Laurence Tubiana, European Climate Foundation
Laurence Tubiana, Leiterin der European Climate Foundation und wichtige Unterhändlerin des Pariser Klimaabkommens aus dem Jahr 2015, hält das für vorgeschoben. „Gerechtigkeit in der Wissenschaft ist sehr wichtig“, sagt sie kurz nach Robinson. „Aber an den IPCC-Berichten sind zum Beispiel hoch qualifizierte Wissenschaftler aus Indien beteiligt.“ Klimadiplomatie habe es ohnehin schwerer als noch vor ein paar Jahren, so Tubiana. Geopolitische Konflikte und steigende Lebenshaltungskosten hätten die Klimakrise aus dem Fokus gedrängt, Geld werde eher in Aufrüstung als in Klimaschutz und -forschung investiert.
Dazu kommt, dass viele „Entwicklungsländer“, als deren Fürsprecher sich zum Beispiel Indien gibt, am ursprünglichen Zeitplan festhalten wollen. Adão Soares Barbosa aus dem südostasiatischen Inselstaat Timor-Leste, Vorsitzender der Gruppe der Least Developed Countries, betont in Antalya: Der nächste IPCC-Bericht müsse pünktlich veröffentlicht werden, wenn die Weltgemeinschaft die Erderwärmung bis zum Ende des Jahrhunderts wieder zurück zur kritischen 1,5-Grad-Grenze bringen wolle.
Ob es die Rückendeckung für den IPCC in den Abschlussbericht dieser Klimakonferenz schafft, ist noch schwer einzuschätzen. Der erste Entwurf, den die türkische COP-Präsidentschaft am Montag vorgestellt hat, enthält eine solche Formulierung – allerdings liste er praktisch alle Forderungen einzelner Staaten auf, auch solche, über die noch lange keine Einigkeit bestehe, schränkt Soares Barbosa ein.
Mary Robinson baut auf Deutschland: Bundesumweltminister Carsten Schneider (SPD), der am Montag in Antalya angekommen war, hat versprochen, in den Verhandlungen über die Abschlusserklärung den IPCC, die Klimawissenschaft und das 1,5-Grad-Ziel zu verteidigen.
There is no planet B
Die Klimakatastrophe braucht unsere volle mediale Aufmerksamkeit. Dafür bündelt die taz seit Jahren ihre Kräfte und begleitet Konflikte und Fortschritte auf allen Kanälen. Und das schon lange: Die taz hat über radikale Klimaveränderungen berichtet, als andere Medien noch treu von unendlichem Wachstum sprachen. Und sie macht weiter, wenn andere ihre Berichterstattung zurückfahren. Unsere Artikel sind und bleiben frei zugänglich – ohne Paywall, dank über 52.000 freiwilliger Unterstützer*innen. Wir sind der Überzeugung, dass es kritische Informationen im Netz geben muss, die nicht kostenpflichtig sind. Gerade zum Thema Klimaschutz. Nur wenn unser Journalismus so viel wie möglich gelesen wird, kann er gesellschaftliche Veränderungen bewirken. Aber das geht nur, wenn sich unsere Leser*innen an dieser Idee beteiligen und den taz-Journalismus mittragen. Sind Sie schon dabei? Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: « Il y a tout à raconter sur ce petit territoire de l’Artois » : Maxence Voiseux, réalisateur de « Gabin »
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Michaël Mélinard
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Pendant dix ans, Maxence Voiseux a suivi l’évolution de Gabin, un enfant de l’Artois désireux de travailler dans le monde rural. Un premier long-métrage fascinant en forme de récit d’apprentissage.
Pour son premier long-métrage documentaire, Maxence Voiseux a pris du temps. Celui d’observer, dix ans durant, de ses 8 à ses 18 ans, l’évolution de Gabin, un gamin de l’Artois, une région du Pas-de-Calais.
Gabin poursuit aussi une plongée dans la famille Jourdel, débutée par le cinéaste avec le grand-père. Ici, la relation fusionnelle avec sa mère, fermière, tranche avec le lien paternel plus tendu. Avec ses choix de récit, Maxence Voiseux dessine un film d’apprentissage passionnant, qui interroge les logiques de transmission et la ruralité.
C’est le troisième film que vous consacrez à la famille Jourdel, pour quelles raisons ?
Maxime Voiseux
Documentariste, réalisateur de « Gabin »
Ma famille est originaire du Pas-de-Calais. Je n’y suis pas né, mais j’ai enduré les vacances familiales chez les grands-parents, les Noëls interminables, les vacances de Pâques avec le grand-père à l’église. C’est un endroit que je n’aimais pas trop et avec lequel je me suis réconcilié par le cinéma. J’ai commencé à faire des films avec le grand-père de Gabin. Il...

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120393.title: Wahl zur Bundespräsidentin | Ilse Aigner: Ganz nett bald im Schloss Bellevue
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120393.author: Christoph Ruf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120393.text:
- Kommentare
- Wahl zur Bundespräsidentin
Ilse Aigner: Ganz nett bald im Schloss Bellevue
Ilse Aigner soll Bundespräsidentin werden. Eine Politikerin, die vor allem durch Worte auffällt, die sie selbst nicht ernst nimmt, wie unser Kolumnist weiß.
Kann es eigentlich sein, dass die Anforderungen an das politische Spitzenpersonal ähnlich stark gesunken sind wie die Exportchancen deutscher Verbrennerautos?
Als ich hörte, dass Ilse Aigner (CSU) Bundespräsidentin werden soll, wunderte ich mich noch dezent. Als ich las, wie hymnisch sie gelobt wurde, schon mehr. Die Sozis überschlugen sich von »sehr gute Bundespräsidentin« bis »perfekte Kandidatin«, was vor allem den Schluss zuließ, dass sie aus den eigenen Reihen auch niemanden gefunden hätten, zu dem einem mehr einfallen würde als »nett«. Neben »bodenständig« war das die Vokabel, die in den Gazetten so oft zu lesen war, dass ich mich fragte, wann meine Freunde und ich endlich ins Schloss Bellevue ziehen dürfen. Wir finden uns wechselseitig auch ganz nett.
Als ich dann aber las, Aigner »stehe für Wertschätzung«, habe ich mich nur noch gewundert. Vor rund zwei Jahren habe ich angefangen, mich bei allem, was ich zum Umgang mit den drei vermaledeiten Buchstaben lese, zu fragen, wem es nützt. Und meistens komme ich zum Ergebnis: der AfD. So auch hier.
Christoph Ruf ist freier Autor und beobachtet hier politische und sportliche Begebenheiten.
Dass man sich ungern in einen Raum begibt, in dem feixende AfD-Leute sitzen, kann ich nachvollziehen. Aber kann es darum gehen, wenn man Wahlergebnisse lesen kann? Was hätte es Aigner gekostet, die Einladung der AfD, ihre Fraktion im Bundestag zu besuchen, anzunehmen und dort ihrer Kernkompetenz gemäß ein paar Allgemeinplätze loszuwerden? Oder die anwesenden Damen und Herren nach allen Regeln der Kunst zu beleidigen? Das muss doch auch Spaß machen.
Alles wäre jedenfalls besser gewesen, als nicht hinzugehen. Denn das bedient das Narrativ von den Demokraten, die ihre eigenen Spielregeln missachten, wenn es ihnen in den Kram passt. Dass das längst mehr ist als ein Narrativ, sieht man an der immer lächerlicher werdenden Kampagne gegen die Regierungsbildung in Berlin. Doch die bayerische Lady beging dann auch noch die bodenlose Frechheit, gleich noch die Linke-Fraktion ebenso zu ignorieren. Passt in den Zeitgeist. Und lässt mich die Aigner-Freundin Monika Gruber zitieren: »Geh’ scheiß’n«
Gut zu wissen ist es da allerdings, dass die künftige Bundespräsidentin selbst findet, man brauche hierzulande »einfach einen breitestmöglichen Konsens und eine Zusammenführung der Gesellschaft« und dass sie sich selbst für »eine Brückenbauerin« hält. Was man halt so redet, wenn man längst den Anspruch aufgegeben hat, dass das eigene Handeln irgendetwas mit dem eigenen Geschwätz zu tun haben sollte.
»Oft bleibt sie beim Bekannten, beim Ungefähren, es fehlen lange Linien, das gewisse Etwas, das tiefer schürft«, las ich dann doch noch beim ZDF. Aufschlussreich, denn plötzlich versteht man auch die Begeisterung aus den Reihen der SPD. Dort scheinen mittlerweile einige verstanden zu haben, dass sie mit einem Parteivorsitzenden, dem noch nie ein origineller Satz über die Lippen kam, endgültig untergehen. Doch da sich die SPD zu Tode regiert hat, scheint als alternatives Angebot zu Pattex-Lars in Hubertus Heil auch wieder nur einer gefunden worden zu sein, der sein ganzes politisches Leben lang die Gedanken anderer ausgeführt hat.
Nichts zu sagen zu haben, mag reichen, um Bundespräsidentin zu werden. Es ist allerdings etwas dünne, um einer ausgebluteten Partei neues Leben einzuhauchen.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: DR Congo’s rival peace efforts fail to halt violence in the east
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
DR Congo’s rival peace efforts fail to halt violence in the east
Diplomatic efforts struggle to end fighting in eastern DRC as civilians continue to bear the cost of conflict.
Bukavu, DRC – For residents of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the succession of diplomatic initiatives meant to end years of conflict is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the violence unfolding around them.
In North and South Kivu provinces, fighting between the Congolese army and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), an armed and political coalition led by former President Joseph Kabila, has continued despite international efforts to secure a settlement. Civilians remain exposed to attacks, displacement and the disruption of essential services.
The latest escalation has raised questions about whether negotiations in Washington and Doha can deliver security on the ground, and whether the separate diplomatic efforts are sufficiently coordinated to make progress.
“One meeting follows another, and they all end up being much the same,” said Blaise Chasumba, a resident of Bukavu, the provincial capital of South Kivu. “But the real peace that the warring parties are dangling before us is far from becoming a reality on the ground. We continue to lose our loved ones and our homes.”
A conflict with deep historical roots
The Washington Accords, signed in December 2025, seek to address tensions between the DRC and neighbouring Rwanda. The Doha process, by contrast, is intended to resolve the conflict between the Congolese government and the Congo River Alliance (AFC), which includes the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group.
The distinction is important: an agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali cannot, on its own, resolve the confrontation between the Congolese government and armed groups operating inside the country.
The Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed by the DRC government, the AFC and M23 on November 15, 2025. In August 2026, representatives of the two sides, alongside Qatar, the United States, Togo, the African Union Commission and Switzerland, agreed on a road map to advance negotiations and establish a mechanism to review implementation. Fighting has nevertheless continued.
The roots of the conflict stretch back decades. The 1994 genocide in neighbouring Rwanda and the flight of former Rwandan soldiers and militia members into what was then Zaire helped create the conditions for successive wars. The presence of armed groups linked to the genocide, and the emergence of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), became a persistent source of tension between Kinshasa and Kigali.
The First and Second Congo Wars, which began in 1996 and 1998, drew in several neighbouring countries. Although the conflicts formally ended, disputes over land, political representation, citizenship and control of natural resources continued to drive violence in the east.
M23 emerged in 2012 after a mutiny by former members of the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP). The group had been integrated into the Congolese army under a March 23, 2009 peace agreement, which its leaders later accused the government of failing to honour. The United Nations and conflict researchers have documented the movement’s origins in the breakdown of that integration process.
The diplomatic landscape has since become more complicated. Established in October 2026 under Kabila’s leadership, the FRN says it has succeeded the AFC and assumed its commitments. The precise relationship between the new coalition and the earlier AFC/M23 structure remains important when assessing who is represented in the negotiations.
On the battlefield, an offensive in early November underlined the fragility of the diplomatic process. FRN fighters advanced through Kahuzi-Biega National Park and along National Road 3, a strategic route linking Bukavu with areas farther north.
Conflict monitoring reports said the fighters captured several localities, including Bitale and the centre of Bulambika on November 8 . The Congolese army said it had halted the advance at Bulambika and was preparing a counteroffensive. Local and military accounts differed over the extent of the fighters’ territorial gains.
Diplomatic commitments, limited progress
The fighting has driven further displacement and placed additional pressure on communities already struggling with years of conflict. Humanitarian organisations have warned that conflict is also making it harder to maintain essential services.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said it had reduced its staff presence in the Bunyakiri health zone, relocating some personnel to Bitale and Bukavu as the security situation deteriorated.
“We remind all parties to the conflict of the importance and the obligation to respect and ensure the protection of healthcare facilities, civilian populations and humanitarian staff, in accordance with international humanitarian law,” MSF said in a statement sent to Al Jazeera.
The Congolese armed forces, known by their French acronym FARDC, have blamed recent attacks in North and South Kivu on the Rwandan army and fighters allied with the FRN. The army says it is preparing operations to recover lost positions.
Rwanda denies supporting armed groups in eastern DRC, citing the presence of the FDLR as a security threat. The dispute has remained central to tensions between the two countries.
In a resolution adopted in February 2025, the UN Security Council condemned M23’s offensive and described direct support and participation by the Rwanda Defence Force. It called on Rwanda to end its support and withdraw its forces from Congolese territory. The resolution also condemned support provided by Congolese forces to armed groups, particularly the FDLR, and called for the group’s neutralisation.
The African Union (AU) has acknowledged the gap between diplomatic commitments and conditions on the ground. In a communique issued after a Peace and Security Council meeting on October 26 , it said implementation of commitments under the Washington and Doha processes remained limited. It called for better coordination between the initiatives and urged inclusive, nationally owned dialogue.
The AU’s assessment points to a central weakness in the peace efforts: Agreements and diplomatic meetings have not translated into a sustained improvement in security. The bloc has stressed that a lasting settlement requires political dialogue involving wider sections of Congolese society, including women, young people and civil society organisations.
Civilians demand a voice in the peace process
For some Congolese, negotiations between governments and armed groups are not enough. They want a broader political process that addresses the grievances sustaining the conflict.
Dieumerci Mungu Akonkwa, North Kivu coordinator for Action for Democracy and Development in the Congo, said the negotiations had yet to produce tangible improvements for civilians.
“Since these negotiations began on the ground, there has been no progress. All that is happening is that the lives of peaceful civilians are being cut short. The war continues to create displaced people, and women are being raped,” he said.
Akonkwa called for an inclusive national dialogue, pointing to proposals put forward by Catholic and Protestant church leaders. Such a process, he argued, could bring political actors and civil society into discussions that extend beyond negotiations between the government and armed groups.
The challenge is not only to secure commitments from the parties to the conflict, but to address the local disputes, weak state institutions and impunity that have helped sustain violence in eastern DRC. Without progress on those issues, a political agreement risks leaving the underlying causes of insecurity unresolved.
For residents, however, the immediate measure of progress is simpler: whether the fighting stops, essential services remain available and families can return home.
Chasumba said people were also waiting for those responsible for the destruction to address their losses.
“We are eager to see compensation for the damage caused by the war. Unfortunately, at this rate, we can see that we are in for a long-running saga, full of twists and turns,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.
But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.
Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.
According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.
“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”
The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.
So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.
While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.
In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.
Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.
The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.
“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

https://taz.de/47-Billionen-US-Dollar-Sc.title: 4,7 Billionen US-Dollar Schaden: Diese Länder trifft die Klimakrise am stärksten
https://taz.de/47-Billionen-US-Dollar-Sc.author: Malte Steinmüller
https://taz.de/47-Billionen-US-Dollar-Sc.text:
4,7 Billionen US-Dollar Schaden: Diese Länder trifft die Klimakrise am stärksten
In den vergangenen 30 Jahren verursachte klimabedingtes Extremwetter laut einem Index über 900.000 Tote. Einige Staaten sind besonders betroffen.
Dominica belegt den traurigen ersten Platz: Der karibische Inselstaat war über die vergangenen drei Jahrzehnte global am stärksten von klimabedingten Extremwettereignissen betroffen. Regelmäßig verwüsten Wirbelstürme die Insel mit ihren 70.000 Bewohner*innen. Der Hurrikan Maria im Jahr 2017 sorgte allein für über 100 Todesopfer und Schäden in Höhe von 1,9 Milliarden US‑Dollar – 270 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts.
Das ist Ergebnis des diesjährigen Klimarisikoindex, der am Dienstag am Rande der Weltklimakonferenz im türkischen Antalya vorgestellt wurde. Das Projekt der NGO Germanwatch untersucht jährlich, welche Staaten am stärksten von Extremwetterereignissen betroffen sind, beruhend auf Daten von der Weltbank und dem Internationalen Währungsfonds. Analysiert werden Todesopfer, betroffene Menschen und wirtschaftliche Verluste der einzelnen Länder.
Extremwetter betraf 5,5 Milliarden Menschen
Stürme, Überschwemmungen, Hitzewellen und Dürren gab es laut dem Index in den vergangenen 30 Jahren weltweit fast 10.000 Mal. Diese Extremwettereignisse betrafen insgesamt 5,5 Milliarden Menschen direkt und forderten 916.000 Menschenleben. Allein im vergangenen Jahr verursachten insgesamt 367 Extremwettereignisse 35.000 Todesfälle und wirtschaftliche Schäden in Höhe von 158 Milliarden US-Dollar.
In den vergangenen 30 Jahren beliefen sich die wirtschaftlichen Schäden inflationsbereinigt auf über 4,7 Billionen US-Dollar, so der Index. Allerdings betrafen die Klimafolgen nicht alle Länder gleichermaßen, sondern insbesondere einkommensschwache Länder. Und die haben gleichzeitig am wenigsten zur Klimakrise beigetragen.
Auf Dominica folgt im Ranking der südostasiatische Staat Myanmar. Allein der Zyklon Nargis sorgte dort 2008 laut dem CRI für den Tod von fast 140.000 Menschen und Schäden in Höhe von 6 Milliarden US‑Dollar. Nach Myanmar listet der Index die Länder Honduras, Libyen, Haiti, Grenada, die Philippinen, Nicaragua, die Bahamas und Indien auf.
Einige der Staaten wurden besonders häufig von Extremwetterereignissen heimgesucht, andere von außergewöhnlich extremen. „Die Klimaforschung belegt eindeutig, dass der Klimawandel die Risiken für beide Gruppen erhöht“, so der Bericht.
Deutschland im oberen Viertel der betroffenen Länder
Deutschland gehört im 30-Jahre-Index mit Rang 34 zum oberen Viertel der am stärksten betroffenen Länder. Von 1996 bis 2025 gab es in Deutschland demnach mehr als 33.000 Tote durch Wetterextreme, vor allem durch Hitzewellen. Die Sachschäden, die insbesondere durch Stürme und Flutkatastrophen entstanden, summierten sich demnach auf inflationsbereinigt 133 Milliarden US-Dollar. Volkswirtschaftliche Folgeschäden seien dabei noch nicht einmal eingerechnet.
Die Autor*innen des Berichts zum Index warnen: „Die Zahl der Todesopfer und die wirtschaftlichen Kosten von klimabedingten Extremwetterereignissen werden weiter steigen.“ Deshalb appellieren sie für mehr Klimaschutz und finanzielle Unterstützung armer Länder. Im vergangenen Jahr betrafen die Extremwettereignisse vor allem Jamaika, Sri Lanka, Spanien, Thailand und die Philippinen.
There is no planet B
Die Klimakatastrophe braucht unsere volle mediale Aufmerksamkeit. Dafür bündelt die taz seit Jahren ihre Kräfte und begleitet Konflikte und Fortschritte auf allen Kanälen. Und das schon lange: Die taz hat über radikale Klimaveränderungen berichtet, als andere Medien noch treu von unendlichem Wachstum sprachen. Und sie macht weiter, wenn andere ihre Berichterstattung zurückfahren. Unsere Artikel sind und bleiben frei zugänglich – ohne Paywall, dank über 52.000 freiwilliger Unterstützer*innen. Wir sind der Überzeugung, dass es kritische Informationen im Netz geben muss, die nicht kostenpflichtig sind. Gerade zum Thema Klimaschutz. Nur wenn unser Journalismus so viel wie möglich gelesen wird, kann er gesellschaftliche Veränderungen bewirken. Aber das geht nur, wenn sich unsere Leser*innen an dieser Idee beteiligen und den taz-Journalismus mittragen. Sind Sie schon dabei? Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ICE agents pepper spray pregnant US citizen in California, video shows
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levin
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident.
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a chaotic encounter.
Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, said in a press conference on Sunday evening that she is part of a group of local residents who monitor ICE sightings, and that she had gone to the jail parking lot after agents were spotted in the area.
A commotion erupted when ICE agents moved to arrest a man who, it appeared, had just been released from the jail, video shows.
Footage filmed by Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera, captured a tumultuous scene as several people protested the agents making the arrest. The circumstances of the man’s arrest were not immediately clear, and he has not been identified. Agents wore law enforcement vests and ICE badges, and at least two of them had masks covering their faces.
It was unclear what exactly happened right before Vargas Andrade’s arrest, with the sound on the footage repeatedly cutting out. One woman was heard screaming at the agents to get away from her and another cursed at the agents, telling them, “You should be embarrassed … you guys are so fucked up.”
Vargas Andrade had her phone in one hand as she and an agent then appeared to bump into each other, footage showed. That agent then grabbed her and started to handcuff her. Another agent then pulled out what appeared to be a pepper-spray canister and pointed it at the direction of Vargas Andrade and her husband who was filming.
The footage partially captured the agent deploying the pepper spray, though it was difficult to discern how long he sprayed it and where the chemicals landed. Soon after, the footage captured Talavera shouting, “She’s pregnant with child!” as the agents moved to detain his wife. Seconds later, two agents took Vargas Andrade to the ground where she was handcuffed on her stomach with her hands behind her back, before one of the agents moved her onto her side.
Vargas Andrade was taken into custody and transported to an ICE field office in Stockton, according to her attorney, Patrick Kolasinski. Vargas Andrade’s sister had called for an ambulance, which then arrived at the ICE facility and transported her to a hospital, her family and a local advocate said at the press conference.
Vargas Andrade said officers had told her she was accused of assaulting an ICE agent, an accusation she denied. She was released later that day, and she has not been charged with any crimes, according to Kolasinski.
Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to inquiries on Monday. A spokesperson for the Department of Justice (DoJ) declined to comment. A spokesperson for the Stanislaus sheriff’s office, which runs the jail, said sheriff deputies were not involved in Vargas Andrade’s arrest.
“They threw me to the ground, they maced me, then they handcuffed me,” Vargas Andrade recalled to reporters on Sunday night. “I told the ICE agent … ‘I’m pregnant, so don’t put your hands on me.’ … They right away threw me on the floor … I was burning. I couldn’t breathe. The mace went up my nose.”
Another ICE agent then gave her water to wash her face, she recalled.
“I got scared,” Talavera said. “I was like, what if she has a miscarriage?”
Vargas Andrade said she was particularly worried because she had suffered two previous pregnancy losses, but she said doctors did an ultrasound after the incident and did not identify any concerns.
The encounter happened amid reports of increased ICE activity in California’s central valley region, which is home to the state’s agricultural industry. DHS and the justice department have repeatedly accused anti-ICE protesters of assaulting agents, though many of those prosecutions in California have fallen apart in federal court.
“We’re not going to stop helping the community even though this happened,” Vargas Andrade said. “We want our immigrants to feel safe here.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Exclusive: Bernie Sanders on Why It’s Vital for Democrats to Replace Chuck Schumer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Exclusive: Bernie Sanders on Why It’s Vital for Democrats to Replace Chuck Schumer
In an interview with The Nation, the progressive icon says that the Senate leader is “way out of touch with where the American people are at.”
Exclusive: Bernie Sanders on Why It’s Vital for Democrats to Replace Chuck Schumer
In an interview with “The Nation,” the progressive icon says that the Senate leader is “way out of touch with where the American people are at.”
US Senator Bernie Sanders, who inspired and helped to elect many of the young insurgent candidates who surfed this month’s Democratic “blue wave,” announced Tuesday that he will not support New York Democrat Chuck Schumer’s bid to lead the party’s majority Senate caucus in the next term of Congress.
The move by Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats and who jumpstarted progressive politics with two bids for the party’s presidential nomination, highlighted the need to break with status-quo agendas after a national election result that was broadly read as a cry for change from the American people.
While Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for a decade, retains significant support within the caucus, Sanders argued in an exclusive interview with The Nation that it is vital for the party to do more than simply oppose the administration of Republican President Donald Trump. He said that Democrats must offer a bold domestic and foreign policy vision that replaces Schumer’s cautious centrism with bolder progressive leadership from a senator such as Maryland’s Senator Chris Van Hollen, who says he has begun reaching out to fellow senators as part of a potential leadership challenge.
—John Nichols
THE NATION: You’ve known Chuck Schumer for a very long time. Obviously, you don’t have a lot of personal antipathy toward him. What made you decide to announce that you would not vote to make him majority leader?
SANDERS: Chuck and I grew up, literally, in the same [Brooklyn] neighborhood. I am older than Chuck, but we went to the same elementary school, the same high school. We were on the Banking Committee together when I was first elected to Congress. So I have known Chuck for a long time, and I like Chuck, personally. He’s a very nice guy.
But, I think, in this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is. On issue after issue, I think he is just not in tune with where his constituents are at.
THE NATION: What issues stand out in that regard?
SANDERS: You can start off with US military aid to Israel. I think that’s a very emotional issue for people in the Democratic caucus. Many of us, including myself, think that [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has committed genocide on the Palestinian people in Gaza, that Netanyahu is a war criminal, and that the United States should not provide another nickel of military aid to Israel, period.
And I think that basically on other issues Chuck is a guy who wants to tinker around the edges. Is Chuck prepared to fight for what the American people want, which is dealing with massive levels of income and wealth inequality by imposing a billionaire tax — a tax on a billionaire’s wealth so that we can adequately fund childcare, make public colleges and universities tuition-free, and build the millions of units of affordable housing that we need? Is that where Chuck is coming from? I don’t think so.
On AI, Chuck was the minority leader and did nothing significant to address what is the most transformational technology in the history of the world being pushed by a handful of multibillionaires. The American people are deeply concerned [about data centers and the rapid development of artificial intelligence]. The elections show that. Chuck was not there.
Those are just some of the issues that, I think, Chuck has not been leading on.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
THE NATION: The polls show that the Democratic Party is not all that popular. Donald Trump is very unpopular, but the Democratic Party is not all that highly rated.
SANDERS: The Democratic Party, in some polling, is less popular than Trump, correct?
THE NATION: That’s been the case. So, is it your view that it is important for the Democratic Party to show that it actually recognizes that there was a vote for change?
SANDERS: Absolutely, John, and I think for two reasons.
Number one, so many of our people are hurting. Sixty percent of our people live paycheck to paycheck. You have millions of elderly people who don’t know how they’re going to retire with dignity. We have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country.
And, number two, I’ll tell you this: Trumpism is not just an American phenomenon. All over Europe, they are seeing the growth of right-wing parties, and the collapse of center-left parties. And I think working people throughout Europe, throughout the United States, are looking at their governments and asking: Do you know that we exist? Do you understand the pain that we are experiencing?
To my mind, it’s not only a question of whether Democrats have to address the enormous economic pain that working families are now experiencing — and their concerns, as they look to the future, that AI may take their jobs, that their kids are likely to have a lower standard of living than they do. It’s not only that we have to deal with those economic issues to help address the pain and anxiety that people are feeling. It’s that if we do not address that pain and anxiety, I worry about the future of democracy. I think people will say: Trump failed us. We gave Democrats an opportunity. Now, they failed us. What we really need is a strong man who will get things right. That’s the history of fascism around the world.
So I think it’s not only the need to address economic pain. Government has finally got to address the issues that working families experience. And if we fail again, and more and more people give up on government, I worry about the future of democracy.
THE NATION: Do you have a candidate in the race for majority leader?
SANDERS: Chris Van Hollen has indicated he’s interested.
THE NATION: And you would support him?
SANDERS: Yes.
