https://hellgatenyc.com/eight-dead-in-br.author: Nick Pinto
https://hellgatenyc.com/eight-dead-in-br.text:
Six adults and two children were killed Wednesday afternoon when a three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a construction site next door. Eighteen other people were injured in the collapse or responding to it. One of them remains in critical condition, Mayor Zohran Mamdani reported at a press conference Thursday afternoon.
Many of the people impacted by the collapse are immigrants, the mayor said, including from Trinidad, Colombia and Mexico. One victim was a 26-year-old father from Ecuador, Today reported. José Luis Caguana Cosquillo leaves behind his pregnant wife and their first child.
"A tragedy of this magnitude demands a comprehensive and thorough investigation that includes both the construction site and the building which collapsed," Mamdani said. But at this time, City officials said, the cause of the collapse has not been determined. It could well have something to do with the demolition and excavation of the building site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue, work that was permitted and ongoing when 1321 Flatbush collapsed, taking with it one side of the neighboring building.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ekow Eshun outlines his curatorial vision for the next Site Santa Fe biennial
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Under the curator Ekow Eshun, the upcoming 13th edition of the Site Santa Fe International Biennial, There Are Other Worlds (11 June 2027-10 January 2028), will aim to reflect how artists open up new ways of understanding the world, potentially inspiring connection and kinship amid the complexity of our times. The exhibition’s citywide programming will span more than six venues, bringing together more than 40 artists from over 15 countries. The biennial is due to include new commissions by the US artists Cauleen Smith, Sanford Biggers and Edgar Arceneaux, the New Mexico-based Diné artist Raven Chacon and the Canadian artist Lotus Kang.
Founded in 1995, Site Santa Fe is one of the US’s key contemporary art events, showcasing international artists while building on New Mexico’s history and social fabric. Eshun—who chairs the Fourth Plinth in London’s Trafalgar Square and is the curator of the touring British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers (touring the UK until June 2028)—is drawing inspiration from the region.
“New Mexico has a layered history, including colonial settlements, but also in the 20th century it had artistic communities that found something here that allowed them to think with expansiveness,” Eshun tells The Art Newspaper. “It is the site of settlement, world-making and self-discovery.”
Beyond New Mexico, Eshun’s vision explores how artists challenge, interpret and shape reality. “We live in a time of divisiveness, uncertainty, inequality and environmental crisis,” he says. “I am inspired by how, in contrast, artists hold complexity and contradictions, inviting us to look beyond binary positions and consider other ways of seeing the world.” These might include imaginative, psychological, emotional and sensory worlds.
The sprawling exhibition is structured into three sections, the curator explains, conceived as “interlocking territories”. The first, “Worlds Beyond”, explores sensory and psychological perception, drawing on the legacy of the Transcendental Painting Group that was active in New Mexico in the 1930s and 40s. “I am interested in how artists look beyond the physical world and can be inspired to think metaphysically, psychologically and emotionally,” Eshun says. He cites the participating Danish Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson, who thinks with scientific precision while creating works that have both sensorial and emotional impacts.
The exhibition’s second section,“Worlds in Common”, draws on New Mexico’s history of utopian settlements to explore “how artworks may enable us to move beyond hierarchies of power or status and conjure connection or kinship, finding imaginative ways in which we can relate to each other”, Eshun says. He cites the work of Chacon as an example, which uncovers histories of displacement in the Americas, but also turns to connection and memory as routes to reimagining assertions of place.
The exhibition’s third section,“Worlds Alive”, will focus on interactions with nature, considering “the planet as a living territory where all the creatures may have a say in how we live collectively”, Eshun says. He is particularly interested in artists who imagine a relationship with the planet beyond extractivism and grounded in connection across organisms. The participating Colombian artist Delcy Morelos, for instance, reflects on the earth as a physical and ethical territory and a space for aesthetic adventure.
The line-up of participating artists, spanning generations and geographies, reflects the curator’s intention to create a locally rooted biennial with an international scope. “The biennial exists in conversation, not isolation,” Eshun says, adding that community programming will be key. Nearly half the artists are from the US, including Arthur Jafa and Nan Goldin, while five, such as the Indigenous artists Rose B. Simpson and Cannupa Hanska Luger, are based in New Mexico. The exhibition will also include a large contingent of international participants, such as Louise Giovanelli (UK), John Akomfrah (Ghana/UK), Sandra Vásquez de la Horra (Chile), Shilpa Gupta (India) and Tavares Strachan (Bahamas), among others.
While touching on pressing issues, Eshun hopes the biennial will also carry a sense of possibility, empathy and even optimism. Artists, he says, “offer no answers but may open new ways to see, imagine and engage with the present”.
- 13th Site Santa Fe International: There Are Other Worlds, 11 June 2027-10 January 2028, various venues, Santa Fe, New Mexico

New York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market. Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams expect to bring in at least $2.04bn collectively from their auctions in the Big Apple this month, with sales potentially exceeding $2.4bn, slightly above last year’s estimates for the period.
The confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for New York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026. Global auction sales were up 70% year on year at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips in the first six months of the year, thanks in part to the enduring appeal of single-owner collections and major estates.
That consignment strategy will be on full display at New York’s blockbuster auctions next week. Single-owner collections allow the houses to rebrand regular seasonal auctions as can’t-miss, once-in-a-lifetime events, and craft marketing campaigns around not just the works on sale but also the legacies of the collectors.
Sotheby’s boasts the highest collective estimate of the auction houses, projecting more than $1.1bn, which would be a house record for a marquee sale season. Around 40% of that total is attributed to the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, a fully guaranteed group of 12 Impressionist, Post-Impressionist and Fauvist paintings expected to sell for around $450m, making it the highest-value single-owner collection on offer this season across the city.
The collection was assembled by the Argentine sugar magnate Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his wife, María Elena “Nelly” Arrieta de Blaquier. Blaquier faced charges relating to the kidnapping of suspected left-wing activists during Argentina's 1976-83 military dictatorship. He denied the allegations and died in 2023 without standing trial. The 12 paintings have been consigned by the couple’s five children; the auction on 18 November will immediately be followed by Sotheby’s multiple-owner evening sale of Modern art.
“The market is very much moved by these collections,” says Allegra Bettini, Sotheby’s head of Modern evening auction. “Collectors today like to understand a narrative and see where works are coming from to understand the taste of how they all hung together.”
When the works in the Blaquier-Arrieta hoard were acquired, mostly in the 1960s and 70s in Europe, collectors could still purchase museum-quality works by Modern masters from commercial art galleries. That is no longer the case, Sotheby’s specialists say, even with a seven-figure budget. The Blaquier-Arrieta family rarely, if ever, loaned works for public display. Until Sotheby’s put them on view in its galleries at the Breuer Building on the Upper East Side, few of the 12 consigned works had been on public exhibit or offered on the market in decades.
The trove’s headline lot is Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (1890), one of the final works the artist painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in the months before his death. It carries a staggering estimate of around $180m and, because it has been guaranteed, is sure to exceed the current auction record for a Van Gogh of $117m (including fees), set by Orchard with Cypresses (1888) at the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York in 2022.
“It’s hard to not want to just touch and feel these brushstrokes because it is so alive,” Bettini says, gesturing to the leaves of the trees in the painting. “There's an intensity to it that really brings us into this landscape with the artist.”
Another possible recordbreaker is Arlequin (1888–90) by Paul Cezanne, which is estimated to sell in the region of $120m. The late harlequin painting is the only example from Cezanne’s series still in private hands, according to Sotheby’s. The current auction record for a Cezanne work, also set during the Paul Allen sales at Christie’s, is $137.79m.
Other standout works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection include paintings by Camille Pissarro, Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Sotheby’s will also offer works from the collections of oil tycoon Armand Hammer, Seattle property developer Richard Hedreen and his wife Elizabeth Hedreen, and cable television pioneer Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth Baum.
In Midtown at Christie’s, the leading lot of the season is Wassily Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken (1922-23), from the artist’s Bauhaus period. Once part of the Guggenheim collection, it was purchased by its current owners—reportedly the billionaire, art-dealing Nahmad family—at Sotheby’s in 1986. It is estimated to sell for between $60m and $80m during the 20th-century evening sale on 17 November.
With the same estimate and on offer during the same sale, Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915-16) was once part of the collection gathered by Serge Sabarsky, the late art dealer who co-founded the Neue Galerie in New York (the beloved Austrian restaurant on the museum’s ground floor is named for him). Leading the 21st century evening sale is an untitled 1983 work by Jean-Michel Basquiat that references a drawing on paper by Leonardo da Vinci and is estimated to sell for between $30m and $50m.
Christie’s is also offering a wide variety of works from the holdings of well-known collectors, among them the music executive Clive Davis, the billionaire businessman William Koch, and more works belonging to the late Museum of Modern Art trustee Agnes Gund that will benefit her foundation. Also on offer is a group of seven works including Old Master, Modernist and post-war artists understood to have been consigned by Jeff Koons. Altogether, the auction house expects to take in between $823m and $1.1bn during its November sales in New York.
Despite recent stock market volatility following the “blue tsunami” during the US midterm elections earlier this month and concerns over a Democrat-controlled Congress’s regulation of artificial intelligence and datacentre development—heightened by recent revelations about chipmaker Nvidia’s president Jensen Huang being embroiled in a spy scandal—stocks show early signs of stabilising. Christie’s specialists are similarly optimistic ahead of the November auctions.
While fluctuations in the stock markets can influence the art market over the longer term, the immediate impact on high-end auctions tends to be limited. Particularly for evening auctions, where lots are estimated to sell for seven-, eight- and nine-figure sums, potential buyers are often wealthy enough to be insulated from the day-to-day fluctuations of the stock market.
“The art’s quality is going to supersede any day in the market. People aren’t day-trading Picassos,” says Kat Widing, Christie’s senior vice president, senior specialist in post-war and contemporary art, and head of the 21st-century evening sale.
Collectors are “looking at these works over months, and they’re thinking through these major purchases”, she adds. “These would be additions to major collections that are quite significant. With those two things in mind, I’m still very optimistic.”
Phillips expects to bring in between $80.4m and 128.7m in New York this month, with its auctions led by Amedeo Modigliani’s limestone sculpture Tête (1911-12), estimated to sell for between $28m and $35m after having been in the same private collection for more than 50 years.
Bonhams estimates it will sell at least $40m worth of art in November in New York, with most of that total coming from a collection of five fresh-to-market Constantin Brâncuși bronzes that were held in the same private collection for decades after being acquired from the artist’s estate. Collectively, they are expected to fetch $25m.

https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.title: Mayor’s Office Backs Two New Hell’s Kitchen Tenant Unions, As Residents Push for Repairs
https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.text:
Share This Article
Tenants organizing across 31 Manhattan buildings in foreclosure are the latest to see support from Mamdani’s newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants.
Since January, the newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants has made it its business to support tenant unions across the city.
Now, city-employed tenant leaders are working with two new tenant unions in Hell’s Kitchen, where residents are asking for help in securing repairs and stewarding their troubled rent stabilized properties through a potential future sale.
The majority of tenants in the impacted buildings have come out in support of the union effort—a milestone, organizers say, that helps them get the attention of both their landlords and the city—and could represent another chance for the Mamdani administration to steer distressed affordable housing into the hands of tenants’ preferred buyer.
One of the unions represents tenants in 31 buildings owned by Arthur Haruvi and Peter Hungerford, which launched on Saturday, where tenants stood with city leaders outside 408 W. 56th St., where they say cooking gas has been out for 722 days. The residents are demanding repairs and a seat at the table when it comes to the future of their dilapidated buildings, now in foreclosure and bankruptcy.
“The two years without cooking gas has had a big toll. My family, and especially myself, like to cook during the holidays. We can’t cook Thanksgiving and Christmas meals on a hot plate,” said Luis Pelaez, who has lived in the building for 34 years.
There are 357 open housing code violations across the 478 units facing foreclosure, according to analysis by Housing Conservation Coordinators.
Tenants say that Peter Hungerford has responded to their request to meet, and they hope to go to the bargaining table in the coming weeks. Hungerford did not respond to City Limits’ requests for comment.
On Saturday, tenants of landlord David Ohebshalom will launch their own tenant union for nine buildings (including both rent stabilized and market rate units) on West 47th Street, alongside the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants head Cea Weaver.
Ohebshalom’s brother Daniel has made headlines before: he did jail time in 2024 for failing to comply with court orders to repair hazardous conditions at two buildings in Washington Heights.
Can tenants influence a sale?
Third time’s the charm?
Since January, the newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants has tried to influence the sale of two major portfolios of rent stabilized housing in New York. But each time, efforts to steer the buildings to preferred buyers have stumbled.
Early this year, officials intervened too late to stop the bankruptcy sale of 5,000 units from prior owner Pinnacle to private landlord Summit. And in July, housing officials backed the bid of preservation group Spatial Equity to buy 850 units in East Harlem, only to see their offers turned down and the portfolio go up for foreclosure auction this week.
Tenants in the Haruvi-Hungerford buildings say that their immediate concerns are securing repairs and maintenance, including restoring cooking gas and addressing pests. Some of the buildings are also included in a class action suit by Housing Rights Initiative against Peter Hungerford’s PH Realty Capital, which accuses the company of overcharging tenants in 18 buildings by $15 million.
But residents know they face a precarious position with their buildings in foreclosure. “If our buildings go up for sale we need a say in who buys them and the terms of that purchase,” said Joseph Di Salle, a resident at 450 57th St.
Tenants and their allies in city government have limited control over what ends up happening to their buildings in such scenarios. But some have credited the work of unions with pushing new landlords into concessions, like when Summit real estate forgave back rent for former Pinnacle tenants shortly after taking over.
The mayor’s housing plan includes some measures that can help tenants assert more control over their buildings when they go up for sale. Tuesday, he signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law, a measure that would give some city-approved buyers first dibs on distressed rental properties before they hit the wider market.
Those attempts to influence ownership, and the city’s overt support for tenant unions, has rubbed some property owners the wrong way, saying it “vilifies” them. And at least one developer that the administration championed recently, in the sale of three debt-riddled rent stabilized Crown Heights buildings, has a less than stellar maintenance record of its own, The City Reporter reported Tuesday.
But others see a clear role for City Hall to play.
With the Hell’s Kitchen buildings, Charlie Dulik of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants said that the city could coordinate code enforcement, come to the bargaining table with tenants, or liaise with the landlord for the Haruvi-Hungerford tenant union.
The tenants have not, as of yet, asked for support in steering their homes to a preferred buyer. If they asked, “we would absolutely talk about it and see what we can do,” said Dulik.
To get traction, get the majority of tenants on board
The Hungerford-Haruvi buildings fit the profile for the kind of properties most likely to get City Hall’s attention. The portfolio is vast, mostly rent stabilized, and connected to a former member of the city’s worst landlord list. It also has a tenants union.
And its members on Saturday, wearing freshly pressed royal blue T-shirts, said that a majority of tenants across 10 Hell’s Kitchen buildings in the Haruvi-Hungerford portfolio had signed on with the union.
Ten blocks south, the West 47th St. Tenants Union also declared that it has the majority support of tenants in nine buildings between 8th and 9th avenues, and are calling on their landlord Ohebshalom and his management company to address rat, mouse, and pest infestations, as well as ongoing maintenance needs.
The 50 percent threshold—getting at least half of a building or buildings’ tenants on board with the union—is key, tenant leaders said, indicating that they will have significant bargaining power.
“Supporting tenant unions and majority tenant unions is incredibly important,” said Dulik, wearing a freshly screenprinted Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants jacket.
Getting to a majority of tenants has become standard practice in the field, advocates say, in part to a growing national tenant movement. The Mamdani administration has been exploring ways to give tenant unions official legal status and recognition and allow them to sue, similar to how the National Labor Relations Board recognizes labor unions.
“There’s going to be more of an emphasis on majority unions for sure, but there’s also going to be an emphasis on portfolio-wide organizing because that’s when you can make the most changes,” said K Agbebiyi, director of communications at Housing Justice for All.
Hell’s Kitchen is one of the city’s most expensive neighborhoods, with smaller walk up buildings nestled between luxury towers.
“Neighborhood tenant unions and community-based organizations are anchors for neighborhood stability,” said Alejandro Coriat, director of borough organizing for Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal. “It is what kept Hell’s Kitchen, some parts of Chelsea, and some parts of the Upper West Side affordable for working class people for a very long time.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Philadelphia city council investigates sudden closure of oldest natural history research institution in the Americas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Adam Schrader
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs. The university’s president will now testify under subpoena before Philadelphia’s city council on 16 November, answering questions about the sudden closure and what will happen to the museum’s valuable collection of more than 19 million specimens.
While many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, says Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there. She says that people have been asking: “Is this safe?” “Can I see it?” “Can I book an appointment?”
Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five. The invertebrate palaeontology collection manager recently left for a job at the American Museum of Natural History. “There is no plan to replace her," Betancourt tells The Art Newspaper. Endowed curator posts in entomology and palaeontology have gone unfilled for years, she adds.
Founded in 1812, the Academy describes itself as the oldest natural history research institution in the Americas. It opened its museum to the public in 1828 and, in 1868, put Hadrosaurus foulkii on view as the world’s first mounted dinosaur skeleton. Its millions of specimens include plants collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, John James Audubon’s birds and Thomas Jefferson’s fossils.
The Academy became a Drexel affiliate in 2011, while retaining its status as a separate non-profit with its own board. Drexel recently told the city council it had “stepped in as a partner” that year, when the Academy “faced severe financial distress”.
The city council passed a resolution on 17 September to investigate the Academy’s closing. The resolution calls institutions like the Academy “part of the cultural fabric of the city” and says its shuttering would especially affect area residents “for whom the museum is a fixture of the neighbourhood”. An initial hearing took place on 26 October, which Drexel’s president did not attend.
At the hearing, representatives for Drexel cited the building's "substantial capital needs" and told the city council that public exhibitions need a new model, "almost certainly in a different location".
Sarah McAnulty, a squid biologist and Save the Academy organiser, says city council members asked Drexel representatives to check their numbers. "If all you need to keep the public museum open is a million dollars, what the hell are we doing here?" she says, describing the city council’s reaction.
Staff learned of the Academy’s closure at a morning meeting on 1 September, Redfield says. Most staff were laid off by 1 November, and many people "found out they were let go in a report by The Philadelphia Inquirer", she adds.
Redfield says the museum drew more than 60,000 visitors in its final 12 days of public hours. "That's not enough time to shut down a lifetime of scientific and educational work," she adds. "I planned to retire at the Academy and don't have any backup plans." Now she is volunteering.
"Unfortunately, volunteer labour is essential to most natural history collections, but it’s not sustainable,” Betancourt says. “The fact that the volunteer manager was initially slated for termination and had to be reinstated shows Drexel has no idea how these collections function."
Betancourt adds that the Academy's social media accounts have been inactive for two months and staff do not have access because Drexel controls them. The Academy's director of marketing and communications was let go with the closure. Betancourt says the university may not realise that communications and education staff connect the collections with the public and potential benefactors, "otherwise, the collections work in darkness”.
The William Penn Foundation has offered a year of funding to replace Drexel's subsidy for the museum. "The foundation has not received a response to our offer," a spokesperson told the Inquirer. Drexel later stated that it had not received a "formal proposal with a defined level of financial support".
Betancourt says Save the Academy wants Drexel to explain "why no capital campaign was undertaken" and "why the scientific community has been shut out of behind-the-scenes negotiations. The closed-door negotiations got us a closed museum. Natural history collections tied to a financially haemorrhaging university are not safe natural history collections.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Artist captures the saga of Luigi Mangione in tweets
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Hannah Sage Kay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
On the morning of 4 December 2024, the Los Angeles-based artist Stanya Kahn opened X (formerly Twitter) to get her daily news digest, when she, like many Americans, was inundated with a mass chorus of tweets—ranging from celebratory snark to unbridled vitriol—about the assassination of United HealthCare’s chief executive Brian Thompson.
“The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions. “At first I was bookmarking them, and then [screenshotting] them, and fairly quickly my thought was to gather these up because the algorithm might start shutting them down.”
Fairly quickly, the Trump administration announced that any celebration of the killing could be criminalised. But with an ever-growing archive and a long-held practice as a time-based media artist, Kahn decided to create a film that chronologically presented the public’s rapidly unfolding response to this now-infamous event.
Titled Deny Defend Depose (2026)—a play on the words scrawled on three shell casings from bullets fired in the shooting, and the strategy invoked by major healthcare providers to reduce payouts and increase profits—Kahn’s film is now screening across the country at artist-run-spaces, cinemas and galleries. The New York non-profit space Participant Inc will screen it on 13 November, with more showings to come.
Originally, Kahn planned to release the film in the lead-up to 9 September, when the state trial of Luigi Mangione was due to take place in New York. Now that Mangione’s 14 August guilty plea—an attempt to avoid double jeopardy—has postponed the state hearing until 10 December, with a federal hearing to follow on 18 December, Kahn plans to continue updating the film with more responses from the public as the saga continues unfolds.
When it all began, she had considered turning the project into a coffee-table book, which would afford a funny inversion of X’s quippy, short-form format. But switching to a film, her primary medium, afforded an opportunity for in-person film screenings, which enabled the originally solitary experience of watching the commentary unfold online to be transformed into a collective viewing experience.
Set to a dramatic soundtrack of acid and jungle, the 30-minute film takes viewers on an emotional rollercoaster. Watching the tweets unfold in sequence together, the audience collectively holds its breadth as anticipation builds to the moment the suspect is revealed as Mangione, laughs as tweets comment on his attractiveness or the Monopoly money found in his backpack, and sighs at the devastating state of healthcare in the United States when statistics regarding industry salaries and investment patterns, or personal anecdotes about life-threatening denials, are shared.
Just like Kahn was glued to X that morning in late 2024, viewers of her film are often transfixed as they relive their reactions to the still-unfolding story at top speed.“The poignancy of such a broad spectrum of the American public responding in kind to what was basically a public political assassination felt like a rupture, especially in party-based politics,” Kahn says. “It cut across the entire political spectrum and the common ground that suddenly emerged in this flashpoint seemed like a new beacon for potential mass movement, because it was a unity that emerged spontaneously and instantaneously, it wasn’t something that got hammered out in time.”
The outpouring of affection for Mangione has been staggering, Kahn says. “Without blinking,” she adds, “people were in full-throat applause of [an alleged] murderer.”
Attention from the media and public has remained steady since the early days of the manhunt, Mangione’s arrest and the trial, with comparisons to Robin Hood, lookalike contests and wanted posters for other healthcare company executives. While the extent of the public’s celebration of Thompson’s killing took many by surprise, Kahn sees this reaction as evidence of just “how deep the pain and anger and frustration is in this country about the evilness of the healthcare system and its inaccessibility”. (Per capita spending on healthcare in the US is double the average of other wealthy countries, and has been increasing faster than inflation for decades.)
Thompson’s killing and its aftermath are hardly a black-and-white tale of righteous moral vengeance. Though some originally attempted to paint Mangione as disaffected and radicalised, his Ivy League education and privileged upbringing told a different story. And the responses to the event “weren’t just coming from more radical spaces”, Kahn says. While capturing their reactions in real time and reviewing the posters’ profiles, she found, “it was literally just ‘every man’—people with five followers and five million. It was regular people because they were pissed.”
- Stanya Kahn’s Deny, Defend, Depose screens on 13 November at Participant Inc, New York and on 12 December at Slash Art, San Francisco

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/carchedi-mar.title: Guglielmo Carchedi Was a Pathbreaking Marxist Economist
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/carchedi-mar.author: Joseph Choonara
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/carchedi-mar.text:
Guglielmo Carchedi Was a Pathbreaking Marxist Economist
Guglielmo Carchedi, who died in October at 85, was one of the great Marxist thinkers of our time. His early work on the new middle class and his later work on value theory and crises still offer the Left powerful tools.
In October, the radical left lost Guglielmo Carchedi — “Mino” to his friends and comrades — who died in his sleep at the age of eighty-five. He was one of the great Marxist thinkers of our times.
I first met him in London a few years after the economic meltdown of 2007–9, at a conference I organized for the journal International Socialism to explore the dynamics of that crisis. He spoke patiently and calmly, setting out his views with authority and an unwavering confidence in the power of Marxist theory. I heard him many more times over the next few years, always speaking with the same measured style. On occasion, he ended his presentations with a shy smile and the Latin “QED,” quod erat demonstrandum: “that which was to be demonstrated.”
It was always a delight when our paths crossed. Often I would encounter him in conjunction with Michael Roberts, with whom Carchedi would form a close personal and intellectual relationship.
The partnership was a fitting one. Roberts, himself a fine political economist, complemented Carchedi’s theoretical subtlety with a keen eye for a potential audience and a flair for showmanship, qualities long evident on Roberts’s indispensable blog. In turn, for Roberts, Carchedi was a mentor in the realm of dialectics and Marxist value theory. Together they produced a stream of articles; an edited collection, World in Crisis: A Global Analysis of Marx’s Law of Profitability; and a coauthored book, Capitalism in the Twenty-first Century Through the Prism of Value.
Carchedi was a kind and modest man, generous with his time when younger Marxists sought advice from him. He was refreshingly uninterested in whether those he spoke to worked in the academy or were simply left militants with a thirst for theory, as I was when we first met. He saw his work not merely as addressing a series of intellectual puzzles but as a contribution to the struggles of the working class.
It is a great boon that new generations can continue to benefit from his wisdom through his writings. Here I will focus on some of his early contributions, which deserve broader appreciation.
Middle-Class Problems
The writing partnership with Roberts has helped win Carchedi a new readership. However, few among the younger generation of Marxists are aware of his early contributions to class theory, especially on the nature of the middle class.
One of his first articles, “On the economic identification of the middle class,” appeared in 1975 in the journal Economy and Society. A second piece, “Reproduction of social classes at the level of production relations,” appeared in the same publication a couple of issues later. They would form two chapters of a book, On the Economic Identification of Social Classes.
After much searching, I managed to get hold of a battered secondhand copy that North Staffordshire Polytechnic had marked “discarded from stock.” As with many niche academic texts of the period, the printers made the plates from the output of an electric typewriter. Only in 2024 did the publisher, Routledge, again make a facsimile of the text available.
Carchedi’s contribution to class theory appeared in the shadow of better-known works by two authors grappling with similar problems. The first was the Greek-French Marxist Nicos Poulantzas, whose Classes in Contemporary Capitalism appeared in English in 1975. The second was Erik Olin Wright, whose first major foray into class theory, Class, Crisis and the State, appeared in 1978. Carchedi’s account, I would argue, offered a more convincing resolution than either of its major rivals.
The new middle class has been a thorny problem for Marxist theory. Karl Marx saw capitalists and workers as the major contending classes within capitalism. He saw the former as the rulers of such societies and the latter as their potential adversaries, capable of overthrowing the rule of capital and beginning the process of forging a communist society.
There was, Marx acknowledged, a substantial petty bourgeoisie, consisting of smallholders of capital, such as shopkeepers or artisans, along with their rural counterpart, the peasantry. Yet as capitalism came to predominate, it would, as Marx put it, “cut up” members of these groups “into two persons,” forcing them to adapt to the new society by operating as both capitalist and worker.
There was no reason to imagine the petty bourgeoisie would vanish, but over long periods of time, the two key classes of capitalist society could begin to absorb such groups. This happens, for instance, when a peasant becomes successful enough to start hiring and exploiting wage labor. Conversely, it happens when a peasant can no longer reproduce themselves without turning to wage labor and subjecting themselves to exploitation at the hands of a capitalist.
But where did this leave the new intermediate layers that modern capitalism created, such as the managers and supervisors that large enterprises required, or technicians and engineers? They worked for a wage, just like workers, but their role set them apart from the mass of wage labor. For some, this called into question the whole Marxist approach to class — or at least blurred beyond recognition the lines demarcating the classes of capitalism.
Poulantzas had sought to resolve this issue by presenting a very restrictive conception of the working class, focused on “productive” workers (those who generate profit for capital) involved in creating material commodities. He assigned anyone who did not meet these criteria — service sector workers, those working in the sphere of circulation, and so on — to a “new petty bourgeoisie” on the grounds of their economic position. To this, he added “political” criteria, allowing him also to thrust managers into this new class, and “ideological” criteria, allowing him to add mental laborers.
As Wright complained, Poulantzas’s approach would make about 70 percent of the US labor force of the time petty bourgeois, many of them on the grounds of ideology and politics. To regard, say, teachers or nurses as petty bourgeois seems particularly out of tune with today’s reality: such groups are clearly subject to the degrading power of capital and are often at the forefront of workplace struggle.
Wright’s own alternative was to deal with these ambiguities through a notion of “objectively contradictory class locations,” avoiding forcing groups such as managers into either the class of capitalists or workers. However, Wright’s approach introduced a complication. He sought to apply his approach both to groups caught between capitalists and workers in the workplace, such as managers, and to other groups — semiautonomous wage-earners and small employers — he identified as lying between the traditional petty bourgeoisie and either workers or capitalists.
This unnecessarily complicates the position of the petty bourgeoisie, whose very nature allows them to shade into the two major classes. The new middle class is a distinctive type of formation, requiring a different approach.
Wright himself would come to reject elements of his earlier contribution. In his later work, he suggested that he had previously overemphasized criteria such as autonomy in identifying class locations at the expense of exploitation.
However, from the mid-1980s, Wright increasingly drew on analytical Marxist thinkers such as John Roemer rather than on Marx’s own approach to exploitation. Roemer was skeptical of the value theory Marx developed in Capital, recasting exploitation as a matter of the different assets that individuals possess. As well as capitalist property, such assets could, in Wright’s new class model, be “organizational assets” or “skills.” The result was a fragmentation of the class structure, leading to myriad different class locations.
Carchedi’s Alternative
Carchedi offered a way out of this morass, drawing on Marx’s Capital. Groups such as managers in modern enterprises must perform two contradictory functions within capitalist production. These are not simply different technical functions; they are social functions, reflecting the imperatives of rival classes.
On the one hand, managers perform some functions of the “collective worker,” including coordinating the labor process, something necessary in any large, complex workplace, in any type of society. On the other hand, they also perform “global functions of capital,” roles of control and surveillance necessary because the workplace sits within a class-divided society. As Carchedi wrote, they are a special group of waged employees forming a “hierarchically organized ensemble, “who collectively perform what used to be the function of an individual capitalist” alongside activities appropriate to the collective worker.
These contradictory functions combine differently in different concrete jobs, influencing whether sections of the new middle class side with workers in struggle or align with their capitalist employers. The configuration of these functions is not static; it shifts with technological change, management culls, and restructurings.
For those Marxists who paid attention, notably Bob Carter, Carchedi’s theory would form the basis for later work, both theoretical accounts of the new middle class and empirical studies of workplaces. It provided a missing link between the labor process analysis that Harry Braverman pioneered in the early 1970s and a sophisticated Marxist class theory.
From Class to Value
Carchedi’s early work on class may superficially seem disconnected from his later work on political economy. However, there are clear links. These become apparent in an exchange with Wright in 1989, which appeared in the collection The Debate on Classes.
Here Carchedi criticized two elements of Wright’s methodology. The first was Wright’s embrace of analytical Marxism’s claim that there is no distinctive Marxist method, that the methods of mainstream social science will suffice. In place of this, Carchedi emphasized a dialectical approach.
This meant acknowledging the crucial roles of social structures, which develop independent of the will of particular individuals. However, these structures are not static but subject to dynamism and change.
This concern with method would persist. It is no coincidence that his 2011 book, Behind the Crisis, opens with a heading: “The need for dialectics.” Almost all of Carchedi’s major writings contain a discussion of method, emphasizing Marx’s dialectical standpoint.
Second, Carchedi reasserted the centrality of Marx’s value theory. Here he would offer another pioneering contribution, as one of the progenitors, along with Alan Freeman and Andrew Kliman, of what its proponents came to call the Temporal Single System Interpretation of Marx.
When analytical Marxists such as Roemer and Wright claimed Marx’s value theory was flawed, they were scrutinizing a modified version of the theory.
For Carchedi, their approach drew heavily on an approach pioneered by figures such as Piero Sraffa, which revived elements of the approach of to the labor theory of value of Marx’s predecessor, David Ricardo.
This “neo-Ricardianism” treated production not as a social and historical process but as a primarily technical one, in which a set of commodities gives rise to another set of commodities. The exploitation of labor ceases to play any distinctive role in creating new value. Neo-Ricardians, conceiving of the economy in this way, could model it through a set of simultaneous equations.
As Carchedi pointed out, one of the key weaknesses in this approach was its neglect of the concept of time. Neo-Ricardians unrealistically assumed that the prices of the outputs of a given cycle of production were the same as the prices of the equivalent inputs into that cycle. Carchedi insisted on reintroducing time, following Marx in resisting seeing capitalism as a system in static equilibrium.
One advantage to this approach was that it helped Carchedi to resolve what Marxists call the “transformation problem.” Marx’s Capital proposes that the value of commodities reflects the labor time that their production typically requires. This includes both the “living labor” of the workers producing them and the “dead labor,” the labor that workers expended in the past to create the material means of production that the process uses up.
This had implications for the rate of profit, the ratio between profit and investment. For Marx, living labor had the distinctive role of creating new value. Because labor can do so in excess of the cost of its reproduction (the wage), this gives rise to profits.
But because the ratio of living and dead labor varies between branches of the economy, Marx’s approach implied a different rate of profit in each. Yet even in Marx’s day, economists observed that profit rates tend to converge over time. Marx reconciled theory with reality through his transformation of values into “prices of production.”
Capital migrates toward branches of the economy where profit rates are high, disrupting the price level as social demand and supply shift. Were this process to reach its conclusion, it would redistribute value between capitalists such that each receives the same average rate of profit on their investment. In fact, as Carchedi showed, this was only a tendency, and new disruptions upset any potential equilibrium long before the system could reach it.
Many critics, starting with Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1896, followed by Ladislau von Bortkiewicz, Paul Sweezy, and Ian Steedman, have faulted Marx for considering only how this transformation of values into prices of production affects the outputs of production, without also transforming the value of inputs. For those working with an atemporal, equilibrium model, such as the neo-Ricardians, making this further transformation allowed them to detach the system of prices of production from value theory altogether.
Carchedi argued that no such detachment was necessary. When capitalists obtain inputs for a new cycle of production, the value they advance is simply the price of production with which they left the previous cycle. This was what Carchedi termed their “social value.” Prices of production are, he proposed, not merely “determined by values but rather are their concrete form of existence.”
Falling Profit Rates
The hallmark of great Marxist political economy is to synthesize the often rather abstract discussions of value theory with an empirical understanding of a dynamic, changing, and crisis-prone system. This was very much on display in what I consider Carchedi’s finest work, Frontiers of Political Economy. Here Carchedi clarified and extended Marx’s approach in Capital while seeking to apply it to contemporary capitalism.
The result is dazzling. Carchedi’s book deals with the intricacies of price formation in the context of uneven and complex processes of intercapitalist competition, first on the national terrain and then on a global scale, where, for instance, wage levels differ sharply. Besides the transformation problem discussed above, he investigated a range of controversies, such as precisely which forms of labor do and don’t produce value and how to account for different skill levels among workers.
At the center of the book, a chapter on “Growth, crises, inflation and crashes” develops themes that would become prominent in his work. Here he focused on Marx’s “tendency of the rate of profit to fall” (TRPF).
Capitalists must advance an ever-greater mass of capital, in the form of dead labor, to grab their share of the pool of profit that the system generates. But because only living labor generates new value, the scale of the employed workforce and the extent of its exploitation ultimately limit the size of this pool. The more dynamic capitalism is in mobilizing a greater amount of dead labor through automation and the expansion of capital, the more this tends to choke off future profits relative to investment, helping pave the way for crises.
The TRPF has been a source of considerable controversy among Marxists. For some, it is an unnecessary distraction from value theory. For others, it is so hedged with counteracting tendencies that no one can grasp an overall pattern. For others still, the empirical evidence has falsified it.
Carchedi argued that the TRPF should remain at the center of crisis theory. It was, he maintained, the ultimate expression of the contradictions of capitalism. This was because, as Marx had proposed, the very processes that impel capitalism forward — exploitation, competition, accumulation — can, through the TRPF, begin to undermine future accumulation.
In his account, Carchedi acknowledged various counteracting tendencies, such as the intensification of exploitation from the 1980s, but argued that, in the long run, the TRPF overpowered these. It might also appear that financial expansion had injected new dynamism into capitalism. Yet for Carchedi, this reflected how the TRPF in productive sectors encouraged capital to shift into the sphere of finance, feeding speculative bubbles and ultimately financial crises. The meltdown of 2007–9 was not, in this account, a purely financial phenomenon but one ultimately rooted in the productive economy, the realm of workers’ exploitation and the site where their potential power concentrates.
Carchedi’s Legacy
I have only touched on a few elements of Carchedi’s contribution. His career saw him explore many other themes, ranging from the class nature of European integration to the relationship between value theory and artificial intelligence. It is far better that the interested reader consults such works for themselves to understand their richness and diversity. Doing so will also make clear the passion that motivated him.
On that, let the final word go to Carchedi himself, from his acceptance speech on receiving the World Marxian Economics Award in 2021. Contrasting the 1960s and ’70s, a time of great hope for those on the radical left, with the present period, he said:
An economic and financial crisis of major proportions is again knocking at the door; the destruction of our natural habitat proceeds unchecked; the divide between the poor of the world and the absurdly rich has never been so great; the dark clouds of a new world war are gathering on the horizon; right-wing ideologies resurrect and even fascism is raising its ugly face again. These are the dangers the new generations will have to face. The difficulties ahead for them will be immense. But the contradictory nature of the system is such that each time capitalism wins, the anti-capitalist forces regroup and counterattack with new forms of resistance. My hope is that my work will be of some help in their struggle.

https://citylimits.org/local-leaders-dem.title: Local Leaders Demand Accountability in Deadly Building Collapse, And What Else Happened This Week in NYC Housing
https://citylimits.org/local-leaders-dem.author: Jeanmarie Evelly

Share This Article
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday that the city has identified six “entities” involved in the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., and that inspectors are checking roughly 160 other work sites across the city where those companies are also involved.
City officials are promising a full investigation into the cause of the deadly building collapse in Flatbush, Brooklyn, which killed eight people and injured 18 others earlier this week.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday that the city has identified six “entities” involved in the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., where officials say crews were doing excavation work Wednesday afternoon when the three-story apartment building next door, at 1321 Flatbush Ave., collapsed.
The Department of Buildings (DOB) is now inspecting roughly 160 other construction sites across the city where those six entities are also doing work, according to the mayor—part of a “comprehensive and thorough investigation” into both properties.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said in a briefing Thursday.
A City Limits review of public properties records found two previous building violations issued to the Bedford Avenue construction site: one in March for crews doing demolition work without required “overhead protection,” and another in April for continuing construction while a stop work order was in place. The contractor named in those violations, N Tech Design of America, did not immediately return a request for comment.
The site is owned by two limited liability companies, FF1632 LLC and JS1024 LLC, which bought the property for nearly $4 million in 2024. The owner and developer of the site, Robert Fischman, did not respond to voicemails left at his place of business Friday.
Fischman had city approval to demolish a one-story building on the site and construct a new three-story building, according to DOB records. He had also submitted plans to build a nine-story building, which were not yet approved.
“If there’s any changes to either the excavation that’s done, the foundation that would be in place for a larger building, those adjustments would have to be made as part of the longer-term approval,” said DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tighani at a press conference Friday.
The adjacent three-story apartment building that collapsed into the construction site, 1321 Flatbush Ave., had 98 open violations on record with the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development, including for things like unsafe electrical wiring and a leaking ceiling.
Attempts to reach the owner—listed on city records as Isolag Realty Corporation, which is registered with the state under the name Olufemi Falade—were unsuccessful.
Local leaders, including Flatbush City Councilmember Farah Louis and civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton, planned a vigil near the scene of the tragedy Friday to demand accountability for the disaster.
The eight fatalities included two children, officials said.
“This could have been any one of us,” Sharpton told reporters, according to a video of the event shared online. “This should not go for two or three days of mourning, and then we go about our business. We don’t know when the next house will collapse.”
Here’s what else happened this week in housing—
ICYMI, from City Limits:
- The number of homeless students attending the city’s public schools declined by 10 percent during the 2025-2026 school year compared to the year before, but remains stubbornly high, with more than 138,000 kids who went without stable housing.
- The city is earmarking an extra $25 million to hire 300 additional outreach workers and open more low-barrier shelter beds this winter, after a brutal freeze killed 18 New Yorkers last year.
- Tenants organizing across 31 Manhattan buildings in foreclosure are the latest to see support from Mamdani’s newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants.
ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:
- A Columbian father and his 9-year-old daughter were among those killed in the Flatbush building collapse, according to Gothamist, which spoke to relatives about how the family had been fearful of federal immigration enforcement in recent months.
- The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office has opened an investigation into the collapse, the New York Times reports.
- Councilmember Farah Louis introduced a bill that would require the city to come up with a plan for addressing vacant rent-stabilized apartments, according to The Real Deal.
- Mayor Mamdani signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law, amNY reports.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/bernie-democ.title: Democrats Did Their Best Bernie Impression in the Midterms
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/bernie-democ.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/bernie-democ.text:
Democrats Did Their Best Bernie Impression in the Midterms
Put their 2026 midterms side by side with previous campaigns, and it’s clear: Democrats won in red states by sounding less like Democrats and more like Bernie Sanders.
The 2026 midterms saw historic gains for socialists and progressives. So, perhaps unsurprisingly, the Democratic Party’s corporate wing is hurriedly spinning the result as a victory for centrists and “moderates.”
Largely lost in this is the way that the Left has transformed what it actually means to run as a Democratic moderate or a centrist. Because looking at this year’s campaigns, there is no doubt that even the most uninspiring “moderate” candidates were taking several pages — whole chapters, really — from the books of Bernie Sanders, Zohran Mamdani, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
It’s worth recalling that before 2025, standard Democratic campaign rhetoric was all about “defending democracy,” railing against extremism and authoritarianism, and advocating for abortion rights — all good things on their merits, but (with the exception of abortion rights) largely abstract ones that are not as animating or as high a priority for the majority of voters as their basic pocketbook concerns.
Just look at former President Joe Biden’s big kick-off speech for his reelection campaign, which was almost completely devoid of an economic message but heavy on talk of “MAGA extremists” and the “soul of America.” In fact, the absence of an economic message was a constant left-wing criticism of the party through the Biden era, including from this very magazine.
This has now completely shifted. While Democratic candidates in 2024 ran by far most of their TV ads on abortion, with immigration coming a distant second, this year, the overwhelming focus of their ad spending was “affordability,” dropping $401 million on the topic — a full quarter of their $1.5 billion total spend.
And where did the “affordability” frame come from? Well, both Democratic and Republican members of Congress happened to start spamming that word in their emails to constituents right after socialist Zohran Mamdani won the New York City Democratic primary with a campaign that put affordability at its very center.
But it’s more than just coming up with a pithy new word describing voters’ struggles with the economy. A number of the moderate candidates who won in red states sounded oddly like Bernie Sanders, railing against billionaires and the ultrarich, the corrupting influence of money in politics, and swearing off corporate money.
The clearest example of this was Texas Senator-elect James Talarico, who said that the fundamental divide in US politics was “top versus bottom,” called billionaires “the only minority destroying America,” charged that “for fifty years, billionaire megadonors have been buying politicians” like his opponent who then “rig the rules of the economy,” and who said that “we already have class warfare in this country” in the form of “the billionaires waging war against the rest of us” — a line almost directly borrowed from Bernie Sanders. He was rewarded for it by winning by one of the biggest margins of the night and doing it in one of the reddest states in the country.
The corporate center has tried to square this by simply retconning Talarico as one of them, a moderate, as Matthew Yglesias dubbed him. They point to the fact that he moved away from some of his support for trans rights, embraced an “all-of-the-above” energy policy, and eschewed Medicare for All in favor a public option (though the idea that’s a “centrist” or “moderate” policy would be surprising to anyone with a memory longer than five or six years).
But even if Talarico wasn’t viewed by nearly half of all Texas voters as “very liberal” on the eve of the election (and as “somewhat liberal” by a further 27 percent), this is a pretty hard sell.
To see why, look at Colin Allred. Just two years ago, Allred, a former NFL player, civil rights lawyer, and congressman, launched his own Texas Senate run with a campaign widely characterized as a “centrist” one against Republican Ted Cruz.
What did that campaign involve? Allred cast the GOP as having become too extreme and told conservatives who believed in the rule of law and the Constitution that they should vote for him. He proudly touted his US Chamber of Commerce endorsement. He “was unable to successfully develop” an economic message against Cruz and made abortion and reproductive rights “central to” and the “banner of” his campaign instead. During their debate, he hammered Cruz for supporting an abortion ban and being soft on the January 6 rioters, calling him a “threat to democracy” and only offhandedly mentioning he cut taxes on the rich. Again, these are all important issues but were unconnected to voters’ economic struggles.
The result: Cruz won by 8 points, nearly quadrupling his winning margin from six years earlier.
Going Red in Red States
This was not something unique to Texas and Talarico’s “moderate” campaign there. It was the case in every red state that Democrats just won a Senate seat in.
Take a look at Annie Andrews’s campaign that made her the first Democrat elected to a South Carolina Senate seat in twenty-eight years. Andrews hammered her initial opponent, the late Lindsey Graham, for “sell[ing] out to big money” and for being “willing to take food off our kids’ plates” and gut Medicaid “just so he can deliver tax cuts to billionaires,” and called on him to refund donations from Jeffrey Epstein–linked billionaires. She swore off “corporate PAC money” and pledged to “rein in the influence of corporations and billionaires in our elections.”
When Graham died and was replaced by his sister, Darline, Andrews hammered her for the same thing. Andrews called her “handpicked and bought by big corporations,” attacked her for doing the bidding of a data center industry spending millions of dollars of dark money to get her elected, and pointed to the $27 million that “outside Super PACs” had spent to support her. She won by nearly 5 points.
This was a very different campaign than the one former corporate lobbyist Jaime Harrison ran against Lindsey Graham six years ago. Since Harrison was relying on corporate bundlers and billionaire donors to raise obscene amounts of money to outspend Graham, he couldn’t and didn’t launch any of these attacks — in fact, Graham turned it around on him, complaining that outside dark money was flooding in to support the Democrat. Harrison’s attacks on Graham were focused on the idea that voters couldn’t trust him, because he had gone back on his word in supporting Donald Trump’s 2020 Supreme Court pick. He lost by 10 points.
Or look at Josh Turek, who won Iowa by four points against GOP candidate Ashley Hinson. Turek constantly talked about how Washington was full of millionaires “looking out for billionaires” and that he was “not one of them,” nor did he take corporate PAC money or was “owned by billionaires” (even as he quietly did take money from some billionaires). Iowa’s Republican senators and, he implied, his opponent, were “just looking out for billionaires and large corporations.”
During a debate, in attack ads, and in a Des Moines Register op-ed, Turek took aim at Hinson’s personal wealth, complaining that she had “gotten richer in her time in Washington” while slashing social spending on working-class Iowans, slamming her for her stock ownership, and saying that “we have a corruption crisis that’s leading to an affordability crisis because we’re sending people like Ashley Hinson up to DC” to line their pockets.
Not even Sanders went this hard against his wealthy opponents.
Then look at Michael Franken’s campaign for an Iowa Senate seat four years earlier. Though Franken prominently swore off corporate PAC donations, there was no talk of billionaires or wealth inequality. Franken appealed to “that middle segment who want logical, pragmatic, smart, dedicated, national servants to work for them,” and ran on a message that “we need to put country over party” and “people over politics.” He jabbed at his opponent’s age and long tenure in office, framed himself as defending democracy and minority rights, particularly those of women, whose right to an abortion he frequently brought up. And he ended up losing by 12 points.
Over in Mississippi, where prosecutor Scott Colom eked out a shock win to become the state’s first black senator, he did it by similarly assailing his Republican opponent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s donations from “millionaires and billionaires” out of state and accusing her of throwing tens of thousands of Mississippians off their health insurance “to look out for people in California and New York,” specifically “billionaires and millionaires” there, by giving them a “billionaire tax break.” He ran on raising taxes on the rich and getting rid of corporate subsidies for billionaires, and hit his opponent for staying silent on data centers being pushed by “AI billionaires” while being backed by a pro-AI super PAC.
This did not happen two years earlier, when Ty Pinkins (who ran, to some controversy, as a third-party candidate this year) ran for the other Mississippi US Senate seat, once again eschewing any kind of bold economic message in favor of warning that “our very democracy is being threatened” by people attacking its “institutional safeguards,” in his announcement. Pinkins said his platform revolved around the vague motto of, “You talk, I listen, we do,” which he explained (in even vaguer terms) meant, “I can listen and hear what’s important to their communities,” and then “do what’s necessary to move these communities and our state forward.” That campaign lost by nearly 30 points.
A particularly instructive example is Sherrod Brown in Ohio, who lost reelection to his Senate seat by nearly 4 points in 2024, then won the other Senate seat this year by just under 5 points. Despite a long-standing and deserved reputation as a populist, Brown said very little about millionaires and billionaires two years ago, other than that they should “pay their fair share” into Social Security — even as they were spending massive amounts to defeat him, which they did.
In 2026, more or less the official motto of Brown’s campaign was “Workers Before Billionaires,” a phrase he put in press releases, merchandise, tweets, Substack posts, reels, TikToks, and video after video. Compare his demure response two years earlier to a question about Republicans backing personally wealthy candidates — “That’s who they are . . . I guess I’m not surprised by that” — to what he said about his 2026 GOP opponent, Jon Husted: “The disdain, the contempt they have for work and for workers tells you everything.”
This time Brown, who called for a tax hike on billionaires, went in on Husted’s connection to the ultrarich and what the campaign characterized as his “corruption”:
- “Clevelanders have seen time and time again how Husted bows down to billionaires and corporations while leaving hardworking Ohioans behind.” (August 29)
- “Jon Husted’s for sale and the billionaires and corporations pouring millions into this race know it.” (September 21)
- “Ohioans have watched Jon Husted put billionaires and corporations before working families time and time again.” (October 3)
- “From Elon Musk to Donald Trump, billionaires are spending hundreds of millions of dollars against me because they know they can buy Jon Husted’s votes.” (October 29)
For good measure, Brown ran at least three separate TV ads hitting Husted for taking more money from Les Wexner, the disgraced Epstein-connected Ohio billionaire, than anyone else in Congress.
It is hard to make the case that nothing has changed when the same candidate ran a completely different campaign just two years later.
Finally, take a look at North Carolina, home to the second largest US financial center after New York, and where former governor Roy Cooper beat the Republican candidate by nearly 20 points. “Time to elect a senator for everyday people, not billionaires,” Cooper said after winning the primary, a theme he came back to over and over again, whether saying that “we don’t have the billionaires they do,” that his opponent was “fighting for the billionaire friends he made while working as a Big Oil and utility company lobbyist in DC,” or hitting Trump’s bill “that gave tax cuts to billionaires” and had “driven healthcare premiums up.”
Again, Cooper has a well-established reputation as a moderate, but this kind of rhetoric simply bore no resemblance to the Senate campaign run by another moderate, former state Supreme Court Chief Justice Cheri Beasley in 2022. Beasley centered her campaign on abortion rights and health care generally, and talked about diversity and reforming the criminal justice system to fix the “disparities” that exist within it while touting her support from law enforcement. There was no talk of billionaires or dark money, since Beasley herself was backed by twenty-three billionaires and won her primary by being boosted by various out-of-state PACs. She lost by 3 points.
This is borne out by research by Eric Blanc. Going through candidate websites in 2024 and 2026, he found that while billionaires were referenced in only 19 percent of candidates’ websites two years ago, this year they featured in 78 percent. Meanwhile, research by the Center for Working Class Politics found that less than 20 percent of the candidates in 2024 attacked corporations, billionaires, or Wall Street for their role in the affordability crisis.
Admitting Defeat in Victory
The fact that these candidates used populist rhetoric doesn’t necessarily mean they are populists, or even progressive. A number of these candidates have taken money from the billionaires they decry, including Talarico, and did not necessarily run on very ambitious policies. Meanwhile, Cooper is a multimillionaire himself, and like several others, did not run on taxing the rich, for all the class-war-style rhetoric that was thrown around.
But it does mean that Democratic moderates have tacitly accepted what voices on the Left have been saying for years, which is that the Bernie Sanders pitch — of a corrupt, rigged system pitting billionaires and corporations against working Americans — has broad appeal that cuts across geographic, racial, and, yes, sometimes even partisan lines.
Whatever they may tell you now, centrists did not always feel this way. Third Way cofounder Matt Bennett, for instance, was one of the corporate centrists insisting that there was nothing remarkable about any of this, because Sanders was not “the first Democratic (adjacent) candidate to use populist rhetoric in the modern era.” This will be news to Third Way circa 2016, whose president celebrated Sanders’s loss in the Democratic primary that year, because if “liberal populism doesn’t win Democratic primaries,” then it can’t “be the path back for a party” in a general election, and showed that “voters are angry, but they don’t want to focus mainly on billionaires.”
Likewise, Matthew Yglesias today may mock clueless young people thinking “Bernie Sanders invented the idea of campaigning on economic fairness themes.” But back in 2016, he listed Sanders’s plans to “soak the rich to a much greater extent” as one of the supposedly risky, radical ideas that made “the vast majority of the party’s elected officials and interest group leaders” worry about him. Stances like that were “not popular,” Yglesias wrote, and made him unelectable, compared to Hillary Clinton’s “relatively modest, overwhelmingly popular tweaks to the tax code.”
Something interesting is happening here. For years, frustrated socialists and progressives have been arguing that opposition to billionaires, soaking the ultrarich, and getting money out of politics are the centrist positions: that Americans across all walks of life — white or black, college-educated or not, liberal or conservative, in blue, red, or purple states — were pretty united on this, regardless of their exact views on things like immigration, guns, or trans kids in sports. Whatever the pundits are saying, centrist candidates seem to have finally acknowledged that’s the case.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/possible-lov.title: Possible Love Is a Cinematic Masterpiece About Class
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/possible-lov.author: Kap Seol
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/possible-lov.text:
Possible Love Is a Cinematic Masterpiece About Class
Lee Chang-dong doesn’t have the same profile as fellow South Korean directors like Bong Joon-ho and Park Chan-wook, but his latest film should change that. Possible Love is a powerful study of class in the wake of a shattering real-life strike defeat.
Possible Love is yet another masterpiece that South Korean director Lee Chang-dong has brought to us, after an eight-year hiatus since his last film Burning (2018). Unlike his younger Korean peers, such as Bong Joon-ho (Parasite) or Park Chan-wook (Old Boy and No Other Choice), Lee, now seventy-two, has often found himself confined to the independent film scene outside South Korea, where he has usually enjoyed modest commercial success.
Deeply rooted in humanity and class relations, Lee’s films deserve a wider audience beyond the ranks of art house aficionados (including Barack Obama, who named Burning among his favorite movies of 2018). Lee’s 1999 film Peppermint Candy weaves the life of a young man into the breakneck pace of South Korean capitalism, showing how innocence loses ground to violence, avarice, and lust. Burning explores the ways in which capitalism preys on and consumes poor young men and women.
Netflix’s funding and global distribution of Possible Love will likely expand Lee’s global reach. However, it has also revealed the maestro’s inability to raise further funds in South Korea, whose media giants — mostly outgrowths of chaebol conglomerates such as CJ ENM or Lotte Entertainment — no longer appear to be willing to bankroll Lee’s bold and unapologetic portrayal of South Korea’s economic system.
The Living and the Dead
For Netflix, Possible Love is a prestige project: an opportunity to bring home an Oscar with a highly accomplished director while reversing a viewership slump and enhancing its brand. Possible Love premiered theatrically in South Korea in September, meeting the Academy’s country-of-origin eligibility deadline. The streaming platform has also made Lee’s previous films available for its subscribers.
Possible Love is set against the aftermath of the 2009 brutal crackdown on the seventy-seven-day strike against massive job cuts at SsangYong Motor (fictionalized in the film as SP Heavy Industries). After crushing the strike, management and the government pushed through one of the country’s first massive layoffs by slashing 50 percent of SsangYong’s blue-collar workforce. In the film as in real life, workers refer to their laid-off colleagues as “the dead” and those who managed to escape the cull as “the living.”
Through the crackdown, corporations and the conservative government set a precedent for mass layoffs. After the defeat at SsangYong, corporations could cut jobs by invoking broadly defined criteria of managerial exigency. The repercussions of the strike and its vivid suppression resonated deeply throughout South Korea.
The strike even became part of the backstory of Squid Game, Netflix’s gamified portrayal of capitalist suffering. In his review of the series, Lee Chang-kun, a leader of SsangYong’s labor union, summed up the experience of an agonizing and prolonged factory occupation:
Out of the blue, we were left with no option but to squat at the factory. We first attempted to turn to each other to survive together. However, we were thrown into a life-or-death situation, often with no other option but to betray and dupe each other. At least once, as in Squid Game, we each had to hurt our closest friends.
Many workers or their family members have since died by suicide or from stress-related conditions such as cardiac arrest. There was probably no better place for Lee to begin Possible Love than the funeral of one such worker.
Anger and Betrayal
In the film, Ho-seok (played by Peppermint Candy star Sul Kyung-gu) was one of the remaining seven hundred striking workers who faced the violent police raid. He had been a welder, proud enough to name his son “Iron.”
Having been injured in the crackdown and subsequently jailed, he has been drained of his blue-collar mettle and sense of purpose, leaving him with simmering feelings of anger and betrayal. His wife, Mi-ok (Secret Sunshine star Jeon Do-yeon) is a good-hearted, innately resilient former seamstress who does her best to hold the family together against all odds in the wake of her husband’s layoff.
At this point, documentary director Ye-ji — played by Cho Yeo-jeong, almost typecast as the seemingly innocuous upper-class woman after her similar role in Parasite — encroaches on Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s fragile universe with her camera lens. A daughter of a small-business owner turned parvenu, Ye-ji is married to Sang-woo (Hope star Zo In-sung), a private equity investor born into generations of wealth and power.
Ye-ji attempts to love Mi-ok and Ho-seok because she believes herself to be a good person. While she is probably sympathetic to Ho-seok and his family, she is strikingly lacking in empathy for their situation. Her superficial innocuousness is pernicious.
Ye-ji’s interest in laid-off workers from SP Industries began during a vacation at a resort in the middle of the Qatar desert, maintained by workers who, her husband tells her, labored hard behind the scenes. Ho-seok is a subject Ye-ji wants to capture through her camera before he disappears into obscurity.
Ye-ji’s husband, Sang-woo, is kind and well-mannered, probably because he has little reason to be otherwise. In his line of business, everything seems impersonal, reduced to numbers and valuations. Although he possesses greater worldly insight than his wife, he need not concern himself with the consequences of his spreadsheets for people like Ho-seok, who remain invisible to him.
There seems to be nothing Ho-seok can do better than Sang-woo. The latter is the better husband, always supportive of his wife, both morally and financially. He is also the better athlete, having tutored the welder’s son in tae kwon do, the sport in which Ho-seok was once a varsity athlete.
To add insult to injury, he is even a superior musician who can play the oboe while Mi-ok sings at karaoke. Ho-seok keeps his guard up around Sang-woo, but he seems to be free of personal jealousy toward him, as though he instinctively feels that the rift between them is one of class rather than individual attributes.
Rather, what has traumatized Ho-seok is the experience of his coworkers, who are now divided into the living and the dead. He has feelings of envy toward the living; they can still throw a fancy birthday party for their children. Emotionally overwhelmed, Ho-seok cannot open up during a group therapy session, where one of the dead laments that they were defeated despite being on the right side.
Impossible Love
It is painful to watch Ho-seok, especially if you understand how strikes and campaigns are defeated — how they implode before they can fizzle out or are violently crushed. We do not walk away from our collective struggles because we abruptly come to fear or love our adversaries. We walk away because we have grown disillusioned or lost trust in the people beside us.
It is before Ye-ji’s camera that Ho-seok finally breaks down in tears and confesses his deepest fear that his wife and former coworkers will discover the anger and sense of betrayal he has kept deep inside. Words like “solidarity” or “resistance” have been reduced to hollow shells of what they used to mean to him.
