It is also when Ye-ji finally lowers her intrusive camera, perhaps stunned by the scene, or perhaps realizing she can never genuinely understand (or love) her subjects. Her very innocuity is a form of violence against Ho-seok and Mi-ok. “That’s enough!” both Ye-ji and Mi-ok yell after Ho-seok’s moment opening-up. The two couples part ways.
Director Lee appears to have built the narrative around one of the Ten Commandments, “You shall not covet,” which appears at the beginning of the film. Ye-ji has even coveted Ho-seok’s agonies. For Ho-seok, that suffering still constitutes part of his own dignity. After opening up, he appears to regain part of his strength.
When Mi-ok asks for the first time in the film about their future, “What shall we do?” he answers, “We will keep living on.” “It will rain tomorrow,” his wife says. “It hasn’t today,” her husband replies, as if that were how he has put himself together day by day since the strike was crushed.
Possible Love is difficult to watch because it relentlessly makes you uncomfortable, if not downright pained. Ho-seok is not an idealized figure: he is a wavering worker, trapped in divisions within his own class, rather than a bold and brave militant taking on his boss and the system. However, this makes his character all the more real: like Ho-seok and the film itself, we are all multilayered beings defying any simple definition.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Four Days Without Cell Service? For This Adventure-Seeking New Yorker, It Was Bliss
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Gothamist Sponsor
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
New Yorkers often pride themselves on their navigation expertise: whether it is finding a commute with the fewest subway transfers or the best way to secure a reservation in a packed restaurant. But when it comes to exploring the world outside of the five boroughs and checking off bucket list trips, this isn’t always the case. Questions like, “How do I pack for hiking at the Grand Canyon?” and “where am I going to find space to store all this gear?” start to creep in. If you've ever wondered how to make an outdoorsy adventure more feasible, keep reading.
For Nicole Goulet, a New York City trauma surgeon and surgical intensivist, spending so much time in the hospital caring for COVID patients led her to seek quiet moments outside of the city. In 2021, Nicole signed up for a four-day, three-night backpacking trip to Death Valley with Wildland Trekking, an Intrepid Company. She arrived with the understandable nerves of a first-time backpacker and left with something she hadn't known she needed: the freedom of being disconnected.
“I loved it so much that when we were walking out of the park that final day, I got sad to have to turn my phone back on again,” Nicole recalls. “At that time, I always needed to have my phone on because of work, so it was an amazing feeling to just not even have the option to have my phone on as there was no service for four days.” (Note: all Wildland guides carry emergency communication devices, which include a satellite phone and/or a GPS locator/texting device.)
On this trip, Death Valley delivered a surprise: four inches of snow in the middle of a Californian desert that is famous for being one of the hottest and driest places in North America (via NPS).
Another high point (pun intended) from her Death Valley trip was reaching the peak of their hike after traversing the mountains and rock formations. “It was so quiet, peaceful and stunning. It was an amazing feeling since in NYC and the hospitals, I am constantly surrounded by people. This and the beautiful sky full of stars are things we do not get to experience in the city.”
Exploring an International Dark Sky Park like Death Valley National Park offers a striking contrast to the bright lights and bustling energy of everyday life in the city, giving guests the opportunity to reconnect with the stillness of the natural world.
Since her first trip, Nicole has been on many trips with Wildland to parks including Yellowstone in 2024 and Yosemite in 2023 and again in 2026. She now takes annual treks with her mother each year. “The trips with my mom are normally either portered or animal assisted because she cannot hike with a large heavy pack, but loves to hike and also camp in the middle of nowhere in a tent!”
Nicole spotlights the Wildland community as a highlight of her trips throughout the years. “You get to meet a great group of very interesting people no matter what trip you take. You also get to know amazing trip leaders. I met Liz Lucas on my very first Wildland trip to Death Valley, we remained in contact and then I got to catch up with her again on this last trip to Yosemite. Liz is such an amazing guide, and I was so inspired by her on that first trip.”
Liz’s own path into the outdoors began with the California Conservation Corps Backcountry Trails program, where she found a love for guiding and public land stewardship. Her journey then took her to New Zealand where she further immersed herself in the outdoor industry, and she has now worked with Wildland as a guide for over five years.
She describes the rewarding experiences that come with being a Wildland guide, saying “I find that when I am out on the trail with guests, I get the honor of witnessing them regulating their nervous systems. I see a childlike awe of the world around us, and an increase in self-awareness and capability that they didn't know they had.”
Liz says that Wildland guides are there for guests every step of the journey, no matter their experience or skill level. “While there can be concern about having the right gear, we provide a robust packing list and advise on what is necessary for the trip. A guide will take on all logistics and will give you a plethora of information ranging from natural interpretation to human history.”
In terms of multi-day gear, Wildland provides nearly all of the necessities, including backpacks, trekking poles, tents, sleeping pads, sleeping bags, cooking gear, eating utensils and more. (Check out their website for additional gear-related details.)
For day hiking, according to Liz, the essentials are straightforward: “Good footwear, good snacks, enough water and a good attitude will put you in the top tier of new hikers in National Parks.” All things that can easily fit in city dwelling of any size!
Ready to trade the city hustle and bustle for a sky full of stars? Wildland Trekking offers backpacking trips, horse/llama/porter supported hikes, inn-based hiking tours, basecamp hiking tours and day hike tours in National Parks and Wilderness Areas worldwide. Get ready for your next big adventure! Find out morehere.

https://gothamist.com/news/f-and-g-lines.title: F and G lines grind to a halt as signal issues slows Friday night rush
https://gothamist.com/news/f-and-g-lines.author: David Giambusso
https://gothamist.com/news/f-and-g-lines.text:
F and G trains have ground to a near halt the MTA said Friday evening, resulting in delays throughout the transit system.
Signal issues were once again the culprit according to city and state officials, this time during the Friday night rush. Passengers were spilling out onto the streets at stations along the two lines in Brooklyn.
At 7:30 p.m. the MTA reported there was no F service between Brooklyn and Manhattan and no G service between Church Avenue and Bedford-Nostrand Avenues.
The stoppage followed delays on the 4 and 5 trains earlier in the day after officials said a passenger was struck.
The subway delays also came as the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the nation amid a communications meltdown at the federal level.

https://gothamist.com/news/faa-meltdown-.title: FAA meltdown strands NJ Gov. Sherrill at Dem conference in Denver
https://gothamist.com/news/faa-meltdown-.author: Ryan Kost, Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/faa-meltdown-.text:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is among the thousands of travelers stranded after an air traffic control breakdown that grounded all flights nationwide for more than five hours Friday.
Sherrill left New Jersey late Thursday and was expected to return Friday evening, a spokesperson said. She’s now expected back sometime Saturday morning.
The governor was among a number of prominent Democrats who went to Denver to attend the “What’s Next” conference, a meeting about the future of the party. U.S. Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, who ran for president in 2020 and is seen as a possible 2028 contender, was also at the conference.
The Federal Aviation Administration stopped all flights Friday afternoon, citing a “temporary telecommunications outage.” It lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m., but not before the stoppage had resulted in more than 7,500 canceled flights and more than 25,000 delays, according to FlightAware.
The region’s airports, including Newark Liberty, will likely see longer delays than the rest of the country as flights resume. Dartmouth engineering professor Vikrant Vaze told Gothamist that’s because the area has heavy demand, limited runways and crowded airspace.
More than a thousand flights at Newark, JFK and Laguardia were canceled as of Saturday morning and passengers were still facing long delays, according to FlightAware, a national flight tracking site.
Lt. Gov. Shirley Emehelu, who was only just appointed on Monday, has been serving as acting governor while Sherrill is away. Emehelu replaced Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September, after an investigation substantiated a sexual harassment complaint against him and other allegations surfaced that he had made women on his staff uncomfortable.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/beef-rancher.title: The Politics of Beef in the 2026 Midterms
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/beef-rancher.author: Nicholas Brown
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/beef-rancher.text:
The Politics of Beef in the 2026 Midterms
Beef has long symbolized the promise of American material abundance. The midterms illustrated the political consequences of failing to deliver it.
In 1840, following the devastating economic contraction of the Panic of 1837, Whig presidential candidate William Henry Harrison defeated incumbent Martin Van Buren by promising “Two dollars a day and roast beef” for every worker. His opponent, meanwhile, was derided for offering workers just “fifty cents a day and French soup.”
Nearly two centuries later, Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom has become the first black person elected to the United States Senate from his state since Reconstruction.
Many pundits have identified the pivotal moment in his campaign: an advertisement mocking Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for responding to soaring beef prices by telling Americans, “You have so many proteins to choose from.”
Colom’s punch line: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
Harrison had promised American workers roast beef. Colom made the inability to afford it an indictment of the Republican Party.
Mississippi wasn’t an isolated case. From Texas’s historic Democratic sweep of statewide offices to extraordinary Democratic gains in Kansas, the 2026 midterms revealed the political consequences of the Trump administration’s failure to manage the American beef economy.
Caught between two constituencies with conflicting interests — cattle ranchers struggling to sustain their businesses and consumers increasingly unable to afford beef — the administration failed both. Meanwhile, immigration policies threatened the workers responsible for processing the country’s cattle.
The result was a political nightmare for Republicans and a lesson for progressives and leftists about the difficulty of delivering the material abundance that American workers have long been promised.
The Beef Market Is Broken (for Everyone)
Beef occupies a special place in the American social contract. It has long symbolized material abundance: the promise that an ordinary person ought to be able to afford the occasional steak. Beef, according to a famous industry campaign, is “What’s for dinner.”
Heading into the midterms, Republicans found themselves caught between two constituencies, both struggling, with conflicting interests. On one side were America’s 622,000 cattle ranchers, of whom nearly 90 percent have only twenty cows on average. In 2018, roughly three in four identified as Republican. Many struggled financially with rising input costs, which resulted in the lowest national herd per capita in recorded history. Consumers, meanwhile, faced beef prices up 111 percent since 2019.
Ranchers need higher cattle prices to sustain their businesses, while consumers need lower beef prices to continue buying it. As Bloomberg reported in late 2025, “The Beef Market Is Broken for Everyone.”
High prices normally induce cattle ranchers to raise more cows. But ranchers have been forced to prepare their heifers for slaughter instead of raising baby calves due to climate-change-induced water shortages and rising primary input costs (namely feed, fertilizer, and fuel — all driven higher by droughts, tariff disputes, and the war in Iran). Last month, Bloomberg reported that more than half of our country’s cattle live in areas suffering from droughts — meaning many of them will have to be sold for slaughter earlier than ranchers would prefer. And even if ranchers want to rebuild their herds, it takes three or four years of financial risk to do so.
The Failure of Republican Beef Policy
Through much of the second Trump administration, Republicans chose a policy of supporting domestic ranchers with high beef prices, implicitly asking consumers to change their eating habits: “Pick another protein.” They were aware, however, that if beef prices rose too much, they’d face a political crisis.
In late 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that cattle ranchers “would be doing just as they’ve done for the past 20 years — Terrible!” if not for his 50 percent tariff on Brazilian cattle coming into the United States. He noted, though, that “it would be nice” if cattle ranchers also understood that “they also have to get their prices down, because the consumer is a very big factor in my thinking.”
While tariffs supported high beef prices, this ultimately proved politically untenable after beef prices continued to surge.
In August, Trump announced an expansion of the quota for imported lean beef trimmings eligible for reduced tariff rates. The goal was to increase imports of lean beef trimmings used to produce ground beef, bringing down beef prices before the midterm election.
Cattle prices subsequently fell roughly 15 percent from their May levels, exposing producers who had purchased cattle at elevated prices to substantial financial losses. Although other market forces also influence cattle prices, the administration’s decision to expand imports certainly contributed to the reduced value of ranchers’ herds.
Imagine you spent $50,000 to buy cattle in April. Now, their market value has fallen $7,500, or 15 percent. If you borrowed money to make the purchase, that decline would represent an even larger percentage of your own investment. When your cows reach market weight — or when you can no longer afford to feed and water them — you will be forced to sell. And if the prices don’t recover, you will lock in those losses.
At the same time, the policy shift came too late to benefit consumers; retail beef prices continued to surge heading into the midterms.
This is likely because consumers don’t immediately see the benefits of increased supply. The process requires importers to purchase and ship the beef, the imported beef to arrive and receive customs approval, the meatpackers to blend the imported and domestic beef, and the ground beef to move to wholesale distribution. After that, the supermarkets receive the shipment and adjust their prices. Just importing the beef takes two to eight weeks.
While cattle prices crashed, consumers paid even higher prices at the supermarket. The administration had failed struggling cattle ranchers without ensuring the ordinary American could afford to eat a steak.
Texas: When Cattle Country Rebels
The consequences were particularly striking in Texas, where Democrats swept statewide offices in a historic electoral breakthrough.
In August, following the expansion of the in-quota allowance for beef imports, Republican Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller broke from Trump, warning that some Texas Republicans would lose statewide offices in November due to rural voter outrage. In fact, Democrats ended up winning every statewide Texas office, including his seat after he lost to his Republican challenger in the primaries.
Some of the state’s most remarkable swings toward Democrats occurred in counties with significant cattle-ranching economies. Kleberg County swung approximately 28 points toward Democrats relative to 2024, Brewster County 24 points, and Wilbarger County 16 points. While these shifts were comparable to the roughly 26-point Democratic swing statewide, they were substantial relative to the approximately 7.5-point swing across rural Texas more broadly.
These results do not prove that cattle prices caused ranchers to abandon the Republican Party. The election was a referendum on the Trump administration, and voters had plenty of reasons to reject its candidates.
But the Democratic gains in cattle country suggest that the administration’s agricultural policies may have broken a key part of the Republican coalition.
Kansas: The Workers Behind the Beef
Beyond the consumers in Mississippi and the cattle ranchers in Texas, there was another constituency caught in the administration’s contradictory beef policy: the workers who process American cattle.
The meatpacking industry, which handles the slaughter and processing of livestock, depends heavily on immigrant labor. In September, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducted raids around meatpacking plants in Kansas, the second-largest meat-processing state. Many of these plants were already on the verge of closing because the herds they could buy were too small to continue operating profitably. ICE raids caused further shutdowns and delays, as immigrant workers stayed home out of fear of arrest. Without workers, the supply of beef fell, and beef prices continued to rise.
Kansas’s three largest meatpacking counties — Ford, Seward, and Finney — swung 39, 52, and 37 points toward Democrats, respectively, compared with a roughly 21-point Democratic swing statewide relative to 2024. The Kansas Reflector reported that they were the three counties that helped the Democrats take the Kansas Senate seat, even though less than one in four voters in these counties are registered Democrats.
While the Trump administration increased beef imports in an attempt to lower consumer prices, its immigration policies threatened the workforce responsible for processing this beef. Ranchers faced losses on their cattle; consumers worried about affording steak again; endangered meatpacking workers faced uncertainty about their livelihoods.
Given these widespread grievances, it’s not surprising that a Kansas Senate seat turned blue for the first time since the Great Depression.
The Price of Breaking the Social Contract
Beef prices alone did not determine the 2026 election — high gas prices and the war in Iran drove a lot of political messaging and actual voting. Texas and Mississippi have distinct political histories, and voters had plenty of reasons to reject Republican candidates beyond the cost of hamburgers.
But beef offers a useful lens through which to understand the election. The Republican Party had built a coalition promising to defend rural producers, restore working-class prosperity, and protect traditional American abundance. But its beef market policies broke each of those promises.
When the administration tried to protect domestic producers, it left consumers with unaffordable groceries. When it tried to help consumers, it hurt ranchers. And its immigration policies threatened the workers essential to the entire industry.
Ultimately, the administration asked all three constituencies to accept a lower standard of living.
For centuries, the ability of ordinary Americans to afford beef has been part of the country’s informal social contract. It is a small expression of a larger promise: that even if inequality explodes to unprecedented heights, economic growth should trickle down into tangible improvements in everyday life.
In 1840, William Henry Harrison understood the political power of promising workers roast beef. In 2026, Republicans discovered the political cost of telling them they could live without it.
For progressives and leftists, the lesson is that governing for working-class prosperity requires more than promising lower prices or higher wages. It requires understanding how the goods Americans depend on are actually produced and developing policies capable of expanding supply while protecting the livelihoods of the workers and producers as well as the natural environment that make that abundance possible. Republicans learned the political cost of failing to deliver roast beef. The Left now has to figure out how to put it back on the table.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-palace-for-.title: 'A palace for the people': Historic, grand Loew's theater reopens in Jersey City
https://gothamist.com/news/a-palace-for-.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/a-palace-for-.text:
It’s showtime again at the Loew’s Jersey Theatre.
The historic venue opened in Jersey City nearly a century ago, just steps from what is now the Journal Square PATH train station, as one of five “Wonder Theatres” built by Loew’s in the New York City area. It had been closed for the past five years, undergoing a $130 million renovation that was decades overdue.
Now the public is finally being welcomed back inside. This weekend’s grand reopening features two sold-out concerts — from the Trey Anastasio Band on Friday and The War on Drugs on Saturday.
The reopening is being touted as a triumphant moment, a key milestone to restoring Journal Square’s place as the beating heart of Jersey City.
“ This theater is beautiful,” Mayor James Solomon said when he and other dignitaries gathered for a ribbon-cutting Monday. “We call it a palace for the people, and that's our vision for it.”
But amid the glitz and glamor inside and outside the venue, a tense uncertainty hangs in the air over what role — if any — the volunteers that kept the Loew’s alive for decades will have in its future. The group saved the building from demolition, but with a major entertainment company taking over the venue, the local residents who’ve cared for the theater for decades say they’re concerned about what the community’s role in the theater will be in the future.
Saved from the brink
The Loew’s was on the verge of being demolished in 1987. A developer wanted to use the property to build an office complex, and city hall supported the plan.
Community members rallied against the proposed demolition, forming what would become the Friends of the Loew’s to speak out at public hearings and advocate for the theater’s preservation.
“A number of concerned citizens, myself included, came together when Jersey City's official redevelopment policy called this place a dying dinosaur that needed to be torn down, and we didn't think that was right,” said Colin Egan, the director of the Friends of the Loew’s.
The city purchased the Loew’s in 1993, effectively ending the demolition threat. Egan and his group then faced a new challenge: They needed to get the theater into decent enough condition that it could host shows, so that it could be part of the community again.
"Even though it was in fairly good shape by the standards of a lot of old theaters, it had been closed at that point for six or seven years,” Egan said. “A lot of deferred maintenance in the decades before that.”
The Friends of the Loew’s turned to volunteers to do major construction inside and out of the building. They patched the roof, tore down walls that had divided the main hall, rebuilt the projection booth and dressing rooms, replaced all the seats and more.
Robert Policastro, an artist who volunteered for the Friends group, recalled chasing pigeons out of the building’s clock tower, where a copper statue shows Saint George fighting a dragon, and the shoestring budget they had to work with.
“ We used to have a guy out here with a Brillo pad trying to get the original copper,” Policastro said.
It took the volunteers years to do, but by 2001 the Loew’s was stable enough to host events again. For the next 20 years, the group hosted a variety of programs. Big-name musicians including Sufjan Stevens, Bright Eyes, Courtney Barnett and Kurt Vile graced the stage. Stephen King and George R.R. Martin came for book signings. Local arts groups were allowed into the space to put on their own shows. And classic film nights offered the chance to see a movie for just $8, with popcorn sold for $1.
The Jersey City Redevelopment Agency is the branch of city government in charge of the Loew’s. Denise Ridley, the chair of the agency’s board, is also the president of the city council. She called the reopening “momentous” at Monday’s ribbon-cutting, and said the effort should be a model for Jersey City.
“ I'm looking forward to more projects in this city where we honor the past while embracing the future,” Ridley said.
Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment, the same company that owns the Philadelphia 76ers and the New Jersey Devils, took over the venue’s lease in 2021. The company closed the Loew’s that year to embark on the massive renovation project.
Bruce Wheeler, the general manager of the Loew’s for Harris Blitzer, said the work was more than just restoring the look of the place. Plumbing, electric and HVAC systems were all updated through the project.
“All those things are brand new, things that the public will never see to really make this a comfortable space,” Wheeler said.
The restoration effort created 525 union jobs, according to Pat Kelleher, the president of the Hudson County Building and Construction Trades Council. Kelleher said the project was a point of pride for many workers, because it is so unique.
“ It shows what the building trades can do,” Kelleher said. “We usually build high-rises, warehouses. This is the marquee of the city.”
The work isn’t quite done. The theater's historic organ is still in the building, but it's not yet back in service. New movie screens have been ordered. And the massive chandelier that previously hung in the lobby is still undergoing its own restoration. All of those pieces are set to be done next year, Wheeler said.
The heart of the city
Thomas Zuppa, who represents Journal Square on the Jersey City Council, said he could remember seeing Casablanca in the Loew’s with his wife years ago, when they only had one restaurant in the neighborhood to choose from for dinner before the show.
The anecdote is a reminder of how drastically Journal Square has changed, with even more development on the way. Zuppa said the neighborhood is experiencing a renaissance, and he expects the renovated Loew’s will be key to anchoring a sense of community and vibrancy amid the changes.
“ I cannot believe that many years ago, many prior administrations ago thought that this building wasn't worth saving,” Zuppa said.
Journal Square is among the fastest growing and changing neighborhoods in Jersey City. Solomon said Journal Square can and should be the thriving heart of the city, and he said having the Loew’s at its best will be key to making that happen.
The Loew’s calendar will be highlighted with stops by acclaimed musicians and comedians. Sean Saadeh, the chief programming officer for Harris Blitzer, said the Loew’s will fill a unique role in the company’s portfolio, which also includes the Prudential Center in Newark.
Saadeh said there’s already strong interest from acts in performing at the Loew’s, and he said it gives Harris Blitzer the ability to book shows that aren’t good fits for arenas or stadiums. The Loew’s will effectively replace White Eagle Hall, another historic Jersey City venue, in the Harris Blitzer portfolio. NJBIZ reported that HBSE chose not to renew its lease on White Eagle hall earlier this year.
“It brings a unique opportunity in the area on the Jersey side, and building artists on the Jersey side I think is really important to us,” Saadeh said. “It’s vital to build artists at this level in Jersey so that they have some history here, so that when they're at the arena level it's not the first time they're in the marketplace.”
Solomon said he's hopeful that some established local legends will take the stage.
“I want Springsteen to come,” Solomon said. “Let's see if we can get The Boss in the Loew’s.”
As part of the agreement with Harris Blitzer to operate the Loew’s, the theater is committed to host community events 55 days of the year. The first of those is scheduled for Dec. 2, when Solomon said the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra will perform for free at the Mayor’s Holiday Concert.
“You're going to have the best shows, the best entertainment, but we in the city also have 55 community programming days,” Solomon said. “We're going to be able to bring in people that represent the best of Jersey City Arts, that speak to the diverse communities of Jersey City and bring them into this extraordinary palace.”
What happens to the Friends?
Who gets to decide what events fill those 55 community dates has become a point of contention. As of now, there is no formal relationship between the city and the Friends of the Loew’s.
Solomon said it's important to him that the Friends of the Loew’s remain involved with the theater. He said negotiations are ongoing to formalize an agreement on what the organization’s role will be moving forward.
“They helped save the building. They have great programming,” Solomon said. “It's us working together on the details of it, which we're making progress, and I have confidence it'll be all finalized shortly.”
Those negotiations are centered on the structure of the Friends of the Loew’s board, according to Egan, and what representation the mayor and city council may have on it. Egan said he’s “guardedly” optimistic that the Friends of the Loew’s will be allowed to guide community programming in the future and he’s encouraged by Solomon’s praise for the group.
But he said he’s increasingly concerned as time goes on with no deal to bring the group back into the Loew’s operation.
“ Here, grand architecture isn't meant for the wealthy and elite, it's meant for everyone, and great performance is supposed to be available at a good price to everybody,” Egan said. “And in the Loew’s, it also has meant the people saved it, rolled up their sleeves and renovated it, and operated it for 20 years for the people as a community place.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-akehu.title: Europe Relies on Illegal Pushbacks to Deter Migrants
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-akehu.author: Calum Jacobs
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-akehu.text:
Europe Relies on Illegal Pushbacks to Deter Migrants
Pushbacks are a tactic to violently force migrants back across borders. European authorities recognize that the practice is illegal, but this hasn’t stopped pushbacks from becoming increasingly common along the EU’s external boundaries.
In the video that precipitated his most recent arrest, Daniel Thomas, founder of the Patriot Platform group, can be heard telling someone on a dinghy in the English Channel, “You’re in English territory, this is England,” before proceeding to rather unsuccessfully slash at their inflated vessel. Thomas’s version of English history presumably doesn’t credit it as the first nation to adopt a comprehensive organization for saving lives at sea (later the Royal National Lifeboat Institution), whose routine rescue operation Thomas was interrupting and whose activities, members, and members’ children have been threatened by Thomas and his far-right associates. When Thomas and his group refer to “taking Britain back” to when it was “great,” they must mean to before the 1536 Offences at Sea Act, which brought maritime crimes into common law, or at least to before the 1854 Merchant Shipping Act, which provided rewards for lifesavers at sea, and whose contemporary update Thomas was arrested on suspicion of offending against.
It doesn’t take much effort to paint Thomas as a man with only one oar in the water. But the sad fact is that his was only an attempted civil enactment of what has become European border regimes’ de facto policy: the migrant pushback.
According to the European Commission, pushback refers to “various measures taken by states which result in migrants. . . . being summarily forced back to the country from where they attempted to cross or have crossed an international border without access to international protection or asylum procedures.” As many have pointed out, “pushback” is an essentially euphemistic term, often masking the specific violent mechanics involved in each case.
In his new book, Along the Watchtower: Dispatches from Europe’s War on Migration, journalist Nathan Akehurst charts the development of pushback as a tactic of immigration control at Europe’s borders, alongside the camps, militarization, surveillance, and externalized enforcement introduced by European states and institutions since the peak in irregular migration to the EU in 2015 (and, in fact, in the decades prior). Akehurst deftly weaves this account with testimonies of survivors of these borders, interviews with the organizations and people who work in and against this system, and his own experience as a volunteer with search-and-rescue operations in the Mediterranean and beyond.
Cases of pushback detailed by Akehurst, as well as in the Black Book of Pushbacks compiled by the Border Violence Monitoring Network, include violent assault, strip search, family separation, sexual violence, dog attacks, detention, abduction, destruction of possessions, use of electric discharge weapons, intimidatory gunfire, ship maneuver resulting in capsize, abandonment in rough waters, and, yes, the stabbing of inflatable vessels. Over 40 percent of recorded cases involve minors, and, while it is impossible to say exactly how many deaths can be attributed to pushbacks, it is almost certainly in the hundreds. These pushbacks have been recorded at almost every EU border, from Turkey-Greece to Poland-Belarus, Finland-Russia to Morocco-Spain, Serbia-Hungary to Libya-Italy, on land and at sea, and even within the Schengen Area supposedly without internal border controls.
From the evidence Akehurst painstakingly gathers in his book, it is impossible to conclude that these pushbacks take place without the knowledge, tacit sanction, and even participation of EU border agency Frontex.
After International Law
Pushback is illegal. It violates the individual’s right to claim asylum under international law and constitutes a deportation without trial. Pushbacks at sea also seem to contravene the universal duty to render assistance to those in distress, enshrined in the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and the 1974 International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea. Given the typical state of repair of the vessels that irregular migrants use to cross, for example, the Mediterranean, their capacity, and the typical condition of the individuals concerned (Akehurst reports multiple instances of pregnant or unconscious passengers), one would think that this duty would kick in automatically for any state agent in a seaworthy boat coming to meet them.
These conventions are only the latest legal formulation of a nautical norm probably as old as seafaring itself. Xenophon’s Hellenica records that it was the failure of the six Athenian generals to rescue shipwrecked soldiers after the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE that prompted their trial and execution by the Athenian democracy. In Roman Law, the Lex Rhodia, codified by Justinian I but likely already over a thousand years old by that point, protects the duty to rescue by establishing the principle that any damages from jettison must be compensated by contributions from all those saved (the law of the general average). Similar conventions are present in the medieval pan-Mediterranean compendium the Consolato del Mare and were brought into the new “maritime law” of various states in the seventeenth century. As the concept of “international law” developed in the eighteenth century, influential Swiss jurist Emer de Vattel argued that there was a right of entry into port for a vessel in distress, and that this right existed notwithstanding the opposition of the coastal state. So universally established was the duty to render assistance, so ingrained in the psyche of European sailors, that Nazi Admiral Karl Dönitz felt obliged to issue an order forbidding such rescue after German U-boats repeatedly went to the aid of sunk Allied vessels and most famously attempted to rescue British and Italian survivors of the ocean liner Laconia (when they were attacked by American aircraft).
One can also tell different stories of Europeans’ behavior at sea. The same Rhodian law of the general average was relied upon by the owners of the slave ship Zong when they filed an insurance claim for the loss of 132 enslaved Africans thrown overboard when the ship ran low on drinking water. The same Vattel published an opinion justifying settlement of North America by Europeans who, “finding land of which the savages stood in no particular need, and of which they made no actual and constant use, were lawfully entitled to take possession of it and settle it with colonies.” The development of maritime and international law in the early modern period is inseparable from the development of European colonialism. European states established laws for their mutual conduct and the rights of their people, and in the same sweep drew the physical and ideological lines beyond which they would not apply: the persons who would not be legal subjects and the peoples who did not meet the criteria for statehood, and who could therefore be brutalized. The law was a technology concurrent to military force, economic extraction, and administrative imposition by which Europeans established sovereignty over distant land, in a process Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari would call “territorialization.”
At Europe’s borders today, exceptions to its “universal” human rights are still being made. The border as Akehurst describes it has become a bitter, one-sided contest between rival regimes of law. Civil and humanitarian groups, of national and international composition, fight for the application of international but also national maritime assistance and asylum law. They are obstructed by international lawfare. (Akehurst cites cases of search-and-rescue volunteers being charged with offenses such as smuggling and espionage. The cases can halt and frustrate rescue operations for years but rarely make it to court, spurious as they are.) Meanwhile, European governments cooperate to maintain states of exception for persons they deem deserving and outsource their lawmaking violence to foreign state and non-state actors. This is not a conflict between state sovereignty and international law but rather between different transnational agents attempting to undermine each other’s governance over social relations in a geographical area — in Deleuze and Guattari’s language, territorializing and deterritorializing actors.
Parallel to post hoc legal justification runs a tradition of European thought, from Diogenes to Franz Kafka, which examines the law not from the perspective of its writer but from the perspective of its sufferer. For the woman experiencing her twentieth pushback at the hands of men with guns in EU-funded patrol vehicles or the teenager in his second year in an offshore detention center waiting to hear whether his asylum claim will be successful, or whether it is even still “under review” at all, what good would be an invocation of the European origins of humanitarian law? The monolith they encounter just is the law. And this monolith, this Castle, this “Fortress Europe” is getting more formidable each year as the death rate rises. How did we get here?
Strange Bedfellows
Along the Watchtower contains a fascinating and timely history of European politics since the millennium, one that turns received wisdom on its head. The familiar story is the competition between liberal Europeanists, who favor increased powers for pan-European institutions, perhaps with the end goal of a supranational European state, and Euroskeptics, who want to maintain nation-state sovereignty as they see it. But Akehurst argues that what characterizes recent developments in Europe is a strategic accord, or at least a confluence of interests and convergence of policy, between these two factions.
In the economic and political crisis in Europe after 2007, amid mildly rising levels of irregular migration, the Europeanists sensed an opportunity to consolidate the European project with two key material tools of statehood: an army and a border. A minor agency, based in Warsaw as a favor to new EU member Poland, proved to be the answer. This was Frontex, and it quickly grew from a budget of €6 million in 2004 to €90 million in 2014. After the “migrant crisis” of 2015, it was supercharged, and its 2025 budget was over €1 billion of taxpayer money. It is now the EU’s largest agency. The number of its Standing Corps, the EU’s first uniformed service, is set to reach ten thousand next year. They have been increasingly equipped like a military force. Meanwhile, Europeanist politicians such as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have toured borders from Poland to Greece and claimed them as “European borders,” capable of being “defended” only by diverting money and power toward the coordinators in Brussels.
In this project, the Europeanists found strange bedfellows in the European far right, on an upward trajectory since 2007. They traditionally opposed European centralization and what they saw as the resulting importation of liberal values into the national body politic. They too spotted an opportunity, and one they too were able to escalate after 2015: to reframe economic downturn and national decline as the fault of immigrants and an overly permissive immigration system. As they started to gain power in countries like Austria and Italy, they worked with European institutions to bring about their desired treatment of migrants. It turned out that Brussels’s liberal values were up for sale, and not for a high price. Through bilateral state agreements, partnerships with illiberal external regimes like in Tunisia and Turkey, and victories for the border lobby within the EU, the far right secured the militarized “hot spot” system that Frontex was only too happy to enforce. This system, in turn, funnels irregular migrants into certain dangerous pinch points, from which emerge the spectacles of large groups of people pushing at fences or overcrowded dinghies making landings, which the far right then uses to campaign on.
And so, von der Leyen and far-right Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni will come together for a photo op on Lampedusa, and both have endorsed the EU’s New Pact on Migration and Asylum that took effect this year. The far right get their ritual violence and their spectacle, and the Europeanists consolidate their transnational power. Whether each side believes they are strategically outmaneuvering the other is by the by: the result is washing up at the shores of the Mediterranean every day. (British pro-Europeans optimistic about Andy Burnham’s recent interventions on reversing Brexit ought to be cognizant that this is the EU to which they would be returning.)
So we are stuck in a vicious cycle of immiseration. Every migrant that fails to get through the border proves that Fortress Europe is working: every migrant that succeeds only proves that more resources, more surveillance, more emergency powers are required. Deeply unpleasant regimes and warlords pocket their fees for maintaining Europe’s external border, which they then use to conduct their own internal repressions, producing more refugees. The arms and surveillance technology companies, often in a revolving-door relationship with European agencies, enrich themselves to the tune of billions of dollars, which they use to lobby for more investment in arms and surveillance technology. The far right surges in Germany, France, Britain, and all over Europe as voters choose the real thing over the milquetoast versions of migrant demonization offered by liberal and social democratic politicians unable to resist the trap their enemies have set for them. Historic landscapes of Europe, Africa, and the Near East, gateways of ancient exchange and adventure, mountain passes, river valleys, and coastlines get covered in barbed-wire fences, tents, and patrolling soldiers. And the Mediterranean continues to groan with blood: the latest count is over thirty five thousand lives lost since 2014.
People Keep Moving
And still people move. It shouldn’t be unfamiliar to Europeans that people move: after all, they’ve always done it. The stories of the European imagination are littered with travelers, voyagers, and migrants: from Homer’s Odyssey to the skaldic poets, from Sadko in the byliny to the Celtic immrama. Without naively imagining this movement as always benevolent, and whatever its rationale, we can recognize that the arduous journeys have been respected; their human cost commemorated; the miracle of rescue honored. In Greek myth, the Aegean Sea is named for the life lost in it. We don’t know all the names of the people who have died in the Mediterranean in the last twelve years. The ones we do know are thanks to the tireless work of legal advocates, humanitarian campaigners, and migrant self-organizations. Akehurst interviews volunteers from I Have Rights in Samos, Mission Wings in Bulgaria, Medical Volunteers International in Serbia, Sea-Eye in the Mediterranean, and many more. We can situate their work in the legacies of civil and socialist opposition to the state, given their utilization of those material concessions won by previous struggles and inscribed within bourgeois law to defend and enact visions of human life beyond capitalist systems of violence. What Akehurst doesn’t give as much detail on is the relation — actual or optimal — between these groups and socialist parties working within national contexts. Nor is his book a theoretical account of the political economy of contemporary migration — a new left-wing popular introduction to which would be welcome. Nonetheless, the stories of these campaigners and the author’s sometimes joyous, normally mad encounters with them and the people seeking safety resonate long after the final chapter.
There are more traditions in Europe than just the imperial, and they include the civil organization of lifesaving at sea, kept alive today by search-and-rescue groups in the Mediterranean. The sea, that “howling infinite,” is not an easy place to territorialize. There is a natural disrule, and everything is more dangerous. This is why it lends itself more to the mythic mode than the juridical. Right-wingers accuse migrants of exploiting this danger in order to claim rescue and asylum. But the reverse is true: it is the European authorities that exploit the remoteness, lack of oversight, and hazard of the water in order to prevent legitimate asylum claims. It should concern us all whether what prevails on the Mediterranean, in the English Channel, and around the world is the law of assistance to those in distress or the law of the pushback.
While we have much to thank these first responders for, they won’t be enough on their own. As migration increases with climate breakdown and capitalism at war, it behooves us all to defend human movement and facilitate its safety. The alternative is becoming increasingly clear: the Mediterranean as mass grave, from the bloody outcrop of Ceuta to Trump hotels on the ethnically cleansed beaches of Gaza; a Europe without enough firefighters to tackle its wildfires, relying on the water cannons of border guards; and a thousand Daniel Thomases in brown shirts patrolling the Channel.
Against such a future, and the present powers who would midwife it, we must build a politics capable of pushing back.

https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-ca.title: Gov. Hochul calls on Duffy to resign after FAA meltdown grounds nation's flights
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-ca.author: Ryan Kost
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-ca.text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul called on U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to resign or be fired after a communications failure grounded all flights across the country Friday, leading to thousands of flight cancellations and delays that continued well into Saturday.
“Sean Duffy must resign, or President Trump must remove him immediately,” the governor said in a statement Saturday morning.
“From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch.”
The governor, who has been battling Duffy for years over transportation funding, said the secretary has been “more focused on starring in his own reality show,” a reference to a YouTube series Duffy filmed that followed his travels across the country with his wife, Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy, and their nine children.
The Federal Aviation Administration halted flights nationwide Friday afternoon, citing a telecommunications outage. The stoppage was lifted later that evening, but still resulted in more than 7,500 flights being canceled and another 25,000 delayed, according to FlightAware.
On Saturday morning Duffy told reporters that a contractor working for the FAA was switching “telecommunications lines from old copper wire and they were bringing it over to fiber” at an undisclosed, “remote” location. The shutdown apparently flooded the system’s routers causing alarm at the FAA.
“When we see that, your safety is paramount,” Duffy said. “We shut down the airspace.”
Hochul called for a congressional investigation into the causes before the start of the holiday travel rush, but said Duffy had to go now.
New York’s Democratic leadership has been feuding with Trump’s transportation department for years over air safety and transportation funding.
The Trump Administration has repeatedly gone after public transportation funding in New York and been shut down in court. Duffy's agency has moved to kill Manhattan’s congestion pricing program, funding for theSecond Avenue subway and funding for the construction of new train tunnels under the Hudson.
In May 2025 a shortage of air traffic control personnel led to delays, confusion and chaos at the region’s airports. Sen. Chuck Schumer said at the time that Duffy’s department had “has failed spectacularly” in regard to safety.
Just last month, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was among a group of 25 lawmakers who asked Duffy and the FAA to pause the rollout of a new AI-enabled air traffic management tool called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories.” The new tool was built through a “12-year, $875 million contract,” according to the lawmakers’ letter, but they argued “there has been little transparency” about how the tool was tested.
Duffy said Friday that the tool had nothing to do with the outage, calling the two “completely disconnected.”
The White House referred questions to the transportation department Saturday. The Department of Transportation did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
This story has been updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/expansion-pro.title: Expansion proposal for Brooklyn plants fuels data center fears
https://gothamist.com/news/expansion-pro.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/expansion-pro.text:
The owner of a pair of floating power plants near Sunset Park, Brooklyn wants to expand the facilities, prompting protests from environmentalists who fear they could be used one day to power data centers.
The Gowanus Generation Station and nearby Narrows Generation Station are peaker facilities that are only activated during periods of peak demand. Such plants produce a disproportionate amount of pollution. But environmentalists' goal of closing the peakers has run into the reality of the downstate grid, which is under strain and largely dependent on fossil fuels since the closure of the Indian Point nuclear facility.
The owner of the plants, AlphaGen, submitted an expansion plan to Con Edison earlier this year, stating that it expects the company's operating permit will be extended past 2029. Alarm over that proposal grew in recent weeks when a company that owns, invests in and operates data centers, DigitalBridge Group, bought AlphaGen’s parent company for more than $1 billion.
“Sunset Park is not a dumping ground for dangerous energy projects,” said State Senator Andrew Gounardes, who joined a protest Thursday over the expansion plans. “Big Tech has the resources to invest in clean energy and help lower our utility costs, but instead, they’re doubling down on polluting a community that has already carried the burden of projects like this for decades. We demand investments that move us forward and we won’t stop fighting until we get them.”
AlphaGen’s expansion proposal “recognizes the realities of current power technology and the need to balance reliability with sustainability,” Curt Morgan, CEO of AlphaGen said in a press release. He added that the plan is intended “to start a conversation about supporting cleaner technology as a bridge to a zero-emissions future.”
But environmental activists who rallied near the Gowanus Generation Station said there is no conversation to be had. They want the peakers shut down entirely.
“ We can't let big tech get a wish list of gas plants, and we can't let them throw Sunset Park residents under the bus just so that they can continue to pad their profits,” said Santosh Nandabalan, organizing director at New York Communities for Change.
The Gowanus Generating Station is a floating 260-megawatt natural gas power plant on barges in New York Harbor. The facility houses 32 turbines on four floating platforms.
The nearby Narrows plant is a 322-megawatt floating peaker plant that consists of 16 turbines on two barges.
AlphaGen wrote it wants to replace the units on all six barges with three new power barges that will deliver a total of 819 megawatts. The company said it will reduce emissions by more than 50% through the upgrade.
"New York City's electric grid is facing a growing reliability gap as older infrastructure retires and demand continues to rise," Morgan said in a statement.
Under the 2025 Peaker Rule, both Brooklyn plants were scheduled for closure by last July. But the state grid operator determined that the plants needed to remain open until May 2029 for grid reliability, citing surging demand from electrification and heat waves.
According to the federal government’s accountability office, peaker plants produce 1.6 times more sulfur dioxide, high levels of nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter than baseload plants that run continuously. Rapidly activating the peakers during times of maximum demand results in less efficiency and more pollution.
AlphaGen spokesperson Aaron Gruen said in a statement that its proposal had no connection to data centers and that it had yet to submit a formal plan to a state regulator.
“New York’s grid operator has found that New York City needs new, dispatchable power by the mid-2030s to replace aging plants and maintain reliable service as electrification of buildings and vehicles increase electric demand,” Gruen said. “The Gowanus proposal would replace 1970s-era units with more efficient, lower-emitting turbines, and if it moves forward, AlphaGen will work alongside the state, the city and our neighbors in the Sunset Park community.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-speciali.title: NYC's specialized high school test stalled by technical problems, DOE says
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-speciali.author: Christian Santana
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-speciali.text:
A number of students were unable to access and finish the Specialized High School Admissions Test on Saturday due to a technical issue, city officials said.
In a statement, the New York City Department of Education said it would reschedule the test after the test's vendor, Pearson, reported technical problems.
"I understand and share the frustration of our students and families," Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said in a statement. "I have spoken with the vendor and shared this frustration, and they have assured me the issue has been corrected."
The department said testing will continue as planned on Nov. 15. It did not elaborate on the nature of the issue or how many students were affected, and Pearson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.
School officials said students who were unable to finish the test would be automatically rescheduled, and that families would receive follow-up information by the end of the day on Monday.
Testing on a new date will not affect any student's score or consideration for admission to a specialized high school, according to the department. Students who finished and submitted a test on Saturday are also eligible to retake the test if they choose, the department said.
In a joint statement on Saturday, a group of city and state lawmakers demanded a thorough and transparent investigation into the issue.
“The DOE may point to its testing contractor, Pearson, but accountability cannot be outsourced,” read the statement from Councilmember Susan Zhuang, Assemblymember William Colton, state Sen.-elect Larry He, and Assemblymembers-elect Joyce Xie and Joey Saban. “The DOE selected the vendor, oversees the process, and is ultimately responsible for ensuring that every student receives a fair and reliable opportunity to take this examination.”
“Under mayoral control, the buck stops with City Hall and DOE leadership,” the statement read.
The SHSAT is administered to eighth and ninth graders in New York City and is used to determine admission to eight of the city’s nine specialized high schools.
This story has been updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/some-in-ny-fr.title: Some in NY fret about being hit by the AI bus. Others are trying to board it.
https://gothamist.com/news/some-in-ny-fr.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/some-in-ny-fr.text:
In a conference room in Manhattan on a recent afternoon, a speaker named Claira spoke to a captive audience about the benefits of using an artificial intelligence agent as a personal assistant.
Claira would know — she herself is one.
The bot, appearing on a large screen, had caramel-color skin and bouncy, curly hair, and is the first ever Afro-Latina, multilingual virtual assistant to hit the market, according to Abran Maldonado, who helped invent her.
Claira was designed, Maldonado said, to bring a multicultural perspective to the AI space, which too often leaves Black and brown voices out of the mix.
Maldonado has showcased Claira across the globe, but in this case relied on the bot to help keynote last week's Latino AI Summit, in front of dozens of attendees who were mostly Latino and Black.
“It’s about visibility,” Claira told Gothamist in an interview. “When people see an Afro-Latina AI, it challenges the idea of who belongs in tech and opens the door for inclusive innovation.”
The Latino AI Summit, the in-person iteration of a forum that also has been featured online, is one of several efforts cropping up in the city designed to empower Black and brown people to get jobs in the AI world, hear from experts about how AI is changing the workforce, and build personalized tools that people can apply to their daily lives or jobs.
Other organizations are pushing similar initiatives, also with an eye toward reaching those often on the sidelines of the tech landscape, an arena at the center of attention, with the upcoming initial public offering of AI giant Anthropic set for Wednesday and expected to value the company at more than $1 trillion.
The Knowledge House in the Bronx provides coding and design training for underserved young people interested in the burgeoning AI economy. For adults, the Rev. Al Sharpton’s AI Fluency Initiative teaches people without tech experience the basics of AI. There, the mission is simple: It's to "close the digital divide and put the power of these tools in the hands of the people," the group states on its website.
The imperative is crystal clear to Michal Tapia, the cofounder of the Latino AI summit, which was held at Civic Hall and Berkeley College in Midtown. AI will play a major role in our future, whether people like it or not, she said.
The key now, she said, is making sure that people of all ethnicities and backgrounds are involved in the builders’ room.
“AI is happening, and it's either we get on the train, or we get left behind,” Tapia said.
A mixed view of the future
Early research on the impact of AI on Black and brown communities is a mixed bag.
A disproportionate number of Black workers hold jobs that are likely to be automated by AI, including in transportation, production and administration roles, according to a report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility.
And Black workers may already be feeling the squeeze. In a 2025 report from Jobs for the Future, a national nonprofit that influences education and workforce systems, found that 67% of Black survey respondents said they feel like AI is already impacting their jobs, compared to 57% of white survey respondents.
The report also found that more Black respondents said they feel like they need to gain new skills due to the impact of AI on their work than the overall sample of people surveyed. More than half of Black respondents in the same survey said they already use AI tools daily or weekly, compared to about 40% of all respondents.
Latinos, likewise, are underrepresented in the tech space. About 19% of the U.S. workforce is Latino, according to a report from the Kapor Foundation, which publishes research on racial equity and technology issues. But Latinos fill just 3% of board seats, 5% of executive leadership roles, and 6% of technical roles across the country’s largest tech companies, according to the same report.
To stay in the game, Maldonado said in an interview, it’s essential for all jobseekers to market themselves as AI-literate.
No matter what field you’re in, your resume should change, Maldonado said. The section that used to list skills in programs like Microsoft Office and the Adobe Suite, now should list proficiency in AI tools like Claude, Codex and Google AI Studio.
And instead of updating a resume every couple of years, jobseekers should update it once a month — that’s how fast the relevant AI tools change, he said.
But even ChatGPT, an AI chatbot, is becoming antiquated, he said. Baseline prerequisites for jobs of the future will include things like knowing how to use Claude projects, an AI work space and Cowork, a tool that helps people complete tasks. And ultimately, he added, administrative tasks should be delegated to an AI agent.
The best thing a person can do to prepare themselves for the changing workforce, Maldonado said, is to always be learning.
“Putting our heads in the sand is not the move,” he said. “ You have to tinker. You have to try these things out.”
Schools will also have to meet the moment, experts say — and some already are. Alpha School, for example, are K-12 schools with programs across the country that provide kids training on AI tools.
“ Kids are scoring through the roof ... the level of fluency and literacy that they have,” Maldonado said.
These curriculums need to be available in all schools, not just those that are predominantly white or wealthy, tech experts argue. Taylor Shead, founder of a company that develops AI-driven education, in the Jobs for the Future report, emphasized “prevention over intervention.”
“Equity and access mean meeting people where they are—going to the systems Black learners and workers are in,” she wrote in the report.
Kara Emery, the director of data science at the AI Hub of NYU’s McSilver Institute for Poverty Policy and Research, said time will tell how these things shake out.
“A lot of these projections of what AI will potentially impact are just that,” Emery said. “Projections on the future of what this technology might be able to do.”
The fear, said Emery, is that AI could make the already staggering racial income inequalities worse. But, Emery emphasized, people have a say in how things unfold.
There are “preparations and things that can be done now to try to protect against what could be a continuation of this wealth gap,” she said.
‘We are rapidly losing our jobs’
Summit attendee Fradely Delacruz, a computational scientist student and a professional data architect, said she is already feeling the economy change beneath her feet.
“Women of color specifically, we are rapidly losing our jobs in the STEM space and the research and development space,” Delacruz said. We’re “losing our jobs in huge amounts.”
Delacruz said she doesn’t entirely blame AI, which she feels is only exacerbating existing social systems and prejudice.
But, she said, half the battle is making sure all people have access to resources and information about what technology is up and coming and how it’s being designed.
“ When AI came, it kind of felt like there was other people who knew about it before we did,” Delacruz said. “By the time we're catching on, we're like, ‘Oh, we're not even part of the conversation.’ I think it's really important to position ourselves in community as innovators.”
Emery said she is seeing Black and brown New Yorkers rising to the occasion.
“ These communities aren't just sitting on the sidelines waiting for these things to have a negative impact,” Emery said. “They really have the agency.”
Not everyone is quite as optimistic.
David Gabeau, who created an online interface of AI companies in New York, is an AI entrepreneur who worked at tech-driven companies like Snapchat and Lyft before eventually starting his own company, which he has since retired.
Gabeau, who is Black, said that his race was one of the reasons he was inspired to work in tech. He said he felt like the social media he consumed growing up was based on Black culture, and he wanted to contribute to the technology’s design.
But after years of working in the space, he now fears that AI is only broadening social inequities across racial lines.
“People [working in AI] are going to get so, so so wealthy,” Gabeau said.
It’s my biggest fear, he continued, that “there will be no forcing function to spread the wealth, and that it will massively and drastically create a divide between the have and have nots.”
After spending 10 years in New York, Gabeau recently moved to San Francisco to get closer to the epicenter of AI.
There, he said, he recently spent an afternoon wearing a 4 pound headset that scanned his brain while he watched videos and answered questions. The effort was for a company that is working on using AI to develop a tool that’s akin to telepathy: the tool converts your thoughts into text without the need to type.
Gabeau said he was paid about $50 for his troubles, although he participated for the sake of his own curiosity. But the experience was an eye opener, Gabeau said. The other people in the room, many of whom were Black and brown, seemed to be there because they needed the money.
“These people's thoughts are gonna have helped create and train the AIs,” Gabeau said. “And they're definitely not gonna receive the benefits of this company getting very big.”
“It was a little predatory,” he added.
But Emery, the NYU researcher, said that sometimes the most outsize fears about AI come from within the tech industry itself. We should be wary, she said, of taking the promises of these companies’ success at face value.
“ This narrative of the inevitability of what these technologies will become is something that's often pushed by those who are currently in the big companies building them now,” Emery said.
She said the right combination of policy, education and a diversity of innovators working behind the scenes is key to preventing existing inequalities from worsening.
And Delacruz, one of the students who attended the summit, said she’s eager to put her skills to use. But at this point, she said she still feels unseen.
“They don't see the scientists and the researchers that are Black and brown and Latinos and Afro-Latinos. They don't know we exist, but we're here,” Delacruz said. “Well, let's look at the people who are professionals and let's collaborate.

https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-love.title: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind
https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-love.author: Stephanie Wambugu
https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-love.text:
What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind
"Requiem" is a fitting self-elegy for the painter, precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.
Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.
The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.
The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows.
Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman.
During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice.
The back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood. She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right.
The archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making important interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism.
“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “Alabama” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it.
But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience.
Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, and the Shanghai Museum on November 16 signed a Memorandum of Understanding cementing the two institutions’ commitment to collaboration via exhibitions, research initiatives, and curatorial exchange. Met director and CEO Max Hollein and Shanghai Museum director Chu Xiaobo signed the document at People’s Square, at the Shanghai institution.
The MoU extends a partnership begun between the two museums in 1980, when the Shanghai Museum took part in the Met’s exhibition “The Great Bronze Age of China.” Since then, the institutions have exchanged loans for a variety of exhibitions; their first cooperatively organized exhibition, “Recasting the Past: The Art of Chinese Bronzes, 1100–1900,” took place last year at both venues.
“The friendship between the two institutions, spanning more than four decades, is built on a shared passion for art and cultural heritage and mutual trust,” said Chu in a statement. “The MoU will further strengthen cooperation in collections, exhibition planning and scholarship, enabling Chinese audiences to experience artistic treasures from around the world while introducing more international visitors to the rich Chinese civilization. The partnership will help foster dialogue and mutual understanding between different cultures.”
“Our collaboration with the Shanghai Museum is rooted in a shared belief in the power of art to foster understanding between cultures,” said Hollein in a statement, noting that he had been impressed by Chu’s leadership of the institution. “This agreement reflects the Met’s deep commitment to extending the reach of our collection and cultivating meaningful connections with global audiences. Such rigorous scholarship and international cooperation are central to the museum’s mission, and we are excited to bring our longstanding institutional friendship to a new level.”
The announcement of the collaboration comes two days before the Shanghai Museum opening of “Jewelry: The Body Transformed, Treasures from the Metropolitan Museum of Art,” a traveling exhibition for which the Shanghai Museum provided objects in addition to those from the Met collection. Later this year, the Met will loan five works for a show at Shanghai Museum titled “Sonorous Silence: The Painting and Calligraphy of Bada Shanren on the 400th Anniversary of His Birth.”

Forty-five percent of respondents to a survey conducted by the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation and Critical Minded in 2026 felt that current business models are unsustainable without “profound changes” to the funding landscape for arts and culture content. “Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent arts and culture publications across 34 states and the District of Columbia about the financial and free-speech pressures they have faced over the past two years, how they address these pressures, and whether their strategies are sustainable. The results are dire. Nearly 65 percent of respondents indicated that financial support primarily comes from foundation and philanthropic grants, yet more than 40 percent reported a decrease in this category. These grants frequently determine whether publications are able to offer a standard of minimum pay for contributors, which in turn affects a publication’s ability to attract such funding. Publications with annual budgets under $49,000 saw an 83 percent decrease in funding through grants, a likely result of foundations preferring to award money to organizations with nonprofit status. 
One respondent said, “Without nonprofit status, which is difficult and time-consuming for an independent, volunteer-run publication to get, it is near impossible now for us to get grants from state agencies or foundations.” The report also identified a correlation between financial precarity and a publication’s experience with censorship, particularly in the South. “Outlets covering marginalized communities also described how rollbacks to funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion programs have resulted in reductions, further exacerbating longstanding inequities in which cultures are disseminated and discussed,” the report details. 
Overall, the report determined that arts journalism is not supported with the same consistency and resources as other forms of journalism, and yet it is equally vital. “Art in all its forms reflects our experiences of increasingly complicated and challenging times,” the report notes, “and arts journalism helps us understand, document, and share those experiences. It also serves as a platform for the exchange of opinions, arguments, and ideas that can lead to new ways of interacting, understanding, and existing together.”
