https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Mera Aladam
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
- Kuwait’s foreign ministry has condemned the latest Iranian drone attack on its territory. Iran’s army has said it fired a drone targeting the Ali al-Salem Airbase in Kuwait. The General Command of the Bahrain Defence Force has also accused Iran of ongoing attacks on the country, after it said it intercepted a number of aerial attacks on Wednesday.
- The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh. Earlier, the coalition also claimed to have carried out a “precision operation” against Houthi military capabilities as well as destroying 60 military targets across Yemen’s governorates of Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada.
- Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior said that civil defence teams evacuated a multi-storey building in the Gulf country's north west due to a fire. "Civil Defence evacuated a multi-story building in Souq Waqif as a precaution, and extinguished a fire in the building. No injuries were reported," the ministry said in a statement, adding that investigations are underway to determine the cause of the blaze.
- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio cast doubt about reports of an "imminent threat" from Iran on Washington. Rubio also questioned the credibility of sources cited in a CNN report about an alleged Iranian plot targeting the US capital, saying: "Some of your intelligence sources are liars; others are liars and criminals."
- US President Donald Trump said that the US is "doing very well in Iran, to put it mildly" during a visit to the Philippines. Trump's comments come during his meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, where he also announced that Washington is expanding its defence cooperation with Manila.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Garth Cartwright
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.”
Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats.
“Bobby’s songs sound like him talking to you,” says Beth McKee, a New Orleans-based singer-songwriter whose 2009 album I’m That Way celebrates Charles’s songs. She explains his particular gift: “They’re conversational, but never ordinary. He had a way of getting right to the heart of something without dressing it up.”
Robert Charles Guidry was born to French-speaking parents in Abbeville, Louisiana. Aged 14, he heard Hank Williams and Fats Domino on the radio, and despite not playing any instruments, began composing songs in his head to sing in high school bands. At a concert in Crowley, Louisiana, the owner of a record shop noted how the crowd went crazy for a Guidry original called See You Later, Alligator. He called Leonard Chess, the boss of Chess Records in Chicago, and instructed young Robert to sing the song down the phone. Chess signed him on the spot and arranged for a recording session in New Orleans – Robert Guidry became the anglicised Bobby Charles.
Later Alligator (Chess abbreviated the title) scored on the R&B charts and Charles was flown to Chicago to meet Chess, who reportedly said: “Motherfucker! You’re not Black?” To which Charles replied: “No, but I’m Cajun – is that close enough?”
Sent on the road as part of a Chess package tour – with Chuck Berry as headliner – Charles was the only white artist. “I had to eat in the kitchens and back rooms and sleep in the Black hotels with all of ’em,” Charles said in 1995. “Brother to brother, you know. I toured quite a bit until it got weird. A couple of white guys tried to shoot me, ’cos they didn’t want to see me hanging out with the Black guys.”
This, alongside Bill Haley scoring a huge hit with See You Later, Alligator, determined Charles would almost never perform again, and instead he became a songwriter for other artists. Swamp pop was the tag given to the blend of Cajun, country and R&B Charles helped pioneer; swamp pop veteran Allan recalls him influencing the local scene. “Bobby gave me a song called Your Picture, one of my best local hits,” he says, “so he really helped my career. He didn’t take credit for swamp pop – I never heard him use that term – but he showed us Cajuns how we could write our own songs, get this new sound”.
Charles’s relationship with Chess ended acrimoniously, but not long after, an encounter with Fats Domino led to Domino recording two remarkable Charles originals, Before I Grow Too Old and Walking to New Orleans. Both were hits, and in 1961 the New Orleans R&B singer Clarence “Frogman” Henry had another with But I Do.
Charles briefly attempted to run his own label, before settling in Nashville. Busted for drugs, he fled while on bail, eventually drifting into Woodstock, New York. Befriended by the local music community, Charles was introduced to music mogul Albert Grossman – manager of the Band and Bob Dylan – who signed Bobby to his Bearsville label and ensured the Nashville arrest warrant got dismissed. Backed by the Band (except Robbie Robertson), guitarist Amos Garrett and pianist and old Louisiana pal Dr John, Charles’s eponymous 1972 debut album is an outlier: bruised, weary, stoned and very soulful, it’s easily among the finest of that discombobulated era.
Although British broadcaster and writer Charlie Gillett called Bobby Charles “album of the year”, not many got to hear it as Charles’s relationship with Grossman quickly soured. He then joined Paul Butterfield’s Better Days, a band led by blues harmonica player Butterfield, who released two albums in 1973, also overlooked gems. Geoff Muldaur, the band’s lead vocalist, recalls Charles affectionately.
“Bobby had the most beautiful speaking voice,” he says. “French was his first language and he spoke English in a unique way. Actually, everything he said sounded like a song title. I’d be driving us across the US and he’d be speaking and I’d think ‘Write that down, it could be a song!’ He couldn’t play an instrument, so he’d sing us his songs and, at the same time, use his arms to demonstrate the rhythms and changes for when he wasn’t singing. He was very talented.”
When Better Days imploded Charles headed back to Louisiana, settling in a house by the bayou (the area’s swamps) with a pet alligator. Muldaur visited him in 1975 and got a taste of Cajun culture.
“One night Bobby suggested we go hear some music at Jay’s Lounge. On arrival, we headed around the back where I found the locals excited about cock fighting. Bobby introduced me to his friends, saying: ‘We all coon-asses!’” – a broad, rustic term for Cajuns. “Pretty quickly I had enough cock fighting so we went into the lounge: it had a sign outside saying ‘Blues Tonight’. I found Lightnin’ Hopkins and Jimmy Reed performing.”
Charles sang backing vocals on the Band’s live Rock of Ages album, and appeared at their 1976 farewell concert, The Last Waltz. Charles features on the soundtrack album singing a rousing Down South in New Orleans. Inexplicably (but for a recluse, suitably), he doesn’t appear in Martin Scorsese’s concert film.
Charles didn’t issue any new music until self-released 1987 album Clean Water. Here he sang of environmental concerns, focusing on his beloved bayous being polluted. From then on he would occasionally release a new album on his Rice ‘N’ Gravy label, never performing and rarely giving interviews. In 2004 Malcolm Mills of the UK’s Proper Records sought out Charles, so to license his albums for European release.
“I went down to meet Bobby face-to-face in Lake Charles, Louisiana,” says Mills. “He wanted to get to see who he was likely to be dealing with, because he certainly knew how to smell a rat. I passed the test.” A friendship developed, and Mills decided Charles deserved a box set covering his entire career. “I wanted to honour his life and career.”
Everyone I speak to emphasises what a remarkable songwriter Charles was. “His songs are a masterclass in simplicity, not overthinking,” says Richey. “He expressed deep feelings eloquently,” adds Muldaur. For a good example, reach for The Jealous Kind, one of Charles’s most covered songs, in which a brooding suitor is unable to accept his ex-partner has moved on. There are many fine versions – Etta James, Joe Cocker, Delbert McClinton – but none matches Ray Charles’s chilling 1977 effort.
After losing his bayou house to fire, Charles resettled in the remote coastal enclave of Holly Beach. Then, in 2005, Hurricane Rita left him homeless and Charles spent his last years living in a trailer, raging against the music and oil industries.
“Bobby would get angry at the corporations and people who dump shit in the Mississippi river,” says Richey, who befriended Charles when working at the nearby Dockside Studio. “Louisiana’s losing its coastline and, as the oil companies employ so many, people are scared to speak up. Not Bobby: he was furious at those who kill our habitat.” McKee, who Charles invited to sing on his final album, 2010’s Timeless, recalls: “Bobby was wounded. He’d been hurt by the music industry and things like Hurricane Rita.”
Richey notes how Charles “had a dual personality – warm and generous or paranoid and angry, especially when drinking vodka and smoking spliff. He got bitter about all the ripoffs he endured in the industry.” But Richey adds that Charles would still sometimes get back together with Dr John. “I engineered a session they did called Solution for Pollution – sadly it’s not been released – and I recall how happy everyone was in the studio. They’d make music, and he was filled with joy again.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
The New York Times faces backlash over report suggesting a possible link between Iranian dams and underground missile facilities, raising fears US could use the claims to target vital infrastructure.
A New York Times (NYT) story suggesting that some of Iran’s dams and water infrastructure may have been built to support the country’s missile programme has sparked fierce backlash, with commentators warning the report could help justify further attacks on civilian facilities.
The controversy comes as Washington threatens renewed military action against Iran, following months of war that have already left the country’s energy facilities, bridges, water infrastructure and other civilian sites damaged.
“The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said in a post on X.
The newspaper has defended its reporting, insisting it accurately represented the views of its experts.
However, several experts quoted by the publication have publicly challenged the implications of the investigation, questioning the evidence behind the proposed link between dams and military installations.
The controversy has also revived memories of the NYT’s reporting in the lead-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, when the paper’s journalists helped amplify claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction that later proved unfounded.
What did the NYT report say?
Published on Tuesday, the story, headlined “War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason”, examined whether Iran’s extensive network of dams, pipelines and water-transfer projects could be connected to its underground missile programme.
The report cited researchers who observed geographical similarities between the locations of dams and sites targeted by US and Israeli air strikes.
According to the report, some of the water and military experts the NYT spoke to concluded that the “water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup”.
However, the newspaper itself acknowledged, “Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.”
Why is the report causing a backlash?
Critics fear that portraying dams as potentially serving military purposes could provide a justification for attacking infrastructure essential to millions of civilians.
US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have damaged oil facilities, power plants, water reservoirs, bridges, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened further attacks, saying last week that key Iranian infrastructure could be destroyed within three days.
Political analyst Rami Khouri called the NYT report “troubling”, saying it reaffirmed his concerns about US mainstream media being “complicit in the US-Israeli criminal attacks on Iran, just as it was during the war on Iraq decades ago and the ongoing genocide in Gaza”.
“The telltale sign of non-credible wobbly journalism is when conditional words like ‘speculative’, ‘suggestive’, ‘may have developed’, ‘may shed light’, ‘suspect’, and ‘long-term riddle’ occur more often than any definitive, evidence-based facts.”
Khouri said it was “not definitive and verified reporting” and “another attempt to support the US-Israeli urgency to find any reason to carry out more war crimes against Iran” by attacking critical infrastructure.
“Another sad day for US mainstream journalism,” he added.
Why is the story falling apart?
Aside from online criticism from readers and commentators, experts cited in the story have themselves come out against aspects of the report.
Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University’s water institute and a former senior Iranian environmental official, one of the experts cited in the story, challenged the report’s reasoning.
“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” he wrote on X.
“Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles! This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure. The New York Times should know better.”
Madani also questioned the newspaper’s claim that seven experts had supported its analysis. “I’m one of the people quoted in the article, but my comments had nothing to do with dams or missiles!” he added.
Nima Shokri, a water-security expert at Hamburg University of Technology, whose research featured prominently in the investigation, also issued a clarification.
“The proximity of dams to military targets does not establish why those dams were built, nor does it justify attacks on them,” he said on X.
A third researcher quoted in the article echoed Shokri’s comments.
“I fully agree [with Shokri],” Amir Aghakouchak, a water expert at the University of California, Irvine, wrote on X, sharing Shokri’s X post.
“Dams and water infrastructure are essential to civilian life and must never become targets of military attacks. Regardless of their location or potential strategic significance, their primary roles in water supply, food security, energy, and environmental sustainability must not be overlooked. Protecting these critical resources should be a priority, regardless of politics or conflict.”
The newspaper rejected accusations that its investigation could provide a pretext for military attacks.
“Our report on Iranian dams accurately cited research and analysis by seven international experts on Iran’s environment and military presence,” spokesperson Nicole Taylor said.
She added that the NYT’s journalists had sought to explain Iran’s infrastructure investment and the effects of US and Israeli attacks on civilians.
“Framing the independent reporting as a pretext for violence is dangerous,” Taylor said.
One of the story’s co-authors, Sanam Mahoozi, said that “neither I nor our report endorses or justifies attacks on dams or other infrastructure”.
“As a journalist, I welcome rigorous, constructive criticism, but I hope some users will critique the report fairly, based on what was actually written,” she posted on X. The story was co-written with Erika Solomon, the NYT bureau chief for Iraq and Iran.
What has Iran said?
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as “rubbish”, accusing what he suggested was pro-Israel media of promoting narratives reminiscent of the run-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq.
“Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it,” he wrote on X.
Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, accused the newspaper of preparing the ground for further attacks on civilian infrastructure.
“New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” he posted on X.
Why are people questioning the NYT’s credibility?
The controversy has revived widespread criticism of the newspaper’s reporting before the US-led invasion of Iraq, when claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction helped build public support for war.
Judith Miller, a former NYT journalist, was among the reporters whose coverage amplified claims about Iraq’s weapons programmes that subsequently proved unfounded.
In September 2002, Miller co-authored a report claiming Iraq had intensified its pursuit of nuclear weapons, citing US officials who alleged that Baghdad was seeking aluminium tubes for uranium enrichment.
Former Vice President Dick Cheney cited the newspaper’s reporting on aluminium tubes to bolster President George W Bush’s administration’s case against Iraq. The claims were later discredited.
Two months after the invasion of Iraq began in March 2003, Miller co-authored a report citing that US intelligence agencies had concluded that two mysterious trailers found in Iraq were mobile units to “produce germs for weapons”.
However, a year after the US war on Iraq began, the NYT acknowledged serious shortcomings in its reporting on the build-up to war, including its reliance on Iraqi defectors and exiles seeking regime change.
“We have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been,” it said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Emicida participa de congresso sobre batalhas de rima em BH, nesta quinta (19)
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O rapper Emicida desembarca em Belo Horizonte, nesta quinta-feira (19) para participar do 2º Congresso Brasileiro das Batalhas de Rima. O artista ministra, às 19h, a palestra “Qual futuro queremos construir por meio das batalhas de rima?”, no Viaduto Santa Tereza, na região Central da capital. A atividade é gratuita e aberta ao público.
O encontro propõe uma reflexão sobre o papel das batalhas de rima na cultura brasileira, os desafios enfrentados pelo movimento Hip Hop e as perspectivas para os próximos anos. A partir de sua trajetória, Emicida deve compartilhar experiências e discutir possibilidades de construção coletiva para o fortalecimento dessas manifestações culturais.
Antes de alcançar reconhecimento nacional, o rapper construiu parte de sua trajetória nas batalhas de improviso de São Paulo, no final dos anos 2000. O artista ficou conhecido pela habilidade nas disputas de rima, que foram fundamentais para o início de sua carreira na música.
:: Relembre: Emicida recebe título Honoris Causa da Ufrgs e reafirma saberes das periferias ::
Nas redes sociais, Emicida destacou sua relação com o Viaduto Santa Tereza e relembrou a primeira vez que esteve no local, em agosto de 2012, durante a primeira edição do Duelo Nacional de MCs. Na ocasião, realizou um show surpresa no centro de Belo Horizonte.
“Quatorze anos depois, estamos de volta ao solo sagrado do freestyle brasileiro convidando geral pra se encontrar e trocar uma ideia de responsa sobre batalhas de rima, cultura Hip Hop e as perspectivas de futuro que queremos construir coletivamente”, afirmou o rapper, nas redes sociais, ao convocar o público para o encontro.
A escolha do Viaduto Santa Tereza como palco da atividade também carrega um significado para a cultura urbana da capital mineira. O espaço é um dos principais pontos de encontro do Hip Hop em Belo Horizonte e recebe tradicionalmente o Duelo de MCs, competição que reúne artistas de diferentes regiões do país e integra a história das batalhas de rima brasileiras.
Serviço
Palestra com Emicida – “Qual futuro queremos construir por meio das batalhas de rima?”
Data: 19 de novembro de 2026 (quinta-feira)
Horário: 19h
Local: Viaduto Santa Tereza
Endereço: Avenida dos Andradas, região Central, Belo Horizonte (MG)
Entrada: gratuita

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Traumas of Sudan war lead to wave of drug addiction
Anguish caused by conflict sees a growing number of young people turn to drugs.
Khartoum, Sudan – Mohammed Awad never imagined that his life would change so dramatically when war broke out in his home city of Khartoum in April 2023 when he was aged 17.
He found himself displaced and forced out of school, moving from one state to another accompanied by his cousins and searching for a safe place where he could escape the horrors of war.
But what began as a journey in search of safety became the beginning of a personal tragedy, one experienced by millions of people in Sudan who are in the midst of one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises in which killing and displacement have become routine.
“I started taking drugs to forget what I have seen and the horrors I have been through in Khartoum during the first months of the war. My friends and my cousin were killed in front of me,” he told Al Jazeera. “I am trying to recover now, so I can proceed with my education and life.”
The conflict between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group saw the capital become one of the initial epicentres of this power struggle between the two former military allies.
The war trapped thousands of people in Khartoum State in their homes for weeks or forced them to flee, but since the SAF expelled the RSF from the region in May last year, it has now become a haven for millions of people fleeing fighting elsewhere in Sudan. The war has led to a humanitarian catastrophe with at least 59,000 people killed and 14 million people forced to leave their homes in a country with a population of 52 million. Displacement is more than the simple act of moving from one place to another but a journey marked by fear, anxiety and instability with increasingly limited options in life.
For those such as Awad caught in the pressures of displacement and the absence of a supportive environment, drugs have become a way of dealing with an unbearable reality.
“I entered rehabilitation centres many times, and I quickly returned to addiction. I take pills and sometimes weed. I want to stop, but I keep failing over and over again,” Awad said.
The war in Sudan has not only severely impacted individual civilians’ lives but has also torn apart the social fabric of the country. The lack of security and poverty have also led to a proliferation of drugs manufacturing and trade, particularly the highly addictive amphetamine Captagon. According to government officials, areas currently or formerly under RSF control are a particular problem.
Treatment and care
The Qadreen Center for Addiction Treatment is one of the few charitable institutions dealing with the problem in Khartoum, and doctors in the capital told Al Jazeera there is growing demand for their services.
“The centre continues to provide its medical services both before and after the outbreak of the war,” the centre’s director, Lubna Ali, said.
“Following the war, it witnessed a significant increase in the number of cases seeking treatment amid growing needs for mental health and addiction recovery services.”
Since the war has broken out, the centre has treated 10,100 cases ranging from patients in need of psychological support for war-related trauma to those with drug addiction. Ali said 135 such individuals have been treated “in their recovery journey”.
Young people are particularly affected by the war, witnessing horrific violence, displacement, the loss of friends and relatives, interrupted education and quickly declining employment opportunities.
Weakened institutions and a deteriorating security situation have undermined oversight efforts and the ability of health services to respond to the addiction crisis.
Dr Aisha Almobasher, a psychiatrist at the Bitmakaly National Organization, which provides psychological and therapeutic support to individuals affected by war and addiction, told Al Jazeera that some areas of Sudan are worse affected by the drug problem than others.
“The growing number of people seeking treatment suggests that this is more than a passing phenomenon. Many of those struggling with addiction come from areas previously controlled by the Rapid Support Forces, RSF, where, following their withdrawal, drugs reportedly became more widely available and trafficking networks expanded,” she told Al Jazeera.
“In some states, drugs also became a means of attracting and recruiting young people, particularly into the ranks of RSF fighters, drawing many of them onto a dark path.”
Drug seizures
According to a report published by the Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker in March, 19 incidents involving the seizures of drugs or manufacturing facilities were recorded in Sudan from 2015 to 2025 with a notable acceleration since the outbreak of the war.
These figures refer to seizures and estimated production capacity not actual drug consumption. Nevertheless, they reveal the scale of the problem and the transformation taking place in the country’s illicit drug trade.
Major-General (Legal) Mohamed Al-Moatasim Okasha, director of Sudan’s General Directorate for Anti-Narcotics, said its teams have dealt with an increase in drug manufacturing and production since the war began.
They have found advanced drug production facilities in areas retaken from the RSF by the SAF, including areas in and around Khartoum. El-Radom, an area in South Darfur State in western Sudan, has become a well-known cannabis-growing region, he said.
“It remains under RSF control and is expected to return to the control of the Sudanese armed forces soon. Throughout the past three years of war, antinarcotics operations in this area have been suspended with no other authority able to effectively address the problem due to its inaccessibility under RSF control,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Meanwhile, the use and circulation of other narcotic substances have been increasing, particularly Captagon, crystal methamphetamine (ice) and drugs such as tramadol. However, these substances remain less widespread than cannabis and other traditionally prevalent drugs.”
A huge facility for manufacturing Captagon pills was recently discovered by the SAF north of Khartoum, close to an oil refinery that was formerly under RSF control.
SAF forces uncovered drugs manufacturing equipment valued at about $3m. The facility was capable of producing 100,000 Captagon pills per hour with raw materials potentially able to produce 700 million pills.
“These are not merely allegations of drug trafficking, smuggling or distribution. They are evidence of industrial-scale drug production taking place in areas that were under RSF control,” Okasha told Al Jazeera.
“As for drug use among combatants, there have been reports and testimonies indicating that quantities of narcotic substances were found in the possession of captured militia members. This highlights how widespread these substances have become and how readily accessible they are to fighters.”
Drug trafficking and manufacturing have become weapons of war, not just illicit sources of income, and they are directly impacting the conflict between the SAF and RSF, he said. Captagon has become a regional issue with facilities producing the drug in Syria during the rule of former President Bashar al-Assad flooding the illicit market.
While the new government in Damascus is trying to crack down on these facilities in southern Syria, Captagon production is a growing problem in other regional conflict areas such as Sudan.
“Sudan faces this growing threat amid the ongoing conflict,” Okasha said. “Through strong nationwide coordination, we are intensifying seizures and disrupting smuggling, trafficking and production networks. Our mission is to stop the spread of narcotics, protect our youth and safeguard future generations. Combating drugs is a national security priority.”
“The drug problem in Sudan cannot be viewed in isolation. It is a regional challenge, and Sudan is part of a region experiencing a growing drug crisis.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Maracastelo leva às ruas de João Pessoa a ancestralidade e a força das mulheres negras no 11º Arrastão da Consciência Negra
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A força da ancestralidade negra ocupa as ruas do bairro Castelo Branco, em João Pessoa, no próximo dia 20 de novembro. Em sua 11ª edição, o Arrastão da Consciência Negra Maracastelo presta homenagem às Rainhas de Maracatu, mulheres que desempenham papel fundamental na preservação da memória, da espiritualidade e dos saberes das manifestações da cultura afro-brasileira.
Promovido pelo Ponto de Cultura Maracastelo, o cortejo integra as celebrações do Dia Nacional da Consciência Negra e transforma as ruas do bairro em espaço de encontro entre gerações, tradições e expressões culturais. A proposta deste ano é reconhecer o protagonismo feminino na história do maracatu, destacando as mulheres que mantêm vivos os fundamentos de uma tradição transmitida ao longo de gerações.
“O Arrastão da Consciência Negra Maracastelo, que chega à sua 11ª edição em 2026, é, além da culminância da Oficina Maracastelo, a celebração de um processo formativo que envolve integrantes antigos e recém-chegados ao coletivo. É um momento de reflexão e valorização da herança cultural de matriz africana, da ancestralidade negra do maracatu e da importância da luta e da resistência da população negra na construção do patrimônio cultural brasileiro, nordestino e paraibano”, comenta a Mestra Angela Gaeta.
Ela explica que, no universo do Maracatu Nação, as rainhas ocupam um lugar de destaque na Corte Real. Suas coroas, mantos e funções carregam significados que vão além da representação festiva, expressando identidade, ancestralidade e resistência. A homenagem também chama atenção para trajetórias de mulheres negras que, apesar de sua contribuição histórica, nem sempre receberam o devido reconhecimento.
Encontro entre tradição pernambucana e cultura quilombola
A edição de 2026 contará com a participação especial de integrantes da Nação Estrela Brilhante do Recife (PE), agremiação madrinha do Maracastelo, fundada em 1906. Um dos momentos marcantes será a presença de Nana, Dama do Passo da Estrela Brilhante, conduzindo a Calunga Dona Erundina, figura de profundo significado simbólico e espiritual para o Maracatu Nação.
A programação também terá a participação da Mestra Ednalva e do Coletivo Cultural Caiana dos Crioulos, comunidade quilombola localizada em Alagoa Grande, na Paraíba, que levará ao cortejo a tradição do Coco de Roda.
A cultura se eterniza
O Arrastão também representa a culminância da Oficina Maracastelo 2026, realizada durante o segundo semestre no Centro de Convivência da Pessoa Idosa (CCPI), no bairro Castelo Branco.
As atividades proporcionaram aos participantes experiências de formação sobre a história, a musicalidade e os fundamentos do Maracatu de Baque Virado. Agora, os novos brincantes terão a oportunidade de compartilhar com a comunidade o aprendizado construído ao longo das oficinas, integrando-se ao cortejo ao lado dos integrantes mais antigos do coletivo.
Para a Mestra Gaeta, o evento representa muito mais do que uma apresentação cultural. É a celebração de um processo de formação, valorização da herança africana e reconhecimento da contribuição da população negra para a construção da sociedade brasileira: “É também um ato político e educativo de enfrentamento ao racismo estrutural e religioso”, destaca.
Ela ressalta ainda a relação construída entre o Maracastelo e os moradores do Castelo Branco, território onde o grupo desenvolve suas atividades e realiza o cortejo.
“É muito especial levar às ruas do Castelo Branco, nosso território, o maracatu que representa o bairro, ao encontro dos moradores que já aguardam nas portas de suas casas para celebrar conosco. É uma forma de afirmar pertencimento, identidade, memória e resistência por meio da cultura popular”, afirma.
Onze anos de história e resistência cultural
Com atuação na Paraíba desde 2014, o Maracastelo consolidou o Arrastão da Consciência Negra como uma importante iniciativa de valorização das culturas de matriz africana em João Pessoa. Ao longo de onze edições, o projeto mantém a tradição de celebrar o 20 de novembro por meio da ocupação dos espaços públicos, da formação cultural e do fortalecimento das identidades negras.
Reconhecido como Ponto de Cultura pelo Ministério da Cultura, o coletivo desenvolve atividades gratuitas de formação, difusão e salvaguarda da cultura popular, além de ações educativas em parceria com escolas, universidades e organizações comunitárias.
No dia da Consciência Negra, o cortejo reafirma que a cultura também é instrumento de memória, educação e transformação social. Ao levar os tambores às ruas, o Maracastelo celebra as mulheres que preservam a tradição, homenageia a ancestralidade africana e mantém viva uma manifestação que faz parte do patrimônio cultural brasileiro.
A participação é gratuita e aberta ao público.
SERVIÇO
11º Arrastão da Consciência Negra Maracastelo
- Tema: Homenagem às Rainhas de Maracatu
- Data: 20 de novembro de 2026 (sexta-feira)
- Concentração: 15h
- Saída do cortejo: 16h
- Local: Centro de Convivência da Pessoa Idosa (CCPI), bairro Castelo Branco, João Pessoa (PB)
- Entrada: Gratuita
- Realização: Coletivo Maracastelo – Maracatu de Baque Virado

Iran's foreign minister vows 'unforgettable response' if US-Israeli attacks target civilian infrastructure
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei has slammed a recent New York Times report that claimed Tehran was using civilian infrastructure for military purposes.
"The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure," Baqaei said.
"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations, including the recent claims published by The New York Times and the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged 'dirty bomb' propagated by CNN."
Baqaei added that these reports are attempting to "manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities".
"Iran knows well how to respond to any act of aggression and ensure that it is met with an unforgettable response," he further warned.
The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure. During the recent acts of aggression by the USrael against Iran, water storage reservoirs in Khomeyn (Markazi Province), Haftkel (Khuzestan Province), and Bamani (Sirik), as well as desalination facilities on Qeshm Island, in Nikshahr and Tis (Sistan and Baluchestan Province), and in the village of Banji in Jask, were targeted. These attacks disrupted or cut off water supplies to civilian populations and residential areas. Portraying the geographical proximity of civilian infrastructure to military facilities as grounds for designating it a legitimate military target is neither a credible argument nor a substantiated claim. Rather, it is a sinister fallacy intended to legitimize attacks against civilian infrastructure and normalize grave violations of international humanitarian law. Although the United States today appears to maintain, with an air of arrogance and a medieval mindset, that the law need not be invoked when dealing with those who wield the sword, international humanitarian law - particularly Article 56 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions - provides special protection for dams and similar installations. Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations, including the recent claims published by The New York Times and the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged “dirty bomb” propagated by CNN. Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities. Iran knows well how to respond to any act of aggression and ensure that it is met with an unforgettable response. The international community, however, must recognize that silence and appeasement in the face of sinister campaigns to normalize flagrant violations of international legal norms and fundamental humanitarian and moral principles will have devastating consequences - not merely for the region, but for humanity as a whole.
— Esmaeil Baqaei (@IRIMFA_SPOX) November 17, 2026

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’ in speech
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Taz Ali (now) and Kate Lamb (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’ in speech
Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin
Trump and Putin shake hands ahead of Apec welcome banquet
US president Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian president Vladimir Putin, as China’s Xi Jinping looks on, ahead of the welcome banquet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China:
Donald Trump has arrived at the welcome banquet with Xi Jinping:
The newswires are carrying pictures of world leaders arriving for the welcome banquet at the Apec summit, including Russia’s Vladimir Putin:
Putin and Trump could meet informally during Apec summit, Russia state media reports
Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump could have several opportunities to speak during the Apec summit in China, according to Russia’s state news agency, Tass.
Citing Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, Tass reported that the two leaders could exchange words informally at various points during the summit.
They will communicate “on their feet, on the steps, in chairs”, Ushakov reportedly said, suggesting their interactions need not be limited to a formal sit-down meeting.
Xi says he hopes to build 'stable' China-US ties with Trump - state media
Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.
Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
Xinhua reported the following remarks by the Chinese president:
 When I visited the United States in September this year, president Trump and his wife made a special trip to the airport to welcome me, and a grand welcoming ceremony was held.
China is a nation of courtesy, with a tradition of reciprocity. I welcome you back to China and look forward to exchanging in-depth views with you on major issues concerning China–US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape, so as to advance a constructive, strategic and stable relationship between China and the US based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.”
Xi hails ‘unshaken’ China-Russia ties after talks with Putin
in Shenzhen
Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin.
In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
Xi also urged closer political and military ties between the two countries.
 
He said “the two sides should leverage the mechanisms for exchanges between the two countries’ governments, legislative bodies, militaries and political parties, ensuring that the consensus reached by the two countries’ heads of state is effectively implemented”, according to the readout.
In a notable gesture, Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen, reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.

Le procès de sept membres du canal Telegram « Femmeblancherie » s’ouvre devant le tribunal judiciaire de Paris, ce mercredi 18 novembre. Entre des appels aux féminicides et des fichages racistes, plusieurs dizaines d’abonnés sont accusés d’une trentaine de délits, dont « provocation publique à commettre un crime ».
Pendant plus de deux ans, 1 758 abonnés à un canal Telegram ont disserté sur comment mettre au pas les « vaginopodes » – réduisant les femmes à des « vagins sur pattes » –, sur comment lutter « contre la juiverie » ou encore ficher les femmes qui « aiment les nègres ». Fondé en avril 2024, « Femmeblancherie » est au centre d’un procès d’ampleur, dont la première audience est prévue mercredi 18 novembre devant le tribunal judiciaire de Paris.

Irankrieg: Bahrain und Kuwait geraten erneut unter Beschuss
Die Golfstaaten Kuwait und Bahrain geraten erneut unter feindlichen Beschuss. Der Iran hatte zuvor Vergeltung für neue US-Attacken angekündigt.
dpa | Die Golfstaaten Bahrain und Kuwait sind erneut Ziel iranischer Angriffe geworden. Die Flugabwehr Bahrains habe mehrere feindliche iranische Angriffe abgewehrt und die Geschosse zerstört, teilte das Generalkommando der Streitkräfte am Morgen mit. „Der Iran setzt seine feindlichen Handlungen durch feige Attacken auf das Königreich Bahrain fort“, hieß es.
Am späten Dienstagabend hatte zudem das Militär des mit den USA verbündeten Landes Kuwait mitgeteilt, dass die Luftabwehr „Angriffe feindlicher Drohnen“ aus dem Iran abwehre. Explosionsgeräusche seien auf das Abfangen der Drohnen zurückzuführen.
Iranischen Angaben zufolge zielten beide Angriffe auf US-Stützpunkte in den Golfstaaten. In Kuwait habe die reguläre iranische Armee mit Kamikazedrohnen auf Flugabwehrstellungen und Raketenabschussrampen gezielt, berichtete die Nachrichtenagentur Tasnim. In Bahrain sei erneut der Luftwaffenstützpunkt Scheich Issa attackiert worden.
Zuletzt vermehrt Angriffe in der Region
Kurz zuvor hatte das US-Militär einen Angriff auf eine Raketenstellung der iranischen Revolutionsgarden auf der iranischen Insel Gheschm in der Straße von Hormus am Dienstag bestätigt und diesen als Vergeltungsschlag bezeichnet. Die iranischen Revolutionsgarden hatten eigenen Angaben zufolge am frühen Dienstagmorgen eine US-Radaranlage im Golfstaat Bahrain angegriffen.
Ende Februar hatten Israel und die USA ihren Krieg gegen den Iran begonnen, der unter anderem mit Gegenangriffen in der Region reagierte. US-Präsident Donald Trump hat zwar zuletzt immer wieder signalisiert, nicht zu größeren Kampfhandlungen zurückkehren zu wollen. Der Konflikt mit der Islamischen Republik ist jedoch bis heute ungelöst, Verhandlungen stecken seit Monaten in der Sackgasse.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia?
Files show Epstein-linked payments at $582m, far more than previously known, and tie Trump business dealings to suspected money laundering networks.
A leak of more than 15 million internal records from Deutsche Bank has shed new light on its dealings with United States President Donald Trump, the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and other powerful figures.
The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation, published on Tuesday by a consortium of international news outlets, has put Germany’s biggest bank back in the spotlight after years of trying to rebuild its reputation following its failures to prevent money laundering.
Here is what we know:
What was leaked and how did it happen?
Files containing millions of emails, minutes of meetings and internal reports were leaked by two whistleblowers whose identities and links to the institution have been withheld for their protection, according to Le Monde, one of the participating news outlets. The pair told the media groups they believed the bank was engaging in criminal activity and that releasing the documents was in the public interest.
An Indian journalist and a South African journalist obtained the cache, then shared it with more than 230 reporters from about 50 news organisations, including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times and The New York Times, in an internationally coordinated effort.
The material includes some nine million emails, as well as meeting minutes, due diligence reports and financial crime reports dating back to the early 2010s, many of them from the bank’s internal investigations.
The whistleblowers also passed the data to US prosecutors and financial crime authorities, and could be eligible for a reward if Washington prosecutes the bank based on their leaks. Le Monde said the whistleblowers were not paid by the journalists and placed no conditions on how the material was used.
Deutsche Bank said concerns raised by the investigation “date back many years” and that it had since strengthened its controls, adding that it did not expect any meaningful financial impact. The bank’s chairman reaffirmed the board’s support for chief executive Christian Sewing, who has run the institution since 2018.
“Deutsche Bank is a different bank today,” the bank said in a statement.
What do the leaks reveal about Trump?
The files identify more than $3m in transactions involving Trump-owned companies, including payments linked to suspected Russian and Azerbaijani money-laundering networks.
Deutsche Bank extended loans to Trump for years, even after a string of bankruptcies and defaults at his businesses from the early 1990s. By January 2021, it was his biggest creditor, with about $340m in loans to his company outstanding.
That month, following the January 6 assault on the US Capitol by protesters wanting to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s win in the presidential election, the bank ceased doing business with him, according to The New York Times. Trump had claimed the election had been rigged against him, of which there has never been any proof.
The Financial Times reported that the bank inadvertently sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term in office, and never told him about the error. Asked about the disclosure during his visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit on Tuesday, Trump said the bank should not have released that information.
“They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it,” he said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment on his remarks.
The leaked records also reveal special monitoring that the bank applied to Trump’s accounts, and its handling of them has drawn scrutiny before.
In 2019, The New York Times reported that Deutsche Bank had failed to alert US authorities to suspicious transactions linked to Trump. The bank said at the time that none of its investigators had been prevented from escalating such concerns.
What do the leaks reveal about Epstein?
The leaked files list about $582m in transactions linked to Epstein, which were flagged internally as suspicious. That is more than double the amount previously identified as being overlooked or not reported by banks during US Senate investigations. When the Senate findings were released in August, a Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the bank regretted its “historical connection” with Epstein.
Epstein, who was a US financier, became a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after pleading guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, and remained a client until 2018. He died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
Internal emails in the newly leaked cache indicate that senior executives approved Epstein as a client despite his conviction, and kept his accounts open even after warnings about the activities of Ghislaine Maxwell, his former girlfriend and associate. Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein sexually abuse teenage girls. She is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The files also reveal information about payments linked to wealthy Epstein associates such as private equity billionaire Leon Black and Wall Street financier Glenn Dubin.
A review commissioned by Black’s firm previously found he had paid Epstein $158m between 2012 and 2017 for tax and estate planning advice. Black has sought to distance himself from Epstein, repeatedly denying wrongdoing or any knowledge of his abuse of girls and young women.
The leak comes years after the bank paid fines and settlements of more than $200m over its handling of Epstein-related finances. In 2020, regulators fined it $150m for compliance failures linked to Epstein and other high-risk clients, finding that he had held more than 40 accounts at the bank. In 2023, it agreed to pay $75m to settle a suit brought by women who alleged they had been abused by him.
Who else is named in the leaks?
The documents also detail Deutsche Bank’s business dealings in Russia up until Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite concerns raised by some managers.
They include previously undisclosed internal warnings about the bank’s continued dealings with wealthy Kremlin-connected clients despite sanctions and money laundering concerns.
Those named include Russian billionaires Roman Abramovich, the former owner of English football club Chelsea, and aluminium tycoon Oleg Deripaska. Both men were sanctioned by the United Kingdom in 2022. Suleiman Kerimov, another billionaire whose name appears in the files, was sanctioned by the US in 2014 and 2018.
Transactions associated with Rifaat al-Assad, the uncle of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, also appear in the files. Rifaat, who died in January, was convicted in France in 2020 of acquiring millions of euros’ worth of property with funds diverted from the Syrian state.
Other files concern figures connected to the Sarkozy-Libya affair, in which former French President Nicolas Sarkozy was convicted in 2025 of criminal conspiracy over efforts to secure funding for his 2007 campaign from the government of late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Senado adia votação do projeto de ajuste fiscal para quarta (18)
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A votação dos quatro destaques ao Projeto de Lei Complementar 299 de 2026, que trata do ajuste fiscal proposto pelo governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), no Senado foi adiada para quarta-feira (18), a partir das 16h. A mudança foi proposta pelo presidente da Casa, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), devido à apresentação de emendas ao texto que exigiriam uma análise mais ampla que a dos destaques.
Alcolumbre pediu que o relator do projeto, senador Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM), avalie as emendas propostas para que seja realizada a votação de todos os pontos na quarta.
Mesmo sobre os quatro destaques que já estavam em discussão, não havia acordo sobre a votação. A base do governo defendeu que todos fossem rejeitados, evitando prejudicar a proposta original. Porém, o líder do PT no Senado, Camilo Santana, também avaliou que poderia não ter votos suficientes para barrar os destaques da oposição.
Senadores que votaram a favor do texto-base na semana passada não estavam presentes na votação de hoje, como Styvenson Valentim (Pode-RN), Fernando Dueire (PSD-PE), Romário (Sem Partido-RJ) e Veneziano Vital do Rêgo (MDB-PB).
O texto-base foi aprovado no Senado na semana passada por 45 votos a 31. E nesta terça-feira (17) seria realizada a votação dos quatro destaques (propostas de mudanças no texto), antes de o projeto poder seguir para a Câmara dos Deputados.
O ministro das Relações Institucionais, José Guimarães, afirmou que o governo tem um acordo com o presidente da Câmara Federal, deputado federal Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), para pautar e votar o projeto de ajuste fiscal na Casa, na sequência da votação no Senado.
“Com a conclusão do Senado, começa imediatamente a votação da Câmara. Foi um compromisso do presidente Hugo Motta esperar chegar do Senado e votar imediatamente”, afirmou Guimarães.
Motta confirmou que pode analisar o texto na sequência da votação no Senado. E já anunciou que o deputado Mauro Benevides Filho (União-CE) será o relator da proposta.
Destaques
Três destaques foram apresentados pelo PL e um pelo Republicanos.
Proposto pelo líder da oposição, senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), um destaque vai na direção de um ajuste mais duro do que o aprovado no texto-base. A emenda reduz de 2% para 0,6% o limite de crescimento real das despesas federais nos anos em que forem acionadas as medidas de contenção.
A proposta também obriga o Executivo a cortar gastos até atingir, pelo menos, o centro da meta fiscal, mesmo quando o resultado estiver dentro da margem de tolerância. Além disso, permite reduzir ou cancelar despesas obrigatórias, com exceção das obrigações constitucionais discriminadas na Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias (LDO).
O texto-base, por sua vez, blinda de qualquer contingenciamento aposentadorias, pensões, o Benefício de Prestação Continuada (BPC), a folha dos servidores federais e os pisos da saúde e da educação.
O destaque do líder do Republicanos, senador Alan Rick (AC), retira do texto a autorização para que o Executivo limite o uso de créditos tributários por empresas para quitar impostos federais. Pelos cálculos do governo, o dispositivo pode reforçar a arrecadação entre R$ 12,8 bilhões e R$ 18,3 bilhões em 2027.
Uma nota assinada por 119 entidades empresariais pede a exclusão total do trecho. Entre elas estão a Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), a Confederação da Agricultura e Pecuária do Brasil (CNA) e a Federação das Indústrias do Estado de São Paulo (Fiesp), que reclamam que os grandes empresários arcarão com a maior parte do custo do ajuste.
Os outros dois destaques do PL tratam dos repasses a estados e municípios. Um deles tenta derrubar a redução das transferências da Lei Kandir, que cairiam de R$ 4 bilhões para R$ 1 bilhão por ano entre 2027 e 2030, com o pagamento da diferença adiado. Segundo o Comitê Nacional de Secretários de Fazenda, Finanças, Receita ou Tributação dos Estados e do Distrito Federal (Comsefaz), a medida retira R$ 12 bilhões dos caixas locais até 2030.
Por fim, há uma tentativa de derrubar o teto de R$ 3 bilhões anuais para a compensação previdenciária da União a estados e municípios.
Primeiro passo
O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, afirmou, nesta terça-feira, que o pacote fiscal apresentado pelo governo federal é o “primeiro passo” para o ajuste gradual nas contas da União. Ele participou de uma audiência na Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos (CAE) do Senado Federal.
“Eu tenho dito que o governo se comprometeu com superávits nos próximos quatro anos, em todos os anos, crescentes a partir de 2028. Ficou evidente que o único caminho é um ajuste gradual, que respeite o gasto social, mas sem negacionismo com a necessidade de avançar na melhoria das contas”, disse Durigan.

Kuwait slams Iranian attacks on its territory
Kuwait’s foreign ministry has condemned the latest Iranian drone attack on its territory.
The ministry denounced the attacks as "repeated and criminal" and described it as a "direct threat" to the Gulf country's "security and stability".
"The Ministry reaffirms that the continuation of these attacks constitutes a dangerous escalation that threatens the region’s security and stability and undermines diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation and reducing tensions," the ministry said in its statement posted on X.
It added that Kuwait retains the right to "take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty, preserve its security and defend its territory and vital facilities against any aggression or threat, in exercise of its inherent right to self-defence".

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: rich world offering ‘crumbs’ to help poor countries adapt to climate breakdown, campaigners say
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Rich countries accused of offering 'crumbs' to help poor ones adapt to climate breakdown
Damien Gayle
Rich countries have been accused of offering “crumbs” to a fund for the developing world to adapt to climate change at Cop31.
At a pledging session on Tuesday night in Antalya, just $50m was pledged to the Adaptation Fund, compared to $135m pledged in Belém last year.
The Adaptation Fund finances projects and programmes to help vulnerable communities in developing countries adapt to climate change. It has operated since 2010 and is financed largely by government and private donors.
Developing countries have repeatedly emphasised their need for finance from wealthier countries, but negotiations to unlock climate finance have stalled, with wealthier countries saying they are unwilling to make any more spending commitments.
“Rich countries are offering crumbs to the Adaptation Fund while blocking the negotiations that should provide the money countries need,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the climate thinktank Power Shift Africa.
“Listening to ministers praise the Adaptation Fund before giving next to nothing, you have to wonder how they expect it to do the work they say is so important. They applaud it with one hand and starve it with the other.”
Adow said the EU was playing a leading role in blocking new finance commitments, and that its intransigence was “undermining its claim to climate leadership”. “They need to end the blockade on climate finance,” he said.
Adaptation can mean the difference between life and death, said Teresa Anderson, climate justice lead at ActionAid International. “Early warning systems mean people can get to high ground before a flood,” she said. “Resilient farming practices reduce the risk of hunger during droughts. Better infrastructure can cope with cyclones.
“It’s heartbreaking that as the need for adaptation grows, the money on offer is shrinking. This can’t continue if humanity wants to ensure its collective survival.”
California Governor Gavin Newsom was a big presence in Antalya last week, serving as the head of a US delegation that attended unofficially due to President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the international summit.
Widely seen as a top presidential contender for 2028, Newsom’s strong rhetoric in support of a fossil fuel phase out and other top climate priorities inspired hope that there’s a future for the US – the world’s second biggest emitter – in negotiations. That of course, depends on who ends up as the next resident of the White House, but Newsom made big promises regardless, as the head of California – the world’s fourth largest economy.
“The climate crisis is not complicated; it’s a fossil fuel crisis,” Newsom said before he left Cop31 last week. “They have delayed the implementation and the application of the solutions that are already at hand, and they need to be called out, and they need to be held accountable.” He also told the Guardian that California is “100%” behind the coalition of more than 50 countries that’s called for a transition away from oil, gas, and coal.
But California is also falling behind on its pledges, according to a new report from the Environmental Working Group. The state set a goal of transitioning fully to clean energy by 2045 under Newsom’s predecessor, Governor Jerry Brown. By the US nonprofit research and advocacy organization’s analysis, “even if the state returns to its historic pace of building clean energy on rooftops, as well as in greenfield locations, it won’t achieve the goal until 2063 at the earliest”. If things continue to lag that goal won’t be possible until 2069.
EWG relied on a review of California’s electricity usage forecasts and generation data to highlight where things are going wrong, according to the report, and found that robust leadership is needed to get the state – which is already being hammered by the effects of global heating – across the finish line.

Dozens of human rights groups have urged Turkish authorities to release four LGBTI activists ahead of a hearing that is scheduled to have just begun at an Istanbul court.
Four founders of an civil society group, the Social Policy, Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation Studies Association (SPoD), are among dozens of human rights defenders who have been imprisoned or subjected to criminal investigations in a crackdown that began on 12 September, according to the Turkish branch of Amnesty International. It said the operation has targeted activists under a law on associations and for criminal code provisions such as ‘obscenity’.
Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, urged authorities to immediately drop all charges and end attempts to dissolve associations for their human rights work.
“Prosecutions of LGBTI human rights defenders and actions to dissolve associations mark a dangerous escalation in efforts by Türkiye’s authorities to criminalize LGBTI rights and must be condemned and rejected,” she said. “These actions threaten not only the organizations directly targeted, but can also have a chilling effect on independent civil society organizations and human rights defenders more broadly in Türkiye. People must be able to defend LGBTI rights without fear of punishment.”
On the weekend, Turkish LGBTQ+ activists and climate protesters from around the world marched together in Antalya in defiance of the Turkish government’s crackdown.
Cop31 aiming to 'protect mechanisms more than goals' - former Colombian environment minister
Fiona Harvey
The main aim of Cop31 appears to be to protect the UN climate negotiating mechanisms than to achieve real progress, the former Colombian minister in charge of this year’s Santa Marta conference has warned.
Irene Veléz Torres oversaw the Santa Marta meeting in April of more than 50 countries pledging to “transition away from fossil fuels”. Under that “coalition of the willing”, countries are producing roadmaps to phase out fossil fuel extraction and use. Eleven countries have now published such plans, including Germany, France, the Netherlands and Ireland.
However, Colombia’s government has changed since the Santa Marta conference, with Abelardo de la Espriella, a right-wing populist and ally of Donald Trump, taking power. He has dumped many of the environmental policies of the previous government.
Veléz said Cop31 was lacking in ambition. “It’s like the main aim is more to protect the mechanism than to protect the goals or to be more ambitious about the goals … I agree that multilateralism has to be protected, but this is not enough. Protecting the mechanism is not going to save us from overshooting [the 1.5C temperature target of the Paris agreement].”
Colombia hosted the Santa Marta conference because of an exasperation with the slow speed of the Cop process, which proceeds by consensus and so can be held to ransom by bad actors. “The production of fossil fuels continues to be a taboo [at Cops],” Veléz said. “Santa Marta tried to break down the taboo and we made a great success by bringing together 57 governments and more than 2,000 people, but is difficult to bridge to this scenario if it has to go to the negotiations [of a Cop]. It won’t happen in the negotiations.”
Colombia’s change of government means it will no longer take a lead, but the baton has passed to Tuvalu, which will host the next meeting, and Ireland, which will assist. In Colombia, said Veléz, “it’s a 180 degrees change in the political spectrum. We are now being run by a president who has given our sovereignty to the United States. It’s actually very close to the White House and particularly in relation to mining and in relation to fossil fuels.”
The previous administration declared Colombia’s section of the Amazon a “fossil fuel free zone”, but that has been reversed. “So 42% of our territory, which is located in the Amazon Bioma, was going to be free from fossil fuels by 2040, by not allocating any new mining title and by not allocating any new oil and gas contract,” said Veléz. “However, the new government reversed that decision and is basically opening the Amazon for extraction with the risk of creating a new sacrifice zone that will not only affect Colombia but the whole Latin American region.”
This was “terribly heavy” for her, she added. “I have given my heart to social change and environmental justice … We made a government dedicated to social justice and climate action. So to see that all that effort is now going to crumble, it’s just very difficult. And they are doing it very fast.”
This morning, activists from Climate Action Network staged a protest at the Cop31 venue demands polluters pay up, and fill the loss and damage fund set up to help vulnerable countries deal with the fallout from violent weather.
Momentum is growing to get dirty industries to contribute to climate finance. Yesterday, the UK signed a statement backing levies on polluting sectors to help pay for countries to adapt to more violent weather and recover from the damages that follow. No global “solidarity levies” have yet been put in place but a taskforce backed by the French government has suggested raising revenue by adding a small charge to tickets for the most frequent flyers and passengers in business class, as well as charges on crypto-currency transactions.
A push by the automotive lobby in the UK to weaken electric car sales rules could jeopardise the country’s climate targets, my colleagues Jasper Jolly, Jillian Ambrose and Kiran Stacey write. The warning from official advisers comes one week after prime minister Andy Burnham told Cop31 “Britain is back”.
Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.
The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.
In a letter published on Wednesday, the CCC said the UK is “likely to miss” its climate targets if it confirms plans to allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans in the next four years.
Those changes could result in an extra 8.4m tonnes of CO2 pollution a year from the UK by next decade.
I’m not a big one for omens, but we have three official days left of talks here in Antalya and the skies were rather foreboding as we arrived at the venue this morning. All dark and moody.
Let’s hope the metaphorical and literal skies clear.
Debate continues on the global electrification pledge – a key priority set by the COP31 presidency of Turkey to transition to 35% electric by 2035 – with entrenched divisions around whether it needs to be tied to renewable energy.
While parties argue over whether increased efficiency and reduced emissions are enough to drive the pledge even for grids still heavily tied to fossil fuels, concerns are also rising that the rush to build energy-hungry data centers could undercut progress.
The host-country has not just set its sights on expanding electrification but dramatically growing its potential to produce energy: Turkey wants to become the regional hub for datacentres over the next decade – and that will require a great deal more capacity.
Turkey’s datacentre market is already planning a rapid expansion, with construction slated to continue in Istanbul. A market analysis released earlier this year projected significant growth from $715m to $1.79bn between 2025 and 2031. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan promised the country would increase data center capacity to at least 1 gigawatt by 2030 at this year’s Turkey Artificial Intelligence Summit, setting at least 2% of public investment projects toward artificial intelligence projects.
On 5 November, just ahead of the international climate summit, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar recently unveiled a plan for $500bn in energy investments by 2040, which includes $330bn for electrification ambitions. That plan also projects data centers will generate an additional 55 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity demand in that same time frame.
While Turkey is hoping to scale renewables alongside energy consumption, Ümit Şahin Senior Scholar and the Coordinator of Climate Change Studies at Istanbul Policy Center told the Guardian the push for data center expansion could add obstacles.
“The 55 TWh figure is striking,” he said. “Electrification is a sound climate policy, but the planned expansion of datacentres could undermine both electrification efforts and the renewable energy transition by substantially increasing electricity demand.”
Good morning, I’m Ajit Niranjan bringing you the Cop31 liveblog from Berlin. We’re heading into the final hectic days of negotiations, and my colleagues on the ground will be guiding you through the conclusion of these contentious climate crisis talks.
Slow progress as talks enter crucial final stretch
Damien Gayle
Delegates arrived to the Cop31 conference centre under grey skies and showered by a fine drizzle this morning. The weather could have been straight from a school creative writing piece, for these are the final days when the UN climate talks get serious.
Since the chaotic – and unexpected – first draft of the “cover decision” on Monday, progress has been slow in Antalya. It has been difficult to figure out what the story is. Unlike previous Cops, there is no headline-grabbing initiative to follow. The 35 by 35 electrification project lacks glamour. The promise to be an “implementation Cop” has not been fulfilled.
Divisions have been clear, however. They are along similar lines to usual. Who will pay for climate breakdown? All the developing world delegates I speak to here say climate finance is the most important issue. It pervades all discussions. Developing countries, already facing debt crises, want public finance from wealthier countries. But the richer countries say they have their own debt problems, crises at home and security issues that require greater military spending.
It is up to the presidency to find ways to bridge the gap between parties. Typically, presidencies have done this by convening informal negotiations, where high level delegates – often ministers – get together to work out a solution. It dates back to Durban’s Cop17, where the South African presidency staged “indabas”, the Xhosa word for a gathering of tribal elders. Last year in Brazil it was mutirão, a word with Guarani roots that had become co-opted into Brazilian Portuguese.
This year, climate diplomats will be getting together in the divan.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: A sweet treat every day: the best chocolate Advent calendars in 2026
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Marian Bull
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
When I think of Advent calendars, I think of chocolate: tiny treats meted out day by day, and intended to increase, with their sheer volume and delight, the recipient’s level of festive cheer. Luckily for the chocolate obsessive among us (myself included), the Advent calendar landscape is vast. Whether you’re looking for classic nostalgia or bean-to-bar extravagance, you’ll be able to find a chocolate Advent calendar to match your tastes. I’ve done the hard work of testing a bunch of them, and am here to outline the best, brightest (literally, one lights up), and classic favorites for 2026.
- Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for more gift guides and holiday shopping ideas for everyone on your list.
Chocolate that teleports you to Tokyo:
Tokyo Choco Club 12-Day Japanese KitKat Advent Calendar
Opening this Japanese KitKat Advent calendar transported me back to the Tokyo convenience stores that defined my recent trip to Japan that I will never shut up about. It features 12 varieties of KitKats, from a dark matcha to an intriguing sweet potato. I appreciate that each door is filled with multiples of a flavor, so that you can try each variety with friends or family. If you don’t want to give the whole thing to one person, you could also split these into stocking stuffers far more unique than a candy cane or Hershey’s bar. Lauren Gould
Small batch chocolate, with a side of folk tales:
Dandelion Chocolate 2026 Advent calendar
This Advent calendar from San Francisco’s favorite bean-to-bar chocolatier is a lush gift full of considered details. Its circular box holds bonbons and treats from 24 chocolatiers from North America and Japan; it also includes a folding paper star to adorn your house, and a book of Nordic tales, one for each night, that inspired the box’s design. It’s really an exploration of what chocolate can be – from bonbons to caramels to praline. The standout, to me, was a genmaicha praliné, which you can also get in their sublime Japanese Tea Bonbon Collection.
A box of chocolates that reads like a cereal box:
Tony’s Chocolonely Advent calendar
Tony’s is hands down my favorite grocery store chocolate brand, so I was thrilled to dig into their calendar, which carries the brand’s signature playfulness: when you open it up, one side offers a “guide” to each day, and reminds me of reading the back of a cereal box. We get six flavors here, including my absolute favorite: dark milk chocolate with pretzel and toffee. They are even educating us about ethics in the chocolate industry while feeding us our daily treat – there’s a QR code you can scan to learn more about this topic that’s a big part of the brand’s identity.
A European classic:
Toblerone Advent calendar
If you have ever picked up the XL Toblerone bar at duty free, this one is for you. The Toblerone calendar includes mini bars in white, milk and dark chocolate. They emerge from a narrow gold box printed with a Christmas tree that will make you think, hey, the Christmas tree and the Toblerones are kinda the same shape! And this sort of whimsy is what Advent calendars are all about.
A luxury ski chalet, full of chocolate:
Vosges 2026 Haut-Chocolat Advent calendar
This has got to be the most tricked-out edible Advent calendar on the market. Luxury chocolatier Vosges has made an Advent calendar that not only looks like a ski lodge and opens up to offer you a world of chocolate – it also plays an instrumental rendition of Deck the Halls, lights up and comes with its own USB-C charger. Inside the “Grand Cacao Lodge” you will find all sorts of unexpected confections, such as pumpkin seed brittle and chocolate dipped gingersnaps. On the final day, you get all the fixings for a cup of “haute” chocolate: drinking chocolate, plus two types of marshmallows.
Another European classic:
Ritter Sport Advent calendar
Here we have an Advent calendar from perhaps my second favorite grocery store chocolate brand, Ritter Sport. Hiding inside the Christmas tree-emblazoned box are a whimsical assortment of Ritter flavors, from the classic to the nouveau: dark chocolate marzipan, milk chocolate with crispies, milk chocolate caramel and milk chocolate pistachio. These squares are the perfect size for snacking, whether it’s post-dinner or during a mid-afternoon slump.
Justice for milk chocolate:
Lindt Teddy Advent calendar
Listen, I ride for dark chocolate and I always will, but this teddy bear-shaped Advent calendar from Lindt reminded me how right milk chocolate can taste, especially during the holidays. I loved this jaunty bear and all the many shapes of milk chocolate he held. Obviously there’s the classic Lindt truffle, as well as teddy-shaped milk chocolates, and mini milk chocolate balls (that come in pairs). If only they offered a sweater so I could match the bear …
Bon bons that are beautiful inside and out:
Cacao and Cardamom Advent calendar
As you might guess from its name, Cacao and Cardamom specializes in chocolate crafted with creative, bold flavors. This box comes shaped like a home – with a pair of women baking in the windows – and opens up, bureau-style, to reveal Technicolor boxes full of chocolate delights. Cacao and Cardamom is based in Houston, and I loved the Texas flavors imbued into these treats, particularly the Texas-shaped chocolate filled with a subtle barbecue-flavored caramel.
Classic cookie, crazy flavors:
Oreo Advent calendar
There’s something incredibly charming about an Oreo Advent calendar shaped … like an Oreo. (With smiling penguins in front of it!) Each day offers a new flavor of chocolate-dipped Oreo – not exactly the flavors you are used to finding at your local grocery store. My favorites were the caramel and pretzel, and peppermint. Give this to your sugar-deprived niece and don’t tell her parents.
