https://jacobin.com/2026/11/interview-bo.title: Organizing for Tenant and Political Power in Montana
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/interview-bo.author: Benjamin Finegan, Willem Morris
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/interview-bo.text:
Organizing for Tenant and Political Power in Montana
We spoke to a Montana tenant union leader about organizing renters in the state and the midterms victory of Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper, a union leader, and the first elected House Democrat in Montana in three decades.
- Interview by
- Willem Morris
Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper and union leader, flipped western Montana’s US House seat blue in last week’s midterm elections. He is the first Democrat from Minnesota elected to the US House in more than thirty years, having run on a grassroots progressive campaign that brought together labor unions, environmental organizations, indigenous groups, and tenant unions.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez played a significant role in Forstag’s upset victory in the Democratic primary. She endorsed Forstag when he was trailing by 20 points and traveled to Missoula for a get-out-the-vote rally. Missoula County carried Forstag to a narrow primary victory, with Democratic primary turnout increasing 23 percent from 2024.
Bozeman Tenants United (BTU) endorsed Forstag for the general election and campaigned for him in Gallatin County, which had the highest increase in Democratic votes between the primary and general election. The county has recently become a destination for wealthy transplants, driving up housing costs. Since the start of the pandemic, the median home price in Bozeman has nearly doubled to over $700,000.
BTU was formed in 2022 and was a cofounding organization in the national Tenant Union Federation in 2024. Benjamin Finegan was a cofounder of BTU and currently serves as president. Jacobin contributor Willem Morris spoke to Finegan about Forstag’s win and how to organize tenants in Montana.
- Willem Morris Who is Sam Forstag, and why did Bozeman Tenants United (BTU) endorse him in his race for the US House of Representatives in Montana’s 1st congressional district?
- Benjamin Finegan This May, Sam Forstag drove two hundred miles from Missoula to Bozeman to join the picket lines of BTU members on a rent strike at two major mobile home parks, the first major rent strike in Montana in fifty years. Sam really went out of his way to support the strike. He used his social media platforms to rally public support for the strike and raised money for our strike fund. Forstag also committed to a co-governance pledge with BTU. He committed to consulting tenants on policy, maintaining ongoing engagement with the union, and working to hold landlords accountable. That’s who Sam Forstag is. He knows what it’s like to have to choose between gas or groceries in order to pay the rent. He’s also someone who has proven that he will stand with working Montanans against multimillionaires and billionaires. BTU is an independent group of tenants with many different political backgrounds. We have been very selective with our endorsements, avoiding establishment picks from both parties, and have focused mostly on local races. Our decision to endorse Sam was the first time we have endorsed a federal candidate. The vote was nearly unanimous, with enthusiastic support across political differences. Our members remembered that Sam was willing to stick his neck out and fight for tenants during their strike at such a high-risk and high-profile moment.
- Willem Morris Missoula carried Forstag to victory in the primary. Your home in Gallatin County made a significant difference in the general election. Who are these voters in Gallatin County?
- Benjamin Finegan Gallatin County is home to Montana State University in Bozeman. It’s also home to the thousands of workers who staff nearby playgrounds for the ultrarich, Big Sky and the Yellowstone Club. The wealthiest people in the world pay $500,000 to join the Yellowstone Club. Working people serve as their landscapers, cooks, and maids. BTU’s membership comes from these two main groups: students and young professionals centered around the university, and families renting apartments and mobile home parks, many of whom work in the service industry or live on fixed retirement incomes.
- Willem Morris BTU formally endorsed Forstag in September. How did BTU contribute to his race in Bozeman?
- Benjamin Finegan BTU organized our members to vote in large numbers for Sam Forstag, and we led mass canvasses in Bozeman. The majority of tenants that struck the trailer parks this summer voted for Sam. This includes folks who I know are more conservative and have historically voted Republican. One of our members is an older retired veteran who went on strike; he told me, “We are getting chiseled, we are getting gouged, we are being sheared like sheep.” He has voted Republican but was one of the folks that voted for our union to endorse Sam in the election. The solidarity that Sam showed us during the strike ultimately meant a whole lot more to our members than the party label. After our endorsement vote, folks hit the doors to get their neighbors committed to vote for Sam. The union is generally pretty trusted by tenants in our city, even if they’re not members. We have a reputation for fighting for tenants and against landlords. Last year, we won a law for tenants to have the right to counsel before eviction, which got city-funded legal representation for tenants. We have organized to enforce that law. So when we knocked doors, we were able to say: “We’re with the tenant union. We won this law called right to counsel, and you can call this number if you ever are in trouble with your landlord. And we’re trying to get this candidate elected who is willing to fight alongside us, Sam Forstag. We trust him, and you can trust him too.”
- Willem Morris Forstag’s support extended well beyond Missoula and Bozeman. He dominated in Butte, Anaconda, and Glacier County. These three areas are traditional Democratic strongholds where MAGA had made inroads over the last decade. The largest shift for Forstag compared to 2024 was in Butte. Why was Forstag able to succeed in these three counties?
- Benjamin Finegan The AFL-CIO threw down for Sam Forstag. They led impressive turnout operations across the state. Sam comes from the labor movement, and unions organized to send one of their own to Congress. Butte and Anaconda, two old union mining towns, are almost legendary places in our state’s labor history. Sam Forstag ran almost 20 points better than Kamala Harris in these two places. Native American voters were very significant for Sam too. Prominent Native leaders supported Sam, and the Blackfeet Nation and Reservation turned out for Sam in Glacier County. Public lands advocates are always important in every Montana election too. These are the forces that came together and were able to lead Sam to such an important victory.
- Willem Morris What else has BTU been organizing around this year?
- Benjamin Finegan Our bread and butter is organizing tenants to fight and win the changes we need from their landlords and from the government: getting members talking to their neighbors in apartment buildings or mobile home parks; developing leaders; deciding on demands; and taking action together. Our membership needs to be able to stay in their homes, regardless of who wins an election. BTU is also one of the five founding locals of the national Tenant Union Federation (TUF). We came together with tenant unions from the South Side of Chicago, Connecticut, Kentucky, and Kansas City, Missouri, to form TUF. In the last few months, TUF ran a three-month intensive training on tenant union organizing. We trained nearly a thousand tenant unionists from over 130 cities in forty states who learned how to organize tenant unions and fight for their homes. This training series has already been getting results around the country and leading to brand new tenant unions in places like Colorado, Idaho, New York, and in the South, and winning collectively bargained leases, repairs, and rent reductions.
- Willem Morris Four years ago in Jacobin, I tried to think about how environmental, labor, and indigenous movements could start to rebuild the Left in Montana. I left out tenants. What does this election show about the potential power of organized tenants?
- Benjamin Finegan Tenant unions and tenant voters were a significant force in the midterms. And tenants are going to be decisive in 2028 and every election going forward. Tenants make up nearly one-third of all Americans. We are facing higher rents for worse conditions and have less and less control over one of our most fundamental needs. Tenants want the government to take action on capping the rent, and I believe this will continue to mobilize more and more people to the ballot box. I’ll also say that many tenants are poor and working-class people who live off a fixed income or work jobs not typically covered by labor unions. And even for tenants who are fortunate to have a labor union, rent increases can outpace wage increases. Organizing at our homes in addition to the workplace is necessary to have a stable, dignified life. As more tenants unionize across Montana and around the country and control our rent, we will wield more power in the economy too. Last, when tenants unionize their apartment building or mobile home park, they experience collective power together, often for the first time. The experience serves as a training ground for democracy for regular people. It shows them how to negotiate and how to make decisions together. It teaches people that taking risks and exercising power collectively can get results. And they take those lessons to other parts of their life. One of our members is a woman in her seventies who works at a nursing home, and she was elected by her neighbors to sit on the bargaining team for her union. We forced a representative from the corporation that owned their building to come to negotiate. During negotiations, I could see her literally shaking as she talked to this landlord representative demanding that they fix parking lot lights outside her building. Afterward, she told us: “I’ve never felt stronger in my entire life.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-fatally-.title: NYPD fatally shoots driver on Belt Parkway following suspected kidnapping
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-fatally-.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-fatally-.text:
Police shot and killed a man in Brooklyn on Saturday night after responding to reports of a woman trapped and screaming for help from inside a van in Coney Island.
The driver of the van, Omatoyo Neverson, was shot on the Belt Parkway following a police chase. Neverson, 26, was taken to a nearby hospital, where he was declared dead.
The woman was able to flee the vehicle and was unharmed, police said.
“ She has confirmed that she was in the van and was screaming and exited the vehicle before the police officers first arrived,” Assistant Chief Charles Minch, the commander of the NYPD’s Patrol Borough Brooklyn South, said at a press conference.
The incident began at 7:20 p.m., when two people called 911 to report a possible kidnapping in Coney Island at West 22nd Street and Surf Avenue around 7:20 p.m., Minch said.
“ The male caller said that he saw a white van and further stated, ‘There's a girl kicking and screaming in there,’” Minch said. “The female caller stated that she heard the girl saying, ‘Let me go,’ multiple times.”
The callers, while on the phone with 911, saw two uniformed cops and told them about the van. Minch said when those officers approached the vehicle, it took off at high speed down the sidewalk.
The van entered the Belt Parkway, heading east, but was slowed by heavy traffic, Minch said. Officers approached the vehicle and ordered Neverson out, and then broke the front passenger side window when he refused.
“The driver began to drive forwards and backwards, ramming both police and occupied civilian vehicles indiscriminately,” Minch said.
Minch said police then tried to use a taser and pepper spray against the driver, but neither was “effective, and the driver continued to ram nearby vehicles.”
Multiple officers then shot Neverson, Minch said. It is unclear how many officers fired, or how many shots were fired.
The officers pulled Neverson from the van and performed CPR while they waited for an ambulance, Minch said. Neverson was taken to NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn, formerly Lutheran Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.
He had a known history of aggression towards the woman, Minch said.
“ The driver of the vehicle was wanted for an unlawful imprisonment last month and also a domestic assault earlier this month,” Minch said. “The victim in both cases was the female who had been in the white van.”
Investigations are ongoing into both the suspected kidnapping and the fatal police shooting. Minch said the shooting was recorded on police body cameras.
This story has been updated.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-big.title: New York's biggest trash dump is releasing even more methane than thought
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-big.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-big.text:
New York’s largest landfill is pumping a lot of methane into the atmosphere — as much as 90 times the federal limit.
The Seneca Meadows landfill, located in the Finger Lakes region 275 miles from Midtown Manhattan, is leaking copious amounts of methane despite repeated repairs and persistent warnings from state regulators, a new report by the advocacy group Full Circle Future revealed on Thursday.
The analysis was based on documents obtained from the state Department of Environmental Conservation and self-reporting from 16 landfills across New York. It found that six sites, including Seneca, surpassed federal limits.
“I certainly knew that the methane emissions were a big problem, but that is an enormous problem,” New York State Assemblymember Emily Gallagher, who chairs the state’s Solid Waste Management Legislative Committee, said in response to the report’s findings.
In a statement, Department of Environmental Conservation spokesperson Andrea Pedrick-Bird said landfill operators are required to “take appropriate measures and conduct re-monitoring” to ensure any methane leaks or excessive emissions are resolved.
The Full Circle Future analysis concludes that DEC’s process isn’t effectively managing methane emissions. The study notes recurrences of leaks in the same spots.
Methane is a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential that is around 80 times more potent than carbon, according to the EPA. Exposure to the gas is also harmful to humans, contributing to respiratory-related deaths.
Seneca Meadows, New York’s largest active landfill, is the state’s biggest source of methane, according to aerial estimates published in a peer-reviewed science journal, Copernicus.
First opened in 1983 near Seneca Falls — the birthplace of the women’s rights movement — the 400-acres landfill is almost as tall as the Statue of Liberty. About 6% of its annual refuse, or 75,000 tons, comes from commercial sources in New York City, according to DEC’s most recent records.
The site is close to full capacity and was originally set to close at the end of last year. But its owner, Texas-based Waste Connections, has applied to increase the size of the landfill and continue operating through 2040.
Locals have strongly opposed the expansion.
“If you could imagine sticking your head into a dumpster in the middle of an alleyway in New York City on a hot, humid July day, it is like someone sucker punched you in the face,” said Mark Pitifer, an employee at Waterloo Container, a nearby business.
The landfill’s owners, Texas-based Waste Connections, did not return requests for comment.
Federal law requires landfill operators to self-report methane releases. But, according to Full Circle Future, it’s a law with no teeth.
“The most shocking thing for me is that all of this is actually within federal regulation,” said Kimenthrie Finlay, Full Circle’s Director of Research and Analytics and a coauthor of the report. "Most of the federal actions don't really require too much.”
Between February 2024 and June 2025, the Department of Environmental Conservation recorded discharges at the same locations six times. According to DEC correspondence, Waste Connection was told to fix the leak and retest the spot within 120 days.
“These quick patches and fixes don't really stay in place,” Finlay said. “In several instances these fixes didn't work and that same spot kept recurring.”
Finlay said the group’s analysis is likely an underestimate since as much as one-third of the Seneca landfill is not monitored, according to the mapping of testing areas.
Those calling for Seneca to be shut down said that the report is further proof that the pollution outweighs any benefits.
“The only way that we can start to recover from this heinous mountain of trash is to close it right away, cap it, and start dealing with the problem, not consider letting it grow,” said Yvonne Taylor, cofounder of local advocacy group Seneca Lake Guardian. “We need to close this thing. And if we need any more signals, this is it. Time is now. Do it. Close it.”
Seneca Meadows has been running on an expired permit for nearly one year, but continues to operate legally. An administrative loophole allows the facility to continue accepting trash while its expansion application is under review. The site is nearly at full capacity under its original limits.
More than 11,000 surrounding residents are exposed to the emissions from the landfill.
The DEC is hosting a public hearing on Nov. 16 on a statewide management plan that aims to greatly reduce dependence on landfills.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-dj-survived.title: A DJ survived the Brooklyn building collapse: His prized record collection did not
https://gothamist.com/news/a-dj-survived.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/a-dj-survived.text:
In the days after last week's deadly building collapse in Brooklyn, TV cameras and photographers captured hundreds of vinyl records scattered in the rubble.
Most, if not all of them, belonged to one man: Omari Jack, an immigrant from Saint Vincent and the Grenadines who has spent 30 years collecting reggae records and performing vinyl DJ sets under the name Roots Outernational at venues like E-K’s Hideaway in East Flatbush.
Jack said he had lived on the top floor of 1321 Flatbush Avenue for around five years. Jack wasn't home when his building crumbled into a neighboring, vacant lot last Wednesday afternoon, killing eight people, including two children, and injuring 18 others. But he lost a lot of his life's work.
His apartment was home to thousands of records, a collection he estimates to have been worth upwards of $100,000.
“I lost tons of records,” he said. “ I literally had one of the rooms as a music room,” Jack said – a space he called his “headquarters.”
“ I had vinyl in my bedroom closet. I had vinyl scattered in the kitchen area,” he said.
In the days since he lost his home, Jack has seen videos of rescue workers carrying some of his record boxes out of the rubble. But he doesn’t know where any of his belongings were sent — or if they were saved at all.
“ Nobody has contacted me from the city for, like, ‘We found some stuff that is still usable.’ I didn't hear anything like that,” Jack said. “And I don't know who to reach out to either.”
Neither City Hall nor FDNY immediately responded to requests for comment on Sunday afternoon.
'I was hoping it ain’t my building'
When Jack left his apartment Wednesday morning, he said his mind was on an upcoming set he was scheduled to do on Friday night for Global Medz Radio.
“ I left everything in my bedroom organized for the radio show,” Jack said. “I have my boxes ready. I have everything all done. I took out the clothes that I was going to wear at the show.”
Jack was at work when it happened. He said he got a call and rushed home.
“I was hoping it ain't my building,” he said. “ It's rough, man. You know, you, you go to work, you come home and you lose everything.”
He didn’t know any of his neighbors very well. He said that construction in the neighboring lot, where developers were planning to build a nine-story complex, meant his apartment rumbled all the time. “Almost every day, man,” he said.
He’d had his laptop with him that day, along with a hard drive with six terabytes of music on it. Some of his records were being stored with a friend on Long Island.
But everything else — his rare recordings of concerts dating back to the 70s, his books on musicians like Bob Marley and Dennis Brown, his CDs and cassette tapes, his favorite poster of the reggae artist Garnet Silk — was lost when the building went down.
Jack said his sets, which take him from New York to Canada, Barbados and back home in St. Vincent, include records from reggae legends like Johnny Clarke, Garnet Silk, Jacob Miller, Prince Lincoln Thompson and Barry Brown.
One bright spot, he said, was he'd spent much of the week before the collapse backing up the digital version of his collection.
“ Every single day I was just backing up stuff. I don't know if it's intuition was telling me to do this. But I was doing it every day for the past week,” Jack said.
Jack is still living in the hotel that the city placed him in after his home was reduced to rubble. He said he's not sure when he’ll DJ again, and he’s not sure he’ll ever come close to rebuilding what he had.
“ I'm not going to focus on that right now because there's other things to do. It's not possible for me to go back to how I was in terms of all the music I lost,” Jack said. “When the time is right I might collect a little stuff, but that's not my priority.”
For now, Jack is focused on getting his life back together.
A fundraiser show for Jack will be held at E-K’s Hideaway on November 28. And a GoFundMe to help Jack recover from the collapse has been launched by his friend Kelly Uman, a fellow collector and DJ who lives in Montreal.
Uman said Jack, like a lot of collectors, didn't have insurance.
“ It's this really hard thing to document and pinpoint. It's not quite as easy to appraise as, like, jewelry,” Uman said. “It definitely is nuanced, and I've yet to hear of anybody who lost their collection get fully reimbursed.”
She added: "He has to start from zero."
Liam Quigley contributed reporting.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-man.title: NYPD says man murdered his elderly aunt at their Bronx home
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-man.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-man.text:
A 35-year-old man was arrested and charged with murder Sunday after police say his aunt was found beaten to death in the Bronx home the two shared.
Police said officers responded to a call about an assault in progress at 754 Manida Street just after midnight Saturday morning.
When police arrived they found 75-year-old Carmen Nunez unconscious and unresponsive, according to the NYPD. EMS rushed her to Lincoln Hospital, where she was pronounced dead, officials said.
Officers took Joshua Nunez into custody at the scene on Saturday, and charged him with murder, manslaughter, and assault on Sunday morning.
Records show they both lived at the Bronx address where the assault was reported, but police did not provide information about what prompted the attack, or if anyone else was present.
Nunez's attorney information was not immediately available.
There have been three murders in the precinct, which includes Hunts Point and Longwood, so far this year; the same rate as 2025, according to NYPD data. Felony assaults in the precinct have declined by roughly 10% so far this year over last.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: What Are Your Odds of Winning New York’s Affordable Housing Lottery?
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado, Kennedy Sessions, Rachel Holliday Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Good news: You almost certainly have better odds of winning the New York City affordable housing lottery than of getting audited — a 1 in 1,101 chance — or getting bitten by a city dog, a 1 in 2,222 chance.
And you’ve got way better odds of winning a lottery apartment than nabbing one of those Knicks-themed wastebaskets the Sanitation Department gave out in June. Just five people snagged one, out of 125,000 who applied, putting the odds at 1 in 25,000.
Meanwhile, the chances of winning New York City’s coveted and frustrating affordable housing lottery for any one application have been 1 in 510, according to The City Reporter’s analysis of a two-year span using public data. In that time period, the city received 10,250,872 applications and, of that pool, 20,200 households ultimately signed a lease for an affordable, rent-stabilized lottery apartment.
In real world terms, the odds look like this: If everyone in five full subway cars — which carry about 100 people each — applied to Housing Connect, just one straphanger would have won an apartment in the group.
“It’s crazy,” said Brad Greenburg, executive director of the NYU Furman Center, a real estate think tank. “A lot of people apply for more than one [lottery], so it’s not like one person has a 1 in 510 chance necessarily of getting a unit — they might have a much better chance than that.”
The housing lottery is not the only way to find an affordable apartment in New York City, but it is the most accessible option for New Yorkers who are not eligible for, unable to access or don’t want to use other forms of taxpayer-funded housing help, such as rental vouchers or traditional public housing.
In an opaque and complicated system that garners millions of applications a year from New Yorkers desperate to find a stable and affordable place to live, 1 in 510 are the rough odds. (Read our methodology on how we calculated the odds and why we are confident in our findings.)
But the devil’s in the details, and an applicant’s chances can climb or fall steeply based on factors like household income and where they apply.
Frustratingly for those who need affordable housing the most, your chances of winning a lottery apartment were better if you earned more money, according to lottery data compiled between January 2022 and October 2024 and by law submitted by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to the City Council.
This trend was also true when our newsroom first analyzed housing lottery data in 2020.
Generally, the lower the monthly cost of an apartment, the lower the income of the household that is eligible to rent it, and the greater the number of people who apply to live there. The households with the worst odds of all, in the “low income” category — which at the time of the data analyzed was between roughly $78,000 and $124,240 for a family of four — had a roughly 1 in 639 chance of winning, meaning there were 639 applications for every one apartment available in that group.
But in the higher income categories, dubbed “moderate” and “middle” income, the chances were almost twice as good: 1 in 325 and 1 in 398, respectively. Across those two categories, the incomes for applicants spanned about $124,240 to $256,245 for a family of four, depending on the size of the household.
At the same time, of the 20,200 signed leases in the two years analyzed, the majority were awarded to people who were listed in the lowest economic income groups.
Roughly 30% or just under 6,000 applicants who signed leases were in the extremely low income category. Those tenants earned $32,610 for a single person or $46,590 for a family of four.
MORE: What is Area Median Income? The Magic Number Behind Affordable Housing Math in NYC
Applicants considered very low income made up roughly a third of the overall leases. These applicants typically made up to $54,350 for a single person or $77,650 for a family of four. And nearly 24% or 4,735 applicants who categorized as low income won a housing lottery. They made up to $86,960 for a single person or $124,240 for a family of four.
That means that the majority of housing lottery leases were awarded to New Yorkers who make less than about $90,000.
Amira Willingham, who works in e-commerce marketing, felt like she beat the odds in early 2024 when she moved into a Chelsea studio she’d applied to the year before. She was in the low income category, the group with the lowest odds, according to The City Reporter’s analysis. It took years of trying before her number hit.
“As soon as the clock struck on my 18th birthday, I started applying,” the now 25-year-old said. “I was ready to move to any borough, any apartment size.”
Five years passed without luck, but then in 2023 she got a call back for the Chelsea studio. The rent was $1,329.
“There’s literally no world in which I’d be able to live alone for the rent I have,” Willingham said. She previously paid about the same to live with three roommates, and her current building has a rooftop pool, a gym and outdoor terraces.
More Choice for the Wealthiest
Among the lottery applicants earning the most, the odds of winning were the best.
That’s because there are relatively more apartments available for higher-income applicants, fewer of those applicants competing for the units and more choice for those applicants in the form of traditional, market-rate apartments.
“If you’re a renter of that [higher] income you would have market options in a range of neighborhoods,” said Rachel Fee, executive director of the New York Housing Conference, an affordable housing policy nonprofit. “If you’re below 80% [Area Median Income], you’re really priced out of most available housing in New York City.”
Patrick Boyle, senior policy director at Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit that helps arrange affordable housing financing, said the numbers speak to a staggering amount of demand, even when the odds at one income tier appear better than another.
“One in 325 is still pretty long odds,” he said. “Those numbers just highlight that there’s tremendous demand across all income brackets.”
Sometimes, applicants in the higher-income groups make a decision unthinkable to many New Yorkers: They win the housing lottery, then turn it down. Across all income groups, roughly 2,698 applicants rejected a unit, according to the data — most of them by residents in the low income category.
Shay O’Reilly, a nonprofit worker, was one of them. Several years ago, he won a two-bedroom lottery apartment in Flatbush but ultimately said no, in large part because at the time the $2,400 rent was higher than rent-stabilized places on the open market.
“We decided not to go for it just because we were like, ‘We can probably find something that’s cheaper,’ and we did,” O’Reilly said. “In 2020, we ended up moving into a two-bedroom, much closer to Prospect Park.”
The rent at the time for that place, he said, was $2,000.
Preferences in the Lottery
In spite of the hurdles and the cumbersome process to get approved, when applications to the housing lottery are selected, it’s random.
“There is no favoritism. I keep hearing, ‘You got to know somebody who knows somebody,’ or ‘Pay something under the table’ — all kinds of nonsense. But that’s not true. It really isn’t,” said Charmaine Marizan, affordable housing marketing and leasing manager at Fifth Avenue Committee. “It’s a very stringent, fair, highly supervised process by the city of New York.”
But there are factors that add weight to certain applicants within the random lottery, and those built-in preferences influence the odds.
Lotteries often include preferences for certain groups, including city employees, people with disabilities and public housing residents. Of the more than 2 million municipal employee applicants, 3,730 signed leases, giving them an overall chance of 1 in 564.
For NYCHA residents, the odds are some of the highest out of subcategories. Of the 44,702 NYCHA residents who applied to the lottery, no more than 255 households signed a lease. Those odds are roughly 1 in 182.
Across racial groups, the applicants who identified themselves as Pacific Islanders had the best odds: 1 in 444. Meanwhile, the odds for Hispanic residents were roughly 1 in 591; for Black New Yorkers, it was 1 in 524; while white New Yorkers saw odds of 1 in 481. Asian New Yorkers’ odds were 1 in 467 and Native Americans’ odds were 1 in 570.
Some applicants chose not to disclose their race. Their odds were 1 in 568.
The lottery also has a special boost for applicants from the community district where the apartments are located. That last rule, known as “community preference,” used to set aside half of all lottery apartments for locals, but since the settlement of a federal lawsuit challenging the practice, the preference set-aside has dropped dramatically.
Community preference gives an applicant a much better shot at signing a lease. The City Reporter’s analysis found that, with community preference in the time period analyzed, an applicant’s odds are about 1 in 53, whereas without community preference, the odds are 1 in 1,051.
Speaking of location, there are huge variations among neighborhoods as to where there are affordable apartments.
Part of this has to do with where developers are building apartments. Neighborhoods where land-use rules have changed to accommodate more housing may see a boom of buildings that contain affordable apartments, especially if the developers take advantage of tax credits that require them.
For example, the community districts that include Long Island City, Williamsburg and Greenpoint Downtown Brooklyn, East New York and the South Bronx were home to the greatest number of affordable apartments since 2020, according to an analysis of HPD advertised lottery data.
“That’s where all of the affordable housing is being built, and then places like Bay Ridge have not historically produced very many income-restricted units, if any,” Greenburg said.
The community districts containing Staten Island’s Mid-Island and South Shore; Laurelton, Rosedale and Queens Village; Bay Ridge, and Howard Beach and South Ozone Park offered the least amount of affordable housing through the lottery.
Lower Incomes, Greater Demand, Less Inventory
The levels of affordability of the housing that appears on Housing Connect shape who can apply in the first place. There were more apartments geared towards families making more money in a six year period, the analysis of advertised lottery data shows.
From July 2020 to November 2, 2026, just 4% of the 56,271 advertised apartments available on Housing Connect were designated for extremely low-income households. Meanwhile, advertised lotteries for middle-income households made up 39%.
Those numbers didn’t surprise Jumelia Abrahamson, director of programs at University Neighborhood Housing Program, which has helped applicants successfully navigate the affordable housing lottery. The clientele of the organization, which is located in the Northwest Bronx, is typically extremely low income, making under $25,000 per household.
“One of the biggest complaints we continue to hear: most of what’s available on Housing Connect is not available for me,” Abrahamson said. “We’re working with people that are at the bottom of the [income] column.”
That means there is great demand for inventory built for households on the lower end of the income spectrum.
Take one lottery for 45 affordable apartments in Park Slope, Brooklyn. The new building was located on bustling Fifth Avenue and close to the Barclays Center, and its affordable apartments had rent set between $654 for a studio and $2,872 for a two-bedroom. (That is, geared toward very low-income to moderate-income households.)
More than 100,000 applicants entered the lottery — most in the first two weeks of the 60-day application period, which closed in December 2025.
“I’ve been doing this a long time, and I’ve never seen those numbers that fast. I was amazed,” said Marizan, of the Fifth Avenue Committee, which oversaw the lottery.
While only qualified applicants — those whose household size and income match the requirements — should apply, the process of whittling down from the full applicant pool to the people who are verified as eligible to then sign leases can be complicated.
All the information an applicant includes in their application must be manually confirmed when and if an applicant’s number is picked in the lottery.
That process is onerous, time-consuming and frustrating for both the potential tenant and the lottery specialists trying to match apartments with people, as The City Reporter detailed in our guide on what happens when you go through the lottery.
Lots of people get that first call back, but very few actually sign a lease. In the case of the Park Slope building, Marizan’s team looked at 500 applicants within different categories. All 45 households they selected signed leases.
When It Works
Other reasons for missing out on an apartment can be maddeningly slight: A missing document, or income just over or under the limit.
That’s what happened to Dutch de Carvalho, an arts educator, professional dancer and content creator who had been applying to the housing lottery for years; at one point, he counted filling out 196 applications. When he finally got a call back for an apartment, he waited for months to be told he was $400 short on income — and ineligible.
“I got rejected at the last minute,” he said.
But later that year when the native Manhattanite got a different call back for another lottery apartment — after five months of paperwork — he signed a lease and moved in.
“It’s really life changing,” he said. “I’m not worried every month about if I can pay my rent. I’m able to help out my family.”
When he shared the news about the apartment on his feed it went super-viral. His first video drew 1.1 million views; a subsequent apartment tour has drawn 9.8 million.
“People who live in our city are desperate for affordable housing and our city government does not make it easy to understand the affordable housing process,” de Carvalho told The City Reporter. “I think when people are able to hear first-hand accounts of what it is like to apply, the steps involved, etc. and actually see someone receive a unit, it’s going to spark interest.”
Content about the lottery, including tips, tricks and advice from those who won, has an avid audience. The Reddit community for discussing it, r/nychousinglottery, has 25,000 visitors a week. The hashtag #nychousinglottery on TikTok has more than 20 million views.
In Chelsea, as thrilled at Willingham is with her affordable studio, she thinks maybe she can hit the lottery twice. She’s continued applying to other Housing Connect apartments in the hopes of leveling up: her sights are on a one-bedroom in Brooklyn.
“It doesn’t always work for everybody,” she said, “but when it works, it really works.”
Additional reporting by Haidee Chu.

https://empire.streetsblog.org/advocates.title: Advocates Urge Gov. Hochul To Order Outside Overhaul of Car-First State DOT
https://empire.streetsblog.org/advocates.author: Austin C. Jefferson
https://empire.streetsblog.org/advocates.text:
More than two dozen advocacy groups want Gov. Hochul to convene an outside panel to overhaul the state Department of Transportation, saying the agency’s highway-first approach to transportation planning and road design has left New York with unsafe, costly roads it can’t maintain and too few alternatives to driving.
“We are at an inflection point where the transportation policies and practices of the past do us great disservice. We must do better,” the transportation, environmental and disability justice groups wrote in their letter issued on Monday.
Advocates accused the state of expanding highways it already struggles to maintain, using financial formulas inherited from an era that prioritized building more roads over upkeep. 
Nearly every county, town, village and city in the state has an under-funded backlog of deferred maintenance and safety work on local roads and bridges, the letter charged. The state’s five-year capital plans lack project-level funding for non-MTA transit, intercity passenger rail and aviation, while its Active Transportation Strategic Plan focuses on procedure over commitments. Upstate transit systems, meanwhile, face structural budget deficits, the groups said, noting that the Capital District Transportation Authority is in its third year of service cuts despite record ridership.
The letter thanked Hochul for suspending NYSDOT’s plans to widen Cross Bronx Expressway as part of the Five Bridges project, but said the flawed planning assumptions persist that led to that proposal happening in the first place. The groups listed several other projects they said reflect the agency’s car-first, approach to planning:
- The $1.5 billion widening of the Van Wyck Expressway to John F. Kennedy International Airport.
- Lane additions on the Belt Parkway and FDR Drive funded by the MTA capital program.
- A $1.4 billion proposal to widen Route 17 in the Catskills, which relies on flawed traffic forecasting. 
- A botched environmental review of the proposed Kensington Expressway cap in Buffalo.
- The agency’s habit of blocking local requests for Complete Streets safety projects in places such as Amityville, Woodstock and Lewiston.
The next steps, the group’s said, are to address the practices that produced the highway widening proposal with an independent, transparent review of state DOT, followed by changes in how the agency plans, spends and delivers projects. 
The groups want Hochul to establish a panel of outside experts to examine why and how the state expands highways and to recommend ways to speed up safe, affordable travel options regardless of where people live or their age, income or disability. The panel should include people who understand the need to reduce vehicle miles traveled and highway development, and someone with a background in turning around an underperforming agency or company.
Advocates likened their requests to similar overhauls at other struggling agencies, like the Office of Cannabis Management.
“I think this is an entirely realistic ask,” said Betsy Plum, executive director of Riders Alliance. Transportation belongs in the same conversation as housing, groceries and child care, Plum said, because when driving is someone’s only practical option, car payments, insurance, gas and repairs become bills they can’t escape. And people who can’t drive because they are too young, old or disabled still have important places to travel to.
A rep for Hochul’s office said she will review the letter. One important state lawmaker said he is open to discussion. “I will always review feedback from community advocates,” State Senate Transportation Chair Jeremy Cooney (D-Rochester) said in a statement, adding that he will continue to invest in solutions that serve all New Yorkers.
The groups acknowledged that New York has led the way in highway removals, citing the West Side Highway, the Sheridan Expressway, the Rochester Inner Loop and Interstate 81 in Syracuse, but said the removal policy is inconsistent as the agency simultenaously plans highway expansions elsewhere.
States including Virginia, Minnesota, Vermont and Massachusetts have all pursued policies that deprioritize cars and highways, the letter said, citing a Brookings Institution study that ranked New York 49th among the 50 states on transportation planning, investment and accountability practices.
Adie Tomer, a senior fellow at Brookings Metro and co-author of that study, said a panel is a fitting tool to repair NYSDOT because the structure of a state transportation agency evolves over decades and isn’t built for rapid decisions. Blue-ribbon commissions have led to governance reforms at other state transportation agencies, he said, pointing to Illinois. Whether a panel succeeds depends on political will, Tomer said, because the governor and legislators have to be willing to act on its recommendations.
The study found that state DOTs often fail to publicly justify how they select projects. “What’s often not transparent is how they decided on those projects,” Tomer said.
Case study: Rochester
Reconnect Rochester Co-Executive Director Cody Donahue said state DOT has been a long-running frustration for his group and the city’s Safe Streets Coalition. On Monroe Avenue, also known as Route 31, in Brighton, Donahue said NYSDOT proposed a road diet, but ignored hundreds of comments asking for bike lanes and lower speed limits.
Because the state must sign off on projects that need its funding or approval, Donahue said, designs proposed by consultants and localities often wind up blocked or diluted. State DOT sets priorities in regional transportation plans, including whether projects keep multimodal upgrades and whether money goes to highway expansion, he said.
Rochester has seen the best and worst of state DOT. Donahue said he’s glad DOT supports removing the Inner Loop urban highway, but wants the same support for lower speed limits, raised crosswalks and protected bike infrastructure.
Rochester safe streets advocates marked this year’s World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims on Lake Avenue, by some measurements the deadliest road in New York. The stretch of the road owned by state DOT has seen eight deaths and 80 injuries in the past decade, but the city must go through the state to make any major changes there.
“We want them to be a partner in improving Lake Avenue, and not standing in the way of good ideas,” Donahue said.
Monday’s letter came as the state prepared its next five-year capital plan and state DOT works on a long-range “2050” planning documents.
Signatories included Transportation Alternatives, Riders Alliance, the Sierra Club’s Atlantic Chapter, the Center for Disability Rights of New York State and the New York Bicycling Coalition.
The coalition’s breadth shows how widely the problem is felt, from transit riders and disability rights advocates to environmental and street safety groups, Plum said. 
“We want more time in our days. We want more money in our pockets, and we want a safe way to get where we need to go,” she said.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Administration Touts Compliance With Class Size Law as ‘Huge Step Forward’
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Michael Elsen-Rooney, Chalkbeat, Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
New York City public schools not only met the state-mandated targets to shrink classes, they surpassed the goal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Friday.
Nearly three-quarters of classes across New York City’s public schools are capped at 20 to 25 students, depending on the grade.
The city cleared the state’s benchmark for two reasons. First, state lawmakers moved the goal post when they agreed in June to give the city more time to comply with the law, requiring 70% of classes meet the caps this school year instead of the original target of 80%.
Additionally, the city made a change in which classes it counted toward class-size compliance. Officials added to the calculation for the first time “cluster” classes in elementary schools — courses like science, art, physical education and music that are not taught by students’ typical classroom teacher. Without counting cluster classes, 69.5% of classes would have met the caps, schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said, just shy of the new requirement.
Unlike last year, city officials are no longer exempting any classes from the size limits, after agreeing with the teachers union to pay a financial bonus of up to $8,500 to certain teachers whose classes were excused from the requirements.
All classes must meet the class size mandates by the 2029-30 school year.
Granting the city a two-year extension to meet the mandates came after months of lobbying from Mamdani, who maintains a close relationship with Gov. Kathy Hochul and was desperate to cut spending amid a budget deficit. State legislative leaders said they were satisfied with Mamdani’s plans to recruit new teachers and build additional space for the most crowded schools.
Samuels said the improving class size compliance rates are a “huge, huge step forward” during a visit Friday to Brooklyn’s M.S. 582, which received funding to hire four additional teachers. “Simply put: More attention for our kids, more one-on-one time from their teachers.”
Counting Art, Gym and Music Classes Gave NYC’s Compliance Rate a Crucial Boost
The city did not previously count elementary school cluster classes because the Education Department didn’t have the ability to track those classes’ sizes, officials said. But this year, the city updated its reporting capabilities to count those courses, which turned out to be a big boon to the city’s overall compliance rate.
Physical education and “performing group” courses like band and dance are capped at 40 students. Nearly 100% of those classes are under their caps, according to the new city data.
City officials said they also started counting middle and high school “exam prep” courses for the first time, but didn’t immediately explain what qualifies as an exam prep course or provide a breakdown of what percentage met the state requirements.
Including those new courses pushed the city’s compliance rate up to 73%.
New Hires, Declining Enrollment and Union Penalties Helped Shrink Classes
City officials credited a $244 million investment last spring that helped schools hire some 1,900 teachers to reduce class sizes. The year before, the city shelled out roughly $400 million to help schools hire an additional 3,700.
Despite the extra investment, the city’s overall teacher headcount actually went down slightly compared to last year, from about 69,900 to 69,400. (That’s still about 5,000 more teachers than the city had two years ago.)
At M.S. 582, the funding helped the school significantly reduce class sizes, in some cases cutting them to 20 students down from about 30, said Principal Jeffrey Merced. The math class Samuels toured included 15 students, though a few were absent.
The hiring has been a boon for the school, Merced noted, allowing more opportunities for small group instruction. There are other benefits, too. A new cluster teacher, hired with extra class size funding, is offering photography lessons. Several students with professional cameras trailed Samuels through the school on Friday.
“What really helped us was the manpower,” Merced said.
For now, the Education Department is picking up the tab for new hires, but Merced is “very worried” the costs will one day have to come out of his own budget. His school’s enrollment ticked up this year, which brings additional money, and he hopes the school will have enough resources to maintain its staffing levels in the future.
Declining enrollment has likely also helped the city shrink classes. Officials did not immediately share enrollment figures for this school year, but city projections anticipated a 20,000-student drop this year, according to a Chalkbeat analysis of the data. (The enrollment projections don’t include students in prekindergarten programs, or District 75 schools for students with complex disabilities.)
Union officials believe that imposing a financial penalty for exemptions from the law — the bonus of $8,500 for teachers whose classes were excused from the state caps — helped coax the city to meet the mandate. Principals are also eligible for pay bumps of up to $10,000 for bringing class sizes into compliance, though Samuels did not say how many will receive them.
Officials said they offered no exemptions this year, down from 10,000 the year before, which helped schools meet the state’s 60% requirement last year.
The pay bonus remains in place for next year, when the city will have to hit 80% compliance, union officials said.
Broad Progress Across the City, but Nearly 500 Schools Still Lack Space
The progress on class sizes stretched across almost the entire city, with 31 of the 32 geographic districts increasing their percentage of classes under the caps.
There was one notable exception: Brooklyn’s District 13 dropped from 78% of classes under the caps last year to just 59% this year. Education Department officials didn’t immediately respond to questions about what led to the surge in class sizes in that district, which spans from Brooklyn Heights to Prospect Heights, Fort Greene and parts of Bedford-Stuyvesant.
Districts’ class sizes varied widely, from a high of 92% of classes under the caps in District 32 in Bushwick, Brooklyn, to a low of 56% in District 26 in northeast Queens.
At the poorest city schools, an average of 90% of classes were under the caps, while 57% of classes were under the caps at the wealthiest schools. Education officials and experts have repeatedly raised equity concerns, as high-need schools stand to benefit least from the new investments in smaller classes.
There are still nearly 500 schools that city officials say do not have enough space to bring all their classes under the caps.
Michael Elsen-Rooney is a reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Michael at melsen-rooney@chalkbeat.org.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

After leading South London Gallery (SLG) since 2001, Margot Heller will step down as its director in May 2027 to work as an independent curator and adviser. Heller offered the following statement in a press release: “The South London Gallery has been a huge part of my life and I believe passionately in its importance. After twenty-five years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career.”
Heller previously worked as a curator, before serving as director of the Southampton City Art Gallery between 1989 and 1996. She then became Director of Exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery in 1996 and also worked as freelance curator before joining SLG.
During her tenure at SLG, Heller tripled the gallery’s footprint, refurbishing and adding a neighboring house and fire station to the institution’s complex. She also facilitated the development of a publicly accessible garden in the gallery, designed by Mexican artist Gabriel Orozco.
Heller also curated solo shows by major artists at SLG, including those by Superflex (2009), Tatiana Trouvé (2010), Rashid Johnson (2012), Lawrence Weiner (2014), Thomas Hirschhorn (2015, Katharina Grosse (2017), and Haegue Yang (2019), among many others.
Her time at the gallery also saw SLG set up its Communities and Learning programme, and support emerging artists through its Post Graduate Artist in Residence Programme for 12 years. “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own,” said artist and SLG board member, Alvaro Barrington, in a statement.
Heller also helmed SLG’s leadership of the pioneering Louis Vuitton Young Arts Project (2010) which marked a collaboration between Tate, Whitechapel Gallery, the Royal Academy, and Hayward Gallery. Before Heller departs, she will curate the first solo show by Dutch artist Mark Manders at a London institution. The exhibition will be on view at SLG from 23 September 2027 to 9 January 2028.

Latinx Art’s New Visionaries
Arlene Dávila on the rallying cry of contemporary Latinx artists, Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal, and Martin Puryear’s quiet revolution.
Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”
Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.
—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor
Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. | Arlene Dávila

https://hyperallergic.com/meet-natalie-w.title: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer
https://hyperallergic.com/meet-natalie-w.author: Sarah Cascone
https://hyperallergic.com/meet-natalie-w.text:
Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer
The artist is among the few shooting on the company’s 20x24, creating otherworldly double-exposure self-portraits with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film.
WHATELY, Mass. — The text message said to head around back to the barn, an only slightly ominous-looking structure with heavily weathered wooden siding, tucked off a winding road in Franklin County, Massachusetts. Inside was one of the world’s only 20x24 Polaroid Land Cameras — sometimes referred to as the Giant Polaroid — and the artist Natalie White, shooting with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film long past its expiration date.
A muse and model-turned-photographer, performance artist, and feminist activist, White just debuted 15 of her unique large-format Polaroids in Natalie White: Strange Magick, a selling exhibition at Phillips Los Angeles. The images are colorful and dreamy, close-up portraits of the artist with an otherworldly quality. Each photo is a double exposure, an unpredictable process that creates ghostly effects with White’s hands and fingers overlaid atop her face.
To achieve this, White leaves the film in the camera after pushing the shutter, takes a second shot, and hopes for the best.
“We’re giving all control to the negative,” White told Hyperallergic. “We always joke that there’s a little magical man painting inside the camera who decides what the double exposure is going to look like.”

https://hyperallergic.com/the-met-and-th.title: The Met and the Shanghai Museum Sign Collaborative Agreement
https://hyperallergic.com/the-met-and-th.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/the-met-and-th.text:
The Met and the Shanghai Museum Sign Collaborative Agreement
The collaboration comes just weeks after MoMA, Paris’s Centre Pompidou, and Hong Kong’s M+ Museum embarked on a similar alliance.
Fluorescent foliage, crisp breezes, dogs in sweaters, and international museum partnership announcements — one of these is not like the others, but you can check them all off on this autumn's bingo card. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan and the Shanghai Museum have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) codifying their relationship ahead of a dual-collection historic jewelry exhibition opening at the Shanghai institution this week.
The MoU between the two museums was announced less than three weeks after the Museum of Modern Art, Centre Pompidou in Paris, and M+ Museum in Hong Kong publicized their collections alliance at the end of October, further illustrating an institutional shift toward resource pooling, joint acquisitions, and other collaboration initiatives popularized in the wake of pandemic-induced budget deficits.
The Met and the Shanghai Museum, which have worked together on myriad projects and exhibitions since 1980, stated in a press release that their shared goals in scholarship and presentation advancement will manifest through “exhibitions, research initiatives, and curatorial exchange.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Assembleia Legislativa paulista exibe série Terreiros Urbanos, do Brasil de Fato, nesta quinta-feira (19)
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A série documental “Terreiros Urbanos em São Paulo”, do Brasil de Fato, será exibida na Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo (Alesp) nesta quinta-feira (19), a partir das 18h, no auditório Teotônio Vilela. A exibição foi proposta pela Bancada Feminista do Psol e será seguida de bate-papo, integrando a programação do Mês da Consciência Negra da Casa.
A série “Terreiros Urbanos em São Paulo” traz a força das lideranças femininas nas religiões de matriz africana no estado de São Paulo, revelando os terreiros como territórios vivos de resistência, pertencimento e transformação social, a partir do papel central das mulheres nas religiões de matriz africana.
Segundo um conto da cosmologia africana, os Orixás masculinos tomavam decisões sobre a humanidade sem ouvir as Yabás, como são chamadas as divindades femininas. Como retaliação, Oxum tirou a fecundidade das mulheres e da natureza, e o mundo colapsou. Então os Orixás descobriram que nenhuma decisão poderia ser tomada sem a visão das mulheres.
São cinco episódios pautados na liderança de mulheres que delineiam os eixos temáticos que atravessam a série: Mãe Alessandra Ribeiro: disciplina e espiritualidade; Mãe Luciana Bispo: política de cuidado; Mãe Claudia Rosa: acolhimento e resistência; Mãe Neide Ribeiro: território e legado; e Ekedi Eloiza Lourenço: zelar pelo sagrado.
Entre a periferia da capital, o interior e o litoral, a série apresenta histórias guiadas por mulheres à frente dos terreiros, que são tanto guardiãs da memória quanto transmissoras de saberes ancestrais que sustentam práticas culturais, espirituais e comunitárias herdadas da diáspora africana.
Todos os episódios podem ser conferidos no YouTube do Brasil de Fato:

Exibição do Documentário Terreiros Urbanos em São Paulo
Local: Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo – Auditório Teotônio Vilela
Endereço: Av. Pedro Álvares Cabral, 201
Horário: das 18h00 às 22h00

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Estudantes fecham a Faria Lima em protesto contra pressão do mercado por ajuste fiscal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Luís Indriunas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Em frente à escultura da Baleia, símbolo dos grandes investidores do mercado financeiro, estudantes e integrantes dos movimentos populares fecharam a avenida Faria Lima, em São Paulo, contra os juros altos e a pressão do mercado financeiro por ajuste fiscal.
“Nós, da União Nacional dos Estudantes [UNE], convocamos esse dia de luta, um dia nacional que está acontecendo em vários estados, em várias capitais, outras cidades. Mas, especificamente aqui em São Paulo, foi o primeiro ato que nós organizamos. Nós estamos aqui na ‘Baleia da Faria Lima’, no coração do mercado financeiro brasileiro. Nós estamos aqui hoje para demarcar a nossa posição contra o mercado financeiro que submete o nosso governo a pressões”, disse a presidenta da UNE, Bianca Borges, ao vivo para o Conexão 2ª Edição, da Rádio Brasil de Fato.
Com gritos como “vem para a rua contra o ajuste”, o ato começou por volta das 17h30. Aos poucos, os manifestantes foram ocupando as pistas da avenida. Por volta das 19h, a avenida ficou fechada para carros no sentido zona sul.
Além de cartazes contra o ajuste fiscal, havia dizeres contra os super-salários, pela taxação das grandes fortunas e contra os juros altos. Com a rua fechada, bandeiras dos Estados Unidos e de Israel foram queimadas. A polícia usou gás lacrimogênio para liberar uma das pistas.
A votação dos quatro destaques ao Projeto de Lei Complementar 299/2026 estava marcada para esta terça (17) no Senado, mas foi adiada para quarta-feira (18), a partir da proposta do presidente da Casa, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), devido à apresentação de emendas ao texto que exigiriam uma análise mais ampla que a dos destaques.
“Nós estamos apoiando as emendas das bancadas do PCdoB, do PT e do Psol, que tiram saúde e educação da limitação de gastos. As emendas que propõem a taxação de grandes fortunas, que propõem a taxação de lucros líquidos e dividendos, porque nós acreditamos que se tem que haver ajuste, que ele comece por quem contribui pouco no desenvolvimento do Brasil”, acrescentou a presidenta da UNE.
Borges também rebateu as críticas de parte da esquerda de que a mobilização no momento seria precipitada. “Em primeiro lugar, sem dúvidas, esse é o momento de se posicionar, porque o PLP do ajuste fiscal está sendo proposto e votado agora. E o próprio presidente Lula fez uma série de pronunciamentos nos últimos meses, inclusive no dia da sua vitória histórica, no dia 25 de outubro, que quer governar ao nosso lado. Então nós estamos ao lado do governo para combater o mercado financeiro, para combater a especulação financeira, que é tão danosa ao nosso país. As manifestações são democráticas, não são manifestações contra o governo, são manifestações contra aqueles que querem pôr a pressão do mercado para limitar o crescimento das despesas e nossos direitos sociais.”
No final, um grupo de estudantes seguiu em caminhada, ocupando uma das faixas da avenida, acompanhados pela Polícia Militar, até a estação de trem.

https://hyperallergic.com/beer-with-a-pa.title: Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts
https://hyperallergic.com/beer-with-a-pa.author: Jennifer Samet
https://hyperallergic.com/beer-with-a-pa.text:
Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts
The Ivorian-born painter works only at night, when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest.
Last month, just a couple of weeks before Ouattara Watts’s solo show opened at Karma, I was directed to knock on the cracked glass door of his Bushwick studio. We met in the late afternoon, which is when his studio time begins. The Ivorian-American artist has coffee and a light evening meal, and works all night, before returning home to sleep during the day. To learn why Watts works only at night, one need only look at his paintings. He views art as a portal to the divine; night is when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest, and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest.
Although a gallery representative had told me Watts would be putting “finishing touches” on the paintings for his exhibition at the time of our meeting, I came to realize that he thinks about the work, and his process, without a beginning or end. The centrifugal energy of his rhythmic compositions does not obey edges. Totemic forms continue beyond the bounds of the canvases; arrows point in varying directions; seed pods are split open to reveal concentric circles. His compositions are stained and dripped fields populated by a lexicon of imagery and symbols, developed over the past four decades. They include coffee beans, sacred books, musical notes, serpents, bursting petals encased in atoms, diagrammatic cubes, and mathematical codes.

Artnet reports that the pioneering feminist artist Eleanor Antin, now ninety-one, filed suit against her dealer Richard Saltoun, in New York Supreme Court on July 29. Antin has accused Saltoun, who has galleries in London, Rome, and New York, of refusing to return nearly 180 of her works unless she hands over “hundreds of thousands of dollars.”
In her complaint, Antin calls Saltoun Gallery “faithless servants” and demands it either send her art back or pay her at least $975,000, plus punitive damages. Antin is being represented by her son, Blaise Antin, through a power of attorney.
Saltoun came to represent Antin by sub-consigning works from Ronald Feldman Fine Arts, Antin’s long-time gallerist. Antin and Feldman separated in January 2023, which, according to the complaint, was encouraged by Saltoun, who allegedly demurred on the topic of a written agreement covering his representation of Antin.
In the three years since, Saltoun sold nothing of Antin’s, except the pastel Death and the Maidens 2 (1974–75), in June 2023 at nearly half the price set by Ronald Feldman. The business relationship between Antin and Saltoun was terminated earlier this year, and the gallery claimed it had returned everything of Antin’s, but her archivist found at least 179 works still in the gallery’s possession.
Saltoun’s lawyers responded with a “possessory lien,” demanding $454,313.89 in commissions on sales to three European museums that the complaint says never occurred. Saltoun asked for damages for reputational harm, because the Antin family had requested that the museums showing her retrospective remove his name from the wall labels. New York’s Arts and Cultural Affairs Law designates consigned art as trust property, meaning it cannot be subject to a consignee’s lien. The complaint argues that the work is being held hostage.

https://hyperallergic.com/rip-to-the-nat.title: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act
https://hyperallergic.com/rip-to-the-nat.author: Greg Werkheiser
https://hyperallergic.com/rip-to-the-nat.text:
RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act
The Act survived Republican and Democratic administrations, recessions, and wars, but its health declined precipitously this year after a devastating bout of congressional malpractice. There’s still time to save it.
The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the beloved American law that spent six decades giving communities a voice in federal decisions affecting the places that tell their stories, died shortly after its birthday following a brief but devastating bout of congressional malpractice. It was 60.
Born on October 15, 1966, with unanimous bipartisan support and signed into law by then-President Lyndon B. Johnson, NHPA was conceived in response to a national epidemic of federally sponsored demolition. Americans discovered that an astonishing 50% of the nation’s 12,000 historic buildings and landmarks documented in an inventory begun by the Civil Works Administration in 1933 had been demolished amid federally supported urban renewal and highway development — a breathtaking path of destruction dubbed “the death mask of America.”
NHPA’s central proposition was modest: Before the federal government or a developer damaged or destroyed an important part of America’s heritage, it simply needed to stop, look, and listen.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Sugestão de Lula de reunião entre EUA, China e Rússia reforça defesa do multilateralismo, avalia professor
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A reunião trilateral entre China, Estados Unidos e Rússia para tratar do fim da guerra na Ucrânia, segundo o premiê canadense, Mark Carney, teria sido sugerida pelo presidente Lula durante encontro entre ambos nas Filipinas, na Cúpula da Asean. A proposta foi apresentada diretamente a Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin e Xi Jinping durante conversas telefônicas realizadas no meio deste ano. Carney elogiou publicamente a ideia de Lula.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Gustavo Menon, professor de relações internacionais da Universidade de São Paulo (USP), observa que os dois líderes têm apostado no multilateralismo e que Lula, em cada oportunidade, reforça essa mensagem publicamente.
O analista observa que é preciso “revisitar as estruturas do sistema multilateral” e atualizá-las de acordo com a realidade contemporânea. Isso inclui, por exemplo, uma ampla reavaliação da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) e seu papel. “A rigor, não estamos falando da mesma correlação de forças do pós-guerra. Existem muitas novas vozes”, pontua.
Menon lembra da Conferência de Ialta, em 1945, que “desenhou e orquestrou o sistema multilateral” que operaria a partir daquele momento e destaca que “algumas pessoas têm especulado” que a cúpula da Cooperação Econômica Ásia-Pacífico (Apec) seria uma reedição da conferência do pós-guerra. “Devemos ver Trump, Putin e Xi juntos a partir de esforços do premiê canadense e de Lula em um mundo em conflagração”, ressalta.
Nesse sentido, o professor pondera que é difícil fazer alguma previsão do resultado dessa articulação idealizada e debatida pela comunidade internacional. “Não sabemos ao certo como as pautas serão costuradas. Chamo aqui a atenção para alguns elementos: além da guerra na Eurásia, há a guerra contra o Irã. É um movimento de cruzamento de crises e, por isso, essas potências, de fato, deveriam sentar à mesa e pactuar os diálogos multilaterais”, defende.
Na avaliação de Gustavo Menon, a expectativa sinaliza, idealmente, para a construção de uma ordem internacional que deve ser multipolarizada e obedecer a princípios de equidade “para maior participação de atores de países emergentes e dessas economias do chamado Sul Global”.
