Kazachgate draait rond het versneld wetgevend werk (de afkoopwet) op maat van Chodiev en op vraag van toenmalig Frans president Sarkozy. Frankrijk wilde in 2010 een belangrijke exportdeal beklinken met de Kazachse dictator Nazarbajev. Die eiste in ruil dat de strafklacht tegen zijn vriend en medestander Patokh Chodiev (en bij uitbreiding het Kazachse trio) in België zou vervallen. De afkoopwet was het vehikel dat daarvoor moest dienen.
Hoe komt Didier Reynders daarbij in beeld?
De entourage van Sarkozy ging voor de operatie op zoek naar medestanders binnen de MR waar Didier Reynders op dat moment nog oppermachtig was. De advocate van Chodiev maakte (onder meer) ruim 700.000 euro over aan voormalig Kamervoorzitter en MR-minister (wijlen) Armand De Decker en eveneens forse bedragen aan Étienne des Rosaies, een naaste medewerker van Nicolas Sarkozy.
In een vertrouwelijke nota schreef Des Rosaies onder meer dat hij zich via Armand De Decker verzekerd had van de unanieme steun van MR voor de afkoopwet en van de bevoegde ministers, waaronder Didier Reynders. Étienne des Rosaies had ook meermaals contact met Reynders’ rechterhand Jean-Claude Fontinoy.
Ondanks een rits zeer concrete aanwijzingen en harde documenten besliste de parlementaire onderzoekscommissie-Kazachgate, meerderheid tegen oppositie, dat er geen ongeoorloofde beïnvloeding van de wetgeving was geweest. Reynders en Fontinoy konden opnieuw gerust adem halen.
Maar ook ander onderzoek binnen de Belgische Staatsveiligheid werd afgeblokt?
Het eerste dossier waar Nicolas Ullens binnen de afdeling economische contraspionage mee te maken kreeg, was het dossier over de verkoop en de verhuur van het Rijksadministratief Centrum in Brussel (RAC). Het reusachtige gebouw aan de Brusselse Pachecolaan, in de schaduw van de Financietoren, was lang eigendom van de overheid.
De constructie die werd uitgewerkt voor de verkoop en verhuur maakte de Belgische schatkist vele tientallen miljoenen lichter, terwijl vastgoedontwikkelaar Breevast drie keer langs de kassa passeerde: de overheid verkocht het RAC voor veel te weinig geld, betaalde vervolgens een te hoge huur en liet enkele jaren later de federale politie het RAC voor 18 jaar huren, opnieuw tegen een veel te hoge huurprijs.
Nota’s van de staatsveiligheid die Apache kon inkijken, tonen hoe verschillende bronnen vele jaren terug al waarschuwden voor een systeem van verregaande corruptie dat in de steigers werd gezet door de omstreden vastgoedlobbyist (wijlen) Koen Blijweert en Jean-Claude Fontinoy, rechterhand van Didier Reynders.
Verschillende bronnen waarschuwden voor een systeem van verregaande corruptie dat in de steigers werd gezet door de omstreden vastgoedlobbyist (wijlen) Koen Blijweert en Jean-Claude Fontinoy,
Ook dat dossier werd volgens Nicolas Ullens afgeblokt door Didier Reynders. Finaal werd Ullens overgeplaatst naar de afdeling salafisme. Maar ook daar botste hij op dossiers waarin Didier Reynders een hoofdrol speelde. Het belangrijkste daarvan is het dossier van de bevroren Libische tegoeden.
Vele jaren terug al waarschuwden bronnen voor een systeem van verregaande corruptie dat werd opgezet door vastgoedlobbyist Koen Blijweert en Fontinoy
Welke rol speelde Reynders daarbij?
In maart 2011, na de val van Kadhafi, werd op vraag van de VN-Veiligheidsraad 12,8 miljard euro, afkomstig uit Libië, bevroren op rekeningen bij Euroclear Bank in Brussel. Jaarlijks verdween 300 miljoen euro aan interesten op dat bedrag naar Libië.
Via een informant kreeg Nicolas Ullens te horen dat Didier Reynders kamp koos in de strijd tussen de twee rivaliserende Libische clans en Libische tegoeden zou overmaken in ruil voor smeergeld. Grote bedragen zouden via tussenpersoon Robert Claushuis richting Reynders en Fontinoy zijn gestroomd.
De zaak kwam aan het licht in de nasleep van het faillissement van GSDT, een vzw van prins Laurent. De vzw zou een deel van de Libische kust herbebossen, maar de Libische staat zegde het contract eenzijdig op. De rechter oordeelde dat Libië de prins 50 miljoen euro verschuldigd is, maar de prins had de grootste moeilijkheden om dat geld los te krijgen.
Zijn vzw ging intussen in vereffening en Reynders weigerde de interesten op de tegoeden te gebruiken om de prins te compenseren. Verschillende mensen boden vervolgens hun diensten aan prins Laurent aan om het bedrag in Libië los te peuteren, in ruil voor een zeer forse commissie. Een van hen was Robert Claushuis.
Voor Ullens was het verbod van zijn chef om verder te werken op het dossier de druppel. Overal waar hij op Reynders en Fontinoy botste, werd hem het werken onmogelijk gemaakt. Hij nam ontslag bij de Belgische staatsveiligheid en stapte naar het gerecht. Zoals hierboven vermeld: de onderzoeken werden geseponeerd aan de vooravond van de benoeming van Didier Reynders tot Europees Commissaris.
Naast het Libische dossier bevatten de gelekte whatsappberichten ook aanwijzingen over linken tussen Didier Reynders en Rusland?
Er zijn verschillende dossiers die aanwijzingen bevatten over relaties tussen Reynders en Rusland. Zo is er het dossier over de illustere edelman, baron Ernest de Laminne de Bex.
In zijn middeleeuwse kasteel in Wezembeek-Oppem herbergde hij tot voor kort de diplomatieke club Cercle International Diplomatique et Consulaire (CIDIC), een pleisterplaats voor edellieden, ambassadeurs, ereconsuls, bedrijfsleiders, politici, magistraten, advocaten, officieren van het leger, verantwoordelijken van inlichtingendiensten en vertegenwoordigers van het hof.
Jarenlang bracht De Laminne de Bex in zijn kasteel diplomaten en spionnen uit het Oosten samen met hun westerse counterparts, onder het genot van een goed glas wijn.
Er zijn verschillende dossiers die aanwijzingen bevatten over relaties tussen Reynders en Rusland
Apache documenteerde, samen met Humo, de schimmige relaties en duistere activiteiten van De Laminne de Bex in Georgië en Kazachstan, zijn schijnbaar uit het niets opgebouwde vastgoedimperium en de verhalen over wapenhandel en deviezensmokkel.
Hoewel De Laminne de Bex op de radar van de inlichtingendiensten stond en Russisch geld doorsluisde naar de Franstalige extreemrechtse populistische partij Parti Populaire, kreeg hij van Didier Reynders een adellijke titel en werd hij tot twee keer toe erkend als ereconsul in België.
En Ernest de Laminne de Bex appte met Didier Reynders?
Op 5 januari 2020 maakt de Laminne de Bex niet enkel zijn beste wensen over en wenste hij Didier Reynders alle succes als Europees Commissaris, hij meldde hem ook dat hij graag eens persoonlijk met hem zou praten over de aantijgingen van Nicolas Ullens en over “een tegenoffensief om een einde te maken aan de laster”. Opvallend daarbij: De Laminne de Bex ‘tutoyeert’ Didier Reynders in het bericht – “j’aimerais bien t’entretenir de vive voix” - wat getuigt van een nauwe relatie tussen beiden.
Baron-spion de Laminne de Bex wilde Reynders graag persoonlijk spreken over de aantijgingen van Nicolas Ullens en over 'een tegenoffensief om een einde te maken aan de laster'
Reynders stond ook dicht bij de Russische oligarch Oleg Deripaska?
Begin september 2025 heropende het Brussels parket een geseponeerd onderzoek naar witwas waarin de Russische superoligarch Oleg Deripaska centraal staat. Dat gebeurde nadat Apache een reactie vroeg aan het Brussels parket, na een uitgebreid onderzoek over twee stichtingen van Deripaska in Ukkel en de directe relatie met Didier Reynders.
Heropende?
In 2014 tekende de antiwitwascel in haar jaarverslag tot in de kleinste details een witwasschema uit rond een Ukkelse kunststichting. De naam werd niet genoemd maar het ging om de vzw Bruno Lussato et Marina Fédier. Deripaska, een nauwe medestander van de Russische president Vladimir Poetin, had de stichting opgericht en Didier Reynders behoorde tot de nauwe vriendenkring. De antiwitwascel vermeldde toen al “nauwe banden tussen de betrokkenen en politiek prominente personen in Rusland en België”.
Didier Reynders was niet enkel kind aan huis in de kuststichting, zijn voormalige adviseur Constantin Chariot was directeur van het museum van de stichting. Hij had een volmacht op de rekening van de vzw. Het gerechtelijk onderzoek dat daarop volgde stond Deripaska’s aanvraag voor een “gouden paspoort” in Cyprus in de weg. Zo’n paspoort moest de Russische oligarch vrije doorgang binnen de Europese Unie verzekeren.
Ondanks subtiele bedreigingen vanuit de entourage van Deripaska aan het adres van de antiwitwascel werd het dossier snel geseponeerd. Didier Reynders was op dat moment als minister bevoegd voor Buitenlandse Zaken, Buitenlandse Handel en Europese Zaken.
Apache en Humo stelden vast dat de voorbije jaren vanuit de centrale vzw 878.000 euro werd versluisd naar een andere Brusselse vzw. Die werd opgericht en bestuurd door personen die nauw verweven zijn met Russische desinformatiecampagnes of betrokken zijn bij grootschalige financiële operaties die duidelijk het stempel van het Kremlin dragen.
Didier Reynders was kind aan huis bij een museum van een stichting van Oleg Deripaska. De antiwitwascel vermeldde toen al 'nauwe banden tussen de betrokkenen en politiek prominente personen in Rusland en België'
Kunst en antiek lijken een belangrijke rol te spelen in de zaak-Reynders.
Constantin Chariot werd indertijd naar eigen zeggen enkel als getuige verhoord in het onderzoek naar de vzw van Oleg Deripaska, maar antiquair Olivier Theunissen bij wie Jean-Claude Fontinoy om de haverklap antiek aankocht, werd intussen wel in verdenking gesteld. Nicolas Ullens omschreef de techniek om wit te wassen via de aankoop van antiek als de methode-Guéant, genoemd naar de voormalige rechterhand van de Franse ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy die ook prima contacten onderhield met Didier Reynders.
De methode-Guéant komt erop neer dat antiek of kunst wordt aangekocht aan een lage prijs en vervolgens voor een zeer hoge prijs wordt doorverkocht. Die meerprijs is de facto het smeergeld om dingen gedaan te krijgen. Theunissen wordt door Nicolas Ullens expliciet genoemd als verbindingsofficier tussen Didier Reynders enerzijds en Nicolas Sakozy en Claude Guéant anderzijds.
Zijn er andere technieken die Reynders of Fontinoy zouden hebben gebruikt?
Omdat Reynders decennialang een zogezegde PEP (Politically Exposed Person) was waarvan de financiën in principe extra in het oog worden gehouden, zou Reynders al die tijd via Jean-Claude Fontinoy hebben gewerkt.
Een tweede manier van witwassen loopt via vastgoed. Jean-Claude Fontinoy vergaarde de voorbije decennia een zestigtal, vaak zeer dure en indrukwekkende woningen in de buurt van Namen. Daarbij zouden geregeld betalingen, deels in cash zijn gebeurd.
Nicolas Ullens beschrijft onder meer hoe Fontinoy in 2019 een cocktailfeestje hield voor de vzw Les Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie, met vooral antiquairs onder de genodigden, ter gelegenheid van de viering van het zestigste pand dat hij in zijn bezit had gekregen.
Welke rol speelde die vzw Les Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie?
Eind 2019 bracht Apache uit dat de vzw rond Fontinoy voor minstens 75.000 euro sponsorgeld had ontvangen van bedrijven die in principe niets te maken hebben met een vzw die zich, zoals de naam zegt, bezighoudt met de opsmuk van de mooiste dorpjes in Wallonië. Het ging onder meer om baggerbedrijf DEME, havenbedrijf Rent-A-Port en projectontwikkelaar Immobel. DEME en Rent-a-port zijn in handen van de Belgische holding Ackermans & van Haaren.
De Paradise Papers leerden onder meer dat de Belgische overheid via investeringsvehikel BMI participeerde in de vennootschap Infra Asia Development Limited, met zetel op de Britse Maagdeneilanden, een notoir belastingparadijs. Via dat vehikel werd een grootschalig havenproject in Noord-Vietnam uitgebouwd. BMI participeerde in de vennootschap op de Britse Maagdeneilanden, samen met Rent-A-Port. De voorzitter van de raad van bestuur van BMI was Jean-Claude Fontinoy.
Een vzw rond Fontinoy die zich bezighoudt met de opsmuk van de mooiste dorpjes in Wallonië.ontving voor minstens 75.000 euro sponsorgeld van bedrijven die daar niets mee te maken hebben
Waarom zou projectontwikkelaar Immobel een toeristische vzw sponsoren?
Twee vennootschappen gelieerd aan de beursgenoteerde projectontwikkelaar stortten elk 1.000 euro op de rekening van de Waalse vzw. Het gaat om Allfin Group en Immobel Group Lotinvest. Het eerder genoemde RAC werd door de Belgische overheid verkocht aan projectontwikkelaar Breevast en Immobel.
In een nota van de staatsveiligheid stond over die aankoop dit: “Bij de Regie der Gebouwen is de man die beslist overduidelijk Jean-Claude Fontinoy, maar zijn inschatting is niet bepaald rationeel: hij koppelt zijn akkoord aan een geheime betaling van een miljoen euro.”
Over het onderzoek dat het parket van Namen startte naar Les Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie werd niets meer vernomen.
Fontinoy wordt ook genoemd in een soort spin-off van een grootschalig onderzoek naar mogelijke fraude bij de verkoop van Europese overheidsgebouwen
Niet enkel Immobel, ook andere projectontwikkelaars vonden hun weg naar de vzw Les Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie?
Apache bracht onder meer een getuigenis over drie betalingen van ongeveer 25.000 euro aan de vzw door een projectontwikkelaar. Die moest voor een vastgoedproject enkele vierkante meters terrein van de NMBS – waar Jean-Claude Fontinoy op een cruciale positie zat – overkopen.
Recent werd duidelijk dat de speurders ook een onderzoek voeren naar een andere vzw waar Fontinoy bij betrokken was?
Het gaat om een onderzoek in de schoot van de investeringsmaatschappij van de federale overheid (SFPIM). Jean-Claude Fontinoy was jarenlang voorzitter van dochteronderneming SFPIM International. Er zijn wel wat parallellen met wat er gebeurde binnen de vzw Les Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie.
De vzw Les Amphitryons, die zich officieel bezighoudt met gastronomie en de kunst van het sigarenroken, ontving stortingen van SFPIM International. De voorzitter van de vzw was ook adviseur van Fontinoy binnen SFPIM International. Volgens de speurders dienden de stortingen als vergoeding van prestaties “voor de voorbereiding van een dossier rond financieringsaanvragen aan de SFPIM door de adviseur van de voorzitter”.
Apache bracht onder meer een getuigenis over forse betalingen door een projectontwikkelaar aan een vzw rond Fontinoy
Het onderzoek is een soort spin-off van een grootschalig onderzoek naar mogelijke fraude bij de verkoop van 23 gebouwen van de Europese Unie aan de Belgische investeringsmaatschappij SFPIM voor in totaal 900 miljoen euro.
Is vastgoed finaal de rode draad in de zaak-Reynders?
Het is zeker niet het enige element, maar wel een belangrijk. Met Fontinoy had Didier Reynders zijn mannetje binnen zowel de NMBS als de Regie der Gebouwen. Met de verkoop van overheidspatrimonium en publieke gronden werden de voorbije decennia in België sloten geld verdiend.
Het kransje ‘Vrienden van het Vastgoed’ dat daarbij telkens weer in beeld komt of kwam, is bekend. Ze dineerden in chique restaurants, en frequenteerden elkaar in de luxueuze villa van wijlen Koen Blijweert in Megève om deals te maken en zaken te bespreken die het daglicht schuwen. Belangrijk daarbij is dat het netwerk telkens opnieuw tracht om zowat alle (traditionele) politieke partijen mee in bad te trekken. De voorbije twee decennia expliciet ook de relatief nieuwe partij N-VA.
Het volstaat om te herlezen hoe die partij haar hoofdkantoor in Brussel verkreeg om zicht te krijgen op de manier van werken. Ook het fameuze etentje in ’t Fornuis op uitnodiging van vastgoedlobbyist Erik Van der Paal – waar naast het bijna integrale toenmalige Antwerpse college een aanzienlijk deel van het netwerk te gast was – maakt duidelijk hoe het werkt. Het is allerminst toevallig dat naast Jean-Claude Fontinoy ook zijn (toenmalige) “socialistische” tegenhanger Luc Joris aanwezig was.
De man waarvan recent geheime opnames uitlekten waarin hij zelf spreekt over de betaling van smeergeld?
Luc Joris stond jarenlang heel dicht bij Elio Di Rupo en de PS. Bij de afwikkeling van de overname van de omstreden projectontwikkelaar Land Invest Group en bij concrete projecten van de groep zou smeergeld zijn betaald, of beter: beloofd smeergeld niet zijn betaald. Land Invest Group was een samenwerking tussen de directe entourage van Bart De Wever en de Luikse PS.
Het dossier illustreert perfect hoe verschillende politieke partijen – ook al zijn ze ideologisch elkaars gezworen vijanden – voor elkaar zwijgen. Die aanpak leidde er indertijd zelfs toe dat N-VA samen met de PS stemde tegen het opheffen van de parlementaire onschendbaarheid van de gevallen Luikse PS-coryfee Alain Mathot.
Die “Belgische methode” maakt dat Didier Reynders anderen in zijn val dreigt mee te slepen, mochten werkelijk alle stinkende zaakjes waarin de naam van Didier Reynders of die van Jean-Claude Fontinoy valt tot op het bot worden uitgespit.
Een dossier zoals Land Invest Group toont hoe verschillende politieke partijen – ook al zijn ze ideologisch elkaars gezworen vijanden – voor elkaar zwijgen
Zijn er dan nog veel andere zaken?
In het boek De clan Reynders lijst de Franstalige onderzoeksjournalist Philippe Engels de schimmige dossiers rond Reynders en Fontinoy grotendeels op. Hij beschrijft daarin onder meer ook hoe Jean-Claude Fontinoy personeel (en geld) van de NMBS zou hebben gebruikt om verkiezingscampagnes van Didier Reynders te ondersteunen.
Ook de rol van Fontinoy bij de investeringen (en de gigantische meerkost) bij de bouw van het NMBS-station Luik-Guillemins wordt uitgebreid belicht. Net als de relatie tussen Fontinoy en Albert Karaziwan, de baas van de Semlex Group die voor honderden miljoenen euro paspoorten en andere identiteitsdocumenten leverde aan verschillende Afrikaanse landen.
Een ander bijzonder gevoelig dossier is dat van de bouw van de Belgische ambassade in Kinshassa door bouwgroep Willemen. Het is een van de dossiers die Nicolas Ullens al in 2019 noemde waarbij Didier Reynders smeergeld zou hebben ontvangen. Net zoals in andere zaken was er sprake van een juridisch vooronderzoek, maar dat leverde niets op.
Jarenlang leken alle affaires van ‘Teflon Didier’ af te glijden, maar zijn in verdenkingstelling maakt ontsnappen deze keer een stuk minder evident
Liggen de kaarten nu anders?
Jarenlang leken alle affaires van ‘Teflon Didier’ af te glijden maar zijn in verdenkingstelling, net als die van Jean-Claude Fontinoy en antiquair Olivier Theunissen, maakt ontsnappen deze keer een stuk minder evident. Ongetwijfeld heeft Reynders nog steeds medestanders, ook binnen het politionele en justitiële apparaat.
Ook de voornoemde “Belgische aanpak” waarbij andere partijen mee in bad worden getrokken, zet gigantisch veel druk op het dossier.
Daar staat tegenover dat de talrijke onthullingen en bewijzen die bovendrijven in verschillende media het bijzonder moeilijk zullen maken om het deksel helemaal op de pot te houden.

https://www.propublica.org/article/east-.title: “We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans Hospital in Crisis
https://www.propublica.org/article/east-.author: Eric Umansky, Joel Jacobs, Hokyoung Kim
https://www.propublica.org/article/east-.text:
This was not normal. But nothing had been normal at East Orange since President Donald Trump returned to office last year and set his sights on the VA.
The behemoth agency, which traces its roots to the Civil War, is both the country’s largest healthcare system and one of its most effective. It provides 9 million veterans what is essentially socialized medicine, often for free, under the cover of the American flag. The doctors, nurses and other staff are employed by the government.
Despite the occasional scandal and persistent short-staffing, studies have shown that the VA — where the doctors coordinate with one another and have deep expertise on veterans’ needs — has better outcomes than private care.
But in his second term, Trump has moved aggressively to upend this system, embracing a decades-long conservative campaign to effectively kneecap the VA’s government-run healthcare and shift veterans toward private doctors and hospitals.
Under Trump, the VA has increasingly acted like an insurer, paying doctors in the community for vets’ care. This, the reasoning went, would allow the government to cut thousands of needless bureaucrats while giving veterans more choices if the VA can’t provide the care.
Do You Have Information About the VA That We Should Know?
We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our reporting team.
Eric Umansky
I’m looking for tips on the VA’s care of veterans, and I’m particularly interested in hearing from healthcare providers and others who work at VA hospitals. Contact me with tips by email or securely on Signal. I take confidentiality seriously.
“We love our veterans,” Trump said during an Oval Office photo op shortly after his inauguration. “We are going to take good care of them.”
Days after that pronouncement, a memo leaked showing the administration was considering sweeping job cuts at the agency. “Things need to change,” warned Doug Collins, Trump’s new VA secretary, in a video message to staff.
After pushback from vets groups and others, the administration retreated from its threat of mass layoffs. But it found another, less attention-getting way to shrink the VA.
If Trump’s appointees couldn’t lay off employees, they would make work conditions so untenable that staffers would leave on their own.
The administration canceled the contracts of the agency’s unions — citing national security concerns. They ordered remote staffers back to the office. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency demanded employees report what they had accomplished each week. And the administration offered staffers early retirement packages and other incentives to quit.
Throughout it all, the VA’s leadership said front-line medical workers would be immune from any cuts. But amid the upheaval, many left anyway.
Six months after Trump entered the White House, the VA had 3,800 fewer doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of his term, according to the department’s own data. While the losses made up a small percentage of overall employees, the drop compounded longstanding shortages — and contrasted sharply with a hiring spree under President Joe Biden that had begun to address them. Many of the front-line workers who quit in Trump’s early days have never been replaced. Instead, the VA has eliminated thousands of open positions, including doctors, nurses and other providers.
The administration has denied that it is hurting veterans’ care. “There’s actually an excitement about what’s going on,” said Collins, a former personal lawyer for Trump, in congressional testimony this spring. A spokesperson said the eliminated jobs for healthcare providers were simply “not needed.”
That is not what we have found. Over months of reporting, ProPublica has watched the East Orange VA Medical Center — a typical agency facility — spiral downward. The hospital and its affiliated facilities in New Jersey lost nearly a tenth of the staff they had when Trump took office.
Over the past two years, a VA watchdog report shows, the number of roles with “severe shortages” in East Orange has tripled, from around 30 to roughly 90. Among them: oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, cardiologists, anesthesiologists, critical care doctors, nurses, mechanics, cleaners — nearly every job that makes a hospital run.
“It’s scary,” one East Orange administrator said in a meeting this year. “We have no one.”
It’s not just there. According to the VA’s watchdog, nearly all VA hospitals — 97% — reported having severe shortages of doctors. (The agency argues that the report — titled in part, “Staffing Shortages” — is simply about shortages of candidates and not actual staffing.)
The exodus of healthcare providers has increasingly forced veterans into the private care program — called Community Care — that the Trump administration has pushed. Amid soaring caseloads there and what a government report describes as “insufficient staffing,” many vets have been facing interminable waits.
ProPublica and other outlets have previously detailed problems with particular areas of VA care under Trump, such as mental health. But our reporting suggests far more care for veterans is being put at risk.
At East Orange, the damage wrought by the administration’s approach has cut like a scythe across nearly every area of the hospital.
Wound care is harder to get, since the nurses who specialize in it have mostly gone. The standard tests for blood clots weren’t available for most of the year, because there were no technicians. Even radiation treatment was stopped for months, after one of the key specialists left.
“Care has gotten worse for the patients,” said one doctor. “The services available. The wait times. We’re not providing the care that we wish we could.”
Another doctor, who recently quit, recalled how vets coming in with chest pains couldn’t get cardiac tests for months. “It felt dangerous practicing in a place like that,” said the physician, who, like others, declined to be named for fear of retribution. “That’s something you don’t want on your conscience.”
VA employees across the country told ProPublica they are seeing remarkably similar issues at their hospitals.
In Albuquerque, New Mexico, short-staffing forced the hospital to take many of its beds offline and stopped it from operating on severe heart attacks. Surgeries — on lungs and spines — have also been suspended for months at the VA hospital near St. Petersburg, Florida. At both hospitals, government reports found, Trump’s touted private care program was also overwhelmed and understaffed, further fueling delays in care.
Surgeries and other critical care have also been delayed at the Minneapolis VA. A staffer there shared a friendly looking notice tacked to a bulletin board in May: “No SOD coverage” — meaning, no surgeon on duty — “until further notice.” Radiation treatment was also suspended there because one of the machine’s operators quit. A Minneapolis doctor recalled that meant having to put a vet with cancer-riddled bones on a rattling ambulance ride every day, rather than simply wheel him down the hall. The doctor said each bump on the winter roads caused the vet excruciating pain: “It was miserable.”
A longtime oncologist who works with VA hospitals around the country told me, “Care is collapsing from the inside.”
Starting in July, ProPublica repeatedly asked the VA about evidence we’d found that short-staffing is hurting veterans’ care. We asked to interview Collins and the leadership of East Orange. The VA did not make them available. Nor did it address the specifics ProPublica shared on care.
In a general statement, the VA said care has improved under Trump. “This Administration is solely focused on measuring VA’s success by how well it serves Veterans,” said agency spokesperson Quinn Slaven. He cited a record number of appointments for both direct and private care over roughly the past year. Slaven also noted that the private care program began under the first Trump administration and was also embraced by the Biden administration.
As for East Orange, Slaven said the facility is outperforming private hospitals on certain metrics, such as diabetes care and some cancer screenings. Slaven also said more appointments were completed in fiscal year 2025 — which ran from October 2024 through September last year — than in any year of the Biden administration.
Citing privacy law, the VA noted it could not address individual cases without a waiver from the patient or appropriate family member. While ProPublica spoke with veterans’ family members and loved ones, none chose to sign.
We did, however, also ask the VA about the general issues surrounding those cases — such as East Orange’s OR being closed — and the agency did not respond.
In speaking to us, family members expressed surprise about their loved ones’ care. Falchetto’s brother, Tony, knew his brother had appendicitis, but hadn’t known that the OR in East Orange was closed. “Oh my god,” Tony exclaimed when I told him that his brother didn’t get timely care.
This story is based on internal documents, emails, agency data, recordings and interviews with more than two dozen current and former VA staffers, along with veterans and their families.
Contrary to the administration’s rhetoric, what emerges is a portrait of an institution in trauma.
“It Felt Like Bullying”
As soon as Trump was reelected, healthcare providers and other staffers at East Orange could feel the barometric pressure plummeting and the storm arriving.
The incoming administration’s plans for federal employees had long been clear. “We want to put them in trauma,” said Russell Vought in 2023, before he became Trump’s chief of the Office of Management and Budget. “We want them to not want to go to work.”
Just days into the new administration, officials imposed a rigid return-to-office policy, even as many staffers — from schedulers to radiologists reading digital scans — had shifted to remote work in recent years. An internal agency watchdog later wrote that the edict caused a “system shock” at East Orange, whose outdated infrastructure and long-mothballed rooms couldn’t handle the influx.
“I love working with vets, and I’ve never wanted to work anywhere else,” said one medical provider at East Orange who rattled off a list of edicts. “You’re this little person, and the full weight of the federal government was on you. It felt like bullying. It was very, very stressful.”
That May, Collins appeared before Congress and promised that the administration would not cut care: “We’re going to maintain VA’s mission-essential jobs, like doctors, nurses, claims processors, while phasing out nonessential roles, like interior designers and other things — DEI.”
Two months later, the agency touted the loss of nearly 30,000 staffers. “VA is headed in the right direction,” Collins said in a statement announcing the losses. It was hard to know if the remaining staff agreed, since officials canceled the VA’s employee satisfaction survey.
Among the most essential staff at VA hospitals have long been the specialty doctors, with their years of extra training. Recognizing their importance — and their potential to earn far more in the private sector — bipartisan legislation, which Biden signed into law in January 2025, allowed the VA to pay top-notch doctors more than the standard government rate.
But under Trump, the department didn’t use that authority for more than a year — even as more and more specialty doctors were leaving.
So, amid the departmental tumult, East Orange’s doctors began to exit, and they often weren’t replaced.
Six months into the administration, East Orange was down five psychologists, two of its four general surgeons and 18 nurses, among others, according to data obtained through a public records request.
Winter Comes to East Orange
A half dozen oncologists and surgeons told me that delaying treatment by more than a month and a half was problematic. At the least, they said, the delays almost certainly made his last weeks more painful. One told me he gives patients in Dennis’ condition radiation “within hours.” (ProPublica is withholding the veteran’s last name at the request of his family, which wants to maintain their privacy.)
Other veterans at East Orange faced the same dynamics: They were shunted to private care after their VA doctors and others left — and then they got stuck in the system since the office that handles private care — Community Care — was so overloaded. “That volume just keeps going up,” one administrator said at a meeting last November. The reason for the increased referrals to Community Care? She explained: “We just do not have the providers to provide the care.”
That winter the short-staffing and its effects spread across East Orange.
Staff were told via email that because of “urgent nurse staffing levels,” eight of the hospital’s roughly 60 general admission beds were being “taken out of service.”
“That was a big chunk of our beds,” said one of East Orange’s doctors. “I don’t recall ever having to close that many.” Without beds, the doctor explained, veterans often “stay in the emergency room, which is not ideal.” Indeed, studies have shown that leaving patients in the ER is dangerous and results in higher mortality rates.
A vet at one of East Orange’s campuses wrote to Trump complaining about short-staffing. He soon received a response signed by the president. “Every American owes our veterans an eternal debt of gratitude,” Trump said in the one-page letter, “and under my leadership, they will always have the loyalty, respect, and support they have earned and so dearly deserve.”
Around the same time, the hospital also had to shutter its operating room.
In December, part of the operating room’s air flow system had malfunctioned, contaminating the surgical instruments. Breakdowns like this weren’t unusual. East Orange was built 70 years ago, and its infrastructure showed it. But now the hospital mechanics who kept it all running were quitting. In interviews, they cited the same downward spiral that healthcare staffers did: As coworkers left, the staff who remained had to pick up the load, further increasing the strain of their jobs.
This put even more strain on a department that was already “severely understaffed” before Trump, said Irvin Webb, who worked as an air systems technician before he left the VA in May 2025. As a result of the departures, he said, repairs ended up taking longer. (Air conditioning equipment mechanic and air conditioning equipment operator were both among the many East Orange positions categorized as having severe shortages in this year’s VA survey.)
Medical staff felt the impact. One doctor calculated that the OR has been down nine times over the past year — compared with once the year before.
After the air flow malfunction in December, the OR was out of action for roughly three weeks. It then reopened for planned surgeries but remained closed for emergency and off-hours surgery for more than another month.
Then, on Feb. 12, Falchetto came to East Orange with a burst, gangrenous appendix.
He arrived in the early evening. Doctors noted that he had abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea, and described the results of Falchetto’s CT scan as “worrisome.” The doctors wrote that Falchetto needed surgery, but, as one physician noted, there was a “lack of OR capability.” And so, despite his life depending on quick intervention, Falchetto had to leave the hospital that was treating him.
At about midnight, East Orange arranged for Falchetto to be transferred to the VA hospital in Manhattan. It’s less than an hour away. But Falchetto ran into yet another problem: Instead of arranging an emergency transfer, the administrators scheduled him to be moved when the transport unit started its morning shift around 7.
“Imminent Risk to Patient Care”
It’s impossible to say for certain whether short-staffing caused Falchetto’s death. He was severely ill when he arrived at East Orange and may have died even if he got proper, timely treatment. But he didn’t get that.
“If I were the family, I’d sue everyone,” one of the doctors involved in Falchetto’s case told ProPublica. “He should have been operated on immediately.”
By last spring, managers at East Orange were sending increasingly dire alarms internally. One email in March — just a few days after Falchetto died — warned that the shortages were preventing proper care.
The crises began coming in quick succession, one more desperate than the next.
Both of the hospital’s orthopedic surgeons left. And wound care became a particular problem. The East Orange VA previously had three nurses who specialized in the area. By this spring, just one remained, according to East Orange staffers. She would have to commute dozens of miles between East Orange’s hospital and its satellite clinics and nursing home.
“I’m not going to have time for anything,” the nurse told colleagues in a meeting about the changes.
A few months later, a veteran arrived at East Orange with a diabetic ulcer — essentially an open wound — on his left foot. His records state that the wound “significantly increased in size” but that he hadn’t been seen by a wound care specialist amid shortages.
It was the VA’s nearby nursing home — which the agency calls a community living center — that raised the starkest alarm. A message to the staff on April 10 warned of an “extreme shortage of CLC nursing staff with an imminent risk to patient care.”
An administrator wrote in the message that the nursing home was taking emergency action to cut the number of veterans allowed at the facility from 192 to 180. Soon the cap was reduced again, to 170.
What that meant is that vets who qualified for spots would be mostly turned away.
Typically, the East Orange hospital could function as a kind of temporary overflow facility for the nursing home. And the nursing home could do the same for East Orange, taking some patients when the hospital was full.
But now neither could handle any more. On May 20, a notice went out to staff saying the hospital couldn’t accept patients from the nursing home that day.
What’s more, 17 veterans who needed admission were instead housed in the ER. Other hospitals also sometimes do that, but at East Orange the problematic practice went from rare to “far more common,” one doctor involved recalled. They were stuck there at least a day. “They’re in bed all day,” said the doctor. “It’s essentially a cot.”
“People Are Falling Through the Cracks”
The day after the ER pileup, Collins, the VA secretary, arrived on Capitol Hill to testify again. He bristled when he was asked about how staff cuts and eliminated positions were affecting care.
“There is nothing they cannot hire,” Collins told the lawmakers. If hospitals need a doctor, “they hire the doctor.”
Soon after, Collins quietly imposed staffing caps. What’s more, even when hospitals do have the authority to hire, the pall hanging over the agency now has impacted recruiting. As ProPublica reported last year, many doctors have turned down VA job offers amid the ongoing turmoil. Nearly 4 in 10 of the roughly 2,000 doctors offered jobs from January through March last year rejected them. That is quadruple the rate of doctors rejecting offers during the same time period in 2024.
At the time of Collins’ testimony, the VA had around 5,100 fewer doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of the Trump administration, a 3.4% drop. Under Biden, by contrast, the VA had been staffing up.
At East Orange, staffers told me the hospital had no vascular techs for most of this year, meaning there was no one to run tests on arteries and veins. And on the oncology ward, internal records show the team assigned to help patients navigate their treatment was down to just one nurse.
The providers who have stayed have been overwhelmed by vets’ needs — a dynamic that employees say is playing out in VA hospitals across the country. “People are falling through the cracks, and now they’re not getting help,” said one primary care physician at a VA clinic in Missouri.
“I’ve been working from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.,” she said. “I’ve had to take mental health breaks because I’ve been so stressed. I’ve been near suicidal. It’s not normal.”
Coins, Not Care
On a late August morning, a smattering of black SUVs and police cars pulled up to a VA campus near East Orange. Collins and a gaggle of aides stepped out of the caravan and went inside.
The VA secretary visited two departments. One was the chaplains’ unit, which, like so many units within East Orange these days, is “severely understaffed,” according to an internal presentation. (Collins is an ordained Baptist minister and once served as a Navy chaplain.)
The other was the residential PTSD unit. Staffers had arranged for Collins to meet with veterans, messages show. The event was not open to the media, but, according to staff and a vet who were there that day, Collins sped through the visit and did not stay long to speak with the vets.
On his way out, Collins stopped for a moment to talk to a veteran without legs in a wheelchair. After Collins strolled away, I asked the veteran what they discussed. “He just thanked me for my service and gave me one of these,” said Willie Johnson, showing me a commemorative coin that says, “Secretary of Veterans Affairs, Douglas A. Collins.”
I asked Johnson whether he had noticed changes in care since Trump returned to office. “Oh yes,” he said, noting that even food has gotten worse (among the positions with severe shortages at East Orange: food service worker).
The day after Collins’ visit, an email went out to staff. A “particularly meaningful part” of the visit, the email from a top administrator said, was the opportunity to recognize the service of five employees with Collins’ coin.
Among the recipients was the head of the maintenance department — the diminished unit that’s struggled to keep the operating room open.
Last week, as we were preparing to publish this story, a doctor at East Orange told me of a development: a backup generator had failed, and the OR was closed yet again.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!’ The last of the great Australian showmen – photo essay
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Words by Tereasa Trevor and photographs by Liz Ham
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
My uncle Teddy Trevor remembers Casey Nelson, a fellow showman, spruiking his double-jointed horse to sideshow punters in the 1960s. The horse, Nelson warned, was “showing here for the last time”. “Too late, too late will be the cry, when Happy Harry has passed you by,” he called. The act continued for another two decades.
I’ve been hearing stories like this my whole life. Ted laughs at Casey’s line as he pours another cup of tea and passes the biscuits at the kitchen table of the family home in Brisbane. At 91, after a lifetime in Australia’s travelling shows, he has no desire to quit the showgrounds yet. While their mid-century heyday may have passed, these grounds are still the lifeblood of his friendships and family.
Ted feels blessed, he says, to belong to two great show families: the Trevors, circus people on his father’s side, and the Fosters, sideshow people on his mother’s. Born on the showgrounds in 1935, he comes from more than eight generations of show folk.
Ted’s grandmother Cora Trevor performed an iron-jaw act, hanging upside-down and spinning grown men by her teeth, including her 14-stone (88kg) acrobat father. My great-grandmother Alice Foster, known as LuLu, arrived in Australia in 1913. She was a widow with six sons and a daughter. Lulu kept her whole family fed while running a dancing duck as a sideshow act.
Uncle Teddy’s own entry into work coincided with the second world war, which brought the showgrounds to a halt. He started his career selling fabric door to door from my grandmother’s vardo caravan. As a young man in the 1950s, he worked with my uncle Frank Foster, promoting Slim Dusty’s tent show on the sideshow alley. Those days were hectic. “You start at nine in the morning, you don’t finish till after 11 at night, and you do a show every 20 minutes,” Ted tells me.
“The show was a big event for the town,” Ted says – the biggest day of the year for some places. The men wore suits, hats and ties, the women their best dresses. “Now they go in a pair of shorts and thongs,” he says.
Teddy says the atmosphere of the sideshow was what everyone came to the show for. He can still recite the lines they used to entice the crowds: “The Slim Dusty show is just about to start! Australia’s top country-and-western recording star, the only Australian to top the hit parade in England, our only gold record-holder, is on this next big program. Hurry boys, hurry girls, get your tickets now! The cowboys, the cowgirls, the knife-throwers, the jugglers, you’ll see and meet them all on the inside.”
Uncle Teddy says that between the advent of TV, RSL clubs offering sideshow talent a new touring strategy, and state-based showground permits hindering showpeople from pivoting beyond the scope of their trade (for example, a clown joint can only do clown business), the landscape of the showgrounds drastically changed in the early 1970s.
Performers could sing half a dozen songs at an RSL, Ted tells me, “for what three or four days and hundreds of songs paid them on a sideshow”.
Participator numbers also declined, while costs climbed, he says. The big rides came in, worth millions. “The showgrounds are saturated with equipment now,” he says. “There’s no more ground available, so there’s no permits for the young showman.”
The cost escalated, too. “They’re charging $12 for a game on the clown joint. It’s all ridiculous,” he says. In Ted’s day, it used to be “only four bob [40 cents] to go and see the show”. Some shows were three shillings, and a shilling for a child. As he puts it: “The money was sort of nothing.”
In the last couple of years, I had seen Uncle Teddy posting diary-like entries on Facebook, sharing his memories along with photographs It led me to ask him some more questions.
Uncle Teddy often says: “I’m sorry you were born a bit late to see the action.” It’s clear he thinks I’d have loved it. He describes the camaraderie of the sideshow community, with everyone pitching in when they were needed. “Everyone’s got to do their own thing,” he says. “The stars have got to get out in the middle of the night and knock pegs in if a storm’s coming up.”
“I always loved the showgrounds because of the people,” Ted says.
 
My cousins still travel the showground runs, working joints, food trucks and rides. The skills of a modern showman are totally different from the past.
“Today you buy a $2m ride and you don’t have to be a showman,” he says. “People either like the ride or they don’t. It’s just got to be a spectacular ride, a thrill ride, and they’ll queue up and go on it … it’s a different ballgame.[Showpeople] don’t have to get up and tell a tale. They just say, ‘Next ride, hurry now, get your tickets for the next big ride,’ and that’s it.”
These days, Uncle Teddy visits his friends and family at the Beenleigh or Brisbane shows, and chats on the phone to his friends across Australia. “You get friends in different towns. You meet their kids, and when you get old, you meet their grandchildren, and they all become like family.”
I take my own child to the Royal Easter Show when it’s on in Sydney, and the moment I spot a laughing-clown joint, I half expect to see Uncle Teddy come around the corner, his eyes sparkling, a joke on his lips and coins jingling in his waist pouch. I tell them the stories Ted told me, alive with dancing ducks and my iron-jawed great-grandmother. Their eyes widen the way mine did at Ted’s kitchen table, and the show rolls on to another generation.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | Is art market regulation too much of a ‘good thing’?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexander Herman
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Anyone who says the art market is unregulated probably has not spent much time in an auction house compliance department. At the big houses, such departments might consist of half a dozen full-time personnel tasked with ensuring that the business can digest what has become an expanding layer cake of government regulation in the art sector.
In the European Union (EU) and UK, this includes regulation around money-laundering, data protection, imports and exports, artist resale rights, a growing economic sanctions regime, endangered species, firearms and complex tax reporting. The UK has additional obligations around ivory and issuing annual “modern slavery” statements.
Focus on the goal
None of these areas of control seem objectionable at first glance. But a careful observer must consider two things. Does the imposition of regulation achieve the intended goal? And, if it does, does it need to apply across the board, both up and down the market, to all participants?
In 2015, the British Art Market Federation undertook an analysis that listed 167 laws and regulations impacting the UK art market. The organisation’s current chair, Tom Christopherson, tells me that the impact of laws and regulations has increased considerably since then. Sophisticated players, with their compliance teams and in-house lawyers, may be able to spot trends, change course and avoid falling foul of the many rules. But what about the small fish?
Consider anti-money laundering regulations, which were extended to the art market by the EU and the UK in 2020. Absolutely nobody wants ill-gotten gains to proliferate in the art market. But despite negative stereotypes and hearsay around “dodgy dealings”, I have yet to find convincing evidence of money laundering in the European art market that could have justified such an expansive regime.
Registration issues
In the UK, data from HMRC (the official tax, payments, and customs authority) shows that more than 200 art market participants have been fined for violating the rules from the date enforcement began in 2022 to September 2025. None of these infractions involved the actual laundering of money, merely the failure to register with HMRC or to report material changes. (One gallery failed on additional grounds relating to risk assessments, due diligence and staff training.) Many of those fined are small operations, such as a toy soldier shop in London that featured in a recent Financial Times story on this topic.
With registration and reporting obligations, the onus falls on market participants. The scope of an offence can extend well beyond laundering itself. With the art market now a “regulated sector”, failure to report suspicions around, for instance, activities that could conceivably be connected to the funding of terrorism is now a criminal offence. An east London art dealer was caught under this new “failure to report” offence in 2023 and sentenced to two-and-a-half years behind bars.
Another area involves sanctions, far less simple than checking customer names against a list of oligarchs. The Russia sanctions list continues to grow by the month; in the UK, it consists of nearly 2,000 individuals and 1,000 companies—with additional lists for countries including Belarus, Iran and Libya—often with a multitude of transliterated names.
Also in the UK, an offence exists that goes beyond dealing with listed sanctioned individuals to exporting or “making available” luxury goods (including art) to anyone “connected with Russia”. This offence was used recently to charge the gallery Hauser & Wirth, along with its shipping company. Judge Tony Baumgartner of Southwark Crown Court dismissed the case in July, having found that the prosecution had failed to make a case that the individual to whom the work had been shipped was indeed “connected with Russia”, as he was no longer ordinarily residing in that country.
We all understand the benefit of regulation when it comes to saving lives, protecting the environment and smothering criminality in high-risk markets. But whether every piece of regulation is justified for the art world remains to be seen—or, rather, proven.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/r.title: Raid! Hochul Leaves MTA Holding $200M Bag
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/r.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/r.text:
Gov. Hochul let Mayor Mamdani (inset) pay $200 million less in contributions to the MTA, which she was supposed to supply. But she didn't, hence this graphic. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
The Hochul administration robbed the MTA of $200 million in bus operating funds in a secret maneuver to shore up the first budget put forward earlier this year by the Mamdani administration, a bombshell report from an Albany watchdog group shows.
As part of a budget deal that closed a $4-billion city budget gap, Gov. Hochul allowed Mayor Mamdani to reduce the city’s annual payment to the MTA’s bus division by $200 million — money that Hochul initially said she would cover from the state’s massive budget, but ended up being covered by the transit agency itself, according to the report from Reinvent Albany.
“The MTA is not the piggybank of the state and the city whenever they need to find money to pay for some other priority,” said Rachael Fauss, Reinvent Albany’s senior policy analyst, who wrote the report. “[These] funds are supposed to be dedicated and safe for the MTA. The MTA Bus aid in this case is supposed to be protected under a 2004 agreement between New York City and the MTA. Transit riders are the ones who get hurt, who are too often asked to pick up the bill to balance the budget.”
The raid became clear over many months and in ways that could easily elude sharp-eyed observers — even those who, as Robert Caro once said, turn every page.
For instance, on May 12, Hochul and Mamdani announced an agreement on “$4 billion in gap-closing support” from the state to the city. At the time, neither lawmaker specifically cited that $200 million of the city’s regular payment to the MTA would be forgiven or deferred as part of the package.
“Indeed,” as Reinvent Albany’s report put it, “the announcement made it sound like the $4 billion was ‘new state assistance’ to the city.”
And the city’s May 2026 Financial Plan Reconciliation – which reflects changes to the budget after the Hochul-Mamdani pact – shows the $200 million savings for the city as “State Aid for MTA” (see the screenshot below):
Throughout the spring, everyone — including the city and state comptrollers — asserted that the state would indeed pay the city’s $200-million contribution to MTA Bus.
A similar report a month later by state Comptroller Tom DiNapoli also said the $200 million reflected “city-funded MTA-related costs” that would now be picked by “by the state.”
By late June, however, the fiscal watchdogs figured out that they’d been had.
“The [budget] reflects a corresponding one-time reduction in the expected city subsidy reimbursement, which will be covered by MTA resources,” the document states. “Despite the reduction in city reimbursement, the MTA Plan continues to provide the resources necessary to maintain current bus service levels for customers.”
Advocates are not convinced. First, Reinvent Albany pointed out that the plan itself shows that predicted deficits have worsened, despite the 4-percent fare and toll increases in 2027:
Second, the raid undermines public trust.
“Raiding public transit funds or trying to balance the city budget on riders’ backs makes New York less affordable and erodes trust in our government,” said Danny Pearlstein, the spokesperson for Riders Alliance, which has supported regular fare hikes. “MTA enforcement agents recently got so aggressive that they assaulted bus rider Kyle Taylor over a $3 fare, so it’s pretty clear our transit system needs the missing $200 million and the governor should make it whole. Raising fares while raiding funds is not the policy New Yorkers expect from our transit champions in public office.”
Fauss added that those “champions” may appear that way in public, or to some reporters, but this particular shell game suggests a different portrait is in order.
“The MTA is getting $200 million less than it is supposed to from New York City — all while the governor could claim credit for helping the city to balance its budget,” she said. “Furthermore, none of this was written down in the state budget agreement. We had to dig through the financial records to even figure out what happened here.”
The $200-million MTA loss more or less wipes out the revenue it anticipated from next year’s fare and toll hike, Reinvent Albany added, which will make it harder for Mayor Mamdani to realize his signature campaign promise of buses that are both fast and free:
Streetsblog reached out to City Hall and the governor’s office for comment on Friday. We will update this story if we hear back.

He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop," which was a hit at the NYC Fringe Festival in 2016, and “SUV: The Musical” in 2007. https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Future of NYC Teen Therapy Service Uncertain Amid ‘Independent Evaluation’
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Trenton Daniel, Healthbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Healthbeat. Sign up for their public health newsletters at healthbeat.org/newsletters.
One of New York City’s more high-profile efforts to tackle the youth mental health crisis after the pandemic appears to be in limbo, and Health Department officials refuse to say whether they plan to renew a service that has drawn scrutiny.
Teenspace launched under former Mayor Eric Adams in November 2023 to provide local teens with free therapists by text, phone or video chat. The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene signed a three-year contract for $26 million with the platform.
Roughly 52,000 teens had signed up for Teenspace as of April 2026, Health Department officials told Chalkbeat. About 80% of the registered users were students of color in the first two years of the program, they added. Teletherapy services such as Teenspace are hailed as an innovative way to help teens confront stress, anxiety, and depression in a way that feels comfortable for them: by texting. For some New York City teens, the platform was their first encounter with a therapist.
The Teenspace website says the program will run through November 2026.
The contract with Talkspace, the New York-based company that oversees Teenspace, was scheduled to end in September but was amended to add two years, according to the city contract portal.
Parent advocates have long raised concerns that health officials haven’t done enough to protect teens’ privacy on the Teenspace platform. They alleged that Teenspace collects user data and shares it with third parties for marketing purposes without their knowledge. The Health Department says that after advocates raised privacy concerns in 2024, it worked with Talkspace to create a privacy policy specific to Teenspace.
“They really should have been doing their due diligence,” said Shannon Edwards, a digital marketing consultant and founder of an online platform called AI for Families. “The work should have been done. It should have been understood.”
Neither the New York City Department nor Talkspace would answer questions about the contract. Rachel Vick, a Health Department spokesperson, said the agency “is in the process of an independent evaluation to review the demonstration project and its outcomes. NYC Teenspace will continue to serve clients while that process continues.”
Talkspace spokesperson Alana Morales referred questions to the Health Department.
One of the program’s biggest champions was then-New York City Department of Education Chancellor David Banks. In a recent interview with Chalkbeat, Banks said he wasn’t paying attention to the initiative. “I don’t know where it really went. I don’t know how impactful it is now.”
Though youth well-being has remained a major concern among mental health professionals since the pandemic, there are signs suggesting improvement. In September, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced that it had seen gains concerning youth mental health and suicide risk factors. Among such risk indicators: Persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness had improved from 33% to 40% from 2023 to 2025.
Public Records Show Advocates Compelled Health Department Officials To Respond
After the contract was inked three years ago, privacy advocates sent Adams, Banks, and the health commissioner a letter expressing their “deep concerns” about Teenspace sharing users’ personal information with third parties.
Leonie Haimson, a critic of education technology who has long raised concerns over privacy issues, said it took advocates nearly a year of fighting to get the Health Department to improve the platform’s privacy policy. Public records she obtained and shared with Healthbeat showed that Health Department officials and Talkspace executives, including its CEO and a lawyer, were looking into the group’s inquiries about the use of trackers to monitor user data. Talkspace said it agreed to remove the trackers from the Teenspace website “as well as trackers not necessary for website operations or security,” records from December 2024 show.
In an email that same month to the Health Department, a Talkspace lawyer wrote that the company had taken measures “above and beyond what is normally required by even the more stringent public privacy standards.” He also noted the company hired an outside privacy law firm and “an outside pixel expert firm to independently and objectively scrutinize our privacy practices, policies and pixel usage, which was a material expense undertaken to help New York City DOH/DOE gain clarity on all of our practices.” In response, Talkspace revised its Teenspace privacy policy.
The advocates were irritated that the Health Department hadn’t taken a closer look at the Teenspace privacy protections before the contract was awarded.
“I just don’t think New York City is doing the job that it should be doing to really safeguard the privacy of children and teens in New York City,” Haimson said
Privacy concerns have continued to dog Teenspace.
At a City Council oversight hearing in April, Councilmember Rita Joseph (D-Brooklyn) wanted to know if any of the Teenspace data collected were being “shared or sold” with third parties.
“The data is protected,” Marnie Davidoff, an assistant commissioner with the Health Department, said. “The data that is used is only for service provision. There is no other allowable use of the data.”
The Health Department says it had privacy protections in place before parent advocates raised their concerns and had protected student data by including several contract stipulations. Among them: keeping client data confidential during and after the completion of the city’s contract, prohibiting the use of data for any purpose other than providing mental services, and requiring data to be destroyed after 30 days if the user did not start therapy.
Chalkbeat Senior Reporter Alex Zimmerman contributed to this story.
Trenton Daniel is a reporter covering public health in New York for Healthbeat. Contact Trenton at tdaniel@healthbeat.org or on the messaging app Signal at trentondaniel.88.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/s.title: Signal Problems: MTA Reports Delays On Multiple CBTC Upgrade Projects Amid Data Center Threat
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/s.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/s.text:
Signal work is not getting done any faster these days. Photo: Marc A. Hermann/MTA
It’s all red signals ahead.
New York’s efforts to upgrade signals on five subway lines are months behind schedule, MTA officials revealed on Monday, with none of the new signals set to come online until 2028 at the earliest — as data centers pose a looming threat to the agency’s efforts to complete the projects with less money.
With the exception of the recently commenced A/C signal upgrades between Downtown Brooklyn and Ozone Park, each of the MTA’s individual signal upgrade projects is now running late:
The Fulton Street-Liberty Avenue project, which upgrades the signals alone the A, C and E lines between 59th Street and High Street, was scheduled to come online in the first quarter of 2027 and now won’t do so until the fourth quarter of 2027.
The Queens Boulevard Line East project, which upgrades signals on the F train between Union Turnpike and 179th Street, was scheduled to come online in the second quarter of 2027 and now won’t be in service until the second quarter of 2028.
The Crosstown project, which upgrades signals on the G and F trains between Court Square and Church Avenue, was scheduled to come online in 2027 on the north piece of the line and 2028 on the south piece, and now won’t be online on either line until 2028.
The problems plaguing the communications-based train control upgrades vary by project, but mostly relate to software issues, train compatibility issues and design plans for how to safely change signals over from the old system to modern computerized signals, according to the MTA executives in charge of the upgrades.
This is most apparent on the Eighth Avenue project. An MTA executive said it was all ready to go, but that the agency found that the track geometry it fed into the computer that controls the train under CBTC was not accurate.
“We can see some issues in some of the testing,” said Mark Roche, the deputy chief development officer at MTA told the Capital Committee. “We can see there’s one silly thing that happened in the project that we have to correct. As the trains run down the system they’re telling us, ‘This curve is a bit bigger than you told us, this hill is steeper than you told us.’ The accuracy of the survey that we gave the computer is now telling us back [that] there’s something a bit strange here.”
Switching trains over to being controlled by computerized signals without accurate track geometry could lead to the same problems that snarled the Queens Boulevard West line in 2022, when the agency activated CBTC and experienced up to 20 signal malfunctions per day on the line.
“We could turn this system on now, it’s ready to go,” Roche said. “But you’d have lots of problems so we’re not gonna turn it on. On the QBL West we probably turned it on too soon, we’re not going to do that again.”
The MTA is running into problems with maintaining the existing signal system on the easternmost portion of the Queens Boulevard line. The agency chose to the legacy signals in place when it designed the new system. Its leaders found it difficult to ensure that an interlocking using CBTC software can respond quickly enough to provide safe and reliable service.
On the Crosstown line, Roche said the agency found a combination of physical work issues and planning issues. The MTA discovered much more serious tunnel damage and leaks, which took the agency a year to fix as it got to work installing new signals.
“State of good repair and discovering state of good repair problems on these projects is a major issue to make these happen quickly,” he said. “We’re finding too many things wrong with the system.”
But the agency also seems to have bitten off more than it can chew with its plans for the project. Roche told the committee that the contractor performing the work for the agency originally pitched the MTA on doing a “cutover” — the term for when a subway system moves from its legacy signals to modern signals all at once, instead of in phases as is usually done.
Despite agreeing to that, the MTA later determined that the idea wouldn’t work, and now has to work with the contractor on a phased cutover plan while the signals are being installed.
“One of those ideas was we could cut this project over in one go,” he said. “On the first day it’s non-CBTC, on the second day it’s CBTC. We’ve not been able to prove that’s a good idea. So we’ve slowed down the project. We’ve worked with [the contractor] to say hold on, let’s cut this over in five or six pieces, let’s spend a little more time.”
The MTA had some good news, too. Its leadership said that the physical work of ripping up tunnels and installing new track has gone according to plan. “The civil work, the track, switch, infrastructure — that is very much going on schedule,” said MTA Construction and Development President Jamie Torres-Springer. “The stuff that disrupts our customers, we are managing those very effectively.”
Roche also pointed out that the MTA has cut the cost of signal upgrade projects on a per-mile basis by about 33 percent, when looking at the Crosstown and Fulton-Liberty projects compared to the per-mile cost for the 7 train, QBL West, Culver, Eighth Avenue and QBL East projects.
There is a touch of grey in that silver lining though, as Roche said that everyone’s favorite boogeyman, data centers, are threatening to drive up the prices for CBTC upgrades. “We are seeing a massive competition with data centers,” said Roche. “The cables, the equipment is getting more expensive. We have a huge competition on the market with data centers.”
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/t.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/t.text:
How excited were we all earlier this year when Gov. Hochul and the state legislature passed a law allowing New York City to finally rein in the worst of the worst super-speeders?
We were very excited because the law would finally marry the city’s speed-enforcement camera system to real accountability: the city could order the installation of speed-limiting devices inside cars whose drivers got more than 15 school-zone speed-camera tickets in one year.
We’ve heard virtually nothing from the Mamdani administration on its plans to implement the law, but the City Council took a step forward last month when Council Member Kayla Santosuosso (D-Bay Ridge) introduced an actual bill to require the mayor to create and launch such an enforcement regime by the end of May 2027.
As loudly as that clock is ticking inside my head, it appears to be a lullaby for everyone else in town. Every day, I refresh the list of supporters of Santosuosso’s bill, and every day, I’m disappointed by how few members of the supposedly safety-conscious Council have signed on, and by how little urgency Speaker Julie Menin is exhibiting. I’m not panicking yet, but the bill is stuck at just 19 of 51 Council members, so I’d thought I’d use one of those hyperlinked sentences to remind our esteemed lawmakers whathappenswhenspeedingdriversarenotreinedin: theykillus.
The Department of Transportation has also pointed out that drivers with 16 speed-camera tickets are twice as likely to be involved in a crash to begin with. Once they get to 20 such tickets, they’re four times as likely. Thirty tickets? Fifty times as likely.
You get the idea. But does the City Council? Pass Intro 1153 now.
In other news:
If only more judges understood the Department of Transportation’s authority to make roadways safer — but Brooklyn Judge Inga O’Neale did by tossing a lawsuit by a random NIMBY against bike lanes on Brooklyn and Kingston avenues. (Reddit)
A hit-and-run driver hit someone in Brooklyn — and the cops said he was just “lying in the roadway.” Really? Sounds like the only thing lying is that preliminary report. (NYDN)
We always refer to The New York Post as our favorite tabloid, despite all the problems we have with its suburban, windshield perspective on the streetscape, but we do have to give at hat tip to former Mayor Bill de Blasio and Gov. Hochul for their appropriately critical, yet honest, best wishes in this Post birthday video.
Meet a real New York City hero: Lord of Bench. (Jacobin)
Our Open Plans colleague Jackson Chabot celebrated the victory of the mayor’s “government efficiency” ballot referenda with WNYC.
And the Post and Streetsblog covered Gov. Hochul’s “raid” on the MTA. (Our graphic was better.)
Following up on our own coverage of the cost of owning a car, Hunters Point Ledger did a nice visualization: The cost of owning a car for one year is the same as nearly 6,000 subway rides, or daily subway or bus commutes all year long for 12 people (more if they only have to go into work four days a week).
A part of the long-closed East River Esplanade will reopen this week. (Patch)
Meet the perfect location for a sandwich shop, which I’m happy to open and operate if I can get some backers. (West Side Rag)
Food for thought: Queens BP Donovan Richards wants to close fast-food restaurants for housing. (Queens Eagle)
And, finally, in case you missed it, “Saturday Night Live” took on the horse carriage “issue.” It’s not a perfect sketch, but it’s a reminder that the only time I wish I was working at SNL instead of at Streetsblog is when the entire cast breaks out in Broadway show tune parodies when debating the transportation issues of the day:
