https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: This Muslim civil rights group defended pro-Palestine protesters. Then Florida labeled it a terrorist organization
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sanya Mansoor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Omar Soboh, a student at the University of Florida, was organizing a campus panel about Islamophobia when he found out one of the groups being represented had suddenly been blacklisted by the state. Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization. The university’s Arab Students’ Association decided to cancel the event, and Soboh, who is Palestinian American, was disheartened.
“Our existence itself is political,” he said.
In July, Governor Ron DeSantis approved legislation giving five state officials the power to designate groups as “domestic terrorist” organizations. Once the designation goes into effect, as it did on 5 November for Cair and its Florida chapter, it can trigger debilitating penalties for the group and its supporters under state law.
The threat of these punishments effectively forces designated groups to shut down, said Cair. In turn, the group has sued Florida officials, including DeSantis, in federal court with the help of the American Civil Liberties Union, alleging violations of free speech and due process. Cair-Florida’s website homepage is now pitch black, except for a note stating that staff has suspended operations because of the “baseless and unconstitutional enforcement” of Florida’s law.
“For the first time in over twenty years, Florida Muslims cannot call their community’s leading civil rights organization for help if they experience a hate crime at their mosque, illegal discrimination in the workplace, violent bullying in school, or any other acts of bigotry,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, national deputy director at Cair, in a press release.
The shutdown has already affected Muslims in the community, as Cair-Florida can no longer provide pro bono legal services for discrimination and immigration cases, leaving local attorneys scrambling to pick up the pieces. Civil rights advocates fear Cair’s targeting is only the beginning of Florida exploiting its power to cripple all kinds of lawful advocacy, especially the pro-Palestinian movement.
“It’s entirely unprecedented for state governments to attempt to shut down organizations by branding them as terror organizations,” said Shirin Sinnar, a law professor at Stanford University who co-authored an amicus brief for Cair in a related case. “This sends a message to the Muslim American community, as a whole, that this organization, which has defended your civil rights, is no longer able to do that.”
The effects of the shutdown amid a rise in Islamophobia
Cair and its Florida chapter are the main civil rights organization for Muslims in the state, focusing on immigration, discrimination and free speech cases, know-your-rights workshops, voter mobilization and Islamophobia research. Cair-Florida, which employed about 12 staff members and eight contractors, has fought for prisoners’ access to halal meals and pro-Palestinian students’ right to protest. Cair’s national division took Muslim Americans’ grievances about federal “no-fly lists” to the supreme court – and won.
State officials have argued in legal filings, without clear evidence, that Cair and its Florida chapter have been operating as a front for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood, “all while masquerading as run-of-the-mill civil rights organizations”.
Cair denies these claims and has never been charged with or convicted of any crime. The group has been outspoken against extremist violence by groups like the Islamic State. Instead, Cair says, Florida is using the new law to “punish their perceived political enemies” and that the organization is being targeted for its religious missions and advocacy.
Aside from Cair, Florida also applied the domestic terrorist designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and “antifa” – a vague umbrella term for far-left-leaning and anarchist anti-fascist groups and individuals. This aligns with the Trump administration labeling “antifa” and certain branches of “the Muslim Brotherhood” as terrorist groups, alongside its targeting of leftist and pro-Palestinian activists.
Tactically, Florida’s focus on Cair reflects an attempt to go after one of the most marginalized groups first, said Sinnar: “The whole point is to establish a precedent with the most disfavored of organizations – the one that few people in the state will rally to defend.” Then, that power can be weaponized against other groups, she added.
Florida’s targeting of Cair comes amid rising Islamophobia in the US – and the pushback against it. That includes a growing crackdown on pro-Palestinian activism, felt most sharply by students facing discipline and immigrants threatened with deportation. Islamophobic attacks also colored Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s run for Senate – with Trump referring to him as a “jihadi” and his Republican opponent falsely linking him with the Muslim Brotherhood.
But El-Sayed’s victory, after leaning in to his Muslim identity and pro-Palestinian values, reflected that Muslims are building electoral power, regardless.
In January, El-Sayed will become the first Muslim US senator, joining a record-breaking seven newly elected Muslims in Congress. Civil rights advocates argue that electing progressive and Muslim lawmakers at the state level can help fight back against Republican-led legislatures and governors enforcing terrorism laws.
This has already happened in Texas, which flipped blue on election night. Governor Greg Abbott, who issued a proclamation last year declaring Cair a terrorist organization, and attorney general Ken Paxton, who sued Cair in an attempt to shut down the organization, both lost their seats to Democrats. Incoming Governor Gina Hinojosa said she will reverse Abbott’s designation in an interview with the Washington Post last week and Paxton recently dropped his lawsuit against Cair. The Muslim Legal Fund of America, which is representing Cair in its Texas lawsuit against Abbott’s designation, said that “it’s pretty clear this case is probably not going to go much further”.
However, it may be too late for an electoral solution in Florida, said Abdullah Sheikh, a community activist who tried to rally opposition to the state’s domestic terrorism program before the legislation hit the governor’s desk. While he’s typically an optimist, he now worries: “The legislature has zero incentive to do anything at this point.” A repeal would need to win over both chambers and the governor, all of which Republicans control.
Florida serves as a “cautionary tale for other states”, he said, to squash these measures before they become law.
The chilling effect sets in
In a normal year, Cair-Florida would have scheduled meetings with elected officials right after the midterms, but that didn’t happen this year.
Before the designation even kicked in, Cair and its Florida chapter had already restricted activity in the state by pausing donor outreach, cancelling active recurring donations and suspending plans for its three annual “life-sustaining” fundraising galas. A Florida-based IT company that Cair was relying on to relaunch a website tracking Islamophobia terminated its relationship with the group. Cair-Florida’s lawyers had already been turning away new prospective clients.
Earlier this month, a federal court rejected Cair-Florida’s request to operate while litigation continues; the organization has since appealed to the US court of appeals. In the meantime, Muslims across the state are feeling a chilling effect. “The mosques now are scared of their own shadow,” said Sheikh.
He has spoken with board members at more than a dozen mosques across central Florida, many of whom are now wary of programming, outside of prayers, that could be perceived as political. Some mosque leadership has told Sheikh they don’t believe Florida will designate them as terror organizations, though they’re wary that growing anti-Muslim hysteria means the government will “look for any excuse” to take away their non-profit status.
In Cair’s absence, individual lawyers are trying to help Muslims and pro-Palestinian advocates who need legal help. But “the void left behind by Cair-Florida’s absence is far too large to be filled by the good-hearted local attorneys that are trying to help the community”, said Jalal Shehadeh, a Palestinian American lawyer who serves on the boards of many legal organizations, including the Florida Muslim Bar Association. “We can only do so much.”
Shehadeh, who frequently fights cases related to the pro-Palestine movement, is anticipating a higher caseload because of Cair-Florida’s suspension. He pointed out that Cair lawyers who were focused on civil rights cases cannot be replaced with private attorneys, who may lack the time and not be able to front the legal costs that Cair does. “Most often the people that need help are the ones without resources,” Shehadeh said. “These individuals don’t have the ability to fork up $10,000 to hire a good attorney.”
Salma Khan, a Muslim American, reached out to Cair-Florida three years ago after a video of a man verbally harassing her went viral. It was the obvious choice, she said, explaining that she grew up in Fort Lauderdale and was familiar with Cair’s presence at mosques and schools; they helped students request Eid off and encouraged fundraising during Ramadan. Cair provided Khan with attorneys after she was harassed, as well as advocacy staff who raised awareness about her case online. Learning that Florida had designated Cair a domestic terrorist organization has made her wonder what will happen to Muslims who rely on the organization to protect them as they speak out against the government.
“Who else is going to be labeled that?” she said. “What will happen to our community?”
Soboh, at the University of Florida, felt hopeful about Muslims breaking ground in the midterms and believes the courts will ultimately rule in Cair’s favor. But he’s worried about the void left by Cair’s absence, and even his own career path.
He dreams of attending law school and working at a civil rights non-profit; he interned at Cair-Florida this summer. “I just want to protect my community and people,” he said. It’s still important for him to “fight for what he believes in”, he said, but he’s feeling more cautious since the designation went into effect.
“It’s made me associate doing work for the Muslim community as being something that is controversial,” he said.

https://taz.de/Wirtschaftswissenschaftle.title: Wirtschaftswissenschaftler zu Einkommen: „Die Leute sind zufriedener mit ihren Einkommen“
https://taz.de/Wirtschaftswissenschaftle.author: Hannes Koch
https://taz.de/Wirtschaftswissenschaftle.text:
Wirtschaftswissenschaftler zu Einkommen: „Die Leute sind zufriedener mit ihren Einkommen“
Markus Grabka sagt, für die Mittelschicht sei das Problem der Bezahlbarkeit eher ein gefühltes. Hart bleibe es aber für Gruppen am unteren Rand.
taz: Herr Grabka, die Ungleichheit zwischen niedrigen und hohen Einkommen nehme hierzulande ständig zu, heißt es oft. Sie dagegen schreiben, dass die Einkünfte nicht weiter auseinanderdriften. Woher kommen die unterschiedlichen Bewertungen?
Markus Grabka: Entscheidend ist, welchen Zeitraum man betrachtet. In ihrem neuen Verteilungsbericht schreibt die gewerkschaftliche Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, die Ungleichheit der Haushaltsnettoeinkommen sei seit 1992 deutlich gestiegen. Das ist ein alter Hut, was wiederholt berichtet wurde. Neu ist, dass sich die Einkommen in den vergangenen Jahren bis 2024 kaum noch auseinanderentwickelt haben.
arbeitet als Verteilungsforscher am Deutschen Institut für Wirtschaftsforschung in Berlin.
taz: Die Böckler-Stiftung schildert die Lage eher düster. Ist Ihr Blick beim Deutschen Institut für Wirtschaftsforschung möglicherweise zu optimistisch?
Grabka: Das glaube ich nicht. Die zentrale Information ist diese: Die inflationsbereinigten Nettoeinkommen der Privathaushalte wuchsen zwischen 1995 und 2024 im Schnitt um 30 Prozent. Gleichzeitig sind die Leute zufriedener geworden mit ihren Einkommen. Auch der Anteil der Sparer hat in den letzten 20 Jahren um 15 Prozentpunkte zugenommen. Selbst Haushalte mit niedrigen Einkommen können zum Teil sparen. Also ist die Lage nicht so schlecht, wie sie dargestellt wird.
taz: Warum wuchs die Polarisierung der Einkommen spätestens seit 2020 nicht mehr?
Grabka: Niedrigverdiener profitierten von der wiederholten Anhebung des Mindestlohns, die häufig über der Inflationsrate lag. Außerdem änderten die Gewerkschaften ihre Lohnpolitik: Statt gleicher prozentualer Lohnsteigerungen für alle Gehaltsgruppen setzten sie größere Anhebungen für Geringverdiener durch. Am oberen Rand dagegen entwickelten sich die Einkünfte von Selbstständigen zeitweise schwach. Während der Coronapandemie blieben viele Geschäfte ja lange geschlossen, und die Eigentümer verdienten wenig.
taz: Um 30 Prozent seien die Einkommen gestiegen, sagen Sie. Haben die Privathaushalte auch im Vergleich zum Wirtschaftswachstum profitiert?
Grabka: Ja, das ist an der Lohnquote zu sehen. Diese zeigt, welcher Anteil der Wirtschaftsleistung den Beschäftigten zugutekommt. 1995 lag sie bei rund 72 Prozent, heute sind es knapp 74 Prozent.
taz: Warum sind viele Leute mit ihren Einkommen zunehmend zufrieden?
Grabka: Offenbar können sie sich mehr leisten, unter anderem durch gute Lohnabschlüsse der Gewerkschaften. So hat die Kaufkraft zugenommen, obwohl die Preise in den Supermärkten seit fünf Jahren deutlich gestiegen sind. Für die Mittelschicht ist das vermeintliche Problem der Bezahlbarkeit deshalb eher ein gefühltes als ein reales. Tatsächlich leiden allerdings die Gruppen am unteren Rand, beispielsweise Singlehaushalte mit Kindern oder Zuwanderer. Dort ist das Armutsrisiko weiter hoch.

https://taz.de/Reform-des-Sorgerechts/!6.title: Reform des Sorgerechts: Kein Umgangsrecht mehr für gewalttätigen Elternteil
https://taz.de/Reform-des-Sorgerechts/!6.text:
Reform des Sorgerechts: Kein Umgangsrecht mehr für gewalttätigen Elternteil
Die Bundesregierung will Kinder besser vor häuslicher Gewalt schützen. Familiengerichte sollen gewalttätigen Eltern den Umgang ganz verbieten können.
afp | Die Bundesregierung will Kinder besser vor häuslicher Gewalt schützen. Wer als Elternteil gegen den andern Elternteil gewalttätig wird, kann künftig ganz vom Umgang mit dem Kind ausgeschlossen werden: Eine entsprechende Reform des Sorge- und Umgangsrechts beschloss das Bundeskabinett am Mittwoch in Berlin. „Familie muss ein sicherer Ort sein“, erklärte Bundesjustizministerin Stefanie Hubig (SPD). Die Reform soll außerdem Kinderrechte und die partnerschaftliche Kinderbetreuung nach einer Trennung stärken.
„Kinder leiden mit, wenn ein Elternteil dem anderen Gewalt antut“, sagte die SPD-Politikerin. Deshalb müssten Familiengerichte häusliche Gewalt künftig „nach engen Kriterien“ berücksichtigen, wenn sie über das Sorge- und Umgangsrecht entscheiden. „Wo es zum Schutz des betroffenen Elternteils nötig ist, kann der Umgang mit dem Gewalttäter ganz ausgeschlossen werden“, sagte Hubig. „Das Umgangsrecht darf nicht die Tür öffnen für neue Gewalt.“
Schon nach geltendem Recht sind Familiengerichte verpflichtet, häusliche Gewalt zu berücksichtigen. Ausdrückliche Regeln, wann der Umgang mit dem Kind bei Partnerschaftsgewalt ausgeschlossen werden kann, fehlen bisher jedoch.
Kinder haben ein Recht auf Schutz vor Übergriffen und Gewalt
Das ändert der nun beschlossene Gesetzentwurf. Familiengerichte sollen den Umgang auch dann ausschließen können, wenn dies zur Abwehr einer Gefahr für Leben, Freiheit oder sexuelle Selbstbestimmung des gewaltbetroffenen Elternteils unerlässlich ist. Der Gesetzentwurf stellt ausdrücklich klar, dass Kinder ein Recht auf Schutz vor Übergriffen und Gewalt haben – auch davor, Übergriffe und Gewalt gegen enge Bezugspersonen mitzuerleben.
Ministerin Hubig sprach am Mittwoch von der größten Reform des Kindschaftsrechts seit Jahrzehnten. Das Gesetz enthält zudem eine klarere Definition des Begriffs „häusliche Gewalt“. Sie umfasst jede körperliche, sexuelle, psychische oder wirtschaftliche Gewalt, die innerhalb der Familie vorkommen. Dazu wird ein Kriterienkatalog formuliert, an dem sich Gerichte orientieren können.
Das Gesetz gewährt auch Kindern ab 14 Jahren neue Mitbestimmungsrechte. So sollen sie ein eigenes Recht auf Umgang mit Großeltern, Geschwistern und anderen engen Bezugspersonen erhalten, wenn der Kontakt ihrem Wohl dient. Darüber hinaus sollen getrennt lebende Eltern in ihrem jeweiligen Betreuungszeitraum über Fragen des täglichen Lebens allein entscheiden dürfen – etwa darüber, ob das Kind zum Ballett geht oder krank zu Hause bleibt.

https://taz.de/Mahnmal-fuer-die-Opfer-de.title: Mahnmal für die Opfer der DDR-Diktatur: Denen, die sich nicht brechen ließen
https://taz.de/Mahnmal-fuer-die-Opfer-de.author: Klaus Hillenbrand
https://taz.de/Mahnmal-fuer-die-Opfer-de.text:
Mahnmal für die Opfer der DDR-Diktatur: Denen, die sich nicht brechen ließen
Ein neues Mahnmal in Berlin soll an die Opfer der kommunistischen Diktatur erinnern. Die Linkspartei war bei dessen Grundsteinlegung nicht erwünscht.
Die Koalitionsverhandlungen im Land Berlin zwischen Linken, Grünen und SPD sind noch nicht beendet, da kann die designierte Regierende Bürgermeisterin Elif Eralp (Linke) bereits einen Pflichttermin wieder streichen. Der Verband der SED-Opfer verbittet sich die Teilnahme eines linken Senatsmitglieds bei der Grundsteinlegung für das Denkmal für die Opfer der DDR-Diktatur.
„Die Linkspartei ist die SED nach drei Umbenennungen“, sagte dazu Dieter Dombrowski (CDU), Vorsitzender der Union der Opferverbände Kommunistischer Gewaltherrschaft zur Begründung der taz. Es gehe nicht darum, einzelne Personen zu bestrafen, doch wer in eine Partei eintrete, respektiere auch deren Geschichte, sagte Dombrowski. Sein Verband steht für rund 40 Organisationen von DDR-Opfern, er selbst saß wegen „ungesetzlichen Grenzübertritts“ vier Jahre hinter Gittern.
Die Grundsteinlegung des an die DDR-Opfer erinnernden Denkmals am Spreebogen im Berliner Regierungsviertel ist nach den Worten von Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer (parteilos) für das erste Halbjahr 2027 vorgesehen. Am Dienstagnachmittag präsentierte Weimer den kurz zuvor von einer Jury gekürten Siegerentwurf. Auf einer Fläche von elf mal elf Metern streben 121 Stelen aus Aluminium zehn Meter in Höhe.
Unterbrochen wird diese preußisch anmutende Ordnung von quer und schräg liegenden Stelen, die für diejenigen stehen sollen, die sich der Diktatur nicht beugten. „Formation und Aufbruch“ heißt das Denkmal aus der Hand von Bea Meyer und Michael Grzesiak vom Leipziger Architekturbüros ZILA. An dem Wettbewerb hatten sich 23 Teilnehmer beteiligt.
Nicht „irgendein Denkmal“
Weimer nannte die Präsentation in den Räumen des Bundesamts für Bauwesen und Raumordnung einen „wichtigen Tag für die Erinnerungskultur in Deutschland“. Schließlich gehe es nicht um „irgendein Denkmal“, sondern um einen „Erinnerungsort für die kommunistische Diktatur“. Er erinnert an die 250.000 in der DDR Gefangenen und die mehr als 300 Todesopfer an der innerdeutschen Grenze sowie die Hunderttausenden, die zur Zeit der sowjetischen Zone in Internierungslagern eingesperrt worden waren.
„Menschen wurden gebrochen“, sagte Weimer. Für die Bundesbeauftragte für die Opfer der SED-Diktatur, Evelyn Zupke, sende der Stelenwald ein Signal aus: „Wir vergessen Euch nicht!“ Opferverbandsvertreter Dombrowski nutzte seinen Auftritt für eine Spitze gegen sämtliche linken Vorstellungen: Er nannte den Bau „eine Mahnung an all jene politischen Kräfte, die noch immer an sozialistischen Utopien festhalten“.
Das geplante Denkmal reiht sich in eine Erinnerungslandschaft in zentraler Position in Berlin ein, die den Opfern der nationalsozialistischen Diktatur gewidmet sind. Dazu zählen neben dem Stelenfeld für die ermordeten Juden Europas die Mahnmale für die in der NS-Zeit verfolgten Sinti und Roma sowie die Homosexuellen, die Zeugen Jehovas und die Opfer der „Euthanasie“-Morde. Ein weiteres geplantes Denkmal soll den während der Nazizeit verfolgten Polen gewidmet sein. Am 11. und 12. Dezember diesen Jahres entscheidet eine Jury über dessen Gestaltung. Im Regierungsviertel fehlt noch das Einheitsdenkmal, dessen Bau sich mehrfach verzögert hat.
Das Mahnmal für die Opfer kommunistischer Gewaltherrschaft in Deutschland, so der offizielle Titel, hat eine lange Geschichte. Schon 2015 unterstützte der Bundestag eine solche Erinnerungsstätte. Vier Jahre später beschloss das Parlament die Errichtung eines zentralen Mahnmals. Damals stimmten Union, SPD und FDP zu, die Grünen und die AfD enthielten sich. Die Linkspartei, in Feindschaft verbunden mit den DDR-Opferverbänden, lehnte die Pläne ab.
Der Begriff „kommunistische Gewaltherrschaft“ sei in Bezug auf die DDR „unverhältnismäßig“, sagte die Linken-Abgeordnete Simone Barrientos damals. Es handle sich um einen „Kampfbegriff“ von Gegnern linker Ideologie. Zudem stelle der geplante Titel „das in der DDR zweifelsfrei geschehene Unrecht auf eine Stufe mit den unfassbaren NS-Verbrechen und relativiert diese“.
Eine solche Gleichsetzung lässt sich dem Siegesentwurf des Denkmals allerdings nicht entnehmen. Für dessen Errichtung sind laut Kulturstaatsminister Weimer 5 Millionen Euro im Bundeshaushalt vorgesehen.

https://taz.de/Cyber-Angriff-auf-Eishock.title: Cyber-Angriff auf Eishockey-Weltverband: Russische Propaganda-Parolen auf der Webseite
https://taz.de/Cyber-Angriff-auf-Eishock.text:
Cyber-Angriff auf Eishockey-Weltverband: Russische Propaganda-Parolen auf der Webseite
Mitten im Streit um eine Teilnahme Russlands an Wettkämpfen ist der Eishockey-Weltverband Ziel einer Hacker-Attacke geworden. Einer russischen?
dpa/taz Mitten in der hitzigen Debatte um eine Rückkehr Russlands zu Eishockey-Wettbewerben ist der Weltverband IIHF von Hackern angegriffen worden. Der IIHF bestätigte am Dienstagabend, dass er das Ziel einer Cyberattacke geworden sei. Die Homepage des Verbandes ist seitdem (Stand Mittwochvormittag) „vorübergehend“ nicht aufrufbar.
Übereinstimmenden Medienberichten zufolge wurde die Webseite offline gesetzt, nachdem dort zuvor das Bild russischer Eishockeyspieler samt einer Propaganda-Parole zu sehen war. Der IIHF bestätigte zunächst nicht, dass es sich um einen russischen Hackerangriff handelte.
„Wir verurteilen diese Aktionen aufs Schärfste und ergreifen die erforderlichen Maßnahmen, um den Ursprung des Angriffs zu ermitteln und unsere Systeme wiederherzustellen. Unsere Plattformen werden wieder online gehen, sobald wir sicher sein können, dass sie geschützt sind“, schrieb der Weltverband auf der Plattform X.
CAS-Urteil mit heftigen Folgen
„Der IIHF setzt sich weiterhin entschlossen dafür ein, die Integrität unserer Organisation zu wahren und unseren Sport zu schützen“, hieß es zudem.
In der Eishockey-Welt gibt es große Aufregung, nachdem der Sportgerichtshof CAS Ende Oktober entschieden hatte, dass russische Teams trotz des weiter andauernden Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine wieder an Wettkämpfen teilnehmen dürfen. Kanada hatte der Auswahl Russlands daraufhin keine Visa für die U20-WM ausgestellt. Moskau will in der Causa erneut vor den CAS ziehen.
Deutschland als Gastgeber der Eishockey-WM 2027 drängt auf eine schnelle Entscheidung in der Frage um eine Teilnahme der Russen. Die Bundesregierung will aktuell keine Aussage über eine mögliche Visa-Verweigerung treffen. Sie hält aber ähnlich wie der Deutsche Eishockey-Bund (DEB) eine Ausrichtung der WM bei einer Teilnahme Russlands für unmöglich. Mehrere Länder um Weltmeister Finnland wollen nicht gegen russische Mannschaften antreten.
Der DEB und auch der deutsche Staatsminister für Sport, Ronald Rauhe, hoffen nun auf eine generelle Suspendierung der Russen durch den IIHF mit deren deutschem Präsidenten Franz Reindl.

https://taz.de/Landtagswahl-in-Schleswig.title: Landtagswahl in Schleswig-Holstein: Platzhirsch vor schwieriger Regierungsbildung
https://taz.de/Landtagswahl-in-Schleswig.author: Esther Geißlinger
https://taz.de/Landtagswahl-in-Schleswig.text:
Landtagswahl in Schleswig-Holstein: Platzhirsch vor schwieriger Regierungsbildung
Schleswig-Holsteins Parteien bringen sich für die Landtagswahl im April in Stellung. Im nächsten Landtag könnten bis zu sieben Fraktionen sitzen.
Der Platzhirsch trat als letzter auf die Lichtung: Mitte November kürte die CDU Schleswig-Holstein ihren Vorsitzenden Daniel Günther zum Spitzenkandidaten für die Landtagswahl im April 2027. Damit haben die demokratischen Parteien im Land ihr Personal und zum größten Teil auch ihre Wahlprogramme aufgestellt. Noch unklar ist, wer die AfD anführt.
Schwieriger als der Wahlkampf wird vermutlich die nächste Regierungsbildung. Denn im künftigen Kieler Landtag könnten bis zu sieben Fraktionen sitzen.
„Wir sind bereit für einen richtig guten Wahlkampf“, verkündete Daniel Günther beim Landesparteitag, zu dem die Nord-CDU Friedrich Merz als Gast eingeladen hatte. Während der Bundeskanzler mit seiner Rede nur mäßigen Applaus erntete, war die Zustimmung für Daniel Günther umso deutlicher: Mit knapp 97 Prozent wählten die Delegierten ihn erneut zum Spitzenkandidaten.
Günther versprach im Gegenzug, das Traum-Ergebnis von 43 Prozent bei der Landtagswahl 2022 zu halten oder gar zu übertreffen. Schließlich könne es nicht das Ziel sei, die Messlatte zu unterlaufen: „Wir sind nicht beim Limbo, sondern wir sind beim Kampf um Demokratie und Freiheit, und den werden wir gewinnen“, so Günther.
Beliebtester Ministerpräsident Deutschlands
Dass die CDU wieder zur stärksten Fraktion im Landtag wird, scheint einigermaßen klar. Daniel Günther gilt als beliebtester Ministerpräsident Deutschlands, die Zustimmungswerte für die CDU sind gut. Dennoch sinken sie zurzeit: Bei einer Umfrage von Infratest dimap im April lag die CDU bei 33, bei einer Befragung von Insa im Juli nur noch bei 27 Prozent.
Um erneut ein Ergebnis zu erzielen, das nahe an eine absolute Mehrheit heranreichte, dürfte die AfD – wie 2022 – nicht in den Landtag einziehen. Doch danach sieht es nicht aus. Im April stand die rechte Partei laut Infratest bei 15 Prozent, im Juli maß Insa 18 Prozent. Damit würde die AfD die Grünen überholen, die als zurzeit zweitstärkste Fraktion mit der CDU regieren.
Geht es nach der grünen Spitzenkandidatin Aminata Touré, wird ihre Partei bei der Wahl noch stärker als bisher. Tourés erklärtes Ziel: Sie will Ministerpräsidentin werden. Es gehe nicht um eine Entscheidung zwischen CDU oder SPD, sagte sie beim Grünen-Parteitag Ende September in Neumünster. „Es ist kein Zweikampf, sondern ein Dreikampf.“
Touré versprach einen eigenen grünen Stil: „Wir sind nicht die SPD und reden das Land schlecht. Wir sind nicht die CDU, die auf ein Weiter-so setzt. Wir sind die Grünen, die etwas verbessern wollen.“ Neben Klima- und Naturschutz setzt die Partei stark auf soziale Themen – das Feld, für das Touré als Sozialministerin steht. Bei der Frage, wer die größte soziale Kompetenz mitbringt, wetteifern die Grünen mit der SPD und den Linken.
Daniel Günther (CDU), Ministerpräsident
Die SPD hatte ihren Spitzenkandidaten Ulf Kämpfer bereits vor einem Jahr bei einer Urwahl bestimmt, die Partei ist damit schon länger im Wahlkampfmodus. Entsprechend verband Spitzenkandidat Kämpfer seine Gratulation an Daniel Günther zum guten internen Ergebnis mit einer Abrechnung: Nach fast zehn Jahren CDU-geführter Landesregierung falle die Bilanz verheerend aus. Die Wirtschaft sei kaum gewachsen, es herrsche Verkehrschaos und die Kommunen würden durch Rekordschulden gedrückt.
Gegen die „offenen Baustellen und offenen Rechnungen“ der CDU setzt die SPD auf die Formel „Einfach, bezahlbar und gerecht“. Ob das ankommt? Die SPD hat in den vergangenen Jahren mehrere Desaster-Wahlen erlebt, bei der Landtagswahl 2022 kam sie auf 16 Prozent. Die Umfragen aus diesem Jahr sehen die Partei bei zwölf beziehungsweise 15 Prozent.
Wenn die AfD in den Landtag einzieht, würde es für Ulf Kämpfer und seine Fraktion nur für den vierten Platz reichen. Die Rolle der Oppositionsführerin könnte sie an die AfD abgeben – wenn sie nicht anstelle oder zusätzlich zu den Grünen als Koalitionspartnerin der CDU gebraucht wird.
Welche Koalitionen im Landtag möglich und wie viele Parteien dazu nötig sind, hängt stark davon ab, wie die kleineren Parteien abschneiden. Für die FPD ist die Abstimmung im April eine Schicksalsfrage. Die Liberalen sind nur noch in vier Landtagen vertreten, 2027 stehen zwei Wahlen an. Bundes-Parteichef Wolfgang Kubicki glaubt daran, dass die FDP sowohl in Schleswig-Holstein als auch in Nordrhein-Westfalen gut abschneidet. Aber wenn nicht, „dann war es das“, sagte er Anfang November.
Linke könnte wieder in Landtag kommen
Während die FDP ums Überleben kämpft, erleben die Linken eine neue Blütephase: Zum ersten Mal seit 2009 könnte die Partei wieder in den Landtag einziehen, die Umfragen sehen sie bei sechs beziehungsweise sieben Prozent. Das Spitzen-Duo Johanna Klitschmüller und Finn Luca Frey setzt auf Themen wie bezahlbares Wohnen, gute Löhne und die Rückkehr des Neun-Euro-Tickets.
Eine „stärkere Entlastung der Menschen“ und Politik für den Mittelstand verspricht der SSW. Der Südschleswigsche Wählerverband ist als Vertretung der dänischen und friesischen Minderheiten von der Fünf-Prozent-Hürde befreit und damit sicher im Landtag. Laut den Umfragen schafft das Team um Spitzenkandidat und Fraktionschef Christian Dirschauer zwischen fünf und sechs Prozent.
Bei der AfD deutet sich eine Kampfabstimmung zwischen Nicole Baer und Karsten Ambrosius an, die beide mit eigenen Listen antreten wollen – auf der Liste von Ambrosius steht unter anderem Kevin Dorow, aktiv in der AfD-Nachwuchsorganisation „Generation Deutschland“, deren Rolle er mit einem Motto der Hitlerjugend beschrieb, die Staatsanwaltschaft ermittelt deswegen. Nach den Kandidat:innen soll im November auch ein neuer Landesvorstand gewählt werden.

https://taz.de/Fenchel-Eine-Liebeserklae.title: Unterschätztes Gemüse: Give me Fenchel!
https://taz.de/Fenchel-Eine-Liebeserklae.author: Laura Catoni
https://taz.de/Fenchel-Eine-Liebeserklae.text:
Unterschätztes Gemüse: Give me Fenchel!
Die weiße Knolle mit ihrem Anisaroma hat hierzulande einen schlechten Ruf. Unsere Autorin kann das nicht verstehen. Eine Liebeserklärung.
Ungläubig schaut meine Freundin Anni mich an, als ich eines Abends bei ihr eine Fenchelknolle aus meiner Fahrradtasche hole, um sie in ihrer Küche in Streifen zu schneiden. Ich hatte den ganzen Tag nur Ungesundes gegessen und sie kurz vor meiner Abfahrt noch in meinem fast leeren Kühlschrank gefunden. „So komme ich heute wenigstens zu ein paar Nährstoffen“, rechtfertige ich mich. Schließlich gilt Fenchel als Heilpflanze, enthält unter anderem Vitamin C, Eisen und Kalium.
„Aber Fenchel?“, fragt Anni mit einem Blick, als hätte ich eine Stinkfrucht auf ihre Arbeitsplatte gepackt. Sie kenne Fenchel nur im Tee oder als Karnickelfutter.
Egal wem ich hierzulande von meiner Fenchelvorliebe erzähle, fast jeder rümpft die Nase. Die meisten haben Fenchel noch nie pur geschweige denn roh gegessen. Welches Geschmackserlebnis ihnen entgangen ist! Dank ihrer ätherischen Öle und ihrem Anisaroma schmeckt die Knolle süßlich und würzig zugleich, sommerlich-kräuterig-frisch und doch auch ein bisschen wie Weihnachten. Mit jedem Blatt, das man ihr abnimmt, wird ihr Fleisch zarter und nussiger. Trotzdem: So wie Haferbrei bei vielen der älteren Generation Kindheitserinnerungen an Mangel und geschmacklosen Schleim auslöst, weckt das Wort Fenchel bei Menschen wie Anni Erinnerungen an Kotzschüssel, Bauchschmerzen und öde Stunden im Bett.
Dabei liegt hier ein Missverständnis vor. Der Geschmack, den Fenchelfeinde mit kranken Kindheitstagen verbinden, gehört zum Fenchelsamen, dessen Aroma deutlich intensiver ist als das der Knolle. Die schmeckt weniger lakritzig, dafür fruchtiger. Ratgeberseiten wissen um das missverstandene Gemüse und titeln „Fenchel: die unterschätzte Power-Knolle“, eine Foodbloggerin schreibt vom Fenchel als ihre „späte Liebe“, und auf Reddit fragt eine Userin, wie man „Fenchel möglichst unfenchelig zubereiten“ kann.
Für den Start der Konfrontationstherapie empfiehlt es sich, den Fenchel zunächst mit Zwiebeln in Olivenöl und anschließend einem Schuss Gemüsebrühe zu dünsten. So verliert er ein wenig seines Anisgeschmacks und bekommt eine angenehme Milde. Mein Tipp: anschließend mit frischer Pasta und Kirschtomaten in eine Pfanne schmeißen, mit Zitrone, Salz und Pfeffer abschmecken und danach mit Parmesan bestreuen.
Hat die Pasta geschmeckt, können sich Fenchel-Newbies an eine meiner absoluten Leibspeisen heranwagen: Orange-Fenchel-Salat. Zusammen mit Olivenöl, Salz, einem Schuss Weißweinessig und Walnüssen sorgen die Würzigkeit des Fenchels und die Süße und Säure der Orangen für einen Kontrast, der auf der Zunge ähnlich gut funktioniert wie bei Melone und Schinken.
Der Salat, den die meisten meiner Freund*innen noch nie gegessen haben, steht bei meiner deutsch-italienischen Familie regelmäßig auf dem Tisch. In Italien ist Fenchel ein so fester Bestandteil der Küche wie in Deutschland Kartoffeln oder Gurken. Schon 1873 schrieb der kochbegeisterte französische Schriftsteller Alexandre Dumas über Süditalien: „Man isst Fenchel wie Sellerie, und nicht selten trifft man auf einfache Leute, die ein Bündel Fenchel unterm Arm mit sich tragen, die sich daraus, mit etwas Brot, ein Mittag- oder Abendessen machen.“ Auch bei meinen Verwandten in Rom gehört der Fenchel in fein geschnittenen Streifen zu den Basics wie Brot und Olivenöl, die fast immer auf dem Esstisch zu finden sind, egal welches Gericht folgt. Wem die puren Streifen immer noch zu fenchelig schmecken, kann sie in eine Marinade aus Zitronensaft, Olivenöl, Salz und Pfeffer tunken.
Für alle, die diese Ideen nicht überzeugen konnten, bleiben mir nur Oberflächlichkeiten. Mit seinen feinen grünen Haaren (nicht wegschmeißen, sondern als Finish verwenden!) bringt der Fenchel schließlich seine eigene kleine Frisur mit. Und mit ihren nach oben gerichteten Stängeln erinnert manche Knolle an ein menschliches Herz. Schließlich heißt Fenchel auf Italienisch – kein Scherz – „finocchio“. Ein Gewächs, das sich so nennt, kann man doch nur liebhaben.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal
Letter alleges possible conflict of interest in Lutnick not adding Megaspeed to US trade blacklist.
Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into whether United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his position to help Cantor Fitzgerald, an investment firm controlled by his two sons, avoid financial losses amid the scandal involving Jensen Huang at artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia.
In the five-page letter dated November 17, House Democrats notified Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald and Howard Lutnick’s son, that they are requesting information to ascertain whether “any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.
Al Jazeera has reviewed the letter.
The letter was authored by Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who is the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, Gregory Meeks of New York and the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California. It asks if the company’s financial exposure influenced Lutnick’s decision to keep Megaspeed off the US Entity List, a trade blacklist.
Megaspeed is attached to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who reportedly had an affair with now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week.
The US adds companies to the Entity List if it determines they pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy.
“The Secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC,” a Commerce Department spokesperson said in a statement in response to the letter, which was first reported by the Financial Times.
Cantor Fitzgerald denied the claims in the letter, saying it holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia. Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients, according to the Reuters news agency.
The firm also said it has no role in US export control or Entity List decisions.
Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four government agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not.
Reuters also reported that senior White House officials have discussed whether Lutnick should be pushed out.
On Tuesday, Huang, in his first public statement after he stepped down from Nvidia, said he would be “honored” to return as CEO, but the company’s board during its earnings call later in the day ruled out bringing him back.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.title: 2,000-Year-Old Wall Paintings and Mosaics Depicting Animals and Mythological Figures Unearthed at Ancient Roman Site in Mérida, Spain
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.text:
Fifty years after the Huerta de Otero site in Mérida, Spain, was first excavated in 1976, archaeologists are still making new discoveries. According to Hoy, a local daily newspaper, excavations have been intermittent, only picking up steam in 2019.
The latest discovery at the approx. 1.2-acre site, of which only 15 percent has been excavated so far, involves mural paintings from around the mid-1st to mid-2nd centuries CE, depicting animals like lions, deer, and various types of birds, along with mythological figures like a satyr. Archaeologists also uncovered a new, well-preserved mosaic to go along with one of Huerta de Otera’s most well-known discoveries, a large, multicolor Medusa mosaic floor uncovered in 2023.
Ancient Romans established a colonia, known as Augusta Emerita, in the area around 25 BCE. The site is made up of remains of a sprawling Roman-era residence, baths, and roads. The latest discovery involved excavating more of the remains of an opulent home belonging to a wealthy family. “We’ve encountered a tremendous surprise: extraordinary mural paintings,” Pepe Vargas, who oversees archaeological work at Huerta de Otero, told Hoy. Vargas also noted a courtyard peristyle covered in mosaics.
Excavation work at the site was possible due to a vocational training program, the Barraeca Professional School, overseen by the Mérida City Council. The current cohort included 12 local students trained as archaeological laborers for three months and then worked in the field at Huerta de Otero for nine months. A new group of trainees will likely start in January, according to Hoy.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: ‘Opposites don’t attract’: Adam Grant on how to strengthen friendships and make new ones faster
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Elle Hunt
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
Here’s a stat to ruin your day: of all the people you would call a friend, research suggests only about half would reciprocate.
The thought might make you want to wipe your contacts list and start afresh. But let’s look on the positive side, suggests Adam Grant, the Wharton organisational psychologist and New York Times bestselling author of Originals, and Hidden Potential.
“It means there’s some people that we don’t think of as friends, who see us as friends – so we may have more potential connections out there than we realise,” Grant says. The trick, he adds, is to understand the part these relationships play in our lives, the wavelength we share and what they need to thrive.
In his new book Vibe: The Secrets of Strong Connections in a Lonely World, Grant describes four platonic bonds: associates (transactional ties, who exchange resources), allies (who align on purpose and compatible goals), pals (who have the same idea of fun, and how to have a good time) and companions (connections based on care).
People can belong to more than one category, but understanding why we connect can help us to strengthen existing bonds and forge new ones faster, Grant says. It also helps us to let go of unrealistic expectations.
In an ebullient audio call – beginning five minutes late, as Grant warns is his habit – he explained how compatibility and constant contact are overrated, what we can learn from penguins, and the surprisingly simple step to building community.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
How do you define “vibe” compared with other aspects of connection, such as compatibility?
I think about a vibe as the quality of connection between people. Fundamentally, that’s about alignment – in the moment, of energy; and then over time, of needs, goals, interests or values.
Research shows that the foundational ideas of compatibility in western culture are at least partially false. Opposites don’t attract. People with supposedly complementary traits don’t actually get along better or end up closer – whether you’re talking about marriages or friendships or work collaborations. And, although similarity does attract people together, it doesn’t bond them.
It seems that, in general, we overrate compatibility – and maybe reciprocity, too, if half of our friends wouldn’t call us friends.
The fact they don’t reciprocate feels depressing, but for me, writing this book, it set the stage for the importance of distinguishing between different kinds of bonds.
Part of the reason there’s so much asymmetry in friendships is that people have different ideas of what a friend is. Some people, if they’ve met you a second time and liked you, will call you a friend; other people reserve the term for a much smaller circle of people, whose whole extended family they’ve met, or who they can pop in and visit unannounced.
I think that the language that we use to describe our relationships is often just too vague and broad to capture anything meaningful.
Instead of friends, you split relationships into four categories: pals, allies, associates and companions. What are the advantages of thinking this way?
It’s a little bit of a reorientation. In the west, we tend to build nuclear families and nuclear friendships. We treat our romantic partner as our No 1 ally, pal and companion, even though we know, empirically, that puts undue strain on the relationship. We do the same thing to our “best friend”, supposing that we can rely on them for everything.
That’s a lot of burden to put on a handful of people. It’s also assuming that all the skills that you look for – collaboration, playfulness, compassion – are going to be co-located in the same person, which is not always the case.
We’re happier when we have a “balanced portfolio” of bonds, you write. How clinical do we need to be about it?
We don’t always have to be explicit – sometimes that can backfire. I’ve had some highly entertaining conversations since Vibe came out, with various people asking: “What do you think we are?” I’ve discovered that a bunch of people I see as allies see me as a pal.
Writing the book, I thought about alignment, as in: both you and I agree that we’re allies, or pals. What I now understand – and there’s some evidence to support this – is that it’s fine if I seek allyship from you, and you’re looking to me as a pal. In functional relationships, we don’t have to play the same roles in each other’s lives, as long as we’re both aware that those are the roles we’re playing.
How does categorising our bonds allow for them to change and grow?
When people expect to progress through linear stages – from stranger to acquaintance to friend to best friend – they often end up on different wavelengths.
One thing I’ve seen consistently is when people have kids, they lose pals because, between family and work, they don’t have a lot of time just to hang out and have fun. But that can cut relationships off unnecessarily.
You meet someone new, you like them, you think that maybe you could become allies or associates – but you feel like you have to become pals first, and your free time is dedicated to your family. That closes the door to a deeper bond, as opposed to finding a different way of going about it: you could collaborate professionally, or sit down and have a heart-to-heart, without going to a bunch of dinners together first.
I think thinking in these terms frees us from the perceived pressure to progress friendships the way we did as teenagers, from “we know each other from school” to “we hang out outside of school” to “we tell each other everything”.
I imagine these categories can also relieve some expectations, too – for example, if you’re a new parent. Instead of comparing your “mom friends” negatively against your old, “real” friends, you can opt to see them as your allies in parenting.
That is such a compelling reframe. Because we’re more selective about our relationships in adulthood, I think we have this unrealistic aspiration that everybody we choose to spend time with is going to be someone we become close to. Certainly in the US, if you don’t feel like there’s a meaningful, personal connection, the zeitgeist says unfriend, unfollow, ghost, go no contact. But allies and associates can play a significant role in our lives – for example, our kids’ friends’ parents. They might not be people that we would confide in or chill with, but they can be role models for our kids.
On the flipside, I realised that, since becoming a parent, I’d been ignoring potential pals because I didn’t see having fun and hanging out as having a meaningful role in my life any more. But it’s really nice to have people in your life that you don’t need anything from, who don’t want anything from you – where the sole purpose of spending time together is the joy of the interaction itself.
How does this framework extend to building community?
Our social networks have gone from these densely interwoven webs to, now, individual hubs with disconnected spokes. In the book, it’s drawn as a bicycle wheel, but in real life it would fall apart: they’re just spokes that don’t go anywhere.
If we want to build a village or have a real sense of community, the first thing we can do is actually introduce our friends to each other. It’s one of the most overlooked ways to strengthen bonds, because it takes what are isolated, one-on-one connections and builds group solidarity around them.
A lot of people are struggling to find their group right now. We don’t have as many third places as we used to, and we also don’t frequent them the same way. I think, if you can’t find your group, form it.
Many people will be cheered by your finding that sharing memes, reels and links is a valid and effective way of maintaining connection.
A lot of people dismiss that back-and-forth as trivial, because it feels low effort. Sometimes it is just spamming each other with random junk from the internet, but when you take the time to send something to a specific person because you thought they would enjoy it or find it meaningful, that’s a gesture of care. It’s a bid for connection, or reconnection. It says to the other person: “I remember what you loved, I paid attention to your interests, and you’re the person that I wanted to share this with.” That’s a much more meaningful way to show people that you’re thinking of them than just saying: “Hey, how are you?”
It’s called “pebbling”, after the ritual among some penguins, which collect pebbles to present to potential mates. The first step is to pick the pebble that’s going to be meaningful. Sometimes it’s a bit of nostalgia, a reminder of something you shared in the past: “I just came across this photo of us together 10 years ago, and I wanted to let you know I miss you.”
How do we balance those lightweight check-ins with meaningful interactions and quality time?
I wish we had better data on that. My hunch is it probably depends on the kind of bond.
Frequent interaction is overrated for sustaining connection, and dormant ties can re-enter our lives and actually prove really meaningful bonds, even if it’s been months or years since we last interacted. My hope is to free people from the shackles of these expectations that we need to be in constant contact in order to be close.
For example, when we graduated, one of my college roommates and I made a pact. We put something on the calendar, six months out, with the agreement that either of us could cancel, anytime, but we had to reschedule. It’s kept us close for the last – gosh – 23 years.
What’s one more thing we can do to improve our relationships?
From reading the research, people carry these implicit expectations – about friendship in general, or each other – but never talk about them. One person is afraid that the other person expects a weekly call and a monthly lunch when they’re actually thinking: “I’m good with once a year.” Neither of them realises that the other is comfortable with less frequent, more meaningful interactions.
People don’t have those conversations nearly enough – but a relationship in which you can’t be candid is actually not a real relationship, it’s a charade. People are operating under a delusional belief that if they just tiptoe around disagreement, they can keep the peace. What that does is keep other people at a distance.
Conflict can actually bring us closer. This was startling to me: a dozen experiments have shown that when people are prompted to confront a friend, relative or colleague with the truth that they’ve been holding back, a week or two later, on average, most people feel closer to that person they confronted, and that person hearing it feels closer to them.
We can also begin by opening the door: “If I’ve ever done anything that upset or hurt you, I want to know about it.” To prove to each other that we can raise those things, and actually trust each other more afterwards – that’s how real bonds get strengthened over time.

https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/f.title: Mary Miss’s Long Fight to Keep Public Art Alive
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/f.author: Emily Watlington
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/f.text:
In the early decades of postwar America, public art tended to be seen as the pallid stepchild of architecture and design. Steel, bronze, or stone abstractions sited in front of modernist buildings were denigrated as “plop art,” or even more damningly as “the turd in the plaza.” And, accordingly, public artists were relegated to the province of decoration or historical commemoration while public responses to their art ranged from indifference to outrage over the expenditure of public money.
Then, in the 1980s, public art was jolted by a revolution. Rebelling against the tradition of the static monument, a group of young artists aspired instead to explore how art in public spaces could encourage connection, reflection, and interaction among viewers who didn’t necessarily have an art education. They created mazes, placed mirrors in the landscape, and drew lines in the snow. An extension of the boundary-breaking experiments of avant-garde artists of the 1970s, this new public art slowly began to gain acceptance from funders, developers, government officials, and general audiences.
Among the most adventurous of these pioneers was Mary Miss. Raised in the American West, she was interested in the tensions between rural and urban landscapes, the built and unbuilt environment, and the ways in which people navigate their path through the spaces of the modern world. By 1988, she had created an impressive roster of temporary and permanent projects that challenged the conventional definitions of public art. That year saw the creation of one of her most celebrated works, a waterside park titled South Cove (1984–87) in the newly created Battery Park City development at the bottommost tip of Manhattan. Created on a former landfill site, this work incorporates natural plantings, rocks, walkways, trellises, wooden pilings, a circular jetty, and an overlook that cantilevers over the edge of the Hudson River. Brilliantly weaving together architecture, landscape, and references to Manhattan’s maritime history, it remains a much-loved intervention in the urban landscape.
The year she made South Cove, Miss sat down with curator Patterson Sims at the 92nd Street Y for a wide-ranging discussion of her work and her views on public art. When he prodded her to speculate on the future of this new way of creating art for the public, Miss replied, “I think we’re just beginning to see what the possibilities are.” Then, reflecting on the support provided for such projects by the National Endowment for the Arts, she added, “I think they’ve started something that can’t stop.”
The irony of this faith in the NEA is not lost on Miss today. This spring, sitting in the Tribeca studio she has occupied since 1970, she recalled the enthusiasm of her younger self with what seemed like envy. “I was still feeling so optimistic,” she says. “I hadn’t been beaten down yet.”
Now a seasoned practitioner, her dedication to public art and dialogue remains intact, but has been tempered by the realities of politics, economics, and societal change. She has endured bureaucratic meddling; watched lofty rhetoric butt up against budgets, architects, and physical and technical limitations; experienced the shrinking and politicization of public money; and seen one of her signature pieces dismantled. In the course of her long career, she’s worked on numerous proposals that haven’t come to fruition, and at times put up with nonpayment and the theft of her ideas.
Yet, while these conditions might have deterred a less determined artist, Miss has responded by adapting: She shifts gears, rethinks her basic premises, and finds a new way. Her current project, “City as Living Laboratory” (CaLL), takes the idea of public art away from its dependence on gatekeepers and experts and returns it to the communities in which it’s created—a testament to her resilience and her remarkable capacity for reinvention.
IT TAKES A SPECIAL kind of person to operate successfully—and continually—as a public artist. Miss was born in New York City in 1944, but spent a peripatetic childhood moving around the country, with extended stays in Colorado and Florida as the family followed her father, who was in the military. She recalls a formative childhood memory of sitting in the back of an old Chevy and watching the scenery spin by. Fences laid across the fields whizzed by in a fine filigree and then gradually disappeared as the urban landscape took over. Such experiences sparked an enduring interest in vernacular forms and quotidian materials. They also provided a metaphor she has frequently invoked of public art as a wide net that stretches across barriers and connects people.
After getting a BA from the University of California, Santa Barbara, Miss came East and enrolled in graduate school at the Maryland Institute College of Art in Baltimore. However, she did not find the faculty very receptive to her interests, so she spent a year out of residence in Colorado. There, she did outdoor projects that contained the germ of her subsequent public work before returning East to New York City in 1968. It was an exciting time to be an artist: While the city itself was struggling economically, cheap rents made it a paradise for the era’s avant-garde. Miss fell in with a group of young women, among them Hannah Wilke, Elizabeth Murray, Nancy Holt, and Alice Aycock, who were challenging the orthodoxies of a male-dominated art world that was still fanning the flames of formalism. Miss recalls, “We figured, OK, you guys aren’t going to play with us. We’ll figure out another way.”
Miss’s early works, extending ideas of the ordinary yet defamiliarized spaces she had begun to explore in Colorado, were constructions using common materials that challenged viewers’ perceptions and sense of space. Some were indoor sculptures comprising bits of rope, ladders, stairs, or barbed wire. Others, using similar materials, were set outside in open fields and on hillsides. She generally eschewed urban contexts, and her modest approach was a marked contrast to the massive works of earth-movers like Michael Heizer and Robert Smithson, for whom an unpeopled landscape provided an empty canvas to be reshaped into a giant sculpture. Instead, Miss’s works were designed to alter viewers’ perspectives as they moved through and around the site, discovering unexpected vistas and pathways.
One work from this period, Perimeters/Pavilions/Decoys (1977–78), temporarily installed across four acres at the Nassau County Museum in Roslyn, New York, embodied the kind of paradoxes Miss was pursuing. Three towers and two semicircular mounds drew viewers forward, but the bulk of the work was not visible on the surface of the land. Instead, a ladder between the mounds invited viewers underground, where they encountered a series of corridors, doors, and slotlike windows.
The work caught the eye of the formidable critic Rosalind Krauss, whose now-classic 1979 essay “Sculpture in the Expanded Field” helped launch Miss into the limelight. In it, Krauss laid out a framework for understanding the movement of sculpture beyond the realm of the object and into an entanglement with architecture and landscape. She opened the essay with a description of Perimeters/Pavilions/Decoys, using it to illustrate the deconstruction of the idea of sculpture and its replacement, the idea of the field. In her typically abstruse fashion, Krauss noted, “Thus the field provides both for an expanded but finite set of related positions for a given artist to occupy and explore, and for an organization of work that is not dictated by the conditions of a particular medium.”
Miss was grateful for the attention, but remarks wryly, “I don’t know what she was interested in, and I didn’t know then what she was talking about. And she obviously didn’t really mean the ‘expanded’ field, because as soon as I started doing that, I went off her radar.” In fact, while Krauss’s essay mapped a set of formal relations, Miss was expanding the field of art to address human concerns.
The artist’s attention shifted from rural to urban settings, particularly to New York City, where she lived and worked. Her projects involved deep research into a site’s history, context, and present use, and these issues helped shape her concepts. For instance, when she was invited to work with the architects who were renovating the Union Square subway station in 1992, she delved into the archeology of the station and discovered how greatly original features like stairs, lighting fixtures, mosaic tiles, and turnstiles had fallen into disrepair or been altered or replaced over the years. She created 125 red framing elements that marked these changes, highlighting historical details that passersby might otherwise miss. At Battery Park City’s South Cove, pilings, blue ships’ lanterns hung on wooden lampposts, and native rocks and plants bring New York City’s residents back in touch with the area’s previous life as an important port. In a playful touch, the shape of the overlook platform deliberately mimics the crown of the Statue of Liberty, which is visible across the water.
In 1989, Miss embarked on a pivotal project—one that recently made headlines. She was invited by the Des Moines Art Center to create something in the nearby Greenwood Pond. Once an important community gathering place, the pond had deteriorated and become overrun with green algae. She started by researching the site, speaking with local ecologists, historians, and Meskwaki Nation elders. Miss discovered that the site had once contained a wetland, and that it, like most of Iowa’s wetlands, had been drained and tilled for agriculture. She also investigated the history and lives of the Meskwaki tribe, which had once occupied this land.
From that research, Miss decided to restore the pond while transforming it into a kind of demonstration wetland, using forms that echoed Native American lodges and earthen mounds. This work, titled Greenwood Pond: Double Site (1989–96), comprised a network of paths, canopies, and mounds, including a wooden pavilion following the curve of the shore as well as an elevated lookout and a walkway that plunged below the surface, allowing visitors to sit beneath the water level. As a newly restored wetland, it welcomed birds, insects, wildlife, and native plants in an educational display of biodiversity.
For this project, Miss collaborated with a wide range of community members and groups. She reflects that Greenwood Pond: Double Site “was kind of a fulcrum for me, because I was able to have a scientist, the Science Center, the Founders Garden Club, the Parks Department, the museum, all in conversation. It was a different way of working.”
For Jenny Dixon, director emerita of the Noguchi Museum and the inaugural director of the Public Art Fund, this “different way of working” is what makes Miss “a major figure in this field.” Dixon, who has known Miss since the 1970s, adds that “you just can’t make a piece of public art in your studio. There has to be another piece to it, whether it’s community, architecture, the space, the site, the environment. Mary’s not one-dimensional.”
With Greenwood Pond: Double Site, Miss began to shift from her earlier focus on land and history to the kinds of ecological issues that subsequently have become her primary focus. “In the wake of climate change,” she remarks, “artists need to help redefine nature. I’ve long claimed that the city is nature and we are living in it.”
But the project was also pivotal for a less happy reason: While the work was enjoyed by the public and maintained by the Art Center through various administrations, by 2024 it had fallen into disrepair. Kelly Baum, the Art Center’s director, informed Miss that the work would need to be dismantled because the Art Center did not have the $8 million necessary for restoration and future maintenance. A public uproar and lawsuit ensued as Miss attempted to force the museum to raise the funds to save the work. In the end, a settlement was reached: The work was taken down, and Miss was awarded $900,000, a portion of which she earmarked for a newly established fund to support threatened site-specific art works.
AT LEAST GREENWOODPOND: DOUBLE SITE was realized and lasted for 29 years. For Miss, the 1990s were marked by increasing frustration as many projects that had consumed considerable time and effort never came to fruition. These included projects for New York City; Los Angeles; St. Paul; St. Louis; and Long Beach, California. Many other projects that did see the light of day were then altered or diminished by the architects and planners with whom she was working.
Then came September 11, 2001. Miss’s studio was in the shadow of the Twin Towers. She recalls that her place “was covered with dust because the windows had been open. We had to come in and clean everything.” Deeply aware of the need for collective mourning, she soon came up with the idea of creating a temporary project to establish places where people could gather and lay flowers. Working with architects Elliott Maltby and Victoria Marshall, Miss named the work Moving Perimeter: A Wreath for Ground Zero (2002). She was struck by the motley nature of the temporary barriers and fences—composed of wood, chain link, concrete, and pipe—that kept out people making a pilgrimage to the site. Her idea was to paint some of these blue and replace others with new sections of fencing, seating, planting, and blue lights in order to create a movable perimeter that would grow denser and smaller as the exclusion zone decreased. It would operate as a place for people to gather and connect and share the profound sense of loss that was enveloping the city.
After years of struggling with bureaucracies, distant deadlines, and ultimately rejections, this project was an eye-opener for Miss. Although it was never realized, it still allowed her to rethink what public art could be: If it was temporary, it could be executed quickly and flexibly. And it would help if it relied on willing participants rather than reluctant bureaucrats to give the work meaning. “Wait a second,” Miss says she realized at one point. “There’s a way I can function instead of just waiting to get something built. You just need to take charge.”
While she was still working on some large-scale permanent projects during this period, she began to think in terms of interactive, collaborative, open-ended works that left a light footprint. This culminated in 2010 with the inauguration of CaLL, based on a concept that went all the way back to her idea of art as a net stretched across communities or even whole cities. She describes CaLL as “the idea that artists, working in collaboration with scientists, engineers, planners, and communities, can have an essential role to play in addressing the pressing environmental issues of our times.”
Over the past 15 years, CaLL has evolved into a series of different practices, including workshops, urban walks, programs, and community-initiated projects. The most ambitious of these is an initiative with the city of Milwaukee called WaterMarks (2015–). Working with ecologist Eric Sanderson, she has focused on the city’s complex relationship with water. A source of life, water also poses dangers from flooding, contamination, and aging infrastructures. WaterMarks involves going into neighborhoods to explore their specific relationship to water, engaging local residents, artists, and public and private institutions along the way. The project coalesces around a set of markers, 25-foot poles wrapped with solar panels and topped by illuminated blue letters chosen by the community.
These poles map out the nexus for educational and artistic projects that center on local stewardship of water. For instance, at Milwaukee’s Acosta Middle School, students chose the letter A for their marker, standing both for Acosta and, in this Latino area, agua, or water. In a series of walks with experts through the neighborhood, students learned about the area’s water history, its green infrastructure, and the need for storm water management in an urban environment. A green space created on a remediated slice of abandoned industrial wasteland became the Green Tech Station, designated with the letter G. This is a site for development, demonstration, and education about green infrastructure projects relating to the management of invasive species, pollutants, and flooding. The letter H designates the Harbor View neighborhood, where enjoyment of water includes activities like swimming, fishing, and kayaking.
So far, WaterMarks has 14 markers in place. Together they form what Miss describes as an atlas of water for the city. Rising above the network of markers is a 350-foot stack in the center of the city’s water treatment plant that has been repurposed as a beacon, with changing colors that warn residents when they need to restrict their water usage to avoid possible sewage overflows into Lake Michigan. “One really wonderful thing that’s come out of this 10-year project,” Miss says, “is that there’s a collective of people who are going to take it forward.”
WaterMarks is the most fully realized of CaLL’s undertakings, but the ideas it exemplifies appear in projects in other cities as well. In Boulder, Colorado, in 2007, Miss worked with climate scientists to map the potential disaster of the long-anticipated “500-year flood” with metal discs on trees, fences, and buildings that charted predicted water levels. In Indianapolis in 2014, Miss worked with local organizations to install along the White River more than 100 markers and mirrors that employed technologies like apps, webcam projections, and websites to provide information on the river’s history and ecology.
Building on Miss’s earlier projects in Manhattan, CaLL has also undertaken several initiatives in New York City. Broadway: 1000 Steps, initiated in 2009, is an ongoing reenvisioning of the city’s longest street as a “green corridor” equipped with hubs that provide text, images, and technology designed to engage the public in dialogues about environmental issues. In 2016, CaLL started Rescuing Tibbetts Brook in the Bronx. This project focuses on a plan to unearth a long-buried stream that now feeds into the sewer system and diverts it to a corridor adjacent to the Major Deegan Expressway, where it can become a new linear park.
Miss is currently working in Corona, Queens, on Cloudburst. This project charts the path taken by water during recent devastating flooding events in this low-lying immigrant neighborhood and helps residents understand the dangers as well as the mitigation efforts being undertaken by the city’s Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). CaLL has organized an advisory committee comprised of local residents and institutions, which will work with the DEP to pinpoint problems and needs. Central to Cloudburst are walks, either led by experts or self-guided, that explore the area’s ecology, specifically its water problems and possible solutions. In a move reminiscent of the markers set up in Milwaukee, beneath trees along the path, CaLL has placed benches with signs that invite passersby to connect to informative recordings via the internet.
But it’s the templates these projects create that are the most meaningful—at least for Olivia Georgia, who has been executive director of CaLL since early in its inception, in 2010. “It’s a model that can be refreshed, enhanced, and amplified by other artists,” she says. “We can’t imagine what the other artists’ projects will be. We set the table for them, but they have to figure out how to use the instruments in the tool kit we have assembled.”
Miss came up as part of a generation benefiting from federal support for the arts; but since that time, the tides have very much turned. She recently had grants canceled by both the National Science Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts. “They’re saying, ‘No science. No climate change,’” she explains, adding that this backlash makes it all the more important to find self-sustaining ways to help people connect to environmental issues. “I’ve had to really change my practice. I loved doing the Des Moines project. I love doing these projects that cost a lot of money. But now I’m trying to find a different way…. I’ve gone from this young woman who wanted to be acknowledged as an artist and who wanted to be able to make a mark with the work that I did, and I’ve ended up wanting this CaLL work to continue. That’s what I would really love to be able to leave behind.
“I really got beaten down in the ’90s,” she reflects, “and yet I ended up in this place. I did come out from under it. I’m glad I reached my optimism again.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/eu.title: EU Countries Renew Call To Exclude Russia from Venice Ahead of 2027 Architecture Biennale
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/eu.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/eu.text:
Ten European Union countries are demanding “further and sustained efforts” from the European Commission to keep Russia out of the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennial, according to Rapporteur.
The report cites a diplomatic note signed by Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, which says Moscow’s presence on the prestigious cultural stage risks normalizing its war on Ukraine. “In light of the current geopolitical realities… there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” the note reportedly reads. The group urged the European Union to take measures against Russia’s participation ahead of a meeting of EU culture ministers on Thursday and Friday.
Russia returned to the Venice Biennale in May for the first time since invading Ukraine in 2022, to the condemnation of politicians, artists, and cultural workers worldwide. (In 2024, Russia did not participate, choosing instead to lend its pavilion to Bolivia, which does not have a dedicated exhibition space on the Biennale grounds.)
An open letter circulating this year addressed Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco directly. “The claim that ‘culture is above politics’ is never neutral. In the case of contemporary Russia, this formula has become a political instrument used to promote aggression and advance state agendas while disguising them behind the language of cultural exchange and dialogue,” the letter read. It was signed by Pina Picierno, an Italian politician who serves as vice president of the European Parliament; Francesca Thyssen-Bornemisza, a collector who runs an art space in Venice; and artists Ragnar Kjartansson and Tomás Saraceno, among others.
The European Commission was among the most high-profile voices urging the Biennale’s organizers to exclude Moscow from the exhibition, even threatening to cancel a €2 million grant to the Biennale. (In July, it did suspend the grant.) In a March statement, the Biennale said it “rejects any form of exclusion or censorship of culture and art.” The European Commission consequently withdrew its funding.
Critics were quick to point out that the Biennale’s stance in 2026 appeared to contradict statements it issued in support of Ukraine in 2022, after Russia’s artistic representatives shuttered its Pavilion in protest of the Kremlin-led invasion.
The 2026 Russian Pavilion was the target of protests during the vernissage, including a joint demonstration from the Russian dissident band Pussy Riot and the feminist activist group FEMEN. The protest spilled onto the broader Biennale stage, as pavilions including Japan, Finland, the UK, France, Belgium, Austria, Italy, and the Netherlands saw temporary closures, shortened hours, or staff walkouts during the opening weekend. The pavilion was open during the preview period (May 5–8) for live performances tied to its exhibition, “The Tree Is Rooted in the Sky,” but ultimately closed from May 9 through the remainder of the Biennale, with digital documentation of the performances presented on screens installed in the building’s windows.
In an interview months later with the Italian publication Corriere della Sera, Buttafuoco doubled down on his decision to include Russia. “The Biennale is independent; I’d do it all over again for the Russian pavilion,” he said, adding that, “With us, art wins.”
The upcoming Venice Architecture Biennale is set to open to the public on May 8, 2027, following preview days on May 6 and 7, and runs through November 21, 2027. The theme is “Do Architecture — For the Possibility of Coexistence Facing a Real Reality,” curated by Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu.
ARTnews has contacted the Venice Architecture Biennale organizers for comment.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/capital.title: Dans GTA, tout n’est pas à prendre, mais tout à comprendre
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/capital.author: Marion d’Allard
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/capital.text:
Dans GTA, tout n’est pas à prendre, mais tout à comprendre
Il y a d’abord le mur des chiffres. Vertigineux. GTA VI, avant même sa sortie officielle, concourt en démesure dans un monde de l’industrie culturelle que le dernier opus des studios Rockstar domine littéralement. Huit ans de développement, 12 studios mis à contribution, plus de 4 700 professionnels mobilisés, concepteurs, ingénieurs, artistes, acteurs…
Au bas mot, 15 millions de précommandes et 1,5 milliard de dollars encaissés avant même son lancement, de quoi amortir les 2 milliards investis. Un record, encore. GTA écrase tout sur son passage, remisant la concurrence au rang de spectatrice d’une lame de fond mondiale, contrainte de repousser – ou d’avancer – toutes les sorties prévues pour éviter d’être plongée dans l’ombre de l’éclipse.
La déflagration n’est pas qu’économique. Elle est culturelle, bien sûr, elle est sociologique, aussi. Elle est donc politique. Ce 19 novembre n’est pas un jour comme les autres. Ainsi, la plateforme RH Remote, qui équipe nombre d’entreprises en logiciel RH, dit avoir observé, au niveau mondial, une hausse de 32 % du nombre de jours chômés posés.
La sortie, il y a plus d’une décennie, du cinquième opus de la saga GTA avait donné lieu à un flot ininterrompu de critiques. Les conservateurs de tout poil dénonçaient pêle-mêle un scénario subversif, violente diatribe contre le capitalisme états-unien – il en est pourtant le pur produit –, la violence des personnages et son supposé impact sur la santé mentale des joueurs.
Les paniques morales d’hier ont abdiqué face à l’évidence : la déambulation d’un couple de gangsters dans une Miami fantasmée où tout est permis ou presque tient lieu de catharsis. Dans un monde en crise permanente, la transgression est un aussi un sauf-conduit.
Il ne s’agit pas de verser dans le soutien béat. Les salariés de l’industrie du jeu vidéo en savent quelque chose, sous pression permanente, obligés d’aligner les heures de travail sans contrôle ni contrepartie, victimes de discrimination antisyndicale… Non, dans GTA tout n’est pas à prendre. Mais tout est à comprendre.
Le journal des intelligences libres
« C’est par des informations étendues et exactes que nous voudrions donner à toutes les intelligences libres le moyen de comprendre et de juger elles-mêmes les événements du monde. »
Tel était « Notre but », comme l’écrivait Jean Jaurès dans le premier éditorial de l’Humanité, le 18 avril 1904. 122 ans plus tard, il n’a pas changé.
