https://taz.de/Hohe-Energiepreise/!62311.title: Hohe Energiepreise: Wie in EU-Ländern der Preiswucher bekämpft wird
https://taz.de/Hohe-Energiepreise/!62311.author: Mathias Brüggmann
https://taz.de/Hohe-Energiepreise/!62311.text:
Hohe Energiepreise: Wie in EU-Ländern der Preiswucher bekämpft wird
Preisdeckel, Übergewinnsteuer, freiwillige Preisbremsen, Energiegeld an ärmere Menschen: Die Maßnahmen zum Senken der Energiekosten sind vielfältig.
Die Brücke der Freundschaft macht dieser Tage vielen Freude: Wer mit dem Auto über die 252 Meter lange Stadtbrücke fährt, die Frankfurt/Oder mit Słubice verbindet, kann auf der polnischen Seite sehr günstig tanken. 5,95 Złoty, umgerechnet 1,35 Euro, kostet an der Dyskont-Tankstelle der Liter E10-Benzin. Auf der Frankfurter Seite lag der Benzinpreis bei 2,159 Euro am frühen Nachmittag. In Polen galt am Mittwoch der Maximalpreis von 5,99 Złoty landesweit für Benzin, für Diesel 7,65 Złoty (1,734 Euro).
Polens linksliberale Regierung hat einen Benzinpreisdeckel erlassen. Finanziert wird der mit den Einnahmen einer Übergewinnsteuer, die der nationalkonservative Präsident Karol Nawrocki am 1. Oktober abgesegnet hat – im Gegensatz zu den meisten Gesetzen aus der Regierungskoalition im Sejm.
Das Gesetz sieht eine Steuer von 60 Prozent auf Übergewinne vor. Sie betrifft Kraftstoffhersteller und Unternehmen mit einer Lizenz für den Kraftstoffhandel. Erfasst werden Übergewinne, die diese Unternehmen zwischen dem 1. März 2026 und dem 31. März 2027 erzielen. Das Gesetz ermöglicht zudem vorübergehende Senkungen der Kraftstoffverbrauchsteuer und der Mehrwertsteuer.
Während die Regierung im östlichen Nachbarland Deutschlands die Spritpreise begrenzt und inzwischen auch über Preisdeckel für Gas und Strom berät, greift im westlichen Nachbarland sogar die Energiewirtschaft selbst ein. Der französische Ölkonzern TotalEnergies hat bereits im Juli den Preis für Benzin und Diesel an seinen Tankstellen gedeckelt: auf höchstens 1,99 Euro für Benzin und 2,25 Euro für Diesel. Das gilt laut Total-Chef Patrick Pouyanné „solange der Konflikt dauert“ an der Straße von Hormus.
Selbst das ärmste EU-Land hilft seinen Bürgern
Der französische Staat indes verkauft seit 1. November Diesel aus seinen strategischen Reserven und senkt so den Preis um 12 bis 18 Cent pro Liter an Tausenden Zapfsäulen. Damit die Mineralölwirtschaft das auch umsetzt, hat Finanz- und Wirtschaftsminister Roland Lescure Tankstellenbeteiber ins Ministerium einbestellt: „Denn wir wollen ganz genau darauf achten, dass die Franzosen und Französinnen von der Freigabe eines Vermögenswerts profitieren, der ihnen gehört und der zu einem günstigeren Preis erworben wurde.“
In Belgien legt das Wirtschaftsministerium die maximalen Treibstoffpreise wöchentlich fest. Tankstellen dürfen billiger verkaufen, aber nie teurer. Als Heizbeihilfe wird der Preis für maximal 1.500 Liter Heizöl pro Haushalt mit maximal 300 Euro subventioniert, sobald der Preis 1,775 €/l Heizöl erreicht oder übersteigt. Mit Heizöl heizt gut ein Drittel der belgischen Haushalte. In Portugal wurden die Verbrauchssteuern für Treibstoff gesenkt. Finanziert wird das durch eine Übergewinnsteuer von 33 Prozent.
Die tschechische Regierung setzt täglich Preisobergrenzen und kann per gerade beschlossenem Gesetz Strompreise für Abnehmer regulieren und die überhöhten Einnahmen von Stromproduzenten deckeln. Das ärmste EU-Mitgliedsland Bulgarien schützt seine Ärmsten: Statt per Gießkanne an alle, gibt es 50 Euro für die Bezieherinnen und Bezieher von Niedrigeinkommen. Strom- und Fernwärmepreise werden für die Bevölkerung nicht erhöht.
Während die europäischen Nachbarn die Spritpreise deckeln und ihre Bürgerinnen und Bürger angesichts hoher Energiekosten entlasten, werden in Deutschland eher die Menschen kontrolliert: Wer auf der Brücke der Freundschaft über die Oder zurück nach Frankfurt fährt, bekommt es wieder mit der deutschen Überwachung zu tun: in Form von Innenminister Alexander Dobrindts (CSU) angeordneten europarechtswidrigen Grenzkontrollen.

Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all-time
AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.
Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the biggest initial public offering of all-time, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June.
The AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.
The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped anticipated demand.
Anthropic had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece.
The blockbuster offering puts Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers from rival AI firm OpenAI, on track for a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, which would make it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla.
Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT.”
Anthropic’s market debut has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the rollout of AI.
Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI in the expectation that it will usher in revolutionary changes in business and society.
AI-related investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to a technology insights company Gartner, and companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the US stock market.
The spending frenzy has stoked debate about whether Big Tech is funding a future gold mine or a speculative bubble similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.
Jay R Ritter, an expert in IPOs at the University of Florida, called Anthropic’s valuation unprecedented for such a young company.
“Investors are excited about its software, which may allow drug companies to find drugs capable of preventing cancer and dementia within ten years,” Ritter told Al Jazeera.
“Thirty years ago, the internet was the next big thing. It has changed our lives. Today, artificial intelligence is the next big thing,” Ritter said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgence
Pennsylvania records eighth measles death of 2026, a day after the US formally loses its 26-year elimination status.
An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-related fatality in the northeastern state this year.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the death on Wednesday and said it had been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
While the department did not publicly identify the individual who died, it said they were a resident of Clinton County, in the centre of the state.
The latest death comes shortly after the United States formally lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for nearly 26 years.
That status indicated that measles was not endemic to the US, meaning no single strain had circulated continuously for 12 months or more.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a branch of the World Health Organization, updated the US’s designation on Tuesday after reviewing transmission data from the country.
The US is grappling with its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of November 12, the CDC had counted 5,412 confirmed cases since the start of the year.
Pennsylvania, meanwhile, reported 1,589 cases across 46 of its 67 counties. The state’s health agency pledged to continue its aggressive response to the outbreak.
“Approximately 300 DOH staff are proactively working with residents, community organizations, and health care providers to combat the measles outbreak in the Commonwealth through access to fact-based information and access to the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine,” the department wrote in a news release.
The agency also said state health officials have administered more than 11,500 MMR vaccine doses in 2026, including more than 7,200 shots in pop-up clinics since the outbreak erupted in late April.
Experts say vaccine hesitancy in recent decades has contributed to the rising number of cases.
Measles is highly contagious and can spread quickly, particularly when someone coughs or sneezes. The virus can survive for up to two hours in the air, and an estimated 90 percent of those who are not immune will catch it upon exposure, according to medical authorities.
Critics point to leadership under US President Donald Trump as contributing to the measles outbreaks.
One of Trump’s cabinet officials, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has questioned the efficacy and safety of vaccines like the MMR shot.
He also said in an interview with NewsNation that the MMR vaccine “contains a lot of aborted foetus debris and DNA particles”, an unsubstantiated claim.
Still, he encouraged vaccination in a social media post on Tuesday, following PAHO’s decision to revoke the US’s measles elimination status.
“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he wrote.
The CDC also said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.
Before taking office in early 2025, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Though it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff.
Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.”
So is Meester: the actor still best known for playing the Upper East Side’s ultimate ice queen in Gossip Girl is one of the few who can pull off “career woman with a heart of stone” with enough zest to overpower cliche. One believes, even accepts, when Meester’s Hannah, dressed in FBI office drag and glasses almost campy in their unsexiness, refuses both hugs and the suggestion of paid rest following the death of her mother, instead opting for the assignment in Montana because she feels “constantly overlooked and underestimated, nobody sees me coming”.
Guarding Stars, adapted from Katherine Center’s novel by Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith, is so named for the unenviable – at least, to the no-nonsense Hannah – task of protecting celebrities as opposed to, say, defusing IEDs in Afghanistan. Is it ever plausible that Meester, forever shaded with peak millennial resting bitch face, toted an assault rifle in the Middle East (as doctored pics helpfully suggest)? Absolutely not, but Meester is an amiable and capable salesman of a woman perpetually unimpressed, particularly when she jiujitsus a skeptical Jack Stapleton (Padalecki) to the ground.
As an action movie star akin, as best as I can tell, to John Krasinski-as-Jack Ryan, Padalecki is perfectly suitable – grizzled, wearing aviator sunglasses, voice 20% huskier than usual and just the faintest whiff of the narcissism of a real People’s Sexiest Man Alive. There’s an immediate spark to the two leads – one a fake action hero, the other too vigilant for her own good, both lonely. But it is mostly a testament to Meester’s sparkling intelligence – you know she knows what’s up – that one happily glosses over 1. Why Jack needs a bodyguard (a stalker, I guess?) and 2. Why Jack immediately insists that his bodyguard also plays his fake girlfriend for Christmas (mom has cancer).
No matter! Hannah promptly gets a makeover straight out of the Sundance catalog (somehow, not one of the movie’s many clear brand sponsors) and bunkers down at the ranch with Jack’s ailing mother (Andie MacDowell, bringing the movie equivalent of simmering homemade stew), gruff father (Shaun Johnston), wary brother (Noah LaLonde) and rodeo queen sister-in-law (Siobhan Williams). Also, a handful of kids and some horses, all creatures that lone-wolf Hannah would ordinarily neutralize in less than two minutes. Meester/Hannah instead make slow, steady inroads on the verboten realm of “the personal” with enough sincerity and self-awareness to puncture one’s perhaps military-grade sap defenses. (That the obligatory grief/trauma reveal hits harder than expected – which is to say, it hits at all – is thanks largely to the savvy use of camcorder footage, an instant nostalgia trapdoor for this film’s core audience of elder millennials.)
It’s not that Guarding Stars is tinkering much with the recipe; it checks the same boxes and clears the same hurdles as any other holiday romcom – mollifying snowball fight, awkward “fake” kiss, unconvinced family, late-stage family blow-up and romantic revelations – but with the swiftness and action sequence flourishes of a professional athlete. Or, perhaps more accurately, an ex-army bodyguard adept at the tuck and roll. Female hyper-competence, it turns out, pairs well with holiday cheer, and when it’s Meester once again taking no prisoners, you have my attention.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Fleur Hargreaves
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Mahmoud Khalil sues US Justice Department over failure to disclose correspondence with immigration judge
Former Columbia University graduate student Mahmoud Khalil sued the US Department of Justice (DOJ) on Wednesday for its failure to disclose documents showing what correspondence government officials may have had with the immigration judge and the appeal panel in his case.
This follows the administration’s failure to comply with a Freedom of Information Act request Khalil submitted in May, on the heels of a New York Times investigation that revealed his case was expedited and resulted in the recusal of members of the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA).
In April, the BIA issued what it called a "final order of removal" for Khalil, meaning he could be deported from the US. However, he is not permitted to be re-arrested while his free speech case in federal court continues.
The judges who make up the BIA do not operate as an independent judiciary. The BIA falls under the control of the executive branch of government - in this case, the Trump administration. The same applies to all immigration courts, which operate under the purview of the DOJ.
“The Trump administration is determined to deport me to deter others from speaking out for Palestinian liberation, so they rigged the immigration court against me,” Khalil said in a statement on Wednesday from his lawyers at NYU Immigrant Rights Clinic, the Center for Constitutional Rights, and Van Der Hout LLP.
“Now they’re trying to conceal their misconduct. I’m suing to shed light on their lies, corruption, and disgraceful disregard for constitutional rights.”
Khalil had sought records and documents showing what involvement, if any, members of the appeals board, other federal officials, or private actors had in the immigration judge’s decisions.
His case, his lawyers said, was treated "abnormally at every level".

Nommé en 2024, le ministre délégué à l’Europe Benjamin Haddad multiplie les positions et déclarations proches de l’extrême droite. S’il fallait encore quelque preuve sur les passerelles entre le macronisme et l’extrême droite, le ministre Benjamin Haddad en donne la preuve chaque jour. https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: EU governments approve trade deal with Indonesia to offset Trump tariffs
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
EU governments approve trade deal with Indonesia to offset Trump tariffs
The deal, initially concluded in 2025, will see both sides remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products.
European Union governments have approved the signing of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indonesia aimed at offsetting the impact of United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
The Council of the European Union’s decision on Wednesday also allows the deal to be applied provisionally. Both sides will remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products, and Indonesia’s 50 percent duty on EU cars will be eliminated within five years.
The deal will tie one of the world’s top economic blocs more closely to the fourth most populous country.
“These agreements will make it easier for European businesses to trade and invest, remove tariffs on almost all goods traded between the EU and Indonesia, and save businesses an estimated €600 million [$658.3m] annually in customs duties,” said Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee.
Indonesia has been negotiating a free trade and investment agreement with the EU since 2016. However, relations became strained after the European Commission decided to phase out palm oil from transport fuel by 2030 and imposed anti-subsidy duties on Indonesia’s biodiesel exports.
Both sides want the agreement, initially concluded in September 2025, to be applied as swiftly as possible. Indonesia will graduate from the EU’s generalised scheme of preferences on January 1, 2027, after which its exports will no longer benefit from preferential tariffs, the Council said in a statement.
The EU and Indonesia will now sign the agreements, which will then be submitted to the European Parliament for approval.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.
The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.
Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.
When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.
Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.
Anthropic’s main expenditure listed in its investor prospectus is computing power from datacenters. The company has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.
Anthropic is the first company at the forefront of the generative AI boom to go public, and its performance is likely to affect investors’ enthusiasm. Its competitor OpenAI was slated to hit Wall Street later this year, but CEO Sam Altman has said that the company opted to delay its IPO until it can overcome safety concerns.
Anthropic’s IPO comes during a volatile time for AI and the stock market. Last month, the industry saw a broader slowdown, with share prices dropping at several companies amid growing concern about the technology. Then, last week, Nvidia, which designs the chips AI companies use to power their chatbots, was racked with a scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang resigning after reports of multiple extramarital affairs.

His case gained global attention.
Khalil is married to a US citizen and used to be a US Green Card holder. When he was arrested, plainclothes ICE agents said his student visa and Green Card had been revoked.
Khalil was locked up in an ICE prison for 104 days, causing him to miss the birth of his first child, until a federal judge ordered him released while the government's case against him played out.
In July, he sued senior Trump administration officials, the conservative think tank, The Heritage Foundation, and the pro-Israel doxxing groups Betar and Canary Mission, seeking damages for unlawful conspiracy and a bid to "terrorize and make an example" of him.
In September, he launched a federal lawsuit against Columbia University, on the grounds that it allowed people like him to be discriminated against, harassed, and ultimately arrested by US immigration agents.
And last month, Khalil asked the highest court in the US to hear his case, arguing the government is trying to shut down a federal judge's ability to intervene when free speech rights are curtailed.
Should the Supreme Court take up the case, it would have wide-reaching implications for all the noncitizen US residents caught up in the Trump administration's pro-Palestine speech-related immigration crackdown, including Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri.
In June 2025, it was a New Jersey federal judge who ordered Khalil's release from immigration detention after more than three months in custody. Khalil was not deemed a danger or a flight risk, and the Trump administration's use of a rare foreign policy threat provision to arrest him was considered by the judge to be too vague.
In its appeal, the US government claimed the federal judge had no right to intervene as Khalil's immigration case played out, given that the Trump administration wanted to deport him.
While immigration cases in the US are heard by DOJ-aligned immigration judges, federal judges, by contrast, are independent.
The DOJ is currently run by President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer, Todd Blanche.

https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/c.title: Cartoons from the frontlines
https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/c.author: Cartoon Movement
https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/c.text:
Ruslan Pikhota is a Ukrainian frontline cartoonist and an active-duty officer in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Before the full-scale invasion, he spent 15 years working in children’s publishing in Kharkiv. He volunteered in February 2022, served as an infantryman on the Donetsk and Kharkiv fronts, and was wounded near Bakhmut. He now serves with an unmanned systems unit.
Since the spring of 2022, he has created more than 550 drawings in trenches, dugouts, ruined buildings, and between military duties. His work documents frontline life, drone warfare, fear, loss, brotherhood, absurdity, and the black humour soldiers use to endure war. His English-language book, Smile under the Roar of Cannon Fire, was published in 2025, and his drawings have been shown in Prishtina, Geneva, and Grenoble. He is now developing this archive into a three-volume visual diary of the war.
We are delighted to welcome Ruslan to Cartoon Movement! As an introduction, we asked him to select what he considers to be his ten most telling drawings made at the front lines.
Drawing No. 519 — FOUR IN THE MORNING
At the front, you constantly feel Death nearby, until it begins to seem like another member of the unit. I imagined the beginning of their day at four in the morning: the soldier starts with coffee, while Death takes a strange pet for a walk.
Drawing No. 393 — WHEN YOU’RE IN A TRENCH
A soldier sitting in a trench always wants more behind him — more artillery, more armour, more aircraft. I drew a very simple infantry feeling: you are one small person in a hole in the ground, and suddenly no amount of support seems excessive.
Drawing No. 533 — WHEN THE SKY FILLS WITH MACHINES
When I first went to war, the sky was mostly empty. A few years later, it had become crowded with reconnaissance drones, FPVs, bomber drones and interceptors. The soldier remained, but the war around him changed.
Drawing No. 564 — WHEN MACHINES BECOME PREDATORS
When two FPV drones suddenly rise in front of a soldier, they stop looking like machines. In that instant, the mind reads them as something alive — predators preparing to strike.
Drawing No. 527 — WHEN DRONES CHANGE THE FOREST
Through drone cameras, I have seen entire battlefields wrapped in fibre-optic cable, birds’ nests made from it, and our own drones caught in cables left by others. The moose is invented, but the new web spreading across the landscape is real.
Drawing No. 541 — THE SEASONS OF WAR: AUTUMN
This drawing is rooted in what happened to my platoon near Kurdiumivka in December 2022. Under fire, we dug shallow shelters in the frozen ground and covered them with plastic, but when the temperature rose to 1°C and rain began, they filled with water while shelling and assaults continued. We remained there for 19 days; when we were finally pulled back to rest, only five of the original twenty-four men were still with the platoon.
Drawing No. 419 — BOTH RIFLES JAMMED
During an assault, Amigo, a soldier of Ukraine’s 3rd Assault Brigade, found his rifle jammed just as the Russian soldier facing him discovered the same thing. Rapira, another soldier from the brigade, intervened and saved Amigo. I later turned the real incident into a short comic: the black humour is invented, but the absurdity that produced it was not.
Drawing No. 562 — PILA: A MODULAR PROBLEM-SOLVING SYSTEM
Pila, a soldier of Ukraine’s 3rd Assault Brigade, lost an arm in the war. I did not want to portray him as a victim, so I imagined his prosthesis as a modular system — a weapon, a bottle, a flower or a fork, whatever the situation requires. Dark humour does not erase trauma; sometimes it gives a person control over it again.
Drawing No. 362 — MOTHER OF GOD: OKHMATDYT
After Russia’s missile strike on the Okhmatdyt Children’s Hospital in Kyiv on 8 July 2024, I saw a photograph of a woman comforting a young patient. I redrew the photograph and transformed it into an icon of the Mother of God and Child. Some events leave no room for satire; they can only be witnessed and remembered.
Drawing No. 396 — THE FIRST DAY AFTER THE WAR
I imagined the first day after the war at the Swallow’s Nest in Crimea. Russia’s war against Ukraine began in Crimea, and it will end there; the soldier has put down his weapon, but learning to live after the war will be another long journey.

Hi!
We did not have a newsletter last month (we were on summer break), so it’s about time for an update! Below you’ll find our latest news, cartoon collections, and the most popular cartoons of the month. Enjoy! And no newsletter is complete without promoting our other newsletter, our daily editor’s choice.
Cartoon Movement at the Dutch Journalism Festival
The Dutch Journalism Festival (Nederlands Journalistiek Festival) is taking place on September 18 and 19 in Deventer, the Netherlands. The two-day festival features panels, workshops, movie screenings and live journalism. Cartoon Movement is also present with the workshop we delevoped for DELIAH: The Importance of Humour for Democracy: Good Humour versus Bad Humour
Unfortunately, the workshop is already fully booked. If you are interested, we did a similar workshop at the International Journalism Festival in Perugia in April, which was recorded:
Also, if you are planning to visit the festival, several Dutch cartoonists will be drawing live on Saturday to see who can make the best cartoon.
The state of democracy, in cartoons
The Kettering Foundation has published a collection of international cartoons with different perspectives on democracy. The collection, with cartoons from 19 renowned cartoonists, was put together by Tjeerd Royaards (cartoonist and editor-in-chief at Cartoon Movement), Terry Anderson (executive director at Cartoonists Rights), and Patrick Gathara (2026 CFK Global Fellow).
Satire translates complex political realities into stories, images, and jokes that ordinary people can engage with. In doing so, it lowers the barriers to political participation while creating space for critique that is often less threatening to audiences than overt political argument.
Patrick Gathara
