https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Unpardonable Malpractice of Pete Hegseth
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Michael T. Klare
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Unpardonable Malpractice of Pete Hegseth
Yes, the defense secretary has committed impeachable offenses. But he’s also just really, really, really bad at his job.
The offenses cited by Representative Thomas Massie (R-KY) in commencing impeachment proceedings against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth—that he initiated and sustained the war with Iran without required congressional approval, conducted military operations in Yemen and the Caribbean without such approval, and eroded protections for civilians trapped in overseas war zones—are all valid and fully justify his removal from office in accordance with constitutional precepts. But however worthy, they fail to capture his essential, unpardonable offense: strategic malpractice when commanding troops in battle.
Hegseth himself has been very outspoken about the need to cleanse the armed services of incompetent generals and admirals (many of whom, he claims, received their promotions as the result of some sort of affirmative action process) and to retain only those able to fight and win. “The previous administration wanted politically correct generals,” he told an assembly of junior officers on September 30. “We only want the top performing generals. It’s not just pass or fail…. The best move on, the worst do not.”
Secretary Hegseth wants us (and every member of Congress) to believe that he ranks among the successful generals and so should be retained. After berating Massie (“a disgruntled and defeated congressman”) and others during his unapologetic Pentagon press conference on November 10, Hegseth sought to defend his record as the ultimate commander of US forces. “By every measure,” he said of the war against Iran, “we achieved a historic military victory.”
But this is sheer fabrication. Were Hegseth to hold himself to the same high standards he supposedly set for his generals, he would have to say: “By every measure, we achieved a total fiasco in Iran,” and hand in his resignation.
To fully appreciate the magnitude of Hegseth’s incompetence, let’s recall the tasks he was assigned when ordered by President Trump to commence hostilities against Iran on February 28. As indicated by Trump in a prerecorded video address that morning, Hegseth was given four overriding objectives: (1) to eliminate, forever, Iran’s ability to construct a nuclear weapon; (2) to eliminate Iran’s ability to manufacture and launch long-range ballistic missiles; (3) to eliminate Iran’s ability to project power in the region, whether with its own military or via proxy forces like Hezbollah and the Houthi rebels; and (4) to eliminate the Iran problem altogether, by killing off Iran’s top leadership and igniting a popular rebellion.
Hegseth set out to achieve these goals with unrestrained vigor. The US military alone struck 13,000 targets in Iran during the first 38 days of fighting, and its Israeli partners struck many thousands more. From the administration’s perspective, it was a total win. In a press statement released on April 8, following the announcement of a ceasefire (that was to prove temporary), the White House declared that “the greatest fighting force the world has ever known has met those objectives with overwhelming strength and lethal precision.”
Among the war’s ostensible accomplishments: “Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal and production capacity has been razed…eliminating its ability to project power.” Also, “Iran can no longer arm terrorist proxies.” And, although the regime was still clinging to power: “What’s left of [it] is desperate, dejected, and in denial.”
For Hegseth, this was a “decisive military victory.”
But, in fact, it wasn’t: Not one of Trump’s stated objectives was achieved by Hegseth and the forces under his command. Not one.
To begin with, the Iranian regime has remained intact and (so far as can be determined from afar) remains as entrenched as ever, with no signs of an imminent popular rebellion.
Although the Iranians have made no visible move to reconstitute their uranium enrichment program (a prerequisite for manufacturing a nuclear bomb), they have demonstrated no inclination to surrender their existing stockpiles of highly enriched uranium or to renounce their enrichment efforts entirely.
And Iran’s regional clout—now buttressed by its apparent capacity to disrupt the Persian Gulf oil flow at will—appears enhanced, not diminished.
Most significantly, Iran’s ability to project power with missiles and long-range drones remains robust, as demonstrated by repeated strikes on US bases in the region. As if to prove this point, the Iranians struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17, killing three US Army service members and destroying or damaging vital military equipment.
The Iranians have also continued to strike tankers attempting to traverse the strategic Strait of Hormuz without their approval, sharply constricting the world’s oil trade and keeping diesel and gasoline prices high.
From any perspective, then, the Hegseth-run war on Iran has been a total fiasco, failing to achieve a single one of its stated objectives. For these reasons alone, the self-styled “secretary of war” should resign. But the war was more than a failure: It entailed a massive strategic disaster, one whose vast dimensions are only beginning to be calculated.
The Strategic Calculus
How do you measure a strategic disaster? We begin, properly, with an intelligence failure, followed by military miscalculation and geopolitical retreat—all adding up to an astonishing contraction of America’s global clout.
Let’s start with intelligence failure, the origin of so much of the sorrow to come. Hegseth and his top lieutenants began with the assumptions that (a) the Iranian military was no match for the technologically superior US military, and (b) the Iranian regime was fragile and would be swept away once its top leaders were killed. Neither assumption has proved even remotely accurate: The Iranian military has demonstrated a remarkable degree of resilience under fire, able to inflict far more damage on US forces than was ever thought possible; and the regime has proved equally resilient, able to reconstitute itself after the loss of its top leadership on the first day of fighting.
Some of this leadership myopia can be attributed to Trump’s ebullience after the successful January 3 US seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in Caracas, and to the overly optimistic assessment of the regime’s fragility given to Trump on February 11 by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a pivotal White House meeting. From the accounts by Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman of The New York Times, we know that Vice President JD Vance and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, warned of possible risks in starting a war with Iran, but that Hegseth assured the president of a rapid US victory. With this assurance, Trump took the plunge.
But this is only part of the story. Hegseth was clearly so blinded by his faith in “the greatest fighting force the world has ever known” that he failed to consider the potential strengths of his adversary—the very first responsibility of a capable commander. The Iranians may have possessed a third-rate navy and air force, but they had also developed a substantial missile- and drone-production capacity and had hardened their launch facilities against possible attack. More importantly, the Iranians had clearly studied US military tactics and prepared for Hegseth’s air and missile bombardment by decentralizing their command and combat capabilities around the country, allowing them to absorb a massive US-Israeli assault and still conduct punishing retaliatory strikes.
By predicting a swift US military victory, moreover, Hegseth saw no need to account for the possible consequences of Iranian retaliatory strikes against Persian Gulf oil shipping. Why worry about oil tankers’ safety if the war would be over in a matter of weeks? Evidently, no one in Hegseth’s inner circle foresaw the possibility of recurring Iranian drone strikes on vital ships and oil infrastructure, depriving the world of approximately one-fifth of its daily petroleum supply and sparking economic hardship around the world.
Surely, those responsible for such a mammoth intelligence failure should be removed from their posts—including those at the very top.
From intelligence failure we move to military miscalculation, another lethal command deficiency. If, like Hegseth, you believe you command the greatest fighting force that ever was, you might be forgiven for a touch of overconfidence when going into battle against a demonstrably weaker power. But when your hubris endangers the lives of your soldiers and their ability to fight, you are unfit to lead.
Most egregious, of course, is Hegseth’s failure to learn from Ukraine about the devastating impact of one-way attack drones on contemporary combat. Anyone who has followed the Ukrainian conflict—and this should have included every senior US military official—knows that drone warfare has transformed the battlefield, placing any unprotected asset at extreme risk of being targeted and attacked by long-range assault weapons, like the Iranian Shahed-136 drones employed by Russia in great numbers.
Yet Hegseth deployed tens of thousands of US soldiers, along with some of America’s most advanced military systems, at bases in the Gulf area within easy range of Iran’s own fleet of Shahed drones. Yes, those troops and weapons were protected by America’s advanced interceptors, such as Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles—but never in sufficient quantities to knock down all of the drones and missiles pitted against them. The unsurprising result: 18 US lives lost, over 800 wounded, and billions of dollars in damage to weapons and equipment.
And then there is the critical issue of interceptor use. To defend US facilities in the Gulf (along with the energy assets of US allies in the region), the Pentagon fired off a substantial share of its available supply of Patriot and THAAD air-defense missiles, leaving US bases elsewhere at greater risk of potential attack. According to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Republican-leaning Washington think tank, the US fired between 1,000 and 1,400 Patriot interceptors during the first weeks of the war, representing about half of the total US inventory at that time; it also expended 190–290 THAAD missiles, or two-thirds to three-quarters of its prewar inventory.
To stem the losses at US bases in the Middle East, Hegseth reportedly ordered US commanders in Europe and Asia to ship scarce Patriot and THAAD batteries from their areas of responsibility to the Gulf, substantially weakening US air and missile defenses in other likely hot spots.
Replacing all those expended missiles and bolstering US air defenses around the world will cost this country tens of billions of dollars and take years to accomplish, Pentagon officials acknowledge.
Add all of this up, and the outcome includes what should be termed geopolitical retreat, or reduced US political clout in the Gulf and elsewhere. As Trump and Hegseth made clear in the opening days of the war, a major US objective was to demonstrate that America’s global reach and power were greater than ever. “[The Iranian] regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump declared on February 28. A victory there, coming on top of the seemingly cost-free intervention in Venezuela, would again demonstrate Washington’s capacity to project power and overcome adversaries worldwide. But the Iran venture failed, severely damaging US credibility.

It will take a long time to calculate all the consequences of this geopolitical setback, but we can begin with Washington’s apparent failure to eliminate all Iranian threats to the untrammeled flow of Persian Gulf oil. Ever since the world economy became dependent on the Gulf’s oil output, in the early Cold War era, protection of the Gulf oil flow has been viewed in Washington as a vital US interest. Following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, President Jimmy Carter told Congress in 1980 that Soviet forces were now “close to the Straits of Hormuz, [thereby posing] a grave threat to the free movement of Middle East oil.” Any attempt by Moscow or some other power to block that flow, he asserted, “will be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the United States of America, and such an assault will be repelled by any means necessary, including military force.”
In accordance with this edict, Carter established the US Central Command (currently responsible for the fighting with Iran) and installed a permanent US military presence in the region. His successors, beginning with Ronald Reagan and continuing with the two Presidents Bush, have cited this so-called Carter Doctrine to justify repeated US military intervention in the Gulf. Over time, the US role in safeguarding “the free movement of Middle East oil” has become a defining feature of America’s global dominance, along with the US military presence in Europe, Japan, and South Korea. But the Iranians have demonstrated an invincible capacity to disrupt that flow, throwing into question a core component of America’s claim to global hegemony.
The US failure to subdue Iran has also undermined America’s dominant status in the other major foci of its hegemonic sway, Europe and Asia. Not only has Iran demonstrated that a medium-sized power can, under the right circumstances, hold a much more powerful force at bay—a feat no doubt being closely studied by Russia and China—but also, by eliciting such a wanton expenditure of advanced US munitions, it has actually left the US less well-equipped to counter those rivals in any future conflicts. According to that same CSIS study on US missile use, the Pentagon consumed a large share of its offensive strike weapons during the opening weeks of the war, including approximately one-third of its prewar inventory of Tomahawk cruise missiles and one-fourth of its Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles.
No doubt there will be other negative consequences from this geopolitical retreat, some possibly of equal concern, but we already know enough to conclude that Hegseth’s combat malpractice has resulted in a severe strategic debacle.
This, combined with his intelligence failures and combat miscalculations, would, in other countries and at other times, result in his forcible removal from office. With this not in the immediate offing, despite calls for his impeachment by prominent Democrats and Republicans in Congress, Hegseth should pay homage to the martial ideals he holds so dear, take personal responsibility for the debacle, and resign.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.title: Oklahoma Drops Murder Charge Against Richard Glossip, Avoiding Third Trial
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.author: Liliana Segura, Jordan Smith
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.text:
Less than a month before he was scheduled to stand trial a third time, accused of a murder he has always sworn he did not commit, Richard Glossip on Thursday agreed to plead guilty to a lesser charge, a final step toward bringing his three-decade legal saga to an end.
Glossip, 63, was twice convicted and sentenced to death for the 1997 murder of his boss Barry Van Treese inside Room 102 of the rundown motel the Van Treese family owned on the outskirts of Oklahoma City. A 19-year-old maintenance man named Justin Sneed admitted to killing Van Treese, but he insisted Glossip put him up to it. Sneed, who is currently serving a life sentence, escaped the death penalty by becoming the star witness against Glossip.
During a brief hearing that was originally scheduled to address pretrial matters, Oklahoma County Court Judge Natalie Mai instead accepted a plea from Glossip to accessory after the fact and dismissed the murder charge against him. With members of Van Treese’s family looking on from their seats in the jury box, Glossip stood to answer a series of routine questions to confirm that his plea was voluntary. Mai did not ask any specific questions about the crime itself.
Under Oklahoma law in place at the time of the killing, the maximum punishment for accessory after the fact was 45 years. Taking into consideration the decades Glossip spent on death row and credits earned for good behavior, Glossip’s attorneys say he would have been eligible for full release in 2016 and should serve no more time behind bars. But defense lawyers did not reach an agreement with the state as to a proposed sentence. In a statement released after the hearing, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who once expressed deep concerns about the state’s case against Glossip, made clear that his office will be seeking additional prison time.
Ultimately it will be up to Mai to decide if Glossip should be sentenced to time served or if any additional punishment is warranted.
The contours of Glossip’s plea are remarkably similar to a behind-the-scenes agreement made in 2023 between Drummond and Glossip’s lead attorney Don Knight. At the time, Drummond told Knight that if a court were to overturn Glossip’s conviction, he would resolve the case by accepting a plea to accessory after the fact in exchange for time served – and a promise that Glossip would not sue Oklahoma for anything related to his arrest and incarceration.
But after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Glossip’s conviction in 2025, finding that it was rooted in false testimony and prosecutorial misconduct, Drummond, who by then was running for governor, did an abrupt about-face, announcing he would once again prosecute Glossip for first degree murder.
In the year and a half since then, it has become glaringly apparent that prosecutors from Drummond’s office are grossly ill-equipped to take Glossip’s case to trial. Since his original trial in 1998, the state has lost or destroyed evidence, numerous witnesses have died, and prosecutors have conceded that their own star witness — who has sought to recant his testimony multiple times — can’t actually be expected to remember what happened the night of the killing.
“For 30 years, Richard Glossip has maintained his innocence,” Knight said in a statement after the hearing. “After nearly executing him 9 times, the State of Oklahoma has now dismissed the murder charge against him. This morning, to finally put this matter to rest, Rich pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact. We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society.”
Glossip had originally been charged as an accessory after the fact for initially failing to give police information about the killing. The night Van Treese was killed, Glossip said, Sneed woke him up around 4 a.m. by knocking on the wall of his apartment, which was adjacent to the motel’s office. Standing outside with a black eye, Sneed told Glossip he had chased off some drunks who had broken a window in one of the motel rooms. According to Glossip, he asked Sneed about his black eye, and Sneed flippantly replied, “I killed Barry.”
According to Glossip, it wasn’t until the next morning, when Van Treese was missing, that he realized Sneed might have been serious. Still, Glossip didn’t tell the cops right away; he said his girlfriend suggested waiting until they figured out what was going on.
But Sneed told police Glossip was the mastermind behind the plot to kill Van Treese, and, with no other evidence tying Glossip to the crime, Sneed’s statement became the basis of the state’s case. At Glossip’s 1998 trial, prosecutors said that he had taken advantage of the younger, more vulnerable Sneed, offering him money to kill their boss so that Glossip could take over the motel. “Glossip encouraged, aided and abetted and sent Mr. Sneed off to do his dirty work,” then-prosecutor Fern Smith told the jury.
But this story began falling apart not long after Glossip arrived on death row. A video of Sneed’s police interrogation cast serious doubt on the state’s version of events, revealing coercive questioning by Oklahoma City detectives who pressured Sneed into implicating Glossip.
Glossip’s defense failed to present the tape to the jury, which led an Oklahoma court to overturn Glossip’s first conviction based on ineffective assistance of counsel. Although a second jury convicted him and sent him to die in 2004, doubts over Glossip’s guilt continued to grow.
Glossip subsequently came close to execution many times and may well have been executed if Drummond hadn’t intervened upon taking office in 2023. He ordered an independent investigation into the case, which concluded that rampant prosecutorial misconduct had infected Glossip’s conviction. Drummond asked the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals to overturn the case. When that failed, joined Glossip in asking the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing that Sneed – whom the state has described as its “indispensable witness” – had lied on the witness stand.
Drummond’s concessions about the flaws in the state’s case and his unprecedented advocacy on Glossip’s behalf made his announcement in June 2025 that he would seek to retry Glossip for murder all the more shocking. According to Glossip’s lawyers, the decision also betrayed the long-standing agreement with Drummond to resolve the case and set Glossip free.
After that, Drummond essentially washed his hands of the case to focus on his ultimately failed attempt to become Oklahoma’s next governor, handing off prosecutorial duties to other lawyers in his office. Prosecutors declared that they intended to use the same discredited evidence to try Glossip a third time and spent months fighting to keep him in jail. Despite those efforts, Mai ordered Glossip’s release.
With a December 2026 trial date looming, tensions between the two sides have ratcheted up. Glossip’s lawyers have complained about prosecutors failing to turn over evidence as required under the law. Prosecutors have tried to limit what the defense can present to jurors at trial regarding the history of the case – including asking Mai to bar any mention of Drummond’s previous advocacy on Glossip’s behalf.
Glossip’s sentencing hearing is scheduled for December 17.
Since his release, Glossip has “been living a peaceful and law-abiding life,” Knight said in his statement. “We look forward to an opportunity to show why returning him to custody would not serve the interests of justice, and to ending this nightmare for Rich and all concerned.”
After the hearing, Glossip and his wife, Lea, stood with Knight to address reporters. Glossip thanked Knight and Lea for their support. “It was a hard day,” Lea told The Intercept, “but Richard and I are both people of faith.” She expressed that “today marks a meaningful step toward finally bringing this case to an end. We are both deeply grateful for the tireless efforts of his legal team.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

https://hellgatenyc.com/humpback-whale-h.title: All Up in My Krill
https://hellgatenyc.com/humpback-whale-h.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/humpback-whale-h.text:
Humpback whales are, for all intents and purposes, the most fêted representation of the baleen whales. Long, lean, and limber with a distinctive and sometimes eerie manner of speaking, the humpback stars in hit films of both recent vintage (1986's "Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home") and contemporary homage (2026's "Whalefall"), its aura more beguiling than a classic celluloid star's and representative of the ocean's untold depths—mysteries that humans are still only just beginning to understand. 
And so when a humpback whale appeared in New York Harbor Thursday morning, the city understandably went bananas. The whale took a jaunt up the Hudson, getting as far as Pier 45 in Greenwich Village, and spawning a ton of euphoric social media videos, including this one, in which the whale appears to be breaching on-rhythm to "Empire State of Mind." But the young humpback whale that showed up on city shores is so much more than a vehicle for human ogling, or even a projection of our wildest dreams: It is an indicator of the wonderful ecosystem rolling beneath the tides. According to Gotham Whale, New York's whale conservation source of record, the humpback appeared in the Upper Bay of New York Harbor, an unusual area far from its normal stomping grounds below the Verrazzano-Narrows, because it was likely tracking a school of Atlantic Menhaden—silvery coastal fish in the herring family to us, "the most important fish in the sea" to the aquatic whippersnapper who ventured towards our shores to brunch upon them.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: A lipsmacking journey from kisses galore to tears of despair – How Do We Find Love? review
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Eddy Frankel
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath.
The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.
The first exhibition begins, like so much love, with a single kiss – a gaunt couple locking lips on a 15th-century Italian vase. They don’t look too thrilled about it but, hey, that’s the reality of love. Sometimes it’s not great. The show then takes you on a salivary journey through every possible kind of kiss: political, maternal, interracial, divine, familial.
Allegories of righteousness and peace give each other an awkward peck in a William Blake watercolour, the infant Christ and St John the Baptist hold each other close in an Anthony van Dyck painting. Then a priest kisses a nun in a Benetton ad, the USSR’s President Brezhnev kisses East German leader Honecker, Cupid kisses Psyche. And that’s before you even get to the bulk of the show with its snogs by Edvard Munch, Wolfgang Tillmans and – obviously – Rodin, whose carved marble canoodle dominates the middle of the exhibition. It’s enough to give you chapped lips.
What they want you to see is the vast complexity of kissing, to understand its different histories and implications. So they show it through a postcolonial lens, a religious lens, a political lens, and so on. But kisses are not some underexplored, subconscious thing – they’re universal. We think about our kisses, we remember them, treasure them, long for them. The whole thing just feels obvious, like someone telling you the plot of a movie you’ve already seen.
There are works that deal with love more widely – including a Tracey Emin neon that says “The Heart has Its Reasons”, as if anyone on Earth needs to see another Tracey Emin neon. But they feature no actual kissing. The concept isn’t bad, and neither’s the execution, but in the end there are only so many images of people necking you can hack before you get mental jaw ache. It’s a whole exhibition of people locked in embraces, a whole show of painterly PDAs, and it wears thin.
The second exhibition, Ecstasy and the Aftermath, tackles the joy of new love, the despair of heartache, and everything in between. That’s where it really falls apart. There are some good works: a Somaya Critchlow nude, a set of deeply romantic and poetic Judy Chicago prints, a Jane Hayes Greenwood painting of leaking, breast-like plant forms, the Marina Abramović and Ulay video of him on the verge of unleashing an arrow into her heart. But the theme is so broad it sends you spinning.
There are works about motherly love, romantic love, desire, the gaze, heartache, grief. There are photos of people dancing in queer nightclubs, because community is a form of love. There’s a Paloma Proudfoot ceramic of gossiping mates, because really liking your pals is love, too. There’s so much to explore, each of those themes could have been a whole exhibition in its own right, but it’s all just been squeezed into one room.
The only way this could have worked is if they’d narrowed the focus. Or if they’d deleted all the wall texts, got rid of the faltering conceptual themes and restrictions and just whacked together a bunch of artworks about desire, adoration, romance, heartache and snogging and let you make your own way through it.
But if you want to know what love is, these two shows do actually provide a pretty good answer. Sometimes it’s beautiful, sometimes it’s joyful, but more often than not, it’s a bit of a mess.

https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.author: Ben Berke, John Moritz, Anastasia Lennon
https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.text:
On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.
Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.
He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.
Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.
The company never came.
A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.
In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.
Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.
ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts.
Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views.
But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction, further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.
The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.
At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”
The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”
Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms.
As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.
In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.
Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” said New London Mayor Michael Passero.
Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt.
The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.
“They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.
Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunity disappear. One project alone, Vineyard Wind, directly employed a total of more than 3,700 full- and part-time workers — most of them from Massachusetts — over eight years of development and construction, according to the developer.
During peak construction activity, as many as 300 union members worked onshore in southeastern Massachusetts for the project, the first large offshore wind farm fully permitted by the federal government. The wind farm was completed this year.
Longshoreman Onix Vazquez, 34, worked full-time tying up barges and moving turbine components on and off New Bedford’s wind pier. He grew up a few blocks away and said he had struggled to find lucrative work until Vineyard Wind began hiring from his union.
Vazquez’s hourly wage of $50 was nearly double what he previously earned unloading occasional shipments of tangerines and juice concentrate. It allowed him and other members of his historically Black union to make down payments on houses, pay off medical bills and for the first time take their families on out-of-state vacations.
“Most of us have to get other jobs for now or collect unemployment,” said Kevin Rose, president of New Bedford’s longshoremen union, which put about two dozen members to work on the project.
The union had been planning to rebuild its nearby meeting hall, which was demolished a decade earlier when work grew scarce. But the next developer to lease New Bedford’s wind pier has delayed its project indefinitely. The union members have put the plans for their new hall on hold.
Vazquez said he now works a seasonal job in the cranberry industry for much lower pay.
“They don’t see that it affects us, the ones that work the projects,” he said.
In response to questions about the impact of the administration’s actions on American offshore wind workers, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior repeated criticisms of offshore wind as an expensive and unreliable source of energy.
“The reality is that the Biden administration lured companies into these projects with the promise of millions of taxpayer dollars in subsidies to make these offshore wind projects viable,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The view is more nuanced on the ground. New Bedford’s fishing industry is generally critical of wind farm development because fishermen worry about disruption to fishing grounds.
But fishing catch limits keep boats tied to docks for much of the year. Work for wind farms gets them out to sea and helps pay the bills.
Over the past few years of construction, Vineyard Wind paid about $11 million to 55 fishing vessels from New England and an estimated 60 to 70 fishermen, according to the developer. (The figure also covers fuel.) The fishermen look out for protected species, guard exposed underwater cable as it’s being laid and log information for the developer.
Some fishermen say they will work in offshore wind for as long as they can.
“The scallop boats need the extra revenue,” said Patrick Walsh, 37, a fifth-generation fisherman who plans to rejoin his father’s fishing business when wind work wraps up. “The worst thing for a boat is to sit. Those boats are made to work.”
Wind farm work made it possible for him to buy his first house, he said.
“Fishing would pay bills, and wind was going in the bank.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: AI helps conservators uncover lost details in William Merritt Chase painting
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Annabel Keenan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When William Merritt Chase’s painting A Comfortable Corner (around 1888) entered the conservation studio, the painting was carrying more than a century of history on its surface—including the interventions of conservators who had treated it decades earlier. Artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to a restoration endeavour that has peeled back some of those interventions.
The newly restored painting, which is part of the collection of the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, will be on display in its exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End (14 November-21 March 2027). The Parrish has an especially deep connection to Chase, who was not only a prominent figure in Gilded Age New York but also spent time on Long Island’s East End, where the museum is located. Today, the Parrish holds a substantial body of Chase’s work, alongside archival material donated by the artist’s family.
A Comfortable Corner depicts a woman reclining in an elaborately furnished interior, dressed in a deep blue kimono and holding an uchiwa fan.“A Comfortable Corner is an important work within William Merritt Chase’s oeuvre as it depicts a specific moment in 19th-century art and Chase’s own period with influences of art and design from Japan,” says Kaitlin Halloran, the museum’s associate curator.
Over the years, at least two restorations substantially altered the appearance of the painting, including a significant effort in the 1960s. Among the changes made were the addition of a heavyweight, almost burlap-like lining, retouching and blotchy inpainting, and the use of uneven varnishes. Some of these interventions changed the surface texture of various areas or discoloured over time. Working with conservator Suzanne Siano and her team at Modern Art Conservation, the museum set out to determine what restoration was needed to get the painting ready for the exhibition.
A crucial piece of evidence to guide this process arrived in the form of an early photograph of the painting. The black-and-white image, understood to have been taken before the 1960s restoration, showed that more of the composition had once been visible than what had survived in the painting. The work had apparently been reduced in size during the 1960s restoration, perhaps to fit a new stretcher or because damaged edges were folded over and effectively removed.
The photograph also revealed details in the composition that had disappeared. A curl of hair beneath the sitter’s ear was missing; parts of a decorative screen had become faint or vanished; and some delicate passages had been overpainted with heavier marks. The conservation team also found evidence of pentimenti—changes made by Chase himself—that were not apparent in the earlier photograph, adding another layer of complexity.
“It is difficult to establish whether all of these changes resulted from earlier conservation,” Siano tells The Art Newspaper. “Some of it may have stemmed from a misreading of what the conservator was seeing. They may have been cleaning toward what they believed to be the original surface when, in fact, some of what they removed may have been changes or additions made by the artist.”
Using AI, the historical photograph was combined with a colour image of the painting to create a composite showing areas where the two diverged.
A tool, not a solution
“Although we are reasonably adept with Photoshop, we felt it was worth seeing what AI could offer,” Siano says. “It proved very helpful, largely because of its speed. It was not instantaneous, but it was considerably faster than assembling the comparison manually.”
The resulting image helped the team identify areas that warranted closer examination. One important discovery concerned Chase’s signature, which had become extremely faint, with some of its letters apparently covered by overpaint. Because Chase’s signature is relatively abstract, Siano believes it may have been mistaken for part of the carpet pattern during the earlier restoration.
The project, supported by a Bank of America grant, illustrates both the possibilities and the limitations of AI in conservation. “Tasks that once took considerable time can be completed more quickly, and AI can provide additional information for us to weigh,” Siano says. “Ultimately, however, conservation is carried out by a highly skilled individual or team, and we do not expect that to change.”
Siano stresses that they did not simply reinstate every discrepancy identified by the software. The historical photograph was neither high-resolution nor necessarily a record of the painting’s earliest state. Instead, the information the photograph provided was assessed alongside magnified examination, ultraviolet imaging, knowledge of Chase’s materials, and comparison with his other works.
“Conservation is a combination of science, art history, craft, manual skill and artistry,” Siano says. “AI is none of those things.”
The Chase painting was the first time Siano’s studio had used AI as an aid in the conservation of a painting. “In terms of determining how to conserve a painting, we think AI’s use will remain very case-specific. We do expect it to become increasingly valuable as a research tool, however: for example, in helping to locate historical images or relevant source material.”
Ultimately, Siano says, “the judgments conservators make are nuanced and subtle, and we doubt those qualities can be replicated by a machine”.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Group biography follows Lee Miller, Pablo Picasso and friends on holiday in the South of France
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Matthew Gale
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony. Each person lies at the heart of a network, opening the potential for an exponential chain of many walk-on parts. Rooted in the photographs of what author Anna Thomasson rightly terms the “fleeting community” of a late summer holiday in 1937, A Vast Horizon succeeds remarkably in marshalling a complex tapestry of egos, events, ideals and disappointments.
The individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose. They were drawn to the South of France by their inter-linked friendships and by “le peintre soleil”, Agar’s witty characterisation of Picasso. As Picasso urged everyone to work, half the witnesses took photographs. Maar, Man Ray and Miller were the relaxing professionals; snapshots were added by Agar and Penrose. Thomasson has searched through this rich, if scattered visual archive of a moment through which photography (as Roland Barthes recognised in Camera Lucida) “mechanically repeats what could never be repeated existentially”. Their hedonism caught in this moment defied the political instability and totalitarianism, with civil war already a year old in Spain.
Plunged into war
From this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war. For each of them it constituted a restructuring of values—not as hoped for by the Surrealists, but as enforced by the destructive triumphalism of Nazi extremism. Here the account turns to Paul Éluard’s transformation of a love poem for Nusch into a litany for “liberty” that captured the spirit of resistance (copies were even dropped over Occupied France by the RAF). Equally powerful was Miller’s reportage of the savagery of combat and, eventually, the revelations of the concentration camps. In this way, the book touches upon the transience of bodies captured in photography: those at Hotel Vaste Horizon were willingly posed for the camera and exchanged in partnerships, before growing fragile through wartime deprivation.
There was no reciprocal gathering in the post-war period. As a result, Thomasson traces the endgames, as each of the participants ages in varying degrees of dignity, creativity and despair. Those bodies displayed on the beach in southern France become the distant, optimistic opposite to the tragic, haunting corpses of Buchenwald; it is little wonder that Miller, the photographer in both cases, would never fully recover from the experience of witnessing such deliberate inhumanity.
While the lives of many of these central figures are, to varying degrees, familiar—from autobiographies (Agar, Man Ray, Penrose) and biographies (Éluard, Miller, Picasso)—Thomasson’s synthesis draws on recent research and extensive reading. A particular strength is the rebalancing of longstanding gender biases and assumptions. The repositioning of Ady Fidelin, the double-marginalised Guadeloupean woman, is especially timely; drawing on fresh scholarship, she is given greater presence and somewhat rescued from simply being Man Ray’s model. Nusch Éluard is also brought more sharply into focus. Substantial traces of these women’s own voices remain to be found, however, confining them to an unknowability ascribed to their devotion to their partners, although this may be overstated in the suggestion that, in 1946, Nusch Éluard “died in the service of Paul [Éluard]’s pursuit of freedom”.
Words over pictures
Late on Thomasson cites Emily Dickinson’s belief that veracity is “more affecting, if told indirectly”. This emerges as a foundational conceit in a volume inspired by photographs but in which only four are reproduced. Instead of showing, the author presents often highly evocative descriptions of what she sees in a wide range of images that the reader is not shown. This is a surprising decision for a narrative stimulated, as we are told, by the author being drawn into “their distant world by their photographs”.
With such a limitation on images, the book’s cover photograph assumes disproportionate significance. Where the British edition favours Agar’s photograph of Maar, Picasso and the Éluards at Juan-les-Pins, Miller’s picnic photograph of “half-naked women sitting among fully clothed men”—the jarring nature of which introduces the whole narrative—appears on the cover of the US edition. Although unaltered when reproduced inside the volume, on the cover the half-naked torsos are rather ineptly airbrushed. That the publishers chose to manipulate a famous 90-year-old image seems an unfortunate undermining of an otherwise compelling narrative of artists embracing freedom before disaster struck.
ª A Vast Horizon: Artists and Lovers, Freedom and War, by Anna Thomasson, published by Pegasus Books, 304pp, 4 b/w reproductions, $29.95 (hb), 7 July

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-luigi-mangio.title: The Luigi Mangione Protest Documentary You Need to See
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-luigi-mangio.author: Julianne Escobedo Shepherd
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-luigi-mangio.text:
During the trial of Luigi Mangione, much of the coverage was focused on three women called the Mangionistas: Whether they are extremists, whether they should have press passes, whether they are simply bubbleheaded fangirls swooning over an objectively hot convicted killer. But much of the sensationalist, often sexist coverage has obscured the deeper issues that the murder of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson has pushed to the surface: The fact that in a nation as wealthy as the U.S., citizens are regularly dying or, at best, going into debt, due to the exorbitant cost of healthcare—and will, as of next year, be left even more vulnerable thanks to Trump's Medicaid cuts, which threaten coverage for nearly a million New Yorkers and institute work requirements to obtain basic coverage. 
"Bigger Than Luigi," Miléna Mikael-Debass's short documentary showing this week at DOC NYC, hones in on this topic so cogently it's a feat that the Emmy-winning director was able to fit so much in its 16-minute runtime, capturing snapshots of the lives of four people from the demonstrations outside Mangione's hearings in lower Manhattan. There is Shane, an ER doctor whose activism extends beyond the City courthouse to Albany, where he advocates for single-payer healthcare system and rallies at the state legislature to pass the New York Health Act; Breigh, a paralegal and true-crime fan from Philadelphia who is adamant about Mangione's right to a fair trial; Jonni, an activist and organizer who lost his brother due to inadequate healthcare; and Celeste, an Italian American New Yorker and grad student with a similar spinal affliction to Mangione.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Museum heists on the rise: are new criminal markets, motives and tactics evolving?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Riah Pryor
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Europol’s warning that museum thefts are becoming more violent and frequent could hardly have been better timed.
Published on 24 August, its report, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists, was followed within days by a string of high-profile thefts. On 27 August thieves stole a “priceless” Bronze Age hoard from Spain’s Museum of Villena; the same day a robbery at Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts netted a diamond necklace worth several million euros. On 8 September thieves broke into the Musée Renoir on the French Riviera, with two works by the artist still missing.
There are plenty of regulations. The real problem is the lack of effective enforcement
“We have observed a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023,” says Jean-Yves Goriou, the head of the EU Organised Crime Unit, within Europol’s European Serious and Organised Crime Centre (ESOCC). Precious metals and stones, as well as Chinese cultural artefacts are identified in the report as increasingly popular targets, a trend which the report argues can be attributed to the objects’ high financial value.
“Some buyers in China will bid on these objects—sometimes to astronomical levels—but when they cannot acquire them legitimately, there appears to be a market for stolen Chinese treasures,” says Christopher Marinello, the founder and chief executive of Art Recovery International. He disagrees however, with the report’s claim that they “are likely to be easily sold on the art market”, arguing that “there are plenty of regulations on the books, many of which place significant burdens on honest dealers. The real problem, in my view, is the lack of effective enforcement of those regulations.”
Louvre’s €88m loss
The concentration and visibility of attacks, particularly against museums holding exceptionally valuable jewellery and precious metals, certainly feels prominent on the public agenda—boosted perhaps by the recent anniversary of the 2025 heist of €88m worth of jewels from the Musée du Louvre in Paris.
However, given that many museum thefts have historically remained unreported—often due to embarrassment or to prevent highlighting security vulnerabilities—“the lack of substantial consistent data has long made it a challenge to establish a workable sample size”, says Julian Radcliffe, the director of the Art Loss Register.
“In the sense of volume of crimes [against museums], there’s not been a change,” says Robert Read, the head of art and private clients at Hiscox insurance. He adds that around 50% of insurance claims continue to stem from accidental damage but adds that there does appear to be a shifting set of motivations at play. “Whereas financial value has long been understood as the key driver of such crimes, there is a sense that items could be being stolen to order, used as collateral, or even just to embarrass public institutions or governments,” he says.
Europol’s research describes a shift from the “traditional trafficker” towards an “emerging aggressor”. The former is characterised as a specialist, non-violent offender operating within a structured criminal network focused on cultural property. The latter is an ad hoc and decentralised perpetrator, prepared to use high-risk violence and operate across criminal markets, rather than concentrating exclusively on cultural property.
Organised networks
“A lot of these trends [in the Europol report] are not new, but they’re arguably occurring on a more pronounced or regular scale,” says Julian Radcliffe.
Certainly, the possibility of items being stolen to order by organised networks and with an eye on art market trends (notably the surge in demand for Chinese antiquities) has drifted in and out of public debate over museum thefts before. In 2016, for example, members of an organised gang were jailed for £57m worth of Chinese and rhino horn thefts from several UK museums and auction houses. Similarly, there is established understanding that the illicit trade in antiquities can involve networks spanning multiple types of criminality.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/farc-colombi.title: Inside Colombia’s FARC, as Victory Gave Way to Survival
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/farc-colombi.author: Oliver Dodd
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/farc-colombi.text:
Inside Colombia’s FARC, as Victory Gave Way to Survival
Tanja Nijmeijer’s memoir tells of how Colombia’s FARC was forced into a long and painful retreat. Her account of its political setbacks suggests that power doesn’t always flow from the barrel of a gun.
In the early hours of September 23, 2010, Tanja Nijmeijer was awakened by a bomb in a FARC guerrilla camp in the Colombian jungle. The strike landed on her commander’s bunker, followed by screams from her comrades. Moments later, dozens of aircraft roared above and launched another wave of bombs. Nijmeijer grabbed her rifle and dived into her foxhole. As the ground shook around her, she closed her eyes, tensed her body and thought: Aquí fue — this is it.
Seven years earlier, when the Dutch internationalist had first entered the jungle to join the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC), the war looked very different. She remembers it as “the calm before the storm,” with abundant supplies, comparatively large and settled camps, and a degree of security.
Nijmeijer’s autobiography, Into the Jungle, recently published by Pluto Press, traces her trajectory from guerrilla warfare to the negotiations that produced the 2016 peace agreement and the troubled transition that followed. Yet what makes the memoir especially politically revealing is that Nijmeijer joined the FARC at almost exactly the moment when the war started to change so decisively against it.
Stark Disparities
Initially traveling to Colombia in order to teach English to the children of the rich, Nijmeijer quickly encountered the extreme inequalities dividing Colombia. She witnessed gated communities, stark disparities separating the northern part of capital Bogotá from the south, and the concentration of wealth and power among an elite while poorer neighborhoods suffered neglect and repression.
Nijmeijer came into contact with FARC militants through her work and began to question the dominant image of the guerrillas as little more than “narco-terrorists.” Instead she encountered people prepared to sacrifice their lives in pursuit of a revolutionary project. Gradually developing a socialist outlook, she began to recognize that the ruling class was blocking any prospects of meaningful, peaceful change. She increasingly regarded armed struggle as not only legitimate but necessary and was convinced that the guerrillas could “take power and plant the seed for a new world.”
Although it was not apparent then, when Nijmeijer went into the jungle, the FARC’s decline was already underway. Right-winger Álvaro Uribe won the presidential election in 2002 on the back of mounting hostility to the FARC following the collapse of the 1999–2002 peace process. Harnessing hegemonic narratives that portrayed the FARC as having acted in bad faith and merely exploited the peace process as an opportunity to expand, Uribe promised a “military solution,” relying on massive US support through Plan Colombia to modernize the armed forces.
By late 2003, seven months after Nijeimer went into the jungle, the counterinsurgency offensive organized through Plan Patriota had reached Sumapaz, where military operations targeted guerrilla fronts in a region central to the FARC’s strategic plan for surrounding Bogotá. Areas over which the FARC had historically enjoyed complete control were now being contested.
The guerrillas later discovered evidence of around sixty helicopter landing sites, army surveillance of guerrilla roads and infrastructure, and reconnaissance teams operating inside jungle territories that the insurgents had assumed were impenetrable.
The state’s expanding war chest enabled significant increases in military personnel, specialized mountain battalions, and airpower. This was supported by satellite imagery and geospatial intelligence, communications interception, and other technologies challenging the guerrillas’ traditional reliance on rugged terrain as a form of defensive protection.
The military’s expanding reach is already evident earlier in Nijmeijer’s account, when she describes the penetration of her units by infiltrators who pulled various stunts as part of a tactic to undermine morale — unlocking weapons, defecating in huts, and cutting up the guerrillas’ rubber boots. The result was that “nobody trusted anybody else.”
Whereas in the past, counterinsurgency campaigns were temporary, with troops eventually withdrawing due to budget cuts and other constraints, now the Colombian army established a permanent offensive presence and pursued the guerrillas into rearguard zones and jungles, closing in on commanders once thought invulnerable.
The shifting conditions led the FARC’s leading military commander, Mono Jojoy, to declare before a crowd of five hundred guerrillas, “Thanks to President Álvaro Uribe Vélez, we are going to learn how to live as guerrilla fighters again! We must go back to basics.”
Improvements in airpower gave the state forces a decisive advantage. Vehicles disappeared, supplies and comforts were reduced, marches replaced a comparatively settled life, and concentration gave way to greater mobility and dispersion. “Our days of easy living,” as Nijmeijer puts it, “were over.”
For the FARC, going back to basics meant adopting an increasingly defensive posture: land mines, often described as a “weapon of the weak,” became an especially useful tool for slowing the encroachments of army patrols. However, they also caused civilian casualties and left the FARC exposed to criticism for disregarding human rights.
To reduce the risk of interception when communicating with urban militants, the guerrillas began sending encrypted messages via satellite internet. But this wasn’t a comprehensive solution. Air surveillance, increased extensively under Plan Colombia, could still intercept such communications. They had to switch off the equipment whenever an approaching plane was suspected, but the introduction of small, largely undetectable drones enabling real-time surveillance in 2006 made it harder to know when they were being watched.
The transition to a more defensive mode of operating affected daily life. Camps were built with deep foxholes; smoking and flashlights were prohibited after dark; vines were strung along paths so fighters could navigate without light; fireflies were used as improvised illumination. The nightly hour of cultural activities, essential for political education and boosting morale, became a thing of the past in Nijmeijer’s units. Meanwhile, massed forces of guerrillas were restricted — a setback from the FARC’s war of movement strategy at the end of the 1990s, in which large concentrations of troops overwhelmed military bases.
Isolation
True, this was a form of adaptation. Yet adaptation increasingly meant preserving the guerrilla organization under adverse conditions rather than recreating the offensive possibilities of the previous decade. Nijmeijer recounts, “The war changed, and it changed in the army’s favor.”
The psychological impact is described in a way that military histories and government documents rarely capture. Nijmeijer recalls the “pure terror” as bombs drop around her, with nowhere to run for safety, and no visible opponent to shoot at, only the hope that the jungle canopy might offer some protection.
Having to be constantly on the move, often in treacherous terrain, had its physical costs. Long marches left the guerrillas hungry and low on calories, and illness and fatigue, inevitable in such conditions, spread and grew more difficult to overcome. The army had repeatedly blocked Mono Jojoy’s attempts to meet up with Manuel Marulanda, the FARC’s founder and long-standing leader. Nijmeijer describes the resulting two-month march through particularly arduous territory on inadequate rations, which left her body aching so badly that she could barely manage to endure the night watch.
The psychological and physical impact had broader organizational repercussions. Demoralization deepened, and desertion rates increased, which the counterinsurgents exploited to the full. One guerrilla defector recorded the coordinates of Raúl Reyes’s location while sitting on the FARC leader’s bed. Iván Ríos, then the youngest member of the FARC’s secretariat, who had decided to remain with a guerrilla front to tackle problems of indiscipline and disorganization, turned up dead alongside his girlfriend — killed by his own head of security, who hoped to collect a lucrative bounty. Even people imagined to be staunchly politically committed ended up deserting and providing crucial intelligence.
As my own interviews with various former FARC leaders confirm, from around 2007, the counterinsurgents took the FARC by surprise, systematically hiding tiny GPS trackers in items that the guerrillas relied upon to survive. They identified stores in guerrilla areas and forced merchants to cooperate and even pressured family members and the children of guerrillas, as revealed in an interview with a retired strategic intelligence analyst in the Colombian navy. The trackers guided precision strikes on guerrilla camps, such as in the case of Mono Jojoy, whose boot concealed a GPS tracker.
Nijmeijer reflects that “if I had to pinpoint a moment when I began to see we wouldn’t take power by military means, it would be some time before Mono’s death in 2010.”
Yet her growing recognition that the FARC could no longer take power militarily was also linked to the organization’s broader political isolation.
As many former FARC commanders have admitted, kidnapping and extortion, justified by the organization as “revolutionary taxation,” inflicted enormous political costs and enabled the ruling classes to paint it as a group of terrorists and bandits, especially in urban areas where most people were based.
The FARC’s communications strategy — deemed a complete failure by Nijmeijer — also left it politically vulnerable. The state had dedicated task forces whose entire purpose was to undermine the FARC’s claim to political legitimacy. According to Nijmeijer, FARC leader Manuel Marulanda had decided “there was no good reason to respond to falsehoods the state made up.”
Given that the FARC was overwhelmingly rooted in the countryside, and the country was increasingly organized around the big cities, political communication was fundamental. Yet Nijmeijer recounts how long the FARC ignored this issue.
Nijmeijer concludes that while the conflict had no straightforward military victor, the FARC “certainly lost the ideological battle.”
Negotiations
The FARC’s strategy had always theoretically left open the possibility of negotiations alongside the more ambitious goal of taking power through a popular insurrection.
But as the FARC faced military blows and narrowing strategic possibilities, the idea of a negotiated settlement gained prominence.
In November 2011, the FARC’s supreme leader — Alfonso Cano — was assassinated by the counterinsurgents, the first time this had occurred in the organization’s half-century history, a moment Nijmeijer remembers as a “heavy blow” that left even the more radical commanders Iván Márquez and Jesús Santrich sitting in stunned silence, repeating, “We have to go on, anyhow.”
While the FARC was capable of sustaining the war over many more years, its influence had been significantly weakened. Key figures, including Nijmeijer, no longer realistically envisaged taking power through a popular insurrection and the point of war, they saw, was to win it, not simply endure it.
Unable to foresee victory or a realistic possibility of retaking the strategic initiative nationally, the FARC turned to negotiations from a position of relative weakness. The state only agreed to talks on the condition that changes to its fundamental economic model were off the cards — thus leaving intact the exploitative social relations that sustained the conflict.
Ultimately, from the perspective of a former guerrilla fighter who experienced firsthand the FARC’s military reversal, the book reveals that political power does not necessarily grow from the barrel of a gun. To be sure, the FARC became one of Latin America’s most powerful communist organizations, with many thousands of guerrillas, control over territory, and access to an enormous war chest. And yet, this capacity to sustain an insurgency did not translate into nationwide appeal or a credible strategy for taking power.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-yamaz.title: A Childlike Devotion Runs Through Godzilla Minus Zero
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-yamaz.author: Eileen Jones
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-yamaz.text:
A Childlike Devotion Runs Through Godzilla Minus Zero
It’s heartwarming the way Takeshi Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment to that ultimate destructive monster, Godzilla, into Godzilla Minus Zero.
There’s a familiar but always thrilling moment in Godzilla Minus Zero when Godzilla is fighting the newer, faster, entirely more visually glamorous monster King Ghidorah — an immense three-headed, golden-ray-shooting dragon that seems set on destroying the human race — and Godzilla is losing. In fact, it seems Godzilla is beaten and dying.
But then Godzilla goes deep and dredges up the last of his prehistoric mojo and comes back to win the brutal kaiju battle. Godzilla the destroyer from the sea becomes Godzilla the hero and savior of the Japanese protagonists watching in wide-eyed terror. All the viewer’s childhood love of Godzilla, who lumbers around on big, squat feet like a crude, clumsy dinosaur based on some devoted but impractical kid’s drawing, surges to the fore.
Writer-director-CGI effects master Takeshi Yamazaki seems highly motivated by such lingering childhood feelings. He cautions us in interviews, in a caringly paternal sort of way, to remember that though Godzilla fights King Ghidorah, it’s not because he sides with human beings: “He can’t become humanity’s friend.”
Oh, we know. But many small children aren’t entirely on the side of humans either. Personally, I was all for the animals as a kid and relentlessly pretended to be an animal for years before the US educational system crushed it out of me. And most little children are united, at least for a few years, in a love of dinosaurs that borders on obsession. Though I’ve known a few kids who loved and identified with cars and trucks and industrial vehicles more than adult people.
Yamazaki seems to understand all that. He says he opted to revive King Ghidorah and have him wreak havoc on Yamazaki’s own hometown of Matsumoto in the first scene of destruction in Godzilla Minus Zero, then fight the climactic epic battle with Godzilla because, fifty-five years ago, he was a seven-year-old kid in Matsumoto eagerly awaiting a revival screening of the Godzilla movie sequel Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster from 1964. The promotional flyer specifically promised, “King Ghidorah attacks Matsumoto!”
But he was terribly disappointed when “the monster finally appeared [and] all he did was clip the roof tiles of the city’s castle before flying off.”
Yamazaki said, “I was so frustrated, so heartbroken. . . . I held a grudge for years.”
But ultimately, it’s heartwarming the way Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment and frustration into making the gorgeous and emotionally compelling Godzilla Minus One, released in 2023 and Godzilla Minus Zero, currently playing in theaters. It goes a long way toward explaining the immense critical and popular appeal of both.
Yamazaki was stunned by the global success of the first film, which he claimed he never expected to get such a warm reception beyond Japan. Its embrace by mass audiences in the United States was especially surprising, since we’re notorious for refusing to see “foreign films” requiring us to read subtitles. But a grand exception is made in the case of Yamazaki’s Godzilla films.
And Yamazaki isn’t conciliating American feelings either. Given the subject matter, it wouldn’t make any sense.
In Godzilla Minus Zero, the characters representing the US military brass in post–World War II Japan are all sinister, arrogant conquerors clearly up to no good, always plotting ways to harness additional power and further subjugate the Japanese. Even the lowly GIs stationed in Tokyo are portrayed as a disturbing alien presence — jittery, full of directionless aggressivity, vaguely looking for trouble. One American soldier chews gum with a manic ferocity.
The satirical portrayal of this platoon looks a lot like British filmmakers Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger’s 1946 take on American GIs in A Matter of Life and Death, and Powell and Pressburger were being conciliatory to the United States in a “hands-across-the-pond” manner. Their GI Joes, killed near the end of World War II, arrive in heaven all hopped up on a similarly strange, angsty energy and immediately scramble over to a suddenly revealed vending machine stocked with Coca-Cola.
Set in 1949, Godzilla Minus Zero has no humor of that kind. It’s a somber film entirely preoccupied with the relentless calamities besetting Japan: World War II, the US nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, living in postwar poverty and wreckage, the Godzilla attacks in Godzilla Minus One, and the King Ghidorah attacks in Godzilla Minus Zero. The character of Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), the elderly biologist who found the charred bodies of his family in the aftermath of the bombing of Hiroshima, miraculously comes through all the mayhem, exclaiming bitterly, “And again, I survive!”
He joins forces to face the King Ghidorah threat with Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), director of the government’s Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, who has to put together the reluctant team that will fight this new monster. Former kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who flew the mission that apparently destroyed Godzilla in the previous film, is hoping — in vain — to avoid having to go up against King Ghidorah. Kōichi has married Noriko Ōishi (Minami Hamabe), a survivor of a previous Godzilla attacks, and together they’ve adopted war orphan Akiko (Sae Nagatani). The investment in their new family gives them a great stake in escaping any further life-threatening calamities.
Director Yamazaki particularly wanted a woman represented among the experts on the disaster team, so he created the character of Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist with a useful theory about King Ghidorah’s attraction to lightning storms.
Godzilla Minus Zero has that typical sequel effect of moving away from a streamlined narrative toward a complicated one involving more monsters, more characters, more plotlines, more everything. There are promising story developments that aren’t fully explored and are presumably there as starter plotlines for sequels, such as the way living “Godzilla cells” are affecting humans, with a handful of scientific subjects who’ve survived contact with Godzilla but are now manifesting mutations. Noriko wears an eyepatch to cover her one reptilian yellow eye, and she also has Godzilla scales and spikes beginning to grow on one shoulder-blade, hidden by her clothing.
Still, the film maintains that basic rhythm also remembered from childhood when watching old Godzilla films: big action scenes full of exciting destruction and terror interspersed with far duller but somehow reassuring meeting scenes when characters representing science, government, the military, and the model family unit regroup to try Plan B, Plan C, and so on. Yamazaki hasn’t come to challenge the genre conventions but to fulfill them and render them more beautiful.
He makes vast CGI action sequences as sensational as it’s possible to make them, and it seems churlish to complain that, though generally magnificent, it’s still so much goddamn wearying CGI. It’s a generational viewership problem, really. I don’t think young people miss the sense of imprinting off of physical reality that once defined the film medium.
But the figure of Godzilla has such lasting, surefire appeal, it’s hard to quell the basic moviegoer longing to see him again. As Yamazaki put it about his own lifelong obsession,
As a kid, it was just: monster, cool, scary, amazing. Making these films now, I understand how much anxiety Japanese audiences were carrying when the first film came out in 1954, and how the monster’s shape matched that fear exactly. . . . Godzilla was never just a cool monster that wrecks things; he’s always carried the weight of the nuclear question, of war. The more I make these films, the more I feel that weight, and I think it’s exactly why people are still drawn to him.
Godzilla brings his fear-shaped silhouette into contemporary times as we’re “drifting toward conflict” on a global scale, in Yamazaki’s view. He meant the sequel to be weightier and more complex: “It’s entertainment, but I wanted it to leave something heavy behind, too.”
Yamazaki’s ability to unite fond nostalgia for Godzilla movies past, reaching back to childhood, with intensified modern angst forged in twentieth-century horrors that only grow over time, creates a riveting emotional combination. The third sequel is guaranteed, but it’s easy to imagine Yamazaki’s Godzilla movies maintaining their global appeal for as long as we’ve got a habitable globe to stand on.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/capitalism-w.title: Under Capitalism, Even Kids’ Playtime Is Alienated
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/capitalism-w.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/capitalism-w.text:
Under Capitalism, Even Kids’ Playtime Is Alienated
Capitalism turns children’s play into preparation for work, but it cannot fully contain what play makes possible. In her new book, Susan Ferguson explores how the openness and pleasure of play can help us imagine other ways of being together.
A central concern of feminist Marxist theory and practice has been how to understand the relationship between paid and unpaid labor. Marxist feminists have drawn on Karl Marx’s observation that capital leaves workers to ensure their own reproduction, a process that depends on their instinct for self-preservation. They have shown how capitalist accumulation depends on reproductive labor, work that has fallen primarily to women. But what, exactly, is being reproduced? Workers must replenish their strength so that they can work again the next day; importantly, reproduction also encompasses bearing children and creating future labor power.
But it does not stop there of course: children must then be shaped into capable workers, a process that does not happen by itself and in which social reproduction is by no means simply left to the workers themselves. For anyone who has attended school, and perhaps even more so for those of us — myself included — who are now experiencing school all over again through our children’s education, it is more than apparent that school is, in many ways, an institution designed to socialize children into their future roles as wage workers.
As E. P. Thompson writes in Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism, schooling can be understood as an acclimatization to the factory’s temporal discipline. Today, however, this involves more than the straightforward discipline Thompson identified. It also entails producing flexible, self-directed learners who can seamlessly retrain and acquire new skills in an ever-changing and volatile labor market.
Playtime for Future Workers
Despite this recognition of the importance of shaping working-class children in particular ways, children, and their role and position within capitalism, have remained marginal concerns within Marxist theory, as well as within feminist social reproduction theory. Perhaps this is precisely because children are not regarded as workers: neither productive nor reproductive.
