https://gothamist.com/news/having-a-job-.title: Having a job doesn’t save you from going hungry in NYC, report finds
https://gothamist.com/news/having-a-job-.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/having-a-job-.text:
More than half of 1.3 million New Yorkers who visited food pantries last year were working but still didn’t earn enough to feed their families, a new report found.
The new findings from the Robin Hood Foundation, an anti-poverty group, show how unyielding food insecurity remains across New York City, even as the Trump administration makes cuts to its federal food assistance program known as SNAP. More than 26,500 New Yorkers have lost their monthly food assistance this year under new work requirements and fewer families are applying for the benefit, city numbers show.
Robin Hood found 39% of pantry users worked full time, 12% worked part-time and 4% had a working spouse or partner. Most of those remaining did not work due to a health reason or were 65 years or older.
“Work really isn't a guarantee against hunger. Many New Yorkers are working. About 55% are either working themselves or living with a family member who works, and they're still having a hard time making ends meet,” said Sarah Oltmans, chief of grant strategy for Robin Hood.
The report found 15% of New Yorkers relied on pantries in 2025, a slight increase from the year before.
Nearly half the people who visited pantries experienced financial shocks. That could mean needing to cover a major expense, losing income or losing a job, the report said. The report also said food pantries play a critical role to help New Yorkers out of poverty.
“We're seeing that pantries are really filling these gaps that the paychecks aren't able to do,” Oltmans said.
The numbers reflect steadily rising food insecurity across the city, where one in three New Yorkers either ran out of food or were worried about running out of food last year. But emergency food advocates said the numbers could get worse as changes to SNAP take full effect and federal changes to Medicaid rules start pushing people off the public insurance program and leave families with even fewer resources.
“People will skip meals. They'll rely on friends and relatives. They'll borrow money. We see a lot of people taking on increased amounts of credit card debt,” said Leslie Gordon, CEO of the Food Bank of NYC, a hunger relief group.
“By the time individuals and/or households turn to our food assistance network, they've already exhausted a lot of these other coping strategies.”
Gordon said pantries are also closely monitoring the drop in how many people are applying to SNAP, not just those who already lost their monthly benefit. The thousands of New Yorkers who lost their benefit under the work rules, can reapply to receive at least three more months of assistance.
“It's the new policy and requirements, along with the fact that people are just anxious and fearful,” she said.
Undocumented New Yorkers are not eligible for SNAP but their U.S. citizen children are. But immigration enforcement crackdowns and recent federal changes around how immigration officials weigh a green card and visa applicant’s use of public assistance when deciding whether to approve their cases, known as the public charge rule, is having a chilling effect on New Yorkers wanting to sign up for a benefit they’re entitled to.
The Mamdani administration this year increased funding for 700 food pantries under its Community Food Connection program, and added pet food at 22 locations.
But Gordon said pantries “can’t fill the gap” on their own. For every one meal provided by a food pantry, SNAP provides nine.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Lights Out: Broken NYC Streetlights Surge As Repair Times Get Longer, Data Shows
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Jose Martinez, Kennedy Sessions
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City is taking longer to fix broken streetlights, with the average time to complete repairs hitting its lowest rate on record, city data reveals.
An analysis by The City Reporter of Department of Transportation data found the number of 311 complaints for out-of-service streetlights has surged to 27,609 so far this year — a 6% increase from 2025 and 23% increase from 2024. The outages are causing safety concerns among residents and elected officials, who point to the risk of traffic crashes, crime and trips and falls in the dark, especially as the sun sets earlier during this time of year.
Some streetlights have been out for months, and several New Yorkers said their requests for service from the city have often dragged out or gotten no response.
“The setting, when you come out [of] the train station, it’s almost like a horror flick,” said commuter Jonny Pastrana on Wednesday night at Flatbush and Ocean avenues in Brooklyn, where a light pole across from the Prospect Park subway stop had long been out. “The lights is off. ‘Thriller’ video, yeah, that’s what it feels like.”
The Mamdani administration is aware of the problem, stating in the latest Mayor’s Management Report that last fiscal year, DOT took action to fix broken streetlights within 10 days just 76% of the time — the lowest rate ever and the first time it had sunk below 90% in almost 20 years. The report cited a combination of “increased demand and repair complexity” for the growing delays.
The city’s 311 system has received nearly 180,000 complaints for broken streetlights since 2021, DOT data shows. Out of the five boroughs, Brooklyn and The Bronx topped the list, with 43,150 and 41,689 complaints, respectively.
The intersection of Flatbush and Ocean avenues, where Pastrana was walking, has rung up the most streetlight repair requests out of any spot in the city during that period, with 295. The Ed Koch Queensboro Bridge followed with 208, while 195 complaints were logged from Riverside Drive and West 116th Street in Manhattan.
While the number of broken streetlight complaints so far in 2026 is down 31% from the five-year high of more than 40,000 in 2022, DOT spokesperson Vin Barone acknowledged the most recent winter factored heavily into the repairs backlog.
“Well-lit streets are essential to the safety and comfort of New Yorkers and they deserve nothing less,” he said. “This winter’s historic snowstorms and freezing temperatures took a toll on our aging street lighting infrastructure — some of which dates back to the early 20th century.”
‘It’s Like Pitch Black’
Bay Ridge resident Dimitri Kontakos said one streetlight on his 81st Street block between Fourth and Fifth avenues remained out of commission after a January snowstorm until crews removed the light earlier this month.
He compared the drawn-out response to “pulling teeth.”
“At night, it’s like pitch black,” Kontakos said. “I get that they’re busy and I understand it’s not going to happen the next day, but it’s frustrating for sure.”
Brendan Bolger, 80, said he and neighbors on Dahlgren Place in Bay Ridge have repeatedly contacted 311 about two streetlights that have been out for months, leaving him to feel “a little leery.”
“They said there were major problems with the light further down the block, that it’s a lot more work than just changing the bulb,” he said.
The Mayor’s Management Report, essentially a report card for city agencies, said streetlight repairs “vary by case.”
“Some repairs are straightforward, such as replacing a luminaire or changing a fuse, while more complex cases may involve electrical issues at the base of a pole, foundation work, utility obstructions or ConEd coordination to restore power,” it said.
In a statement, Con Edison said it works with the city to “get streetlights back in service as soon as possible, as we have a shared commitment to public safety.”
‘Bread-and-Butter’ Constituent Services
DOT’s Barone said the city has committed to replacing all LED lights citywide as part of its Vision Zero plan to eliminate traffic deaths. The Mamdani administration is also aiming to develop a connected streetlight network in the coming years to automatically detect outages and speed up repairs while improving visibility in high-risk locations, including beneath elevated trains and highways.
State Sen. Andrew Gounardes said he and City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso — both Democrats who represent Bay Ridge and parts of Dyker Heights — have asked DOT to conduct a “thorough review” of the streetlight repair backlog because of what they said were more than 130 inoperable lights in Brooklyn Community Board 10 as of the end of October.
“Those are typically very easy things to solve. It’s like a bread-and-butter constituent service case,” Gounardes said. “Someone calls in, ‘This is a problem, here’s my 311 number, can you help me figure it out.’ We do — usually, it’s pretty routine.”
At Flatbush and Ocean avenues, Fox White said the broken lights add to the stress of crossing a “gnarly intersection.”
“This area in general is just kind of dark,” White said. “I don’t notice the streetlights in particular, but it does make the area kind of gnarly.”

https://hyperallergic.com/how-should-we-.title: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
https://hyperallergic.com/how-should-we-.author: Ed Simon
https://hyperallergic.com/how-should-we-.text:
How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy.
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for.
When the “Monument Against Fascism” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque.
Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.

https://hyperallergic.com/shahzia-sikand.title: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work
https://hyperallergic.com/shahzia-sikand.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/shahzia-sikand.text:
Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work
With work by Shahzia Sikander and Hylozoic/Desires, “Between Salt and Earth” simultaneously probes and defies the violent and extractive legacies of British imperialism across Asia.
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Earth presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires.
The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Public School Enrollment Falls 3%, With Further Decrease Expected
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat, Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
New York City’s public schools lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers the Education Department released Monday.
That leaves the nation’s largest school system with about 766,900 students, from kindergarten through senior year, as of Oct. 31, with several contributing factors leading to the drop: falling birth rates, families leaving the city and a slowdown of immigration into the five boroughs under President Donald Trump.
Over the past decade, the city has lost about 200,000 students, or nearly 20%.
Enrollment in city-funded preschool programs was up slightly, thanks to the rollout of a new program for 2,000 2-year-olds this year as well as an uptick in 4-year-olds signed up for prekindergarten programs.
What the dip means for school budgets remains murky. Historically, when schools have fewer students than projected on their roster, the Education Department claws back money in the middle of the school year. But since the pandemic, the city has largely kept school budgets steady despite enrollment declines. Officials declined to say whether they planned to continue that policy, known as being “held harmless.” Since 2020, New York City has spent nearly $2 billion to prop up budgets at schools with declining enrollment.
Any changes to wind down that policy could be politically explosive, as schools could have to cut back on after-school and other enrichment programs this school year and eventually let go of teachers. When former Mayor Eric Adams proposed phasing it out, the blowback was so intense that City Council members apologized for giving him the green light. (The decision was later rolled back.)
In his first budget deal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani kept school budgets whole, though some experts warn that approach is inequitable because it allows schools with declining enrollment to spend significantly more per student than other campuses.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has repeatedly raised concerns about declining enrollment, saying that the city will need to look closer at closures or mergers for schools too small to offer a full array of courses. Already, the city is floating proposals to close two small schools in Harlem and one in Brooklyn, as well as merge two sets of schools in the Bronx and Brooklyn, according to public documents. Those plans are expected to be voted on by the Panel for Educational Policy over the next two months.
“We’ve started to have conversations in communities,” Samuels told the Chancellor’s Parent Advisory Committee last week. “It doesn’t mean it’s not going to be tough sometimes, but they have been going pretty well.”
Enrollment is projected to continue declining. By the 2034-35 school year, the city is predicting that the student population will fall by another 130,000, according to demographic projections from the School Construction Authority.
The declines in New York City mirror national trends. Thirty states have seen public school enrollment declines since 2014. Many large school systems — including in Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia and Houston — are also grappling with sharp drops.
Mamdani’s administration pointed to some efforts to help bolster city schools, including reducing class sizes, which is required by state law and has likely been aided by declining student headcounts. Aside from continuing some of his predecessor’s initiatives, Mamdani has yet to articulate a vision for the public school system. He has focused more on his affordability agenda and expanding his free 2-K program, which expects to add 10,000 more seats next year.
When the city’s free preschool programs for 2-, 3- and 4-year-olds are included in the enrollment tally, the total is 863,100, according to the Education Department’s preliminary data. That was down about 2.6% from the previous year.
Chalkbeat New York Reporter Michael Elsen-Rooney contributed.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

https://hyperallergic.com/olivia-reaveys.title: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality
https://hyperallergic.com/olivia-reaveys.author: Bryan Martin
https://hyperallergic.com/olivia-reaveys.text:
Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality
Everything is a treasured scrap for Reavey to pull from in her unorthodox black-and-white photography.
Olivia Reavey moves at breakneck speed. Her silver-gelatin-analog printing process is frenzied and intense: Black-and-white prints are cut into irregular quadrilaterals with crumpled edges, then hung unframed and loosely fixed to the walls with clips, pins, and other supports. But this is not just slapdash; everything here is intentionally energetic and playful, with images asserting the body’s formal pleasure captured in film.
Many bare their flesh but are often obfuscated or appear with objects: a broken branch covers a male’s buttocks in “Stick” (all works 2026); a wooden lever protrudes from a woman’s pubic area, captured in the reflection of a mirror in “Untitled.” The penetrative and phallic elements here are obvious, but also read neutrally in a recurring tension between eroticism and form — shapes and tonal values outweigh anything provocative.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Progress Stalls in Reducing 911 Calls for NYC Students in Emotional Distress
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Abigail Kramer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Crystal Roach felt her hands shake as she ordered an Uber. Her thoughts were racing, imagining her 6-year-old son, Zai, confused and afraid. She pictured his little wrists in handcuffs, and it felt hard to breathe.
Roach had just gotten off the phone with a guidance counselor from Zai’s school — P.S. 11, in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn. Zai had recently been diagnosed with autism. At home, he was funny and affectionate, saying “I love you” and doing silly dances to make Roach laugh, even though he didn’t like being hugged or touched. But for months, he’d been having meltdowns in class and the lunchroom, throwing pencils and books, tearing up papers, hitting other kids or teachers.
School staff called Roach nearly every day, she said, telling her she had to pick up Zai (a family nickname) immediately. Roach told them she couldn’t keep leaving work. She was a single parent and a nanny, and her boss was losing patience.
But this call — in April 2026, near the end of Zai’s first grade — was different: The school had called a mobile crisis team, which in turn called 911. Police and an ambulance were on their way. If Roach didn’t get there first, they’d take Zai to an emergency room. No one could tell her which hospital.
The idea of not knowing where Zai was felt intolerable. Roach frantically dialed her mom and an aunt, trying to find someone who could get to Zai faster.
When she pulled up to the school, there was a police car parked in front. That’s when her fear shifted to disbelief, she said. “I just kept thinking: ‘Cops? For a 6-year-old?’”
New York City schools are only supposed to call 911 on students in the most extreme circumstances. Under city regulations, school staff must do everything they can to de-escalate a student’s behavioral or mental health crisis themselves — only resorting to 911 if someone is at imminent risk of serious physical harm.
When schools do call 911 — incidents known as “child in crisis” calls — police typically show up first, containing students until EMTs arrive. Hundreds of times each year, kids end up in handcuffs — some of them as young as 6 and 7 years old.
In the wake of a 2013 lawsuit, the city adopted rules aimed at reducing child in crisis calls, including quarterly reporting requirements and crisis intervention training for schools. In 2023, after an investigation by ProPublica and The City Reporter, the New York City Council passed a law requiring police to document whether schools had attempted to de-escalate a crisis before involving EMTs or cops.
But while the number of calls dropped after the lawsuit was settled, progress has largely stalled. New York City schools continue to call 911 on students in emotional distress well over 2,000 times a year.
Child in crisis calls are far more likely to happen to students with disabilities and Black students, and they frequently involve very young kids. Since 2016, when the city first started tracking the numbers, schools have called 911 more than 5,000 times on children who were less than 10 years old, according to city data.
Families and mental health providers say that hauling kids to hospitals is traumatic, humiliating and often counterproductive. In most cases, students wait for hours in crowded ERs, only to be evaluated and sent home without treatment, advocates say.
“Calling 911 doesn’t make anything better at school the next day,” said Nelson Mar, a senior attorney at Legal Services NYC who is working with Roach to secure special education services for Zai.
Mar also led the 2013 lawsuit that prompted the city to adopt its first formal limits on schools’ use of 911. But while the settlement led to gains, he said, it failed to address the root causes of child in crisis incidents. Despite federal laws requiring school districts to serve students with disabilities, most city schools lack the training and resources to support kids who’ve experienced serious trauma, or whose disabilities manifest in disruptive behavior.
By the time a situation escalates to the point where school staff consider calling 911, they’ve likely missed countless opportunities to help a kid succeed, advocates and educators say.
In a March 2026 letter to the Mamdani administration, Mar and other advocates urged the city to expand behavioral interventions in city schools. Among their recommendations: Staff each district with specialists who can help schools create detailed behavior plans for struggling kids; train teachers to understand common behavior patterns in neurodivergent students; and expand initiatives like the Path program, which uses evidence-based strategies to support students with emotional disabilities in general education classrooms.
When schools have more tools, they can become more “healing-centered and less punitive,” Mar said. “There needs to be a culture shift.”
How Bureaucracy and Punishment Left a First Grader Without Help
Zai’s troubles started near the beginning of first grade. When school staff first raised concerns about his behavior, Roach trusted they wanted what was best for him, she said. Zai’s big sister had attended P.S. 11 and left with a wall full of achievement awards.
Roach enrolled Zai in therapy and took time off work to sit in his classroom. On the school’s advice, she requested an evaluation for an individualized education program — a document that could entitle Zai to special education services to help him regulate his meltdowns.
But the evaluation was delayed for months, long beyond the legal deadline, despite Roach’s repeated emails pleading with the school to speed up the process. As the delays stretched on, she said, Zai’s meltdowns became more frequent and the school’s response more punitive.
He came home calling himself “a bad kid,” something he heard from a teacher, Roach said. He often had to miss recess or eat lunch alone, as a punishment for something he’d done on a previous day.
Desperate for help, Roach took Zai to a neurologist, who diagnosed him with autism.
Based on that diagnosis, Zai’s school could have provided him services through a “504 plan,” using its discretionary budget to assign him a one-on-one paraprofessional who’d help him calm down when he got agitated. They also could have sought help from the district to create a detailed behavior plan identifying Zai’s triggers and strategies to prevent his meltdowns.
“They didn’t do any of that,” Roach said.
In an occurrence report from April, P.S. 11 Principal Abidemi Hope wrote that the school had tried several interventions for Zai, “including my direct involvement as principal, At-Risk counseling services, and structured morning and afternoon check-ins with support staff.”
Despite these efforts, Hope wrote, Zai’s “behaviors have continued to escalate in both frequency and severity, surpassing the school’s capacity to safely manage them within the general education setting.”
To Roach, it seemed like P.S. 11 just wanted to get rid of Zai, even before completing his assessment or providing him with a full set of services.
“He was just seen as a problem child,” she said.
It’s not unusual for kids with difficult behaviors to be pushed out of general education schools. According to a data analysis released last week by the New York City Independent Budget Office, almost 30% of students classified as having emotional disabilities are placed in separate, special-education schools run by District 75.
Overwhelmingly, they end up concentrated in a handful of schools where attendance and graduation rates are among the poorest in the city — and where they are even likelier to be subject to a 911 call.
A Team Meant To Prevent 911 Calls Made One Instead
In the last decade, the city has launched several initiatives designed to make schools less punitive and more supportive, including healing-centered schools, the “mental health continuum,” and restorative justice programs.
Proponents say those programs benefit all kids, not just those with serious mental health or behavioral struggles. But they remain small and marginal, frequently losing momentum and funding when political priorities shift.
More recently, city officials have encouraged schools to make use of mobile crisis teams — mental health professionals who can respond in anywhere from a few hours to a few days to triage struggling students and help them connect to longer-term services if necessary. One of the teams’ explicit goals is to keep people in crisis away from unnecessary encounters with police and trips to the ER.
When P.S. 11 staff told Roach about the crisis team program, she thought it sounded like a good idea.
On the day the school called the team, Zai had a meltdown after a change in his schedule, flipping tables, throwing classroom materials and punching a teacher in the stomach, according to a school occurrence report. The teacher took Zai on a walk around the school to help “settle his nervous system,” the report said. They encountered another staff member, who began to question Zai about misbehavior on the previous day. Zai ran away and sat on a bench.
Zai was calm and back in class when the crisis team arrived later in the day. When he was pulled out to meet with the two crisis responders, along with Hope and other school staff, however, he got upset again. Zai kicked Hope, then drew a picture of her, scribbled over her face and wrote, “Weak, you should die.”
In the crisis de-escalation plan that P.S. 11 filed with the city last year, staff are instructed to remove distressed students from the environment that is setting them off and attempt to have a conversation “exploring the student’s point of view.”
Those steps were not taken in the incident with Zai. According to the report, staff reprimanded him, instructing him to speak politely as his behaviors began to escalate. Hope — who was the focus of Zai’s behavior — remained in the room as he started to throw erasers and books at her and push away staff members who tried to intervene. That’s when the mobile crisis team called 911.
VNS Health, the nonprofit agency that deployed the crisis team, declined to comment, citing client privacy. Neither the principal nor Education Department officials responded to specific questions about Zai’s experience.
In an emailed statement, spokesperson Onika Richards wrote, “Under no circumstance is 911 ever called simply for a student’s behavior — or to cause student arrest or pressure to transfer out of our schools. 911 is only called as an alternative, when an emotional or behavioral crisis has exceeded the ability of the school staff to address it safely.”
She added, “Our students are children who need support, not children who should be criminalized or handcuffed.”
When Roach arrived at Zai’s school, she found him standing silently, surrounded by two police officers, the two members of the crisis team and Hope. Two more officers were coming through the door.
Her worst fears were relieved: Zai was still in the building, he was unhurt and he wasn’t wearing handcuffs. But he looked scared and small, rocking back and forth and flicking his fingers in the way he does to soothe himself when he’s upset.
“What crime did he commit?” she asked later. “I have a 6-year-old child that was treated more like a criminal.”
After the 911 call, Mar helped Zai transfer to P.S. 20, another school in Clinton Hill, where he was assigned a paraprofessional within weeks. When he got overwhelmed or appeared to be escalating, staff gave him choices about where to go, including rooms stocked with calming tools such as Legos and sensory toys.
In the three months before school broke for summer, Roach said she picked Zai up early only once — after he saw a police car outside the school and panicked.
Abigail Kramer is a New York City-based journalist. You can reach her at: abigailkramer@gmail.com.

Rare Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction
Christie's withdraws a Frida Kahlo painting following protests, Sotheby's says heirs of contested Van Gogh agreed to a deal, and more in today's art news.
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic's writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.
Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction
Works by the Swedish spiritualist and abstract art pioneer, who asked that her paintings remain unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944, have not come up for auction in more than three decades. That's about to change with the emergence of “Ser III No. 5” (1920) at the Stockholm-based house Bukowskis, which estimates the oil and graphite on canvas will fetch up to 8 million SEK (~$791,000) in its upcoming November 18–19 sale. Controversy has long followed the legacy of the late artist, with some arguing that her works should be kept together rather than sold and commercialized.
Sotheby's Settles Dispute With Heirs Who Contested Van Gogh Sale
After the heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer requested the withdrawal of Van Gogh's “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (1890) from a sale at Sotheby's, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe, the family has reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with the work's consignors, said a Sotheby's statement shared with Hyperallergic. But will the dispute put a damper on sale results? We'll find out tonight when the painting, valued at $180 million, goes under the hammer.

The critic plays buzzword bingo with the terms that defined late ’60s sculpture
“I am thinking of the terms ‘post-Minimalism’ and ‘dematerialization’—of how they have become entrenched within the lexicon of contemporary criticism. I am thinking of the extreme disjunction between the strategic value of those terms and their capacity to signify.”
In “Sense and Sensibility: Reflection on Post ’60s Sculpture,” published in Artforum’s November 1973 issue, Rosalind Krauss cast a retrospective glance on the avant-garde at the turn of the decade, attempting to free the work of artists such as Richard Serra, On Kawara, and Dorothea Rockburne from the prescriptive shadow of the era’s prevailing catchall terms. Krauss’s essay builds from the notion that historical context alone is an inadequate substitute for more meaningful evaluations of an artwork’s function. The critic argues further that in referring to late-1960s sculpture through the descriptors “post-Minimalism” and “dematerialization,” one defines the art exclusively through its deepening or supplanting of earlier conventions. This approach traps the critic in an “infinite regress of negation,” describing historical lineages rather than any “positive” content of artworks.
Krauss goes on to contrast the work of “dematerialists” like Sol LeWitt, Mel Bochner, or Richard Tuttle with the “objectless” cohort of Robert Barry, Joseph Kosuth, and Douglas Huebler. This opposition allows the critic to interrogate the varied positions artists take to either uphold or confound the viewer’s understanding of a “private mental space . . . in which meanings and intentions have to exist before they could issue into the space of the world.” Unlike the Abstract Expressionists, who believed their canvases were realizations of some truth held in an “inviolable” interior self, artists like Bochner and Rockburne often challenged notions of language and sensation as internal constructions, instead highlighting their shared social nature in their work. Others, like Serra, attempted to challenge preconceived notions of self through conflicts with the body, forcing viewers to confront the instability of perception through encounters with space and corporeal scale. In each case, these “post-Minimalists” and “dematerialists” attempted to leave behind historical context as a site for generating meaning in their work, and instead chose to find new pathways for complicating and deepening the viewer’s understanding of reality, often without historical precedent.
Read “Sense and Sensibility: Reflection on Post ’60s Sculpture” from the November 1973 issue of Artforum.
–Theo Belci

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/in.title: Trump Accepts Artistic Gift from India Just Months After Branding it a “Hellhole” Country
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/in.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/in.text:
Traditional Indian art and crafts were in the spotlight as Indian prime minister Narendra Modi arrived at the ASEAN Summit and meeting of Quad leaders, which concluded yesterday in Manila, the capital of the Philippines. It was organized by Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which includes 11 countries in the region, whose populations total almost 700 million.
Modi gave out gifts to all the leaders in attendance. Philippines president Ferdinand R. “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. got a hand-knotted Kashmiri carpet. His wife, Marie Louise “Liza” Araneta-Marcos, received a Pashmina shawl in a papier-mâché box. Donald Trump took home a golden Pichwai painting from Nathdwara, Rajasthan, while Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese is the proud new owner of a piece of Jaipur blue pottery.
And the gift-giving went on. Modi gave a Katan silk stole in a Sadheli box to Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi. He bestowed a rose quartz elephant with gold work upon Lao PM Sonexay Siphandone. To Singapore’s PM he conveyed a traditional gond painting. He delivered a Chola bronze sculpture to Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto.
The Nathdwara school of miniature painting, of which Trump was given a representative gift, flourished during the 18th and 19th centuries in the village of the same name in southern Rajasthan, as the Times of India wrote in 2008, on the occasion of an exhibition organized by the Archer Foundation at Amdavad-ni-Gufa, a gallery in Ahmedabad, India. A group of priests had moved a treasured idol of Shrinathji to a new temple there in 1672, explains the Times, after Mughal emperor Aurangzeb destroyed a number of the Goswamis’ temples. Shrinathji is considered a form of Krishna.
In the large example given to Trump, visible in an Instagram post by the Indian government, eight women in gowns surround an extravagantly dressed central figure sporting a halo, against a backdrop of highly stylized trees and sky. Gold, seemingly Trump’s favorite color to judge by his Oval Office decor, is abundant.
Trump received his offering even though he arrived late, only on Tuesday, as the summit was wrapping up, and, according to the New York Times, “he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.” This, says the newspaper, leads to a “widespread belief” among ASEAN leaders “that the United States is not a reliable partner.”
But Trump got his gift just the same. He is also not one who is known for his attitude toward preserving the arts and culture, having, for example, initiated Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) campaign, which resulted in the gutting of the Institute of Museum and Library Services, and having moved more than once to completely defund organizations like the National Endowment for the Arts.
But he is a man known to love gifts from foreign leaders, even a superjumbo jet from the nation of Qatar meant to serve as Air Force One, despite its not being technically outfitted for the job and despite that country’s history of support for the Muslim Brotherhood. During the midterm election campaigns, Trump attempted to smear Minnesota’s then–Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed with association with the group, calling him a “jihadist.”
He also accepted the gift despite calling India a “hellhole” in April on the Savage Nation talk radio show.

                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Diretor da PF cita ‘quebra de confiança’ e afirma que afastamento de delegados no caso Master não tem relação com conteúdo de relatórios sobre ministros
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O diretor-geral da Polícia Federal (PF), Andrei Rodrigues, afirmou nesta quarta-feira (18) que os delegados responsáveis pelos relatórios sobre ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) no caso Banco Master perderam as funções de chefia por quebra de confiança, e não pelo conteúdo dos documentos. A declaração foi dada em audiência pública conjunta das comissões de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) e de Segurança Pública (CSP) do Senado.
Segundo Rodrigues, a equipe deveria ter apresentado a ele minutas dos relatórios de inteligência, que depois seriam enviadas ao presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin. Em vez disso, os delegados assinaram e inseriram as primeiras versões no Sistema Eletrônico de Informações (SEI) da PF. O diretor-geral disse ainda que determinou a reformulação dos relatórios porque os documentos não atendiam aos requisitos estabelecidos por Fachin.
“A questão da confiança não guarda relação com conteúdo dos relatórios. Nenhuma. A relação foi quebrada porque houve determinação do diretor da Dicor [Diretoria de Investigação e Combate ao Crime Organizado e à Corrupção] para apresentassem minuta e isso submetido a mim para apresentar ao Fachin”, disse.
“Para surpresa de todos, não houve apresentação, houve a subida desses relatórios para o sistema SEI da PF. Aí reside a quebra de confiança. A equipe não confia no diretor e o diretor, obviamente, passa a não confiar nessas pessoas que estavam em cargo de chefia”, acrescentou.
Os delegados Daniel Mostardeiro Cola e Wedson Cajé Lopes perderam as funções de chefia depois de participar da elaboração dos relatórios, que reuniam citações aos ministros Alexandre de Moraes, Dias Toffoli e Kassio Nunes Marques. As novas versões devem ser individualizadas e incluir todos os ministros da Corte citados no material analisado pela PF.
O senador Alessandro Vieira (MDB-SE), autor dos requerimentos que convocaram a audiência, contestou a justificativa. Para ele, os documentos foram elaborados com base em informações de investigações policiais e, por isso, não deveriam depender de aprovação administrativa. Rodrigues respondeu que os relatórios foram pedidos diretamente a ele pela Presidência do STF e não foram produzidos no exercício regular da atividade investigativa.
O diretor-geral afirmou ainda que oito delegados assinaram os relatórios inseridos no sistema sem autorização. De acordo com ele, nenhum foi retirado das investigações, e todos permanecem nas mesmas unidades, inclusive o delegado que comanda um dos inquéritos. A única mudança, segundo Rodrigues, foi a não recondução às funções de confiança.
Envio a Fachin
Durante a audiência, Rodrigues anunciou que enviará a Fachin um HD com os dados usados na elaboração dos relatórios. Além das versões refeitas, o diretor-geral disse que deixará à disposição do presidente do STF os relatórios originais.
“Vai ter o HD com todo o material de onde extraímos, para que, enfim, a assessoria do presidente, o presidente possa eventualmente fazer as pesquisas que quiser fazer”, informou.
Segundo Rodrigues, a ordem para refazer os documentos não resultou na exclusão das versões anteriores, que seguem guardadas no sistema da PF e poderão ser examinadas pelo STF. “Ninguém apaga um processo, estão lá, assinados, preservados, que na minha avaliação não são adequados”, afirmou.
O diretor-geral sustentou que a revisão buscou preservar a legalidade das investigações, já que a PF não pode investigar ministros do STF sem autorização da própria Corte. Caberá ao Supremo, segundo ele, decidir se as informações justificam a abertura de novas apurações ou o arquivamento.
“A Polícia Federal não tem absolutamente nada para esconder de ninguém, não está perseguindo, não está protegendo, está cumprindo o seu papel legal e constitucional”, declarou.
Ministro defende decisão
O ministro da Justiça e Segurança Pública, Wellington César Lima e Silva, que também participou da audiência, defendeu a PF e afirmou que as decisões de Rodrigues seguiram a lei.
“Como se vê da resposta do diretor-geral, não teria ocorrido nenhuma demissão, nem punição disciplinar. O que teria ocorrido, foi uma opção da direção da Polícia Federal, de não reconduzir aqueles dois delegados à função de confiança”, disse Lima e Silva.
O ministro sustentou que o diretor-geral tem o direito de promover mudanças na corporação e que todas as funções investigativas foram mantidas. “O Ministério da Justiça supervisiona a Polícia Federal, não a dirige”, ressaltou.

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: GTA 6 : sous le capot, la décadence de nos sociétés capitalistes
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Aurélien Soucheyre
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
Jeu de tous les superlatifs, GTA 6, qui sort ce jeudi 18 novembre sur console, suscite un immense engouement. Attendue comme une claque technologique, avec un monde ouvert ultraréaliste, cette histoire de gangsters appartient à une saga qui s’est toujours évertuée à parodier le néolibéralisme, au risque d’en devenir l’un des principaux vecteurs.
Avez-vous déjà entendu parler de Jay Norris ? Ce gourou de la Silicon Valley, autoproclamé démiurge de la tech, pseudo-philanthrope en réalité milliardaire vorace, PDG de LifeInvader, présente son tout nouveau smartphone lors d’une grande messe télévisuelle. Michael De Santa, l’un des personnages principaux incarné par le joueur ou la joueuse dans GTA V, regarde l’événement depuis son canapé.
La veille, il a piégé le téléphone du champion des Gafam en s’infiltrant dans ses locaux. Tranquillement, il appelle Jay Norris sur son portable. Surpris, le faux prophète répond, ce qui déclenche la bombe : son visage explose en mondovision. Un crime parfait, spectaculaire, mené un verre à la main depuis le confort d’un salon. Voilà l’un des immenses doigts d’honneur que le jeu vidéo GTA V envoyait au visage du capitalisme américain, en 2013.
Depuis, les seigneurs de la tech à la Mark Zuckerberg et Elon Musk ont pris le pouvoir. Et un certain Donald Love, magnat de l’immobilier et des médias rêvant d’un...

https://taz.de/Erfinderin-des-Badeanzugs.title: Erfinderin des Badeanzugs: Die Nixe mit der zu knappen Bademode
https://taz.de/Erfinderin-des-Badeanzugs.author: Elke Wittich
https://taz.de/Erfinderin-des-Badeanzugs.text:
Erfinderin des Badeanzugs: Die Nixe mit der zu knappen Bademode
Schwimmstar, Modestar und Filmstar: Die Australierin Annette Kellerman war Anfang des 20. Jahrhunderts das, was man heute Influencerin nennt.
E ine Influencerin mit eigener Modelinie, eine Sportlerin mit späterer Karriere als Filmstar, dazu Autorin von Ratgeber-Büchern und Varieté-Star – das Leben der 1886 geborenen Australierin Annette Kellerman enthält viele Stationen, die heute Teil des Promi-Daseins sind.
Dabei sollte die Frau, die maßgeblich dazu beitrug, dass Frauen die damals als angemessen geltende Schwimmkleidung, also Kleider und Pumphosen aus schwerem Material, gegen Badeanzüge eintauschten, eigentlich Pianistin werden. Die elterliche Musikschule war sehr erfolgreich, aber Annette hasste das ständige Üben. Sie wollte lieber Tänzerin werden, doch durch eine Rachitis-Erkrankung musste sie schwere Beinschienen tragen. Ärzte empfahlen schließlich Schwimmunterricht.
Dort, wo heute die Oper von Sydney steht, lernte Annette in einem flotierenden, mit Holzlatten vom Hafengelände abgetrennten Becken das Schwimmen. Begeistert war die Siebenjährige von der Idee jedoch nicht, sie hatte große Angst vor der Tiefe und erinnerte sich in ihren unveröffentlichten Memoiren, dass man sie schreiend ins Wasser tragen musste.
Nachdem sie schwimmen gelernt hatte, machte ihr der Sport immer mehr Spaß, als Teenagerin trainierte sie schließlich in einem Bad, das auch vom zweimaligen Schwimm-Olympiasieger Freddie Lane frequentiert wurde. 1901 wollte sie zum ersten Mal an einem Wettkampf teilnehmen, ihre Mutter hielt das jedoch für ein unschickliches Vorhaben. Freddie Lane überzeugte Annettes Eltern jedoch, indem er auf ihre bemerkenswerte Kondition und Ausdauer hinwies.
Die australische Meerjungfrau
Prompt gewann sie ihr erstes Rennen über 45 Yard, rund 41 Meter, und startete im Dezember 1901 bei einem Schwimmfest. Wieder gewann sie, allerdings waren es Fotos ihrer gewagten Sprünge vom 15-Meter-Brett, die sie zum ersten Mal in die Presse brachten. Dass sie dabei einen ärmellosen, nur bis zu den Knien reichenden Badeanzug trug, machte sie für die Fotografen sicher noch interessanter.
1902 wurde sie zweifache Meisterin von New South Wales. Nach einem Auftritt im Melbourner Aquarium, wo sie zur Begeisterung des Publikums mit Fischen schwamm und Kunststücke zeigte, trat sie unter dem Beinamen „Australian Mermaid“ auf. Die Presse berichtete ausführlich über ihre Shows, aber auch über ihre Erfolge als Langstreckenschwimmerin, die sich bald bis nach Europa herumsprachen.
1905 reisten Annette und ihr Vater nach Großbritannien, wo sie mehr als 20 Kilometer in der Themse schwamm. Die Strecke war natürlich nicht abgesperrt, die australische Meerjungfrau musste sich zwischen Schiffen und Dampfern ihren Weg durch den stark verschmutzten Fluss suchen.
Die britischen Zeitungen reagierten begeistert, ein Boulevardblatt nahm sie unter Vertrag. Auch auf den europäischen Varietébühnen wurde Kellerman zum Publikumsmagneten: In riesigen Wassertanks zeigte sie eine Mischung aus Schwimmen, Ballett und spektakulären Sprüngen, die ihr hohe Gagen einbrachte.
Mode- und Filmstar
Dass sie mehrmals daran scheiterte, den Ärmelkanal zu durchschwimmen, schadete ihrer Popularität nicht. Vielmehr wurde sie auch in den USA zum Star, wozu sicher auch ihre unter dem eigenen Namen vermarktete moderne Badekleidung beitrug. Und ihr Talent zur Selbstvermarktung: Sie erzählte zwar gern, dass sie 1907 an einem Bostoner Strand wegen ihres engen Badeanzugs verhaftet worden sei, aber in zeitgenössischen Presseberichten und Polizeiakten ist darüber nichts zu finden – im Gegensatz zu ihren Verhaftungen wegen zu schnellen Fahrens.
Ab 1909 wurde Annette Kellerman zusätzlich zum Filmstar. Von „Neptune’s daughter“ (1914) sind nur noch Ausschnitte erhalten, „A daughter of the gods“ (1916) gilt als verschollen. In beiden Filmen trat sie nackt auf und zeigte gefährliche Stunts. Wenn sie nicht gerade filmte, veröffentlichte sie Schwimm- und Beauty-Ratgeber. 1924 spielte sie zum letzten Mal in einem Film namens „Venus of the South Seas“.
Von der Verfilmung ihres Lebens mit Esther Williams in der Hauptrolle zeigte sie sich jedoch enttäuscht, obwohl sie die Produktion beraten hatte. 1956 kehrte sie mit ihrem Ehemann James Sullivan nach Australien zurück, wo sie 1975 im Alter von 89 Jahren verstarb.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120398.title: Queerness | Lutz van Dijk: Die Tugend der Dickköpfigkeit
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120398.author: Bodo Niendel
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120398.text:
- Kultur
- Queerness
Lutz van Dijk: Die Tugend der Dickköpfigkeit
»Wer einen Menschen rettet, rettet die Welt«: Dieser Satz aus dem Talmud passte sehr gut zum queeren Aktivisten Lutz van Dijk, der jetzt gestorben ist.
Lutz van Dijk hatte eine ungewöhnliche Ausstrahlung, ja, eine Aura. Er fesselte einen Saal innerhalb weniger Augenblicke. Die Menschen hingen an seinen Lippen. Das lag nicht nur an seinen Geschichten, sondern auch an seiner Zugewandtheit, seinem ansteckenden Lachen und seiner tiefen Liebe zum Du. Was ihn mit dem Theologen Martin Buber verband.
Vielleicht hat er nicht nur ein Leben gelebt, sondern gleich mehrere. So viel passt in diese Biografie, diese Begegnungen, Kämpfe und Geschichten. Er war Menschenrechtsaktivist, Pädagoge, Historiker, Schriftsteller, Friedensaktivist und nd-Autor. Noch im ersten Halbjahr dieses Jahres ging er mit dem zweiten Band seiner Autobiografie auf Lesereise durch Deutschland, in mehr als 25 Städten. Dass er diese Reise trotz seiner fortschreitenden Parkinson-Erkrankung auf sich nahm, ist bezeichnend. Er wollte auch ein Zeichen gegen das Erstarken der neuen Nazis setzen. An seiner Seite war sein Mann, Perry Tsang. Gemeinsam hatten sie über Jahrzehnte ein Leben gestaltet, das von Liebe, Solidarität und selbst gewählten Familien, von Wahlverwandtschaften geprägt war.
Meine erste Begegnung mit Lutz liegt viele Jahre zurück. Ich hatte ihn zu einer Konferenz eingeladen, die wir im Rahmen der Parada Równości, der Parade der Gleichheit organisierten, Pendant zum Christopher-Street-Day in Warschau. Die Parade war damals von Verboten bedroht. Erst der Europäische Gerichtshof hob das Verbot des damaligen Bürgermeisters Lech Kaczyński auf.
Wirklich herzlich begegnet sind wir uns in der Internationalen Jugendbegegnungsstätte Auschwitz im Jahr 2017. Ich war auf Bildungsreise mit dem Internationalen Auschwitz-Komitee. Er hatte eine Lesung im Goethe-Institut in Krakau. Dem promovierten Historiker und ehemaligen Mitarbeiter des Anne-Frank-Hauses in Amsterdam lag die Erinnerungsarbeit an die Verbrechen des Faschismus sehr am Herzen. In der Gedenkstätte Auschwitz bot er eine Weiterbildung zum Thema »Queere Opfer im KZ« an, die sehr gut besucht war.
Seine Beharrlichkeit führte ihn schließlich bis in den Bundestag. 2018 initiierte Lutz eine Petition für eine eigene Gedenkstunde für die queeren Opfer des Nationalsozialismus zum Holocaust-Gedenktag. Zunächst wurde sein Anliegen vom Bundestagspräsidenten Wolfgang Schäuble zurückgewiesen. Doch Lutz ließ nicht locker.
2023 wurde die Gedenkstunde Wirklichkeit. Bärbel Bas von der SPD war nun Bundestagspräsidentin. Die von ihm verfassten Lebensgeschichten von Mary Pünjer und Karl Gorath, vorgetragen von Maren Kroymann und Jannik Schümann, machten das Schicksal Verfolgter sichtbar. Diese dicht gedrängte Stunde – weiterhin abrufbar auf der Seite des Bundestags – war sein Meisterstück. Bewegend, wie die Schicksale vermittelt wurden. Traurig, dass die Verfolgung queerer Menschen auch nach 1945 in beiden deutschen Staaten fortbestand.
Lutz war ein queerer Aktivist, aber eben nicht nur das. Er schrieb gegen Antisemitismus und Rassismus, gegen autoritäre Regime und die Festung Europa. Und er war ein radikaler Pazifist, der niemals eine Waffe in die Hand genommen hätte. Auch nach dem russischen Angriff auf die Ukraine hielt er an dieser Überzeugung fest. Das brachte ihn in Konflikt mit Menschen, die angesichts des Krieges zu anderen politischen Schlussfolgerungen kamen. Und auch mit manchem Medium, für das er schrieb, so zum Beispiel der »Taz«. Aber Lutz gab seinen Pazifismus nicht auf.
Er veröffentlichte in seinem Leben mehr als 50 Bücher. Besonders seine Jugendbücher machten tabuisierte Themen zugänglich. Die Lesereisen durch Schulen und Bibliotheken strahlten aus und prägten viele Menschen. Seine pädagogische Arbeit mit Kindern, die als »besonders schwierig« galten, prägte seinen Blick auf die Welt: Niemand sollte abgeschrieben, ausgegrenzt oder seiner Würde beraubt werden. Sein Beamtendasein als Sozialpädagoge hängte er an den Nagel, sein Aktivismus war ihm wichtiger. Der Verfassungsschutz beobachtete seine Friedensaktivitäten argwöhnisch.
Lutz lebte unterschiedliche Formen des Zusammenlebens der »Regenbogenfamilie« zu einer Zeit vor, in der solche Lebensmodelle noch kaum gesellschaftliche Anerkennung fanden. Familie war für ihn von Wahlverwandtschaft geprägt. Perry war ihm in den letzten Jahrzehnten sein treuer Gefährte. Aber, dies macht Lutz in seiner Biografie sehr deutlich, guter Sex nicht nur mit einem Mann, zum Beispiel in der Schwulensauna, waren ihm sehr wichtig.
2002 gründeten Lutz und Perry gemeinsam HOKISA (Homes for Kids in South Africa) ein Kinder- und Jugendhausprojekt für HIV-positive Kinder und Jugendliche in einem Township bei Kapstadt. In einer Zeit, in der die südafrikanische Regierung wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse zu HIV und Aids infrage stellte und lebensnotwendige Medikamente vielerorts nicht verfügbar waren, sorgten sie dafür, dass die benötigten Medikamente ins Land kamen. Zahlreiche Kinder verdankten ihm ihr Leben.
Perry hat HOKISA gemeinsam mit Lutz aufgebaut und getragen. Zur Eröffnung kam Friedensnobelpreisträger Desmond Tutu, mit dem er bis zum Lebensende befreundet war. Das Projekt besteht bis heute. »Wer einen Menschen rettet, rettet die Welt« – dieser Satz aus dem Talmud hätte kaum besser zu seinem Leben passen können. Im Juni habe ich Lutz für »queer.de« interviewt. Auf die Frage, was ihn trotz aller Widerstände habe weitermachen lassen, antwortete er: »Beharrlich sein bis zum Dickkopf kann in der Tat eine Tugend sein.« Das war Lutz.
In einer unserer letzten Whatsapp-Nachrichten war er sofort bereit, sich gegen antisemitische Unterstellungen gegen die Berliner Linke und Elif Eralp einsetzen. Er bat mich, ein Zitat von ihm für Eralp in den sozialen Medien zu verbreiten. Aber auch wenn er im letzten Bundestagswahlkampf zur Wahl der Linken aufgerufen hatte, war ihm Parteipolitik fremd. Ihn verbanden Freundschaften in viele parteipolitischen Richtungen. Er war ein sehr talentierter Netzwerker.
Unsere letzte gemeinsame Veranstaltung fand im Juli bei der Rosa-Luxemburg-Stiftung statt. Zusammen mit Petra Pau stellte Lutz den zweiten Band seiner Autobiografie vor. Der Saal war wieder einmal bis auf den letzten Platz gefüllt. Lutz war bereits deutlich von seiner Parkinson-Erkrankung gezeichnet, doch der Saal klebte an seinen Lippen. Petra Pau hatte ihn kurz zuvor in Südafrika besucht.
Er ist am 17. November im Beisein seines Mannes Perry Tsang in Amsterdam selbstbestimmt aus dem Leben geschieden, so wie er es sich gewünscht hatte. Er wurde 71 Jahre alt. In seiner letzten Nachricht schrieb er: »Da ich meinen Körper der Wissenschaft zur Verfügung stelle, wird es keine Beerdigung geben.«
Etwa zehn Bücher habe ich von ihm rezensiert, nicht ihm zuliebe, sondern weil sich mich bewegten. Lutz war Philanthrop und für unsere queere Community eine Ikone, die nachhallen wird. Da bin ich mir sicher.
Wer Lutz’ und Perrys Lebenswerk HOKISA unterstützen möchte: Informationen und Spendenmöglichkeiten gibt es unter: www.hokisa.de
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US admits ‘substantial’ change to extradition request translation for leftist activist
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Timothy Pratt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US authorities have admitted altering the translation of an extradition request for James “Fergie” Chambers from English into Spanish, attributing violent and illegal actions to the wealthy activist and philanthropist that were not in the original.
Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
In a notification sent to Spain’s ministry of justice, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) cites three of the examples of legally significant alterations revealed in the Guardian’s reporting on the issue, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”.
The notification arrived to defense attorneys, the prosecutor and a three-judge panel on Tuesday as the judges were deliberating whether to grant the US extradition request, leading the defense team to file a motion calling for a halt in the proceedings and a new translation.
The US has now admitted to three of the alterations detailed in the Guardian’s reporting, and calls the fourth “an acceptable translation”. One of them involves introducing the word “fire” in describing late 2023 protests against Elbit, an Israeli weapons manufacturer. Two of the three charges in the criminal complaint against Chambers are related to the protests – where nothing was set on fire.
Other changes involved adding the Spanish words for “violent” and “detonate” when the original English text did not have them.
According to documents seen by the Guardian, the Trump administration notified Spain of the alterations on 12 November, the day before a hearing involving Chambers’s attorneys, the three judges and the prosecutor – but the notification only reached all parties on Tuesday.
The unusual chain of events caps off weeks of unsuccessful efforts by the defense team to get the high court to pay attention to the issue and order a new translation.
The Guardian’s reporting on the issue was based in part on a 3 November motion that Chambers’s attorneys filed with the court, identifying a dozen alterations to the original criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request.
However, the judges responded to the motion by saying “the translation offered by the requesting country’s authorities should be considered trustworthy” and that no action was required, according to Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team.
Then, during the hearing, the judges denied the defense team’s request to admit into evidence a 345-page report prepared by a certified Spanish translator identifying what were now 30 “incriminating changes” the US had made to a machine-made translation.
The judges also denied the attorneys’ request to present the translator as a witness in the hearing. Meanwhile, the prosecutor dismissed the issue dismissively, referring to “supposed translation errors”.
These and other prejudicial notions with specific legal implications form part of the prosecutor’s report on the case, which in turn influences the judges deciding on the extradition request, Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian.
“I think the fact that the US recognizes what it has done shows that they were trying to fool the judges,” said Martínez. “This should touch the pride of the Spanish justice system.”
Spanish law and the extradition treaty between the US and Spain require extradition requests to be translated into Spanish by the requesting country. Martínez notes in the defense team’s motion filed on Tuesday that a 2003 extradition request from Turkey wound up being denied due to errors in translation – after defense attorneys took the case to Spain’s constitutional court, alleging violations of due process.
“We might wind up doing the same,” Martínez said.
A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers is also heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Enterprises. He sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023 and has been funding an estimated 100 progressive and humanitarian projects in 20 countries since then.
Chambers’s views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media, including his public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
If the court’s decision on the US request is affirmative, Spain’s council of ministers can reverse the outcome. This means Chambers’s extradition may be among the last decisions made under Pedro Sánchez, the socialist prime minister, before national elections on 29 November.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mt.title: New York City’s Transit System Has the State’s Greatest ‘Underground Museum.’ Here’s Why It’s Worth Visiting.
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mt.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mt.text:
New York has the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum, the Frick Collection, and countless other great art institutions. Yet one of the city’s most well-rounded ones is an “underground museum” that can be found largely in the subway, with certain pieces also visible at Metro-North and Long Island Rail Road train stops.
That was the terminology used by Tina Vaz, director of the MTA’s Arts & Design program, in a talk held this past Friday at the PMC Studio as part of Art Week NYC, a festival of programming put on across the city by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.
“This is a dynamic transit environment, but even in all of the noise and movement and motion, the works get through and people connect with them,” Vaz said. She cited a survey in which 80 percent of respondents said they noticed the artworks at MTA, Metro-North, and LIRR stops, which have been done by artists ranging from William Wegman to Yayoi Kusama. That people were aware of these works, Vaz said, is “double proof of concept.”
Vaz’s latest commissions are by artists Ivan Forde, Trevor Paglen, and Howardena Pindell, who are respectively in the process of making new works for the Broadway Junction subway stop and the Metro-North’s Southeast and Botanical Garden stops. Forde and Pindell joined Vaz on Friday to discuss their commissions.
Forde’s, a mosaic called Bedtime Story for Brownsville: The Fish Who Carried the Moon (2026), grew out of his sketches and poetry. In his mosaic, the Moon is what he called a “main character.” “The Moon has lost her way, and she fell into the sea,” he said. “These fish, they come and they help her, and they guide her back to the sky … It’s really thinking about structures of epic poetry.”
Pindell is making a glass installation based on photographs she took over the course of a day at the New York Botanical Garden. “Once they were developed, I cut them into sections and laid them out along part of the station wall,” she said. “Then, there were arrows put in.” Through the installation, “you are seeing the inside of the garden, both the domed building as well as along the paths.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Estamos ainda na ponta do iceberg’, diz cientista política sobre um ano do escândalo do Banco Master
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Gabriela Carvalho
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Há exatamente um ano, o Caso Master tinha início com a liquidação do banco decretada pelo Banco Central, arrastando autoridades de diversas esferas em um esquema que gerou prejuízos de mais de R$ 76 bilhões no sistema financeiro do país. Um dia antes, em 17 de novembro, o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro foi preso em Guarulhos quando tentava deixar o país em um jatinho particular.
Nesta quarta-feira (18), a Polícia Federal (PF) entregou ao presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Edson Fachin, documentos com menções a ministros da Corte e a parentes deles no caso Banco Master. Os documentos foram refeitos por determinação do comando da PF, depois do afastamento dos delegados que coordenavam as investigações e preparavam a versão original.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a cientista política Rosemary Segurado considera “estranha” a determinação da revisão de um relatório que já havia sido feito. “Parece que os delegados da PF que estavam realizando essa investigação tinham colocado foco na participação de um ministro do STF nas relações com Vorcaro. Contudo, nos últimos meses, descobrimos que outros ministros supostamente tiveram relação com Vorcaro”, afirma. “Resta saber se esse relatório vai trazer de fato todos esses supostos envolvimentos”, pontua.
Segurado pondera que, ao longo deste ano, muitas informações tiveram que ser levantadas e dá destaque para o comportamento do banqueiro, que, em muitos momentos, tentou dominar a narrativa ao ameaçar delações, que, no entanto, não apresentaram novas informações. “Nas mensagens do celular dele havia informações mais relevantes”, aponta.
Na avaliação da cientista política, o Caso Master pode ter ainda informações não reveladas. “É um escândalo que envolve valores muito altos e muita gente. Era preciso corromper muitas autoridades para fazer esse acúmulo de recursos. Então, é difícil dizer isso, mas acho que estamos ainda na ponta do iceberg”, conclui.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/educatio.title: Mouvement lycéen : avec plus de 3 000 conseils de discipline en deux mois, le gouvernement sort un nouvel outil répressif de sa manche
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/educatio.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/educatio.text:
Le gouvernement met en œuvre tous les outils répressifs à sa disposition pour intimider les lycéens en lutte. Aux violences policières, aux fichages et aux gardes à vue s’ajoutent déjà 3 000 sanctions disciplinaires.
Puisque la matraque, les lacrimo, les inculpations et les interdictions de manifester ne suffisent pas, le ministère de l’Éducation a sorti de son arsenal une autre arme pour faire taire les lycéens. Entre septembre et le 1er novembre, environ 3 000 d’entre eux sont passés en conseil de discipline pour leur implication dans le mouvement, a indiqué le ministre Édouard Geffray sur RMC le 18 novembre.
À Paris par exemple, une « quinzaine d’élèves » ont ainsi été exclus définitivement de leur établissement, sanction disciplinaire la plus élevée, et ont été « rescolarisés » dans un autre établissement de la capitale.
Un courrier pour « renforcer et systématiser les sanctions disciplinaires »
Ce recours aux sanctions administratives est une décision politique. Dans un télégramme envoyé le 13 novembre, le gouvernement a demandé aux recteurs de renforcer et de systématiser les sanctions disciplinaires à l’encontre des élèves et des personnels de l’Éducation nationale participant à des blocages de lycées.
Parmi les actes visés par ces procédures, figurent les appels « à la violence, dégradation des biens, blocage de l’accès à des espaces intérieurs de l’établissement, violence physique ou verbale envers des personnels, etc. », selon l’AFP qui a consulté ce texte.
Concernant les personnels de l’Éducation nationale, il y a une « quinzaine de procédures disciplinaires ouvertes », a dénombré Édouard Geffray. Elles visent « des agents » qu’il accuse d’avoir « complètement erré par rapport au devoir de neutralité ».
À cette orgie de sanctions disciplinaires s’ajoutent « plus de 1 000 plaintes » pénales déposées pour des « violences », a précisé le ministre, estimant ensuite devant les sénateurs à 266 le nombre de personnels de l’Éducation nationale blessés depuis le début du mouvement.
« Volonté de réprimer » ce « mouvement de masse »
« Je ne suis pas neutre parce qu’il y a une accélération de l’autoritarisme », a réagi auprès de l’AFP Virginie Prégny, professeure à Paris et élue CGT Educ’action, lors d’un rassemblement intersyndical « contre la répression dans l’Éducation nationale » organisé le même jour devant la Sorbonne.
Elle a accompagné à un « entretien préalable à sanction » une surveillante (AED), accusée d’avoir eu « l’air de pousser les élèves à bloquer », « sans aucun fait matériel », a-t-elle déploré, craignant que le contrat de cet agent ne soit pas renouvelé. « Les conseils de discipline tendent les choses », a déploré François, professeur à Paris et militant FO, estimant qu’il y a une « volonté de réprimer » ce « mouvement de masse » par les gardes à vue et les sanctions disciplinaires.
Le 12 novembre déjà, la présidente de la région île de France, la LR Valérie Pécresse, avait annoncé la suspension de plusieurs aides facultatives aux lycéens exclus de leur établissement pour violences ou dégradations. À défaut de mettre enfin les moyens nécessaires dans la rénovation des lycées, elle a également décidé de proposer à des proviseurs d’installer des caméras de surveillance à l’intérieur de leurs établissements.
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://taz.de/Fiktionalisierte-Doku-Wie.title: Film „Wiener Blues“: So ein Menschenleben währt halt nicht ewig
https://taz.de/Fiktionalisierte-Doku-Wie.author: Katharina Böhm​
https://taz.de/Fiktionalisierte-Doku-Wie.text:
Film „Wiener Blues“: So ein Menschenleben währt halt nicht ewig
Der Film „Wiener Blues – The Loneliest Man in Town“ von Tizza Covi und Rainer Frimmel porträtiert den Musiker Al Cook. Der spendet Wärme in der kalten Jahreszeit.
Mit einwandfreier Frisur und einem Weihnachtsbaum im Gepäck betritt Alois Koch die Szenerie, ein Wohnhaus im 3. Wiener Bezirk. Hier wurde der später als „Al Cook“ österreichweit bekannte Blues-Musiker 1945 geboren, hier ist er nie weggezogen, und seine Wohnung im ersten Stock macht den Anschein, als läge das 21. Jahrhundert noch in ferner Zukunft.
Die Stufen ins Untergeschoss nimmt Cook eine Spur leichter. Sie führen zum Raum, der alles beherbergt, was sein Leben bis heute erfüllt. Schrankwände voller Vinyl und CDs, Elvis-Devotionalien, an den Wänden Porträts der Delta-Blues-Legende Robert Johnson und von seiner geliebten Sylvia. Anders als Al sind sie alle schon tot.
Behutsam geht er einen Stapel Platten durch: Ma Rainey, Son House, Wynonie Harris, Robert Johnson und Lonnie Johnson, dessen Stimme die Stille umgehend füllen wird: „So tired of sighin’, so tired of cryin’, I’m so tired of livin’ all alone“. Vielleicht fühlt Al den Song jetzt noch etwas mehr als früher, jedenfalls richtet er den Blick bald gen Himmel, so gut das eben geht in einem fensterlosen Kellerraum. Er ist der letzte verbliebene Mieter in diesem Haus.
Der Film
„Wiener Blues – The Loneliest Man in Town“. Regie: Tizza Covi, Rainer Frimmel. Mit Alois Koch, Brigitte Meduna u. a. Österreich 2026, 86 Min.
„Wiener Blues“ reichen ein paar Minuten und man ist voll eingestimmt auf die Welt des Al Cook. Welcher Generation man sich selbst auch zurechnet, man möchte diese Zimmer auf knarzenden Dielen durchschreiten, alles darin in Ruhe betrachten, mit der gleichen Vorsicht behandeln, wie dieser Mann es tut. Und fragt sich doch etwas ratlos, was darauf noch folgen mag.
Stromausfall an Heiligabend
Das Wunderbare, das Tizza Covi und Rainer Frimmel mit ihrem achten Film, „Wiener Blues – The Loneliest Man in Town“, gelingt: Sie verbinden Wehmut und Melancholie so nonchalant mit einer wohldosierten Portion Lebensmut, dass man die Erzählung über Al Cook beschwingter verlässt, als man hineingegangen ist. Dabei zeigt die fiktionalisierte Cook-Dokumentation einen stoischen Mann. Einen, der seine Haltung aber so entwaffnend vertritt, dass man sich möglichst oft ein Beispiel daran nehmen will.
Als an Heiligabend der Strom ausfällt, spielt Al die Gitarre kurzerhand selbst. Als bald darauf zwei windige Typen an seine Tür klopfen und ihm in breitem Wienerisch nahelegen, auszuziehen, bevor der neue Eigentümer das Haus abreißt, der Herr würde sich das natürlich bezahlen lassen, belässt Cook es erst mal bei verhaltenem Schnauben. Im Unterschied zu den sonstigen Rahmenbedingungen ist der Handlungsstrang um seine prekäre Wohnsituation fiktiv, wenn auch realistisch.
Als gesichert gilt, dass er ein Mann seiner Zeit ist, wie man ihm nicht mehr oft begegnet. Al Cooks Welt ist nicht nur die des Blues. Auch Butterbrote auf Porzellantellern, die Gelben Seiten, seidene Morgenmäntel und eines Elvis-Fans würdige Mengen an Haarspray haben darin Platz. Cook lebt allein, aber kultivierter, als moderne Menschen vor Publikum es gern von sich behaupten. Dieser Typ trägt das glitzernde Nadelstreifensakko am Weihnachtsabend einfach für sich.
Aktionismus oder gar Kämpfertum gehen ihm ab
Er hat zudem ein Alter erreicht, in dem man bestenfalls begriffen hat, dass so ein Menschenleben nicht ewig währt. Irgendwann schlägt Cook das angebotene Geld nicht mehr aus. Aktionismus oder gar Kämpfertum scheinen ihm völlig abzugehen. Ehrlich gesagt: Es ist entlastend. Die realen Probleme um Wohnraum in den Großstädten dieser Welt werden so ausnahmsweise mal denen überlassen, die sich hoffentlich wählen lassen, um sie zu lösen. Und: Covi und Frimmel bringen so Dynamik in die Geschichte. Auf dem leicht gebogenen Rückgrat ihres Protagonisten kann der Film unerwarteten Ufern entgegengehen.
Allein das Wiedersehen mit Als Ex-Freundin Brigitte ist die Sache wert. Ihre gemeinsame Zeit liegt gut ein halbes Leben zurück, und weil man die eigenen Befindlichkeiten dank näherrückendem Ende nicht mehr so lächerlich ernst nimmt, fallen ihre Begegnungen umso geradliniger aus.
Offene Fragen werden endlich gestellt: „Jetzt sog’ einmal, warum hast du mich damals einfach so mir nichts, dir nichts sitzen lassen?“, und mit Ideen zur Beziehungsgestaltung wird nicht lange hinterm Berg gehalten: „Deshalb hob’ i dir vorschlagen wollen, dass …“ Als virtuoser Flirt gehen solche Dialoge eher nicht durch. Sie sind rührend und von entwaffnender Ehrlichkeit.
Empfohlener externer Inhalt
Wir würden Ihnen hier gerne einen externen Inhalt zeigen. Sie entscheiden, ob Sie dieses Element auch sehen wollen:
Trailer „Wiener Blues“
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung
Anstatt ihren Freund Cook ungebremst drauflos erzählen zu lassen, hat Covi ihm ein grobes Drehbuch vorgelegt und ihn die Dialoge dann improvisieren lassen. Der Film entwickelt Komik, ohne sich dafür spürbar anstrengen zu müssen. Alles scheint so, als hätte auch das Regieduo die Ruhe gepachtet (wohinter meist echtes Können steckt).
Obwohl ihr Protagonist gegen Ende des Films kaum anders wirkt als zu Beginn, spürt man die wachsende Beinfreiheit, die in seinen Alltag Einzug hält. Es zieht Al ins Reisebüro oder zum Herrenausstatter, und er lässt los, etwa wenn er Fremden begegnet, um ihnen seine Platten, altes Equipment oder Möbel zu überlassen. Belege eines Lebens, das den Blick wieder nach vorne richtet.
Ob sein Weg den „Karl May des Blues“, wie Cook, der noch nie in den USA war, tatsächlich genannt wird, doch noch ins Mississippidelta führen wird, gerät darüber fast zur Nebensache. In seinem Buch „Mystery Train“ zitiert Musikjournalist Greil Marcus seinen Kollegen Stanley Booth damit, dass Können und Kompetenz im Blues eine Notwendigkeit seien. Die wahre Stärke des Bluesmusikers aber läge darin, dass er sein Leben akzeptiere, ein Leben, für das er nur zum Teil selbst verantwortlich ist. Möglich, dass Al Cook seinen Idolen in Wien doch näher gekommen ist als gedacht.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen
