https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Charlotte Higgins
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world.
At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in some of his religious paintings, including the Ghent altarpiece, these are the sum total of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.
In a manner profoundly different from Ryman’s works, Van Eyck’s portraits pull you from our world into his. The precision of his physiognomies is dizzying. In his portrait of his wife, Margaret, recently conserved and on loan from Bruges, she regards you with a steady gaze, her lips firm and decisive. Between her cheek and ear is a blemish, a slight discolouring of the skin; her left eyebrow is bisected by a scar. Her headdress contains seven layers of frothing lace that you want to pinch between your thumb and finger. What must it have been like, to look back at this vision of yourself, in a world in which mirrors were luxury items (and mostly convex, like the one that famously hangs at the back of the Arnolfini portrait)?
We know it’s her, because a very detailed inscription in the painter’s hand on the original frame tells us that “my husband Jan completed me on 15 June 1439” and that “my age is 33 years”. By some stroke of painterly enchantment, is it Margaret herself addressing us? Or is the “me” the painting – a mere arrangement of oil paint on a panel of Baltic oak? The inscription concludes with the words “as I can” – Van Eyck’s motto, a phrase that hovers between extreme modesty and great boastfulness.
All the portraits have something of this uncanny hyper-realistic quality. The pockmark on the slightly shiny, reddish young skin. The lines around the eyes and crinkled cheeks of the old scholar in his red robe, and his ear, purplish with age. The scar between the eyes of the stubbled Baudouin de Lannoy, who worked alongside Van Eyck at the court of Philip the Good, the Burgundian ruler of the Low Countries. The individual hairs of a fur collar as they brush the skin of the neck; the intricate whorls of an ear. You feel that if these people reached out their beringed fingers and tugged you through the frame, you could walk about with them, in the streets of Ghent or Bruges of the 1430s.
Perhaps the most arresting of these faces is the portrait of Jan de Leeuw, who, like Margaret, gazes straight at the viewer. He has such a modern-seeming face that it’s hard to shake the impression that he might have sat beside you on the morning commute. Like Margaret, he has his original frame, around which Van Eyck has painted words that translate as: “Jan de Leeuw who, on Saint Ursula’s day, opened his eyes for the first time, 1401. Jan Van Eyck has counterfeited me. It can be seen when he began 1436.” Beautiful precision, all the more satisfying because the Van Leeuw in question can be found in Bruges’ city archives: from a family of goldsmiths, he was himself the inspector of the goldsmiths’ guild at the time of the portrait. Everything checks out: he’s holding a gold ring.
Except that it doesn’t. Like all the works in the exhibition, its apparent “truthfulness” turns out to be a trap, its mirror-like reality a game of illusion and deceit. “He counterfeited me” – the word is “gheconterfeit” – is such a strange word to use, especially of a man who assessed the quality of gold. In its 15th-century context, it was an ambiguous word, says show’s co-curator Nicholas Flory, also “used in documents to describe a true likeness or reliable copy of a real thing”.
But Van Eyck is also deeply unreliable. The painted words are a trompe l’oeil, convincing you they are inscribed in brass. The man’s name, which means “lion”, actually appears as a cute pictogram, as a little joke. To add to the confounding, certain letters of the inscription are made to look as if they are standing out in relief. If you take these and treat them as Roman numerals, they add up to the dates crucial for the painting: 1401 and 1436. In other words, the portrait, which at first seduces with its “reality”, turns out on second glance to be a highly artificial, self-conscious construct. The paint counterfeits metal for its goldsmith sitter, and sets puzzles for the viewer. The ring De Leeuw is holding is so terribly real – and also, so desperately fake.
The Arnolfini portrait is another example of apparent clarity melting swiftly away to complete bafflement. It is one of the best known works in the National Gallery, so familiar to British art lovers that it is possible to forget how strange it is. For centuries, this image of a man taking hold of a woman’s hand was known as the “Arnolfini marriage”, because it was assumed to commemorate an actual wedding ceremony. In the 1930s, Erwin Panofsky posited that every item in the busy domestic interior (the oranges, the wooden overshoes, the mirror, the dog, the burning candle and the guttering candle in the beautifully painted chandelier) was weighted with matrimonial symbolism.
But in truth, no one even knows for sure whether it represents members of the mercantile Arnolfini family (the identification was made based on 16th-century inventories in which the picture said to portray “Hernoul le fin” or “Arnoult Fin”, which were thought to be corruptions of the name Arnolfini). And more recently, many critics have pulled back to accept a more straightforwardly materialist interpretation of the scene: the oranges, the ridiculously voluminous green dress, the fine furnishings, are all markers of status, rather than symbolic as such.
As for the inscription – it reads: “Johannes de eyck fuit hic [was here] 1434”. Again, it seems so clear – but where on earth is “here”? Does it mean Van Eyck was witness to some actual event that he depicted? Or that he painted himself as one of those figures dimly visible in the convex mirror? Or that the main figure is actually a self-portrait, and that this pale man with the large hat and flared nostrils – also the subject of a second portrait in the show – is Van Eyck himself? The inscription breaks the fourth wall: it seems to be hovering on the picture plane itself. So is “here” the metaphysical “here” of the artist’s imagination?
There is one certain self-portrait of Van Eyck, and that, characteristically, is another trick. It is not in this exhibition, but rather in a religious work in the Groeningemuseum in Bruges, the Virgin and Child With Canon Joris Van der Paele. Van Eyck hid in his painting in a tiny image of himself – identifiable by his paintbrush – reflected in the metal shield of Saint George. The ageing canon has removed his spectacles, perhaps the better to appreciate the supernatural vision of the Virgin and child.
The National Gallery’s show opens with a work from its own collection that is frequently regarded as a self-portrait. The realist details are bewitching, intimate: the bloodshot red eyes, the fine lines around them, the stubbled cheeks, the exuberantly painted red hat. On its original frame is painted a signature (“Jan van Eyck made me on 21 October 1433”) along with the motto “as I can” – the position of which, where one would often find the name of the sitter, helps build the case that the work depicts the painter himself. Here, the writing appears to be deeply incised into the surface, playfully implying that the frame is of solid gold, rather than the gilt that it really is.
The more you crane and gaze at these paintings, admiring the wrinkles and the spots and the all-too human flesh, the more you trip up on Van Eyck’s tricksiness. The slippage between being fooled by the illusion and recognising that you are being fooled is part of the pleasure. The more you look, the more you feel you’re having a conversation with the painter – and that he is having the last laugh.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
In a new Al Jazeera Originals film directed by Awad Joumaa, Israeli soldiers describe the psychological toll of the genocide in Gaza, yet many express no remorse.
Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and graphic descriptions of combat.
If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, support is available through international crisis helplines.
“I think our army is the most moral army in the world.”
Itay Sagi, a reservist in the Maglan unit, describes killing Hamas fighters inside Israel after October 7, 2023.
“I didn’t choose to kill people. I had to,” he says.
His grief is for his friends. Sagi wants to go back and fight. He does not mention the Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Boris Shtonda, who served with an Israeli special forces unit, lost a leg when an explosive device detonated inside a building in Gaza in November 2023, killing four of his friends.
“We lost our friends, we lost our families, we lost everything,” he says.
The Israeli soldiers in the film “Gaza Syndrome” speak of nightmares, panic, addiction and Israelis who died by suicide. They speak, too, of wanting to return to fight. In hours of testimony, the Palestinians of Gaza are almost entirely absent.
The overwhelming weight of Israel’s war has fallen on Palestinians in Gaza: their children, homes and hospitals. Israeli forces have killed at least 74,700 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, according to Al Jazeera reporting. In September 2025, an independent UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed genocide in Gaza. The soldiers in this film are part of those forces.
Guy Zaken, a military bulldozer driver, told an Israeli parliamentary committee that soldiers had to “run over “‘terrorists’, dead and alive, in the hundreds”. His co-driver, Eliran Mizrahi, spent 186 days in Gaza demolishing homes and died by suicide two days before he was due to return. “He got out of Gaza, but Gaza did not get out of him,” his mother told CNN.
The question is not whether the Israeli soldiers’ psychological injuries are real. It is what psychological injury means when it is joined to denial, impunity and the absence of remorse.
Psychological crisis
In The Wretched of the Earth, the mid-20th century psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon observed that colonial violence inflicts severe psychiatric trauma on both the colonised and the perpetrators. When soldiers carry out systematic destruction and violence, the psychological toll cannot be separated from the political structure that enables and ignores it.
An Al Jazeera Investigative Unit examination of more than 2,500 Israeli soldiers’ social media accounts documented wanton destruction, abuse of detainees, and the use of Palestinian civilians as human shields.
The scale of the psychological crisis is growing. Nearly 30,000 Israeli soldiers and security personnel wounded since October 7 have entered the Defence Ministry’s rehabilitation system, the ministry said in October.
About 63 percent have psychological injuries, with thousands formally diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress reactions following prolonged combat exposure. The Israeli army says 22 soldiers died by suicide in 2025, one more than in 2024, up from 17 in 2023. An Israeli parliament Research and Information Center report recorded 279 suicide attempts between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 percent of the deaths by suicide in 2024.
Mohanad Mustafa, a scholar of Israeli society, told Al Jazeera Israel faces “a psychological crisis among thousands of soldiers, but no moral crisis”.
He says many soldiers feel no remorse for violations of international law. “This indicates a very significant moral decline in Israeli society.”
Israel’s public culture has helped make that denial possible. Oren Ziv, an Israeli journalist with +972 Magazine, says soldiers he interviewed described “an atmosphere of revenge, that everything is allowed”. They could shoot if they saw movement, he says, or if they were bored, and “nobody will investigate it”.
Daniel Bar-Tal, a political psychologist, says soldiers in Gaza still confront Palestinian suffering “to some extent”, even when they deny it or refuse to see it.
This suppressed awareness, he said, creates a quiet, internal fracture, a psychological burden that deepens precisely because the trauma cannot be fully acknowledged or resolved without confronting the suffering of those they harmed.
Ashira Darwish, a Palestinian trauma therapist and survivor of severe trauma and torture who created Active Meditation to heal from full-body paralysis, believes Israeli soldiers can enter Gaza, shoot children and burn homes only by suppressing their own humanity. She and other trauma experts emphasise that returning reservists undergo a severe psychological transition when re-entering civilian life after engaging in continuous combat.
“Someone who can exterminate an entire people while sitting there laughing will carry a psychological impact.”
Darwish describes reservists returning from Gaza to a hospital, office or school within a week or two. She warns of anger, substance addiction, domestic conflict, and sudden outbursts of violence as untreated combat trauma manifests in everyday interactions. “Where are they supposed to go with everything they have done?”
Israel’s Observatory on Femicide recorded 34 femicides in 2025, a 48 percent rise from 23 in 2024. Firearms were the most common weapon for the first time. Women’s groups warned early in the war that combat trauma and expanded access to guns could heighten the risk of domestic violence. There is no official data proving that returning soldiers caused the rise, and the Observatory found no link between licenced guns and femicide. The warning is about a society saturated with weapons, fear and impunity, not a claim that every soldier becomes violent at home.
Impunity
In Qusra, a Palestinian village south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the film finds the other end of that impunity. Abdul Azim al-Wadi, a former head of the village council, says Israeli settlers killed his brother Ibrahim and nephew Ahmad, shot two of his sons and burned his son’s and daughter’s homes.
“The occupation army is the continuation of the settlers’ attacks,” he says. “They play the role together.”
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.
The same impunity is visible in Gaza. In NAZA, a documentary built on anonymous testimony from Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, sources describe civilian deaths factored into military decisions and targets watched inside their homes. The Israeli army called NAZA a “manipulative depiction of reality”.
In March, Israel dropped charges against five soldiers accused of sexually abusing a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention facility.
A few do not accept the orders to serve in the army. Itamar Greenberg chose military prison over conscription. Iddo Elam said: “I do not want to hold a weapon towards innocent people.”
Their refusal matters because it shows the violence is not inevitable, and neither is the story Israel tells about it.
Bar-Tal offers his country a choice: “Cut the violence or cut the narrative.”
So far, it has chosen neither.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: IA : Anthropic, l’entrée en Bourse de tous les dangers
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Pierric Marissal
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
Entre les soubresauts financiers autour de l’IA générative et les déboires du géant Nvidia qui font craindre un effondrement des valeurs tech, l’entreprise créatrice de Claude, dont le modèle économique repose sur un pari financier, se lance en Bourse le 19 novembre sous le regard effrayé des spéculateurs du monde entier.
Anthropic, créateur de l’IA générative Claude, prépare son entrée en Bourse ce jeudi. Pourtant, le contexte n’est pas vraiment favorable. En l’espace de deux semaines, des milliards de dollars de capitalisation ont fondu au Nasdaq, le marché où sont cotées les entreprises de la tech états-unienne qu’entend rejoindre Anthropic.
Alors le groupe a revu ses ambitions à la baisse. Il espérait peser 2 000 milliards de dollars de capitalisation boursière et vise désormais 1 500 milliards de valorisation. En vendant 956 millions d’actions (plus que les 825 millions initialement prévues), à 83 dollars le titre, cela permet néanmoins à l’entreprise de récupérer 79,3 milliards de dollars.
Si l’entreprise se lance en Bourse malgré ce contexte à haut risque, c’est que, sur les neuf premiers mois de 2026, la perte nette d’Anthropic s’élève à 104 milliards de dollars. Pour rentrer au Nasdaq, le créateur de Claude a dû publier auprès de la SEC, le gendarme de la Bourse états-unien, un long document économique mettant fin, comme ce fut le cas pour SpaceX cet été, à l’opacité financière entourant l’entreprise.
Un modèle économique toujours pas viable
Cette perte colossale (à hauteur de plus de 70 milliards) est principalement liée à l’inscription dans le bilan comptable d’obligations (donc de la dette) convertibles, souscrites notamment auprès d’Amazon. Cela veut dire qu’une fois payés les intérêts, l’entreprise pourra, selon ses moyens, soit rembourser l’emprunt, soit transformer cette dette en actions. Alors évidemment, Anthropic met plutôt en avant la croissance impressionnante de son chiffre d’affaires, multiplié par 12 en un an. Mais celui-ci augmente plus lentement que ses dépenses en puissance de calcul.

https://taz.de/Stoerungen-bei-Microsoft/.title: Störungen bei Microsoft: Hang zum Bürokratismus, garniert mit einer Portion Schiss
https://taz.de/Stoerungen-bei-Microsoft/.author: Steffen Grimberg
https://taz.de/Stoerungen-bei-Microsoft/.text:
Störungen bei Microsoft: Hang zum Bürokratismus, garniert mit einer Portion Schiss
Die Abhängigkeit vieler systemrelevanter Institutionen von Microsoft & Co ist verheerend. Können die Öffentlich-Rechtlichen überhaupt noch ohne?
D as gute alte Telefon hat als Kommunikationsmittel im Kontakt mit den Pressestellen öffentlich-rechtlicher Sender ja schon länger ausgedient. Wer doch noch anruft, kann mit einem freundlichen „Schicken Sie uns das bitte per Mail“ rechnen. Das ist Hang zum Bürokratismus, garniert mit einer guten Portion Schiss. Wie das zu den laufenden Reformen im ÖRR passt, wo alles so agil und modern werden soll, weiß nur der Nah-und.
Welche Schmach muss es da letzte Woche für die Pressestelle des WDR gewesen sein, über den dpa-Meldungsverbreitungsdienst ots melden zu müssen, dass „aufgrund der weltweiten Störungen bei Microsoft die WDR-Kommunikation derzeit nicht per E-Mail erreichbar“ sei. Ja, mehr noch, man möge gefälligst anrufen!
Die telefonäre Posse ist dabei nur die Spitze eines Eisbergs. Denn die Abhängigkeit vieler „systemrelevanter Institutionen“ von Microsoft & Co ist immens. Oder konkreter formuliert, systemrelevant. Und das geht weit über Mailprogramme und Telefondienste hinaus. (Dieser Text entsteht übrigens mit Microsoft Word, wird aber nicht über Outlook verschickt und ich mache heute auch keine Teamsschalte mit der Mitbewohnerin!)
Wenn das System dann mal relevant hustet, wie Ende vergangener Woche bei Microsoft, steht vieles still. Oder wie der ARD-Vorsitzende Florian Hager Anfang des Jahres in einem Interview auf die Frage: „Das heißt, wenn Microsoft den Stecker zieht, ist die ARD weiter arbeitsfähig?“, zugab: „Es würde natürlich dazu führen, dass Dinge anders und erheblich langsamer laufen. Aber wir sind mit Microsoft in Verhandlungen über Themen wie Datenhoheit.“
Die Abhängigkeit von US-Konzernen
Tja, was nützt halt ein Vertrag mit Service Level Agreement von 99,9 Prozent, wenn es eben nur eine Zusicherung in die hohle Hand ist? Der Grad der Abhängigkeit, der nirgends wirklich transparent gemacht wird, ist vermutlich riesig. Immerhin ist die Frage mittlerweile angekommen, warum wir uns in Deutschland so von den US-Konzernen und ihrer im Wortsinn kritischen Infrastruktur abhängig machen und diese auch noch fürstlich dafür bezahlen.
„Also für mich ist das keine Frage, für mich ist das fahrlässig. Digitale Erneuerung und digitale Souveränität, alles für den schmalen Beitragstaler“, sagt die Mitbewohnerin.
Denn die Gefahr ist ja nicht nur, dass beim nächsten Ausfall der WDR wieder ans Telefon gehen muss, sondern dass durch gezielte Manipulation der weltumspannenden Dienstleistungstrusts systemrelevante Einrichtungen von Krankenhäusern über den ÖRR bis zu Supermarktkühlschränken systematisch lahmgelegt werden.
Nach dem guten alten Motto des passiven Widerstands der Arbeiter*innenbewegung gegen die Besetzung des Ruhrgebiets vor gut 100 Jahren: „Alle Räder stehen still, wenn Dein starker Arm es will!“ Dagegen ist jetzt aktiver Widerstand im Sinne von Umsatteln der heutigen Verantwortlichen nötig. Nicht nur, aber gerade auch bei den Öffentlich-Rechtlichen und allen anderen Medien, deren Teams am Microsoft-Tropf hängen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Charting the world’s biggest IPOs as Anthropic overtakes SpaceX
The AI company behind Claude raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering ever, at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, despite fears that AI could threaten humanity, protests over energy-hungry data centres and concerns about an AI investment bubble.
Five years ago, Anthropic raised $124m from its first investors. On Wednesday, it priced its shares at $83 each, valuing the company at roughly $1.5 trillion and making it the world’s 12th-biggest company, just behind Tesla. Its shares begin trading on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.
Demand far outstripped expectations. Investors reportedly sought six times as many shares as were available, and Anthropic sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million it had planned, at a price above its expected range of $70 to $78.
What is an IPO?
An initial public offering (IPO) is the process by which a private company sells shares to the public for the first time by listing on a stock exchange. The company raises money by issuing new shares, and existing owners, such as founders and early investors, can sell some of theirs.
To prepare, the company hires investment banks to value it and run the sale. The banks write a prospectus explaining its business, finances and risks.
Executives and bankers then pitch the shares to big investors to gauge demand before setting the price. Early investors are usually barred from selling for several months after the listing.
How much is Anthropic worth?
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. It develops AI models under its Claude brand, making most of its money by selling businesses access.
Its growth has been extraordinary. In May 2026, Anthropic raised $65bn from private investors at a valuation of $965bn. Its IPO price values the company about 55 percent higher.
Anthropic confidentially filed for an IPO in June and made its registration statement public on October 26.
Its revenue reached $33.2bn in the first nine months of 2026, including $17bn in the third quarter. That represents rapid growth from the previous year, although the company continues to spend heavily on computing infrastructure.
Its November prospectus also reported a net loss of $104bn over the first nine months of the year, largely driven by non-cash accounting adjustments, and disclosed nearly $901bn in computing and infrastructure commitments.
Biggest IPOs in history
Anthropic overtook SpaceX, which raised $75bn in June by selling shares at $135 each, valuing Elon Musk’s rocket, satellite and AI company at $1.75 trillion. SpaceX’s total rose to $85.7bn after it sold extra shares following its listing.
In July, South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix raised $26.5bn when it listed on the Nasdaq, the largest US listing ever by a foreign company. It now ranks third.
Saudi Aramco, which held the record before SpaceX, is now fourth. The state-owned oil giant raised $25.6bn on Riyadh’s stock exchange in December 2019, at a valuation of about $1.7 trillion.
The rest of the top 10 are Alibaba (2014), SoftBank (2018), NTT Mobile (1998), Visa (2008), AIA (2010) and Enel (1999).

How Nvidia’s CEO Flirted With Oblivion
A tech titan’s dopey affair with a suspected Chinese agent could upend the economy.
Will the AI boom that currently powers the stock market—and pretty much the whole economy—be brought low by one tech exec’s inability to keep it in his pants? Nervous investors sent Nvidia’s stock skittering downward after hours Wednesday in the wake of reports that the already scandal-infected company CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an executive who reports to him—and that Nvidia’s board was about to send him packing. Huang wound up sparing them the trouble by announcing his resignation Thursday.
This was all, of course, on top of his recent admission that he’d had an affair with a Chinese executive at the tech firm Megaspeed with the same last name who the US government says is a Chinese spy. Many observers thought that Huang would somehow survive the revelation of the Chinese spy affair, but evidently two affairs is one too many to overlook.
A CEO having a fling with a subordinate is an egregious HR nightmare, to be sure, but it was the affair with apparent Chinese Ministry of State Security employee Alice Huang that raised actual geopolitical concerns. Had the Nvidia CEO (knowingly or unknowingly) passed along information to her or lobbied for an easing of restrictions on plans to export chips to China at least in part on her behalf? Was he so gullible that he didn’t realize she was a spy? Or could he have known, and thus committed some light (or possibly heavy) treason?
But the whole Huang fiasco looks like it could be far more than a sex scandal with a side of espionage. Some company critics are suggesting that Nvidia’s “China problem” goes well beyond Huang’s bad spy romance. We know that Nvidia sold some $4.6 billion worth of chips to a Megaspeed subsidiary, ostensibly intended for a Malaysian data center. But Culper Research, a small short-selling shop that produced an explosive report on Nvidia back in May, says that this is just the tip of the iceberg: Culper estimated that at least 20 percent of the company’s compute revenue in the 2026 fiscal year may have come from illicit sales of its most advanced chips to a network of sketchy companies in Southeast Asia that have in some instances diverted the chips to China, contravening the US export ban.
According to Culper, “Numerous experts told us that Nvidia has long possessed the means to detect diversions”—including post-sale technical tests of server IP addresses and latency time, which could prove that the chips were physically in China. The implication is clear: Either Nvidia knew about the diversions and did nothing, or it didn’t even bother to check, almost certainly because company leaders didn’t want to know. (Culper Research acknowledged in its report that it was shorting Nvidia stock, which means that it benefits if it goes down.)
Ed Zitron, a tech muckraker and AI-boom skeptic contends, based on Culper’s research and his own, that “Nvidia is an untrustworthy company inflating its revenues with deals that range from dodgy to outright illegal.”
Culper’s broad-ranging accusations haven’t exactly been at the center of the media coverage of the scandal. A Wednesday New York Times profile of the man behind Culper mentioned them only glancingly, but you can rest assured that reporters at the Times and elsewhere are hard at work trying to corroborate the Culper research—and so are congressional investigators. In other words, as big as the Nvidia scandal is now, it could get a lot bigger.
And of course there’s the not-inconsiderable political angle. President Donald Trump was first informed of Huang’s affair with a spy about a year ago, and was reminded again by Marco Rubio just prior to a trip Trump took to Beijing back in May. Trump was evidently so unbothered by the fact that the CEO running the firm that provides the essential infrastructure for the AI boom, whose most powerful chips are so cutting-edge that it is forbidden to sell them to China, might be compromised by Chinese intelligence that he went ahead and invited Huang on his trip. As the Times put it, in its deadpan prose, “Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market.” (Trump also harbors his own conflict of interest, having brokered a deal for the United States to share between 15 and 25 percent of Nvidia’s revenues derived from China sales.)
Trump continues to insist that he knew nothing of any of this until “not too long ago.” As far as he’s concerned, Huang is “an amazing guy” who, as far as Trump knows, hasn’t “done anything wrong.” He went on to offer the perplexing explanation that Huang “dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” On Sunday, after Huang had publicly confessed to having an affair, Trump assured reporters that the CEO was “an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
It’s unlikely that Huang has even one convincing explanation for his actions. But what Huang did have was a crisis PR firm—run by Risa Heller, who famously also represented former (and greatly disgraced) Democratic Representative Anthony Weiner, and which he hired around the time the Times first raised questions about his association with Alice Huang in an article more than a year ago. Presumably, Huang (Jensen, that is) thought that he was about to be enveloped in a scandal of his own making. The Times article, titled “A Mystery C.E.O. and Billions in Sales: Is China Buying Banned Nvidia Chips?,”not only featured several photos of Huang and Huang, er, networking in Taipei; it also made a pretty convincing case, if an implicit one, that Nvidia should have known that Megaspeed was not exactly on the up-and-up. The article closed with a memorable vignette, noting that when a Times reporter visited the headquarters of Megaspeed’s subsidiary Speedmatrix in a Malaysian mall, “three employees inside did not answer despite repeated knocks. A woman eventually emerged for lunch and identified herself as an administrator. She said she had no contact with her bosses. When asked what the company did, she said, ‘It’s not clear.’ ”
You might have thought that this report, which sketched out many of the basic elements of the scandal that now saturates the financial media, would have been a huge deal at the time. But the world only really stood up and took notice when we learned last week that Huang was literally fucking someone who seems to be a Chinese spy.
But the scandal’s salacious aspects aren’t the key issue here, largely because of who Jensen Huang is. He wasn’t just any CEO, just as Nvidia isn’t just any company. Huang was the de facto “key man” of the second-biggest company in the world by market cap, after Apple. Many tech industry observers regarded him as an indispensable figure in the rolling AI boom, and he apparently concurred, having made no effort to groom a successor. Oops.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
As for the $4.2 trillion company he cofounded, it isn’t just a supplier of the chips that make the AI boom possible; it’s widely considered the “central bank of AI.” Its outsize market valuation has left it deeply entangled in a web of circular finance with companies ranging from tech giants like Meta and OpenAI to smaller companies like the cloud-computing rentier CoreWeave. Nvidia will often invest billions of dollars in companies that in turn buy billions of dollars worth of chips from it. It’s all a bit reminiscent of writer Brandy Jensen’s definition of “modern friendship [as] just sending the same $20 back and forth via venmo, forever.” The Economist, noting that Nvidia pledged more than $70 billion in investments in start-ups over three years and offered $300 billion in financial support to customers, warns that “the more of this boom they finance, the more of any bust they will have to bear.”
And the more of this boom they finance, the more likely that a scandal like the one they now face could trigger an AI market crash that could quickly spread to other stocks and take down the economy itself. As Charlie Warzel of The Atlantic notes, “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation. Huang is too big to fail.” And now he has.
But Nvidia isn’t the only company that is, as Warzel and Matteo Wong put it in an Atlantic essay last year, “load-bearing” for the economy. So are the other giant firms at the top of America’s corporate heap, many of which have become monstrously large in recent years. Concentration of economic power has increased dramatically. At the end of 2015, the top 10 firms in the S&P 500 represented roughly 19 percent of the market cap of the total index, according to RBC Wealth Management; by the end of last year the top 10 represented nearly 41 percent, a record. (My own back-of- the-envelope calculations suggest the number is a few percentage points higher today.)
Meanwhile, the diversity of these top firms has decreased as the AI boom has inflated the top tech firms and pushed older stalwarts like GE and Johnson and Johnson off the list. Currently, after Apple and Nvidia, the next five-largest US companies by market cap are all tech firms, with most of them, including Alphabet (the parent company of Google), Microsoft and Meta, heavily invested in AI—and all are large customers of Nvidia. If Nvidia falls, so will they, and we’ll all suffer the collateral damage. Hey ChatGPT, are we all screwed?

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Michele Goodwin
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Scott Colom’s Historic Victory
The Mississippi Democrat’s win is more than a joyous occasion—it’s redemption.
On Wednesday, Scott Colom was declared the victor in the hotly contested United States Senate race in Mississippi. Colom, a lawyer and district attorney, will become the first Black person from Mississippi to hold a US Senate seat in more than 140 years. Colom’s victory against the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith was declared after close ballot-counting. Upon learning of this, I sat in my office and wept, reflecting on childhood summer visits to Mississippi, where my maternal great-grandfather lacked running water and electricity. He died while I was in law school—never having had running water.
Pundits will point to Colom’s important win as particularly noteworthy for several reasons. For example, in 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked his candidacy to become a federal judge by withholding the “’blue slip’ required under Senate Judiciary Committee practice to advance Colom’s judicial nomination, despite support from fellow Mississippi Republican Sen. Roger Wicker,” reported The Advocate. And in 2024, Donald Trump swept the state, defeating Kamala Harris by almost 23 points—a jump in voter support from his 2020 and 2016 victories in the state. Commentators will also likely frame Colom’s victory as a response to the very real economic hardship Americans are facing given Trump’s disastrous policies. All are true.
However, Colom’s victory means something much more profound and earthshaking—perhaps even greater than the presidential victory of Barack Obama, who failed to receive more than 43 percent of the vote in the state in both of his elections—especially for many Black Americans with a legacy tied to Mississippi. For those of us who share this lineage, Colom’s victory is not only a repudiation of Donald Trump but also of the horrific political and social machines that drove American slavery and Jim Crow. For centuries—not decades—Mississippi was a proud “slave state.” It embraced and profited from the enslavement of Black people and fought hard to keep its status quo.
In its 1861 declaration of secession—“A Declaration of the Immediate Causes which Induce and Justify the Secession of the State of Mississippi from the Federal Union”—state lawmakers affirmed, “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world. Its labor supplies the product which constitutes by far the largest and most important portions of commerce of the earth.” Mississippi referred to enslaved Black people as “products” that were “peculiar to the climate verging on the tropical regions, and by an imperious law of nature, none but the black race can bear exposure to the tropical sun.”
Mississippi saw enslaved Black people as essential to its economy and ways of being. Its declaration of secession points to a degradation in being denied owning people rather than the immorality of human bondage, rape, forced pregnancy and childbearing, and the cruelties of family separation and the whip. Even after the Civil War, in which Mississippi’s losses were high (all of its enlisted Ole Miss students died fighting for the Confederacy), the state refused to ratify the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery and involuntary servitude. In fact, it wasn’t until 2013 that the state did so—148 years later.
Even while it could not block Black people’s newly ratified constitutional freedoms, Mississippi erected barriers nonetheless. It was the first state to enact notorious Black Codes, barring Black people from freely engaging in labor contracting. It passed harmful apprenticeship policies, snatching Black children away from their parents on dubious claims of neglect. These practices condemned Black children to slavery under the guise of apprenticeship to plantation owners. Mississippi lawmakers also imposed fines on Black people who traveled and stood together on public streets, calling this vagrancy.
Despite all of these barriers to equal participation in society, newly freed Black Americans in Mississippi came into office, helping to enact policies that resulted in public education for all and even property rights for married women. That window was closed abruptly when the United States Supreme Court dismantled Reconstruction by upholding segregationist laws and granting its imprimatur to “separate but equal” strategies.
Mississippi welcomed the end of Reconstruction and profited from it with coercive sharecropping practices and convict leasing. Aspects of those legacies linger. For example, it must be noted that Black Americans today represent more than half of Mississippi’s prison population, while representing only 38 percent of the state’s entire population.
The horrors of Mississippi’s Jim Crow–era are hard to turn away from. Featured in award-winning documentaries like Eyes on the Prize, detailing among other things Mississippi’s brazen and violent citizens’ councils that organized against Black voting rights; in films like Mississippi Burning, which narrates the tragic killings of three young civil rights workers—Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner, and James Chaney; in song, Nina Simone’s Mississippi Goddam comes to mind, as well as Billie Holiday’s Strange Fruit, capturing the chilling terror of lynchings; in the testimony of Fannie Lou Hamer at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, when she spoke of being arrested and beaten by law enforcement after attempting to vote—and in the terrifying image of Emmett Till on the cover of Jet magazine after his bloated, beaten, and tortured 14-year-old body was lifted from the Tallahatchie River. His murderers, Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam, were acquitted in barely an hour by an all-white jury. They later confessed in Look magazine.
Colom’s victory must be understood against a complex backdrop, where Black people fled Mississippi during the Great Black Migration to never return given a legacy of cruelty and hate. And one where so many remained like Colom and his forebears, committed to fighting for democracy in a state that they toiled to build and where quite literally, the blood of their ancestors was spilt.
For me, Colom’s victory is a balm or salve on scars carried across generations—on the backs of grandparents and great grandparents. Of my grandmother’s siblings who fled Mississippi, she was the only one who would cross the Mason Dixon line, to drive south to visit family. Sadly, this took courage. Several of her siblings simply could not. My summers in the South, especially the visits to Mississippi, left an indelible mark.
Whether they are residing now in the state or are the offspring of the hundreds of thousands who fled north in the greatest migration, Colom’s win is more than a joyous occasion for the Black Americans who remain connected to Mississippi. It is the closest to redemption that the state and perhaps the United States has come to in modern times.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.title: Hegseth Dodges Impeachment, for Now. And Tom Morello on Fighting for the World You Want
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.text:
Secretary of defense Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment on Tuesday, but his future is anything but secure as an enraged Democratic caucus prepares to take control of both the House and Senate in January.
“Tick, tock! Get ready, asshole, because we’re coming,” Congress member-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., warned Hegseth at a press conference on Wednesday. Ojeda told The Intercept that he planned not only to impeach Hegseth but also to bring criminal charges against him.
On Tuesday, the House declined to move forward with impeachment proceedings introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., which accused Hegseth of multiple “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Massie accused Hegseth of illegally waging war against both Iran and Yemen and of overseeing extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean.
This week on The Intercept Briefing, co-host Jessica Washington speaks with Nick Turse, Intercept senior national security reporter and editor of Tom Dispatch, about Hegseth’s legacy as “secretary of war.”
“Hegseth can spin it any way he likes,” says Turse. “He can use the troops as a shield, claiming that indictments of him are indictments of them. But in the end, he’s got a lot to answer for on his own, and none of it’s because he’s doing a good job.” Turse adds: “It’s because he’s committing high crimes.”
Co-host Jordan Uhl also sits down with musician and guitarist Tom Morello to talk about his new album “Everyone Gets Everything They Want” and his decades-long fight against forever wars and his resistance to fascism.
“My career has basically been rebellion as self-care,” says Morello. “But in this day and age, every act of art is an act of resistance. Every truth spoken is a light in the gathering darkness. And every song sung has the potential to be a trumpet of a bulwark against the rising tide of authoritarianism to help sound the bell for current and future generations to continue to fight for a more just and peaceful and decent planet.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Jessica Washington: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing, I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter for The Intercept.
CNN: Republicans banded together and they killed this effort to impeach Pete Hegseth and largely stayed united. And the final vote here was 211 to 204.
NBC: Republicans uniting to block them from moving forward following Hegseth’s fiery rebuke of the outgoing congressman who introduced them, Thomas Massie.
ABC: The Republicans sticking together have essentially tabled or moved this resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, where it’s expected under Republican control these articles of impeachment will die. Pete Hegseth, for the moment, will not be impeached by the House of Representatives under this effort by Kentucky Republican Congressman Thomas Massie. Not a single Republican colleague joined him. All the Democrats stuck together, but there were not enough.
JW: On Tuesday night U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment as House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky.
Rep. Thomas Massie: We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings. There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective. The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.
JW: That’s Congressman Massie speaking at a press conference about the articles of Impeachment he introduced against the embattled Cabinet Secretary. This is how Hegseth responded:
Pete Hegseth: As for the articles themselves, Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen, every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs. We destroyed terror regime’s capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator into handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job. And it is a job well done.
Joining me now to break it all down is Nick Turse, senior national security and foreign policy reporter for the Intercept and editor of Tom Dispatch.
Nick, welcome back to The Intercept Briefing.
Nick Turse: Thanks for having me on. It’s great to be here.
JW: Before we dive in, I also want to let listeners know we have a special interview with Tom Morello, the musician and original member of Rage Against the Machine.
Tom Morello: My job from day one is to try to make one guitar sound like a riot and to have my music be a contributing factor to social justice movements at home and abroad.
JW: So stay tuned for that conversation
All right, Nick, to start. What’s your reaction to Secretary Hegseth dismissing Massie’s impeachment articles, claiming:
Pete Hegseth: What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.
JW: and that Massie is punishing him for a, “job well done”? What is your response?
NT: To start, it’s laughable. For half an hour at a press conference on the morning of the impeachment vote, Secretary Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight impeachment charges. He repeatedly claimed that the effort to impeach him was just a stunt by one disgruntled congressman.
But, as we came to see, more than 200 members of Congress voted with Massie. So no, this wasn’t one man’s vendetta. When the new Congress is sworn in I think we’re going to find that the number in favor of impeaching him is only going to grow. And consequently, I think the list of high crimes and misdemeanors against him is also going to grow.
There’s almost a limitless list of high crimes that Hegseth can be charged with, and there are crimes within crimes. Waging unlawful wars in Iran and Yemen and Venezuela and specific war crimes within them that Hegseth may also be culpable for.
The boat strikes in and of themselves are criminal, and then there is, for example, the double tap strike on the first attack on a so-called drug boat, which is a crime in its own right.
Hegseth can spin it any way he likes. He can use the troops as a shield, claiming that indictments of him are indictments of them. But in the end, he’s got a lot to answer for on his own, and none of it’s because he’s doing a good job. It’s because he’s committing high crimes.
JW: High crimes and misdemeanors to a layperson, even to me, is not exactly indicative of what these actual crimes are. So what were the actual charges that Massie leveled against Hegseth?
NT: There were three charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution. There was a charge related to Operation Rough Rider, which is the 2025 war in Yemen, which caused a tremendous number of civilian casualties. It’s become a forgotten conflict at this point.
The boat strike campaign which experts say are extrajudicial killings. There’s also a charge related to Hegseth’s efforts to undermine efforts at minimizing the possibility of civilian casualties. So these are some of the high crimes and misdemeanors of eight charges that Massie put forth.
JW: You just mentioned the drone strikes on so-called “narco terrorist” boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which to your estimate have killed more than 240 civilians. Those strikes, from my perspective, have gotten far less media attention than the Iran war, and obviously part of that is that much of what the U.S. is doing and who they’re targeting in open waters is shrouded in secrecy. But, how unprecedented are these strikes, and are these actions considered war crimes?
NT: The boat strikes, as you said, have largely been overtaken by the Iran war. But during his Pentagon press conference, Hegseth made a full-throated defense of his actions that actually drew attention to the unprecedented nature of the boat strike campaign.
Hegseth said that the charges that the American military targets civilians are a lie, and that the only people that target civilians are the terrorists that the U.S. hunts down. That itself is an outright lie. The U.S. boat strike campaign has only targeted civilians. Only. Not some, not inadvertently, not maybe. These are all civilians, period, full stop.
These summary executions of more than 240 people are a significant departure from the standard practice in the long-running U.S. war on drugs, in which law enforcement agencies detained suspected drug smugglers and then brought them to trial on criminal charges.
Experts in the laws of war, Pentagon officials that I’ve spoken with, and members of Congress from both parties say that Hegseth’s boat strikes are illegal, that they’re extrajudicial killings. The military is not permitted to deliberately target civilians, even suspected criminals.
Interdiction in these cases is possible. It’s preferable. It’s legal. We don’t execute suspected criminals in this country, or when the police do, it’s supposed to be a crime. If there was a declared war, these boat strikes might be war crimes, but no war exists, and there is no plausible legal justification for the strikes. And outside of armed conflict, the legal term for premeditated killing is murder. That’s what’s happening. That’s what Hegseth is responsible for, outright murder.
JW: Massie has not called Hegseth a war criminal or used the term murder like you have, but he did have this to say about Hegseth when discussing the articles of impeachment.
Thomas Massie: You won’t find a reference to war crimes. What I do say, though, is because he’s violated the international norms of war and violated our own conventions of war, he’s put our own soldiers and sailors at risk. When you go back for a second kill on people who are clinging to wreckage, you’re encouraging our adversaries to do the same. That’s why those laws — those international laws — are on the books.
JW: Nick, what did you make of Massie’s response just now?
NT: We were the first outlet to report that double tap strike in September 2025. It caused a firestorm in Congress for the very reason that Massie’s talking about.
He’s right. Double tap strikes on helpless shipwrecked people, they’re in contravention of the U.S. military’s own law of war manual, and they undermine respect for the laws of war and encourage enemies to give Americans no quarter, which is a war crime, and a war crime that Secretary Hegseth has openly called for and advocated.
I’m going to out myself as a lapsed historian here, but to emphasize that this is a longstanding norm in armed conflict I’d mention that a great rallying cry of the Revolutionary War — the American Revolution —was “Remember Paoli.” It’s a town in Pennsylvania where British Redcoats reportedly offered no quarter and massacred American forces.
Back in 1777, this was considered a major breach of the laws of combat. This is what Secretary Hegseth has advocated [that] we are doing in these types of double tap strikes, executing those who are injured those who are surrendering. That’s outright barbarism.
JW: We were just discussing civilian casualties in the boat strike —intentional civilian casualties. I also wanted to talk about what happened in February when the United States conducted an airstrike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran. That strike killed at least 150 people, most of them children.
Now, U.S. officials said the strike was caused by a “targeting error” where the military mistook the elementary school for an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval base. What did this horrific incident tell us about how the military has been operating under Hegseth when it comes to civilian casualties?
NT: This horrendous attack — a massacre of children — was the predictable result of Pentagon policies that The Intercept has been spotlighting since the spring of 2025, just after Pete Hegseth came to office. Hegseth made it inevitable that something like this mass killing of children would happen.
We reported that immediately upon taking office, he began dismantling what is known within the military as CHMR, the shorthand for Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response, basically undermining everything he could that restrains the military in favor of his favorite dictum, which is lethality.
A group of Democratic lawmakers told Hegseth in July in a letter directly to him that this gutting of CHMR had left the Pentagon unable to comply with the law and also its congressionally mandated responsibilities to protect civilians. This is precisely what military officials told us would happen months earlier, and it all came to fruition.
These criticisms were echoed in another report that we revealed in July that found that Hegseth had gutted the premier center devoted to preventing civilian casualties in war zones, the Pentagon’s own Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. Its workforce was slashed from 40 personnel in January of 2025 to just nine at the end of last year.
Last week we published an exposé that quoted six current and former defense officials who served under Hegseth, and one of them was the former senior advisor to this Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. This former official Wes Bryant, served eight combat deployments calling in airstrikes on ISIS and other post-9/11 entities.
Then he served under Hegseth until he was pushed out for blowing the whistle on policies that would undermine protections for civilians. Bryant told me that Hegseth is conducting what he called, “state terrorism.” He said Hegseth is “100 percent a war criminal,” and that he needs to be prosecuted.
JW: To that last point, and I really don’t like to play devil’s advocate, but from my understanding, you choose to refer to Hegseth by his self-styled title, Secretary of War, and if I understand you correctly, your argument is that there’s no need to sugarcoat what the U.S. military is doing. The Army is not in the business of defense. It’s in the business of war.
Is there an argument to be made that Hegseth is simply stripping back the facade of the U.S. military as anything other than a war machine, or is he really changing how the U.S. operates in the theater of war and in the world?
NT: I take a lot of heat from from readers on social media and in my email inbox about this, and readers plead with me not to bend to Hegseth’s will and call him the Secretary of War, which is, as you said his preferred title.
But I’ve really jumped at the chance for the reasons that you mentioned. When Hegseth unilaterally renamed the department, it gave me license to do what I’d wanted to do for years to call it as it’s seen, as it’s experienced in the world. For years out in the field, I found it grating whether I was in Vietnam or Cambodia or Libya and Somalia, to talk to victims of U.S. military violence about the so-called Department of Defense. The DoD says this. The DoD spokesman says that. I don’t think these people cared about it, but I absolutely did.
The Defense Department made war on the world, killing, wounding, and displacing millions of people not in the defense of anything. It was an aggressive war-making organization, plain and simple.
I hate using milquetoast euphemisms, but journalistic conventions handcuffed me. I couldn’t go off on my own and start calling it “Department of War.” But when they freed me up to give readers a more accurate assessment of what they do now under Hegseth and what has been done since they changed the name going back to the 1940s, I took the opportunity that I was afforded.
Attacking an elementary school in Iran is an act of war and maybe a war crime. It’s not a defense of the United States or in defense of the United States. That’s the reason why I use that title.
JW: Do you think that Hegseth has changed what the department is? Did it becoming the Department of War change something fundamental about it, or is that what it’s always been? And then is Hegseth changing anything about the actual way it operates?
NT: Hegseth has pulled the veil off of what the department does. I think in a very real sense, he’s undermined protections on civilians that were only just starting to perhaps take hold. The Center of Excellence that I mentioned earlier only just came into existence and was needed because the Pentagon has a long history of attacking civilians whether purposefully or inadvertently as “collateral damage.”
So the Defense Department always did what the Department of War does now, but there were some measures that were perhaps just starting to take hold, and Hegseth has undermined them completely.
JW: I think to your point, yes, Hegseth has lifted the veil off of what this department does. It is a department that makes war on the world. But he’s also made that worse and deadlier for civilians around the world.
And, obviously on Tuesday, Republicans killed the possibility of Hegseth being impeached by the current Congress. But come January, there’s going to be a new Congress dominated by Democrats. Now, before the vote on Massie’s articles of impeachment, Massie had this really interesting argument actually for why Republicans should join him in impeaching Hegseth. Let’s hear that clip.
Thomas Massie: I’m being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing somebody, really. You don’t go to prison. You don’t go to jail. You don’t pay a fine. OK, when the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious.
JW: He went on to say.
Thomas Massie: The Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection. They’ll be able to say what he’s actually done, the things that he has ignored, the things that he did that caused civilian casualties, the way he’s ignored the laws, and then there’ll be a full, robust trial over in the Senate.
JW: Nick, what do you make of Massie’s remarks, the failure of this vote now, and what do you think might be coming in the next Democratic-led House and Senate?
NT: So Hegseth was very fixated on Massie having a grudge against Trump, which he had transferred over to the war secretary. But Massie, as we heard there, throughout the process, was very vocal that he was doing Hegseth a huge favor. Massie suggested that his impeachment resolution was the legislative equivalent of a mercy killing, calling it a much gentler version of what the Democrats would do when they take control of Congress in January.
The Democrats can rain down relentless hellfire on Hegseth. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. They can paper the Pentagon with subpoenas.
Representative Yasmin Ansari, who filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth in the spring, told me that Hegseth surviving Massie’s impeachment only opened him up to a plethora of ways for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session. Specifically compelling to testify under oath before Congress and before the American people.
She emphasized that he’s “not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration,” her words, “but also one of the most unpopular” on a bipartisan basis. What she believes is going to happen is that Hegseth is going to be hauled up before Congress, and he’s just going to be battered incessantly.
This is probably going to grow so great that he’s going to become toxic to the administration. Representative-elect Richard Ojeda of North Carolina told our colleague Matt Sledge just after the impeachment vote the new Democrats are spoiling for a fight with Hegseth. He said “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted.”
I personally think that Hegseth might relish this rhetorical combat on Capitol Hill as a prelude to a potential presidential run. But, I think at some point it’s going to become untenable for him to actually preside over the Pentagon.
JW: I was at a press conference where Richard Ojeda was as well, and he had even more colorful language for Hegseth.
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda: Make no mistake about it, the 120th Congress, he will not be so lucky. Tick, tock! Get ready, asshole, because we’re coming.
JW: They certainly seem to have plans to really target Hegseth and Massie might have been right that he was trying to offer a mercy kill. But we’re going to have to leave it there.
Nick Turse, thank you so much for joining me on the Intercept Briefing.
NT:: Thanks so much for having me.
JW: After the break, my co-host Jordan Uhl speaks to musician and guitarist Tom Morello about his new album “Everyone Gets Everything They Want” and using his platform to fight fascism.
[Break]
Jordan Uhl: “Every act of art is an act of resistance,” says the legendary musician Tom Morello. Fighting for social justice and against fascism has been a staple of his art and career, from his work with The Nightwatchman to Rage Against the Machine to Audioslave.
And he’s at it again with his new album “Everyone Gets Everything They Want.” The track “Adjourn it” denounces the rising tide of racism and anti immigrant bigotry.
The song features Serj Tankian of System of a Down and Morello’s 15 year old son, Roman.
Tom Morello joins me now.
Tom, thanks so much for joining us on The Intercept Briefing.
JU: Tom Morello, it is an honor. Thank you so much for joining us on the Intercept Briefing
Tom Morello: It’s my pleasure. Thank you very much for having me
JU: Tom, you have a long history of activism, infusing that into your music and your art, and creating space for activism-oriented concerts and events like Power to the People. Your new album follows that tradition. It’s called “Everyone Gets Everything They Want.” Can you tell us about this new album, the themes that you explore on it, and if there are plans for future Power to the People festivals as we head into the presidential cycle?
TM: My career has basically been rebellion as self-care — rock and roll, especially in these troubled times. But in this day and age, every act of art is an act of resistance. Every truth spoken is a light in the gathering darkness. And every song sung has the potential to be a trumpet of a bulwark against the rising tide of authoritarianism to help sound the bell for current and future generations to continue to fight for a more just and peaceful and decent planet.
“Everyone Gets Everything They Want” is the 22nd album of my career. All 22 of those records have been built around a single purpose: that history is not something that happens, history is something that we make. Standing up in your place, in your time, in your place of work, whether it’s in a recording studio, whether it’s at the carpenter’s union, whether you’re a student, whether you’re an unhoused person, whether you’re a politician, is doing what you can with what you’ve got to try to be an advocate and an agent for a more just and peaceful planet.
JU: We are coming off of a massive rout in this election. Voters made it clear how they feel about this growing fascist movement in this country. But coming out of it, while some people are relieved, some people are happy, there are already intra-party debates over the policy priorities and leadership.
Unsurprisingly, we are seeing the pundit class rush to quell people’s enthusiasm, insisting the left does not have a mandate and that the moderate policy is the answer. What is your response to that?
TM: I was the scheduling secretary for United States Senator Alan Cranston for two years, so I got to see how the sausage is made from inside the sausage factory, and it is worse than you could possibly imagine. While it is encouraging that here and in Hungary and in Serbia and in Brazil that the people have resoundingly said no to fascism but the idea is not to have a kinder, gentler oligarchy. The idea is the liberation of humanity. The idea is securing a planet — a healthy planet — for our children and grandchildren, generations to come.
One thing that is encouraging in those other countries and in our most recent election is in addition to the terrible corporate Democrats who are also represented, there’s a new breed of politician. We have a socialist mayor in New York City. We have a socialist mayor in Los Angeles, the two biggest cities in our country.
The young people are once again the hope of the future. Rather than having me, a musician of a certain age saying, “This is what you should do,” I think that the main thing I can do is listen to what they have to say and encourage them in their efforts to build that more just and more peaceful planet.
JU: Do you have any thoughts on who should lead in the House and the Senate? We’re seeing calls for Schumer to step aside. Maybe if it’s new blood, maybe it’s Chris Van Hollen. Do you have any thoughts on who should lead Democrats in the Senate?
TM: My thoughts of people who should lead in the Senate are not elected in politics. And likely your show would be thrown off the air if I were to name them. [Laughter.]
Obviously the Chuck Schumers and Hakeem Jeffries are just awful continuations of the awful policies that got us in this to begin with. You can trace it back to Clinton with the crime bill and with NAFTA, and the abandonment of the working class that got us in this mess to begin with.
But again, I also think that it’s important to aim for the world you really want without compromise, without apology, and to not just go, “OK, well this is going to be better than the slippery slope to obvious this 50 percent clown show, 50 percent fascism that is the Trump administration.”
But what is the world you really want, and how do you build that? Not just what is a glazed-over version of what we’ve had, a reheated version of the terrible policies of both parties that got us in this situation of nearly environmental collapse and right-wing white Christian nationalism.
One thing I will say is that, there has been some reckoning that needs to be pushed even further of dealing with America’s original sin. The paradox of this country, which is demanding liberty while embracing white supremacy. That is the story of our country from day one in that some people’s lives just matter a lot more than other people’s lives, both at home and abroad. And a full rejection of that we’ve seen in some other countries, we’ve seen in part of the electorate here, and in some of the elected officials.
In my view, Election Day is harm reduction. I always vote. I vote my conscience, unless it is a contested election, and then I vote for the absolute most harm reduction.
To go beyond that and be like, “What’s the world you really want, and how do we fight for it?” That doesn’t just happen on Election Day. That happens the day after Election Day, and the day after that.
Since I was 17 years old, I have been in the trenches of grassroots organizing via rock and roll to try to do what I can in my small way with a Marshall half stack to liberate humanity. And that work has only just begun.
JU: I want to touch on that. I live in Los Angeles, and we just watched California voters reject a billionaire tax. This was a fight you were directly involved in. You performed at a rally here in Los Angeles in the spring. How do you make sense of that? You’re talking about these socialist gains, and we’re seeing this—
TM: It’s easy to make sense of it. It’s money in politics. I’m a fan of sports. Every World Series game, every football game had 72 ads paid for by tech billionaires and featuring the heroes of the California Democratic Party saying, “Please don’t tax the billionaires, whatever you do.”
This is a firsthand account. I was the scheduling secretary for a U.S. senator. Let me tell you what I scheduled. I scheduled phone calls for him to ask rich dudes for money. That’s what the schedule was.
We would go to a hotel, and there were like 10 payphones in a row. I would commandeer them, and I would call up the first guy and say, “Can you hold for the senator?” He’d get on the phone and ask that rich dude for money. Nine more calls in a row, Republicans, Democrats, corporate people, whatever.
Then they would start again, and we would spend the whole day doing that. Those guys are bought, sold, and totally beholden to the oligarchs that have their hands on the lever of power. So the reason why that tax failed was because how much money did they spend? If they had put as much money into healthcare for Californians as they did in trying to reject the billionaire tax, we’d be a lot better off.
JU: Over $300 million by a handful of billionaires. It’s absolutely staggering.
I want to look ahead. You and through your music, you’ve always been ahead of the curve waiting for folks to catch up. So what are the emerging fights that you see now that people need to get plugged in on? Is there something that stands out?
TM: I would say one thing is to not sink into a complacency when there’s a euphoria in the aftermath of a in my view somewhat surprising rejection of to the level that we’ve seen of Trumpism. But that’s just the beginning. We’ve already seen, as you mentioned, the right-wing of the Democratic Party asserting their hold on, like, “Hold on now. Hold on now.”
What people need to realize is the world isn’t going to change itself. That is up to you. That is up to me. While that may sound like a daunting sentence and a daunting task, the good news is whenever the world has changed in progressive, radical, or even revolutionary ways, it has been changed by people who didn’t have any more money, courage, power, intelligence, influence than anyone listening or watching this right now. The world is changed by average, everyday, ordinary people standing up in their time, not just at the ballot box, but in all that intervening time. Change comes from below. When change is real, it comes from below. It comes from you and me. That’s what I’ve been singing about and screaming about in my songs for an entire career. But I think that just that realization that we are agents of history, not just on election day, but beyond.
JU: The song “Unconquered” on your album features Kneecap, the Irish rap trio who have been very vocal at their shows for the liberation of Palestine, and they faced backlash, losing gigs, revocation of visas. Macklemore, same thing, speaking out about Palestine. We are in a moment right now where artists are using their platform for a critical human rights issue, a moral issue, and they are being punished.
What do you make of this backlash from the industry, from venue owners, from the billionaire class?
TM: First of all, welcome to my life. There’s nothing new about that. From Rage Against the Machine to my own political organizing, the pushback is real when you threaten centers of power and established orthodoxy in that regard.
The one thing that artists should remember is that you don’t put down your First Amendment rights when you pick up a microphone or a guitar. A lot of people are like, “Just shut up and dribble in sports,” or, “Just shut up and play music.” I would encourage all artists, don’t leave behind who you are and what you do.
But not just artists. As journalists, whatever your job is, don’t leave behind your convictions in your vocation. Those artists, Kneecap and Macklemore, have done it, and they’ve paid a price. Well, thank God. If you are making music that everyone can like hold hands to and skip around, you’re probably making pretty shitty music.
But those artists have stood up at a critical juncture. They are the Rage Against the Machine of now, fearlessly standing up for an oppressed people in a time where the world pushes back, and they don’t give a fuck. That should not just be Irish rappers and Pacific Northwestern rappers, but everybody should be emboldened by that and realize that they’re on the right side of history.
JU: Tom, before we let you go, we know you’re pressed for time. Any final thoughts?
TM: Thank you for your service, and The Intercept’s service in doing what you do. I think that you guys are upholding a long tradition of confrontational journalism, which the world needs now more than ever.
And also I’ve just started. I had hoped maybe around this time in my career we’d be living in the anarcho-syndicalist utopia that perhaps we imagined in the pre-choruses of some Rage Against the Machine songs long ago. That not being the case, though, I’m in it to win it. And I’ve only just started. My job from day one is to try to make one guitar sound like a riot and to have my music be a contributing factor to social justice movements at home and abroad.
JU: Tom, thank you so much for joining me on the Intercept Briefing
TM: Thank you very much.
JW: That’s Intercept Briefing co-host and contributor Jordan Uhl and musician and guitarist Tom Morello.
And that does it for this episode.
