Seth Stern is the director of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation.
Before the effort to impeach him failed Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth lashed out at a group he despises even more than “beardos” and “weirdos”: the press. His security team threatened to physically remove journalists from a news briefing, Hegseth’s first in several months, if they didn’t maintain decorum.
It’s nothing new for Hegseth. He may want to pump soldiers up with testosterone, but he’s spent the last couple years trying to neuter the Fourth Estate. It’s unfortunate that his unconstitutional attacks on journalists were not part of the official case for removing him. Next time, they should be. And Congress should not stop with Hegseth.
The impeachment resolution Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., brought against Hegseth included eight articles, alleging that the so-called Secretary of War acted illegally in military campaigns in Iran, Venezuela, and the Caribbean, among other things. The resolution touched on free speech violations – Article VI is about Hegseth’s retaliation campaign against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for reminding troops of their right to refuse illegal orders – but it didn’t mention the press.
A recap is in order: In February of 2025, Hegseth’s Pentagon evicted the New York Times, NBC, Politico, and NPR from their dedicated workspaces in the building, replacing them largely with sycophantic right-wing outlets like Breitbart and One America News Network. Some elements of the fawning right-wing press were on full display during his Tuesday press conference: “How does it make you feel,” asked a reporter from an outlet called Real America’s Voice, “when our own politicians don’t support taking out the narco-traffickers that kill their own constituents?”
Months later, Hegseth concocted a requirement that journalists who wish to access the Pentagon pledge not to solicit unauthorized information from the government, under threat of losing their credentials. Dozens of reporters from outlets across the political spectrum turned in their access badges rather than comply. They were replaced, once again, by loyalists who could be counted on to treat Hegseth and his fragile ego with kid gloves.
A judge soon struck down the pledge policy as an unconstitutional effort to force out disfavored journalists. The Pentagon immediately issued new restrictions on unauthorized disclosures that were, in some ways, even worse than the originals. The judge rejected that policy too. Hegseth also imposed a requirement for reporters to be escorted around the Pentagon, which is still working its way through the courts.
Hegseth’s Pentagon cracked down on the military’s newspaper, Stars and Stripes, barring it from briefings and demanding it stop publishing “woke” content. After all, it used to run columns from that well-known leftist Ann Coulter. His Pentagon then fired key personnel and otherwise did everything it could think of to try to turn Stars and Stripes into a propaganda organ unrecognizable to its readership – mostly troops, veterans, and their families.
It gets even pettier: Hegseth’s staff barred press photographers from briefings after they published pictures of him that he found unflattering.
Hegseth’s illegal war on transparency has extended not just to reporters but also to their sources. He forced staff to take unreliable polygraph tests to identify leakers until the White House itself halted the effort after a Trump loyalist complained about being targeted. He’s formed a joint task force with the Justice Department to push for prosecution of leakers and adopted President Donald Trump’s alarming habit of equating national security reporting to “treason.”
There will almost certainly be another effort to impeach Hegseth in the next Congress, if not sooner. Censorship may not be the lede — alleged international war crimes understandably tend to take the spotlight over other infractions — but it also shouldn’t be an afterthought.
While Congress is at it, remove Brendan Carr too
And while they’re impeaching wartime censors, Congress shouldn’t forget about FCC Chair Brendan Carr. He has defied federal law, the First Amendment, and the FCC’s own rules and guidelines in his incessant efforts to turn the agency into Trump’s journalism police. And critical reporting on the Iran war – which the Republican party now apparently agrees deserved criticism all along – has been one of Carr’s most frequent targets.
At the beginning of the war, after Trump fumed at accurate coverage he disliked, Carr – who wears Trump’s gilded face as a lapel pin and sips from a mug depicting himself as Trump’s pit bull – promptly reposted the president’s attack. He warned that broadcasters airing “hoaxes and news distortions” should “correct course before their license renewals come up.”
An emboldened Trump responded the same night, posting that outlets spreading “fake news” about the war should “be brought up on Charges for TREASON,” adding that he was “thrilled” Carr was investigating the licenses of media outlets across the country.
Then, after April’s purported ceasefire, CNN reported a statement from Iran’s Supreme National Security Council claiming victory. Trump took to Truth Social to announce a purported investigation into whether CNN committed some unspecified crime by publishing the quote. Carr piled on, accusing CNN, which the FCC does not regulate, of pushing a “hoax headline” that “requires accountability,” implying that licensees who aired similar reporting would face his wrath. But the statement was real. Trump just would’ve preferred CNN air a different one.
Of course, Carr’s censorship campaigns are myriad and many have little to do with the war. But his arguably most egregious (and impeachable) offense did, albeit indirectly.
Last year, Carr inexplicably stalled the FCC’s consideration of then-CBS News parent Paramount’s merger with David Ellison’s Skydance until Paramount paid $16 million to settle Trump’s frivolous lawsuit over “60 Minutes’” editing of an interview with Kamala Harris. He approved the merger two days after Trump said he’d received his dirty money. Essentially, he aided Trump in laundering a bribe through the courts.
Carr – who knows better, having once written that editorial judgment “should be beyond the reach of any government official” – also used his leverage over the merger to give himself and his delegates a seat at CBS’s editors desk, extracting unconstitutional editorial concessions from Ellison’s team. CBS has since been widely criticized for softening its coverage of Trump’s agenda, including (among other things) echoing administration narratives on the U.S. military operations like the war in Iran and the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
Facilitating likely bribery is the epitome of an impeachable offense. Republicans might not vote for impeachment, but after all the backlash Carr has received from the right, they also can’t credibly accuse Democrats of some kind of partisan witch hunt. Congress should not let the opportunity to hold Carr accountable pass them by.
Lawmakers need to acknowledge that the reporters the administration called traitors got it right all along, and that those who attempted to censor wartime journalism did a disservice to the Constitution and the American people. Hegseth and Carr should both be impeached, with the press they tried to muzzle freely reporting on every minute of the proceedings.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/subp.author: C. Frances
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/subp.text:
The Trump administration quietly broadened its crackdown on campus pro-Palestine protests over the summer, moving to ensnare one of the largest unions in the country in a case revolving around alleged incidents of vandalism.
The national headquarters of the American Federation of Teachers, or AFT, received a grand jury subpoena in August as part of an ongoing federal investigation into protests at the University of Michigan. Twelve pro-Palestine activists have been charged with felonies in the case.
The subpoena against the AFT, which has not been previously reported and was obtained by The Intercept, shows the administration casting a wider net in its investigation into student protesters than was previously known.
The Graduate Employees’ Organization, or GEO, an AFT local at the university, also received a notice to provide information and testimony to a grand jury around the same time, according to a copy of the previously unreported subpoena obtained by The Intercept.
The effort to draw a powerful, liberal union into a case that revolves around spray-painting charges represents a dramatic escalation in Donald Trump’s war on the left.
“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations that are taking stances against fascism, against the government, and anything that’s counter to their ideology,” said Natalie Chen, who serves as GEO’s communications director. “This is perhaps another ‘in’ for them to broaden their attack
on labor.”
Subpoenas to Crush Dissent
As pro-Palestine protests swept campuses across the country in 2024 and widespread demonstration broke out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this year, the Trump administration has sought to paint left-of-center protest, nonprofit work, and labor organizing as a nefarious far-left conspiracy, even labeling some activists and groups as terrorists.
Critics of the administration’s crackdown on Palestine solidarity and protests against ICE see moves like the ones against AFT and GEO as part of an effort to silence dissent.
“Historically, federal grand jury subpoenas have been used against social movements and political dissent to gather information, to isolate individuals, and of course to try and prosecute people,” said Xavier de Janon, executive director of the National Lawyers Guild. “What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed, which many people see clearly goes way beyond what they’re supposedly trying to prosecute.”
Activists at the University of Michigan said the effort to extract information about students from the union was an attempt to further target pro-Palestine protesters and their relationships with labor organizers.
The grand jury subpoenas came as part of a case that has seen a dozen protesters become caught up in serious federal charges against the students, dubbed “the Michigan 12.” They allege that protesters committed illegal acts like vandalism as part of a pressure campaign seeking to push university officials to divest school holdings tied to the Israeli genocide in Palestine.
The subpoenas against the GEO and AFT were requested by federal prosecutor Margaret Smith with assistance from FBI agent Kara Phipps — two federal officials deeply enmeshed in the investigation into the Michigan 12. (The Department of Justice declined to comment for this story.)
GEO Under Fire
The subpoenas were issued as the GEO was already reeling after its president, Hiab Teshome, was charged with felony embezzlement by local prosecutors working in conjunction with the University of Michigan Police Department.
Authorities alleged that Teshome, who was a bargaining team member in the middle of intense contract negotiations between the union and the school, misused organizational funds to purchase laptops for a campus club.
In a statement, the GEO called the charges meritless and characterized them as an attempt to limit protected union activity. Teshome was later cleared of any wrongdoing by the university’s student government, and the charges against her were thrown out by a judge.
Federal prosecutors issued the subpoenas the same day the charges against Teshome were dismissed, leaving activists little time to regroup.
Although GEO is not mentioned in the federal indictment against protesters, the AFT chapter is a prominent member of the Tahrir coalition, a pro-Palestine student collective that is referenced repeatedly in federal filings and characterized by prosecutors as having ties with defendants.
Broad in Scope
The scope of the information requested of the unions by the federal government is broad. GEO and AFT are being compelled, according to the subpoenas, to surrender information including complete membership rolls, payroll records on officers, reimbursement policies, audit reports, and all transcribed minutes on membership and executive board meetings of the University of Michigan local since January 2023.
The American Federation of Teachers has more than 1.7 million members and more than 3,000 local chapters.
After receiving the subpoena, GEO immediately obtained attorneys and filed a motion to quash the order. The national office of the AFT, however, has not publicly acknowledged receiving the directive or stated whether it intends to comply. (AFT did not respond to requests for comment about the subpoenas, including whether the union would be complying.)
Teshome, the GEO president, believes that the subpoena against the AFT may be an attempt by the federal government to circumvent the local union and force the national organization to comply.
“GEO has taken the stance that we will do everything in our power to protect the data and the information of our membership,” Teshome said. “I think that this is a strategy that the federal government is using in order to try to actually receive the information that they are trying to get by usurping us as a local union and going instead to AFT national.”
Additionally, Teshome likened the GEO’s case to similar surveillance activities conducted by federal agents against trade unionists in Minnesota as part of the Trump White House’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, a presidential directive that attempts to criminalize leftist political organizations.
“All of the repression we are seeing across the country is the federal government’s attack on anyone who has political thought,” Teshome said. “Michigan is no different than all of these other cases in that we are one of the testing grounds for NSPM-7 and how much oppression can be applied through the federal government in order to demobilize and disorganize.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Exhibition explores how the fisherman-turned-artist Alfred Wallis inspired leading British artists
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.
Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.
Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.
A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once said to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.
The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.
Scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.
The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a new direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott says, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.
Scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”
• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027

https://hellgatenyc.com/a-new-film-festi.title: A New Film Festival Looks at Life Beyond Rikers
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-new-film-festi.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-new-film-festi.text:
Shortly after Edwin Santana was released from prison in 2017, he picked up his phone and began making what would become his first-ever documentary: "Closing the Last Penal Colony."
The last penal colony in question was Rikers Island, where Santana had spent time as a young man. While in prison, he didn't know much about the movement to close Rikers, and now that he was a free man, he started filming a movement that was urgently trying to shut down a place that had wounded him deeply. 
"I know the horrors firsthand, but it was only when I came home did I see that there was a massive movement centered around the issues I experienced, even all these years later," he told Hell Gate. "It was amazing to see people like myself, the formerly incarcerated, people who felt like they didn't have a voice, that they should even be ashamed of their own voices because they were incarcerated, leading this movement."
Santana had seen Rikers Island depicted in film, either glorifying the violence or as this unimaginable hellhole. But he'd never seen anything that actually put Rikers in the context of a long history of incarceration and bondage in New York City. 
"I wanted to see where Rikers came from," Santana said. "How did it even get here?" 
His documentary, which traces the history of Rikers Island—from a military training ground during the Civil War (including New York's segregated regiment of Black soldiers), to a modern massive jail complex literally built by prisoners, to the movement to close it—isn't the most polished documentary. Santana knows, two years after its release, that it would be a lot better if he made it today. But he also knows it reflects the mindset and experience of someone who just came out of a system that had inflicted harm on thousands of young people like him, and which still, stubbornly, hasn't closed. 
Santana's film is now one of the centerpieces of A Future Beyond Rikers Film Festival, which is taking place this weekend at the Maysles Documentary Center in Harlem, beginning Friday evening.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/populis.author: Peter Certo
https://inthesetimes.com/article/populis.text:
We Just Witnessed a Populist Blowout
In Tuesday’s midterm elections, voters rejected Trump’s billionaire-backed politics and attacks on working people. The winners need to show that a different kind of politics can deliver.
Peter Certo
For years, Americans have been viciously divided according to race, religion, immigration status and gender identity by politicians dead set on making us fight each other rather than them. In a year where real people’s struggles were impossible to ignore, that effort fell short.
It’s hard to overstate the scale of Democratic victories in this year’s midterm elections.
Voters broke for Democratic candidates by margins scarcely anticipated by even the party’s rosiest polls—often in deep red states and congressional districts that few seriously thought were competitive. Democrats will now control a commanding House majority and hold a significant edge in the Senate as well.
This was a decisive rejection of Trumpism — and it happened on a significantly tiited playing field.
Before the election, Supreme Court justices aligned with President Donald Trump gutted what remained of the Voting Rights Act, only the latest in a series of rulings limiting fair access to voting and representation. At Trump’s urging, Republican-led statehouses unleashed an unprecedented flurry of mid-decade gerrymanders designed to maximize their partisan advantage and disenfranchise their critics. Billionaires poured vast sums into races — and trillionaire Elon Musk spent over $400 million alone, more than George Soros has spent on elections his entire life.
And that’s not even getting into the concerns, often stoked by leading Republicans themselves, that the administration would try to cancel results, deploy National Guard or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to cities, or otherwise meddle in the election.
None of it was enough for voters who’ve spent years now watching events in their lives spin out of control.
Trump’s tariffs made life miserable for farmers, manufacturers, and consumers while his allies slashed safety net programs to fund tax breaks for billionaires. The war in Iran, which Trump launched shortly after promising no new wars, sent the price of fuel skyrocketing.
Lawless ICE agents terrorized immigrants and citizens alike and shocked the conscience of people across the political spectrum. And a data center boom spiked power bills and disrupted communities across the country, all to power a technology CEOs vowed to use for replacing people’s jobs and surveilling their day to day life.
In the races that mattered most, populist candidates spoke to these concerns directly.
Candidates who backed data center restrictions and moratoria flipped red governorships and/or Senate seats in Ohio, Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, and beyond—while voters directly passed their own local moratoria in dozens of communities.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated a shockingly Islamophobic opposition by focusing relentlessly on taking U.S. foreign and domestic policy alike back from billionaires. In Maine, Troy Jackson toppled longtime Sen. Susan Collins by embracing his working class identity and supporting Medicare for All. And in a state that became emblematic of ICE’s abuse, Peggy Flanagan ran away with a victory in Minnesota calling to “rip ICE apart.”
But to sustain these gains, these winners — and the leaders of their party — will need to follow through on the promises voters entrusted them with.
In the two years Trump has left, they’ll need to be held accountable to claw back the enormous funds Trump and the GOP have set aside for ICE and Pentagon and put them back into programs to make sure struggling Americans have food and healthcare—areas which are only set to see further cuts as more provisions of the “Big Beautiful Bill” take effect.
They should embrace their powers of investigation not only to crack down on the administration’s unprecedented corruption, but also to make tech CEOs answer for foisting AI and data centers on Americans and to hold corporate price gougers accountable for raising the cost of groceries, healthcare and rent. And they’ll need to rapidly repair our civic infrastructure to get money out of politics and put ordinary people back in it.
If our next leaders can’t deliver as promised, the politics of scapegoating will come roaring back. It won’t be easy, but the voters are watching. And this November they spoke loud and clear.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.title: Organizing Beat Out Democratic Conventional Wisdom
https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.author: Hamilton Nolan
https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.text:
Organizing Beat Out Democratic Conventional Wisdom
Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterms showed why the old playbook should be thrown out of the window—and that the Left is on the march.
Hamilton Nolan
A decade ago, I went to Texas to write a profile of the Democratic candidate running in the reddest congressional district in the United States. He was a local gadfly, and had been given no resources from the national Democratic Party beyond a handshake. The story was meant to be a lark — a farcical, lighthearted tale of mankind’s capacity to forge ahead into impossible tasks.
Yet that is not the lesson I found. As I wandered the dusty neighborhoods of Amarillo, I began to wonder why this place was assumed to be intractably, unchangeably Republican. This was a town with a lot of immigrants and working people trying to stay on the right side of the poverty line. It was a place where you could imagine plenty of people being attracted to the Democratic platform. The folly I saw was not the man who took on the uphill task of running, but the party that had written this place off as a lost cause, unworthy of any effort. What that deep red Texas district needed was not resignation — it needed organizing.
This is why political consultants will never change the world. They look at the seething ball of humanity that makes up a political district — a writhing mass of hopes and dreams and desperation, covered in fluctuating layers of repression and ignorance and inspiration — and they see a neat column of numbers. They see a set of fixed quantities. They see politics as the art of running towards the favorable numbers and away from the bad ones. They do not see that that entire grand edifice of numbers can be reversed. It can be smashed, with breathtaking speed, if the real people in the real places change their minds.
The data-driven model of politics that rules the United States, that governs the spending of the Democratic Party, that starts with the status quo and cautiously wonders if it can move a single space on the policy chessboard, is vulnerable to those who understand that all of that data can be changed. It is vulnerable to those who know how to organize. 
The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterms was, in one sense, no surprise — President Donald Trump is historically unpopular and dismissive of political advice, and he carried his entire party to doom like an insane mother who jumps off a bridge with her baby clutched to her chest. Democrats have taken back control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, where they will hold firm majorities, and a new class of socialists and progressives is headed to Congress.
The most striking element of the whole thing, to me, was the natural experiment that was carried out between the states of Texas and Florida. Both are huge states that have been Republican strongholds for so long that they became deep red-coded in conventional wisdom, despite the fact that their populations are racially and economically and culturally diverse. They are both places where the raw material of Democratic political power has been suffocated by a lack of adequate resources and organizing.
Last night, we saw what adequate resources could do. James Talarico turned Texas blue by winning his Senate race against Ken Paxton after the most expensive non-presidential race in U.S. history. Talarico’s campaign raised nearly $150 million and took advantage of maximal support from the national Democratic Party to overcome an even more grotesque sea of spending by Tesla CEO (and world’s richest person) Elon Musk in support of Paxton, his debased opponent. In Florida, by contrast, former union organizer and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member Angie Nixon upset the party’s handpicked candidate in the primary, and then came within three points of winning the general election (the best performance by a Florida Democrat in a Senate race since 2018) by pursuing nonstop ground-level organizing while being significantly outspent the whole time.
In Texas, deemed by conventional wisdom to be a macho Republican stronghold, a decidedly non-macho Democrat won with the help of a flood of national resources. In Florida, deemed by conventional wisdom to be a stronghold of Trumpian racists and rabid anti-communists, a Black woman DSA member who knew how to organize came shockingly close to winning. What’s the difference there? The difference is that one candidate got the resources and the other didn’t. Angie Nixon did not win, but with time we may admit that she performed an even greater service for the Democratic Party by proving that their idea of what is and is not possible in red states is wrong. 
As soon as Election Day is over, the battle to write the narrative begins. Whoever is able to persuade the bulk of the party and the public of their own narrative can take control of the direction of the party as we turn towards the next presidential election. This battle for control of the Democratic vision is more pronounced right now than it has ever been in my lifetime. Now, for the first time in decades, the left wing of the Democratic Party is not a bunch of fringe outsiders begging for scraps. The Left is surging and ascendent. The next two years will not just be about thwarting the deranged and retrograde ambitions of MAGA world; they will be a fight for the steering wheel of the Democratic steamroller.
For centrists and moderates, there is always the same narrative: Centrism was vindicated. We must run to the middle. The path to victory lies in extending a hand to disaffected Republicans. This is the story they will tell about what just happened. But in fact, the real narrative, the one that follows the surges of political electricity, is this: Trump squeaked into office after the last Democratic president seemingly went senile and withdrew his candidacy abruptly. Two years of raving lies, fascist insanity, blatant corruption, and a violent racist purge carried out by Nazi-esque White House officials has left people pissed off. The need for real change, deep change, structural change, is obvious.
Zohran Mamdani’s election as mayor in New York City has energized a socialist movement inside of the Democratic Party that is getting stronger, more widespread, and better organized with each passing day. This group arises not from the business world or the consulting world but from social movements, from unions, from activism — and it therefore approaches politics with an organizing model that the “raise corporate money and pour it into negative advertising” model of campaigns struggles to defeat. More than any time in living memory, The Political Left as broadly understood is organized, popular, smart, and determined.
The Left is not confined to coastal big cities. It’s everywhere. The legacy of the wheezing Democratic establishment is that they lost to Trump and got us here. The Left is cleaning up their mess — thanks in large part to a capacity for ignoring conventional wisdom and doing things that politicians are not supposed to do, lest they isolate the fabled suburban swing voters who seem to grow less and less real with each passing election.
The real problem for the Democratic establishment is that U.S. democracy requires deeper changes than they are willing to countenance, and their failure to support the pursuit of those changes will ultimately result in the further erosion of Democratic power. The 2026 midterms were worthy of celebration for all of us. They were a sign of hope for America’s future. But for the Left, they are not going to be a ceiling. They are going to be a trampoline.
