https://inthesetimes.com/article/voting-.title: The Hour Before Dawn
https://inthesetimes.com/article/voting-.author: Jesse Hagopian
https://inthesetimes.com/article/voting-.text:
The Hour Before Dawn
With the Voting Rights Act gutted and education under attack, building democratic power must reach beyond the ballot box—and into classrooms and the streets
Jesse Hagopian
In 1980, conservative strategist Paul Weyrich made a startling declaration during a speech in Dallas: “I don’t want everyone to vote.”
Weyrich, a leading strategist of the modern conservative movement and co-founder of the Heritage Foundation, explained, “Elections are not won by a majority of people. They never have been from the beginning of our country, and they are not now. As a matter of fact, our leverage in the elections quite candidly goes up as the voting populace goes down.”
Weyrich’s battles over political power did not end at the ballot box. He also saw education as a crucial battleground. In a 1999 op-ed, he claimed “political correctness” ruled schools and universities with “totalitarian ambitions.” His solution was for conservatives to build a “complete, separate, parallel structure” of “schools, universities, media, entertainment, everything.”
More than 40 years after Weyrich’s infamous voting remarks, Donald Trump has waged battles on these same two fronts. In 2020, on conservative talk show Fox & Friends, Trump warned that greater “levels of voting” would mean “you’d never have a Republican elected in this country again.” His administration has also sought to restrict what students can learn, threatening to withhold federal funding from schools that teach about systemic racism in ways it opposes and attempting to prohibit DEI programs in schools. Trump has simultaneously worked to dismantle the Department of Education while directing more public money toward private schools through voucher programs.
The message is clear: Limit who can exercise democratic power in the present, and limit what people learn about how previous generations expanded it.
The Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais represents the latest chapter in a centuries-long effort to restrict political participation whenever it threatens the existing distribution of wealth and power. The tactics have changed — from literacy tests and poll taxes to racial gerrymandering and voter suppression laws — but the goal of limiting political participation remains.
The case began when Black voters challenged a Louisiana congressional map that created just one majority-Black district out of six, despite Black residents making up nearly one-third of the population. A federal judge found that the map likely violated the Voting Rights Act by diluting Black voting power, prompting the Republican-controlled legislature to draw a second majority-Black district. But a group of self-described non-Black voters challenged the new map, arguing that creating the second majority-Black district amounted to unconstitutional racial gerrymandering. 
In a 6 – 3 decision on April 29, the Supreme Court struck down the new map and effectively gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits racial discrimination in voting. As voting rights journalist Ari Berman explained, the ruling served to “effectively kill the last remaining tool of the Voting Rights Act,” following earlier Supreme Court decisions in 2013 and 2021 that weakened its protections.
The consequences have reshaped the 2026 midterm elections. Following Callais, Republican-controlled legislatures in Louisiana and Tennessee redrew congressional maps to eliminate majority-Black districts, including the district representing much of Memphis.
In Alabama, the Supreme Court allowed the state to use a map that eliminated a second district in which Black voters had an opportunity to elect their preferred candidate. Florida enacted a new congressional map designed to shift four Democratic-leaning districts toward Republicans. Meanwhile, a federal appeals court in Georgia overturned a 2023 ruling that the state’s electoral maps discriminated against Black voters, ordering the case reconsidered under the new, more restrictive standard. With additional redistricting battles already taking shape for 2028, the struggle over who gets to exercise political power is far from over.
In her dissent, Justice Elena Kagan warned that “The Voting Rights Act is — or, now more accurately, was — one of the most consequential, efficacious and amply justified exercises of federal legislative power in our nation’s history.”
The Callais decision arrives amid a broader assault on democracy. Across the country, lawmakers are redrawing electoral maps to dilute Black and brown political power, erecting new barriers to voting, attacking independent election administration, criminalizing voter registration efforts and undermining public confidence in elections themselves. These attacks are part of a broader effort to prevent the vast majority of people from exercising meaningful political power.
But democracy is about more than casting a ballot every few years. It depends on people having the freedom to learn, deliberate, organize, protest, advocate, and govern collectively. Achieving a democratic society requires a public empowered to decide not only who holds political office, but also how to govern the wealth, resources and institutions created by our collective labor.
It’s no wonder then why attacks on voting rights and education so often travel together. Limiting teachers’ ability to show students how social movements have expanded democratic rights and challenged concentrated political and economic power constrains the possibilities people can imagine for the future.
As veterans of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) warned in their response to the Callais decision, these attacks are part of a long historical effort to “control the vote. Control the outcome. Control the future.” Few people are better positioned to remind us why. SNCC organizers risked — and, in some cases, gave — their lives to secure the right to vote.
But “voting alone has never been sufficient,” they said. The movement that won the Voting Rights Act never imagined democracy as something that happened only every few years inside a voting booth. Voting mattered because it was one tool — among many — that ordinary people could use to build democratic power. As the SNCC veterans explained, movements must also “build power beyond” the vote through organizing, coalition building, political education and institutions capable of challenging unjust laws and holding those in power accountable long after Election Day. Voting rights have never been gifts handed down by enlightened leaders. They were victories won through collective struggle.
During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved Black communities and their allies fought to transform emancipation into political power. Their organizing helped secure the 15th Amendment in 1870, prohibiting states from denying the right to vote based on race. Reconstruction demonstrated that voting rights were inseparable from broader struggles for public education, economic opportunity, safety and full participation in society.
For a brief period, the United States moved closer to becoming a multiracial democracy. Black voters helped elect Black legislators across the South, establish public schools, expand public services and reshape political life. Yet Reconstruction was ultimately defeated by a campaign of racial terror and political reaction led by former Confederates and their allies. 
Today’s battles over voting rights are the latest manifestation of that counterrevolution.
Nearly a century later, the Civil Rights Movement launched what many historians have called a Second Reconstruction.
In 1964, SNCC helped lead the Mississippi Freedom Summer campaign through the Council of Federated Organizations, a coalition that brought together SNCC, the Congress of Racial Equality, the NAACP, and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Alongside thousands of Black Mississippians who had been organizing for years, they built Freedom Schools, organized voter registration drives, developed local leadership and helped establish the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party to challenge the state’s all-white Democratic delegation. They faced bombings, beatings and jail cells, and the murders of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner.
Yet the movement persisted.
Freedom Summer helped expose the brutality of Jim Crow to the nation and laid crucial groundwork for passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But its lessons extended far beyond voting.
Freedom School students studied Black history, examined social inequalities, debated current events and imagined a more democratic future. Organizers recognized that people needed not only the right to vote but also the knowledge, confidence, and political understanding necessary to exercise power.
Reflecting on the movement decades later, SNCC veteran Courtland Cox explained that the struggle was never simply about access to the ballot. Rather, it sought to create “space for millions of Americans to participate in the political and economic life of this country.”
Voting rights are about more than elections. They are about who has the power to shape the conditions of their lives. They are connected to struggles for quality schools, affordable housing, healthcare, labor rights, clean air and water, public investment and economic justice. This is precisely why attacks on voting rights are so often accompanied by attacks on education.
Those seeking to restrict popular power understand the power of history education and see it as dangerous. When students learn about Reconstruction, they discover that formerly enslaved people fought to dramatically expand democratic rights in a nation that had never lived up to its democratic claims. When they learn about Freedom Summer, they discover that ordinary people challenged systems of oppression that seemed permanent. When they learn about the Civil Rights Movement, they discover that rights are rarely granted voluntarily by those in power; they are won through, as SNCC puts it, “courage, radical imagination and readiness to act.”
If young people understand these histories, they may begin to see themselves not simply as spectators to politics but as participants in shaping the future. That is precisely why educators must refuse to lie about the past and teach honest history about the Black Freedom Struggle and movements for collective liberation. Through the growing Teach Truth movement, educators, students, and communities across the country are organizing against book bans and curriculum censorship. Teachers are refusing to surrender to laws and political intimidation designed to erase the history of systemic racism and its enduring impact on American society. Instead, they are teaching the truth about the long struggle for voting rights and the grassroots movements that challenged slavery, segregation, and racial injustice. They are helping students understand that democracy has never simply been handed down from above. It has been expanded by ordinary people organizing together to demand it.
Paul Weyrich’s call for a “complete, separate, parallel structure” of schools and media lives on in today’s MAGA movement, with its push for school privatization through charter schools and private school vouchers while restricting the teaching of systemic racism in public schools. Yet decades before Weyrich’s declaration, SNCC and other Freedom Summer organizers had built their own parallel institutions from below — not to privatize public education, but to challenge the segregation and white supremacy of Mississippi’s schools and society. The irony is striking: Today’s MAGA movement champions alternatives to public schools while seeking to suppress the alternative education that SNCC’s Freedom Schools were created to provide — teaching that white supremacy can be challenged, that ordinary people can transform society and that education should empower young people to fight for a more democratic world.
In this time of rising authoritarianism, the lessons of SNCC veterans are vital. “We have seen darker nights than this one,” the SNCC veterans’ response to Callais reminds us, but “we do not pretend that this moment is ordinary.”
This metaphor from SNCC veterans is a fitting one for our own time:
Yes, it is late, and it’s dark outside. But it is 3 a.m. This is the hour when the body is most vulnerable. The hour when the future feels uncertain. The hour when many lose their way. But it is also the hour before dawn. A new world isn’t guaranteed. But it is possible. And it’s already being imagined, organized and fought for.
The hour before dawn has never belonged to spectators. It has always belonged to those willing to organize despite uncertainty and to imagine a freer society before it seems possible. That is the inheritance the veterans of SNCC have entrusted to us.
Jesse Hagopian is a Seattle educator, an editor for Rethinking Schools magazine, a founding steering committee member of Black Lives Matter at School and serves as the director of the Teaching for Black Lives Campaign for the Zinn Education Project. His most recent book from Haymarket Books is Teach Truth: The Attack on Critical Race Theory and the Struggle for Antiracist Education. Jesse is editor of More Than a Score: The New Uprising Against High Stakes Testing and co-editor of the books, Teaching for Black Lives, Black Lives Matter at School and Teachers Unions and Social Justice.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-keep-new-.title: Opinion: Keep New York Storm Batteries Ready
https://citylimits.org/opinion-keep-new-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-keep-new-.text:
Share This Article
“Storms are not waiting for regulators. New York can use community batteries on ordinary days without sacrificing the people who depend on them during the worst ones.”
Earlier this fall, a slow-moving nor’easter flooded New York’s coast, toppled hundreds of trees on Long Island and in the Rockaways and knocked out power to tens of thousands of homes across the Northeast. In July, record heat and holiday storms interrupted service to about 173,700 Con Edison customers. Westchester communities suffered the most storm-related outages.
When the lights go out, many New Yorkers turn to community centers, shelters and senior centers. More of those buildings now have batteries, often paired with rooftop solar, that can keep fans, phones and medicine refrigerators running. After Hurricane Sandy, the city’s RISE:NYC program built eight solar-and-battery microgrids in Staten Island, Brooklyn and the Rockaways for that purpose.
These batteries could also help the grid on hot afternoons, when electricity demand spikes. Utilities and private companies already pay some battery owners to release stored power. Connect enough batteries and they can work together as a virtual power plant.
But a shelter cannot sell the same electricity it needs for an emergency. If a utility drains its battery during an evening peak and a storm arrives the next morning, the shelter may have nothing left. New York’s utility rules provide no common way to protect backup power while selling the remainder. Facilities that serve medically vulnerable residents, older adults and families without money for generators have the most to lose.
That is an energy justice problem. Residents of historically excluded communities often face greater exposure to extreme heat and outages while having fewer resources to leave, replace spoiled food or power medical equipment. Publicly funded batteries should protect those residents first. They should also earn revenue that can support maintenance and community services when no emergency exists.
Community organizing taught me that resilience plans fail when institutions design them around equipment instead of the people who will depend on it.
New York has 528.7 megawatts of installed storage, including 268.2 megawatts in smaller local projects, according to the Department of Public Service. Yet utility peak-demand programs enrolled only about 68 megawatts of battery relief in 2025. Con Edison held dispatch rights to 185 megawatts; the other major utilities held none.
Not every unenrolled battery can participate, but the disparity shows that New Yorkers do not have equal access to the benefits of shared storage. The Public Service Commission should require every major utility to offer one set of terms for batteries that serve two purposes. Eligible sites should include hospitals, shelters, cooling centers, senior facilities, schools, houses of worship and community organizations that provide essential services during outages.
First, each site should keep a protected reserve that utilities cannot use. Small facilities could use a standard reserve set by facility type, while hospitals and other complex sites could document their needs through a detailed study. Utilities could buy only the energy above that floor.
Second, routine dispatch should pause when the National Weather Service warns of hazards the Commission determines pose a significant local outage risk, such as hurricanes, coastal flooding or damaging winds, giving batteries time to recharge. Third, a hospital, shelter or cooling center should be able to leave a grid event without penalty when safety requires it. Utilities should report each override so regulators can deter abuse.
Utility companies and ratepayer advocates may object that these protections reduce the power available to the grid and add verification costs. They are right about the tradeoff. A battery with a protected reserve offers less capacity than an unrestricted one. But reliable capacity is worth more than capacity a facility will not enroll because the contract threatens its emergency mission. Standard rules also cost less to negotiate and audit than a different agreement for every building.
The timing matters. New York aims to reach 6,000 megawatts of storage by 2030, and state law promises disadvantaged communities a fair share of clean-energy benefits. Every project signed under different terms makes a statewide standard harder to adopt later. Residents should ask the Public Service Commission and their utilities to protect community reserves, publish participation data and include frontline organizations when writing the rules.
Storms are not waiting for regulators. New York can use community batteries on ordinary days without sacrificing the people who depend on them during the worst ones. The Commission should set that bargain now.
Jessica A. Campbell is a community organizer and clean-energy policy student in Yale’s Financing and Deploying Clean Energy certificate program.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/south-africa.title: South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/south-africa.author: Zwelinzima Vavi
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/south-africa.text:
South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
The African National Congress is losing its working-class base. The beneficiaries: parties of the Right. South Africa’s local elections expose the fallout of three decades of economic failure — and the need to rebuild working-class power.
While the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia.
With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place.
The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order.
The ANC’s Historic Failure
The defeat of apartheid was an extraordinary achievement. We won universal suffrage, democratic institutions, constitutional rights, and legal protections for workers. Those victories were won through generations of sacrifice and collective struggle, and they must be defended. But political apartheid was defeated while the economic structures inherited from apartheid remained largely intact.
The liberation movement historically brought together different classes and social groups united against racial oppression. That unity was indispensable to apartheid’s defeat. But national identity does not abolish class contradictions. Instead of using democracy to transform the ownership and control of the economy in the interests of the majority, the ANC increasingly became an instrument through which a new elite could enter and benefit from the existing economic order.
The ownership and control of the commanding heights of the economy were never fundamentally transformed. Land ownership remained extraordinarily unequal. The former Bantustans, created as reservoirs of cheap African labor, were never provided with the productive economic foundations needed to overcome their inherited poverty.
Over time, the ANC came to treat the advancement of an emerging black capitalist class as evidence of economic transformation. A narrow layer of businesspeople accumulated wealth, in some cases extraordinary wealth, through access to political power, state contracts, and opportunities created by the Black Economic Empowerment policy, while the overwhelming majority remained excluded from meaningful economic power.
The ANC’s adoption of neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s deepened this problem. The language of economic liberation gave way to investor confidence, competitiveness, and market reform. Brutal austerity, liberalization, and dependence on private investment displaced the redistributive ambitions of the liberation struggle.
We were repeatedly told that economic growth would eventually deliver employment and redistribution. We were also told that redistribution must wait for economic growth and the development of the productive forces. But if redistribution had to wait while productive capacity developed, why did South Africa simultaneously deindustrialize?
We have become what I have described as a “warehouse economy.” We export raw materials and insufficiently processed mineral wealth, allow other countries to manufacture finished products, then import those products for domestic consumption. We export jobs embedded in raw materials and import unemployment embedded in finished goods.
Factories have closed while warehouses have remained open. South Africa continues to extract enormous mineral wealth without developing the productive industries capable of turning that wealth into decent employment on the scale required.
It is a very painful fact that, after decades of mass unemployment and deindustrialization, the poor are now poorer and more numerous than under apartheid. In the second quarter of 2026, South Africa’s official unemployment rate stood at 33.6 percent. Including people who want work but have stopped actively searching, the rate was 43.8 percent. Among young people age fifteen to twenty-four who were in the labor force, unemployment reached 62.8 percent.
This crisis has meant the destruction of hope for millions of people. It has also been accompanied by the weakening of the organized working class. Mass unemployment undermines bargaining power, makes workers afraid to exercise their rights, and encourages casualization and precarious employment. A worker who knows that thousands of unemployed people are desperate for a job is in a much weaker position to resist exploitation.
The crisis has also fragmented the working class itself. Millions of people are unemployed, casually employed, working in the informal economy, or moving between different forms of insecure work. Traditional trade unions organize only a section of this wider class.
The working class cannot be reduced to people fortunate enough to receive a regular pay slip. The unemployed, precarious workers, labor-broker workers, informal workers, women carrying the burden of unpaid care, and young people who have never had secure employment must all be part of the social movement capable of transforming South Africa.
At the same time, the combination of austerity and extreme corruption has resulted in the decay of the state and the collapse of public services. Municipalities have become centers of patronage, political competition over tenders, and the accumulation of private wealth. Water systems collapse, roads deteriorate, sewage flows through communities, and public transport becomes increasingly unreliable. It has become normal for even middle-class areas to go for weeks or even months without water, while the poor live among stinking piles of uncollected refuse.
The crisis is also visible in the ANC’s conception of the state. A developmental state cannot simply outsource development and then claim the credit. It requires public institutions with the capacity to plan, build, maintain infrastructure, and provide services directly.
South Africa has developed a system in which government contracts out essential functions while state capacity deteriorates. The result is an expanding network of contractors, consultants, and intermediaries whose accumulation depends on public expenditure, while the institutions responsible for serving the people become weaker.
The tragic reality is that the ANC’s neoliberal policies have not simply failed to resolve the economic crisis. They have also undermined the credibility of the very idea of democratic transformation, opening the door to right-wing demagoguery.
Corruption and the Destruction of Political Authority
Economic failure has been compounded by the degeneration of political leadership. The ANC once insisted that leadership required exceptional qualities: political understanding, integrity, discipline, courage, humility, service, and sacrifice. Its own document, “Through the Eye of the Needle,” expressed the idea that leadership should be earned through commitment to the people rather than acquired through personal ambition.
Today the competition for leadership largely revolves around factions, access to resources, control of organizational structures, and the distribution of positions. Political office has become a route to private accumulation.
This cannot be understood merely as a series of individual moral failures. It is connected to a political culture in which access to the state and public wealth becomes a route to private economic advancement. Where the public sector is treated as a source of tenders and contracts rather than an instrument for meeting social needs, the distinction between political leadership and business accumulation becomes blurred. The result is a profound loss of moral authority.
When working people see leaders acquiring enormous wealth while unemployment rises, schools deteriorate, hospitals struggle, and the water supply fails, they inevitably begin to lose confidence in the institutions that claim to represent them. The ANC’s electoral collapse is therefore not mysterious. It is the political expression of a much deeper social, economic, and organizational failure.
At the same time, trade unions have been divided, and some have become very corrupt, as corrupt as the ANC. The capacity of unions and community organizations to develop working-class leaders has weakened. Organizations have often concentrated on internal contests or debates between established political figures instead of building the democratic power of ordinary people. Political education, once central to the union movement, has declined. With the exception of Abahlali baseMjondolo, the two-hundred-thousand-strong movement of the urban poor, community organizations have lost much of their former strength, with many collapsing completely.
The Right Advances
A rapidly growing Right has been very successful in redirecting legitimate popular anger away from those responsible for generalized social suffering and toward African and Asian migrants. Fascist organisations such as Operation Dudula and March and March have built movements around violent hostility toward African migrants. In communities devastated by unemployment, crime, and failing services, they offer a simple explanation: foreigners are responsible for the crisis. Political parties have increasingly adopted the same language. Like many centrist parties elsewhere in the world, the ANC made a profound error of political judgment in indulging organized xenophobia rather than opposing it.
The two parties that have surged forward in these elections, ActionSA and the MKP, have both actively supported the xenophobic street thuggery that forced up to 150,000 migrants, including refugees and other documented migrants, from the country in a matter of months.
This right-wing mobilization, which includes fascist elements, does not only target migrants. It increasingly argues that South Africa has too many rights, that the Constitution should be changed to do away with some of these rights, and that strong leaders should be freed from democratic constraints.
The result is a political paradox. South Africa faces one of the most severe crises of unemployment and inequality anywhere in the world, yet the electoral beneficiaries of popular anger are largely forces advocating policies that will deepen inequality as they redirect anger toward vulnerable minorities.
Renewing the Left
The Left is also in crisis. For decades, the South African Communist Party (SACP) presented itself as the socialist component of the ANC-led alliance. Yet it remained politically committed to governments that implemented austerity, privatization, and other neoliberal policies. Its leaders participated in those governments while continuing to speak in the language of socialism and working-class liberation. The contradiction between revolutionary language and participation in the administration of neoliberal capitalism became increasingly difficult to ignore.
This contradiction has never been satisfactorily resolved. Earlier this year, the SACP proposed convening a “Conference of the Left,” inviting organizations including the ANC and Zuma’s MKP, which had been on the streets with the xenophobic mobs. How could a conference claim to unite the Left while including a governing party responsible for decades of neoliberal economic policy and a political formation associated with state capture, ethnic chauvinism, and xenophobia? The independent South African Federation of Trade Unions (SAFTU) considered the invitation carefully and decided not to participate. Other progressive organizations, such as Abahlali baseMjondolo, took similar positions.
Working-class unity is indispensable, but it must be based on principles and a shared program. A Left that abandons its defining commitments in pursuit of alliances with corrupt or reactionary organizations will not resolve the present crisis. It will only deepen it.
Rebuilding Independent Working-Class Power
The answer cannot be to demand that workers and the poor continue supporting political organizations that have repeatedly failed them. Nor can we respond to the advance of the Right with moral denunciations while leaving the underlying conditions of life unchanged.
South Africa needs a new working-class political project rooted in a credible program of economic transformation. But no program, however coherent, will succeed without organized social power. A genuine working-class political alternative must emerge from renewed organization, political education, democratic debate, and collective struggle.
The principles of such a movement cannot be negotiable. It must be independent of employers and the capitalist state, committed to socialism and worker democracy, and resolutely opposed to racism, xenophobia, sexism, patriarchy, and ethnic chauvinism. It must be internationalist in its outlook and rooted in the everyday struggles of workers and poor communities.
Rebuilding working-class power also requires reconnecting workplace struggles with those of communities. Water is a workers’ issue. Electricity is a workers’ issue. Public transport, housing, health care, education, gender-based violence, and the climate crisis are all workers’ issues.
The struggles of an employed factory worker cannot be separated from those of an unemployed young person, a mother trying to feed her children, a shack dweller fighting for water, or a community resisting the destruction of its environment.
The organizations capable of creating a new political alternative will have to emerge from these connected struggles.
South Africa’s democratic transition was a great victory for popular movements across the world. The possibility that its political future could now be shaped increasingly by xenophobic and authoritarian forces should concern everyone committed to democracy, equality, and international solidarity.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-public-sc.title: NYC public school enrollment drops yet again, even as some schools overflow
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-public-sc.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-public-sc.text:
New York City’s public school enrollment declined once again this fall, a trend that’s already added pressure to school budgets, and accelerated calls for closures and mergers that can be divisive in local communities.
As of this month, 863,100 kids were enrolled in the city’s public schools, including the city's 2K, 3K and 4K programs, according to a preliminary count released by the Mamdani administration on Monday.
That’s a 2.6% decline from last year and part of a downward trend that has continued for more than a decade. The exception to that was in 2023, when public schools saw an influx of migrant students.
According to city data, the school system has lost roughly 200,000 students over the past ten years, even as it has expanded public early childhood programs.
Experts have said the decline is driven by lower birth rates and families with children leaving the city. The decline is not unique to New York City: dwindling public school enrollment is affecting school districts and upending education budgets across the country.
Some of the steepest enrollment declines have been concentrated around central Brooklyn, the Bronx and Washington Heights, according to a report the city comptroller released last month. Schools chancellor Kamar Samuels has said 30,000 students attend small or underenrolled schools.
But enrollment is not declining evenly across the nation’s largest school system. Highly sought-after schools in parts of Manhattan and Brooklyn are exploring additions to accommodate students, even as schools in adjacent neighborhoods see their rosters shrink.
Samuels has called the enrollment decline one of the system’s biggest challenges. Over the summer, he convened working groups in five districts across the city to develop community-driven solutions to the intertwined issues of declining enrollment, class size, and segregation.
“We have to figure out what is the thing that we are going to do on behalf of our most marginalized young people, oftentimes, but on behalf of every single child in your district,” Samuels said at the time.
Samuels has said he expects to form similar working groups throughout the city.
Small schools are expensive because they still need enough administrators and teachers to oversee and instruct students. At the same time, many small schools can’t afford art programs, advanced courses or extracurriculars, putting their students at an educational disadvantage.
Ana Champeny, vice president for research at the Citizens Budget Commission, said the enrollment decline shows a “worrisome trend leading to schools that are too small to be efficient or effective, underutilized buildings, and ultimately, funding inequities between schools.”
Champeny said the city should end its practice of funding schools based on previous enrollment levels – known as “hold harmless” – that’s been in place most years since the Covid pandemic, and that more mergers and closures have to be on the table.
But past efforts to merge and close schools have been explosive, and decreasing funding for schools can cause a political backlash.
Mamdani administration officials did not respond to questions about whether there would be funding cuts related to declining enrollment this year.
City Hall spokesperson Penelope Birnbaum said the enrollment numbers underscore the need to address the city’s affordability crisis, and emphasized the investments made in free childcare, including 2K.
“With this enrollment data, we’re seeing the implications of the affordability crisis in real time – birth rates are down, immigration has slowed, and New Yorkers are leaving the city they love,” said Birnbaum. “We’ve taken major steps towards building a city that is affordable and livable, including through the launch of 2-K this fall, but this data is proof that we cannot stop or slow down.”

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-falls-fur.title: MTA falls further behind on $2B in upgrades to NYC subway signals, consultant finds
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-falls-fur.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-falls-fur.text:
The MTA has fallen further behind schedule on a massive effort to upgrade aging signal technology that guides trains on some of the city’s busiest subway lines, according to a report published Monday by a consultant for the transit agency.
The signals will replace 1930s-era technology with new systems designed to allow trains to run faster and closer together. The agency’s consultant last year found the signal upgrades had faced months of delays, and the new report found that unanticipated infrastructure repairs and software issues have pushed the installation back even more.
The report stated the upgrades to signals on the A, C and E lines running along Eighth Avenue were running 15 months behind schedule and wouldn’t be completed until January 2029. The consultant reported another eight months of delays in the project to add new signals on the F and E lines in eastern Queens, which is also expected to wrap in January 2029. And the effort to upgrade the signals on the G line, which has caused regular service disruptions for riders, is delayed another 14 months and a final determination for a complete date is still being considered, the report found.
The consultant noted the new signal technology was expected to be operational months before each project wraps. The construction timelines published in the report also include other technical work.
MTA officials last year blamed delays in signal upgrades on contractors the agency hired and a lack of engineering expertise in the field of signal work. The agency earlier this year said the delays in the G line work were in part due to leaks that workers found in the Greenpoint Tube under Newtown Creek, which took a year to repair.
MTA construction chief Jamie Torres-Springer said Monday that riders were already seeing benefits from the disruptions to G train service, noting the agency has added new elevators and modern subway cars to the line.
“I just want to be clear that as we’re doing this work, the benefits to riders accrue incrementally even before we get to turning on the CBTC program and it’s a good new story in that way,” Torres-Springer said.
He said the delays to the Eighth Avenue project were “primarily due to software issues” and the "unavailability" of time to test the technology on subway tracks.
Dr. Nabil Ghaly, a signal technology expert who issued the report for the MTA consultant at the agency’s committee meeting, said it was difficult to upgrade New York City’s subway signals because the system runs around the clock.
“The [independent engineering consultant] recognizes that implementing [communications-based train control] on an existing transit system that operates 24/7 presents operational, technical and physical complexities,” Ghaly said.
The consultant estimated the combined cost of the three delayed signal projects at more than $2 billion. The MTA earlier this month also started work on another $2 billion project to upgrade the signals on the Fulton-Liberty line, where the A and C trains run in Brooklyn and Queens.
Modern signals are already operational on the entire lengths of the L and 7 lines. The MTA also completed an upgrade to the signals on the F line in Brooklyn last year.
Officials said they plan to release a new report on Wednesday that lays out the MTA’s vision of implementing the new signal technology on every subway line.

https://citylimits.org/new-federal-rule-.title: New Federal Rule Threatens Housing for Thousands of NYC Families With Mixed Immigration Status
https://citylimits.org/new-federal-rule-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-federal-rule-.text:
Share This Article
Advocates say they intend to fight implementation of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule, which they say could force some 2,500 New York households to give up their federal housing assistance or separate from family.
On Nov. 10, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued a final rule requiring households in federally funded public housing to verify citizenship, potentially affecting thousands of families with mixed immigration statuses.
The new rule, which was proposed earlier this year and would go into effect on Dec. 14, tightens eligibility requirements for federal rental assistance for immigrants especially.
Currently, undocumented immigrants are not eligible for federal housing subsidies. But they are allowed to live in federally subsidized properties—like New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) buildings—with other qualifying family members in what’s called “mixed-status” households.
Those households pay a higher percentage of the rent to account for the ineligible family member, receiving what’s known as “a prorated rate.”
Under the new rule, every member of a household that receives federal rental assistance—including those with Section 8 vouchers, or who live in Section 9 public housing—will be required to provide proof of their citizenship or an immigration status that’s eligible for federal subsidies, as outlined in federal regulations called Section 214.
Even immigrants who are in the United States legally could be at risk under that requirement, experts said.
“People can be in the United States lawfully, but they are not necessarily eligible for rental assistance under Section 214,” explained Lucy Newman, the supervising attorney of Legal Aid Society’s public housing unit, adding, “that’s a really significant part of this.”
Immigration statuses that are eligible for federal housing assistance include green card holders, asylees or refugees, survivors of human trafficking, self petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act, immigrants admitted for lawful temporary assistance, amongst others.
Non-eligible immigration statuses include U visa holders, DACA recipients, TPS holders, and undocumented immigrants.
Newman explained that on average, three out of four members of New York City’s mixed-status households have an immigration status that’s eligible for federal assistance, and warns that the new rule could trigger those eligible members to move, or force them to separate from loved ones.
A coalition of 22 state attorneys general, including New York’s, wrote a letter to HUD Secretary Scott Turner in April opposing the rule change, which would impact 2,500 mixed-status households in New York.
“We and other activists are working on delaying or stopping the implementation of this, including considering legal action,” Newman said.
Public comments submitted in opposition of the rule argued that it’s unnecessary because non-eligible household members don’t receive federal subsidies, and that it would displace households without freeing up assistance for others.
“It is actually more expensive to fund fully eligible households, because the subsidy has to cover all of the people in that household,” Newman explained. “If this rule goes into effect, the overall situation is they end up helping fewer people because the program will cost more.”
According to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan policy group, nearly 80,000 people in 20,000 households nationwide could be at risk of losing their homes; 96 percent are people of color, including 86 percent who are Latino.
After California and Texas, New York State has the third-highest number of mixed-status households in public housing.
NYCHA, which administers a Section 8 program as well Section 9 public housing developments, did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the rule change. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development, which also administers Section 8 locally, referred questions to the mayor’s office.
In a statement to City Limits, Mayor Zohran Mamdani expressed his opposition to the rule, while reassuring New Yorkers receiving federal housing assistance that last week’s announcement will not result in an immediate change to their subsidy.
“In New York City, we believe everyone deserves a safe, affordable place to call home, regardless of where they were born or their immigration status,” Mamdani said. “The City is evaluating every available option to defend New Yorkers and protect their access to housing. Because no one should live in fear of losing their home because of where they come from.”
The Division of Housing and Community Renewal (DHCR), which is part of the New York State Homes and Community Renewal and oversees some Section 8 programs, said it will “continue to analyze the potential impact of these proposed changes.”
In an interview with FOX, HUD Secretary Turner referred to the rule as closing a “decades-old loophole.”
“We are ending the subsidization of Biden’s open borders, upholding the rule of law, closing the decades-old ‘mixed status roommate’ loophole, and safeguarding American taxpayers’ dollars,” a HUD spokesperson said in a statement to City Limits, saying the change will free up $218 million in subsidies for “fully eligible American households.”*
But housing advocates note that no subsidies are currently offered to people who are not eligible for the program.
“Mixed-status families subsidize HUD housing for everyone else,” said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, director of the Evictions Initiative Project and managing attorney at the National Housing Law Project.
“If these families are forced to leave, there will be less funding available for HUD-assisted housing, which reduces the housing supply and worsens the housing crisis for everyone,” Tran-Leung added. “This is especially important in a place like New York, where there is definitely a shortage of housing, and especially a shortage of affordable housing.”
Still, she and other housing advocates are urging people to be patient and remain calm.
“There is a danger of families self-evicting right now, even though they have the right to stay where they are,” Tran-Leung emphasized. “They don’t yet have to leave until this rule goes into effect, and advocates are trying to think or trying to push different avenues for potentially blocking or delaying that effective date.”
Housing attorneys explained that after Dec. 14, should the rule take effect, tenants would have 90 days to prove their eligible immigration status. Even if a housing authority decides that someone doesn’t qualify, advocates emphasized, residents still have due process rights.
“That’s another thing we want to stress: there is supposed to be a process that happens, so it should not be just something that happens overnight,” Tran-Leung explained.
Advocates linked the rule change to the Trump administration’s aggressive crackdown on immigration. HUD attempted to advance a similar policy in 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term, but President Joe Biden later withdrew it.
“What we see is Trump and HUD exploiting economic crises to destroy the federal housing programs by sowing division and scapegoating immigrants,” Tran-Leung said.
Another implication of the rule, Newman explained, is less stability for immigrant New Yorkers who are on the brink of obtaining legal status.
“We’ve had clients who over the span of 18 months are now green card holders,” she said. “There are many people who are living in those households who may be able to adjust to an eligible immigration status in the near future.”
For now, however, Newman said, “people need to know that until it goes into effect, nothing has changed. They should not move, or evict out of fear.”
*This story was updated after initial publication to include comment from HUD.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/will-lawrenc.title: Heading to Congress, Will Lawrence Still Has Some Questions
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/will-lawrenc.author: Liza Featherstone
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/will-lawrenc.text:
Heading to Congress, Will Lawrence Still Has Some Questions
The election of left-wing environmental activist Will Lawrence to Congress from Michigan offers hope for American democracy. But in a conversation with Jacobin, the congressman-elect is sober about just how much our system can change.
Will Lawrence has been part of every anti-oligarchic organizing effort that has mattered over the last two decades: Barack Obama–era climate activism, Occupy Wall Street, Sunrise Movement, housing justice, the Bernie Sanders campaigns, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), and resistance to artificial intelligence data centers. Before the recent midterm election, the thirty-six-year-old East Lansing, Michigan native was exactly the sort of candidate who, according to conventional wisdom, could maybe beat establishment Democrats in liberal blue districts but would lack traction against the Right in a general election.
Yet on Election Day, Lawrence proved that conventional wisdom wrong. He flipped a Republican seat in Mid Michigan and is now headed to Congress.
Lawrence is not the only one showing that an anti-oligarchy, pro-working-class politics can succeed in purple and red America. From Maine to Montana, Bernie Sanders–style politics beat Trumpism across the nation. In Washington, DC’s incoming Congress, Lawrence, reached by phone while walking through the tunnels of Capitol Hill, joins numerous “regular people, many of whom are complete outsiders,” newly taking their place in Congress.
They’re not just “regular” in the sense of not being billionaires. They’re also not career politicians. They “owe nothing to anybody” in power, Lawrence emphasizes, and they “have a mandate to root out corruption, get money out of politics, deliver economic security for their constituents, stop stupid wars, and stabilize the climate.”
But Lawrence has serious questions about what’s possible in this moment.
“We can undo everything that Trump has done,” he vows. “We can undo the Big Beautiful Bill. We can restore SNAP [the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program], Medicaid, and the ACA. We can take action to lower prices in certain sectors,” he says:
And yet, economic volatility will continue. People will continue to feel that the future is looking worse. And we’ll still be stuck with the questions of, “What is America’s global role in the twenty-first century? How do we deal with the billionaires, the oligarchs, at the commanding heights of the economy?”
He pauses, aware that he’s brought down the mood. I feel a bit superficial bringing us back to the elections, asking how he won his congressional seat, but it turns out not to be a change of subject or tone. Lawrence’s refusal of sunny platitudes continues.
“Acknowledging the despair and disillusionment that people feel as rational and legitimate, and then drawing on those who have come before, to remember that people have dealt with adversity, uncertainty, and volatility and have fought back against the powerful of their time to win the rights and freedoms and quality of life that we have until recently enjoyed,” is crucial, he says. “The social compact of the New Deal era was fought for and won with blood.”
Lawrence’s parents, like my own, worked at Michigan State University, and I’ve spent a lot of time in his hometown, a land grant university town bordered by flat cornfields on one side and Lansing, the state capitol, on the other. I’m not surprised his bleak honesty and capacious politics could draw Michiganders together.
Lawrence unseated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, a Trumper who staunchly supported the war in Iran and opposed extending the Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits at the beginning of this year. The district backed Donald Trump in 2024 but has flipped so often that it is regarded as a bellwether for the presidential election.
“There are a lot of bad people,” Lawrence continues,
and a lot of reasons to feel disillusioned when bad people manipulate their way into having a lot of power. And yet we have it inside of us to become the better versions of ourselves, to build a better version of our society. [The campaign] was all about that: giving people a reason for hope, creating space for community, for people to make friends and get to know each other, challenge each other, challenge themselves to take action and to take responsibility.
“And it did,” he allows, passing the hopium pipe for just a second, “make me feel more optimistic about democracy. There is some juice left.”
Lawrence isn’t calling himself a socialist these days. He let his DSA membership lapse, which he announced during the campaign, wanting to focus, he told CNN at the time, on uniting the district. He said that he wanted his constituents to feel he represented and was listening to them, rather than any specific organization.
Whether he was wearing his green-and-white Spartans hat at the tailgating parties on Michigan State’s massive campus, where the student vote shapes elections more than it does anywhere else in the nation; or canvassing or conducting town halls across the district, in small cities and towns like Grand Ledge and Brighton — this approach clearly resonated, winning over independent voters and even Republicans.
“The more I continued with the campaign,” he tells Jacobin, “the more I just chafed at some of the attempts to label me as ‘socialist,’ ‘communist,’ or whatever, in a way that was about making people fear me.” So he decided, “Let’s just focus on the values and the issues. When we start there, there’s tons of common ground.”
As he points out, he’s not alone among the incoming left wing of the party in taking this approach. While the new Congress includes New York City socialists Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, it also includes Lawrence’s fellow Michigander, incoming Senator Abdul El-Sayed, who beat a Republican with a Bernie Sanders platform and no “socialist” label; or Troy Jackson in Maine, who did the same.
“With this incoming freshman class that is large and historic,” Lawrence says, “people identify themselves in a variety of ways: progressive, moderate, none of the above. But everybody campaigned on the same issues. And they feel a mandate to deliver change.”
It has been striking to see the continuity, across the country, of Sanders-style issues in the winning candidates’ platforms: Medicare for All, taxing the rich, childcare, defunding the war machine, a moratorium on AI data centers. It is a mandate against billionaires and for the common good. And, Lawrence suggests, there may be a variety of ways to express that:
For the self-identified Left, my push is not to get too hung up on labels or making assumptions about others based on their labels. . . . The project of reconstituting the social and political compact for the twenty-first century has to be based in the bid for a supermajority of the people of this country. And there is no supermajority of this country who currently identifies with any common label. So, we have to be willing to listen beyond that and then find new symbols and perhaps new labels that allow us to establish that majority.
Lawrence feels strongly about changing the direction of foreign policy, and this incoming class has a mandate to do that, probably for the first time this century. But he’s very worried about whether it can be done — and not for the reasons I’m expecting, like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and defense lobbyists.
“For me, this is one of the lessons of Joe Biden’s administration, which I do really believe tried to do something good for the American working class and wanted to deliver on economic security,” yet was “so militarist and hawkish.” He points to the administration’s position on Israel and Palestine: “It completely undid the coalition that Bernie and Biden supporters had painstakingly built together for the sake of building a united front to defeat Trump.”
Lawrence is worried about whether, in America, we can have peacetime social democracy. “Social democracy without a Cold War posture is unproven,” he says. “Social democracy was forged in the context of the Cold War. And in the attempt to reforge a social democracy [today], there will be those, like in the Biden administration, who believe that a new Cold War is a natural part of that project.”
He’s right: During the Cold War, workers’ material gains — including civil rights for black Americans — could often be framed as part of an anti-communist argument that capitalism could deliver a better life for the working class than communism. And a state of permanent war readiness fueled the economy, bringing billions of federal dollars into defense spending and creating millions of good jobs.
Lawrence worries that many Democrats still can’t separate militarism and social democracy, that they believe that ongoing war can “clarify the resolve and the sense of national purpose, but also that it’s the only way that we can have an economy which is prosperous, with a broad-based growth that includes a strong deal for the working class.” That won’t cut it today, he says: “I don’t believe that that will work for the twenty-first century, because the conditions of the political economy are different. It’s not 1946 anymore. And we’re not going to recreate the economic conditions that existed then. So we have to find a different way.”
One of the fights that politically shaped Lawrence, a Sunrise activist, was the campaign for the Green New Deal during the Biden administration; it seems possible that an energy transition off fossil fuels could contain the seeds of that “different way.” Maybe in Congress, Lawrence can help bring those ideas back to political life.
Maybe. But he’s certainly not overpromising. It’s jarring to talk to a politician who has thought so deeply about the perils and limitations of our moment and speaks so frankly about them. Not only does Lawrence not think perpetual geopolitical conflict can deliver for Americans. (Americans, squeezed by gas prices during the war in Iran, seem to agree.) “I really don’t want to see World War III. It’s as likely as not that that’s where things are headed,” he warns. “Preventing that is one of my main missions.”

https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.title: Man charged with murder in shooting at NJ vigil that left 1 dead, 4 injured
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.text:
A New Jersey man is facing murder charges in connection with a shooting at a candlelight vigil in Elizabeth last month that left one person dead and four others injured, prosecutors announced Monday.
Travon Holmes, 29, is charged with first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder and four counts of attempted murder, according to the Union County Prosecutor's Office.
The shooting happened around 9:30 p.m. on Oct. 26 during a candlelight vigil at the intersection of Elmwood Place and Irvington Avenue in Elizabeth, authorities said.
Five people were shot, including 26-year-old Steve Scott of Edison, who was pronounced dead at the scene. The four other victims were taken to a local hospital for treatment, officials said.
Holmes was arrested Friday, Nov. 13, in Elizabeth and is being held at the Essex County Jail, prosecutors said.
The investigation remains ongoing. Attorney information for Holmes was not immediately available to Gothamist.

https://gothamist.com/news/united-airlin.title: United Airlines says system outage affecting departing flights is resolved
https://gothamist.com/news/united-airlin.author: Phil Corso
https://gothamist.com/news/united-airlin.text:
United Airlines said it has resolved a widespread technology outage that affected some departing flights Monday evening.
The airline acknowledged the outage in a post on X shortly before 5 p.m.
"We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," the first post said.
In an update shortly after 6 p.m., it said the issue had been resolved but did not say what caused it or how many flights were affected.
The outage comes just three days after a nationwide ground stop caused thousands of flight cancellations and delays, including at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark airports. Federal officials attributed that disruption to a telecommunications failure.
It also comes as customers of several major banks reported trouble accessing their online accounts Monday. There is no indication the outages are connected.
United advised passengers to check their flight status through its app or website.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://gothamist.com/news/can-talking-t.title: Can talking to protesters help the NYPD avoid clashes? One expert sees promise.
https://gothamist.com/news/can-talking-t.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/can-talking-t.text:
The NYPD’s new plan for policing protests will encourage police officers and civilian leaders to communicate directly with demonstration organizers, the mayor and the police commissioner said Monday.
This dialogue-based approach to protests has been implemented in London, Columbus, Ohio and Portland, Oregon. New York will be the largest U.S. city to try the approach.
Scholars who have studied and designed such strategies say the change could build trust between police and protesters, help police get more reliable information if trouble starts, and help avoid heavy-handed policing tactics.
“I think it's a very positive move. It is a reform that I think is grounded in logic,” said Professor Clifford Stott, a British scholar whose expertise is crowd behavior and public order policing.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced Monday the department would disband the Strategic Response Group, a controversial unit that responds to mass demonstrations but is also trained in counterterrorism response. With the announcement, Mamdani made good on a campaign promise to rejigger how the NYPD responds to protests.
If implemented correctly, the new approach could be an important step for the NYPD to more effectively police demonstrations, but there are inherent risks involved, Stott said.
Critics have long complained that officers assigned to SRG are trained in counterterrorism operations while they also respond to protests protected by the First Amendment. Mamdani said that will no longer be the case.
“The need to combine an anti-terrorist response with a protest response is no longer needed,” he said. ”I think that the move towards a dialogue-led approach is absolutely in line with what needs to be done.”
In addition to civilians and officers tasked with communicating with protest organizers, the plan will also create a new unit of NYPD officers who will make arrests at demonstrations if necessary.
‘Community dialogue’
Stott, who helped develop the model in Columbus, said if police are actively communicating with demonstrators, officers will likely not have to rely on tactics like encircling protesters or deploying gas to disperse crowds.
Those tactics have been prohibited under the plan Mamdani and Tisch unveiled Monday.
By communicating with protesters, police are also better able to identify a small number of people in a crowd who might veer into committing crimes, Stott added.
“It certainly makes it easier because there is a more cooperative relationship between police and crowds, protest organizers,” Stott said. “And through that collaborative relationship, it becomes much easier for the police to understand where people are present who are beginning to disrupt the harmony.”
He added that if protesters trust police more, they’re more likely to share valuable information with officers.
“So the quality of their information goes up exponentially, and their awareness of potentially disruptive situations occurs much earlier than it might otherwise,” Stott said.
He added that dialogue with protesters could also prompt demonstrators to de-escalate situations on their own.
The approach is not without its risks, Stott said. This will be the first time the NYPD will rely on civilians to communicate with protesters, which could create problems when there are both protesters and counter-protesters, he said. Proper training and management could help, he said.
An overhaul of the practices has strong support from some city lawmakers, including Councilmembers Chi Osse and Lincoln Restler.
Restler told Gothamist Monday that the plan laid out by Mamdani and Tisch on Monday is modeled after best practices in cities like Columbus.
“Unfortunately, on too many occasions, there is an antagonistic dynamic between the NYPD and protesters,” Restler said. “I really am hopeful that having civilian leads kind of managing the engagement with the folks protesting can avoid antagonistic dynamics and prevent issues from escalating.”
New unit
In the statement announcing the changes Monday, Tisch said she backs the reforms in part because they will keep both New Yorkers and officers safe.
“I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat,” Tisch said.
In addition to banning the practice of police encircling protesters, the new rules block the use of tear gas and long guns by officers. The department will also create a new unit called the Patrol Support Division, staffed with trained officers who will be tasked with making arrests at demonstrations if necessary.
The plan drew some criticism by progressive groups because of the creation of the new unit.
The Justice Committee, a progressive police reform advocacy group, said in a statement it was pleased with “first steps” by Mamdani, but was concerned the reforms could be a rebranding of SRG.
“We have serious questions and concerns related to whether what’s being called 'disbanding the SRG' may turn out to be rebranding and reshuffling SRG officers and functions,” Loyda Colón, the executive director of the Justice Committee said.
The Legal Aid Society also commended Mamdani on the changes, but said in a statement the new plan would need “vigilant oversight” to ensure the tactics used by SRG are not repeated.
Police unions who represent officers in the Strategic Response Group are also skeptical of the shift, but for different reasons.
“Mayor Mamdani is showing his true colors: He's willing to put your safety and police officers' safety at risk to appease his radical base,” Patrick Hendry, the president of the Police Benevolent Association said in a statement. “So the next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/l.title: London’s Car-Free Oxford Street Is a Lesson for Mamdani’s Fifth Avenue Redesign
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/l.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/l.text:
Fifth Avenue closed to traffic on some weekends around the holidays in years past, as seen here 2022. Photo: Kevin Duggan
Mayor Mamdani should take a page out of London’s successful pedestrianization of Oxford Street, and banish cars from Fifth Avenue in Midtown and other shopping hubs as the holiday season rounds the corner, advocates said.
The British capital saw surges in foot traffic, spending and international visitors after the city removed cars from the globally famous retail corridor last month.
“The numbers are in: footfall *and* spending are up on Oxford Street,” London Mayor Sadiq Khan posted on Bluesky on Nov. 9. In the larger West End area, spending increased by 13 percent in the first six days of the conversion.
Three weeks ago, city transportation officials in the Big Smoke banned buses, taxis and even bikes from a roughly 0.6-mile stretch of Oxford Street. The intervention was a decade in the making and six years late under Khan’s mayoralty, and aimed at improving street safety, cutting pollution and revitalizing ailing businesses on the strip.
Livable streets advocates on our side of the pond immediately seized on the promising data to bolster the case for pedestrianizing Fifth Avenue, Manhattan’s dominant shopping artery and the city’s closest equivalent to Oxford Street. The idea dates back to 2017, when ex-Mayor Bloomberg’s former DOT Commissioner Janette Sadik-Khan proposed pedestrianizing three of the strip’s five lanes for 25 blocks south of Central Park, while leaving the remaining two lanes for buses.
But business titans along the ritzy row have foiled successive efforts by both mayors Bill de Blasio and Eric Adams to reclaim space from cars. Mamdani now has a chance to stand up to the monied interests and follow London’s lead, advocates said. “New York, it’s time to pedestrianize Fifth Avenue,” said Doug Gordon, a co-host of the War on Cars podcast.
In recent years, the city has closed the corridor to traffic on some December weekends to make room for holiday shopping crowds. But former Mayor Eric Adams scaled those events back, despite a 6.6-percent bump in spending during the car-free days.
One street safety advocate said the upcoming holiday season provides an opportunity for Mamdani to go bigger than his predecessors and set the tone for pedestrian-first shopping streets throughout the Big Apple.
“I’m optimistic that the numbers [on Oxford Street] will continue to remain pretty high and it’s something that New York should be taking very seriously,” said Samir Lavingia, the second vice chair of Manhattan Community Board 5, who noted he’s not speaking on behalf of the board. “I would love to see him lead with something visionary in Midtown,”
Lavingia suggested that Mamdani could start with an entire month of a car-free Fifth Avenue, and later bring the conversion to other busy shopping areas, like SoHo or Williamsburg. “That would be a good way to kick it off,” he said. “For people to change their behavior, it needs to be multiple days in a row.”
Two mayors have attempted to redesign Fifth Avenue, starting with de Blasio’s busway in 2020, which would have banned through-traffic for private vehicles between 57th and 34th Streets.
After big business fat cats pushed back against the idea of banning through-traffic, de Blasio watered down his proposal to allow through-traffic for private vehicles. But even the diluted plan never made it out of the planning phase before he left office.
The Eric Adams administration at first proposed a different plan with bus and protected bike lanes, before ditching the cycle path and releasing a $350 million overhaul called the “Future of Fifth.”
The plan would have widened sidewalks while preserving the majority of the roadbed for private cars. It would have also slowed bus commutes by cutting the dedicated bus lanes from two to one. The proposal received strong support from the Fifth Avenue Association, an influential group representing businesses and institutions along the corridor like the Trump Organization, St. Patrick’s Cathedral and Bergdorf Goodman.
London rerouted buses away from Oxford Street ahead of its pedestrianization. Relocating buses away from Fifth Avenue could be a challenge, since its double-wide bus lanes serve as a key south-bound surface transit artery connecting to all other boroughs, and nearby Madison Avenue serves the same function for buses heading north.
Lavingia said if Mamdani wanted to move buses elsewhere, he could work with the state-run MTA to look at alternatives in its upcoming borough-wide bus network redesign. “It’s an opportunity for the mayor to say, ‘look, I would love to see the buses off of Fifth Avenue to pedestrianize it,” he said.
The Adams administration wanted to start construction in 2028, but it’s unclear if Mamdani’s Department of Transportation still plans to move forward with the redesign. A DOT rep declined to specify the agency’s plans for Fifth Avenue, and instead cited Commissioner Mike Flynn’s Vision Zero Reimagined platform that called for more pedestrian-focused designs in the city.
“The Mamdani administration will be developing the city’s first-ever pedestrian-priority and pedestrian-only districts and we look forward to sharing more soon,” said Vin Barone. A spokesperson for the Fifth Avenue Association said it was still too early to measure success on Oxford Street, but its CEO emphasized the pressing need for more sidewalk space.
“Everyone can see Fifth Avenue pedestrians deserve wider, more attractive and sustainable sidewalks,” its CEO, Madelyn Wils, told Streetsblog. “We have studied many global examples that prove the value of investing in streetscape projects that increase the quality of conditions for pedestrians.”
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-new-day-arr.title: A new day arrives on Brooklyn's Flatbush Avenue as redesign gives bus riders priority
https://gothamist.com/news/a-new-day-arr.author: Carol Chen, Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/a-new-day-arr.text:
City officials on Tuesday unveiled an overhaul to a stretch of Flatbush Avenue designed to speed up commutes for tens of thousands of bus riders.
The redesign revolves around two new bus lanes in the center of the road between Grand Army Plaza and Livingston Street, where passenger cars are now banned 24 hours a day. Six concrete bus boarding islands were installed to make it easier for riders to board. The changes pushed most car traffic into a single lane in each direction.
Crews also added 36 new bike racks to the street, as well as fresh bus shelters, benches and leaning bars at every single bus boarding island, according to the city transportation department. The changes removed 41 parking spaces, but also added new loading zones for trucks and deliveries on side streets.
The city transportation department also said the new bus lanes will speed up commutes on the B41, which previously averaged 4 mph along the corridor. City officials claimed the upgrades would help 120,000 daily riders, which also includes those who use the nearby B67, B45 and B103 routes.
The redesign is the most ambitious bus lane project the city transportation department has completed since Mayor Zohran Mamdani took office at the start of the year.
“Flatbush Avenue is the foundation for the future of bus service in New York City … Bus riders are tired of waiting — waiting for the bus that never comes, waiting for the bus to crawl through traffic and waiting for government to care about their precious time,” Mamdani said in a statement.
The changes cover only about a mile of Flatbush Avenue, but officials plan to eventually implement similar redesigns that give buses priority all the way to Kings Plaza. The transportation department is also mulling an overhaul to Grand Army Plaza to make the traffic circle more hospitable to pedestrians.
The new bus lanes prohibit regular vehicle traffic but allow emergency and paratransit vehicles to use them.
Bus riders on the B41 bus said they already noticed a slight improvement in their commutes
Monica O’Neill, 30, who rides the route every other day to get to work, said “traffic goes a little bit faster than usual” since the buses no longer have to stop in front of restaurants and shops.
Some locals were still getting used to the new street design, having never seen a bus island where riders wait to board in between lanes of traffic instead of the sidewalk.
Nadine Barry, 45, worried that cars would crash into the boarding islands.
“I think pedestrians…are the first priority,” she said. “Because living in New York, New York is always congested.”
Workers at Antonio’s Pizza on Flatbush Avenue were up in arms about the bus lane, claiming it’s already pushed customers away from the slice shop.
“This place used to be full around 12 o’clock with all the construction guys, plumbing guys,” said Arlind Kirkuti, 20, who’s worked at the shop for five years. “Now they can’t even find parking, so they don’t even stop by no more.”
Sy Hannan, who runs a painting business in the area, said he might have to charge more for jobs in the area because it takes longer to find parking and haul his equipment to the location.
“If I had to work for one of these people, I'd have to park several blocks away and haul my gear, and that costs the client more,” Hannan said.
