TEFAF Maastricht, the European Fine Art Foundation’s Dutch art fair, has shared its 2027 lineup. It will take place at Maastricht’s MECC, a major convention center, and is set to include an international roster of 277 galleries. Participating galleries hail from Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East, and Asia.
The fair will include two special sections: Showcase, which features nine emerging dealers, all showing at TEFAF for the first time, and Focus, which features seven galleries that focus on a single artist or curatorial idea. 2026’s Focus featured French Realist painting, African Modernist ceramics, and abstract expressionism. The fair is known for art by European old masters, but it also includes modern and contemporary art, including photography, jewelry, and works on paper.
Some of the newcomers for 2027 include Galerie AB and Galerie Édouard Ambroselli, (France); Gallery Arte y Ritual (Spain); Galerie Bei Der Albertina (Austria); Butchoff Antiques (UK); Hazlitt (UK and US); Xavier Hufkens (Belgium); Thomsen Gallery and Martos Gallery (US); and Thaddaeus Ropac (UK, France, Austria, Italy, South Korea). Three new Focus galleries include Daguet-Bresson from France, Edel Assanti from the UK, and Repetto Gallery from Switzerland.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Two PhDs, Three Classes and One EBT Card: A CUNY Adjunct’s Struggle to Make Ends Meet
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Aisha Baiocchi
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
At 37, and with two PhDs, Juliana Nalerio relies on SNAP and Medicaid to get by while teaching as an adjunct professor at the City University of New York.
Nalerio is one of the 11,000 part-time faculty, some earning as little as $7,000 a course, who make the country’s biggest urban public university run.
She teaches one class in the History department at City College, and two English courses at Queens College. This semester, that’s 70 students across three classes. Between Harlem, Flushing and her home in Astoria, Nalerio spends eight hours each week on the commute alone.
GET THE CUNY SCOOP: Subscribe to our new weekly newsletter covering the City University of New York
“I keep telling myself that next year will be better, and if I keep teaching well, and trying to write, it will turn into something more stable,” she told The City Reporter.
In the last two decades, universities across the nation have become more reliant on non-tenure track part-time professors, mostly working on contracts that span less than a year. CUNY is no exception; in fact it is at least 10% ahead of the national average, with part-timers making up 52% of instructional staff.
Glenn Colby, a senior research officer with the American Association of University Professors said he’s observed a steady increase in contingent hires since the 2008 financial crisis, one that’s only continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and the Trump administration’s research budget cuts and attacks on universities.
“The driver of it all is institutions trying to deal with the uncertainty around finances, which is tied to student enrollment and state funding,” Colby said. “And as those issues fluctuate, institutions try to deal with it by saying, well, we’re gonna hire people on contingent appointments because we’re not certain about the future.”
The majority of adjuncts in the United States are highly educated and comparatively underpaid, according to a national study by the College and University Professional Association for Human Relations. Universities are most likely to use adjuncts to teach liberal arts, and nationally they are likely to hire women and minorities for adjunct positions at a much higher rate than full time.
“Adjunct faculty play an indispensable role at CUNY, enriching the educational experience of students through their teaching, expertise and dedication,” university press secretary Noah Gardy said in a statement. “Recognizing the vital role they play, our current labor contract with the PSC significantly increased compensation and continued investments in greater stability and access to health insurance.”
At CUNY, enrollment numbers are rising, but still haven’t passed pre-pandemic highs. Fundraising drives have been heralded as successful, but the university still has a massive $7 billion maintenance backlog as colleges endure floods, leaks and broken elevators.
Against that backdrop, adjunct professors make financial sense for cash-strapped universities. Part-time faculty can also include working professionals who bring on-the-ground experience into the classroom, a significant bonus for CUNY’s pre-professional programs and schools.
‘I Do Unpaid Labor’
But adjuncts like Nalerio may be left out by this model.
Last year, packing advanced degrees from Stanford University and the University of Salamanca in Spain, Nalerio made just $36,000. It is less than a third of what the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says is the average annual income for someone with a doctorate.
According to the most recent Poverty Tracker report by the nonprofit advocacy group Robin Hood, Nalerio’s income puts her well within New York City’s “low income” range, experiencing similar material hardship to those living below the poverty line.
“My goal was never to make a lot of money. I spent a lot of time learning to teach, research and write. But now I’m presented with this problem: the work I’ve trained to do doesn’t line up with the reality of the work right now. So I can do unpaid labor, and hope it gets better, as I do, or leave it all together.”
While dividing her time between campuses in Flushing and Harlem might seem like a burden, this semester is actually easier than last semester, Nalerio says, because her classes in the two boroughs are stacked on different days. The Spring semester had her rushing from her morning Harlem course out to Flushing by the late afternoon, every Tuesday and Thursday, at the mercy of the 7 train and the weather.
Each of the three classes Nalerio teaches this semester is different, and she designs the coursework herself. She has an introductory women and gender studies class, a composition class for international students learning English, and a civilizations after 1500 class at City College, which she’s been teaching the longest.
Brutal University Math
The economics can be brutal. For each course, Nalerio is paid for three teaching hours, and one non-teaching hour, which includes time spent talking to students, grading, and course planning. According to this formula, Nalerio is working only 12 hours a week, with a full 28 hours left over to work other jobs and boost her income.
But that accounting is ludicrous, adjuncts say. Preparing course materials and grading student work takes far longer than an hour a week.
“If you have 70 students on two campuses it is literally impossible,” Nalerio said. She barely has time to eat between classes, much less find another part-time job.
Nalerio’s workload is determined by a union-negotiated contract: adjunct faculty can teach up to nine hours on one campus, and one additional section at another campus, which cannot exceed six hours. She teaches as many course hours as she can, always hoping to pick up more work to pay her bills — but is still working full-time while living on a part-time salary.
“My benefits are also dependent on my course load each semester,” she said, “but I don’t have time to keep track of the 75 students and the Tetris that they’re playing with my pay and my benefits and my life.”
Gardy, the spokesperson, said “CUNY adjunct pay remains highly competitive for a public university” and will be “nearly 75% above the national average” when a new contract goes into effect next summer.
Roommate Life
A full-time assistant professor at the City University teaching the same course load as Nalerio would earn a starting salary of at least $57,000, with generous health and retirement benefits.
Jasmine Bayron, a Hunter College adjunct with a PhD, said it isn’t uncommon for part-timers to struggle to find time for other jobs. Bayron has a number of side gigs, which she tries to set up a year in advance in case any of her courses falls through. Like Nalerio, she also has roommates.
“It’s kind of crazy to spend your entire life in school and then you can’t afford to live by yourself,” Bayron said.
MORE: Past Due – Why CUNY Adjuncts Can’t Get Paid On Time
Colby suggested universities underpay adjuncts because the job pool for contingent labor is so large and little attention is paid within higher education to working conditions for part-timers.
“It’s a challenge to get a full-time faculty position if you don’t have experience teaching and so one thing people do is say, ‘Well, I’ll do this so that I have it on my CV that I’m an experienced teacher.’ But then it becomes a permanent situation for a lot of people,” he said.
‘Their Education Matters’
Five years into adjuncting, Nalerio is still figuring out if it can be a permanent situation for her.
She started teaching at CUNY during her last semester at Stanford in 2022, and says she continued after receiving her PhD because she has New York roots and “drank the Kool Aid” of the university’s mission to serve working class students.
“These people are relying on me — they’re young people with lives,” Nalerio said. “Their education matters. It is an important step, and they’re really important. Serving them is a full-time job.”
Nalerio customizes courses to her students, this past week changing a lecture for her history course at Queens College to better include the large contingent of Latinos in the classroom and showing a documentary about white masculinity in her gender studies class after noticing the students seem disconnected from the original course material.
“I feel a sense of purpose doing it,” she said. “And I know I need more stability, but I love it, and I love the students.”
But Nalerio hasn’t found stability in years. Since coming to New York in 2022, she’s only been able to sublet since because her income is so low and inconsistent that she hasn’t qualified to rent an apartment in her own name.
MORE: ‘A Joke’ Missing State Aid Leaves CUNY Students Stressed
She can’t always afford to eat. She got a dog, for her mental health, and enrolled in SNAP to lift some of the stress off, but she’s still “just getting by.”
The CUPA-HR study found universities pay adjuncts the most in disciplines for which they use them the least, like engineering and architecture. Melissa Fuesting, the report’s co-author, pointed to high demand for graduates of engineering and other programs with direct career placement. A career path for liberal arts can be more difficult to find.
While representatives at CUNY’s Professional Staff Congress have suggested Nalerio apply for administrative jobs at the university, and she’s thought about leaving academia altogether, her heart is set on teaching. She loves ideas, her students, and the institution.
“It’s a one-sided affair,” she said. “Its very clear CUNY doesn’t love me back.”

The Trellis Art Fund, a private foundation in New York, has announced its 2026 Stepping Stone cohort. Each of the twenty artists honored will receive $40,000 installments over two years, totalling in $800,000.
The Stepping Stone grant program was founded in 2024 and awarded $20,000 to artists with promising practices. The nominating committee is composed of more than sixty-five curators, historians, artists, and other art-world professionals.

Kader Attia, curator of the seventh edition of the Kochi–Muziris Biennale (KMB), has announced the focus of the upcoming exhibition will be “the relationship between dreams, memory and repair.” The show will run from December 12, 2027 to March 31, 2028 in the Indian port city of Kochi, Kerala.
In a press release, Attia set the “unpredictability” of dreams and art against AI’s “increasingly predictive logic,” which destroys “our sovereignty over the sources of our dreams.” He also traces the emergence of dreams and memories back through human evolution, where, as a physically weaker species amid the wildness of nature, we began to gather and share memories. According to Attia, the increasing complexity of technology has overtaken human control in how and where our memories develop and are used.
“The art world is one of the last spaces where society co-individuates itself,” Attia says. “Our subjectivity is fragmented, like the internet, an intensely fragmented landscape, yet there we are tracked by the algorithm. Exhibitions are important because they produce emotions, activating new traces in our minds. That is how we produce traces for the future. In the same way we are the traces of our ancestors and of the millions of anonymous subjects who preceded us.”
Attia routes his reflections on thought and subjectivity through the history of Kochi’s harbor—one of India’s largest ports and a historic center for colonial European trade. Despite the lasting “dream of empire” which persists in the mind of Koichi’s residents, the curator argues that it’s possible to reverse exploitative legacies through art.
Dr. Venu V, chair of the Kochi Biennale Foundation, said, “Kader Attia’s multi-layered proposition sets a compelling tone for Kochi–Muziris Biennale 2027. By engaging with history, memory, colonial legacies, and the possibilities of repair, it makes art not merely an aesthetic experience but a means of reflection, dialogue, and understanding.”

Swiss video artist Pipilotti Rist has been named the winner of the 2027 Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts, presented by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Rist will receive the honor in a ceremony taking place April 8, 2027. She will receive a $100,000 cash prize and will undertake a residency at the school that spring.
“Pipilotti Rist has spent four decades using digital tools to dissolve the line between screen, body, building, and landscape,” said MIT Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan in a statement. “Her immersive multimedia installations slow us down, return us to our bodies and the spaces we occupy, and gather us into shared experience, rather than fragmenting our attention.”
Rist is known for her pathbreaking immersive video and light installations investigating the relationships between the body, nature, and technology. Among her most recognized works is 1997’s Ever Is Over All, in which she walks down a city street smashing car windows with a flower; the piece served as the basis for Beyoncé’s 2016 “Hold Up” music video.
“I am kissing your Institute and your feet,” said Rist in a statement. “I am immensely touched and grateful to have this trust and investment in ideas I’ve yet to conceive. I’m honored to receive an award that has been granted to so many of my heroes, and look forward to collaborating closely with the brilliant minds at MIT.”
Established in 1974, the Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts at MIT recognizes important contributions by artists in all fields, and is intended to fund their future creative endeavors. Past winners include David Adjaye, Santiago Calatrava, Agnes Denes, Olafur Eliasson, Isaac Julien, Jeff Wall, Bill Viola, and Pamela Z.

https://www.artforum.com/news/yayoi-kusa.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/yayoi-kusa.text:
Subscribe to

An “Infinity Net” painting by Yayoi Kusama brought in $15.1 million with fees at Sotheby’s in New York last night, setting an auction record for the late artist. The work had arrived to the block carrying an estimate of $10 million to $15 million; the hammer came down at $12.5 million before fees. Artnews reports that the sale followed a four-minute battle between two unnamed clients, both bidding by phone.
The painting, titled No. 3P.B., 1960, is a rare early example of Kusama’s “Infinity Net” series. Begun in 1958, the series is characterized by dense abstract fields of dots swirling across large-scale monochrome canvases. More broadly, it is emblematic of the artist’s obsessive focus on repetition, also embodied in her “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” which gained popularity with the rise of social media, thanks to their selfie-friendly nature. Kusama painted the rich red No. 3P.B. shortly after moving to New York. It was shown in the Whitney Annual of 1961, a forerunner of the Whitney Biennial.
The artist’s previous record was set in 2022 by another early “Infinity Net” work, the white Untitled (Nets), 1959, which went for $10.5 million with fees at Phillips. Since Kusama’s death this past August at the age of ninety-seven, nearly thirty of her works have come to auction. No. 3P.B. was a highlight of the Now and Contemporary Evening Auction, which raked in $268.7 million with fees, an increase of 50 percent over last year’s event. The sale was followed immediately by a single-lot auction of works from the collection of the late Ted and Ruth Baum, which pulled in nearly $110 million with fees, bringing the night’s total to a whopping $378.7 million with fees. Tomma Abts, Firelei Báez, Sam Francis, and Jonas Wood are among the artists who set records alongside Kusama.

Anti-Monuments to Trump
How do we memorialize the Trump era? Plus, an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act, and having a beer with Outarra Watts.
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument.
Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”
Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.
—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy. | Ed Simon

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Raft of New Penalties Eat at Outdoor Dining Owners
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Katie Honan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Restaurant owners could face dozens of new fines as part of the city’s new year-round outdoor dining program, adding more than 10 times the number of penalties faced under a previous version of the program.
Despite a vow by Mayor Zohran Mamdani to cut red tape across city agencies, businesses could face 36 individual violations through the program, from improper winterization coverings to blocking clearance. The changes also include moving up closing time from midnight to 11 p.m.
“You never want to see more small business fines,” Andrew Rigie, the executive director of the New York City Hospitality Alliance, said.
He warned against steep penalties — which start at $200 for the first offense and then rise to $500 for those after — that could discourage more restaurants from taking part.
“The city shouldn’t be using small businesses as an ATM,” he added.
The city’s Department of Transportation, though, says the new fine structure was created to make it easier for restaurant owners to be compliant and stay in the program.
“Outdoor dining has become a beloved part of New York City’s streetscape, and our new year-round program will make it easier for more restaurants to participate by reducing costs associated with the seasonal program,” an agency spokesperson, Will Livingston, said in a statement.
“Our goal is not to issue violations but bring restaurants into compliance with standards set to preserve quality of life for New Yorkers — like establishing clear pedestrian paths, requiring clean, and accessible setups — and that’s why we have a 30-day grace period for restaurants to fix issues before any violation is written.”
The existing outdoor dining program has just two types of penalties for restaurants in the program, which caused confusion for the DOT, restaurants, and at the administrative hearings where violations were dealt with, he added.
Year-round outdoor dining was approved by the City Council in August, increasing the pandemic-era program that helped keep bars and restaurants afloat during indoor shutdowns.
The mayor signed it into law shortly after.
Fans and foes of the new fine structure sounded off last week at a hearing on the new change, sharing a large menu of suggestions.
Stacie Johnson, the district manager of Manhattan’s Community Board 4, had concerns over what constitutes a “clear path” around outdoor cafes.
“The intended clear path for pedestrians on the busiest streets and avenues is being severely encroached upon due to changes in interpretation,” she wrote. “The situation would worsen if a new law permits café enclosures without careful guardrails.”
Some welcomed more violations, so long as they were properly enforced — and not added in as the cost of doing business for restaurants.
Other people expressed concerns over the fully-enclosed structures — which are in demand during cold winter months — noting how dangerous it could be for immunocompromised New Yorkers.
“Outdoor seating must be safe and accessible for ALL disabilities, not just physical ones,” Talia Miele, who posted that she’s disabled with immune deficiency issues, shared online.
Sandra Jaquez, the president of the New York State Latino Restaurant Association, said she fields calls all day long from owners struggling to stay open.
But she was concerned with the increased number of potential fines, even if it provides clarity for the program. She was also concerned about the curfew for outdoor dining changing from midnight to 11 p.m.
“That really could hurt a lot of businesses,” she said about the new time limit. “That one hour, it is significant for us when it comes down to making a profit or losing that night.”
She said the fines could scare businesses away.
“We actually advocated very much to make this program permanent, it was a lifesaver — post-Covid we saw it was something that could be beneficial for some restaurants,” she said.
“Now some of these fines that are just attached to this, it makes it kind of irrelevant to even have this outdoor dining.”

https://hyperallergic.com/how-american-g.title: How “American Gothic” Took On a Life of Its Own
https://hyperallergic.com/how-american-g.author: Lauren Moya Ford
https://hyperallergic.com/how-american-g.text:
How “American Gothic” Took On a Life of Its Own
After decades of collecting pop culture riffs on the iconic 1930 painting, Wanda M. Corn traces the work’s canonization and the life of its maker Grant Wood, whose story remains largely overlooked.
You already know the image by heart: Two stern figures stand before an old wooden house. To the left, a blonde, blue-eyed woman wears an apron and a somber expression. Beside her, an unsmiling man in glasses and overalls grips a pitchfork. Since it was first exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1930, Grant Wood’s painting has joined the ranks of art historical touchstones and shown up in countless ads, books, and memes. But what made this unassuming image so popular, and why does it continue to captivate us today?
In The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon (2026), art historian and curator Wanda M. Corn provides some compelling answers. The author began writing about Wood’s painting in 1981, and she has spent decades amassing an archive of “American Gothic”-related imagery that tracks the farm couple across General Mills cereal ads, Gordon Parks’s 1942 portrait of African-American janitor Ella Watson during his fellowship with the Farm Security Administration, magazine covers, COVID-era cartoons, and other surprising riffs. Her book traces the painting’s history from the controversy behind its creation and the bitter fallout it brought to its hapless maker through to its transformation into a pop culture cornerstone and a symbol of Wood’s home state.

https://hyperallergic.com/eleanor-antin-.title: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works
https://hyperallergic.com/eleanor-antin-.author: Phillip Pyle
https://hyperallergic.com/eleanor-antin-.text:
Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works
The artist filed the complaint six months after terminating her relationship with dealer Richard Saltoun.
Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun. The complaint was filed in New York State Supreme Court on July 29, six months after the artist terminated her relationship with Saltoun’s namesake gallery, which operates locations in New York, London, and Rome.
Filed by the 91-year-old artist’s son and attorney-in-fact, Blaise Antin, and her studio, Paranoid Productions, the suit claims that Saltoun “initially purported to agree to return all of the works it held” upon their business separation at the gallery's London location on January 16. News of the lawsuit was first reported by Artnet.
Saltoun claimed in February that the gallery had returned all of Antin’s works to her family, according to filed documents. However, later that month, the artist’s archivist, citing an inventory produced by Saltoun himself, allegedly discovered that Antin was still missing at least 179 works, the majority of which were still held at the London gallery.

https://hyperallergic.com/vilcek-foundat.title: Vilcek Foundation Launches Open Call for 2027 Grants Offering $200,000 in Funding to US Nonprofits
https://hyperallergic.com/vilcek-foundat.author: The Vilcek Foundation
https://hyperallergic.com/vilcek-foundat.text:
Vilcek Foundation Launches Open Call for 2027 Grants Offering $200,000 in Funding to US Nonprofits
The foundation invites applications from mission-aligned arts and science organizations for grants of up to $20,000 through March 31, 2027.
This week, the Vilcek Foundation announced its third annual open call for grant applications. The organization invites nonprofits whose work aligns with the foundation’s mission to elevate immigrant contributions in the United States and foster an appreciation for the arts and sciences to apply for funding now through March 31, 2027.
The foundation will award a total of $200,000 to US-based nonprofits as a part of its 2027 grants cycle. Individual organizations may apply for a grant of up to $20,000.
Applicants should lead innovative initiatives that generate measurable impact within and beyond their immediate communities. Strong applications demonstrate both a unique vision and clear plan of action for uplifting immigrants, the arts, or the sciences. Qualifying organizations must be recognized as tax-exempt under Section 501(c)(3).
The Vilcek Foundation is actively expanding the geographic reach of its grantmaking with the goal of supporting organizations across all US states and select territories. The 2027 grant cycle aims to support nonprofits based around the country, including those in the following locations not previously represented in the foundation’s grantmaking: Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Iowa, Mississippi, Nevada, South Carolina, South Dakota, West Virginia, Wisconsin, American Samoa, Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and the US Virgin Islands.
Since its founding in 2000, the Vilcek Foundation has remained steadfast in its philanthropic mission. To date, the foundation has provided more than $7 million in grants to nonprofits in 40 states, two US territories, and Washington, DC.
Earlier this month, the foundation announced the 12 organizations receiving funding as a part of its 2026 grants cycle. Situated across the country, the 2026 grantees include the Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts; Counterpublic, whose Triennial is currently on view in St. Louis; Delaware Contemporary Arts; and the Japanese American National Museum.
The 2027 Vilcek Foundation grant period will run from September 1, 2027 through August 31, 2028.
Organizations may apply for either project support or operating support.
Interested nonprofits should submit applications via the foundation’s Grants Portal by 11:59 pm (ET) on March 31, 2027.
For full eligibility requirements and application details, visit vilcek.org/grants.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: ‘O legado do teatro fica no corpo do ator’, diz Marcelo Drummond sobre trajetória de Zé Celso
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: BdF Entrevista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
Após uma luta de muitos anos capitaneada pelo Teatro Oficina Uzyna Uzona, companhia fundada pelo saudoso Zé Celso Martinez Corrêa, a Prefeitura de São Paulo oficializou o Parque Municipal do Rio Bixiga, no centro da capital paulista. A área destinada ao parque fica no cruzamento das ruas Jaceguai e Abolição e pertenceu por cerca de 40 anos ao Grupo Silvio Santos, que pretendia desenvolver projetos imobiliários no terreno.
Ao BdF Entrevista, o ator e diretor Marcelo Drummond, companheiro de Zé Celso e tutor da obra do artista, relata que um dos momentos emblemáticos dessa trajetória ocorreu no sétimo dia da morte do fundador do Teatro Oficina, quando os integrantes da companhia, impedidos de entrar na área, plantaram na calçada da rua um ipê, presente da atriz Fernanda Montenegro por ocasião do casamento de Zé Celso e Marcelo Drummond.
Foi durante essa mobilização na calçada que surgiu a promessa decisiva do promotor de Justiça Silvio Marques, do Ministério Público de São Paulo, para viabilizar o projeto. Drummond conta que Marques esteve no local e, ao cumprimentá-lo, disse: “Olha, eu vou fazer esse parque. Eu não sei como, mas eu vou fazer”. A promessa se cumpriu quando recursos de uma ação judicial, que, segundo o ator, giraram em torno de R$ 65 milhões, foram destinados à Prefeitura de São Paulo para a compra do terreno.
A resolução do impasse trouxe um sentimento de profundo reconhecimento por parte de Marcelo Drummond e da equipe do teatro. “É um cara que faz pela cidade. Eu sou muito grato por ele ter feito uma coisa dessas. Ele ter olhado para a luta que era”, avalia.
A luta pelo parque se conecta com o histórico de resistência e preservação do prédio do Teatro Oficina. Para Drummond, todos esses movimentos se confundem com a própria vida de Zé Celso.
Drummond também fala sobre o legado do companheiro, que tem orgulho de levar adiante, embora pondere que nem sempre isso é plenamente possível. “O legado do teatro fica no corpo do ator. O legado do teatro está na gente continuar fazendo teatro. O fato de continuar fazendo teatro é o legado”, afirma. O ator relembra como a trajetória de ambos se entrelaçou há mais de quatro décadas e fala sobre saudade. “Muitas vezes eu sinto falta dele como uma direção, mas aí aquilo me inspira. Eu procuro me inspirar no que eu imagino que ele faria”, relata.
Marcelo Drummond busca, no momento, organizar livros que reunirão textos antigos de Zé Celso, “desde os tempos de Araraquara”, incluindo escritos inéditos do diretor. “‘O Banquete’ a gente fez, ‘O Fedro’ a gente não produziu, mas ele fez o filme. Então, esses textos vão sair. Tem muita coisa do Zé para sair, que é o legado dele, obviamente”, ressalta.
Questionado sobre a missão de manter a memória de Zé Celso viva, Drummond afirma que é um compromisso que levará para o resto da vida. “Mais do que herdar, eu sou um tutor de uma obra. Mais do que herdeiro, porque é uma delícia ter aqui essas coisas todas, mas é também um fardo. E eu preciso botar isso para fora. Preciso botar que as pessoas conheçam”, resume. Nesse sentido, cita um trecho de “Bacantes” (texto clássico cuja montagem conduzida por Zé tornou-se antológica): “A dor é doce e o fardo é leve”.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Cézanne ‘Arlequin’ Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby’s, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
Paul Cézanne made his name painting apples and mountains. But on Wednesday night, the artist’s somewhat severe picture of a teenager in costume became one of the most expensive Cézannes ever sold at auction, after selling at Sotheby’s New York for $111 million with fees.
Arlequin (1888–90), a colorful painting of a young man in a red-and-black diamond-patterned costume, hit the block at Sotheby’s during its dedicated evening sale for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection. The painting hammered at $99 million.
It failed to beat the previous record of $137.8 million set by La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888–90), which sold at Christie’s in 2022 as part of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen‘s collection. Still, once auctioneer Oliver Barker sold Arlequin tonight, a round of applause followed.
Sotheby’s didn’t publish an estimate for Arlequin prior to the sale, though the painting was expected to bring in around $120 million.
The figure in the painting is Cézanne’s son, Paul, dressed as Harlequin, the mischievous character from Italian commedia dell’arte theater. He wears a pointed hat and an elaborate white collar, and holds a slender baton as he walks across a sharply tilted floor. For someone dressed as a comic character, he looks surprisingly serious.
Cézanne painted the picture in Paris between 1888 and 1890, when he was experimenting with a series of theatrical subjects. There are only four paintings in the group, and Arlequin is the only one still in private hands. The others are in museums, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., the Pola Museum of Art in Japan, and the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.
The painting comes with quite a history. It passed through the hands of several of the great dealers of the early modern art market, including Ambroise Vollard and Paul Rosenberg, before become part of Lord Victor Rothschild’s collection during the 1930s. His son, Lord Jacob Rothschild, later inherited it, and in 1975 it was sold through London’s Lefevre Gallery to Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier.
Before leaving for Argentina, the painting appeared in major exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1929, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1952, and the Tate Gallery in London in 1954. After the Blaquiers bought it, it all but disappeared from public view for half a century.
Sotheby’s had guaranteed the painting before Wednesday’s auction, promising the sellers an undisclosed amount regardless of the outcome. It also secured an irrevocable bid, meaning at least one prospective buyer had committed to bidding before the auction began.
Such arrangements are increasingly common at the top of the art market. According to an analysis by the art-market data firm ARTDAI, just 19 guaranteed Cézanne lots make up 63 percent of the hammer-price value in its database of 640 Cézanne sales. In other words, a small number of exceptionally expensive pictures drive much of the artist’s auction business.
The record-setting Cézanne, La Montagne Sainte-Victoire, hammered at $120 million in 2022, more than twice the price achieved by the artist’s next most expensive auction result, a still life that fetched $60.5 million at Sotheby’s in 1999.
Of course, that auction record doesn’t tell the whole story. A version of Cézanne’s The Card Players was reportedly sold privately to Qatar for around $250 million in 2011, a reminder that some of the biggest deals in the art world never reach a public salesroom.
Arlequin was one of 12 paintings offered from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection on Wednesday, alongside Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which had been expected to fetch around $180 million and ended up selling for $190.4 million.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: EUA querem retomar ideia de ‘áreas de influência’, mas China tem dado as cartas do jogo global, avalia analista internacional
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Todos os olhares do mundo estão voltados para a histórica reunião trilateral entre Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin e Xi Jinping. Previsto para acontecer nesta quinta-feira (19), em Shenzhen, na China, o encontro terá como tema central a busca por uma solução para o fim da guerra na Ucrânia.
Em entrevista ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Gilberto Maringoni, professor de relações internacionais da Universidade Federal do ABC (UFABC), pondera que a reunião entre as três potências acaba ocultando situações igualmente importantes das relações bilaterais entre elas. “A questão do chip e do livre comércio interessa muito à China, e quem quer bloquear o livre comércio com as tarifas são os EUA. E eles foram pródigos em pregar isso há muitos anos. Só que a China se tornou a fábrica do mundo e não quer mais sanções como os EUA vêm impondo”, pontua.
Do ponto de vista geopolítico, aponta Maringoni, Trump chega para essa reunião enfraquecido após a derrota nas eleições de meio de mandato, que deu vitória ao Partido Democrata. Além disso, o presidente estadunidense não tem conseguido lidar com a guerra no Irã, que tem imposto a ele sucessivas derrotas, inclusive na avaliação de aliados. “É um atoleiro do qual ele não consegue sair. Os preços do petróleo aumentaram muito por causa dos bloqueios no Estreito de Ormuz e de Bab El-Mandeb. Ele chega muito enfraquecido em um cenário em que quem dá as cartas é a China, circundada pela Rússia, que está em guerra com a Ucrânia. Nós entramos numa fase multilateral do mundo e não mais com uma potência hegemônica”, argumenta.
No período pós-Segunda Guerra, quando foram realizadas conferências para costurar a nova ordem mundial, o Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) dos EUA representava mais de 40% do PIB mundial. Hoje, ressalta o analista, representa apenas 18%. “Existe um equilíbrio muito maior e um redesenho global que não repetirá o desenho da Segunda Guerra Mundial, com a fundação da ONU [Organização das Nações Unidas]. Uma das coisas que o Xi Jinping quer levar é a mudança de regras dentro da ONU, ampliação do Conselho de Segurança, ou seja, um mundo multilateral. Isso pode abrir espaço para o Brasil, se ele se colocar numa rota de desenvolvimento. Por isso, essa reunião é muito importante”, avalia.
Com relação à postura da China diante das outras duas potências que vivem atualmente conflitos importantes, Maringoni observa que as “grandes potências muito raramente entram em guerra ou choque aberto” entre si. E isso se dá por interesses estratégicos. O professor aponta que a China forneceu tecnologia de informação ao Irã e a Rússia esté envolvida com a Ucrânia.
“No caso ucraniano, a China não se mobilizou na questão das tarifas, mas passou a abrir seu comércio de energia para comprar petróleo russo. Há, sim, uma sinergia entre as potências, em especial as que gravitam em torno da China”, avalia. “Nesse sentido, não acho que a China esteja à parte. É ao contrário. A China está no centro do jogo. Por outro lado, os EUA querem retomar a política da Guerra Fria de que as potências têm sua área de influência definida”, resume.
