Houthis hit Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund skyscraper
The skyscraper housing Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) in Riyadh was damaged on Thursday by a Houthi strike, the kingdom has confirmed.
The strike destroyed windows across seven to eight floors of the tower, Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, and bent part of its metal facade, according to a Reuters journalist. Video footage shared from the Saudi capital showed crews already working to replace the glass.
The attack is the second time this month that the Houthis have struck at the heart of Saudi Arabia’s image as a safe investment destination. PIF says it has around $1 trillion in assets. Earlier this month, the Houthis struck Aramco Tower in Riyadh.
“One of the towers of the Financial Center in Riyadh was targeted in a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, causing material damage but no injuries -praise be to God,” the Saudi authorities said in a statement released on Thursday.
The press release included an image showing notable but relatively minor damage to the PIF headquarters. Video footage appeared to show a missile slamming into the 80-storey tower, but Middle East Eye could not independently verify the footage.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
In the wake of the United States midterm elections, attention has turned to whether Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will be able to preserve his cabinet-level position once Congress’s new Democratic majorities are sworn in.
Already, the Fox News host-turned-military-chief has faced mounting calls for his removal from office.
But analysts question the extent to which Hegseth’s impeachment would affect military policy under President Donald Trump.
“Ultimately, the secretary of defence is a powerful participant in shaping a war,” said Jasmine El-Gamal, a former Middle East adviser in the Pentagon.
El-Gamal, however, believes targeting Hegseth alone would not be enough to secure accountability for decisions like launching the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hegseth holds significant power in directing the US war effort, she explained, but he also works hand-in-hand with the president and his advisers.
“Calling him merely an ‘executor’ understates that power, while calling him its sole architect understates the president’s power and obscures where particular decisions were actually made,” El-Gamal said.
Facing impeachment
Since he was sworn in on January 25, 2025, Hegseth has overseen some of Trump’s most controversial international campaigns, including the war on Iran and a series of deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.
Both campaigns have been accused of violating international law. The Iran war, in particular, became a political albatross for Trump’s Republican Party during the midterm race.
A poll earlier this month found that 44 percent of US voters said they were less likely to vote for a midterm candidate who supported the war.
That number dwarfed the 13 percent who said they were more inclined to vote for such a candidate, by a ratio of more than three to one.
The Democratic Party scored a thumping victory in the November 3 midterms, flipping both the House of Representatives and the Senate from Republican control.
Less than a week later, Hegseth faced a push for impeachment, led by outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie.
Among the eight articles of impeachment Massie filed were accusations that Hegseth had dismantled fundamental safeguards to protect civilian lives, leading to incidents like the bombing of an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed at least 120 children.
But the impeachment proceedings were shelved on November 10, after the Republicans’ lame-duck majority in the House voted 211 to 204 to block the measure. Eleven Democrats were absent for the vote.
Scrutiny of Pentagon chiefs
Hegseth is hardly the first Pentagon chief to face pressure to leave office following a dismal election for his party.
In November 2006, Republicans likewise suffered a midterm rout amid a groundswell of voter ire over the US-led wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Both chambers of Congress that year flipped to Democratic control.
Within a day of the vote, then-President George W Bush announced that his defence secretary, the late Donald Rumsfeld, would resign. He cited the Iraq war in his remarks.
“I recognise that many Americans voted last night to register their displeasure with the lack of progress being made there,” Bush said of the conflict.
Hegseth, however, has resisted calls for his resignation. In a five-minute video posted two days after the midterms, Hegseth dismissed his critics as “deep-state radicals” obsessed with “political theatre”.
“They attack us because we are effective. It’s not going to work. We will not back down,” Hegseth said. “We put America and the war-fighter first, always and without apology. And that fight continues in the lame-duck Congress.”
His message of defiance included an appeal for the military to “stay the course”, including in the war against Iran.
“I’ll assure you, we have only just begun to fight,” Hegseth added. “We are more determined than ever, more resolute than ever to finish what we have started.”
A key role in the war
Some of the criticism, however, has come from within Hegseth’s own party. Vice President JD Vance, for instance, said the “real reason” the Republicans lost the midterms is “obvious to almost everyone”.
“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on social media.
Hala Rharrit, a former US diplomat who spent 18 years in the State Department, was among the officials who resigned before Trump took office for his second term, in protest of the US involvement in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
She explained that Hegseth would have been critical in guiding some of the Iran war’s most divisive moments.
The bombing of the Minab elementary school, for example, took place on February 28, the first day of the conflict.
Rharrit said Hegseth and other senior Department of Defense (DOD) officials would have drawn up the initial strike lists before advising Trump on the targets for final approval.
“I suspect that Trump would not get into the granularities of which targets to strike on day one,” Rharrit told Al Jazeera.
“Hegseth and others in DOD had a lot to do with those precise decisions, which also runs through lawyers.”
She also drew a line between decisions taken by Hegseth and Trump and the losses the US and its allies have endured since the war began.
Iran has retaliated against US and Israeli attacks with strikes across the Middle East. At least 23 US service members have died in the conflict, and 865 were wounded.
“Ultimately, they are both responsible, not just for the strikes in Iran, but also for making American service members and diplomats throughout the region sitting ducks,” said Rharrit.
Congress reasserting its authority?
Throughout the war, Congress has had the power to pull the emergency cord and stop the fighting, according to Brian Finucane, who served as a legal adviser in the State Department from 2011 to 2021.
Under the Constitution, “the overwhelming bulk of war powers belong” to the members of Congress, he said.
He sees the midterm results, in part, as a backlash to the Trump administration’s expansive use of executive power.
After all, critics say officials like Hegseth have offered Congress relatively little transparency in the military’s overseas actions.
“We’ve seen sort of the apex of presidential unilateralism under Trump,” Finucane said. “I think it has reminded Americans of why the Constitution gives Congress, not one man, the power to take the country to war.”
The incoming Democrat-led Congress has pledged to use its power to check Trump’s war-making powers and confront Hegseth over his policies.
In the final days of the midterm race, Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who is now in line to become the first Black speaker of the House, told supporters that Hegseth’s days were numbered.
“In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Jeffries said.
He has since described himself as a “hard yes” on impeachment proceedings against the Pentagon chief.
But El-Gamal cautioned against treating the impeachment vote as the only path to accountability.
“Impeachment is just one constitutional accountability mechanism,” said El-Gamal.
She pointed to congressional investigations and the legislature’s “power of the purse” — its authority over federal spending — as two other avenues for reining in Hegseth and Trump.
El-Gamal added that November’s blocked impeachment motion “was not an acquittal nor a vote resolving the allegations” of war crimes in Iran and elsewhere. She anticipates the new Congress, once sworn in, will continue to pursue those allegations.

Houthis hit Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund skyscraper
The skyscraper housing Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) in Riyadh was damaged on Thursday by a Houthi strike, the kingdom has confirmed.
The strike destroyed windows across seven to eight floors of the tower, Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, and bent part of its metal facade, according to a Reuters journalist. Video footage shared from the Saudi capital showed crews already working to replace the glass.
The attack is the second time this month that the Houthis have struck at the heart of Saudi Arabia’s image as a safe investment destination. PIF says it has around $1 trillion in assets. Earlier this month, the Houthis struck Aramco Tower in Riyadh.
“One of the towers of the Financial Center in Riyadh was targeted in a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, causing material damage but no injuries -praise be to God,” the Saudi authorities said in a statement released on Thursday.
The press release included an image showing notable but relatively minor damage to the PIF headquarters. Video footage appeared to show a missile slamming into the 80-storey tower, but Middle East Eye could not independently verify the footage.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Reuters reported that three sources said the building was struck by a missile while the kingdom said it had dealt with the incoming missile threat and that debris had fallen.
Sources on the ground in Riyadh told MEE that they were awakened by a massive explosion around 5am.
Heart of the kingdom
A direct attack on PIF strikes at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s efforts to diversify the kingdom’s economy away from a total reliance on oil exports and attract foreign investors to Saudi Arabia.
The strike was the latest in a Houthi air campaign targeting Saudi Arabia's civilian infrastructure, including airports, commercial buildings and energy installations.
The attacks come as the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government in Yemen struggles to stem a Houthi advance that is now threatening Aden, the provisional capital of the Saudi-backed government.
The strikes come as the kingdom continues to look for international support to counter the Houthis. The commander of US Central Command (Centcom), Admiral Brad Cooper, met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on Thursday.
The two sides "reviewed bilateral relations, particularly in the military fields, and discussed regional developments", the media outlet said.
MEE was the first to reveal the high-level visit, in which dozens of senior US military advisors also arrived in Riyadh to advise Saudi Arabia on air defence.
Diplomats and officials in the region say Saudi Arabia has no appetite to engage the Houthis in talks at the moment, and is gearing up for a protracted war.
The kingdom gathered western partners in Riyadh this week, asking them to turn on the weapons spigot to help it, three western officials familiar with the meetings told MEE.
The sources said that Saudi Arabia is seeking weapons supplies to “deter” Houthi attacks, as it prepares for a drawn-out conflict.
“Saudi Arabia is in the market,” one of the officials told MEE.
The long-running civil war in Yemen fell dormant in 2022 after a ceasefire was implemented but reignited in recent months.
The Houthis have made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed and are nearing Aden.
More than 1,600 people have been killed in the latest round of fighting, with more than 300,000 displaced, according to the United Nations.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz faces a deepening water crisis
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz faces a deepening water crisis
Fuel shortages and the loss of access to wells have left residents dependent on unsafe water.
Taiz, Yemen – Qaid al-Sharaabi waited three days before it was his turn to receive a tanker of clean water.
But the delay is not the only problem. He says he now has to pay more – the result of the Houthi siege on Taiz, in southwestern Yemen.
“This is the second time since the siege began a month-and-a-half ago that I’ve had to pay twice the price for a water tanker,” al-Sharaabi told Al Jazeera. “I’m afraid that if things continue like this, more residents will resort to using unsafe water.”
The United Nations children’s agency (UNICEF) says that water production in Taiz has nearly halved, while more than 800,000 people are reported to be cut off from humanitarian assistance.
The crisis has left the city reeling, even as government soldiers try to defend it, in the latest round of fighting to hit the area since the war in Yemen started in 2014.
Hospital administrators are warning of a public health disaster, while government officials are unsure how much longer they will have the funds needed to carry out even limited services.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has long suffered from severe water shortages.
But, according to Wafiq al-Aghbari, director-general of Taiz governorate’s Local Water and Sanitation Corporation, the crisis “intensified in 2015, with the first siege imposed on the city by the Houthis, and continued to worsen year after year, as the suffering of the city’s residents grew”.
He said the crisis has deepened since the Houthis laid siege to the city again in October, after they made advances against government forces in the countryside around Taiz.
Before the war started in 2014, al-Aghbari explained, Taiz received about 20,000 cubic metres (700,000 cubic feet) of water per day from six large wellfields, which had supplied the city and its immediate surroundings for years.
But only one of those wellfields is inside the city limits, and before the war, it had only been used in emergencies.
By 2015, Taiz had lost access to all five of its external wellfields, which had either fallen under Houthi control or were on the front lines, leaving the city reliant on its emergency wells.
But work in the past few years to dig additional wells and rehabilitate existing sources had brought daily production capacity up to 5,000 cubic metres (175,000 cubic feet) – still just 14 percent of the city’s estimated daily needs.
Tightening siege
The Houthi encirclement of Taiz in October led to the Iranian-backed group seizing control of Hadhran al-Dhabab, an external wellfield that had been partially restored in August 2025.
The situation has led to the water corporation losing 3,200 cubic metres (112,000 cubic feet) of daily production capacity – 1,200 cubic metres (42,000 cubic feet) after pumping stopped from the Hadhran al-Dhabab wellfield, and a further 2,000 cubic metres (70,000 cubic feet) after wells inside the city stopped operating because of a shortage of diesel. The corporation is now able to produce only 1,800 cubic metres (63,180 cubic feet) a day from the emergency wells that it can still operate.
Al-Aghbari said the consequences of the siege had extended beyond the widening gap between water supplies and demand.
Funding and supplies for the city’s charitable water distribution points, known as “sabeel”, have also been disrupted, because of shortages of fuel and water.
According to al-Aghbari, the subsidised distribution points had previously provided up to 1.5 million litres (396,000 gallons) of fresh water a day, alongside a further 1 million litres (264,000 gallons) of untreated water.
“The water corporation has entered a major financial crisis as a result of the loss of most international and local funding for its operations, at a time when the corporation is also under immense pressure because of the growing shortfall in meeting local water needs,” al-Aghbari said.
He added that this was especially problematic because more residents cannot afford to buy commercially-supplied water as a result of the worsening economic situation, and become more dependent on the free water distribution points.
The owner of one commercial water tanker, who did not want to give his name for security reasons, said that prices had risen sharply at the beginning of the siege, from 18,000 riyals per tanker (about $12 at parallel market rates) to 30,000 riyals (about $20).
He continues to try to pick up water from the Hadhran al-Dhabab wellfield, but said that the process had become difficult.
“[That is] because of the consequences of the siege, including the inspection procedures imposed by the Houthi group … which last for hours,” he said. “Sometimes we are prevented from entering and remain outside the city for more than a day, on the grounds that there are risks because of heightened military and security tensions.”
The Houthis have denied responsibility for the closure of roads into Taiz. Human Rights Watch has said that residents, aid workers, and UN officials had blamed the armed group for shortages in the city.
Contaminated water
The consequences of the siege have gone beyond its humanitarian and economic impact, with serious implications for public health, according to Dr Abdulqawi al-Shamiri, the director of Taiz’s al-Taawun Hospital.
He warned of “serious health disasters because of the interruption of safe water supplies that residents used to obtain from groundwater fields outside the city”.
Al-Shamiri said water from the emergency wells within the city had “long been unfit for human use, as a large proportion of it has become contaminated, or is hard water containing high concentrations of salts”.
He explained that the contamination was the result of sewage mixing with water because of poorly maintained sewage networks, and rubbish dumped in streets and floodwater channels. The Houthis, al-Shamiri said, have prevented waste from being transported to a landfill outside the city.
According to an internal report from the governorate’s Cleaning and Improvement Fund, close to half of the city’s rubbish is going uncollected.
Residents are contracting illnesses such as cholera and acute diarrhoea as a result, Al-Shamiri said.
“The rubbish quickly decomposes into extremely dangerous bacteria and chemicals that increase the existing contamination of the city’s well water, making it unfit for human use,” al-Shamiri said. “Unfortunately, however, most people are being forced to use it under the current circumstances because of the difficulty of accessing clean, safe water.”

https://apache.be/2026/11/04/vlaamse-ado.title: Vlaamse adoptiedienst verzon fabel van Nepalese tapijtkinderen
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/vlaamse-ado.author: Hari Prasad Sacré
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/vlaamse-ado.text:
De Vlaamse adoptiedienst Interadoptie haalde kinderen uit Nepal om hen zogezegd te redden van kinderarbeid in de tapijtfabrieken. Maar hun broers en zussen bleven in Nepal, en geen van hen werd ooit een tapijtkind. Documenten tonen dat de dienst bewust kinderen met familie koos, en dat toezichthouder Kind en Gezin daarvan op de hoogte was.
Interadoptie bracht in de jaren 90 zeven kinderen uit Nepal naar Vlaanderen, officieel om hen te behoeden voor kinderarbeid in de tapijtfabrieken. Ik ben een van hen en ik ken het verhaal van vijf anderen. Elk van ons had nog familie, waaronder minstens één ouder en broers en zussen. Bovendien bevat mijn eigen dossier onjuiste en vervalste informatie en heeft mijn eerste moeder nooit toestemming gegeven voor adoptie.
Via het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie kreeg ik inzage in mijn adoptiedossier en in de briefwisseling tussen Interadoptie, Kind en Gezin en de bemiddelaar S.S. in Nepal, tussen 1992 en 2000. Die documenten tonen hoe de fabel van de tapijtkinderen de wanpraktijken verhulde.
“Rijp voor kinderhandel”
Dat er in Nepal risico’s waren, wist de adoptiedienst al vroeg. In een verslag aan Kind en Gezin uit 1994 schrijft Interadoptie: “Dit land is duidelijk ‘rijp’ voor kinderhandel en private adoptie.”
Elk van de kinderen die Interadoptie naar Vlaanderen bracht had nog familie, waaronder minstens één ouder en broers en zussen
De dienst stelt daarom voor om de Belgische ambassade en Bal Mandir, het staatsweeshuis in de hoofdstad Kathmandu, te verwittigen dat adopties niet privaat mogen gebeuren. Zo wil men irreguliere adopties buiten de erkende diensten om tegenhouden. Maar de waakzaamheid richt zich enkel naar buiten. Het eigen kanaal blijft buiten schot.
Want in hetzelfde verslag staat ook dit:
“Onze gevolmachtigde ter plaatse […] overweegt nu en dan een adoptie van een half-weeskind of achtergelaten kind in een hospitaal. De wachtlijsten met Bal Mandir schieten niet op en hun briefwisseling spreekt enkel concreet over donaties voor hun tehuizen.”
Lees die zinnen samen en de redenering wordt zichtbaar. De officiële weg naar wezen zat vast, en andere organisaties boden hogere donaties. Dus zocht de dienst een andere weg. Via de contactpersoon die Bal Mandir voor Interadoptie had aangeduid, mevrouw S.S., kwamen kinderen buiten het weeshuis in beeld. In de zes adopties die ik ken, ging het altijd om half-wezen. Deze kinderen hebben nog een levende ouder, broers, zussen en grootouders.
De fabel van de tapijtkinderen
Hoe verantwoordde de dienst haar keuzes? Een inspectieverslag van 1994 rapporteert de motivatie van de dienst als volgt:
“In Nepal wordt de adoptiedienst echter geconfronteerd met het feit dat de kinderen in de weeshuizen dikwijls een beter leven hebben dan de kinderen die bij hun ouders verblijven. […] ‘Tapijtkinderen’ worden al vanaf 6 jaar tewerkgesteld in tapijtfabrieken […]. Om die reden en in het belang van het kind opteert de adoptiedienst ervoor om geen kinderen uit weeshuizen te adopteren maar wel kinderen die het risico lopen om in zo'n tapijtfabriek te worden tewerkgesteld.”
Kinderarbeid in de Nepalese tapijtindustrie was in de jaren 90 echt. Het kreeg internationaal ook veel aandacht. Dat maakt de fabel zo overtuigend. Een goede fabel heeft altijd een kern van waarheid. Maar de adoptiedienst gebruikte het beeld van de tapijtkinderen en kinderarbeid om kinderen los te wrikken van functionerende families met een slinkse retoriek.
De adoptiedienst gebruikte het beeld van de tapijtindustrie om kinderen los te wrikken van functionerende families met een slinkse retoriek
Nepalese gezinnen worden in dat beeld neergezet als een risico-omgeving. Kinderen in een weeshuis zouden het beter hebben dan kinderen die opgroeien bij hun ouders. De adoptiedienst slaagt er zo in om de logica dat een kind bij zijn familie hoort volledig om te draaien. Het Nepalese gezin wordt verdacht gemaakt en opgevoerd als een omgeving waaruit het kind gered moet worden.
Daarnaast verschuift de focus van weeskinderen naar risicokinderen met familie. De dienst kiest uitdrukkelijk niet voor kinderen uit weeshuizen. Wie bewust geen wezen adopteert, adopteert intentioneel kinderen die nog familie hebben. Zo komen kwetsbare gezinnen die door een moeilijke periode gaan plots in het vizier van transnationale adoptie.
Tot slot sluit het gezegde ‘in het belang van het kind’ elk kritisch gesprek uit. Wie dat argument inroept, maakt tegenspraak moeilijk. Wie kan er tegen zijn dat een kind niet in een fabriek moet gaan werken?
Broers en zussen nooit actief in de tapijtindustrie
Wij, Nepalees geadopteerden, kennen elkaar. Van zes van ons ken ik het verhaal en de families. Telkens gaat het om kinderen die werden weggehaald uit families waar ze nog ouders, grootouders, broers en zussen hadden. Die broers en zussen bleven in Nepal. Geen van hen kwam ooit in een tapijtfabriek terecht. Het risico waarvan wij gered moesten worden, was nooit een reëel gevaar in hun leven.
Het risico waarvan de geadopteerden gered moesten worden, was nooit een reëel gevaar in het leven van hun broers en zussen
Dat de redenering rond de tapijtkinderen niet klopte, zag Interadoptie trouwens zelf in. In een brief aan mijn adoptieouders uit 1994 schrijft de dienst: “Men kan zich wel afvragen wat er met de andere kinderen gebeurt.”
Daarmee erkent de dienst het gat in het eigen verhaal. Als één kind gered moest worden van de tapijtfabriek, gold dat risico evengoed voor zijn broers en zussen. Toch bleven zij in hetzelfde gezin, met dezelfde ouders en dezelfde armoede. Dat Interadoptie hen liet waar ze waren, toont dat de adopties nooit een antwoord waren op het risico van kinderarbeid.
De geadopteerde bleef achter met de vraag waarom net hij of zij weg moest, terwijl de broers en zussen bij hun ouders konden opgroeien. Op die vraag heeft het reddersverhaal geen antwoord.
Internationale basisregel niet gerespecteerd
Dat het ook anders kon, blijkt uit een verslag van een vergadering met de vicevoorzitter van Bal Mandir in oktober 1996. Bal Mandir adopteerde lange tijd enkel wezen. “Sinds kort komen ook verlaten kinderen in aanmerking, maar enkel als ze niet door familieleden kunnen opgevangen worden.”
De vicevoorzitter van Bal Mandir noemde de private adopties via ngo’s “handel”, winstbejag zonder projecthulp of nazorg
Het officiële Nepalese kanaal zocht dus eerst naar familie. Bal Mandir paste daarmee toe wat internationaal als basisregel geldt. Een kind komt namelijk pas in aanmerking voor adoptie in het buitenland als zorg in de eigen familie of gemeenschap onmogelijk is. De Speciale VN-rapporteur voor de verkoop van kinderen rekent in een rapport uit 2016 het negeren van dat principe tot de praktijken die van een adoptie een verkoop van kinderen maken.
De bemiddelaar van Interadoptie, mevrouw S.S., koos telkens voor kinderen die nog familie hadden. In hetzelfde gesprek noemt de vicevoorzitter van Bal Mandir de private adopties via ngo’s “handel”, namelijk winstbejag zonder projecthulp of nazorg. Ook Interadoptie volgde die private weg bij zeker zes van de zeven dossiers. Dat die weg niet zonder risico was, wist de dienst zelf. In het verslag van de vergadering schrijft Interadoptie dat adoptiegezinnen bij private adopties “voor moeilijkheden kunnen komen te staan” bij het Nepalese ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken, “zoals bij onze twee laatste dossiers”.
Nazorg als ‘controle’
Ook na de adoptie bleef het reddingsverhaal de keuzes van de dienst bepalen. Een inspectieverslag van Kind en Gezin uit 1993 beschrijft hoe Interadoptie omging met nazorg:
“Nepal vraagt nazorgrapporten tot het kind 18 jaar is. Er worden hiervoor geen huisbezoeken gebracht. Inspectie deelde mee dat dit geen nazorg is […]. De adoptiedienst stelde dat als er problemen zijn bij de adoptiegezinnen zij dit wel verneemt, van de groepsverantwoordelijken […]. Bovendien is er ook een financieel probleem. Wie zal deze huisbezoeken betalen? En zullen adoptanten dit als een controle beschouwen.”
Het comfort van de adoptieouders woog zwaarder dan de noden van het kind
Nepal vroeg opvolging tot het kind volwassen was. Interadoptie zag geen nood aan huisbezoeken. Problemen zou de dienst wel horen via de groepsverantwoordelijken, adoptieouders die per land activiteiten organiseerden. Daarnaast speelden de kosten en de vrees dat adoptanten bezoeken als controle zouden ervaren. Het comfort van de adoptieouders woog zo zwaarder dan de noden van het kind. De dienst beloofde nadien de nazorg beter uit te bouwen, maar de huisbezoeken zijn er nooit gekomen.
De nood aan nazorg was er wel degelijk. Deze kinderen waren weggehaald bij familie die bleef bestaan en moesten met dat verlies leren leven. Het reddingsverhaal liet daar geen ruimte voor. Wie als gered wordt voorgesteld, krijgt immers weinig ruimte om verlies te verwerken.
Wat deed de toezichthouder?
Kind en Gezin wist van bij het begin van de risico’s in Nepal. Volgens een inspectieverslag uit 1993 begon de samenwerking met Nepal “op vraag van kandidaat-adoptanten […], die absoluut een Nepalees kindje wilden adopteren”. Toen dat koppel na zes maanden nog geen toewijzing had, wilde het toch vertrekken. “De verantwoordelijke van de adoptiedienst kon hen niet tegenhouden.”
Niet de nood van een kind in Nepal, maar de wens van Vlaamse adoptanten zette de samenwerking met Nepal in gang
Het is een schoolvoorbeeld van wat het Vlaamse expertenpanel rond transnationale adoptie in 2021 vaststelde, namelijk dat het systeem vraaggestuurd was. Niet de nood van een kind in Nepal, maar de wens van Vlaamse adoptanten zette de samenwerking met Nepal in gang.
De toezichthouder ontving ook het verslag waarin Interadoptie Nepal “rijp” noemde voor kinderhandel. De eigen inspectie noteerde dat de dienst in dat land bewust geen wezen adopteerde, maar kinderen met familie. Waarom greep de toezichthouder niet in?
Na zeven adopties stopte Interadoptie de samenwerking met Nepal. Uit de documenten blijkt niet waarom. Wel valt op dat de stopzetting kwam kort nadat de private route problemen opleverde in twee dossiers bij de Nepalese overheid.
Hari Prasad Sacré dankt de binnenlands geadopteerden die gestreden hebben voor het inzagerecht. “Zonder hun moedige strijd had ik deze analyse niet kunnen schrijven. Daarnaast dank ik de medewerkers van het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie. Ik ervaarde een grote bereidheid en zorgvuldigheid om de documenten te verzamelen en ter beschikking te stellen.”

https://apache.be/2026/11/04/adoptiedien.title: “Adoptiedienst wrikte Nepalese kinderen los van hun families”
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/adoptiedien.author: Kasper Nollet
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/adoptiedien.text:
Een Vlaamse adoptiedienst voerde in de jaren 90 bewust adopties uit op Nepalese kinderen met families, onder het valse voorwendsel dat er een risico bestond op kinderarbeid. Toezichthouder Kind en Gezin was daarvan op de hoogte en greep niet in. Dat schrijft onderzoeker Hari Prasad Sacré, die zelf in die periode geadopteerd werd uit Nepal, in een gastbijdrage op apache.be op basis van interne documenten die ook Apache kon inkijken.
In het kort
- Tussen 1992 en 2000 bracht het Vlaamse adoptiebureau Interadoptie zeven kinderen uit Nepal naar Vlaanderen.
- Inspectieverslagen en correspondentie tussen Interadoptie en Kind en Gezin (vandaag het agentschap Opgroeien) tonen aan dat Interadoptie bewust niet-verweesde kinderen uitkoos ter adoptie, schrijft adoptieonderzoeker Hari Prasad Sacré in een gastbijdrage op apache.be.
- De kinderen werden gescheiden van hun familie onder het valse voorwendsel dat ze behoed moesten worden voor kinderarbeid in de Nepalese tapijtenindustrie.
- Kind en Gezin wist volgens Sacré af van de mistoestanden, maar greep niet in. Zijn gastbijdrage komt op een moment dat er veel kritiek is op hoe Vlaanderen het onderzoek naar de historische wantoestanden in de adoptiesector voert.
Tussen 1992 en 2000 vonden in totaal zeven adopties plaats in Nepal die georganiseerd werden door de Vlaamse adoptiedienst Interadoptie. Adoptieonderzoeker en taalpedagoog Hari Prasad Sacré was een van die zeven adoptiekinderen.
“De Vlaamse adoptiedienst Interadoptie haalde kinderen uit Nepal om hen zogezegd te redden van kinderarbeid in de tapijtfabrieken. Maar hun broers en zussen bleven in Nepal, en geen van hen werd ooit een tapijtkind”, schrijft hij in een gastbijdrage op apache.be. Kind en Gezin, de dienst die destijds toezag op interlandelijke adopties, was daar volgens Sacré van op de hoogte. Toch greep de overheidsorganisatie niet in.
“De juridische en ethische kaders uit de jaren 90 zijn heel anders dan vandaag. Als we de praktijk van vroeger toetsen aan de kennis en normen die we vandaag hanteren, zouden deze adopties wellicht niet hebben plaatsgevonden”, reageert Dries Cludts, woordvoerder van Opgroeien, het agentschap dat in 2019 ontstond uit de fusie van Agentschap Jongerenwelzijn, Kind en Gezin en een deel van het Vlaams Agentschap voor Personen met een Handicap.
Eind april 2026 besliste de Vlaamse Regering om interlandelijke adopties definitief stop te zetten. In 2027 zal er nieuwe wetgeving in voege treden.
De beslissing van de regering kwam er na jaren van kritiek op het systeem. In verschillende dossiers bleek dat achtergrondinformatie niet klopte of dat documenten vervalst waren. Soms was er zelfs sprake van kinderhandel.
Een kind uit het binnenland adopteren blijft wel nog mogelijk, al gaat het daar om een zeer beperkte groep en zijn de voorwaarden verstrengd.
Tapijtindustrie als voorwendsel
In 1992 vat Interadoptie zijn activiteiten in Nepal aan op vraag van Vlaamse kandidaat-adoptieouders “die absoluut een Nepalees kindje wilden adopteren”, staat in een inspectieverslag uit 1993. Om aan hun verzoek tegemoet te komen, zou Interadoptie daarvoor samenwerken met het Nepalese staatsadoptiebureau Bal Mandir. Interadoptie schakelde een Nepalese bemiddelaar in, een vrouw met de naam S.S.
In een brief uit 1994 aan Kind en Gezin schrijft Interadoptie dat het bewust kiest voor niet-verweesde kinderen of voor kinderen die worden achtergelaten in ziekenhuizen
In een brief uit 1994 aan Kind en Gezin schrijft Interadoptie dat het bewust kiest voor niet-verweesde kinderen of voor kinderen die worden achtergelaten in ziekenhuizen. Uit een inspectieverslag van datzelfde jaar van Kind en Gezin staat te lezen hoe Interadoptie die keuze motiveert.
De adoptiedienst zou geconfronteerd worden met “het feit dat de kinderen in de weeshuizen dikwijls een beter leven hebben dan de kinderen die bij hun ouders verblijven”. Zogenoemde ‘tapijtkinderen’ zouden al vanaf 6 jaar tewerkgesteld worden in tapijtfabrieken. “Om die reden en in het belang van het kind opteert de adoptiedienst ervoor om geen kinderen uit weeshuizen te adopteren maar wel kinderen die het risico lopen om in zo'n tapijtfabriek te worden tewerkgesteld”, klinkt het in het inspectieverslag.
De kwestie van kinderarbeid in Nepal in die periode is reëel. “Maar de adoptiedienst gebruikte het beeld van de tapijtkinderen en kinderarbeid om kinderen los te wrikken van functionerende families met een slinkse retoriek”, schrijft Sacré. “Nepalese gezinnen worden in dat beeld neergezet als een risico-omgeving.”
De adoptiedienst slaagt er volgens hem zo in om de logica dat een kind bij zijn familie hoort volledig om te draaien. “Het gezegde ‘in het belang van het kind’ sluit elk kritisch gesprek uit. Wie dat argument inroept, maakt tegenspraak moeilijk. Wie kan er tegen zijn dat een kind niet in een fabriek moet gaan werken?”
Hij wijst erop dat een kind pas in aanmerking komt voor adoptie in het buitenland als zorg in de eigen familie of gemeenschap onmogelijk is. “De Speciale VN-rapporteur voor de verkoop van kinderen rekent het negeren van dat principe tot de praktijken die van een adoptie een verkoop van kinderen maken.”
De impact op de kinderen en hun families in Nepal is groot, schrijft Sacré. “Wij, Nepalees geadopteerden, kennen elkaar. Van zes van ons ken ik het verhaal en de families. Telkens gaat het om kinderen die werden weggehaald uit families waar ze nog ouders, grootouders, broers en zussen hadden. Die broers en zussen bleven in Nepal. Geen van hen kwam ooit in een tapijtfabriek terecht. Het risico waarvan wij gered moesten worden, was nooit een reëel gevaar in hun leven.”
Kind en Gezin op de hoogte
Na zeven adopties stopte Interadoptie in 2000 met adopties uit Nepal. Het is niet duidelijk waarom. Volgens een inspectieverslag uit 1993 begon de samenwerking met Nepal “op vraag van kandidaat-adoptanten […], die absoluut een Nepalees kindje wilden adopteren”. Toen dat koppel na zes maanden nog geen toewijzing had, wilde het toch vertrekken. “De verantwoordelijke van de adoptiedienst kon hen niet tegenhouden.”
“Kind en Gezin wist van bij het begin van de risico’s in Nepal”, schrijft Hari Prasad Sacré
“Kind en Gezin wist van bij het begin van de risico’s in Nepal”, concludeert Sacré. “Het is een schoolvoorbeeld van wat het Vlaamse expertenpanel rond transnationale adoptie in 2021 vaststelde, namelijk dat het systeem vraaggestuurd was. Niet de nood van een kind in Nepal, maar de wens van Vlaamse adoptanten zette de samenwerking met Nepal in gang.”
“Opgroeien erkent dat vragen over adoptie en afstamming voor betrokkenen erg gevoelig kunnen zijn. Daarom vinden we het belangrijk dat iedereen die daar behoefte aan heeft zijn of haar verhaal kan delen”, reageert de woordvoerder van agentschap Opgroeien.
Hij zegt dat het agentschap deze adopties vandaag wellicht zou hebben afgekeurd. “De juridische en ethische kaders uit de jaren 90 zijn heel anders dan vandaag.” Intussen heeft de Vlaamse Regering beslist om interlandelijke adoptie stop te zetten, beklemtoont hij. “Dat besluit past binnen de fundamenteel veranderde kijk op interlandelijke adoptie.”
Vragen bij onafhankelijk onderzoek
De gastbijdrage van Sacré komt op een moment dat er grote kritiek is op de manier waarop Vlaanderen het onderzoek naar de historische wantoestanden in de adoptiesector voert. Critici beschuldigen het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie (VCA), dat in 2023 de opdracht kreeg om wantoestanden te onderzoeken, van belangenvermenging.
Critici beschuldigen het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie, dat in 2023 de opdracht kreeg om wantoestanden te onderzoeken, van belangenvermenging
Enkele van de medewerkers van de voormalige adoptiediensten zijn immers ondergebracht in een adviesraad van het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie. Ook vinden critici het een probleem dat het VCA nog contact onderhoudt met partnerorganisaties die zelf betrokken waren bij omstreden adoptiepraktijken. Verschillende geadopteerden deden bij Apache al hun verhaal over hun ervaringen met het VCA-onderzoek.
Bovendien hebben enkele van de onderzoekers die werden ingeschakeld als onafhankelijke experts kritiek op de werkwijze van VCA. Drie academici haakten inmiddels al af omdat ze niet akkoord zijn met onder meer een verplichte geheimhoudinsclausule en een gebrek aan inspraak.
Een van de belangrijkste vragen waarmee veel geadopteerden vandaag zitten, is waarom het de overheid aan moed ontbreekt om voormalige adoptiediensten verantwoordelijk te stellen voor hun daden, zegt Sacré aan Apache.
Hari Prasad Sacré is blij met het voortschrijdend inzicht van het departement Opgroeien. “Dat deze adopties in de huidige regelgeving afgekeurd zouden worden is een mooie eerste stap van erkenning. Maar de levens van ons en onze families zijn onomkeerbaar getekend door de falende kaders van de jaren 90. Welke herstelmaatregelen plaatst de overheid hier tegenover?”

Exhibition of the week
Nicole Eisenman 
  
A free display beside the seaside from the witty and imaginative sort-of-figurative artist.
 
Turner Contemporary, Margate, from 14 November to 11 April
Also showing
The Last Human Kiss
 
Snogging galore by Wolfgang Tillmans, Tracey Emin and other contemporary romantics.
 
Sainsbury Museum and Art Centre, Norwich, until 11 April
Roman Scotland 
  
Images of classical gods, tombs of fallen legionaries and mysterious relics of Pictish life in a journey to the edge of the Roman empire and beyond.
 
National Museum of Scotland, Edinburgh, from 14 November to 18 April
Beyond the Streets 
  
In spite of the title, this is very much a celebration of street art and culture starring Shepard Fairey, Goldie, Jenny Holzer and many, many more.
 
Saatchi Gallery, London, until 5 May
Dialogues: Wilhelmina Barns-Graham x Haroun Hayward 
  
A contemporary artist goes head-to-head with the noted modernist who died in 2004.
 
Hales Gallery, London, until 18 December
Image of the week
We found Tate Britain’s new exhibition, Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, an “epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings” of the co-habiting modernists. Read the full review
What we learned
The brilliantly bolshie artist Ryan Gander lambasted practically everyone
Jill Posener’s cheeky, feminist photography served as a rebuttal to 80s misogyny
Epstein survivors were overwhelmed by messages of support at pop-up art exhibition
The Vatican houses a collection of Indigenous treasures questionably ‘gifted’ to it
Masterpiece of the week
Head of Christ Crucified by the Master of Liesborn (Johann von Soest?), probably early 1480s-1490
The blood streams over Christ’s deathly white face in a vivid, almost Hammer horror contrast between gore and pallor. It flows in thick rivulets from the crown of thorns that has been mockingly forced on to his head. The initials INRI on a piece of paper fixed to the cross stand for “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” in Latin, and the cruel crown rams home the barb. Christ bears the laughter and the physical pain with patience and dignity, lowering his eyes in sorrow as he waits for his earthly body to die. The stark, simple shock of this image comes from an age in which Europeans were encouraged to identify with Christ, to imagine themselves suffering alongside him. At the same time this artist’s explicit focus on flowing blood may serve a theological function: the central moment of the medieval Mass was the miraculous transformation of bread and wine into the actual body and blood of Christ. According to the philosopher Thomas Aquinas this took place literally: the bread and wine kept their “accidental” appearance while changing their “essential” nature. This painting is part of an altarpiece from Germany, but not all Germans were convinced by such ideas. In the early 1500s Martin Luther would rebel against the miracle of transubstantiation, and against art like this which he regarded as idolatry.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke, Alexander Morrison, David Clack
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
As Tate Britain opens Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, a major show exploring these pivotal figures in British Modernism in a new light, Ben Luke visits the show and takes a tour with the exhibition’s co-curator, Thomas Kennedy.
The Lagos Biennial opens this weekend in the Nigerian city and this fifth edition is called The Museum of Things Unseen. Its three curators are Furen Dai, Chinyere Obieze and Sam Hopkins, and Ben speaks to Chinyere and Sam about their concept for the biennial.
And this episode’s Work of the Week is a group of plaster sculptures created by the Belgian artist Constantin Meunier for his magnum opus in Brussels, the Monument to Labour. Meunier’s work is at the heart of a new exhibition at the Petit Palais in Paris called Brussels 1900. Ben talks to Davy Depelchin, head curator of the 19th-century paintings and sculptures department at the Musées Royaux des Beaux-Arts, Belgium, who is one of the curatorial team organising this vast show.
- Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, Tate Britain, until 11 April 2027
- Lagos Biennial, 14 November-6 December
- Brussels 1900, Petit Palais, Paris, until 25 April 2027

The Class War Midterms
The legacy of Bernie Sanders’ presidential runs was on full display in Democrats’ titanic midterm election results. The message from voters is clear: deliver on economic populism.
Miles Kampf-Lassin
The day after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) released a video that encapsulated the left electoral movement he helped bring to life.
Set to David Bowie’s iconic song “Starman,” the video shows Sanders clasping hands with many of the candidates he endorsed this cycle. Not only did Sens.-elect Adbul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), Troy Jackson (D-Maine) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) — along with more than 50 U.S. House and downballot victors backed by Sanders — win their races, they were instrumental in delivering Democrats’ sweeping tidal wave in this year’s midterms.
Far more than just a flex, the video served as a reminder of how deeply Sanders — the iconoclast democratic socialist leader — has transformed U.S. politics over the past decade. After more than 30 years of shouting his message from the sidelines, Sanders’ call to take on the billionaire class, tackle wealth inequality and guarantee universal healthcare is now the incandescent core of a new economic populism that is redefining how candidates run and govern.
The incoming class of Sanders disciples — along with a legion of newly minted winners who embraced key aspects of his platform — will hold greater sway in Congress than progressives have seen in a lifetime. Democrats took back control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in dramatic fashion, with a mandate to turn the page on Trumpism and enact an agenda squarely focused on uplifting the working class. 
For President Donald Trump and Republicans, the outcome was ruinous. As Ryan Grim of Dropsite News pointed out, it turns out starting an illegal war in Iran that drives up gas prices while covering up a child sex predator ring and engaging in never-before-seen levels of corruption is not a successful gameplan for retaining power — especially when you promised during your campaign to end foreign wars and bring consumer prices down.
But that’s not all voters were furious about. Sending armed gestapo-like forces into cities to kidnap and kill U.S. residents shocked the country and led to a nationwide resistance movement that coalesced labor and grassroots organizations. The colossal buildout of data centers in communities across the country, along with the unchecked development of artificial intelligence (AI) by hyperrich tech oligarchs on a mission to rule over our lives, sparked widespread anger and opposition. And voters are reeling from the impact of a full-scale war on working people — epitomized by the GOP’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which is ripping away lifesaving food and healthcare programs to enrich the wealthiest Americans and supercharge Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Trump made this all possible, and his party paid the price.
But now the real fight begins. There is a push and pull between every election, with the party in power losing seats and the other gaining, until the cycle repeats itself. The only way out of continuing this historical trend is for Democrats to use their newfound leverage to make clear they’re unafraid to bring about real fundamental change.
When it comes to bringing legislation to the floor, as Democrats will be able to do in both houses of Congress next year, Sanders’ policy program is a good place to start. The majority of Americans support Medicare for All, a billionaire wealth tax, expanded Social Security, a $20 per hour minimum wage, a national data center moratorium, free public college, enhanced union rights and an end to U.S. military aid to Israel.
Even if Republicans try to block such attempts, or President Trump promises to veto them, showcasing Democratic backing of these massively popular measures would help polarize the country and show which party is actually out of step with what Americans want from the government. As Sanders told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes two days after the midterms: “Our job is to be bold. Trump wants to veto stuff? It’s his privilege. We’ve got to distinguish ourselves from the Republicans.”
The emphasis on corporate greed and a rigged economic system has trickled down from Sanders to all levels of Democratic politicians. In his victory speech, Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) said, “We just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system: in this state, in this country, power belongs to the people.” That wasn’t simply a winning message — Talarico smoked his Republican opponent by 12 points in a state where a Democrat hadn’t won a Senate seat since 1988.
Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-endorsed candidates also had a historic showing, with more than 50 scoring wins up and down the ballot. That includes newly-elected members of Congress Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Chris Rabb (D-Penn.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif). They’ll join fellow DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), taking the total number of socialists in the House up to eight — the most in U.S. history.
And this new crop of socialists is following the path being laid by New York City Zohran Mamdani, a DSA member who has helped reorient the Democratic Party around a politics of affordability. Following the results, Mamdani told reporters that voters gave Democrats “a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power.” 
But taking bold action will require real leadership, something elites in the party establishment have shown themselves unwilling (or unable) to adopt. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), in line to become House Speaker and Senate Leader, respectively, have both expressed caution about moving too fast or putting forward bills that could be considered too ambitious, including Medicare for All.
At least seven incoming Democratic senators have so far refused to commit to supporting Schumer in the upcoming leadership vote, and even incumbent Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) told Bloomberg, “no one should be committing to anybody as the next Democratic leader” unless they put forward a plan to enact an aggressive progressive agenda, adding: “we need commitments.”
With the incoming Democratic House caucus swelling to more than 250, socialists and left-wing members will hold less sway than if there had been a narrower margin, yet that shouldn’t impact the urgency of demanding the party take a fighting approach that shows which side it stands on. The donor class set aflame billions of dollars over the midterms and still couldn’t blunt voters’ hunger for a break from the status quo.
The pro-corporate Third Way set is already calling for Democrats to rush to the center, but it’s clear that class war-style populism came out on top this election — and points the way forward to building a durable coalition that can replace the failed authoritarian old guard clinging to power in the White House.
It will take a revitalized labor movement and energetic, broad-based grassroots organizing — not just more sympathetic elected officials — to steer U.S. politics in the direction of working people’s interests. But there’s no doubt the terrain has moved in favor of such a shift.
While Sanders didn’t win when he ran for president, he inspired a generation that’s now taking power. Let’s not blow it — he’s proven, as Bowie sang, that he knows it’s all worthwhile.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/mayor-j.title: “Sewer Socialism” is Ascendant in America’s Big Cities
https://inthesetimes.com/article/mayor-j.author: Rebecca Burns
https://inthesetimes.com/article/mayor-j.text:
“Sewer Socialism” is Ascendant in America’s Big Cities
As the next mayor of Washington, D.C., Janeese Lewis George will join other local leaders who say they’ll look to the public sector to help solve their cities’ housing crises.
Rebecca Burns
Following a night of historic victories for Democrats in Congressional and state races, you’d be forgiven for overlooking a stunning development in local politics: Beginning in January, multiple major American cities will be governed by self-described democratic socialists.
In Washington, D.C., City Council member Janeese Lewis George will become the city’s first new mayor in more than a decade, after winning a June Democratic primary to succeed retiring three-term Mayor Muriel Bowser. In Providence, Rhode Island, 27-year-old State Representative David Morales will become the city’s youngest-ever mayor, after beating incumbent Brett Smiley in a September primary. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, County Commissioner Yousef Rabhi handily defeated incumbent mayor Chris Taylor in the city’s mayoral primary and was elected in a landslide on Nov. 3.
And in Los Angeles, City Council member Nithya Raman is expected to oust Mayor Karen Bass. (Like Lewis George, Morales and Rabhi, Raman is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, although the group’s national body nearly voted to revoke her endorsement over her ambiguous support for the Palestinian Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement.)
Along with New York’s Zohran Mamdani and Seattle’s Katie Wilson, this new generation of left-wing municipal leaders are reviving the moniker of “sewer socialism,” a label embraced by early 20th century socialist office-holders in Milwaukee who built modern sewage and wastewater treatment systems, public parks and the nation’s first municipal public housing. Like their forbears, today’s sewer socialists say they’re laser-focused on demonstrating that the public sector can deliver everyday necessities — including housing.
Just days before the November election, Lewis George hosted a packed tenant town hall in a church on the city’s northwest side, where she invited renters to share their housing horror stories.
The crowd obliged, detailing stories of bedbug, roach and even raccoon infestations, as well as dangerous elevators and retaliatory property managers — including in affordable housing subsidized by the city.
“We know we can’t allow negligent landlords to operate in D.C., and we certainly can’t allow them to operate on the government’s dime,” Lewis George responded to applause from the crowd.
In order to deliver dignified and affordable apartments to those being priced out of the nation’s capital, Lewis George has proposed creating a new municipal office of social housing, similar to that now operating in Seattle. Where federally funded public housing is reserved for low-income residents — and can’t be significantly expanded without changes to federal law—local governments are exploring new avenues to build publicly owned, mixed-income housing with stable rents. “Social housing” is more of an umbrella term than a singular model, but many advocates take inspiration from Vienna, where nearly 50% of the population lives in apartments owned or subsidized by the city.
In April, the Washington Post editorial board denounced spending taxpayer money on social housing as “untenable in this economy,” calling instead for a rollback of eviction protections and other safeguards for renters in order to coax wary developers into building more.
Lewis George has maintained that boosting private-sector building is important, too: In an April editorial for Greater Greater Washington, she wrote that while once skeptical of new construction in the name of affordability, she now believes that “increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical.” Alongside new social housing, her housing platform calls for reforms to zoning restrictions and permitting in order to meet her overall goal of building 72,000 new homes in the city over the next five years.
But Washington currently spends more than a billion dollars annually on affordable housing, much of that going to subsidize private-sector landlords promising to build and maintain apartments for low-income residents. Key programs like the city’s Housing Production Trust Fund have faced accusations of inefficiency and favoritism toward political insiders. A 2021 report from the city’s Office of Inspector General found that D.C. officials had misspent nearly $82 million in funds earmarked for extremely low-income residents, including by overpaying certain private developers.
Meanwhile, the city has a dearth of more than 37,000 rental homes available and affordable to very low-income households, according to the National Low-Income Housing Coalition. While D.C. has an overall housing shortage — the worst in the nation as a percentage of its total housing stock, according to Freddie Mac’s estimates — that gap also reflects apartment construction tilted towards luxury housing.
Could the public sector prove a better vehicle for providing truly affordable housing at the scale required?
Will Merrifield, a housing attorney who ran for D.C. City Council in 2020, believes that incentivizing the private market to provide enough affordable housing is a “losing battle.” In order to build, developers often rely on private equity investors who expect hefty returns, pushing project costs up higher. When local governments step in to provide “public equity” instead, investors’ foregone profits can translate into greater affordability — and keep publicly subsidized housing in the hands of the public. Now the director of the non-profit Center for Social Housing and Public Investment, Merrifield hopes to help map out how Washington could provide a “public option” for renters.
One influential model exists just outside the city, where in 2021, Montgomery County, Maryland, created a $50 million revolving loan fund backed by municipal bonds. Drawing on that fund, the county provides low-cost construction loans to developers in exchange for an ownership stake. Once a project is completed, the developer repays the loan, and the county reinvests the money in new projects. Some 6,000 units are in various stages of development; because the projects are mixed-income, rents from higher-income tenants subsidize lower ones. While this approach keeps ongoing costs down, the lack of additional subsidies means fewer affordable units.
Merrifield emphasizes that Washington and other municipalities must grapple with those trade-offs in order to design social housing programs that balance speed, scale and deep affordability.
“Social housing is expensive because it’s expensive to produce housing in this country,” he says. “But it’s necessary if we’re going to reclaim economic development from the real estate investor class.”
At the October tenant town hall hosted by Lewis George’s campaign, renters living in buildings owned by one of the city’s largest affordable housing landlords made the case that the city is not getting its money’s worth — and that residents are paying the price.
Since the spring, tenants in buildings owned and managed by prolific developer Buwa Binitie have been organizing a citywide campaign, pushing for repairs in their buildings as well as an end to new public dollars or contracts for their landlord.
“One of the things we want this new administration to realize is that [Binitie’s company] has been cited for hundreds of thousands of dollars [in fees for violations],” said William Bates, a resident of a senior building managed by Binitie, during the town hall. “What we want is for him not to be able to get more properties.”
In September, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued Binitie over “shocking” conditions at another one of his buildings, including broken elevators in the 10-story building, exposed electrical wiring and stairwells contaminated with human waste and debris. The 166-unit Delta Pearl building was rehabbed and re-opened in 2023 as “luxury affordable housing,” using $18 million from the city’s Housing Production Trust Fund.
The Dumas Collective, the real-estate conglomerate Binitie founded in 2006, comprises a development company that has secured a total of $444 million in public subsidies, encompassing “financing from nearly every public capital source available,” according to the firm’s website. A property management arm oversees more than 1,000 apartments in D.C., which have collectively racked up more than 1,600 code violations between them, according to a review by City Cast DC.
A major donor to outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser, Binitie served for eight years as the chair of the D.C. Housing Finance Agency, which awards tax-exempt bonds and low-cost financing to affordable housing developers. While Binitie has said that he recused himself from decisions involving his own projects, he appears to have been investigated for an alleged conflict of interest, according to reporting by the Washington City Paper.
A separate investigation by the paper revealed that the District forfeited $3 million of federal low-income housing tax credits in 2024, in part due to a swap of newer credits used to “bail out” one of Binitie’s older projects, which had suffered delays and budget shortfalls.
Binitie’s political connections also created a bizarre scene this fall, when the lawyer defending him, former D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine, crashed a press conference where tenants were urging the City Council not to grant public land to the developer for a new project. The council tabled the bill that would have awarded Binitie development rights.
Binitie did not respond to a list of questions from In These Times. In a September statement to WUSA9, a representative of the Delta Pearl acknowledged the serious conditions but said that “prolonged court delays and widespread rent delinquency have pushed this affordable housing property into a severe financial crisis.”
Nathan Hunter-El, a former resident of Binitie’s Capitol Vista apartments and a leader in Empower DC, a tenant organizing coalition, says the campaign is “not just about one bad actor.” Tenants are also fighting to overhaul a system they say lets scofflaw landlords stay in business.
For example, they are advocating passage of legislation that would make it easier to hold serial bad actors accountable, including by wresting control of properties through the courts when owners refuse to address conditions threatening tenants’ health and safety.
That’s where a new office of social housing could play a role, says Damiana Dendy, a housing organizer for D.C. Jobs with Justice who is working with tenants in buildings owned by Binitie’s companies. City intervention to acquire and preserve troubled affordable housing portfolios could actually represent a more effective approach than continuing to throw taxpayer money at emergency intervention and enforcement in subsidized buildings.
“Right now, we’re just hemorrhaging money to these slumlords,” Dendy says.
While a transformation of the private housing market may sound quixotic, the public sector we take for granted today is, in part, the legacy of yesterday’s municipal socialists, says labor historian Shelton Stromquist.
The provision of basic services like clean water and sanitation were part of a struggle to put “a new kind of floor under what people could expect in daily life,” says Stromquist, whose book, Claiming the City: A Global History of Workers’ Fight for Municipal Socialism examines the legacy of local left-wing governments in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Today’s municipal socialists have an “inheritance,” Stromquist says, and an opportunity to “expand that public sector in new directions, beyond the limits that it faced in the past.”
