https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-parents-a.title: NYC parents are leaving work over childcare costs. Free care could help, report says.
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-parents-a.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-parents-a.text:
Working moms are disproportionately leaving their jobs or cutting back their hours because they can’t afford to pay for childcare, a new report says. And that’s hurting businesses and New York City’s economy.
The findings were released Tuesday by the think tank 5Boro Institute at Citizens Union and the Boston Consulting Group, which measured the anticipated economic impact of providing free childcare. New York City began rolling out free care for 2-year-olds this fall, starting with 2,000 seats, as part of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Gov. Kathy Hochul’s push to make childcare universal. Earlier this month, Hochul also signaled she’d be open to raising taxes to fund childcare expansion.
About 15% of New Yorkers surveyed this year had to change their work situation after becoming parents, the report said. Most changed their work hours and 25% left the workforce altogether, costing about $1.7 billion in annual income. Of the parents who left or lost their jobs, 73% were women, half were Black or Hispanic, and 43% earned under $50,000 a year. The report was based on surveys with about 3,000 parents so did not offer historical comparisons or similar statistics in other cities.
The report said offering 35 hours of free childcare a week could generate up to $6.5 billion in annual economic value for the city — matching or exceeding what it would cost to make it free. Most surveyed parents said that’s the model they would prefer. The city covers only about 30 hours of free care for 3- and 4-year-olds but offers up to 50 hours a week for 2-year-olds. The Mamdani administration estimates universal childcare will cost $6 billion annually.
“We felt like it was really important to make sure all New Yorkers understood that public investments in childcare benefit the entire city by benefiting the economy,” said Grace Rauh, executive director of Citizens Union, a good-government watchdog group.
Rauh said when parents are offered free childcare, “that's money that would've otherwise been going out the door to pay for childcare that is now in their pocket. The savings would allow them to spend money on housing, food, transportation.”
It also allows parents the option to return to work. The survey asked unemployed parents if they would return to work if they had free childcare, and 22% said they would. Of those who said they would, 95% were women. Many of them said they wanted to work in healthcare, food services and education, the report said.
“If they had the choice, these women would rather be working,” Rauh said.
“We know that women disproportionately bear the responsibility for a lot of child-rearing, a lot of domestic activities in the home. I think this figure really bears that out and shows how disproportionate the impact of having a child is on women in particular.”
Ruth Vargas, 25, said she would have gone back to work and enrolled in school if she were offered 35 hours of free childcare for her twin 2-year-old boys. She was their primary caretaker until they were about 18 months, which prolonged her return to work. She was finally able to secure a childcare voucher for their care and is working as an administrative assistant.
“I wanted to go back to college, and I kept trying to look for alternatives on how I could go back, maybe online, and then I realized that my kids needed me 24/7, and I was very frustrated because I wanted to just do something,” she said. “I wanted to feel human again when it came to Ruth as just me and not Ruth as being a mom and a caregiver all the time.”
Childcare costs parents an average of $21,000 a year in the city and many parents go into debt to cover the cost, the report said.
Federal guidelines suggest childcare costs shouldn’t exceed 7% of a household’s budget.
But it can make up more than a third of the budget for New York families earning less than $50,000 a year. Even for families making more than $200,000, childcare can cost 13% of their income, the report said.
Rauh said when parents leave the workforce, “ their earnings leave, the money that they spend in our local economy leaves with them.”
One in two surveyed parents who left the city in the last three years cited the cost of living and childcare as a driving factor.
High childcare costs don’t just harm parents, but businesses, too, the report said. More than half the parents who were surveyed missed at least one day of work in the past three months due to childcare issues and on average lost three to four days of work and up to five partial days in the same time period.
For workers who get paid by the hour, that can come out to 10.9 million missed hours of work or roughly $360 million in lost earnings a year, the report estimated.
“If you have an employee who you've invested in, you have trained them, they are rising up the career ladder, they're becoming more valuable to you as an employee, and then they're pulling out or pulling back, reducing their hours or leaving the workforce entirely,” Rauh said.
“That's a real loss to you as a business and an employer.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-b.title: NYC Council bill pits Amazon against Teamsters union in fight over delivery workers
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-b.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-b.text:
In the shadow of StuyTown, Gabrielly Sierra-Moreno adjusted her blue, Amazon-branded vest and lifted a box half her size. As she hauled the Amazon packages from a truck with the Prime logo to a push cart destined for the apartment buildings, she weaved around a dozen other workers wearing similar outfits.
“ Since I'm very tiny, it's kind of hard for me,” said Sierra-Moreno, cracking a grin. "But I’m able to manage it. I'm starting to get a little muscle.”
Despite the ubiquitous Amazon branding, Sierra-Moreno, 21, and her colleagues don’t actually work for the online retail giant. They’re employees of Brimela Routes Corp, one of more than 40 delivery service providers bringing Amazon packages to New Yorkers’ doorsteps.
That arrangement — where workers like Sierra-Moreno deliver Amazon packages without officially working for the $2.8 trillion e-commerce giant — is the subject of a major battle pitting City Hall against Amazon and its contractors. The Delivery Protection Act would ban these third-party arrangements and force companies like Amazon to hire its delivery workers directly. A majority of the City Council supports the bill and Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he’ll sign it if it passes.
Supporters of the bill, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, the powerful transport union with about 1.3 million active members, argue the current structure shields Amazon from liability, leads to lax safety standards and dilutes the power of unionized workers.
Amazon, alongside business groups and the National Urban League, say the measure would decimate a network of small businesses, about a quarter of which are owned by Black or Hispanic entrepreneurs. Amazon has already spent millions of dollars lobbying against the proposal.
“There's people today that I employ that will be overlooked if this bill passes through,” said Julissa Alvarez, the owner of Brimela Routes Corp. “ Amazon is not going to be forced to hire my employees. They’re going to have to go through the whole pipeline process, which is going to be devastating for many of our employees.”
Sierra-Moreno said she likes that she knows her boss personally and that they can communicate in Spanish. She said her schedule is flexible and she has easy access to paid time off. “ I wouldn't want them to get shut down,” she said.
But workers for other delivery service providers, or DSPs, feel differently. They allege their employers often cut corners to save money, like deferring maintenance on their vehicle fleet and renting out budget vans.
“ Nine times out of 10, there's something wrong with my van,” said LeAnn Rivera, a driver for Excell Logistics, which operates out of Amazon’s DBK1 warehouse in Woodside, Queens.
Rivera said she recently had a van that kept rolling even after she pulled the emergency brake to park.
Samuel Mangual, another Excell Logistics driver at DBK1, said he’s also dealt with faulty brakes and other issues that can force him to abandon his route.
“I've been on a road where my van door didn't close,” he said. “So now I'm sitting in a van where I can't make the rest of the deliveries because I'm afraid someone might be able to steal it, along with my belongings.”
Some drivers said the contractor model allows both Amazon and the third-party companies to evade responsibility.
“Right now, if any accident happens to one of us drivers, Amazon claims the DSP is responsible,” said José Huerta, a driver with Fast Track Delivery Inc. and union organizer with the Teamsters. “The DSP, on the other hand, says no, that it’s Amazon that’s responsible. In other words, they just blame each other.”
Excell Logistics did not respond to a request for comment. A representative for Fast Track Delivery denied their vans were unsafe. “Vehicles identified with safety-related defects are grounded and removed from service until the necessary repairs are completed and the vehicle is cleared to return to operation,” said Amar Patel, the company’s president.
Many of the workers say that drivers delivering Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans should be able to make direct demands of the e-retail giant.
In December, Teamsters Local 804 organized with over 200 drivers at Amazon’s Queens warehouse to demand better safety standards and higher pay in a union contract.
Drivers, who typically work 10-hour shifts delivering up to 230 packages a day, say they’d like to see an increase in their average pay of $24 an hour and better protections from layoffs.
“Why do I have their uniform if I’m not their employee,” Huerta said.
Amazon is spending millions of dollars to oppose the bill. The online investigative site New York Focus reported Amazon has spent an unprecedented amount of company money on a lobbying effort, pouring millions into a group called the Five Borough Jobs Campaign. City data shows the Five Borough Jobs Campaign has spent over $8 million dollars lobbying against the bill this year.
In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company is “committed to the local small business partners who work with us every day to provide fast, reliable delivery for New Yorkers.”
The legislation as written would “undermine that commitment – threatening the small businesses that deliver to customers, putting the jobs of more than 5,000 of their employees at risk, and forcing us to consider relocating delivery operations outside of the city,” Nantel said.
Marc Morial, the president of the National Urban League, the historic civil rights organization headquartered in New York City, said the third-party delivery companies are being treated unfairly as “a political football.”
“ They've taken out loans, they've taken out debt to build these businesses, and they're going to be wiped out,” Morial said. “Where are the reparations for the small business owners, the Black-owned business owners, the Latino-owned business owners that are going to be eliminated because of this bill?”
Amazon is a “diamond partner” of the National Urban League, meaning they’ve given the organization more than $1 million. A spokesperson for the organization said financial contributions do not influence their policy positions.
The council bill, championed by Queens Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, currently has 35 co-sponsors, well past a majority.
Council Speaker Julie Menin said her office was working “around the clock” to get the bill to the finish line. At a press conference last week Menin said her staff was working on some changes to address legal concerns.
“To be clear, we are going to be regulating Amazon,” Menin said. “We will be the first city in the country to regulate Amazon in a very significant way.”
Orin Starn, an anthropology professor at Duke University who did fieldwork as an employee at an Amazon warehouse until he was fired, said that if the bill passes, it will likely be seen as a model for other cities.
“That makes something like a giant city [taking] action at the municipal level to try to hold Amazon to account so important,” he said.
Alvarez, the owner of Brimela Routes Corp, said she’d be supportive of reforms that mandate better oversight and benefits but don’t blow up the entire system of third-party contractors. She said she feels swept up in a crusade that the mayor and city councilmembers are waging against big companies like Amazon.
“ What about me? I am also one of your constituents,” she said. “Are you trying to kill my business, my family, my dreams, my opportunity to help the community?”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/m.title: Mayor Mamdani Mulls Motor Vehicles In Central Park
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/m.text:
Prior versions of these "horseless" carriages (left) were really big compared to pedicabs. File art
He’s putting the electric carriage before the horse. Or, more accurately, after.
Having approved the end of horse carriage rides in Central Park, Mayor Mamdani now says he will study the feasibility of replacing those throwback rides with electric tourism vehicles — ostensibly restoring cars to the idyllic car-free roadway inside the world’s most famous park.
The news came as part of an announcement on Tuesday that outlined his administration’s plan to support horse-carriage workers, whose industry is being phased out by 2028. The announcement was thin on details, but said the administration would “commission a feasibility study examining electric carriages and electric pedal-assist bicycles as potential alternatives within Central Park, as well as electric carriages along the park’s perimeter.”
Advocates — especially those who had spent decades trying to get cars out of the park — were stunned.
“This is just crazy, it’s really sad to think that Mamdani would be supporting reintroducing motor vehicles into Central Park,” said Ken Coughlin, who led the fight. “I don’t want to have to spend another 26 years trying to get them out.”
And Upper West side Council Member Gale Brewer agreed, adding that the idea would “open the door to a whole new fleet of commercial electric vehicles.”
“The Central Park Conservancy, Transportation Alternatives, New Yorkers for Parks, the pedestrian safety community, and the overwhelming majority of New Yorkers who use the park every day are united against swapping one safety risk for another by introducing large electric vehicles into a park that is predominantly pedestrian,” she said.
After the mayor’s statement was released, the Central Park Conservancy also quickly warned that the cars would “return [the park] to a more dangerous past.”
“Adding heavy electric vehicles to Central Park that cater almost exclusively to tourists would come at the expense of the regular New Yorkers who run, walk, bike, and stroll through it — and who worked for decades to get cars out of the Park,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe the better solution is a reformed, well-regulated year-round pedicab fleet. There are bills before the City Council right now that would do just that.”
The idea to replace horse-drawn carriages with carriage-looking vehicles is not new. When the City Council voted to enact the horse carriage ban, Council Member Vickie Paladino (R-College Point) rallied in front of City Hall to push for the “timeless” carriage-like cars. Paladino even sent her Council colleagues a 10-page slide deck to convince them on the feasibility of deploying the Disney-esque cars.
“We envision bringing that same timeless appeal to Central Park through a fleet of 68 elegant, vintage-style electric [low-speed vehicles], operated by professionally trained drivers wearing tailored, period-inspired uniforms,” said Paladino’s presentation, which was first reported by Hell Gate.
Last month, Streetsblog reminded would-be Paladinos that a proposal to bring the electric cars to the park has been around since Bill de Blasio got elected in 2013 with some big help from well-financed horse carriage opponents.
At the time, those foes rolled out — literally — their vision for a post-horse world: an electric buggy that looked like a Model T on lasix:
Cars were banned from the Central Park Drive in 2018 after a long campaign by cyclists and street safety advocates. Coughlin, who led the charge then and still advocates for a safe park, said adding these electric carriages would be a “foot in the door” to let all vehicles back in.
This is a breaking story. We reached out to City Hall for comment and will update if we hear back.

https://taz.de/Pro-und-Contra/!6224492/.title: Pro und Contra: Soll man in der Schlange stehen?
https://taz.de/Pro-und-Contra/!6224492/.author: Ambros Waibel und Carolina Schwarz
https://taz.de/Pro-und-Contra/!6224492/.text:
Pro und Contra : Soll man in der Schlange stehen?
Amsterdamer haben erfolglos gegen die Dauerschlange vor einer Frittenbude geklagt. Warum aber will man da hin, wo eh schon so viele andere sind?
JA!
W er jede Schlange im Leben umgeht, weiß nicht, was er verpasst. Kürzlich habe ich die leckerste Yuxiang Style Eggplant meines Lebens gegessen. Im Tontopf geschmorte Aubergine, butterweich mit viel Knoblauch, Essig und fermentierter Bohnenpaste.
Das Berliner Restaurant war mit seiner Neueröffnung bei Tiktok viral gegangen, was ich natürlich nicht mitbekommen habe, aber die Schlange, die sich jeden Tag vor dem neuen Laden bildete, hatte mich neugierig gemacht. So wie eigentlich jede Schlange es tut.
Wenn ich durch Berlin oder als Touristin durch eine andere Stadt schlendere und sehe, wie sich eine große Gruppe Menschen vor einem Laden sammelt, möchte ich sofort wissen, worauf sie wartet. Warum sind so viele Menschen bereit, sich bei Wind und Wetter die Beine in den Bauch zu stehen? Das muss sich doch lohnen. Und nicht selten denke ich dann: Hier will ich auch sein.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Natürlich macht es mir auch keinen Spaß, stundenlang irgendwo rumzustehen und auf etwas zu Warten. Doch meine Angst etwas zu verpassen, ist größer. Und: In der Schlange stehen, will gelernt sein. Es gibt Mittel und Wege das Nichtstun angenehmer zu gestalten, als Teil der experience.
Zuerst gilt es, den Hype eine Weile zu beobachten, um herauszufinden, wann die Schlange am kürzesten ist. Und es braucht Vorbereitung: Niemals ausgehungert anstellen, und wenn, dann nur mit Snacks in der Handtasche. Und warum den Aperitif nicht schon beim Warten nehmen? Ein Bier vom Späti reicht da vollkommen aus. Während man das Menü studiert, lässt sich die Vorfreude auf das bevorstehende Erlebnis ausreizen.
Wichtig ist, die Wartenden vor einem nicht als Gegner:innen zu begreifen, die vor einem den Platz ergattern, sondern als Community. Wir alle wollen gleich gemeinsam etwas erleben, warum nicht ein bisschen ins Gespräch kommen? Und wenn es nichts zu reden gibt, können Spiele die Wartezeit verkürzen. Manchmal reicht ein simples Ich-sehe-was-was-du-nicht-siehst, der Partyklassiker Never-have-I-ever aus. In Lissabon habe ich in einer Restaurantschlange das Handyspiel HeadsUp kennengelernt, ein Gruppenratespiel mit verschiedenen Kategorien. Das spiele ich nun seit sieben Jahren.
Auch für mich gibt es beim Warten Grenzen. Vor einem Schuhladen oder einer Konzert-Location übernachten, ist selbst mir zu viel. Aber wer weiß, was ich dabei verpasse. Vielleicht habe ich nur noch nicht richtig verstanden, wie das geht – das Schlangestehen über Nacht.
Vor dem chinesischen Restaurant in Berlin ist mittlerweile keine Schlange mehr. Man kann einfach reingehen und die aromatische Aubergine genießen – was ich immer wieder tue. Ohne Schlange hätte ich sie wohl nie probiert. (Carolina Schwarz)
NEIN!
Das Leben beginnt ungefragt. Wenn man Glück hat, wird man freudig erwartet. Am Ende gibt es keine Alternative, man muss gehen. Die Frage, ob ich die Zeit dazwischen in der Schlange verbringen will, um etwas zu ergattern, was auch viele andere wollen, ist in dieser Perspektive einfach zu beantworten: auf gar keinen Fall. Best things in live are free und ohne Anstehen zu haben.
Dass in einer Überflussökonomie, in der ich mein bisheriges Leben verbracht habe, die Verknappung eines Guts einen gewissen Thrill gibt, kann ich dabei durchaus verstehen. Aber ich finde es schöner, auf Wiesen zu grasen, wo noch keine Herden hingetrieben worden sind. Ich liebe die Entdeckungen und die Schleichwege. Ich fahre an Orte, die niemand sehen will, und sobald aus Schwammerlsuchen Waldbaden wird, bin ich raus (passenderweise gibt es eh immer weniger Pilze).
Ist mir dadurch etwas entgangen? In dem Sinn auf jeden Fall, dass meine Erfahrungen oft nicht teilbar sind. Ich muss sie, wie einst ein Dichter sagte, „im Busen bewahren“. Zumindest eine Zeit lang. Denn echte Entdeckungen bleiben nie Geheimtipps, wobei dieser Begriff eh schon alle Warnleuchten aufblinken lässt.
Unvergessen etwa der Moment, wo man uns in dem angesagten Restaurant nach zwei Stunden mitteilte, unser „Slot“ sei nun vorbei und wir müssten gehen. Wer lässt sich so ein zweites Mal abfertigen? Wer stellt sich zwei Stunden irgendwo in der Kälte an, um dann möglicherweise gar nicht reingelassen zu werden? Ist das vielleicht schon ein Training für apokalyptische Zeiten, in denen lebensnotwendige Güter nur nach langer Wartezeit zu ergattern sein werden?
Die Schlange, wäre ein Gedanke, hat aber doch etwas Demokratisches: Alle bekommen eine Chance, Fair Play, dieses angelsächsische Lebensgefühl eben. Ich will das nicht wegdrängeln, erinnere mich aber auch an den italienischen Großvater, der seinen Enkeln angesichts einer disziplinierten Touristenschlange in Venedig erklärte, „seht ihr, so sind sie, die Menschen in anderen Ländern, ordentlich und geduldig. Aber wir sind Italiener, und wir sind nicht so.“
Ich bin kein Italiener. Aber ich bin auch nicht so. Ich kriege Nervenkrisen in Schlangen, und Schweißausbrüche. Ich will da raus und nicht hinein, egal welches Paradies am Ende auf mich wartet. Ob’s am Ende für das Richtige reicht, werde ich dann rausfinden, wenn es Zeit ist – und jedenfalls ohne Anstehen. (Ambros Waibel)
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Isabelle Ferreras
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.
When the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm is to leave, it is a clear sign that corporate governance in the industry is broken. Each departure takes with it the very knowledge needed to steer these systems safely.
As policymakers, tech workers, trade unionists, members of parliament and experts from a wide range of global institutions, including the Vatican and the UN, gather in London this week to discuss AI safety, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: we cannot regulate AI safely from the outside if the companies building it remain autocracies on the inside.
Regulatory debates remain trapped in a narrow mindset where governments treat AI either as a consumer product to be tested for defects or as a geopolitical race to be won by relaxing rules on business. This is the logic of Ursula von der Leyen’s EU digital omnibus, which delays implementation of rules enshrined in the EU’s landmark 2024 AI Act that set out specific safety requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems. Corporate lobbies encourage this framing of a trade-off between safety and innovation by arguing that legislation imposes too many burdens.
This is a dangerous path. AI is not merely a software product; it is a technology of government. Yet inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google, a handful of executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models that shape millions of lives.
As the Oxford legal scholar Jeremias Adams-Prassl, who pioneered research into the gig economy and is leading research into automated work in Europe, has shown, algorithmic management already monitors, evaluates and dismisses workers across the socioeconomic spectrum, often without any human oversight.
In a democratic society, the exercise of governing power requires the consent of the governed. Yet corporate law still treats firms as the property of shareholders, and the labour investors, who put their intellect, health and lives into the firm, as subordinates. To align AI with the public interest, we need a dual strategy: alongside solid public regulations on AI “from the outside”, we need to enter the corporate black box and force corporate governance into alignment with democratic principles.
Legislators must move forward on three critical reforms. First, in AI development, they must protect and empower those who build AI models. Governments must outlaw non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, and enact robust whistleblower protection. Tech workers also need a collective standing over corporate strategy, independent channels to report safety breaches and formal representation inside frontier labs before models are deployed.
The second reform relates to AI deployment. Remember what happened at Meta over the summer: Mark Zuckerberg’s firm faced a backlash from employees after Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp introduced a tool that tracked staff keystrokes, mouse clicks and content displayed on computer screens to collect data for training its AI models. Not only were workers worried that privacy and consent was in ruins, they worried their jobs were on the line.
Legislators must establish a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI. No algorithmic system that monitors, evaluates or disciplines workers should be deployed without prior negotiation. At national and EU level, we need to consider collective bargaining on AI deployment and veto rights for works councils or trade unions, backed by independent technical experts and a strict ban on automated firing.
Third, across the economy, we must democratise boardrooms and reward firms that refuse to concentrate power at the top. Legislators should mandate worker-elected directors on boards, moving towards dual-majority governance in which strategic decisions require the consent not only of capital but of labour.
As Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, have shown, technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity: institutions decide who benefits and who pays. Extending democracy into the firm is not an old battle over power for its own sake, but a practical necessity for more ethical judgment. Aligning AI with the good of workers and society requires more wisdom than closed executive rooms can offer. It needs what the Yale political theorist Hélène Landemore calls “democratic reason”, the collective intelligence of diverse, deliberating voices, brought to bear on corporate decision-making.
Left to self-regulation and the occasional whistleblower, AI governance will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy. Accountability and aligment begins with giving those who build these systems and those whose work they govern an enforceable voice, from the code floor to the boardroom.
- Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Jonathan Liew
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast.
Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-life business proposition; a legitimate going concern with profits and a bottom line and a plan for the future.
Eventually a new vision emerged – LIV 2.0 – announced at a triumphant press conference at the Trump National course in New Jersey. In future, LIV would belong to the players, who would become equity partners in the tour, forgoing guaranteed purses in return for something far more valuable: an idea, a stake in the future enterprise, with all its untapped potential. Upon signing their lavish contracts, most of these players had spoken warmly of LIV’s values, its commitment to holistic growth of the game, and if ever there were an opportunity to demonstrate their commitment to the breakaway tour, it was now. Amusingly, most of them decided to walk away and plot a route back to one of the world’s more liquid golfing tours.
Can it really have been true? Was it really just about the money all along? For all LIV’s grandiose mission statements, its talk of innovation and creative disruption, its mode of operation was never that artful or artfully disguised, and nor did you need a deep well of sympathy for the existing golfing establishment to see it. Golf was not dying when LIV came along. It was not irretrievably fractured, on its last legs, in need of rescue. LIV fulfilled no urgent need beyond the inelastic impatience of Yasir al-Rumayyan, and his yearning to possess by shock doctrine what he could not obtain by incremental manoeuvre.
There was no great innovation here, no act of generational genius, as much as the credulous golf press and business media clambered over themselves to indulge Norman and his outlandish claims, to anoint al-Rumayyan the “new king of golf”. As it turned out, Spending Lots Of Money To Buy The World’s Best Golfers is not a hard or clever thing to do (at least until the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz sends your oil revenues spinning deep into the second cut). Particularly when the reason for your interest is less as a robust investment vehicle and more because You Just Really Like Golf.
And why do rich, powerful men love golf? Fresh air. Oneness with nature. Don’t say social segregation. Peace and quiet, the solemn and noble pursuit of personal fulfilment. No riff-raff. No! It’s obsession, it’s tradition, it’s triumph and disaster, it’s the world in a little white ball. It’s a shrine to moneyed heritage. Stop it! It’s not! It’s camaraderie, it’s freedom, it’s exercise, it’s a game of infinite angles and unfathomable skill that – unlike snooker and darts and table tennis and all the other sports of which this is also true – also incorporates a kind of moral code, a way of living.
Most of golf’s rules and customs are less about the adjudication of a sporting contest and more about an assertion of values, and the implied exclusion of those who fail to live up to them. No phones at Augusta. Respect for the putting line. Calling a penalty on yourself. Drinks in the clubhouse. Collared shirts and tailored legwear. Your approval for membership must be proposed and seconded by existing club members. More than virtually any other sport in existence, golf is continually posing the question: are you our kind of person? Prove it. Prove it.
At the elite levels, perhaps this manifests itself as a kind of affected and immaculate reserve: an acceptance of and comfort with the world as it is, or at least the world as it is presented to you. There is no great tradition of golf activism, no golf Kaepernick or golf Osaka or even a golf Cantona. Rory McIlroy has been elevated to deity status for the apparently remarkable act of being quite nice. But of course he still accepted the offer to play a round with Trump at his course, indeed regarded it as an honour and privilege, was utterly baffled at the idea that anyone might deem it a political act, because ultimately golf exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled.
And above all, it manifests as an effortless ease around money, which is not really supposed to be talked about, even though it’s everywhere. Other sports have league tables and medal counts; golf has a “money list”, and so naturally when LIV began its campaign of disruption there would be no real reckoning. In theory, it was the perfect moment for golf to reflect on its role in the world: its celebration of wealth and privilege, its environmental impact, who it takes its money from. Instead, the PGA reasoned that the way to respond to LIV’s money was with more money, better money, more sustainable money.
And so, under the former NFL executive Brian Rolapp, the PGA Tour has marched unapologetically into a new world of private equity, increased prize funds and untrammelled greed. A new top-tier Champions Series. “Signature events” with smaller fields and no cuts. A player equity programme, based in part on fan engagement and media visibility, an extension of the core idea of Trumponomics: for those best able to leverage it, attention equals currency, power, money. LIV may have lost the war. But it may just have won the argument.

https://taz.de/Erstes-Basketball-Museum-.title: Erstes Basketball-Museum Deutschlands: Das Spiel, seine Ikonen und viele vergessene Geschichten
https://taz.de/Erstes-Basketball-Museum-.author: Katarina Schubert
https://taz.de/Erstes-Basketball-Museum-.text:
Erstes Basketball-Museum Deutschlands: Das Spiel, seine Ikonen und viele vergessene Geschichten
In Berlin entsteht das Basketball-Museum „28.15“. Es soll den Sport und seine Geschichte näherbringen. Was noch fehlt, sind Räumlichkeiten.
Es regnete in Strömen, dennoch fanden am Dienstagabend mehr als 100 Leute den Weg ins Besucherzentrum des ehemaligen Flughafens Tempelhof, wo sie etwas ganz Besonderes erwartete: die Besichtigung eines Basketball-Courts, sechs Stockwerke über der Abflughalle und direkt unter dem Dach gelegen. 1947 von der US-Armee erbaut, diente er lange Jahre ihren Soldaten als Spiel- und Trainingsstätte. Heutzutage ist das in Türkis und Orange gehaltene Feld baufällig und gehört zu den zahlreichen sogenannten Hidden Places Berlins. Man bekommt es also eher selten zu sehen.
„Viele haben schon einmal von diesem Basketball-Court gehört, aber gesehen haben sie ihn noch nie. Die Leute kamen nach der Besichtigung alle ein bisschen glücklicher zurück, hatte ich das Gefühl“, sagt Henning Harnisch später am Abend. Er ist Vizepräsident des Basketballvereins Alba Berlin und Projektleiter des Basketball-Museums „28.15“. Letzteres hatte auch die besondere Besichtigung mitorganisiert, die im Rahmen der Veranstaltung „Was fliegt denn da? Basketball in Berlin vor und nach 1989/90“ stattfand.
Noch befindet sich das Basketball-Museum „28.15“ im Aufbau. Die Idee, ein eigenes Museum zu gründen, hatten Harnisch und Alba-Geschäftsführer Marco Baldi bereits vor zwei Jahren. Benannt nach den Maßen eines europäischen Basketballfelds – 28 mal 15 Meter –, soll das Museum aber nicht nur die Geschichte Albas abdecken. Es gehe generell um die Welt des Basketballs, erklärt Harnisch begeistert. Denn: „Wir haben so eine reiche Kultur, das ist so ein schönes Spiel, so vielfältig aufgeladen. Sei es der Freiplatz-Basketball, Männer und Frauen, Mädchen und Jungen, Ost und West, die Rolle der US-Amerikaner, die Mode, seine Ikonen.“
Es gebe so viel zu erzählen. Das zugänglich zu machen, sei das Ziel des Museums. „Bis jetzt existiert so ein Museum in Deutschland ja auch noch gar nicht, deshalb ist es an der Zeit, sich geschichtlich damit auseinanderzusetzen, wo dieser Sport in Deutschland eigentlich herkam“, sagt Harnisch. Er selbst war zwischen 1987 und 1997 Nationalspieler und wurde 1993 mit dem deutschen Team Europameister.
Es wird noch nach einem Raum gesucht
Räumlichkeiten hat Alba für sein Museum noch nicht gefunden, das sei aber nur eine Frage der Zeit. Und soll nicht heißen, dass das Projekt stillsteht. Zurzeit gibt es einen eigenen Podcast namens „Hangtime History“ sowie einen Newsletter, außerdem ist das Museum in den sozialen Medien vertreten. Hauptfokus sei jedoch die Arbeit mit jungen Menschen, deshalb geht „28.15“ auch in die Schulen.
„Unser Traum ist es aber, dass wir irgendwann einen eigenen Ort haben, an dem wir einen außerschulischen Lern- und Bildungsort schaffen können“, sagt Harnisch. „Einerseits wollen wir die Möglichkeit bieten, etwas über den Sport zu erfahren, andererseits sollen die Schüler*innen lernen, wie man sich journalistisch und künstlerisch darüber austauschen kann. Das ist die große Idee.“
Solange es diesen Ort aber noch nicht gibt, seien solche Veranstaltungen, wie sie nun am Tempelhofer Flughafen stattgefunden hat, umso wichtiger. Auch weil sie für Themen Sichtbarkeit schaffen, die sonst nicht so präsent sind. Die Anwesenden bekamen jedenfalls an diesem Abend nicht nur die Gelegenheit, sich den US-Court und eine Ausstellung über die Geschichte des deutschen Basketballs anzuschauen, sondern auch mit ehemaligen Spieler*innen wie Frank Menz oder Inge Laabs ins Gespräch zu kommen.
Letztere spielte in den 1970er Jahren für das Nationalteam der DDR und freute sich, dass jetzt auch deren Erfolge die angemessene Aufmerksamkeit bekommen. 1966 gewannen die DDR-Frauen EM-Bronze, ein Jahr später wurden sie Vierte bei der WM, das beste WM-Ergebnis eines deutschen Frauenbasketballteams bis zur WM dieses Jahr, bei der die deutschen Frauen etwas überraschend erneut Vierte geworden sind. „Basketball gab es in der DDR schon lange, und der war international auch sehr erfolgreich, was aber viele so nicht wissen“, erzählt die heutige Trainerin.
Schlaglichter auf vergessene Geschichte zu lenken, ist auch Henning Harnisch wichtig. „Ich wusste selbst nicht viel über die Erfolge der DDR-Frauen und war dann positiv erstaunt, wie erfolgreich sie waren“, gibt er zu. 1969 wurde dem Basketball von der DDR-Sportführung allerdings die Förderung entzogen, die Erfolge blieben daraufhin aus. „Diese Geschichte wollen wir unbedingt zugänglich machen. Ich finde es sportpolitisch wichtig, dass junge Menschen davon erfahren“, sagt er. Das Interesse am Dienstagabend war auf jeden Fall groß. Sogar zur Überraschung von Harnisch selbst. „Irgendwie treffen wir da gerade einen Nerv“, glaubt er.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Stuart McGurk
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.
It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.
The two had become fast friends since they met at Power Slap 17, which took place last October in Saudi Arabia. They host a podcast together, called The Slappy Hour (sample chat: “I had questions for his chin … but the chin question’s gone”). “As the sport’s so new, it’s great to have someone to bounce ideas off,” said Robinson. It’s not uncommon for competitors to destroy each other on stage, then later compare notes. When I spoke to Damien “the Bell” Dibbell, an affable 24-year-old American heavyweight whom many consider the greatest slap-fighter alive, he mentioned that he met his best friend, Duane “the Iron Giant” Crespo, after knocking him unconscious in the second round.
In the Crowne Plaza, conversation veered from recent rule changes – beards were now limited to a few millimetres, much glorious facial hair had been lost – to a controversial incident in Power Slap 21 when Anthony “Kiing” DeFrank had refused to alter his stance after being accused of “turtling”, breaking the rules by tucking his chin flush into his neck to receive the slap. Despite his protests, he was disqualified. Word was he’d never slap again.
Seen from a certain perspective, Power Slap is less a sport in its own right than one whittled down from other sports: think football reduced to penalties or rugby with just conversions. Like boxing, it is a combat sport, separated by gender and weight divisions (from flyweight to super-heavyweight). Unlike boxing, competitors are forbidden from dodging or blocking the blows. Like darts, Power Slap is turn-based. Unlike darts, contestants effectively take turns at being the board.
The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.
This is a sport precision-made for our moment. It is designed to be viewed on TikTok and YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, one thumb-swipe at a time. Power Slap’s CEO, Frank Lamicella, a former corporate lawyer from New York, will happily admit it was created with short attention spans in mind. The only real buildup comes in the contestants’ walk to the stage and the brief seconds they spend rehearsing their slap before striking, like snooker players feathering a cue. A round lasts a couple of minutes; titles can be decided in seconds. As every action is a potential knockout, the highlights come pre-packaged. It is nothing but highlights.
Since its launch in November 2022, Power Slap has gained 4 million YouTube subscribers. On TikTok it has more than 9 million. Perhaps even more importantly – though admittedly unverifiably – Power Slap claims that clips of the sport have racked up 25bn total views across all online platforms. Its live events are now held almost every month, in locations from Las Vegas to Abu Dhabi.
The founder of Power Slap is Dana White, the man behind the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), whose accomplishments include organising a cage fight on the White House lawn to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Donald Trump is such a fan of White that he recently asked him to be his press secretary. (He later claimed he was just kidding.)
White expects Power Slap to be the biggest sport in the world soon. In explaining its appeal, he likes to invoke the school playground: no matter what kids are up to, when a fight breaks out, everyone watches. Violence is a universal language. Or, as he told a podcast last year, “everyone understands a slap”. He sells “holy shit moments”, he said, and Power Slap has more than most.
According to White, Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade. The companies lining up to plaster their name over Power Slap include energy drink suppliers such as Monster Energy and cryptocurrency platforms such as VeChain. Erectile dysfunction drug company Rugiet recently sponsored Power Slap’s action replay.
Power Slap is not without its detractors, many of whom deem it less a sport than violence for the hell of it. The Brain Injury Association of America has demanded its immediate end. Chris Nowinski, CEO of the Concussion Legacy Foundation, has wondered: “What’s next, ‘who can survive a stabbing?’” Even podcaster Joe Rogan, a noted proponent of UFC – itself criticised for brutality – has called Power Slap “free brain damage”.
In Belgrade, Robinson was confident but apprehensive. Power Slap 22 marked the first time the competition had been held in Europe. It was only his second Power Slap, having risen through the less glamorous UK scene where they slap over a barrel. He wanted to do his local scene proud. His opponent the following day was Pavol “Glitch” Horelican, an undefeated Slovakian. Yet his long-term goal was taking down Dibbell, the Apollo Creed to his Rocky. “He’s an ungodly genetic freak,” Robinson told me. “He’s probably the perfect slap-fighter.” In Serbia, the two went out for dinner, though they were careful not to talk tactics.
Both Robinson and Kenny had been at the hotel for the best part of a week, fulfilling various media duties. One of the challenges, it turns out, for a sport that is both ultra-collegial and ultra-violent, is ramping up aggression when required. For his pre-fight face-off with Horelican earlier that day, Robinson did his best with the required pantomime smack-talk, but his heart wasn’t in it. He’d taken him out to dinner, too, and even taught him how he tenses his muscles to prepare for a slap. (Kenny was aghast: “What the fuck you doing?”)
In the hours before the fight, Robinson told me, he planned to work himself into a state of frenzy by imagining Horelican responsible for the death of his entire family, a sort of John Wick-plus. Kenny, the Canadian, said he would be aiming for a Zen state, through meditation.
Roughly speaking, the history of sport is a story of compression and contraction, or at least the growing understanding that we all have homes to go to. Many events began as endurance contests: boxing matches went on until one person could no longer stand; Test cricket could span weeks. (One match, between England and South Africa, lasted 12 days and was eventually abandoned as England had a ship to catch.) Before the modern marathon, the Victorians followed “pedestrianism”, six-day walking races during which competitors steadily consumed beef tea. By the dawn of the TV age, most competitive sports required only small tweaks, rather than total reinventions, to accommodate themselves to the new medium. Football kick-off times changed, table-tennis balls were very slightly enlarged. Now that we have arrived at the viral clip stage of human culture, we have new requirements. Hence Power Slap.
The first professional slap, as far as anyone can tell, took place a little over a decade ago. A Californian man called Raymond Hernandez ran a touring expo called The Ink Masters Tattoo Show and wanted some non-tattoo-based entertainment. He had recently toured Japan, and remembered a segment from a gameshow that made him laugh: five men in a circle, each taking turns to slap the man to his right – last man standing wins. Hernandez decided two men were enough. Stripping an activity down to its studs was in slap-fighting’s DNA from the start. At an expo in Lubbock, Texas, in early 2015, Hernandez placed the competitors either side of a folding table and explained the entire rulebook. Slap.
The first man slapped the other across the table without much impact; the second slapped back and knocked his opponent out. Hernandez hadn’t arranged for anyone to catch the falling fighter. “We never thought you could get knocked out by a slap,” he has said. The footage, recorded on a smartphone, went viral. ESPN and Jimmy Kimmel got in touch. Slap fighting was born.
It wasn’t until 2017 that Dana White first became aware of slap fighting. Sitting in a meeting room at UFC’s head office in Las Vegas, White, as CEO, was supposed to be discussing matchups and pay-per-view deals, yet his attention was elsewhere: specifically, on a social media video of two large Russian men taking turns to slap each other. The production value was not high – to White it looked like it had been filmed in a barn – yet it had racked up almost 400m views. At the time, those were Justin Bieber numbers.
At UFC, White had built a reputation on turning violence into entertainment. UFC is a very-few-holds-barred cage-fighting contest that combines kickboxing and wrestling undertaken with minimally padded gloves. In 1995, the senator John McCain labelled it “human cockfighting”. By 2001, UFC was on the verge of bankruptcy when White, along with Vegas casino magnates Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta, bought it for $2m. They codified the rules, received athletic commission approval, and self-funded a reality TV show to promote it. It became a juggernaut. In July 2016, the trio had sold UFC for $4bn, though White stayed on as CEO. Not long after seeing the video of the Russian men slugging each other in a weirdly compelling ritual, White called the Fertitta brothers and asked: “Wanna do it again?” It was a historic moment. “I don’t know another example where this has happened, where you take one YouTube video and you build an entire sport around it,” Lamicella told me.
Owing to the pandemic, it wasn’t until March 2022 that they put together a closed-doors pilot in Las Vegas. It consisted of 25 bouts involving more than 40 fighters over two days, and its aim was, among other things, to firm up the rules. By then, other slap-fighting competitions, with varying standards of safety and showmanship, had formed in Poland, South Africa and the UK. There was even an American upstart called SlapFight Championship. Power Slap, with more buying power, snapped up the best fighters.
The rules boiled down to three main fouls. No stepping – meaning no heel lift, feet square, to reduce a strike’s power. No clubbing – meaning no striking with the heel of the palm and no contact anywhere but the cheek. And no flinching. They also limited the number of rounds. At SlapFight Championship, they initially went on until someone won, which usually meant a knockout. One fight lasted 27 rounds before doctors stopped it. One man’s eye had swollen shut.
For Lamicella, the pilot event in Vegas brought home one major realisation: they were going to need a hell of a lot of cameras. More than 30, he reckoned, to capture the full majesty of the sport. “You have the shot, the slow-mo, the super slow-mo, the aerial shot, the shot of the feet, every which angle,” he told me. “It looks simple, but the production budget is huge.”
White followed the same formula as UFC. After obtaining regulatory approval from the Nevada State Athletic Commission, he launched a reality TV show to promote it, Power Slap: Road to the Title, to air on basic cable network TBS. The show did not last long once footage emerged of White, in an irony that was lost on no one, slapping his wife in a nightclub. TBS cancelled the show after the first season.
There is no typical route into “slap”, as those in the sport call it. Robinson, who had never previously competed professionally in any combat sport, discovered it online during lockdown. Then and there, he decided, for reasons he finds hard to fully articulate, to become the best slap fighter in the world. His podcast co-host, Kenny, had been making $30 a match in Canadian wrestling when a recruiter asked him: “You wanna get slapped?” After asking how much it paid – $5,000 with another five if he won – it turned out that, yes, in fact, he did.
Some journeys are more colourful. Peter “the Alligator All G” Truchlik, a former international arm-wrestling champion, was talent-spotted by Power Slap promoters who came across YouTube videos of him bending nails, tearing books and slapping watermelons into oblivion. Vasilii “Dumpling” Kamotskii, who competes in the super-heavyweight division, found the sport by chance. At a strongman festival years before, the Siberian farmer had entered both a slap-fighting and a dumpling-eating contest, won both, and got a new side-hustle and a new nickname to go with it. His first Power Slap paycheque was $25,000 and three goats.
No one I spoke to slapped full-time. Even reigning heavyweight champion Dibbell, who sells slap-based merch (phone cases, hoodies, T-shirts) on the side, has a day job as an air-conditioning repairman. Robinson is a lift engineer by trade. He enjoys the work. It teaches him a lot about people. Surprisingly often, he says, he’ll attend a broken lift only to find those stuck inside have ended up fighting, breaking it further still. “A different type of cage match,” he laughs.
Robinson is short and sturdy, with a trim beard and a seriousness only punctuated by a laugh that seems to arrive by accident, as if he’s been caught off guard. He is a man easily obsessed, and his obsessions make him easy to like. Before slap fighting, his passions flared and burned out. As a younger man, he compulsively collected things such as coins and cards, before moving on to driving simulators, buying everything from the chair to the steering wheel to the gearstick. By his mid-20s, he was on to chess, setting up two monitors at work, one permanently on chess.com, playing four or five hours a day (he has since left that job), before moving on to darts, joining leagues, spending hundreds on the exact type of board and arrow, “trying to work my way up”.
Each time, what ended the obsession was the dispiriting realisation he would never be the best. Chess came to an abrupt halt when he realised he was 20 years late, having failed to start aged five.
His gift for Power Slap had been staring him in the face the whole time. He grew up on a rough estate in Stalybridge, was punched and slapped his fair share, yet he never so much as bruised. His party trick as a teen: to let people punch him as hard as they could. This was not his proudest hour, yet he eventually realised it was his superpower. When he saw slap fighting on YouTube in lockdown, he thought: where can I do this?
He contacted Josh Skeete, who by 2022 was just getting a UK slap-fighting scene, which would later be called BritSlap, off the ground in Liverpool. Skeete had encountered his fair share of resistance. At first, the fighters and wrestlers he contacted to take part told him to get lost; slap fighting wasn’t a sport. Others seemed interested. He hired refs – who could ensure the fighters’ feet didn’t move and the striker’s aim for the cheek was true – and a medical team, yet soon realised he needed to hire catchers, too. At early events, fighters brought along a friend for the job, but they would often get so wrapped up in the action, they’d forget to actually catch the falling fighters.
For his first slap fight, at BritSlap 3 in early 2024, filmed without an audience in a TV studio in Liverpool, Robinson competed in jeans. Looking back, he reckons his technique was all over the place, his body motion all wrong. Still, by the judge’s decision, he won. He was hooked. “I was all in. I was addicted. That was it for me. I thought: now I’m gonna conquer the world.”
He had only told his partner, Shannon Hilton, that he was taking part a few hours before. She spent the intervening time watching YouTube videos, becoming ever-more horrified. “She was livid,” Robinson told me. When he returned and told her he’d won, she had been so angry, she’d already decided to deny him victory, and had told everyone he had lost.
Slap fighting is so new that nearly every aspect of training and technique must be invented. Prior to his second BritSlap fight, in October 2024, Robinson prepared mostly with regular gym work, while also honing his technique by slapping pads held by a friend. He got some odd looks in a PureGym while those around him did pilates. He won his fight, knocking his opponent out with the very first slap. But to become the best in the world, he needed more.
The demands on the slap fighter are particular. Unlike boxing, the rules dictate that competitors cannot place one foot behind the other to help generate force. So Robinson sought out a sport in which competitors throw while seated, and found one: Paralympic discus. He found a Paralympic discus trainer who taught him how to generate torque from his hips. The motion suited him: unlike taller US slap fighters, who prefer horizontal bear-claw swipes, Robinson, at 5ft 7in, is mostly slapping upwards.
His feet weren’t allowed to lift – but what, he wondered, if they could roll? Other slap fighters wore cowboy boots to aid this. Power Slap has no rules regarding footwear. Under the guidance of his personal trainer, James Reed, Robinson began studying the heel-to-toe rolling techniques that surfers use to change direction. He realised the tendon in his slapping arm, his right, was more important than the muscles. In his van, any time he was parked, Robinson pumped a hand-grip with his right. To strengthen that hand, he looked to rock climbers, who do finger exercises with their hands submerged in uncooked rice. “The burn you get off that is insane,” says Robinson, who mostly does it while watching Netflix. When he saw an actor deliver a slap on screen, he’d think: amateur.
At the gym, he’d slap a punching bag. At night, in his garden, he’d practice by slapping the head of a boxing mannequin. At first, his neighbours thought the sound was gunfire. By BritSlap 5, in May last year, now at Boxpark in Liverpool with a crowd of more than 1,000, Robinson knocked another opponent out with his first slap. Power Slap soon came calling. Skeete became his manager.
To fully appreciate the power of a well-honed slap, I attended the Resilience Training Centre in Stalybridge, a small gym in a former factory that recently became the first in the UK to offer dedicated slap-fight training. I held a pad at head height as a slender young man, who was competing in a forthcoming BritSlap, practised his slaps. With each, my arm was almost wrenched from the socket. I declined Robinson’s kind offer to receive his slaps next, but I can confirm: Robinson’s slaps do sound like gunfire.
When it comes to brain injuries, just how dire is Power Slap? The bad news is that participation virtually guarantees head trauma. But its defenders note that this trauma comes in limited portions: five scheduled blows for title fights. Robinson points out that he might take more than 100 blows in a boxing match. In Power Slap, the most common injuries happen to the slapper – pulled biceps, fractured wrists, even broken arms, because, unlike boxing, where your gloves cushion the blow, the combatant is putting all their force into connecting with a solid object.
Still, the solid object in question happens to be the opponent’s face, and the unabashed aim is to render that opponent unconscious. It is this that drives online views. Power Slap offers $10,000 bonuses for knockouts, typically doubling a fighter’s purse. Robinson has honed his technique to this end. He slaps upwards, making the head move quicker, the brain deforming inside the skull. “The science of knocking someone out isn’t how hard you hit them,” he told me. “It’s how fast you can make that brain accelerate.” Robinson has yet to be knocked out, but notes the “flashes” of white light he gets each time he is struck.
Sometimes, after a knockout, competitors have to be reminded what happened. At Power Slap’s test event, a competitor named Chris Kennedy was knocked unconscious by the first slap he took, and asked, upon waking, “Got knocked out doing what?” After being knocked out in Power Slap 6, in Las Vegas, Sheena “the Hungarian Hurricane” Bathory woke up in an ambulance. She had to be informed why she was in Las Vegas, and that she had won (her opponent had committed a clubbing foul). Slap fighting’s one fatality occurred in 2021, at PunchDown 5 in Poland, when Artur “Waluś” Walczak suffered a brain bleed and died several weeks later. It was his third slap fight of the evening. (“In any combat sport, fighting more than once in an evening is insane,” says Robinson.)
When I asked Lamicella about the dangers, he noted the comprehensive medical tests, including brain scans, that every fighter must pass before each fight. He also compared Power Slap, favourably, to both boxing and UFC. “If our doctor was on the phone, he would tell you the big issues in boxing are not the big knockouts. It’s all the little jabs, the continuous punches, the sparring. That’s where the people really get hurt with things like brain bleeds,” he said. He added that their “hospital transport number” was “a lot lower than UFC”.
One of the few medical studies of Power Slap was carried out by Raj Lavadi, a neurosurgeon at Indiana University School of Medicine, who studied footage of 333 strikes across 78 matches and found 79% of fighters showed an observable sign of concussion. “The frequency with which you observe these signs is shocking,” Lavadi told me.
Lavadi also pointed out the brain scans don’t count for much. “A brain scan is great for certain things,” he said. “But I don’t know if it really protects the fighter. Like, is that it?” Crucially, while a brain scan can pick up conditions ranging from blood vessel abnormalities to fractures, it would not pick up the onset of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease most likely caused by repeated blows to the head, which is linked to symptoms ranging from memory loss to dementia. “You can really only diagnose that in autopsy,” he said.
At the event in Belgrade, participants spoke about the fighters who could take a slap without much reaction and who could not – who could “eat it”, in slap parlance. They also spoke about a “chin-meter” – like a battery bar they think of depleting with each knockout, making the next knockout more likely. Both Robinson and Kenny mentioned light heavyweight Ron “the Wolverine” Bata. It was time for him to retire, they felt. “He doesn’t look the same, he looks like he gets hurt more and more now,” said Kenny.
When I mentioned the undetectable onset of CTE to Robinson, he said he’d already given himself a knockout limit. Twice and he was out. He understood the long-term impact multiple knockouts could have. He was a father of three, with a fourth on the way. He mentioned a quote from Dibbell, the reigning champion he hoped to topple. “He said, ‘If you’ve been knocked out before, I’m not the man to fight’, and that’s the truth.”
Every Power Slap clip is its own microdrama. Each has suspense and violence, triumph and disaster. It doesn’t much matter if you watch in horror or with glee: the algorithm will note that you watched and will suggest you watch more.
Nearly all begin with a closeup on the face of someone waiting patiently to be struck, and you realise how strange this is. It is not like watching a live execution, but it’s also not like watching penalties. The closest analogue is probably corporal punishment. As they wait, slap fighters grimace manically, looking terrified. This grimacing is often used for the thumbnail images on social media, but it is not just a product of fear. Forming this expression engages their trapezius muscles, or traps, bracing the neck and upper back, aiming to spread the impact of the blow to come. You feel their pain before they do.
The striker will first place their hand on their opponent’s cheek, in a way that almost seems tender, to get their measure before they swing. They will do wind-ups, slowly motioning the real strike, and must declare beforehand when it comes – on one, two or three.
For a sport that doesn’t allow flinching, let alone blocking, slap fighters put just as much training into defence as they do attack. What exactly works seems woolly. Most agree having strong neck and jaw muscles helps, though most don’t copy Hayden “the Cowboy” Johnson, who lifts kettlebells with his teeth. Robinson uses a jaw exerciser. He’s managed to develop bulging temples (“a right meathead,” he laughs).
The hardest part, most will tell you, is training yourself not to flinch, especially for those with a combat background, who’ve spent their lives learning how to dodge. The penalties for flinching are serious. After a flinch, the striker is allowed to slap again. Three flinches in the same round, or four overall, means disqualification. Light heavyweight Logan “Kill Shot” Greenhalgh once lost a title fight to a flinch. Some use the Muay Thai technique of punching water in a barrel, keeping their eyes open through the splashes. It’s perhaps only Aaron “Colossus” Turner who trains with snakes, putting his face to the glass and trying to stay still when they strike. (It didn’t work – Turner was disqualified in his last match for flinching.) Most, including Robinson, just get someone to slap them with foam pool noodles.
Yet even here, Robinson has innovated. What if, he wondered, he could take the impact out of a slap by moving his face, rolling with it, at the exact moment of contact? Could it be done? In that fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a second? He looked towards Formula One, where drivers train their reactions with a multicoloured three-pronged spinning device – they must grab the colour of the prong their coach calls out while it spins in mid-air. “We’ve spent hours doing that,” laughs Reed, his trainer. In real time, as he is struck, it seems as if Robinson is flinching. YouTube commentators always claim it. It’s only in slow motion you realise he isn’t. He moves at the millisecond a blow arrives. Robinson now proudly calls this his signature move.
The most-watched Power Slap clip is an 18sec YouTube short, with almost half a billion views. It is not a knockdown. It is called “Eviahn ATE this slap with ease!” Eviahn “the Waterboy” Scott takes a blow, and celebrates wildly, like a goalkeeper who’s just pulled off a fingertip save to preserve a precious lead. The camera cuts to a giggling Dana White, looking like a child who’s seen an adult almost slip over. Then it’s time for the replay. In Power Slap, the slow-motion replays almost always focus on the exact motion of impact, the flesh on the face not so much absorbing the blow as spreading it, rippling from it, like a sheet caught by a breeze.
The second-most-watched clip is a knockdown. It has been viewed 371m times, this time on TikTok. It is called, “Jewel Scott #knockouts hit different #powerslap #slap”, and sees Scott’s opponent, Anthony Green, drop to the ground like a ragdoll.
We think of dopamine as a pleasure chemical, yet neuroscientists will tell you it is not. It is, instead, the molecule of desire and anticipation. It makes us watch to the end, it makes us flick to the next, but it does not bring joy. It is also why they compare social media’s infinite scroll to slot machines.
At the Belgrade Arena, on 30 July, several thousand spectators filed in for PowerSlap 22. The sport is still new in Europe. In Las Vegas, I’m told, the vibe is a cross between British darts and American wrestling, the ramp-up between each slap eliciting hollers and cheers and boos. In Belgrade, the mood was one of amused interest.
Before it began, young fans flooded to the front to beg autographs from a couple of fighters walking the floor. Once the lights went down, it took on an air closer to a Vegas magic show than a prize fight. A light show strobed, a black stage without borders in the arena’s centre was lit up by neon podiums at either end – Power Slap’s equivalent of a fighter’s corner, where each competitor would retreat for one minute to recover after each blow – and in the centre, a glowing podium rose from the ground to a height of around 3ft, the padded plinth over which all slaps would take place.
A sharply suited MC kicked things off by introducing the sponsors. The night’s “monster knockouts”, we were told, were brought to us by Monster Energy (“unleash the beast!”). VeChain was the crypto token partner – and also the medium in which the $10,000 knockout bonuses would be paid. The night’s prediction odds were brought to us by Polymarket.
The first fight was both the most thrilling and disturbing, as Darren “the Tarantula” Godfrey, bearded and liberally tattooed, took on the fresh-faced Daniyar “Shreder” Toktarov in the middleweight division. Both wore trainers, Power Slap-branded tracksuit bottoms, and Power Slap-branded T-shirts. Godfrey was knocked down in both the first and second rounds, something most fighters don’t recover from. On the second occasion, Godfrey stayed down until the referee counted to eight. He retreated to his corner, then returned to the podium. On Godfrey’s second slap, he knocked Tokarov out, his head connecting sickeningly with the central podium as he dropped. It was replayed in slow, then super slow, motion on the arena’s screens. No one in the audience appeared to wince. Most clapped and cheered.
When Robinson entered the arena, he set about stirring up the crowd, whipping both arms upwards. The lights strobed, La Roux’s In for the Kill vibrated from the speakers. The arena’s screens listed the circumference of the competitors’ necks (19in for Robinson, 20in for Horelican) and the size of their hands, measured thumb to pinky (8in to 9.5in). Horelican, who had won the coin toss, slapped first, but to little effect. The strike wasn’t clean, hitting Robinson on the neck: a clubbing foul, a point deduction.
Before his strike, Robinson rubbed his hands in chalk. He gave Horelican a mirthless wink. And then, drawing on all his 6am starts, his hours of studying footage, his months of tendon training, his garden slapping, he put it all into a single motion that lasted milliseconds, a sharp twist of torso, a brutal whipping blow upwards.
Horelican went down, blood gushing from his mouth. Robinson raised both palms, the universal symbol of: are you not entertained? Robinson had burst a blood vessel in his opponent’s mouth – remarkably, a Power Slap first. Medical staff wiped the blood from his chin, but they couldn’t stem the bleeding. Horelican didn’t seem dazed, but a replay showed his eyes rolling back, sickeningly, as he fell. He couldn’t carry on.
For several minutes after Horelican left the stage, Power Slap staff half-heartedly mopped the blood from the arena’s floor by pushing towels with their feet. Robinson had won, one slap closer to the title. Not long after, he called Shannon, as he always does post-fight, to let her know he was OK.
When I spoke to Robinson recently, he was one step closer still, having recently competed in Power Slap 25 in Abu Dhabi, beating Jujhar “Tiger” Singh in the second round. Though he wouldn’t get a $10,000 knockout bonus – his first slap failed to knock his opponent down and Singh was disqualified in the second round after consecutive clubbing fouls – he had moved up two places in heavyweight rankings, to six. His partner was still coming around, he said, slowly but surely. This time, she’d even allowed a viewing party at their home. Though he added: “I was told she was basically peeking from behind the door in the kitchen on the first slap.”
Her view of the sport likely wasn’t helped by another serious injury a month before. At Power Slap 23 in Texas, Jake “Rock Hard” Hager was left with one eyeball ruptured and a retina detached. His team stated that, after two surgeries, he retained some sight in the eye. Dana White described it as one of the most severe injuries in the sport he had seen.
Not long ago, I spoke to Shannon. She still remembers her first reaction to the sport: “How can someone stand there and take a blow?” Before every fight, she says, an entire week of dread, a 50/50 chance that her partner gets hurt. But she remembers, too, his early determination. Even back when Robinson was in BritSlap, “he’d watch Power Slap and say: ‘I’ll be there one day.’ I said there’s no way you’re going there! It looks brutal.” But, so far, he’s proved he can do it. “I’ve never had a reason to doubt him. I think that’s what changed my opinion.”
Still, at the recent watch party, she couldn’t stand to watch him be hit. She turned her back to the screen, and asked those around her: “Is he still standing? Is he still standing up?” She is yet to see him compete in the flesh. But if Power Slap was held in London, she allows that she might. Their eldest daughter, who’s 11, has become quite the fan. “She loves it,” says Robinson. “She thinks I’m some kind of local celebrity. You know: my dad’s on Google!” It sounded almost quaint.
