Ernstige kwetsbaarheden blootgelegd in software voor gebruik eID
door Jan Walraven
Een Amerikaanse onderzoeker heeft veiligheidsproblemen ontdekt in de browser-extensie van Connective. Met dat stukje software van Nitro Software Belgium kunnen Belgen met hun eID online inloggen, documenten ondertekenen of ook Itsme activeren. De extensie in de Google Chrome-webbrowser telt twee miljoen gebruikers. Nitro heeft de problemen intussen opgelost, weliswaar bijna 150 dagen na de eerste melding door onderzoeker James Arnott van het Amerikaanse cyberveiligheidsbedrijf Bay Area Labs.
Arnott stelde zijn bevindingen voor op DEF CON, een jaarlijkse conferentie in het Amerikaanse Las Vegas, en in een uitgebreide blogpost. Via de door Arnott ontdekte kwetsbaarheden kon in principe elke website toegang krijgen tot de gegevens van de identiteitskaart − inclusief de pincode − wanneer die via de kaartlezer ingelezen werd. Arnott legde ook bloot dat een potentiële aanvaller via de Connective-extensie vanop afstand computercode kon uitvoeren op de computer van gebruikers, ook als de kaartlezer niet verbonden was. De potentiële impact hiervan is moeilijk in te schatten, want zo “kan het bijvoorbeeld gaan om spyware of ransomware die al wordt geladen door simpelweg de verkeerde webpagina te bezoeken”, schrijft Arnott in een e-mail aan Apache.
Onder meer bij de ingebruikname van Itsme, de authenticatie-app in handen van vier Belgische grootbanken en drie telecomoperatoren, moeten gebruikers de extensie van Connective gebruiken. Hetzelfde geldt ook voor onder meer het gebruik van je eID met Doccle, de tool waarmee particulieren, zelfstandigen en bedrijven online hun administratie kunnen regelen, en die naar eigen zeggen gekoppeld is aan meer dan 150 bedrijven en overheidsinstellingen.
In zijn blogpost legt Arnott uit dat de veiligheidsfout het in principe mogelijk maakte dat een aanvaller bijvoorbeeld een vals Itsme-account op naam van een slachtoffer kon aanmaken en dus in diens naam transacties en dergelijke zou kunnen uitvoeren, met alle mogelijke gevolgen van dien. Dat een stukje software dat zo belangrijk is voor Belgische burgers dergelijke kwetsbaarheden vertoont, noemt Arnott reden om de wettelijke veiligheidsvereisten te verstrengen.
In een officieel statement benadrukt Nitro dat het om “een kwetsbaarheid, geen inbreuk” ging. “We hebben geen aanwijzingen gevonden dat er misbruik is gemaakt van deze kwetsbaarheden. De kwetsbaarheden zijn gemeld aan het Centrum voor Cyberveiligheid België en we hebben gedurende het hele proces nauw met hen samengewerkt.” Volgens Nitro is het probleem nu verholpen en zijn klanten die de huidige versie gebruiken beschermd. Een woordvoerder van het Centrum voor Cyberveiligheid België benadrukt dat niet Nitro, maar wel de onderzoeker het Centrum op de hoogte bracht.
Aan Apache bevestigt Arnott dat ook hij geen aanwijzingen heeft dat er misbruik van de kwetsbaarheden is gemaakt, “maar dat komt alleen omdat we geen manier hebben om dit te controleren”. Hij voegt er nog aan toe dat het bij Nitro “ontzettend lang heeft geduurd” om deze problemen op te lossen, ondanks zijn aandringen en hoewel een oplossing volgens hem veel sneller geïmplementeerd had kunnen worden. Na de eerste melding duurde het volgens hem 146 dagen totdat Nitro de problemen effectief opgelost had. Nitro vroeg hem om zijn bevindingen pas wereldkundig te maken zodra ze de oplossing hadden doorgevoerd. Hij vroeg een ‘beloning’ (bounty) voor zijn werk en Nitro zou hem 200 dollar hebben aangeboden, maar hij wil die niet aanvaarden.
Om Apache te kunnen lezen moet je niet inloggen via eID, gewoon jaarlijks of maandelijks je abonnement betalen volstaat. Oef! En dat geld proberen we zo goed mogelijk te besteden. Bijvoorbeeld door niet langer elke maand een pakje euro’s over te maken aan Google. We hebben het er in deze blog al enkele keren over gehad, maar nu komt het stilaan in een stroomversnelling: de migratie van onze cloudopslag naar Nextcloud.
Wat we nu al zeker kunnen zeggen, is dat Google op dat vlak een beetje op Donald Trump gelijkt: het maakt migratie allesbehalve gemakkelijk. Om het overzetten van ruim 600 gigabyte aan documenten, e-mails, … toch zo vlot mogelijk te laten verlopen, rekenen we op de expertise van Tactic asbl. Deze vzw zal ook onze Nextcloud-omgeving ‘hosten’ en onderhouden.
Maar maakt Apache zich dan niet afhankelijk van Tactic, vraag je je misschien af. En dat is een terechte vraag. Hier ligt net het voordeel van opensourcesoftware als Nextcloud: als we niet meer tevreden zijn over de ene aanbieder kunnen we gewoon aankloppen bij een andere. Of kunnen we zelf de opensourcesoftware hosten op een eigen server – nu al doen we dat voor sommige zaken. De software blijft dezelfde, enkel de aanbieder verandert.
Rekening houdend met de vakantieplannen van onze ploeg, mikken we erop dat we vanaf midden september in Nextcloud aan onze artikels en nieuwsbrieven schrijven en schaven. Daarna openen we meteen enkele andere werven. Zo willen we onder meer het Amerikaanse Mailchimp, het programma waarmee we nieuwsbrieven versturen, vervangen door het opensource-alternatief CiviCRM.
En volgende week hebben we een videogesprek gepland met de mensen van Bonfire. Zij ontwikkelen opensourcesoftware waarmee we hopelijk de Apache-community een boost kunnen geven. Het Duitse magazine Jacobin toont nu al de mogelijkheden van dit “eigen sociale netwerk”. Daarover later hopelijk meer!
Om zijn afhankelijkheid van big tech af te bouwen werkt Apache aan een eigen app. Wil jij ons een zetje geven? Dat kan met een donatie op BE55 5230 8045 8444, of door een aandeel in onze lezerscoöperatie te kopen via apache.be/bouw-mee. Bedankt.
Ludieke luddieten maken verzet tegen big tech weer leuk
door Jan Walraven
“Fuck, fuck, fuck AI.” Veel duidelijker wordt een slagzin niet. Begin juli vierden actievoerders in New York een week lang The Summer of Ludd. En ‘vierden’ is wel degelijk het juiste woord, als we het verslag van Janus Rose voor technologieniewssite 404 Media mogen geloven.
Het festival was niet gewoon een zoveelste protestmars, maar wou eerst en vooral aantonen dat we geen sociale media en dominante techplatformen nodig hebben om elkaar te ontmoeten én plezier te maken.
De Luddite Renaissance kondigde de acties niet aan op sociale media, wel via affiches en mond-aan-mondreclame. Van het theatrale tribunaal en de vele getuigenissen tegen pakweg de “criminele praktijken” van OpenAI werden geen korte video’s voor TikTok of Instagram gemaakt. Want: The Event is the Medium, zoals de titel van het enkel op papier verkrijgbare manifest duidelijk maakt.
Ja, er verschenen wel nieuwsartikels met enkele foto’s, maar je moest er vooral écht bijzijn. Bijvoorbeeld om te zien dat de nieuwe generatie luddieten, die al enkele maanden onder verschillende namen actief zijn in New York, niet enkel haar inspiratie haalt bij de originele brekers van machinale weefgetouwen in het negentiende-eeuwse Engeland, maar ook bij de Nederlands-Belgische ‘kabouters’. Deze geweldloze, anarchistische protestbeweging voerde begin jaar 70 ludieke acties tegen onder meer consumentisme en voor natuur en milieu.
(Terzijde: als iemand ‘luddiet’ als scheldwoord gebruikt omdat je niet zomaar Claude gebruikt om te weten hoe je een potlood slijpt, laat die persoon dan dit artikel uit ons archief lezen.)
Zal een als kabouter verklede New Yorker die een iPhone aan grut slaat Mark Zuckerberg doen twijfelen of hij wel nog een giga-datacenter moet bouwen? Wie weet! Janus Rose ziet alvast in de kolderieke en absurdistische sfeer het onderscheidende karakter van deze nieuwe luddieten: geen cynisme, wel het pure plezier van protesteren tegen iets dat onontkoombaar lijkt. En een oude smartphone symbolisch offeren, is eens iets anders dan AI-ontwikkelaars als Anthropic die massaal tweedehands boeken opkopen om die in te scannen en tegelijk te vernietigen (de rug wordt ervan gesneden om ze makkelijker te kunnen scannen). Hoe ouder het boek, hoe liever, want daar staat zeker geen door AI gegenereerde nonsens in, in tegenstelling tot wat tegenwoordig op het wereldwijde web verschijnt. Zeldzame boeken zijn het meest gegeerd. Kwestie van hun taalmodel nog “slimmer” te maken. En eenmaal vernietigd, worden ze nóg zeldzamer.
Maar terug naar de nieuwe luddieten. Zij willen voorbijgangers geen complex aanpraten of veroordelen omdat ze werkelijk alles aan Google Gemini vragen of soms te lang door hun Instagram-feed scrollen, maar vooral tonen dat we ook zonder big tech kunnen. En dat dit verzet geweldig plezant kan zijn. Dat is misschien de beste overredingstactiek om zich bij deze onafhankelijkheidsbeweging aan te sluiten en mee te werken aan offline ontmoetingsplekken.
Het is een les die we bij Apache ook ter harte kunnen nemen. Uiteraard geven we onze onafhankelijkheidsstrijd tegen big tech niet op, maar dit gaat om meer dan technologie. Onze Franstalige collega’s van Médor en ook van het Portugese Fumaça hebben dat al langer begrepen: zij organiseren op regelmatige tijdstippen ook échte, offline ontmoetingen met hun lezers, zoals we in een artikel voor Apache Magazine schreven.
Ook de Europese Commissie lijkt er (althans soms) op gebrand om big tech het lachen te laten vergaan. De Commissie heeft Google (nogmaals) twee boetes opgelegd van in totaal 890 miljoen euro omdat de techgigant zijn machtspositie misbruikt. Ten eerste door in zijn zoekmachine voorrang te geven aan eigen producten en diensten, en ten tweede door het voor app-ontwikkelaars te moeilijk te maken om gebruikers naar goedkopere aanbiedingen buiten de Google Play Store te leiden.
Die nieuwe boete is Donald Trump wel (weer) in het verkeerde keelgat geschoten. Hij heeft al gedreigd met hogere importtarieven voor de EU, waarmee hij nogmaals de nauwe banden tussen de Amerikaanse techsector en het Witte Huis in de verf zet.
Het is lang niet de eerste (noch laatste) keer dat de Commissie Google aanpakt wegens oneerlijke praktijken. Begin juli bevestigde het Hof van Justitie een boete van ruim 4 miljard euro voor het misbruik van de dominante positie van zijn smartphone-besturingssysteem Android. Het beroep van Google mocht dus niet baten.
Ik schreef deze blogpost trouwens op een Lenovo Thinkpad X240, bouwjaar 2013, die stof lag te vergaren op onze redactie. Aangezien we met Apache op zoek zijn naar alternatieven voor de diensten van big tech en daarbij zoveel mogelijk willen kiezen voor opensourceoplossingen, moeten we ook af en toe experimenteren, bijvoorbeeld met een alternatief op Linux gebaseerd opensourcebesturingssysteem. Dat we zo een dertien jaar oud toestel nieuw leven kunnen inblazen, is mooi meegenomen.
Ik koos ervoor om Linux Mint te installeren ter vervanging van Windows 10. En dat ging verbazend vlot. De naar hedendaagse normen oeroude laptop doet weer wat hij moet doen. Gezien zijn ouderdom verwondert het niet dat hij soms wat hapert, maar dat is niet erg als je het toestel als een prikkelvrije computer beschouwt en gebruikt. Ideaal om zonder al te veel afleiding deze blogpost te schrijven.
Eerst had ik trouwens de meest geavanceerde versie van Linux Mint geïnstalleerd. Die bleek echter te zwaar voor de dertien jaar oude hardware. Met de lichtere Xfce-versie van Linux Mint loopt alles veel vlotter. Linux Mint wordt aangeraden als de beste Linux-optie voor gebruikers die Windows gewend zijn. Als Mac-gebruiker is het dus wel wat aanpassen aan de interface, maar door enkele simpele aanpassingen kan je de gebruikerservaring iets meer op die van een Apple Macbook laten lijken. Een simpel voorbeeld: de knoppen om een venster te sluiten of minimaliseren kan je links bovenaan zetten zoals op een Macbook.
Het zal nog even duren voor alle collega’s op een laptop werken die draait op Linux, maar dit experimentje toont alleszins dat het niet onmogelijk is. En dat opensourcetoepassingen ook een ecologische optie kunnen zijn: alweer een laptop van de schroothoop gered.
Vlaamse Microsoft-factuur verdubbeld tot 22,6 miljoen euro
door Jan Walraven
De Vlaamse overheid gaf vorig jaar ruim 22,6 miljoen euro uit aan Microsoft-diensten. Dat is een verdubbeling ten opzichte van 2023. Dat blijkt uit een antwoord van Vlaams minister-president Matthias Diependaele (N-VA) op een parlementaire vraag van Kris Verduyckt (Vooruit). De voorbije drie jaar spendeerde de Vlaamse overheid net geen 50 miljoen euro aan Microsoft.
Van de 22,6 miljoen euro die Vlaanderen in 2025 betaalde, ging bijna 8 miljoen naar clouddiensten. De resterende 14,6 miljoen euro ging vorig jaar naar de licenties om de programma’s van Microsoft te mogen gebruiken.
In die 14,6 miljoen euro zit ook de kost van 5.000 Copilot-licenties verrekend. In 2025 bedroeg het totaalbudget voor de uitrol van Copilot binnen de Vlaamse overheid 1,93 miljoen euro. Zoals Apache eerder schreef, komt daar dit jaar nog eens 3,65 miljoen euro bij voor de uitrol van 5.000 extra Copilot-licenties.
De uitgaven voor Microsoft gebeurden binnen de bestaande raamovereenkomsten, die nog lopen tot 2029, geeft minister-president Diependaele aan.
Terwijl Digitaal Vlaanderen een nieuwe aanbesteding voor de ICT-raamovereenkomsten voorbereidt, zet de Europese focus op digitale soevereiniteit de keuze voor Amerikaanse technologieleveranciers op scherp. Daar zit het bruuske optreden van Donald Trump voor iets tussen, maar ook een recente uitspraak van het Amerikaanse Hooggerechtshof zorgt voor onrust.
Is op vlak van gegevensbescherming het gebruik van Amerikaanse clouddiensten nog te verantwoorden, nu er eigenlijk geen onafhankelijke Amerikaanse toezichthouder meer is?
De geopolitieke context, maar ook de modus operandi en de daaruit vloeiende machtsconcentratie die big tech zo big maakt, noopt Apache tot een koerswijziging.
Zoals we een maand geleden hebben aangekondigd, wordt een overstap naar de opensource-toepassing Nextcloud in plaats van Google Workspace ons eerste wapenfeit. We gebruiken al een tijdje beide oplossingen naast elkaar, maar in de komende weken bereiden we een volledige migratie voor.
Dat zal wat voeten in de aarde hebben – en dat terwijl collega’s van welverdiende vakantie genieten – maar het is ook een goed moment om ons overstromende digitale archief op te ruimen. Hebben we echt nog een kopie van een draft van een artikel uit 2017 nodig?
De cloud mag dan wel efemeer klinken, het gaat wel degelijk om fysieke, energie- en waterslurpende infrastructuur, zoals ze onder meer in Henegouwen maar al te goed beseffen.
We gebruiken sinds kort de opensource-berichtenapp Signal om dagelijkse updates over onze onderzoeken te versturen. En dat wordt blijkbaar gesmaakt, want het aantal leden in onze Signal-groep groeit razendsnel. Op deze pagina leggen we graag uit hoe jij je ook kan aanmelden.
Verandering doet meestal wel een bitje pijn – pun intended – maar het helpt om te weten dat we er niet als enige mee bezig zijn.
Voor een artikel dat in het herfstnummer van Apache Magazine zal verschijnen, mocht jouw verslaggever langsgaan in de Brusselse hackerspace, waar digitale doe-het-zelvers tonen dat technologie ook leuk kan zijn en dat een door een AI-chatbot gegenereerde afbeelding niet het toppunt van digitale creativiteit is (alsof dat nog bewezen moest worden).
Ja, opensourcetoepassingen zijn plezant. Wie experimenteert nu niet graag met een robotstofzuiger?
Bij de meeste Belgen doet de naam Hyves wellicht geen belletje rinkelen. In Nederland ging de nostalgiemeter wél in het rood bij de aankondiging dat het sociaal netwerk een tweede leven krijgt. De Telegraaf had de primeur: met Hyves gaat moederbedrijf Mediahuis de concurrentie aan met de Facebooks en Tiktoks van deze wereld. Hyves was in Nederland begin jaren 2000 nog de populairste socialenetwerksite, maar gaf dertien jaar geleden de strijd tegen de Amerikaanse concurrenten op. Drie jaar eerder, in 2010, had Telegraaf Media Groep (TMG) nog 43,7 miljoen euro veil voor het platform. TMG werd inmiddels opgeslorpt door Mediahuis, de Belgische uitgever van onder ander Het Nieuwsblad en De Standaard.
Mediahuis ontkent dat de reanimatie door nostalgie werd ingegeven, maar probeert het te verkopen als ethisch alternatief voor big tech. De uitgever plaatst Hyves’ herrijzenis nadrukkelijk binnen twee trends. Enerzijds speelt het in op toenemende kritiek op de schadelijke effecten van de verslavende algoritmes van grote platformen, anderzijds surft het mee op de golven van de beweging die pleit voor meer Europese digitale autonomie.
“Hyves wil het anders doen”, klinkt het. Maar wie de gebruiksvoorwaarden en privacyverklaring leest, ziet meteen dat je dit best met een korrel zout neemt. Hyves wordt een zoveelste advertentieplatform voor Mediahuis, zoals elke ‘mediamerk’ dat eigenlijk is. De gegevens die Mediahuis over gebruikers van Hyves binnenhaalt, kunnen gebruikt worden om ook de advertenties op andere sites van Mediahuis op maat van gebruikers te snijden.
Of het nu van Mediahuis of DPG Media is: op basis van de gegevens die de uitgevers verzamelen, krijgen gebruikers ‘gepersonaliseerde’ reclame te zien: surveillance capitalism in de Lage Landen. Op kleinere schaal, maar in essentie blijft het hetzelfde verdienmodel als dat van Facebook, Instagram, … (Moederbedrijf Meta lanceerde tot grote tevredenheid van de beurs een ‘persoonlijke’ AI-agent voor zijn gebruikers en daarmee wil Meta uiteraard ook gebruikersgegevens opslurpen en gebruiken.)
Het Nederlandse platform voor onderzoeksjournalistiek Follow the Money ontdekte bovendien dat gebruikersgegevens van Hyves gewoon verwerkt worden via Amerikaanse software. Ondanks de belofte van “een overwegend Europese technische architectuur”.
Een commercieel mediabedrijf dat gebruikers wil insluiten op een commercieel sociaal medium. Denken we echt dat dit een oplossing is? Een stukje macht van vooral Amerikaanse big tech afknijpen en overdragen aan commerciële bedrijven van ‘eigen bodem’? Nochtans toont een andere krant van Mediahuis dat het ook anders kan. Lezers van NRC konden de voorbije weken de queeste van techjournalist Marloes de Koning volgen om de krant aan het open sociale web toe te voegen. Het leidde tot een plan om een NRC-server te openen op Mastodon, waarop “mensen van binnen en buiten NRC met elkaar in gesprek kunnen gaan, onder onze eigen voorwaarden en op onze infrastructuur”.
Mastodon is onderdeel van het fediverse, een verzameling van alternatieve sociale netwerken die onderling verbonden zijn. Zoals bij e-mail maakt het niet uit of je nu een account hebt bij NRC of bij een andere dienstverlener: je kan met anderen in gesprek gaan. (En van dienstverlener wisselen als je ontevreden bent.) Om dit mogelijk te maken, rekent dat fediverse op het ActivityPub-protocol; een set van regels over hoe systemen met elkaar moeten communiceren.

			Next article : « Seen and heard – French youth on the (…) »
	
		
Archive selection
In response to the student protests, the French government has initiated a public consultation via a digital platform. If that sounds familiar, it could be because it’s exactly what it did, in 2019, in response to the Gilets Jaunes protests. ‘Right at the outset they warned they would only consider contributions submitted online,’ Magali Della Sudda and Grégory Rzepski write in this month’s edition. ‘But, in fact, the authorities never responded to the exercise at all.’ Pretending to listen has a long history. Even the idealistic Estates General of French Renewal, a huge public consultation exercise organised in 1945 by the National Council of the Resistance (CNR), was quickly sidelined by Charles de Gaulle.
Elsewhere, Italy’s far right is being outflanked by an even further right; Pierre Daum reports from the Algeria-Morocco border; in Cameroon, the AI revolution looks more like poorly paid, precarious work for Western firms. https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: This Guy Could Change the Direction of the Supreme Court
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
This Guy Could Change the Direction of the Supreme Court
Texas’s newly elected attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has the power to end the state’s role as a pipeline for the most toxic high-court cases.
The most important legal development from the midterm elections happened in Texas. Nope, I’m not talking about the election of James Talarico, or the Democrats’ newfound power to block Donald Trump’s judicial appointments. That stuff matters, of course, but the single biggest change to what happens in the courts over the next two years probably comes down to Democrat Nathan Johnson, the new attorney general for the state of Texas.
The Texas AG’s office has been ground zero for many of the most destructive legal battles Republicans have fought and largely won over the past generation. The outgoing Texas AG is the guy who lost to Talarico for the Senate, Ken Paxton. Paxton has been suing abortion providers who send mifepristone (the “abortion pill”) to his state. He has attacked trans people, immigrants, and the environment. He tried to single-handedly block Joe Biden’s agenda from ever being enacted in Texas, and has generally been a despicable menace who uses the law to promote bigotry. Paxton has been at the post since 2015. Before him, the Texas AG was Greg Abbott (the Texas governor who just lost to Gina Hinojosa). Before him, John Cornyn held the role; he’s the outgoing Republican senator whom Paxton beat in the primary. Cornyn replaced Democrat Dan Morales as AG in 1999. Republicans have literally controlled this post this whole century.
What makes the person who occupies this post particularly influential is that the Texas attorney general is always backed up by the Texas solicitor general, who has the job of arguing the AG’s cases in court. The Texas AG, rather than the governor, is also the one who appoints the SG. Past Texas solicitors general include Johnathan Mitchell—who is the guy who had the bright idea to set bounty hunters on abortion providers—and… Senator Ted Cruz.
All of this matters because a disproportionate number of this Supreme Court’s worst, most corrosive cases originate in Texas. That’s because of a quirk in Texas’s judicial structure that allows for easy and flagrant judge-shopping. In other states, the initial judge presiding over a federal lawsuit is chosen by lottery from among the available judges in the district where the lawsuit is filed. In Texas, the presiding judge is whoever happens to run the courthouse in the place where the case is filed. That means that the Texas AG can pick the judge who will rule on any given case by filing the case in the right mailbox. For the past few years, the judge of choice for culture-war issues has been the “emperor of Amarillo,” the reactionary misogynist Matthew Kacsmaryk. For the past 20 years, the judge of choice for immigration issues has been reactionary bigot Reed O’Connor.
Sometimes, a case might end there, with a favorable ruling from one of these handpicked judges. But if the losing party appeals—and, the Texas AG and SG are often counting on this—they can defend their case in front of the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Fifth Circuit is the most conservative appellate court in the country, by some margin. It is full of people openly auditioning for Supreme Court appointments, and in the Trump era that audition has devolved into judges’ ruling in the most insane way possible. Fifth Circuit judges like James C. Ho, Stuart Kyle Duncan, and Andy Oldham are truly some of the worst people the system has to offer.
From there, once the next inevitable appeal arrives, it’s a straight shot to the Supreme Court, where whatever legal monstrosity the Texas AG cooked up is often enshrined into national law by the six Republican justices. What starts in Texas rarely stays there.
This is why replacing the Texas AG with a Democrat is so important. It stops a bunch of lawsuits before they even start. It greatly diminishes the evil the people on the Fifth Circuit can do. It deprives the conservatives on the Supreme Court of some of the cases they need if they want to change the law. Other Republican attorneys general who survived the blue tsunami will surely try to pick up the slack for Texas, but because other states lack the unique judge-shopping structure available in Texas, those surviving AGs are unlikely to be as effective as the Texas AG has been. Moreover, as Ian Millhiser points out, the attorney general offices in other states (like Louisiana and Mississippi, which are the other two states in the Fifth Circuit) are fundamentally smaller than Texas and don’t have as much money. “[T]hey will likely only have the resources to bring a fraction of the number of partisan lawsuits filed by Paxton.”
You don’t have to take our words for it. Just listen to conservative legal commentator Josh Blackman bemoaning the loss of the position in a post-election article in Reason:
I would suspect that all of the conservative strategic litigation cases brought by Attorney General Paxton will be dismissed. Indeed, it is conceivable that the new Texas Attorney General would not defend the Texas Ten Commandments Law if cert is granted.… The Texas Attorney General will also not bring original jurisdiction actions before the Supreme Court of Texas. Going forward, all of the strategic forums in Texas will be severely underutilized.
To de-jargonize some of the gobbledygook: “original jurisdiction actions” refer to cases where Texas sues some other state for, say, “election fraud”; “strategic forums” refer to the judge-shopping Texas AGs traditionally do; and “strategic litigation” is whatever antidemocratic cultural nonsense people like Josh Blackman can think up next. As Sean Rankin, head of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, put it in an interview with Politico, “We took the head of the snake.”
With that head gone, the Texas AG will no longer be the force for pure evil that it has been. There’s a lot of bad stuff the office will cease to do. The other side of the coin is the good stuff the AG can do. Nathan Johnson has already said he will end the out-of-state prosecutions of abortion providers and restore a “respect for the rule of law,” which was something that was severely lacking under his predecessor. But I will dare to hope for a little more than a mere restoration of respect. Texas is the corporate home of a number of companies that haven’t been regulated or investigated at the state level during this century, among them: ExxonMobile, McKesson Pharmaceuticals, AT&T, Oracle… and the entire Elon Musk cinematic universe, including Tesla, SpaceX, and Twitter.
That’s right, Nathan Johnson is poised to become Elon Musk’s worst nightmare: a Democrat with jurisdiction. Musk and his companies fled California after Tesla was sued for civil rights violations there. Do we think he stopped allegedly violating workers’ civil rights when he got to Texas? I don’t think so, and I bet Johnson doesn’t think so either. The judge-shopping door swings both ways, and all Johnson needs is one favorable district court judge in, say, Austin, and he can haul Musk before a jury of his new neighbors.
Think about all the work New York Attorney General Tish James (who won a third term last week) has done trying to hold the Trump crime family accountable. Think about all the work Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has done trying to hold police accountable. Think about all the work California Attorney General Rob Bonta (who just won a second term) has done trying to hold ICE accountable. Now think about the fact that we added new Democratic AGs in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas (defeating Republican Kris Kobach, who would have been the worst AG in the country if Ken Paxton did not exist).
And now we’re adding Johnson in Elon Musk’s home state of Texas to the illustrious array of Democratic crime-fighters. This, my friends, is a full-on “Avengers, Assemble” moment—and they are “on your left.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while plans continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.
While most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly launched, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebranding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly announced Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.
Regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo shows at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.
This market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.
"We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh says. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market."
That step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh says, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.
Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the company following a growing market. “Our last new fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”
Frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a new collecting cohort.
New structure, new horizons
Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the company run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a new company founded by Emanuel called Mari.
Mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of DCT director-general Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.
This multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. It should also ensure Frieze's plans align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.
Luxury destination
The arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.
How measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no plans to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.
The luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.
Rebalancing the canon
Stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.
The fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

https://www.propublica.org/article/georg.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
https://www.propublica.org/article/georg.author: Doug Bock Clark
https://www.propublica.org/article/georg.text:
In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.
The board sets the swing state’s election rules, oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.
Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.
The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes.
At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA, Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.
At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.
The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.
EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.
“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”
The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.
“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.”
Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday, in part to discuss personnel matters.
In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.
“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for amazing performances, not threats of termination.”
In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run.
Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and affiliated groups.
King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.
“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.”
When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.
Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to EIN.
Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed questions, put a post on X celebrating EIN’s work with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer anyone?”
Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”
EIN has been deeply entwined with conservatives’ efforts to reshape Georgia elections since at least 2024.
That year, ProPublica’s reporting revealed, EIN members secretly pushed a rule through the State Election Board allowing local officials to potentially delay certifying the state’s vote count. A court subsequently struck down the change, which experts had warned could enable county election boards to disrupt certifying the election if Trump had lost.
In late 2025, the board played a role in instigating the Trump administration’s unprecedented effort to reinvestigate alleged 2020 voting irregularities, formally asking the Justice Department to obtain Fulton County election records subsequently seized by the FBI. It was a move pushed by the EIN. The affidavit authorizing the raid cited Johnston and King as witnesses. The affidavit also cited a report put together by an EIN researcher compiling activists’ debunked allegations of fraud.
In recent months, EIN’s allies and participants at the state board pushed counties to use ELLY, a tool developed by an EIN member, to search voter rolls for signs of fraud and purge suspect registrants.
ELLY aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources, but doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers or full dates of birth. As a result, voting rights groups have said, ELLY often erroneously flags legitimate voters.
Nonetheless, before the midterms, the State Election Board’s investigative staff pressured Chatham County, a Democratic stronghold, to purge more than 200 registered voters that the tool identified as questionable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported.
After the election, a Forsyth County election board member who is also a member of EIN submitted ELLY data questioning the validity of over 60 ballots, including four cast by people who were supposedly dead. ProPublica found that all four were, in fact, alive. The board rejected the challenges.
EIN members and state board officials have defended ELLY’s accuracy.
The EIN’s connections to the board carry additional importance in light of last week’s election results, in which Democrats wrested control of all statewide offices and the state House from Republicans. The House appoints a member to the State Election Board, opening the door to change.
Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms ran on a platform that promised a new approach to the election board.
“The State Election Board has become mired in political games, conspiracy theories, and partisan interference,” the platform stated. Bottoms’ platform pledged that she would “work with the General Assembly to eliminate the current State Election Board and replace it with a stronger, more independent election oversight structure that is insulated from partisan manipulation.”
Fervier is part of the board’s four-member Republican majority, but he has clashed repeatedly with Johnston, King and Mills and has effectively been relegated to a member of the minority at times.
Emails and communications between board members and staff obtained by ProPublica via public records requests show that Fervier and other board members who oppose steps supported by the EIN have been excluded from some board hiring decisions.
Earlier this year, Fervier publicly accused Mills of going beyond what the board had authorized in calling for the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to intervene to assess the security of the state’s voting machines.
“Activists should not control the board,” he told ProPublica. “I’m really looking forward to this meeting because I think that we’re going to address some issues that should have been addressed awhile ago.”

https://inthesetimes.com/article/counter.title: The Enemies List
https://inthesetimes.com/article/counter.author: Alberto Toscano
https://inthesetimes.com/article/counter.text:
The Enemies List
The Trump administration’s war on the Left is designed to suffocate dissent.
Alberto Toscano
One year ago, in the wake of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, the White House ramped up its campaign against left-wing dissidence.
The government weaponized the legally dubious category of “domestic terrorism” when, on Sept. 22, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order against “Antifa,” designating it as a domestic terrorist organization. Three days later, Trump issued a national security memorandum declaring that the “‘anti-fascist’ lie has become the organizing rallying cry used by domestic terrorists to wage a violent assault against democratic institutions, constitutional rights and fundamental American liberties.” It instructs federal agencies to devise a national strategy to preempt, disband and prosecute those “networks” and “conspiracies” that supposedly seek to undermine and overthrow the U.S. government.
This strategy framed the prosecution in the “Prairieland” case, in which nine activists were charged in relation to a solidarity noise protest outside an ICE detention center at which an officer was shot, in circumstances that remain disputed.
But as Adam Federman reported for In These Times and Type Investigations in March, FBI records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request show that the bureau investigated an alleged Dallas-area antifa group years earlier, in 2018, and closed that investigation after finding it posed no threat to national security.
In June, eight of the Prairieland defendants were sentenced to a cumulative 450 years in prison. The sentences were largely for actions deemed “material support” for terrorism. Perhaps most egregiously, Daniel Rolando Sanchez-Estrada, who was not present at the demonstration, was given 30 years for moving a box of anarchist zines, which was construed as conspiracy to corruptly conceal documents.
The same month the protesters were sentenced, antifa was again invoked in the federal charges levied against 15 members of Direct Action Minnesota for their role in anti-ICE protests. Just as Prairieland prosecutors depicted black clothing at demonstrations as evidence of terroristic intent, the use of the messaging app Signal was understood as proof of conspiracy in the Minneapolis case.
These cases demonstrate the grievous effects of applying the legal and ideological arsenal of counterterrorism to left-wing activism, imagined as a vast conspiratorial network (“Antifa”). They are also one front in something larger: a counterterrorism crusade that functions as a miniature version of the economic warfare that has been deployed against nation-states such as Cuba, Iraq and Iran. Its aim: to suffocate any opposition — abroad and at home.
The Trump administration’s efforts to repress opposition have always been international in scope. While domestic terrorism is not covered as such by any existing law, designation as a foreign terrorist organization or specially designated terrorist group has momentous consequences — not least for U.S. citizens or residents accused of providing material support. The desire to paint antifa as an heir to the fantastical Soviet-managed “terror network” that preoccupied the CIA in the 1980s explains the decision to designate four marginal European groups as terrorists in November 2025.
The economic siege against Cuba has also been accompanied by an effort to link the U.S. Left to nefarious foreign puppet masters. In an improbable regurgitation of high Cold War propaganda, contemporary Cuba has been reimagined as America’s dystopian nemesis.
The State Department released a 100-page report, widely suspected to have been produced by the AI platform Claude, under the bombastic title “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism.” The transparent aim is to tie the effort to turn Cuba into a docile dependent through economic (and eventually also military) warfare to the mounting campaign to persecute political dissidence at home.
Turning history on its head, the report’s first lines declare: “For nearly seven decades, the Cuban regime has waged a sustained campaign of subversion against the United States.” The conspiratorial imagination is on overdrive: despite its poverty and almost total asymmetry of power vis-à-vis the United States, Cuba has orchestrated “a vast hemispheric network.” It has infiltrated “the highest reaches” of the United States and established “a revolutionary infrastructure designed to turn America against itself.” This infrastructure has co-opted everyone from Karen Bass to Barack Obama, the Black Panther Party to the People’s Forum, Amy Goodman of Democracy Now! to myriad university departments and civil society organizations.
As scholar Charisse Burden-Stelly has argued, this pastiche of red scares past is a form of “anti-communist governance” — one that combines public authority and self-censorship “to penalize, regulate, censure and criminalize ideas and beliefs that challenge racial oppression, economic inequality and class antagonism by labeling them ‘communist.’”
These increasingly delirious declarations are not trying to consolidate or manufacture consent; they seem meant for internal consumption within the echo chambers of the White House Situation Room and the MAGA mediasphere.
Unfortunately, without commensurate resistance, force without consent can go a long way. Behind the fantastical façade is the as yet unimpeded project — nationally and regionally — to maximize the impunity of capital while suppressing any alternative vision of collective life and welfare.
That international reach was on full display at the “Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism,” a conference hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington, D.C., in July. In his keynote remarks, Rubio lambasted a media and academic establishment that he presented as treating left-wing violence as a “protected class unto itself” and declared: “It is time to crush this evil forever.” He launched into a vituperative portrait of violent leftists as resentful enemies of Western greatness and civilization.
For Rubio, the menace to be snuffed out is “a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good … perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.”
The sentiment was echoed with characteristic shrill hyperbole by White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, who asked the audience to reflect on why no one attending antifa protests looks “normal”. His answer contained a familiarly fascistic theory of leftist ideas manifesting as physical degeneracy: “Every one of them … has scarred their body and their appearance in many different ways, to the point in which their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.”
But behind the rhetoric about the revolt of the weak — which, like the anti-communist pastiche of the Cuba report, is of very old vintage — lies a focused, and terribly contemporary, strategy of repression. Miller emphasized the need to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest, and prosecute” the nodes of the new terror network.
This counterterrorism architecture projects any single act of so-called left-wing violence as linked to all others both ideologically and materially. Its latest target is the Italian anti-fascist hacktivist collective and digital service provider Autistici/Inventati (translated as Autistic/Invented), also known as A/I.
A/I was founded in 2001, in the context of the antiglobalization movement and the mobilization against the G-8 in Genoa, and provided services like blogs, mailing lists, email and website hosting to groups and individuals with whom it felt a broad political affinity.
On August 26, A/I was named a specially designated terrorist group by the State Department, alongside Palestine Action — the direct action group whose designation as a terrorist group by the UK government has been the object of sustained protest and challenge — and the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement (Masar Badil). But the designation does not concern any actions the collective has carried out. There are no indictments pending against it in either the United States or Italy. Rather, the State Department alleges that its digital infrastructure facilitated acts of “left-wing violence,” from railway sabotage in Europe to the resistance against Cop City in Atlanta, as well as communications among groups ranging from Rose City Antifa to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party.
The designation’s effect, as intended, was swift and drastic. In Italy, where a U.S. designation has no legal standing, A/I was debanked by Banca Etica. The bank declared that notwithstanding its opposition to this campaign against its client, it could not risk the consequences to its other 130,000 accounts should the Treasury Department’s secondary sanctions affect the bank’s access to Visa, Mastercard, Nexi and dollar exchanges.
The outsize power of the U.S. government and the dollar in the international financial system, specifically in monetary transactions, means banks exercise anticipatory overcompliance to avoid risk. The effect is to turn any opponent into an economic nonperson, with all the social and political consequences that entails.
A/I disbanded to shield its former clients from persecution. Shortly before, the collective said the Trump administration had targeted it in a kind of “hybrid warfare.”
Perhaps the most worrying aspect is the absence of any concerted effort by Italian or European institutions to defend the collective’s right to free expression, which is also a right to the digital infrastructures that make it possible. As the collective Sabot Media observed, U.S. sanctions create a “perimeter of fear” around those they target, one that operates in advance of and in lieu of the law.
This crusade builds upon the anti-Palestinian, anti-migrant and anti-Muslim legal provisions that were crystallized by the so-called “war on terror” — when the terror lists were born.
As the academic Lisa Bhungalia rightly notes in her work on the “asphyxiatory violence” of contemporary imperialism, the current wave of repression is “a depository of past decades that build one upon the other rather than … a radical departure from that which came before.”
To face this moment, an internationalist Left must maintain and repair the infrastructures of resistance. The threat is not only a frontal assault or Trump and Miller’s fascist verbiage, but also the kind of suffocation that uses the silent violence of money and law to snuff out any liberatory alternative to the status quo.
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
ALBERTO TOSCANO is the author of Late Fascism: Race, Capitalism and the Politics of Crisis (Verso) and Terms of Disorder: Keywords for an Interregnum (Seagull). He lives in Vancouver.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Tate’s Bloomsbury group exhibition throws fresh light on early British enthusiasm for Van Gogh
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.
Vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers. The Bloomsbury group, named after the London quarter where they lived in the early 20th century, began as an informal collective of progressive artists, writers and intellectuals.
As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing new and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”
Bell and Grant were both also very close to the art critic Roger Fry, who in 1910 curated the pathbreaking London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists, inventing the term Post-Impressionism. This show introduced Van Gogh to a British audience.
As so often with the Bloomsbury group, sexual relationships were complex and intertwined. In 1907 Vanessa had married the art critic Clive Bell, but it was always an open marriage. Two years later she started a relationship with Duncan Grant, producing a daughter, and they then continued to live together.
Duncan Grant, however, was homosexual, having numerous lovers, including a male cousin and Vanessa’s brother. To add to the complications, Vanessa later had a brief relationship with Roger Fry. The quip about the group was that they were “living in squares [in Bloomsbury], painting in circles and loving in triangles”.
The Bloomsbury relationships may seem bewildering to outsiders, but the key point to bear in mind with the current Tate exhibition is that Bell and Grant shared a home for over 50 years. Initially they lived in London, and, from 1916, partly at Charleston farmhouse in rural Sussex.
It proved to be an enduring artistic partnership. They influenced each other, and they, in turn, were influenced by modern European artists, such as Van Gogh, along with Paul Gauguin, Paul Cezanne, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.
Grant, who studied art in Paris in 1906, may have then come across the work of Van Gogh. What is more certain is that Bell discovered Van Gogh in 1909, in a group exhibition at London’s New Gallery, which included a single painting by the Dutchman. She once described it as “a lovely little Van Gogh of flowers in a jug”.
The still life had been lent by Thomas Fisher Unwin, a London publisher who, with his wife Jane, had in 1896 been the first Briton to buy a Van Gogh after the artist’s death. This was a flower still life, probably one with a black background which has always been in private collections.
Post-Impressionism and Provence
But what was most influential for Bell and Grant was Fry's first Post-Impressionist exhibition in 1910. Including around 30 works by Van Gogh, it was the first chance for Londoners to see more than an odd painting by the artist.
This was a heady time for the Bloomsbury group. Bell later recalled: ”That autumn of 1910 is to me a time when everything seemed springing to a new life - a time when all was a sizzle of excitement, new relationships, new ideas, different and intense emotions all seemed crowding into one’s life.”
In 1912 both Bell and Grant had paintings in Fry’s second Post-Impressionist exhibition. They also co-designed the catalogue with Fry, and Bell helped hang the show. This time there was only a single Van Gogh, but it was again the Fisher Unwin flower still life, which Bell had known from four years earlier.
Bell, Grant and Fry all loved the south of France, where Van Gogh had also worked, and they visited regularly from the 1920s. Fry helped a friend buy a farmhouse in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just a few hundred metres from the asylum where Van Gogh had stayed in 1889-90. On one occasion Grant visited Bell, who had bought a house just outside Cassis, on the Mediterranean coast. Grant described the surrounding landscape as “far more extraordinary than St Remi [sic]”. Both artists were well aware of Van Gogh's connection with Provence.
How then did Van Gogh’s art inspire Bell and Grant? They never set out to simply imitate his style, but were nevertheless powerfully influenced by his work and that of the other Post-Impressionists. The two British artists began to paint with heightened colours, simplified forms and strong lines.
The links can also be seen in individual pictures. Bell’s View into a Garden (1926, Bolton Library & Museum Services) includes two empty chairs, which were probably a reflection of Van Gogh’s pair of paintings of his own chair and the armchair of Gauguin (the picture of his own chair had been bought by London’s National Gallery three years earlier, so would have been well known to Bell).
In 1911, the critic Frank Rutter described Bell’s Chrysanthemums (1920, Tate, although not in the current exhibition) as “undoubtedly influenced by Van Gogh”. Its dark background echoes the Van Gogh still life which Bell had seen some years earlier.
Decades later, in 1946, Grant wrote to Bell about visiting a Van Gogh exhibition in Copenhagen, “a splendid show”. He added: “I really feel that artists should resist to the death having their works reproduced in colour. It really has been the death of Van Gogh. It’s only when one sees the originals that one realises what a very lovely & personal colour sense he had… I really do not believe in his madness as an artist at all.” Van Gogh remained in the minds of the couple for the rest of their lives.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Holding Trump Accountable Is Not Optional for Democrats
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sasha Abramsky
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Holding Trump Accountable Is Not Optional for Democrats
Yes, the party must focus on the economy. But that is inextricably linked to a focus on corruption.
Heading to the airport Tuesday morning, I lucked out on my Lyft driver. He was a middle-aged African American man, listening to the news coverage of the impeachment proceedings against Pete Hegseth. He was horrified that a man like Hegseth—someone willing to embrace clearly illegal orders to, for example, turn the military against civilians, and eager to deny people promotion based on the color of their skin and/or gender—had so much power; and he was salivating at the prospect of the self-proclaimed “Secretary of War,” whom he denounced in fiery language as a dyed-in-the-wool racist, finally being held to account. To restore America’s global reputation, he insisted, there had to be accountability. And that accountability should begin, but not end, with Hegseth’s impeachment.
I asked if he thought that the incoming Democratic majority should focus on investigations and impeachments, or on legislation intended to provide an economic boost to struggling Americans? “Do both!” my driver exclaimed. “You can chew gum and walk down the staircase at the same time.”
Amen to that.
Polls showed that two issues were dominating voters’ minds in the midterm elections. The first, more “normal” concern, was bread-and-butter economics: inflation, high interest rates, job insecurity, the destabilizing impact of AI, the difficulty in finding affordable housing, the increasing cost of healthcare. But the second was different: corruption and its degrading effect on our democracy, as well as the damage done to government institutions by the incompetent and cruel leadership of men such as Hegseth.
After 10 years of the Trump cult, America’s voters, in overwhelming numbers, finally saw through the con. They intuited, at long last, that their government was being shamelessly tapped for private profit, and that a man elected as the ultimate outsider was, in fact, consolidating a new elite strata, in large part propped up by unqualified hires such as Hegseth, infinitely more venal and brutal than the “establishment” they had replaced.
These two issues, of course, are intertwined. In the sort of sultanistic kleptocracy that Trump is running—backed up by mediocre loyal foot soldiers, such as Hegseth, who owe their status solely to their undying fealty to Trump and Trumpism—the suffering of ordinary Americans as a result of, say, high tariff-induced and war-induced inflation, represents a glittering set of opportunities for grifters to move in and capitalize on the crisis, for influence-peddlers to sell their wares, for backroom deals that exempt companies from tariffs in exchange for lining the pockets of Trump and his princelings. Addressing one without the other will never lead to the sort of cleansing moment that America so desperately needs—and is demanding—in order to truly enter the post-Trump era.
Come January, of course, Democrats should focus on rolling out a new social compact. They need to offer voters an expanded social safety net—a new Fair Deal—paid for by appropriately taxing America’s emergent oligarchy and its ill-gotten gains. Make Elon Musk, Zuckerberg, Altman, and the other tech-lords pay their fair share, and suddenly—precisely because wealth is so grotesquely concentrated—you have a whole lot more money to stabilize Social Security, move toward healthcare access for all, build more public housing, expand nutritional programs, and much else besides.
But simultaneously, Democrats must also be relentless in hammering home to Americans that, while they are fighting the good fight, Trump and his shrunken claque of GOP congressional enablers, with the ludicrous Jim Jordan at the helm, are still mired in extremism—stonewalling, grifting, or simply prattling on about vanity projects such as the (now-not-so) Triumphal Arch. That means holding public hearings on all the corruption and criminality, all of the unconstitutional, violent actions, and all of the self-dealing of this gang of crooks.
There is debate over exactly which members of the administration can be impeached, but at least some legal analysts think that in addition to elected officials and cabinet members, high-ranking, non-Senate-appointed officials can be subject to this sanction too. On that assumption, Democrats should start by aggressively investigating new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller’s white nationalist ties; his orders for ICE to meet arrest quotas, which have resulted in an epic level of violence against noncriminal immigrants; his decision to send shock- troops into cities such as Minneapolis, Chicago, Charlotte, Portland and Los Angeles; his vastly cruel project of ramping up deportations—more than 25,000 to date—to third countries with atrocious human rights records; and, court orders notwithstanding, the shipping of people, via third countries that are a party to the scheme, back to homelands where they could well be tortured or killed.
With the exception of Trump, there is no man more dangerous to the ongoing viability of the multiethnic, diverse, American democratic experiment than Miller—no man more willing to push the country toward civil conflict to pursue his fanatical political ends. Democrats should lay this all out for the American people to see—that Miller isn’t just a shmuck but that he is a shmuck on a Constitution-wrecking mission—and then impeach him. Dare the GOP survivors in the Senate to not convict this odious man and drive him from office; and, if they take up that dare, make them wear their spineless decision as a scarlet letter heading into the 2028 and 2030 election cycles.
Similarly, since the GOP-led Congress failed to impeach Hegseth this week, impeach him in January. Add to the list RFK Jr, Todd Blanche, and Kash Patel, all of whom have flagrantly abused their offices—whether through promoting quack medical cures at the urgings of financial donors or siccing the vast investigative and legal powers of the DoJ and FBI on Trump’s “enemies”—and then force the Republicans in the Senate to choose sides. These men are all low-hanging fruit, as strong candidates for impeachment as any public officials in US history. If the Republicans remaining in the Senate come 2027 can’t muster the strength to pick off these cabinet members, the public will, I suspect, be entirely unforgiving over the coming years’ election cycles.
And, above all, Democrats need to investigate Trump and his family’s endless self-dealing. Lay out in easy-to-understand detail how the con works: how the billions of dollars flow in via crypto scams; corrupt real estate deals; illegal “gifts”; strong-arm, mafiosi-like tactics deployed against corporations and overseas governments; the endless demanding of tribute; the pay-to-play understandings with companies looking to secure government contracts.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Document all of this and convict the Trumps beyond any reasonable doubt in the court of public opinion. But don’t immediately trigger an impeachment vote; don’t give the GOP an excuse to say this is all Trump Derangement Syndrome. Instead, let the Trump clan twist on the end of the investigative rope for a while as the full scope of their criminal actions is laid bare for the world to see. And then force the Republicans themselves to take the initiative, as—when push came to shove—GOP senators in 1974 did in pushing Nixon to resign: force them to either make their peace, even after the midterms drubbing, with who and what Trump and his self-dealing family is, with all the electoral fallout this will likely lead to for the GOP in 2028 and 2030, or to finally and definitively cut ties with Trump’s mobster government and agree to vote to convict him. Make those Republicans with capacious ambitions for high office—the Josh Hawleys and Ted Cruzes, for example—beg to be allowed to turn a corner on the Trump era that the party’s cravenness and opportunism have inflicted on the world.
In short, make the GOP cry uncle. Make the party that brought us Trump be the one that has to deliver the coup de grâce to the man and his kleptocracy.
