What Democratic Socialists Can Learn About Endorsing a Presidential Candidate in 2028
The Democratic Socialists of America has gained increasing electoral influence. After the Left’s success in the midterms, the group could make an impact in the upcoming presidential race—if organizers take lessons from previous cycles.
David Duhalde
Will there be a socialist presidential standard bearer in 2028? The answer may be coming soon, as every four years, it seems, U.S. presidential candidates announce earlier and earlier.
After the Democrats’ drubbing of Republicans in the midterms, attention is turning to the future role of the Left in American politics. With the largest number of socialists entering Congress in U.S. history, and progressives winning up and down the ballot, across the country, a lane is open to vie for the highest office in the country.
White House contenders launching sooner than ever was one of the reasons the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) leadership passed a measure at its September 2026 meeting allowing the body to make a presidential endorsement ahead of DSA’s 2027 summer convention. Proponents of the measure argued that any serious campaign for president would launch well before DSA convention delegates assemble and vote in the middle of next year.
The DSA leadership vote was not unanimous. And the division between having the DSA national leadership board or its convention delegates vote on a presidential endorsement also occurred in the 2020 race. My 2022 piece, “Democratic Socialists and the U.S. Presidency in the Neoliberal Era,” included below, provides historical background for DSA’s previous interventions in White House races with special attention to Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) second run.
The 2028 White House race likely will be the first in a decade and half without President Donald Trump on the ballot. This open contest puts the nominations of both major parties up for grabs. For the Democrats, one candidate being floated by media outlets, politicians and left organizers as a possible contender is Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), an open democratic socialist and DSA member. At this summer’s DSA Summit in Chicago, some members held a gathering with the goal of drafting her to enter the presidential race, which received coverage in the mainstream press. On Nov. 9, a new organization called Ready for AOC was launched to encourage Ocasio-Cortez to run and build out the infrastructure for a possible campaign.
Ocasio-Cortez has options — she could stay in Congress, challenge an increasingly unpopular Senate Democratic minority leader Chuck Schumer, or set her sights on moving to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. Should she run for president, it would not be unprecedented.
First, Sen. Sanders’ two presidential campaigns demonstrated that there is a lane for a democratic socialist to put up a real fight in the Democratic nomination process. Second, DSA has gone through a presidential endorsement process before where the candidate was popular with its base but also had clear and vocal skeptics.
OR Press has graciously allowed In These Times to republish my history of DSA around the organization’s 2020 presidential endorsement process for Bernie Sanders — and the organization’s orientation towards the primary and general elections — from the book Power Concedes Nothing. The chapter features a number of parallels to questions facing DSA today.
These similarities include, but are not limited to, DSA lacking a longstanding endorsement process for president; the democratic socialist presidential candidates having serious detractors in DSA over single issues; and debates over whether an online poll can best determine popular support among the organization’s base.
But there are some critical differences, too, especially for DSA. Ocasio-Cortez, unlike Sanders, is a DSA member, and publicly renewed her membership recently. DSA’s reach is also now wider and stronger in the political arena than ever before. Eight DSA-backed candidates are set to be sworn into Congress next year, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a fellow DSA member, has become a popular figure and national star. DSA can offer a deeper volunteer operation to Ocasio-Cortez in 2028 than it could for Sanders during either of his runs.
This electoral success has led, since 2020, to tens of thousands of people joining DSA. This year, DSA surpassed the Socialist Party of America as the largest anti-capitalist group in U.S. history, reaching more than 130,000 members.
Hopefully this chapter can help readers both in and outside DSA understand the organization’s endorsement process and the choices facing the broader Left today.
Democratic Socialists and the U.S. Presidency in the Neoliberal Era
— — —
DSA in 2020: From the thick of it to the sideline
Thousands of Democratic Socialists of America members poured tens of thousands of hours into electoral work in 2020, and their collective efforts were an important factor in Sen. Bernie Sanders’ bid for the presidency. DSA members also contributed — in some cases decisively — to the victories won by progressive and socialist candidates running for local and state office, and several seats in the House of Representatives. During the course of these efforts the organization continued the explosive growth it experienced beginning in 2016, reaching over 87,000 members by the end of 2020.
When it came to the main event, however — the fight to deny Donald Trump and the racist authoritarian bloc behind him a second term in the White House — DSA as an organization officially sat on the sidelines. As the largest and fastest growing socialist organization in the United States, the decision to sit out of one of the most consequential presidential elections in decades had reverberations throughout the left, as well as within its own ranks.
It caused confusion, led to criticism, and provided no clear direction to thousands of potential volunteers. It may also have created tensions with other parts of the left. It meant DSA did not connect itself to any of the formal anti-Trump coalitions or informal alignments that involved the overwhelming bulk of progressive groups and individuals — especially in the labor movement and communities of color. While some of those formations gained influence and credibility among working-class people and communities of color who joined the effort to defeat Trump, DSA squandered the opportunity to do the same. Only some of that damage was mitigated by the decision to take part in the U.S. Senate run-off election in Georgia in January 2021.
The reasons for the decision to not endorse and help elect Biden are not simple. It did not flow from the organization or its leadership being united on a particular view about how U.S.-based socialists relate to electoral politics and mass movements. The reality behind DSA’s decision lies in a wider series of external events confronting a group facing unprecedented membership growth and untested internal processes.
The decision must also be contextualized within the history of how DSA has handled White House candidacies since 1980, and in the political evolution of the organization’s membership. Especially important are the ways that internal decisions leading up to the organizational endorsement of Sanders during the primary race run set the conditions for a “Bernie or Bust” resolution without proper consideration of the possible consequences.
In the fraught period ahead, neither DSA nor the broader left can afford to repeat these kinds of mistakes. Although the decision was a political error, the events that unfolded afterwards offer lessons that will serve DSA and the left. This article is my attempt to tell that story and draw out those lessons.
DSA and presidential elections: 1980-2012
The evolution of DSA’s presidential endorsements since 1980 informed how the group landed at a nonendorsement in the 2020 general presidential election. Regardless of what those who support and critique DSA’s 2020 decision say, both sides exaggerate how much a nonendorsement strayed from DSA’s previous stances. Still, the choice in 2019 to pre-empt any possible endorsement of a Democrat other than Sanders later down the line was unprecedented for DSA and its predecessor organizations.
DSA was birthed in 1982, out of the merging of two socialist organizations — the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee (DSOC) and the New American Movement (NAM). Leading up to the 1980 presidential election, DSOC led a coalition project dubbed the “Democratic Agenda” that brought together labor and other mass organizations. Their goal was to curtail rising neoliberalism and defend a New Deal coalition on its last legs by backing Senator Ted Kennedy in his bid to wrest the Democratic nomination from incumbent President Jimmy Carter. They were unsuccessful, and after President Carter secured the party nomination, he went on to lose to Ronald Reagan. DSOC — much as DSA would do 40 years later — did not endorse a candidate for the general election after Kennedy lost the nomination.
DSA went in nearly the opposite direction in 1984 and endorsed the consensus pick of Walter Mondale — Carter’s former vice president and running mate in 1980 — in the general election after making no endorsement in the primary. Jesse Jackson ran in the primaries that year, and the decision to not endorse the progressive movement candidate was reflective of some demographic traits and political choices of early 1980s DSA. The organization remained heavily white and with a large Jewish membership that prioritized relationships with labor leaders. Jesse Jackson’s sympathies for Palestinians and reported anti-Semitic comments did not help him, but neither did a DSA leadership generally unconnected to Black and other people of color – led social movements.
When Jesse Jackson ran again in 1988 at the tail end of Reagan’s presidency, DSA enthusiastically joined his campaign efforts along with many other progressives, socialists, and communists. He won three times as many delegates as in 1984, and the relative success of his campaign and the Rainbow Coalition gave hope to many that a multiracial national movement could spring from his campaign. However, the lack of a democratic Rainbow organization, Jackson’s own personal agenda, and other factors dampened hopes about a new democratic alliance against racial capitalism. Jackson would go on to lose the Democratic nomination, and Reagan’s vice president, George H.W. Bush, would go on to win the 1988 presidential race.
The fortunes of DSA and the broader left steadily declined from the Reagan era into the Bill Clinton administration. In 1992, Clinton became the first Democratic president since Carter, and rose to power championing a “Third Way” politics that blended socially liberal and fiscally conservative policies, reflecting the rightward shift in the country and growing neoliberal hegemony. DSA’s influence, already waning from the mid-1980s, further sank through the 1990s and early 2000s. During this entire period, DSA did not endorse presidential candidates, partly because of the lack of major presidential candidates that challenged neoliberal hegemony in the White House.
In 2000, Ralph Nader’s candidacy for president on the progressive Green Party ticket inspired millions of votes. However, DSA did not endorse him either. The organization lacked unity and many members thought that Al Gore — Bill Clinton’s vice president and Democratic nominee for the presidential race — would obviously prevail. George W. Bush’s victory was a wake-up call to many that conditions could get even worse.
Four years later in 2004, after DSA membership was largely divided between Howard Dean or Dennis Kucinich in the Democratic primaries, John Kerry won the nomination and DSA promptly endorsed him in the general election. It was the organization’s first presidential endorsement in 16 years. Although Kerry was hardly progressive, DSA believed that he was the only candidate who could defeat Bush in the general election, and that was top priority.
Many members went to work to elect Kerry or to unseat Bush. Hardly any members actively supported Ralph Nader’s independent run that year, drawing lessons from 2000, when many believed that Nader split Democratic votes and was partially responsible for Bush’s victory. This experience is important because it mirrors the conditions in 2020 in some important ways, and a much smaller and very different DSA chose a different path than they would 16 years later.
Kerry lost that election, but after making our first endorsement since 1988, DSA would take some critical steps to modernize its electoral structures including getting a political action committee (PAC) so it could spend money on federal races.
After an eight-year Bush presidency that launched endless wars, DSA and other left formations threw their weight behind Barack Obama’s historic campaign. Although Obama was masterful at using social movement rhetoric and building a multiracial electoral coalition, his time in power did not break with neoliberalism and DSA declined to re-endorse him in 2012. DSA did however publicly state that his re-election would be better than the victory of his Republican challenger, Mitt Romney.
The 2016 election and the Sanders era
At the end of Obama’s two-term presidency, DSA still had not endorsed a presidential contender in the primaries since 1988. Bernie Sanders would soon change that. Once the senator from Vermont began sending out feelers to test his viability as a candidate, groups like DSA and the Progressive Democrats of America (PDA) began circulating petitions urging him to run for president. While on the surface, the self-described democratic socialist seemed like an obvious candidate for DSA to rally behind, there were a few other factors that led to our support.
First, even before Sanders’ run, there was a renewed and growing interest in socialism across the country. The devastation brought on by the 2008 financial crisis, growing inequality, the increasing inability of neoliberal policies to meet the material needs of people, and the far distant memory of the Cold War and anti-Soviet propaganda were among many factors that contributed to a growing openness to alternatives to capitalism, especially among younger people.
In addition, eight years of right-wing attacks and labeling of Obama as a socialist not only had zero detrimental effect on his reelection, but those attacks arguably backfired as his moderate policies defanged the foreign specter of “socialism” in the eyes of many, especially with the working-class people of color who supported him and were the target of socialist organizations like DSA.
Lastly, campaign finance laws had changed significantly since DSA’s first major support of Sanders’ Senate run in 2007. The Supreme Court ruling in Citizens United greatly expanded the ability of nonprofit organizations with a 501(c)(4) designation such as DSA to spend money supporting specific candidates during campaign season. This gave DSA more freedom to independently support a candidate in whatever way and with whatever messaging we chose than if we coordinated with the candidate’s official campaign.
DSA launched a supportive independent expenditure operation called “We Need Bernie” that engaged chapters and brought in new members throughout 2015 and 2016. The decision to do that was brought forward by DSA’s National Political Committee (NPC), and won widespread approval at the 2015 national convention. This was partly because of Sanders’ political stances, but also because of his prior relationship with DSA since our support of his 2006 Senate race.
While Sanders’ 2006 US Senate candidacy brought some press coverage and helped slightly grow the membership, DSA continued to be of only very limited political relevance. For several years, DSA hardly broke 6,000 dues-paying members. After Bernie lost the primary election in 2016, DSA unsurprisingly declined to endorse Clinton by name but embraced the “Dump Trump” effort. Few of us imagined he would win, but correctly saw his authoritarian streak and attacks on the voting rights of communities of color, among other threats, as extremely dangerous. His surprise Electoral College victory shocked the progressive world to its core, and his presidency quickly proved to be just as scary and dangerous as his campaign was. This horror sparked thousands of new activists, especially millennials, to join organizations like DSA, PDA, and new formations like Our Revolution and Indivisible in droves. This crowd of new socialists and radicals transformed DSA. After the inauguration and the Women’s March in January 2017, it was clear that progressives were mobilizing at an unprecedented scale.
The next few years would see DSA’s numbers swell into the tens of thousands, but what was more important was how the character of DSA changed with this influx of new members. The influx ranged from experienced leftists coming from other anti-capitalist formations to the newly introduced to socialism who lacked any background in the left movement and its history. This change in the size and character of DSA is crucial to understanding how the “Bernie or Bust” resolution came to pass, and how we eventually declined to throw the full weight of the organization into the 2020 general election.
It is important to note that after 2016’s loss, while Sanders and organizations like Our Revolution focused a lot of their work on efforts to reform Democratic Party structures and processes — especially after controversy around the party’s 2016 presidential primaries and superdelegates — DSA remained absent from these struggles. After our 2017 convention, we began shifting away from our legacy of intra-Democratic Party work to begin supporting the formation of a new workers party. This dynamic is critical to understand as it was a harbinger of how DSA could appear much more in lockstep with Bernie than was actually true.
The road to ‘Bernie or Bust’
The broader history of DSA endorsements laid out up to this point makes it clear that DSA has not consistently endorsed presidential candidates in primary or general elections. Sometimes we did the former and a few more times we did the latter, but most often we endorsed no one at all. People on all sides of the debate surrounding our 2020 nonendorsement of Biden have falsely made it seem like DSA had a long history of either formally endorsing or informally backing the Democratic nominee. This misunderstanding inaccurately colored the debate throughout 2020.
DSA’s ultimate backing of Sanders’ second presidential run started in 2018 when the national organization and its chapters began having discussions about an endorsement. Although the external perception might have been that DSA was fully behind the race before Sanders declared, this was not the case. The hesitation from DSA members to re-endorse Sanders were multifaceted, but all were rooted in the fact that this organization was different from the one that had backed him in 2016.
Some members felt that throwing down in the presidential elections would overextend DSA’s capacity, and that new formations like Our Revolution could handle it on their own, especially since many DSA members would volunteer as individuals anyway. Others felt that Sanders had missed the mark on sex worker rights by voting for the anti-sex-trafficking legislation SESTA-FOSTA and disliked his foreign policy positions. Sanders’ consistently poor showing with African American voters and disconnect from surging Black social movements also caused some supporters in DSA to wonder if he had learned anything from 2016.
We also knew that Sanders could not win without his grassroots base, which DSA was a very important part of, and DSA would have been marginalized if we didn’t endorse his campaign. If we supported Sanders, we had to figure out how to do so while being clear about the differences between his social democratic program and our democratic socialist vision. We did not have unity around how to demarcate that difference while still supporting him.
Organizationally, the new DSA also lacked any consensus on how to select a presidential campaign to get behind. Historically, only the National Political Committee (NPC) would determine a handful of national endorsements. By 2016, DSA had developed an internal culture and process where major endorsements came from local chapters, so that endorsements were more democratic and had local buy-in. After local chapters vetted and nominated candidates, a National Electoral Committee made up of volunteers from around the country would analyze the races further, and eventually the National Political Committee would decide whether to endorse the candidate. Chapters could only nominate candidates running in their jurisdiction, which was determined by assigning zip codes to every chapter. Notably, under this new process, DSA’s Vermont chapter did not submit Bernie Sanders’ 2018 US Senate race for an endorsement and the National Political Committee quietly acquiesced.
However, this process applied only to local and state races, and we still lacked a formal method for endorsing national candidates. For decades, the de facto practice was that the NPC would make presidential endorsements without any clear process that incorporated chapter input. In 2015, the convention resoundingly reaffirmed that body’s decision to back Sanders. However, three years later when we started having discussions about backing Sanders’ 2020 run, DSA had grown and changed. Members were more accustomed to having input in endorsements, and had practice through the local endorsement process outlined above. Leadership understood this, and had to balance these new expectations and culture with a tight timeline.
DSA’s national convention is where the decision to endorse Sanders was supposed to happen, but that was slated for August 2019, less than a year before the primary elections would take place. If a decision wasn’t made until then, DSA would miss valuable time needed to prepare for its independent expenditure operation. Given how slow things moved in the volunteer-led and short-staffed organization, the desire to endorse before the convention made sense. A compromise was reached that DSA would send a poll to all members asking if we should endorse Sanders. The results of this poll would inform the NPC in their decision-making process.
At a late January 2019 NPC meeting, they voted 10 to 3 to form an exploratory committee to begin the process to endorse Sanders. They told the membership:
“Included in this announcement will be a political rationale for why we are considering Bernie Sanders and no other candidate in the Democratic primaries. This rationale will make clear that we are not rubber-stamping Sanders, but instead that we have high demands on him politically, and that we will push Sanders towards our positions as much as possible.”
A few days later, the poll went out via email and about a quarter of DSA’s then roughly 53,000 members voted. Nearly 75% of the voters supported backing Sanders. The NPC interpreted this as buy-in to back Bernie ahead of the upcoming biennial convention. While the NPC had promised that the upcoming preconvention gatherings would still debate backing Sanders, they voted to endorse before all those gatherings could be completed. The fact that the poll offered no alternative to Sanders alongside the endorsement being made before the debates at the preconvention gatherings could take place left a sour taste in some members’ mouths.
So much of this situation was unprecedented. The scale of our decision-making process and expectations around engagement from DSA membership in 2019 had no parallel in our organization’s history. At the time this was taking place, I was the political director at Our Revolution, and we endorsed Sanders almost immediately after he announced his candidacy. I stayed away from commenting on DSA’s process because of my role at Our Revolution, but privately, I thought the process chosen was a poor one. I have since contended that DSA should have built an endorsement process that incorporated its rules for a special convention as outlined in our constitution. In that scenario, chapters representing a certain percentage of the membership can call for a national gathering to address whatever issue they deem important. It would have been better to encourage chapters to nominate presidential candidates for the NPC to consider. It is hard to imagine such a mass of chapters or members not choosing Bernie, but they would have had the option between him and other candidates inside and outside the Democratic Party.
By the time that DSA’s August 2019 convention rolled around, the NPC had already endorsed Sanders and we had already launched our independent expenditure operation under the banner of “DSA for Bernie”. The “Bernie or Bust” resolution — formally called the “In the Event of a Sanders Loss” resolution — began circulating ahead of the convention. Some DSA members in swing states signed a letter against it. A handful of members, including myself, also spoke on the floor against it. We argued that it would prematurely tie the organization’s hands in the event of complex scenarios such as Sanders getting a vice presidential nod. Supporters of the resolution contended that we should aim high and that planning for these other scenarios meant we were giving up ahead of time. On all sides of the debate, we could not overcome the resounding feelings that the only endorsement a socialist organization could make would be for Bernie Sanders.
The resolution overwhelmingly passed at the convention. This vote outcome formally meant that DSA would only back one Democrat in the primary or general election: Bernie Sanders. Many of the supporters of the proposal would not realize its far-reaching effects until much later. It hurt DSA’s ability to work with other mass organizations during the general election, and paralyzed the organization around the general presidential election as the COVID-19 pandemic, surging mobilizations against police violence, and growing right-wing violence changed the political landscape in unforeseeable ways.
‘DSA for Bernie’ and the general election
Once the NPC made the decision to endorse Sanders back in March 2019, DSA launched an independent expenditure operation in its support of Sanders’ 2020 run under the banner of “DSA for Bernie.” The independent expenditure was a distinct legal body that was technically separate from DSA, but obviously connected and coordinated.
In order to carry out this massive independent electoral effort, DSA would have to spend serious resources. The proposal to spend $100,000 on access to voter databases and staffing for “DSA for Bernie” proved controversial because we have limited resources as a smaller, nonprofit organization, and our members have strong and opposing opinions about how that money should be spent. One of the selling points was that DSA could keep data on volunteers and voters in order to plug them into our longer-term work after the election. This investment of DSA resources could then help the organization expand its reach both in the short and long term, especially in areas where the Sanders campaign didn’t have a physical presence. In the end, after much deliberation and discussion, “DSA for Bernie” got the fiscal support it needed from the organization.
The nature of the presidential primaries made it so that the first few states to vote required nearly all the Sanders campaign’s attention. This provided an opportunity for DSA to be one of the main mobilizers of Bernie supporters in states where the campaign could not dedicate much of its early time, such as California, Texas, and Massachusetts. DSA, maybe more than any other non-union group, led Sanders volunteers on canvasses and phonebanks in those places. In the end, “DSA for Bernie” had huge metric success, although we felt that we didn’t do enough to support building power with local organizations in the places we operated. Overall, “DSA for Bernie” engaged with 91 out of 199 chapters to knock on 576,000 doors, identified 40,000 Bernie supporters, and gained over 15,000 members during the campaign.
DSA’s investment in internal infrastructure and the independent campaign helped Sanders’ showing in the primaries and helped our organization grow. DSA did not just work alone, but also collaborated with the coalition People Power for Bernie. This alliance was made up of some of the movement nonprofits that backed Sanders in 2016 and new additions such as Sunrise Movement, Our Revolution, and Dream Defenders. The formation stayed together after the primary, although DSA exited once Bernie lost.
In April 2020, Bernie Sanders lost the Democratic primary elections for the second time in four years. This time, however, he was much more ready to enthusiastically endorse his opponent, partially because the stakes were so much higher. Donald Trump was mishandling the COVID-19 pandemic by denying basic science and allowing countless deaths; emboldening and encouraging right-wing violence, and showing no commitment to respecting the democratic will of voters in November should he lose. These and other compounding crises gave massive pressure for groups to rally behind the Democratic nominee despite their hesitations over Joe Biden.
Biden was a deeply flawed candidate for the left to rally around under normal circumstances. He was frozen in time, and was steadfast against the issues that were dearest to Bernie supporters, such as Medicare for All and student debt cancellation. Like his Democratic predecessor Barack Obama, Biden also seemed uninterested in courting the Left’s vote, and was happy to leave that work to Sanders and other prominent progressives.
DSA was very influential, and big, so there was lots of outside pressure to break with our resolution and endorse Biden. I knew that the National Political Committee would not overturn the will of the convention. One important consideration that was missing from all sides of the debate was that Joe Biden did not want a DSA endorsement. Both the DSA members who did not want to endorse him and the comrades who did seemed to avoid the assessment that an endorsement might actually hurt him. Biden was interested in appealing to the center, not the left, and a socialist stamp of approval could have undermined his campaign strategy. The degree to which the debates around an endorsement avoided this led me to believe the debates were much more about public posturing than actual political assessments.
The essential point was that once Bernie dropped out of the race and endorsed Biden, DSA did little — if anything — to mobilize against a Trump presidency. In public statements, DSA was critical of both Biden and Trump while admitting that Trump was worse, but the NPC lacked any mandate or consensus to overturn the resolution. DSA then declined to stay on the People Power for Bernie coalition as it rebranded to the United Against Trump coalition, even as they hired former Sanders 2020 labor coordinator and prominent DSA member Jonah Furman to staff the alliance. In May, the NPC voted down board members of the Socialist Majority Caucus (which I was a part of) in their effort to push chapters in swing states to consider discussions about voting for Biden. Jennifer Bolen, an NPC member, summed up the majority stance when she wrote that the effort “violated the spirit” of the “Bernie or Bust” resolution and “sound[ed] like an endorsement” of Biden. So while the rest of the left and progressives began struggling with the real choice between Trump and Biden, DSA was frozen. DSA even abstained from efforts framed only around defeating Trump because many argued that those efforts were de facto pro-Biden, since he was the only candidate that could beat Trump.
It was one thing for DSA not to endorse Biden. That was predictable and consistent with previous actions. Declining to do anything related to the general presidential election had dire consequences and was the wrong decision.
On April 12, 2020, DSA tweeted “We are not endorsing Joe Biden.” It went viral, amassing over 16,000 retweets and 90,000 likes. Our Revolution, on the other hand, also did not endorse Joe Biden but made no such public proclamation about their decision. Providing no information of what the organization would actually do besides not backing Biden left DSA open to criticism from other leftists and from moderate and right-wing critics. DSA’s poor messaging alienated its allies and sowed tensions within the membership, especially less active members who were not plugged into the endorsement process. It was difficult for them to understand exactly what had gone into the decision making, and this gave space for leftists to criticize DSA’s inaction on platforms as prominent as the New York Times. Whether this was done with the hopes of actually influencing DSA to change the decision or not, it allowed its critics to shame DSA and hurt its reputation. DSA eventually did send out guidance on how to approach the 2020 elections, but it was in September and sent privately to chapter leaders. No public clarity was offered as the uprising of the summer swept the country and the threat of political violence increased.
As the political situation grew worse going into the fall, some members felt the lack of a position was unsustainable even if changing DSA’s stance was impossible. To address this, I joined with others in October to publish a letter expressing our concerns with a possible Trump victory. We avoided mentioning Biden. We asked others to sign on and sought to create a vehicle for members to openly express their concerns. We also sought to provide organizing opportunities for members who wanted to do electoral work to plug into as individuals. These opportunities were focused on down-ballot races with the aim of turning out Democratic voters key to defeating Trump. We viewed this not just about messaging but about organizing, and we strove to be different from the previous open letters and articles, which seemed more focused on demonstrating righteousness to others than influencing DSA to change their stance.
Our effort was greeted both with praise and scorn. Those primarily concerned with removing Trump from the White House were more sympathetic. Many of those who had voted enthusiastically for the “Bernie or Bust” resolution were less happy. Some members even lied and said we were pushing DSA members to campaign for Biden, which was objectively false. There was a feeling that we were trying to get around the convention resolution and that using our DSA titles implied an endorsement. This argument rang hollow to me, because the resolution just prevented endorsing a Democrat besides Sanders, and did not bar individual DSA members from doing electoral work. Most active DSA members, even those who were against our letter, believed that the resolution closed off any possible presidential endorsement, but the author of the resolution said that it left the door open for the endorsement of a third-party candidate.
People inside and outside of DSA understood that the only choices were Biden or Trump. The Green Party received 75% fewer presidential votes between 2016 and 2020, despite higher turnout, and only two DSA chapters endorsed Howie Hawkins’ race. They were both promptly chastised for doing so outside of a formal national process. Our national formation should have owned that there were two choices and the majority of working people were picking Biden. We should have not shied away from publicly and significantly helping to defeat Trump, even if that meant electing Biden, because those were the only two real choices facing working-class voters.
Although DSA and Sanders’ rise had coincided, this relationship grew more distant and awkward as time went on. While prominent democratic socialist elected officials such as Sanders, Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Jamaal Bowman pushed turnout for Biden, their own organization was absent. A few days before the election, Sanders, Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, and Bowman joined with many other liberal-left mass groups for an online turnout rally in support of Joe Biden. DSA, whose rise paralleled many of their careers and had helped elect many of them, was not at the event. Our absence was glaring and hard to forget.
After November
Thanks to the tireless work of progressive and left organizations, Joe Biden defeated Donald Trump without DSA’s help in the November general election. In doing so, he flipped the state of Georgia, which had not been won by a Democrat since Bill Clinton’s win in 1992. The turnout that propelled Biden’s victory there also pushed the two US Senate races into runoff elections, since no single candidate received the majority of votes. With the “Bernie or Bust” resolution no longer holding DSA back, the organization mobilized against the GOP incumbent senators. DSA deployed volunteers in the runoff elections and contributed to the successful effort to stop Republicans from gaining those two seats, all without ever making an endorsement.
This shift demonstrated to me that DSA was willing to be part of the type of coalition politics needed to defeat the far right. DSA matured through our experience of 2020, and we have learned through democratic struggle how to make better political interventions and plan for different scenarios. Even beyond the election, as of August 2021, DSA has continued its foray into mass politics and electoral engagement through logging over a million phone calls to swing-state US senators in support of the labor law reform PRO Act. This kind of coalition work highlights that DSA is ready to be part of broader social movements.
Looking forward
At the August 2021 DSA convention, two years after our fateful gathering where the “Bernie or Bust” resolution passed, we faced no hard questions about presidential endorsements. However, over 1,000 delegates in attendance debated electoral strategy more broadly and struggled over the question of how DSA should relate to elected officials we champion who in turn endorse corporate Democrats in other elections. To my pleasant surprise, an amendment to the electoral strategy resolution calling for DSA to discourage our electeds from doing this only got 40% approval and failed.
This demonstrates that DSA members understand that elected officials play a different role than our organization in defeating the far right, and that we need to employ a multitude of tactics on a variety of fronts in order to do that. We need to provide flexibility for officeholders such as Cori Bush — a socialist in a purple state — to work to defeat the far right by working with whomever they deem necessary, and that calculus changes based on time, place, and conditions. Socialists should avoid solutions and blanket decisions that are devoid of an analysis of the particular conditions and scenarios at play. The willingness of delegates at our 2021 convention to move away from pre-emptive rules and resolutions is a healthy sign of a maturing democratic socialist movement.
Since 2019, I have not encountered anyone who voted against the “Bernie or Bust” resolution and regretted it. I have, however, encountered plenty of people who did vote for it and later admitted that it was an error. DSA’s involvement in the Georgia runoffs and the results of the 2021 convention are positive signs of a move away from sectarianism and toward a more popular front understanding.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/ndaa.title: Congress Might Sneakily Use Lame Duck to Deeply Intertwine the U.S. and Israeli Militaries
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/ndaa.author: Josh Ruebner
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/ndaa.text:
Josh Ruebner is policy director of the IMEU Policy Project and author of the forthcoming book The United States and Palestinian Nakba: A Transnational History, 1947-1950.
After President Biden’s unrelenting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza helped pave the way for President Trump’s reelection in 2024, Trump’s own foolish decision to launch an Israel-backed war against Iran played a large role in putting Democrats back in control of both chambers of Congress — a fact Vice President JD Vance diagnosed in no uncertain terms.
Now Democrats and Republicans alike have the opportunity to demonstrate they’ve finally learned the lesson voters have tried to deliver to both parties over the last three years: The American people do not want to be entangled and complicit in Israel’s aggression and atrocities. Their first opportunity to heed that call is arriving sooner than one might expect.
Right now, the House Armed Services Committee and Senate Armed Services Committee are engaged in an informal but highly consequential conference to finalize the text of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which sets policy for the Pentagon. A disturbing provision in current versions of the texts passed by the House and Senate committees would integrate Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon procurement process at an unprecedented level — opening a back door to almost untraceably send billions of taxpayer dollars to Israeli weapons makers without congressional oversight. The House bill would create a new “executive agent” position within the Pentagon to steer this integration—a level of amalgamation that exceeds collaboration with nations in NATO.
Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle are opposing this provision. On Tuesday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen and nine other Democratic senators, plus independent Bernie Sanders, demanded it be removed. In the House, Democrat Ro Khanna and Republican Thomas Massie have made clear they will also try to strip the NDAA of this measure. In doing so, they are representing what the vast majority of Americans want—and their colleagues should take note.
In our August polling with Data for Progress, 75 percent of Democratic voters oppose this provision, as do 58 percent of independents and 42 percent of Republicans. In addition, polling shows a majority of Americans now want to see taxpayer funding to Israel reduced or ended. Passing the NDAA with this measure would mean that even if Congress zeroed out annual weapons funding to Israel, currently at $3.3 billion per year, in the State Department budget — earlier this year, 103 Democratic representatives joined Massie in a move to do just that — there could still be a major increase in actual dollars flowing to Israeli companies that the American people never hear about.
The negative repercussions extend beyond funding Israeli weapons makers (some of which are government-owned) with our tax dollars. This sort of integration could allow for Israeli weapons and surveillance technology that have been tested on Palestinians to be used in the U.S. to advance the Trump administration’s cruel mass deportation program. Israeli weapons maker Elbit Systems’s U.S. subsidiary is expected to install more than 300 surveillance towers along the U.S.-Mexico border, developed from its technology deployed along portions of Israel’s apartheid wall in the West Bank.
Melding Israel into our government procurement process should also set off alarm bells in the U.S. national security world. The Washington Post reported earlier this year that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vetoed Biden’s decision to send U.S.-Israeli co-produced missile systems to Ukraine three years ago for Ukraine’s war against Russia, even though the missiles were paid for by American taxpayers. The integration measure proposed in the NDAA would massively expand the scope of weapons over which the Israeli government could exercise a unilateral veto.
Congress should be unwinding intelligence cooperation with Israel, not only on the moral grounds that no part of the U.S. national security apparatus should assist in genocide, but also because Pentagon officials raised the threat of Israeli spying to its highest possible level earlier this year. But instead of diminishing our intelligence sharing with Israel, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence’s FY27 Intelligence Authorization Act, which is typically incorporated into the final NDAA version, includes a provision (Sec. 618) actually mandating the president engage in even more intelligence cooperation.
This should give us pause because of the faulty nature of Israeli intelligence and the way Israel used this intelligence to build a case for dragging the United States into war. It was reportedly Israeli intelligence that claimed the Iranian government could be overthrown within weeks, if not days, of Trump launching the war. Instead, Trump and Netanyahu are now stuck in a quagmire, and the war has imposed a terrible cost on the American people, U.S. servicemembers, and people across Iran and the region. Energy prices around the world have skyrocketed, the cost of the war has already exceeded $2,000 per U.S. household on average, and the U.S. is running low on interceptor missiles that will take years to replenish.
None of this seems to concern the main backers of U.S.-Israel military and intelligence integration, like Foundation for Defense of Democracies President Mark Dubowitz. In a column published in Israel Hayom, the right-wing newspaper owned by the Israeli-American GOP megadonor Miriam Adelson, Dubowitz said: “Israel and the United States should deepen their military, technological, intelligence, and economic integration to such an extent that inflicting financial harm on Israel would also carry a significant cost for Washington.”
In an interview, Dubowitz added that the U.S. and Israel should be so intertwined that any accountability measure against Israel, such as sanctions being enacted by American allies in Europe, would “impose costs on the U.S. itself.” In no uncertain terms, advocates for the integration envisioned in the NDAA want to try to make it impossible for the U.S. to disentangle itself from a regime that is increasingly perceived by many as a rogue actor.
The NDAA is usually considered a “must pass” bill in Congress — in fact, Congress has passed annual defense authorizations for 65 consecutive years. But Congress is under no statutory obligation to pass it this year, and doing so without stripping these provisions to become even more entrenched with supporting Israel would be an immediate betrayal of the will of voters. At a time when even Republicans are openly admitting the midterm election was a referendum on U.S. support for Israel, it would be an unforgivable choice for Congress to pass an NDAA with these integration provisions. If Republicans use their committee majorities to force their inclusion in the bill’s final text, Democrats have every bit of leverage to filibuster and block the bill’s passage in the Senate, which requires 60 votes.
Saying no to bringing the U.S. into a closer relationship with Israel in just about the most expensive, opaque, and dangerous way imaginable should be the easiest political decision Congress makes during its current lame-duck session.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Paris Photo’s digital sector offers ‘soft photography’ and vital context
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarp Kerem Yavuz
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.
The world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.
This year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.
The digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as New York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.
Noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.
Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.
Yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.
Vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.
The New York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.
Meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.
Given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.
Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.
- Paris Photo, until 15 November, Grand Palais, Paris

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/isra.title: Israel Used a U.S.-Made Missile to Kill Six at Gaza’s Nasser Hospital
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/isra.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/isra.text:
Throughout Israel’s war on Palestine, doctors Thaer Ahmad and Feroze Sidhwa spent months at Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis, where they provided care as volunteers and survived a raid and an airstrike on the complex. On Wednesday evening, they were in an Uber in New York headed to a screening of their film about their time in Gaza when they realized Nasser was the target of another Israeli airstrike.
“They just hit Nasser again,” Ahmad said, turning from the front seat toward Sidhwa. “I think Rizk is dead.”
He was referring to Dr. Rizk Abu Shaaira, an experienced surgeon and fixture of the Palestinian medical community whom both had worked alongside at the hospital and who appears in their film “American Doctor.” When Israel attacked Nasser Hospital on Wednesday — for at least the seventh time since the genocide escalated in 2023 — Abu Shaaira was one of the six people killed.
As the doctors arrived at a theater in Westchester for their screening, they received a flood of messages, photos, and video from their colleagues at Nasser, showing smoke-filled departments and wrecked operating rooms. The attack forced the closure of the hospital’s emergency, surgery, radiology and laboratory departments, hospital officials said.
Six people were killed in the airstrike, according to Gaza health officials, and 52 others were wounded, said Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders. Israel said it had used a precision-guided missile to target a Hamas commander.
One video showed a body bag holding Abu Shaaira, who had been working a night shift in the surgical ward, one of several floors severely damaged in the airstrike. Sidhwa, who worked directly with Abu Shaaira during his time volunteering at Nasser, described the 52-year-old father as a colleague who was “enthusiastic about everything” and “loved surgery.”
Another image showed unexploded ordnance launched at the hospital that medical workers had placed atop a stretcher, bearing the label “GBU-39/B” – a model of guided missiles manufactured by U.S. company Boeing. Israel purchases this precise missile model using funds from the U.S. State Department.
“That’s not complicity,” said Feroze when asked about the U.S.-made missiles used in the attack. “That’s active participation in the murder of physicians and other healthcare workers.”
Wednesday’s attack on Nasser Hospital, which serves a population of about 1.3 million people, is the fourth Israeli strike on a hospital since the so-called ceasefire agreement in October 2025. It is the seventh on the Nasser complex, including a double-tap strike in August 2025 when Israeli warplanes struck the hospital twice within minutes, killing first responders and journalists. Sidhwa had been volunteering at Nasser during an earlier airstrike on the complex in March 2025 violating an earlier ceasefire. That strike killed multiple people, including a 16-year-old boy.
When Ahmad volunteered at Nasser in early 2024, a part of the hospital’s pediatric ward was still damaged from an Israeli tank shell that flew through a window, killing Donia Abu Mohsen, 12, while she received care from a previous airstrike that killed her family. During his stint, Israeli soldiers raided the complex and detained several doctors with whom he worked; they remain imprisoned without charge. Ahmad said his colleagues at Nasser told him that upon hearing the first booms on Wednesday, they knew immediately, due to familiarity, that they had been hit by an Israeli attack.
“Something that has troubled us so much is how normalized the targeting of these hospitals has become for Palestinians serving their communities,” Ahmad said. “They knew what was going on right away.”
Since returning from their time treating patients in Gaza, both Ahmad and Sidhwa have lobbied members of Congress to support the Block the Bombs Act, a House bill that seeks to prohibit the sale of certain arms to Israel that are tied to violations of U.S. and international human rights law. Among the weapons subject to the ban is Boeing’s 250-pound GBU-39. With a new Congress soon to be controlled by Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns touting support for the bill, both Ahmad and Sidhwa called on lawmakers to act.
“If our Congress upheld international humanitarian law, as well as U.S. domestic law, Dr. Rizik would still be alive,” Ahmad said, “and there wouldn’t be a surgeon who lost both of his legs in this bombing.”
The Israeli military claimed in a series of statements posted to social media that it had targeted a senior Hamas commander and other Hamas members who were “hiding” in the hospital and that the strike was meant to “eliminate the threat they posed.” The military did not specify the actual threat nor address the killing of Rizk, patients, and other civilians by “precision-guided missiles” it claims to have deployed to mitigate civilian harm. Israel alleged Hamas was operating out of the hospital’s second floor, but provided no evidence beyond a computer-rendered video. At least six Israelis have been killed in Gaza since the start of the so-called ceasefire, the Israeli military has said. Israel has killed more than 1,400 Palestinians in that time, according to Gaza health officials. The United Nations said that among those reported dead are at least 340 children.
In a statement to The Intercept, the Israeli military repeated its claim that Wednesday’s strike was targeting a Hamas commander, but it declined to confirm whether the alleged target of their strike was killed or comment on the civilians killed in the attack.
President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, tasked with rebuilding Gaza, called Wednesday’s attack a “tragic loss of life” but went on to repeat the Israeli allegation that Hamas carries out “continued exploitation of hospitals and other critical civilian infrastructure for military purposes.”
Sidhwa called the Board of Peace statement on Hamas’ alleged embedding in hospitals “bullshit,” adding that he has seen no evidence of Hamas embedding its fighters within any hospital in Gaza, a recurring observation by international doctors who volunteer in the strip.
“Show me one example,” Sidhwa said. “I would love to see a single photo, a single video, a single testimony from a Palestinian. Literally anything. It’s just completely absurd.”
Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders said in a statement that it was “appalled and outraged” by Israel’s attack, adding that its doctors had to operate on two of their colleagues and another patient injured in the strike. The group referred to its earlier decision in January to temporarily halt its teams’ operations at Nasser, citing reports of “armed men in different areas of the large compound of the hospital,” and said similar incidents have taken place more recently. Even so, the group said, this does not justify Israel’s attack.
“Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” the group said. “In no conceivable circumstances can attacks on functioning hospitals in Gaza be treated as normal or acceptable.”
The strike came days after the board issued a rare condemnation of the Israeli government for its blockade of humanitarian aid from entering Gaza in the aftermath of a storm that wiped out thousands of tents, killing four people. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rebuffed the criticism and blamed Hamas for not disarming. Israel, meanwhile, continues to occupy about 70% of the Gaza strip, extending beyond the yellow line, a border drawn in the ceasefire agreement that is meant to mark where Israel can operate its military, and launches attacks on the strip on a weekly basis, all violations of the agreement.
“The same military who’s blocking the necessary supplies, as a middle finger to you, decides that they’re going to bomb a hospital,” Ahmad said. “I’m sure behind closed doors everybody is fuming and reeling, but unless people are ready to actually hold the Israelis accountable, actually use their leverage, nothing is going to change.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Healthcare company opens art gallery near Los Angeles
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Scarlet Cheng
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
AltaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its new 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).
AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them currently placed in its offices and clinics.
“Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), said in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”
In recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.
“The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”
Some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.
AltaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.
The first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.
She says she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.
It has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she says. The company has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.
Down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".
The other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/hake.title: The Hegseth Vote Was Jeffries's First Big Test. He Failed.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/hake.author: Eoin Higgins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/hake.text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
Democrats rolled into Washington this week fresh off a generational sweep election on the promise of affordability for Americans and accountability for the Trump administration.
But on Tuesday night, Democrats in the House failed the first test of their incoming majority. An impeachment resolution introduced Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., targeting Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, one of the main architects of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, provided Republicans with a chance to score an early victory.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the chamber’s Democratic leadership failed to take advantage, as 11 Democrats missed a critical vote that would have kept the resolution alive. The attempt failed by a slim margin, 211 to 204; Massie told The Intercept on Wednesday that even if the missing Democrats showed up he was sure House Speaker Mike Johnson could have rallied his members and made up the difference anyway. Until the new term begins, the chamber is still controlled by the GOP.
Nonetheless, the vote was a chance to send a message to the White House. One was sent: that of a disorganized, dysfunctional caucus. Other Democrats sought to take advantage of the misstep, noting that they were unwilling to miss the vote—Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas said she rerouted around traffic, and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York made it the day after back surgery.
“No matter what, I wasn’t going to allow traffic to keep me from that vote,” Crockett told MS NOW. “It was just that important to me.”
When asked about the absences, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was present for the vote, offered only “someone may have had a health issue” as an explanation.
House members who missed the vote blamed a number of factors for their absence, including traffic. On Wednesday, all of those same House Democrats save Rep. Haley Stevens (Mich.) began to offer explanations. Rep. Jonathan Jackson (Ill.) told TMZ DC that his “traffic jam”-related absence was “inexcusable.” He wasn’t the only one to blame traffic — Reps. Marilyn Strickland (Wa.) and Laura Gillen (N.Y.) also cited D.C. gridlock as the reason they missed the vote; Rep. Julia Brownley (Calif.) said she was “rushing” to the vote but missed it. Reps. Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), Lou Corea (Calif.), and Frederica Wilson (Fla.) were all out of town.
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (N.M.) offered a front-facing video apology to constituents. Rep. Steven Horsford (Nev.) took “full responsibility” in a floor speech. And Rep. Brittany Pettersen (Colo.) acknowledged that she was at a super PAC event and said there was “no excuse” for missing the vote.
Expressing regret is a good start. It shows these lawmakers are aware that their actions are antithetical to where their voters are at this moment and are adjusting accordingly. It’s not enough.
Leadership was asleep at the wheel. As whip, Rep. Katherine Clark should have kept the caucus in line. (It’s worth noting that Clark officially launched a bid for majority leader last week.) A number of reps who blamed traffic were previously at an event hosted by the group Elect Democratic Women, which receives some of its funding from AIPAC. The event overlapped with the impeachment resolution vote; Clark is a cofounder of the group.
“Republicans just blocked the House from impeaching Pete Hegseth,” Clark posted on X after the vote—failing to take responsibility for her party’s own lack of discipline.
Democrats missing a vote to hold one of the main figures in the war on Iran accountable so they could attend a fundraiser is so tailor-made for progressive complaints over the state of party leadership, it’s hard to believe.
Jeffries tried to spin the vote as only a temporary reprieve for Hegseth, but he didn’t telegraph much willingness about holding his caucus to account.
“I haven’t had a conversation with anyone on the floor team about what may or may not have happened in terms of the Hegseth resolution, but this is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” he told Politico. Most critically, he accepted no responsibility for the stunningly bad optics of having members of his caucus no-show, even if it likely wouldn’t have moved the needle.
This never should have happened in the first place. It was the result of a series of decisions by Jeffries and Clark about the vote that made clear it wasn’t important.
Momentum lost can’t be regained. If Jeffries doesn’t understand that, he’s not the man for the job purely on tactical grounds, and he should lay no claim to being a party standard-bearer to steer us through the next two years of Trump’s America.
Jeffries and his party seem doomed to repeat the past. In 2009, when President Barack Obama came into the White House on the back of a change election that gave Democrats huge majorities in Congress, including a filibuster-proof supermajority in the Senate, the party hobbled itself out of the gate by preemptively declining to pursue justice for the many crimes of eight straight years of George W. Bush.
“We need to look forward as opposed to looking backwards,” Obama told ABC News’s George Stephanopoulos in January 2009, effectively ending any hope of accountability for the outgoing administration’s torture program and myriad other misdeeds. The ramifications of that decision arguably led to the war on Iran, a bipartisan immigration-deportation regime, and the end of Roe.
Now, with a Republican president who is hated even more than W—something that would have seemed impossible to imagine almost 18 years ago—the Democratic Party’s establishment wing appears ready to repeat those failures. Taking on Trump and his corrupt, violent administration was one of the main messages that flipped House and Senate seats across the country but the party’s current leaders are allergic to action.
Entrenched Democrats also don’t seem interested in any sort of accountability. Stevens, the Michigan Democrat who broke ranks with her party and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for Senate rather than back Abdul El-Sayed, was under pressure in the days before and after the election, with even establishment kingmaker Rep. Jim Clyburn signaling openness to expelling her from the caucus. By Tuesday morning, Pelosi — always in touch with party leadership — seemed to throw cold water on the idea: “I’m not supporting kicking her out…. Let’s focus on the very positive.”
This is such a complete misunderstanding of the mood of the electorate, one wonders if it’s intentionally obtuse. Democratic voters don’t want the party to rest on its laurels, they want blood. Anyone who’s been to a liberal rally since the start of the second Trump term can tell you that the signage is calling for, at minimum, accountability, not immediate compromise.
If Democrats rubber-stamp Jeffries as speaker and fail to adopt a more aggressive legislative and investigative approach, frustrations within the caucus and among the base will only continue to mount.
Jeffries is downplaying dissent, but this is more than just a battle between two wings of the Democratic Party. Democrats in New York have been looking to unseat the leader for years, frustrated with his closeness to AIPAC and financial institutions. He’s the kind of Democrat the base is fed up with, and that exasperation is widespread; polling shows just how deeply unpopular he is.
Now, multiple incoming and incumbent Democratic reps have told reporters that constituents and activist groups are demanding they not vote for Jeffries as speaker.
There is an alternative gaining steam: Rep. Ayanna Pressley, the Massachusetts progressive and member of the original “Squad” who were first elected in 2018. Pressley has an uphill battle and has not yet announced that she’s interested in the job. The left is interested.
Voters gave Democrats a clear mandate on Election Day for what they want to see in Washington. Holding this administration accountable should be one of the top priorities. If the party fails to do all it can to advance that goal, it will once again earn its reputation for preferring failure to action. We should all push the next Congress to act as the exception to that rule—and they can start by picking a new speaker to meet the moment.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
