https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New contemporary art centre coming to University of California, San Diego
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Angella d'Avignon
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027. Housed in the university’s new Triton Center, the Strauss Family Gallery will include four indoor exhibition spaces and an outdoor sculpture terrace. Free and open to the public, the Strauss will host exhibitions, commissions, artist residencies and public programmes that encourage collaboration between artists and UC San Diego researchers and scholars.
Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential. "The Strauss represents a long-term commitment that the university is making to contemporary art and sees it as an integral part of the university's intellectual and public life," she says.
In 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego. (Matthew, who made his money in real estate, died the following year.) Represented artists in the gift include Carrie Mae Weems, Fred Wilson, Zhang Huan and Sabine Moritz.
The Strauss’s new David and Claire Guggenheim Gallery will serve as the public entrance and a space for exhibitions, gatherings and an artist-in-residence programme focused on digital artists, while the two-story Gray Box will accommodate large-scale sculpture, moving-image installations and performances.
The 3,043-sq.-ft Black Box will be equipped for immersive video, sound, sculpture and performance; and the White Cube will provide a more conventional gallery setting for works from the Strauss Family Foundation, travelling exhibitions and collaborations with collections in San Diego and beyond.
Taylor calls the Strauss the first "ground-up museum" at UC San Diego. Pointing to existing spaces on campus like the Mandeville Art Gallery (open for nearly 60 years) and a black-box theatre in the music department, she says the Strauss will strive to be part of the landscape of both the campus and San Diego at large. But the Strauss will play a unique role—with commissions, curatorial research and exhibitions in collaboration with artists from across the globe.
UC San Diego’s Stuart Collection, which includes sculptures installed across campus, has already established a public art presence at the university. The Strauss will now give artists a dedicated space for exhibitions, commissions and research.
“We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve," Taylor says. "The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom."
Taylor's greater vision is to engage the community through public programming and student involvement. The Strauss plans to engage both established and emerging artists, particularly in the digital space, and support the development of their work. "We're looking at how we can bring artistic inquiry into university teaching and research," Taylor says.
This could include incorporating exhibitions and artistic methodologies into existing courses, giving students opportunities to participate in curatorial research and creative projects, and developing collaborations across the university. Taylor points to potential partnerships with UC San Diego’s Qualcomm Institute, the Interdisciplinary Computing and the Arts programme, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Goeddel Family Technology Sandbox as examples of the range of possibilities.
"We see the Strauss as more of a platform than a container for a collection," Taylor says. "We do have a collection, but our goal is to be a platform for research and critical inquiry—and for challenging assumptions."

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Why Progressives Are Backing Chris Van Hollen
The senator netted key endorsements from progressives, activists, and unions in his quest to oust Chuck Schumer. But he still faces an uphill battle.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen jumped into the race for Senate majority leader Tuesday night, providing a clear progressive challenge to what New York Senator Chuck Schumer had hoped would be a smooth transition into the leadership post following big Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
Even as Schumer—who has led Senate Democrats since 2017—claimed that he maintains more than enough support to prevail in an expected early December caucus vote, Van Hollen indicated in a Thursday night interview that at least 10 of his colleagues had already expressed interest in his bid. And he said he hopes to have serious conversations in coming days with senators of every ideological bent, background, and region.
Van Hollen received immediate support from Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, one of the highest-profile newcomers to a Senate Democratic caucus that now has 55 members—and could grow to 56 if Mary Peltola wins in Alaska. Peggy Flanagan, the new senator-elect from Minnesota, added her endorsement of Van Hollen on Friday morning. The Marylander also attracted support from activist groups, a key union, and prominent progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who had already signaled his preference for Van Hollen, and who celebrated the Marylander’s announcement as a step that would help build “a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”
Van Hollen, a Capitol Hill veteran and savvy election strategist who had been exploring a 2028 presidential bid, has emerged as a progressive favorite in the leadership race with Schumer for a variety of reasons, including his vow to provide “not a penny” of funding for the war in Iran. He has also argued that Senate Democrats should push for wage hikes, taxes on the rich, reining in AI, and a new approach to campaigns that rejects money from AIPAC, crypto interests, and influence-purchasing billionaires.
Reflecting on the 2026 election results—which saw Democrats take control of the House and Senate and make huge gains in states that as recently as two years ago had backed President Trump and right-wing Republicans—Van Hollen declared on Thursday, “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies—but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people.”
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” added the senator. “This is not about any one person—it’s about answering the call of the American people.”
Van Hollen followed that message up with interviews in which he promised to challenge a rigged system that has stalled progress on everything from Medicare for All healthcare reforms to a foreign-policy shift that would “end the American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel.” In particular, he focused on the role that big-money influence on politics plays in undermining workers and unions while benefiting billionaires and expanding wealth inequality.
“We saw a huge outburst of democracy on Election Day—red states, blue states, purple states—and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty,” the senator told MS Now. “It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people, led by a corrupt political system.”
El-Sayed, for whom Van Hollen campaigned in an August primary where the Michigander beat centrist Haley Stevens, has long encouraged Van Hollen to mount a leadership bid. And he was quick to jump on board Thursday.
“Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All,” said El-Sayed. “Senator Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”
Flanagan also cited sentiments in her home state to make the case for Van Hollen. “Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership,” she said. “I believe Chris Van Hollen is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind.”
The Working Families Party, which is influential in the politics of Schumer’s New York State, has expressed opposition to his leadership bid. So have high-profile progressive and activist groups such as MoveOn and Indivisible. And climate activists with the Sunrise Movement called Thursday for Schumer to “STEP ASIDE as Senate Majority Leader in favor of Senator Chris Van Hollen.”

The 600,000-member International Association of Machinists union, which had previously called on Schumer to stand down, gave Van Hollen’s bid an enthusiastic boost.
Describing Van Hollen as “a proven champion of working people who will fight to unrig an economy stacked against working families,” Machinists International Union president Brian Bryant said, “Senator Van Hollen understands this is a fight of Workers vs. Billionaires and has the courage to deliver the change voters demanded. Workers did their part on election night. Now it’s Senate Democrats’ turn. Senator Van Hollen is the right choice.”
The momentum for Van Hollen is real, but the final choice rests with Democratic senators, many of whom remain closely tied to Schumer. The Maryland senator acknowledges that he has a lot of work ahead of him, but he continues to argue, “We shouldn’t have a coronation.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Shanghai’s art week finds buyers in a selective market
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alex Wang, Lisa Movius
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.
“I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.
Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and new spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.
“Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” says Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”
Hsu says he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this new era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”
Along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the new boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.
The 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a new acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.
At West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.
Dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she says.
Hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.
At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.
Also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.
Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, says that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.
He suggests that the growth of new art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang says, adding that Shanghai remains an important entry point for collectors from across mainland China.
Hsu says the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Midterms Were a Revolt Against ICE. Democrats Need to Remember That.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Felipe de la Hoz
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Midterms Were a Revolt Against ICE. Democrats Need to Remember That.
Voters made their disgust with Trump’s war on immigrants clear. Now, with the fanatical Stephen Miller given even more power, Democrats must take on the administration.
With the final votes being counted in the 2026 midterms, electoral contests have given way to the usual and infinitely more annoying postelection debate over what the results mean. Did the Democrats triumph purely because of anger at the high price of gas? Was it because Black voters rose up against the Trump administration’s efforts to disenfranchise them? Was it a nationwide repudiation of MAGA on economic and cultural fronts? Do the people want another FDR?
These discussions, fun as they are for commentators (I know, glass houses), rest on the shaky premise that an election in an ultra-diverse, vast country of over 340 million people electing politicians at every level of government can speak with anything like a unified voice. But the rush to form a consensus that voters are driven above all by one singular factor also tends to paper over a host of other significant factors. For instance, most of the postelection analysis so far seems to have largely glided past one of the most directly visible examples of Donald Trump’s authoritarian excesses: the broad crackdown on immigration, speech, and political organizing helmed by ICE. This is despite the fact that revulsion at the crackdown can probably help explain not only the complete reversal of Republicans’ 2024 gains among Latinos but also broader Democratic turnout across the board.
It would be a mistake not to see the ICE invasion of Minneapolis, and the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good, as an inflection point in the country’s political thinking—not only in terms of the attack on immigration itself but also as such an open and militarized display of the administration’s authoritarian designs that it could no longer be ignored. Conversely, the resistance to ICE also proved that the administration was not invincible and was vulnerable to bleeding public support—and led to the biggest revival of the movement to abolish ICE since Trump’s first term.
Trump himself was questioned on this by Ross Douthat, Bari Weiss’s latest smooth-brained acquisition at the shell of 60 Minutes, where he said he might have been “too tough” on immigration enforcement. This unsurprisingly appeared to be a manifestation of Trump’s reflex to just agree with whomever he’s in front of, as almost immediately afterward he named Stephen Miller, the architect of this barbaric effort, the new White House chief of staff—a move not unlike replacing the control rods in a nuclear reactor with just more plutonium to see what happens.
The thing about Trump is that he is intrinsically, fundamentally a racist and has been for his whole life—an attitude learned from his developer father, who was infamously named alongside Donald in a federal civil rights case for refusing to rent to Black New Yorkers. He is, however, a different type of racist than Miller. Trump is the prototypical white Queens uncle racist, the sort who latently believes that Black people are less intellectually capable and Mexicans are simple, good workers who are exploitable and expendable, but is ultimately happy to transact with anyone as long as they serve his direct material interests. Miller, on the other hand, is a blood-and-soil racist, a man whose every impulse and action is warped through the prism of his deep, ideological bigotry.
In making Miller the chief of staff, Trump is ensuring that the latter approach wins out, if only because a matchup between relative indifference and zealotry will almost always result in a victory for the zealot. Trump can spend the next two years keeping the grift spigot going and enriching himself while letting Miller et al. mind the store. He’s in such a hermetic information bubble that he almost certainly does not and could not grasp the volume of disgust at Miller’s crackdown, particularly since the media narrative is already downplaying its importance to this enormous electoral loss.
No matter what, it will be hard to dislodge Miller. Trump, over a decade in public life, has proved mainly that he is committed to certain overarching tenets—his enrichment, his vanity, petty grievance and retribution, social hierarchy—but otherwise completely erratic in decision-making and personnel decisions. Apart from his family, other people do not seem entirely real to him, so he can command absolute loyalty from wretched underlings but is always prepared to toss them by the wayside the moment he thinks it’s advantageous. He has already dumped several people involved with his unpopular immigration actions, including former DHS secretary and noted puppy slaughterer Kristi Noem and fun-size Nazi Greg Bovino, the one-time Border Patrol commander responsible for the aggressive occupations in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.
Miller, though, has been a remarkably consistent presence by Trump’s side since his first campaign, far outlasting Miller’s own former boss Jeff Sessions, who spent about a year and a half as attorney general (a long tenure in Trumpworld, as it would turn out). He seems to have entered that rarefied inner circle status just below family (the Tiffany tier, if you will).
For his part, Miller, who, if nothing else, is a tactical operator, must realize that the time he has to see through his vision of a paramilitary-enforced white America is dwindling. There will be significant pressure for Democrats to at the very least launch inquiries into ICE’s conduct. There are rumors about growing support for Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen as Senate majority leader. If his name rings a bell, it might be because Van Hollen made headlines for traveling to El Salvador to demand to see his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García at the notorious CECOT gulag at a time when no one had seen him—or indeed the other dozens of men unlawfully sent there—alive since their rendition. A majority leader Van Hollen is not likely to forget about ICE.
Whatever guardrails still exist, Miller is liable to try to remove them completely and let the authoritarian train run unimpeded until Congress and the courts actually throw some obstacles on the tracks. He has at least the financial ability to do so, given the MAGA Congress’s mammoth appropriation for immigration enforcement just earlier this year. Yet we’re already seeing centrist pundits and party apparatchiks performing a sleight of hand, saying that the new majority must prioritize “kitchen-table” issues rather than accountability work—a prospect that will only get more ridiculous if and when ICE and its corollaries do not moderate, and perhaps just get more sadistic. As with the other questions of accountability, corruption, and weaponization of government, it should be easy to make the case not just that they are just as needed as economic justice but are inextricably tied together with it.
I don’t think that the millions of voters that handed Democrats historic victories will need much convincing that the $70 billion handed to ICE and CBP—as the Iran War was in its fourth month and after the killings of Good and Pretti—could be better used elsewhere, or that the administration’s current enforcement posture has torpedoed industries from agriculture to construction to biotech, imposing long-term costs on the American economy writ large. Not that the argument has to or should be purely an economic one; there was true, tangible, national rejection of the administration’s targeting of longtime residents and contempt for constitutional principles and basic decency. Articles in the vein of “I supported Trump’s deportation efforts, and then my wife was detained” have become so common as to basically be a trope now.
Dragging DHS officials from the secretary down before congressional committees; having a Church Committee–style dedicated investigative team uncovering the extent, mechanics, and executors of DHS abuses; referring some to criminal prosecution or civil penalties, including the prospect of impeachment; and both clawing back DHS funding and putting some stricter limits on the spending that still exists (while broaching the conversation of full abolition) are not only moral and constitutional imperatives but at this point likely political slam dunks.
The post-2024 pundit consensus that the slim Trump victory had definitively indicated a popular appetite for mass and indiscriminate deportation and the unrestrained surveillance and enforcement apparatus to support it has been proved pretty conclusively wrong. Even those voters that ostensibly did support it were backing a version of it that existed mainly in their own imaginations. As the election showed, many of them have come to detest or at the very least disavow the operations in practice.
Miller, like all dogmatists, will stop only when he’s stopped. As they settle into power, the new Democratic majorities must understand this as part of their mandate.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Trump and Vance Are Using War to Enrich Their Cronies
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Trump and Vance Are Using War to Enrich Their Cronies
A new report shows how the pair is robbing Venezuela blind on behalf of one of their donors.
On Monday, while laying out his case for impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie made the grave accusation that Hegseth was deploying the military not for national defense but for plunder. “I do have a message to the troops. This secretary has used our troops to go seize oil for large corporations in America. You shouldn’t be used like that. You signed up to pledge your life for this country if need be, and that obligation shouldn’t be diminished to stealing oil for big corporations,” Massie said.
On one level, this indictment seems hardly noteworthy; Donald Trump has repeatedly gushed about the riches the United States is gaining from controlling Venezuelan oil since he kidnapped Prime Minister Nicolás Maduro at the start of this year. Speaking at the United Nations in September, Trump boasted that the US had signed with Venezuela “the biggest oil deal in world history,” guided by the philosophy “to the victor belongs the spoils.”
Massie’s accusation of theft is merely an acknowledgement of Trump’s own words. What’s more notable is Massie’s reference to the accomplices in the theft—the big corporations.
On Wednesday, Reuters published an explosive report offering more evidence of what Massie was talking about. The investigation focuses on the relationship between Vice President JD Vance and John Addison, an executive at the trading giant Vitol.
Addison is a patron of both Vance and Trump. In 2020, he donated $300,00 to a super PAC supporting Vance’s successful Senate run in Ohio. Two years later, Addison and his wife gave $7 million to PACs working to elect Trump and Vance to the White House.
According to Reuters, Vance and Addison met at a resort in Montana on December 27, 2025, one week before the United States invaded Venezuela to kidnap Maduro. The news service reports:
Vance and Addison talked about Venezuela, according to the person, who was given an account of the meeting from Addison. Vance was particularly interested to know how quickly Venezuelan crude could be sold if the US hypothetically gained control of the country’s oil supplies, the person said. Addison assured Vance that Vitol was uniquely placed to do that job.
Vance and Addison deny that this meeting took place, although flight records show they were in Montana at the same time. Prior to the meeting, Vance had commended Addison to Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Reuters notes that Addison has confirmed “that on Jan. 5—two days after the operation that unseated Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and killed up to 100 people—US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called him at his desk in Houston with an irresistible offer.”
Wright circumvented normal rules for government contracts designed to ensure competitive bidding and transparency. Instead, according to Reuters, he quickly signed a sweetheart deal that gave “Vitol and its rival Trafigura…special licenses to sell Venezuela’s oil.… the companies have since earned hundreds of millions of dollars marketing the crude.”
On the very day Reuters published this blockbuster report, Trump, displaying his characteristic freedom from shame, tasked Vance with investigating corruption in states and cities governed by Democrats.
Vance as a corruption fighter is a bad joke. His ties with Addison and Vitol cry out for congressional investigation.
California Representative Mike Levin posted on X.com that
Congress has a duty to act. We should bring Secretary Wright, Vitol, and Addison in to testify under oath. We should demand the phone records, emails, and flight logs. We should find out whether anyone got a heads-up about a military operation. And we should require open, competitive bidding before any company profits from our foreign policy.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
This is a reasonable demand, but should be extended to Trump’s entire foreign policy. With former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang engulfed in a scandal over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, the salient question becomes whether the Trump administration gave him protection and turned a blind eye to Nvidia’s circumvention of a US export ban to China. Huang and Nvidia have been major donors to causes near and dear to Trump’s heart, such as his inauguration and his garish White House ballroom.
The backroom deals behind the war with Iran also demand congressional scrutiny. Speaking to sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, Trump justified the war by saying “the people we are looking to protect,” which is “basically the Middle East,” are “tremendous investors in our country. They spend trillions of dollars in our country.”
One of the biggest beneficiaries of these investments from the Middle East is Trump himself. In an interview for 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, columnist Ross Douthat asked about the seeming corruption inherent in the fact that Trump’s sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump help “manage a cryptocurrency company called World Liberty Financial” that is “also partially owned by investors connected to the government of the United Arab Emirates.” Trump responded by saying “every president has a problem…going back to George Washington.” Very gently, Douthat noted that the sheer scale of Trump’s conflicts of interest dwarfs previous presidents’.
In 1935, Maj. Gen. Smedley Darlington Butler wrote a book titled War Is a Racket, a title that has a new resonance in the Trump era. Trump’s foreign policy is rancid with corruption. He is clearly setting policy, including the wars he’s launched, to benefit cronies who have lavished largesse on him and his inner circle. The incoming Democratic Congress won a landslide because the public is sick of Trump’s corruption and wars. It’s of paramount importance that Congress use its investigatory powers to shut down Trump’s racket.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The End of Russell Brand's Rape Shtick
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Laurie Penny
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The End of Russell Brand’s Rape Shtick
The British celebrity kept reinventing his image to try to cloak his predations.
Foreign rapists are not, apparently, all created equal. Years of fearmongering about notional predators penetrating the US border don’t seem to count when the culprits are rich and famous and British. This week, born-again YouTube grifter and alleged comedian Russell Brand received a 10-year sentence in England for rape and sexual assault. Today, apex manosphere grifter Andrew Tate and his unimportant brother will appear in a Florida court pending extradition to the United Kingdom on rape and human-trafficking charges. These are men who got away with staggering feats of sexual violence not only in plain sight but also on large public platforms—getting away with it, in fact, was the gimmick. Performative misogyny wasn’t incidental to their appeal. It was their shtick from the start.
Everyone knew about Russell Brand. Not just everyone at the BBC in 2009 or everyone on liberal Twitter in 2012, but everyone who, at any point in the past several decades, watched him leering and groping and degrading women live on air. “Did Russell Brand go too far this time?” has been an open tab in British public discourse for my entire adult life. He swaggered around the BBC in a skinny scarf cackling about his conquests like some sort of sex pirate—an erotic swashbuckler who would never be square enough to ask before grabbing or take no for an answer. Everyone loves pirates; yes, they’re violent criminals, but that’s fine because they’re on the right side—namely the side where, to quote the leader of the nominally free world, “when you’re a star, they let you do it.”
How much violence and corruption should powerful men be allowed to perpetrate? How many rules do they get to break? How long do we let them laugh at the concept of individual and democratic consent? The moral questions shape our politics on a fundamental level. The #MeToo movement still casts a deep shadow over culture, and the misogyny of the modern right is not your mother’s misogyny. It’s new, reactive, and openly vengeful—after all, if women were allowed to take the rule of law into their own hands by asking men to stop raping them, men should get to overthrow the democratic consensus and wreck the global economy just to show us they still can.
That wounded, weaponized patriarchy is still in power—for now. Millennial and Gen Z men are in the unlucky position of having to foot the bill for a thousand years of male privilege that they never got to enjoy because they happened to hit adulthood just when the music stopped and the reckoning began. These men have proven easy marks for self-serving Gordon Gekkos of the attention economy like Brand and the Tates and the president of the United States.
But something has changed. We’re now in the backlash to the backlash to the backlash. It’s been a good few weeks of consequences for men who model that vengeful, nihilist masculinity, where power is its own reward and the rules only apply to losers. Russell Brand was one of the very first. In the early aughts men wanted to be him; women wanted to fix him; non-binary people wanted to know how he got his hair like that. All the while, he lapped up the attention, indulging his particular fetish for sexually degrading women live on air where they had to keep smiling. His personal aura has shifted through the whole spectrum of charismatic criminality from Jack Sparrow to, lately, David Koresh. He’s always been the patron saint of getting away with it—a wrong’un so devoid of integrity that he could and did relentlessly alter his personality so as to attach his coercive control circus to any movement that could offer him a moral alibi and an army of adoring fans. When it was cool to be anti-capitalist, he was suddenly a revolutionary figurehead, until those of us who actually went to the meetings started pointing out that he never did.
Brand first attempted to retcon his cheeky-neighborhood-crotch-grabber persona in the 2010s by identifying as a sex addict—as a sinner in need of saving, a sick boy in need of healing, rather than an adult man in charge of his own behavior. I remember him claiming to have been cured, as so many coercive men do, by “the love of a good woman”—as opposed, presumably, to the bad women who let him degrade them. The good woman in question, Jemima Khan, has spoken today about the abuse she suffered at his hands, and his ex-wife, Katy Perry, has only commented that Brand belongs in jail.
And yet Brand is clearly convinced that he is the victim here—a martyr to vile mind-virus #MeToo purity politics, which are of course very different from the down-home purity politics he’s pushing these days. His latest incarnation is as a born-again YouTube guru, complete with salt-and-pepper ponytail and linen shirt, taking the knee for God on stage for cash and applause at Turning Point USA. The alt-right is certainly a more welcoming place for professional sex pests. Among the lost boys of the manosphere, Brand, like the Tates, groomed an army of angry minions ready to rush to his aid as a brave free speech defender. Now that consequences have come calling, inevitably, wokes like me are being told that this is all our fault. We are the ones who somehow made him do it, along with every other outrage that dark-triad Svengalis perpetrate against public decency.
I will not waste energy arguing with this, having finally learned that when someone wants to fight a version of you they made up, it’s best to leave the room and let them get on with it.
More interesting is the insistence we are now seeing in the online blood-gutters where chemtrail-huffing tech moguls and their flying monkeys now control the discourse that this conviction represents a miscarriage of justice—mob rule that degrades the rule of law. In the maelstrom of #MeToo, this is what women were accused of doing when they denied wrongdoers their day in court, but now that those days are here, the same procedural outrage persists. The absolute importance of the rule of law, of course, is conveniently forgotten when it’s your own side that runs militantly afoul of it. The alleged journalist Michael Tracey has made it his business to reveal the identities of Brand’s accusers, just as he tried to expose Jane Doe in the ongoing frat-house rape cases at Cornell University. Feminist scholar Catherine MackInnon wrote that the crime of rape is defined not by women’s experience of violation but by the level of violence men consider acceptable. Here the question isn’t whether sexual violence happened but whether we consider it a crime.
At his trial, Brand didn’t dispute the events—but he still seems to believe he did nothing wrong, and millions of people agree with him. The fact is that a great many ordinary people seem to think that violence is the price women should expect to pay for casual sex, and that women who claim otherwise are the real villains. Brand and his online corps of enablers seem to think that if a young girl goes to a celebrity’s dressing room, he gets to do whatever he wants to her; that his reputation will always be more important than her dignity and safety. They seem to think that sex is disputed territory in a war between men and women—a violent, dirty thing men do to women who are foolish enough to let them.
Brand, the Tates and their ilk groomed millions of supporters for cash and cover stories. Their fans know whom they are defending, just as the millions of Americans knew what they were choosing, in 2016 and 2024, when they showed the world that they would rather elect a rapist than a woman. But persecution fantasies are part of the playbook of modern fascism. Brand has every incentive to position himself as a martyr, a figure unfairly punished for doing what every man would obviously do if he only had the balls.
This is, of course, nonsense. Most men and boys are not abusers-in-waiting, and most have far more in common with the victims of Brand and Trump and the Tates and every other professional wrong’un. But that’s the whole point of this weaponized, wounded patriarchy. It’s integral to the recruiting strategy of modern fascism to persuade millions of men that they are no more than temporarily embarrassed sex criminals, who owe their allegiance to the venal and shameless.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: After a year off, the ADAA's New York fair returns with a new name and revamped layout
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Since 1989, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA) had hosted its Art Show, which brought member galleries from across the country together for an annual fair in New York. Last year, the ADAA cancelled the 2025 fair less than four months before it was set to open, citing a need to take a “strategic pause” to reevaluate how to best serve its members.
This week, the newly-renamed ADAA Fair returns to the Park Avenue Armory (until 16 November), the first solely under the leadership of Kinsey Robb, who joined in 2024. Despite the new name and a few tweaks, it remains the same fair, she says.
“It’s a continuation. It's an evolution,” Robb says. “It is still a small-scale collegial fair of the members, so that hasn't changed either. It's just adapting into the environment and the time that we're in.”
One of those new aspects is a smaller exhibitor list. This year, 63 galleries are participating, around 12 fewer than the last edition. The intention was to give the fair more focus in a time when dealers and collectors alike are complaining of "fairtigue", both due to frequency and size (Art Basel Miami Beach, the largest art fair in the Western Hemisphere, will also scale down participating galleries this year).
The hiatus “gave us an opportunity to look at the oversaturation of fairs that were happening at that time, and the fatigue that people were feeling,” Kinsey says. “This scale feels nice to me.”
The reduction allows for a larger space around the circular bar at the center of this year’s fair, affording attendees more space to move and cut through the three-aisle expo. Visitors naturally found themselves socialising at the centre of the fair during the opening gala for the Whitney Museum of American Art on Thursday (12 November), which was well-attended despite the stormy weather and even a tornado warning in New York City. (During the ADAA fair's hiatus, its longtime preview night partner and beneficiary, the Henry Street Settlement, teamed up with the Independent fair.)
The partnership with the Whitney Museum has brought in a new, often-younger crowd, participating dealers say; works on display, meanwhile, skew heavily toward Modern and post-war secondary-market material rather contemporary works.
“I think deeply about the ecosystem of the art world, and how we all are connected,” Kinsey says. “Even if we all are in our own lanes or bubbles, we are all essential to each other in service of the art and in service of the artist.”
The dealers participating range from stalwarts like Hirschl & Adler and Kraushaar Galleries, founding members of the ADAA who participated in the Art Show’s inaugural edition in 1989, to first-time exhibitors like Alexander Berggruen, Sargent's Daughters, Piero Atchugarry, Nicodim and Hollis Taggart.
Taggart has run his namesake gallery for nearly 50 years but only recently became an ADAA member, he says, allowing him to apply for and participate in the fair for the first time. He says that in the first few hours of the opening gala, he saw a great crowd of visitors, often from the surrounding Upper East Side, different from the crowd that comes to the openings in Chelsea, where he has a space. The gallery is presenting a dual stand dedicated to two women Abstract Expressionist painters: Michael (Corinne) West and Teruko Yokoi.
“I think it's very mixed, it’s a bifurcated market,” Taggart says of the art market leading up to the fair. “There’s so many daily events that happen politically and financially, like the meltdown with Nvidia. I think the market's OK, but when you consider world events, it's a miracle that it's still as good as it is.”
The most valuable transactions reported to date at the fair are Agnes Pelton’s The Well of Peace (1932), which had an asking price of $2.4m, and Beauford Delaney’s Untitled (Paris) (1986), which was priced at $1.6m, both from the stand of New York-based dealer Jonathan Boos.
Another Upper East Side local, Kraushaar Galleries, reported the sale of two paintings for six-figure sums, as well as several works priced below $2,000. James Barron Art says it sold works by Beverly Pepper, Kenneth Noland and Kikuo Saito, each priced between $40,000 and $85,000, while Yoshii Gallery sold several works priced between $6,000 and $80,000. The Chelsea-based gallery and advisory firm AH Arts sold a work on paper by Helen Frankenthaler for $75,000. The international gallery Perrotin sold two Susumu Kamijo paintings priced between $30,000 and 45,000. Jessica Silverman from San Francisco reported eight sales from its presentation of new works by Julie Buffalohead, ranging in price from $22,000 and $50,000.
The Tribeca-based dealer Charles Moffett, who previously took part in the 2024 edition, says he appreciated the 2025 break and how the ADAA doesn’t pressure members to take part. During the opening gala, Moffett’s gallery sold two paintings by Lily Stockman priced at $20,000 apiece, and three paintings by Julia Joe priced at $30,000 each.
“With so many of the fairs, once you're on the hamster wheel, it's like, go go go. You apply every year, and if you don't apply or if you decide to sit out a year, you go to the back of the line,” Moffett says. “I'm just grateful that this feels more like an organisation that wants to see the best for each gallery.”
- ADAA Fair, until 16 November, Park Avenue Armory, New York

https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-a.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-a.author: Corey G. Johnson, Brandon Roberts
https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-a.text:
A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”
Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.
In a letter to the department’s inspector general, the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.
Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why.
In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.
At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures.
Read More
It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025.
Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.
The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.
“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.
The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds.
ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies.
Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency. 
The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said.
Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.
HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote. President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term.
ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”
Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses.
Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database, a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Should Not Give an Inch to the Lame-Duck Congress
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Should Not Give an Inch to the Lame-Duck Congress
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent makes the case for Democrats to block Trump’s attempt at judiciary-stuffing. Plus, boycott Harry Potter!
Donald Trump and the Republican Congress have confirmed 57 new federal judges over the last two years. Now, with Republicans on the way out, Trump is demanding that Congress confirm another 25 judges during the lame-duck session.
That’s a tough ask. Confirming judges takes a lot of Senate time and resources, both of which the Republicans might prefer to use for whatever other fell priorities Republicans may have before they are removed from power. It’s also worth remembering that the government runs out of funding (again) on December 11, and figuring out how to avoid (another) government shutdown should probably take priority for Republicans over confirming lame-duck judges.
Adding to the challenge is the question of whether Democratic minority leader Chuck Schumer will be in a deal-making mood when it comes to judges. On the one hand, Schumer allowed a number of Republican-aligned judges to be confirmed at the end of Joe Biden’s term in order to give Biden the “record” for the largest number of judges appointed in one presidential term. On the other hand, Schumer is facing increasingly loud questions about his leadership, and his ascension to majority leader is far from assured. If Chuck caves now—on the budget, on judges, on anything—the calls for his head will only get louder. I don’t think it’s in Schumer’s best interest to help Trump confirm 25 judges in the lame duck and then turn around and ask Democrats to give him the gavel in the new Congress.
Of course, outgoing Senate majority leader John Thune doesn’t need the Democrats to confirm a slate of new judges. He has the votes in his own caucus to do this, assuming retiring or defeated Republican senators are willing to give Trump a parting gift even though he’s ruined their careers.
But I do think if Republicans confirm 25 new federal judges in the lame-duck session, that becomes another data point to convince Democrats to confirm no new federal judges for the last two years of Trump’s term.
Now is the time for judicial hardball, and I hope Democrats get this memo.
The Bad and the Ugly
- Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 3,000 votes in their Mississippi Senate race. Hyde-Smith conceded, saving us all from a weeks-long court battle to confirm her defeat. My mother is a Black woman who was born in Clarksdale, Mississippi, in 1950. Watching her react to a Black person being elected as senator from her home state for the first time in 145 years has been one of the joys of my life.
- In Alaska, Senate candidate Mary Peltola now has more votes than both Dan Sullivans combined, further obviating the Department of Justice’s antidemocratic lawsuit aimed at overturning the election, and making even more of a mockery of Trump’s wild claims that all of one Dan Sullivan’s votes should be given to the other. Peltola still hasn’t quite breached the 50 percent barrier, which is the point at which the state shuts down the ranked-choice voting process, but there are still more votes to count.
- Remember when Trump said he would accept the results of the election after his party got walloped? Yeah, that didn’t last a week. On Monday, Trump asked on Truth Social, “Does anybody really believe this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote.” An authoritarian goon does not change his spots so easily, and everybody who thought he did deserves another time-out in the dunce chair.
- The Kennedy family joined the lawsuit to block Trump’s arch, saying that the monstrosity would disturb and diminish John F. Kennedy’s gravesite at Arlington. I have watched enough movies to know that you should never disturb the ancestral burial grounds if you can possibly avoid it.
- Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. At the sentencing hearing, Justice Joel Bennathan said, “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” I don’t have a joke here. This is just a perfect and true statement.
Inspired Takes
- Not gonna lie, I have enjoyed the Pope Leo experience. In The Nation, Victor Gaetan writes about how Pope Leo has gone to war—against war. Specifically, Pete Hegseth’s wars.
- In The New Republic, Perry Bacon makes the point that the “groups” that centrists and Democratic consultants maligned over the past few years are the reason Democrats won the midterms.
- Jamelle Bouie has a great article on the new “Southern Strategy” that helped the Democrats win in the South. Maybe next time the Democratic Party could actually invest in that strategy and give these candidates some money.
Worst Argument of the Week
OK, I think I understand what happened with the Pete Hegseth “impeachment” situation, and I think there‘s a lot of confusion out there that’s causing Democrats to get criticized unnecessarily. TLDR: This wasn’t the real Hegseth impeachment effort. The real one will be coming in the next Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Here’s what happened. Representative Thomas Massie submitted articles of impeachment for Pete Hegseth on eight charges (mostly relating to the war in Iran and the extrajudicial killings Hegseth has overseen). Massie is a Republican from Kentucky who has been vocal about the Epstein files—so vocal that Trump backed Massie’s primary challenger, Ed Gallrein, who defeated Massie in the primary and won Massie’s seat last Tuesday. Massie is on his way out, and the impeachment articles were a parting gift to an administration he hates.
Trying to impeach Hegseth now, in the lame-duck Congress, was a stunt. And a stupid one.
In any event, there was a procedural vote this week on whether to send the articles of impeachment to the full House (which is still controlled by Republicans) or leave it with the House Judiciary Committee (which is still controlled by Republicans). The option to send it to the full House (which is what Democrats ostensibly wanted) was defeated 211–204, with only Massie breaking party ranks and joining Democrats in the losing effort. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans “missed” the vote. Many people have pointed out that if the 11 Democrats had shown up, the measure would have passed (many of these people skip over the fact that if the seven Republicans had shown up to counter the Democrats, the measure would have failed). Since the Democrats have a history of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory, a firestorm over weak Democratic leadership erupted online.
Here’s the thing that I think is important to remember: Hegseth was never going to be impeached by this Republican-controlled Congress, and there were two legitimate dangers in trying to force it:
- No investigation
- Double jeopardy
There is a lot of potential evidence that Pete Hegseth has committed high crimes and misdemeanors, but Massie, acting on his own, was not in a position to provide any of it. Hegseth needs to be investigated by the House Judiciary Committee; that will not happen as long as Republicans control Congress. But I will bet all the money in my grabbable area that he will be investigated, once Representative Jamie Raskin is in charge of the Judiciary Committee. Impeaching him now, without that investigation, looks like a political stunt spearheaded by a bitter politician because it is. After Raskin gets ahold of the gavel, it will look a lot different.
And that might matter, legally speaking, because we might get only one shot at this. Look, I don’t believe that “double jeopardy”—the prohibition against prosecuting somebody twice for the same crime—should apply to impeachment proceedings. But, as I must regularly remind people, I don’t happen to have a seat on the Supreme Court. If you impeach Hegseth now, and he gets acquitted, can you impeach him six months from now for the same crimes? I think so. But I don’t know so. And I don’t want to give John Roberts, Clarence Thomas, and Samuel Alito an opportunity to answer that question for me.
Is it a bad look for 11 Democrats to “miss” a vote on impeachment so soon after the midterms? Sure. The optics are not good. The communication from the Democratic leadership on what really happened is worse. But by the same token, the “optics” around doing a rushed impeachment—a rushed impeachment that is destined to fail in front of a Republican-controlled House—are arguably worse.
If I were in the leadership chair (and I’ll note that’s yet another job I don’t have), I’d have told all my members to opt out of Massie’s vainglorious charade.
Democrats will impeach Pete Hegseth when they have their ducks in a row. They don’t need a Republican who has been booted out of Congress to lead the charge.
What I Wrote
Soo… I have the cover story in the December issue of the magazine. You can read it online here. It’s about how Democratic presidential hopefuls should campaign on court reform in 2028, and what will happen to their entire agenda if they do not.
I also wrote about how Texas has a new Democratic attorney general who will become the regulator of first resort of Elon Musk and his companies.
In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
I’m not going to watch the new HBO Harry Potter series. I’m not going to watch it because the creator of Harry Potter, J.K. Rowling, is a drooling transphobic bigot.
There are a lot of artists and creators who are problematic in some obvious and heinous way. Rowling has committed no crime, but where she stands out to me is that she’s made being a bigoted scumbag her entire personality. It’s not that she’s said a few anti-trans things, here or there. It’s that she’s happily become the face of the anti-trans movement in the UK. It’s that she uses her money and power and influence to fund anti-trans organizations that try to erase trans people from public life. She works, tirelessly it would seem, to menace trans people and manipulate the laws against them. When you support a J.K. Rowling project, you are directly supporting her financial efforts to hurt trans people. Why would you do that?
And here’s the thing about boycotting Rowling media products: It’s easy. There are so many evil people in the world whose products have been integrated into our lives in ways that make it almost impossible to excise them. I hate Jeff Bezos, for example, but pretending Amazon and The Washington Post don’t exist is really hard. I don’t support the actions of the Saudi Arabian government, but it has major investment stakes in Uber and the company that makes football video games. And, speaking of football, I believe I’ve already discussed my ongoing issues with loving a sport that is based on my favorite athletes’ getting repeatedly concussed into early oblivion.
But Harry Potter? A Harry Potter television show? I can cut Harry freaking Potter out of my life with almost no downside. If the question is, “Watch a television show or stand with transgender people?,” it’s the easiest call in my otherwise complicated journey of trying to be a moral person in an immoral world.
“What’s on HBO tonight, honey?”
“Transphobus Maximus!”
“Umm… what else is on HBO?”
“Well, John Oliver comes on in about an hour.”
“Cool, let’s watch LITERALLY ANYTHING ELSE until then.”
It’s not hard. Just don’t watch Harry Potter and let trans people live their best lives.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: The late Los Angeles artist Betye Saar receives heartfelt send-off at the Getty Center
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Jori Finkel
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children. But the memorial to Betye Saar this week at the Getty Center did just the opposite, setting into relief how powerfully she managed to balance—even integrate—acts of mothering and artmaking. (She also managed to earn her bachelor’s degree at the University of California, Los Angeles in 1949, a time when there were few Black students.)
Earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday. The tone was sombre and celebratory, ending with her brother-in-law Bennie Maupin on saxophone and the band Bayou Bump leading a procession, as Saar had wanted.
One of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch. “She was as impactful and skilful as a family matriarch as she was a gifted artist. She gathered us together whether it was in a back yard or public park. She kept our family history in the forefront of our minds and in the public eye—you can literally see our family in her artwork,” he said, referring to assemblages where she incorporated family snapshots or memorabilia.
Johnson also celebrated Saar’s sense of humour and adventure, noting that she learned to belly dance early on and showed off her dance moves in June when she was honoured by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) at its Party in the Garden gala.
His tribute followed one by MoMA director Christophe Cherix, who recalled Saar’s studio in Laurel Canyon being “unlike any other studio I had ever seen…overflowing with treasures, almost archaeological, with objects patiently waiting sometimes years or even decades to be gathered, recognised [and] assembled into works of art”.
Saar’s longtime home and studio in Laurel Canyon is where she developed her deeply spiritualist, Black-centred, female-empowered vision through printmaking and assemblage, most famously using a windowpane to organise the esoteric, celestial images that make up the 1969 work Black Girl’s Window. It is also where she raised her three daughters: the sculptor Alison Saar, the mixed media artist Lezley Saar and the writer Tracye Saar. Early on they liked to pretend the wheel of their mother’s printing press was the helm of a pirate ship, and they have said in interviews they are happy they survived without losing a finger or hand.
The veteran Los Angeles collector Joy Simmons, who recalled bringing her week-old daughter Naima to a Saar opening at the Jan Baum gallery in 1981 (“I was not going to miss this opportunity to celebrate a Black woman opening up at a white woman’s gallery”), described the Saar creative lineage, which extends to grandchildren who work in the arts today.
“To Alison, Lezley, Tracye and the whole family: I’ve watched three generations of Saar women make this city’s art history something special. Betye’s work belongs to museums now,” Simmons said, “but I know her proudest moment and her proudest accomplishment is all of you.”
