https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Frieze Artist Award reimagines endangered Lebanese site
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.
Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.
Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.
Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”
Similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”
The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser says.
Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser says.
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone, Jared Rutecki, Vernal Coleman
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Crushing Debt: Chicago’s mismanagement of pensions and heavy reliance on borrowing over decades have created an unrelenting financial burden.
- Vicious Cycle: To solve its annual budget crunch, more borrowing is used to fill in holes, including back pay for firefighters and payouts for police misconduct.
- Strained Services: Solutions to crises involving public health lack the funding that can improve the lives of Chicagoans, and basic inspections for sidewalks and restaurants fall short.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.
Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.
Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.
No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.
New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.
According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.
Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion, saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months.
Chicago’s Pension Systems Are Less than 50% Funded
The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded.
Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.
The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.
“Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance.
Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.
But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data.
That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson.
It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.
In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden.
Chicago’s Debt Payments Were the Largest Category of the City’s Budget in 2026
With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation — Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.
The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.
The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.
Amid the finger-pointing, Johnson acknowledged the bind facing his administration and the city as a whole. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch,” he said.
Watching the annual struggles of city officials to climb out of its money pit leaves many residents feeling more than a little uneasy about what comes next.
“It is the feeling that people get when they max out their credit card and they’re barely paying the minimum,” said Alderperson Andre Vasquez, who represents the 40th Ward and speaks often of growing up in a family that struggled to pay the rent every month. “You’re behind on your utilities. So you get mail every month, letting you know you’re behind.
“And at some point, you’re not even gonna open the envelope anymore, because the feeling of dread, even trying to see it, is a challenging one. That’s how people in Chicago feel.”
Unhealthy Fallout
When Johnson ran for mayor in 2023, he repeatedly emphasized his commitment to invest in the city’s neighborhoods in order to build a healthier city. Central to his message was a pledge to reopen six mental health clinics closed by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel when he faced his own budget pressures in 2011.
Those closures fueled a terrible cycle, Johnson has said. Chicagoans in desperate need of counseling and medication instead found themselves in crisis, forced to call 911 for help or struggle alone.
But during Johnson’s time in office, the city has reopened just two clinics. The city’s lack of capacity has forced nonprofit organizations to pick up the slack, despite their own funding woes and staffing challenges.
Johnson, who has touted his record of investing in “historically underserved communities,” is promising to open another clinic in 2027. But fulfilling that promise hinges on the outcome of a court fight over whether Chicago can levy taxes on social media companies like Facebook and YouTube.
“The need is big and growing,” said Mark Ishaug, CEO of Thresholds, a nonprofit group that specializes in community care. “We don’t have enough money, and what we do have is being threatened.”
Hemmed in by the city’s budget, Johnson has worked to expand mental health services outside the traditional clinic setting by offering counseling at libraries across the city several times a week and launching a “street psychiatry” program focused on unhoused Chicagoans.
Chicago’s wide range of public health needs often have solutions that require money the city lacks.
In recent years, for example, the Public Health Department’s food safety programs have been “not in substantial compliance,” according to a 2025 state audit. The department has had to prioritize restaurants and other eateries that are considered high risk while lower-risk establishments are inspected less frequently. But even that effort falls short. State law requires three inspections a year for high-priority eateries, yet that happens at only 15% of those, records show.
Inspections also were at the center of a 2023 City Council proposal to prevent lead poisoning, especially among the city’s vulnerable children living in aging or neglected housing. More than 600,000 houses and apartments, the majority of the city’s homes, were built before 1978, when lead paint was banned by the federal government. Lead paint poses a hazard in 99% of homes built before 1978, officials have said.
One solution suggested by an alderperson would’ve mandated that the city inspect every Chicago home or apartment every five years for lead paint and other health hazards. But the proposal would have required the Public Health Department to hire 600 new inspectors, more than doubling its total workforce — and its budget. Ultimately, not a single hearing was held on the idea.
This March, the issue came up again, when the City Council created a working group to develop a plan to proactively inspect all Chicago homes offered for rent. The first step would be a study and recommendations within six months. But that deadline passed without any public progress, despite several community meetings.
The department’s current efforts to address child lead poisoning underscore the impact of budget pressures.
The department receives more than 1,000 notifications each year about children with lead poisoning. Each report kicks off a complicated remediation process, involving multiple city departments, designed to identify and remove the lead source from the child’s home. Health department nurses work with the families to monitor their children’s health and assess whether the city’s abatement efforts are working.
Public health records provide a snapshot of workloads for caseworkers during the first quarter of the year, with several handling more than 200 cases at a time. “Concerns remain for case managers with persistently high caseloads,” wrote a supervising nurse in an April email to department leaders.
A department spokesperson said it reaches out to all families in these situations, “providing at minimum direct outreach and educational materials.” More than 96% of families that are contacted get a home visit from department staff. The spokesperson did not say what percentage of families the city is able to reach.
In the coming months, Public Health will have to do even more with its limited budget. The state of Illinois has lowered the threshold for elevated levels of lead in the blood, which will lead to increases in positive tests.
Coupled with the city’s efforts to expand blood tests for children in areas on the South and West sides, even more families are expected to enter the queue for case management.
Patchwork Solutions
Felicia Nalls-Bradley just wanted to get to work. It was her first week on the job.
But she tripped over an uneven sidewalk on the South Side in 2022. As she fell, she struck a fence and suffered injuries to her head, neck, shoulders, hands and back that required surgery and almost a week in the hospital. Records describe the path as “unreasonably hazardous,” with a 2-inch difference in elevation between two portions of the walkway.
She sued the city for negligence and settled for $400,000 last year. It was one of more than 350 sidewalk-related cases the city has settled since 2010, records show. The city has paid at least $16.1 million to resolve such claims during that period.
Records and deposition testimony from those cases describe a largely reactive maintenance system that relies heavily on residents to report problems.
A city engineer testified in a sidewalk-injury deposition in 2024 that Chicago does not routinely inspect its sidewalks. He also said that employees investigating a complaint are not expected to identify other hazards nearby.
In separate testimony in 2017, another engineer said the city responded to about 13,000 sidewalk maintenance requests annually but had only a handful of crews rotating across Chicago to make repairs.
The engineer’s testimony in another case contrasted his professional desires with the limitations of his resources. “In a perfect world I would like to do that, yes,” he said about inspecting every sidewalk complaint.
He then added a caveat: “This is the real world.”
Injuries — and lawsuits — are not the only consequence of poor sidewalk maintenance. Iliana Haven, who uses a power wheelchair and scooter because of a neuromuscular condition, said they regularly encounter obstacles as they struggle to get around.
A thwarted trip to the Puerto Rican People’s Day Parade exemplified their problems as they encountered broken and uneven sidewalks on their scooter. After being unable to find a passable route, Haven called family for help.
It took about 30 minutes for relatives to find Haven. Family members returned home to get a motorized wheelchair, which could more easily carry Haven to the event. But it had nearly concluded by the time everybody got through the entrance gate. Haven appreciated the help and took it with good humor, but the ordeal highlighted a lesson.
“It is a rule of mine to never leave anywhere by myself if I can help it,” Haven said.
They also understand the frustration of others challenged by sidewalks. The lack of access impacts businesses in the end, they said.
“There’s a huge number of disabled people in the city of Chicago. We would love to go and spend our money,” Haven said. “We can only do that if we can leave our house.”
The Debt Burden
After declaring that he would run again for mayor in next year’s election, Johnson gathered the media in early October to tout what his administration called a success story, a concrete example of his commitment to building up neglected areas of the city.
Under bright skies, he cut the ribbon on seven new two-flats in North Lawndale, a West Side neighborhood that has seen its population dwindle and its crime rate remain stubbornly high. The only way to reverse those entrenched trends, he said, is to create safe, affordable new homes that will allow Chicagoans to “put down roots and build wealth.”
The homes were built on city-owned vacant land; they also were built on more city debt. The Johnson administration used $5.4 million from the $1.25 billion Johnson borrowed in 2025 to fund housing and economic development projects across the city.
The debate over that borrowing crystalized Chicago’s current governing dilemma: Should it reduce its dependence on debt or address crucial needs for Chicagoans? And is it possible to do both?
Some alderpersons warned the city could not afford to borrow another $1.25 billion and questioned the wisdom of a payment schedule that avoids paying any principal until 2028. If that debt is not retired until 2055, as scheduled, taxpayers will have paid more than $98.9 million in interest costs alone, records show.
That borrowing is at the heart of Johnson’s attempt to expand the city’s economic capacity and invest in neighborhoods that have long been ignored by City Hall. His administration defends the borrowing by saying there is a plan to pay it back with a new approach that doesn’t affect taxpayers. Nearly four dozen tax-increment financing districts are set to expire by 2039, allowing more than $2 billion to flow back to the city, Chicago Public Schools and other taxing districts in coming years, records show.
Some alderpersons remain skeptical of Johnson’s budget strategy, and his overall financial stewardship was dealt a significant setback when Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch resigned Friday. She described a deep rift with the administration over how to portray the city’s finances.
“The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about the City’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate,” she wrote to Johnson. “I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve.”
The city responded by criticizing her job performance, saying she had been “largely absent” as Johnson’s team worked on its 2027 budget.
In the aftermath, alderpersons are seeking an audit of city finances. A majority already have been sparring with Johnson over borrowing.
They moved in September to make it harder to take on new debt by requiring the votes of at least 30 alderpersons, not just a simple majority from the panel of 50. Johnson blasted that change, saying it would stop investment flowing to neighborhoods like North Lawndale, and vetoed it.
Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said Johnson faces hard choices as he tries to implement his agenda.
“I give the mayor credit for having aspirations to make housing more affordable and to expand behavioral and mental health care,” Marlowe said. “These are all noble goals. But the city can’t afford it.”
Less than two weeks later, Johnson was back at City Hall, giving his 2027 budget address and outlining his plans to fill yet another large gap. Among his solutions again was a corporate tax, which once again was deemed dead-on-arrival by key alderpersons. But the City Council may have no choice but to go along with Johnson’s plan for more borrowing.
He proposed borrowing $481 million in 2027 to cover the cost of resolving lawsuits alleging that police misconduct led to wrongful convictions and deadly pursuits. If approved by the council, it would mark the second straight year that the city has borrowed to cover its bills, a move that financial experts consider a sign of worsening financial distress.
Marlowe said the city has no choice but to borrow to cover those costs, calling it the “least bad option” available to the city.
But Joseph Ferguson, who heads the Civic Federation, a nonpartisan budget watchdog group, was unimpressed by Johnson’s presentation. He’s seen a pattern over decades in which city officials plan to make it through the next election cycle or the next budget fight without looking toward lasting solutions.
Johnson’s plan, Ferguson said, shifts costs onto future taxpayers and only manages to “dig the city deeper into a financial hole.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/demo.title: The Future Is Bright for the Democrats, as Long as They Don’t Have to Interact With the Public
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/demo.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/demo.text:
Clutching a Shake Shack bag in the Denver airport Saturday, Lis Smith held forth on her “do’s and don’ts” for the Democrats. Do: Focus on cost of living and accountability for the excesses of the Trump administration. Don’t: Prioritize revenge on Trump before hitting your affordability goals.
“The voters who helped us get this majority were voters that said we want you to lower our costs, we want you to listen to us, we want you to root out corruption,” said Smith, a prominent strategist for the centrist wing of the Democratic Party. “We’re living in the middle of a cost-of-living-crisis, and if you’re not talking to voters about that issue, not meeting them where they are in terms of their anger at the system, at both the economic and political system, like, you’re doing it wrong.”
Smith was among the flotsam and jetsam of exhausted Democratic politicos swirling about Denver International Airport in a surreal coda to a gathering she’d helped organize: a two-day conference of moderate and center-left Democrats exploring the future of the party, aptly dubbed “What’s Next.”
It was organized by the self-styled pragmatists of Majority Democrats, a hybrid political action committee and super PAC bankrolled by the hedge fund tycoon Stephen Mandel and his wife, Sue, and co-signed by the Searchlight Institute, a centrist think tank launched by former staffers of John Fetterman who have sought to quash the party’s focus on more left-leaning policy. The conference was seen as a practice ground for stump speeches from potential 2028 presidential candidates, heavy on party unity and light on ideological debate.
Within the confines of the Mission Ballroom complex in Denver’s River North neighborhood, it was a safe space for hopefuls like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Texas, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, and Sen. Corey Booker of New Jersey to test out their lines for next cycle — before they have to go in front of the public.
But now, it was stuck.
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop order, throwing the nation’s airports into chaos and canceling thousands of flights. As the situation was unfolding, Buttigieg joked onstage that he’d be available to help anyone looking to rebook their flight. On Saturday, 24 hours later, that joke might have been less funny to the likes of Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, who told The Intercept he had been unceremoniously deplaned from a flight canceled at the last minute.
Despite the airline chaos, Smith was feeling good. To her, the attendees represent the future in a post-Blue Tsunami landscape — and you better not call them the establishment.
“Majority Democrats does not consider itself a centrist organization,” said Smith, who worked on Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential run, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s 2018 reelection campaign, and Cuomo’s 2021 response to sexual harassment allegations. “So we want to be an alternative to the stale establishment that puts up candidates like Joe Biden or like Andrew Cuomo for mayor.”
Smith said she welcomed it when “What’s Next” became the scene of early shots in a battle over Democratic leadership in the Senate. On Thursday, the first night of the conference, at about 7 p.m. Mountain time, news broke that Sen. Chris Van Hollen — a Maryland Democrat, conference invitee, and rumored 2028 hopeful — planned to mount a challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for party leadership.
“I think a little democracy in the United States Senate caucus is a good thing,” he said at his first press conference on the matter on Friday. “I think it’s important that we give Senate Democrats a choice. We gave voters all over the country a choice, and they chose change.”
Van Hollen, who has differentiated himself from Schumer with his critical stance on Israel, told reporters he had decided to abandon a go for the White House in 2028 in favor of shaking up the party’s presence in the Senate.
It was a slight departure from the celebratory mood in Denver, where the words “big tent” were frequently bandied about. At the airport, Smith told The Intercept she and other organizers were as surprised as anyone by Van Hollen’s announcement. “We invited Van Hollen just as we invited anyone who was on the list of potential 2028ers,” she said. “But what better place to do it, I guess!”
Aside from Van Hollen positioning himself as a progressive challenger to Schumer, there was a noted absence of the party’s left flank. The progressives who did make the invite list stayed on message with the “takes all kinds” approach to Democratic victory.
“It’s a really good time to be a Democrat right now,” said Morris Katz, a campaign adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and, later, to Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner. “I think if you look at the historic wins that we had across the country and the way those candidates spoke, they sound a lot more like Bernie Sanders in 2016 than Hillary Clinton in 2016.”
But not everyone was feeling the love. Shelby Green, an organizer for a campaign in Florida to turn the state’s bankrupt Brightline railroad service into a public asset, criticized the conference organizers for having few Black women speakers on the main stage. She spoke bitterly of what she described as the party’s failure to properly support Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate who narrowly lost her contest for Senate in Florida.
“They waited until just weeks before the election to do a get-out-the-vote push, when they should have been doing voter registration,” Green said. “I think there should have been a space to apologize to Angie Nixon and to apologize to the South and say, ‘I’m sorry we underinvested, what can we do to make sure we don’t miss the ball next time?’”
Perhaps the most heated moments came when the conference attendees were forced to interact with members of the public — particularly those who disagreed with them.
On Friday morning, moments into a sit-down interview on the main stage between Jessica Tarlov, a token Democrat on Fox News, and New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, heir apparent to the Democratic leadership in the House, a small group of protesters stood up and started to shout for some of the left-wing policies that had gone largely unmentioned inside the conference.
“When is it time for Medicare for all?” one protester called out, prompting boos and jeers from the crowd. “When is it time for an arms embargo?”
As the protesters were ushered out, Jeffries began to speak of the honor he felt at “the trust placed in us by the American people.”
“Nobody trusts you!” another protester called out.
The conference shielded its attendees from most of the dissent. On the drive into the city on Thursday morning, The Intercept spotted a gaggle of protesters from the group Indivisible hoisting a huge banner on a highway overpass declaring “No Schumer Coronation,” objecting to the New York Democrat’s presumed rise as Senate majority leader. The group reappeared outside the convention center on Friday morning alongside protesters from Sunrise Movement demanding a Green New Deal, while police in riot gear milled around an armored vehicle looking bored and over-equipped. Onboard a shuttle bus ferrying conference-goers from their hotels to the convention center, one battle-hardened Democratic operative derided the protesters as “wacktivists,” expressing a distaste for the so-called “groups” blamed by many in the Democratic establishment for dragging the party left on social issues, to its detriment in 2024.
On the street corner on Friday morning, Tammy Butters, a retired teacher, told The Intercept that she was merely there to encourage those inside to not “chicken out” of holding the Trump administration accountable.
“There’s all this talk of compromise and talking to the other side, and I get that,” Butters said. “But I think we the people are screaming for accountability, and accountability and affordability are not separate issues. We are capable of doing both.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Gillian Jakab
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
Uncanny Correspondences
The radical choreography of Trisha Brown
The Uncanny Choreography of Trisha Brown
After a career spanning five decades, and 10 years after her passing, the choreographer and dancer is having a moment.
In 1982, the dancer Trisha Brown started an unorthodox correspondence with the musician and performance artist Laurie Anderson. Anderson’s debut studio album, Big Science, had just been released, and Brown, emerging as one of the leading dance artists of her generation, had choreographed a 10-minute duet to the song “Sweaters.” She sent it to Anderson by videotape without sound. Anderson then composed a new score for Brown’s dance and mailed back a cassette with the music. And with that, Brown set in motion the latest in a series of multimedia collaborations, not just with Anderson but with the artist Robert Rauschenberg, that would result in her masterwork, Set and Reset.
In October 1983, Set and Reset premiered at the Brooklyn Academy of Music’s Next Wave festival. The dance opens on Rauschenberg’s sculptural set Elastic Carrier (Shiner), a rectangular prism flanked by two pyramids. The first movements are projections of newsreel-style found footage—traffic, baseball, a monkey—shifting onto the fabric forms that rise to make way for the performers as they appear. Two stagehands enter holding a dancer horizontally overhead, charting the stage perimeter as she walks on a wall that isn’t there. It’s a witty quotation of one of her earlier works, 1971’s Walking on the Wall. Meanwhile, Anderson’s score—part sci-fi, part groovy rhythm—keeps the dancers in motion. They break away in different directions, each doing a variation of the piece’s basic movement phrases. Straight limbs slice the air, punctuating slinky hip swivels with geometric precision. Individuals relate to one another like a Fibonacci sequence in nature, in mathematical patterns so seamless that one doesn’t register the equation behind the pine cone’s spiral. This cascading energy, simultaneously fluid and structured, epitomizes Brown’s movement language.
This past February, the Trisha Brown Dance Company performed Set and Reset on the BAM stage of its premiere—a reprise that marked a major stop in the company’s ongoing “Dancing With Bob” tour celebrating Rauschenberg’s centennial. The double bill includes Merce Cunningham’s Travelogue and is taking Brown’s dance company all over the world, from Beverly Hills to Chicago, Vienna to Paris.
Much has changed since Set and Reset’s debut four decades ago. In the early 1980s, Brown benefited from substantial federal funding. In 2025, as part of the Trump administration’s attack on cultural institutions, the National Endowment for the Arts revoked a major grant intended for the tour. Now her company must lean more heavily on private funds, such as from the French jewelry company Van Cleef and Arpels. But so deep-seated is Brown’s choreography in the postmodern canon that watching the piece today, one can sense its constancy, as though Brown were in the translucent wings of Rauschenberg’s set directing it. When Anderson’s voice proclaims “Long time no see” over her electronic score, it is now a greeting to these old friends. No worries that neither Brown nor Rauschenberg are alive; Set and Reset reaches them as a séance of sorts, made easier by the staying power of their legacies.
Born in 1936 in Aberdeen, Washington, Trisha Brown graduated from Mills College in 1958 with a degree in dance. She learned improvisation techniques from Anna Halprin in San Francisco before making the inevitable crossing to New York City. When she arrived in the early 1960s, Brown took classes at the Merce Cunningham studio and worked answering phones there. That’s how she met Rauschenberg: “This man used to call named Bob Rauschenberg, and I had the greatest conversations with him,” she told David Sears in a 1982 interview for Ballet Review. It would be another decade before they officially collaborated, but Brown admired Rauschenberg’s dynamic stage designs for Cunningham and others, as well as his exhibitions pushing the limits of sculpture and painting. (“I was bowled over that anyone would put a bed on the wall and put some paint on it,” she said of one of the artist’s early “combines,” Bed.)
Brown eventually graduated from Cunningham’s reception desk and matriculated into the street school broadly referred to as New York’s downtown art scene. She was a founding member of the Judson Dance Theater—the now-legendary avant-garde collective that rejected the drama of early modern dance and championed a democratic, pedestrian form of movement. Under the roof of Judson Memorial Church, Brown trail-blazed what we now refer to as postmodern dance along with people like Yvonne Rainer, Steve Paxton, and Simone Forti. By the 1970s, Brown wasn’t under the roof so much as outside or even on top of it. Her 1971 Roof Piece and her “equipment pieces,” such as Man Walking Down the Side of a Building (1970), liberated dance from theaters and set it loose in galleries, lofts, parks, and in front of buildings. When Brown’s Walking on the Wall was performed on the exterior of the Whitney, it was Rauschenberg who supplied the equipment.
As the 1980s approached, Brown’s work began to change. A transition from site-specific dances to a cycle of proscenium pieces posed new questions of perspective and audience. While Brown’s dances were welcomed by mainstream concert venues like BAM and backed by conventional art-funding sources, they retained their experimental edge. It was in this era that Brown opened her company to men and began documenting not just her finished pieces but her creative process on video. It was also in this period that she developed Set and Reset.
At once wild and precise, playful and deadpan, Set and Reset respects the choreographic categories that came before it even as it defies them. The veteran critic Deborah Jowitt once noted that “it’s always been one of the high aspirations of modern dance not to move like the person you started with.” Martha Graham broke away from her teachers at the Denishawn school in the 1920s. Graham’s disciples—the generation of Merce Cunningham and Paul Taylor—then distinguished themselves in turn against their inherited gospel. In Set and Reset, as the name implies, Brown marked herself out as one of the true innovators of dance movement in the 20th century. By that point, it seemed like her movement came, as Brown once put it, from “Heaven.”
The heaven that Brown may have had in mind, as Susan Rosenberg expertly shows in her book Trisha Brown: Choreography as Visual Art, was her childhood in the rural beauty of Washington State. Of course, the inspiration might have come from somewhere else, too. But Brown’s work was, as Rauschenberg once noted, “just about as personal” as one can get: “She’s right on the edge—I mean if she weren’t so eccentric, it would be too autobiographical, but she is such an unpredictable person, actually, that even if it is autobiographical, it looks abstract.”
It’s this personal quality that fed Brown’s artistic relationships, including in the making of Set and Reset. Despite privileging structure, logic, and mathematical precision, her principles of motion had at their core a collaborative element—one born out of her interactions with others. The paradigmatic example is what Brown called “memorized improvisation,” which she used to create Set and Reset. Generating spontaneous building blocks of movement from her body and engineering them into a choreographic flow, she then had her dancers execute the material in the studio, down to the last square inch, before encouraging them to improvise from it—“play with visibility and invisibility”—over and over until a new set of movements emerged. “Brown felt that instinctual behavior brought up tenderness and sort of a sabotage aspect to the work. You get all kinds of things happening outside the confines of the original, rigorously organized material. [Set and Reset] was really one of the first times that humor was an element of the work—high jinks, exuberance all showed up and were then committed [to the choreography],” recalled Carolyn Lucas, a former dancer with the company and its current associate artistic director. “She said at one point of the dancers, ‘I couldn’t keep them out of the work.’”
With her outside collaborators, Brown also cultivated equally intimate exchanges, such as her VHS-for-cassette-tape dialogue with Anderson that prompted the making of Set and Reset. The composer dubbed it “electronic closeness,” a kind of Snapchat ahead of its time. Brown got just as close with others, like Rauschenberg, but each time through different means. In Brown’s own words: “In Set and Reset, the communication between [Bob and me] was direct, almost as if he lived inside of me, or me inside of him. There were correspondences that were uncanny.” Brown was not just aware that her collaborative demands ran deep; it was her consciously imposed condition, her sine qua non of the artistic relationship. “One factor in all of my collaborations is that I work with friends of mine,” Brown told The Brooklyn Rail in 2005. “You need to know if they’re going to go ballistic at the drop of a hat or not. You have to know if they’ll be able to deal with it.”
Brown did not completely blur the borders of music, visual art, and dance in her work. Nor did she insist on the complete autonomy of each of these art forms the way Cunningham, Cage, and Rauschenberg had done. What she did do was bring each discipline into a quasi-familial relationship characterized by both proximity and distance. In Set and Reset, Brown would send Anderson weekly videos of new movement phrases as Anderson worked on the score. Rauschenberg labored over the set and costumes at a greater distance from the other two, insisting that “the sturdiest kind of collaboration happens when you allow all the participants as much freedom as they can absorb.” Out of this practice came Elastic Carrier (Shiner) and his silk-screened city images on the dancers’ costumes. Grayscale, they are in contrast with Rauschenberg’s projected moving images, forming the kind of two-way flow that characterized Brown’s practice.
After a career spanning five decades, and 10 years after her passing, Trisha Brown is having a moment. The reprise of Set and Reset, in a tour honoring one of her closest artistic partners, stands as a testament to her legacy, not by imparting it to those around her but by pulling them into it. Her work is powerful enough to jump generations. Her set of movements are still in motion, and her collaborators—some alive, others now dead—span nearly half a century of American art, music, and dance. Some of her collaborators will need to be reached by séance; others are immediately accessible. But their sheer number is both the proof of Brown’s achievement as a choreographer and the reason why Set and Reset feels as fresh today as it did back in 1983.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Reem Al Mubarak: What We Left in the Sandbox
Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027
In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.
The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
Shaikha Al Mazrou
Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027
In 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.
She receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside new commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.
All Manner of Experiments
NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027
In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Said established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.
All Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.
The exhibition at the New York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Said’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.
A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.
Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean
Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027
The Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.
This investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).
Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.
Vantage Point 13
Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November
The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.
Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.
The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu shows life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.
Artist’s Rooms: Walid Siti; Shezad Dawood; Lulua Alyahya; Afrah Shafiq; Bani Abidi
Jameel Arts Centre, Dubai
The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.
One room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.
Bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.
Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.
New Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.
Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.
The sky held it, the earth remembered
Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December
The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.
In Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.
The work—a new iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—shows how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.
Devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.
In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.
The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.
The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.
Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.
Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril
In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt.
First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.
Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees.
As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story.
Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.
In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed.
Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments.
Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011.
But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security.
In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.
Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials.
Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets
Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.
They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase.
But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially.
The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection.
By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease.
The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.
Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008.
But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics.
Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation.
Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just months before she lost her bid for reelection.
The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and significantly reduced the annual budget gaps.
In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a temporary hole in the 2027 city budget.
The Financial Toll of Police Misconduct
The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals, misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a politically powerful police union.
After a massive outcry greeted footage of McDonald getting shot 16 times while he walked away from officers, the federal government launched a probe that in 2017 found ample evidence that the department routinely violated the constitutional rights of Black and Latino Chicagoans.
In 2019, the Chicago Police Department agreed — under the oversight of a federal judge — to change the way officers are trained, supervised and disciplined. In taking so long to address a pernicious problem, a succession of city leaders set up Chicago for a huge financial hit.
The true scope of police misconduct and what it will cost the city is only now becoming clear.
From 2019 to 2025, as the city scrambled to fill budget holes, it agreed to pay nearly $730 million to resolve lawsuits alleging officers committed a wide range of misconduct, according to a WTTW News analysis of city records. The most expensive cases involve wrongful convictions that sent Chicagoans now declared innocent to prison for decades, as well as botched raids and police pursuits that violated CPD policy and led to injuries, according to that analysis.
In 2026 alone, Chicago has spent more than $277 million to resolve lawsuits alleging police misconduct, records show. That includes nearly $100 million to resolve 90 lawsuits filed by people who allege they were wrongfully implicated based on evidence gathered by former Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was convicted in 2013 of taking bribes. He has denied wrongdoing.
Johnson has urged the City Council to borrow an additional $481 million to cover the costs of resolving more lawsuits, with $260.8 million earmarked for 17 people wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. A judge determined Guevara told “bald-faced lies” while under oath in 2017, a fact that will be presented to any jury asked to determine whether the city should be held accountable for claims of misconduct. He has repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself when pressed to testify in civil cases.
Another 25 lawsuits naming Guevara remain pending.
Guevara is now one of the most notorious members of the Chicago Police Department, costing taxpayers more than any other officer, including former Cmdr. Jon Burge, who tortured and beat more than 100 Black men from the 1970s to the 1990s, city officials have acknowledged.
Records show that Guevara, who retired from CPD in 2005 and lives in Texas, collects an annual payout of $91,000 from the city’s depleted police pension fund.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Nomad art and design fair lands at Abu Dhabi’s Modernist former airport terminal
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.
“Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” says the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”
This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.
Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.
Bellavance‑Lecompte says that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.
Another important development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something new can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte says.
For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte says. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.
• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.title: ICE Shot Pepper Spray Into a Car in a Traffic Stop, Then Broke a Detainee’s Collarbone
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.text:
Jose Rosito Roca Estrada and his friends were on their way to work in a van on June 27, when a car in front of them slammed on its brakes, forcing them to crash into it and ricochet backward on the busy highway.
Three more cars surrounded theirs, and an estimated 10 to 12 officers poured out. The agents screamed at the men to get out of the vehicle despite traffic whipping by, Roca Estrada and fellow passenger Elvis Manuel Mejia told The Intercept. The stalemate ended with the sound of shattering glass and an asphyxiating cloud of chemicals flooding the car.
According to a new federal lawsuit and photos from the scene shared with The Intercept, federal agents smashed the car’s back windows and “sprayed the occupants with pepper spray through the lowered side windows.”
Officers then dragged a scared and temporarily blinded Roca Estrada from the car. “I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator. “They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me because they were asking very personal questions.”
The June attack is one of six stories described in a lawsuit brought by several groups — including the American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia, the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, the Legal Aid Justice Center, and multiple law firms — alleging widespread “unlawful and dangerous” warrantless arrests by immigration officials in Virginia.
On behalf of Roca Estrada and other plaintiffs, the groups are suing the Department of Homeland Security, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director of ICE David Venturella, and ICE D.C. Field Office Director Robert Guadian. They’re asking the court in the Eastern District of Virginia to force DHS to comply with congressional limits on warrantless immigration arrests and prohibit the agency from making immigration arrests without legally required individual assessments.
“They have a mandate from the Trump administration … to get creative and make arrests, however they see fit,” said Sophia Gregg, an immigrants’ rights attorney at the ACLU of Virginia. “The agents are ill-trained, and even when they do violate the law, there are no consequences.”
Roca Estrada said that the officers demanded to search his pockets, and when he declined, an agent threw him to the ground headfirst and dug his knees into his upper back. He remembered screaming as pain began to radiate through his collarbone. An X-ray reviewed by The Intercept would later confirm it was broken.
According to Roca Estrada and the lawsuit, officers began to punch and hit him in the back, eventually twisting his arm to place him in handcuffs and into the vehicle. Roca Estrada said that nurses who examined him after the alleged assault told him that blood had filled his lungs, and the lawsuit notes he was diagnosed with a broken clavicle and a lung injury. At no point, the lawsuit alleges, did officers ask the necessary questions to determine whether Roca Estrada was deportable or whether he was a flight risk.
Immigration officers are only supposed to make warrantless immigration arrests if they have determined “probable cause” to believe a person is unlawfully present likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. But in an effort to meet the Trump administration’s nationwide quota of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, the lawsuit alleges, the Department of Homeland Security has chosen to pursue an unlawful policy and practice of “arrest-first, investigate-later” — leaving a trail of traumatized victims who should have never been arrested in the first place.
In the first year of the Trump administration, immigration arrests drastically increased in Virginia. According to the lawsuit, in 2025, ICE made “970 arrests each month in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — nearly five times the average monthly arrest volume in 2024.”
Reached by The Intercept, a DHS spokesperson said that agency had “arrested Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, an illegal alien from Guatemala,” using Roca Estrada’s full name even though The Intercept had not provided it, but denied that its officers “fractured a detainee’s collarbone.” The spokesperson did not deny that officials had deployed chemical weapons, saying, “staff relied on their training to gain compliance.”
“Claims that agents did not properly identify themselves are FALSE. When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement,” wrote the spokesperson. “At NO time were any of the detainees thrown to the ground during the arrest. Allegations that our officers fractured a detainee’s collarbone during the arrest are FALSE.”
Six weeks after Roca Estrada’s arrest, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona was home caring for her 4-year-old sister in Norfolk, Virginia, when she found out ICE had detained her fiancé, his brother, and his brother-in-law.
It was another traffic stop, and Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and recent high school graduate, had to go pick up their abandoned car. There, according to the lawsuit, an ICE officer demanded her identification, refused to let her get her wallet, and accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle. They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.
Eventually, ICE allowed another sister, 15, to come pick up the 4-year-old, then took Ramirez Corona into custody. She sat in “handcuffs, ankle shackles and a waist chain” for hours, according to the lawsuit, until her 15-year-old sister was able to bring her birth certificate — showing she was a natural-born U.S. citizen.
The lawsuit argues that Ramirez Corona’s arrest exemplifies an out-of-control trend of warrantless and often nonsensical arrests. Stephen Miller, then homeland security adviser and now the White House chief of staff, directed agents to “just go out there and arrest,” and the department seems to have complied.
“More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July 2026 did not have a criminal record,” the plaintiffs note. “And more than 500 people detained by ICE since January 2025 are U.S. citizens — another likely undercount — like Ms. Ramirez Corona.”
The same month that Roca Estrada says that federal agents temporarily blinded him, broke his collarbone, and beat him until his lungs filled with blood, Congress approved another $72 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrant advocacy groups warned ahead of the funding vote that additional money for ICE and President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown would mean more people would suffer a fate like Roca Estrada’s — or worse. The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars.
Physicians for Human Rights and the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center documented over 412 incidents of misuse of force by law enforcement agents at immigration protests from June 2025 to May 2026, including the use of chemical irritants like pepper balls and pepper spray — the same family of weapons Roca Estrada and Mejia suspect was set off in their car.
In ICE custody, 52 people have died during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, according to Human Rights Watch, while use-of-force by guards remains largely unknown.
“We have received many more reports of violent use of force against people,” said Jeff Migliozzi, the communications director for Freedom for Immigrants, which runs the National Immigration Detention Hotline, referencing hotline numbers from June and July. “The overwhelming forces of intimidation and fear and retaliation, the M.O. of ICE has not changed. But certainly, as more people are detained, there’s more incidents [of violence].”
The DHS spokesperson claimed that Roca Estrada and everyone arrested along with him were offered medical care but declined, adding that “one of the detainees indicated that he had a prior shoulder injury.”
Roca Estrada tells a very different story.
He says he spent the next month tossed between detention centers in Virginia and West Virginia. Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets. He said he largely went without medical care despite agonizing pain that prevented him from laying down at night.
Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.
“After medical personnel offered to document his injuries and consult a forensic physician, officers abruptly removed him from the hospital and returned him to detention,” the lawsuit alleges. “For weeks thereafter, Defendants failed to provide the promised follow-up care.”
According to the lawsuit, none of this should have happened because Roca Estrada never should have been detained in the first place.
The suit alleges that immigration officers never asked the 24-year-old “about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status, where he worked, how long he had lived in Virginia, whom he lived with, whether he had family or community ties in the United States, or similar questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Other stories in the lawsuit follow a similar pattern. Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, a 24-year-old woman from Guatemala, was detained in Centreville, Virginia, during a traffic stop around 6:00 a.m. with her husband. She alleges that masked officers blocked her car at a traffic light and forced her and her husband from the vehicle.
The officers falsely claimed that her husband had a deportation order, according to the lawsuit. But when her husband asked questions about the stop, Us Lopez alleges an agent pepper-sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their weapons.
According to Us Lopez, officers did not “inquire about her immigration status, ask where she lived, inquire about her family, ask about her ties to the community, or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Instead, she claims that officers ignored her as she explained that she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order in place, and allegedly mocked her requests for answers and legal assistance.
For Roca Estrada, his physical injuries and trauma left him unable to work for a month. While he was detained, he also lost his apartment and had his personal belongings sent back to Guatemala without his consent, according to the lawsuit.
“The way that I was arrested … and the immense pain that I had to go through during this whole experience,” said Roca Estrada. “What happened to me was not just.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
