https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-econo.author: Clara E. Mattei
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-econo.text:
Anwar Shaikh Gave Us an Emancipatory Economics
Anwar Shaikh, who died in October at 80, showed how capitalism really works: profit drives it, competition is a war, and crisis is the norm. Economist Clara Mattei argues that his work remains a guide to changing the world.
Writing about someone who has changed your life and to whom you owe so much is much more difficult than I would have thought. It is impossible to feel capable of delivering even a fraction of what it would take to fully honor the human and intellectual memory of Anwar Shaikh.
I met Anwar at a moment of great intellectual insecurity for myself that he helped me overcome. Now, in front of this blank page, that insecurity is back. At the same time, this state of mind allows me to fully reconnect with the memories of our first encounters and the development of a mentorship and friendship that has deeply shaped me as a scholar and as a person.
Grounding Theory in Historical Analysis
It was 2015, and I was struggling to pursue the research for my economics PhD in Pisa, Italy. It had been a tough couple of years: after a five-year university degree in philosophy and history, the doctoral program had thrown me into hardcore economics courses. There were intense examinations in mathematics, econometrics, statistics, microeconomics, and game theory, which I had survived by studying nonstop and memorizing formulas that I would obsess over at night, half awake, half in my dreams. After so many examinations and so much peer pressure, it took me a while to find a subject I could feel passionate about.
Economics, as my course textbooks presented it, was a dry, abstract discipline, all about technique and not much about intellectual stimulation. I felt demotivated and especially out of place. Was I ever going to be fit for this?
I cared deeply about social justice and critique of the system — I read Karl Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts and Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation — but none of it seemed to fit the current canon of scientificity. My supervisor, Giovanni Dosi, suggested I work on austerity, and I agreed, but I could not find an approach that was not so deeply economistic, focused only on debt and growth.
Finally, while desperately roaming the library, I found an article on Fascist economics in 1920s Italy. I realized its deep affinity with contemporary economic policies in Europe, especially Italy. That day, I had a moment of awakening and decided to embark on archival research to trace the genesis of these policies in the thought of the economists who were advising Benito Mussolini.
The research was challenging. I adhered to no specific methodological framework. To make sense of things, I realized I had to surpass the narrow limits of what history of economic thought, economic history, or economics meant for the profession.
In my scholarly journey, I had found supportive mentors — Nicola Giocoli, Alessandro Nuvolari, and George Peden, for example — but there was clearly not much space for me in Italian academia, especially within economics. I was not doing enough of what economics was supposed to look like, but to maintain my motivation, I could not conform.
This is when an email from Anwar changed my life forever. It read: “Dear Clara, I could not stop reading your paper once I started! It is excellent, and I hope you continue to pursue the parallels between the post-WWI rationale for austerity and the subsequent reincarnations in the 1980s and again now. Congratulations on a fine piece of work.” I remember gasping with happiness and a sense of recognition that I had never felt before. Really? A scholar like Anwar was taking my research seriously? And in an economics department?
In his role as chair of the Economics Department at the New School for Social Research, Anwar was responding to an exploratory email I had sent just a week earlier, inquiring about a visiting scholar position. I had only recently discovered the existence of a department where Marxian economics was part of the canon, where economics seemed to be about substance as well as technique. In that email, I had attached a chapter of my dissertation, but I had no expectation whatsoever that Anwar was going to open the file.
But he did, and from then on he would continue to make clear the importance of understanding the history of economic thought as integral to the analysis of capitalism itself. He wrote again inviting me both as a visiting scholar and to give a talk on my work to the department. That email exchange was a real turning point in my life’s journey.
When I arrived in New York City in September 2015, I went to Anwar’s office hours. His wisdom and generosity were traits that struck me immediately. He was not teaching that semester, but I would stop by his office to get his feedback on some ideas.
The week before my scheduled department talk, he told me: “You know, we are hiring, and you should apply.” The message was implicit: take this talk as an opportunity to showcase your work. At that point, I was exhilarated. The amount of adrenaline I felt leading up to that 4 p.m. Tuesday seminar was something I would never experience again.
Anwar fought hard for the department to hire me. I only learned this after I had begun working as an assistant professor of economics at the New School. He believed in me so strongly. I still have a hard time understanding why and have never felt worthy of such high esteem.
My dear colleague Ying Chen, whom the department hired at the same time as me, and I were both so lucky to have his support. We will miss those lunches, sharing different varieties of spicy Chinese food over conversations both fun and serious.
A Life’s Mission
In the summer of 2016, right before I moved to New York to start teaching, I helped organize a couple of stops for Anwar’s book launch in Italy. The stops were at the International University College of Turin and at my alma mater, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa. Anwar had just published his masterpiece, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises.
There is one conversation with him I will remember forever: We were sitting at a café on the Po River, and he started telling me about the commitment and devotion it had taken him to produce his book. It had taken him over thirty years to completely reset the foundations of economics and the study of capitalism. He told me that escaping the traps of dominant economic theory was a sacrosanct mission to change the world, that deep study carried enormous transformational weight, and that it required sacrificing a lot of worldly distractions.
He emphasized that he had supported me so strongly because he had seen potential in my research and in my devotion to it. He believed I could make a critical contribution to the study of capitalism and the political dimensions of economics. The connection between so-called pure economics and fascism that I was unveiling was for him key to unsettling some accepted truths about our economic system.
It was then that I promised him I would persevere. And in times of demotivation, his words are always there to motivate me.
I spent another six years developing my book, The Capital Order. I always wondered whether the final result lived up to his expectations, but luckily, he did seem proud.
It was really thanks to Anwar’s influence and mentorship that I was able to give a sturdy theoretical foundation to the archival research, tracing its roots in the deep tendencies of our economic system. I also wanted the archival research to bolster the systemic analysis, especially of the deeply political forces that shape our economy. More generally, the book is the product of the intellectual milieu of the department Anwar introduced me to. The intellectual stimulation and methodological insights I received, including from colleagues like Duncan Foley, completely transformed it.
I remember the long conversations on the phone with Anwar during the COVID-19 lockdown, in which he meticulously commented on my interpretation of Ralph Hawtrey’s theory of inflation and explained how best to measure rates of exploitation and profit. His comments, often critical, were not easily digestible, and I would take them bit by bit and dissect them with Aditya Singh, my loyal research assistant, who was also Anwar’s student.
Neither the Perfect Nor the Imperfect but the Real
What Anwar has gifted us all is his formidable lens through which to interpret capitalism and challenge the mainstream. He offered a lucidity about the systemic tendencies of our economic system and a holistic approach that, as many, including Vivek Chibber, have already stated, bears comparison with that of Karl Marx himself.
In my years working at the New School, I attended two of Anwar’s graduate courses. I experienced firsthand how he was able to translate the titanic amount of knowledge in his book into effective pedagogical tools.
His story of the chicken pot pie, for example, embodies his capacity to convey the nature of capitalism in an intuitive and lasting way. Once Mary sold her chicken pot pie hobby to a business, it did not matter what was in the pies, which became full of hormone-treated chicken; what mattered was their price. With an image that stuck, Anwar explained the fundamental logic of value as being completely detached from use value, from those qualities that made the chicken pot pie so good.
Anwar delivered, like no one else, the antibodies against bourgeois economics, against those “theories” that only help hide rather than explain. In his book, as in his classes, students learned to wear different lenses through which to look at the economic world. They came to understand the slick capacity of the “perfectionist” and “imperfectionist” approaches to idealize markets, competition, and progress.
Shifting from one framework to another, examining their explanations of inflation, profits, and unemployment and their policy implications, Anwar was able to deliver a scathing critique of both neoclassical (perfectionist) and Keynesian (imperfectionist) economics. He tore down the edifice not just of neoclassical economics but also of its supposed Keynesian alternative with grace and precision. He unmasked how they shared much more than one would think, especially a common backbone of idealization and an urge to get back to perfection, which Keynesians thought state intervention could achieve.
As he put it in his brilliant interview with the Institute for New Economic Thinking: “The notion of imperfection is a dual of perfection; you can’t speak of imperfection unless you are implicitly paying allegiance to perfection, and I do not want to be trapped in that space.” He also recalled something I had felt deeply myself: “When I started as a graduate student, I was surprised to discover that the representation of the world was an idealized fictitious form that makes no sense to me, and that as an economist you had to accept that, then spend your time showing how the world is imperfect.”
That is why his blackboard did not have just these two possibilities: next to the perfectionist and the imperfectionist, there was a third column that had vastly more explanatory power. Anwar was not content with merely modifying the existing framework but spent thirty years rebuilding the foundations of economics from scratch. What he built was revelatory. And it had to start from real observation, from confronting the naked reality of capitalism.
Real economics, he liked to call it: an approach that vindicated and expanded, both theoretically and empirically, the most important intuitions of Adam Smith’s, David Ricardo’s, and especially Marx’s analysis, without calling it Marxist. In this, Anwar was adamant and would not accept compromises. He thought it important to get out of the niche, to avoid the self-sectarianism typical of heterodox economists.
As a matter of fact, he disliked the term “heterodox” for exactly that same reason: identifying yourself as an antithesis to the orthodoxy weakens the capacity of real economics to stand on its own feet and gain hegemony. As he wrote in the introduction to his book: “Its object of investigation is neither the perfect nor the imperfect but the real.”
Profit as the Engine
Anwar’s whole economic edifice rested on one crucial intuition that, paradoxically, the perfectionist and imperfectionist paradigms had disregarded: profit drives all the system’s dynamics; it is the engine of the whole economic system.
The incessant quest for profits drives investment and economic growth. Profit shapes supply (firms produce with the goal of making a profit) and aggregate demand (purchases of inputs, plant, and equipment, and the hiring of workers and their capacity to consume). As he put it concisely in the slides he shared with me: “The profit motive always remains central, and its dominance creates the force field that shapes and channels microeconomic and macroeconomic outcomes. This is the proper meaning of the invisible hand.”
He reappropriated the meaning of Smith’s invisible hand not as a metaphysical myth of the eternal efficiency of the market but as the expression of those profit imperatives that operated through real competition. Through the lens of the profit motive, Anwar drew a few fundamental intuitions.
First, class struggle is at the heart of the system, and technological dynamism is one of its expressions. Modern economic analysis reduces capital to durable wealth and understands profit as a reward for abstinence and entrepreneurial search. Against this, Anwar reminded us that capital had nothing to do with the qualities of the commodity. Instead, it had everything to do with capitalism’s specific historical process — potentially infinite accumulation — and the class strugglethat grounds it.
Indeed, profit mirrors surplus labor, and as he says, the existence of surplus labor is a “social outcome.” He writes: “Surplus product only arises when the length of the working day exceeds the working time to reproduce the standard of living of the employed worker, that is, only when surplus labor is performed.” Technological progress is no proof of the fairy tale that capitalism exists to maximize consumer satisfaction with ever better commodities. To the contrary, firms invest in new technology to squeeze more surplus out of their workers and to cut costs below their rivals’. In real competition, firms that fail to do so don’t survive.
Second, the real rests on a conflictual structure, precisely the one that neoclassical economists seek to erase in favor of a harmonious scheme that persuades us to believe we live in the best of all possible worlds. Far from the “ballet” of perfect competition, it is a war of all against all.
The business literature showcased extremely well how the profit motive played out through real competition. In Anwar’s words, “Firms set prices; they try to survive; some win; some don’t; they use tools to attack each other. Roughly 70 percent of firms die within the first three years.”
As Chibber has pointedly discussed, this theory led Anwar to deconstruct traditional leftist understandings of the dysfunctions of capitalism. Capitalism’s violent outcomes do not stem from monopoly power “corrupting” competition; they arise precisely out of a system working as it should, driven solely by the quest for profit.
Third, crisis is the norm under capitalism, an expression of crucial recurrent patterns or “gravitational tendencies” that emerge out of the very dominance of the profit motive itself. As Anwar put it, “The history of market systems reveals recurrent patterns of booms and busts over centuries, emanating precisely from the developed world.” These include the great depressions of the 1840s, the Long Depression of 1873–1896, the Great Depression of the 1930s, the stagflation crises of the 1970s, and the great global crises of the 2010s. In this long-run perspective, excessive financialization was merely the trigger of the 2008 crash; its underlying cause was a crisis of profitability.
Anwar’s real economic framework can also explain other devastating features of our economic system, including the structural economic plunder of the Global South and permanent warfare as a stimulus to profitability that does not risk subordinating the profit motive to social goals. Such subordination is correctly seen as a threat to the capitalist order and labeled “socialistic.” My work on austerity’s structural role in managing capitalism — by repressing wages and preserving the social relations underpinning profitability — is charged by this theoretical insight. Indeed, it underscores how capitalist governments must find the “right” stimulus policies — those that do not challenge market dependence or the command of private investment.
Turbulent Gravitation
These observations are important to avoid easy misunderstandings. Anwar was not a determinist. The patterns he discovered were important to guide systemic knowledge but did not eliminate agency.
Rather, Anwar developed a multidimensional structure of influence that is at once hierarchical and deeply historical. This is the significance of turbulent gravitation: a relatively small set of operative principles can explain a great variety of economic phenomena, without reducing the dynamics of capitalism to mechanical laws. There are observable patterns in the system — but humans can organize and change the system through political action.
This is the deeply historical and political approach that runs through Anwar’s analysis. He repudiated the bourgeois distinction between, on the one hand, “ahistorical laws” and, on the other, the “contingencies” of history. One must understand that classes, through their historical agency, create the very imperatives upon which they act, even as those imperatives bind them.
This is particularly important when it comes to the “gain-seeking behavior” that defines capitalism as a particular social form. The imperatives of profitability are not simply external laws bearing down on historical actors, nor are they merely the outcome of individual choices. Class relations and competition produce them historically, even as they confront those actors as real constraints that shape their actions. The beauty of Anwar’s economic analysis is that he could identify the underlying regularities of capitalism without abstracting them from the historical relations of class and agency through which actors continually reproduce them.
This also speaks to Anwar’s particular relationship to empirical data. He was emphatically empirical, but not a positivist. His argument was that classical assumptions are consistent with empirical reality.
He understood that data are never innocent. Data are not simply a collection of preexisting facts waiting for an observer. As he writes, “Theory intervenes not merely in the interpretation of events but in their very representation (and occasionally in their suppression, as we know only too well).”
His example of unemployment is particularly telling: the official definition counts someone as employed if they did any work at all for pay or profit. Such a definition masks a much bleaker picture of the realities of unemployment and underemployment as structural features of the system.
Anwar’s historical proclivity, expressed in his attention to social relations, is particularly clear in his passion for Michał Kalecki’s famous 1943 article, “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” which we discussed at length on many occasions. He thought this was one of the most important pieces of political economy ever written, as it clearly stressed one of the strongest Marxian intuitions: capital not only produces unemployment — it fundamentally depends on it.
Keynesian economics, with its utopian delirium of ignoring exploitation, had depoliticized the economy. It failed to realize that its goal — full employment — was technically possible, but that only a fascist dictatorship could achieve it without undermining capitalism. Indeed, only under fascism can you forgo the impersonal discipline of unemployment because political discipline is firmly in place.
I draw heavily on these conversations in my most recent book, Escape From Capitalism. Anwar reviewed it in detail and wrote a final blurb for it: “A book for the times. Mattei takes aim at the notion that the forces which regulate market and social outcomes are socially neutral. Mattei argues that we need to reject this framework, to ‘politicize our lives to participate in the transformation of the material and social reality around us’ at the local and global level.”
Anwar’s approach deeply inspired the book, and I try to bring it to life for a broader, nonacademic audience. I carry forward his conviction that economics is a social science and therefore a historical and political science.
I especially carry forward what I understand to be the fundamental Shaikhian spirit: it is only by explaining how capitalism really works that we can sharpen our tools to overcome it. Indeed, Anwar’s work has inspired generations of young people and won international acclaim.
“Don’t Give It Up”
Anwar was extremely supportive of my embarking on the journey to the University of Tulsa. He gave a brilliant opening lecture at the inaugural conference of the Center for Heterodox Economics there, which I had organized. He remained deeply supportive throughout the turbulent times at the university and when I began setting up the independent Forum for Real Economic Emancipation (FREE).
I helped organize a wonderful retirement celebration for Anwar, which produced a special issue on his work in The New School Economic Review. Afterward Anwar enjoyed his new home at the lake in Amherst, writing, fishing, cooking, and visiting friends like Robert Pollin.
We spoke on the phone often. Anwar had helped create the intellectual ethos of the New School for Social Research Economics Department and had opposed academic hierarchies all his life. He was appalled at the administration’s attacks, like firing tenured and untenured faculty members and blocking PhD admissions, which were effectively dismantling the department.
His recorded words at the retirement party ring true to all of us:
The important thing about democracy is that you have a voice. It does not mean you have to agree with me. You have to have a voice, and you constantly need to protect it, and you have to act on it. Look around you — no department anywhere has this kind of voice. So don’t give it up. No matter what they do. They are going to try to make you give it up. Don’t give it up. Go and strike if you have to. Close the place down.
Carrying the Work Forward
Iremember the shock of that phone call in which he told me he had cancer. I pretended it wasn’t real: his voice was so combative that it seemed impossible that anything could beat him. To the very end, as he heroically fought his devastating illness, he remained focused on his scholarship and on the possibility of delivering an abbreviated version of his masterpiece, updated with new empirical data.
Anwar’s archives at Bard College reveal letters that Joan Robinson and Nicholas Kaldor wrote to him in the 1970s, already recognizing the power of his work. Fortunately, Anwar leaves behind a considerable number of students, now spread across the world. A recent piece by Nikos Chatzarakis perfectly exemplifies their power to speak of his breakthroughs. As his former student Juan Santarcángelo, now a professor in Argentina, has forcefully put it, “Anwar will never truly die; he will live on in each of us and in those who were lucky enough to know him.”
It is our task to carry his paradigm forward, advance it, and spread it widely, publishing and making his work available in many different forms. This is something to which I intend to devote considerable energy in the coming years.
Anwar was one of the most powerful thinkers of our time. His legacy finds an especially important place in this historical moment, when the violence of capitalism is rampant and the thirst for radical political change so strong. The massive archive that his youngest student, Nicholas Anderson, has digitized, now held at Bard College, is a treasure that we need to cultivate and explore in detail.
It is Anwar’s real economics, and its potential for full emancipation, that we need to keep alive as a guide to collective action and the possibility of change. This is what we are trying to do at FREE, an assembly-based project for empowering education and concrete postcapitalist alternatives that is spreading globally. I hope many more people will join us in this collective endeavor for a humane, profit-liberated future.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump's Made-for-TV Cabinet
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump’s Made-for-TV Cabinet
The secretary of transportation was a reality-TV “star” and a Fox Business cable host. But when the American aviation system was grounded, he lost it.
Twenty years ago, Sean Duffy was a washed-up reality-TV personality competing in lumberjack contests and making ends meet as a small-town district attorney in northern Wisconsin. Then, the 2010 Tea Party election wave swept him into Congress. But Duffy wasn’t exactly satisfied with the new gig. He grumbled about the pay—$174,000 annually—and, in 2019, he quit to become a lobbyist and the cohost of a cable show on the Fox Business channel.
This turned out to be an unexpectedly shrewd choice. Duffy was glib, good-looking, and on cable news, and that was enough to convince Donald Trump—who, as we all know, thinks that being glib, good-looking, and on cable news automatically qualifies you to run essential sections of the federal government—to nominate the Wisconsinite as the nation’s 20th secretary of transportation. Unfortunately, like so many of the score of Fox hosts who have gotten Trump administration gigs as cabinet secretaries, czars, ambassadors, and Justice Department hangers-on, Duffy was woefully unprepared to do the job.
That was abundantly clear last Friday, when Duffy was called upon to explain the FAA’s decision to bring the nation’s aviation system to a halt. In the same week that another Fox alum, “War Secretary” Pete Hegseth, narrowly escaped impeachment, Duffy was thrust into the limelight as a bumbling sidekick for Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, himself a former mixed martial arts prizefighter. At a moment of national anxiety, Duffy defaulted to the talking-head formula, which imagines that any crisis—no matter how serious—can be addressed with a word salad of implication, insinuation and invective.
Duffy’s performance was so miserable that it provoked an immediate demand for his removal from New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who called to mind the cabinet secretary’s former career as a “star” of MTV’s The Real World: Boston and his recently launched reality travel series The Great American Road Trip. “Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency,” said Hochul, adding, “From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch.” Richard Clarke, a former counterterrorism official in Republican administrations, labeled Duffy and Mullin’s double act “perhaps the worst crisis communications press conference I’ve ever seen.”
Facing questions about whether the grounding of 14,000 flights and the disruption of travel plans for millions of Americans might have resulted from software problems, cyberattacks, or rogue AI agents, Mullin mused about how “you just can’t rule out anything at this point” and complimented his absent boss. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” he declared. “He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead.”
That pronouncement provoked major head-scratching when Mullin turned the microphone over to Duffy, whose performance reminded everyone that “the leadership of President Trump” involves installing Fox hosts in positions where they inevitably get in over their talking heads. In no time, they are mismanaging wars and national emergencies with the sort of deer-in-the-headlights desperation that inspires confusion rather than confidence.
On Friday, and then again in a follow-up press conference on Saturday, Duffy made excuses, muddled explanations, and griped about how he didn’t have enough money to do his job—even though he’s a Republican cabinet member in a Republican administration with perhaps the most subservient Republican Congress in US history at his disposal.
On this weekend’s Saturday Night Live, “Weekend Update” anchor Colin Jost reflected on how “the FAA suddenly and mysteriously grounded all US flights yesterday” and then—barely containing his laughter—explained, “The scary thing by far about all these flights getting grounded was the messaging from the normally dependable Trump administration. First, they said it was a telecommunications outage as of now. Why add ‘as of now’? No one wants to hear, ‘Your child is safe—as of now.’ Then Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the whole situation was the result of a contractor upgrading copper wire to fiber optic cable. So, one guy switched out one wire and took out all planes? I think that’s literally a scene from the movie Airplane!”
Just as jarring was Duffy’s wild-eyed ranting about how Congress was not providing sufficient funding to upgrade communications systems and airports. During the Friday night press briefing, Duffy repeatedly demanded $50 billion in new money—even though he had a hard time explaining precisely what he’d done with the $12.5 billion his department got last year for air traffic control improvements, and even though Duffy had been asking just a day earlier for a mere $30.1 billion for aviation upgrades.
Instead of making a compelling case for necessary infrastructure investment, Duffy appeared to be grabbing numbers out of the sky. CNN headlined a report: “Messaging failures worsened the air traffic freeze and sowed distrust in government.” When Duffy attempted to hold another briefing on Saturday, microphone feedback created such a mess that the Irish Star newspaper declared, “Sean Duffy forced to halt ‘clown show’ press conference due to technical glitch.”
On a more serious note, newly elected US Representative Fred Wellman (D-MO) announced, “I’m calling for a full investigation of this failure and the resignation of Secretary Duffy. We will find out the damage that his incompetent leadership has done to our air traffic system. Instead of filming reality TV shows he should have been ensuring the safety of Americans.”
The calls for accountability will keep coming. No one seriously doubts that America has underfunded infrastructure projects that must be addressed—on the ground and in the air. But everyone who is serious about these issues is entertaining fresh doubts about whether Sean Duffy’s TV experience has prepared him for this reality.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: ‘Aboriginal people were the backbone of this state’: rediscovered photographs reveal life inside the 1946 Pilbara strike camps
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Rosamund Brennan
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Troy Eaton lives in Pippingarra, near Port Hedland, where the Pilbara’s multibillion-dollar mining industry looms large. “It’s a mecca of mining,” says the Nyamal man. But his family’s mining history stretches back long before the arrival of today’s resources giants.
In September, Eaton took the long drive from Pippingarra to Perth to see some of those early pioneers: his ancestors, who established their own mining ventures in the Pilbara some 80 years ago.
On the walls of Lawrence Wilson Art Gallery at the University of Western Australia (UWA), he saw colour photographs of women sifting minerals with shallow tin yandies, and men wielding picks and shovels beneath vast blue skies. Among them were his grandmother, Kakaya Lucy Mitchell, his great-grandmother and other relatives, captured in photographs he had never seen. “It’s a bit emotional … just reminiscing on what it was like in their time,” he says.
“They look healthy. They look happy. There was a sense of pride looking at it, because they was doing something that they could never believe, most probably in their lifetime – taking control of their own destiny.”
The photographs feature in Strike Camps: The Photographs of John Wilson, an exhibition documenting the independent mining communities established after the 1946 Pilbara strike, when about 800 Aboriginal workers walked off pastoral stations over appalling conditions and meagre wages. Many were paid only in rations of tea, flour, sugar and tobacco.
The walk-off soon became more than a labour dispute. Hundreds of workers established camps near Port Hedland and Marble Bar, building spinifex shelters and setting up schools. Over the following years, they supported themselves by mining tin, beryl and other minerals, as well as pearl shelling and collecting buffel grass seed.
The camps offered them a measure of freedom from pastoralists’ control and the chance to raise families on their own terms. In 1952, their mining company, Northern Development and Mining, produced minerals worth £70,000.
The anthropologist John Wilson photographed the camps in the late 1950s and early 1960s, conducting fieldwork alongside his wife and fellow anthropologist, Katrin. Both have since died, and this year their daughter Bu unearthed a cache of slides beneath a wardrobe in the family’s Fremantle home, helping reunite an archive of some 350 colour images.
The UWA art historian Darren Jorgensen, who co-curated the exhibition, had spent years searching for Wilson’s photographs. They form what he calls “the most substantial collection of pictures” of the camps, documenting Aboriginal self-determination 20 years before the Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill, the 1966 strike that became a turning point in Australia’s land rights movement.
Jorgensen believes the Pilbara strike remains less well known partly because it lacked a defining image, unlike Wave Hill’s famous photograph of Gough Whitlam pouring soil into Vincent Lingiari’s hand. Yet the communities Wilson photographed had achieved something remarkable: at a time when Aboriginal people in Western Australia were still denied the vote and subjected to discriminatory laws, “they were making international mining deals and shipping off barrels of columbite to Singapore”, he says.
Alongside 35 photographs, the exhibition features two short films that use generative AI to animate scenes of work and everyday life in the Pilbara camps. Created by the exhibition co-curator and UWA fine arts head, Vladimir Todorović, the films were developed in consultation with descendants of the strikers.
The strike itself was carefully orchestrated. As early as March 1945, more than a year before the walk-off, Nyamal organiser Clancy McKenna and Nyangumarta lawman Dooley Binbin travelled between remote pastoral stations, distributing makeshift calendars drawn on food packaging, including jam-tin labels, so workers could count down to the planned walk-off on 1 May. With the help of white prospector Don McLeod, they coordinated a strike that spread across more than 20 stations and some 10,000 sq km. Both Aboriginal leaders were jailed, but the strike gathered strength.
The walk-off lasted three years, making it the longest recorded strike in Australian history. But the workers’ right to remain in their camps was contested. In 1949, when authorities ordered families to dismantle their homes at Twelve Mile near Port Hedland, the strikers protested in writing, warning that the closure could reignite the dispute. The government subsequently withdrew the order. The strike ended that year with improved pay and conditions at two stations but unfulfilled promises of wider reform. Some returned to work on sheep and cattle stations; others stayed in the communities they had built, which endured for decades.
Eaton’s grandfather Putangaja Ernie Mitchell became a key leader, coordinating mining operations and negotiating with government officials. Mitchell’s daughter Doris, who also attended the exhibition opening, remembers growing up in the camps, where children sifted ore and traded tins of minerals for lollies. Welfare authorities once labelled her a “neglected child”. “But I wasn’t neglected,” she says. “As children, we grew up with many parents.”
Yet even within the mining cooperatives, control remained contested. In 1959, Mitchell and fellow leader Peter Kangkushot Coppin broke with McLeod amid disagreements over how earnings were used, with workers receiving rations rather than cash. Wilson photographed a meeting as the movement split. “They didn’t get any money in their hands,” Doris recalls.
Mitchell and Coppin continued the mining cooperative known as Pindan, while McLeod’s supporters formed another, Nomads. Both groups went on to establish pastoral enterprises: Pindan’s successors at Yandeyarra and Nomads at Strelley, where an independent Aboriginal school established in 1976 still operates today.
One of the last surviving strikers, Nyamal elder Captain Mudjawariny Wilson, is now in his 90s and living in aged care in Roebourne. His daughter Ursula, an exhibition co-curator, brought him to Perth for the exhibition’s opening, where he recognised himself working as a young man in the photographs. “When I first looked at the pictures, I stood there and had tears in my eyes,” Ursula recalls.
For Eaton, the photographs tell a story too often overlooked. “We always hear doom and gloom stories, but we don’t hear any great stories like this,” he says. This year, he notes, Rio Tinto celebrated 60 years of Pilbara operations; his ancestors were mining there decades earlier. “Aboriginal people were actually the backbone of this state.”
Eighty years after the strike began, Eaton is working to establish an Aboriginal-owned mining venture in the Pilbara, pursuing the same independence his grandfather’s generation fought for.
“I need to finish that journey,” he says. “Because my grandfather and those guys started it back then, right? And that journey continues to this day.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: 'It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person': Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.
It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.
“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Not
many gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.
Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”
Informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.
Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.
Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”
As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”
The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?
Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.
And the most recent?
A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.
If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?
I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.
Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?
My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.
What do you recommend doing outside the fair?
November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.
What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?
Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.
What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?
The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/flavio-bolso.title: The Scandal of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Escape Won’t Fade Away
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/flavio-bolso.author: Felipe Antunes de Oliveira
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/flavio-bolso.text:
The Scandal of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Escape Won’t Fade Away
Shortly after losing the Brazilian presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro fled the country with help from a Trump operative and a former Mossad agent. The newly elected US Congress needs to investigate Washington’s role in this shady exfiltration job.
To exfiltrate means “to smuggle [an intelligence agent, soldier, etc.] out of an area under enemy control.” The term belongs to military jargon, rather than to political commentary. Nevertheless, the Brazilian media has been using it to describe the sudden removal of former presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro from Brazil’s territory a couple of days after he lost the second round of this year’s presidential elections.
José Roberto de Toledo, a veteran journalist, was probably the first to use the word “exfiltration” in relation to Flávio Bolsonaro, in his influential weekly podcast. The circumstances of Bolsonaro’s escape seem to come directly out of a spy film. Smuggled in the middle of the night across the border with the active participation of a former Mossad agent and US government officials, he reappeared in Florida and pledged to take the details of his escape to his grave.
An exfiltration is not an act of political sympathy. It is an extremely risky operation to preserve an asset from being captured by the enemy. On the one hand, the exfiltrated asset enjoys safety when he finally reaches his destination; on the other, the exfiltration makes all masks fall, and the fugitive’s true allegiances become transparent.
For that reason, if Flávio Bolsonaro was indeed exfiltrated to the United States, this episode should figure side by side with the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as a blatant example of US neo-imperialism in Latin America. The political and legal responsibilities for this case cannot be brushed under the carpet of history and will certainly come back to haunt Brazil-US relations for decades to come.
A Very Suspicious Escape
The details of Flávio Bolsonaro’s escape from Brazil are not entirely known. So far, The New York Times has reported that Jason Miller, a White House operative, arranged the luxury private jet that Bolsonaro and his family used (at the cost of almost one million reais, paid for by an American corporate account).
The party crossed the border with Argentina through means that are not yet entirely clear, most likely by land, on the night of Tuesday, October 27, near Foz do Iguaçu. Brazil’s top Sunday night TV news show, Fantástico, revealed that a former Israeli intelligence operative accompanied the fleeing Bolsonaro family. From the Argentinian border location of Puerto Iguazú, the disgraced former presidential candidate took a private jet to the United States, stopping in Ecuador for refueling and avoiding Brazilian airspace.
Arriving in the US, Flávio Bolsonaro landed at the infamous Miami–Opa Locka Executive Airport, used six decades earlier to prepare for the US-supported Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba, one of the worst historical examples of direct US imperial aggression in Latin America. Upon arrival, despite presenting his canceled diplomatic passport, Bolsonaro received “parole status” and was escorted by a motorcade to an undisclosed location.
Who Takes Responsibility?
Donald Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was quick to deflect responsibility. “We didn’t facilitate anything,”claimed Rubio in a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting a few days after the fact. He knew that confessing the exfiltration would mean exposing the State Department to serious internal and international reckoning.
Flávio Bolsonaro himself told The New York Times he would take the details of his fleeing “to the grave.” In an open letterreleased after his arrival in the United States, he compared himself to figures like José Martí and Charles de Gaulle and denounced the election result. He also thanked Argentine President Javier Milei “for his courage, sense of justice, and legality” and expressed his gratitude to Trump “and the wonderful American people” for hosting him.
By fleeing Brazilian justice, Flávio Bolsonaro has secured protection, at least for now, from having to answer for his alleged crimes in two different investigations. More important, as long as he is safe in the United States, it becomes more difficult for Brazilian investigators to prove the precise nature of his ties to Washington.
He is not the first person to have claimed US protection in suspicious circumstances. His younger brother Eduardo has been agitating from Texas for the Trump administration to impose sanctions against his own country, while the former head of the Brazilian intelligence agency under Jair Bolsonaro is also on US soil, having dodged immigration enforcement under very mysterious circumstances.
However, Trump and Rubio cannot shield Flávio Bolsonaro from justice and history indefinitely. It took decades for Washington’s involvement in military coups across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s to be proven with overwhelming evidence. A comprehensive apology is yet to materialize.
Hopefully, we will not need to wait that long this time. A newly elected Democratic-controlled Congress should hold US officials accountable for any interference in the Brazilian democratic process. It should clarify whether US taxpayers’ money was used to facilitate Bolsonaro’s escape from justice and whether he promised his eventual US handlers any specific information or advantages, beyond his public pledges to give the US preferred access to Brazilian rare earths.
In due course, Flávio Bolsonaro must be extradited, and cables and intelligence documents pertaining to this case should be declassified, so that the Brazilian and American people can finally learn what really happened on the night of October 27.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum extend loan of Asante regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Ghana
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.
The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.
“The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” says Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.
The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.
The gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.
“The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.
The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trujillo-dic.title: The Dominican Government Uses Zionism to Whitewash Trujillo
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trujillo-dic.author: Simón Rodríguez
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trujillo-dic.text:
The Dominican Government Uses Zionism to Whitewash Trujillo
The Trujillo dictatorship was obsessed with “whitening” the Dominican Republic. But despite its record suppressing Afro-descendants, today’s Dominican government paints Trujillo as a fighter against discrimination because of his solidarity with Israel.
On August 24, the Dominican government announced its adherence to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) definition of antisemitism. President Luis Abinader, a businessman of Lebanese descent, made the announcement at the opening ceremony of the Sixth Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism,held in Santo Domingo by the US-based Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM). Abinader also promised to invest 50 million pesos (approximately US$852,000) in the construction of a Jewish museum in Sosúa, in the north of the country, where 747 European Jewish refugees settled during the 1940s.
The foreign ministry statement announcing Abinader’s decision included a defense of the Trujillo dictatorship (1930–1961) as a supposed opponent of discrimination, hatred, and religious intolerance. Rafael Trujillo, whose dictatorship was fanatically racist, perpetrated a genocide against the Haitian population along the Dominican border between late 1937 and early 1938 and was obsessed with “whitening” the Dominican Republic, whose overwhelming majority was and continues to be of African descent. The government’s invocation of Trujillo’s legacy is key to understanding its real motivation in pledging allegiance to the IHRA definition of antisemitism.
The Dominican government is an unconditional ally of Israel’s apartheid regime. One of its first measures upon coming to power was a statement in 2020 in favor of establishing the Dominican embassy in Jerusalem. In 2023, the Santo Domingo International Book Fair had the Israeli embassy as guest of honor. An agreement with Mekorot, Israel’s state-owned water company, to design a national water management plan was signed, and there is also Israeli cooperation with the Dominican office for the technification of irrigation. President Abinader has drawn inspiration from the Israeli wall system that encloses Gaza and Palestinian communities in the West Bank for his own border wall with Haiti, and he has relied on the purchase of Israeli weapons to drive the largest arms buildup in the country since the Trujillo dictatorship. The government also relies on Israeli technologies for internal repression, having used Pegasus spyware against a journalist who was investigating corruption.
The current Dominican government’s claim to oppose discrimination runs counter to all evidence. It has refused to introduce legislation against hate crimes and incitement to racial or religious hatred. The Penal Code, which took effect in August 2026, defines the crime of discrimination but effectively eliminates any penalty for discriminatory actions justified on religious grounds or in which the legitimate exercise of a legal authority is invoked, which amounts to the legalization of discrimination. The 1943 law banning the Vodou religion, enacted by Trujillo, remains in effect and is used to persecute Afro-Dominicans and Haitians. Meanwhile, a 1962 law prohibiting the glorification of Trujillo and Trujilloism is not enforced. Neofascist paramilitary groups that praise Trujillo, Benito Mussolini, and Adolf Hitler operate openly and collaborate with the police to repress the Left and Haitian communities.
In this context, Abinader, like Trujillo, claims to oppose antisemitism in order to whitewash and further his own racist agenda.
In Service of Genocide
CAM, which promoted the Dominican adoption of the IHRA working definition of antisemitism, is linked to the Israeli foreign ministry. Both its CEO, Sacha Roytman-Dratwa, and its editor in chief, Barney Breen-Portnoy, have worked in communications for the Israel Defense Forces. Senior Israeli officials, such as the country’s current president, Isaac Herzog, have served on its advisory board. The organization has promoted the criminalization of the slogan “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free,” following the example of the Austrian government in 2023. The Jewish Council of Australia has considered CAM’s summits on antisemitism to be part of an effort to silence criticism of Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people by equating it with antisemitism.
In its statements, CAM has defended Israel’s military actions in Gaza, describing them as an exercise in self-defense. Conversely, the International Association of Genocide Scholars has described Israel’s actions and policies in Gaza as crimes against humanity and war crimes and has stated that they meet the legal definition of genocide.
Among the organizations that initially affiliated with CAM was the Clarion Project, an anti-Islam lobby that has been classified by the Southern Poverty Law Center as a hate group.
For the Dominican government, hosting a CAM event and adhering to the IHRA definition serves four main purposes: it reaffirms its political subservience to US foreign policy, contributes to whitewashing the image of its ally Israel, portrays the Dominican regime as opposed to discrimination, and attempts to rewrite history to present the Trujillo dictatorship as the initiator of an alleged antidiscrimination policy upheld today by Abinader. There is indeed continuity between the Trujillo dictatorship and the current regime, but in a different sense.
One Hand Washes the Other
The statement from the Dominican foreign ministry announcing the adoption of the IHRA definition of antisemitism asserts that “the Dominican Republic underscores its ongoing commitment to the fight against all forms of hatred, discrimination, and religious intolerance, a position it has consistently maintained since 1938, when the Dominican state was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees.” The Dominican government goes on to urge all governments to take measures to “prevent hatred, intolerance, and discrimination in all their manifestations.” These are curious statements in light of Dominican history, not least the last six years of rule by Abinader’s right-wing Modern Revolutionary Party.
That the Dominican government considers itself the heir to the Trujillo legacy is an important admission. President Abinader, named in the Pandora Papers leaks for having offshore accounts, has also admitted to sharing the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, who ruled the country with an iron fist from 1966 to 1978 and before that was one of the main ideologues and officials of the Trujillo regime. Since 2021, Abinader has been enforcing an undeclared state of exception to carry out mass deportations of Haitians, including the systematic use of arbitrary detentions based on racial profiling, raids without warrants, and militarization of hospitals and their use as immigration detention centers, as well as widespread violence by migration agents, including murders, torture, forced disappearances, and sexual violence.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Chuck Schumer Is Yesterday’s Man
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Chuck Schumer Is Yesterday’s Man
The Senate Democratic leader just keeps showing why he needs to be replaced.
If you want to ruin a boisterous celebration, just hand over a microphone to Chuck Schumer. The Senate Democratic leader is the ultimate buzzkill, adept at deploying a droning voice that can turn giddy jubilation into existential dread.
November 3 was one of the happiest nights Democrats have known in decades, as the sheer size of the party’s victory in the midterm elections became apparent. After a decade of Trump dominating public life as standard-bearer of the Republican Party, here at last was proof that the public, even in red states such as Texas and South Carolina, were fed up. Beaten down as they were by frustration at the GOP pushing a hard-right agenda, Democrats could finally entertain the hopes of a better future.
But the brief remarks Schumer delivered that night were a reminder that Trump and the Republicans were only part of the problem the country faces. There’s also the disheartening fact that the Democrats are led by political dinosaurs who have no understanding of the urgency of the current moment.
Schumer is now facing a challenge for the post of Senate majority leader from Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen. Schumer’s election night speech offers clear evidence as to why Van Hollen deserves to win.
Schumer started with a question: “How did he win?” His answer: “First and foremost, we focused on American families and their pain and their needs, their suffering. They are not having a good life, and they are worried about the future for themselves and their children.” Schumer summed up the election as being about three issues: costs, chaos, and corruption.
What’s notable among this vague litany of complaints are all the issues left out that produced heated debate and no shortage of voter anger: the Iran War and its role in destabilizing the world economy, US support of Israel as a factor in the war, the rise of AI and data centers, and the outsize roles of tech plutocrats like Elon Musk in corrupting the political system.
Schumer expressed surprise that the Republicans “embraced Trump” and “followed Trump over the cliff as some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs.” For most people, talking about “extraneous things” would not make the list of Trump’s thousand worst offenses, so it was puzzling why Schumer felt it necessary to highlight in a short victory speech.
Schumer ended his peroration with a puzzling metaphor: “The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.” As commentators such as Jon Stewart and Sam Seder pointed out, these words were more likely to generate confusion than inspiration. What exactly is the “red brick wall”? Further, walls are usually reduced to rubble, not a pile of bricks. If the bricks still exist, then the red wall can be rebuilt.
Seder rightly noted the absurdity of Schumer’s amazement at congressional Republicans’ loyalty to Trump, given that anyone who has been sentient for the last decade should have noticed that Trump easily won the GOP presidential nomination three times in a row and turned the party into his personal cult. There are few facts more obvious in American public life than that the Republican Party is completely subservient to Trump. But it’s a fact that Schumer still has a hard time accepting or acknowledging.
Partly, this is because Schumer is deeply committed to ancien régime restoration. He still seems to see Trump as a regrettable anomaly who will one day disappear and allow those most mythical creatures, the “reasonable Republicans,” to return. In this worldview, Democrats such as Schumer have to keep signaling they are ready to work with Republicans in order to hasten the return of normal politics. This is why Schumer can only talk about politics in the most abstract of terms (costs, chaos, and corruption) rather than specifying real areas of disagreement.
Schumer has been quite candid about this strategy. In March 2025, he caved in to Republicans during budget negotiations, making concessions that angered his fellow Democrats. Explaining his thinking in an interview with The New York Times, Schumer said his goal was to wait till Trump’s approval ratings have dropped below 40 percent:
And when he went below 40 percent in the polls, the Republican legislators started working with us. He was at 51. He’s now at 48. We’re gonna keep at it until he goes below 40. Look, I talk to a lot of these Republican legislators. I’ve worked with them. Some of them are Trump devotees. But many of them don’t like him, don’t respect him and worry about what he’s doing to our country. Right now he’s so popular they can’t resist him. I mean, so many of them came to me and said: “I don’t think Hegseth should be defense secretary or R.F.K. should be H.H.S. But Trump wants him. He won.” The Republicans would like to have some freedom from Trump, but they won’t until we bring him down in popularity. That happened with Bush in 2005. It happened with Trump in 2017. When it happens, I am hopeful that our Republican colleagues will resume working with us. And I talk to them. One of the places is in the gym. When you’re on that bike in your shorts, panting away next to a Republican, a lot of the inhibitions come off.
This theory of latent Republican moderation rests on nothing more than locker-room conviviality—hardly the basis for a meaningful political agenda. We will now have an empirical test to see if Schumer’s theory is correct. Trump’s approval ratings went below 40 percent in April and have generally stayed well under that threshold. The Republicans suffered a wipeout in the midterms. Yet there is no evidence that the GOP is moderating. In the wake of the midterm trouncing, House Republicans picked Jim Jordan, a hard-right Trump loyalist, as their new leader. The House held a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who brought the motion to the floor, was the only Republican to vote for it. That near-total GOP opposition, and the fact that 11 Democrats failed to show up for the vote, was enough to kill the effort. Massie himself had been defeated earlier this year in the Republican primary and is leaving Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Like many centrists, Schumer fashions himself as a realist. In truth, he’s a fantasist whose theory of politics rests on a world that no longer exists, if it ever did.
Beyond his fetishization of bipartisanship, Schumer’s substantive political commitments are also out of tune with the current urgent moment in politics. In an interview with The Nation, Senator Bernie Sanders listed three areas where Schumer is out of touch: Israel/Palestine, taxing the wealthy, and AI. Sanders described Schumer as someone who “a guy who wants to tinker around the edges” rather than fight for systematic change. In other words, Schumer is yesterday’s man, which is reason enough to support Chris Van Hollen as a replacement.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many new sides to his works
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
There is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a new and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.
But we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.
Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.
The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).
Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.
Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.
Some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” says Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.
Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, says Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.
The London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory says has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects new research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.
Arnolfini not Arnolfini?
Just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.
The Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory says the diminutive roster is, in fact, the big attraction.
“There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory says. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.
• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.
Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.
Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely new one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.
Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.
Multiple Arnolfini portraits
Kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.
Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.
Other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-
Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he says. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.
The implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.
The exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.
“I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens says of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).
Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, says Martens).
Beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert says: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”
