https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Scott Reyburn
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?
“It’s important to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.
The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.
On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.
Of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).
The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.
That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.
The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?
Luxury playground?
“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.
The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.
But maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.
Tax breaks
Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.
The ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.
Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.
Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?
Young people priced out
Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?
The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a New York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.)
“It is important for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”
The main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always
Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.
In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.
Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.
After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Want to Upend “Citizens United”?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Moore
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Want to Upend Citizens United?
Check out the Montana Plan.
Want to Upend “Citizens United”?
Check out the Montana Plan.
On November 3, two-thirds of Montana voters approved a measure that strips corporations of the power to spend money on elections, striking a blow against corporate political cash in a state that went for Donald Trump by 20 points in 2024.
Initiative 194, known as the “Montana Plan,” is a first-of-its-kind ballot measure that rewrites state law so that “artificial persons”—such as corporations, nonprofits, unions, and trade associations—are no longer allowed to spend on candidates, PACs, or ballot measures. Advocates hail the plan as a novel legal strategy to bar corporate and dark money from influencing elections, and say that versions are being pursued in more than 30 states.
The measure passed by 66 to 34 percent, making Montana the second state, after Hawaii, to use its power over corporate charters to sidestep the US Supreme Court’s 2010 decision in Citizens United v. FEC. The ruling, which held that the First Amendment prohibits the government from restricting independent political spending by corporations and unions, relied on the claim that spending not coordinated with a candidate cannot corrupt; now candidates are permitted by the Federal Election Commission to raise money for their allied super PACs, and in practice frequently coordinate with them. Over 465,000 Montana voters voted on the initiative, which was greeted with a lawsuit from the Montana Republican Party and conservative groups on election night, before the race was called.
The initiative’s approval came as the 2026 elections smashed spending records. AdImpact tallied $11.9 billion in media spending nationwide, making this the most expensive election on record for political advertising. Outside spending on federal races, by groups like super PACs that pay for things like ads and mailers, was projected by OpenSecrets to reach $3.9 billion, a record for a midterm. The nonprofit also calculated that dark money flowing into federal races surpassed $1.5 billion, more than in the 2024 presidential cycle.
Voters this year noticed. An AP poll of midterm voters found that government corruption was the factor most mentioned in the survey as “crucial” in their choice for Congress, followed by the cost of living. More than half of midterm voters pointed to corruption as a main concern in the poll, conducted by the nonpartisan SSRS.
The Montana Plan redefines the powers the state grants to artificial persons, like corporations and nonprofits, to no longer include spending in elections—harnessing the legal distinction between constitutional rights and charter powers that are issued by states. Rather than restricting corporate speech rights, which Citizens United protects, the statutory Initiative 194 changes Montana’s code so that the state no longer grants artificial persons the power to spend on politics. Corporations and covered entities would no longer be allowed to contribute to any candidate, political party, or political committee in an election in Montana, including state and local ballot initiatives. Backers say that corporations remain free to advocate for candidates without giving money.
The measure applies to companies chartered in the state as well as out-of-state companies and nonprofits, so a Delaware corporation or a Washington, DC, nonprofit will be barred from unloading cash in a Montana election. Political committees, including super PACs, can still spend in the state, and individuals can still give to them—but corporations, nonprofits, and other artificial persons can no longer contribute to those committees. The new law does not apply to individuals, government bodies, or the distribution of news or commentary, unless the outlet is controlled by a party, PAC, or candidate.
A company, nonprofit, union, or other group found to be in violation would forfeit its charter privileges, including limited liability, and would be required to pay back its spending, regardless of whether it won or lost in the contest. The legal theory behind the plan, dubbed the Corporate Power Reset, was developed by Tom Moore, senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, who compiled a tracker of ballot initiatives and state bills introduced or being considered. Montana supporters say that once the law is in effect, disclosures listing the donors behind spending groups in the state will be names of real people, not corporations or dark-money groups.
The law is set to take effect on January 1, 2027, and legal challenges are underway that could be bound for the US Supreme Court, where the case would pit long-standing legal precedent for states’ authority to define corporate powers against the ruling in Citizens United. The Montana lawsuit, filed by the Institute for Free Speech on behalf of the state GOP and conservative groups, argues that the law violates the First Amendment by barring them from spending to communicate about candidates and ballot measures.
The nonprofit behind the initiative, the Transparent Election Initiative (TEI), says it anticipated the legal challenge and is prepared to defend the plan while helping other states advance their own versions.
“What I’ve been saying to folks for two years now is, there is a solution,” said Jeff Mangan, a former state legislator and Montana commissioner of political practices who is TEI’s founder and president, of the flood of corporate and dark money in elections.
“I started at the beginning of 2025, doing a listening session across the state, just asking folks about how they felt about money in politics, and if they’re ready for a change,” Mangan said. “I always led with the same question: Do you believe there’s too much money in politics? Everyone said yes.”
Since Citizens United, he said, people had been told that “there’s nothing you can do unless you have an amendment to the Constitution or the Supreme Court overturns it.” When he outlined the plan building on the state’s authority over corporations “to change the way corporations spend in elections, which will affect dark money and the amount of money going into our politics,” he said, “people got excited about it and wanted to collect signatures.”
TEI’s all-volunteer signature drive collected more than 50,000 signatures from all 56 Montana counties, above the 30,121 valid signatures required, with more than 600 volunteers helping the initiative qualify for the ballot. Mangan said TEI aimed to show the measure could make the ballot without the paid signature gatherers that have become commonplace for campaigns.
He pointed to the surge of corporate money this cycle. “The amount of money this year alone is staggering,” he said. Public Citizen recently found that 40 percent of the $1.8 billion that corporations have spent since the Citizens United ruling came in the 2026 midterms. The scale of the spending was inescapable, Mangan said, in recent Montana races like the 2024 Senate contest between Democrat Jon Tester and now-Senator Tim Sheehy, which set a national record for per-voter spending. He points out that billionaires are free to form PACs, just with their names attached. “They choose to spend anonymously through C4s or keep it dark for a reason,” he said, referring to 501(c)4 nonprofits.
A 2018 documentary about secret spending in Montana politics, Dark Money, was a regular feature of the signature drive. TEI showed the movie about a dozen times around the state, Mangan said, including a screening in Helena with remarks from the filmmaker, Kimberly Reed, who is from there.
Volunteers from other groups joined to put the Montana Plan in front of voters. The League of Women Voters of Montana’s members gathered signatures and hosted voter education events around the state, said Bonnie Lorenzen, the group’s president.
“The League of Women Voters of Montana chose early on to endorse the Montana Plan because it aligned perfectly with the League’s goal to ensure that our government serves the people, not wealthy special interests,” Lorenzen told The Nation. “We believe this is best attained by promoting transparency in government and eliminating dark money, which is what the Montana Plan aims to do.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
“Our elected officials need to be responsive to their constituents who elect them, not to corporate entities financing their campaigns,” Lorenzen said.
Former Republican governor Marc Racicot endorsed the Montana Plan, calling it “a brilliant idea,” along with Tester and Gary Buchanan, a former independent candidate for Congress. Groups applauding the plan included the cross-partisan Issue One, Free Speech for People, and Craig Holman, government affairs lobbyist for Public Citizen. Opposition to the ballot initiative came from groups including the Montana Chamber of Commerce, the Montana Mining Association, and the Montana Petroleum Association, as well as the state GOP. In April, the Montana Supreme Court unanimously dismissed a challenge from business groups that would have barred I-194 from the ballot, ruling that citizens have a right to go through the initiative process.
In May, Hawaii became the first state to enact a law based on the Corporate Power Reset framework, when Act 11, passed with near-unanimous support in the state House and Senate, was signed by Governor Josh Green. The law takes effect July 1, 2027, though it faces two federal lawsuits: one from the free-market think tank Grassroot Institute of Hawaii, and a second from the massive dark-money lobby the US Chamber of Commerce.
Bills based on the Corporate Power Reset were introduced in nearly 20 states this year, after New York was the first to introduce the legislation in late 2025. The New York Assembly bill was sponsored by Assemblyman Micah Lasher, now a US representative-elect, and the Senate bill by Senator Kristen Gonzalez; both bills were left in committee.
“We’ve always said it has to be a local solution, it has to be a state-by-state solution,” Mangan said of others seeking to pass the plan, whether through ballot initiatives or state legislatures. The measure’s spread across the map, he said, shows it has been “embraced by folks across the political spectrum.” After the plan’s resounding passage in Montana, he sees people thinking, “Oh, we can actually do something, rather than just saying we can do something.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Yayoi Kusama sets $15m record as Sotheby’s opens New York mega-sales
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a new auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.
Kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a new auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).
The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.
Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.
Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.
One of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.
Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.
The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.
The top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.
It was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.
Not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.
After the sale, Sotheby’s said works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.
“When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, said following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—says it all.”
On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-domestic-.title: Opinion: Domestic Violence is a Key Driver of Homelessness for NYC Families
https://citylimits.org/opinion-domestic-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-domestic-.text:
Share This Article
“It is time to start thinking outside the box/apartment and offer a solution to homeless victims of domestic violence.”
Today, more than 16,000 families, including 28,000 children, are living in New York City’s shelter system.
Unfortunately the number one reason is domestic violence, accounting for 20 percent of entries into the family shelter system. This incredible and sad statistic greatly out weighs traditional factors, such as overcrowding (11 percent) and eviction (also 11 percent). It is estimated that one third of all the families in the system are families suffering from domestic violence, and the city’s 54 domestic violence family shelters are insufficient.
As a result, city shelters designated for domestic violence are saturated, and many families are directed to the regular shelter system. By not being in a DV shelter, these families are not receiving the support that they and their children need to deal with this trauma, and the help needed to obtain permanent housing.
Perhaps even more disturbing is the fact that 40 percent of felony assault cases in the city since the COVID-19 pandemic are related to domestic violence. This has resulted in nearly 20 percent of all new intake at the family shelter system being related to domestic violence.
The quick release of defendants—whether through automatic bail schedules, rapid pretrial release, or early prison discharge—exposes domestic violence victims to immediate physical danger, psychological trauma, and coercion. Because domestic abuse is uniquely characterized by ongoing power dynamics and escalating patterns of control, rapid release often strips away the critical time window victims need to secure safety.
As a former deputy commissioner at the New York City Department of Homeless Services and a vice president for supportive housing at Women in Need, I believe the key to reducing this trend in domestic violence is to greatly increase the amount of supportive housing for DV victims.
There are presently over 6,000 vacant apartments in the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA), and I believe that DV victims should be given priority in filling them.
In addition, a novel ideal would be to create a program to match DV families with NYCHA residents who have several bedrooms, but now live alone. In this way the DV families could help pay the rent for the single, often elderly person, who has more than enough space at this point in their lives.
We could call this program Adopt a Family. This would be a win/win situation for all those involved. A prior report from the Independent Budget Office estimated that nearly one third of NYCHA’s nearly 180,000 apartments, or 57,000 units, are under occupied. Of those under occupied apartments, half were headed by a senior citizen.
It is time to start thinking outside the box/apartment and offer a solution to homeless victims of domestic violence.
Robert Mascali is a former deputy commissioner at the New York City Department of Homeless Services and a vice president for supportive housing at Women in Need.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trum.title: Inside the Trump Administration’s War on the International Criminal Court
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trum.author: Ashley Gate
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trum.text:
A New World Order
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has once again attacked the global system of laws, norms, and principles instituted to place limits on international armed violence. Advocating for a return to might-makes-right barbarism during a keynote speech on Friday, Rubio threatened to use military force against the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities. Warning that if the ICC was “foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city’s charters against his legions. … ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”
Rubio’s effort to undermine the principles and rules that regulate the means and methods of warfare and the humanitarian protection of civilian populations, sick and wounded combatants, and prisoners of war is part of the Trump administration’s wide-ranging effort to upend the rules-based international order that the U.S. has championed — but often failed to abide by — since World War II.
Speaking before the conservative Federalist Society at the National Lawyers Convention in Washington, D.C., Rubio disparaged the ICC as a “fake court” and “an unelected world tribunal, which claims to supersede the laws and constitutions of sovereign states, even those who never signed up for it.”
Rubio’s tirade was the latest salvo in a long-running campaign against the ICC by President Donald Trump’s administration, which has vowed to cripple the court. In October, after former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, Trump — who has relentlessly campaigned for the award — was enraged and derided the South African jurist as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of.”
Hours after the award was announced, the U.S. imposed sanctions on the ICC. These latest sanctions are intended to turn the judicial organ into an economic pariah. They prohibited the court from conducting dollar-denominated transactions, froze its U.S.-based assets, and barred the judicial body from using the U.S. banking system or working with American institutions — effectively blacklisting the court.
The ICC was created by the international community to investigate and prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the crime of aggression — when one country uses armed force against another without legal justification. The Hague, Netherlands-based court is unique as a permanent judicial organ capable of prosecuting anyone, infantry soldiers and sitting heads of state alike, for humanity’s gravest crimes if they are committed in the territories of its 125 member states. The ICC is critically a court of last resort that will only intervene when domestic jurisdictions either fail to hold their own service members and political leaders accountable, or when state parties to the court call for an investigation.
While the Trump administration’s timing in sanctioning the ICC was notable, this latest strike against the court is just one facet of the Trump administration’s yearslong campaign to — in the words of Rubio’s State Department — “dismantle” it. The effort dates back to 2020, when the first Trump administration imposed sanctions on ICC officials after the court opened an investigation into alleged U.S. war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Afghanistan.
Overturned by the Biden administration in 2021, the first round of U.S. sanctions against the court were replaced last February by a new series targeting the court’s chief prosecutor, its two deputy prosecutors, and six of its judges. All of these judges had either investigated the actions of U.S. nationals in Afghanistan or were part of the ICC’s decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for their co-perpetration of “the war crime of starvation” and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Though the litany of prior U.S. sanctions against the court impacted the lives of those nine individuals and their families — cutting them off from their bank accounts, emails, and blocking their travel — the actions were piecemeal and did not fully upend the work of the court.
Now, all of the ICC’s U.S.-based partner organizations have six months to completely cut ties with the court or face legal retribution. What’s more, since the current global economic system is built upon the U.S. dollar, international — particularly European — organizations often preemptively abide by U.S. sanctions even if their workings fall completely outside of America’s jurisdiction. For example, when the French company Axa terminated its life and health insurance contracts with the ICC on October 1, the insurer reportedly cited the escalating campaign by the U.S. against the court.
Absent the implementation of effective countermeasures — like amending and enforcing the EU Blocking Statute, which can shield EU individuals and businesses from “unlawful” third-country sanctions — this latest move by the U.S. may not kill the ICC, but it will cut off the judicial organ’s blood supply.
Victors’ Justice?
For over 80 years, the U.S. has enjoyed the privilege of proscribing — and not necessarily abiding by — international law. American representatives served as the chief arbiters of the post-World War II Nuremberg and Tokyo military tribunals that prosecuted Nazi and Japanese war criminals, which are seen by many in the field as the birthplaces of modern international criminal law. American arbiters, notably U.S. Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, led the victors of the Second World War as they tried and prosecuted their former adversaries for novel notions of wrongdoing, including crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. These newly defined criminal acts form the bedrock of the ICC’s jurisdiction.
At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, all 25 major Japanese leaders were convicted, with seven receiving death sentences. Judge Radhabinod Pal of India argued for the acquittal of all 25. In his dissent, he complained that the tribunal dispensed victors’ justice. He said that America’s atomic strikes on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were among the most criminal acts of the conflict, yet immune from prosecution.
Indeed, the international criminal justice system was never intended to hold the U.S. or its allies accountable. And in the decades since, consecutive U.S. administrations have wielded the nation’s political and military strength to avoid any semblance of international legal oversight.
Although relations with the court have oscillated over the course of Democratic and Republican administrations, the U.S. has always been wary of the court’s potential jurisdiction over American nationals. From the court’s conception, in which the U.S. played a role, the global hegemon has continuously shown its disdain for the court’s territorial jurisdiction. While the ICC cannot prosecute any American nationals for their actions in the U.S., it does have jurisdiction over acts undertaken, by U.S. nationals or otherwise, within the territories of its member nations including Afghanistan, Libya, and Palestine.
Under the Clinton administration in the 1990s, the U.S. was one of only seven drafting nations to initially veto the Rome Statute — the international treaty that created the ICC — due to its concerns over the court’s territorial jurisdiction. Later, in 2002, the same year the ICC was established, the George W. Bush administration signed the Hague Invasion Act into law. The act, which is still in effect, grants the president the legal backing to use military force against the court in order to free any U.S. or allied person held or imprisoned by the ICC. The Bush administration subsequently pressured dozens of countries to agree to never transfer U.S. nationals to the ICC, and threatened to cut military assistance, cease counterterrorism operations, or cut humanitarian aid if these states did not comply. Though relations with the ICC thawed somewhat under the Obama administration in the 2010s, the U.S. has never shown a substantial interest in joining the court and has worked for years to restrict its jurisdiction.
The Trump administration’s courtwide sanctions on the ICC are, however, a far leap beyond the pressure campaigns against the court and its member states by prior U.S. administrations. While the Trump administration cares little for the thin veneer of justice that prior U.S. administrations sought to maintain, the ongoing campaign to “dismantle” the ICC is just one piece of a larger effort by the current administration to ensure the U.S. military can act with impunity.
Soon after taking office, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered a mass purge of senior judge advocates general. Among their many functions, JAGs historically educated military leaders on the laws that prohibit the use of the U.S. military in domestic law enforcement and ensured commanders were aptly informed of the international legal obligations to protect civilians and prisoners of war. When asked about the mass layoffs in February 2025, Hegseth explained that the action was taken to remove potential “roadblocks to orders that are given by a commander in chief.”
In a concerted effort to further “maximum lethality,” Trump and Hegseth additionally gutted the Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence and the broader Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program in the early months of 2025. The budding program, which the majority of U.S combatant commanders urged Hegseth to maintain, was established in 2022 to prevent, reduce, and respond to civilian casualty incidents. Stark cuts to the program’s manpower and funding coincided with a rise in civilian casualties reported in U.S. military operations in Iran, Yemen, Somalia, and in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
When taken together, the administration’s cuts to internal legal mechanisms and policy programs intended to maintain law and protect civilians, as well as its ongoing attempts to dismantle the ICC, can be seen as two aspects of a larger campaign to eradicate all avenues of military oversight.
The Fight for Justice Will Continue
The sweeping courtwide sanctions against the ICC are formidable for the same reasons they are survivable: They aim to isolate the court from its broad system of support. The international criminal justice system depends on evidence. This evidence is not found in The Hague; it is brought to it by an array of local, national, and international investigators, researchers, watchdogs, and atrocity survivors.
The evidence needed to confirm the genocide in Palestine; the U.S. bombing of the elementary school in Minab, Iran; and the extrajudicial killings of fisherman in the Caribbean would not exist without the networks of dedicated researchers, local journalists, and courageous survivors. And the work of these people, while critical to the court’s functions, will continue, even if the court is dismantled brick by brick.
The ICC has strongly condemned the U.S. sanctions. ICC President Tomoko Akane has said that the court will “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.” Pillay has also used the publicity stemming from her Nobel Peace Prize to showcase the court’s work. She further dedicated her award to “all the survivors of international crimes” as well as the international jurists “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”
In his speech on Friday, Rubio took aim at those very jurists, declaring that the U.S. would never submit to the “sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats.” He claimed that this “global elite” was using international law as “an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.” This was, in fact, a stark about-face for Rubio, who was an advocate for international law during his 14 years as a U.S. senator. He even co-sponsored a resolution encouraging other nations to support the ICC’s investigations of Russian war crimes in Ukraine.
Rubio claimed that those who advocate for the restraint of law over all nations are anti-American. “For these people — the fundamental purpose of the law, American law and international law alike, is to weaken the United States,” he claimed. “It is to hinder the American government’s ability to defend American interests at home and abroad.” He continued, “There is nothing — there is nothing — in our history or the history of any other great nation that requires us to recognize the authority or legitimacy of any of these ridiculous ideas.”
Prior to Rubio’s speech, however, Pillay offered up a differing vision of America. In her estimation, Americans are not the singularly self-interested, lawless, reprobates envisioned by Rubio but a people who eschew limitless violence and value humanitarian principles. “I know,” she said, “that Americans support the principle of ending impunity for these serious crimes and that they support justice and accountability.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-inspectio.title: NYC inspection blitz halts construction at sites tied to fatal Brooklyn building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-inspectio.author: David Brand, Joe Hong
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-inspectio.text:
New York City buildings inspectors have halted construction completely or in part for at least five projects tied to a pair of engineers in the wake of a fatal Brooklyn building collapse, a Gothamist analysis shows.
The Department of Buildings issued the full and partial stop-work orders during an ongoing safety inspection blitz targeting companies and individuals contracted to work on a Flatbush excavation site where a neighboring apartment building collapsed and killed eight people on Nov. 11. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the sweeps would hit around 160 projects involving six different firms.
The department declined to provide details about all the properties it is inspecting, but a Gothamist review reveals that the agency has targeted at least 24 jobsites in four boroughs tied to engineers involved in the Flatbush project.
City records show the Department of Buildings visited projects handled by engineer Jieming Wang and his New Jersey-based LMW Engineering Group. They also inspected projects where MD Ariful Islam and his Queens-based RI Consulting Services drafted city-approved structural plans or performed safety monitoring.
Wang was the licensed engineer who submitted structural drawings and plans for supporting the adjacent buildings during excavation of the Flatbush project involved in last week’s building collapse. Wang’s drawings, which were approved by city plan examiners, did not call for steel bracing or foundational support known as “underpinning” at the site of the collapse, as Gothamist reported on Friday.
Islam was hired to conduct monitoring of the excavation and shoring work at the site as special inspector, according to city documents. Islam applied to withdraw from the project on Nov. 12, a day after the collapse, but Department of Buildings spokesperson Andrew Rudansky said the agency has not yet approved his request.
Wang and Islam did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A person who answered the phone at Wang’s office extension last Friday immediately hung up after a Gothamist reporter identified himself.
City building inspectors issued partial stop-work orders at four of the job sites, including the conversion of a Greenwich Village parking garage into a luxury condo complex and the development of a new six-story apartment building next to the 7 train tracks in Woodside, Queens.
Just one of the stop work orders involves excavation – the focus of the investigation into the cause of the building collapse in Flatbush.
In the case of a planned four-story apartment building in the Bronx, inspectors halted all construction after first finding broken safety fencing around an excavation site on Sunday, according to complaint data on the buildings department website.
An inspector returned Tuesday and issued a full stop-work order after the project’s general contractor “refused inspection of active site and ordered me to [leave] the premises with threats of locking me on the inside,” according to another complaint posted to the agency site.
Rudansky declined to provide more details about the safety blitz after Gothamist shared findings on the inspection locations and stop-work orders.
“To protect the integrity of our ongoing investigation and the related safety sweeps, we are not providing additional information about the targets, scope, or results of the sweeps at this time,” Rudansky said.
He repeated previous written statements he provided to Gothamist in which he said it was the responsibility of the project engineer — in this case, Wang — to determine “whether the plans have considered factors relating to their site-specific design and ensuring those plans are code compliant and safe for construction.”
It does not appear that any of the inspection sweeps sites identified by Gothamist are linked to the same owners of the Flatbush project. A limited liability company tied to Robert Fischman and Judy Swimer received approval to construct a three-story apartment building on the lot in 2025.
They applied to build a nine-story complex with a ground-floor grocery store in September but the city has yet to approve or reject the application.
Fischman and Swimer did not respond to phone calls or visits to their Brooklyn homes.
Engineer Jieming Wang
Building department records show city inspectors visited at least 17 projects that list Wang and LMW Engineering as the engineer who submitted structural and excavation plans, or other site-safety designs. Those projects include the high-profile conversion of a Greenwich Village parking garage at 332 West 11th St. into a luxury, six-story condo complex. The city issued a partial stop-work order to halt all exterior work at the site after finding unsafe scaffolding on Nov. 15, records indicate.
The project was previously targeted in a round of inspection sweeps following the near-collapse of a Midtown office building earlier this summer. Inspectors at the time were focusing on projects that contracted with the company Barone Steel, the same steel installation and fabrication firm that worked on the Midtown building.
Developer Charles Dunne did not respond to an email seeking comment about the order to pause work at the garage conversion site.
Inspectors also halted some interior work at a new six-story apartment building at 56-12 Roosevelt Ave. in Woodside, Queens, on Nov. 16 after seeing a construction worker standing on an interior scaffolding without a safety harness, buildings department records show. Building documents list Wang as structural engineer for the project.
The property is owned by a limited liability company tied to general contractor Green JJ Management and its owner Danny Chang.
Reached by phone Tuesday, Green JJ Management administrator Helena See said the company took over the plan from another firm.
“We did not choose that engineer. We purchased the property with that plan,” See said.
Property records show Chang’s company acquired the site in November 2024. Documents filed with the Department of Buildings and signed by Chang show his company began notifying neighboring owners of upcoming demolition work in February 2025.
See said she found Wang to be a competent engineer. But the collapse, she said, “is a very unpleasant thing to hear.”
Inspectors visited another Wang project at 1021 Summit Ave. in the Highbridge section of the Bronx twice in the wake of the disaster. The address is the site of a proposed new four-story apartment building. The buildings department halted all exterior work at the construction site on Nov. 12 after an inspector noted that scaffolding did not meet city code requirements, records show.
In a brief phone interview, building owner Jeton Rugovaj said the partial stop-work order was “no big deal” and that city inspectors were focusing on small problems rather than “structural stuff” in their safety sweeps.
Officials also inspected a job site at 54-47 Little Neck Parkway in Douglaston, Queens, three times since the collapse. The department halted all facade and exterior work after finding safety hazards, like loose netting above a neighboring school playground and missing guardrails, on Nov. 13, according to agency data.
Building records list Wang as the engineer for foundation and earthwork for that project, which is owned by Harvest Church of New York on the border of Queens and Nassau County.
Harvest Church did not respond to emails about the stop-work order.
Special Inspector MD Ariful Islam and RI Consulting Services
The buildings department also targeted projects involving Islam, the special inspector at the Flatbush construction site. He is a licensed engineer whose company RI Consulting Services has submitted designs for various other projects across the five boroughs.
Cityapproved documents list Islam as the engineer who designed the excavation safety plans for a planned four-story apartment building at 58 West 184th St. in the Bronx.
Records show the buildings department issued a partial stop work at the project following a construction enforcement sweep on Nov. 15.
An inspector returned on Tuesday and issued a full stop-work order after the project’s general contractor blocked the inspector from entering the site, according to a complaint on the building department website.
The site is owned by a limited liability company linked to real estate investor Dean Massari, according to property records. Massari did not respond to a phone call or text message seeking comment.
Inspectors visited another Brooklyn site where Islam designed the excavation support plan on Nov. 13, records show. The buildings department did not stop construction during the visit.
The agency issued a permit for foundation work at the address, an attached two-story house on Montgomery Street in Crown Heights, the same day.

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-is-fed-.title: New York Is Fed Up With Chuck Schumer
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-is-fed-.author: Holly Pretsky
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-is-fed-.text:
When did New York voters begin to turn on their five-term U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer? 
Was it when he squandered Democratic leverage to hash out a deal to avoid a government shutdown last year? (Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called that move a "betrayal.")
Or perhaps it was his April vote, along with just six other Democrats, to continue sending military bulldozers to Israel, at a moment when Americans are increasingly fed up with Israel's war in Gaza.
Maybe they thought Schumer had lost touch with reality when he refused to endorse Zohran Mamdani last year, a decision that was echoed in his failure to recognize other progressive juggernauts across the country before the 2026 midterms.
Or perhaps Schumer's appeal has been steadily ebbing for years, as his longstanding coziness with Wall Street feels wildly out of step at a time of surging economic populism and anger at a "rigged system." Schumer's daughters' employment at Facebook, Amazon, and, no kidding, OpenAI, certainly looks corrupt.
Whatever love we once felt for the avuncular retail politician known for his annual visits to each of New York's 62 counties, his high school graduation speeches, and his parade grand marshaling, New York is over it. 
In his home state, his job approval rating bottomed out at 27 percent in February, according to Marist. A more recent Quinnipiac survey had him at 36 percent, but still underwater with 54 percent of New Yorkers polled disapproving of the job he's doing. "Poll after poll suggests that the American people want real change," Senator Bernie Sanders said at a recent press conference with Senator Elissa Slotkin as they called for new Senate leadership. We reached out to Schumer's team to run all this by them, and we'll update this story if they respond.
