https://gothamist.com/news/greenpoint-ma.title: Greenpoint man accused of groping jogger stands trial after years of neighborhood concerns
https://gothamist.com/news/greenpoint-ma.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/greenpoint-ma.text:
A Greenpoint man with severe mental illness who has faced repeated accusations of harassing, assaulting and groping people in the neighborhood stands trial this week in Brooklyn.
Christopher Boissard’s allegedly aggressive behavior has divided the North Brooklyn neighborhood for years. Gothamist previously spoke with more than a dozen community members who expressed deep ambivalence about how to balance Boissard’s mental health needs with their own safety.
According to city officials and court records, Boissard, 35, has repeatedly cycled between psychiatric hospitals, substance abuse treatment and incarceration over the years. He is currently detained on Rikers Island.
Boissard’s trial comes just weeks after a man with a documented history of mental illness allegedly stabbed and killed a woman running on a path in South Brooklyn. While it is rare for people with psychiatric conditions to commit violent crimes, the cases that do occur often raise concerns about the city’s ability to properly care for people who need mental healthcare.
Boissard stands trial on sexual abuse and forcible touching charges. He faces up to four years in prison if convicted of the most serious offense.
Assistant District Attorney Taylor Tesher said in her opening statement Monday that Boissard grabbed a runner’s breast as she jogged past him on July 5, 2024. The touch was brief, the prosecutor said, but “it still stripped away her sense of safety.”
“She could not believe this happened to her,” Tesher said.
Greenpoint residents previously told Gothamist that Boissard’s physical aggression made them feel deeply unsettled in their own neighborhood. Similar, random acts of violence or belligerence by people seemingly in mental distress in public places like sidewalks, parks and subway cars have stoked concerns from the East Village to Bed-Stuy.
Amanda Gauthier, the jogger, had never seen Boissard before that day, the assistant DA told jurors. She reported the assault to police to ensure it didn’t happen to anyone else, the prosecutor said. Tesher then told the jury that they would learn other information about Boissard that would make his intent “all the more clear to you.”
Boissard was convicted of forcible touching in 2021, according to the state’s sex offender registry, which classifies him as a “sexually violent offender and predicate sex offender.” Whether jurors find him guilty in this case will likely depend on whether they believe he intended to touch Gauthier in order to gratify himself or degrade her. He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him.
Defense attorney Natalia Mata didn’t deny that Boissard touched the runner. But she said it was a “hit,” “swipe,” or “swat,” and not a grope.
“On July 5, 2024, Christopher Boissard had no sexual intent. Not to degrade. Not to abuse. Not to fulfill his sexual desires,” the Brooklyn Defender Services attorney said.
Mata said Boissard can’t verbally communicate because he is deaf. She said the runner was moving very quickly and that the encounter happened “in the blink of an eye.” She also told jurors not to judge what Boissard’s intentions were that day based on any testimony they may hear from people who have had encounters with her client in the past.
“No one is saying you have to like Mr. Boissard,” she said.
Boissard, dressed in a checkered, button-down shirt and blazer, followed the proceedings through two American Sign Language interpreters, occasionally groaning or gesturing animatedly. His mother sat behind him in the gallery.
Gauthier, 30, breathed deeply and occasionally dabbed her face with a tissue during approximately three hours of testimony Monday afternoon. She told the jury that she started running in college to cope with anxiety — that when she runs, she feels like she can breathe.
On the day she encountered Boissard, she said she was training for the New York City marathon. It was an “easy run” on a path she knew well, she said, so she was jogging at a slower than usual pace and listening to a podcast.
As Gauthier turned onto Manhattan Avenue near the north end of the neighborhood, a man “put his arm up,” she said. She ran into his arm, she said, and then his hand touched her left breast “almost like the pledge of allegiance.” The jogger said it felt “like his hand was palming my breast” and that she felt “intense pressure afterward.” She recalled shouting “What the hell?” and swatting his hand before running away.
Defense attorney Johnny Castellanos questioned whether Boissard made any sexual gestures, spit at Gauthier or exposed himself before, during or after touching her chest. She said she didn’t remember seeing that.
“To me it wasn’t an accident, because it seemed like he intentionally put his hand up,” she said.
Since the incident, Gauthier said, she has continued to run regularly — both on her own and with a team. But she said she wears headphones less and is more vigilant than she used to be.
“Two years ago, before this happened, I guess I was a little more naive,” she said. “Now I am definitely more attentive.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a new bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.
Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).
Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.
“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.
Central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”
Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, launched in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is currently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.
“A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”
The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” says Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.
Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.
“There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”
In El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”
Independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” says Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.
Sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.
Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.
Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo says. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”
- Sutura, 18 November-22 November, various locations, Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, El Paso, United States

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/athens-polyt.title: The 1973 Athens Polytechnic Uprising Still Matters Today
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/athens-polyt.author: Christos Avramidis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/athens-polyt.text:
The 1973 Athens Polytechnic Uprising Still Matters Today
In November 1973, Greek students occupying the Athens Polytechnic painted “USA Out” and “NATO Out” on its gate, protesting decades of US interference in Greece. Today US bases there still tie the country to Washington’s wars.
A military dictatorship had ruled Greece for more than six years when, in November 1973, hundreds of student occupied the Athens Polytechnic, transforming their university into a center of resistance. Thousands of workers, school students, and ordinary citizens soon joined them.
On the pillars of the Polytechnic’s central gate, a student painted two messages in large letters: “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.” Within days, on November 17, a military tank would smash through that same gate. Why were young Greeks risking their lives to overthrow the military dictatorship also demanding the withdrawal of the United States and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)?
The answer lies in the three decades preceding the uprising. During those years, Greece experienced Nazi occupation, British military intervention, civil war, and the consolidation of an anti-communist political order that American assistance sustained. The Greek ruling class was all too happy to allow US interference to consolidate its own rule.
The Resistance That Britain Opposed
During World War II, Greece developed one of Europe’s largest resistance movements. The communist-led National Liberation Front (EAM) and its armed wing, the Greek People’s Liberation Army (ELAS), mobilized hundreds of thousands of people and came to control much of the Greek countryside.
EAM was far more than a guerrilla organization. In the territories it liberated from Nazi occupation, EAM established institutions of popular administration, organized schools, and introduced new forms of political participation. In 1944, women were able to vote and stand as candidates in elections the resistance organized, years before they gained equal voting rights in national Greek elections.
By the time German troops withdrew in October 1944, the resistance had become one of the most powerful social and political forces in the country. But Winston Churchill’s government was determined to prevent the communist-led movement from dominating postwar Greece.
The confrontation centered on the future of the armed forces. Under British supervision, the Greek government demanded the disarmament of ELAS while retaining military formations associated with the government in exile. EAM rejected an arrangement that would leave its supporters disarmed in the face of potentially hostile forces.
In practice, the leadership of EAM and of the Communist Party of Greece had an ambivalent stance toward the British army and British agents operating on Greek soil. They had cooperated with the British against the Nazi occupation. But they were deeply skeptical of British intervention in liberated Greece. Events after the German withdrawal from Athens confirmed their suspicions: the forces of liberation (EAM/ELAS and their allies) would have to fight a new battle.
On December 3, 1944, an enormous, initially peaceful demonstration gathered in central Athens. Police opened fire, killing demonstrators and wounding many others.
The Athens police chief, Angelos Evert, later acknowledged ordering the shooting. He had remained in charge of the police during the Nazi occupation, maintaining relations with the occupying authorities as well as contacts with British intelligence. The massacre marked the beginning of the December clashes, which Greeks call the Dekemvriana.
British troops clashed with ELAS in the streets of Athens, using tanks, artillery, and aircraft. Their Greek allies included formations containing former members of the Security Battalions, which had collaborated with the Nazi occupiers in the struggle against the resistance. Militants who had fought the Nazis now faced the British army — and, fighting alongside it, former collaborators of the occupation.
Churchill himself arrived in Athens on Christmas Day to intervene in the political negotiations. The British military campaign eventually defeated ELAS in the capital. The Varkiza Agreement, which the government and EAM signed in February 1945, then required the resistance to surrender its weapons.
The Left had suffered a military defeat and now had to accept a political settlement from a position of profound weakness. Its supporters would soon discover how little protection that settlement provided.
White Terror and the American Takeover
Widespread persecution of the Left, which Greeks remember as the White Terror, followed the disarmament of ELAS. Armed right-wing groups, often operating with the tolerance or cooperation of state authorities, targeted people associated with EAM. They murdered and tortured former resistance fighters or drove them from their homes. State authorities imprisoned many more.
Contemporary figures that EAM compiled recorded 1,289 murders, 31,632 cases of torture and physical abuse, 84,931 arrests, and 265 rapes between February 1945 and March 1946. United Nations documentation later cited these figures, but they originated with the persecuted movement rather than an independent nationwide investigation.
The political climate was hardly conducive to a free electoral contest. The government scheduled elections for March 1946, while thousands of leftists faced imprisonment, displacement, intimidation, and restrictions on political activity. The communist-led left boycotted the vote, arguing that the conditions made meaningful democratic participation impossible.
The Right emerged victorious. A referendum later that year restored King George II to the throne, consolidating the monarchy’s influence in the postwar political order. Greece descended into full-scale civil war.
By 1947, however, Britain could no longer afford to sustain its intervention. The United States took its place.
President Harry Truman requested $400 million in assistance for Greece and Turkey, declaring that Washington would help free peoples resist communist domination. In Greece, this meant massive military assistance to the government fighting the communist-led Democratic Army of Greece (DSE).
American weapons, money, and military advisers helped determine the outcome of the war. During its final stages in 1949, Greek government aircraft dropped American-supplied napalm on Greek territory, targeting communist positions in the mountains of northern Greece. The United States had used napalm during World War II, but its deployment in Greece preceded Washington’s much better-known use of the weapon in Vietnam.
Government forces defeated the DSE in 1949. For their supporters, however, the end of the war did not bring freedom.
The state sent thousands of leftists to prisons and remote island camps. The camp on the island of Makronisos became particularly notorious for its system of torture, beatings, forced declarations of repentance, and ideological reeducation. The contrast with the treatment of Nazi collaborators was striking, with far higher numbers of executions.
One execution became a symbol of that political order. Nikos Beloyannis had been a communist resistance fighter during the Nazi occupation. The authorities arrested him after the civil war, and a military court sentenced him to death. A photograph of him smiling with a red carnation during his trial became famous internationally, while an international campaign demanded that the Greek government spare his life.
Nevertheless, on March 30, 1952, a firing squad executed Beloyannis and three other communists.
Their deaths reflected the determination of the postwar Greek state to eliminate what it regarded as the communist threat, despite the formal restoration of parliamentary institutions. That same year, Greece joined NATO.
Much of Greece’s political elite had fled the country during the Nazi occupation, while significant sections of its economic elite had collaborated with the occupying forces. After liberation, the former returned to power, while much of the latter retained its economic influence. The restored ruling establishment built new mechanisms of repression and presided over a new era for Greek capitalism, keeping wages low and suppressing trade unions. US imperialism, which had taken the reins from its British counterpart, underpinned this new configuration of forces. In the postwar years, US interference would take many forms; at the same time, the Greek left would prove much more resilient than anyone could have predicted.
When the American Ambassador Intervened in Greek Elections
American influence went beyond supplying weapons. Declassified US diplomatic documents reveal direct American intervention in Greece’s electoral arrangements.
In March 1952, US ambassador John Peurifoy informed Washington that the American embassy’s political intervention and a public statement had blocked the introduction of proportional representation. The American ambassador was candidly discussing his government’s efforts to influence the electoral system of a formally sovereign democracy. The elections four years later vividly illustrated the political consequences of Greece’s unusual electoral arrangements.
In the 1956 parliamentary elections, the opposition Democratic Union won 48.15 percent of the popular vote, compared with 47.38 percent for Konstantinos Karamanlis’s conservative National Radical Union.
Yet Karamanlis secured 165 parliamentary seats, while the opposition received only 132. The party that won fewer votes formed the new government.
The opposition alliance was not a communist electoral front. It brought together centrist and left-wing forces against the conservative government. Even this broad parliamentary challenge failed to dislodge the Right.
Two years later, the United Democratic Left (EDA) became Greece’s second-largest parliamentary party, demonstrating the continuing electoral strength of the Left despite years of persecution. The result alarmed the conservative establishment and reinforced its fears about the political consequences of a more open democratic system.
The Monarchy, the Para-State, and the Road to Dictatorship
The Greek monarchy was far from a ceremonial institution. The palace intervened repeatedly in political affairs, exercised substantial influence over the armed forces, and helped shape the composition and survival of governments. Alongside the formal state existed an extensive anti-communist security apparatus and networks of right-wing organizations, some of which maintained close relations with elements of the police, military, and intelligence services.
Greek and American security agencies also cooperated during the Cold War in covert structures, including a clandestine stay-behind network called “Red Sheepskin.” These networks formed part of the country’s anti-communist security architecture, although their existence alone does not establish responsibility for every episode of political violence.
In 1965, King Constantine II’s confrontation with the centrist Prime Minister Georgios Papandreou over control of the military precipitated a government crisis. Papandreou had won a substantial parliamentary majority in 1964, yet his government collapsed amid royal intervention and defections from his own party. Greeks call these defections the Apostasia.
The conflict was particularly revealing because Papandreou was no communist revolutionary. He was a moderate centrist politician operating within the parliamentary system. Nevertheless, his attempt to exercise authority over the military collided with the monarchy and the security establishment.
By April 1967, Greece was approaching another national election. The army intervened before voters could go to the polls.
The Colonels and Their American Allies
On April 21, 1967, a group of military officers seized power. They suspended the constitution, banned political parties, imposed censorship, and arrested thousands of political opponents.
The dictatorship established a system of exile and torture that particularly targeted communists, trade unionists, students, and other opponents. Its leaders justified their seizure of power as necessary to prevent a communist takeover.
The precise extent of American foreknowledge of the coup, and of individual US officials’ involvement in it, remains contested. But the documentary record of Washington’s subsequent military cooperation with the dictatorship is extensive and undisputed.
The Johnson administration suspended deliveries of certain major weapons systems. The suspension, however, was only partial, and restrictions on military deliveries were gradually eased. An October 1969 memorandum for President Richard Nixon acknowledged that the United States had delivered approximately $100 million in military equipment to Greece as grant assistance between April 1967 and June 1969. During the same period, the dictatorship held political prisoners in camps and prisons, and torture and repression continued unabated.
American officials had a clear understanding of the nature of the dictatorship. They also regarded Greece’s position in NATO, its military installations, and its strategic location in the eastern Mediterranean as important to American interests.
The contradiction was evident. Washington publicly called for constitutional government while maintaining significant military ties with a dictatorship that had abolished it.
Greece was not an isolated example. In Spain, the United States had signed military agreements with Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in 1953, securing access to bases in exchange for financial and military assistance. The protection of Western strategic interests could coexist with the survival of authoritarian governments.
The Tank at the Athens Polytechnic Uprising
By November 1973, the Greek dictatorship was facing growing opposition. On November 14, students occupied the Athens Polytechnic and established a makeshift radio station. Their broadcasts called on the population to join the struggle for freedom. The most famous slogan of the uprising was “Bread, Education, Freedom.”
But the messages painted on the pillars of the university gate revealed another dimension of the revolt. They read “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.”
For the protesters, these demands were inseparable from their struggle against the dictatorship. They had grown up in a country where American military assistance had helped defeat the communist left and where political prisoners had endured years of persecution. US diplomats had intervened in its domestic politics, and Greece’s military dictatorship maintained close relations with Washington. Thousands gathered around the Polytechnic.
In the early hours of November 17, the dictatorship sent tanks against the occupied university. One crashed through the main gate. Police and soldiers violently suppressed the uprising. Historian Leonidas Kallivretakis has documented twenty-four confirmed deaths associated with the events, many of them in the streets surrounding the Polytechnic.
In Greek popular memory, the uprising became the decisive event that brought down the dictatorship. Strictly speaking, however, the dictatorship survived for another eight months.
On November 25, hard-line military officer Dimitrios Ioannidis overthrew dictator Georgios Papadopoulos and established an even more repressive military government. But Greek society had watched police and soldiers kill young people who had demanded freedom. The apparent restoration of military control could not erase the political consequences of the uprising.
American officials continued to maintain diplomatic and military relations with the new junta, despite their awareness of its repressive character.
US diplomatic reporting from 1974 acknowledged the resentment directed at Washington and the widespread Greek belief that American support had contributed to the dictatorship’s survival. The new rulers also maintained their interest in relations with the United States while seeking international support for their rule.
The junta finally collapsed in July 1974, after it organized a coup against Cyprus’s president, Archbishop Makarios III, triggering the crisis that culminated in Turkey’s invasion of the island.
Democracy returned. But the legacy of the Polytechnic uprising extended far beyond the overthrow of the colonels.
The Bases That Never Left
The anger against foreign intervention remained a powerful force in Greek politics after the restoration of democracy. In August 1974, even conservative Prime Minister Karamanlis withdrew Greece from NATO’s integrated military command structure in protest over the alliance’s response to Turkey’s invasion of Cyprus.
The decision reflected both the government’s security concerns and the extraordinary public anger surrounding the Cyprus crisis.
Greece returned to NATO’s military command in 1980.
In October 1981, Andreas Papandreou, the son of Georgios Papandreou, led the Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) to victory. PASOK won 48.07 percent of the vote, the highest share in the party’s electoral history. Its program had promised a fundamental change in Greece’s relationship with the United States, including the removal of American bases and withdrawal from NATO, but neither happened.
In 1983, Papandreou’s government signed a new agreement regulating the American military presence. The country remained in NATO, and American facilities continued operating.
More than fifty years later, Greece remains an important part of American military strategy. Successive governments have expanded defense cooperation with Washington, including agreements granting American forces access to facilities across the country. Among the most significant is Souda Bay, on the island of Crete, a major logistical and operational hub for the US Navy and Air Force in the eastern Mediterranean.
The implications became particularly visible during the American attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025.
Greek news outlets reported that American KC-135 aerial refueling aircraft operating from Souda Bay supported the mission involving US B-2 bombers. According to these reports, aircraft departing from the base participated in refueling operations over the Mediterranean.
In March 2026, the United States, Israel, and Iran were once again locked in military confrontation. Greece’s defense minister, Nikos Dendias, publicly discussed the possibility of attacks on military facilities and the measures the government had taken to protect Souda Bay and other critical infrastructure.
The Greek government has stated that Greece is not participating in operations against Iran. But the strategic importance of American military facilities on Greek territory has made questions about their use, security, and accountability increasingly consequential.
The Polytechnic Uprising Lives On
Every November 17, tens of thousands of Greeks take to the streets to commemorate the Polytechnic uprising. The annual march traditionally ends outside the American embassy. Even the statue of Harry S. Truman in Athens became a target of protest. Over the decades, demonstrators repeatedly attacked it and attempted to bring it down, sometimes succeeding.
The monument to the president whose doctrine had initiated America’s postwar intervention in Greece became a recurring symbol of opposition to that intervention.
The dictatorship fell in 1974. Parliamentary democracy returned, and governments of different political orientations have held power since then. Yet the country continues to host military facilities that form part of Washington’s wider strategic presence in the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
For generations of Greeks, the Polytechnic has represented not only the struggle against military dictatorship but also the demand that the country’s future should be decided by its own people.
Fifty-three years after the uprising, the words students painted on the pillars of its gate remain part of an unresolved historical debate. A tank smashed the gate. The demands written on its pillars survived.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-plans-new.title: MTA plans new subway signals for ‘the whole damn system, finally’
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-plans-new.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-plans-new.text:
The antiquated technology that guides subways will be upgraded on every mile of subway track by 2050, MTA Chair Janno Lieber said Tuesday, unveiling a plan to address the leading cause of delays for millions of commuters.
Lieber shared the plan during an event at WNYC’s Greene Space, saying the new signals will change service for the better.
“[We’re] accomplishing what people have talked about in general terms but never really laid a detailed plan for, which is going to resignal the whole damn system, finally,” Lieber said. “This is the key to unlocking more and better service.”
Much of the city’s subway system relies on signal technology that dates back to the 1930s. In some cases, transit dispatchers cannot know the exact locations of trains.
Modern technology, called communications-based train control, uses automated systems to drive trains, allowing them to travel faster and closer together.
Over the last two decades, the transit agency has upgraded the signals on the entire lengths of the L and 7 lines, as well as a section of the F line in Brooklyn. Work is ongoing to modernize the signals on sections of the A, C, E, G and other parts of the F line, but each project is far behind schedule.
But MTA officials say they’ve learned lessons from the ongoing work and are now charting a course to add modern signals to every inch of tracks over the next 24 years. A report published by the transit agency states the 1 and 4 lines in the Bronx will be the next to get signal upgrades. It marks the first time the MTA has announced a plan to modernize subway signals in the borough.
“These are two lines with legacy signal equipment at or well beyond its useful life and due for investment,” the report said.
The numbered lines, which were originally built by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company decades before the MTA was formed, are the oldest train lines in the system. The report also said that rolling out the technology on the 1 and 4 lines will for the first time coincide with “the arrival of new subway cars, allowing us to test and refine the system immediately.”
The new trains will come equipped with CBTC technology, which will shave time off getting the signals up and running.
Alyssa Cobb Konon, deputy chief development officer for planning at the MTA’s construction department, said the transit agency has proven it can install the technology in the subway system while still running trains 24/7 and that it now feels more confident it can implement the new signals systemwide.
The report outlines details of every project the MTA will tackle in each decade leading up to 2050.
In the 2020s, it will continue projects currently undergoing CBTC installation and renew existing modern signals on the L train that are reaching the end of their useful life. In the 2030s, the MTA will bring the technology to 10 additional lines, half of which are the numbered lines. In the 2040s, it will bring CBTC to the seven remaining lines.
“Our approach will be flexible enough to be nimble,” the report said. “If one project gets delayed or other work makes a corridor impossible to modernize for a while, we will pivot to an alternative to constantly deliver better service for riders.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/s.title: Shoppers Rejoice! The Flatbush Avenue Bus Lanes Are Officially Open
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/s.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/s.text:
DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn announces the Flatbush Avenue bus lanes are officially open. Dave Colon
You can’t spell “business” without “bus.”
Department of Transportation Commissioner Mike Flynn and a key Brooklyn business representativethrew cold water on some merchants’ claims that Flatbush Avenue’s new bus lanes threaten their livelihoods, during a Tuesday ribbon-cutting where the pair highlighted transit improvements that will boost commerce and bring more people to the popular retail corridor.
Flynn and a clutch of elected officials, advocates and DOT employees merrily opened the new bus lanes on Flatbush, which run down the center of the street from Grand Army Plaza to Livingston Street — where they connect to the existing Livingston Street busway, thereby creating about 1.5 miles of the dark red lanes in each direction.
The commissioner noted that 55,000 daily bus riders traverse the stretch between Grand Army and Livingston every day. Those passengers will now see their commutes and trips for leisure or important appointments become quicker and far more reliable, while pedestrians will benefit from fewer and slower private cars.
“The design separates bus lanes from general traffic lanes,” said Flynn. “That means riders are no longer suffering from commutes slowed by double-parked cars or general traffic, and commuters are not losing time as busses weave into and out of the curb lane for pickups and drop-offs. This will help Flatbush feel less like a busy highway and more like a calm neighborhood street that’s easier to cross.”
As with any street redesign project on a thriving commercial corridor, purveyor-critics of the Flatbush bus lanes have said that rebalancing the street to favor public transit users will kill their businesses. The owners of Antonio’s Pizzeria and El Gran Castillo complained about the project in August. But Flynn pointed out that DOT research has found that the vast majority of people shopping on this piece of Flatbush do not drive cars to the area.
“We want to move busses faster, we also want to make it easier to do business in New York City, and we want small businesses to succeed,” Flynn told reporters. “It’s definitely a consideration. We did a pedestrian intercept survey, we sent our street teams out and found that about 92 percent of folks on Flatbush arrive by walking or transit.”
The Flatbush redesign didn’t ignore local businesses. DOT updated curb regulations on and around the street to encourage turnover, added metered parking and designated new loading zones to clear the curb for delivery trucks. Flynn emphasized that people often mistake street redesigns’ attendant traffic and construction headaches as a new and permanent status quo — especially when the project involves a street that must carry traffic during construction.
“This is one of the largest and most complex projects that we’ve done in this way,” he said. “Typically, you would do something like this as a capital project, and it would take years. But we’ve been able to deliver it in months. Because you have to stage the construction and the traffic patterns change, there’s always that period that’s a little less comfortable, and there’s some inconveniences. I think what we’ll see as people adjust to it is that it’ll become the new normal. And I think businesses should see, like we found, the vast majority of their customers are arriving on foot or are bus riders.”
Flynn was hardly alone in singing the praises of the bus lane as a potential business booster.
“I think this project is bigger and more transformative to the benefit of all the users of the district, people coming from afar, people using the neighborhood to get to A and B,” said North Flatbush Business Improvement District Executive Director James Ellis. “We’re a very transit-rich district, and we want to recognize that. But we also recognize that there needs to be some of these changes to make the district more hospitable.”
Ellis echoed Flynn’s observation that the construction itself could temporarily disrupt business owners and that people get used to doing things a certain way.
“Dealing with change is a pain, specifically with some of the businesses we’ve heard from that have been there a long time, running their business the way they’ve been running for a long time,” he said. “Change is real, and we’re sympathetic to that. But we also hope that these transformative changes that are coming will make the experience for everybody and they’ll see the benefits in the long term.”
As a representative of business interests up and down the Flatbush corridor, Ellis is perfectly positioned to understand whether the elimination of 41 parking spots on a mile-long corridor makes the difference between a lively shopping district and a ghost town. His verdict? The bus lane could attract more people to the area.
Council Member Lincoln Restler, who represents the northernmost end of Flatbush, told reporters that he avoided Flatbush before the city added the new bus lanes and traffic calming measures. Ellis later referred back to Restler’s remarks.
“I think locally we’re going to see neighbors be more attracted to coming here,” he said. “We heard from other some other speakers, Flatbush was something to maybe avoid at times, unless you had to, unless you had to make that connection to a train or a bus, or make that doctor’s appointment, or meet friends at the arena for a game. Hopefully, now with it being a little bit more hospitable and more like visitable, we’ll see even neighbors coming around to use this system more frequently.”
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://gothamist.com/news/tenant-in-col.title: Tenant in collapsed Brooklyn building warned landlord of cracks, lawsuit says
https://gothamist.com/news/tenant-in-col.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/tenant-in-col.text:
A Brooklyn musician made homeless when his apartment building collapsed into an adjacent construction site is suing his landlord and several construction firms, claiming he warned them about cracks near the Flatbush Avenue building's entrance.
In a complaint filed in Brooklyn Supreme Court late Monday, tenant Dengane Omari Jack said he “photographed those cracks, and reported the condition to the landlord or management responsible for the building” in October, weeks before the disaster claimed eight lives, including two children, and injured several others.
Jack claims the owner, Olufemi Falade, shrugged off the complaint, responding “that the condition was not the landlord's fault or could not be fixed” and that he “failed to arrange a timely and adequate structural investigation, obtain necessary protection or repairs, or take appropriate steps in response to the reported condition and the ongoing adjoining excavation.”
Falade owns the property through a limited liability company called Isolag Realty Corp. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development documented 98 violations at the four-unit building, including unsafe electrical wiring and an inadequate water supply to the sprinkler system, before its collapse.
The lawsuit also names the owners of the adjacent construction site – limited liability companies tied to Robert Fischman and Judy Swimer – and a host of companies and individuals involved in the project, including general contractor Townhouse Builders, subcontractor Elite Concrete, structural engineer Jieming Wang of LMW Engineering and special inspections agency RI Consulting Services Inc.
Falade did not immediately respond to a phone message seeking comment Tuesday.
The building where Jack lived at 1321 Flatbush Ave. crumbled into the adjacent construction site at around 4 p.m. Nov. 11, taking the facade of another adjoining apartment building with it. Rescue operations continued into the next day as first responders searched the debris for survivors and the deceased.
“Our client obviously sends condolences to the families of all those killed, and best wishes to all those injured,” said Jack’s attorney Scott Epstein in a phone interview Tuesday. “The loss of his residence and the entirety of his worldly possessions has traumatically affected him.”
The city’s Department of Buildings has not yet determined the cause of the fatal collapse and has launched a safety inspection blitz at other projects handled by the same firms as the Flatbush project. A Gothamist analysis found that inspectors visited at least 24 sites associated with LMW Engineering and RI Consulting Services and halted work at five.
LMW Engineering, RI Consulting Services, Townhouse Builders, Elite Concrete, Fischman and Swimer did not respond to requests for comment about the collapse.
Fischman and Swimer received approval to construct a three-story apartment complex on the lot after demolishing a single-story commercial building. They sought approval to build a nine-story complex with a first-floor grocery store in September, but the city had not yet signed off on the plan before the collapse.
The city’s Buildings Department halted demolition work at the site in March after observing missing safety precautions. The department then fined the development team $10,000 for proceeding with the demolition despite the order.
Building records show the apartment building next door was in bad shape before it collapsed. A preconstruction report documented the “poor” condition of the side facade overlooking the construction site, though the engineering firm that prepared it noted it could not access the building.
Excavation safety plans prepared by LMW Engineer’s Jieming Wang called for steel support beams, known as rakers, at every location along the perimeter of the lot except at the collapse site.
Tenants living at 1321 Flatbush Ave. dealt with problems in the building long before the fatal collapse. The building cycled through the city’s tax lien sale process for unpaid municipal debt at least five times in the last decade, court and property records show.
Falade also has a dubious track record as a landlord.
A judge sent him to jail for 12 days in 2006 for violations at a different building.

https://gothamist.com/news/astoria-board.title: Astoria board eyes plans for 3 high-rise towers on Steinway Street
https://gothamist.com/news/astoria-board.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/astoria-board.text:
Three proposed high-rise apartment buildings on the southern end of Astoria’s Steinway Street, set to be reviewed by the local community board, have become a lightning rod over the neighborhood's redevelopment future.
While several other high-rise buildings are planned for the same stretch of Steinway Street, home to many one- and two-story shops and shuttered businesses, these three are among the few that require public review and government approval to move forward.
The proposals have raised questions and concerns among wary neighbors about the pace and accessibility of real estate development in the neighborhood, amid a boom in luxury high-rise construction.
Evie Hantzopoulos, the chair of Queens Community Board 1, said she’s received over 100 letters detailing concerns about the projects ahead of the board meeting, at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday at the Marquee Astoria, 25-22 Astoria Blvd.
“ People are concerned, No. 1, that the majority of these apartments that are being built are not going to be accessible to working-class and immigrant communities,” Hantzopoulos said in an interview. “ I think (there’s) just concern that it is gonna become a neighborhood only for the wealthy.”
One project includes two apartment buildings—one nine stories and the other 12—on the corner of 34th Ave at 34-14/22 Steinway St., by the developer Schuman Properties. Together, the buildings would total 243 units, about 61 of which would be designated as affordable. Commercial space would occupy the first floor.
The community board will review another proposal for a 17-story, mixed-use building across the street at 34-49 Steinway St., by ZD Jasper Realty. The building would have 214 apartments, about 54-64 of which would be reserved for affordable housing, and also include commercial space and a “community facility.”
Details about specific rental prices were not immediately available. Schuman Properties declined to comment and ZD Jasper Realty did not respond to a request for comment.
Critics of the projects worry rents will be too high, and that even the required affordable housing will be out of reach for many of the neighborhood’s working-class immigrant residents.
Rana Abdelhamid, the founder and executive director of Malikah, a neighborhood anti-violence group, said the projects don’t “necessarily guarantee true affordability for our communities.”
Malikah is among several local organizations, including Chhaya Community Development Corporation and the Astoria Tenants Union, that have signed onto a letter to the community board asking them to withhold support for the proposals, pending an investigation of the displacement impacts of the projects and “binding, enforceable commitments to deeply affordable housing.”
Other projects are on tap in the area. Just north of 34th Ave., another developer submitted an application to the Department of Buildings in March to construct a nine-story building with 74 units at 32-73 Steinway St., according to the Real Deal. Next door, at 32-75 Steinway St., another developer submitted an application for an eight-story building with 65 units.
In July, another developer submitted an application for a 19-story building with 99 apartments at 35-13 Steinway St., just south of 35th Avenue.
Those developments don’t require community board consideration, since they don’t require changes to the city’s current zoning rules.
But to move forward, the three proposals at 34-14/22 and 34-49 Steinway St. will need to be reviewed by the community board and borough president before the city’s planning commission and City Council consider them. The proposals do not need community board approval to move forward in the rezoning process.
The community board meeting will also be livestreamed on YouTube. After gathering testimony, the community board’s land use committee will meet again to discuss its recommendations to the board, and the board will vote on the proposals in December.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdanis-plan.title: Mamdani's plan to wind down carriage horse industry takes shape
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdanis-plan.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdanis-plan.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled some basic details on how his administration plans to help carriage horse drivers transition to other careers once the industry’s ban takes effect — but the union representing the drivers remains highly skeptical that they won’t be left high and dry.
According to City Hall, the plan would give the industry’s 200 carriage drivers and stable hands access to career training programs at LaGuardia Community College, offering entrepreneurship support, connections to employers and tuition assistance. The city would also facilitate medallion buybacks.
The details come just weeks after the City Council voted in support of a bill that would shut down the city’s 160-year-old horse carriage industry by June 2028. Carriage drivers said they felt betrayed by the move, and it was not immediately clear how the city would help them find new careers.
Mamdani has repeatedly pledged not to leave the workers behind, but Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said all of his proposals could “quickly be abandoned” if the city faces a fiscal crisis and needs money for other things.
“That would leave hundreds of horse-carriage workers, owners and family members on the curb with nothing at all,” he wrote in a statement, adding that the union still planned to file a federal lawsuit against Romanch’s Law — the bill that would shutter the industry.
Mamdani said his administration would continue working with TWU Local 100 to develop a full transition blueprint by April 2027. He also planned to commission a feasibility study to see whether electric carriages and pedal-assist bikes could be potential alternatives for Central Park tours.
Romanch’s Law — named after the teen tourist who died this summer after he was thrown from a runaway horse carriage — also stipulates rules for the horses as the industry shutters, barring owners from selling or transferring them for slaughter or for use in other horse-drawn carriage businesses.

https://gothamist.com/news/plan-for-will.title: Plan for Williamsburg business district fuels fight over future of pricey neighborhood
https://gothamist.com/news/plan-for-will.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/plan-for-will.text:
When Katie Denny Horowitz became the North Brooklyn Parks Alliance's executive director in 2019, she started thinking about different ways to raise money for parks maintenance in Williamsburg.
Local residents, she said, were complaining that the parks and surrounding streets were filthy, and existing city services weren’t meeting the demand of the neighborhood, which had seen a major uptick in development.
The answer Horowitz arrived at, with the backing of others, is a proposal to create a Business Improvement District, or BID, in which property owners within a certain area pay into a dedicated fund for extra street cleaning and neighborhood beautification projects, like adding plants, lighting and public art to streetscapes.
“ You have more businesses attracting tourism, attracting shoppers, attracting diners and you have tens of thousands” of new residents, said Horowitz, describing the neighborhood now known for its eating, drinking and shopping scenes. “All those people are bringing with them things like trash [...] The city's budget isn't necessarily increasing at the same time to be able to pick up the trash faster,” she added.
Horowitz and other local leaders, including Councilmember Lincoln Restler, are leading the push for the proposed Northside Williamsburg BID, which would run from Grand Street to North 15th Street, and Bedford Avenue to the East River.
But getting it off the ground is no sure thing. The proposal has been met with pushback at community meetings, where opponents frame the business improvement district as another sign that Williamsburg is becoming a haven for wealthy and upscale brands.
Property owners have objected to the extra monthly fees. Dues would be based on the size of their holdings and property assessment, which could add hundreds or even thousands of dollars on top of the owners’ existing property tax bill.
“This BID is being developed with the wealthiest landlords and interests that will prioritize privatization and profit over the community’s well-being,” a Change.org petition against the BID states. “Northside BID threatens to alter the very fabric that makes Williamsburg unique and inclusive. The BID will decimate any below-market commercial or residential spaces that exist.”
The pushback has extended into the courtroom. A residential property owner has sued the Northside Improvement District Steering Committee, its chair, Ward Dennis, the city, and other other affiliated groups. The petitioner, who filed suit under the names of multiple limited liability companies, claims that the voting, which is already underway, was initiated prematurely and has strayed from the city’s official process to form a BID.
The proponents are undaunted.
Restler called the lawsuit “totally frivolous and irrelevant” and said he does not expect it to prevent the BID proposal from moving forward.
If adopted, the Northside Williamsburg BID would be New York City's 79th business improvement district – and larger than many of the others.
The money, according to Restler, would go toward funding a few dozen workers for special trash pickups within the designated area on a daily basis, along with public safety efforts, streetscape improvements and business assistance.
The process of getting there, however, is circuitous. Unlike some ballot measures, there is no official election day or deadline to cast a ballot, according to the Northside BID’s website.
For the BID to be enacted, a majority of the assessed properties in the area have to vote in support of the proposal. But the city’s Small Business Services, which green-lights proposals, said it considers votes from other community members as well, and generally looks for “broad-based support.”
In the case of the Northside Williamsburg BID proposal, the steering committee first began distributing ballots in October 2025 and voting is ongoing. If and when enough support is garnered, the proposal will be brought before the community board, the City Council and the borough president for approval. With their sign-off, the measure would then go to the mayor’s office, for one last swipe of a pen.
“Our job now is to try to get the majority of folks on the ground to believe in that solution and to give it a try,” Horowitz said.
But some residents, like Anthony Dassaro, are vehemently opposed. Dassaro said he feels like he’s being forced to pay for a service he doesn’t want.
Dassaro, 58, said he has lived in Williamsburg, in the bounds of the proposed BID, his entire life, long before the neighborhood became a commercial shopping district with luxury storefronts.
The area near North Sixth Street and Berry Street now features a Chanel, a Hermes, a WeWork and a Whole Foods. But he notes it used to be home to meatpacking plants.
“ You would see during the day the skinned cows on hooks hanging in the street,” Dassaro said. “There would be dumpsters of bones from the cows,” and people would “feed their dog with those bones.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-s.title: When the U.S. Military Implemented AI, Civilian Deaths Rose
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-s.author: Namir Shabibi
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/ai-s.text:
This story is published in collaboration with Airwars.
On a balmy night in 2019, 35-year-old Barakat was on his way home, driven by friends through the ancient, mountainous Syrian village of Barisha, one among the previously abandoned Byzantine “Dead Cities.”
“I was with my best friends. They wanted to drop me off at home,” the father of five later told NPR. Barakat and his two companions had finished their day’s work as agricultural laborers at an olive press. “We had pumpkin seeds and bought coffee on the road and were having fun.”
Unknown to them, a fateful military operation was occurring nearby. Three hundred meters away, a team of U.S. special forces was raiding the compound of Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.
As the attack unfolded, most U.S. surveillance and reconnaissance assets were trained on the compound itself. Yet, known to few at the time, a new set of artificial eyes had been introduced to U.S. warfare in Iraq and Syria. Computer vision target detection, part of the Pentagon’s algorithmic warfare program known as Project Maven, enabled the military to recognize enemy personnel and vehicles through AI-assisted fusion and analysis of images and video.
As Barakat’s vehicle headed south through Barisha, Maven’s AI detected a vehicle that the U.S. military’s human eyes had missed. The ground commander then proceeded to call in the attack.
“At that moment, the helicopters arrived. Suddenly, we were hit. I didn’t know what was going on. I was just trying to escape death,” Barakat told NPR. His right arm was blown off, with his left hand partially disabled. His friends, Khaled Mustafa Qurmo and Khaled Abdel Majid Qurmo, were killed.
The U.S. military ultimately rejected Barakat’s claim of harm. The results of a second Pentagon review, opened after an NPR investigation, were never released.
A spate of articles have hailed this as the year of AI warfare — from Ukrainian drones to Israel’s algorithmic decision support systems. A recent project that I worked on tracked how the rapid and potentially dangerous introduction of AI is transforming every part of the “kill chain.”
The AI-powered attack on Barakat may have occurred seven years ago, but new research has shown that many of these systems had been fielded years earlier than previously known, prompting questions about the extent of artificial intelligence’s role in historical attacks — and how it has already impacted civilian harm.
Maven’s Dawn
The role of Maven in the 2019 Baghdadi attack was only revealed this year in journalist Katrina Manson’s book “Project Maven,” which charts the development of U.S. algorithmic warfare through the program of the same name.
Project Maven sought to create the algorithms and platforms to fuse real-time data from multiple feeds — among them drones, radar, satellites, and text — to conduct detect threats, run pattern-of-life analysis, and track targets, in the service of accelerating military targeting.
The U.S. military initially tapped Google as a technology partner for Project Maven. But Google pulled out in 2018, following protests about its involvement in AI targeting, and Palantir stepped in.
Maven’s most revolutionary aspects were twofold: the creation of a “single visualization tool” — in this case, Palantir’s Maven Smart System — to house the feeds, fuse them and turbocharge decision-making, better known as “decision support systems.”
The second transformative aspect was the training of AI algorithms on vast amounts of images and full motion video generated from drone surveillance and other aerial and space-based sensors — a collaborative effort involving multiple defense contractors, initially led by the Pentagon. Maven algorithms would then be deployed into conflict theaters and applied to data streams to detect objects or targets, in technology known as “computer vision.”
Since their introduction to the Iraq and Syria conflicts in December 2017, as reported by Manson, just how many of the U.S. strikes undertaken were aided by Project Maven algorithms remains classified. But some analysis is possible.
December 2017 also saw the introduction of Maven AI to Somalia, at Baledogle Airfield where U.S. special forces were stationed, according to Manson’s reporting. At that point, the U.S. had run a covert campaign of special force raids, kidnappings, and drone strikes in Somalia for over a decade, targeting insurgent groups opposed to its allies — most prominently al-Shabab.
Maven’s AI models were first trained on thousands of hours of drone footage from the country. Its integration lead, Colin Carroll, told Manson that Somalia was “more of a free-for-all” than other higher-profile American conflicts at the time, such as Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan. Manson writes that “the operational risks of messing up weren’t as high,” and that Maven’s detection mistakes were “how crews got better.”
The initial aim wasn’t accuracy: Maven’s algorithms got its detections wrong more often than not, as Manson reported. Instead, the goal was to get analysts used to having their jobs made easier by the tireless, unblinking stare of computer vision. And it was a major step to the ultimate prize of getting the broader military hooked on AI — a goal that U.S. military planners appear to have met.
Earlier this year, the U.S. deputy secretary of defense wrote to Pentagon leaders to announce that Palantir’s Maven Smart System would be made a program of record, locking in use of the technology across the U.S. military.
The Pentagon remains tight-lipped about AI’s role in given strikes, save for occasional authorized leaks or disclosures to select journalists. Therefore establishing the role of AI in civilian harm in a large enough sample of cases to draw significant conclusions is nigh impossible.
But data from the civilian harm watchdog Airwars — which has tracked alleged U.S. strikes in Somalia since 2007 — gives some understanding of what happened after computer vision was integrated into U.S. targeting.
In the two years up to the introduction of Maven in December 2017, Airwars documented 64 strikes attributed to U.S. forces in Somalia. In the two years after, that number rose to 153.
This unsurprisingly coincided with a spike in civilians being harmed. In the 64 strikes in 2016 and 2017, Airwars documented a minimum of 25 civilians killed and a further eight injured. In the two years after the introduction of Maven, the civilian kill count rose to a minimum of 79 — a more than threefold increase.
There were other factors that contributed toward these trends. Shortly before Maven was fielded in 2017, President Donald Trump designated part of the country as an “area of active hostilities.” Previously, any U.S. strike in Somalia required near certainty that the intended target was present and civilians would not be harmed, but these rules were loosened. The Trump administration also reordered the military structure, making it easier for strikes to be signed off lower down the chain of command. At the same time, private contractors came to be used more extensively.
But this dramatic increase in strikes is consistent with the goals of Project Maven — which include finding more targets, and accelerating the targeting cycle.
At the very least, there is no evidence, as advocates claim, that the introduction of AI reduced harm or made targeting more accurate. In the two years before Maven’s introduction to Somalia, civilians were reported killed or injured in roughly 1 in 7 alleged U.S. strikes. In the two years after, that rose to more than 1 in 5.
In striking similarity to Barakat’s case, less than a year after Maven’s deployment in Somalia, on August 2, 2018, U.S. Africa Command struck and killed four individuals it claimed were “terrorists” in a vehicle. Amnesty International found that three civilians had been killed, prompting the command to declassify its assessment in a disclosure to The Intercept — revealing the military didn’t know the identities of those killed.
“Critical Juncture”
This week could mark a decisive moment for the use of artificial intelligence in war. At the United Nations conference on Certain Conventional Weapons, nations will decide on adopting a mandate to begin negotiations on a new treaty to regulate autonomous weapons.
“We are at a critical juncture,” said Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of the group Stop Killer Robots, a campaign group. “The vast majority of states worldwide are in favor of a new legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons systems.”
“The first and important step in setting norms for the limits of AI-enabled, accelerated use of force is the mandate to negotiate legally binding rules for autonomous weapon systems,” said Elke Schwarz, a professor of political theory at Queen Mary University of London.
Target identification AI models, such as Maven, would not be covered by current negotiations since the U.N. definition of autonomous weapons demands that a single system both autonomously select and strike a target.
“There is a whole separate [UN] process for AI in the military domain,” van Rooijen said, “and [for that] we are nowhere near a treaty process.”
What played out in Somalia in the years after Maven’s introduction — a surge in the number of strikes and associated civilian harm — is similar to trends tracked in other recent military confrontations by actors known to use AI-powered systems.
The joint U.S.–Israeli attack on Iran ushered in a new era of AI-powered warfare. In the initial 40-day assault, the U.S. and Israel declared they struck more than 17,000 targets — a pace of warfare unparalleled in modern conflict. Airwars found that on every single day, Iranian civilians were reported killed or injured, in a total of 264 tracked civilian harm incidents.
In Somalia, the current Trump administration has already launched nearly four times the number of airstrikes than that of the Biden administration in its entire period in office, with reports of grave consequences for civilians. Last November, a U.S. airstrike reportedly killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children. No investigation appears to have been launched into the attack and, when asked by The Guardian, U.S. officials declined to provide its casualty assessment of the incident.
How machine-learning algorithms have contributed to targeting errors is compounded by misleading statements by militaries using AI.
One such case was U.S. Central Command’s response to a March 2026 investigation by Airwars and The Independent into the first known victim of an airstrike in which the use of AI-assisted targeting was acknowledged. The military command claimed that it had “no way of knowing” whether the strike in Iraq had relied on machine-learning algorithms, despite its chief technology officer initially claiming that it had.
Next Chapter in AI Warfare
Meanwhile, another, quieter development is underway that seems poised to further transform AI-powered warfare. Initiated by the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the U.S. military is planning to embrace more complex versions of already-fraught computer vision models.
The “first generation” of models applied AI object detection algorithms to images and video feeds. However, in the “next chapter,” the NGA and private contractors have been training models to spot anomalies, thus detecting not just known threats but also potential ones.
As the NGA director explained last year, it could be an adversary truck that’s out of place, or a weapons manufacturing facility that has become very busy or fallen quiet.
“Anomaly detection,” as it is known, takes computer vision one step further, by deciphering objects or targets from imagery and then applying machine reasoning to a scene to determine whether changes indicate potential threatening activity.
But computer vision-based targeting models have been plagued by inaccuracy, and therefore risks of civilian harm.
When deployed in new terrain, and where uncertain environmental conditions hinder its abilities to recognize and flag objects, the first generation of Maven models exhibited a detection accuracy below 30 percent, according to Manson’s book. At times it was less than 10 percent.
Treaty process aside, the distinction between autonomous weapons — narrowly defined — and AI-powered target identification may be one without a meaningful difference. In 2024, a Maven military exercise aimed at achieving 1,000 targeting decisions in an hour, which translates per operator as a decision to select or dismiss a target every 72 seconds.
When decision support systems serve targeting intelligence to military analysts at such intensity, the human in the loop becomes meaningless, argues Schwarz, the political theory professor.
“The use of AI target identification systems in recent conflicts in the Middle East has accelerated targeting to the point where no human decision-maker in the loop can make a truly meaningful decision, thereby becoming the proverbial cog-in-the-(killing)-machine,” she said.
“In creating an illusion of human judgment, AI-enabled targeting systems are perhaps an even more problematic technology than fully autonomous ones.”
In response to questions from Airwars and The Intercept, a Palantir spokesperson said Maven’s “superior technology is critical to both deterrence, the avoidance of wars, and the protection of civilians in the case of war.”
“Thanks to [Maven Smart System],” the spokesperson continued, “the U.S. military is now better able to protect the American people from those that seek to harm us, and is better prepared, if necessary, to win wars in a responsible, precise, and technologically-dominant manner.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
