https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-investig.title: NYPD investigating alleged sexual assault of NYU student near freshman dorm
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-investig.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-investig.text:
Police are investigating the alleged sexual assault of a 19-year-old NYU student in Greenwich Village over the weekend.
Police confirmed reports that a man allegedly assaulted the woman around 9:58 p.m. Sunday near Bleecker and Mercer streets, where NYU's John A. Paulson Center also serves as a first-year residence hall.
NYU is not conducting its own investigation because the alleged assailant is not a member of the university community, according to the school. The university says it is cooperating with the NYPD and providing support to students.
“The safety and wellbeing of our students will always come first,” said Wiley Norvell, NYU's senior vice president for university relations and public relations, in a statement. “Our focus is supporting our community and assisting the NYPD in its investigation. We strictly protect the privacy of anyone who comes forward.”
No arrests have been made, according to the police.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: Twelve gift ideas for hosts so you never show up to the party empty-handed
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Tobey Grumet Segal
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
The golden rule of holiday party going is simple: never show up empty-handed. Whether you are going for a sit-down dinner or just popping in for a drink, a small token of your appreciation is non-negotiable. But how do you best shop for the hostess (or host) with the mostest in your life? We checked in with a few etiquette experts to help you up your gifting game this season.
Thankfully, you don’t have to spend a fortune when choosing a hostess gift – especially since many of us tend to have multiple parties to attend. “I think bringing a small gift for your host or hostess is such a thoughtful gesture, especially during the holidays when so much time and care goes into welcoming family and friends,” said Shauna Varvel, author of Provence Style and owner of Le Mas des Poiriers, a farmhouse estate in Provence. “It’s a simple way to show your appreciation, and it doesn’t have to be extravagant to feel special.”
Nick Leighton, co-host of the etiquette podcast Were You Raised By Wolves?, suggests bringing something that will not give your already-busy host more work. “Flowers that need a vase? Something that has to go into the oven or freezer? Something you expect them to serve or pour at their party? All not great choices,” he said.
So before you head out for holiday party season, take a gander at these thoughtful, original gifts that will let your host or hostess know you really care.
- Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for more gift guides and holiday shopping ideas for everyone on your list.
Yes, you can still bring wine
It may feel a tad lazy, but spirits and wine are really just fine. David Jubé, founder of The Gourmet Host, suggests a bottle meant for later. “Say: ‘This one is for you, not tonight’ as you hand it over, so the host never feels obliged to open it against a menu they have already planned,” he says.
This mid-priced bottle of Pinot Noir comes straight from Oregon’s Willamette valley. It’s a round, berry-forward red wine perfect for dropping temperatures that tastes even better with a slight chill. I like to put it in the fridge and take it out a few minutes before serving, so just tuck it into the back of your host’s fridge, out of reach of greedy partygoers, so they can enjoy it another time. (If you want to bring something without alcohol, consider this beautifully packaged NA bubbly Blanc de Blanc from Elton John Zero.)
From Francis Ford Coppola to your favorite host or hostess: this two-bottle gift set is the perfect nod to both wine and movie lovers, and includes a full-bodied Zinfandel and a fresh-tasting Vermintino. It comes in a pretty black gift box so they can display it without having to open it – it can sit on a shelf until the time is right
This African-produced gin brings a little whimsy to any home bar – and it is likely something your hosts would not necessarily buy for themselves. A hint of citrus makes it an excellent addition to a Negroni, and it captures the holiday spirit for spritzes and a seasonal G+T.
Refresh their pantry
Edible gifts are always a nice gesture and they can be plenty crowd pleasing as well. If you want to arrive with something besides wine or if you know the host doesn’t drink, Jubé thinks these types of gifts are among the best ways to contribute without overstepping.
On a recent trip to Tuscany, I found myself pleasantly surprised at how flavorful the region’s olive oil is. Bold, spicy and a little peppery, it’s meant for dipping or to be used as a finishing oil. And because the product goes through such rigorous certification, it’s a little pricier than your normal, supermarket bottle. A grand gesture for the foodies in your life, who will really, truly appreciate it.
For the spice-loving hosts in your life, set aside the Carolina Reaper hot sauce gift set and switch to something a little more nuanced. These mini bottles of Fly By Jing’s best-selling condiments are not for the faint-hearted – but they will add an extra kick to eggs, rice, salad dressing and even ice-cream.
Atlas is known for its variety of coffees from around the world and this sampler gift set hits the sweet spots. Choose from whole beans or ground, with highlights from Costa Rica, Kenya, Peru and India. We especially love it for its sustainability efforts and the informational postcards that come with each pouch of coffee.
Make it nice!
Tablescapes are all the rage, so bringing something to dress up a spread is always helpful. “A great hostess gift is a little indulgence, something lovely they may never buy for themselves but are thrilled to have,” said Kelly Gaudreau, a Long Island-based tabletop and home styling expert.”
I use my salt cellar daily, and though it tends to stay in the kitchen, I also like putting it on the table during dinner parties so guests can help themselves. This petite, ceramic container comes with a lid and a small, Nanmu wooden spoon. And it is much more dramatic (and nicer to look at) than a salt shaker.
Small, charming and unexpected, I love these gorgeous bejeweled cocktail picks by artist and jewelry designer Presley Oldham. The partnership with Quattro Gatti gin, which is produced in Italy using Umbrian juniper, makes these a limited edition – and the most enticing way to spear olives for those holiday party martinis.
For me, holidays equal red wine. And I love having an everyday wine glass that is as chic as it is sturdy. Give this refined set of two crystal Pinot Noir glasses because Riedel knows drinkware. You can also use them for a robust Nebbiolo and even aperitivo time.
Don’t forget the pets
“Here’s one of my pro tips,” said Leighton. “If the host has a pet, buy for them. This has a 100% success rate.” Here are a few creative ideas to get you started.
after newsletter promotion
Get personal with this adorable, waterproof collar for any sized pup. Made from lightweight, easy-to-clean material, you can also add charms to spell out a name or nickname to further customize it. Choose from 14 different colors to make it truly theirs.
Bring a little extra holiday joy with this ceramic, hand-painted holiday keepsake that doubles as an ornament. Just find a photo of your host’s pet, upload it on Etsy, then make sure to proof the image before they ship it. They’ll surely appreciate the thought behind this gift, even if their pet doesn’t.
As a cat owner, I can attest to the allure of the floppy fish. Felines, and even small dogs, can’t get enough of the life-like wiggling motions and I especially like these from Tooge because the 3D printing is so realistic. The fish also come with a small bag of catnip, for the most discerning or hard-to-please kitties. Bring them to any party and watch the pets lose their minds.
Make their house a home
“A great host tends to have a well stocked pantry and all of the hosting essentials, so they can be hard to gift for,” said Amber Mayfield Hewett, event planner, author of recently released entertaining book, Your Turn to Host. “With this in mind, I turn to the little details that hosts will appreciate.”
A Sonic Editions gift card is my secret weapon for any hard-to-gift-for host. A curated website for fine-art photography, they will be able to choose from a vast archive of limited-edition, gallery-quality prints. Themes swing wildly from music, film and sport to travel, fashion and culture. I would tell you to check out the website yourself but there’s so much to look at, you may miss the next party.
Chances are, your host’s tea towel drawer could use a small refresh. These adorable tea towels are a great addition to the mix. Made from Geoweave, a proprietary material that the brand says is highly-absorbent, odor-resistant and quick-drying, these towels really marry form and function. This festive Frenchies design is part of a series that includes labs, poodles, doodles and dachshunds, to name a few.
Give the gift of scent with this beautiful, violet room spray from Antica Farmacista, known best for its bespoke scents at the Beverly Hills hotel and the Ritz-Carlton. A luscious combination of holiday memories such as toasty creme brulee, florals and a hint of cognac, it smells as good as it looks and they can use it in any room for a little hint of fancy.
“I love giving candles during the holidays because they’re something everyone can enjoy,” said Varvel. And I know that in my home, candles are always welcome, especially during the holidays. I like gifting these deep red oxblood tapers from H&M Home. They come in three different shapes, including two different sized spirals, and they are surprisingly affordable. And if you’d rather spare your host’s tablecloth from errant wax drips, I am obsessed with Party Favor, a Champagne fizz-scented candle (in a jar) from Minnesota-based Nose Dive.
It’s alive!
Mariah Humber, a certified etiquette expert, likes “to opt for host gifts that truly feel like a gift that can be enjoyed later rather than something the host feels obligated to tend to in the moment”. So why not give them something that needs care, just not immediately.
Yes, sourdough IS a living thing. And this starter set will allow your hosts to ease into their baking journey with a fresh, active starter paired with a stoneware crock. For sourdough newbies perhaps intimidated by the idea of a ball of living gloop sitting in their fridge, the set includes care and feeding instructions.
This affordable, organic kit comes with a humidity tent to let anyone easily grow their own mushrooms at home – right in the box. It is a simple way to learn how to grow fungi: just mist it daily with the included spray bottle and your hosts will be harvesting their own shrooms (not the psychedelic ones) in about 10 days.
Fresh flowers can be a pain when you are in the middle of hosting, so bring a nice potted plant instead. I adore these pretty, purple calla lilies because they are still a flower, but can be safely put aside with no further attention needed. They come ensconced in a washed grey wooden planter and you can choose from a small or larger size. (A word of caution: if your intended recipient has a plant-curious pet, you might want to skip this, as these plants are toxic for both dogs and cats.)
Other gift ideas you might enjoy from the Filter, the Guardian’s guide to buying fewer, better things:
- Gift ideas for the person who already has everything and personalized gifts
- Global gifts that Americans are missing out on
- Advent calendars for everyone, including chocolate and food lovers

Since Supreme Court Justice Ralph Fabrizio began presiding over criminal cases in the Bronx in 2010, attorneys on both sides of the bar have objected to his conduct.

https://citylimits.org/rent-stabilized-e.title: Rent-Stabilized East Harlem Buildings Fail To Sell At Auction, Leaving Tenants in the Lurch
https://citylimits.org/rent-stabilized-e.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/rent-stabilized-e.text:
Share This Article
Despite the Mamdani administration’s efforts to avoid the auction block, a large portfolio of former Emerald Equities’ buildings went up for sale—but failed to attract any bids at foreclosure auction, throwing tenants into an uncertain future and raising alarm about the health of the city’s rent-stabilized housing stock.
Ideally, “we shouldn’t even be going to an auction,” organizer Sergio Sorza lamented.
Tenant leaders, community organizers, and members of the East Harlem Community Land Trust were huddled in the hallway outside a Manhattan courtroom, still abuzz with the frenzy of a dozen foreclosure auctions that concluded in rapid succession last Tuesday.
They were a bit shell-shocked.
“I’m pissed,” said Vic Washington, a tenant of a building on East 103rd Street included in the auction.
It’s part of a nearly 900-unit portfolio of 39 mostly rent-stabilized buildings, once owned by Emerald Equities’ Isaac Kassirer, many of which went up for foreclosure sale last week, despite the efforts of Washington, her tenant union, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration.
Of the 27 buildings in the portfolio up for auction over the past two weeks, 26 attracted no bids. One building on East 114th Street sold for $826,000, splitting the tenants and throwing their plans—to steer the properties to their preferred buyers, who could work to preserve the apartments—into uncertainty.
It’s another twist in the Mamdani administration’s efforts to intervene in the sales of distressed affordable housing.
“It makes it more challenging, but we’re up for the challenge,” said Washington, who also works at the El Barrio Community Land Trust.
Tenants in five Emerald Equities buildings on East 103rd Street won a rent strike in 2025 before expanding their organizing across the rest of the real estate group’s portfolio and starting a “buyer beware” campaign.
Tenants called for a responsible owner—preferably a nonprofit that would help them turn some of the apartments into affordable coops—to take over. The city took notice, and backed a bid from preservation buyer Spatial Equity.
But the city’s efforts to push for a sale failed, as the creditor, Sabal Investment Holdings, rejected Spatial Equity’s offers of $68 and $110 million in July and October, according to reporting by both City Limits and Gothamist.
If banks holding the roughly $250 million in debt on the properties hoped for a better deal at auction, it didn’t materialize Tuesday. Instead, tenants are back to the drawing board, trying to get repairs on their neglected buildings.
“We are disappointed that one of these buildings was apparently purchased by a third party, assuming this sale goes through,” said Matt Latterner, a staff attorney at Legal Services NYC working with the tenants. “We do have a tenant’s association in this building and we are prepared to stand by those tenants as they seek to get repairs and fight the illegal overcharges.”
‘Going once, going twice… back to the plaintiff.’
At foreclosure auctions, investors can bid for buildings on the cheap, looking for financial upside.
But one after the other, as Emerald Equities’ buildings were announced on consecutive Tuesdays this month, auctions closed without a bid, sending them back to the bank for just $500 apiece.
At auction, bids must clear the “upset price”—a figure that matches the size of the judgement the bank holds. Only one building, 417 East 114th St., a skinny three story walk-up that looks out over Thomas Jefferson park, sold at auction, for $1,000 above the upset price of $826,000.
It was sold to a bidder, “Matt,” who, according to court papers, bid on behalf of 135th Place LLC, a group linked to Isaac Badalov, who owns one other building in Rockaway, according to Who Owns What. Attempts to reach representatives from LLCs associated with Badalov and his business address were unsuccessful.
While the tenants hope the scarce interest from buyers leaves the door open for nonprofit ownership, it alarmed landlords.
The prices of heavily rent-stabilized buildings like those in the Emerald Equities portfolio are flagging. “Nobody wants to own these buildings,” said Kenny Burgos, CEO of the New York Apartment Association.
Burgos’s group says that New York’s rent stabilization policies, including 2019 changes to state law that made it harder for owners to deregulate buildings, have limited landlords’ ability to increase rent to keep pace with expenses and repairs.
Banks are not in the business of operating housing, Burgos said, and are looking for the best deal—but don’t realize just how little interest owners have in these buildings. “The banks are still in this disbelief stage that the values have fallen so drastically,” he said.
But tenants say it’s because Emerald Equities neglected the buildings, destroying their value. They complain about pests, mold, heat outages, and unsafe conditions across the portfolio, which had 2,300 open housing code violations as of this summer.
“I think what we’re looking at is an unprecedented reckoning for how these buildings have been managed,” said Cami Dominguez, a staff organizer with Community Voices Heard.
Washington said that Emerald Equities and the banks have no one but themselves to blame, taking out an irresponsible level of debt, hoping to be able to take some of the units out of rent stabilization—until reforms in 2019 that closed rent-raising loopholes foiled their plans.
“These banks overleveraged their hand. They over-lent to a clearly irresponsible landlord who wasn’t able to properly steward these buildings, and now the tenants are facing the brunt of that,” said Washington.
Nonprofit owners may face some of the same challenges as their for profit peers, with rising maintenance and insurance costs.
“Purchasing or rehabbing rent stabilization is hard. The amount of money in it is really hard,” said Brian Peters, executive director of the El Barrio Community Land Trust. “So anybody who’s going to commit to it, it’s got to make financial sense. And clearly, for a for-profit entity, it’s not making sense—99 percent of people [are] saying this doesn’t make sense to buy at these prices.”
The mayor’s original plan makes sense to Peters—have a preservation buyer come in, with city support, and spin off some of the buildings on East 103rd Street for a community land trust, which would own the land and govern it through a resident board, managed by El Barrio.
Putting distressed rentals in the hands of community groups and trusted nonprofits is a pillar of Mamdani’s housing plan—and he just signed a bill, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, that may open up more opportunities for groups like Peters’ to buy.
“The goals are different. The money is different,” said Peters. “For non-profits, it’s just used to maintain the building. It’s not going anywhere.”
But groups like his need financial support from the city to be able to afford the high costs of preserving housing.
The mayor’s office has intervened strategically to try and push vulnerable portfolios of housing to preferred buyers, as they tried earlier this year with more than 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments formerly owned by Pinnacle Realty.
Those efforts have seen mixed results. Even when sales don’t go their way—as was the case with the Pinnacle units—tenant unions say their organizing helped them extract key concessions from new ownership.
But the scale of the problem in rent-stabilized housing, according to Burgos, outpaces the city’s resources to preserve them.
“Lost in all of this is that tenants get stuck in limbo,” said Burgos.
“Policy after policy ignores the underlying math,” he added. “[The mayor] will not be able to intervene and scale to every building…that is a futile effort.”
What’s next for tenants?
Going to auction throws tenants into another round of uncertainty, and each day in ownership limbo is another lived in poor conditions.
With most of the buildings back in the bank’s hands, tenants hope to resurrect their vision of a preservation buyer and a community land trust. A court-appointed receiver currently manages the buildings.
“We might not today have the power to influence the sale, but the majority of tenants coming together to understand the conditions and chart their own path forward, that’s what the tenant union is doing,” said Dominguez.
With little to show from the foreclosure, tenants are hoping that Spatial Equity’s $110 million offer now looks more appealing to the banks.
“It’s just adding extra steps, but the fight is still one and the same,” said Sorza, who works for the nonprofit Community Voices Heard.
For tenants in 417 East 114th St., the lone property that sold, the uncertainty is compounded by their uncoupling from the rest of the portfolio.
“We said ‘buyer beware’… we’re going to be on their necks,” said Washington. “Whoever buys these buildings is going to inherit a lot of violations, a lot of work that they’re going to be doing, and a whole lot of organizing that’s been behind each and every tenant in this building.”
Where the Mamdani administration and Spatial Equity want to go from here remains to be seen. Spatial Equity head Teg Sethi did not respond to requests for comment.
“The Mayor’s Office is proud to support the tenants of the East Harlem Tenants Union as they organize for better living conditions and more control over the future of their homes,” said Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants’ leader Cea Weaver in a statement.
With Pinnacle’s portfolio now in private hands and Emerald Equities’ buildings up for grabs, it’s not yet clear if the administration’s plans to steer more affordable housing into community hands will work.
“They’re developing a strategy. It’s in progress,” said Dominguez.
When new owners Summit, who bought the Pinnacle portfolio, agreed to make repairs in bankruptcy court, the Mamdani administration claimed a partial victory.
Washington said she isn’t ready to call that a win.
“Let’s get the show on the road. Let’s get these buildings fixed,” she said.
“The amount of concessions that some of my neighbors have had to make is more than enough,” Washington added. “Some of us, some of my neighbors, don’t have doors. They don’t have ceilings that are working properly. Their apartments are not comfortable. They don’t have cooking gas. They don’t have heat. I think we’ve made enough concessions.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexandra Martinez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.
In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Oorganisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.
“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.
The campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.
For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.
Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.
And yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.
“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”
According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.
Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.
“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.
Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.
The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.
As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.
Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.
For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.
“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mokhtefi-alg.title: The American Woman Who Joined Algeria’s Socialist Experiment
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mokhtefi-alg.author: Julia Harte
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mokhtefi-alg.text:
The American Woman Who Joined Algeria’s Socialist Experiment
Elaine Mokhtefi has died. The Jewish New Yorker was the only American to serve in Algeria’s government after independence, and she spent a decade at the center of the Third World revolution.
Within days of arriving in Algeria, months after its liberation from France in 1962, Elaine Klein knew she was there for the long haul. “The experiment to create a new socialist country from the impoverished colony, the tremendous task of building a state respected in the international arena, was daunting,” she later wrote. Yet, “My gut told me that I would settle here.”
Her intuition was correct. For more than a decade, the Jewish New Yorker was the only American in Algeria’s new government. She assumed a range of roles — reporter, translator, envoy — as the former French colony established itself as an international haven for resistance groups, political dissidents, and anti-colonial organizers. Klein was not the only one taking on new responsibilities. A national program of popular self-management, or “autogestion,” was implemented soon after the revolution, giving the Algerian people ownership of the farms, businesses, and buildings abandoned by fleeing European settlers.
A coup led by military chief Houari Boumédiène overthrew the first postcolonial government. The autogestion experiment largely ended, though Boumédiène kept trying to close Algeria’s wealth gap and resist economic subordination by the Global North. Klein also continued to cover progressive and socialist assemblages around the world on behalf of the national press agency, Algérie Presse Service. When the Organization of Latin American Solidarity gathered in Cuba in 1967 to form a united front against US imperialism, she attended a press conference where Stokely Carmichael called “white Western imperialist society” the “common enemy” of all the delegates present and declared, “Our struggle is to overthrow this system which feeds itself and expands itself through the economic and cultural exploitation of nonwhite, non-Western peoples.” Klein took the opportunity to invite Carmichael to visit Algeria later that year: his first trip to the African continent.
Into the early 1970s, she served as a sort of domestic ambassador for other Black Panthers and leaders of international revolutionary movements who flocked to open offices in Algiers, a city dubbed the “Mecca of Revolution” by Pan-African Bissau-Guinean poet Amílcar Cabral and the “third world capital” by Klein. Her work brought her under the scope of a vast CIA operation aimed at uncovering foreign involvement in domestic protest movements within the United States. The FBI’s COINTELPRO initiative helped drive a wedge between the international wing of the Black Panther Party, which Klein helped establish, and their US-based counterparts. After more than a decade in Algeria, Klein herself was forced to leave when she refused to spy on a friend for the Boumédiène regime.
Her idealism, however, never wavered. Until her death this September, she followed an irrepressible impulse to stand with other humans fighting for freedom and self-government, no matter where they were. And despite the remarkable role she played in some of the twentieth century’s most historic anti-colonial, social ownership, and civil rights movements, she never thought of herself as anything more or less than a world citizen.
Revolution in the Third World
Klein first encountered the Algerian anti-colonial movement at the 1952 May Day parade in Paris. She had moved to France months earlier, after being pushed out of her job in New York with the United World Federalists (UWF). The UWF, part of an emerging “world government” movement that aimed to eradicate war and establish a system of global justice, had fractured due to internal divisions and external pressure from US authorities, a process that would recur with many causes Klein championed over time.
After moving to Paris, she began learning the history of decolonization in North and West Africa through work as a French–English conference interpreter. In 1960, the year that eleven African countries — including nine former French colonies — became independent, she helped organize a congress in Ghana, the first African state to shake off colonial rule. There she developed a fast friendship with Frantz Fanon, whom the Algerian provisional government had recently named their ambassador to Ghana.
Back in New York later that year, Klein met the Algerian provisional government’s representative to the United Nations. He hired her on the spot to write promotional material and lobby for Algerian independence at the United Nations. On December 19, 1960, those efforts would pay off when the General Assembly voted 63–8 to recognize Algeria’s right to self-rule. (The United States and twenty-seven other countries abstained.) As Mokhtefi later told me, the unexpected job was a long-awaited opportunity for “digging in” and “getting my hands dirty” in the decolonization cause that she had long supported.
When France recognized Algerian independence in the summer of 1962, a brief power struggle ensued inside the National Liberation Front, the party that had led Algeria’s revolution. One of the Front’s original leaders, Ahmed Ben Bella, and Boumédiène, the head of his army, took control of Algiers in September. Klein arrived in October and started working for the tourism authority, a largely theoretical job in a country that would receive no tourists for years to come. Upon learning she was from New York, Ben Bella’s press and information adviser hired her as his assistant. From there, she was transferred to the government’s secretary general, an office that produced agendas, reports, and press releases for meetings of Algeria’s cabinet. Finally, she was moved to Algérie Presse Service, where she wrote daily op-eds and became the entire “English desk.”
Ben Bella was an outspoken adherent of Third Worldism, the anti-imperialist, anti-racist movement through which current and former colonies united to resist oppression by European powers as well as, eventually, the American and Sino-Soviet blocs during the Cold War. Third Worldists, as political scientist Robert Malley put it, had an “uneasy coexistence” with the Eurocentrism and cultural superiority embedded in some Marxist theory; Friedrich Engels in 1848 had described France’s conquest of Algeria as “an important and fortunate fact for the progress of civilization.”
Yet following the 1962 exodus of French colonists, or “pieds noirs,” socialists from around the world flocked to Algeria, drawn by the revolutionaries’ vision of a more democratic, egalitarian state. These foreigners would become known as “pieds rouges” after Ben Bella’s overthrow ousted many of them from Algeria too. Among them was the Greek Trotskyist Michalis Raptis, aka Michel Pablo. While leading the Fourth International during the 1950s, Pablo had devised a counterfeit-money scheme to buy weapons for Algerian revolutionaries on the world market and had established an arms factory for them in Morocco.
Soon after Pablo arrived in independent Algeria, he became an economic adviser to Ben Bella, presiding over the campaign of “autogestion” that put the nation’s resources under popular control. Modeled on similar experiments in Cuba and Yugoslavia — countries that also sent medical teams to Algeria to help replace the European health care personnel who had fled — Algeria’s self-management program established worker-run committees to oversee the farms, industrial enterprises, and estates left behind by the colonial regime. After attending an Algerian congress on industrial self-management in 1964, the Trotskyist French militant Daniel Guérin wrote that the event had been “dominated” by the emergence of “a working class, of a socialist awareness.” Ben Bella himself embraced socialism at public rallies and within his government, opening a National Office for the Support of the Socialist Sector.
This enthusiasm was short-lived, however. Ben Bella’s other advisers persuaded him to fold the socialist sector support office into the agricultural ministry and to exert more central control over the self-managed farms, giving rise to a corrupt bureaucracy. While the National Liberation Front continued to publicly tout Algeria as a self-managed socialist state, the country slipped further from that ideal. “Power and increasing adulation isolated [Ben Bella] from a truthful examination of events,” according to Klein. “He launched new national projects every day, but neglected the measures required to implement them; he created offices and agencies that functioned in name only.” Ben Bella also began to take more punitive measures against domestic dissidents, arresting, torturing and banishing those who criticized him.
Three years after Algeria had won its independence, Boumédiène led a coup in which Ben Bella was arrested. It was the result of an internal power struggle more than an ideological rift; Boumédiène would continue to pursue some of the same progressive social policies and redistribution measures as his predecessor. But many pieds rouges, including Pablo, were branded foreign atheists and forced out of Algeria. Klein stayed, even though she had joined popular protests against the coup. Her fluency in English and French — a rare combination in postrevolutionary Algeria — had made her useful to the foreign affairs minister, Abdelaziz Bouteflika, a key ally of Boumédiène. “Hope remained that one day everything would be put right,” Klein later wrote. “And we all went back to work.”
Panthers, Trotskyists, and G-Men
In the summer of 1969, two years after she had invited Carmichael to Algeria and shown him around the country, Klein received a call that another Black Panther leader was in Algiers — and needed her help establishing a permanent presence there. Eldridge Cleaver had fled the United States several months earlier after exchanging shots with Oakland police the night of Martin Luther King Jr’s assassination. For Klein, who had protested racial segregation in the United States since college and reported on the rise of the Black Panther Party for the Algerian press, the opportunity to work for the Panthers was thrilling. As with many in the Third Worldist movement, she saw anti-racist and anti-colonial activism as inseparable.
Klein helped formalize Cleaver’s status in the country by involving him in the world’s first Pan-African Cultural Festival, which she organized in Algiers soon after his arrival. She also helped Cleaver and other Panthers establish the party’s international branch there, and accompanied his wife Kathleen on a speaking tour back in the United States. As Cleaver settled into Algeria, he took a more militantly anti-American stance and strengthened the Panthers’ Third World, anti-colonial bona fides through new alliances with figures such as North Korea’s Kim Il Sung and the Palestinian Fatah leader Yasser Arafat. In a 1971 interview with a San Francisco radio station, Cleaver proudly claimed that Black Panther members serving in Vietnam had switched sides, fighting against the US war effort there.
These moves clashed with the priorities of the US-based Panthers, who, depleted of personnel and funds by the number of Panthers who had ended up in prison, were trying to put more resources into peaceful community service programs. In March 1970, as part of its COINTELPRO effort to “expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize the activities of black nationalist, hate-type organizations and groupings,” the FBI’s second most powerful official recommended that the Bureau send Cleaver a letter “aimed at inflaming the dispute” by telling Cleaver he was being undercut by US-based Black Panther Party leaders. One year later, as Cleaver was on the brink of completely falling out with one such leader, Huey Newton, J. Edgar Hoover endorsed a plan to send Cleaver and Newton spurious correspondence designed to “provoke the existing difficulty” between them. One fake letter purported to show Newton denouncing Cleaver to Boumédiène.
Tensions between the Algerian government and the Black Panthers, meanwhile, had been building, exacerbated by the Panthers’ disinclination to integrate into Algerian society. There was also a fundamental contradiction between the goals of the Algiers-based Panthers and those of the Algerian government. For Cleaver, the Black Panther Party had a singular objective: overthrowing the US government. But Algerian leaders wanted to limit their military aid to freedom fighters trying to liberate their countries from foreign colonization.
The mutual frustration between the Algerian authorities and their American guests peaked in August 1972. That month, members of the Black Liberation Army, a splinter group started by former Black Panthers who had rejected Huey Newton as too moderate, hijacked a Delta flight from Detroit destined for Miami and landed it in Algiers. They planned to donate their $1 million ransom from the airline to the international Black Panthers, but Algerian authorities confiscated the funds and returned them to Delta. When Cleaver demanded the money, local police raided the Panther villa and took their weapons. Cleaver was never officially deported, but with other Panthers also leaving Algiers, he decided to leave.
To extract Cleaver from Algeria, Klein enlisted the help of none other than Michel Pablo, who had fled to France after Boumédiène’s 1965 coup. The former Fourth International secretary and Ben Bella adviser who had once counterfeited money to supply arms to Algeria’s revolutionary army sprang into action once more to help a different kind of revolutionary leave Algeria. Pablo gave Klein the number of a “passer” who could meet Cleaver at the Geneva airport and covertly drive him over the border into France. Pablo also supplied her with a “classy British passport with a photo of a Black man who could have been a younger Eldridge,” as Klein wrote in her memoir. She arranged a safe house for Cleaver and helped him find French lawyers to petition for his asylum there.
Klein’s own position in Algeria was becoming more precarious under Boumédiène’s regime. In 1972, security agents asked her to spy on a friend of hers who had married Ben Bella, and she refused. Two years later, Klein herself was forced into exile from the country to which she had devoted her life. But she had a companion by her side. Two years earlier, a mutual friend had set her up with Mokhtar Mokhtefi: a dashing hero of the Algerian Revolution, who was also rapidly growing disillusioned with the authoritarian turn of the post-independence leadership. When Mokhtefi ended up in France, Mokhtar followed, and they lived there for two decades, doing a mix of odd jobs — from making jewelry to writing children’s books — before moving to the United States in 1994.
As she forged a new life first in Paris and ultimately in New York City, Algeria underwent its own identity crises and political convulsions, straying even farther from the socialist ambitions that had defined its early years of independence. When Bouteflika — the Boumédiène-aligned foreign affairs minister who had used Klein’s translation services in the 1960s — became president of Algeria in 1999, he shored up his power by enriching a small group of oligarchs at the expense of the general population.
Twenty years into his presidency, Bouteflika was forced out of office by the largest popular opposition movement in Algeria since the revolution that had launched his political career sixty years earlier. On November 1, 2019, the sixty-fifth anniversary of the start of the revolution, tens of thousands of demonstrators who called themselves the Hirak (Arabic for “movement”) surged through Algiers to protest Bouteflika’s final efforts to cling to power. “Algeria will take back its independence,” they chanted in Arabic, clapping in time to the syncopated rallying cry. Young and old Algerians waved flags as they marched in the streets or banged on pots and pans from their windows in solidarity.
Among the protesters thronging the main streets of Algiers so densely that it was almost impossible to move, Elaine Klein — now Elaine Mokhtefi and ninety years old — could be seen in the crowd, glowing with excitement and cheering on the Hirak with the slogans of the new revolutionaries.
“I’ve Started to Talk, and I Don’t Stop”
I first visited Mokhtefi at her Manhattan apartment in 2021, when I emailed her out of the blue to ask if I could interview her for a book I was writing about Americans who had traveled abroad to join revolutionary liberation movements. We spoke for several hours about the remarkable trajectory of her life and the causes she and Mokhtar continued to support after moving back to the United States. It was a lonely repatriation for Mokhtefi, at first: “There was nobody to tell what had happened, neither about the Black Panthers, nor about the Algerian war. Everyone seemed very far from all that.” But she and Mokhtar were not idle. “We had to contribute,” she said. “We had to show that we were still responsible world citizens.” They joined Palestinian liberation demonstrations, climate justice marches, and visited encamped protesters at Zuccotti Park several times during the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement.
Mokhtar died in 2015, forty-three years after he and Mokhtefi first met. Writing her memoir, Algiers, Third World Capital: Freedom Fighters, Revolutionaries, Black Panthers, Mokhtefi told me, had saved her from a pit of grief that she feared might swallow her up. But ever since it was published in 2018, “and I went on these tours, and I saw that people were really interested in what I had lived,” she continued, “I’ve started to talk, and I don’t stop.”
I stayed in touch with Mokhtefi as I continued working on my chapter about her. In 2022, I went to Algiers to visit prominent sites from her time there and interview former Algerian revolutionaries whose paths had crossed with hers. Eventually she met my partner and daughter, and I got to know many of her friends. Every time we saw each other, I marveled at how busy her social life and traveling schedule remained, even as she grew frailer and memories eluded her more often. In August, I visited her apartment one last time to attend a party she threw to celebrate receiving Algerian nationality in recognition of her service to the nation. By then, I had a copy of my own book to give her.
A few weeks later — three days before her sudden death — she emailed me, telling me she had started reading my book from the beginning, but that about halfway through the second chapter, “I couldn’t hold myself back, I had to read about me. I just wasn’t capable of waiting my turn. What an experience . . . Thanks, merci, gracias, saha as the Algerians say, the works. I felt so full of myself, validated well beyond any merit.”
She told me how lucky she felt that we had entered each other’s lives. Then she added, “I will read the other chapters and see your perspective through to the end, and with such pleasure. With love, Elaine.”

Two landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have come up with plans rivaling Trump’s proposed triumphal arch at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., Dezeen reports. The students, Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, based their two alternative designs on previous historical proposals for the site.
In the first proposal, Dvorak and Geitner replace a central roundabout, which is currently filled with turf, with a large pool of water and add a natural-stone perimeter inscribed with the words “belonging and unity.”
The second proposal replaces the grassy roundabout with a straight boulevard that connects Memorial Avenue to the nearby Arlington Memorial Bridge. Two circular fountains flank the roadway, housed in low-lying stone mounds replete with planters. During commemorative events when the bridge is closed, the complex would be flooded to create a single pool of water.
Dvorak and Geitner noted that the fountains’ “geometries arise from the site’s historic proposals, combining concentric circles, intersecting alignments, and formal planting into a composition that acknowledges history whilst creating its own present identity.” They added, “In this way the landscape becomes a physical record of its own change.”
After attending a GSD seminar taught by Charles A. Birnbaum, a founding partner of Washington, D.C. nonprofit the Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF), Dvorak and Geitner were inspired to base their work on public participation and historical inquiry—elements they found lacking in the government’s planning process.
“By recognizing Memorial Circle’s implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design’s capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape,” they said.
Trump’s gilded, neoclassical arch has come under fire by various parties for blocking views to Arlington National Cemetery. Construction, which was set to begin in September, is currently on hold; Judge Tonya Chutkan temporarily blocked the work earlier this month.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Imogen Tilden
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different.
Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.
My photography is collaborative. I brought some visual ideas to the shoot, and Meg brought her own ways of moving and expressing herself. The photograph developed between us. I took references from art history: Jenny Saville’s nudes and Lucian Freud’s work have inspired me, along with the sense of flesh and physical presence in Rubens’ paintings.
I lit her in a painterly way and used a canvas backdrop. As I was photographing her, I found myself getting lower down. I wanted the body to have a real presence in the photograph, to become the portrait itself. It was Meg’s idea to scrunch her belly in that way. I asked her to look away so that her face wouldn’t be the first place your eye went. I love how fleshy the image feels. Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate who someone is. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture.
Meg loved it and was delighted when the image was selected to be displayed in the National Portrait Gallery. Her nude modelling is only a small part of what she does – most of her time and energies go into raising awareness about overconsumption and the “tat” that fills our lives and ends up in landfill. She’s a superstar on TikTok!
“Fat women’s femininity is [often] stripped from them and … I am masculinised and called brave for just existing in this body. When I am life modelling, I feel the most feminine and deeply in touch with myself. I am proud to take up space and represent people who often are not,” she says.
My commissioned work specialises in boudoir and nude photography. Coming to this has been a personal journey. I was very critical of my body – I was one of those women who couldn’t look in a mirror. For me, being behind the camera was also a way of avoiding being in photographs. I liked having that control. I started out doing headshots, but when you run your own business, you need to be visible. I became frustrated with all the negative feelings I had about myself, and one day I stripped off and I took my own photographs of my nude body. And when I looked over the images I was shocked to realise that I didn’t hate them. In fact I thought they were beautiful.
And then I noticed a change in myself. I was walking down the street taller. I wasn’t wearing cardigans to hide my arms. And I realised that maybe I can help others. I don’t think a photograph can resolve someone’s relationship with their body, but it can be one part of seeing themselves differently, feeling more connected to their body, or recognising that they are worthy of being seen.
But there is a tension in my work between beauty standards and how women want to be seen. Much of the boudoir photography I do sits in that culture that shapes how women think they should look and what makes a body beautiful or desirable. But who decides what makes a body either of these things? Women’s bodies don’t exist to meet someone else’s expectations of beauty or desirability, which change over time. There is room for wanting to feel sexy, but whose idea of sexy are we working towards?
When I make or look at a nude photograph, I ask what the pose, light, colour and composition are communicating. Whose perspective is shaping the image, and how much say does the person being photographed have in how they are seen?
With Body Like Mine, I want to give more space to people’s own accounts of living in their bodies, particularly where those experiences differ from what others assume when they look at them. The next person I’m photographing lives with endometriosis, and another participant is experiencing memory loss. I want us to explore how those experiences might be expressed in a photograph, guided by what each person wants to share.
Before we photograph, I ask each person to choose a few words that describe what they would like us to express together. Those words give us a starting point for the images. Meg’s were “real”, “joyful” and “free”.
Body Like Mine is part of the Winston Taylor photo portrait prize exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, London, until 17 January. siornaphotography.com; @siornaphotography
Siorna Ashby CV
Born: Blackpool, 1983
 
High point: Having my photograph of Meg Foster, Body Like Mine, selected for the National Portrait Gallery’s Winston Taylor photo portrait prize 2026 exhibition.
 
Top tip: Talk through boundaries before artistic nude or boudoir photoshoots, and keep checking in as you work. Make it easy for someone to change their mind, and be ready to adapt a pose, change direction or put the camera down.

Make America Function Again!
Who is going to fix all the things the Republicans, corporations, and tech titans broke?
The thing about bills is that they always come due. Americans are starting to see the true price of years of Republican malfeasance, corporate greed, and rushed reliance on unproven artificial intelligence systems. That price looks like e-mail outages. It looks like nationwide flight ground stops. It looks like data breaches, malware attacks, and the enshittification of every product, good, or service available for purchase.
America is not a failed state—not yet at least. In the scholarship, a “failed state” is one that has lost its monopoly on the legitimate use of force, and one that cannot provide basic public services. We’re not there yet; our extrajudicial murder force, ICE, still technically acts under the color of government authority. And the government, at the federal as well as state and local levels, still has the ability to provide services: We can maintain the electrical grid, support a transportation network, and (mostly) deliver clean drinking water to those lucky enough to have homes and not live in Michigan. We just screw up the delivery of those services with increasing and alarming frequency.
The United States is not failed, but it’s far from functional. We’re a nation held together by duct tape and super glue. Everybody can see the cracks forming, and people are starting to realize that there is nobody minding the store. There are a few heroic individuals holding their fingers in the dam, and we’re all just hoping the dam doesn’t break today.
Everyone knows the broad contours of how we got here. Republicans run for office on the claim that government cannot work, and then spend their time in power destroying government just to prove that they were right. Neoliberals help Republicans by ceding critical government functions to the private sector, which in turn ignores the public good in an all-consuming chase for greater margins and profits. Occasionally things get so bad that the people elect leaders who are modestly responsible—who fix things just enough that the next guy (and it’s pretty much always a guy) can come in and complain about taxes and Black people and get elected to wreck the government again.
The latest version of this cycle has been especially damaging because the second Trump administration was captured by people who had a plan to destroy the government (Project 2025), and Trump then went ahead and empowered Elon Musk as the chainsaw-wielding destructor. With a truly breathtaking lack of knowledge or care, Musk did serious harm to the functioning of the government by firing career professionals who actually understood how everything worked. Everybody can complain about the incompetent rogue’s gallery of cabinet secretaries Trump has appointed, but it is the loss of these institutional experts that has done the most damage to the United States’s ability to work properly. The grounding of every plane in the country is just one of the more obvious consequences of Musk and his DOGE initiative, but there are many others.
Musk is also the bridge between the dysfunction of our government and the dysfunction of our society more generally, because he is one of the eight to 10 oligarchs who have amassed power at an unbelievable scale. We live in a world where if one of these guys (and once again, they’re all guys) has a bad day, everybody has a bad day. If one of them decides to bump chips with a spy, entire industries can be manipulated. If one of them changes the algorithm, our whole perception of reality can be warped. We have global “key man risk.”
And then there’s the tech these oligarches have helped create. The problem is not that we’re reliant on technology; humans have always relied on technology, whether that technology was a spearpoint or a fish hook or Uber Eats. The problem is that the tech is no longer made to be reliable. The tech is made to make money. Everything is designed either to break or become obsolete so we have to buy a new thing.
Then that nondurable tech is integrated into a bunch of other nondurable tech so that if one thing breaks it can cause a cascade of failures. Somebody introduces a bug into a hardware system, and suddenly we cannot access our bank accounts. Somebody installs a new router, and suddenly the airplanes cannot fly. Somebody hacks into a software program and suddenly all the refrigerators in the supermarket stop working.
Oh, and just in case you think I am merely listing petty inconveniences, the National Security Agency’s internal communication system went down while I was writing this.
The monopolies controlled by the oligarchs and the integration of their tech into everything we use combine to destroy our system resiliency. If one system fails, entire systems fail. The tech bros always claim to have various contingencies, but because of conglomeration, we don’t have backups for when those contingencies fail.
On top of all of this, these same oligarchs are pushing to incorporate artificial intelligence into everything. This is a technology that few people understand, and worse, the ones who do understand it are warning us that they can’t control it. We’re also using the AI to replace human workers, so when the AI breaks, our only choice is to ask the AI how to fix it. Wonderful world we’re building here.
All of this political, corporate, and technological dysfunction has a natural endpoint: People will get hurt; people will suffer. Some might eventually die. Hell, we have managed to bring back measles. There is no clearer indication that things no longer work the way they should than people getting sick from a disease previous generations worked hard to eradicate.
What naturally follows from this gross incompetence is social unrest. Once people can’t reliably go about their daily lives without hassle, the pitchforks and torches come out. We’re seeing a little of this already. In the midterm elections, people who were willing to suffer Trump’s racism, misogyny, thievery, buffonery, incompetence, and incontinence decided to vote for Democrats for the first time in their lives because they couldn’t afford gas and eggs.
The affordability crisis is a symptom of the deeper rot in our society. Things don’t work. Things are expensive and still don’t work. Things that worked yesterday might not work tomorrow—and the update you’ve been forced to download to make it work might brick your whole system.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
A political leader could rise by running on a platform restoring functionality to our daily lives. I’d hope that such a leader would be a progressive, but I’ll remind readers that fascists and authoritarians have earned a lot of supporters over the course of history simply by making things, like trains, work. Running on an agenda of making things work properly is usually very popular, and it gets more popular the crappier things are.
I also want to be clear that I’m not talking about an institutionalist platform—I have lived through the Joe Biden era of restoring competency to government and found it lacking. I’m talking about a radical, populist platform that improves people’s daily lives and kneecaps the kleptocrats running the joint. Everybody’s flights didn’t get canceled because Sean Duffy is an incompetent boob (though he is an incompetent boob). Everybody’s flights got canceled because there was some stupid problem caused by our long failure to invest in our infrastructure—and when there was a problem, rich people were able to opt out of the entire system and charter their way home. Markwayne Mullen was literally able to fly to a football game (football teams also saw their travel prioritized, for honestly no good reason) while regular people were still sleeping in airports with their children.
Making America functional again means prioritizing the needs of people over the needs of investors. It means paying more attention to purchasing power than to quarterly profits. It means valuing durability over planned obsolescence. It means busting monopolies and restoring consumer protections. It means testing experimental technologies before they are approved for wide-scale use instead of treating every American as a beta tester or lab rat. It means being able to fill a prescription provided by your doctor without having to spend two hours on hold with your insurance company. And, for the love of humanity, it means regulating AI.
It’s one thing for stuff to break. Entropy is undefeated, but enshittification is a choice. Things are breaking because a small cadre of people have decided it’s more profitable for things to break than it is for things to last. We’re not suffering because of the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune. We’re suffering because we are paying for the fortunes of others. My computer is more expensive because AI is buying up all the RAM. My water is more expensive because AI is sucking up all the water. And all the while my e-mail sometimes doesn’t work, probably because of some AI assistant I never even asked for.
You know how most zombie movies depict “the day” the zombie plague becomes active and society is destroyed? There are always planes falling out of the sky and car crashes and fires, and the hero ends up surviving because they were functionally off the grid that day by some happenstance? The problem with these movies is that societies don’t collapse in a day (well, maybe Pompeii, but that’s an exception). They fall apart over a long period of time. Things stop working; people adjust and make workarounds, and soon enough nobody can remember what it was like when that thing worked. And within a generation or two, you go from reading a scroll in a Roman library to using the paper with the weird markings on them for kindling.
We need to make America functional again—before nobody remembers how to fix it.

https://gothamist.com/news/dna-and-photo.title: DNA, photos could link alleged Central Park serial rapist to 3 assaults, prosecutors say
https://gothamist.com/news/dna-and-photo.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/dna-and-photo.text:
The man who allegedly raped a woman in Central Park in October will likely be linked to two additional, similar incidents in the park through DNA and photographic evidence, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Manhattan assistant district attorney Maxine Rosenthal told the court that DNA swabs from the genital areas of three different women matched that of 30-year-old Dereck Rivera-Deleon, who was extradited from Florida to New York City and arraigned on two counts of predatory sexual assault.
One of the counts stems from the Oct. 24 assault, in which prosecutors said Rivera-Deleon threatened a 39-year-old woman at knifepoint, took her into Central Park near East 67th Street and East Drive, and sexually assaulted her. A witness later identified him in a photo array, Rosenthal said.
According to prosecutors, the other count is connected to a nearly identical incident on July 18, 2021. The victim in that case identified Rivera-Deleon in a photo array “as the man who took her into Central Park and engaged in a forceful sexual encounter,” but police were unable to locate him at the time, Rosenthal said.
Investigators are also working to connect Rivera-Deleon to a rape that was reported in the park in October 2023, where the victim also identified him in a photo array, according to prosecutors. Rosenthal told the court that DNA collected from an anal swab in the 2023 case matched the DNA collected from the victim in the October 2026 case.
Rosenthal said Rivera-Deleon fled south after the most recent incident because he saw himself on the news and realized that police were looking for him. He was taken into custody last week at a Burger King in Miami by NYPD detectives assigned to the U.S. Marshals regional fugitive task force, police said.
Rivera-Deleon did not speak throughout the brief proceeding, and did not enter a plea. He was dressed in a white T-shirt and sneakers, and his feet were shackled and chained together.
Rivera-Deleon’s defense attorney, Cara Mazor, argued for the judge to set “some amount of bail” because he has a limited criminal history, with one arrest from 2015.
But Judge Shirin Zarabi, citing the “seriousness of the allegations,” ordered him held in jail without bail as the case proceeds.
Rivera-Deleon will be back in court on Nov. 23. His lawyer declined to comment outside the courtroom.

https://citylimits.org/betting-platform-.title: Betting Platform Kalshi Pledges $1M to NYCHA Health Careers Program, Amid Gambling Lawsuit With State
https://citylimits.org/betting-platform-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/betting-platform-.text:
Share This Article
Kalshi’s million dollar commitment will support the NYCHA Health Corps, which offers public housing residents a pathway to jumpstart health careers.
A career training program for the city’s public housing residents is getting $1 million from an unusual source: Kalshi, the prediction market company recently sued by New York State for allegedly operating as an illegal and unlicensed gambling platform.
Kalshi’s million dollar commitment establishes the Kalshi Public Housing Health Fund, and will be rolled out over the next four years to support NYCHA Health Corps, a program run by the New York City Housing Authority that provides public housing residents with experience and training in public health careers.
“I’ve been in elected office for about 14 years, and I never had a company come to me and say, ‘We want to invest $1 million in public housing,'” said Congressman Ritchie Torres, who announced the partnership with Kalshi at NYCHA’s Andrew Jackson Houses in the South Bronx earlier this month.
Public housing residents currently involved in the program describe it as a pathway to jumpstart health careers—in anything from social work, environmental justice, and even beekeeping—and as a way to give back to their communities.
Still, some advocates expressed alarm at the involvement of Kalshi, which was sued in July by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, who accused the company of sidestepping its obligation to pay taxes owed by licensed mobile gambling platforms—taxes used to fund public services, like schools and programs for underserved youth.
Ramona Ferreyra, founder of Save Section 9, a coalition of tenants advocating to keep private management companies out of public housing, described the partnership as “wild.”
“My understanding of the issue is that Kalshi is bypassing our tax laws around gambling, and if they are doing that, it means the state is losing revenue,” Ferreyra said. “If the governor and the attorney general feel that Kalshi is causing us to lose revenue, why is a congressman partnering with them and validating their behavior?”
But Torres and public housing residents say the $1 million injection provides critical support for an important public service program.
All of the money from Kalshi will be used on living allowances for public housing residents who participate in NYCHA’s Health Corps program, according to Alex Zablocki, the executive director of the Public Housing Community Fund (PHCF), a nonprofit that NYCHA created in 2016 to facilitate public projects funded by private donors.
“What’s so special about Kalshi’s contribution is that they’re coming in with four years of funding, which gives us confidence that we can continue the program over the next few years,” Zablocki said.
Participants work up to 40 hours each week in jobs that broadly focus on chronic disease prevention, family wellbeing, and social determinants of health.
The program is in partnership with AmeriCorps, and participants receive standardized living allowances of $22,000 over a period of roughly 10 months, which is paid out every two weeks. Interested applicants can apply on NYCHA’s website here.
Now in its second year, the health program will swear in up to 35 public housing residents across the city this December, who will be placed at one of roughly 20 public agencies and nonprofit sites citywide that partner with NYCHA, including the city’s Health Department, NYC Health + Hospitals, and local nonprofits.
“The goal is to place about two-thirds of our graduates into full-time jobs, which could be at any of our health partners,” Zablocki said. Along with access to direct pathways to public health careers, participating residents can also receive professional development training.
“There’s a variety of jobs and careers, and they could also get further certifications or education, for things like social work licenses,” Zablocki said.
Tina Aurice Johnson, a 59-year-old resident of NYCHA’s General Grant Houses in West Harlem since birth, told City Limits she learned of the program through her role as an appointed member to the NYC Environmental Justice Board.
“I got involved in all the work I’ve been doing to improve my community, and help it prepare for extreme weather conditions” fueled by climate change, Johnson said.
Over the last 10 months, she was paired to work as a habitat specialist with The Bee Conservancy, an environmental non-profit that’s focused on saving bees, and manages pollinator gardens across the city.
“All the work that I did in the gardens were on NYCHA campuses,” Johnson said, adding that her role included planting, weeding and learning about bees and soil.
“Through this program I’ve learned so much about public health and I’ve begun to see it as a framework for environmental justice,” she added.
At the announcement of the partnership, Rep. Torres, who was raised in NYCHA’s Throgg’s Neck Houses in the Bronx, described the program as a way for residents to become “healthcare providers who have roots in our community,” and “who have earned the trust of our community.”
“The million dollars from Kalshi is not charity, it’s an investment in healthcare access as a human right,” Torres said.
Kalshi launched in 2021 as the first federally regulated prediction market platform, and allows users across the country to make predictions and bets on outcomes of future events—anything from rates of inflation and unemployment to the weather.
Headquartered in New York City, the company’s vision is to “allow people to capitalize on their opinions,” according to its website.
The recent lawsuit against Kalshi follows an investigation by Attorney General James, which accused the prediction market of being “an illegal, unlicensed gambling operation,” that exposes New Yorkers, including those younger than the legal gambling age of 21, “to serious personal and financial risk.”
Torres told City Limits that “prediction markets are a new technology, and with new technology comes a need for regulation.”
“The federal government has to figure out how we’re going to regulate it, how we generate tax revenue from it, and how we ensure that there’s consumer and investor protection,” the congressmember said. “Those are questions that Congress is actively thinking through.”
PHCF declined to comment on the ongoing litigation, and Kalshi did not respond to City Limits’ request for comment.
Kalshi’s $1 million commitment to the health program follows the company’s $3 million partnership with the nonprofit Housing Works, which aims to expand healthcare access and strengthen community services for thousands of New Yorkers, announced in October.
