https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers said that a clash with the Hindu festival Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to exhibitors rehanging around one-third of their stands, rather than 75%-100%.
The mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to match bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).
For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” said Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand, including photographs by Ronny Sen, and rehung around 50% of it.
Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a new buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.
In the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.
Subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send PDFs prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” said the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.
With India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox said this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.
Also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that showed at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (New York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).
Several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. Director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair but closing a few more sales could make it great”.
By and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works, struggled. Niru Ratnam did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Amal Gosh to cover stand and shipping costs, though Ratnam noted that he made some sales towards the end of the week.
One of the clearer litmus tests for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff said she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.
The gallery did however sell a $16,000 painting installation by Dhiya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's former chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff said.
Speaking of Picasso, one 1930s painting by the Spanish master was brought by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery brought a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, this only convinced director Hugo Cobb to only double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he said.
As many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes are local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by pride in local culture, and familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff."
Further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art market hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes to ship works in and out of this country. As Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan said, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in work. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".
Meanwhile, issues of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one anonymous dealer noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".
India's art market growth indeed appears to be domestic success story, in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.
While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, collectors covet international names at the expense of local talent, India protects and supports its own artists and its ecosystem—representatives from a growing number of new Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.
While India might not yet be ready for an international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which will help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer moment.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/seattle-hilt.title: The Longest Hotel Strike in Washington State History
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/seattle-hilt.author: Diana Varenik, Natascha Elena Uhlmann
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/seattle-hilt.text:
The Longest Hotel Strike in Washington State History
After 85 days on the picket line, workers at Seattle’s Embassy Suites won a historic strike victory. Workers achieved big pay increases, lower barriers for health care eligibility, and highly sought-after protections for immigrant workers.
You’d be forgiven for worrying, twelve weeks into a strike, that the boss is hell-bent on waiting you out. But after more than eighty days on the picket line at Seattle’s Embassy Suites by Hilton in Pioneer Square, Aspen Desmarais was undeterred. “I can live on a budget,” she said. “Been doing it since day one.”
After eighty-five days, on September 10, workers won the longest hotel strike in Washington state history. Their union, UNITE HERE Local 8, represents four thousand hospitality workers in Oregon and Washington.
Desmarais, a strike captain and bartender at the hotel, worked to keep others motivated throughout the fight. She and her coworkers were “tired of people talking down to us and not treating us with respect,” she said, “when we’re the reason that place stays running the way that it does.”
Hilton’s offer, two weeks into the strike, of one cent per hour over its previous proposal helped fuel outrage. The union held open bargaining, so members heard the offer firsthand. “I [felt] frustrated and disrespected,” Desmarais said. “Especially with how much hard work my coworkers put into making sure the hotel and its guests have clean spaces and stays that are welcoming.”
Fritzie Corral, an Embassy Suites breakfast attendant, had only worked at the hotel for two months before walking out. As the strike went on, she said, her son worried that she had made a mistake in taking the job.
“You see other employees that decided to stay in the hotel working,” she said. “Even during that time, I still believed I made the right choice. It’s my right to voice out what I feel and to fight for my rights.”
Hilton did not respond to requests for comment.
Protection From ICE
Workers won significant pay increases, lowered barriers for health care eligibility, and highly sought-after protections for immigrant workers. Hilton, which manages the hotel, drew protests earlier this year for housing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and for cutting ties with a Minneapolis hotel that canceled ICE bookings during Operation Metro Surge.
The union’s leaders criticized Hilton throughout the strike for dismissing contract language that would protect immigrant workers. “With ICE-related killings in the news for months causing immigrant workers to worry, why is Hilton refusing to give immigrant workers’ union a heads up if ICE is staying at the hotel?” Local 8 President Anita Seth asked Business Wire.
Ultimately workers won a commitment from Hilton not to punish workers who call out due to an immigration enforcement surge, plus language binding the hotel to an expedited resolution process in such an event. Workers who lose their work authorization due to immigration enforcement will now be able to return to their jobs if their work authorization is restored within four years, and to retain their seniority for up to two.
Desmarais told Labor Notes that making sure immigrant coworkers missing work because of ICE “knew they would have a job still and a safe place to come back to” was the “most important” win strikers fought for.
Starting in 2027, housekeepers will make over $31 an hour — a giant step above the $17.63 an hour that housekeepers make on average across the country, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The new contract makes them the highest-paid housekeepers in the state, according to the union. Embassy Suites workers classified as “tipped” will now make $1 more per hour than the city’s minimum wage.
Health care eligibility was also a core demand for the union. Many hotel workers under collective bargaining agreements must meet a minimum threshold of hours worked to qualify for health benefits in a given period. Seasonal layoffs, a hallmark of hotel work, often mean inconsistent coverage for workers and their families.
The new contract replaces the month-to-month eligibility standard with an annual threshold of 1,250 hours, or around twenty-four hours a week, to qualify.
Mass Cancellations
The strike coincided with five of the six World Cup soccer matches held at Seattle’s Lumen Field this summer, directly across from the Embassy Suites. World Cup–related leverage helped produce quick contract wins this summer for service and hospitality workers in Philadelphia, New York, and Los Angeles, but not so in Seattle.
How did strikers there keep up the pressure for another sixty-three days after the games ended? The hotel’s proximity to Lumen Field makes it a destination for football fans when the season starts in September. On game days, the hotel sets up a bar facing the stadium. Workers set up a separate picket line mere feet away from the customers and urged fans not to cross.
In between sporting events, Desmarais said solidarity from other union workers played a big role.
Combined pressure from Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway (BNSF) railworkers (represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen Division 518) and sympathetic elected officials pushed Sound Transit to move its contract to another hotel with no promise of return. The transit agency had maintained a block of rooms for the BNSF workers who operate its commuter rail — accounting for twenty-five rooms nightly, or roughly $18,500 in weekly revenues, according to Local 8, and a significant portion of the hotel’s income during low-traffic winter months.
Embassy Suites workers like Desmarais worked hard to push Sound Transit and other hotel clients to honor the picket line. “There was one day I had to make over ninety phone calls,” she said. “For the most part, it was actually a pretty positive reaction.”
Teamster sanitation and United Parcel Service workers also refused to service the hotel during the strike. Corral reported seeing the hotel’s director and assistant director hauling garbage out during the World Cup. “It felt so rewarding,” said Desmarais. “Yeah, you have to get your hands dirty and not just do paperwork. I think it gave them a real experience of what we have to deal with.”
Corral said community solidarity was key in getting Hilton to concede. Strikers’ church groups joined the picket line. So did several Seattle elected officials and even some hotel guests. Guests also brought workers donuts, contributed to the strike fund, and left Google reviews urging hotel management to “come to the table” and “sign the contract already.”
One temp worker walked off the job after only an hour to join the picket line. Corral said such displays of solidarity made workers “more motivated to keep on.”
Many workers worried about money, the future of their jobs, and their families while on strike. But when someone was scared or upset, there was always another worker to help uplift them, said Corral: “We’re like family.”

Christie’s pulled a Frida Kahlo canvas from a November 17 evening sale in New York just hours before the auction was to begin after a group raised concerns that it was considered part of Mexico’s heritage and thus not legally allowed to leave the country. In accordance with the 1984 establishment of Mexico’s cultural patrimony law declaring her works national monuments, the artist’s work is not permitted to permanently leave Mexico without permission from the country’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL).
“In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research,” said the auction house in a statement. “We look forward to selling this work at a later date.”
Titled Congreso de los Pueblos por la Paz (Congress of Peoples for Peace), the contested canvas was painted by Kahlo in 1952 to commemorate a pacifist assembly in Vienna that same year.
Spanish daily El País reports that the organization Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection) has been pressuring INBAL over the work on the grounds that it is part of the trust of Casa Azul created by Kahlo’s husband, Diego Rivera, following her death in 1954, and is “part of the legacy left to the people of Mexico.” According to the petitioning collective, Rivera left explicit instructions that works and objects included in the trust not leave Casa Azul, Kahlo’s birthplace and the couple’s longtime home, which is today a museum devoted to her work.
How the painting came to leave Casa Azul is unclear, though INBAL told Mexican daily Excélsior that it is thought to have left the country before the establishment of the trust, and thus before the establishment of the patrimony law.
Artnews reports that Christie’s, which has since wiped the painting’s provenance from its site, initially listed Galería Ramis Barquet, based in Monterrey, Mexico, and New York, as the work’s earliest owner. The gallery subsequently sold the painting to an individual who then sold it to the current owner for $2.6 million at a 2020 auction conducted by Sotheby’s.
According to the New York Times, Casa Azul is looking into the timeline of the painting’s disappearance from its collection, while INBAL has asked Christie’s to provide documentation proving provenance.

https://gothamist.com/news/hakeem-jeffri.title: Hakeem Jeffries gets party nod as House Speaker, but NYC's left remains wary
https://gothamist.com/news/hakeem-jeffri.author: Ryan Kost
https://gothamist.com/news/hakeem-jeffri.text:
U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries moved a step closer to becoming speaker of the House of Representatives Wednesday, even as two democratic socialists in New York City’s congressional delegation voted against him.
House Democrats backed Jeffries 251-11 in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote, multiple news outlets reported. Jeffries, who ran unopposed, will have to wait until the full House votes to officially claim the gavel, but there’s little doubt now that he’ll become the country’s first Black speaker.
Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, two members of the Democratic Socialists of America, released a statement with five other members-elect from outside New York explaining their decision to vote against Jeffries’ nomination.
“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the group said. “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”
Jeffries, who represents New York's 8th Congressional District in Central Brooklyn, is seen as a centrist who has been reluctant to embrace some of the DSA’s platform, most notably its criticism of Israel. Jeffries waited for months to endorse Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral run last year, even as he faced off against former Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Republican Curtis Sliwa.
Wednesday’s nomination comes after months of pushback from Jeffries’ left, much of it from his own city. In June’s primaries, Avila Chevalier unseated Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom Jeffries had endorsed. At Valdez’s primary-night party, her supporters chanted “You’re next!” when Jeffries appeared on a TV screen. Earlier, City Councilmember Chi Ossé, a DSA member, had briefly moved to challenge Jeffries himself but backed off.
Ultimately, Jeffries won the nomination easily. No challenger came forward, and two of the city’s most prominent progressives, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, stood by him.
When asked by reporters about the democratic socialists’ comments, Jeffries said he was looking forward to working with all members of his party.
“It’s an honor to be serving with a majority of 260 members from all across the country,” he said. “People who have different perspectives, and we embrace that, but we’re gonna work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people.”
The New York City Democratic Socialists of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

https://hellgatenyc.com/vanity-fair-timo.title: The Timothée Chalamet Vanity Fair Profile Makes Me Sick
https://hellgatenyc.com/vanity-fair-timo.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/vanity-fair-timo.text:
It's Wednesday, you deserve a treat, like an episode of the Hell Gate Podcast! Listen here or watch here.
The cover story of Vanity Fair's Holiday Issue, a profile of Timothée Chalamet, is excruciating.
I can sympathize with its writer, Vanity Fair's "senior editorial director," (whatever that means) Mark Guiducci. An A-list celeb like Chalamet has little incentive to do anything the broke, failing media wants these days. He calls the shots, even to a legendary magazine like VF. Like an emailed excuse to a college professor, Guiducci drops a few references to the constraints he's working with: He's only got 90 minutes before Chalamet heads to Yankee Stadium to watch them get creamed by the Tampa Bay Rays, and he uses a few of them to eat a Lenwich; Chalamet is rigorously media-trained, and he and his publicists have dictated several "no-go zones" in advance, including his relationship with Kylie Jenner; the photoshoot in Iceland has already occurred.
And so, Guiducci begins the piece with expectation-setting: Nothing noteworthy will happen, because "it's dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days." There especially will not be a gaffe like the one made earlier this year during the Oscar campaign for "Marty Supreme," where Chalamet (arguably correctly) noted opera and ballet as mediums with waning mainstream appeal. That actually caused discourse, and who wants that? And anyway, that was said in a videotaped interview with another actor (obviously). This is a magazine profile.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most important artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.
Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a new dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.
Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most important museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a new institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.
Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
Tiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.
Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.
Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)
Hungarian National Gallery
Szent György tér
In Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.
Working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s new Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.
Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
The MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.
Left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.
The Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)
Hungarian Parliament
Kossuth Lajos tér
The Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.
A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.
Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969)
Hungarian National Gallery
Szent György tér
Now regarded as one of the most important artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.
Judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.
Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
Goya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.
An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”
Can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)
Id. Antall József rkp
In the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.
Comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.
Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)
Vasarely Museum Budapest
Szentlélek tér
For the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.
Schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
Hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.
A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.
Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)
Ludwig Museum
Komor Marcell utca
During the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.
A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterm-resu.title: Did Moderate Democrats Really Outperform the Left? No.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterm-resu.author: Matt Bruenig
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterm-resu.text:
Did Moderate Democrats Really Outperform the Left? No.
Contrary to what centrist pundits might say, assessing how moderate and left-leaning Democrats performed in the midterms is no simple task. But however you slice the data, you can’t make the case that moderates meaningfully outperformed the Left.
Democrats did well in the 2026 midterm elections. According to the current tally, they gained forty-one House seats, eight Senate seats, and five governorships. Democratic candidates of all types had success, making it difficult to easily point the finger at this or that faction for blowing the election.
This has generated some frustration among factional partisans because such partisans are heavily invested in the idea that their style of politics is electorally superior to the politics of other factions. They can’t point to winners and losers to support their positions because, in this election, everyone was a winner. So they are forced to make their case by analyzing margins of victory, which is hard to do well and full of uncertainty even when it is done well.
In this piece, I walk through various approaches to quantifying candidate-specific performance to provide a sort of primer on how to think about this and successfully navigate the deluge of election pseudo-statistics.
I. Raw Vote Share
The most obvious, though naive, way to distinguish between winners is to look at their raw vote share. If one Democratic candidate won 51 percent of the votes cast in their race and another won 70 percent of the votes cast in their race, then, at a glance, it seems like you could say that the 70-percent candidate performed better than the 51-percent candidate.
Certainly the 70-percent candidate did better, but this is not the same thing as performing better. When pundits talk about performance, they are trying to isolate the effect the candidate’s own characteristics had on the election results. Raw vote shares do not do this because raw vote shares reflect other factors as well, including the underlying tendencies of the voters in that area. In other words, it’s possible that the 70-percent district leans more Democratic, and the 51-percent candidate would have also gotten 70 percent in that district.
II. Expected Vote Share
To isolate the candidate-specific effects, you have to establish some kind of baseline figure for what the election results would have been in a hypothetical version of the race where the candidate was a “generic” Democrat. The difference between the actual results and these “expected” results is then assumed to reflect the unique characteristics of the candidate.
This is not an easy thing to do, and most of the efforts I see in the discourse are ridiculous.
A. Uniform Swing as Expected Vote Share
The most common approach to quantifying expected vote share is to determine how vote shares changed nationally from the prior election and then assign that change uniformly across every voting area in the country. This is what Kevin Deluca did in the following graph.
It may look sophisticated, but, as the caption explains, all Deluca did was go through each of the twelve states and add 7.5 points to Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential result in that state. This is his entire model for expected vote share. The difference between this expected vote and the actual vote is then used to declare underperformers and overperformers.
The simplicity of this model is very charming and no doubt explains why I see it more than any other: anyone who can add and subtract is capable of running the model. But does it really make sense to suppose that, if you ran a generic Democrat in every Senate race in the country, each of them would have received a Harris+7.5 vote share?
Even if one were to suppose that all of the noncandidate differences between these states and races could be fully captured by Harris’s 2024 presidential result, why would equal performances by generic Senate candidates show up as equal changes in percentage points? Wouldn’t it make more sense for equal performances to show up as equal changes in percent of the 2024 non-Democratic share that was converted to the 2026 Democratic share?
To see what I mean, imagine two House districts, one where Harris got 80 percent of the vote in 2024 and another where Harris got 20 percent of the vote in 2024. If you put equally-performing generic Democrats in those districts, what would you expect the result to be?
The uniform-swing approach says that we should expect them to add the same number of percentage points. So, for example, we should expect the 80-percent district to become a 90-percent district and the 20-percent district to become a 30-percent district. In this scenario, both districts moved equally by 10 points. But to move 10 points in the 80-percent district, you have to persuade 50 percent of the non-Democratic voters. Moving 10 points in the 20-percent district only requires persuading 12.5 percent of the non-Democratic voters. Why would we expect one generic Democrat to be four times as persuasive as another generic Democrat? How is that equal performance?
The premise of the uniform-swing model, which is that equal performance equates to equal percentage points, is nonsensical on its face. Clearly, the number of points an equal performer can move will vary state to state and district to district by the share of the electorate that is even capable of being moved. Simple linear regressions using the House and Senate results provide some empirical support for this point.
There are at least two other big problems with this approach to modeling expected vote share.
First, a uniform vote swing would make sense only if you were modeling generic Democrat versus generic Republican. But these Senate races do not have generic Republicans in them. Maine’s Troy Jackson ran against a thirty-year incumbent in Susan Collins, while Texas’s James Talarico ran against a scandal-plagued nonincumbent in Ken Paxton. The difference between actual vote share and expected vote share would capture the combined candidate effects of both the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate.
So, for instance, if Troy Jackson runs 2 points behind the uniform-swing expected vote share, that could be because he has negative candidate effects, because Collins has positive candidate effects, or because of some combination of the two. Likewise, if Talarico runs 2 points ahead of the generic-versus-generic expected vote share, that could be because he has positive candidate effects or because Paxton has negative candidate effects. By construction, the uniform-swing approach assumes that the relative overperformance or underperformance of Republican candidates is uniformly zero.
Second, different districts have different demographic compositions, which should generate different swings even with equally-performing generic Democrats. For example, here’s what percent of each racial group voted for the Dems nationally in 2024 and 2026.
As we can see, the vote swing varies by racial group. Given this variation, the only way equally-performing generic Democrats would generate uniform vote swings in every voting district is if every voting district had the same racial demographics. They don’t.
Race is the most obvious example, but other demographic variables like income and education vary across districts and also drive differential vote swings separate from anything having to do with candidate effects.
B. Overlapping Elections as Expected Vote Share
The second most common approach to quantifying expected vote share is to compare a specific Democratic candidate’s vote share to the vote share of other Democratic candidates running for other positions within the same voting area. So, for instance, you might compare how one statewide candidate did to how other statewide candidates in that same state did.
This approach avoids some of the problems of the uniform-swing approach. It does not require us to clumsily extrapolate from prior election results. By construction, it controls for demographics and other sorts of variation between different groups of voters because it compares how different candidates did among the exact same voters in the same year. No longer are we stuck having to wonder whether Michigan 2024 is comparable to Michigan 2026 or whether Michigan 2026 is comparable to Texas 2026. Instead, this approach just compares Michigan 2026 to Michigan 2026.
But this overlapping-elections approach still has some of the same problems as the uniform-swing approach and some unique problems of its own.
Like the uniform-swing approach, the overlapping-elections approach effectively assumes that Republican candidates never underperform or overperform. But this is obviously untrue. In Texas, Senator-elect Talarico (Dem) received 55.1 percent of the vote while Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (Dem) received 52.8 percent of the vote. The overlapping-elections approach would say that Talarico overperformed by 2.3 points, or, alternatively, that Hinojosa underperformed by 2.3 points.
But these numbers don’t allow us to reach any such conclusion. After all, another explanation would be that Talarico and Hinojosa performed exactly the same while Talarico’s opponent, the scandal-plagued first-time Senate candidate Ken Paxton, underperformed by 1.15 points and Hinojosa’s opponent, the twelve-year incumbent Greg Abbott, overperformed by 1.15 points.
The overlapping-elections approach is also unable to determine the absolute quality of the candidates in a given geography, only their relative positions to one another (if that). The uniform-swing approach presumably uses national averages on the theory that a large sample across many geographies provides a more reliable indicator of what the average candidate quality is. But if your dataset only includes a handful of overlapping races, it’s quite possible that a disproportionate share of the candidates in your dataset (even, potentially, all of the candidates in your dataset) are underperformers or overperformers. A senator who runs slightly above a governor or the combined House vote could be an overperformer, but they might also be an underperformer surrounded by even greater underperformers. This approach cannot distinguish between the two.
Another unique problem with the overlapping-elections approach is that it assumes that the only reason a voter would split their ticket — e.g., vote for a Democrat for senator and then a Republican for governor or House of Representatives — is because of the different characteristics of the candidates running in the various races.
But this is not true. A voter might also split their ticket because of differences in the powers of the various offices they are voting on. A voter who typically supports Republicans but dislikes Donald Trump and wants to rein in his power may support a Republican for governor while supporting a Democrat for the House. That same lean-Republican voter, while supporting a Democrat for the House, might support a Republican for the Senate, given that senators serve six-year terms while all House representatives come up for reelection again in 2028.
Even if only a small percentage of voters think in this (quite rational) ticket-splitting way, it’s enough to completely swamp most of the point differences we see in these overlapping-election results, especially when you add in the other problems identified above.
C. Regression Models
One of the least common approaches to quantifying expected vote share is also the most sophisticated: regression models. Rather than assuming a uniform swing or looking at overlapping elections, throw a variety of variables into a model that spits out an expected vote share for each geography. The difference between what the model outputs and the actual vote share is then presumed to be driven by candidate effects.
As far as I know, the two main sources for this approach are Split Ticket, which is now at The Argument, and Strength in Numbers led by G. Elliot Morris.
In this election, the Strength in Numbers approach showed no real difference between the various ideological groupings of House candidates. If anything, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates overperformed the average Democrat.
Split Ticket, which uses a different regression model, reached a similar result, with only the Blue Dogs and Justice Democrat candidates posting performance results (slightly) distinguishable from zero.
The Economist also published the results of a model it apparently put together for the election. According to this model and its candidate groupings, moderates outperformed expectation by less than 1 point while progressives underperformed expectation by the same amount.
The main problem with this modeling approach is just that it is not totally clear what variables should be included in the models. This is why they all differ from one another.
Another problem, which plagues all of these expected-vote approaches, is that not all candidate effects are related to ideology. Candidates might do better or worse because of their identity, e.g., being a Muslim. They might do better or worse because of their personality, e.g., being charismatic or not. Indeed, as we can see in the scatterplots above, the differences between candidates in each bucket far exceed the average differences between the candidate buckets. This problem is especially relevant when it comes to candidate selection, e.g., when voting in a Democratic primary, because it suggests that the nonideological aspects of candidates completely swamp the ideological aspects.
Arguably, these problems could be waved away if the various models all reached similar conclusions about candidate quality and did so at margins too large to plausibly deny. When it comes to the progressive-versus-moderates question, these three regression models do basically reach similar conclusions, which is a null conclusion. What departures we see from null in some of the models on some of the candidate groupings are so small that any grains of salt completely eradicate them.
III. Where That Leaves Us
Obviously, most discourse participants don’t care about any of this and are happy to move around whatever chart they see that shows that science proves their politics is the best politics. But among pro-moderate pundits who do care at least some about maintaining a defensible argument on the merits, what I have seen lately is a proposal of sorts in which pro-progressive pundits agree that moderates do better than progressives in exchange for pro-moderate pundits agreeing that the gap is very small. Both Jonathan Chait and Matt Yglesias have gone this route after the election. In more recent exchanges I’ve had with Yglesias, he seems to retreat a bit further toward acknowledging that the moderate advantage can’t be reliably demonstrated in the data but that it rests on strong theoretical foundations.
The problem with these strategic retreats is that the difference between zero and nearly-zero is not going to be big enough to convince anyone to abandon policy initiatives that they think are important, especially given that policy popularity changes over time in part due to the advocacy of policy partisans. If the current electoral penalty of advocating single-payer health care over expanding Obamacare subsidies is 1 point or less, it would be crazy for someone who believes single-payer health care would dramatically improve society to give it up, especially when the alternative of attempting to persuade some voters to change their minds on that, which includes running candidates who argue for it, also exists.

The Pan-African Biennale (PAB) and the Center for Architecture have announced a joint initiative to launch an open-access digital archive to celebrate architecture from all fifty-four African nations. There is currently no such archive focused on architecture with representation from across Africa and its global diasporas.
Curated by PAB, which had its inaugural exhibition this year in Nairobi, the archive will include publications, research, and other documentation together with commissioned essays, poems, and criticism. According to a press release, the platform will eventually also feature oral histories, interviews, and site soundscapes recorded with architects and communities. The Center for Architecture will provide the project’s institutional framework and administration.
“African architecture has been studied, photographed and filed elsewhere, by others, for too long,” said Omar Degan, founder and executive director of PAB. “This archive reverses that. What Africa produces, on the continent and across its diasporas, stays open, is written from within, and is read on our terms. That is what shifting the center means in practice.”
Work from biennale exhibitors will appear in early iterations of the archive, including that of Maissa Architectures (Gabon), Bled El Abar Collective (Tunisia), RAAS Architects (Ethiopia), Moralo Designs (Botswana), Nicolas Patience Basabose (Democratic Republic of the Congo), Sylvain Bobossi-Bizon (Central African Republic), and Mokhethi Gerard Rampeta (Lesotho).
In spring 2028, the two organizations will collaborate on a related exhibition at the Center for Architecture, in New York, featuring projects from the biennale and allowing audiences to relate African architecture to social, cultural, and environmental issues.
Jesse Lazar, executive director of AIA New York and the Center for Architecture, emphasized that the project will broaden global conversations around built environments, adding, “Through this partnership with the Pan-African Biennale, the Center for Architecture has an opportunity to help preserve and share an extraordinary body of architectural knowledge while creating new opportunities for learning, research, and dialogue across borders.”

https://gothamist.com/news/3-high-rise-t.title: 3 high-rise towers in Astoria? 'Not the affordable housing' residents have in mind.
https://gothamist.com/news/3-high-rise-t.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/3-high-rise-t.text:
The Marquee Astoria's chandelier-adorned ballroom was the setting for the local community board’s public hearing on plans for three high-rise apartment buildings proposed for the south end of Steinway Street.
The fancy decor, however, did little to mask the Queens crowd’s visceral reaction to much of what they heard. Many in the audience jeered, booed and buzzed as the project developers presented their plans and answered questions.
Attendees said they worried the new housing would be too pricey for many already living in the neighborhood – echoing concerns frequently heard in communities across the five boroughs where developers are pushing new housing developments.
"This is not the affordable housing that our community is really needing," community board member Christina Chaise said to applause from some attendees.
The discussion on Tuesday evening centered on proposed 12- and nine-story buildings by Schuman Properties on Steinway Street and 34th Avenue, and a 16-story building across the street, at 34-49 Steinway St., by ZD Jasper Realty.
The developers for both projects did not provide projected rental prices for the apartments at the three buildings. But at least a quarter of the apartments in all three buildings would be reserved for income-restricted affordable housing, as required under Mandatory Inclusionary Housing requirements.
Based on figures from 2025, rents for those apartments would range from $1,130 to $3,370, depending on the apartment size and tenant's income. And they would be available to individuals making between 40% and 80% of the city's median income, between $45,400 and $90,700 for individuals and up to $140,000 for families, depending on the size.
But angry residents voiced concerns that even the required affordable housing units would be out of reach for working-class Astorians. The neighborhood’s median income as of 2024 was $93,460, about 11% higher than the city median income, according to the NYU Furman Center, a housing policy and research institute.
“Developments that have been pitched here and approved generally are doing more than the minimum,” community board member Frank Fredericks told the developers.
Some board members welcomed the new apartments, nothing their hope that the development could boost business in a struggling section of the commercial corridor.
“I like to see in general the residential being built in this area,” community board member Richard Khuzami said. ”It's going to help support some of the commercial. It's been a challenge to have healthy commercial down there."
But other residents voiced concerns that the new developments would raise rents for the small businesses in the area.
“The only way I can support this development is if it goes way deeper into affordable housing,” said Alfredo Hernandez, a neighborhood resident. “I also would only support it as well if it includes small business spaces with long, affordable leases. Because I’m really tired of walking around Steinway and there’s so many out-of-business stores.”
Representatives from Schuman Properties declined to comment on the criticisms of their project. Jasper Wu, of ZD Jasper Realty, said his firm has already adjusted the proposals, such as the unit count, based on feedback from the community board.
“I understand there’s a lot of strong reactions to it,” said Wu. “I understand people care deeply about the community… We’re definitely open to feedback. I’m sure there’s going to be more feedback from this. And we’ll take it and we’ll process it and we’ll respond.”
The community board will vote on the projects next month, after which the proposals move to the borough president, city planning commission, and the City Council for review.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, New York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.
“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the new attribution.
The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.
Llanes Serrano says the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.
The early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano says that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.
Julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s new chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day says.
Llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s new conservation studio, says XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.
The process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the new 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she says. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.
A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.
Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-anthropic.title: Anthropic’s IPO Is a Bid to Manufacture Confidence
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-anthropic.author: Clark Randall
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-anthropic.text:
Anthropic’s IPO Is a Bid to Manufacture Confidence
The firm behind AI software Claude is offering shares to the public. It’s meant to boost confidence in Anthropic’s future at the moment when most Americans are turning against data centers.
Anthropic, maker of artificial intelligence software Claude, is going public this Thursday. The initial public offering (IPO) could top the record SpaceX set earlier this year, once a concurrent private stock placement is counted. In February, Anthropic raised capital at a $380 billion valuation, and it is now seeking buy-in at $1.4 trillion. The rise has only been matched by the demand from investors, as Bloomberg reported the IPO road show was oversubscribed by six times the available shares. In other words, institutions will be crowding out individual investors vying for early gains.
Anthropic aims to raise $64 billion from the IPO in a nontraditional coming-to-market event. It has already been widely noted how the IPO’s role has changed over the last decade, with the flipping of public and private functions. Previously companies went public when their growth depended on it, raising capital from the public in order to continue expansion. But today, exponential growth takes place across multiple rounds of buy-in for private credit and venture capital (VC) funds. When those investors are ready to sell, the IPO works, in part, as an exit opportunity. Meaning: the people in the know, inside Anthropic, are rushing to market in order to offload their shares at peak value into your hands.
Anthropic is aware of the problem with how this looks. For this reason, out of its IPO of 825 million shares, over 800 million (97 percent) are fresh issuance — newly formed slices of the company that dilute previous shareholders’ stock but have the benefit of providing capital upfront to the company. This is not a normal distribution for a large IPO but does mimic the earlier framework of SpaceX — that is, another company that oriented its price and offering around retail interest. Essentially, these companies are duping investors with the facade of fresh issuance as proof of internal confidence, understanding that selling pressure will spike in the months after the firm goes public.
Obscure lockup terms mark out twenty-three liquidity events — days when insiders can sell shares — beginning on the first day of trading. Typically, early investors would wait six months to a year before being able to sell. The thinking is presumably the following: increase public confidence by smoothing out the change of hands, in order to avoid a deluge of shares going live at any one time.
Forever Young
In preparation for going public, Anthropic filed its S-1 prospectus document with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The tech-and-VC All-In Podcast with Chamath Palihapitiya and Jason Calacanis opened its post-S-1 commentary with David Sacks by calling this the greatest wealth-creation event in the history of Silicon Valley. Indeed, more than a thousand Anthropic employees are in line to make $10–$100 million post-IPO. Calacanis followed up by questioning whether this was the “greatest business in the history of capitalism.” Irony aside, I found the comment thought-provoking. Could it be that Anthropic is the greatest misallocation of capital and the greatest company capitalism has ever produced?
This is one of an array of dialectics defining the development of American frontier AI labs. Together they merge imagery from utopic and dystopic futures: we are told that these developments will either eliminate half the workforce, or “create more jobs than they destroy”; solve the climate crisis, or burst the environmental constraints of water, electricity, and critical minerals asunder; they’re either a word-order prediction machine, or an army of banal geniuses. We might be either in the first inning or the ninth: Who can tell? The element in common is that few people in the public eye hold any position in between these extremes. Bifurcated opinion is an accumulation mechanism for these companies; the unknown is the elixir of their success. The moment they become a known quantity is the moment when corporate accounting standards mean something.
Palihapitiya of All-In demonstrates the value of AI by citing the fact that a company like Microsoft has grown its revenue by two-thirds ($198 billion to $332 billion) in the past four years without increasing its workforce. The company recently sent buyout offers to 60,000 employees: revenue per worker has skyrocketed, and yet it still sees dead weight everywhere. It’s a story seen across the tech industry. Torsten Slok at Apollo recently found that revenue per employee in the sector is up around 40 percent since the 2022 turning point in AI and has flatlined in the S&P’s remaining 493 companies.
We can assume 2022 really was the turning point, after ChatGPT was introduced to the public that November. Yet what happened a month earlier was, I’d argue, far more important to Slok’s findings. Elon Musk acquired Twitter in October 2022, and within the week he halved its workforce and issued work-intensity ultimatums to thousands more. A 7,500-person company was reduced to a little over 1,000 staff. On Twitter (soon renamed X) and in the media, most speculated about the collapse of user experience and platform viability. Instead, nothing really changed; vulgar and racist tweets were widespread, explicit usage of the platform proliferated, but if we’re being honest, nothing collapsed in the way we expected. Bluesky, save for a cohort of academics, has not supplanted X as the place where news headlines are disseminated.
Slok’s headline read “No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector,” but this fabricated an impact where it was yet to be observed. The tech sector, led by Musk and backed up by the Effective Altruism crew thereafter, slashed employees and found an unfortunate truth about “bullshit jobs” — that millions of prestigious white-collar positions weren’t materially involved in the production process. The apparent productivity gains owed rather less to a revolutionary AI workforce.
The Spectacle of an AI Economy
As Anthropic comes to market, we might look for insight from Guy Debord’s Society of the Spectacle. A Marxist and prominent figure among the French situationists in the 1960s, Debord saw the circulation of images as a final evolution in the accumulation process. Surplus ultimately finds itself reinvested as signage, representation, and aesthetics as opposed to the productive economy.
Leading up to the IPO, Anthropic deployed a yearlong advertising campaign stretching from the Super Bowl to the FIFA World Cup and every major TV event in between. The tagline? “Keep Thinking.” Over a Rolodex of apocalyptic images, the voices of everyday Americans can be heard questioning the future of AI, saying things from “If they end up taking all the jobs, then what does it really mean to work?” to “Could AI help people stop feeling misunderstood?” The images shift from catastrophe to connection, showing mothers holding daughters and whales breaching water.
Debord wrote in 1967 that “the spectacle is the nightmare of imprisoned modern society which ultimately expresses nothing more than its desire to sleep. The spectacle is the guardian of sleep.” Essentially, the spectacle exists as a way of whispering to society: keep sleeping. In response, a revolutionary leader like Malcolm X used to warn his audiences that they must wake up and think for themselves — the subtext being that society will dictate what thoughts are permissible, in order to control how they act.
The irony today is that capital no longer cares what we think. We are free now, liberated (encouraged even) to think whatever thoughts we’d like. Our aggregated impressions, worries, and conundrums are catalogued and commodified. We can all be communists, socialists, or anti-capitalists at heart; anything, so long as we keep thinking using their models.
When we fear that AI means the end of critical thinking, we may be fearing the wrong thing. Claude and ChatGPT are not the end of our capacity to critique or analyze. If anything, the opposite is true: we enter a mind-numbing labyrinth of critical thoughts, questions, and opinions. These are anti-relational machines, not anti-thinking ones. I was on the phone with my dad the other day; how cool is it, he said, that he can put an image of his struggling plants into ChatGPT and get back a protocol for caretaking. I asked, what would you have done before? I’d probably have called my brother, he answered.
AI and Big Tech capital integrated the lessons of postmodernist discourse with surprising effectiveness. Back in a 2013 blog post, author and media theorist Nathan Jurgenson called this the “anti-capitalism-capitalism” of Silicon Valley. Thus far, the debates surrounding Anthropic chief Dario Amodei’s obsession with extinction-level AI events have been somewhat surface-deep. Skeptics like Ed Zitron and Steve Eisman of The Big Short believe it’s a smoke screen for regulatory capture by a company with no economic moat around it. Others take it literally. It’s both and it’s neither: it’s the construction of a discursive world, a spectacle, that distracts us from confronting the distributional politics of AI’s advancement.
Dual-Zone Economy
In 1987, the stock market crashed on Black Monday at the behest of newly automated computer-programmed trading algorithms, which simultaneously sold stocks as they began to fall due to the macro environment. Some of the conditions from back then again seem familiar — what was then a skirmish with Iranian forces is today a full-blown war; again today, the dollar is weakening both nominally and politically, and global energy markets are stressed. Still, after crashing 20 percent, the indexes finished in 1987 slightly higher than they started it. The temperature of the times blew hot and cold.
That same year, German automaker BMW introduced “dual-zone automatic climate control” into its premium vehicles. For the first time, the driver could dial the heat up as their passenger turned the air conditioning on. By the turn of the millennium, most models included some iteration of this. Industry commentators at the time dubbed it “the marriage saver.” The same moving car could now hold two divergent conditions. Today Anthropic chief Amodei, fellow AI kingpins like Sam Altman, and newly disgraced former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang are sitting on each other’s laps in the driver’s seat and running it hot, even despite last week’s drawdown. But we’re in the passenger seat, and the data says it’s cold as can be in here. These companies are public or will be public soon; they, more than anything, will decide the fates of our retirement accounts; their collapse would spell a more widespread recession. They expect us to join them for the ride, for the sake of the marriage.
And yet the recent US midterms saw forty of forty-one ballots related to data centers reject them by wide margins. Capitalism’s greatest business is, as Karl Marx predicted, birthing its own gravediggers. Deskilled white-collar labor, though highly paid, is learning of its own immateriality. Working-class Americans are saying no to having their communities repurposed for the sake of technological progress. AI’s advancement and its discontents, as a particular technological revolution distinct from others, are setting the stage for a once-in-a-century kind of cross-class, cross-identity, cross-party opposition.

https://www.artforum.com/news/laura-hopt.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/laura-hopt.text:

The Center for Curatorial Studies, Bard College (CCS Bard), in Annandale-on-Hudson, New York, has announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the winner of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence. The honor, awarded annually since 1998, recognizes “outstanding curatorial achievements of individuals who have advanced the field of exhibition-making through dedicated service, boundary-pushing creativity, and innovative vision,” per a press release, and is accompanied by a $25,000 prize.
A contemporary arts curator for more than thirty years, Hoptman has led the Drawing Center since 2018. In her capacity as executive director there, she has introduced a wide audience to the work of artists rarely exhibited in the US, as well as to little-known drawings by established artists. She previously spent eight years as a curator in the Department of Painting and Sculpture at the Museum of Modern Art, New York. Before that, she was an assistant curator in MoMA’s Department of Drawings, where she curated the landmark exhibition “Drawing Now: Eight Propositions,” centering figurative drawing.
“Laura’s longstanding curatorial practice has furthered new art historical analysis and international recognition of drawing as a creative medium and social practice,” said Tom Eccles, executive director of CCS Bard, in a statement. “Her international projects have reexamined the legacies of an array of artists through new and creative frameworks. What is often forgotten is how consistently Laura has demonstrated a boldness and bravery in championing artists across many institutional structures. CCS Bard is honored to award Laura’s achievements at the 2027 Gala, recognizing her excellent work in contemporary exhibition-making.”
Hoptman will be presented with the award at CCS Bard’s upcoming spring gala, to take place in New York on April 12, 2027.
