https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-tests.title: Mamdani tests new strategy to punish bad NYC landlords in latest lawsuit
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-tests.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-tests.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani says the city has a new tool in its fight against bad landlords: a legal maneuver typically used to punish fraud.
The city’s Law Department on Tuesday sued landlord Barry Singer in Bronx Supreme Court, arguing that he and the limited liability companies he controls violated the New York False Claims Act by evading more than $1 million in fines and emergency repairs completed by the city’s housing agency at 10 of his apartment buildings. Singer is a longtime fixture of the public advocate’s annual “worst landlord list,” ranking third on the most recent roster after accumulating thousands of open housing code violations.
The False Claims Act typically allows city and state governments to sue contractors, healthcare providers and other entities that submit fraudulent invoices or requests for repayment. Companies found guilty are required to pay triple damages for their misconduct.
The new city lawsuit contends that a section of the legislation also empowers it to sue any person or company who “knowingly and improperly avoids” paying money they owe, as in the case of Singer and unpaid fines levied by the Office of Administrative Trial Hearings, the Environmental Control Board and the city’s health and housing agencies.
The complaint says Singer could be on the hook for roughly $8 million if found guilty. Singer did not respond to a phone message left with his attorney.
The lawsuit is Mamdani's latest tactic to punish irresponsible landlords and potentially pry buildings away from owners who rack up violations or face financial distress. Since taking office, the mayor has pursued various methods for turning those buildings over to new groups that city officials deem more responsible. Those include intervening ahead of bankruptcy and foreclosure auctions and backing legislation that would give nonprofits first dibs on some buildings before they hit the open market. The efforts have generated support among tenant organizers but elicited furious opposition from landlord groups and their allies.
Mamdani said the city’s usual tactics for holding landlords accountable — violations and fines — has not worked in the case of Singer, and other chronically negligent owners.
“When the same old tools fail to deliver results, we will use new strategies to hold noncompliant landlords accountable and win justice for tenants,” the mayor said in a statement. “Every New Yorker deserves a safe, well-maintained home, and we will use every tool at our disposal to make that a reality across the five boroughs.”
The lawsuit lists 10 buildings with a combined 299 apartments controlled by Singer, many of them located in the Bronx's Allerton, Kingsbridge and Fordham neighborhoods. One 58-unit building at 2500 Webb Ave. has 456 open housing code violations, including 183 deemed immediately hazardous for problems like a leaky roof, broken brick walls and roach infestations, according to city data.
“This is a new playbook,” said Department of Housing Preservation and Development Commissioner Dina Levy in an interview. “This has extreme consequences financially and we are going to keep innovating to finally, at long lost, make them compliant or get out of the real estate business.”
She said the tactic aligns with Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s housing plan, which features a section called “Fix The City” with strategies for punishing “persistently negligent landlords.”
But the city’s legal argument in the new case against Singer remains untested.
In a written statement, Corporation Counsel Steven Banks said he was confident the False Claims Act can serve as a “powerful new tool to seek relief for tenants and hold landlords accountable for the public nuisances they have created in our communities.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/sanchez-psoe.title: Is This the End of Pedro Sánchez?
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/sanchez-psoe.author: Pablo Castaño
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/sanchez-psoe.text:
Is This the End of Pedro Sánchez?
Spain’s premier, Pedro Sánchez, is a famous political survivor, and his Socialists could still top the poll in November’s general election. But while Sánchez has won the trust of many left-wing voters, his allies’ support is fast melting away.
In recent years, Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish government, formed by his Socialists (PSOE) and the left-wing alliance Sumar, has been a reference point for the global left. Rarely among social democratic politicians, Sánchez has become well-known for his confrontations with Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, and for his governing coalition’s progressive social and economic policies.
However, Spain’s government could soon fall into the hands of a new alliance of the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party. At least, this is what almost all polls now suggest, less than two weeks before the general election on November 29.
There are many reasons for the electoral weakness of the PSOE and its further-left allies, now grouped in the Frente Amplio alliance. The broad-left government had already lost its majority in parliament in 2023, forcing it to rely on the votes of regionalist parties. But it has also been hit by its own mistakes as well as a ruthless offensive by traditional Spanish elites.
Here are six reasons why the snap elections on November 29 could force Sánchez from office.
1. Complicated Parliamentary Arithmetic
After the last general election in 2023, Sánchez only remained prime minister thanks to an eclectic coalition of progressive parties and Catalan, Basque, and Galician nationalists, including conservatives. They were united only by fear of a PP-Vox government that would be very hostile to the cultural and national diversity that defines Spain.
Because of the tight electoral results in 2023, the current legislative term has been marked by parliamentary instability and by a no-holds-barred war by the Right against a government that it considered illegitimate from the outset due to its reliance on parties who want independence from Spain. That dependence on conservative formations such as Catalonia’s Junts and, to a lesser extent, the Partido Nacionalista Vasco (PNV) has forced the government to lower its ambition regarding some laws and has cost it important votes in Congress, especially on housing issues.
The most serious parliamentary defeat came this October, when PP, Vox, and Junts together rejected two emergency decrees on housing tabled by the government following the eviction of an eighty-seven-year-old woman in Madrid and the subsequent massive demonstrations for the right to housing. Much of the mobilization centered on the government’s inability to curb rents. However, Sánchez also called this snap election hoping that the debate on housing would distract attention from the migration crisis in Ceuta.
2. Stormy Relations With Catalan Conservatives
Among the numerous parliamentary groups on which the PSOE-Sumar coalition government depended, the one that has set the highest price for its support has been Junts, a Catalan party which supports pro-business economic policies.
This party is led from exile by a former president of the Catalan government, Carles Puigdemont, who until last month feared arrest over his role in organizing the unofficial 2017 independence referendum. Following the 2023 general election, Junts set a price on supporting Sánchez’s investiture as head of government. It said it would only vote to keep him prime minister in exchange for an amnesty law that ended the judicial prosecution of Catalan pro-independence leaders.
The approval of the amnesty law in 2024 unleashed a nationalist campaign by the Spanish right, which considers the pro-independence supporters “coup plotters.” This conflict, too, fed Spanish nationalist party Vox’s electoral rise. The PSOE lost the support of numerous voters, and the Right exploited to saturation the idea that Sánchez has no principles and is capable of doing anything to stay in power. The Supreme Court, controlled by a judiciary heavily tilted to the right, has battled to prevent the full application of the law, but it has ended up being applied by order of the Constitutional Court.
3. Lawfare and Corruption
The justice system has been one of the main arenas of a fierce opposition to Sánchez. Right-wing ideas are clearly overrepresented in the Spanish judiciary: the two conservative judicial associations gather more than 40 percent of judges, while less than 10 percent belong to the only progressive association (the rest are not part of an association or belong to smaller groupings). To this unbalanced picture is added the growing shamelessness of the most reactionary judges in using the justice system for political ends. This is already shown by the judicial harassment against left-wing party Podemos and, more seriously, against Catalan independence supporters.
Various conservative judges have initiated proceedings of dubious justification against Sánchez’s brother and wife, confirming, in the eyes of the right-wing electorate, the idea that the Socialist prime minister is surrounded by corruption. The accusation is especially damaging because Sánchez himself reached the head of government in 2018 thanks to a motion of no confidence after the then-ruling PP was convicted in a serious corruption case. Unfounded accusations against Sánchez’s relatives have been mixed with real cases that have contributed to damaging his popularity: his former number two, ex–Minister of Development José Luis Ábalos, has been sentenced to twenty-four years in prison for taking bribes and awarding public contracts for the purchase of masks during the pandemic, and Santos Cerdán, who was also the PSOE’s organizational secretary, is likewise being investigated for corruption.
4. Insufficient Action on Housing and Inflation
The PSOE-Sumar coalition government has managed, despite its parliamentary weakness, to approve important measures such as increases in the minimum wage, the expansion of paternity leave, a boost to pension rates, and a law — albeit an insufficient one — to regulate rental prices. These added to the labor reform that has reduced temporary employment and the creation of a minimum living income to fight poverty, both introduced during the previous PSOE-Podemos government (2020–23). In addition, the macroeconomic data is good: Spain has for years been top of the table for GDP growth among the major European economies, and unemployment is at its lowest level since 2008.
However, a large part of the working class has seen its standard of living worsen. The minimum wage has risen almost 75 percent since 2018 (from €858 gross to €1,500 per month), but it has not pulled up wages in general: according to the Juan de Mariana Institute, three out of four wage earners earn under twice the minimum. Meanwhile, inflation reached close to 5 percent this October, and food has become 41.5 percent more expensive since 2018. Even more serious is the escalation of rents, rising 43 percent on average in a decade; in large cities, renting an apartment is equivalent to 100 percent of a young person’s income.
The housing situation, which is the main problem for Spaniards according to all polls, translates into more than forty evictions per day, despite the fact that Sánchez promised that this parliamentary term would be “the legislature of housing.” The explosion of the housing movement in recent weeks, which has included the first general strike on this issue in the history of Spain, demonstrates the failure of the coalition government in this key area for the Spanish working class.
5. Immigration and the Rise of Vox
The worsening of the material living conditions of much of the middle and working classes has opened up space for Vox’s racist messaging, which has only in recent years managed to sink roots among the lower-income electorate. The sudden entry of more than seventy thousand migrants into Ceuta (Spain’s North African enclave) on July 30–31 seemed to confirm Vox’s rhetoric, which warns of a supposed migrant “invasion.”
Santiago Abascal’s Vox has turned the rejection of immigration into its absolute priority, with a discourse that connects it with crime, even though the latter has declined while the number of migrant workers has grown. Its radicalism is akin to that of Germany’s ultranationalist Alternative für Deutschland: in 2025, Abascal incited the racist riots in Torre-Pacheco (Murcia), and a spokeswoman advocated the “remigration” of between seven and eight million people, including Spaniards descended from foreigners.
As in other European countries, the conservative PP has contributed to normalizing Vox’s discourse, forming governments with it at the regional level (in Spain’s so-called autonomous communities) and hardening its anti-immigration line. Driven by the reactionary wave that began with Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, Vox is approaching 20 percent in polls, and no one doubts that it will form a coalition government with Alberto Núñez Feijóo’s PP if the results allow it.
6. A Divided and Weak Left
Sánchez could reestablish his coalition government in 2023 thanks to the electoral comeback achieved by his PSOE, but also by Sumar, the formation led by Deputy Premier Yolanda Díaz, which scored 12 percent of the vote. Podemos, which split from Sumar, today has only a small parliamentary representation. For several weeks in October, the alternative left starred in a real soap opera about whether it would form a single candidacy. It was even mooted that such a list would be headed by Gabriel Rufián, of Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC), the most popular politician to the left of the PSOE in all of Spain, despite his pro-independence stance.
Finally, a coalition called Frente Amplio was formed, led by former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau and including fifteen parties. Podemos refused to join the Frente Amplio despite the great similarity between their programs, and now Podemos is polling under 2 percent support. This division has aggravated the disenchantment of the left-wing electorate. It also reduces the chances of a new broad-left majority, since the electoral system penalizes parties with few votes spread across many provinces, such as Frente Amplio and Podemos.
Less than two weeks before the elections, Frente Amplio is aiming for 10 percent of the votes, which would give it between fifteen and twenty seats. But if Colau’s candidacy sinks, even if the PSOE has a decent result, there will hardly be a parliamentary majority willing to keep Sánchez as prime minister. Paradoxically, part of his Socialists’ now-scant hopes lie in the good prospects for Euskal Herria Bildu (in the Basque Country), the ERC (Catalonia), and Adelante Andalucía, three left-wing sovereigntist formations that are growing in the polls and would also vote in favor of Sánchez returning as premier.
But Nothing Is Set in Stone
To these structural factors was added, a few weeks before the elections, a collision between two trains that caused sixty-nine deaths. This was the second high-speed accident in a year, revealing the deplorable state of the country’s railway infrastructure. The disaster prompted the resignation of Transport Minister Óscar Puente, a Sánchez loyalist.
In addition, the accident has weakened one of the PSOE’s main lines of argument: the defense of public services against the “chainsaw” of the Spanish far right, which admires the ultra-free-marketeer economic policies of Argentina’s President Javier Milei.
At the time of writing, almost all polls show a considerable majority for the right-wing camp, but they also detect a recent rebound by the PSOE. Both the Socialists and the Frente Amplio want to believe in a scenario like 2023, in which the charismatic Sánchez’s effective campaign and fears of the Right ended up mobilizing the broadly left-wing electorate.
However, the government parties would today need to recover much more ground during the campaign than they managed in 2023. A long-enduring right-wing campaign to delegitimize the government, Vox’s strength, and the sustained wear and tear of office means that, for now, the most likely outcome is that Spain loses its luster as a model for the Left.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Does an opera have to make sense? 'Einstein on the Beach' at BAM is a chance to find out.
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Earlier this week, Michael Riesman, the 83-year-old music director of the Philip Glass Ensemble, sat at a piano in an upstairs rehearsal space at the Brooklyn Academy of Music. His fingers flew furiously across the keys as he played nonstop arpeggios. The sound echoed through the room.
Riesman sat with his back to nearly a dozen people whose chairs were arranged in a neat semicircle. They were singing in perfect unison, but the sounds floating from their mouths were odd: They sang a series of numbers. “One, two-two, two-three, two-four, two,” they sang staccato, lifting their chins to project the nonsensical lyrics toward the airy room’s ceiling. Riesman, still playing his arpeggios, gave them live feedback: “The twos are a little long,” he said. Then, “the twos are a little late.” Eventually, the twos sounded right. Phew.
This Thursday through Saturday, Riesman, the ensemble, and the chorus will perform the cacophonous number as part of BAM’s 50th anniversary concert of composer Philip Glass and director Robert Wilson’s 1976 opera “Einstein on the Beach.” This is the fourth time a version of the groundbreaking work will be performed at BAM, following previous, fuller-scale productions in 1984, 1992 and 2012. The opera’s four acts are connected by “knee plays,” or intermezzos named after the connective joint. In its original form, “Einstein” lasts over four hours without an intermission, though audience members have been encouraged to wander in and out of the performance at will. BAM will put on a truncated concert version, which runs 2 hours and 35 minutes with an intermission.
Before the rehearsal, Riesman, a tall, silver-haired man who has been part of the Philip Glass Ensemble since 1974, said that he is proud to continue leading a production that “opened the door to a whole new concept of what you could do in an opera house.”
“Einstein” lacks a traditional narrative. Though the German-born physicist appears onstage in the opera, the performances unfolding around him offer largely abstract interpretations of his life and achievements. At one point, a soloist — choreographer Lucinda Childs in the original production — delivers a speech about visiting a “prematurely air-conditioned supermarket.” Over and over, she recalls that “there were all these bathing caps that you could buy.” Somehow, you might connect these happenings to Einstein’s theory of relativity. (If you don’t understand it, don’t worry: Wilson has said over the years that he didn’t know what “Einstein” was really about, either. This clip might help paint a more vivid picture.)
As music director of the Philip Glass Ensemble, Riesman has been tasked with carrying on the legacy of Glass’ work, renowned for its minimalist and repetitive qualities. He said he maintains a deep connection with the hypnotic music of “Einstein.”
“It’s had such a profound effect on people,” Riesman said. “I’ve had people come up to me and say, ‘I just saw “Einstein” and it changed my life. It opened my eyes to something. It made me want to get into this kind of thing.’”
But has there ever been anything else of this kind? As early as the mid-1980s, roughly a decade after “Einstein” premiered at Festival d’Avignon in France, filmmaker Mark Obenhaus heralded the production in a televised documentary as one that “changed forever the image of opera.” In the film, Glass says he and Wilson are offering audiences a “profoundly different way of relating to music theater” than, say, a production of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s “Oklahoma!”
“It’s really only an opera in terms of how it relates to the history of opera,” Riesman said. Wilson, also credited as the show’s designer, establishes early on in the documentary that he refers to “Einstein” as an opera simply “because it means opus, or work.”
The upcoming BAM productions mark the first instance in which Glass, 89, and Wilson, who died last year at 83, won’t be directly involved in putting “Einstein” on at the venue where they met in 1973. (Though Glass plans to attend one of the three nights, as the performances are part of yearlong celebrations of his upcoming 90th birthday.) Riesman joined the Philip Glass Ensemble as a keyboardist after hitting a wall in his career as a professor. He wanted to work in a more hands-on capacity than academia could offer, and what better way than to collaborate with a steady group of musicians? He eventually rose to music director because, as he put it, “I had the talent, the ear and the chutzpah to tell Philip where he could get lost sometimes.” (Riesman noted that his title is still technically unofficial, as he has never signed a contract in his years with the ensemble.)
“I never had a regular job,” he said. “Philip basically became a full-time job, paid my rent, and that’s worth a lot to me. Maybe it took away from my own creative work to some extent … but I did manage to slip in a few pieces.”
The composer envisioned his 1987 album “Formal Abandon” as a dance piece for Childs, his former collaborator on “Einstein.” He has also produced solo piano arrangements of Glass’ film scores. At the upcoming BAM shows, Riesman will perform an original keyboard solo, called a cadenza, that he used to improvise but eventually decided to compose as a set piece. The piece resembles something by Bach, he said, noting that it “has become a very popular number on Apple Music.”
Several singers performing at the upcoming BAM shows are veterans who sang in the “Einstein” revival a dozen years ago, and even back in the 1990s. But a few of them, in their early 20s, are new to the production. That keeps with the “Einstein” tradition, according to Riesman, who noted that many of the original cast members weren’t trained dancers or singers.
The BAM shows are directed by sound engineer Dan Bora, Riesman’s former assistant, who became a member of the Philip Glass Ensemble and started mixing sound for the group when it staged “Einstein” at BAM in 2012. Bora described the 50th anniversary concerts in an interview as “full circle,” but also “a big step forward that I hadn’t really planned on.”
“Sometimes it feels like I happened to be scratching my head when somebody said, ‘Raise your hand if you want to,’” Bora said, laughing.
Neither he nor Riesman seems afraid of putting their own spin on things; in fact, Bora said, he doesn’t consider it his responsibility to preserve what Glass and Wilson created in 1976.
“Einstein” is a meticulously written opera, full of “ones,” “one-twos” and “one-two-three-four-five-six-sevens” that hit exactly when they are supposed to. But it remains permutable as a show. The songs are written to be condensed if needed, as they are in the concert version. The monologues read aloud throughout the four acts have been tweaked over the years. In 1993, one was scrapped entirely when an actor replaced the scripted version with a new speech called “All Men Are Equal.”
“‘Einstein’ is a tabula rasa. It's an empty canvas,” Riesman said. “It’s never going to be Bob Wilson’s performance again, and it’s never going to be the [original] Philip Glass Ensemble’s performance again. And it shouldn’t be.”

https://gothamist.com/news/owner-of-pean.title: Owner of Peanut, scandalously slain NY squirrel, charged with upstate mortgage fraud
https://gothamist.com/news/owner-of-pean.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/owner-of-pean.text:
The outspoken owner of an internet-famous squirrel was arrested Wednesday on fraud charges connected to the animal sanctuary he founded and named after his pet before it was euthanized by New York officials.
Mark Longo, 36, who gained notoriety for his viral videos with the squirrel, Peanut, was arraigned on charges including residential mortgage fraud and second-degree grand larceny in the Southport Town Court near the Pennsylvania border. He pleaded not guilty, according to New York State Police.
Longo built up a following of hundreds of thousands of social-media users by documenting Peanut’s wacky antics. In the closing days of the 2024 presidential race, New York authorities obtained a warrant to seize the critter and a raccoon, which are considered wildlife that can’t legally be kept as pets. The squirrel then bit an officer — and protocol called for it to be euthanized, decapitated and tested for rabies, which came back negative.
The episode became a cause célèbre for JD Vance, Elon Musk and other MAGA supporters while causing an outcry and a wave of violent threats that sent shockwaves through the state Department of Environmental Conservation, Gothamist previously reported.
At the time, state authorities said Longo did not have the proper license to care for a squirrel and a raccoon. Longo was not charged in connection with the incident.
But in recent weeks, Longo and his wife, Daniela Bittner, have both found themselves accused of being on the wrong side of the law.
Along with Longo’s arrest Wednesday, Bittner — who is originally from Germany — was detained by federal immigration authorities in mid-October and is facing possible deportation, according to the Associated Press. Longo has blamed her detention on a paperwork snafu.
On Wednesday, state police accused Longo of using fake pay stubs, letters and application documents to get a $720,000 mortgage. That amount matches the mortgage Longo and two associates received in 2023 for a Chemung County property that became the 311-acre P’Nut’s Freedom Farm Animal Sanctuary.
Longo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Peanut’s death led to hundreds of threats against the state DEC and its top officials, with at least 10 buildings temporarily closing down due to bomb threats.
Among those who left violent voicemails, one man said he wanted to see DEC agents “laying dead in the f—ing street.” Another called for the agents involved in the search to be executed on live television.
As a result, the DEC’s entire workforce of about 3,000 employees was permitted to work remotely for a few days. The agency also pulled back on certain public-facing operations, including so-called deer checks along major thoroughfares to weed out poachers, Gothamist reported last year.
State police say they began their fraud investigation of Longo in December 2024, not long after Peanut’s seizure. The agency says it “received information about financial irregularities involving Longo” then, according to a news release.
In all, Longo faces 14 criminal counts ranging from mortgage fraud and grand larceny — both Class C felonies — to falsifying business records, a lower class E felony. He was released on his own recognizance and is scheduled to return to court in February, police said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.title: Trump Intel Pick Calls $1 Million Bribe for a Pardon a “Complicated Legal Question”
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.text:
Asked at a Wednesday confirmation hearing whether the law allowed people to give the president a $1 million bribe in exchange for a pardon, a White House attorney up for a major intelligence job said it was a “complicated legal question.”
Gary Lawkowski, who advised President Donald Trump in office and on the campaign trail, faced tough questioning from Democrats during his Wednesday hearing to serve as general counsel to the Office of Director of National Intelligence.
The hearing came as Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., sought to rush Lawkowski’s confirmation to the top intelligence posting before the end of the year, when Democrats take over Congress.
Although Lawkowski drew no hostile questions from Republicans, Democratic senators were concerned about Lawkowski’s role in Trump’s pardon spree, as well as his involvement in controversial executive orders that directed federal law enforcement to crack down on the left and designate antifa as a domestic terror organization.
“We’re looking for judgment here,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “And I understand: You were just the lawyer. But so many times, ‘I was just the lawyer’ kind of becomes the default answer.”
Lawkowski’s current position is deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president. He was little known outside the White House before Trump nominated him earlier this month to serve at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, a Cabinet-level department where he would coordinate legal advice for the 18 different agencies making up the intelligence community.
According to a questionnaire, Lawkowski has not held jobs at intelligence agencies before. His prior national security experience involves advising Trump on classified matters over the past two years.
He also has a long-standing relationship with Trump. During Trump’s time out of the White House, he helped provided legal advice to the president’s reelection campaign and defended him from lawsuits brought by people harmed during the January 6 insurrection.
Questioning His Record
During the Senate hearing, Warner criticized Trump’s pardons for January 6 rioters and for crypto mogul Changpeng Zhao. The crypto tycoon’s company Binance was involved in a transaction that benefited one of the Trump family’s crypto ventures.
Lawkowski suggested that prior reporting in the New York Times had exaggerated his role in the pardon process.
“My main focus was litigation and policy,” he said. “I’m actually not our primary pardon counsel. I have worked on some pardon issues.”
Sen. Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, pressed Lawkowski on whether it would be illegal for someone to walk into the Oval Office and hand the president a $1 million bribe for a pardon.
“That’s OK?” King said.
“Well, bribery itself would be a separate statutory crime. How that would interact with presidential immunity would be a complicated legal question that I think the court kind of reserved in that case,” he said, referring to a 2024 Supreme Court decision that granted the president broad immunity from prosecution for official acts.
Another senator zeroed in on Lawkowski’s role in crafting National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, commonly known as NSPM-7, the executive order directing federal law enforcement agencies to target “antifa” and other boogeymen of the far right.
In the written questionnaire, Lawkowski said he was involved in “communications” regarding that order and another that purported to designate antifa — the loose-knit anti-fascist movement — as a domestic terror group. He declined to explain further, citing the confidentiality of his legal conversations with the president.
“There is no basis in law to designate a domestic terrorist organization, but you have claimed the president can just do it anyways based on some magical constitutional authority,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. “Once he’s operating outside the law, are there any limits to how Donald Trump can persecute Americans?”
“I don’t agree with the premise that the president is acting outside of the law,” Lawkowski said. “Of course, the president is constrained by the limits of the Constitution.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: MTA Drivers Taking 50 Sick Days a Year May Be to Blame For Your Canceled Bus
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Jose Martinez
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Close to 1,000 bus operators call out sick in excess of 50 days a year, MTA officials said Wednesday, charging that no-show “bad apples” have left riders hanging on nearly 120,000 trips this year alone.
“Don’t milk the city and state and regional taxpayer so you can sit at home or go to Florida or whatever,” Janno Lieber, MTA chairperson and chief executive, said in response to a question from The City Reporter.
The striking numbers surfaced during a budget presentation at the transportation authority’s monthly board meeting, with Lieber challenging what he described as a “small outlier” of absentee employees to “go find another job.”
Just under one in 10 bus operators take more than 50 paid sick days a year — with limited consequences because of a difficult disciplinary process, Lieber said.
Those days add up to a lot of cancelled trips — and taxpayer money. The MTA said it loses $20 million for every day in lost productivity across its entire workforce.
MTA Chief Financial Officer Jai Patel outlined how most employees are expected to be available for service 227 days a year out of 261 potential workdays.
“In reality, the latest data puts us at about 201 days, with about 19 sick days taken and another seven for workers’ comp and other reasons,” she said.
MTA data shows that as recently as 2013, the number of productive days per employee had climbed as high as 207. That number plummeted to 193 during the COVID-scarred year of 2020, when transit ridership plummeted during the pandemic even as workers kept the subways and buses running.
Officials said the frequent use of sick days comes with a high cost for commuters and the MTA’s finances, citing how the transportation authority has to rely on overtime and reserve bus operators to fill shifts.
But Patel said that some bus operators are “basically whole again” by taking an overtime shift that makes up for sick days.
“We’ve seen that persistently in sort of the bad actors in that sick-leave policy,” she said.
The absentee issue is especially acute among the MTA’s nearly 13,000 bus operators, who make up the largest single group of workers at the transit agency.
“Many of them are doing the right thing and showing up to work day in and day out,” Lieber said. “But about a thousand of the operators are taking a significant number of sick days, over 50 days per year.”
That has amounted to 118,000 canceled trips so far this year, he added, because “there was no bus operator available to drive the bus.”
“It burns everybody else who’s showing up to work,” Lieber said.
Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents the largest number of MTA bus drivers, declined to comment through a spokesperson. The union is in the midst of contract negotiations with the MTA.
“We are working hard to get the TWU contract settled,” Lieber said. “I think we are making progress and I’m not ready to say anything more specific than that, but that is very much a priority.”
The grumbling over canceled bus trips came after the MTA had to contend in recent years with hundreds of operator vacancies that stemmed from retirements, a pre-pandemic hiring freeze and worker deaths. To fill the shortfall, the transportation authority in 2021 began a hiring spree.
MTA Board Member Marc Herbst said he was “shocked” by the high sick-leave numbers.
“If I had a job where I only had to show up four days a week and not even include vacation and personal time, that’s unbelievable,” he said.
The head of an organization that advocates for MTA express bus riders said those who travel between the boroughs and Manhattan are subjected to more crowded carriages and getting pinched in the wallet as a result of driver absences.
“Some people work at odd hours when the express bus may run only hourly,” said Vittorio Bugatti, founder of the Express Bus Advocacy Group. “For those people working at night and heading to Manhattan, they may be forced to take an expensive Uber if they live somewhere where there literally is no alternative like a subway.”
Lieber said it’s very difficult to discipline or fire workers who frequently call out sick. He blamed “too many roadblocks” in the disciplinary process against absentee bus drivers for the low worker-availability rates, saying it’s “really hard to get those people out the door.”
“We need to cut through all that and have a short, predictable disciplinary process,” he said. “It will be fair for them because they will hopefully get the message and come to work.”
“Or they can go get work at another place, they’re not ready to work at the MTA,” Lieber added. “Go find another job.”

https://hyperallergic.com/georgia-okeeff.title: Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in NYC Closet Sells for $4.9M
https://hyperallergic.com/georgia-okeeff.author: Phillip Pyle
https://hyperallergic.com/georgia-okeeff.text:
Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in NYC Closet Sells for $4.9M
Calls to exclude Russia from Venice Architecture Biennale, Public Art Fund announces 2027 program, and more in today's art news.
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.
Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in Closet Breaks Estimates
Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.
EU Countries Call to Exclude Russia From Architecture Biennale
Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.
Public Art Fund Announces 2027 Program
Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.
More in Today’s News:
- Brooklyn artist Julia Jo's "One Fell Swoop" (2026) will be offered at Christie’s evening sale tomorrow, November 19, to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. The New York-based nonprofit has supported unhoused individuals and families in the city through food, clothing, housing, job training, and youth programs since its founding in 1981. "One Fell Swoop" is estimated to fetch between $30,000 and $50,000, though a Christie’s spokesperson told Hyperallergic that “we think it will go for more.”
- Two months before the closing of Ana Mendieta at London’s Tate Modern, the Museum of Modern Art has announced it will present the first retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist in the United States in over 20 years.
- Leading feminist conceptual artist Eleanor Antin has sued her dealer Richard Saltoun, who operates galleries in New York, London, and Rome, over his alleged withholding of at least 179 works.
- After this month’s “blue wave,” President Donald Trump will soon have to contend with a Democrat-majority Congress ready to investigate his culture war tirades against institutions including the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the Kennedy Center.
- This week, the City of Sydney in Australia awarded 40 artists $25,000 “no strings attached” grants in a new initiative aimed at preventing the city from losing “its local storytellers and creative soul.”
- Five works, including 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and 18th-20th century inscribed crosses, were repatriated to Ethiopia following a ceremony in London today, November 18, as part of a new partnership between the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio and the Ethiopian Heritage Authority.

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny.
The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances.
It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days.
The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.
Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on.
Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.
But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.)
The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.”
The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.
“We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.”
Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance.
Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.
“The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.”
In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.”
Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies.
Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined by a series of decisions from previous mayors.
Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit.
The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a commentary in the Chicago Tribune over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”).
Then, in a brief interview with the Chicago Sun-Times on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit.
“If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.”
Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation.
S&P Global, one of a handful of major ratings agencies, released a statement on Wednesday about its “CreditWatch” for Chicago. It cited the intense battle over the budget and an increased likelihood that “the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget.”
That means analysts see at least a 1-in-2 chance of issuing a rating cut in the next three months.
Johnson’s administration has sought to portray Gabrysch as someone who fell short in her duties and mismanaged a major transfer of funds — characterizations she has disputed.
Read More
The mayor has dismissed the conflict that led to Gabrysch’s resignation as a “technical dispute.” When he unveiled his 2027 budget, Johnson and administration officials said 76% of the budget gap would be closed with “structural fixes” — long-term or permanent solutions — that would bring expenses in line with revenues. That could help the city avoid another credit downgrade.
But Gabrysch told the City Council on Oct. 26 that the decision to borrow $481 million to cover the cost of resolving police misconduct lawsuits in 2027 and 2028 changed that calculation, reducing the amount the gap closed with revenue the city can count on in future years to just 56%.
As recently as September, Johnson told reporters the city would not borrow to cover those costs.
If the City Council approves Johnson’s proposal to borrow $481 million, the city’s massive debt burden — which now tops $55 billion — is set to grow for the second straight year to cover the cost of running the city, a sign of financial trouble.
That distress, Johnson has argued, is largely due to the decisions of previous administrations. “It’s no secret: Our city finds itself in a precarious financial situation due to decades of mismanagement,” he said Tuesday.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/s.title: Sean Duffy’s DOT Pitches Congestion Pricing Grants While Trying to Kill Congestion Pricing
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/s.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/s.text:
So now U.S. DOT Secretary Sean Duffy says congestion pricing is just fine, a complete 180 from what the Trump administration had been saying for more than six years. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
President Trump and Secretary Sean Duffy’s Department of Transportation, which has spent two years trying to kill New York City’s congestion pricing program, has exciting news for cities across America: They can apply for grants to launch their own congestion pricing programs.
A triumphant press release from the Federal Highway Administration on Wednesday announced that cities can apply for $100 million in grants for a number of programs that reduce congestion including “HOV toll lanes, as well as congestion, cordon, and parking pricing programs” (emphasis added).
Trump and Duffy have famously warred with the MTA and the Empire State over New York City’s congestion pricing program, which has reduced the number of vehicles in the Manhattan core and provided a reliable revenue stream to fund capital work on the city’s mass transit system.
The federal agency’s reversal clearly surprised MTA Chairman and CEO Janno Lieber. On Wednesday, he interrupted an ongoing press conference after his agency’s monthly board meeting to acknowledge the email and wonder aloud why the FHWA wants more congestion pricing programs around the country.
“Either they’ve been hacked, or Sean Duffy’s been reading the press on this subject, but either way, that’s a pretty remarkable about-face,” said Lieber. “I think it really speaks to the fact that this program has not only survived legally but has been such a success in its implementation.”
The MTA boss was magnanimous in the face of the somewhat maddening news that the proudly anti-congestion pricing administration is now promoting congestion pricing, even as the MTA continues to defend the toll in court from Duffy’s and the president’s campaign to kill it for good.
“In the long run, the fact that the program has been successfully implemented, and the legal fight about it, has been part of making sure the world understands how successful and effective it has been, is actually a net benefit to those of us who believe this kind of initiative is worth the candle,” he said.
After cutting vehicle entries into Manhattan south of 60th Street by 11 percent in its first year, the toll has continued to reduce vehicle entries into Manhattan’s central business district. In 2026, fewer than 500,000 vehicles on average entered lower Manhattan during every month but October, compared to five months that averaged more than 500,000 daily vehicle entries into the Manhattan CBD in 2025.
New York City’s economy has not fallen apart. Furthermore, the MTA has successfully defended the traffic toll in six separate federal lawsuits in the Southern District of New York, two in New Jersey and one state-level lawsuit in New York.
Of course, U.S. DOT is bound by law to offer states and cities the chance to apply for projects to reduce congestion through congestion pricing or cordon pricing. But the law does require Duffy and his agency to award grants for traffic tolls. He and U.S. DOT are free to spend all of their time and money on the other traffic-reduction strategies mentioned in the press release, such as traffic monitoring and on-demand micro-transit.
Still, as long as the federal transportation agency is mentioning cordon pricing, it is as good time as any to remind longtime readers that Duffy pronounces the word “cordon” in a weird way — as cor-DON — which really set off this reporter in early 2025.
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.
"The NYPD will be able to continue to use bicycles as a form of transit," Mamdani said at a press conference about his disbanding of the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. "And what we’ve made very clear is a limitation on the use of bicycles as a weapon or form of aggression.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/unions-schum.title: Why Are Most Union Leaders Silent on Booting Chuck Schumer?
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/unions-schum.author: Eric Blanc
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/unions-schum.text:
Why Are Most Union Leaders Silent on Booting Chuck Schumer?
There is exactly zero reason to believe Chuck Schumer is the man for this moment. Yet most union leaders are not speaking up against him in the fight with Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader.
Why have only four national unions publicly backed Chris Van Hollen against Chuck Schumer for Senate leader? The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, the Office and Professional Employees International Union, National Nurses United, and the National Union of Healthcare Workers have taken Van Hollen’s side in this urgent fight. But where is everybody else?
It’s hard to overstate the stakes. If Democrats once again squander the opportunity given to them by the American people, the lost chance to improve people’s lives — and the ensuing political backlash — could be even worse than what followed the Clinton, Obama, and Biden administrations. Schumer-style corporate politics might as well have been designed in a lab to ensure that Democrats disappoint voters and quickly hand Republicans back the reins of power, perhaps this time under an even more dangerous and effective incarnation of far-right reaction.
Missing the Moment
There is exactly zero reason to believe Schumer is the man for this moment. He’s a pro-Israel war hawk who is deeply embedded with the same billionaires that Democrats — including every single victorious 2026 Democratic Senate candidate in a battleground state — ran against in these midterms.
Want to see the pro-union Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act and other urgent reforms passed within the first hundred days of the next Democratic administration? So do I. But even if Democrats win the presidency and retain Congress, getting this crucial labor law reform enacted will almost certainly require abolishing the filibuster. Van Hollen has explicitly endorsed doing so. As he put it last Friday, the Senate needs to let majorities govern with “fifty-one votes,” rather than keeping the “antidemocratic” filibuster. Schumer, by contrast, has refused to say whether he’d support getting rid of it. Asked directly after the midterms whether Democrats should abolish the rule, he dodged the question.
There’s also plenty a Senate majority leader can do over the next two years, even with Trump still holding the presidential veto. Democrats should aggressively investigate the administration’s corruption and use their control over spending to immediately challenge its worst policies on Iran, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Israel. Even more important, they’ll need to make crystal clear to Americans the ambitious agenda they’ll enact if they win the White House in 2028.
Van Hollen is promising to make the Senate a center of political opposition to billionaire power, putting popular reforms on the table and forcing Republicans to defend their opposition. Schumer is itching to return to the familiar routines of Schumerism: decent policy promises, timid negotiations, and endless excuses for inaction.
Plus, he’s insanely unpopular. A November YouGov poll found that just 23 percent of voters viewed Schumer favorably, compared with 39 percent for Trump. That’s right: the Democratic leader most national unions are so far refusing to buck is substantially less popular than Donald Trump. An astonishing 57 percent of voters view Schumer unfavorably. Only 10 percent want him to remain Senate majority leader, compared with 57 percent who want somebody else.
Why on earth should the party’s future be placed in the hands of someone so widely disliked?
Schumer’s supporters understandably point to the Democratic victories this month. He did help recruit some good candidates, and that deserves some credit. But winning a midterm election amid an unpopular president’s economic and political disasters is a pretty different task from governing successfully afterward.
The Case for Van Hollen
Like Franklin Delano Roosevelt in the 1930s, Van Hollen comes out of the Democratic establishment but is reading the mood of the public and offering a real alternative to politics as usual. He has called for confronting billionaire power, backed Medicare for All, supported ending the filibuster, and taken a much tougher line on using congressional spending authority to end Trump’s war with Iran. He has also pledged to give the new class of insurgent populist senators a greater role in shaping the party’s direction.
Obviously, changing the leader won’t automatically overcome every obstacle to reform. Obviously, switching Senate leaders doesn’t mean the rest of us can sit back and watch the Democrats finally deliver. But there’s a big difference between a leader promising to break with business as usual and one whose career has largely been built around it.
Van Hollen has also shown that he’s willing to take political risks for workers. Don’t forget the case of Kilmar Ábrego García, the sheet-metal apprentice and International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART) member who Trump illegally deported to a notorious prison in El Salvador. Van Hollen personally flew there, met with Ábrego García, and helped lead the fight that brought him back to the United States. You would think SMART leadership would back a leader willing to go to such a degree for one of its members.
Some national unions have so far made clear that they understand the stakes. The Machinists’ president, Brian Bryant, said Van Hollen understood that the fight was one of “Workers vs. Billionaires.” OPEIU likewise sent Schumer a letter urging him to withdraw and make way for another leader, such as Van Hollen. National Nurses United put the point well in endorsing Van Hollen. Its executive director, Puneet Maharaj, warned that Democrats must not squander the opening voters have given them.
Politicking on the K Street Corridor
The reason why more national union leaders aren’t yet saying the same isn’t complicated.
Many of them feel that a significant part of their job is to build close relationships with congresspeople to deliver for their members and fight for pro-worker legislation. If they back Van Hollen and Schumer wins, there’s a real risk that their union might suddenly find that their calls get returned a little less quickly (or not at all), and that important Democratic leaders might no longer listen to their legislative priorities. That’s a valid concern, especially given how Washington currently works.
But it’s also an extraordinarily narrow way to calculate political risk, especially at this moment of crisis. For years now, progressive union leaders have rightly insisted that democracy is on the line, that sky-high economic inequality must be reversed, that the Democrats should stand up for the little guy, and that the labor movement must do everything possible to defeat MAGA and greedy CEOs.
Now union leaders and Democrats have a rare opportunity to actually move the needle in that direction. And it wouldn’t even take much effort. This Senate fight is one of those exceedingly rare moments when a union press release could make a historic difference for working people and the country as a whole.
There’s no excuse for silence. Schumer is seventy-five and faces reelection in 2028 — if he even chooses to run. He’s hardly a permanent fixture of American politics. And Van Hollen is a respected senator who can work across the party’s ideological divisions.
The timidity prevailing on the K Street corridor of downtown DC isn’t an inevitable way of doing politics. Just look at how much bolder unions have been in state-level contests this year. In Michigan, the United Auto Workers (UAW), the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) Michigan, National Nurses United, the Association of Flight Attendants, and United Food and Commercial Workers Local 951 were among the unions that took sides in a fiercely contested Democratic Senate primary, backing Abdul El-Sayed against Schumer’s preferred candidate, Haley Stevens. In Maine, the state AFL-CIO and dozens of local unions went all out for Troy Jackson. And in Minnesota, the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), UNITE HERE Local 17, and others backed Peggy Flanagan against the more establishment-friendly Angie Craig. All three of these Senate winners are now supporting Van Hollen.
Moving away from this bold spirit, most national union leaders currently appear to want to stay silent, hoping to square the circle between the evident anger of their base and their desire not to break with Schumer.
Some of them have framed the issue to me over the past few days as a matter of fighting for the agenda, not the person. But whether they like it or not, it’s precisely that choice of agenda and strategy that’s now being posed by the Senate leadership fight. Everybody knows that who leads the party has a great deal to do with what the party actually does.
It’s a bit disingenuous, too, to suddenly insist that the agenda matters but the leadership doesn’t, given how many national unions came out swinging for Nancy Pelosi when her speakership seemed like it might be challenged in 2018. Back then, the AFL-CIO, AFT, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, SEIU, UAW, the United Steelworkers, and numerous other unions publicly backed Pelosi in her fight to return as House Speaker. Union leaders understand that the choice of congressional leadership matters for the legislative agenda.
Not Too Late
My suggestion to rank-and-file members and local and state union leaders is to look at this Van Hollen–Schumer fight as a test of whether their national leaders are ready to meet the moment. If they’re not able to take even this relatively mild risk to help save the Democrats from themselves, why should we expect them to take on the much bigger, even more consequential risks, like backing anti-corporate candidates for office in 2028 or massively investing in new organizing to unionize America afterward?
National union leaders still sitting this out or leaning toward Schumer should reconsider. In today’s fight for the future of the Democratic Party, national unions have to choose a side. They can stick with the old, corporate-friendly hacks who helped get us into this mess, or stand with those willing to fight against business as usual. There’s no neutral ground here.

Art Bridges has announced that it will give $9.5 million to extend its Access For All Initiative, which has helped 64 museums across the US to offer free admission and community-based programming. The original funding happened over the course of a three-year evaluation period. The evaluation was a success: Art Bridges found that museums were able to attract a “more local, loyal and diverse visitor community,” according to a press release. The support will help 61 of the original 64 museums and will fund the program through 2029.
Attendance at Access for All programs grew by more than a tenth of a percent from the first year to the second, according to the evaluation. Museums that moved towards a free admission model saw a 22% increase on average in attendance. Surveyed program attendees reported declines in barriers to visiting. Lack of time fell from 46% in Year 1 to 27% in Year 3; financial barriers from 28% to 12%; and lack of awareness from 27% to 11%. The Whitney Museum, one of the participants in the initiative, had 67,000 visitors last year for its free Second Sundays, more than double the museum’s usual Sunday attendance.
The Access For All Initiative began in 2024, with $40 million towards museums in 36 states and Puerto Rico. “The strategy behind the second tranche of funding was to give our organizations an off-ramp, so that they could sustain this beyond Art Bridges’s support,” Art Bridges CEO Anne Kraybill said in an interview with ARTnews, adding that “anytime you take something away, it can be hard for the community to understand why. Our initial three-year investment was the proof of concept that a lot of these organizations needed for their local philanthropists to come along.”

https://gothamist.com/news/city-to-demol.title: City to demolish Brooklyn building damaged in deadly Flatbush collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/city-to-demol.author: Phil Corso
https://gothamist.com/news/city-to-demol.text:
New York City officials say they will demolish a Brooklyn apartment building that was severely damaged in last week's collapse of a neighboring building that killed eight people.
The Department of Buildings announced on Wednesday that engineers determined the building at 1323 Flatbush Ave. is too unstable to repair safely. The building was heavily damaged when the apartment building next door, 1321 Flatbush Ave., collapsed into an adjacent construction site on Wednesday, Nov. 11.
“Given the dangerous condition of the building and the imperative to make sure no one else gets hurt, ordering for the controlled safe demolition of the building is the only available option,” Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a statement.
The department said the building's condition has continued to deteriorate since the collapse, leaving its interior exposed to the elements. Engineers determined that allowing workers inside to install supports would put them at risk.
Officials said tenants also cannot return to retrieve their belongings because of unstable floors and asbestos contamination.
The city has since established a fenced-off safety zone around the building and plans to reinforce the neighboring property at 1325 Flatbush Ave. before demolition begins, officials said.
The cause of the deadly collapse remains under investigation, authorities said.
The Department of Buildings is also inspecting more than 160 construction sites associated with companies and individuals involved in the adjacent development project.
City officials said displaced tenants are receiving hotel accommodations through the American Red Cross through at least the end of November.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/greg.title: Greg Abbott Tried to Destroy Muslim Group By Calling Them Terrorists. Texas Voters Balked.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/greg.author: Sanya Mansoor
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/greg.text:
As Texas Republicans pursued their crusade against the Council on American-Islamic Relations, they ran into an unexpected obstacle: voters.
Republicans Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton had carried out their crackdown on the largest Muslim civil rights group in the U.S., hoping to ban CAIR’s operations in the state and label it a terrorist organization. That agenda suffered a crippling blow in the midterm elections, when Democratic candidates beat Abbott and Paxton in stunning upsets — with both their current offices set to be led by Democrats.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa promised to reverse Abbott’s designation of CAIR as a foreign terrorist organization. She told the Washington Post last week, “We have to use public safety measures for public safety” — decrying Abbott’s designation as “nonsense.” Paxton, who lost a bid for an open U.S. Senate seat, dropped a lawsuit, filed in February, that would have banned CAIR from operating in Texas.
“Don’t underestimate the power of the vote to create the administration that creates and enforces these laws,” said Chelsea Glover, a lawyer with the Muslim Legal Fund of America, who is representing CAIR Texas in litigation challenging Abbott’s designation. “Lots of times we don’t think it’s possible but, as Texas has shown, anything is possible.”
The Muslim Legal Fund of America said the lawsuit is ongoing and will be until Abbott’s terror designation is formally withdrawn by Hinojosa.
CAIR’s suit was necessary, said Glover, but acknowledged that the ballot box can be a faster way to shut down bigotry than drawn out court cases.
CAIR welcomed Hinojosa’s promise to walk back Abbott’s proclamation, which CAIR called a “baseless, unconstitutional order.”
The proclamation classified CAIR and its Texas chapter, as well as the Muslim Brotherhood, as foreign terrorist groups; it also banned designated groups from buying or acquiring land in the state.
“When you get the right person in power, who is going to follow the Constitution, it’s like — poof, the designation is gone almost overnight,” said Imran Ghani, director of digital communications for CAIR Texas and operations director for the Houston branch.
Ghani said CAIR Texas noticed a chilling effect after Abbott’s proclamation last November. Some donors stopped giving money, and a few mosques became hesitant to platform CAIR. He said the organization quickly rebuilt trust and also won over new supporters who were invigorated by the state’s targeting of CAIR and wanted to help.
“I tend to look at it rather positively,” Ghani said. “The designation gave CAIR more publicity than we have ever received.”
CAIR Texas officials pointed out that Republican candidates leaned heavily into fabricated fears about Muslims taking over Texas and enforcing sharia law.
“We had to send a strong message,” said Shaimaa Zayan, Austin director for CAIR Texas. “If we allow them to say all of that and stay home that would be a green light for them to continue harassing our community.”
CAIR Texas says the organization scaled up its engagement around the elections this year by showing up weekly to dozens of mosques in Houston, Austin, and Dallas, from August until early October, during Friday prayers, to encourage voter registration.
CAIR Action, the group’s political wing, reported historic turnout for Texas Muslims voting early in a general election—marking a 78.6 percent increase since 2018.
State-Level Bigotry
Republican candidates’ anti-Muslim rhetoric came alongside the state education board approving an anti-Islamic rewrite of Texas social studies lessons and exclusions on a voucher program for K-12 Islamic schools.
Islamophobia has also led to violence against Texas’s Muslim population in recent years. In 2024, the Justice Department sentenced a Dallas man to 37 years in prison after he killed one person and tried to kill four others during a mass shooting at a Muslim-owned business; the FBI said he intentionally targeted Muslims.
While designating terrorist organizations is normally a power reserved for the federal government, Texas and Florida have taken unprecedented actions to allow state officials to apply those labels.
CAIR and its Florida chapter suspended operations in Florida earlier this month after Gov. Ron DeSantis and four state officials designated the groups as domestic terror organizations under a new, unprecedented administrative process approved by the legislature this summer.
The American Civil Liberties Union and CAIR sued DeSantis, alleging free speech and due process violations. The civil rights groups also argued that the debilitating penalties associated with the designations effectively force targeted groups to shut down.
On Monday, DeSantis commented on X about news of Hinojosa’s promised reversal and said, “This would be a huge contrast with Florida, where CAIR has disbanded.”
“Elections have consequences,” said Shirin Sinnar, a law professor at Stanford University.
She pointed out that the different outcomes in Florida and Texas “show the power of electoral consequences on the same issue.”
“A Loaded Gun”
Sinnar cautioned that the federal government may have plans of its own to crack down on nonprofits.
The Wall Street Journal reported on November 6 that the Trump administration is considering an executive order that would list some nonprofits as being tied to terrorists, effectively shutting down their operations.
Sinnar said that while Texas may be backing off from the executive order and lawsuit against CAIR, there’s more work to be done at the state level.
“It’s a good moment for civil rights advocates and communities to push the legislature to repeal the laws that enabled these designations,” she said. “Otherwise, they’re a loaded gun available to be used in the future against CAIR or another disfavored target.”
Those laws include measures that created the category of Texas foreign terrorist organizations and authorized state and local officials, as well as private residents, the ability to bring civil suits against them without having to prove any personal injury.
Youssef Chouhoud, a research scientist for the Texas-based nonprofit Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research, which focuses on issues related to Muslims, said Republicans in the state will likely continue engaging in Islamophobic rhetoric and policies. Attacking the Muslim community was “very much a winning strategy” in the Republican primaries, he said.
Though 95 percent of Republican primary voters said they supported a ballot proposition asking if “Texas should prohibit sharia law,” critics pointed out that the state’s anti-Muslim hysteria has led to an overblown focus on Muslim religious law.
Ghani, in Houston, had left a corporate job for more meaningful work and joined CAIR only about two months before Abbott’s terror designation. He took solace in his five daily prayers and hoped the past would become precedent.
“History has shown this is the path of many civil rights groups,” Ghani said of the persecution — and perseverance — of other civil rights groups like the NAACP in the 1950s and 60s, and the ACLU itself during the McCarthy era.
“It’s a badge of honor,” Ghani said, “to be targeted by extremists in the government.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
