https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: First Rikers Island Demolition Set for 2027 Under Mamdani Plan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The Mamdani administration plans to begin demolishing a lockup on Rikers Island next year, starting with a nearly century-old jail and medical facility, as part of a sweeping new blueprint to shutter the notorious jail complex, The City Reporter has learned.
The biggest obstacle to closing Rikers remains reducing the number of people behind bars. The city’s jail population stood at 6,651 on Wednesday, down from roughly 7,000 during the Adams administration, but still far above the roughly 4,500 people that four planned borough-based jails are designed to hold.
The transition is expected to happen gradually as the borough-based jails come online. The Brooklyn facility is expected to be completed first, in 2029, with people in custody gradually moved there and corresponding beds on Rikers taken out of service.
The Bronx and Queens facilities are expected to follow in 2031, with the final jail, in Manhattan, slated for 2032.
On Rikers, the North Infirmary Command, which opened in 1932, is slated to be torn down in 2027. The facility was closed in June, with some detainees moved to a new medical unit at Bellevue Hospital.
The building has also been the site of deadly medical emergencies and major operational failures in recent years.
Marvin Pines, 65, died there in February 2023 after suffering a seizure. A state review found that Correction Department staff failed to meet minimum supervision standards and that jail medical staff failed to conduct basic assessments and follow-ups. A fire also broke out at the facility in April 2023, prompting an investigation by the city’s Board of Correction that resulted in a dozen recommendations for the department.
The demolition would mark a symbolic step in the city’s long-running effort to close Rikers, signaling that the island’s days as a jail complex are coming to an end.
The city has not explained why it chose North Infirmary Command, known as NIC, as the first building to come down, or identified which of Rikers’ other jail facilities might be next in line for demolition.
Jail Alternatives
The broader blueprint also calls for increased investments in alternatives to incarceration for people awaiting trial and reentry programs.
It also entails expanding support for families who provide housing for former detainees and assistance to people returning home from jail, according to a source familiar with the plan. That program, known as kinship housing, has been run by the Osborne Association, a nonprofit helping formerly incarcerated people.
“They really are focused on the re-entry side of things,” the source said. “Once you get arrested and charged: How do you divert people as soon as possible?”
Reducing the number of people held in city jails has been one of the biggest obstacles to closing and reforming Rikers, according to multiple jail experts.
The average length of stay in city jails jumped to 116 days in the 2026 fiscal year, up from 87 days the previous year, reversing a decline in the prior two years, according to the city’s latest Mayor’s Management Report. Nearly a quarter of people in Correction Department custody had been held for more than a year, with some spending three years or longer behind bars.
It is unclear what the blueprint includes to speed up the processing of criminal cases. Some of those delays are tied to mental health evaluations, dragged-out court cases, and a backlogged legal system.
The blueprint also calls for overhauling correction officer training with help from Amend, a program based at the University of California, San Francisco, that works to change correctional culture through officer and leadership training. The program draws on public health principles and practices adapted from Norway’s correctional system, emphasizing more constructive relationships between officers and people in custody.
But expanding supportive housing for former detainees has been a longstanding challenge for City Hall dating back more than four decades. Previous administrations have struggled to fund new facilities, get neighborhood buy-in, and cover yearly operating costs.
MORE: Ninth Detainee Dies on Rikers Island So Far This Year
As for the close Rikers plan, the Mamdani administration has already put new money behind its effort.
The November financial plan includes $37.9 million in new funding for the Office of Criminal Justice in the current fiscal year, rising to $110.3 million next fiscal year, according to budget records.
The money is earmarked for a range of initiatives that could help reduce the jail population, including defender decarceration units, expanded alternatives to incarceration, kinship housing and reentry programs.
The administration also appears to be moving toward the long-envisioned Renewable Rikers plan, which would transform the island into a hub for green energy and environmental infrastructure once the jails are shuttered.
The concept, championed by advocates and City Council members for years, envisions using the island for projects including solar energy, wastewater treatment, composting and other sustainability initiatives.
The Mamdani administration has already taken steps in that direction.
In June, the city transferred the North Infirmary Command and portions of two other vacant jail facilities from the Department of Correction to the Department of Citywide Administrative Services, which will oversee planning for their future use.
The blueprint comes as Elizabeth Glazer, one of the chief architects of the original plan to close Rikers, has publicly broken with that approach. Glazer, who led the Mayor’s Office of Criminal Justice under Bill de Blasio, argued in a New York Times opinion essay published Tuesday that Mayor Mamdani should abandon the current strategy and instead rebuild or renovate jails on Rikers Island to create safer, more humane facilities.
On Wednesday, City Hall spokesperson Sam Raskin said the administration remains committed to closing Rikers and moving to a borough-based jail system, but he declined to provide additional details about the planned demolition or broader blueprint.
“As the mayor has said, our administration is fully committed to closing Rikers Island and transitioning to a borough-based jail system that is safer and more humane for both people in custody and staff who work in the jails,” Raskin said in a statement. “We will have more to share soon.”

https://hyperallergic.com/is-my-art-funn.title: Is My Art Funny to You?
https://hyperallergic.com/is-my-art-funn.author: Greta Rainbow
https://hyperallergic.com/is-my-art-funn.text:
Is My Art Funny to You?
A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.
Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”
What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.
Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?
The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.
The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.
Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”)
“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.
Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.
“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”
Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.
Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

The Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago has announced a gift of 65 works of art from Chicago collectors Sandra and Jack Guthman. The gift was made in honor of the MCA’s 60th anniversary and includes paintings, photography, works on paper, and sculpture by 54 artists, 13 of whom are new to the MCA’s collection. The Guthmans have now donated 130 works, more than anyone else in the institution’s history.
The gift includes work by several Chicago-connected artists, like Rashid Johnson, Amanda Wiliams, Pope.L, Christopher Wool, Dawoud Bey, Theaster Gates, and Bethany Collins. Johnson currently has a solo exhibition on view at the MCA, while Williams will have a solo show there next year.
Sandra and Jack Guthman made their first donations to the MCA in 1988, and Jack Guthman joined the institution’s board of trustees shortly thereafter in 1989. In 2016, they made a major donation of 50 works, all of which were made by women photographers, in honor of the MCA’s 50th anniversary. These became the subject of “Woman With A Camera,” an exhibition presented at the museum later that year.
“The significance of this promised gift, and the Guthmans’ overall dedication to the MCA, is to be celebrated,” chief of curatorial affairs and deputy director Joey Orr said in a press release. “These artworks will not only help the MCA achieve its provenance goals—they will deepen and expand our publics’ understanding of contemporary art, which is central to all we do.”

https://gothamist.com/news/trump-said-co.title: Trump said congestion pricing would end NYC. Now, his admin wants it in more cities.
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-said-co.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-said-co.text:
President Donald Trump once declared congestion pricing would kill New York City. Now, his administration wants to help other cities set up similar tolling programs for drivers.
The Federal Highway Administration announced Wednesday it is offering $100 million in grants so other cities can implement their own programs to fight traffic congestion.
The agency said in a release that the funding would allow cities with more than 1 million people to apply for the funds to help monitor and manage traffic, create “HOV toll lanes, as well as congestion, cordon and parking pricing programs.” The federal money can also be used on commuter buses, paratransit and micromobility.
Shortly after Gothamist published this article, "congestion" and "cordon" pricing programs were deleted from the Federal Highway Administration's announcement. Cordon tolls are a technical term for a toll imposed on drivers to enter a designated zone, like a central business district.
MTA Chair Janno Lieber reveled in the apparent change of heart.
“ I say they've been hacked or (Transportation Secretary) Sean Duffy's been reading the press on this subject. But either way, that's a pretty remarkable about-face,” Lieber said Wednesday. “And I think it really speaks to the fact that this program has not only survived legally, but has been such a success, in its implementation.”
Last spring, a federal judge declared the Trump administration's efforts to revoke approval for congestion pricing unlawful. The MTA successfully defended numerous other lawsuits seeking to halt the program, which charges drivers $9 during peak periods to drive in Manhattan south of 60th Street. Toll revenue is used to fund public transit.
The U.S. Department of Transportation did not respond to questions about why it appeared to change its view on the tolling program.
“Gridlock is costing Americans time with their families and money from their wallets,” FHWA Administrator Sean McMaster wrote in a release. “This program brings much-needed relief to our most congested metropolitan areas. Alongside building new capacity, the program uses cutting-edge technology to maximize the efficiency of our highways.”
New York City's congestion pricing tolls have been in effect for nearly two years. The MTA reports traffic is down 15% in Manhattan since the tolls were turned on. The agency says the tolls have raised hundreds of millions of dollars used to secure billions of dollars in bonds to fund capital projects.
“It may have taken nearly two years of unquestionable results and repeated losses in court to understand, but we are glad that Secretary Duffy has seen the light," Sean Butler, a spokesperson for Gov. Kathy Hochul, said in a statement. "Congestion pricing works and we welcome any attempt to emulate New York’s huge success."
Lieber reflected on the fight to implement congestion pricing during an event Wednesday night at WNYC’s Greene Space. He said the lengthy process to get it approved under the Biden administration wound up helping the MTA protect the program from Trump's legal attacks.
“There are improvements to air quality documented, a reduction in crashes that injure pedestrians and cyclists,” Lieber said. “There's a dramatic reduction in the number of noise complaints to 311. And even the drivers have shifted in polls because they are recognizing the value of the time they're saving, especially on the crossings in, in and out of Manhattan.”
This story has been updated to reflect the edit of the Federal Highway Administration announcement.

https://hyperallergic.com/a-marquee-week.title: A Marquee Week of Indulgence
https://hyperallergic.com/a-marquee-week.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/a-marquee-week.text:
A Marquee Week of Indulgence
The latest from the fall auctions, museum protests, and tackling the British Empire one video at a time.
My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.
Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work, alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution.
Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.
Really glad they worked that out.
On the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the Museum of Modern Art during an annual benefit for the museum’s Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center last Thursday, calling on filmmaker and honored guest Steven Spielberg to reject the recognition and boycott the museum over Leon Black’s Epstein-related sexual abuse allegations. Cold, biting rain soaked the group of 20 artists and activists outside the gala, and Spielberg hasn’t acknowledged their demands.
All things considered, Iraqi-British data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi’s first-ever book, which was released last week, comes at a most opportune time. The book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026), comes from Chalabi five-year endeavor in examining class inequality in the United States by analyzing the incomes, expenses, tax deductions, systemic barriers, and livelihoods of 10 Americans across the nation. In a recent interview with Hyperallergic’s Lakshmi Rivera Amin, Chalabi noted that journalists themselves often don’t acknowledge or even recognize how their own class upbringing can color their reporting on wealth and poverty, whereas other markers like race and gender are positioned as lenses of understanding.
A new video exhibition on the High Line also tackles greed and indulgence through the lens of the British Empire’s storied trade monopolies and resource theft across South Asia and China. Works by Shahzia Sikander and the artist duo Hylozoic/Desires unpack the British stronghold on salt in India and the empire’s deliberate opium influx in China during the Qing dynasty, while also highlighting historic and speculative subversions that disrupt dominant colonial narratives.
I wasn’t super fond of the High Line’s most recent film installation, but this one sounds more up my alley on a subjective, personal history level. I’m looking forward to checking it out soon — before the weather really turns south — and visiting the Mighty Miniatures exhibition that’s opening this Saturday at the National Museum of the American Indian.
Study Contemporary Art at Sotheby's Institute
Whether you’re pursuing a degree, developing your professional expertise, or deepening your knowledge of contemporary art, discover opportunities to learn from specialists and engage directly with the international art world.
From Our Critics
Stephanie Wambugu
Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem at Boesky Gallery
"O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them."
Amy Levine-Kennedy
American Society of Botanical Artists 29th Annual International Exhibition at the Society of Illustrators
"Here is awe for Mother Earth and her plants — and these botanical artists — and for the meticulous, enchanting detail and outcry that cherish every bud, stem, leaf, petal, bark, seed, blade, stamen, and root."
Phillip Pyle
Octopus and Others: Acts of Collaboration and Poetics at El Museo del Barrio
"The message that passes through could resonate with any of the works that surround it: 'My thoughts have meandered with the footsteps I have walked, heading on this journey to a place I call home.'"
Interviews
Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallergic about her first book, “Ten Lives.” | Lakshmi Rivera Amin
Read More
How Miles Greenberg Got “WAR” Past the Censors

What Else Is Happening?
- At the Bard Graduate Center, design researcher Yelena McLane takes an audience into the world of Soviet design principles through the lens of influential monthly magazine Decorative Art of the USSR (1957–91), a critical platform for diversity and innovation in industrial design, interior decor, crafts, folk art, and monumental and decorative architecture across the Soviet Republics. (Wed Nov 18) [bgc.bard.edu]
- Stewards of local historic and cultural landmarks across Queens share the stories of behind their sites and invite the next generation to engage with the borough’s diverse history in a talk at the Lewis Latimer House in Flushing (Thu Nov 19) [Instagram flyer]
- Perhaps an institutional complement to HBO's Sex and the City, the Museum of the City of New York opens its Photography Triennial devoted to night time hours in the Big Apple. Midnight snacks, the third shift, and NYC's world-famous nightlife scene are centered in this group exhibition of contemporary photography. (Fri Nov 20) [mcny.org]
- Part of Amant’s programming for Sentient Earth, exhibiting artists Emil Martirosian and Rachel Fäth will stage a live electronic sound performance complemented by time-based media touching on the show’s themes of extractive industries and their interference with earth’s natural frequencies. (Fri Nov 20) [amant.org]
- The Whitney celebrates 25 years of artport, its online gallery space for web art commissions, in a phygital exhibition on its sixth floor. (Sat, Nov 21) [whitney.org]
- The Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian opens Mighty Miniatures, a collection exhibition on bite-sized Indigenous art and its monumental role in preserving traditional knowledge, stimulating economic development, and stoking children's imaginations. (Sat Nov 21) [americanindian.si.edu]

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-warns-of-.title: MTA warns of major budget deficit without help from city, state and feds
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-warns-of-.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-warns-of-.text:
MTA officials on Wednesday warned the transit agency will face a half-billion-dollar deficit as soon as 2028 if the city, state and federal governments don’t help balance its books.
The agency’s leaders proposed a balanced budget for next year, which is required by state law. But the financial plan also projects a $585 million deficit in its operating budget for 2028, which could grow to a $979 million deficit in 2030. MTA officials said existing revenues from fares, tolls and taxes aren’t enough to keep up with rising costs for healthcare, wages, fuel and electricity.
MTA Chair Janno Lieber said he hoped the incoming Democratic majority in Congress would approve more funding for the agency. He also called on the city to pay for a larger share of the MTA’s paratransit service.
The city currently covers a majority of the cost to run that program. Lieber said lawmakers in Albany could approve legislation requiring the city to pay a larger share, which could save the state-run agency $300 million annually.
The mayor's office didn't immediately comment on Lieber's remarks.
The MTA’s annual budgets often project deficits in future years. Gov. Kathy Hochul and state lawmakers have, over the past five years, approved marginal tax hikes, including an increase in a payroll tax for large New York City businesses in 2023, to help keep the transit agency fully funded.
The MTA budgets a 4% fare and toll hike every two years designed to align with the rate of inflation. The budget proposed Wednesday said the next increase is planned for March.
Lieber on Wednesday noted that without new funding, the MTA would need to resort to even higher fare hikes, service cuts and headcount reductions to balance its books.
“Those are the only tools the MTA has at its disposal,” Lieber said. “Those are not tools that we ever want to use.”
Lieber also noted the MTA has not received any new discretionary funds from the U.S. Department of Transportation since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025. He argued it wasn’t fair that New York carries 43% of the nation’s mass transit riders but only receives 17% of the federal funding annually allocated for mass transit agencies.
“If we get a fairer contribution from Washington, we might have to borrow a little less money,” Lieber said at a news conference. “So if we get a fairer share from Washington, it too will contribute to the solution and that’s why we’re focusing on it so much.”

https://hyperallergic.com/obits-2/.title: Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89
https://hyperallergic.com/obits-2/.author: Lisa Yin Zhang
https://hyperallergic.com/obits-2/.text:
Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89
In this column honoring those we lost in the art world, we also remember a British painter of bewitching scenes and one of Japan’s greatest manga artists.
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.
Arpita Singh (1937–2026)
Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality
One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year.
"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."

https://gothamist.com/news/alleged-centr.title: Alleged Central Park rapist charged with 2 counts of rape, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/alleged-centr.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/alleged-centr.text:
The man wanted for sexually assaulting a woman at knifepoint in Central Park last month has been charged with two counts of rape and is expected to appear before a Manhattan judge on Wednesday.
Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, arrived in New York City on Tuesday — a week after he was taken into custody at a Burger King in Miami by NYPD detectives assigned to the U.S. Marshals Regional Fugitive Task Force, according to the department.
Police said he attacked a 39-year-old woman near East 67th Street and East Drive around 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 24. Officials said he would also be charged with two earlier rapes in the park, in 2023 and 2021.
The department did not say how investigators linked him to those attacks or release any details about either.
Rivera-Deleon is scheduled to be arraigned in Manhattan Criminal Court. Information for his lawyer is not yet available.
Police said his most recent New York address was in the Wakefield neighborhood of the Bronx.
This story is developing and may be updated.

https://hyperallergic.com/moma-to-host-f.title: MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years
https://hyperallergic.com/moma-to-host-f.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/moma-to-host-f.text:
MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years
The 200-work exhibition will open in December 2027, almost a year after the closing of the Tate Modern’s current retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist.
The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in New York next year. Scheduled to open at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in Manhattan in December 2027, Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective marks the first presentation of Mendieta's overarching career in the United States in over 20 years.
MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London. Comprising around 200 works, including rarely seen formative drawings and newly remastered films, the MoMA exhibition will present Mendieta's artistic process, signature developments, and career milestones in a chronological fashion. Starting with early figurative works completed during her undergraduate and graduate studies at the University of Iowa, the exhibition will follow the artist's subsequent expansion in making and documenting her performance art, as well as her foray into sculpture, installation, and site-specific land art.
Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world. She's best known for her Silueta (1973–80) series, in which the outline of her body (either present or absent) is embedded, extruded, burned, or embellished into various natural environments as a physical and spiritual reunion with the earth. These “earth-body works,” as Mendieta called them, dealt with Mesoamerican and Afro-Caribbean divinity, natural reclamation and life cycles, and the deconstruction of borders.
Presaging Mendieta's groundbreaking Siluetas were transgressive performance pieces centering the use of blood as a signifier of violence, fertility, vitality, and ancestral ritual. Her 1973 performance “Untitled (Rape Scene)” and its photo documentation were created in response to the rape and murder of 20-year-old University of Iowa student Sarah Ann Ottens, whereas her filmed performance of “Untitled (Death of a Chicken)” (1972) graphically referenced animal sacrifice practices associated with Santería.
The retrospective also centers the artist's lens-based work, her sustained interest in organic material, and how her travels, reunion with Cuba, and art residencies sparked major evolutions in her practice. Mendieta's 1981 Esculturas Rupestres (Rupestrian Sculptures) series, 1983–85 fellowship at the American Academy in Rome, and a variety of later works, including a series of ink-wash drawings, are among the highlights mentioned by the museum.
“Ana Mendieta rigorously investigated the physical, conceptual, and emotional potential of materials like soil, sand, water, blood, leaves, wood, and fire to create images that speak across time and geography,” said Beverly Adams, MoMA's Latin American art curator and retrospective co-organizer, in a press statement. “In doing so, she redefined the boundaries between sculpture and action, object and image, and private and public.”
In celebrating Mendieta's punctuated career, the retrospective apparently strays away from the tragic circumstances of the 36-year-old artist's death and the unshakeable speculations that continue to follow. Such is the case with Mendieta's ongoing exhibition at the Tate Modern, which also omitted mentioning the artist's death and the resulting controversy surrounding her husband, artist Carl Andre.
Nevertheless, the artist's own poignant grapplings with loss and rebirth are staged independently of the discourse, underscoring her persisting critical impact in a visual arts landscape that has rarely offered credit to women artists.
Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective will be on view at MoMA from December 12, 2027 to April 15, 2028.

https://hyperallergic.com/edward-said-sp.title: Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever
https://hyperallergic.com/edward-said-sp.author: Moustafa Bayoumi
https://hyperallergic.com/edward-said-sp.text:
Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever
As a new documentary shows, the Palestinian scholar believed an intellectual must always oppose domination while cultivating resistance.
In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die.
While Salloum and Suleiman’s film consists mostly of news clips and film reels, one of Gaza’s elder statesmen, the late Haider Abdul Shafi, does appear briefly twice. In one scene, Abdul Shafi, sitting at a nondescript table, is asked by an interviewer: “Is it your belief that if a Palestinian state was created, there would be lasting peace in the Middle East?” Just as he’s about to respond, the film mischievously cuts away, in an edit loaded with meaning. Palestinians may be seen in Western media, the film is telling us, but they cannot be heard from.
Maiken Baird’s new documentary, Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), joyfully demonstrates how Edward Said was the exception to this semi-official ban on Palestinians representing themselves. Like Salloum and Suleiman, Baird also sifts through reservoirs of found footage, though the result couldn’t be more different. Offering a rough chronology of Said’s life, Baird’s film celebrates him by highlighting his contributions and lasting influence in numerous domains, from literary theory to American foreign policy.
For decades, the Columbia University professor of comparative literature was the most famous, if not the only, Palestinian regularly speaking on American airwaves and writing about the Palestinians in its magazines. Wearing his bespoke suits and contributing classical music criticism to the Nation, Said cut an urbane, sophisticated, and cosmopolitan figure.
But it was his substance, and not his style, that earned him his legacy. As the author of the foundational text Orientalism, Said was one of the most influential intellectuals of the 20th century, and he took the vocation extremely seriously, holding the yes-men intellectuals of the powerful in contempt. As he wrote in his essay “Secular Criticism": “It is not practicing criticism to validate the status quo.” For Said, an intellectual must always oppose domination while cultivating resistance to oppression.
I am one of the fortunate ones. I knew Edward Said personally, having studied under him while I completed my PhD at Columbia University. With Andrew Rubin, another of his students, I edited The Selected Works of Edward Said: 1996-2006 (2019). (A producer of this film contacted me during its early phase for a background discussion on Said and his life, but I had nothing to do with the making of this documentary.) It’s hard to believe that more than 20 years have passed since Said died from leukemia in 2003, but thanks to Baird’s documentary, a new generation can now access his indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight for justice.
With the question of Palestine currently assuming a new urgency around the world, and with Israel’s genocide of Gazans ongoing, the timing of the film feels like a deliberate intervention. To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation. It’s no mistake that, aside from hearing a few interviewers’ questions and small asides, the audio of this 108-minute film consists almost entirely of Said speaking.
Produced with the cooperation of the Said family, the film includes moments from early home movies taken by Wadie Said, Edward Said’s father. The elder Said purchased a movie camera in 1938 and made “incredibly boring” films, according to the younger. By including snippets of these early scenes, Baird does something more than show us a young and gangly Edward Said. The home movies not only invite viewers into the private life of a Palestinian family in Palestine. They also become an assertion of presence against an ideology which demands Palestinian absence.
Young Edward was entirely apolitical. As a teenager, he was expelled for being a “troublemaker” from Victoria College in Egypt and sent by his family to the “puritanical” Mount Hermon School in rural Massachusetts, where, as he says, he was mocked endlessly for his name (“Ed Said. Well, what did he say?”). An elite education at Princeton and Harvard followed, and then a job as an assistant professor at Columbia University. “The professional thing took care of itself,” he says. But after the humiliating Arab defeats of the 1967 war, Said felt a need to reconcile the two parts of himself: an American professor of literature and a Palestinian Arab born in Jerusalem. In the wake of the losses in 1967, his friend Ibrahim Abu-Lughod invited him to contribute an essay to the United States-based magazine The Arab World, and Said wrote “The Arab Portrayed,” his first significant foray into the politics of representation.
In the film, Said describes his decisions to take on the Palestinian cause, and his father’s caution to his son: “I’m very worried about what the Zionists will do to you." In the early 1970s, while living in Beirut, he immerses himself in the Arabic language and literature and associates with some of the preeminent Palestinian intellectuals of the era. The film’s tempo picks up as Said’s star begins to shine more brightly. We watch him being asked borderline racist questions in multiple TV interviews, see him with Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat, and despair with him when the Israeli invasion of Lebanon leads to the expulsion of the PLO from Lebanon in 1982.
Said was the most prominent dissenting Palestinian voice to the 1993 Oslo Accords. He believed the PLO had sold out the Palestinian national movement, only to become “Israel’s enforcer” of the occupation. Baird’s film successfully shows how he went from being a fierce critic of American and Israeli policy to a fierce critic of American, Israeli, and Palestinian leadership. I knew Said at this time in his life, and what the film doesn’t show is the profound sense of isolation he felt while the entire global liberal establishment was telling us that “the conflict,” as it’s euphemistically called, was about to be solved. Needless to say, Said was right.
Music was a grounding force in Said’s life (he was a near-concert-level pianist) and another constant in the film. Baird ends her film with his growing friendship with the Argentinian-Israeli composer Daniel Barenboim. Said and Barenboim began the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra, a musical venture bringing together young Arab and Israeli musicians, in 1999, the same year his essay “The One-State Solution” was published in the New York Times. The essay argued that “real peace can come only with a binational Israeli-Palestinian state.”
In the final years of his life, Said committed himself to such efforts at coexistence. The last scene of this finely tuned documentary is of him playing the piano with passionate intensity. “It’s not our destiny to be refugees," he says via voiceover. "It’s not our destiny to be prisoners of war. It’s not our destiny to be commandos. It’s not our destiny to be an army of occupation. We have a choice.”
There is more than a whiff of optimism in these later positions, and it’s impossible to say where Said would stand today, as Palestinians face their most demanding fight for survival yet. But the fact that his optimism feels somewhat dated today probably tells us less about Said and more about how far away we are now from attaining true and lasting justice for the Palestinians.
Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), directed by Maiken Baird, is screening at various film festivals including the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam, London Palestine Film Festival, Marrakech International Film Festival, and many more. It will be released widely in 2027 by Kino Lorber.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: City Says Pied-à-Terre Tax Will Bring in Half a Billion Dollars, Despite Fewer Bills
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration wound up billing thousands fewer homeowners for his vaunted pied-à-terre tax than they originally believed would be eligible, but he continues to insist it will raise the $500 million that he’d previously predicted.
On Sunday, the Department of Finance mailed out bills to 7,500 households — less than half the 17,000 who got notices last summer saying they were susceptible to the tax because the city believed their properties were not primary residences.
But thousands of targeted owners insisted the city got it wrong, and the administration ultimately granted exemptions to nearly 9,000 properties that were initially pegged for the tax.
The tax applies to two- and three-family homes with what the city determines to be a “market value” of $5 million or more and condos and co-ops the city says are worth $1 million or more. All of the properties that won exemptions would have raised at least $356 million if they’d been declared second homes.
Despite the big drop in the number of properties that actually got billed, the administration stuck with the $500 million revenue figure they say will help plug a budget gap.
City officials explained that the predicted revenue will materialize despite the significant drop in billed properties because those that were ultimately confirmed as second homes had higher market values.
“As Mayor Mamdani has said before, owning a second home worth over $5 million should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable,” Finance Commissioner Richard Lee said in a statement, asserting that the agency “will continue to implement the pied-à-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone.”
Ken Girardin of the Manhattan Institute noted that the 7,500 billed properties fall short of the 10,000 homes Gov. Kathy Hochul had estimated as subject to the tax when she signed off on it in May.
“The governor’s office expected the final number of properties would land around 10,000 and this is the strongest indication yet that the city will come up short,” Girardin said, predicting that “this will make it tougher to close the FY28 budget gap next spring.”
A spokesperson for the governor, Jennifer Goodman, noted the 10,000 households eligible for the tax was merely an estimate, adding, “It’s up to the city to determine how the tax is implemented. I don’t think ‘coming up short’ is fair but I refer you to the city for specific questions here.”
