https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.title: This Counselor Faces Trial for Sexually Abusing 15 Students. California Has Been Warned About Him for Years.
https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.author: Holly McDede
https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Licensed Until Charged: Three educators who were reported to the state for alleged misconduct were allowed to keep working — and to draw new complaints — until they were criminally charged.
- Incomplete Investigation: One was reported for allegedly touching children inappropriately in 2019. California didn’t suspend his credentials until his 2024 arrest.
- Lack of Guidelines: California’s educator licensing agency provides no guidelines to the volunteers who review teacher misconduct cases for determining when and how to mete out punishment.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap, rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas.
But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019. And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them, prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had touched him, too.
The state Commission on Teacher Credentialing also delayed revoking the credentials of two other teachers who were later convicted of sexually abusing students. As with Braff, schools had reported those educators to the agency that determines who can work in California’s public schools. And as with Braff, the commission allowed those teachers to keep teaching — and draw new complaints — until after they were criminally charged, an investigation by KQED and ProPublica found. That includes a middle school math teacher who sent his student a video showing a boy’s genitals and an elementary teacher who touched students’ butts and vaginal areas and placed their hands on his crotch, according to court records.
In each of the cases, state investigators did not interview some of the students who had alleged abuse, according to the students, parents and attorneys who spoke to KQED and ProPublica. Several former agency staffers, including investigators, told the news outlets that, at times, the volunteer panel tasked with assessing teacher accusations overlooked evidence of wrongdoing. That perspective from staff members was backed up by two former members of the panel and two people who served on the state commission that ultimately decides teacher discipline.
After police arrested Braff in 2024, a parent emailed Jeffrey Weinstein, superintendent at Santa Paula Unified School District, where Braff was first accused of sexually abusing students. “Who dropped the ball and allowed this monster to still be around kids?” the parent wrote, according to public records obtained by the news outlets. (Weinstein was not working at Santa Paula at the time students accused Braff.)
In his emailed response, Weinstein blamed the state’s teacher licensing agency. He told the parent that the district had conducted its own investigation and reported the guidance counselor to the state as well as to police. He also said he had reviewed the district’s investigative file and “vehemently disagreed” with the agency’s decision not to revoke Braff’s credentials.
“We sent all the evidence we had gathered,” Weinstein said. “The district did everything in its legal capacity it could.”
Braff is soon to stand trial for sexually abusing 15 students, including 13 from Santa Paula. He has been in jail since November 2024. He has pleaded not guilty and did not respond to a request for comment sent through the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office’s electronic messaging system. His attorney declined to comment.
Braff had previously told Santa Paula Unified administrators that he did not touch students near their private parts or have them sit on his lap — and that he only gave students side hugs, high-fives, fist bumps and taps on the knee, according to the district’s 2019 report to the state.
“Mr. Braff described keeping an office environment where kids can move around; and he would not be closer than arm’s length,” the report said, summarizing the district’s interview with Braff. “It was not his intent to make them afraid but rather feel that there was someone in their corner; someone to talk to.”
Anita Fitzhugh, a spokesperson for the Commission on Teacher Credentialing, said the state automatically revokes teachers’ credentials when they are convicted of sexual criminal offenses. But she wrote in a statement that “unless the applicant or educator is convicted of a mandatory criminal offense, there are no written criteria that set the level of adverse action for educator discipline matters.” She did not answer questions about specific cases or details of the investigative process.
Fitzhugh said the state does not provide any guidelines for those reviewing teacher misconduct cases about when discipline is warranted or the type of punishment that should be meted out. And she said it was the commission’s role to balance “protecting students as well as the legal rights of educators who have been accused but not convicted.”
California’s system of disciplining educators dates to the 1970s, Fitzhugh said, and “a deep and comprehensive review of the educator discipline system, prioritizing student safety in the schools, is in order.”
“We expect the Commission to take this up in the near future,” she said.
Students Not Interviewed
In the summer of 2019, California’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing received a detailed report from the Santa Paula school district about Braff’s alleged misconduct at McKevett Elementary School. The state requires districts to report educators when they resign or are fired after allegations of misconduct. Braff, who had been a guidance counselor at the school for four years, had resigned in the midst of the district’s investigation into complaints by at least seven students that he had touched them inappropriately.
The district told the state agency that it had contemplated but did not initiate any discipline against Braff before accepting his resignation. The district said it appeared, based on student interviews, that Braff “had engaged in at least inappropriate conduct.” Its report to the state, submitted two months after he resigned, included a 20-page summary of the principal’s interviews with at least seven accusers and two witnesses. It also included Braff’s defense and noted multiple inconsistencies in his account of what had occurred.
One fifth grade girl said that during a visit to his office, Braff had locked the door, grabbed her by her hips and forced her to sit on his lap, according to the district’s report to the state of its investigation. She said she did not like being touched and cried every time she had to see him for counseling. The girl requested to transfer to another school, district investigators said, because she wanted to “be away from” Braff.
Two other girls alleged Braff touched them near their “privates,” the district reported to the state. Neither girl was aware of the other’s claim.
One of them, a fourth grader, told the principal that she had been meeting regularly with Braff for counseling since second grade. During those visits, he would make her sit on his lap. She told the principal that Braff tapped her on the leg with his hand “in a way to try to make her feel like she was doing a good job,” but she said the tapping hurt. After two school years of regular counseling, she alleged he started tapping her higher on the thigh, close to her “private.” In contrast, she said a different teacher pats students on the head when they do a good job, according to the district’s report to the state.
The girl, who is now 18, spoke to KQED and ProPublica with her mother and attorney present on the condition that only her first initial, J., be used to protect her privacy. J. said Braff had told her that whatever happened in his office was a secret. She said she had few friends at the school and was terrified of getting in trouble when she reported the person she confided in.
The district’s report to the state included notes from an interview with J.’s former principal, Lydia Olivo, who had left the school before J. and other students complained about Braff. Olivo told Santa Paula investigators that J. was “not always honest,” the report said. Olivo described Braff as a reliable employee who had strong relationships with parents, staff and students. She “seemed surprised that any of this could have occurred while she had been Principal at McKevett,” the district’s report said. Olivo did not respond to calls, emails and texts seeking comment.
During the district’s investigation, Braff acknowledged touching students on the knee. “He explained if someone is crying, he taps on the knee to say they are doing a good job to get the sad feelings out,” according to the district’s report to the state. “When asked to demonstrate, Mr. Braff showed a slap on his own knee.”
Nonetheless, the educator licensing agency appears not to have attempted to reconcile the very different accounts of Braff’s behavior. Informed of Olivo’s characterization of her complaint, J. and her mother told KQED and ProPublica that no one at the state agency had called to ask them about it or sought to verify any details, even though the district’s report to the state included J.’s contact information along with that of the other students.
“If a little girl comes up to you and says something, maybe you should not say that they’re a liar,” J. said.
“They should interview students themselves and not just rely on the school district. Do a legit investigation,” said J.’s mother, who did not know that the state had decided not to discipline Braff until the news outlets alerted her.
Fitzhugh, the spokesperson for the teacher credentialing agency, did not answer questions as to why J. was not interviewed or whether anyone else was. The case was assigned to a staffer whose job description did not include interviewing victims.
At least one other student who had reported Braff for touching her inappropriately also told KQED and ProPublica that no one from the state contacted her about her allegations.
A former agency investigator, who reviewed the district’s report to the state at the request of the news outlets, said she believed the students’ accusations because the district’s investigation described multiple children making similar claims. She also noted the contradictions in Braff’s responses. Cases involving allegations of inappropriately touching students should always be assigned to investigators trained to interview victims, she said.
“Any claim of sexual misconduct should go to somebody who’s going to be making phone calls,” said the investigator, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect her current job. “This man is grooming these children. There’s no other way to look at it to me. Their stories are credible.”
Per state law, the agency staff assigned to look into Braff’s case did not make recommendations about whether or how to discipline him. That recommendation is left up to a little-known group of volunteers who meet monthly at the agency’s Sacramento headquarters to weigh reports from state investigators, school districts, police and others. That volunteer panel sends its recommendations to the 19 commissioners of the credentialing body, most of whom are appointed by the governor.
If the panel does recommend discipline, the commissioners have the final say. However, if the panel decides that no punishment is warranted, the commissioners do not review that case.
Two former investigators at the state agency told the news organizations that the panel’s recommendations did not always align with the evidence they found. “Sometimes, as investigators, we’ll see the recommendations, and we’ll be like, ‘What the hell happened here?’” one former investigator said.
“I Was Consistently Shocked”
Over three days in December 2020, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, members of the volunteer panel, known as the Committee of Credentials, dialed into their monthly phone meeting to address 198 cases of educators accused of misconduct. Among them was Braff, who by then was working in another school.
The volunteers included a retired law enforcement officer, a school board member, a school administrator, an education consultant and several teachers. They had been selected by the commissioners for two-year terms.
State regulations give the volunteer committee broad latitude when assessing allegations of teacher misconduct and recommending discipline to the commission. Unlike jurors in a criminal trial, who need to believe a case is proven beyond a reasonable doubt in order to convict, the committee only needs to find “probable cause” before recommending a reprimand, a far lower standard.
“It’s where a normal and reasonable person would feel that there’s a chance that this person did this,” said Steve Thorpe, the former law enforcement officer who served on the committee when Braff’s case was reviewed. “It’s a low threshold. You know it when you see it.” He declined to comment on Braff’s case.
The fact that Braff’s case was not forwarded to the commissioners, former committee members said, meant the majority of the seven-member panel did not see enough evidence in the district’s investigation and the state’s report to discipline Braff.
One former committee member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of repercussions from the teacher licensing agency, said she tends to scrutinize district investigations because administrators can misrepresent the facts or ask children leading questions.
Another former committee member who served during the Braff case said that they were generally alarmed to hear some fellow members dismiss children as unreliable sources. The person, who declined to comment on Braff’s case, spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.
“I was consistently shocked,” they said. “To have committee members discuss serious allegations as, ‘Well, you know how girls can be. They say all kinds of things they don’t mean,’ is an unacceptable, antiquated point of view. What if we get this wrong? Who are we allowing in the classroom?”
By the time the committee decided against recommending punishment for Braff, he had already been working as a counselor at a different elementary school in Los Angeles for more than a year. (A former student at that charter school would tell police after Braff’s 2024 arrest that the counselor had touched the boy’s thigh near his groin when the two met in his office, according to a court transcript from his criminal case.)
In 2022, nearly two years after the state closed Braff’s case, a school administrator reported to the district that one of the girls who had accused Braff of abuse continued to suffer severe anxiety and could not be in rooms alone with men. Another had attempted suicide multiple times and spent a year in residential treatment, she wrote in an email obtained by KQED and ProPublica.
In his response, an assistant superintendent informed the administrator that the district had previously filed with the state to have Braff’s credential revoked or suspended but the agency chose not to do so. “At this point, I think pursing this matter legally is the best way to address these issues,” he wrote, referring to following up with Santa Paula police.
Santa Paula administrators did not respond to requests for comment.
Two Additional Cases
KQED and ProPublica identified at least two other educators who, like Braff, were reported by their school districts to the state for sexual misconduct but were allowed to keep teaching until they were criminally charged. Each would draw additional allegations of sexual abuse.
As in the Braff case, the volunteer committee in these two cases evaluated much of the same evidence as police, including complaints detailing students’ experiences. And in both cases, investigators with the teacher credentialing agency did not interview some victims.
In one, a Southern California school district shared with the state agency screenshots of messages that middle school math teacher Brashawn Washington had sent to his 11-year-old student, who he regularly contacted through the video game Fortnite. Those messages included a TikTok video showing another boy’s penis. (At his trial, Washington told jurors that he did not send the video to his student.)
The Romoland School District also shared with the state screenshots of Washington’s Google Hangouts chats asking the student if he worked out, calling him “guapo,” or handsome, and sending him kissing emojis.
The boy’s mother had provided the screenshots from her son’s phone to the school in May 2020, according to public records obtained from Romoland. The school district promptly alerted police and began its own investigation, filing a report to the teacher credentialing agency that summer, district records show.
The district included in its report the mother’s contact information, records show. But neither the student nor his mother were interviewed, the mother told KQED and ProPublica. Fitzhugh, the credentialing agency spokesperson, did not answer questions about how state investigators decided who, if anyone, to interview.
A Romoland administrator who said the district shared the screenshots with the state as part of its report did not answer questions about the state’s response.
Washington resigned during the school’s investigation and soon got hired at Pasadena High School starting in the fall of 2020. Washington, teaching virtually at first during the pandemic, continued messaging students over Fortnite despite district policy prohibiting personal contact with students. He had been teaching there for seven months when the volunteer committee recommended a 21-day suspension in March. (Commissioners did not approve the suspension until after school let out.)
State law did not require Washington to notify the Pasadena school district of the recommended suspension. Nor did the teacher licensing agency have to alert his new employer of any discipline if it did not know where he was employed.
Just as his suspension was set to begin in July 2021, Washington was arrested — and the state suspended his credentials indefinitely.
The next year, while out on bail, Washington sent a Pasadena High student images of himself having oral sex with another man, among other messages, according to court records. At Washington’s 2024 criminal trial, that student testified that the teacher had also asked him to share naked pictures of himself when he was 16. Washington told jurors that he did not know the student was a minor. He was sentenced to eight years and eight months in prison for multiple sex offenses, including “annoying or molesting” the Romoland student by sending him the video, as well as producing and possessing child sex abuse material related to minors who were not his students.
A spokesperson for Pasadena Unified did not respond to questions regarding Washington’s hiring or the state’s recommended discipline, but said in a written statement that the district conducts background checks during the hiring process.
Both Washington and his former attorney declined to comment.
A similar pattern unfolded with a San Francisco Bay Area elementary teacher, Matthew Shelton, who was convicted of sexually abusing four students last month.
Shelton had first been arrested in 2007 on charges of sexually abusing students in Napa Valley. Three third-graders had told police he touched their butts or crotches, or made them touch his penis during class.
Shelton was acquitted in that case, but the state’s licensing body did investigate the claims. At the time, Shelton told state investigators that the students had made up the allegations and that he passed a polygraph test, which he had obtained himself. Two of those former students told KQED and ProPublica that state investigators never interviewed them. The agency did not respond to questions about why the students were not interviewed.
In 2008, the licensing agency issued Shelton a confidential written warning, which was expunged after three years, according to trial testimony. That decision meant Shelton was able to keep teaching for the long term; he had already begun a new job in nearby Benicia.
Years later, in 2022, students began accusing Shelton of touching them inappropriately. The Benicia school district and a student’s parents reported him to the state commission in 2023. More students came forward and told police that Shelton had touched their crotch or butt over their clothing; one student said he made her touch his penis when she was in first grade during a school field trip.
Shelton resigned but quickly got a job at another school. As with the other cases, the new school said it had no information about the ongoing investigation. It also had no knowledge of his earlier warning, which had been expunged more than a decade earlier.
This time around, however, things unfolded differently: While the state did not alert the new school about any problems, a parent did. In September, just weeks into the school year, Shelton’s new employer learned from a Benicia parent about the active police investigation as well as the earlier issues in Napa.
Shelton was immediately put on leave. In February 2024, prosecutors charged him, requiring the state licensing agency to automatically suspend his credentials. Unlike in Napa, the agency revoked his license in July 2024 without waiting for a conviction.
Shelton did not respond to requests for comment, and his attorney declined to comment. He is due to be sentenced in December. Benicia Superintendent Chris Calabrese declined to comment on Shelton’s hiring.
There are significant repercussions when the state fails to take disciplinary action. For one thing, it means that other schools receive no indication of a problem. A red flag typically appears next to an educator’s name in a public database when they are punished by the Commission on Teacher Credentialing. But no such warning appears when a teacher is fired or forced to resign without state discipline, leaving their potential future employers in the dark. Nor would a confidential warning letter like the one Shelton received result in a red flag. California lawmakers have tried to address the gap, but their efforts failed.
Student victims, too, suffer long-lasting damage.
One of the students who accused Shelton in Napa told KQED and ProPublica that for years she wished she hadn’t reported him to anyone because she and her classmates were characterized as liars after “we poured out so much.”
“It could’ve been stopped with us, but it wasn’t,” she said. “They didn’t believe us.”
In Braff’s case, the Santa Paula Unified students who had accused him of abuse continued to struggle in school as their former counselor kept getting new jobs in education.
J. told KQED and ProPublica that for years she avoided acknowledging what Braff did to her. “I couldn’t place where all these emotions were coming from. I was blaming everything else except the actual problem,” J. said, referring to the abuse by Braff. “I didn’t want to live anymore.”
J., now a high school senior, has been homeschooled by her mother for almost three years. She said she still has nightmares in which Braff yells at her for “telling on him.”
And she has long faced doubts from others about her account of what happened to her in elementary school. A few years ago, she recalled, a former classmate told her: “Why would they let him go work somewhere else if he did that to you?”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.
But the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in New York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.
Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.
Estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Aquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.
Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.
Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.
The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.
The top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.
One of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.
Mary Cassatt also established a new auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.
Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/p.title: Petitions Push Congressional Democrats to Ditch Dangerous New Transportation Bill
https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/p.author: Kea Wilson
https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/p.text:
A growing chorus of transportation reform advocates is urging the House transportation committee to abandon the massive road funding bill it passed when Republicans had control — even as a key Democratic leader pledges to push it through anyway.
Shortly after the “blue wave” crashed over U.S. shores in this month’s midterms, advocates at Transportation for America launched a petition to urge the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to abandon the five-year, $580 billion BUILD America 250 Act it passed last May, which the group said “utterly failed to rethink or reform our country’s broken and bankrupt approach to transportation funding and policy.”
Organizations and individuals across the country echoed that call to action, pressing House Democrats to seize a historic opportunity to orient America’s single most important transportation law around policies that actually save lives, reduce emissions and fix “crumbling roads and bridges” — and abandon a bill that experts say would do the exact opposite.
Almost as quickly, however, those calls were dismissed by U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen (D-WA), the likely incoming chair of the House committee that oversees reauthorization negotiations.
Larsen told Politico last week that he and his colleagues would “not [be] starting from scratch” in its next round of transportation talks, because “we just don’t have the time” amidst competing concerns, like funding the Federal Aviation Administration in the wake of last week’s nationwide ground stop. (Larsen’s office did not respond to a request for comment from Streetsblog.)
In the midst of a decades-long transportation crisis on the ground, though, the authors of the petition say that response is simply unacceptable – and America simply cannot afford for any version of BUILD America 250 to become law.
“BUILD America 250 … favors the building of highways over the needs of everyday Americans who need a better transportation system,” said Kristina Curtiss, Transportation for America’s senior policy manager. “Now is more important than ever to tell Ranking Member Larsen that he’s wrong.”
What’s wrong with BUILD America 250
Curtiss’s organization isn’t the only one that’s been pushing back against BUILD America 250 since before it passed out of committee in May — which it did, by the way, with broad bipartisan support, and only a single lawmaker from each party voting “no.”
Transportation reform advocates across the political spectrum have been speaking out against the bill for months, which they say doubles down on the worst qualities of its predecessor, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, by slashing billions in guaranteed transit, rail, and multimodal safety funding. The bill also falls short on a number of vehicle safety measures, including undermining truck safety standards and paving the way for the rapid rollout of untested AVs.
Guaranteed highway funding, meanwhile, would actually increase under the law, pushing the national transportation coffers even further into debt than they already are. That’s despite arbitrary new hybrid and EV fees, which experts say aren’t nearly big enough to make a dent in the shortfall — at least while the gas tax remains stubbornly low and highway-building costs remain shockingly high.
Taken together, an analysis by the Georgetown Climate Center this summer projected that the policies in BUILD America 250 would generate an additional 14 to 22 million metric tons of annual carbon dioxide emissions, and result in the deaths of more than 1,050 additional people in car crashes each year, too.
The average American household, meanwhile, would be hit with $270 in new annual transportation costs, even if they don’t drive EVs — in sharp contrast to the $14,170 the American Public Transportation Association says they’d save if they had access to shared mobility options that allowed them to give up their private vehicles altogether.
“All across the country, demands for affordability and accountability rang out louder and clearer than ever [this midterms]” wrote a coalition of 11 New York-based advocacy organizations* in a letter to Democrat leaders. “[This is an] urgent matter that will have lasting cost of living and time savings impacts on millions of New York families for decades to come.”
For Curtiss, though, the biggest problem with BUILD America 250 is simply that it keeps the highway money flowing, even when states keep building expansions that are directly responsible for making congestion, safety, and other transportation outcomes worse.
That fundamental flaw means that a few tweaks and funding shifts won’t be enough to save the legislation — and that Congress must look to models like 2020’s proposed INVEST Act for a better alternative. That bill did require states to measure how their investments would impact access to jobs and services, and adjusted core funding levels to accelerate the transit, biking, and walking projects that are most likely to improve it.
BUILD America 250 does neither of those things.
“[This bill] is built on a foundation that allows states flexibility for how much transportation money they spend, without accountability,” Curtiss added. “Line item edits to this bill won’t be enough to change the fact that it upholds a process that fundamentally values how much money we spend — and doesn’t answer the question of why are we spending this money to begin with.”
A political morass
Still, some advocates fear House Democrats will struggle to negotiate a better alternative to BUILD America 250 – even after the historically-blue 120th Congress takes office in January.
Because the bill passed out of committee with such broad bipartisan support, Curtiss said, standing members will face pressure to stick to their votes, unless a groundswell of constituents urges them to reverse course. And because lawmakers often sacrifice transportation as a bargaining chip in the name of larger bipartisan collaboration, Curtiss fears even incoming committee members will feel pressure to follow their caucus’s deeply flawed approach.
Still, she’s hopeful that changemay already be underway — and an organized opposition could push holdouts over the edge.
“Since the markup in May, we’re hearing committee members change their minds,” Curtiss said. “The tide in the public is shifting, and people are starting to recognize many parts of this bill are bad.”
Even if Larsen does scrap BUILD America 250 and comes up with a better alternative, though, Curtiss said the next transportation bill will face another daunting challenge: getting the executive branch to actually follow that law.
Since resuming office in 2024, the Trump administration has repeatedly hamstrung the nation’s current core transportation bill — the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act — using every legal trick in the book and a few illegal ones to cancel or delay policies it didn’t like. That includes holding hostage one of the nation’s largest transit funding sources, by flat-out refusing to sign a single Capital Investment Grant since taking office.
The battle over BUILD America 250 will prolong that messy fight even more by forcing Congress to pass yet another extension to the IIJA after its current one expires on December 11. Even worse, the last extension used even more legal tricks to kill key transit and rail programs — forcing advocates to mount a parallelcampaign to get the money restored in the midst of negotiations over the next bill.
“One question we often have is, ‘What is the point in writing a new reauthorization bill giving them more money, in a world where they’re not going to even spend the money they already have?'” Curtiss added. “Congress [needs to] use its oversight authority to ensure that the past bill and the future bill are implemented in a way that people can trust … [and that] create outcomes in transportation projects that people are excited for.”
Still, Curtiss argues that Congress can walk and chew gum at the same time – and it can certainly hold Trump accountable on transportation today, while fighting for a bill that will deliver better mobility outcomes tomorrow. And since the next transportation bill will last for at least five years, it’s essential that this Congress level up their ambitions while they can.
“This bill shouldn’t be written by an old Congress,” she added. “We’re looking forward to working with new committee members, who deserve a voice in how we write this reauthorization. It’s unfair to freshmen coming onto district to be handed an old bill that’s going to set them up for failure when they go back and people ask them why they didn’t invest in bike lanes.”
*Disclosure: the signatories of this letter include Open Plans, the parent organization of Streetsblog USA and NYC.
Kea Wilson is Senior Editor for Streetsblog USA. She has more than a dozen years experience as a writer telling emotional, urgent and actionable stories that motivate average Americans to get involved in making their cities better places. She is also a novelist, cyclist, and affordable housing advocate. She lives in St. Louis, MO. For tips, submissions, and general questions, reach out to her at kea@streetsblog.org, or on Bluesky @keawilson.bsky.social.
Six weeks away from taking the House transportation committee gavel, Rep. Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) remains a supporter of Republicans' transportation funding bill.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: 15 Years After Complaints to Authorities, Lawsuit Accuses Brooklyn Doctor of Sex Abuse
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
More than a decade before three women filed a lawsuit accusing Dr. Richard Grazi, a Brooklyn fertility specialist, of sexually abusing patients, one of the plaintiffs took her allegations to state health officials.
The woman, who asked to remain anonymous, spoke to investigators at the state Department of Health around 2011, she told The City Reporter.
She recalled being interviewed alongside several other women who also had complaints about Grazi, a prominent physician in her tight-knit Jewish community.
The interview left her believing that state officials were taking the allegations seriously, but months later she was told that, for reasons the department would not explain, no further action was being taken.
“I was deflated,” she recalled, noting she was 19 when she first saw Dr. Grazi. “It’s not something I’d readily share with other people,” she said of her alleged assault. “A person carries a lot of shame.”
Now, she is among three women suing Grazi, Maimonides Medical Center and Genesis Fertility alleging that the doctor sexually abused them under the guise of medical examinations and that the institutions knew or should have known about his alleged misconduct but failed to protect patients.
The women allege that Grazi exploited his position as a physician to subject them to nonconsensual touching, digital penetration and examinations that served no legitimate medical purpose, according to the lawsuit. They also allege that the examinations were conducted without gloves, a chaperone or appropriate medical staff present.
Doctor Denies Wrongdoing
Grazi, who has practiced in Brooklyn for decades, has not been charged with a crime and denied any wrongdoing.
“Dr. Grazi categorically denies the allegations made against him in this lawsuit,” his lawyer, James Nikraftar, told NBC. “Throughout his career, Dr. Grazi has helped thousands of women build their families. He has treated patients with care and professionalism, and that is exactly what the facts will show.”
Tina Lee, a spokesperson for Maimonides, said, “We cannot comment on active litigation, but can confirm that Dr. Richard Grazi is not a Maimonides employee and does not have privileges here.”
Grazi was previously the director of Reproductive Endocrinology and Fertility at Maimonides Medical Center and founded Genesis Fertility and Reproductive Medicine in Bensonhurst. The clinic, which specializes in IVF and egg freezing, was popular among members of the Jewish community.
Grazi’s medical license remains active, according to state Health Department records.
The state health commissioner has the power to suspend a doctor from practicing pending the conclusion of an investigation if that person poses an imminent danger.
But that rarely happens.
MORE: A 27-Hour Wait for a Hospital Bed? Why Delays Are Growing at New York Hospitals
Patient advocates have long criticized state medical boards for allowing doctors who are under scrutiny to continue to practice while under investigation. The boards usually are heavily made up of doctors nominated by state and local medical societies.
Erin Clary, a Health Department spokesperson, said the state takes “all allegations of medical misconduct seriously” and follows guidelines laid out by state law. The department is prohibited from discussing any investigation, complaint, or prosecution beyond what is published on its website, she added.
A 2025 Newsday investigation found that the state’s system for disciplining doctors had become increasingly lenient, with serious disciplinary actions declining even as the number of physicians practicing in New York grew.
The state received at least 7,900 complaints annually between 2013 and 2023, but took no more than 440 final actions in any year, according to the report.
Newsday also found that the rate of serious disciplinary actions fell by roughly half over the decade ending in 2023.
Eileen Corina, founder and president of Pulse Center for Patient Safety Education & Advocacy, said the case highlights how vulnerable patients can be when they seek medical care, especially when they don’t know what to expect during an examination or where to turn if a doctor crosses a line.
The three women suing Grazi asked to remain anonymous because of the sensitive nature of the allegations.
‘Inappropriate Behavior’ Alleged in 2005 Lawsuit
The complaint alleges that Maimonides and the Genesis Fertility knew or should have known of concerning conduct years earlier because of a 2005 lawsuit filed by former physician Dr. Susan M. Lobel, who worked with Dr. Grazi.
That lawsuit, which primarily focused on a labor dispute, also alleged “inappropriate behavior with female patients and staff.”
Dr. Lobel did not respond to a call and text message seeking comment.
More women have come forward alleging similar abuses since the lawsuit was filed, according to Helene Weiss, who is representing the three plaintiffs. They are considering joining the litigation, Weiss said.
Those women “could have been spared abuse if only the institutions around him had listened years ago,” Weiss told The City Reporter.
Fifteen years after first bringing her allegations to state investigators, the former patient is hoping her lawsuit will bring accountability.
“The doctor should not have a medical license,” she said, “and should not be around women and children.”

https://empire.streetsblog.org/state-shu.title: State Shuts I-81 Ramp — And Starts The Healing Of Syracuse
https://empire.streetsblog.org/state-shu.author: Austin C. Jefferson
https://empire.streetsblog.org/state-shu.text:
A detour from I-81 construction. Photo: Austin C. Jefferson
State officials on Monday permanently closed a ramp on an elevated stretch of Interstate 81 through Syracuse, the first segment to be removed as part of a teardown of the highway that ripped through a thriving Black neighborhood in the 1960s — and the beginning of an effort to heal the city it has divided for six decades.
Monday’s closure is an early step in the long-delayed $2.25-billion I-81 Viaduct Project, which will remove the full 1.4-mile stretch of elevated I-81 — the viaduct itself, plus the ramps that feed it — and route through traffic around the city on Interstate 481, which is to the east of downtown. Federal officials approved redesignating that eastern bypass as the new Interstate 81 in September, and the old route through the city will become Business Loop 81.
Beyond merely removing and renaming highways, the plan’s centerpiece is the “community grid,” a street-level network that stitches together the divided neighborhoods and opens up land for more productive uses, as outlined in the city’s Community Grid Vision Plan. The first goal is maintaining housing for existing residents, who are sometimes displaced when property values rise to reflect the appeal of safer, more livable streets, a concern some residents have raised.
The aim is to repair the damage that highways caused to low-income communities of color in the 1960s, not repeat it.
“We’re getting a very good deal where we’re going to have a chance to make our community whole,” said Assembly Member-elect Mo Brown (D-Syracuse).
Removing the viaduct will free up scarce land for housing and health care institutions, and make way for better streetlights, sidewalks and bike lanes at street level, said Syracuse City Auditor Alex Marion, who said he attended his first public meeting about I-81 in 2008, when he was in high school.
“It’s about the physical structure being a divider in the city and being this wall in the city,” added Alex Lawson, a member of the Moving People Transportation Coalition.
Lawson said he remembers poring over early renderings of the community grid and thinking, “Oh my God, this is going to be incredible.” Seeing it start to happen, he said, is the true milestone from Monday’s ramp closure.
The community grid plan should be relatively seamless since most of the traffic using that ramp was local commuters, Lawson said, because drivers seeking to bypass Syracuse had already switched to Interstate 481 south of the city. State DOT estimates about 10,000 vehicles used the ramp each day. That makes it a natural first piece to remove: a slab of car infrastructure that mostly moved commuters past neighborhoods that have lived with the highway for six decades.
The remaining open question is about funding, Marion said. The city was supposed to receive about $30 million from the federal Neighborhood Access and Equity program for sidewalks, streetlights, trees and bike lanes on streets now buried beneath the viaduct. The Trump administration took back that funding, and the city has not identified a replacement. The state’s share was untouched.
Marion’s office recommended this fall that Congress replace the money, and he’s more optimistic now that Congress will have a Democratic majority.
Lawson, meanwhile, wants something else. On Monday, when crews started taking down the viaduct, there was no celebration or even any public event.
“I do hope that they have some sort of anti-groundbreaking event when they actually tear the viaduct down,” he said.
Before becoming Albany Bureau Chief in late 2025, Austin C. Jefferson was a state politics reporter for City & State NY, covering state government, elections and major legislative debates. His reporting has also appeared in the Daily Freeman, Chronogram Magazine and The Legislative Gazette. Having grown up in the Hudson Valley, he's always happy to argue about where Upstate New York truly begins.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/giorgia-me.author: Scarlett Bain
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/giorgia-me.text:
Depuis la mi-octobre, le mouvement de contestation contre la vie chère a gagné l’Italie. Place forte des mobilisations, Turin se prépare à la journée de grève générale et de manifestation du 20 novembre, à l’appel de la Confédération générale italienne du travail. Lycéens, étudiants, travailleurs et retraités s’affichent unis contre le gouvernement d’extrême droite.
Turin (Italie), envoyée spéciale.
Un café vite fait et Giacomo sort de chez lui pour faire ses courses. En ce lundi matin, l’ouvrier devrait être en poste à l’usine Mirafiori de Turin (Piémont). Mais, pour la cinquième semaine consécutive, ce site historique de Fiat, appartenant au groupe Stellantis, a placé tous ses salariés au chômage partiel.
Giacomo a commencé sur les chaînes de production de la Punto Fiat en 1994. Il a aujourd’hui 69 ans, gagne 1 800 euros par mois et se serre la ceinture. Depuis bientôt deux mois, son salaire est amputé de 30 %. « Mais moi, je suis du niveau 4. Pour ceux en dessous, c’est encore pire », concède-t-il, de son regard bleu désolé.
De la poche de son treillis noir, il sort une feuille A4 pliée. Il s’agit du calendrier des jours chômés. Une date est inscrite en rouge : celle du loyer à payer, près de 700 euros. Dans cette grande ville du nord de l’Italie, « ça reste un loyer imbattable », reconnaît-il, mais « c’est sans compter les factures énergétiques et tout le reste, bien sûr ! ».

https://hyperallergic.com/native-artist-.title: Native Artist Receives $10K Grant to Revive Visor Craftmaking
https://hyperallergic.com/native-artist-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/native-artist-.text:
Native Artist Receives $10K Grant to Revive Visor Craftmaking
Dustin Newman (Unangax̂/Deg Hit’an Athabascan) will use the Walker Youngbird Foundation grant to revive the qayaatx̂ux, or chief visor.
The Walker Youngbird Foundation named Native artist Dustin Newman (Unangax̂/Deg Hit’an Athabascan) the annual recipient of its Núhi grant today, November 19. The Alaskan artist will use the $10,000 award to revive and pass down the endangered craftsmanship behind qayaatx̂ux, traditional closed crown visors worn by Unangax̂ chiefs.
Through technical research with the Anchorage Museum and collaborations with regional hat-makers, Newman will produce a small series of visors to gift to cultural leaders. An intricately decorated hunting hat historically worn by chiefs and high-ranking whaling captains, the qayaatx̂ux began fading into obscurity in the early 20th century due to factors including American colonization. After completing the series, Newman will share the tradition with community members through Camp Qungaayux on the island of Unalaska and the Agdaagux Culture Camp in King Cove, the fishing village where the artist was raised.
"I first started bending visors at 17 with my mentor Okalena Patricia Lekanoff-Gregory at our regional culture camp in Anchorage and Unalaska," Newman told Hyperallergic. "Why I chose to pursue this project through the Núhi Grant was to uplift the status of these visors not as a wall hanging but as a symbol within our communities honoring our culture bearers and community leaders."

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Teachers Union Fires Legal Shot Over Pension Clawback
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The United Federation of Teachers formally announced its intent to sue the main pension fund covering the city’s retired educators over a pension clawback impacting 183 disabled retired paraprofessionals.
The UFT filed a notice of claim with the city comptroller’s office against the Teachers Retirement System on Tuesday, a required move ahead of filing any lawsuit seeking damages from the city. Union president Michael Mulgrew first disclosed the filing in a delegates assembly meeting on Wednesday evening.
“Yesterday we filed a notice of claim, which you have to do when you’re suing the city of New York. We were trying to get to a resolution, and it’s just something I said, I don’t believe it can be done in a timely manner,” Mulgrew said according to a transcript of his remarks obtained by The City Reporter.
”But we’re not going to sit here and just say because TRS and others made a mistake over 20 years ago that these paraprofessionals are going to have their lives completely upset.”
It’s the latest twist in a controversy that dates to mid-June, when more than 180 retired paraprofessionals were informed by the city’s Teachers Retirement System that it would dramatically reduce their monthly payments by as much as half to recoup a portion from their checks going forward to make up for more than 20 years of overpayments.
In those letters, TRS acknowledged that the pension system, not the retirees, was responsible for the miscalculated payments. At the time, UFT officials suggested they might pursue legal action against the pension fund.
But the question of how to address the overpayments, which by some estimates cost the pension fund about $155,000 a month, have roiled the stakeholders of the fund who have competing interests and opinions on how to resolve the issue.
TRS and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have said that the city has a legal obligation to claw back the overpayments. The UFT and retiree advocates have said that recovery efforts are cruel and that the impacted paraprofessionals should be allowed to keep their pensions because the overpayments were a result of the pension fund’s own error.
“The city is one of many parties when it comes to the stewarding of these pensions,” Mamdani said in August. “The Law Department has come forward and identified this as a mistake that took place over many, many years, and the need for us to be in legal compliance to correct that moving forward.”
Law Department spokesperson Nicholas Paolucci said the notice of claim is “under review,” and a City Hall spokesperson said the Mamdani administration had no further comment. A spokesperson for TRS referred questions to the Law Department.
The teachers union has spent the last several months negotiating a resolution with TRS, which agreed to pause any pension clawbacks until January.
The notice of claim that the union filed this week offers a glimpse into the arguments it plans to make in a forthcoming lawsuit.
In the letters that it sent to the retired paraprofessionals and in public statements, TRS has acknowledged the overpayments resulted from its own error.
The UFT stressed the point in its notice of claim, claiming that under TRS’ governing laws, the pension fund has “discretion to ensure that those least able to afford it are not subject to financial harm due to TRS’s own mistakes.”
The Teachers Retirement System board of trustees is scheduled to have its monthly meeting Thursday afternoon. The board is made up of six members: city Comptroller Mark Levine, three teacher members, a representative for the education department’s Panel of Educational Policy, and an appointee from the mayor’s office.
Levine, the steward of the city’s pension funds, has not publicly said how he believes the matter should be handled and has referred all questions to TRS.
The retired paraprofessionals impacted by the payment mishap all retired early due to injuries they sustained on the job, including brutal assaults by students that required surgeries and physical therapy.
The retirees had erroneously been earning pensions equivalent to two-thirds of their final average salaries when, under state law, retirees who are eligible for Workers Compensation are owed just one-third of their salaries. In June, TRS announced that those 183 retirees should have only been receiving pensions equivalent to one-third of their salaries.
Current salaries for paraprofessionals, teachers aides who often work with children with disabilities, tops out at $56,700 per year. The impacted pensioners all retired from their jobs more than 10 years ago, when the top salaries were much lower.
Several who spoke with The City Reporter in August said they were dropping their doctors and prescriptions due to the pension clawback. One retiree living in Florida said his revised pension dropped to less than $1,000 per month, a loss compounded by more than $38,000 in overpayments the TRS informed him it would collect from future checks.
That retiree, Anthony Delgardio, retired from his job in a special education high school in Brooklyn more than 12 years ago after he was attacked by a student. He suffered a concussion and broken bones and continues to struggle with memory loss and mobility issues. When he first received the letter from TRS informing him of the pension rollback, Delgardio assumed it was a scam. He relocated to his sister’s Long Island home to cut back on expenses and is contemplating selling his home.
The City Reporter described Delgardio’s and other paraprofessionals’ dilemmas to Mamdani in September: “We will follow up on that,” he responded.
A distraught Delgardio described his grim financial situation: “I can’t even buy a toothbrush right now.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.title: Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum Names Krist Gruijthuijsen as Next Director
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.text:
The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has named the Dutch-born curator and art critic Krist Gruijthuijsen as its next director. He will succeed Rein Wolfs in July 2027.
Gruijthuijsen, a self-described “artist-driven curator,” will join the Stedelijk from EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art in Finland, where he has been director since 2025, a role he holds concurrently with curator at large at Kunsthaus Zürich.
His vision for EMMA, a respected but relatively low-profile institution outside the Nordic region, included sustained support for artists through project funding, acquisitions and stipends, among more. Speaking to Frieze, he said he envisioned opening up the floor of the Brutalist building by removing its internal walls.
Prior to EMMA, Gruijthuijsen was director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, beginning in 2016. His tenure there included well-received programming, with exhibitions by artists such as Hanne Lippard, Beatriz González, and Hassan Sharif. He also curated “Martin Wong: Malicious Mischief,” which the Stedelijk co-produced and hosted from November 2023 to April 2024.
His return to Amsterdam will also mark a curatorial homecoming, as Gruijthuijsen cofounded the Kunstverein Amsterdam with Maxine Kopsa and served as its director from 2009 to 2012, a role that briefly overlapped with his time heading the MA Fine Arts department at Amsterdam’s Sandberg Instituut (2011-16).
At the Stedelijk, he will oversee the institution’s modern and contemporary art and design strategy and guide collection management and public engagement.
“The [Stedelijk] has long held a special place in my personal and professional life, as it does in the history of modern and contemporary art and design,” Gruijthuijsen said in a statement. “Its remarkable collection and rich legacy carry a responsibility that extends far beyond preserving the past. Above all, they call on us to engage with the present and help shape what lies ahead, with art and artists at the heart of everything we do.”
He continued, “An essential part of my role will be to deepen the museum’s relationship with Amsterdam: to make it ever more open, engaged, and connected to the city and its communities. I want the Stedelijk not only to reflect the world we live in, but also to actively contribute to shaping its future.”

https://taz.de/Prozess-gegen-Patricia-Sc.title: Prozess gegen Patricia Schlesinger: Zulässige Zulagen für die Intendanz
https://taz.de/Prozess-gegen-Patricia-Sc.author: Anna Simbürger
https://taz.de/Prozess-gegen-Patricia-Sc.text:
Prozess gegen Patricia Schlesinger: Zulässige Zulagen für die Intendanz
Im Prozess gegen die Ex-RBB-Intendantin ging es am 4. Tag um Zulagen. Die seien auch auf Führungsebene legitim, sagte ein Unternehmensberater aus.
Der Vergütungsberater Martin von Hören arbeitet für die Unternehmensberatung Kienbaum und hat sich in den letzten Jahrzehnten auf die Beratung von Unternehmen aus dem öffentlichen Sektor spezialisiert. Die Firma Kienbaum hatte auch den RBB beraten, ein variables Vergütungssystem auch für die Hierarchieebene der Direktion und später der Intendanz einzuführen. Am Donnerstag sagte von Hören im Untreue-Prozess gegen die ehemalige RBB-Intendantin Patricia Schlesinger aus.
Schlesinger hatte den RBB 2022 verlassen, nachdem Vorwürfe gegen sie laut wurden. Mit ihr sind Nachfolger Hagen Brandstäter, der ehemalige Verwaltungsratsvorsitzende Wolf-Dieter Wolf und die Justiziarin Susann Lange angeklagt. Bei den Vorwürfen gegen die vier Angeklagten geht es um leistungsbezogene Zulagen, extravagante Abendessen und eine Reise von Schlesinger und ihrem Mann nach London. Die Summe der veruntreuten Beträge soll sich auf 1,8 Millionen Euro belaufen.
Das variable Vergütungssystem sieht für Mitarbeitende auf den höheren Hierarchieebenen einen Gehaltszuschlag oder -abzug vor, abhängig von der Erreichung vorher festgelegter Ziele. Ein solches System war beim RBB bereits seit den 2000er-Jahren für die Ebene der Hauptabteilungsleiter*innen etabliert worden. Weil es Unzufriedenheit über das bestehende System gegeben habe, sei 2017 die Firma Kienbaum kontaktiert worden, um bei einer Reform mitzuwirken, sagte von Hören.
Die Hauptabteilungsleiter*innen hätten die variablen Beträge im bestehenden System als zu gering empfunden. Und: „Es hat keine Möglichkeit gegeben, Ziele zu überschreiten“, sagte von Hören. Die variable Vergütung werde in solchen Fällen vor allem als Verlustgefahr wahrgenommen und führe zu Motivationsproblemen. Das System sollte aber nicht nur für die Hauptabteilungsleiter*innen reformiert, sondern auch auf die Ebene der Direktion ausgeweitet werden. Das Gehalt der Intendanz habe in diesen ersten Gesprächen aber noch keine Rolle gespielt, sagte von Hören.
Wer hat die Zielerreichung evaluiert?
Je länger von Hören spricht, desto mehr entlastende Aussagen macht er für die vier Angeklagten. Auch die gezielten Nachfragen der Kammer und der Staatsanwaltschaft ändern nichts an diesem Eindruck. Ob es ungewöhnlich gewesen sei, ein variables Vergütungssystem einführen zu wollen? Absolut nicht. Ob es im öffentlichen Sektor ungewöhnlich sei? Im Gegenteil, von Hören sieht das System als schlaue Modernisierungsstrategie.
Ob es unüblich war, die Intendanz später auch in so ein variables Vergütungssystem mit einzubeziehen? „Es wäre eher zu begründen gewesen, die Intendanz nicht einzubeziehen“, sagte von Hören. Ob er vom RBB Vorgaben bei der Erstellung des Systems bekommen habe? Nein, er habe größtenteils freie Hand gehabt. Wer konkret das System habe einführen wollen? Der erste Impuls dafür sei aus dem Verwaltungsrat gekommen.
Der Vorwurf, der Verwaltungsrat habe von den Zulagen nichts gewusst, ließ sich so noch nicht bestätigen. Brandstäters Verteidiger Panos Pananis wirft dem Gericht vor, mit diesem Vorwurf lediglich ein Narrativ zu bedienen. Er forderte, das Gericht solle die Anklagepunkte konkretisieren. Bestünde der Vorwurf nun darin, das variable Vergütungssystem überhaupt erst eingeführt zu haben, oder darin, es ohne das Wissen des Verwaltungsrats gemacht zu haben?
Etwas mehr Fragezeichen hatte der Zeuge von Hören dabei, wie und von wem die Zielerreichung bewertet wurde. Die Firma Kienbaum selbst habe dabei nur eine untergeordnete Rolle gespielt, sagte er. Die Staatsanwaltschaft wirft die Frage auf, ob die Bewertung der Zielerreichung teilweise zu großzügig ausgefallen sei: Von 14 Zielen der Direktionsebene im Jahr 2020 und 2021 seien 4 vollständig erreicht und 10 deutlich überschritten worden. Von Hören kann die Frage nicht beantworten.
Für den nächsten Verhandlungstag am kommenden Dienstag ist die Aussage eines weiteren Mitarbeiters der Unternehmensberatung Kienbaum angesetzt.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen
