https://jacobin.com/2026/11/work-freedom.title: How Will We Get People to Work Under Socialism?
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/work-freedom.author: Nick French, Neal Meyer
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/work-freedom.text:
How Will We Get People to Work Under Socialism?
Under capitalism, people are often motivated to work by the threat of destitution. A feasible and desirable socialist system has to get people to work while respecting individual freedom.
- Interview by
- Neal Meyer
With Zohran Mamdani’s rise to the mayoralty of the United States’s largest city and democratic socialists winning more and more elected offices at all levels across the country, there is renewed interest in and excitement about the idea of democratic socialism. But among socialists, there is little consensus on the content of that ideal. Many on the Left describe socialism in terms of greater income redistribution or an expanded public sector, with some socialists even describing their vision as compatible with capitalism.
But we are seeing a growing number of proposals for feasible postcapitalist futures, distinct from both the social democratic welfare states and the state socialist systems of the twentieth century. In a recent article for Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy, Jacobin editor Nick French tackles the question of how a just postcapitalist society could get people to work. French argues that a just socialist society would recognize and enforce a general obligation to work while also protecting individual freedom; he argues that labor markets are the best institutional means to achieving these goals.
Jacobin contributor Neal Meyer recently sat down with French to talk through the case for labor markets, including arguments against “postwork” visions of life after capitalism and appeals to moral motives, and what sort of economic inequalities might persist under socialism. You can listen to their conversation here. This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.
The Duty to Work
- Neal Meyer We could start by talking about why you think people should work. It sounds like a preposterous question, but it actually is an important intervention. You and I are basically the same age; when we were in our twenties, the anarchist, libertarian left milieu was quite popular. I remember, as I was getting politicized, people talking about how people should have the right to be lazy, that we want to live in a postwork future. But in your article, you’re making an argument that people should work — that people have a duty to work.
- Nick French I’ll have something to say about these advocates of postwork socialism or postwork communism. But first, on the idea of a duty to work: it’s very intuitive to most people. In order to produce the things that we need, individually and collectively, we have to engage in labor. That often means doing things we don’t want to do, or spending our time such that we would rather be doing something else. It means exercising our capacities for particular ends to serve social needs. This is a kind of burden, a very significant burden, that is placed on people. My argument is trying to develop the intuitive idea that there are duties of fairness to other members of society. Insofar as you’re able to work — you’re not significantly disabled, or we can make accommodations for people to work — we all have an obligation to contribute to society through our labor. Maybe the more interesting questions about a duty to work are about how we might implement it. Also, people have a lot of objections to the idea that there’s a duty to work based around very valid worries, or even revulsion, at the way the work ethic is deployed in our capitalist society, which is brutally unjust. Oftentimes the reason people are not working is not because they don’t want to, or because they’re just lazy. It’s because they’re actually excluded from the labor market; there’s not enough work to go around. Or they’re not working because they haven’t been provided with adequate educational opportunities, or they’re sick or disabled, and so on. I’m not trying to make the argument that, in our actually existing society, people who aren’t working are immoral, or that we ought to shame people who are unemployed. Rather, the argument is: if we were to construct a fair society, where people have basic economic security, where everybody has equal access to high-quality education, where there are institutions that really do give everybody who can work a shot at getting a good job that pays well and treats them with dignity — in that ideal situation, we should expect everyone to contribute.
- Neal Meyer This is very much a conversation about the obligations we would have to each other in a future society, not our current society.
- Nick French Right. This is an argument in what philosophers sometimes call “ideal theory,” about the principles that would apply in a society that is basically just.
Freedom of Occupational Choice
- Neal Meyer Part of the conception of justice you advance regarding labor is this idea that people should have a right to choose their occupation. Can you say more about that? And then, what’s the contrast you’re trying to draw here? Are there societies where that’s not the case?
- Nick French This is another idea that is intuitive to most people, but it’s important to articulate it clearly. Because when we start trying to come up with a detailed vision of what socialism might look like, it’s important as a North Star to block certain authoritarian possibilities. The idea of freedom of occupational choice is based in the notion that individual freedom, or autonomy, is an overriding value. This is something that’s common ground between the Marxist socialist tradition and the left-liberal philosophical tradition, chiefly as represented by people like John Stuart Mill and John Rawls, who I draw on a lot in this article. It’s very important that we be able to choose how we spend our time and how we exercise and develop our productive, creative, and intellectual capacities. Part of how we do that is with the traditional civil liberties: freedom of speech, freedom of movement, freedom of assembly, freedom of association, the kinds of things people are familiar with from the US Bill of Rights. But freedom of choice of occupation is really important too. In formulating an idea of how I want to live my life, I’m crucially thinking about how I want to contribute to society. What sort of productive capacities do I want to develop and exercise? Do I want to be an engineer or a mechanic, an artist or a writer? These are fundamental to people’s identities in contemporary society. And that’s a kind of liberty that we should hope a socialist society would not just preserve but maximize. When it comes to the potential contrasts or alternatives I have in mind, I’m thinking of societies where people are either prevented from taking on certain occupations or forced to take on certain jobs or occupations in an extensive way, where there’s not much room for people to set their own course in life. There’s formal legal discrimination, when employers discriminate openly on the basis of race or sex. That obviously is a major violation of freedom of choice of occupation. Again, most people in contemporary society would already reject such discrimination; the right to freedom of choice of occupation protects against it. But it also protects against a vision of a more coercive or Stalinist-style socialism, where you have a central authority assigning people to certain jobs because that’s where they are supposedly most needed. We should guard against that as well.
- Neal Meyer You mention in the article that that’s not even how state socialist societies actually handled the labor obligation problem. People had the freedom to choose their occupations to a large extent.
- Nick French That’s right. These societies did have what were called “parasite laws.” The constitutions of the Soviet Union and other state socialist countries enshrined a duty to work, and they had laws on the books that would criminalize not working. If you refused to work at all, you would be punished. But in general, they didn’t tell people they had to work in certain occupations. This is more of a theoretical possibility than something that was actually implemented on a large scale.
Can a Basic Income Free Us From Work?
- Neal Meyer Your article sets up these goals and then walks through a couple of models that you disagree with before presenting your desired option. The first idea you criticize is what people will probably be most familiar with, which is the universal basic income (UBI).
- Nick French To be clear, I’m not arguing against UBI as a policy. I think something like a UBI would be an important part of a socialist institutional framework. What I’m arguing against is the idea that a UBI could free people from the need to work, which is how postwork theorists present it. People might still work out of the goodness of their hearts, or intrinsic joy in certain activities, but there would be no compulsion, or no duty or necessity, to work. Here I’m drawing on Alex Gourevitch, who had a great piece in Catalyst a few years ago arguing against this postwork idea at length. His basic thought is, if nobody’s working because everybody is just taking a UBI, then no one is producing the goods that people would buy with that UBI. So it’s a fantasy that the UBI could free people from having to work. One argument that some postwork thinkers emphasize is that automation can come in, the robots can come in, to do all the work that was formerly done by humans. That’s how we could have no one working and everyone just taking the UBI, because the machines are producing everything we need. I started working on this project before AI was at the top of everyone’s minds, and maybe now a lot of people think it’s more plausible that at least a lot of kinds of work are going to be automated out of existence in the foreseeable future. But I still think — and here again I agree with Gourevitch — that we’re always going to have some people working. Crucially, we’re always going to need people to make decisions and oversee the machines that are doing labor. I also think there are lots of kinds of work, especially care work or “connective labor,” that seem to essentially involve human-to-human interaction: whether that’s health care or childcare or therapy, or the kind of interactions that we take for granted at, say, a bar or a restaurant or a coffee shop. Now, under capitalism a lot of those workers are horribly exploited and not paid enough. But I don’t think an ideal socialist society would get rid of service work. I think those kinds of jobs can and should persist under socialism; workers should just be paid better and treated better and have more say over their working conditions. So even if AI and automation get rid of a lot of work, I think there will still always be work to do, and we need to have an idea of how we’re going to divvy that up and get people to do it.
Can Moral Motivation Do the Job?
- Neal Meyer The second argument you take on is this idea that moral motivation can be a substitute: that people should be exhorted to work harder to do these jobs, and that in a socialist society, these kinds of moral appeals will be sufficient to get people to do the necessary work. What problems do you see here?
- Nick French A natural thought is that, if people have to work and we accept that there’s a duty to work, in a socialist society, we don’t want people to be motivated either by the threat of force or by “the dull compulsion of economic relations,” as Karl Marx put it — i.e., if you don’t work, you’ll starve. Instead, the idea is that we all come together, we democratically decide what work has to get done, and then, because we all see the value in contributing to the social project, we’ll all be motivated by the goodness of our hearts or our sense of duty to do what needs to be done. My view is this seems to imply a very big change in human motivation from what we see today, and that there’s an unrealistically altruistic or moralistic conception of human nature and human psychology at play. Again, to go back to the original argument for a duty to work: work is often something that we don’t want to do. It imposes significant burdens. In choosing to work, I’m often choosing to do something where, if I’m left to my own devices, I would rather do something else. The idea that you’re going to rely on these kinds of intrinsic moral motivations across a whole national or international economy, bringing together people who have no connection to each other, or maybe even have historical conflicts with one another — that you’re going to get them all to work out of a sense of duty — is just unrealistic. I’m not saying it’s impossible. But in setting forward a vision of socialism, we shouldn’t rely on assuming unrealistic changes in human psychology. We should present something that is feasible given human beings as we know and understand them.
Coercion and Compulsion
- Neal Meyer Before we move on to your positive argument, I wanted to go back to the topic of coercion. You’re not saying that all attempts to get people to work are necessarily immoral or wrong or unjust. There are cases where some amount of compulsion may be necessary.
- Nick French I want to separate two issues here. The first goes into the positive case I make for labor markets. We can imagine a just society in which people are motivated in part by monetary gain. There’s not necessarily anything wrong with trying to realize compliance with a duty to work by having a basic income or some social minimum that everyone is guaranteed, but then saying, “Hey, if you want to make more than that, you do have to work.” Then you have different jobs that are paying people different amounts of money. But I’ll come back to that. The second issue is there might be certain jobs that, for various reasons, not enough people want to do, even if you pay them a lot of extra money — either because they require rare skills or talents, or because they involve a lot of drudgery, or because they’re especially hazardous. The classic example is sanitation workers. Maybe the robots will solve that one day; they don’t seem to be doing it yet. But until then, we’re still going to need people to collect and sort garbage. It’s drudgery, and it’s very hazardous work. We don’t want the market to assign that to whoever happens to want to take those jobs. I’m very sympathetic to recent proposals by folks like Lucas Stanczyk and Jan Kandiyali that people might be forced to take these jobs. I’m especially sympathetic to this idea when it comes to a kind of limited rotation. Maybe everyone should have a year or two of national civil service where they have to work as a sanitation worker, or they have to work cleaning hospitals, or something like that — work that involves more drudgery or is more hazardous. That’s a way of fairly sharing more extreme burdens of work. It’s also a way of inculcating a sense of civic duty and solidarity, that we’re all in this together. Where I would draw the line is when it gets to a point that you’re really interfering with freedom of choice of occupation, where you’re forcing people to work for long periods of time, where you’re no longer allowing them to autonomously set the direction of their lives and decide how they want to develop and exercise their creative capacities. There’s some room for a kind of coercive work regime in the kind of socialism I’m envisioning, but it has to be limited so that we are still respecting freedom of choice of occupation.
- Neal Meyer One of the interesting questions, when thinking about the difference between a socialist society and a capitalist society, is: What kinds of jobs do people need to be incentivized to take? Under capitalism, the assumption is people need to be incentivized to take jobs that require a lot of training, or a lot of autonomy and decision-making, or a lot of organizational skills or people skills. These are jobs that, in a socialist society where there was greater equality of opportunity, a lot of people would have the opportunity to get and would want to take. You can think of a whole list of occupations today that people get paid a lot of money to do that have their own intrinsic rewards besides the financial incentive. Under socialism, I would imagine those jobs are not going to pay as much, because a lot of people are going to be willing and able to do them. The jobs that are going to pay a lot are going to be the ones that require a lot of physical labor, that put you at risk, that are onerous or undesirable for many reasons. There’s going to be a kind of flipping of what needs to be incentivized in a transition from capitalism to socialism.
- Nick French That’s how I’m thinking about it. If you have an institutional framework in which firms are collectively owned, where people have equal opportunity in terms of access to high-quality education, and society is really trying to make jobs available to everyone, and also you do have a generous welfare-state social minimum, so that when people are unemployed it’s not an absolute personal disaster — they have that extra leverage. They can walk away from jobs; they’re not desperate to take the first offer that comes into view. We wouldn’t expect as many people to be forced by the market into the more difficult jobs.
The Case for Labor Markets
- Neal Meyer We’ve cleared out some of the alternative ideas about how to handle the work problem in a better society. You come to the conclusion that labor markets have a really important role to play. Could you define what you mean by “labor markets,” and why you think they’re an important part of a vision for socialism?
- Nick French By a labor market, I mean that you have firms — whether they’re public sector firms or cooperatives that are owned or managed by their workers — where people can be attracted to those positions by the offer of a certain wage, and they take those jobs because they offer a certain wage. There can be pay differentials to attract people to jobs and firms where they’re most needed. This fits into a broader vision of market socialism. The core case for this is provided by the moral arguments we discussed, and also the case against the alternatives. Because there is a duty to work — people need to work, and they ought to do so, and we ought to share that burden equally — and because people’s freedom of choice of occupation should be respected, the best way of realizing both of those principles is a labor market. To clarify what I have in mind: Again, this is a socialist society. Obviously, we all have a lot of objections to the way labor markets work under capitalism, which we’ve already talked about. People are forced to take certain jobs because if they don’t, they’ll be on the street; they’ll starve. Also, when they take those jobs, they’re submitting to the tyranny of bosses who are not accountable to them in any way, who are following their own unconstrained profit imperatives. Again, I’m imagining a situation in which the relevant employers are democratically worker-managed firms, or public sector enterprises that are democratically accountable to the public, where workers have strong collective bargaining rights and protections. Once you have those things in place, and once you have a strong social minimum provided by a welfare state — decommodified health care, free, high-quality education, and something like a universal basic income, so even if you’re not working, you have money to spend on clothes, shoes, and so on — I don’t think there’s any objection per se to a labor market. Now, there are practical concerns that you might have about how this all works that I talk about in the paper. One of them is: If you have a really generous welfare state, or a generous basic income, what’s the incentive going to be for people to actually take jobs? We already said we’re not legally forcing people to take certain jobs. If that mute compulsion of economic relations isn’t there, is this really feasible? I point to the evidence from really existing, generous social democracies, in the Nordic countries for example, that seems to show that having more robust welfare states doesn’t negatively affect people’s participation in the labor force or economic growth. So we have good reason to be optimistic that having a very generous social minimum is compatible with a dynamic labor market. That said, I would acknowledge that if you make that social minimum too generous, then at some point you will lose that motivation that’s provided by offering people extra pay to take certain jobs. There’s always going to be some sort of balancing act. Probably, in our ideal socialist society, we’re going to have to do some trial and error to find where exactly that ideal social minimum lies. But I’m confident that we can ensure everyone a dignified existence.
- Neal Meyer People might ask, well, what about those people who can’t work, for whatever reason, or who retire? Presumably they would be offered a higher-than-minimum income.
- Nick French Yeah. Again, actually existing welfare states point in the direction of what a socialist society should do too, which is: if people have disabilities that prevent them from working, or if they’ve reached retirement age, they get an additional stipend above and beyond what they would get if they were working age and not judged to be disabled. That’s a fair way of managing things: to think that there’s some population we define as working age and capable that receives that basic dignified social minimum but also experiences an economic pressure to join the labor force.
- Neal Meyer One thing that might be worth also clarifying here is that, in your version of a labor market for socialism, we’re not talking about the kind of society we live in, where there’s no limit to the amount of income that someone can accumulate. The idea is to have a much more egalitarian wage structure.
- Nick French Definitely. My thought is that you want to allow inequalities insofar as that is necessary for providing everyone the means to flourish. I’m not coming down hard on an exact view about what the most just income distribution looks like. But I do think something like John Rawls’s difference principle is really compelling: you allow for inequalities in wealth and income insofar as those benefit the worst off. Now, the kinds of inequalities that would exist because of pay differentials to get people to take certain jobs are going to be way smaller than exist under capitalism. There are a few reasons for that. One is that I do think people will be more intrinsically motivated in a society that is more solidaristic and where there’s more equality of opportunity. And when more of the economy is under public ownership and less driven by the profit motive, when you have collective bargaining regimes in place that guarantee workers certain minimums and sectoral benchmarks, as we’ve seen in places like Sweden, you’re not going to see runaway pay for executives. We’ve gotten rid of the capitalist class, so you don’t have capitalists hoarding wealth as individuals. So, there’s still inequality, but way less.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as new director
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Senay Boztas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.
Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”
The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.
This success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.
But Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he says. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”
Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.
From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental shows of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he says.
From the Finns, he will also bring an important lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he says: “Less talking, more doing.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Campanha Natal Solidário 2026 vai distribuir 4.500 refeições e brinquedos na periferia de SP
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Afonso Bezerra
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Movimento Brasil Popular em São Paulo está realizando a campanha Natal Solidário de 2026. A iniciativa tem mobilizado 15 cozinhas solidárias para distribuir em torno de 4.500 refeições e brinquedos para crianças nas comunidades periféricas.
Ao jornal É de Manhã, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Raquel Almeida, do Movimento Brasil Popular, conta que a mobilização acontece desde 2023 e que ela define como uma ação de solidariedade carregada do simbolismo que tem as festividades de final de ano. ” É semelhante como acontece nas nossas casas também, onde sempre no dia 24, no dia 25 ,a gente se reúne com a nossa família, a gente celebra, a gente senta à mesa, come uma comida boa, come uma comida gostosa e o Natal solidário nos territórios tem essa finalidade também”, afirma.
Almeida explica que o conceito de cozinha popular vai muito além do local onde é produzido o alimento. “A cozinha popular é esse território de luta, é esse território de organização popular. É o espaço onde a gente vai congregar várias coisas, como o direito à educação, o direito à saúde, o direito ao cuidado das crianças e das mulheres”, aponta. “E a gente faz um dia celebrativo, a gente chega cedo, prepara as refeições, mas também faz essa construção da preparação do ambiente para receber as crianças. A cozinha popular tem esse papel de mitigação da fome nos territórios”, explica.
Este ano, conta Raquel Almeida, a campanha tem focado também na entrega de brinquedos para as crianças. “Essa é uma forma de a gente incluir as crianças, ir no território, brincar com elas, para que as crianças se sintam também representadas nesse processo de solidariedade”, aponta.
As ações acontecerão entre os dias 14 e 19 de dezembro. Quem quiser apoiar o Natal Solidário, pode acessar o Instagram do Movimento Brasil Popular SP onde há um link na bio que direciona para a plataforma Apoia-se.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/ice-.title: ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/ice-.author: Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/ice-.text:
A viral piece of misinformation about iPhone security made its way into official government communications after multiple regional branches of Homeland Security Investigations sent out memos containing false or misleading information, sources told The Intercept.
Staff in at least three regional offices of HSI, a division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, told The Intercept they received memos within the past week warning of the iPhone’s “Live Listen” feature, which the memos erroneously described as enabling all iPhones to capture nearby audio, transcribe it, and transmit it to Apple.
The memos were handed down amid a broader swell of viral social media posts about the feature, which began to bubble up sometime last month, according to the fact-checking website Snopes.
A fourth memo, which was verified by an ICE spokesperson, appears to have broken containment this week when a screenshot of the memo, sent from the “chief intelligence officer” of Chicago’s HSI office began making the rounds on social media. The language in that memo was almost identical to the memos described by HSI officials who spoke with The Intercept on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record.
“The recent Apple iOS 27 update automatically enables ‘Live Listening’ [sic] on Apple devices,” the Chicago memo read. “This means that all iPhones and iPads with this update, both personal and operational, are by default capturing conversations around them, transcribing them, and sending those transcriptions up to Apple for advertising purposes.”
That description gets several key facts wrong, according to Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Klosowski said it conflates the Live Listen feature with commonly held fears of iPhones picking up ambient audio and using it to target users with advertising.
“It feels very much like there are people in the U.S. government who are getting their security advice from TikTok rather than from actual professionals,” Klosowski said. “It’s almost verbatim some of the memeified warnings that I’ve seen. You would hope that government organizations would be providing more concrete, useful, and correct security advice to the people in the government.”
A spokesperson for ICE acknowledged the message with incorrect information about a vulnerability.
“This notice was not accurate and was subsequently corrected,” the spokesperson said. “It was not a formal government cybersecurity advisory. Formal government cybersecurity advisories are disseminated by DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.”
Live Listen, an accessibility feature first introduced in 2014, enables iPhone users to stream audio from their phone’s microphone into hearing aids or headphones synched with the device. The “remote control” feature is newer, first introduced in iOS 26, and allows users to control the feature remotely from a nearby Apple device signed into the same iCloud account.
A spokesperson for Apple declined to directly address the memos or the social media furor around the Live Listen feature, but denied that Apple stores any data from Live Listen, which processes transcripts of captured audio directly on the iPhone.
Actually Securing Your Phone
Just because social media — and some government officials — are propagating fears about Apple audio surveillance doesn’t mean there isn’t anything to do to secure one’s phone.
Though it is a feature intended to help people with accessibility needs, the Live Listen feature can turn your iPhone into a listening device — and Apple provides instructions on how to use your iPhone as a remote microphone.
Bad actors, however, can only use your phone’s Live Listen feature to spy on you if they gain access to your phone or log into your Apple account to read transcripts. If the attackers were to manage any of those feats, the Live Listen feature would be the least of your worries — not a purported security flaw that has already been debunked.
While it’s certainly a good idea to disable the Live Listen feature if you’re not actively using it — as with any feature not in use — there are other practical measures that will likely have a much bigger impact on your phone’s security.
Clean Up Your Apps
One of the ways data can stolen off your phone is through rogue apps hoovering up your contacts and other information.
The first thing to do to minimize this is to go through your installed apps and remove anything that you don’t regularly use. That one time you downloaded a specific app to be able to fly on an airline you haven’t flown on in years? Get rid of it.
A good rule of thumb is if you haven’t used an app in over a month, go ahead and uninstall it. You can always download it again.
In general, get into the habit of removing one-time or limited-use apps as soon as you’re done with them. If you used the Disney World app for maps and ordering food, for instance, you can delete the app as soon as you leave Florida.
Once you’ve narrowed the playing field to apps you actually regularly use, the next thing to do is to limit the permissions that your installed apps have. Your casual gaming apps do not need access to your contacts list, and your grocery store loyalty app doesn’t need access to your camera or microphone.
If you’re not sure about whether an app needs a particular permission to be able to function, the best approach is to disable all permissions and only enable them one by one if the app isn’t working.
Update Everything, Constantly
After you’ve pruned your in-use apps and locked down their permissions, the next step is to make sure you regularly keep them updated. Ideally, you should go into your App (iOS) or Play (Android) store0 at least once a week, and update all your apps regularly.
Speaking of updates, be sure you’re keeping your phone’s operating system up to date, too. Even if you have automatic updates enabled, it’s still beneficial to regularly go into your update settings and manually check.
Even when you’ve updated all of your apps and your OS, you’re not out of the woods quite yet. You also need to stay on top of hardware updates, and make sure your phone can run the latest security and app updates and isn’t vulnerable to any known hardware-based security threats.
These threats are real: In June, older iPhone models like the XS, XR, 11, and SE 2 were found to have a hardware vulnerability that’s not fixable by any measure other than upgrading to a new device.
Thwart Spyware
If you’re worried about sophisticated spyware — like one used by state actors or deep-pocketed corporations — both modern iOS and Android phones come with specialized security modes that you can enable to limit the chances that advanced malicious actors can sink their claws into your device.
On iPhones, you’ll want to turn on Lockdown Mode (by going to Settings > Privacy & Security > Lockdown Mode > Turn On Lockdown Mode), while on Androids, the roughly analogous mode is called Advanced Protection (go to Settings > Security & Privacy > Advanced Protection > Enable Device Protection > Turn On).
Security has traditionally been at loggerheads with usability, and this is the case here: Enabling these advanced security features does come with certain functionality trade-offs. You can’t, for example, use shared albums. It’s up to you to decide if your security concerns outweigh your need to, say, FaceTime with strangers.
Another quick way to thwart some spyware is to regularly turn off and restart your phone. The National Security Agency recommends that you do so at least weekly, but it can’t hurt to do it once a day. This simple trick works because malicious code often lingers in your phone’s ephemeral versus permanent memory, so it’s much harder for spyware and malware to survive a reboot. Rebooting your device would require the spyware to reinfect your device.
All of these tips will help you harden your phone against unwanted surveillance and malicious actors. You may also consider switching your phone over to a more hardened operating system such as GrapheneOS, which provides several added security functionality beyond those offered by Android or iOS.
Phone security, however, isn’t just about tweaking settings or running the right operating system; it requires keeping your wits about you and constantly staying vigilant. The best thing you can do is to not download shady apps or click on unknown links.

This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
