Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Hundreds of NYC Students Still Without School Bus Transportation, Officials Say
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Olander, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
Hundreds of New York City students still lack assigned school bus transportation more than two months into the academic year, education officials told City Council members Wednesday.
Roughly 2,000 students started the school year without bus service, and 467 remained without assigned transportation as of Wednesday, officials said at an oversight hearing. Most of the students initially affected have individualized education programs, or IEPs, that require transportation to and from school.
The figures point to persistent problems in a system that carries about 150,000 students daily, even as officials pour more money into busing. The city spent $2.1 billion on student transportation in fiscal year 2026, up from $1.46 billion five years earlier, and has budgeted $2.28 billion for fiscal year 2027. City officials had warned of potential bus shortages before classes began in September.
Kevin Moran, the Education Department’s deputy chancellor for school operations, acknowledged that “too many families have experienced delays, route changes, staffing shortages or gaps in service.” He attributed some gaps to transportation requests submitted after an Aug. 6 registration deadline, including for students who moved, changed schools or had their transportation needs updated.
Before the hearing, dozens of parents, students, advocates and elected officials rallied on the steps of City Hall to demand better bus service. The gathering, organized by the Road to Better Busing Coalition and ARISE Coalition, featured signs reading “NYC needs better busing” and “Late bus = lost learning.”
Parents described how transportation problems have disrupted their children’s education. Divya Mathew said the bus for her 7-year-old daughter, who attends a private school for students with disabilities, routinely arrived 30 minutes to more than an hour late at the start of the year. The delays threatened her daughter’s speech and occupational therapy services, Mathew said, so she began driving her daughter to school. Mathew said she filed nearly 25 complaints to the Education Department’s Office of Pupil Transportation before the problem was resolved.
At the hearing, Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, who chairs the Education Committee, called unreliable bus service a “perennial issue.” He described a student whose bus arrives an hour before school ends, forcing the family to choose between missed instruction and paying for private transportation.
“It is heartbreaking and unconscionable to receive emails and phone calls that a child didn’t get on the bus because it never came,” Dinowitz said.
Moran said every route that lacked a driver on the first day of school now has one, and the city has offered temporary rideshare transportation to some families awaiting bus assignments. He cited a parent survey showing nearly 90% satisfaction with transportation during the 2025-26 school year.
But staffing gaps remain for students who need additional support. More than 350 students are still waiting for the paraprofessionals their IEPs require to accompany them on the bus, officials said. Paraprofessional shortages have previously left students with disabilities unable to attend school.
Students with assigned routes face problems, too. Councilmember Lincoln Restler said nearly 90,000 bus routes were delayed last school year, about 500 per school day, and said 56,000 students experienced delays of more than an hour.
Restler and Dinowitz are sponsoring legislation requiring the Education Department to publish monthly data on early, late and missed pickups and drop-offs on a public dashboard. The data would go beyond the department’s existing vendor report cards, which initially lacked on-time performance figures. Education Department officials said they support the bill’s intent and want to work with the council on a feasible reporting timeline. Council members discussed the measure Wednesday without taking a vote.
Lawmakers Scrutinize NYC School Bus Oversight
In 2019, the city contracted with Via Transportation to modernize its school bus system, including tracking buses and students and developing more efficient routes. The contract is now valued at $51.7 million, but the promised route optimization software remains unfinished years after its original deadline. Asked why the city still uses older routing software, education officials said the COVID-19 pandemic interrupted development and the department had not been ready to integrate some features into its systems.
Contractor oversight has also drawn scrutiny. A December 2025 comptroller audit found the department failed to consistently use available data to identify problem routes and hold bus companies accountable. The city could have assessed $44.3 million in penalties for violations of GPS tracking requirements during the 2024-25 school year, the audit found, but assessed just $1.7 million.
Drivers must log into the city’s tracking app, which launched in 2024, so families can locate their children’s buses. Moran said officials initially held off on penalizing some bus companies for GPS tracking violations because of technical problems and training needs. The department has since assessed about $270,000 in tracking penalties, he said, and drivers now log in about 93% of the time.
That scrutiny could shape the city’s next round of bus contracts. Last November, the Panel for Educational Policy approved three-year contract extensions after a dispute that threatened to disrupt bus service. The agreements expire in 2028, and City Council members have called for new contracts with companies committed to improving service.
Samantha Olander writes about Newark and New York schools.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gu.title: Guadalupe Maravilla to Offer Midnight Mass Sound Bath at St. John the Divine Cathedral
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gu.author: Maximilíano Durón
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gu.text:
As part of his forthcoming Creative Time commission at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, artist Guadalupe Maravilla will offer a bevy of programming beginning December 18.
Titled Consejos de las Estrellas and presented in collaboration with the Clemente Soto Vélez Cultural and Educational Center, the project comprises a sculptural installation that will “serve as a healing instrument and a place to find warmth and belonging when the holidays deepen the feeling of absence,” as Maravilla told ARTnews when the project was announced in October.
Core to Maravilla’s sculptures is their ability to be activated for sound baths, and Consejos de las Estrellas will offer eight sound baths during its run. Two of them will be staged in tandem with two winter holidays: a Christmas Eve Midnight Mass sound bath, beginning at 11:59 p.m. on December 24, and New Year Cleansing sound bath on January 9. The latter event will be proceeded by an herbal cleansing workshop by Herban Cura, which describes itself as a “healing justice herbalism and ecology school,” per its website.
A cancer survivor himself, Maravilla has long held sound baths specifically for the cancer community and he will offer two at St. John the Divine that will bookend this part of the programming. The first of these, on December 18, will be specifically for cancer survivors, healthcare workers, and caregivers and realized in partnership with the Mount Sinai Tisch Cancer Center. The final one will be staged on February 4, which is also World Cancer Day.
Consejos de las Estrellas will also feature performances by artist-collaborators who will activate Maravilla’s installation. They are Holland Andrews (January 22), Tesora Garcia and Camilo Godoy (January 29), and Jesús Hilario-Reyes (February 6). Maravilla will hold an artist conversation and Tarot reading on January 14.
Additionally, there will be a Three Kings Eve celebration and procession on the afternoon of January 5 with puppeteers from Teatro Sea. The project also will serve as a mutual aid hub, collecting food, clothing, and toy donations during its open hours, Wednesday to Sunday.
Consejos de las Estrellas will be open at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York’s Morningside Heights neighborhood from December 17 to February 7. Opening hours will be Wednesdays to Fridays from 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturdays and Sundays from 12 p.m. to 7 p.m.; the project will be closed from December 31–January 2. Full details for the accompanying programming, which is free and open to the public, can be found on Creative Time’s website.

https://taz.de/AfD-Kandidat-in-Sachsen-A.title: AfD-Kandidat in Sachsen-Anhalt: Siegmunds Schlingerkurs
https://taz.de/AfD-Kandidat-in-Sachsen-A.author: David Muschenich
https://taz.de/AfD-Kandidat-in-Sachsen-A.text:
AfD-Kandidat in Sachsen-Anhalt : Siegmunds Schlingerkurs
Erst wollte er nicht, dann nur im ersten Wahlgang und jetzt doch ein bisschen früher. Das könnte Aktionismus sein, um Aufmerksamkeit zu erzeugen.
D ie AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt zieht die Wahl des Ministerpräsidenten in Sachsen-Anhalt um eine Woche vor; nun soll es der 8. Dezember werden. Der Vorstoß überrascht zwar, dass Ulrich Siegmund seine Ankündigung ändert, aber nicht.
Schon nach der Landtagswahl zeigte er sich, nun ja, flexibel. Denn eines der wenigen konkreten Wahlversprechen lautete: Siegmund regiert nur, wenn seine Partei eine deutliche Mehrheit im Landtag stellt. Doch als nach der Wahl klar war, dass der AfD drei Stimmen fehlen, rückte er davon schnell ab. Die Mehrheit würde sich noch irgendwo im Landtag finden. Er war sich aber sicher, er werde am 15. Dezember im ersten Wahlgang gewählt.
Anfang November klang Siegmund dann nicht mehr sicher. Er wolle auch weitere Wahlgänge offen lassen, sagte er in einem Interview mit der Regionalzeitung Volksstimme. Und jetzt will er sich früher wählen lassen
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Aber weshalb jetzt der 8. Dezember statt eine Woche später? Wenn Siegmund eine Mehrheit mit dem BSW oder abtrünnigen Abgeordneten der CDU sicher hätte, könnte er auch schon jetzt antreten. Oder in der nächsten Woche. Vielleicht lag der 15. Dezember einfach terminlich ungünstig. Wer weiß, ob an dem Tag alle Zeit hatten, die Siegmund für seine dünne Mehrheit braucht. Wenn dann auch noch ein Abgeordneter Siegmund in den Rücken fällt, wäre der auf offener Bühne blamiert.
Oder die Sondersitzung ist reiner Aktionismus, um zu vermitteln, in Sachsen-Anhalt bewege sich etwas. Über Fortschritte bei Sondierungen oder Koalitionsgesprächen kann die AfD nicht berichten. Es gibt keine. Während Mecklenburg-Vorpommern schon seine Regierung hat und bundesweit Medien minutiös über die Koalitionsverhandlungen in Berlin berichten, kann Siegmund nur Videos mit den alten Wahlkampfphrasen hochladen.
Das AfD-Motto „Alles ist möglich“ nimmt Siegmund aber sichtlich ernst. Was immer er verspricht, ein neuer Move ist möglich.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-hou.title: Hakeem Jeffries Aside, Congress’s Left Is Well Positioned
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-hou.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-hou.text:
Hakeem Jeffries Aside, Congress’s Left Is Well Positioned
Hakeem Jeffries will be the next House speaker, a depressing fact for many angry at the Democratic Party status quo. But there is a strong case that the Left is well positioned for fights with Jeffries and the party establishment in the near future.
In a bitter disappointment for the Left, Hakeem Jeffries — the vehemently pro-Israel Wall Street darling who once, bizarrely, did a version of George Wallace’s infamous “segregation forever” speech, only subbing in “Israel” for “segregation” — will be the next speaker of the House of Representatives. The vote wasn’t even close: 251–11, with two members abstaining, something Jeffries’s allies are already celebrating as a sign of his domination of the Democratic caucus.
Going into this election, the members of the expanded Squad — the twenty or so progressives and socialists elected to Congress who may or may not now be known as “The Bloc” — viewed the two years between now and 2028 as a vital, possibly final, chance for Democrats to deliver some actual results for working people and avert future political disaster. Jeffries’s ascension to the speaker’s gavel drastically reduces the chances of that happening.
That’s the pessimistic way to look at it, at least. There is also a rosier perspective.
But to start with, there’s a lot to be pessimistic about. Hakeem Jeffries is a champion of political and economic elites. He and the rest of the House leadership are largely funded by the exact industries — finance, defense, health insurers and pharmaceuticals, the crypto industry, and firms like Palantir — that are militantly against the kind of change that people voted his party into power to see.
His ambitious agenda if Democrats won was to reverse a handful of policies Donald Trump had enacted last year, including ending the Iran war, and simply bring us back to the intolerable status quo ante that produced Trump’s election in the first place. Jeffries is already punting on the budding plan to end the war by defunding it. He has refused to commit to even holding a vote on US aid to Israel, putting him at odds with not just a large supermajority of his party’s own voters but most of the American public.
Jeffries is, in other words, an embodiment of everything people do not like about the Democratic Party, which is more or less what incoming Ohio Rep. Don Leonard told him in a closed-door meeting, a sentiment Jeffries apparently gets. Upon telling the speaker-to-be to his face that his name was “synonymous” with the “low quality” of today’s Democratic Party brand, Jeffries, according to Leonard, nodded.
Socialists and progressives did not even try to mount a challenge to Jeffries, seemingly confirming fears that the blowout margin of the Democrats’ midterm win would, paradoxically, produce a more conservative outcome by shrinking the Left’s leverage. The party’s left-populist wing made the calculation that Jeffries simply had unassailable numbers, thanks in no small part to his lockstep support from the powerful Congressional Black Caucus (CBC), which views the history-making aspect of the first black House speaker as critically important, regardless of that speaker’s actual politics.
Some progressives have also pointed to the lack of viable (or really, any) challenger to Jeffries to explain the failure to move against him, which is partially true. They still could have tried to muster enough members to oppose him that it would make his eventual path to the speakership (for which the actual, full House vote will take place next year) more difficult and eventually wring concessions out of him, as the GOP’s Freedom Caucus did to Kevin McCarthy three years ago.
The counterargument to this is that Republicans in 2023 had a far slimmer majority than the Democrats will have — just nine seats, compared to the Democrats’ eighty-five seats and counting next year — and that they did this on the back of a GOP midterm performance widely viewed as a flop compared to the Democrats’ historic overperformance this year, which Jeffries’s allies like the CBC wasted no time in crediting him personally with.
In any case, the party’s left bloc — which, of course, is still getting its bearings and hasn’t even been sworn in yet in Congress — decided the slim chances of rolling Jeffries wasn’t worth the risk of drawing his ire. The strongest, “steel man” argument for this is that they have done something similar to Zohran Mamdani in New York, who likewise calculated that, given his relatively weak position as a newly elected insurgent mayor, there was no plausible pathway to challenging centrist Democrats in New York, and he would be more successful if he avoided spending political capital on what he viewed as a suicide mission.
That decision saw Mamdani effectively quash a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) primary endorsement against Jeffries last year, both to keep the powerful Democratic leader out of his hair as he got his nascent mayoralty going and because he assessed that such a challenge could not win, and ally himself with centrist governor Kathy Hochul, betting he could accomplish the kinds of legislative victories he needed to succeed as mayor by cozying up to the governor (who holds significantly more power across multiple fronts) than by antagonizing her. Both of those proved to be successful bets for Mamdani.
We’ve gotten some idea of what the consequences for crossing Jeffries could look like from Leonard, who last week revealed party leadership had threatened to make him lose reelection in two years time if he didn’t get behind the Brooklyn Democrat. Other than Leonard, from what we know so far, the others who voted against Jeffries were almost all socialist freshmen in safe blue districts — or, in the case of incoming Reps. Frederick Haynes III and Adam Hamawy, Medicare for All–supporting progressives in safe blue districts.
In other words, the votes against Jeffries are from members who have nothing to lose and in fact could benefit politically in the long run from going on the record opposing someone expected to be a disappointing speaker.
By one view, this failure to block Jeffries will be fatal to the party and to any hope of it pursuing a pro-working-class agenda. Shortly after the result, Corbin Trent, cofounder of Justice Democrats and former staffer to both the Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, had told me his fears that the Democrats would fail “if the same people who drove this bus of the party into the hands of Donald Trump twice” stayed in place, meaning Jeffries and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer. Trent has spread that message elsewhere, including on Fox News, where he appeared to not-so-subtly prod his former boss, Ocasio-Cortez, to be more outspoken in this fight, saying that anyone planning to run for president in 2028 “should be voicing up now.”
As a number of incumbent and incoming left-insurgent lawmakers told me in the process of reporting a forthcoming In These Times piece on the midterm result, a Democratic failure to deliver results, or even to appear to be trying to deliver them, could spark another Obama era–like mass disillusionment that could end up empowering someone much worse than Trump not far down the line. According to the pessimistic view of where things currently stand, we are well on the way to that future right now.
But again, that’s not the only way to assess what happened here.
Jeffries Isn’t Out of the Woods
There is good reason not to swallow wholesale the corporate center’s triumphalism over the vote margin, which the corruption-tainted Rep. Henry Cuellar gloated showed the opposition to Jeffries is just “a small number of votes that are marginalized” and that “this small little group cannot tell the caucus where we need to be at.” Those reasons go beyond the fact that some version of this line is what this crowd has constantly been telling themselves as their grip on the party has slowly faded the past ten years.
In advance of the vote, Jeffries had already moved on his initial, tepid program of Trump reversals by publicly endorsing Bernie Sanders’s Medicare expansion plan over the weekend. Sanders’s proposal — lowering the Medicare eligibility age to fifty-five, including dental, vision, and hearing in the program, and covering all children with it until they turn nineteen — was not something any Democrat brought up or ran on during the midterms. Yet Jeffries’s adoption of it means it’s quickly becoming a consensus position among both the Democrats’ populist and corporate wings since the Vermont senator first brought it up two days after the election.
This would not be a minor reform. It would extend free public health insurance to 3.45 million adults and anywhere from four–seven million kids, depending on exactly how many children are thrown off health insurance in the years ahead by Trump’s Medicaid cuts. It would go much further than the Medicare-related parts of Joe Biden’s popular but never-passed Build Back Better bill, which merely added hearing to the program’s coverage, and would go a long way toward alleviating voters’ cost-of-living concerns, since health care is one of the biggest, most stress-inducing, and sometimes life-ruining costs anyone can deal with in today’s United States.
Left-insurgent lawmakers view the next two years as a unique opportunity: either they pass something that Trump actually ends up signing into law, making good on their election promises and tangibly making voters’ lives better, or Trump vetoes a bunch of things they pass, letting them make the argument to voters in 2028 that they need a Democratic president in the White House. If Jeffries’s movement on this matter holds, it will put socialists and progressives in a decent position to actually pursue this strategy.
Meanwhile, the fact that Jeffries has moved suggests he’s more vulnerable than the numbers today make it seem. Jeffries has, incredibly, a worse approval rating than outgoing Republican House speaker Mike Johnson, and while he at least gets overall positive marks from Kamala Harris voters, liberals, and Democrats — three of the paltry four groups he’s not underwater with — he gets them just barely, unable to muster majority support from any of those three.
More worrying for Jeffries, his congressional district, New York’s 8th, where he will have to contest a primary election in just two years’ time, is deep in DSA territory, in a state and city where the socialist organization has emerged over the past year as a leading political power.
To its immediate north is the 7th district, where DSA member and Mamdani ally Claire Valdez (who just voted against Jeffries) easily bested the Brooklyn borough president for the seat, and at whose watch party DSA members chanted “You’re next!” when Jeffries came on the screen. Bordering its panhandle to the west is the heavily Jewish 10th district, where another Mamdani ally, Brad Lander, comfortably ousted one of the Democrats’ most well-financed and most ardently pro-Israel members of Congress by taking direct aim at his unconditional support for Israel’s genocide. A little further up, and you get to the kingdom of another Mamdani ally and DSA member, Ocasio-Cortez, who eight years ago made her 14th district the final resting place for the career of a different corporate Democrat once tipped to be a future speaker.
In other words, for the sake of his career, Jeffries has to watch his left flank for the next couple years. A misstep, or a series of them, where he ends up looking like the singular roadblock to Democrats’ progressive ambitions, will be a weakness that a future primary challenger will eagerly exploit.
Piling on the pressure is the fact that next year’s Democrat-led Senate is now looking like a far more progressive chamber than usual. Besides Sanders, the country’s most prominent and well-liked socialist, it will feature three of his endorsees (Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, and Peggy Flanagan), all of whom campaigned on Medicare for All, and sixteen others who — however disingenuously — endorsed Sanders’s legislation on the program last year, as well as one other — Ron Wyden — who has come around to the idea in the past year, and vowed to use his coming chairmanship of the Senate Finance Committee to push through an expansion of the program.
It’s notable that the bold idea to risk a government shutdown in order to force Trump to end the Iran war originated from the Senate, and so far has the sign-on of not just Sanders and Chris Van Hollen — who has spent the past twenty-two months courting progressive support for a potential 2028 run — but centrists Michael Bennet and Tammy Duckworth. It’s notable, too, that Jeffries felt he had to go along with the Medicare expansion proposal, another progressive idea that came out of the Senate.
What happens in the Senate majority leadership race could intensify this dynamic. If Schumer — who is more vulnerable than Jeffries and underwater with the left-leaning demographics that still give the future speaker a slim positive approval rating — really is replaced by the more progressive Van Hollen, it may add further pressure on Jeffries, given that he can’t politically afford to look like he’s stymieing the party’s agenda or undermining its resistance to Trump.
None of this is guaranteed, and it’s possible in a few months to a year, this will all read as wildly overoptimistic.
But the opposite, pessimistic case isn’t guaranteed either, and there are reasons to think that the Democrats’ populist wing of socialists and progressives has cards it’s yet to play, as it once more thanklessly drags the party into saving itself. Jeffries’s victory yesterday is certainly a blow for the Left. But it’s not out of the question that in hindsight, it looks more like losing a battle while winning the war.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Artists should receive tax breaks for donating their own work to UK museums, says new philanthropy report
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.
The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.
The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”
In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.
Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a new national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”
Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, says the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.
Charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he says. “The biggest issue seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”
The CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report says.
UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”
Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, says: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.
“Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a new Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: A história se constrói com a força da memória, da imaginação e da coerência
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Leonardo Melgarejo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
Na semana anterior aconteceram dois fatos que me marcaram bastante, e que agora me parecem tão relacionados a este debate que avança na base do governo e nas mídias de todas as cores, contra o ajuste fiscal, que vou me atrever a tentar estabelecer ligação entre eles.
Inicialmente, temos aquela necessidade objetiva de todos os governos. Eles começam com apoios otimistas, mas logo se deparam com críticas e com a necessidade de apresentar resultados que operem contra a erosão da popularidade inicial. E para este governo, com aquele novo congresso, o futuro será complicado. Por isso se tornou urgente obter, ainda este ano, condições para minimização dos problemas que vão ser construídos ou agravados por aquela maioria parlamentar que se anuncia disposta a inviabilizar o projeto Lula 4.
E isso começará no dia da posse, quando o governo passa a ter que cumprir as promessas de campanha, respeitando as normas em vigor.
Para tanto, o governo estima que vai precisar de pelo menos mais R$ 60 bilhões. E sabe que isso não pode ser obtido com base nos aumentos da receita, porque existem compromissos fixos em lei, medidos em percentuais sobre o Produto Interno Bruto (PIB), que sobem com as receitas. E ainda há um limite para este crescimento, amarrado ao antigo teto de gastos, atual arcabouço fiscal, que justifica aquela proposta de ajuste fiscal. Ou seja, o governo está numa sinuca de bico. Não adianta aumentar a receita e não pode cortar nas despesas mais relevantes, como INSS, Saúde e Educação, que crescem vegetativamente mais do que os 2,5% ao ano (do arcabouço fiscal, reduzidos – na proposta de ajuste – para 2% em 2027), porque elas dizem respeito ao programa que o elegeu. Vai ter que recuperar desperdícios, como a isenção de impostos e os incentivos a caloteiros. E ok, bastaria que o Banco Central (BC) reduzisse as taxas de juro, em 1%, que R$ 60 bi por ano seriam transferidos dos rentistas para o caixa do Ministério da Fazenda, e tudo fluiria bem. Mas já está visto que Lula não pode contar com isso.
Então, esta semana o ministro do planejamento, Bruno Moretti, apresentou uma proposta de ajuste fiscal, que procura compatibilizar a governabilidade futura com compromissos sociais e previsibilidade orçamentária. Como essa proposta veio a público sem maiores discussões, algumas bases do governo se sentiram desprestigiadas. E expuseram contrariedades que se somaram à posições da direita, dificultando a situação do governo, para sua aprovação. É verdade que aquelas medidas não são uma Brastemp, e mesmo assim, está difícil sua aprovação no atual congresso. Seu sucesso deverá exigir favores e concessões inconfessáveis, que talvez só venhamos a conhecer no futuro. Além disso, o ajuste fiscal vem sendo apresentado como tão indispensável e tão pressionado pelo tempo, que o risco de inviabilização do novo governo não pode ser descartado.
Sem entrar em detalhes, destaque-se: a partir de 2027 qualquer decisão que envolva este congresso de maioria golpista tenderá a ser contra o governo Lula. E terá o apoio do império, das grandes mídias e seus acionistas temerosos das ações da Polícia Federal e revoltados com o fim das bets e da jornada 6×1. Neste sentido se faz urgente uma visão de futuro. Em síntese, a correlação de forças que já é desfavorável à democracia, tende a se agravar quando os parlamentares eleitos assumirem o congresso.
E está evidente que, mantida a situação atual, o governo Lula não vai conseguir atender a compromissos de campanha que envolvem, entre tantas outras coisas, ganhos reais para o salário mínimo e ampliação de recursos para saúde, educação, segurança, reindustrialização com soberania e proteção ambiental, e outros aspectos de enorme relevância. Então algum tipo de ajuste que amplie a disponibilidade de recursos discricionários, na mão do governo, já em janeiro de 2027, tende a ser essencial. Sem isso o governo lula vai fracassar e talvez nem chegue a 2030. E mesmo que vá até lá, se chegar nas próximas eleições capengando e acumulando frustrações de expectativas, seremos engolidos pela extrema direita 2.0.
O que fazer? Bom, precisamos que o governo Lula tenha sucesso. E sabemos que isso vai depender de seus resultados em termos de ações relacionadas à saúde, educação, segurança, geração de empregos, ganhos reais de renda dos trabalhadores e, principalmente, aceitação e participação popular. Não vai ser moleza, e concordo com a excelente avaliação de Breno Altman. Ele pontuou entre outras coisas (e destaco apenas isso), que já no início de 2027 Lula precisará dizer ao país, claramente, quais brigas pretende comprar, hierarquizando suas relevâncias e chamando o povo a colaborar com a viabilização de pautas que possivelmente deverão incorporar radicalismo até aqui inédito. Vai precisar iniciar no ataque e manter seu exército na rua, cobrando iniciativas e comemorando resultados que dependerão de recursos ainda inexistentes .
Mas independente disso, e já, desde agora, no fim do Lula3, o governo precisa que o congresso aprove suas projeções em termos de limites de gastos e expectativas de receitas, sem esquecer os constrangimentos que se colocam para 2027.
Não será possível mexer no dreno das emendas impositivas, porque o governo precisa da simpatia daqueles/as que se beneficiam delas. Então, ainda que a proposta de ajuste fiscal elaborada pelo ministro Bruno Moretti possa ser melhorada isso não justifica seu abandono. Ela tem méritos, o tempo voa, a direita prefere não votar ou votar contra. E se nos perdermos na busca de algo melhor, sem tempo para negociações e sem pesar o que vai acontecer se fecharmos o ano sem algo que o atual congresso aprove este ajuste fiscal, o pior virá.
A história é repleta de exemplos neste sentido.
Ou alguém esqueceu das conexões entre aqueles movimentos populares que se somaram à estratégia da direita, viabilizando o impeachment de Dilma, a prisão de Lula, a eleição do Coiso e a desmoralização das instituições públicas?
É evidente que se desconsiderarmos as oportunidades de aprendizado com os erros do passado, os acertos do presente não serão suficientes para a estabilidade do futuro. Precisamos olhar para a história como um continuum, e é este o argumento que me faz trazer aqui os outros dois acontecimentos que me marcaram esta semana.
Dia 9 de novembro, no Cine bancários, foram apresentados seis episódios da série documental Passageiros da Fronteira Sul. Trata-se de revisão do ocorrido por ocasião do Plano Condor, quando ditaduras do cone sul articularam ações extraterritoriais, desprezando fronteiras, legislações, acordos e direitos internacionais, monitorando, sequestrando, torturando e eliminando pessoas interpretadas como “inadequadas” aos propósitos de golpistas empoderados nos seus diferentes países, sob tutela do governo dos Estados Unidos. Em Porto Alegre o caso mais conhecido envolveu o sequestro de Lilián Celiberti, Universindo Díaz e seus filhos menores, pela polícia uruguaia, com apoio do DOPS gaúcho e respaldo do Itamaraty. (Recomendo que assistam a série e outros documentos que estão disponíveis aqui, lembrando que seus autores também prepararam material de apoio pedagógico a estudantes e professores do ensino médio e da educação de jovens e adultos (EJA) interessados em compreender “o sentido as características e as consequências do regime cívico-militar instaurado no Brasil em 1964”).
No debate que se seguiu, onde os avanços da extrema direita e a fragilidade do atual momento que vivemos foram destacados, Jair Krischke lembrou que “a memória é a única vacina contra as ditaduras”. Com a concordância de Pedro Isaias Lucas e Omar Ferri, Jair Krischke destacou a permanência de acordos espúrios que tendem a garantir a impunidade a crimes lesa humanidade e que subsistem como sombras entre nós, preparando, sem cessar, novos golpes.
O quase sucesso de Flávio B, bloqueado com participação decisiva da juventude permite entender o interesse dos golpistas, na erosão do capital político representado pela consciência das novas gerações. Isto explica o esforço desenvolvido pela extrema direita, contra a recuperação e a manutenção/exposição de nossa história. Por isso, nossos aspirantes a ditadores e seus associados estão comprometidos com a distorção de percepções sociais a respeito da urgência de assegurar bases que reduzam riscos de fracasso do governo Lula. Se trata de impedir que o governo consiga mitigar efeitos da insatisfação da classe média e da violência da pobreza, que eles criaram e que agora/sempre pretendem atiçar contra governos progressistas como o de Lula. Funcionou bem no impeachment da Dilma e eles acreditam que será possível repetir a dose.
E nós? Nós precisamos enfrentar essa onda e aprender com o passado porque, sem dúvida, a memória é nossa arma mais efetiva.
E assim, pelo rastro da história viva, chegamos ao terceiro evento desta semana. Na noite de quinta feira dia 12 de novembro, nos deixou Isaías Vedovatto.
Agricultor sem terra, liderança do MST, Isaías foi secretário de Estado ajudando a construir a Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Rural e a implantar o recorde de assentamentos ocorridos no RS, durante o governo Olivio Dutra. Mas ele fez bem mais do que isso. Aliás, acredito que Isaias tenha contribuído positivamente com todas as pessoas que tiveram oportunidade de conviver com ele. De certa forma, como é característico de tantos mestres da cultura popular que povoam nosso território, mas são pouco reconhecidos fora de seus círculos, Isaias continuará influenciando pessoas que possivelmente nunca ouviram seu nome. Recomendo a estas, que tentem conhecê-lo e que aproveitem o fato de que nestas semanas as redes de ativistas da reforma agrária, dos direitos humanos, da comunicação popular e da educação do campo estarão repletas de depoimentos que não alcanço repetir ou sintetizar. Sem condições de fazer mais do que isso, vou me limitar a tentar estabelecer uma conexão entre as limitações e dificuldades do governo Lula, seu plano de Ajuste Fiscal, o Plano Condor e um poco do muito que aprendi em conversas e posicionamentos de Isaias, em encontros com amigos do MST.
Isaias sabia escutar, conseguia se colocar no lugar dos outros e sabia fazer perguntas que facilitavam a compreensão coletiva dos temas em debate. Só isso já inspirava confiança. Mas ele também conseguia fazer boas sínteses de conteúdo dos temas em discussão. E usava nisso expressões que vinham das falas dos outros, o que facilitava (e fortalecia) a construção de compromissos coletivos. Liderava, ainda que não se sentisse à vontade com isso. Era modesto e provavelmente diria que estou exagerando nesta sua descrição. Mas sei que muitos/as concordarão comigo.
Em uma avaliação dos sucessos e insucessos da reforma agrária, e vivendo em um dos assentamentos mais exitosos do planeta, ele dizia que a evolução das comunidades assentadas deve projetar a criação de atividades produtivas não relacionadas à agricultura, porque elas motivarão a criatividade e o interesse dos jovens, pelo que virá, pelo que ainda não existe, mas no futuro haverá de ser necessário. Ele também lembrava a importância da geração de alternativas ocupacionais para os idosos, que precisam ser inseridos em atividades coletivas relacionadas ao cuidado, que dispensem o uso da força física e que ajudem a impedir tendencias ao isolamento e à solidão provocada por sentimentos de incapacitação contributiva.
Ele percebia que o fortalecimento de alianças entre as gerações se relaciona a processos de formação que, embora tenham necessariamente uma base técnica, exigem mais do que isso, apontando para eixos de emancipação das comunidades, e não apenas de seus indivíduos.
Lembro que no aniversário de 40 anos da ocupação da Fazenda Annoni, quando os “antigos” estavam sendo homenageados, Isaias fez uma espécie de chamado à juventude. Ele disse: é a vez de vocês. Tenham projetos, tenham coragem, e busquem formas de construir um mundo melhor. Estudem a realidade, aprendam com o passado, mas não se prendam a ela. Se desafiem, tenham paciência e persistência.
Vejo nisso uma lição de história, um mapa de trajetos que de alguma maneira todos percorremos e que dependem da memória e da imaginação. Algo associado à noção de desenvolvimento teorizada por Amartya Sen[1], no sentido de que as sensações de liberdade se expandem com capacidades que se constroem à medida em que os grupos sociais superam limitações comuns e estabelecem identidades definidoras de compromissos de solidariedade, assumindo novos desafios e conectando o que foi vivido ao que pretendem vir a ser. Memória, e imaginação trabalhando em parceria, qualificando instrumentos de seleção partilhada, que reinterpretam o passado e projetam o futuro, demarcando o que deve ser superado e o que deve permanecer. A Reforma Agrária Popular, com agroecologia garantindo alimentos sadios e respeitando os limites da natureza e o plantio de 100 milhões de árvores projetadas pelo MST são alguns dos frutos dessa construção coletiva que, com a simbologia do MST vem influenciando gradativamente as populações urbanas. Isaías é parte desse vasto projeto que, em termos de abrangência, vai alcançar limites que inda não podemos avaliar.
E projeto, aqui, é a palavra-chave, que une os três temas abordados nesta coluna. Para um projeto de vida, um projeto de comunidade, um projeto de nação, precisamos de acordos em relação ao tanto que podemos avançar agora, levando em conta o que aprendemos, os riscos que estamos dispostos a assumir, e considerando que sempre representaremos aqueles/as/aquilo tudo que não tem voz.
Penso que Isaias concordaria com Jair Krischke: a memória é nossa arma contra descuidos que podem alimentar retrocessos, da mesma forma que a imaginação é nossa plataforma para a construção de um futuro que dependerá de nossas convicções e persistência. E os avanços neste rumo serão coletivos, envolvendo jovens e idosos, ou não existirão.
Suponho que o projeto do Governo Lula 4, com as dificuldades que se anunciam, com as negociações penosas que deverão ser feitas diante de campanhas produzidas pela extrema direita, veiculadas pelas grandes mídias e articuladas pelos vendilhões da pátria em favor da ganância do império, precisa ser defendido. E isso vai exigir além de muita energia, a tolerância e a cautela necessárias a quem sabe que o momento é difícil mas que que depende de nós a formatação do Brasil que merecemos.
Do ponto de vista da luta pela reforma agraria popular, que se coloca como um projeto de todos, e que tem potencial para alavancar o a soberania alimentar e o desenvolvimento deste país, agrego imagens do 40º aniversário da ocupação da Fazenda Annoni. A meu juízo elas sintetizam o que tentei expor em palavras.
….
Quando terminei o texto, fiquei sabendo que o senado aprovou, com algumas alterações importantes (para pior), o Projeto de Ajuste Fiscal. Agora o tema vota à Câmara Federal onde se espera que vá ser votado na terça-feira que vem. Até o momento o Governo tem expectativa de acessar $50 bilhões em 2027. E isso é bom, é bastante, e talvez seja suficiente. Veremos. O PL lamentou, o PT comemorou.
Fotos do aniversário de 40 anos da ocupação da Fazenda Annoni.
A memória e a imaginação, o passado e o futuro
A formação emancipatória é um trabalho permanente

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/ice-.title: Everyone’s Talking About Air Travel. No One’s Talking About How ICE Flights Make It Less Safe.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/ice-.author: Tyler McBrien, Jon Nealon
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/ice-.text:
Tyler McBrien is the managing editor of Lawfare.
Jon Nealon is a documentary filmmaker and geospatial journalist.
It’s finally time to talk about air travel safety. High-profile crashes, equipment failures, and last week’s rare nationwide ground stop have thrust a long-overdue conversation about flying to the fore. But the chatter has largely omitted a major factor exacerbating the risk of airline catastrophes: the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies.
With slapdash and violent immigration enforcement as arguably its defining feature, the second Trump administration has mobilized and redirected vast federal resources to hit impossibly high detention and deportation targets. The administration has bent and broken laws, ignored proper vetting processes for new Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits, and slashed mandatory training hours. The results of these dangerous shortcuts have been deadly: 2025 saw the highest number of deaths for people in ICE custody in decades. At the urging of Stephen Miller, now the White House chief of staff, the detention and deportation quotas have pushed ever higher. To meet them has required the rapid transportation of migrants, often via flights.
In the air, as on the ground, speed kills.
Traditionally, the federal government has not owned and operated its own airline, instead chartering flights from private airlines. Reliance on private contractors is not atypical, but in December 2025, the Trump administration broke with past practice and began to acquire its own fleet to complement the private charters.
In less than two years, ICE’s air operation has quietly transformed into a full-fledged domestic airline, adding more traffic to the already crowded skies. Just as the Federal Aviation Administration has failed to keep up with flight capacity at major airports, this shadow network of detention shuffle flights has been operating with a reckless attitude toward safety that befits ICE’s overall reputation. As one flight attendant working on ICE Air flights told ProPublica last year, it’s “only a matter of time” before one of these deportation flights ends in disaster.
According to Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, since Trump’s second inauguration, there have been almost 20,000 individual flights chartered by ICE. Between January 2025 and January 2026, the number of flights inside the U.S. quadrupled. Most of these flights are not actually deportations, but trips shuffling detainees around the country between the hundreds of county jails, state prisons, and privately owned detention centers. Vulnerable migrants are locked in handcuffs, waist chains, and leg irons for the entire trip, unable to unbuckle themselves, violating a federal standard that says a full plane must be evacuated in 90 seconds. ICE Air has quietly removed three safety layers at once — the passenger, the crew, and the airport — and every flight risks triggering an emergency that no one on board could survive.
There was little mention of these risks after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop last week, which Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy blamed on technological upgrades and aging infrastructure.
But an unsafe plane can put anyone at risk, and ICE flights regularly violate FAA safety standards. On ICE’s airliner-size jets, shackled detainees land at one of more than 100 airports in ICE’s expanding network, usually not at major hubs but at small regional airports and airfields. Many of these small, regional airports are not certified by the FAA for planes that size, and some have no fire-and-rescue crews on the ground.
If you live near a small airport in the U.S. and began noticing increased jet noise in the last year and a half, you were probably not imagining things. Your local airfield may be one of the nodes in this network. At the Northeast Alabama Regional Airport in Gadsden, Alabama, for example, over 300 ICE flights have gone in and out since September 2025. The airport, together with the nearby Etowah County detention center, has developed into a transfer node, feeding migrants who were arrested in Alabama, Georgia, and Eastern Tennessee into the major deportation removal hubs centered in Louisiana.
At least five airports in the ICE flight network, including Northeast Alabama, lack FAA Part 139 safety certification, which mandates basic standards like on-the-ground aircraft rescue and firefighting capability. Dozens of other airports have hosted immigration-related aircraft that are sized beyond what their certification index anticipates.
When a small airport falls short of fire and rescue safety minimums, local departments often wait at the airport on standby, further stretching local municipalities’ abilities to keep everyone, even those not flying, safe. As illustrated by numerous videos of federal agents using excessive force or arrest, every encounter between ICE agents and ordinary people brings its own risk of harm. Each chartered flight also brings with it another chance for something to go wrong, and the number of flights keeps climbing. When it does, it could happen at an airport, like Gadsden, with no federal fire-and-rescue requirement and no certification.
Reports that ICE used tools to shield deportation flights from public scrutiny and congressional oversight have only compounded these safety concerns. In May, several Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford raising the alarm about ICE’s reported misuse of “Limiting Aircraft Data Displayed,” a program that allows private aircraft to request that the FAA withhold registration numbers and other identifiable data to block public flight trackers. “ICE’s use of this program to obscure routine government operations and suppress information about deportation flights is out of the scope of this program, and therefore inappropriate and dangerous,” the lawmakers wrote.
For the last 18 months, as this network of flights and airports ramped up, supercharged by windfalls from the so-called “Big Beautiful Bill,” congressional Republicans exercised little to no oversight. Come January, once Democrats take the gavel, a new opportunity for accountability will open up. One legislative option includes closing the loophole that lets ICE’s charter contractors operate airliner-size jets out of smaller regional airports that have no FAA Part 139 safety certification, either by amending the negotiated-charter exemption in federal law, or by demanding that the FAA explain — and if necessary enforce — the rules that appear to require certification for flights of this size.
With the power to legislate comes the power to investigate, and congressional Democrats should make full use of the subpoena. Mullen, Bedford, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, and representatives from CSI Aviation and the other private airlines making millions off of these flights should answer questions in public, at congressional hearings. In addition to Trump administration officials and those profiting from the flights, the American people also need to hear from those on the ground who run these small airports, and the local municipalities all across the country who have been assuming increased public safety risks, both in the skies and on the ground.
In pursuit of its draconian immigration policy, the Trump administration has pushed the immigration system beyond its ability to function safely, which puts all Americans at risk, with migrants at the most vulnerable end of the spectrum. Failing to mention how immigration enforcement contributes to the crisis plaguing air travel only risks prolonging it.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
