https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: These singles gathered in Central Park to swap their exes’ stuff
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
One of the hardest parts of breaking up, especially in this town, is dealing with your ex’s stuff. Most newly-eligible New Yorkers simply don’t have the space for it — in their apartments nor in their hearts.
But of course, one person’s baggage can be another’s treasure, so the upstart dating network Park Bench recently hosted “The Ex-Change,” a mixer of sorts for people to swap mementos.
“The singles that we've talked to are always looking for ways to meet other singles, but in a not explicitly singles-coded way,” said Kasey Luo, a co-founder of Park Bench. This idea had a convenient value proposition: Whether or not you came away with a phone number, you wouldn’t leave empty-handed.
“New Yorkers love free stuff,” Luo said.
Arihant Barajatya — who, for what it’s worth, was one of the few male attendees and the only one game enough to talk to us — was giving away a pair of unisex sweatpants he’d shared with his ex.
“ I don't want anything that reminds me of her now,” he said.
While everything was gratis, the few dozen items people brought, laid out on picnic blankets, covered a range of monetary values. A paperback copy of “2666.” A pack of Marlboro Golds. A navy blue Burberry raincoat with the tags still on.
“I got this Le Labo clutch,” said Brianne Adiola, who was parting with some denim outfits. “I honestly only picked it up because I know Le Labo's expensive.”
But for the people discarding some of these big-ticket items, the benefits were clearly priceless.
When I asked Eliwa Onanga why she was parting with a chic pair of saddle shoes, she said they had nothing to do with an ex and everything to do with her own personal growth.
“ I think there was a time where I felt like I really had to show up super ‘professionally’ at work,” she said. “And I don't necessarily feel that way anymore.”
Margo Hera, who’d recently broken up with her partner of eight years, was giving away a steel sword from the series “One Piece” that could likely fetch three figures.
“ I bought [my ex] this as a present, and she left it,” she said. “It's an anime thing. I've never watched anime. I watched two episodes of the live action with her and I couldn't get into it.”
Read into this what you will, but that wasn’t the only sword-as-a-gift on offer.
“He told me he wanted dangly earrings, so I actually bought these for him,” said Julia Cooper, holding up a pair of sword earrings. “Then he never wore them, and he kinda, like, gifted them back, and I just decided I didn't want anything that reminded me of him at all.”
And that wasn’t the only thing Cooper was giving away for free — she also had some dating advice to offer: “ If you're feeling any sort of negative type of feelings, just break up. If you're spending more of your days unhappy with someone, it's not gonna get better, and the relief that you feel, it's really great.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/corpu.title: Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences.
https://www.propublica.org/article/corpu.author: Colleen DeGuzman, The Texas Tribune, Rachel Denny Clow
https://www.propublica.org/article/corpu.text:
Late in 2024, Corpus Christi, Texas, was desperate for water after years of drought. So city officials hatched a plan to tap millions of gallons of water a day from an aquifer that serves dozens of counties across the Texas Gulf Coast.
The city would drill wells — lots of them.
Corpus Christi’s drilling frenzy alarmed rural residents, who worried it threatened their access to water. They mobilized to create a groundwater conservation district that would regulate drilling and, they hoped, limit how much water the city could pump.
Then Corpus Christi officials came up with a peculiar idea. Fearing the residents’ effort could hamper the city’s ambitious plans to tap significant amounts of groundwater, officials asked a local entity to serve as its well regulator.
The advantages: City Council members appoint that entity’s board of directors, and its staff is made up entirely of city employees.
Since that decision last fall, the entity — called the Corpus Christi Aquifer Storage and Recovery Conservation District — has greenlit every city request to drill more wells. In doing so, The Texas Tribune and KRIS 6 found, it fast-tracked its permitting process for the city and overlooked steps that would have slowed down the process for approving the permits — safeguards its own rules require to protect other well users.
A city-commissioned study released this summer found that the drilling plan could cause land around the wells to sink and water levels in other nearby wells to drop significantly. But by then, the district had already approved permits allowing the city to pump up to about 40 million gallons a day from 20 wells, although the city draws less than a third of that daily on average.
The city defended the approvals. It said the district’s rules let the board decide when it has enough information to sign off on a permit and that before it does so, the city gives estimates of how pumping could affect water levels.
But water experts warn that the amount the city is allowed to pump in such a small area is exorbitant. “It’s absolutely unfathomable,” said Drew Molly, the former chief operating officer of Corpus Christi’s water department.
Molly, who is now chief water officer at Houston’s water department, said the district’s “lightning speed” approval of the city’s permits will cause ripple effects locally and across the state.
In Texas, fights over limited groundwater supplies will likely intensify as the population booms. Groundwater comes from aquifers and makes up more than half of the state’s water supply.
Aquifers stretch underground across counties and, sometimes, across states. The aquifer Corpus Christi draws from serves dozens of communities along the Gulf of Mexico, including some in Louisiana. Overpumping from aquifers is a key concern in Texas because they need rain and time to refill. As droughts get longer, the state’s water plan shows larger drops in groundwater’s availability compared with other sources.
Groundwater pumping must be approached with caution, experts say. In worst-case scenarios, excessive pumping “can wipe an aquifer out,” said Jarrod Reynolds, a groundwater resource engineer.
“It can be a stopgap, it can be a supplement, but it’s something that’s got to be managed,” Reynolds said.
Corpus Christi’s rapid expansion of groundwater wells offers a critical, if not extreme, example of the challenges presented by a patchwork system for regulating the water that cities, businesses and citizens can extract from the ground.
The coastal city of more than 300,000 residents nearly reached a crisis point earlier this year after persistent drought and years of inaction. It was months away from being unable to meet water demand and faced harsh restrictions to conserve supplies.
Drilling for groundwater became an important fix. So when the possibility of tougher regulation loomed in the wake of the rural residents’ efforts, city officials turned to Corpus Christi’s storage and recovery district, an entity created two decades earlier with the power to approve well permits.
The storage and recovery district is one of nearly 100 such groundwater districts in the state, but it’s the only one with City Council-appointed leaders. Most groundwater districts are led by leaders who are either elected or appointed by county officials — an important distinction since counties are not water suppliers, so there is less concern about any conflict of interest.
Corpus Christi leaders insisted in a written statement that the close ties the city shares with its well regulator will not hamstring efforts to protect the aquifer.
“There is no conflict of interest. City employees involved with the District have no personal or financial interest in permitting decisions,” said Ashley Marion, strategic business manager for the city water department, in the written statement. She added that, “The City and District share an interest in protecting and sustainably managing regional groundwater.”
Marion also said the city tracks water levels and physical conditions at the wells and adjusts pumping rates based on daily data and long-term modeling.
But the arrangement has drawn concern from water experts across the state, an outgoing state lawmaker and at least one of the storage and recovery district’s own board members.
“That’s the fox guarding the henhouse,” said Robert Mace, executive director at Texas State University’s Meadows Center for Water and the Environment, which focuses on water and environmental management policy.
“It tells me that the district is looking out for Corpus Christi’s interests and not necessarily the interests of other landowners that might be affected.”
Years of Inaction Lead to a City in Crisis
Corpus Christi’s decision to begin drilling wells reflects how the city’s approach to finding water swings wildly during drought.
The city currently relies on three drought-vulnerable reservoirs for most of its supply. Despite warnings that it needed to diversify its water sources, the city has repeatedly waffled on whether to invest in long-term solutions.
Since 2025, a divided City Council has twice declined to move forward with a city-run desalination plant, even though the state had approved $757 million in loans for the project and Corpus Christi officials had selected contractors to begin the work. The city has said the plant could produce around a third of the city’s daily demand.
After the most recent vote in September, outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott chastised Corpus Christi leaders for having “once again failed to secure reliable water.”
Desalination was not the city’s only missed opportunity to increase its water supply. Two decades ago, Democratic state Sen. Juan “Chuy” Hinojosa authored legislation that created the Corpus Christi Aquifer Storage and Recovery Conservation District. The district’s purpose is in its name: The city had plans to inject and store excess drinking water and treated wastewater underground to save for emergencies. Hinojosa did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
In the years that followed, the district studied the idea, drilled test wells and drew up plans. But nothing ever happened.
As the region’s main reservoirs were drying up in late 2024, city leaders found themselves searching for solutions again. Molly, then the city’s water director, had a “wild idea.” He reached out to John Michael, an engineer long involved in the city’s water projects, to ask if the city could drill wells along the Nueces River, according to a recent memo in which Michael recalled the conversation.
It was possible, and the city quickly started drilling. But this was always supposed to be a temporary solution.
While the wells were “a viable option to supplement water resources during the current drought, I never envisioned that the wells would be used for anything other than emergency supply,” Michael wrote in the June 26 memo.
In a written response to the newsrooms, the city called the groundwater program “a key component” of its strategy to diversify the region’s water supply.
Then officials learned of rural residents’ efforts to form their own groundwater conservation district. This posed a “potential danger” to the city’s plans, said then-Corpus Christi City Attorney Miles Risley at an October 2025 City Council meeting.
So the city moved quickly to ask the storage and recovery district to expand its boundaries to include its well fields outside city limits in Nueces County.
“Do you think we’d be able to carry that out without being biased?” council member Everett Roy asked the city’s water resource manager, Esteban Ramos, as the council debated asking the entity to regulate the wells.
“Yes, I do,” answered Ramos, who is also the storage and recovery district’s general manager.
When the storage and recovery district approved the city’s well permits last year, board members attached several protective requirements, such as creating plans to monitor water quality in its well fields and to reduce harm to neighbors’ wells.
None of those requirements prevented or slowed the city from moving forward with its drilling plans.
The city has not “fully satisfied” some of those requirements nine months later, according to a document two board members prepared for the district. The city said the district asked it to provide more information on its monitoring and mitigation plan. It said it is working with the district to meet the conditions and that the city’s compliance reports are public.
A private research company named Intera raised several red flags about the city’s groundwater pumping in a study the city released in June. It estimated that the ground around the city’s western well fields could sink about 20 inches over the next 30 years.
As water is withdrawn, just a few inches of sinkage can do costly damage to infrastructure, including pipelines, foundations, roads and bridges.
This type of sinkage, caused by compacting sand, rock or sediment, can reduce the amount of water an aquifer can hold long term, according to the American Geosciences Institute.
A drop in the aquifer’s levels would first be felt by rural residents, whose wells are not as deep as the city’s. The study said a drop of up to 100 feet was possible within five years near the city’s wells. In its response to these findings, the city maintained that they are just projections and don’t reflect how much it’s pumping on average.
But the city can easily pump more in emergencies, like when pipes break or during long dry spells.
That’s the fear of rural residents like Scott Barraza, who lives on 20 acres about 20 miles from downtown Corpus Christi with his wife, Julie; teen daughter, Grace; five dogs; three goats; and a horse named Rosie.
He recently purchased a $9,000 water purification system and a trailer to haul water from the city for his family and neighbors. Barraza acknowledges it’s probably excessive but says it’s best to be prepared.
“When you live out in the country, you don’t have a city water supply. Your well is your water supply,” he said.
Molly said the city’s decision to increasingly rely on groundwater rather than investing in a seawater desalination plant means Corpus Christi “basically put all their eggs in a terrible basket.”
Who Guards Groundwater?
What’s happening in Corpus Christi and the surrounding area raises critical questions about how the state manages its limited groundwater resources and who regulates them.
Republican state Rep. Denise Villalobos was so concerned about the unusual dynamic in Corpus Christi that she planned to file a bill to abolish the storage and recovery district in the upcoming legislative session. She also drafted another bill to create, in its place, a more traditional groundwater district that would regulate wells across all of Nueces County.
Then she lost her seat to Democrat Stephanie Guerrero Sáenz in the recent midterm elections. The incoming lawmaker, whose term begins in January, was less certain about her approach when interviewed by the newsrooms, saying she needs to talk with her new constituents first. She said any legislation she supports “must strike the right balance between protecting rural groundwater rights and addressing the urgent water needs of our region.”
In the meantime, some members of the storage and recovery district are starting to push back, including Michael, the engineer. He was appointed to the board five weeks after the district approved the city’s first 20 well permits.
Next month, the board is set to consider a resolution that would cap the city’s pumping to 6.5 million gallons a day — half of the city’s current average — until it meets the regulatory requirements meant to protect the aquifer’s health.
Michael and board member Jeff Edmonds, who is also the city’s director of engineering, proposed the measure, which is set for discussion Dec. 3. They said the current rate of the city’s pumping could cause “irreversible offsite impacts.” They also point to civil penalties the city risks if it continues to not comply with the rules.
For now, the recent water crisis in Corpus Christi has been averted after rains this summer temporarily refilled the reservoirs the city depends on. But projections show the city could be back in a water emergency by September 2029.
It’s a reminder of the reality that faces the entire state. The Texas Water Development Board has said Texas does not have enough water to meet demand if it faces a historic drought.
What’s happening with the storage and recovery district is “a microcosm of examples of what’s happening around the state,” Michael told the newsrooms, because Texas’ population is growing as available water resources are dwindling.
“We have to manage these districts in a sustainable manner,” he said, “and decisions have to be made on science and not emotions.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/a-barnes-noble-s.title: A Barnes & Noble—Sans Bathroom—Hits the East Village
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-barnes-noble-s.author: Christopher Robbins
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-barnes-noble-s.text:
Inside the brand-new East Village Barnes & Noble on Wednesday, Booker Prize-winning author Douglas Stewart signed copies of his latest novel to celebrate the grand opening of the corporate chain's newest location.
Outside on the sidewalk along Avenue A, a group of independent booksellers spread out their wares in defiance. Usually the group, called Armageddon Time, spends their Sundays selling books outside Tompkins Square Park, though they also have day jobs at bookstores around town. Wednesday's gathering was a kind of protest—a "Barnes & Ignoble Book Fair."
"Someone said to me, like, 'It's good because people are turning away from Amazon and going to Barnes & Noble.' What a pathetic fucking choice!" Szczypka said, in between drags of a rolled cigarette. "All of these bookstores have been carrying this flame because there's like, legitimate interest. It's like a community, like a trade, through ups and downs. And then Barnes & Noble comes in like, right at the end, after BookTok and everything else. And their windows are full of commercial literature."

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.title: Repression gegen Linke | Deutschland und USA haben Anti-Antifa-Workshop abgehalten
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.author: Matthias Monroy
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.text:
- Politik
- Repression gegen Linke
Deutschland und USA haben Anti-Antifa-Workshop abgehalten
»Praktiker« aus 31 Ländern trafen sich auf Einladung der USA zu einem geheimen Treffen in Berlin gegen »gewaltorientierten Linksextremismus«.
Das Außenministerium in Washington bestätigte am Dienstag in einer Mitteilung, dass ein gemeinsam mit Deutschland geplanter Workshop zu »gewaltorientiertem Linksextremismus« inzwischen stattgefunden und »Praktiker« aus 31 Ländern zusammengebracht habe. Die zweitägige Veranstaltung habe dem Informationsaustausch und der Koordinierung von Maßnahmen gegen transnationalen linken Terrorismus gedient.
Ein konkretes Datum nennt das von Marco Rubio geleitete Ministerium nicht. Laut einem Protokoll eines hochrangigen Treffens von EU-Innenministerien hatte Deutschland hierzu den 9. und 10. November 2026 in Berlin angegeben.
Das Bundesinnenministerium hält sich dazu weiter bedeckt. Auf eine Mitte Oktober gestellte Anfrage wurde »nd« abermals erklärt, die Planungen befänden sich »in einem frühen Stadium der Planung und Vorbereitung«, Details könnten nicht genannt werden. Eine erneute Auskunftsbitte vom 3. November blieb dann unbeantwortet.
Gegen »antiwestlichen« und »antisemitischem Extremismus«
Erst auf weitere Nachfrage am Dienstag teilte das Ministerium mit, es habe gemeinsam mit den Vereinigten Staaten »zu einem internationalen Praktikerworkshop zum fachlichen Austausch über Phänomenentwicklungen sowie über Ansätze der Prävention und Bekämpfung von gewaltorientiertem Linksextremismus eingeladen«. Weitere Angaben zu Ort, Datum oder Teilnehmerkreis machte es nicht.
Unklar bleibt, ob nur Polizei- oder auch Geheimdienstbehörden eingeladen wurden. Auch konkrete Inhalte des Workshops sind weiterhin nicht bekannt. Die US-Mitteilung behauptet dazu allgemein, linker Terrorismus überschneide sich zunehmend »mit Drogen-Terrorismus sowie antiwestlichem, antikapitalistischem und antisemitischem Extremismus«.
Das Treffen geht auf eine Konferenz zurück, die US-Außenminister Marco Rubio am 16. Juli in Washington ausgerichtet hatte. Das deutsche Innenministerium nahm mit seinem Abteilungsleiter für öffentliche Sicherheit teil und erklärte dort die Bereitschaft, das Folgetreffen in Deutschland auszurichten. Ministeriumssprecher begründeten das Engagement mit der Bekämpfung »linksextremistischer Gewalt«, die auch Deutschland betreffe. Eine Anwesenheit ungarischer Behörden ist wahrscheinlich: Das Land hat Ende Oktober das erste Memorandum zur gemeinsamen Verfolgung antifaschistischer Gruppen mit den USA geschlossen.
»Versuch, an unbekannte US-Aktivisten heranzukommen«
Es ist weiter unklar, weshalb Rubio eine derartige Energie zur Verfolgung linker Gruppen in Europa an den Tag legt. Vor einem Jahr hatten die USA per Präsidentenerlass vier europäische Gruppen als »ausländische terroristische Organisationen« und »designierte globale Terroristen« eingestuft und mit Sanktionen belegt, darunter die in Deutschland verortete Gruppe Antifa Ost. Ende August folgte die Einstufung des italienischen linken Tech-Kollektivs Autistici/Inventati.
US-amerikanische Rechtsexpert*innen vermuten, dass die Terrorlistungen von europäischen Antifa-Gruppen der US-Regierung den Zugriff auf Überwachungsbefugnisse gegenüber eigenen Staatsbürger*innen eröffnen könnten: Können Verbindungen zu einer dieser verbotenen Gruppen konstruiert werden, darf der Auslandsgeheimdienst deren Kommunikation ohne Richterbeschluss abhören. In einem internen US-Memorandum werden auch zwei in den USA ansässige Gruppen namentlich genannt, die angeblich Dienste von Autistici/Inventati (A/I) nutzen: Rose City Antifa mit Sitz in Portland und die für das Recht auf Abtreibung eintretende Gruppe Jane’s Revenge.
Auch der Anwalt Shayana Kadidal vom Center for Constitutional Rights äußerte in einem Interview mit der Tageszeitung »Junge Welt« den Verdacht, die Sanktionen gegen das italienische Tech-Kollektiv Autistici/Inventati (A/I) dienten diesem Zweck. »Es ist ein Versuch, an unbekannte US-Aktivisten heranzukommen«, sagte Kadidal. Nur die betroffene Organisation selbst könne ihre Einstufung anfechten – was etwa im Fall der von deutschen Behörden konstruierten Antifa Ost unmöglich ist.
Scharfe Kritik von links
Dass der Termin des deutsch-amerikanischen Workshops gegen »gewaltorientierten Linksextremismus« trotz mehrfacher Anfragen von Presse und Abgeordneten erst durch eine Mitteilung der US-Regierung bekannt wird, kritisiert die innenpolitische Sprecherin der Linksfraktion Clara Bünger scharf: »Es ist ein Affront gegenüber Parlament und Öffentlichkeit, dass die Bundesregierung Auskünfte zu diesem Workshop konsequent verweigert.« Das öffentliche Interesse daran sei hoch.
»Wer sich mit einer US-Regierung gemein macht, die routinemäßig Völkerrecht bricht, Menschen illegal deportiert und regierungskritische Gruppen als ›Feinde‹ markiert und strafrechtlich verfolgt, muss antifaschistischen Protest aushalten«, sagt die Bundestagsabgeordnete »nd«.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/cantine.title: Restauration scolaire : « Un service public de l’alimentation est essentiel »
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/cantine.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/cantine.text:
Face aux logiques de profit des grands groupes privés, la restauration collective publique peut garantir une alimentation de qualité tout en soutenant l’agriculture locale et la transition écologique. En mutualisant leurs moyens, les collectivités peuvent reprendre la main sur les politiques alimentaires et mettre la commande publique au service de l’intérêt général. Par Philippe Bouyssou, maire d’Ivry-sur-Seine et président de Tables Communes, et Patrice Leclerc, maire de Gennevilliers et président du Syrec.
Une alimentation au profit des enfants et non pour alimenter des profits à des grands groupes capitalistes voilà un des enjeux de la restauration scolaire. La restauration collective publique doit et peut répondre aux défis majeurs de la qualité de l’alimentation, de la transition écologique, de l’évolution des obligations réglementaires… C’est l’objectif de Synergies Communes, créée par des collectivités locales qui font le pari de la coopération entre acteurs publics pour préserver leur capacité d’action et renforcer le service public local.
La restauration collective va bien au-delà de la simple production de repas. Son action touche également la santé, l’éducation alimentaire, l’égalité d’accès à une alimentation de qualité, la transition écologique, mais aussi l’avenir de nos filières agricoles.
Chaque jour, dans les crèches, les écoles, les établissements publics ou auprès des personnes âgées, les collectivités font des choix qui ont des conséquences économiques, sociales et environnementales très concrètes. Que mettons-nous dans les assiettes ? À quel prix ? Dans quelles conditions les aliments sont-ils produits ? Et quelle agriculture souhaitons-nous soutenir ?
Le choix d’une alimentation de qualité accessible à toutes et tous
Défendre une restauration collective publique forte, c’est donc faire un choix politique : celui d’une alimentation de qualité accessible à toutes et tous, et d’une puissance publique capable d’agir sur son territoire plutôt que de subir les seules logiques du marché.
C’est dans cet esprit qu’a été créé Synergies Communes en 2023, sous l’impulsion de Tables Communes et du Syrec, deux syndicats de restauration collective qui produisent à eux deux 58 000 repas quotidiens répartis sur 19 villes d’Île-de-France. Aujourd’hui, Synergies Communes rassemble 23 collectivités dans une pluralité de sensibilités politiques.
Il s’agit de mettre en commun ce qui peut l’être sans jamais renoncer à la capacité de décision de chaque territoire. La coopération public-public n’a pas vocation à uniformiser les pratiques ni à effacer les spécificités locales. Elle permet au contraire à chaque collectivité de s’appuyer sur la force du collectif pour disposer de davantage de moyens, d’expertise et de marges de manœuvre dans la conduite de ses politiques publiques.
Cette coopération permet à la puissance publique de peser sur les choix économiques. Les millions de repas servis chaque année par les collectivités représentent ainsi des millions d’euros d’achats alimentaires.
Cette commande publique peut contribuer à sécuriser des débouchés, donner de la visibilité aux producteurs, accompagner le développement de filières durables et favoriser une alimentation davantage ancrée dans les territoires.
Mettre la commande publique au service de l’intérêt commun
La coopération avec la Coopérative Bio d’Île-de-France illustre concrètement cette ambition. Son adhésion récente au réseau Manger Bio contribue à renforcer une offre biologique structurée destinée notamment à la restauration collective. Pour les collectivités qui rejoignent Synergies Communes, cette dynamique peut faciliter l’accès à des produits bio de proximité et de qualité tout en soutenant des producteurs locaux et en leur offrant des débouchés plus prévisibles et une juste rémunération du travail agricole. La restauration collective participe ainsi à une politique alimentaire qui mêle accessibilité sociale, qualité des produits et transition écologique.
Cette capacité collective permet aussi de développer des solutions qui seraient difficiles à porter isolément. C’est le cas de la Semelog (structure innovante d’économie mixte crée par le Syrec et Tables Communes) qui organise une boucle de réemploi des contenants avec leur collecte, leur lavage, leur stockage et leur traçabilité.
La commande publique cesse alors d’être uniquement un acte administratif ou comptable. Elle devient un véritable outil de politique économique, sociale et écologique. Mutualiser permet de peser davantage pour donner un sens à la dépense publique.
Dans un contexte budgétaire contraint et face à des exigences techniques toujours plus fortes, la maîtrise publique de la restauration scolaire donne des garanties durables que le privé ne peut donner à cause du fait qu’une partie de ses ressources part en rémunération du capital.
Dans une période où de nombreux agriculteurs peinent à vivre correctement de leur travail et où les collectivités doivent répondre à des contraintes financières toujours plus fortes, la restauration collective publique constitue l’un des espaces où se construit une autre logique : mettre la puissance de la commande publique au service de l’intérêt commun.
L’alimentation n’est pas une marchandise comme une autre. Elle touche à la santé, à l’égalité, à l’agriculture, à l’environnement et à notre capacité collective à décider de ce que nous voulons produire et consommer. C’est précisément pour cela qu’un service public de l’alimentation fort est aujourd’hui essentiel.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://hyperallergic.com/iconic-and-ind.author: New York Studio School
https://hyperallergic.com/iconic-and-ind.text:
Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School's MFA Program
NYSS is now accepting applications from independent thinkers and experimenters in the arts.
What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires? Since its founding in 1964, the New York Studio School (NYSS) has pursued this question through an approach to art education grounded in sustained studio practice, rigorous inquiry, and the conviction that artists develop through the ongoing process of making, looking, and thinking.
Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art. Founded by artist and educator Mercedes Matter, NYSS carries forward a tradition of independent thinking and experimentation, offering an environment where artists can challenge assumptions, investigate fundamental questions, and develop their work through direct engagement with materials and ideas.
The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history. Rather than prescribing a single artistic direction, the program provides students with the time, space, and mentorship to pursue their own questions and cultivate their own distinctive artistic language.
At the heart of the New York Studio School MFA program is the relationship between individual practice and collective exchange. Students are assigned private or semi-private studio spaces and select two core faculty artists to serve as their atelier mentors. Through studio visits, group critiques, and ongoing dialogue with faculty and peers, students are encouraged to examine their work from multiple perspectives while developing the confidence and critical awareness to move their practice forward.
The curriculum combines independent studio work with intensive two-week Marathons, drawing courses, Critical Studies seminars, and encounters with visiting artists. The School’s renowned Evening Lecture Series and Exhibitions further connect students to a broad community of artists, writers, historians, and thinkers. Drawing remains a foundational component of the program, informing the study of painting and sculpture and encouraging deeper attention to perception, form, space, and material.
Students in the MFA program are encouraged to engage with the histories of art while questioning established conventions, exploring the relationships between representation and abstraction, and discovering new possibilities through sustained experimentation. The goal is to support the development of an independent, thoughtful, and resilient artistic practice. The MFA program’s second year culminates with a thesis project and exhibition in the School’s historic galleries, connecting a new generation of artists with a building that has been part of New York’s cultural life for more than a century.
For artists seeking a demanding, immersive environment in which to deepen their work, the New York Studio School offers an education built around the essential questions of art-making, and the time, community, and commitment needed to pursue them.
Applications are now open for Fall 2027 admission. For full consideration for admission and financial aid, apply by the Priority Deadline: January 15.
Learn more about the MFA program and apply at nyss.org.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Paved-Over Black Cemetery Could Qualify as Landmark, Commission Says
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Researchers at the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission have determined that an African burial ground in Elmhurst, Queens, that currently sits under an illegal parking lot is likely eligible for landmark status.
“We believe the former cemetery has cultural and historic significance related to the 19th Century Black and abolitionist history of New York City,” Margaret Herman, the commission’s director of research, wrote last month. “Research staff finds that the former cemetery may merit consideration for designation as a landmark.”
The finding is a preliminary step that could help transform a cemetery underneath an empty parking lot into a memorial for the upwards of 300 free-born and formerly enslaved Black New Yorkers buried there.
After The City Reporter revealed that tow trucks hired by the NYPD to remove abandoned vehicles from the streets were dropping cars and trucks there, a host of elected officials called on the administration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani to purchase the site and turn it into a memorial. The lot was soon shut down by the Buildings Department.
In August the Elmhurst History and Cemetery Preservation Society filed a request with Landmarks after the revelation about the parking lot’s use. Herman responded to the group’s president, Mariaelena Giampino, in October revealing that the commission’s research unit agreed the site was likely eligible to be landmarked.
The cemetery was formed in the early 19th century by the founders of what would become the St. Mark African Methodist and Episcopal Church. The church and its burial ground were sold in the 1930s and St. Mark moved a mile away to Jackson Heights. The church continues to serve as steward of the cemetery site and under state law can play a role in determining its ultimate fate. The Rev. Kimberly Detherage of St. Mark’s has called for the city to buy it.
Mamdani Administration Cool to City Purchase
The site is currently controlled by a limited liability corporation that bought the loan of the previous owner after they defaulted on their mortgage when plans to build a luxury co-op building stalled. Over the summer Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. called for the city to step in, and in September pushed the Mamdani administration to protect the site.
On Thursday, Matthew Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for the mayor, said the city has no current plans to purchase the burial ground. He declined to comment on the Landmarks letter. All of the commission’s 10 members are mayoral appointees.
In September, state Attorney General Letitia James also got involved, filing a motion in a pending foreclosure lawsuit demanding that, whatever happens to the burial ground, the bodies be treated respectfully under the state’s Unmarked Burial Site Protection Act.
“The New Yorkers laid to rest at this historic burial ground worked to build this city even while it denied them their freedom,” James said in a statement Wednesday. “Their final resting place deserves respect. I welcome any effort to offer these souls the permanent protection they are owed, including this first step toward landmark designation.”
In her letter, Herman cited that law in noting that the fate of the lot will likely be complicated.
Landmark status, she wrote, “may not be the only or most appropriate tool to achieve that community’s goals.” Landmarked burial sites are usually either on public land or are privately-owned cemeteries that are still in use. She said that moving the remains to another site “would not typically be considered appropriate.”
Herman noted that the Unmarked Burial Site law provides for the involvement of the state’s archaeologist in consultation with the church about “appropriate next steps.”
A spokesperson for the state archaeologist on Wednesday did not respond to a request for comment.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ad.title: Art World Advice Columnists Chen & Lampert Answered Questions as Old as Time
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ad.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ad.text:
The disquieting question of how to be human in the art world came in for special consideration during a talk with advice columnists Chen & Lampert during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.
Together, Howie Chen and Andrew Lampert talked about their individual and collective efforts as artists, curators, and incomparable visionaries whose recurring “Hard Truths” advice columns and accompanying “Hard Choices” interactive quizzes are highlights of every issue of Art of America. Since their debut in 2019, the two writers have mulled pressing questions—can senior citizens be sage social-media ambassadors for museums in need of street cred? should a jilted artist keep applying for grants? is our advice helpful?—while dishing out wisdom for the ages.
At their talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Chen & Lampert reminisced about fielding queries from the past as well as their trip to Las Vegas for a 2025 essay titled “Art and Ecstatic Ambience in Las Vegas’s Neon Vortex.” (A little taste of that, for old time’s sake: “Some writers go on Hajj to Marfa to feel the minimalist wind blow sand into their eyes, while others schlep Brooklinen tote bags as they chase biennials across small European cities. Being earnest art-world advice columnists, we prefer to explore more democratic forms of visual culture—the kind that ribaldly stages a two-hour revue called The Empire Strips Back: A Burlesque Parody.”)
As watchable in the video of their talk above, Chen & Lampert also addressed questions solicited from A.i.A. readers on the fly—among them: “Do mean people in the art world actually like art? If not, what is their motivation?”

https://taz.de/Estnisch-russische-Grenze.title: Estnisch-russische Grenze: Kein kleiner Grenzverkehr mehr in Narva
https://taz.de/Estnisch-russische-Grenze.author: Viktor Spitza
https://taz.de/Estnisch-russische-Grenze.text:
Estnisch-russische Grenze: Kein kleiner Grenzverkehr mehr in Narva
Nach dem versuchten Brandanschlag auf ein estnisches Rüstungsunternehmen will Tallinn die Grenze zu Russland schließen. In der Grenzstadt Narva sorgt das für Unruhe.
Narva könnten harte Zeiten bevorstehen. Die drittgrößte Stadt Estlands liegt direkt an der Grenze zu Russland, die durch den gleichnamigen Fluss verläuft. Über 90 Prozent der rund 52.000 Einwohner*innen gehören der russischen Minderheit des baltischen Staates an. Am Anfang der Woche wurde bekannt, dass Premierminister Kristen Michal Innenminister Igor Taro sowie die Staatskanzlei beauftragt hat, Schritte zu einer vollständigen Schließung der Grenze zwischen Estland und Russland vorzubereiten.
Anlass für diese Maßnahme, die schon am 1. Dezember in Kraft treten könnte, war ein versuchter Brandanschlag auf das estnische Rüstungsunternehmen Threod Systems. Wegen mutmaßlicher Beteiligung wurden acht in Lettland ansässige Personen festgenommen. Ihre Aktionen habe laut estnischem Inlandsgeheimdienst Kapo die russische Spionageabwehr (GRU) koordiniert.
Dass alle Grenzübergänge geschlossen werden könnten, treibt die Menschen in Narva schon seit geraumer Zeit um und sorgt für wachsende Unruhe in der Bevölkerung. Auch eine Rentnerin hat bereits davon erfahren. Sie steht auf dem zentralen Petersplatz, den Reisebusse ständig anfahren und wieder verlassen. An manchen Tagen bilden sich hier lange Warteschlangen.
Der Grenzübergang nur für Fußgänger*innen ist in unmittelbarer Nähe, die russische Stadt Iwangorod auf der anderen Seite des Flusses nur einen Steinwurf entfernt. „Ich bin 71 Jahre alt, meine Schwester lebt in Kingissepp im Leningrader Gebiet, sie ist 76. Wir sind beide nicht mehr die Jüngsten, und die Gesundheit macht uns manchmal zu schaffen. Man mag gar nicht an das Schlimmste denken: Wenn uns etwas zustößt – wer wird uns dann helfen? Der bloße Gedanke daran macht mir Angst“, sagt sie.
Krieg in der Ukraine
Mit dem Einmarsch im 24. Februar 2022 begann der groß angelegte russische Angriffskrieg auf die Ukraine. Bereits im März 2014 erfolgte die Annexion der Krim, kurz darauf entbrannte der Konflikt in den ostukrainischen Gebieten.
Humanitäre und wirtschaftliche Frage
Auch Narvas Bürgermeister Jaan Toots blickt mit Sorge auf die jüngsten Entwicklungen. „Wir müssen die Entscheidung der Regierung abwarten. Meiner Ansicht nach sollte, falls man die Grenzen Estlands tatsächlich schließen will, dies nicht nur einseitig geschehen. In diesem Fall müsste auch die Grenzkontrolle zu Lettland wieder eingeführt werden. Die versuchte Brandstiftung steht schließlich auch mit Bewohner*innen Lettlands in Verbindung“, sagte er am Dienstag.
Laut Toots sei die humanitäre Frage ungeklärt. Schließlich hätten viele Bewohner*innen von Narva und der ganzen Region Ida-Virumaa, zu der die Stadt gehört, Verwandte in Russland, die sie besuchen können müssten.
Zudem sehe er große Probleme auf die Wirtschaft zukommen, die schon jetzt in einer schwierigen Lage sei. Die Fakten geben ihm recht. Landesweit liegt die Arbeitslosenquote derzeit bei 5,4 Prozent, in der Region Ida-Virumaa hingegen bei 9,2 Prozent. Während das Durchschnittsgehalt in Estland sich auf 2.250 Euro brutto beläuft, beträgt es in Narva gerade einmal 1.500 Euro.
Kürzlich wurde der Abbau von 35 Stellen im Zentralkrankenhaus in Ida-Virumaa bekannt gegeben, darunter drei Ärzt*innen. In der vergangenen Woche kündigte der staatliche Konzern Eesti Energia den Abbau von rund 400 Arbeitsplätzen an. Bei der Mehrheit der Betroffenen handelt es sich um Menschen aus Narva.
Eine Grenzschließung wird zu weiteren Stellenstreichungen führen – etwa bei Busunternehmen. Täglich gibt es derzeit noch bis zu 50 Busverbindungen zwischen der Hauptstadt Tallinn und Narva. Laut Angaben einiger Hotels in Narva von Dienstag seien bis zu 20 Prozent ihrer Gäste Reisende gewesen, die es nicht mehr rechtzeitig über die Grenze geschafft hätten. Auch diejenigen, die ihre Wohnungen für die Nacht vermieten, dürften massive Einbußen erleiden. Wechselstubenketten sowohl in Narva als auch in Tallinn haben ihre Schließung angekündigt.
Güterzüge sollen weiter fahren dürfen
Demgegenüber wiegelt Innenminister Igor Taro ab. Die Schließung der Grenze zu Russland werde allenfalls eine geringe Anzahl von Menschen sowie einzelne Unternehmen betreffen. Der Grenzübergang für Güterzüge in Narva solle auf estnischer Seite vorerst geöffnet bleiben.
„Über diesen Weg werden strategische Rohstoffe eingeführt, die sowohl für Estland als auch für Europa von großer Bedeutung sind. Wir werden die Einfuhr für einen gewissen Zeitraum weiterhin gestatten, bis die Unternehmen Alternativen und andere Lösungen gefunden haben. Wir können jedoch keineswegs garantieren, dass Russland in dieser Hinsicht keine Schritte unternehmen wird“, sagte Taro.
Das kann niemand. Aus dem Kreml hieß es am Montag, Russland weise die gegen sich erhobenen Vorwürfe wegen Sabotageakten – darunter auch Anschuldigungen seitens Estlands – zurück und betrachte diese als grund- und haltlos. „Derartige Vorwürfe hören wir nicht nur aus Tallinn, sondern auch aus anderen europäischen Hauptstädten. All diese Äußerungen entbehren jeglicher Grundlage. Es gibt dafür weder Argumente noch Beweise – rein gar nichts. Sie sind völlig aus der Luft gegriffen“, sagte der Pressesprecher des russischen Präsidenten, Dmitri Peskow.
Am Freitag nun wird die Regierung über eine Grenzschließung entscheiden. Solange will die Stadtverwaltung von Narva noch warten, bevor sie ein offizielles Schreiben nach Tallinn schickt.
Ein Mann in den Fünfzigern wartet an diesem Dienstag auf dem Petersplatz auf den Grenzübertritt. Er kommt aus Helsinki und will seine Mutter in St. Petersburg besuchen. Finnland hat alle Grenzübergänge für Fußgänger, Radfahrer, Autos und Busse schrittweise bis Ende November 2023 geschlossen, und die Schließung wurde seither auf unbestimmte Zeit verlängert. „Solche Beschränkungen treffen vor allem die einfachen Menschen“, sagt er. „Und nicht etwa diejenigen, die tatsächlich eine Sicherheitsbedrohung darstellen.“
Aus dem Russischen von Barbara Oertel
