https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-phill.title: Rejecting Equality Is a Long-Standing American Tradition
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-phill.author: Robbie Nelson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-phill.text:
Rejecting Equality Is a Long-Standing American Tradition
The current version of explicitly anti-egalitarian politics adopted by today’s economic and political elites is only the latest in a long tradition of American reactionary thought that insists that all men and women are not, in fact, created equal.
Living in a country whose residents include both the world’s first trillionaire and 1.5 million homeless schoolchildren, the fact of American inequality is hard to miss. Such a reality produces countless justifications, explanations, and plans for ameliorating its worst impacts across the political spectrum. But at its sharpest edge, it also produces a coterie of intellectuals, pseudo-intellectuals, tycoons, activists, and posters who don’t merely attempt to explain or excuse inequality but rather celebrate its fruits and try to consolidate its bases.
Silicon Valley today plays host to the most prominent nest of techno-fascists, neoreactionaries, transhumanists, and “effective altruists” whose obscene wealth allows them to shape political discourse far beyond the strengths of their ideas or their personal charms, such as they are.
But as Kim Phillips-Fein demonstrates in her new book Country of Lords, the current version of explicitly anti-egalitarian politics adopted by today’s economic and political elites is merely the latest in a long tradition of American reactionary thought. Aimed squarely against the premise announced in the Declaration of Independence that “all men are created equal,” this intellectual and political lineage has been carried forward by the lawyers, business moguls, charlatans, and academics who form the primary figures of Phillips-Fein’s sweeping tour of American political history.
Country of Lords is a highly readable book, filled with a cast of colorful characters both well-known and more obscure. It sets forth a counter-history to the sunny, West Wing–style liberal narrative in which the inevitable march of American progress toward equal inclusion only faces obstacles thrown up by the dead weight of tradition or ignorance. Instead, building upon her previous work about the role of right-wing businessmen in fighting against the New Deal, Phillips-Fein shows the strenuous and continuous efforts of reactionary figures not merely to conserve some traditional order but to transform and reestablish new hierarchies in the face of technological, social, and political change.
Action and Reaction
The book is organized into six primary chapters, arranged chronologically and each anchored around a few historical figures and their connected sets of ideas. The New England statesman John Adams and the racist pro-slavery theorist George Fitzhugh might seem an odd pairing, but Phillips-Fein links their attempts to define the roles of their respective political and racial “aristocracies” in the early decades of American Republic. Likewise with the Yale professor William Graham Sumner and industrialist Andrew Carnegie enunciating their own versions of “survival of the fittest” in the context of Gilded Age industrial society.
Next are the “utilitarian racists,” anchored by Lothrop Stoddard and his infamous 1920 book, The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy, a deeply racist cri de coeur (beloved by The Great Gatsby character Tom Buchanan) that identified World War I and the Bolshevik revolution as the tipping points against European colonial power. The interwar period ushered in the age of Henry Ford and his “Gospel of Production,” a corporatist vision of American society in which the unequal unity of proprietors and their loyal workers could box out both the (Jewish-coded) union Reds and the (Jewish-coded) financiers.
The book’s fifth chapter, perhaps its most interesting and certainly its most expansive, takes a broader view of postwar liberalism’s discontents. Particularly potent are the various debates around the rise of intelligence quotient (IQ) tests, standardized college admissions exams like the SAT, and ideas about “equality of opportunity” in the midst of the legal changes called forth by the civil rights movements of the 1950s and ’60s. The author eventually hones in on the scientist-turned-racist-crank William Shockley and the Harvard psychologist Richard Herrnstein, two figures associated with the thesis that IQ is heritable and racially differentiated. Phillips-Fein pairs the race-and-IQ crowd with the libertarians and monetarists represented by the likes of Ayn Rand and Milton Friedman. What united these seemingly disparate figures was their belief that purportedly “neutral” mechanisms (standardized intelligence tests and free-market competition) could separate the “natural elite” from those meant to be ruled. The book ends with an investigation of the antidemocratic strains within Silicon Valley that provide a surprising intellectual continuity between the countercultural 1960s to the corporate consolidation of the 1980s and ’90s to the emergence of hard-right tech anti-humanists that dominate the scene today.
Each chapter could stand on its own, a mini-history of a particular moment and the multiple strands of anti-egalitarian politics that attended it. But, taken together, they paint a larger picture. By fleshing out both the continuities and similarities between inegalitarian ideas across time, some crucial patterns emerge. Idiosyncratic though they may be, these anti-egalitarian thinkers did not develop their ideas in a vacuum. Rather, their politics are deeply responsive to the emerging shape of struggle from below. In other words, reactionary thinkers are always reactive to historically particular assertions of political power from the lower orders.
Although each chapter focuses primarily on conservative ideologues, their antagonists make consistent appearances. In each successive historical moment, new rounds of egalitarian struggle imperiled the ruling order. In response, new reactionary ideologies emerged that sought to both enshrine and update the ideological map of inequality.
The story lurking beneath The Country of Lords is that of an episodic but relatively cohesive American egalitarian tradition. From radical Enlightenment thinkers and indebted Revolutionary War veterans to abolitionists, Knights of Labor to the Socialist Party of Eugene V. Debs, garment workers on the Lower East Side to the NAACP of W. E. B Du Bois, United Auto Workers organizers to civil rights activists and beyond, American history has churned out ceaseless waves of agitators and movements seeking to overturn the social, economic, and political order and establish a more equal future.
The task of the modern reactionary, then, has not been to simply assert the God-given superiority of certain aristocratic families, but rather to counter each successive challenge with an updated and reorganized hierarchy that fits the changing social, technological, and economic landscapes that they encounter. Henry Ford’s worldview was not atavistic but distinctly modern and technologically driven, in the spirit of his age. His model of American corporatism incorporated not only the revolutionary technologies of internal combustion and the assembly line, but also cutting-edge social-scientific research into managing his workers’ lives and bodies on and off the factory floor.
Richard Herrnstein likewise did not subscribe to George Wallace–style Southern segregationism, but rather employed advanced (though subsequently debunked) statistical methods to make his arguments about race and IQ, being careful not to deny the possibility of individual black success stories. In other words, the realities of social mobility, new institutions, and new social attitudes pressurized the shape of these anti-egalitarian ideas.
Almost all of these anti-egalitatarian figures relied heavily on the discursive power of science and technology in both their explanations of inequality and their visions of how that inequality could be leveraged for social good. As the primary modern schema for adjudicating differences between things and producing causal explanations for social phenomena, the natural and social sciences loom large in the reactionary imagination as both threats and resources.
It is telling that almost all of this book’s subjects were not, themselves, born into high privilege. They ranged from working-class immigrants who worked their way up through industry or academia (Carnegie, Herrnstein, Friedman) to the children of middling farmers (Ford, Adams, Sumner) to the children of moderately successful provincial professionals (Fitzhugh, Stoddard). Interestingly, two of the techno-racists (Shockley and Peter Thiel) are the children of prosperous but highly peripatetic mining engineers.
Having gained a vantage point on American society from both outside and inside the elite, these up-and-comers were often able to craft and mobilize ideological concepts that went beyond mere defense of status quo elite configurations. Because of their personal prominence in the American economic or intellectual scene, these individuals had deep investment in both upholding the legitimacy of the system as well as opening that system up to the fresh perspectives of those coming from outside the blue-blood northeastern elite. Potential for upward social mobility of one kind or another is a load-bearing feature of most modern reactionary ideologies, because it both serves to justify the merited existence of a ruling class while also leaving open the possibility of entry. The replenishment of the upper classes and the defanging of disruptive movements from below are the dual goals of these political movements.
Constructing Equality
Because of its particular focus on the history of anti-egalitarian ideas in the United States as well as its slim profile, Country of Lords does not spend much time building up a competing, left-wing account of and response to inequality. While the Left’s primary political task is countering actual inequality in the workplace, social relations, and the state, we also have to develop our own story about the nature of inequality in order to counter some of the key arguments of the reactionaries and their liberal fellow travelers.
There are both empirical observations and normative claims at the heart of this story. First, human beings are not “equal” or equivalent in terms of our physical capacities, desires, and talents. We inhabit different bodies and life experiences. But we assert that human beings do have equal dignity and worth and thus should be given, to the greatest extent possible, equal power to determine our own lives and to participate in decision-making that shapes our societies. The question at play in modern progressive politics is determining which institutions and historical processes can cultivate flourishing egalitarian societies in the context of human diversity and nonequivalency.
Historically speaking, unequal social classes are a pretty recent human social phenomenon, only emerging around twelve thousand years ago during the Neolithic revolution. During this era, the advent of agriculture, livestock domestication, sedentary urbanism, and the complex social division of labor fed into the generation of social surplus. In other words, these societies were able to produce and store more food than was necessary to meet their populations’ immediate needs.
New elites emerged and solidified their ability to command others’ labor, coordinate production and exchange, and make decisions about how to mobilize that social surplus. These new practices enabled the development of larger human populations, more advanced technology, and greater complexity in social, cultural, and economic life.
This rough historical sketch, viewed in a certain way, lends credence to anti-egalitarian arguments: human societies, since the birth of agriculture, have depended in fundamental ways on social hierarchy. In this telling, hierarchical divisions of labor were necessary to produce the technological advancements that have propelled humanity from living as small bands of hunter-gatherers to becoming geo-engineers and star-travelers.
However, the anti-egalitarians err in misidentifying the historically functional inequality of class society as an intrinsic inequality. Unequal power over the social surplus was provisionally necessary for the class system as it has emerged, but, empirically speaking, the actual people in those dominant positions over the course of history have not shared any intrinsic biological, moral, or technical superiority over those they have dominated.
The socialist movement has thus set for itself the most ambitious task imaginable: the construction of systems that sustain a complex divisions of labor necessary for a technologically advanced mass society — which is comprised of individuals who each have unique capacities and desires — while maintaining roughly equal access to social income and roughly equal decision-making power about the production and distribution of social surplus. An equal future cannot simply be wished or asserted: it needs to be built.
Despite Karl Marx’s famous injunction against “writing recipes for the cookshops of the future,” there has been a rash of recent English-language writing attempting to sketch the contours of a socialist future. While each example deserves its own complex treatment — and there are tensions between different visions — the ideas and institutions of democracy lie at the heart of each one.
The particular combination and format of representative and direct democratic decision-making is up for contestation, as is the precise role of markets in economic life. But democratic decision-making is the key mechanism for synthesizing the reality of individual difference with the need for collective deliberation and rough equality of political power. In a socialist future characterized by social complexity, division of labor, technological advancement, civil liberties, rough equality of social income, and rough equality of political capacity, democracy is the indispensable technology.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Iraq’s national museum announces reopening after major renovations
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Hadani Ditmars
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.
Several important artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The new Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.
The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the new government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are plans afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.
Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.
New focus on museums
According to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.
A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.
Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.
Al-Dakhili has also announced that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement says.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Panela do Jazz reúne Amaro Freitas, Spok e Lucas dos Prazeres em shows gratuitos no Recife
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Fátima Pereira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Largo do Poço da Panela, na Zona Norte do Recife, recebe nesta sexta-feira (20) e sábado (21) a programação principal da sétima edição do Festival Panela do Jazz. Com entrada gratuita, os dois dias de shows reúnem nomes como Amaro Freitas Trio, Spok, Lucas dos Prazeres, Neris Rodrigues e O Trombonando, além de artistas de outros estados e representantes das culturas populares pernambucanas.
As apresentações acontecem ao lado da Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Saúde e integram a homenagem aos 100 anos de nascimento do compositor, maestro e multi-instrumentista pernambucano Moacir Santos.
Com o tema “Quilombo Sonoro: Liberdade e Ancestralidade – As Mil Faces das ‘Coisas’ de Moacir Santos”, o festival propõe aproximar a música instrumental brasileira de manifestações afro-brasileiras, valorizando a ancestralidade e a produção musical coletiva.
Na sexta-feira (20), a agenda começa às 17h, com uma roda de capoeira do Centro de Capoeira São Salomão. Entre os destaques da noite estão Silva Barros & Grupo, às 21h10, e Lucas dos Prazeres, que apresenta o espetáculo “Nação do Amor” a partir das 22h30. A programação também conta com o Combo CPM, do Conservatório Pernambucano de Música, e apresentações da Mestra Maria Helena Sampaio com o Afoxé Oyá Alaxé. Antes dos shows, haverá uma mesa de conversa sobre o lançamento da reimpressão do livro de Moacir Santos, com participação de Andrea Ernest Dias e mediação de Débora Nascimento.
No sábado (21), o palco recebe atrações de Pernambuco e de outros estados. A programação começa às 16h, com uma roda de Capoeira Angola do grupo Afromandingas, seguida pelo Cristian Sperandir Trio, do Rio Grande do Sul. Também se apresentam Camila Rocha, de Belo Horizonte, e o Mestre Zezinho de Casa Amarela, com coco de sala e repente.
Entre os momentos aguardados da noite estão o show “Raízes encontra Ouro Negro”, de Spok, às 20h10, e o tributo a Moacir Santos conduzido por Neris Rodrigues & O Trombonando, com participações de Isaar e Arthur Philipe, às 22h. O encerramento fica por conta do Amaro Freitas Trio, que sobe ao palco às 23h50. A programação inclui ainda apresentações do Afoxé Ylê de Egbá, que celebra 40 anos, e da Nação do Maracatu Porto Rico, pelos seus 120 anos.
Além dos shows, o festival mantém uma programação paralela voltada a diferentes públicos. No sábado (21), o Polo Infantojuvenil reúne contação de histórias com Bell Puã, oficina de dedoches, teatro de mamulengo e espetáculos de Mari Bigio e Palhaço Gambiarra.
A Feira Olegarinha de Artes da Mulher também integra a programação, com atividades na Praça Ruy Antunes, no Poço da Panela, nos dias 20 e 21, a partir das 16h e das 14h, respectivamente. O encerramento acontece no domingo (22), no Parque de Apipucos, onde será realizada mais uma edição da feira.
No mesmo dia, o Parque recebe o Cine Panela, das 15h às 21h, com exibição de filmes sobre Moacir Santos, Mestre Batman e Letieres Leite. Entre as produções estão “O Som da Pele”, de Marcos Santos, e “As Travessias de Letieres Leite”, dirigido por Iris de Oliveira e Day Sena. A programação inclui ainda discotecagem e apresentação do Maracatu Sensorial, do Instituto Som da Pele.
A edição de 2026 também contou com atividades formativas realizadas entre os dias 6 e 13 de novembro, em escolas, equipamentos culturais e comunidades do Recife. Oficinas de música afro-brasileira, percussão, empreendedorismo feminino, reciclagem e sustentabilidade fizeram parte da agenda. Nos dias 14 e 15, o festival promoveu roteiros de afroturismo pelo Alto José do Pinho e pelo Morro da Conceição, aproximando o público de iniciativas e manifestações culturais desses territórios.
Idealizado pelo produtor cultural Antonio Pinhêiro, o Panela do Jazz busca ampliar o acesso à música instrumental e promover encontros entre artistas, mestres da cultura popular e diferentes gerações.
“A programação começa nas ações formativas, passa pelas comunidades, movimenta a economia criativa e chega ao palco como celebração coletiva. Queremos que o festival seja compreendido como um circuito cultural que estabelece relações entre música, território e sustentabilidade”, afirma o curador.
O Festival Panela do Jazz tem patrocínio da Neoenergia e do Instituto Neoenergia, por meio da Lei Federal de Incentivo à Cultura, e realização da PRO4, do Ministério da Cultura e do Governo Federal.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/us-w.title: U.S. Drug War in Mexico Fueled More Murders, Violence, and Drug Deaths
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/us-w.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/us-w.text:
President Donald Trump took aim at Mexico last week, in the wake of the rout of his party in the midterm elections. The “INVASION of our Country is taking place again. Huge CARAVANS are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico,” he announced on Truth Social. He lobbed threats of tariffs at Mexico “if they don’t stop them.”
Trump’s renewed anti-immigrant fearmongering — a highlight of the campaign that won him a return to the White House — came as joint U.S. and Mexican military counter-cartel efforts are growing, new details about expanded covert CIA anti-drug operations in Mexico have come to light, and fears of worsening relations and even unilateral U.S. attacks south of the border are on the rise in Mexico.
The Trump administration has, over the last two years, expanded counter-drug efforts across the Americas through a plethora of initiatives from extrajudicial killings of suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean to ground operations by elite troops in Ecuador to enhanced efforts alongside Mexican forces.
“Right now, we have historic cooperation, military-to-military,” self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth said last year. This year, his department established the Joint Interagency Task Force-Counter Cartel to “identify, disrupt, and dismantle cartel operations posing a threat to the United States along the U.S.-Mexico border.” At the same time, the CIA reportedly used a cartel-compromised prosecutor to expand its operations in Mexico after President Claudia Sheinbaum blocked such efforts. (The covert operations only came to light when CIA operatives died during a mission.)
The Trump administration’s latest initiatives are just the latest in a decadeslong string of U.S. security assistance efforts with Mexico that have failed spectacularly, according to a new report by the World Peace Foundation at Tufts University’s Fletcher School released in collaboration with the Costs of War project at Brown University. The analysis, shared exclusively with The Intercept, examines close to 15 years of U.S. and Mexican efforts to combat the drug trade. It offers a stark rebuke of past U.S. efforts, and suggests the Trump administration’s current paradigm for counter-drug policy in Mexico — and counter-cartel policy across the Americas more broadly — is destined to fail.
“U.S. military aid to Mexico in the ‘war on drugs’ echoes the same failures of the ‘war on terror,’” said Stephanie Savell, director of the Costs of War project. “U.S. security assistance in both cases has fueled forever wars marked by protracted militarization, spiraling violence, and widespread civilian harm. These conflicts negatively impact human rights, the economy, and civil institutions.”
Despite billions of dollars in U.S. aid over decades, the human, financial, and political costs of Mexico’s drug war have skyrocketed, according to the new report. The U.S. poured $3.3 billion into Mexico’s interdiction and counter-drug operations through the Mérida Initiative from 2008 to 2021. The researchers found that while Plan Mérida was originally slated to be a shared effort to strengthen government institutions, target crime networks, and reduce cross-border drug flows, both the U.S. and Mexico consistently failed to meet benchmarks, as political will ebbed and flowed and implantation of projects frequently faltered. As a result, in Mexico, drug violence spiked, homicide rates tripled, and government authority crumbled. North of the border, drug demand continued apace and overdose deaths surged, while little was done in the U.S. to stem the flow of firearms and cash that fuels the drug trade.
The authors of the report, Aileen Teague, an assistant professor of international affairs at Texas A&M, and Peyton McGuire, an adjunct professor of political science at Georgia Gwinnett College, detailed the immense human toll of violence in Mexico: more than 460,000 homicides since 2006.
“Despite expanded military deployments under Mérida and its successors, Mexico’s homicide rates reached historic highs between 2016 and 2019,” they wrote, adding: “Civilians have borne the overwhelming share of this violence: massacres, kidnappings, and targeted killings have become widespread.” More than 130,000 people have also been reported missing. Femicides, the term for gender-motivated killings, have also spiked during the drug war. Reported femicides increased from 427 in 2015 to 1,004 in 2021 — a 135 percent increase. Last year, in Sinaloa state alone, 105 women were killed. It was the highest toll in 14 years; 73 of the killings were investigated as femicides.
The massive death toll is directly attributable to the U.S. “Many of these homicides are inflicted by firearms trafficked from the United States, which remain a principal source of weapons used by Mexican criminal organizations,” according to Teague and McGuire. No less than Secretary of State Marco Rubio admitted the same. “Many of the weapons that are in the hands of these cartels are weapons that have been purchased from a source in the United States,” Rubio admitted in 2025. “These weapons have been trafficked.” An Intercept investigation also found that cartels have even been able to procure ammunition produced for the U.S. military.
Despite clear evidence of the carnage and its cause, most violence in Mexico goes unreported and unpunished. Research shows that in nearly 95 percent of cases, violent crimes go unsolved, exposing massive deficiencies in the Mexican government’s ability to deter, investigate, and prosecute organized crime. The carnage, much of it inflicted by cartels, is inextricably bound to declining state authority. Recent reporting by the Wall Street Journal highlighted the control of cartels across Mexico. An estimated one-third of the country’s territory is controlled by criminal groups — such as the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel — according to U.S. government estimates. “This erosion in territorial governance is both a cause and consequence of violence,” write Teague and McGuire.
U.S. and Mexican efforts to target drug kingpins have fractured criminal groups and caused a proliferation of localized conflicts, overwhelming the abilities of local governments and law enforcement to contain them. “In turn, weakened institutions proved unable to contain or deter violence, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which violence degrades state capacity, and diminished state capacity enables further violence,” according to the report.
As local police forces have faltered, military involvement in law enforcement has fueled rampant state violence. Widespread abuses by Mexican security forces, including torture, extrajudicial killings, and enforced disappearances, have been exhaustedly documented by NGOs like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch.
Beyond its direct impacts on victims and survivors and the authority of the Mexican state, violence has also devastated Mexico’s economy. The economic burden of the bloodshed, in just 2021 alone, was almost $200 billion, roughly 15 percent of Mexico’s gross domestic product. That total has since increased to as much as $250 billion or nearly 18 percent of GDP.
In the wake of the failures of the Plan Mérida and similar militarized U.S.-Mexican counter-drug efforts, the Trump administration has pushed Mexico to destroy the cartels using tariffs, immigration enforcement, and threats of unilateral military operations — such as drone strikes — as leverage on Sheinbaum. Her government has made repeated concessions such as deepened intelligence sharing, expediting the transfer of high-profile imprisoned traffickers to U.S. custody, and using U.S. intelligence to kill Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “El Mencho,” leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. This latter operation threw into broad relief the continued perils for Mexico in placating the U.S., as violence then erupted across 10 states, including arson attacks, assaults on security forces, and road blockades.
The violence and instability stoked by the Trump administration in Mexico has been mirrored across the Americas, amid the aggressive diplomatic and military engagement dubbed the Donroe Doctrine, a bastardization of the 1823 Monroe Doctrine. Earlier this year, a report by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project found that “U.S. pressure on organized crime is accelerating the spread of militarized security approaches in the region.” This volatility was set to “fuel an increase in violence throughout the rest of Trump’s term, potentially undermining any short-term improvements achieved through hardline approaches.”
The Donroe Doctrine has been used to justify strikes on civilian boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean; an attack on Venezuela and the abduction of its president; the CIA operations in Mexico; expanded partnerships with Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras, and Panama; joint counter-cartel operations in Ecuador dubbed “Operation Total Extermination”; and increased military and intelligence operations elsewhere in Latin America. It may be utilized to justify military operations in Mexico, too.
Even though Sheinbaum noted the so-called caravan of Central American immigrants was about 2,000 miles from the U.S. border and not moving northward, Trump continued lobbing threats this week. “They will not be allowed in,” Trump said on Monday. “They said that they were going to stop them, and if they don’t stop them, we’re going to put heavy tariffs on Mexico.”
This fearmongering follows the recent promotion of Trump’s xenophobic adviser Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. The chief architect of the Donroe Doctrine, who oversaw the closure of the U.S. southern border and Trump’s mass deportation campaign, Miller has been an advocate of extreme hard-line anti-Mexican policies and has seemed to advocate for even greater militarization of U.S. policy in the Americas. “Cartels that operate in this hemisphere are the ISIS and al-Qaida of this hemisphere and must be treated just as ruthlessly,” Miller said earlier this year, adding that “hard power” and lethal force — not criminal justice — must be employed.
The new report by the World Peace Foundation demonstrates that decades of militarized security cooperation has repeatedly failed. The lessons of the Mérida Initiative, according to the report, indicate that any new policy must focus on the “structural drivers of the drug economy — demand, arms, finance, and institutional weakness — on both sides of the border.”
After decades of futility and bloodshed, Teague and McGuire say that U.S. security assistance to its partner to the south needs a complete reset. “Moving forward,” they wrote, “a more effective U.S.-Mexico (and by extension, U.S.-Latin America) security framework will require a fundamental recalibration away from enforcement-dominant, militarized approaches toward a genuinely binational strategy that addresses the full political economy of the drug trade.”
Neither the White House nor Hegseth’s office responded to repeated requests for comment.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://gothamist.com/news/incoming-ny-r.title: Incoming NY Rep. Constantino isn’t looking to make friends. What are Republicans to do?
https://gothamist.com/news/incoming-ny-r.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/incoming-ny-r.text:
This column originally appeared in The Politics Brief, our weekly newsletter on the people, power and policies that shape New Yorkers' lives.
Sign up to get the full version where you can ask questions, share news tips and weigh in on the conversation. Hits inboxes on Wednesdays.
Anthony Constantino has an — ahem — unusual approach to politics.
The Republican businessman who owns Sticker Mule, an online printing company, will represent New York’s 21st Congressional District next year, after eking out a win to succeed Rep. Elise Stefanik in the state’s North Country. He didn’t get there by playing it safe.
You might’ve seen his rap video baselessly accusing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani of associating with terrorists, or his full album honoring President Donald Trump. Perhaps you saw a clip of his election night victory speech, where he cursed at “evil” reporters and called for Diddy’s release. Or maybe you keep up with his very active X account, where he’s settling scores with GOP leaders who failed to back him in a contentious primary and trying to convince Nvidia to reinstate its embattled ex-CEO.
Now, Constantino is trying to put his mark on the state Republican Party before officially joining New York’s congressional delegation in January. It’s left Republican leaders grappling with the same question: What do we do with this guy?
Liz Joy, the Republican Party’s regional chair for New York’s North Country, has clashed with Constantino for more than a year. The feud has spilled out into the open since the election, with Constantino calling her a “stone cold loser and quite evil” and Joy saying Constantino is "mentally unfit for office."
Joy said Republican leaders have already been discussing potential opponents for Constantino in a 2028 Republican primary.
”The conversations about a primary were already taking place before the election,” said Joy.
Constantino didn’t have the backing of the state Republican Party and most GOP leaders in the 21st District during his bruising primary battle with state Assemblymember Robert Smullen in June. But he did have the support of a far more influential Republican in his red-leaning district: Trump, whose endorsement helped propel Constantino to a primary victory.
Constantino was able to survive the blue wave that overtook much of the country — but just barely. The latest count had Constantino up by 1.6 percentage points over Democrat Blake Gendebien. Stefanik won the same district by 24 points two years ago.
“I think that the election results in NY-21 clearly show that the Republican Party has not embraced Anthony Constantino's style of erratic and bombastic behavior and language,” Joy said.
On X, Constantino said he “banned [Joy] from my race” and won. “All Party Bosses who elevated her should be ashamed of themselves,” he wrote.
Other Republicans say Constantino’s win in the midst of a blue wave is reason enough to give him a seat at the table as the party tries to rebuild.
Former Rep. Marc Molinaro, a Republican who previously ran for governor and won a seat in the state Assembly this year, said voters “desperately want authenticity.”
“[Constantino] does speak to a segment of voters — by the way, not all Republicans — who want people to take on the elites, who want candidates who speak and talk and feel the way they do,” Molinaro said. "And is that the orthodox, traditional candidate for office? No. But there are lessons to be learned there.”
Constantino’s camp didn’t respond to requests for comment. But the congressmember-elect has been outspoken on social media about Republican leaders — including state GOP Chair Ed Cox, who’s led the state party since 2023 and, before that, from 2009 to 2019.
After Constantino declared victory on election night, he took to X at 3:15 a.m. to call Cox “dumb as rocks.”
“I am with the people and insist we rebuild the Party,” Constantino posted. “Fire Ed Cox!”
Cox hasn’t addressed Constantino’s criticism directly, at least in public. But he issued a statement following Election Day calling on the party to “regroup,” saying that now is “not the time for accusations or a circular firing squad.”
The Republican chair’s term runs through September. He’s given no indication he intends to step down before then.
Last week, the party held a virtual meeting with county chairs across the state to shift the focus to the 2027 elections — when Republicans are bracing for a possible ballot measure that, if approved, could clear the way for Democrats in Albany to redraw the state’s congressional map.
On Wednesday, Constantino again took to X to call out “haters” who have underestimated him and are now “doubting if I’ll perform in Congress for my district and get things done.”
“What will it take for my haters to get tired of being wrong and looking stupid?”
We want to hear from you
House Democrats have officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to become speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. What issues should he focus on first when he takes the speaker’s gavel in January?
We'll share responses in next week's newsletter. (Sign up!)
This week in New York politics
- New York City will offer career training and medallion buybacks for horse carriage drivers as part of Mayor Mamdani's plan to wind down the carriage horse industry.
- New York City buildings inspectors have halted construction completely or in part for at least five projects tied to a pair of engineers in the wake of a fatal Brooklyn building collapse, a Gothamist analysis shows.
- Mayor Mamdani declined to endorse Brooklyn native U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as the next Senate majority leader.
- The City Council passed a bill banning surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data.
- Gov. Kathy Hochul called on U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to resign or be fired after a communications failure grounded all flights across the country last Friday.
- A bill in the City Council would force companies like Amazon to hire its delivery workers directly, pitting them against the Teamsters union, which supports the bill.
- Mayor Mamdani selected Eric Thor, who recently served as co-chair of New York City’s chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, to lead the Office of Nightlife.

https://www.propublica.org/article/irs-s.title: The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro
https://www.propublica.org/article/irs-s.author: Avi Asher-Schapiro, Andy Kroll, Alex Mierjeski
https://www.propublica.org/article/irs-s.text:
Top Trump administration officials intervened to help a longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley secure a half-million-dollar payout from the IRS. A company connected to Trump’s media business also got a half-million.
The deal grew out of a little-noticed federal class-action lawsuit filed in 2025 by five individuals and companies. The group got $2.5 million after accusing the IRS of failing to protect their tax information.
The law permits a $1,000 payment to victims for each instance of an unauthorized inspection or disclosure of tax data. In this case, however, the government’s monetary settlement is 250 times higher than what the law calls for given the allegations. Victims can receive more money if they show actual damages, but multiple officials say such cases almost never result in payments approaching this size. These generous settlements have raised concerns because IRS Office of Chief Counsel attorneys were not consulted about the settlement terms, as is standard practice, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.
What’s more, those payouts didn’t resolve the lawsuit. After the settlement was made, two more people came forward seeking to continue the litigation — and both are connected to Trump businesses. One is a retired accountant who worked at the same Trump property as the golf pro. The second appears to be a former lifeguard at a different Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.
Gil Rothenberg, a law professor at American University who ran the appellate section at the Justice Department tax division for 15 years before leaving in 2019, said the deal “is not passing the smell test.”
“It’s not just the amount that I find odd and unusual,” he told ProPublica. “It’s the fact that this settlement amount occurred before any final decision by the district court, and basically the DOJ is giving up any right to appeal.”
The case in question is Safe Harbor International LLC v. Booz Allen Hamilton, Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Department of the Treasury, brought in Maryland federal court. Plaintiffs claim that the IRS and the government contractor Booz Allen failed to implement proper safeguards and were negligent in allowing Booz Allen employee Charles Littlejohn to steal tax records and give them to news organizations, including ProPublica.
President Donald Trump sued over similar claims earlier this year, seeking $10 billion in damages. In response, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization fund” to resolve the case. That settlement was structured to grant the president’s inner circle the authority to green-light payouts of government money to whomever they wanted. The public erupted in outrage. Democratic and even a small number of Republican lawmakers objected to the proposed fund, and the department dropped the idea as Blanche sought Senate confirmation for his position.
Critics fear that the DOJ’s unusual payment in the Safe Harbor case could be a backdoor way to revive something similar to the controversial slush fund. In all, plaintiffs claim the size of the class is “in the tens or hundreds of thousands.” If a significant number of those plaintiffs secured the same payment, the total liability for the federal government could reach into the billions of dollars. A judge has yet to rule on whether to allow the case to proceed.
That group could include other Trump allies and friends. It even “opens the door to Trump himself benefiting from this settlement,” said John Koskinen, who served as IRS commissioner from 2013 to 2017.
Spokespeople for the Justice Department and IRS said they would not comment on a pending case. A White House spokesperson said that the Justice Department is “promoting efficient resolution of cases to avoid extraordinary liability.”
Between 2018 and 2020, Littlejohn, the Booz Allen contractor, leaked confidential IRS data to ProPublica and The New York Times, he has said. The data included years of Trump’s taxes and information on thousands of the wealthiest people in the country.
Do You Have a Justice Department Tip for ProPublica?
If you know about this case and the government’s handling of it, please contact our reporting team. I’m grateful for any documents that sources can share. Protecting sources is something I take very seriously.
Avi Asher-Schapiro
If you have tips about Big Tech and the Trump administration, please get in touch.
ProPublica published stories on the tax-avoidance strategies of the ultrawealthy. The New York Times reported in 2020 on how Trump declared large annual losses to avoid paying taxes. Together, the two news organizations reported that Trump was fighting with the IRS over a long-running audit that could have cost him $100 million.
Littlejohn pleaded guilty in October 2023 to unauthorized disclosure of tax information. A judge sentenced him to five years in prison.
The IRS sent letters to more than 400,000 individuals and businesses to alert them that their taxpayer information had been “inappropriately disclosed” by Littlejohn. As ProPublica has previously stated, we obtained the tax return information of the top 0.001% of individuals by income, a figure in the thousands. Limited information about other entities appears in the records only to the extent that it is related to the group of top earners.
A number of taxpayers who received the notice filed civil lawsuits demanding compensation from the IRS and Booz Allen.
The Safe Harbor class-action initially brought together five such plaintiffs who, at first glance, had nothing in common apart from having received an IRS notice about the leak.
Safe Harbor International is an obscure LLC incorporated in Delaware. It has no website or public presence and was most recently registered to a residential home in Washington, D.C. When ProPublica knocked on the door, the person living there said they’d never heard of the company.
Safe Harbor’s investors include Donald Wilson, who leads a Chicago-based financial trading firm. Last March, the Securities and Exchange Commission dropped a case brought during the Biden administration against a crypto company that Wilson controlled. A few months later, Wilson’s firm said it had invested $100 million in the president’s publicly traded media company, Trump Media and Technology Group, the owner of Truth Social.
A spokesperson for Wilson said he is a passive shareholder in Safe Harbor and “was unaware of this lawsuit until last week and has had no involvement in the litigation or any settlement discussions.” The spokesperson added that there was no connection between Wilson’s Trump Media investment and the SEC’s dismissal. “There was no quid pro quo, and the investment was not made in exchange for any regulatory action,” the spokesperson said.
The other four plaintiffs who ultimately joined Safe Harbor’s suit were Texas-based Alarm Concepts, a Connecticut company called Belpointe Sleepovation Investment, an individual in Texas named Cedrick Williams, and Shelby Lowman, the golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley.
It’s unclear if Trump knows Lowman personally. After Trump bought his Hudson Valley golf club in 2009, the Poughkeepsie Journal reported that he visited nearly every month to oversee renovations. Lowman was already working there as a golf pro and has remained at the club for the past 17 years, according to his LinkedIn profile.
In addition to his work as a golf pro, Lowman paints pastoral scenes of Trump’s golf properties. Trump has autographed copies of Lowman’s paintings to be given out as prizes for golf competitions at the club. The golf club has also posted a photo of Lowman posing with Eric Trump, who runs the Trump Organization.
A spokesperson for the Trump Organization said it “had no involvement in or connection to this lawsuit. To the extent any current or former employees are involved, it is entirely in their personal capacity as individual taxpayers.”
At first, the Justice Department sought to dismiss the Safe Harbor case. A DOJ trial attorney argued, among other things, that the U.S. government was not the proper target for a lawsuit about the conduct of a government contractor. The judge rejected the motion and cleared the way for discovery and potentially a trial.
The plaintiffs in Safe Harbor alleged two unauthorized disclosures of their tax information, which would entitle them to $2,000 each under the statute. To get more, they would have to prove actual damages. But before the case reached the fact-finding stage, the DOJ stopped fighting the case and in August made a unilateral proposal to the five named plaintiffs, labeled an offer of judgment, to resolve the matter by paying them $500,000 each, court records show.
When IRS employees learned about the DOJ’s $2.5 million offer, they pointed out that it was dramatically higher than what the law called for and was not supported by any evidence, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.
What made the government’s offer even more unusual was who made it. The career DOJ trial attorney working the case did not sign the proposed payout, as is typical.
Instead, two Trump political appointees delivered the offer: Brett Shumate, the head of the DOJ’s civil division, and Joshua Wu, the deputy assistant attorney general for the department’s tax litigation branch. (Shumate left the DOJ in early November. He did not respond to requests for comment.)
In the past, the IRS has fought such claims. In 2022, billionaire investor Ken Griffin brought a similar suit against the agency, dropping it a year and a half later after he received an apology from the IRS and a pledge to improve the agency’s data security. Griffin received no money as part of the settlement.
Lowman, Williams and Alarm Concepts did not respond to requests for comment. Reached by phone, Linda Nussbaum, a lawyer for Belpointe, told ProPublica that it was “news to me” that the other plaintiffs in the lawsuit had “ties to the Trump administration.” She declined to comment further on the case.

https://hellgatenyc.com/reuters-guild-st.title: Hundreds of Reuters Journalists Are Ready to Strike
https://hellgatenyc.com/reuters-guild-st.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/reuters-guild-st.text:
Reuters journalists spent Monday voting on whether or not to authorize a strike, after more than a year of bargaining and 11 months working under an expired contract. The result: an overwhelming yes. 
According to NewsGuild of New York, around 96 percent of the almost 300-person Reuters Guild unit participated, and of those voters, 94 percent voted in favor of a potential strike. 
"Our members have given us the authority to call a strike, which is not something we would do lightly," Andy Sullivan, a Reuters reporter based out of the publication's Washington, D.C. bureau, told Hell Gate. "That would involve significant financial hardship for a lot of our members—and also, we're passionate about our work. We would rather not not work, you know. But at the same time, we can't. We need to get paid more than they are offering. It's that simple."
Thomson Reuters did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.title: »The Only Living Pickpocket In New York« im Kino | Ein nostalgisches Gedicht über New York
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.author: Gabriele Summen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.text:
- Kultur
- »The Only Living Pickpocket In New York« im Kino
Ein nostalgisches Gedicht über New York
In »The Only Living Pickpocket In New York« kämpft ein alternder Taschendieb im modernen New York ums Überleben
Wünschen Sie sich auch manchmal, die Zeit wäre stehengeblieben? Sehnen Sie sich auch hin und wieder nach einer Zeit ohne Smartphone, ohne Kryptowährung, ohne Internet zurück? Eine Ära, in der sogar Hehlern und Taschendieben Ehre noch etwas bedeutete? (Zumindest in den Filmen aus dieser Zeit.) Und lieben Sie überdies New York? Also das alte New York, noch lange vor Donald Trump, ICE, der Gentrifizierung – als dort noch normale Menschen leben konnten? Dann sollten Sie sich unbedingt Noah Segans »The Only Living Pickpocket In New York« anschauen, einen Film, der wie aus der Zeit gefallen wirkt, einen Film wie ein nostalgisches Gedicht über New York – obwohl er in unserer Gegenwart spielt.
Das Thriller-Drama beginnt folgerichtig mit dem Song »New York, I Love You But You’re Bringing Me Down« von LCD Soundsystem über den Niedergang des Big Apple: Ein schnöseliger Wall-Street-Banker macht sich bereit für seinen Arbeitstag, nimmt in Ermangelung eines Taxis ausnahmsweise die U-Bahn – und bemerkt erst später im Nobelrestaurant, dass er beklaut wurde. Und zwar von Harry, einem Taschendieb in seinen 60ern, einem Meister seines Fachs – einem Mann, der vieles in seinem Leben falsch gemacht hat, sich aber jetzt rührend um seine schwerkranke Frau Rosie kümmert.
John Turturro spielt diesen Antihelden zurückgenommen und verleiht dem New Yorker alten Schlags so viel Charme und Würde, dass man von seiner Performance nicht genug bekommen kann und nach knapp 90 Minuten mit tiefem Bedauern von ihm Abschied nimmt.
Selbst wenn man ihn dabei ertappt, wie er einem Kind einen Schokoriegel stibitzt, oder erfährt, was für ein miserabler Vater er früher war, kann man nicht anders, als leise Zärtlichkeit für ihn zu empfinden. Und wenn er seine vollständig gelähmte Rosie die Treppen hochträgt, einseitige Gespräche mit ihr führt oder gar für sie tanzt, sprengt das sowieso unser melancholisches Herz.
Das digitale Zeitalter hat auch vor Harrys Profession nicht haltgemacht: Die Menschen haben immer weniger Bargeld bei sich und kaum jemand trägt noch Armbanduhren – oder Fälschungen, wie der von Harry erleichterte Investmentbanker.
Doch eines Abends scheint das Glück auf Harrys Seite zu sein: Er beklaut Dylan (Will Price), der eine gut gefüllte Brieftasche hat und eine sündhaft teure Uhr trägt. Mit der Waffe und dem USB-Stick in der aus Dylans Muscle-Car gestohlenen Tasche kann Harry, der nicht einmal ein Mobiltelefon besitzt, allerdings wenig anfangen. Die Pistole entsorgt er, und sein Stammhehler Ben, ebenfalls unvergesslich verkörpert von einer Hollywood-Legende im Pensionsalter, Steve Buscemi, steckt den Stick arglos in seinen steinalten PC. Der kann ihn jedoch nicht lesen. »So kriegen sie dich«, konstatiert er trocken, in dem von leisem Humor durchzogenen Film.
Wer sie allerdings erst einmal so kriegt, ist Dylan, der verwöhnte Sprössling eines Mafia-Clans, dessen Stick ein Signal sendet. Er kann so Bens PC orten und hat nun eine Spur, wie er seinen Stick zurückbekommt, auf dem sich eine enorme Summe an Kryptowährung befindet.
Spätestens als Dylan und seine degenerierten Mafiafreunde Harry in dessen Wohnung auflauern und ihm damit drohen, der bettlägerigen Rosie etwas anzutun, wenn er nicht innerhalb weniger Stunden den Stick wieder besorgt, weiß Harry, dass er die letzte Tour seines Lebens durch New York antreten wird. Das digitale Zeitalter hat das analoge vollends abgelöst: So etwas wie Ganovenehre kann man von diesen Typen nicht erwarten.
Nun setzt der kluge und besonnene Kopf alles daran, wenigstens für seine Rosie vorzusorgen, wenn er nicht mehr da ist – und seinen letzten Coup zu landen. Dabei hilft ihm unter anderem der kurz vor der Pensionierung stehende Detective Warren, der von einem bestens aufgelegten Giancarlo Esposito gespielt wird. Gegen Ende begegnet Harry der Mafia-Matriarchin, verkörpert von Jamie Lee Curtis, einem weiteren Star des US-amerikanischen Kinos derselben Generation. Ihr Auftritt verleiht dem Abschied von den alten Zeiten noch mehr Gewicht.
Begleitet von einem Jazz-Score, der uns in die 70er zurückversetzt, führt Harrys Weg von der Bronx durch Chinatown, sogar bis nach Queens, einem von der Gentrifizierung infizierten Viertel, das er bislang gemieden hat.
Mit der gleichen inneren Ruhe, mit der Harry der sich wandelnden Welt und deren Widrigkeiten begegnet, fängt Kameramann Sam Levy (»Frances Ha«) die Atmosphäre New Yorks ein, abseits von Touristenpfaden. Er folgt ihm, beobachtet ihn, wie er einer – von Turturros Cousine gespielten – Bettlerin Schmiergeld zusteckt oder in einer herzzerreißenden Szene seine Tochter Kelly aufsucht, die er Jahre nicht gesehen hat.
Diese vielschichtige Geschichte um einen Taschendieb, Solidarität unter »Verlierer*innen« im grausamen Spiel des Kapitalismus, das Altern und den Wandel der Welt fühlt sich bereits beim ersten Schauen wie ein Klassiker an. »Die schlechten alten Zeiten«, wie Harry einmal sagt, sind endgültig vorbei. Mal Hand aufs Herz: Wer von uns Älteren sehnt sich nicht manchmal danach zurück?
»The Only Living Pickpocket In New York«: USA 2026. Regie und Buch: Noah Segan. Mit: John Turturro, Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, Will Price, Tatiana Maslany, Victoria Moroles, Jamie Lee Curtis. 89 Min. Kinostart: 19. November.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: How Conservatives Lost Their Minds Over the “Indian Question”
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Arvin Alaigh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
How Conservatives Lost Their Minds Over the “Indian Question”
Indian Americans seemed to be trending towards the GOP. Then came a ton of racism.
Chris Rufo wears many hats—infamous culture warrior, fellow at the right-wing Manhattan Institute think tank, nakedly cynical enemy of diversity initiatives and Critical Race Theory, serial fabulist. And, since this is 2026, Rufo also has his own podcast, Rufo and Lomez, which he cohosts with Jonathan Keeperman on Blaze TV. This past September, an episode of Rufo and Lomez caused a wave of controversy by its title: “The Indian Question.”
The phrase is a winking provocation, a deliberate throwback to previous generations’ racialized “questions” (the “Jewish question” or the “Catholic question”). But there was nothing funny about Rufo’s message: that Indian Americans’ alleged resistance to assimilation, coupled with their collective capture of elite institutions, such as universities, threatens the cultural heritage of the United States. “Even if there might be trade-offs for keeping some amount of immigrants out who are high-skilled and might be a benefit to the economy, I like having a high-trust society,” Keeperman remarks during the podcast. “I like living somewhere where there is cultural cohesion, where I have this unspoken affinity with my neighbors.”
Of course, this is a childish view of cultural kinship and cohesion—one that fuses trust with skin color, as if all white Americans shared the same values and trusted one another the same. It’s difficult to take figures like Keeperman and Rufo seriously. The former is an erstwhile anonymous Twitter troll, and a friend to open white nationalists such as Steve Sailer. The latter is far more prominent, best known for spreading the racist lie in 2024 that immigrant Haitians in Ohio were eating their neighbors’ cats. But Rufo is nothing if not an opportunist, a shapeshifter who senses where the political winds might be blowing and moves accordingly. John Ganz astutely describes him as “a political entrepreneur… identifying conflicts developing on the right and translating cultural controversies into politically usable concepts and then into institutional campaigns.”
Rufo’s engagement with the “Indian Question” is revealing—if not for its substance, which is just faux-intellectual babble that aims to inflame, then as a sign of the present conservative approach to immigration.
By the end of the 20th century, the debate largely hinged on the axis of good “legal” and bad “illegal” immigration. The latter, it was thought, should be policed; the former wasn’t only tolerated but exalted as a monument of the American promise, a shibboleth held by Democrats and most Republicans alike. That consensus began to crack over the years of the Obama presidency, which saw Republicans repeatedly detonate efforts to substantively reform immigration laws (all while Obama presided over a historic deportation operation).
The last decade of American politics has shattered these shibboleths, thanks to a reinvigorated nativist conservative base powered by the rise of Donald Trump. These days, conservative discourse on immigration is littered with chilling, fantastical concepts such as “remigration” (the forced repatriation of immigrants and their descendants back to their home countries), and “Heritage Americans” (a category that defines “real” Americans on openly racial lines).
Figures like Rufo have long sought to harness this raucous, eliminationist spirit, and inject it into the heart of contemporary Republican Party politics. They’ve largely succeeded, and today, the status quo on immigration has been upended: Over the last year and a half, undocumented immigrants have been subjected to a fascist, murderous blitz; now “legal” immigrants have also come into the crosshairs of conservative politicians.
Two years ago, the Republican Party appeared to be on the brink of a breakthrough with Indian American voters, a historically solid Democratic bloc. Twenty-two percent of Indian American voters supported Trump’s 2020 campaign; that number shot up to 30 percent in his 2024 campaign. If Republicans could have siphoned more Indian American voters this cycle, that could have potentially affected margins of swing seats in states such as Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas. Yet, perhaps owing to the recent surge in conservative anti-Indian rhetoric, Republican gains with Indian American voters have evaporated.
Even as this new consensus was decisively rebuked in the midterms, though, it remains the dominating paradigm of American immigration—and in both interesting and pressing ways, it has touched the politics of the Indian American diaspora as well.
The present anti–Indian American phenomenon began as an outgrowth of an intra-conservative debate about the H-1B visa system, which permits tens of thousands of foreign, high-skilled workers to immigrate to the United States and work for American companies. Indian immigrants account for nearly three-quarters of H-1B visa holders, and have thus become emblematic of both the H-1B system and its alleged “abuse.” Right-wing opponents generally see the H-1B as a mechanism for job-stealing foreigners to enter America through the back door.
Some of the more enterprising firebreathers, such as Steve Bannon, talk about the program as enabling “corporate greed,” shrouding their critiques in a thin tissue of populist rhetoric (for many of this ilk, these were the first—and perhaps only—comments on corporate excess they’ve ever levied). In recent months, the Trump administration, facing historically low approval ratings and anemic enthusiasm going into the midterms, announced further restrictions to the process. As expected, the reforms roused the GOP base, jolting a fresh round of discourse around both the visa and Indian immigration.
Critiques of the H-1B system often blur into outright xenophobia—an unsurprising development when considering how much of contemporary conservative politics is powered by its white nationalist bloc. The best-known example of this came in September, when a Texas Republican candidate named Bo French reposted a photograph depicting a group of South Asian students celebrating a University of Texas–Austin football win. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” he laments. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”
French’s comments attracted widespread condemnation, yet his sentiment was far from exceptional. In January, Aaron Reitz, a former Texas GOP candidate who currently serves as a United States Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, tweeted about the “invasion of un-assimilated & unassimilable Indians,” before calling on the Trump administration to “Deport most. Assimilate the rest.”
Another story from earlier this year, which circulated widely across the right-wing media ecosystem, highlighted the Dallas suburb of Frisco. Around 20 percent of Frisco’s residents are of Indian descent, and many of them are H-1B visa holders, a fact that prompted conservative talking heads to warn of Frisco’s “Indian takeover.” Riled-up activists flooded Frisco City Hall meetings, where they often ripped into Burt Thakur, one of the city’s council members—ironically, an Indian American Trump supporter.
On the federal stage, two of the most vocal critics alleging H-1B abuse are Vice President JD Vance and Republican Texas Representative Brandon Gill. Vance recently referred to H-1B workers as “indentured servants”; Gill, a 32-year-old with a massive and rabid online following, tweeted, “We don’t need to import 7-Eleven workers from India or anywhere across the globe. Hire Americans.”
The profound irony is that both Vance and Gill have married Indian American women; they are fathers to Indian American children. Yet both have gladly offered up their families as tributes to the white nationalist meat grinder sustaining massive swaths of their governing coalitions. Indeed, many others have made this observation in recent months, but perhaps none more noteworthy than the shrill antisemite and white supremacist Nick Fuentes, in a recent jeremiad excoriating the contemporary right’s lack of authenticity.
Vivek Ramaswamy, one of the most contemptuous figures in American politics, is a key figure in this conversation—an exemplar of the tightrope act that today’s conservatives of color are forced to walk. His Indian ancestry was a key liability during his 2024 presidential campaign, and continued to drag down his chances during his ill-fated Ohio gubernatorial campaign. Last December, he took to The New York Times to try to stake some moral high ground, writing that “it is downright unacceptable to spew poison toward Jews, Indians or any other ethnic group.”
Unfortunately for Ramaswamy, this “righteous” declaration is painfully out of step with contemporary Republican politics (to say nothing of his otherwise heinous campaign). Ahead of the election, right-wing pundit Erick Erickson described Ohio’s polling as “pretty bleak,” a fact he partly attributes to how “the white nationalists…don’t want to support Vivek Ramaswamy for governor.”
Ramaswamy ultimately lost the governor’s race by nearly eight percentage points, a humiliating defeat that will usher in Ohio’s first Democratic governor in a decade and a half. “Look at what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan. We’re not going to let that come to our state of Ohio,” he warned at one of his final campaign speeches. It’s a Lynchian scene: a brown-skinned Hindu warning about brown-skinned Muslims, trusting that a political movement, composed of a growing number of white nationalists, will make the distinction between the “good” and the “bad” brown-skinned immigrant.
Yet this dissonance hasn’t slowed an odd set of right-wing influencers of Indian descent from unloading on the H-1B program—and in the process, slipping between the critiques of the visa and Indians writ large. Nalin Haley, son of former South Carolina governor and UN Ambassador Nimrata “Nikki” Haley, is an influencer with over 50,000 followers across social-media platforms, and has frequently called for the complete termination of the program. But his comments, too, have occasionally blasted the Indian nation-state more broadly: “They send cheap labor to the US, buy cheap oil from Iran, and cheap weapons from Russia because they have a cheap government.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Another influencer, one Priya Patel, who boasts a cumulative following of nearly 200,000, has also coupled her critiques of H-1B with scathing comments that implicate her own ancestry. “Not all cultures are equal, and we shouldn’t be importing the third world,” she once tweeted, before later describing India as the “third world.”
To witness these Indian Americans contort their identities to fit the shell of nativist Americanism is absurd, even carnivalesque. Perhaps they feel like they can singe off their Indian inheritances in exchange for unconditional entry into the fraternity of “America.” One quick scroll on their social-media accounts and we’re reminded just how wishful this thinking is—at any given time, you’ll find troll accounts disparaging these Indian American influencers as “jeets,” the preferred anti–South Asian slur of the online right.
In Texas, the anti-Indian fight has harmonized well with an existing Islamophobic panic around “Sharia law” currently possessing Texas conservatives. To right-wing, nativist Texans, it appears that both invasions are two sides of the same coin. In the aftermath of the midterm results, one conservative influencer commented, “This is what happens when you import Muslims and Indians into Collin County,” accompanied by a screenshot showing Collin swinging toward James Talarico (Collin contains part of Frisco, as well as Plano, another city that right-wingers have seized upon in their anti-H1B hysteria).
But the Hindu American Foundation, a noxious organization that has long served the interests of rich, right-wing Indian Americans, is trying to cleave anti-Indian hate from anti-Sharia panic. Not only does it wish to justify the latter, it also cosigns the notion that Hindus are well-suited to combat Sharia—a misguided strategy that only fans the flames of bigotry. And beyond its reprehensible moral approach, it’s a hopelessly naïve effort given the symbiotic relationship between anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim politics—a pathetic appeal that rhymes with those scenes of Ramaswamy begging white nationalists for their support.
As surreal as this entire spectacle remains, it’s not without its material consequences. According to one report by Stop AAPI Hate, the proliferation of anti-South Asian slurs online more than doubled between January 2023 and December 2025. “Threats against South Asians,” the report reads, “comprised 71% of all anti-Asian threats between August 2024 and December 2025.” Just this weekend, a right-wing activist and his followers stormed a Seattle Diwali event brandishing signs that read “Deport All Dot Heads” and “Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians.” Over recent months, following the tragic news of an undocumented Sikh truck driver’s fatal crash that killed three people, Sikh Americans were particularly targeted—both by online right-wing mobs, as well as the Department of Homeland Security. “I can’t wait till ICE swipes your ass with your H1-B and deports you via shipping container,” one anonymous right-winger tweeted to Jyot Singh, a recently elected Sikh American Georgia state representative.
Last month, a 19-year-old neo-Nazi stormed a Hindu temple in Illinois, where he intended to carry out a mass shooting. Miraculously, his rifle misfired and no one was injured. His manifesto, which allegedly derides Black, Jewish, and Indian Americans as “subhuman,” offers a clear glimpse into the ideology underpinning contemporary white supremacist radicalism. According to news reports, authorities found a gas can at the attacker’s home. The label read “Jeet Remover.”

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/allemagne/.title: Deutsche Bank : du capitalisme à la finance spéculative, quarante ans de dérives du géant bancaire
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/allemagne/.author: Bruno Odent
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/allemagne/.text:
S’ajoutant aux multiples scandales qui touchent régulièrement la Deutsche Bank depuis deux décennies, les nouvelles révélations sur les pratiques de la plus grande banque d’outre-Rhin viennent confirmer les ravages occasionnés par sa transformation accélérée, destinée à la soumettre à la globalisation financière dominée par les États-Unis.
Le nouveau scandale qui frappe la Deutsche Bank, à la suite de fuites sur plus de 15 millions de fichiers internes, ne vaut pas tant pour l’implication de quelques illustres têtes d’affiche, comme ces oligarques, qu’ils soient russes, locataire de la Maison-Blanche ou champion du monde des abus sexuels. C’est son caractère systémique qui en constitue la dimension la plus terrible.
L’histoire récente de la plus grande banque allemande, dont la tour de verre domine l’imposante colonie de gratte-ciel qui entourent la Bourse de Francfort, épouse en effet celle d’une transformation radicale de l’économie germanique, à partir du début des années 1990. Jusque-là, la banque n’avait jamais vraiment défrayé la chronique.
Son rôle n’en était pas moins décisif puisqu’elle fut l’un des principaux piliers de ce qu’il est convenu d’appeler le capitalisme rhénan. Entendez : une étroite imbrication des mondes bancaire et industriel, qui va propulser l’économie locale au sommet d’une production industrielle...

Recovering Edward Said’s Voice
Moustafa Bayoumi on a new documentary about the legendary Palestinian critic and activist; plus, can contemporary art make us laugh?
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship. Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.
Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.
—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor
Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever
In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi
