https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.title: Finanzindustrie | Kollateralschäden der Digitalisierung
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.author: Hermannus Pfeiffer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.text:
- Kommentare
- Finanzindustrie
Kollateralschäden der Digitalisierung
Die geklauten Dokumente der Deutschen Bank mögen veraltet sein, gewähren jedoch einen tiefen Einblick in den digitalisierten Kapitalismus. Ein Kommentar
Nach Jahren der Sanierung und Umstrukturierung legt Deutsche-Bank-Boss Christian Sewing ein Rekordergebnis nach dem anderen vor. In diesem Jahr meldet die größte deutsche Bank nach nur neun Monaten bereits einen Nettogewinn von rund 6 Milliarden Euro. Doch seit Dienstag erschüttert ein Datenleck das mächtige Geldhaus. Mehr als 15 Millionen interne Dokumente werden seit Monaten von einem Journalistenkonsortium aus mehr als 50 Medienhäusern vom ZDF bis zur »New York Times« ausgewertet – es dürfte sich um den größten »Leak« einer Bank überhaupt handeln.
Derweil rotiert die mediale Skandalmaschine: Demnach übergab im März 2017 ein Bankbeschäftigter einem Buchhalter der Deutschen Bank im US-Bundesstaat Maine versehentlich Finanzunterlagen zu 1586 Konten von Kunden. Darunter drei von »DT«, wie die Bank intern Donald Trump angeblich nannte. Den geklauten Unterlagen zufolge meldete die Bank den Fall den US-Behörden, beschloss aber, die betroffenen Kunden nicht zu benachrichtigen. Intern sei das als »brillantes Ergebnis« gefeiert worden, der spätere Bankchef Christian Sewing habe per Mail zugestimmt.
Aber es gibt auch schwergewichtige Enthüllungen: Das Leck bestätigt erneut, wie tief Banken in Geldwäscheaktivitäten verstrickt sind. Und dass man wie im Fall der milliardenschweren Übertragung von Aktien des Springer-Konzerns an Mathias Döpfner weiter bereitwillig hilft, Schlupflöcher zu nutzen, um gewaltige Steuerzahlungen zu vermeiden. Sind das die Lehren aus dem Cum-Ex-Skandal?
Die Deutsche Bank weist darauf hin, dass die entwendeten Dokumente »mehrere Jahre alt sind«. Dennoch erscheinen diverse Strafzahlungen, Rügen der Aufsichtsbehörden und Polizeirazzien in der Konzernzentrale, zuletzt im Juli, in einem anderen, grellen Licht. Im September hatte die deutsche Finanzaufsicht Bafin die Beseitigung von Mängeln in der Datenverarbeitung angeordnet. Und erst in der vergangenen Woche erließ die Bafin eine Geldbuße gegen die Deutsche Bank, weil sie bei der IT-Integration der früher staatlichen Postbank gegen das Wertpapierhandelsgesetz verstoßen habe.
Was nicht im Fokus der Skandalberichterstattung ist: Durch das Datenloch in Frankfurt am Main schimmern auch die Zeichen der Zeit. In rasendem Tempo treibt das (Finanz-)Kapital die Digitalisierung der Welt voran. Die Beschleunigung aller Arbeits- und Lebensprozesse, die gleichzeitige Individualisierung der Konsumenten-Klasse und der Schulterschluss mit Regierungspolitikern jeglicher Couleur erleichtern die Geschäfte der Digital-Macht. Als Kollateralschaden nimmt man hin, dass da auch schon mal digitalisierte Unterlagen den Weg aus der Bank herausfinden – wie genau, ist übrigens unbekannt. Oder dass in dieser Woche bei einem Hackerangriff auf das staatliche Melderegister in Dänemark Täter Daten von 8,8 Millionen Menschen abgriffen. Oder dass ausgerechnet der US-Geheimdienst für elektronische Aufklärung und Kryptologie, die NSA, durch einen Cyberangriff schwer gestört wird.
KI-Sympathisant Donald Trump kommentiert die weitere Kaskade von Digital-Ausfällen ungewöhnlich gelassen: »Wenn man groß und mächtig ist und das ganze Geld hat, passieren solche Dinge. Das ist in Ordnung.« Doch wer ist schon so reich und mächtig, außer Trump und der Deutschen Bank?
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: A New Trump Rule on Tax Credits Could Impoverish Thousands of Legal Immigrants
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Bryce Covert
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A New Trump Rule on Tax Credits Could Impoverish Thousands of Legal Immigrants
It’s the latest move in the administration’s all-out effort to deny government benefits to immigrants—even those living and working here legally.
The Trump administration recently proposed a change to tax credits that would, if finalized, significantly impoverish hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants—as well as their US citizen children. It’s the latest move in the administration’s all-out effort to deny government benefits to immigrants—both those who are undocumented and those legally living and working in the United States—in order to make life in the county as miserable as possible for them.
The proposed rule, released by the Treasury Department in August, targets four federal tax credits—the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, the American Opportunity Tax Credit, and the Adoption Credit—that give tax refunds to filers who earn below a certain threshold. The EITC and CTC are by far the largest and most commonly claimed. Over 1 million people live in families that could lose access to the CTC and 602,000 could lose access to the EITC. About 515,000 could lose both.
The immigrants who will be affected by the rule change include the recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals—people who have been living in the United States since they were very young and don’t know any other place to call home—those who have pending asylum applications with work authorization, those with Temporary Protected Status, those with visas for victims of violence and crimes, those with employment and student visas, those granted parole for less than a year, and children who have been abused or neglected by their parents. The average family losing the credits because they are DACA recipients would forgo $4,560 in tax credits per year, amounting to 13 percent of their income. “That is not a drop in the bucket for those families,” Davis said. “They are going to feel that.”
Related Articles
The EITC and CTC have long required a work-authorized Social Security number, which can only be obtained with some sort of legal status. “This is not a credit where a migrant can cross the border and start receiving it in the next day,” pointed out Carl Davis, research director at the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. But while an immigrant with one of the targeted statuses who is married to a citizen will be protected, single parents or people who are married to someone else with one of these statuses will not. Meanwhile, about 523,000 children live in families that could lose the CTC and 279,000 are in families that could lose the EITC. About 90 percent of those children are US citizens. “When a family loses access to a credit like this, it affects everyone on the return,” Davis pointed out. “The kids are going to suffer too.”
The EITC and CTC help working families avoid poverty by giving them income support. Families often use the money to fill gaps in their budgets, buying necessities like food and diapers, repairing cars, paying off owed rent, or paying for their children’s extracurriculars. “They can use the money in the way that’s most effective and most important for their families,” said Kris Cox, director of federal tax policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. These measures have proven effective. Refundable tax credits kept over 10 million people out of poverty in 2025. When the CTC was expanded in 2021, child poverty fell to the lowest level recorded.
The families targeted by the rule change pay taxes to the federal government through Social Security taxes, income taxes, sales taxes, and property taxes, meaning they are still “paying on net to the federal government,” noted Ben D’Avanzo, senior strategist for federal advocacy at the National Immigration Law Center. If the rule were finalized, they would stop getting a benefit they help to fund. It would create “a two-tiered tax system,” D’Avanzo explained, “where immigrants essentially pay higher taxes than other people, without getting the benefits in return.”
The rule could also scare immigrants away from paying taxes after years of the IRS trying to encourage them to file. For the first time, filers will have to correctly report their immigration status on their returns, and the IRS will have to verify it, even though it currently has no system for doing so. In a draft tax form for 2026, the IRS has added a box asking, “At the time you file your return, are you, and your spouse if filing jointly, a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or an alien lawfully authorized to work in the U.S.? (see instructions).” That question has “never been on there before,” Cox said. It has also drafted a new form for claiming the refundable tax credits that askes, “Are you or your spouse a U.S. citizen, U.S national, or qualified alien?”
Such questions could deter immigrants from filing their taxes, particularly after the IRS shared information on tens of thousands of people with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in 2025 (a practice courts have since blocked). “There will be some people who are just frightened about answering any questions related to their immigration status and might feel chilled answering these questions,” said Shelby Gonzales, vice president for immigration policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, even though failing to file could result in criminal penalties. Many immigrants may not know if their particular status is “qualified” for the credits or not; some might need the help of an immigration lawyer to figure it out. “If I am an immigrant, I do not have a card that says, ‘You have a qualifying immigration status,’” Gonzales pointed out. “People are not going to risk this if they don’t know for sure that they fit into one of those categories.”
“It’s unavoidable that people who are eligible for the credits, who remain eligible despite this rule” will end up without them “because of this confusion and fear,” Cox added.
The proposed rule is an outgrowth of changes made in sweeping welfare reform legislation passed in 1996, which for the first time denied this group of lawful immigrants cash welfare. They were “vilified for a conservative agenda,” said D’Avanzo, as “people who do not deserve help, do not deserve the ability to have access to support for their families.” But for the last 30 years, Congress has never applied that restriction to other benefits and programs. “This rule is really upending 30 years of precedent and policy,” Cox said.
If the rule is finalized, it’s likely to face a challenge in court. Congress “clearly thought about this issue and has crafted its own restrictions [for these tax credits], and now the administration wants to go farther,” Davis said. In 1996 Congress also passed legislation restricting the EITC to people with Social Security numbers—which these immigrants have—and there is language in current statute that says noncitizens are eligible for tax credits. “The administration is attempting to usurp Congress’s authority in setting tax law and creating its own rules,” D’Avanzo asserted, “driven not by what the law itself says but by their really deranged anti-immigrant sentiments.”
The administration also had a chance to create these changes legislatively, but it didn’t: Trump’s huge tax-focused reconciliation bill, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed last year with only Republican votes, didn’t include anything limiting tax credits for legal immigrants. At the same time, Republicans did take away some benefits—Medicaid and CHIP funding, Affordable Care Act exchange premium tax credits, Medicare, and food stamps—from a similar group of immigrants, leaving them only available to citizens, green-card holders, and a few others.

The Trump administration has already tried to apply the immigration-related restrictions of the 1996 welfare reform law to other programs, most notably Head Start. Last year, a handful of federal agencies issued guidance saying they would classify the same group of immigrants as ineligible for Head Start enrollment, as well as for access to things like mental health services, domestic violence shelters, adult education programs, and federally funded health centers, deeming these things to also be “public benefits.” The effort has been permanently blocked by the courts nationwide, in part because the judge said the agencies violated procedure in issuing the guidance. But the judge left open the possibility of agencies’ issuing rules similar to what the IRS has proposed for tax credits in an attempt to do it in a more lawful way. “It would not be surprising,” D’Avanzo said, if the agencies try again through rulemaking.
In November, the administration did the same thing to a variety of programs at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, many of which fund affordable housing and homelessness services. The administration has also finalized a rule that prohibits entire families with mixed immigration status—where one or more family members don’t have a qualifying immigration status, even if others do—from living in federally subsidized housing, including both public housing and private apartments that receive rental assistance. Nearly 80,000 people could lose their rental assistance, including 52,500 citizens.
The administration has also finalized a harsh so-called “public charge” rule that will allow immigration officials to deny people’s green-card applications. It gives these officials wide latitude to take an immigrant’s use of nearly any public benefit into account and deem that it’s a negative factor in their quest for legal status. Most of the immigrants who go through that process are not undocumented and have a pathway toward lawful permanent status, but now they will face the choice between keeping benefits that allow them and their families to eat and survive or giving them up for a shot at a green card. Between 1.4 million and 4.1 million people could end up deciding to disenroll from Medicaid and CHIP, including their 1.7 million children who are US citizens. When the Trump administration issued a similar rule during his first term, which was later blocked by the courts, it still led 31 percent of adults in families with at least one family member who did not yet have a green card to forgo benefits. It’s “another way of scaring people who remain eligible for benefit programs from accessing them,” Gonzales said.
On top of all of that, early in Trump’s second administration he rescinded a Biden-era rule that allowed DACA recipients to get health coverage on the Affordable Care Act exchanges, instead blocking them from that option.
This is “a very coordinated effort to take away eligibility for benefit programs,” Gonzales noted. And that is meant to make life as uncomfortable as possible for immigrants in this country, with and without legal status. The Trump administration is using “every lever of the federal government for making immigrants feel unwelcome and unsafe living in the United States,” D’Avanzo said. “The overarching goal is to make it as hard as possible to be an immigrant in the United States.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Peter Bradshaw
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature.
Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. But there is nonetheless such a huge amount of energy, fun, scabrous black comedy, provocative bad taste and film-making style to be had here.
Like Tarantino’s Kill Bill: Volume 2, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth repeats the ideas and characters of the first film a little pedantically, certainly, and the ending is rather truncated – again, I think, a function of the story being spread across film and book. But it maintains a headlong craziness with a flair so few can come anywhere near. It is a movie that once again gives us the brutality and scuzz of Ed Bunker, the urban crime-pastoral of Elmore Leonard, and naturally the classic Tarantino trope of two tough guys rolling up in a car, a little before the appointed hour, but in time for some backtalk and bickering. (Here, some loathsome hitmen argue about the illogical house-numbering sequence on LA’s Mulholland Drive.) Fincher’s direction perhaps speeds things up in the scene transitions, quicker than the chapter-by-chapter prolixity that Tarantino would have favoured. Female characters also tend to keep their shoes and socks on.
The setting is now almost 10 years on from the first film, the Los Angeles of 1977, the time and place of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Boogie Nights, in fact, and also the presidency of Jimmy Carter, though it is only Nixon who gets a namecheck. Sharon Tate is on TV advertising cigarettes. Cliff has grown a moustache and quit the stunt business, having sustained an injury that gives him a slight limp; his old pal Rick Dalton is apparently making a TV show in Australia.
These days, Cliff has moved out of his trailer and lives with his cantankerous old pawnshop-proprietor dad Gus (Peter Weller) and presides over a portfolio of side-hustles. He’s a movie theatre projectionist (like Pitt’s character in Fight Club) at LA’s historic New Beverly Cinema, a coyly proprietorial touch from the screenwriter and the venue’s present-day owner. Cliff tends bar at various joints on various nights of the week, has a gig at a demolition derby, and maintains unofficial connections with the screen acting world, which causes people to recognise him all over the city.
Most importantly, he is a discreet fixer and intermediary for influential people who are being extorted. Cliff is bemused to be contacted out of the blue by smart, willowy talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), a former movie critic once mentored by Pauline Kael, and this would appear to be how Tarantino has taken his idea for a movie critic character that was going to be the subject of his “final” movie. (Personally I was disappointed that the LA Times’s Kevin Thomas isn’t the one to have taken Karen under his wing.)
Karen, with whom Cliff falls passionately in love, introduces him to her client Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), who is currently acting in a TV show with blaxploitation star “Hot” Rod Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). We get a very amusing pastiche-montage of Charlie’s B-picture and TV credits, like the ones for Rick Dalton in the first picture. Charlie is fascinated by Cliff’s military record in the second world war, and Cliff agrees to take on a difficult job for him, his heart softened by the fact that he once had a tendresse for Charlie’s worldly wife Toni (Carla Cugino). So Cliff enters, or re-enters, or maybe just gets further into, a world of violent crime.
The film can only work with the drawlingly imperturbable good humour of Brad Pitt as Cliff. His performance is endlessly watchable and entertaining, but also enigmatic, in that Cliff’s battle-hardened experience of the world has left him with an easygoing carapace of calm. Cliff is essentially surprised by nothing, affected by nothing; this is a function of Cliff’s character and Pitt’s own almost sphinx-like address to the camera. It is Cliff’s inability to be seriously rattled by anything which provides the ironic torsion and charge to the movie. It is Pitt’s great comic creation.

https://taz.de/Forschungsreise-in-die-An.author: Manfred Ronzheimer
https://taz.de/Forschungsreise-in-die-An.text:
Forschungsreise in die Antarktis: Frostige Klimaversprechen
Der Lebensraum der Antarktis ist in Gefahr. Das sieht Dorothee Bär bei ihrem Besuch dort die Woche und will mehr in Forschung investieren. Reicht das?
Dicht gedrängt stehen sie an der Kante des Ekström-Schelfeises und trotzen dem eisigen Wind: Die Kaiserpinguine der Atka-Bucht sind die wohl berühmtesten Nachbarn der deutschen Antarktisforschung. Rund um die Uhr richten sich die Farb- und Wärmebildkameras des ferngesteuerten Observatoriums Spot auf die Kolonie der rund 20.000 Tiere, um ihr Brutverhalten zu dokumentieren.
Doch die Idylle im ewigen Eis trügt. Weil das Meereis infolge der Erderhitzung immer früher aufbricht und schmilzt, schmilzt auch die Kinderstube der Tiere dahin. Hinzu kommt: Junge Kaiserpinguine schwimmen oft Hunderte Kilometer weit über bestehende Schutzzonen hinaus in ungeschützte Gewässer. Ohne einen strengeren, international durchgesetzten Bestandsschutz und konsequenten Klimaschutz droht der ikonischen Art das Aus. Deutschland ist für mehr Schutz, die USA und China dagegen.
Genau an diese Schelfeiskante reiste in dieser Woche Bundesforschungsministerin Dorothee Bär (CSU), begleitet von Hajo Eicken, Direktor des Alfred-Wegener-Instituts, dem Helmholtz-Präsident Martin Keller und ESA-Astronaut Alexander Gerst. Bei minus 30 Grad ließ sich die Delegation auf der auf Stelzen stehenden Neumayer-Station III zeigen, wie dramatisch sich das Erdsystem verändert.
Im luftchemischen Observatorium messen Forschende in der saubersten Luft der Erde den unaufhaltsamen Anstieg von Kohlendioxid und Methan. Die Antarktis wirkt als gigantischer Kühlschrank und Süßwasserspeicher für den gesamten Planeten – gerät sie aus dem Gleichgewicht, steigen weltweit die Meeresspiegel.
Konferenz aus dem Eis
Bei einer virtuell aus dem Eis übertragenen Pressekonferenz am Mittwoch fand Bär entsprechend große Worte: Der Klimaschutz habe für die gesamte Bundesregierung „höchste Priorität“, betonte die CSU-Politikerin. Investitionen in die ökologische Transformation seien kein Bremsklotz, sondern ein Motor auch für die Wirtschaft. „Was die Menschen hier auf der Neumayer-Station leisten, verdient meinen allergrößten Respekt“, erklärte Bär mit Blick auf die monatelange Isolation der Überwinterungsteams. Nur dank dieses Einsatzes ließen sich „wertvolle Messreihen fortführen, die zum Teil bis in die 1980er Jahre zurückreichen“.
AWI-Direktor Hajo Eicken erklärte in der Schalte, wie komplex die Dynamik des schwindenden Eisschildes und der Ozeane ist und warum es lückenlose Langzeitdaten braucht, um Kipppunkte im Klimasystem und deren Folgen für den globalen Meeresspiegel rechtzeitig zu erfassen.
Als „Geschenk der Natur“ bezeichnete es der Meeresforscher, dass die Klimaveränderungen derzeit zunehmende Niederschläge in der Antarktis auslösen. „Das würde bedeuten, dass wir erst mal zumindest für einen kurzen Zeitraum Zeit sparen, in dem Sinne, dass also dem Meer Wasser entzogen wird, das hier in der Antarktis abgelegt wird.“ Der Anstieg des Meeresspiegels würde dadurch gedrosselt.
Dass es der Bundesregierung zumindest bei der Forschungsinfrastruktur nicht an Geld mangelt, zeigt der Blick auf die Flottenplanung: Über 1 Milliarde Euro lässt sich der Bund den Neubau des Forschungs-Eisbrechers „Polarstern II“ kosten, der ab 2030 in See stechen soll.
There is no planet B
Die Klimakatastrophe braucht unsere volle mediale Aufmerksamkeit. Dafür bündelt die taz seit Jahren ihre Kräfte und begleitet Konflikte und Fortschritte auf allen Kanälen. Und das schon lange: Die taz hat über radikale Klimaveränderungen berichtet, als andere Medien noch treu von unendlichem Wachstum sprachen. Und sie macht weiter, wenn andere ihre Berichterstattung zurückfahren. Unsere Artikel sind und bleiben frei zugänglich – ohne Paywall, dank über 52.000 freiwilliger Unterstützer*innen. Wir sind der Überzeugung, dass es kritische Informationen im Netz geben muss, die nicht kostenpflichtig sind. Gerade zum Thema Klimaschutz. Nur wenn unser Journalismus so viel wie möglich gelesen wird, kann er gesellschaftliche Veränderungen bewirken. Aber das geht nur, wenn sich unsere Leser*innen an dieser Idee beteiligen und den taz-Journalismus mittragen. Sind Sie schon dabei? Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.title: Großveranstaltungen | Expo 2035 in Berlin: Sport macht mit
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.author: David Rojas Kienzle
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.text:
- Berlin
- Großveranstaltungen
Expo 2035 in Berlin: Sport macht mit
Der Landessportbund unterstützt die Expo-Bewerbung. Als Standort rückt das Gewerbegebiet Buchholz-Nord in den Fokus.
Eine Weltausstellung sei ein in die Zukunft gerichtetes visionäres Konzept, aber auch ein »offenes Gefäß«, sagt Friedhard Teuffel, Direktor des Landessportbunds Berlin (LSB). Er spricht am Donnerstag auf einer gemeinsamen Pressekonferenz seiner Organisation und der Expo 2035 Berlin GmbH. Der Dachverband des organisierten Berliner Sports hofft, dieses Gefäß mit eigenen Inhalten zu füllen, und schließt sich den vielen Organisationen an, die die Expo 2035 nach Berlin holen wollen.
Für die Befürworter*innen einer Expo in der Hauptstadtregion sind das gute Nachrichten. Erst am Dienstag hatten die Landesregierungen von Berlin und Brandenburg erklärt, dass es keine gemeinsame Bewerbung geben werde. Die beiden Länder hatten lange geprüft, ob die Weltausstellung mit einem zentralen Gelände in Schönefeld stattfinden könnte. Dort habe es aber bei Verkehrsinfrastruktur, Flächenverfügbarkeit sowie planerischer und zeitlicher Umsetzbarkeit mehr Risiken als Vorteile gegeben.
Jetzt muss sich Berlin alleine aufmachen, doch die Suche nach einem zentralen Ausstellungsort ist schwierig. Mit Schönefeld und dem ehemaligen Flughafen Tegel sind schon zwei Standorte aus dem Rennen. Henning Wehmeyer, Geschäftsführer der Expo 2035 Berlin GmbH erklärt, man nehme nun das geplante Gewerbegebiet Buchholz-Nord in Pankow in den Fokus. Das etwa 180 Hektar große Gelände am nördlichen Stadtrand steht bereits im Stadtentwicklungsplan, für Wehmeyer ein großer Vorteil. »Das ist ein Gelände, das sowieso entwickelt werden muss«, sagt Wehmeyer. So sei sichergestellt, dass die Expo-Infrastruktur nachgenutzt werde. Ergänzt werden soll das zentrale Gelände durch »Kiezpavillons« in der ganzen Stadt.
Auch finanziell wirbt Wehmeyer mit der Nachnutzung: Gelinge das mit der Expo, trage der Bund 75 Prozent der Infrastrukturkosten, etwa für die ÖPNV-Anbindung. Diese beziffert er auf rund 700 Millionen Euro. Für das Kerngelände müssten insgesamt 2,3 Milliarden Euro aufgebracht werden. Wehmeyer erwartet 20 Millionen Besucher*innen und Einnahmen von 1,6 bis 2,3 Milliarden Euro, die die Investitionen zumindest teilweise refinanzieren sollen. Die Besucherzahl sei dabei »konservativ« gerechnet.
Zunächst muss aber ein 700-seitiges Bewerbungsexposé an das Bureau International des Expositions (BIE) in Paris gehen, das die Weltausstellungen vergibt. Das soll bis Anfang nächsten Jahres geschehen. Allein die Bewerbung kostet 7,5 Millionen Euro, die Bund, Land Berlin und die Beteiligungsgesellschaft der deutschen Wirtschaft zu gleichen Teilen tragen müssten. Schon vor einer Entscheidung ist die Bewerbung also ein teures Unterfangen. Das BIE entscheidet Anfang 2028 über den Zuschlag. Bislang einziger bekannter Konkurrent ist die US-Metropole Miami.
Was verspricht sich der LSB davon? »Wir wollen unsere Stadt noch viel mehr in Bewegung bringen und dabei auch ganz neue Wege ausprobieren«, sagt der LSB-Präsident Thomas Härtel. Die Expo sei ein echtes Zukunftsprojekt für Berlin mit großer Gestaltungskraft. Die Partnerschaft sei daher eine große Chance für mehr Bewegung. »Die lebenswerte Stadt der Zukunft braucht mehr und neue Bewegungsräume und Bewegungsanreize und der Sport eine noch alltäglichere Präsenz in der Öffentlichkeit.« Das »offene Gefäß« wird also langsam gefüllt.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: E-Bike Battery Safety Bill Heads to Trump After Bipartisan Senate Approval
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The Senate on Thursday unanimously approved a bill sponsored by New York Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand that aims to stem the sale of unsafe e-bike batteries that have ignited hundreds of fires across the city this year.
The bill has twice passed the House and now heads to President Donald Trump’s desk. It requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set safety standards for the lithium-ion batteries that power e-bikes and e-scooters and gives the agency the power to halt the sale, distribution and importation of non-compliant batteries.
Batteries that are not safety certified are susceptible to bursting into flame, a phenomenon that’s resulted in 406 fires and nine deaths in New York City so far this year. The City Reporter has been reporting on this problem since 2022.
The bill passed in the House in 2024 and 2025 where it was sponsored by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-Bronx). But it never made it to the Senate floor because Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, blocked it via a tactic known as a “hold” that allows a single senator to stymie consideration of proposed legislation.
On Thursday Sen. Gillibrand, the bill’s lead sponsor in the Senate, requested a bipartisan unanimous consent on bringing it to the floor for a vote. The bill then passed with support from both Democrats and Republicans.
“We have lost far too many New Yorkers due to underregulated lithium-ion batteries,” she said. “Passing this bill is an important step in preventing future fires. I urge the president to immediately sign this bill into law and for CPSC to meet its requirements.”
Sen. Schumer said the bill’s passage “brings us one step closer to protecting the public and firefighters from the growing hazards of these low-quality and dangerous batteries.”
As the proliferation of e-mobility devices took off with the growth of delivery drivers during the pandemic, the danger of unsafe batteries increased annually. Since 2019, more than 1,600 e-bike battery fires have resulted in 46 deaths and 628 injuries in the five boroughs.
The Fire Department has repeatedly issued warnings about the dangers uncertified batteries pose and has urged the owners of e-bikes, e-scooters and other e-mobility devices to rely only on safety certified batteries.
In 2023, after an alarming wave of battery fires, the city passed a law barring the sale of uncertified batteries. But since then, enforcement of this law has wavered, records obtained by The City Reporter have shown.
Last month a battery fire at a public housing development in The Bronx resulted in four deaths. Then earlier this month a fire in a Sunset Park apartment building resulted in six fatalities, including an 11-year-old boy. The cause of that fire has not yet been announced but fire officials confirmed two charred e-bikes were removed from the building following the blaze.
The deadly role unsafe batteries play in these fires took center stage in the tragic 2023 death of journalist Fazil Kahn when a raging fire erupted in an apartment below him where tenants were charging multiple batteries. Weeks earlier 311 callers had warned the city about this, but there was no response.

‘Completely messed up everything’: Malawi’s fuel crisis causes chaos
Motorists and businesses struggle as shortages disrupt daily life.
Blantyre, Malawi – Finding fuel in Malawi has become a daily struggle, with motorists spending hours, sometimes entire nights, waiting for tankers that may never arrive.
As shortages persist, filling stations across the country have become flashpoints for frustration and violence as motorists compete for dwindling supplies.
Ken Mhango, 40, a car flipper in Blantyre, recently drove to a nearby filling station after a friend told him a fuel tanker was on its way. He had gone several days without fuel.
Twelve people were already waiting when he arrived, but the situation soon turned chaotic.
“Minibus drivers and motorcycle taxi operators started arriving and jumping queues. They were so reckless they didn’t care if they bumped your vehicle. A scuffle erupted and I saw others, especially women, desperately trying to keep their place in the queue. It took me four hours to get 20 litres but others spent the night in the queue,” he told Al Jazeera.
Violence at filling stations
The scramble for petrol has increasingly turned violent in Malawi’s cities and towns. Although the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority publishes daily schedules indicating which filling stations are expected to receive fuel, motorists say uncertainty over deliveries makes it difficult to plan their journeys.
Videos of confrontations have circulated on social media, including footage appearing to show people attacking a man at a filling station. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The mayor of Blantyre has also been sued for assault following an incident at a fuel queue, while an attendant was killed after being struck by a vehicle during a commotion at a filling station, according to local media reports.
Purchases are reportedly rationed to 20 litres (5.3 gallons) a day, while motorists sometimes pay attendants for an additional five litres, Mhango said.
“The whole chaos that this has created is hectic. It is very hectic and it has created an atmosphere of uncertainty. This is happening when money is scarce, you have to make sure that you plan properly to survive,” he said.
On another occasion, Mhango arrived at Nyabadwe filling station in Blantyre at 5pm after joining a convoy of motorists searching for fuel. The tanker arrived at 9pm, and did not leave until 1am.
“My schedule has been completely altered. Now commuting is no longer a norm but a luxury. I have two parcels in town but I can’t even manage to go and get them,” he said.
Unable to find sufficient supplies at filling stations, Mhango turned to the black market. He paid 30,000 Malawian kwacha (about $17.31) for two litres of petrol for his father. On another occasion, he suspected fuel bought for his garage had been mixed with water after an engine malfunctioned.
“The crisis has completely changed and messed up everything. As a businessperson who deals with vehicles at my garage, people are no longer bringing their vehicles any more because of lack of fuel. And we can’t take our equipment to follow the client,” he said.
He added that his business was unlikely to meet its monthly targets, forcing him to consider docking the salaries of employees who assist him.
Black market dangers
Selling fuel without the required permits is illegal in Malawi, but shortages have created opportunities for vendors to sell petrol at inflated prices.
Motorists who need to travel for work, business or medical care are increasingly turning to informal sellers despite the high prices and safety risks.
According to GlobalPetrolPrices, petrol in Malawi costs about $3.24 per litre, more than double the global average of approximately $1.52.
The informal trade has also proved deadly. Authorities have stepped up arrests of illegal vendors, while fires and explosions caused by unsafe fuel storage have killed people.
Earlier this year, petrol vendors and motorcycle taxi operators protested in Lilongwe after a suspected black market fuel seller was burned alive in an explosion following a police chase, local media reported.
Malawi’s Nation newspaper has documented at least six deaths from fuel explosions this year, including incidents involving families and children.
Calls for accountability
The shortages, alongside foreign-exchange problems and electricity blackouts, have fuelled demands for government accountability.
The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) planned nationwide demonstrations on November 17, calling for the resignation of the energy minister over persistent fuel shortages and power cuts.
The protests were postponed after police said they could not provide adequate security because officers were committed to a governing-party parade scheduled for the same day.
Michael Kaiyatsa, HRDC chairperson, told Al Jazeera that the decision reflected “genuine concerns about public safety”, rather than a retreat from the coalition’s demands.
He described the fuel situation as “heartbreaking”, saying its effects extended beyond transport and commerce to people’s access to essential services.
“It affects access to healthcare, education, food, employment and other essential services; ultimately this is a human rights issue,” he said.
“People are struggling to get their children to school. We have small-scale businesses that are losing money. We have employees that are failing to get to work, and ordinary motorists that are spending hours and sometimes entire days just looking for fuel.”
Kaiyatsa said the shortages were pushing people to buy fuel on the black market, not necessarily because they wanted to break the law but because they were trying to meet their daily needs.
“We must therefore be clear that this is the responsibility of the government to ensure that fuel is normalised,” he said.
While acknowledging the dangers of illegal fuel trading, he said law enforcement must respect human rights and due process.
“We have seen tragic incidents recently involving explosions and fires resulting from petrol being kept in homes. These incidents are serious public safety concerns. However, our position is that law enforcement must be exercised within the confines of the law with respect to human rights, proportionality and due process,” he said.
Livelihoods on the line
In a statement issued hours before the planned demonstrations, the Ministry of Energy acknowledged the difficulties caused by the shortages but rejected accusations of government inaction, saying interventions were under way to restore fuel supplies.
“The current fuel supply challenges are largely attributable to a combination of financial, foreign exchange and logistical constraints affecting the country’s capacity to consistently import petroleum products,” the statement said.
For motorcycle taxi operator Tadala Kachingwe in Limbe, the shortage has meant dwindling earnings and depleted savings. He said he could no longer set aside money to buy relish for his wife in the morning.
“The business has been affected because previously, when fuel was available, I could have some savings but now it’s impossible,” he told Al Jazeera.
Getting his motorcycle into a filling station has also become difficult, with minibuses blocking the entrances.
“I have no idea which queue I should be joining because the minibuses have blocked off all sides of entry into the filling station. I will need to pay caller boys to sneak this motorcycle into that filling station,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Religious messages agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.
“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in a 5 April email, marking Easter.
US district judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the first amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of Department of Agriculture (USDA) workers.
The USDA did not respond to a request for comment.
Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’ Christian faith, Thompson ruled.
When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to. “Cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates” are commands that were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted.
Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins’ policy.
Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Série Terreiros Urbanos extrapola debate sobre criminalização para valorizar a liderança de mulheres negras, diz deputada
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Monyse Ravena
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A exibição da série documental “Terreiros Urbanos em São Paulo”, do Brasil de Fato, na Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo (Alesp), nesta quinta-feira (19), foi marcada pela exaltação à valorização da liderança das mulheres negras, que são protagonistas do documentário e dos terreiros apresentados na obra.
A série destaca a força das lideranças femininas nas religiões de matriz africana, revelando os terreiros como territórios vivos de resistência, pertencimento e transformação social, a partir do papel central das mulheres.
A deputada estadual Paula Nunes, da Bancada Feminista (Psol), destacou que é importante debater a criminalização e o racismo religioso contra as religiões de matriz africana, mas que foi algo especial “ver de perto o que é a construção de uma comunidade a partir de lideranças femininas, de lideranças mulheres negras”.
“A beleza do documentário Terreiros Urbanos é, inclusive, extrapolar esse debate. Porque a gente sabe que existe criminalização, a gente sabe que existe racismo religioso, a gente sabe tudo isso. Mas em que momento nós falaremos sobre a importância de valorizar essas histórias, de valorizar esse legado e de reconhecer esses terreiros e essas mulheres como construtoras de comunidade para além dos seus próprios terreiros?”, questionou.
Ela destaca também a importância de mostrar o trabalho de construção dessas comunidades, da preservação da história oral, do respeito a pessoas LGBT+. “Quando eu assisti ao documentário, eu fiquei muito sensibilizada”, afirmou Nunes.
A co-diretora da série, Marcela Reis, ressalta justamente a diversidade, não só de pessoas, que existe nos terreiros, mas de lutas, de saberes, de cuidados. E que formam grandes comunidades.
“A gente viu mulheres que falam muito sobre as pessoas LGBT+ dentro dos terreiros, outras que tocam muito a luta antirracista, outras que o foco é muito com mulheres, com cultura. Mas sem deixar de lado esse esperançar de um futuro, de um olhar para frente, olhando para os antepassados, olhando para o que elas aprenderam. E sonhar uma sociedade onde esses territórios, esses terreiros, que são uma grande comunidade, uma grande família, tenham mais espaço, sejam mais valorizados”, disse.
A co-deputada Mariana Souza parabenizou toda a equipe que participou da construção da série e disse esperar que ela chegue a muito mais gente. “É importante parabenizar todas as mãos que fizeram parte desse projeto. São histórias que nos tocam e nos são muito importantes”, afirmou.
A série “Terreiros Urbanos em São Paulo” tem cinco episódios pautados na liderança de mulheres que delineiam os eixos temáticos que atravessam a série: Mãe Alessandra Ribeiro: disciplina e espiritualidade; Mãe Luciana Bispo: política de cuidado; Mãe Claudia Rosa: acolhimento e resistência; Mãe Neide Ribeiro: território e legado; e Ekedi Eloiza Lourenço: zelar pelo sagrado.
Entre a periferia da capital, o interior e o litoral, a série apresenta histórias guiadas por mulheres à frente dos terreiros, que são tanto guardiãs da memória quanto transmissoras de saberes ancestrais que sustentam práticas culturais, espirituais e comunitárias herdadas da diáspora africana.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-to-pay-12m.title: NY to pay $1.2M to a woman who accused ex-Manhattan corrections officer of sexual assault
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-to-pay-12m.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-to-pay-12m.text:
New York will pay $1.2 million to a woman who sued the state after she accused a former corrections officer of repeatedly sexually assaulting her at a women’s prison in Manhattan, according to lawyers.
The settlement is the first case that closed after the three-year look back period of the Adult Survivors Act ended, lawyers said. The New York law, signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in 2022, allowed alleged victims of sexual assault to file lawsuits after the statue of limitations had expired.
The ASA established a one-year period for these lawsuits to be filed from Nov. 24, 2022 to Nov. 24, 2023.
The lawsuit accused Corrections Officer Leslie Dawkins of sexually abusing the inmate in her prison cell more than 20 times between August 2010 and January 2011, according to lawyers.
Dawkins has also been named in more than 15 other ASA suits, with prison records revealing that the state corrections department had received several complaints from other incarcerated women about the former corrections officer, according to Slater Slater Schulman LLP, the law firm that represented the woman in this case.
The law firm also said that other prison staff and an internal investigation had warned the state about the sexual abuse that occurred at the now-shuttered Bayview Correctional Facility in Chelsea for decades, and that the state failed to address the issue.
“Three years after New York’s Adult Survivors Act lookback window closed, survivors are only now having their day in court after years of unnecessary delays that only serve to retraumatize our clients,” said Adam Slater, a founding and managing partner at the firm. “This outcome shows the State is prepared to accept responsibility and be held accountable for the harm it caused generations of women.”
The law firm said that it is representing 1,200 of an estimated 1,600 people who have filed lawsuits using the ASA after claiming sexual abuse in New York state prisons.
“New York passed the Adult Survivors Act to help survivors of sexual abuse and assault seek justice,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement. “In every matter, the Office of the Attorney General is committed to following the facts and the law where they lead. In this case, the evidence led to conceding the state’s liability and agreeing on compensation.”
Attorney information for Dawkins was not made immediately available.
The story was updated with a statement from the attorney general.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/th.title: The Landing, Beloved Los Angeles Gallery with a Keen Eye for Pairing Historical and Contemporary Artists, Closes After 14 Years
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/th.author: Maximilíano Durón
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/th.text:
The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.
On the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.”
In an Instagram post, Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”
O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to shows of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon reported.
In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo show for the late California artist JB Blunk.
Over the years, the Landing would become known for its pairings of historical and contemporary artists. At the time of its closing, its roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living contemporary artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez).
The gallery was also known for regularly staging off-kilter group exhibitions, with titles like “Rat Bastard Protective Association” (2016), “The Useful and the Decorative” (2017), “New Iconography: Artists Raising Children” (2021), and “Consensual Ennui (2023). The first of these, “3 Women” (2016) took its name from a 1977 Robert Altman film as a way “to create a cross-generational dialogue that explores the intersections of craft and fine art, influence and homage,” per a release. It featured the work of Lenore Tawney from the 1960s and ’70s paired with textile pieces by Tanya Aguiñiga and paintings by Loie Hollowell. The exhibition marked the first time Tawney’s work had been exhibited in LA in nearly 50 years.
In an Artforum review, Erin Kimmel wrote, “The Landing’s handsome, restrained exhibition showcased the exquisite detail of [Tawney’s] works, which reward prolonged scrutiny with seemingly boundless formal revelations.”
To mark its 10th anniversary at its Jefferson Boulevard space, the Landing mounted a two-part anniversary exhibition. The first part, which opened in November 2025, focused on contemporary art and design and featured the work of Ruth Asawa, Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Lyne Foulkes, and Doyle Lane. The second part, which opened this past April, featured gallery artists as well as others who had exhibited there, including Brenda Goodman, Sam Jablon, and Lukas Geronimas.
In a release for part one, O’Brien wrote, “10 Year brings together the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”
The Landing’s closure is the latest in an extended wave of closures that began in mid-2025. Los Angeles galleries have particularly been affected, with Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, and Blum all shuttering, along with the LA outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar.
In his statement on the gallery’s website, O’Brien added, “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future offsite exhibitions, activations, and special projects. Thank you for being part of the Landing’s ongoing narrative.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Emily Carr and E.J. Hughes lead the way at Heffel's $10m autumn auctions
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Larry Humber
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.
“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.
The back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).
Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.
The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.
A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).
A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.
Among the night’s other big-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.
J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.
Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.
The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

https://www.artforum.com/news/the-new-mu.author: Thomas Patier
https://www.artforum.com/news/the-new-mu.text:

The New Museum has announced a multiyear partnership with the Toronto-based Vega Foundation, an organization dedicated to commissioning and supporting video art. It was launched by Elisa Nuyten, a New Museum board member.
The Vega foundation primarily provides opportunities to emerging and mid-career artists who work in film and video. Recent artists who have received Vega commissions include Ali Cherri, Diego Marcon, Martine Syms, and Yuyan Wang. The foundation started in 2022, and has primarily collaborated with Canadian institutions.
Vega’s first commission associated with its New Museum partnership will be a solo show at the institution by the Thai artist Korakrit Arunanondchai, set to open in February. The subject of his exhibition will be the phenomenon of post-Vietnam War-era ghost cinemas in Thailand—venues where monks staged screenings via portable projectors in otherwise dilapidated architecture. The show will take the form of a video installation that includes fog, light, and a soil floor, and will also feature a performance series by Tosh Basco.
“For Vega, supporting artists also means thinking about how their work continues to reach new audiences and find new contexts over time,” said Nuyten in an email to ARTnews, “That’s something I’d really like to see come out of this partnership.”
Massimiliano Gioni, director of the New Museum, said that “Vega’s work creating a network of possibilities for works that might otherwise never be realized is perfectly aligned with what the New Museum was founded to do nearly fifty years ago, giving artists the freedom and resources to take risks, experiment, and pursue ideas that might initially seem strange or even impossible. To me, that is precisely what contemporary art needs.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/make-me-drain-ca.title: I Hereby Volunteer for the Drain Captain Program That I Am Urging the City to Institute
https://hellgatenyc.com/make-me-drain-ca.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/make-me-drain-ca.text:
When there's a big rainstorm coming, the City sometimes sends its residents a warning text: "Help prevent street flooding by clearing leaves and debris from catch basins near your home if it is safe to do so. If you're cleaning catch basin grates, be sure to wear gloves & watch out for traffic."
As the text indicates, the city wasn't built for the type of storms we've gotten in the Anthropocene, the imposing churlish thunderheads that absolutely drench, flooding streets and snarling commutes. The sewer system and its network of thousands of storm drains quickly get clogged with street debris, especially during autumn.  
But for most people, the emergency text is puzzling: Catch basins? Gloves? Traffic? Plus, it's November, the peak of the fallen leaf season. Seems like a lot of work for one person!
But what if the city had a volunteer army ready to clear the city's storm drains, sparing their neighbors from flooding, making sure water doesn't run into basements, pool at bus stops, and make crosswalks unsafe? Call them "The Drain Captains."

https://hyperallergic.com/drawing-center.title: Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award
https://hyperallergic.com/drawing-center.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/drawing-center.text:
Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award
Plus: Joyce Awards winners announced, Agnes Gund's gift to art in schools, and Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami.
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence
The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.
So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.
“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://citylimits.org/like-a-child-agai.title: ‘Like a Child Again’: How Late Night Soccer Gives Busy New Yorkers Time to Play
https://citylimits.org/like-a-child-agai.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/like-a-child-agai.text:
Share This Article
At five public parks, free soccer games continue until 2 a.m., giving workers, students and residents a place to exercise and build friendships. “You forget about life for a good hour or two,” one player said. “You kick a ball around with some of your buddies, feel like a child again.”
At Calvert Vaux Park in Brooklyn, the night doesn’t begin with a referee’s whistle. Players arrive in groups, laughing and passing the ball around as they wait for their games to begin.
For some, it’s an opportunity to exercise after a long day. For others, it’s a chance to reconnect with friends whose busy schedules rarely allow them to meet.
Juan Gomez, a 20-year-old Brooklyn resident, knows that feeling well.
Between school, work and Brazilian jiu jitsu, Gomez said he rarely has time for soccer before late evening. His classes and training can keep him occupied until around 9:30 p.m., leaving little room for another activity.
“A lot of friends that I really don’t have the time, or I don’t really have the chance to see, actually come out and play, and it’s kind of like a big reunion,” Gomez said.
That reunion is made possible by NYC Open Play, a city initiative that keeps soccer fields open until 2 a.m. at five public parks, one in each borough.
Introduced during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the program returned on Oct. 5 after a summer pilot recorded 4,531 player check-ins across 696 field bookings. It offers free pickup games for adults from 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. every night through the end of the month (and will resume in the spring after a winter hiatus).
“The World Cup may be over, but our commitment to a city where every New Yorker can find joy for free continues,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said last month when announcing the program’s extension.
For Gomez, the program provides an affordable alternative to private soccer facilities. Without the late night games, he said he would consider playing at Soccer Roof in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, though the cost can make it less appealing.
“It’s not a bad place to play. It’s just sometimes you know, it’s kind of pricey,” he said.
A familiar field, a different time
For Angel Yax, a 24-year-old electrician from Brooklyn, Calvert Vaux Park is more than a convenient place to play.
“This park brings a lot of memories to me because when I was younger, I used to come here a lot with my boys and my friends, and we used to hang out all the time,” Yax said.
Now, as a working adult, he returns to the same field after spending much of his day on electrical projects. His work sometimes requires him to stay beyond his scheduled hours, leaving evenings as one of his few opportunities to exercise.
Tim Brown, a field host at Calvert Vaux Park who also worked with NYC Open Play during its summer pilot, said he has witnessed players forming relationships through the program.
“I’ve seen a lot of people make friends,” Brown said. “I’ve seen a lot of really cool connections come together in real time just from having the field lights on.”
Finding community after hours in Queens
Across the city at Astoria Park, players described a similar atmosphere, where soccer provides an escape from daily responsibilities and a chance to spend time with others.
Eric G., a 29-year-old Mexican-American resident of Astoria, balances work, college and fatherhood. He said late night soccer fits into a schedule that otherwise leaves him with little time for recreation.
But what keeps him coming back isn’t simply the opportunity to exercise. It’s also the moments he shares with other players.
Eric recalled watching a friend score a bicycle kick, known in Spanish as a chilena, during a game the previous night. “I’ll probably remember that moment maybe in 20 years from now,” he said.
For Anthony Vayeko, 25, those shared experiences have turned regular games into friendships.
Vayeko drives from Elmhurst, Queens, after finishing his workday, usually around 5 or 5:30 p.m. Once home, he showers, eats and prepares to head to Astoria.
He said the late night sessions provide an opportunity that can be difficult to find during the day, when public soccer fields are often crowded or reserved.
“Given how limited the permits are, you know, fields are packed in the mornings and the afternoons,” Vayeko said. “So these late night games definitely give us an opportunity to get some exercise in.”
Over time, the familiar faces at the park have become part of his routine.
“You learn their names, you see each other week in and week out,” he said. “Making friends outside of work, outside of school.”
Playing late can mean getting fewer hours of sleep and feeling sore the following morning. Still, Vayeko said the experience gives him a break from the responsibilities waiting for him outside the field.
“You forget about life for a good hour or two,” he said. “You kick a ball around with some of your buddies, feel like a child again.”
Where the late night games draw the biggest crowds
Calvert Vaux Park in Brooklyn and Astoria Park in Queens have emerged as the two busiest locations during NYC Open Play’s fall season, according to Tarek Pertew, co-founder and CEO of NYC Footy, which coordinates the games.
Between Oct. 5 and Oct. 24, Calvert Vaux recorded approximately 720 of the 1,800 player check-ins across all five parks. Astoria Park ranked second and had been the busiest during the program’s opening week.
Pertew said many participants are workers whose schedules make daytime recreation difficult, including restaurant and hospitality employees, delivery workers and people finishing evening shifts.
It also makes it easier for individuals to participate without organizing a team beforehand. “Most players show up on their own. That’s the point of the program,” Pertew said.
Field hosts organize pickup games as participants arrive, divide them into teams and rotate players so everyone gets time on the field.
For some participants, convenience is another factor. Pertew said transportation after 2 a.m. has not emerged as a significant concern among players so far, noting that many live near the participating parks and that the locations have overnight transit connections.
Still, the program currently operates at just one park in each borough, leaving questions about how easily residents farther from those locations can participate.
Five parks, five boroughs
NYC Open Play operates at five participating parks:
- Bronx: Soundview Park
- Brooklyn: Calvert Vaux Park
- Manhattan: Harlem River Park
- Queens: Astoria Park
- Staten Island: Fairview Park
Each location provides space for seven-on-seven pickup soccer between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. The program is free for adults ages 18 and older. Players can participate individually or reserve a time slot with a team.
To join, participants must visit nycopenplay.com and complete an online waiver before arriving at the field. Individual players do not need to make a reservation. After signing the waiver, they can arrive at a participating park, check in with an onsite field host and join an available game.
Teams can reserve a time slot online, but every player must complete an individual waiver. Team captains or representatives are instructed to arrive at least 20 minutes before their reservation to check in.
NYC Footy coordinates the games onsite, while NYC Parks manages field permits and lighting. Parks Enforcement Patrol officers also maintain a presence at participating locations.
Keeping the connections going
The fall season is scheduled to end in November, with NYC Open Play returning from April through September 2027.
Pertew said NYC Footy is working with NYC Parks to explore additional opportunities for recreational field access across the city. One recent development is a pilot involving temporary lighting at Robert Moses Playground in Kips Bay, which Pertew said followed three years of advocacy for expanded playing hours.
For players at Calvert Vaux and Astoria Park, the program has already provided more than a place to exercise. It has become an opportunity to reconnect with childhood friends, meet new people and make room for recreation in otherwise demanding schedules.
At Astoria Park, field host Dewan Gurung said the program gives New Yorkers a chance to stay active after their daytime responsibilities.
“I think it’s a wonderful program. It needs to keep on running,” Gurung said.
