https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/elon.title: Elon Musk Thinks You’re an Idiot
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/elon.author: Katherine Krueger
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/elon.text:
After the cresting of a blue wave in the midterm elections earlier this month, it’s officially about-face season, and Elon Musk is the latest major figure to predict which way the wind is blowing. During the New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday — which also featured appearances by the war profiteer Palmer Luckey, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Hailey Bieber, I guess — the chief of Tesla and SpaceX appeared by video to recast himself as a political moderate.
“I’m not MAGA,” Musk told columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
This “both parties” lip service is deeply revisionist recent history for the man who became the largest individual political donor in U.S. history in the midterms by spending almost $450 million on Republican candidates, particularly in Texas. Reflecting on that complete and utter waste of unfathomable resources, Musk said he feels “pretty foolish” in retrospect.
“Republicans were routed, and the money I spent — I feel pretty foolish having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” he said. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”
Musk went on to say the Democrats winning the governor and Senate races in Texas is no crisis for the world’s richest man, who infamously moved Tesla from California to Texas to dodge taxes, regulations, and woke. He also expressed his optimism that Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa would actually be “quite moderate” in office.
This reversal is a telling, but not novel, approach as the rats flee the sinking ship of Donald Trump’s presidency and the Make America Great Again ideology made in his image. Just one day after Republicans were shellacked on Election Day, Vice President JD Vance planted his 2028 flag by distancing himself from the administration he’s still part of to declare that the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran was “the reason we lost.” (Trump is reportedly not pleased with Vance throwing him under the bus.) Other Republicans who previously cheered the country into war have also picked up the scent, and now we seem to be left with a war that absolutely no one claims to have wanted in the first place, apparently save for Trump, who said the war was worth losing the midterms.
As with Vance, cozying up to Trump paid extraordinary dividends for Musk, until it became a political liability. Musk knew exactly what MAGA was when it was lavishly benefiting his bottom line, and infamously declared himself “not just MAGA, but dark MAGA” while tipping his custom black-on-black Make America Great Again hat at a Trump campaign rally.
As a special government employee in the Trump administration, the Tesla CEO launched the Department of Government Efficiency, better known by its epic meme acronym DOGE, which took a “slash and burn” approach to the federal government under the banners of increasing “efficiency” and eliminating “fraud and abuse.” Musk empowered a merry band of half-smart racists to lay off federal employees en masse; handed down devastating cuts to foreign aid, killing hundreds of thousands of people around the world; eliminated jobs that undergird the social promises that the things we eat and the medicines we take should be safe; and set scientific research back untold years.
Musk did all this as part of a project to extract even more wealth from the government — he and his businesses have benefited from a staggering $38 billion in public loans, subsidies, contracts, and tax credits over the years — with minimal oversight, and to reshape the work of a functioning federal government into a right wing political project.
The South African businessman, who became the world’s first trillionaire this summer, is deeply invested in eugenics-based causes like the pronatalist movement, which encourages the right kind of Americans to have more kids so “humanity” doesn’t die out. He has pushed the notion that “white genocide” is well underway. When he launched his AI chatbot’s competitor to Wikipedia’s “propaganda,” Grokipedia dubbed itself “MechaHitler,” praised Adolf Hitler, and listed which races it deemed “good.”
This is who Elon Musk is, and he hopes Americans have the memory of a fruit fly when it comes to everything he’s said and done in public. But like the public rejected his campaign to convince us he was cool, we can’t allow this cynical rebrand to proceed as planned.
Musk is an extremist staring down the barrel of years of courtrooms and congressional hearings who knows the Trumpism he once boosted is a spent political force. He’s experienced no dark night of the soul that’s caused him to meaningfully break from the president or from the far right wing, and no serious person should allow him to deploy that fantasy.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-con.title: Don’t Mourn Hakeem Jeffries’s Speakership. Organize.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-con.author: Austin Warrington
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-con.text:
Don’t Mourn Hakeem Jeffries’s Speakership. Organize.
Hakeem Jeffries was elected the next Speaker of the House because the Left simply does not currently have the power to elect a speaker who reflects the progressive mandate we saw in the midterms. Changing that reality, however, is possible.
In the wake of the midterms, the entirety of left-liberal America was jubilant. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, outperforming even the most idealistic predictions. But it was not only the Democratic victories that shocked observers — it was the kind of candidates who won. Democratic socialists had their strongest showing of any election in recent history, winning 169 endorsed ballot measures and seats at the local, state, and federal levels — their strongest showing of any general election in recent history. And the wins by nonsocialist progressives and even many centrists affirmed an agenda championed by democratic socialists, centering economic populism, wealth redistribution, and universal health care.
But then a harsh reality set in: the near inevitability of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the House, a result that seemed to fly in the face of the progressive results we’d just seen. On Wednesday, just eleven Democrats voted against Jeffries in an internal nonbinding vote, including a bloc of five newly elected democratic socialists, joined by two additional Democrats. In a statement on their decision, the no voters cited ongoing negotiations around “Medicare for All, stopping [Immigration and Customs Enforcment (ICE)] terror, getting money out of politics, [and] ending the genocide in Gaza.” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez notably did not join the no votes.
Jeffries is decidedly not a leftist nor a progressive. He is a pro-corporate Democrat who defends Israel and readily takes American Israel Public Affairs Committee money and corporate money. How, in the face of such a resounding progressive message from voters, could there be no clear alternative?
It’s understandable that some on the Left might feel deflated by this outcome. But we can also see the speaker conundrum as exposing an organizing void in Congress, one that the broadly left-leaning forces that felt so heartened by the midterm results have to confront soberly: we simply do not currently have the power, leverage, or internal relationships to elect a speaker that reflects the mandate we just witnessed. Changing that reality will need to start with an honest evaluation of the conditions surrounding the speakership race.
Jeffries has spent years building up to this moment. The relationships he’s nurtured with his careful, deliberate style and results he’s delivered to the Democratic caucus — negotiating important earmarks for Democrats in a Republican-controlled House, leading a multistate campaign to neutralize Republicans’ gerrymandering efforts, and steering increasingly large fundraising hauls to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — were all leading to this moment. Any challenger, particularly one from a rising Left that is at its very beginnings in the halls of power, would be at a massive disadvantage.
Not only that, but any defectors willing to stick their necks out to back an alternative would be putting a target on their back, as Jeffries plays a key role in committee assignments and setting the agenda for the floor. Asking our electeds to risk their ability to successfully carry out their jobs and advance our priorities would be irresponsible without a viable path to success.
Socialists grappling with increasing power in government have to think long-term about how to create the conditions where a majority of House Democrats can back a socialist speaker. The time to start building toward that outcome is now, in Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) working groups and organizing committees across the country. Our bench of socialist electeds needs to be deeper in a way that can build buy-in for our goals among the general public, and we need to continue the work of relationship-building with our existing socialist electeds.
Deepening our bench of electeds happens at every level of government and requires a clear-eyed assessment of what it takes to win races, which usually centers on an ambitious fundraising plan. Designated candidate recruitment organizers can begin by identifying prospective candidates and taking meetings now in anticipation of 2028; ideal candidates have preexisting ties to DSA or a labor union, direct organizing experience, a demonstrated commitment to advancing socialist policies, and a willingness to work collaboratively and meet regularly with chapter leaders once elected.
Creating buy-in and demonstrating the popularity of our agenda among the public requires frequent and honest communication with the public. Rep. Ocasio-Cortez excels at this, making the often opaque operations of Congress accessible to millions through social media. To elect a socialist speaker, we would need to launch a campaign early, educating the public on the mechanisms as well as the stakes of the speaker’s race and building consensus around a candidate. A successful campaign will put us in a strong position when it is time for members to vote, where we can flex our organizing muscle to exert pressure using all of the support we’ve built throughout the course of the campaign.
Most importantly, we will need to continue the work of building relationships with our bloc of socialist electeds across the country. This work is carried out by trusted organizing leaders in regularly scheduled group meetings. It necessitates strong interpersonal skills on both ends, including the ability to manage conflict healthily and negotiate. Chapters with maturing socialist coalitions should connect with the architects of more established programs to take some of the many lessons that have emerged over the years.
What distinguishes democratic socialists from other politicians is that strategizing and organizing don’t stop after election day. The project of building power is year-round and relies on the active participation of skilled organizers working with elected officials. In the past two weeks, Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier have organized canvasses of their constituents, asking them directly what they should prioritize in Congress and who they should back as speaker. This ongoing dialogue with constituents represents a new kind of strategy — one in which elected officials meet people where they’re at to continue the work of organizing outside of an electoral context, facilitating dialogue at the doors and creating trust and buy-in.
This is only a small piece of what it will take to win our agenda, but it is an important and meaningful step toward the kind of politics we should always be practicing: one that centers the needs of working people and ensures their voices echo in the halls of power.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/19/m.title: Mamdani Wants Delivery Apps To Pay If Workers Ride Illegal Bikes
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/19/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/19/m.text:
This delivery worker is using an illegal bike. Mayor Mamdani wants the app company to pay for that, but critics say that's the wrong approach. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Mayor Mandani is pushing a City Council bill to require delivery companies to ensure that their independently contracted workers are using legal e-bikes and mopeds — but delivery workers are concerned that such a law will only result in more workers being deactivated.
On Thursday, Transportation Committee Chairman Shaun Abreu said he submitted the bill “at the request of Mayor Mamdani,” and championed it for holding delivery apps and companies “accountable for the e-bikes that their workers use.”
“My bill will protect deliveristas and pedestrians, while also reducing fire hazards,” Abreu (D-Morningside Heights) said in a statement. “Protecting everyone on our streets will require a comprehensive approach, and getting the dangerous, illegal devices off our streets is critical. We expect companies to uphold a basic standard of safety and legal compliance,” said Abreu in a press release announcing the initiative.
The bill is meant to tackle a two-pronged issue with electric bikes: the fire risk associated with uncertified lithium-ion batteries and the proliferation of illegal e-motos, which are faster and heavier than legal e-bikes.
Fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries that power the delivery boom are up 68 percent from the same period last year — and six New Yorkers have been killed in such blazes. (That figure doesn’t include another six New Yorkers who perished in a Sunset Park fire that may have been caused by the batteries, though that investigation is ongoing.)
But the head of the main delivery advocacy group said she is “deeply disappointed” by an approach that creates policies “without the meaningful input of delivery workers.”
“We are particularly concerned by the continued focus on enforcement without adequately considering the realities of delivery workers’ lives, the impact these policies have on their livelihoods, or the urgent need for a comprehensive, worker-centered transition plan away from unsafe devices,” said Ligia Guallpa, executive director of the Worker’s Justice Project. “Giving enforcement power over the city’s laws to the same app delivery companies that steal workers’ wages and are deactivating workers by the thousands is a recipe for continued worker exploitation at the hands of multi-billion-dollar corporations that only care about profit, not about New Yorkers’ well-being.”
She said the end result of the bill would be that the app companies deactivate more workers, “leaving them without due process and placing the economic burden on workers and their families.”
City Department of Transportation Commissioner Mike Flynn did not address Guallpa’s concerns in his statement, which doubled-down on the need to rein in the apps for allowing workers to ride unsafe bikes.
“Delivery cyclists deserve to work with safe and street-legal devices as they serve our city every day and night and as New York’s delivery landscape continues to evolve, the need for transparency from delivery service companies is long overdue,” said Flynn’s statement. “Ensuring that delivery trips are completed on safe and compliant devices improves safety for all New Yorkers.”
This bill adds to the pile of legislative proposals associated with e-bikes, which are popular among the city’s around 80,000 delivery workers. Vehicles with a motor with more than 750 watts or that can reach speeds of over 25 miles per hour are illegal to ride on the street, but such so-called “e-motos” end up in the city’s bike lanes because of a largely unregulated online marketplace.
The city has worked to crack down on the websites selling these bikes by issuing cease-and-desist letters and sending out inspectors from the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to survey brick-and-mortar locations.
One app company said the bill is misguided — and that the Mamdani administration needs to look itself in the mirror.
“Ultimately, the Administration needs to stop outsourcing enforcement,” said Josh Gold, the spokesperson for Uber, which owns Uber Eats. “It’s still far too easy in New York City to buy illegal devices and to buy devices that require a license to operate without ever getting one.”
It’s not the first time the Council has sought to require app companies to do more about their workers’ equipment. A similar bill in 2023 died. A 2024 Council bill that could have required apps to provide legal and safe bikes for workers was watered down to only cover ancillary equipment.
This is a breaking story and it may be updated. We reached out to City Hall and will update this story when we hear back.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ameriqu.title: Maison de l’Amérique latine : l’Élysée doit agir avant qu’il ne soit trop tard
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ameriqu.author: Tribunes
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ameriqu.text:
La Banque de France a mis en vente le 217, boulevard Saint-Germain, sans imposer à l’acheteur le maintien de l’institution qu’elle loge : la Maison de l’Amérique latine. Associations, parlementaires et ambassadeurs interpellent le président Emmanuel Macron pour garantir la survie de ce lieu emblématique. L’acquéreur doit être choisi fin novembre.
Les deux hôtels particuliers, estimés à près de 100 millions d’euros, abritent depuis six décennies le seul lieu parisien entièrement consacré à l’Amérique latine et aux Caraïbes. Les offres ont été closes le 21 octobre. Sans intervention, l’institution, qui vient de fêter ses 80 ans, risque de se retrouver à la rue.
Afin de garantir la survie de l’institution, soixante-trois associations latino-américaines et caribéennes de France ont adressé ce 7 novembre une lettre ouverte au chef de l’État : « Sauver la Maison de l’Amérique latine ». Lancée par l’Observatoire de l’Argentine contemporaine, l’initiative réunit d’anciens prisonniers politiques chiliens, France Amérique Latine, des collectifs colombiens, uruguayens, brésiliens, vénézuéliens, cubains, équatoriens, péruviens, nicaraguayens et boliviens, mais aussi des festivals de cinéma et de tango, des revues, des séminaires et des associations de psychanalystes.
Elle rappelle que la Maison, placée sous le haut patronage du président de la République, fut inaugurée en 1946 sous l’impulsion du général de Gaulle, en remerciement aux nations qui avaient soutenu la France libre.
Soutenues par un travail bénévole, près de 250 activités y ont été organisées en 2025 avec une participation de 5 000 personnes au Forum de la Maison de l’Amérique latine cette année. Les signataires demandent à Macron d’intervenir auprès du gouverneur pour qu’une clause garantisse le maintien de la Maison sur place.
Le 5 novembre, 47 sénateurs de tous bords, du communiste Ian Brossat au républicain Francis Szpiner, avaient écrit à l’Élysée. Ils soulignent que la subvention de l’État plafonne à 25 000 euros par an et que l’indépendance monétaire de la Banque de France « ne signifie pas une autonomie absolue » sur son patrimoine : un censeur nommé par Bercy dispose d’un droit de veto. La sénatrice Sophie Briante Guillemont a saisi le ministre de l’Économie par une question écrite. Le 20 octobre, les députés LFI de la commission des affaires étrangères, menés par Mathilde Panot, ont alerté Jean-Noël Barrot, jugeant qu’une telle « liquidation » apparaîtrait « comme une opération politique ».
Les ambassadeurs s’en mêlent. Selon l’AFP, le Groupe des ambassadeurs d’Amérique latine et des Caraïbes (GALA) estime que « la France ne saurait laisser disparaître » ce « patrimoine diplomatique et culturel commun ». La pétition de Jean-Marc Laforêt, président de la Maison, approche les 30 000 signatures, dont celles de Michelle Bachelet, Dominique de Villepin, Jean-Marc Ayrault et Bernard Cazeneuve.
Quatre-vingts ans après sa fondation, le sort de la Maison dépend maintenant d’une signature à l’Élysée.
Par Carlos Schmerkin, conseil en édition, ancien prisonnier politique en Argentine et militant associatif.
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.

https://taz.de/Was-wir-vor-GTA-VI-nicht-.title: Meme über Videospiel: Was wir vor GTA VI nicht geschafft haben
https://taz.de/Was-wir-vor-GTA-VI-nicht-.author: Laura Verseck
https://taz.de/Was-wir-vor-GTA-VI-nicht-.text:
Meme über Videospiel : Was wir vor GTA VI nicht geschafft haben
In den 13 Jahren des Wartens auf GTA VI ist nicht nur viel passiert, wie ein virales Meme bezeugt, sondern auch vieles nicht. Welche Probleme es noch zu lösen gilt.
E s ist Zeit, Abschied zu nehmen. Ein Internetmeme hat sein Ablaufdatum erreicht: den 19. November 2026. Am Donnerstag, dem Erscheinungstag von „Grand Theft Auto VI“, begann eine neue Zeitrechnung. Nun gibt es die Zeit vor GTA VI und die Zeit nach GTA VI.
„… vor GTA 6“ gehörte in den vergangenen Jahren zum Inventar der Kommentarspalten sozialer Medien. Wann immer etwas Unvorhergesehenes, Kurioses oder Absurdes geschah, dauerte es nicht lange, bis jemand darauf hinwies, dass auch das noch vor GTA VI passiert sei. Der US-amerikanische Spieleentwickler Rockstar Games hatte 2013 den fünften Teil der Videospielreihe veröffentlicht. Auf den sechsten mussten die Fans 13 Jahre warten. Zuvor wurde der Erscheinungstermin mehrfach verschoben. Aus der gemeinsamen Ungeduld entstand ein Running Gag.
Zu einem Abschied gehört der Rückblick. Doch statt zu fragen, was alles vor GTA VI passiert ist, wäre es interessanter zu fragen, was nicht passiert ist.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Man hätte beispielsweise dafür sorgen können, dass sich Menschen mit durchschnittlichem Einkommen eine Wohnung leisten können. Die von der Ampelregierung versprochenen 400.000 neuen Wohnungen pro Jahr hätten zumindest einmal Realität werden können. Stattdessen wurden bis 2025 nur gut halb so viele fertiggestellt.
Von Alben und Büchern
Selbst Stuttgart 21 hätte vor GTA VI fertig werden können. Der neue Hauptbahnhof sollte ursprünglich schon 2019 eröffnet werden, mittlerweile ist von 2031 die Rede. Während Rockstar Games in der Zwischenzeit eine ganze Großstadt erschaffen hat, arbeitet die Deutsche Bahn noch an einem Bahnhof.
Und dann wären da noch George R. R. Martin und Rihanna. Die einen warten seit 2011 auf den sechsten Band von „Das Lied von Eis und Feuer“, die anderen seit 2016 auf ein neues Album. Aber offenbar können nicht alle Fangemeinden gleichzeitig glücklich sein.
Auch für die Abschaffung des Patriarchats wären 13 Jahre doch eigentlich genug Zeit gewesen. Oder, um die Erwartungen etwas herunterzuschrauben, zumindest um den Gender Pay Gap zu schließen. Frauen verdienten 2025 in Deutschland durchschnittlich immer noch 16 Prozent weniger pro Stunde als Männer. Und auch der Paragraf 218 zum Schwangerschaftsabbruch hätte es in 13 Jahren aus dem Strafgesetzbuch schaffen können.
Was die Politik seit Jahren nicht hinbekommt, versprechen sich manche Frauen nun von einem Videospiel: eine unbeschwerte Nacht. Auf Tiktok etwa freuen sich einige Frauen darauf, am Donnerstag feiern zu gehen. Es seien ja schließlich weniger Männer unterwegs. Endlich ungestört tanzen. Und wenn es keine Partynacht sein soll, dann eben eine Joggingrunde nach Einbruch der Dunkelheit.
Dass sich Frauen von der Veröffentlichung eines Videospiels über organisierte Kriminalität mehr Bewegungsfreiheit im öffentlichen Raum versprechen, ist natürlich erst mal ein Witz. Dass die Vorstellung einer Nacht mit weniger Männern auf der Straße für manche Frauen so reizvoll ist, hingegen weniger.
Erstmals eine weibliche Hauptfigur
Mehr Freiheiten bekommen Frauen mit GTA VI auch in der virtuellen Welt. Mit Lucia Caminos bekommt die Reihe erstmals seit Langem eine spielbare weibliche Hauptfigur. Gemeinsam mit ihrem Partner Jason zieht sie durch die kriminelle Unterwelt des fiktiven US-Bundesstaats Leonida.
Dass jetzt auch eine Frau die Freiheiten genießen darf, die männliche GTA-Protagonisten seit Jahrzehnten für sich beanspruchen, sorgte schon vor GTA VI für Diskussionen. Manche Männer konnten sich offenbar nicht vorstellen, in die Rolle einer Frau zu schlüpfen. Manche Frauen wiederum diskutierten in den sozialen Medien darüber, ob es bereits als Fremdgehen gelte, wenn ihr Partner im Spiel eine Beziehung mit einer anderen Frau führe. In einem Videospiel, in dem man Autos klauen, Banken ausrauben und Menschen erschießen kann, wird ausgerechnet die Beziehung zum moralischen Streitfall.
In den sozialen Medien kursieren derweil Verträge, die das Zusammenleben mit der Freundin nach Erscheinen von GTA VI regeln sollen. Küsse, Umarmungen und Bitten um Hilfe müssen demnach bis zum Ende einer Mission warten. Wer vor dem Bildschirm herumläuft, muss mit Konsequenzen rechnen. Welche das sind, bleibt offen.
Hat die Freundin mindestens 40 Euro zum Kauf des Spiels beigesteuert, darf sie eine Regel streichen. Manche Verträge sehen immerhin eine Entschädigung in Form eines gemeinsamen Abendessens vor. Um die Zukunft der GTA-bezogenen Internetabsurditäten muss einem also nicht bange sein.
Bis zu GTA 7
Wem der Abschied vom Meme dennoch schwerfällt, dem sei ein Blick auf den Instagram-Account der CDU empfohlen. Unterm Motto „Erfolge vor GTA VI“ inszeniert die Partei Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz mithilfe von KI im Stil des Videospiels. Gefeiert wird unter anderem das Ende des Verbrennerverbots.
Mit solchen Trauergästen fällt die Beerdigung des Memes doch gleich ein bisschen leichter. Und wenn die CDU schon in GTA-Zeitrechnung denkt, hätte man da noch einen Vorschlag für die nächste Wartezeit: Laut Frauenhauskoordinierung fehlten im Juli bundesweit knapp 12.000 Frauenhausplätze. Wie schön wäre es, irgendwann in den Kommentarspalten lesen zu können: „Genug Frauenhausplätze vor GTA 7“.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Voters Just Rejected Data Centers and Big Tech. Congress Is Moving Fast to Undermine Them.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Basav Sen
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Voters Just Rejected Data Centers and Big Tech. Congress Is Moving Fast to Undermine Them.
A look at the forces driving the rush for “permitting reform” before a new Congress starts its term.
Despite a populist midterm wave driven by outrage over corruption and inequality, the lame-duck Senate has rushed to advance a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill perpetuating much of what voters just rejected. Instead of waiting for new members to be sworn in, the bill’s bipartisan backers have opted to skip even a committee hearing, rushing it straight to the floor.
Officially called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the bill will deregulate environmental permitting laws to ease the construction of energy projects. Among other changes, it will restrict states from imposing more rigorous standards than the federal government under the Clean Water Act and make it easier for developers to sue the government if their permits are denied for environmental reasons.
This massive giveaway to the polluting fossil fuel and data center industries is bad policy. It will lock in new fossil fuel infrastructure at a time when we need to be cutting back. It will facilitate the buildout of data centers. And it will not reduce energy bills—and may even raise them instead.
Data centers are widely hated nationwide and across partisan lines. Local initiatives to put serious regulatory restrictions on data centers, or outright ban them, passed with wide margins almost everywhere they were on the ballot this November.
Indigenous tribes, environmental justice communities, immigration justice advocates, and historic preservationists are all part of the broad civil society coalition that has formed in opposition to this disastrous bill.
So why are elected officials pushing this bad, unpopular policy? Money is part of the answer, but not the whole thing.
Three of the four senators sponsoring the bill—Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM)—receive large campaign contributions from the oil and gas and utility industries. The fourth, Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), does not, but he and his wife have large holdings of stock in Big Tech companies behind the data center boom.
But there are factors at play as well. The idea that our environmental permitting system is failing to do its job by blocking or delaying too many projects appears to have become conventional wisdom among influential sections of the political, policy, and media elite.
But rigorous, peer-reviewed evidence does not support this conclusion. The available evidence suggests that the primary reasons for permitting delays are understaffing or communication errors, not stringent regulations. Instead, it appears that a kind of mass hysteria has gripped our elites.
Another factor behind the support for BAAJA is deference to corporate agendas. Being “pro-business” is a default ideological position for many US politicians. The American Petroleum Institute, the American Coal Council, and other polluting industry lobby groups support this bill.
So does the tech industry, in spite of strenuous efforts by some to deny it. BAAJA facilitates the buildout of fracked gas infrastructure that the tech industry needs to power its energy-hungry data centers. It also facilitates the buildout of data centers on federal lands, which triggers federal environmental review.
An industry-aligned consulting firm points to provisions in BAAJA that require data centers to pay for their share of the costs of increasing grid capacity. Similarly, an industry-aligned think tank is claiming that BAAJA will protect utility ratepayers from rising bills attributable to data centers.
But this is misleading. It doesn’t account for the fact that many data center developers are already bypassing grid connections altogether and building their own captive gas power plants. The purported ratepayer protection provisions in BAAJA incentivize more off-grid gas-powered generation for data centers, and the permitting deregulation provisions make it easier to build the ancillary gas infrastructure.
Even if they aren’t connected to the grid, these projects can still increase utility bills by driving up demand for natural gas—a potent greenhouse pollutant often obtained by fracking.
It’s noteworthy that the data center industry is not vociferously arguing against BAAJA provisions requiring data centers to pay for the grid updates they need. On the contrary, tech industry interests and business associations with tech industry membership have come out in favor of the bill, giving the game away.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
No self-interested, powerful corporation would push for legislation that actively harms their self-interest. The reasonable conclusion is that BAAJA is backed by—and serves the interests of—Big Tech.
Finally, there’s one more constituency pushing for BAAJA: the far right.
The bill faithfully implements the Project 2025 deregulation agenda developed by the Heritage Foundation. It is part of the far-right agenda to gut landmark environmental laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.
Unsurprisingly, President Trump and his newly elevated extremist chief of staff Stephen Miller are both pushing for the bill’s passage. They obviously support making it easier for their Big Oil and Big Tech friends to ram through polluting pipelines, LNG export terminals, and data centers. They may also recognize that BAAJA will make it harder to block construction of the ICE concentration camps they want to build.
For Democrats to be supporting a bill that benefits Big Oil and Big Tech, silences impacted communities, expedites detention center construction, promotes the Project 2025 deregulatory agenda, and aligns with Trump’s goals—immediately after voters resoundingly rejected Trump and Big Tech in a landslide—is nothing short of a betrayal.
It’s now up to us to stop BAAJA from ever becoming law. If your senator was among the 73 who voted to advance the bill, please call them to voice your displeasure and urge them to oppose it in the next vote. And tell your representative in the House to pledge to oppose the bill, should it be passed by the Senate and go on to the House.

- Sport
- Probetraining
Heimstatt des Pingpong
Unser Kolumnist lernt in einem hippen Prenzlauer Tischtennis-Space die Tücken der Noppe kennen
Ich erhöhe die Schlagzahl: Diese Woche will ich jeden Tag an der Platte sein – bei meinem Versuch, Tischtennis von der Pike auf zu erlernen und am Ende beim Berliner »Tischtennisturnier der Tausende« eine gute Figur abzugeben. »Alles braucht Zeit und Übung«, hat meine Trainerin Domino mir empfohlen. Nun denn, versuche ich es also mit Regelmäßigkeit! Routinen finden!
An meinem freien Montag gab mein Sohn Ruben den Sparringspartner, am Dienstagmorgen wechselte ich vor der Arbeit eine Stunde lang Bälle mit meinem Kumpel René, der selbst in einem Tischtennisverein spielt. Am Mittwoch dann mein erstes Gruppentraining – und damit auch mein dritter Tag in Folge an der Prenzlauer Allee 38, wo in den nächsten Wochen mein Tischtennis-Zuhause liegt: im »Ding Dong Ping Pong Club«.
nd-Redakteur Jirka Grahl probiert sich in verschiedenen Sportarten, diesmal Tischtennis. Im Januar will er beim Tischtennisturnier der Tausende antreten.
Zwischen DM und Späti haben die Ding-Dong-Gründer Waldemar Zeiler und Kian Pariwar ein großes Ladengeschäft zum schicken Tischtennis-Space umgebaut. Fünf Profiplatten stehen bereit, für Stundenpreise zwischen 16 und 25 Euro kann man sich rund um die Uhr einbuchen, Schläger und Bälle inklusive. Es gibt keinen Counter, der Check-in läuft über die App. Neben den Platten hängen iPads und Bildschirme, auf denen man sich seine Ballwechsel im Replay noch einmal anschauen kann. (Ich staune, wie hüftsteif ich auf den Wiederholungen aussehe, wo ich mich doch so dynamisch fühle!)
Tischtennis erlebt einen kleinen Boom, und für viele ist »Ding Dong« eine Alternative zu den Tischtennisvereinen, für die es in Berlin lange Wartelisten gibt. Auch wenn der Laden voll digitalisiert ist, ist es den Gründern vor allem um die Gemeinschaft wichtig: montags Training nur für Frauen, dienstags »Open Playdate« für alle, zudem verschiedene Turnierformate und Ranglisten. »Wir wollen Menschen zusammenbringen, egal welchen Geschlechts, welcher Religion, welcher Herkunft«, sagt Gründer Kian Pawari, der wie sein Kompagnon um die Ecke wohnt – im Kiez.
Tagsüber sitzt Pariwar oft mit seinem Laptop auf einer der Bänke am Schaufenster und arbeitet, so auch am Mittwoch, als ich beim »Time Out«-Gruppentraining Lehrgeld zahle: Wir sind zu viert, ein Mann in meinem Alter, eine Französin und eine Frau, die mir ein paar Jahre älter und ein Stück unbeweglicher erscheint. Wir trainieren Aufschläge, Vor- und Rückhandspiel und am Ende gibt’s ein Turnier: Gegen meinen Altersgenossen gewinne ich, gegen die Französin auch, aber – oje – gegen die Älteste habe ich keine Chance: Sie spielt »Noppe«, einen besonderen Belag, der den Spin des Balles schwerer zu berechnen macht: Immer wieder schlage ich ins Netz, ich verliere 1:2 nach Sätzen. Herrje!
Donnerstagabend, nach Redaktionsschluss, steht schon das nächste Kleinturnier an, die »Charts« im »Ding Dong«. Ich rechne mit dem Schlimmsten. Für Freitag habe ich mich dann mit nd-Fotochef Frank Schirrmeister zu einem Match in der Mittagspause verabredet. Denn ich habe im Redaktions-Chat die Kolleginnen und Kollegen vom »nd« zum Spiel herausgefordert. Davon beim nächsten Mal mehr!

https://inthesetimes.com/article/boiling.title: Boiling Point: The road to war and Ukraine’s uncertain future
https://inthesetimes.com/article/boiling.author: John P. Ruehl
https://inthesetimes.com/article/boiling.text:
Boiling Point: The road to war and Ukraine’s uncertain future
In his new book, Boiling Point, journalist and historian Stephen Kinzer traces decades of US involvement in Ukraine, which helped start one of the deadliest and most consequential conflicts in the 21st century.
John P. Ruehl
This article was originally published by the Independent Media Institute on Nov. 02, 2026. It is shared here with permission.
The narrative surrounding the Ukraine war often marks its beginning on February 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. But the rivalries and political decisions that brought the two countries into conflict stretch back centuries. The start of the Cold War, meanwhile, was the beginning of sustained US efforts to further antagonize Ukraine’s relationship with Moscow.
In his new book, Boiling Point: How America Brought War to Ukraine, author Stephen Kinzer presents an account of how successive US administrations sought to cultivate Ukrainian nationalism and challenge Moscow, helping set the stage for conflict. Instead of viewing the invasion in isolation, Kinzer details Washington’s involvement over decades, from covert CIA operations in Soviet Ukraine during the early Cold War to Ukrainian independence and the post-Cold War tensions with Russia over NATO expansion, which all culminated in the outbreak of war.
Kinzer provides an extensive, detailed account of the history of US foreign policy in the region, without losing sight of the larger geopolitical forces at play. By challenging the conventional narrative of the war’s origins, Kinzer offers a deeply researched perspective largely absent from mainstream discussions.
Understanding the decades of geopolitical competition and political motives that preceded the war is essential to seeing why it began and where it might lead. Any eventual peace settlement will pose difficult questions about territory and security guarantees, as well as Ukraine’s reconstruction and place between Europe and Russia. The war will likely end without resolving Ukrainian and Russian divisions that, as Kinzer describes in his book, US policy helped deepen, leaving both countries and the wider region to contend with the consequences for years to come.
As a journalist, author, and historian, Kinzer has spent decades examining American foreign policy, interventionism, and the consequences of US involvement abroad. His work has appeared in The New York Times and other major publications, and he’s written several books exploring America’s role in shaping international affairs. I spoke with him about the history behind Boiling Point, the choices that might have prevented the war, and what he believes lies ahead for Ukraine.
John P. Ruehl: Your new book, Boiling Point, examines the history of US policy toward Ukraine and Russia, tracing Washington’s efforts since the end of World War II to cultivate Ukrainian nationalism and challenge Moscow’s influence. It looks at how those efforts contributed to the tensions that ultimately erupted into the ongoing war in Ukraine.
To start, could you tell us a little about the book, its central argument, and the history you believe readers need to understand to make sense of the war today?
Stephen Kinzer: One of the points that I hope people will take away from this book is that much of what we have been told about the Ukraine war is wrong. And, in particular, there’s one word we constantly hear about the Russian invasion, and it was that word, really, that set me off after about the 200th time I heard it, and that word, of course, is unprovoked. We always read about that not just the February invasion, or the Russian invasion, or the military invasion, but the unprovoked invasion. Now, you can say a lot of things about this invasion, for example, that it was illegal under international law, just like many American operations have been, but it was definitely not unprovoked. How do I justify that statement? That’s my book.
The book traces 75 years of uninterrupted American plans to turn Ukraine into a battering ram against Russia. This began with the dropping of armed commandos into Ukraine back in the late 1940s, and it continued through a whole series of covert actions leading up to Ukrainian independence in 1991; then the project went into overdrive. [The US] spent huge amounts of money promoting anti-government groups in Ukraine and groups that would support the idea of confrontation with Russia.
That finally exploded. You might make an argument that we did the right thing to provoke Russia and to promote all this nationalist feeling in Ukraine. And I’m okay with that. But before you make any judgment on the justice or nature of the Ukraine war, you should know what happened before.
If you look at a snapshot of… February 24, 2022, you will see what happened. Russia invaded a peaceful country, Ukraine. But that picture should really be seen as just one frame in a very long movie that unfolded over 75 years. My book is an attempt to show you the real background of the Ukraine war.
JPR: Do you think Washington still has a bipartisan commitment to supporting Ukraine, or has it largely achieved what it set out to accomplish and now is unsure about how to proceed, amid the Trump administration’s efforts to negotiate peace?
SK: I think most people in Washington still think the Ukraine war is a great idea. It comes out of a deep-seated hatred for Russia, a belief that Russian expansion or anything good for Russia is bad for the world. I actually think that many Americans consider this war a success. The reason is, we’ve killed a lot of Russians. The fact that tens of thousands of Ukrainians have been killed and their country has been devastated doesn’t really register in Washington.
Most of the people in Washington who are most eagerly promoting this war can hardly find Ukraine on a map. They are not interested in Ukraine. All they’re interested in is Russia. … The result is that Ukraine has gotten wrecked, but for Americans, and I think for some Europeans as well, it seems like a win because it has wounded Russia.
JPR: You write about the CIA’s espionage and covert operations in Soviet territory within Ukraine’s modern borders, particularly during the early Cold War, which created massive tensions. The NATO expansion after the Cold War has been another major source of tension with Russia.
Now, NATO appears less central to US policy under Trump. If NATO’s role diminishes, what other institutions or government agencies might take the lead in sustaining pressure on Russia?
SK: The whole NATO argument is really one of the saddest pieces of this whole story. If Joe Biden had simply stood up and said five words: “Ukraine will not join NATO,” the war would have been avoided. He refused to say that. But the worst part of it is that in private, American leaders all admitted that Ukraine was never gonna join NATO; it’s not nearly ready, and there were all kinds of problems that would take decades [to resolve]. But nobody wanted to say this in public because it would seem like we were responding to Russia, we were intimidated by Russia, and we were doing what Russia wanted. The fear of seeming to grant any credibility to Russia was so great that we refused to do that.
There were many off-ramps for this war, and simply declaring that NATO would not accept Ukraine as a member would have stopped it. What you really need from Ukraine is essentially a peace accord, which was hammered out in Istanbul a month after the war began. Henry Kissinger used to say the same thing — Ukraine needs to be a bridge between east and west. It shouldn’t be a territory that the two sides fight over.
A great model would be Austria. After World War II, to ensure the withdrawal of occupying forces, Austria signed a treaty and inserted, in its constitution, a pledge that it would never join a military alliance and would never have foreign troops on its soil. That has worked great. That should be a model for Ukraine, but Americans don’t like that because it doesn’t smell like victory.
JPR: You dedicate the book to the Ukrainian people and argue that they didn’t really understand the consequences of the policies pursued by the United States and NATO toward Russia.
How do you respond to those who would argue that opposing the United States and NATO policy toward Ukraine amounts to supporting Russian aggression? Beyond reading your book, what evidence or arguments do you find most persuasive in that view, and what convinces people to reconsider the United States’ and the West’s role in the conflict?
SK: I don’t think Russia is seeking to capture Ukraine, much less further territories, but Russia has a fear that is understandable, and that is, they don’t want a nuclear-armed military alliance that they are not a member of right on their border. I pose this analogy: suppose China decided with Mexico that it would open a military base in Veracruz, or suppose Russia would open an air base in Quebec. Would the United States say, “Well, every country has a right to choose its own security partners, so I guess there’s nothing we could do about it.” Of course, we wouldn’t do that. We would bomb those bases. We would never tolerate that. So we’re now expecting Russia to accept something we would never accept.
There is room for negotiation, but only if the United States and the Europeans, who are now really taking on the extreme burden of the war, accept that they have to recognize Russia’s security interests. This is a horrific idea in some European capitals. But in the end, the only way there is ever going to be peace and stability in Europe is if there is a security architecture that takes into account the security interests of all countries, including Russia.
JPR: You discuss Kosovo and the Western effort to separate it from Serbia. Was there ever a realistic possibility of peacefully accommodating separatist sentiment in eastern and southeastern Ukraine after the 2013 – 2014 Maidan Revolution? Or were Ukrainian nationalist forces, Western interests, and Russian influence too deeply entrenched? And what alternative policies might have prevented the current conflict after the end of the Cold War?
SK: The most important off-ramp we had was at the beginning of the post-Cold War period, so around 1990 and the early 90s. Our president then, George H.W. Bush, fully understood this, and he promised Mikhail Gorbachev that he would not promote any eastward expansion of NATO. Soon, of course, Bush was gone; Clinton came in. There was a completely different approach. But there is a perfectly reasonable argument for a neutral Ukraine.
And I’ll tell you, one of the reasons that I got so passionate about this project, I realized later on, well, part of my experience way back in the 1980s, I was the reporter covering the Contra War in Nicaragua. And one thing I took away from that experience is that the war had nothing to do with Nicaragua. It was a conflict between two great powers that chose that poor country as the stage on which they fought. And, of course, [most of] the dead people were just the locals.
The same thing is happening in Ukraine. This war is not about Ukraine. It’s Ukraine that is suffering, and the big powers are holding its fate in their hands. Now, you talk about obstacles to peace. You’re absolutely right about the difference between eastern Ukraine and western Ukraine. Really, they are two countries that got stuck inside the same border by accidents of history. And one of the real sticking points, one of the real difficulties in reaching some kind of a national accord, is that for non-Russian-speaking Ukrainians, those in the western part of Ukraine, being anti-Russian, hating Russia, is a fundamental part of the national patriotic Ukrainian identity. And as long as there are millions of Russians in the country, these other Ukrainians feel they are a fifth column; they’re always going to be promoting enemy interests.
So, any Ukrainian leader who signs a peace treaty runs an immense danger, not only from history, but also from far-right militias that are going to attack them. The cleavage between the two parts of the country is so deep that it’s hard to imagine how they would ever come together, at least without some kind of federalized structure, if not by moving those eastern provinces directly under Russian control.
JPR: Could Ukraine’s postwar frontline resemble the situation between Russia and Georgia after their 2008 war, with an unstable standoff and Russia gradually altering the boundaries? Or do you expect a different outcome in Ukraine?
SK: I think the Russians won’t stop until they’ve consolidated their power over [the] four eastern provinces that they claim. After that, I do think there is a possibility that it could settle into a kind of frozen conflict. That would avoid forcing some Ukrainians to sign an agreement under which part of their territory is surrendered, but it could also end combat. It’s not an ideal solution. I would compare it to what’s happening in Korea. But at least that might be one way to end the conflict without putting people on either side in an untenable position.
JPR: What do you see as Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s political future after the war? Wartime leaders can struggle to retain public support in peacetime. Or do you think he will remain a central figure in Ukrainian politics?
SK: Zelenskyy is really an odd figure who emerged; I have a whole section in my book about how he did this. He was a TV personality. He was a fictional character who led a political party that was against corruption. And then this oligarch who owned the TV station said to him, “You know, we’re going to make that fake party. We’re gonna make it into a real party, and I’m gonna make you run for president.” So, he was about the most unlikely character you could imagine for that job.
And I don’t think he’s gonna wind up being a major figure in the future of Ukraine. Poor Zelenskyy, I think, is in a really difficult position now. Here’s what I think is going through his mind: “So the Americans are yelling at me because I didn’t make a deal. I didn’t accept a compromise with Russia. But when I tried to make a compromise with Russia, just a month after the war started, they stopped me! They told me not to do it. So now I’m being punished for doing what you told me to do.” And I can understand and sympathize with Zelenskyy’s frustration.
JPR: There have been reports of Ukrainian involvement in training militants in Mali against Russian interests, while Ukraine has also continued striking Russian oil infrastructure, despite pressure from Washington to stop. And Ukraine now has a large battle-tested military, even if the country itself is severely weakened. What consequences could this have for Europe and the United States, particularly if the Ukrainians come to feel that the West and the United States have betrayed them?
SK: The situation you’re describing is somewhat analogous to what’s happening in the Middle East; a war that was supposed to be localized has metastasized and is turning up in different incarnations in different places, even far from the nations that were supposed to be the target.
So, I do think we’re gonna wind up with a highly militarized Ukraine. The worst part is that many of the strongest military units are not the actual regular army, but are far-right militias, which proudly use Nazi insignia and proclaim their loyalty to Ukrainians who fought alongside the Nazis and helped participate in the Holocaust. That is going to be a project that Europe’s going to have to deal with.
But I don’t even think Europe is thinking about a postwar yet. I feel like Europe is in a complete delusion. They have the idea that if we just keep pouring weapons into Ukraine and pouring money into Ukraine, somehow the tide will turn. Meanwhile, inside those European countries, there’s tremendous political turmoil. Much of it is based on frustration that the government isn’t using its money to provide schools and other services people want. One reason is that so much money is going to Ukraine.
So, I think you might see resentment [toward] Ukraine growing, and depending on the way the war finally ends or freezes, people will become generally sympathetic to Ukraine, or very hostile to Ukraine. It’s another example of how wars like this set in motion processes that can’t be stopped and can affect international relations for decades to come. It’s really an object lesson in how you should stop and think about long-term consequences before launching foreign interventions.
JPR: What will or what can the EU do if Washington pulls away from Ukraine?
SK: The EU then has two choices. One is to continue its policy, which is ever more war, ever more arms for Ukraine, ever more money, or Ukraine could go back to the agreement that was tentatively reached a month after the war began and accept Ukrainian neutrality. This would be very wise for Europe. It’s foolish for the United States to be promoting war in Ukraine; it’s even more foolish for the Europeans. They are going to face real crossroads, and I fear the rise of radical political parties in Europe will create an even more difficult situation.
So that’s another reason I dedicated Boiling Point to the people of Ukraine; it’s my sympathy for them as victims of a great-power rivalry they don’t want anything to do with.
JPR: What was one of the biggest revelations you had while writing and researching for the book?
SK: The biggest revelation, by far, was my realization of how completely American foreign policy toward Russia and Eastern Europe has been shaped by officials with family backgrounds in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. We had [former] Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. We had [former] National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski. We had a [former] ambassador to NATO, Victoria Nuland. There’s a whole list of these [names] in my book.
So, what you had was a group of children and grandchildren of emigres from Eastern Europe and what became the Soviet Union. These people grew up with bitter, anti-Russian hatred, and that’s quite understandable, frankly, when you look at the history of what Russia has done to those countries. But when those grandchildren and children of emigres decided they wanted to affect American politics and foreign policy, they found themselves unwelcome in the Republican Party, which was then not interested in ideological crusades. So, they became Democrats. And all these people filled the Biden administration, the Obama administration, and the Clinton administration. It’s the only example in the entire history of American foreign policy where all major policies toward one part of the world were shaped by people with family background in that region. They turned the United States into the instrument of their vengeance against Russia, and thereby greatly distorted American foreign policy.
Those diplomats were quite capable. They should have been made ambassador to Brazil, or assistant secretary of state for Asia or something like that. But to place them in these positions where they were able to wreak havoc against Russia in accordance with the long instincts that had been bred into them from childhood is unique, and it greatly distorted American foreign policy. That was really the greatest single revelation I had.
JPR: And that’s a dynamic we really don’t see regarding China and Taiwan.
SK: Absolutely. You don’t see Chinese, let’s say, the children of Chinese immigrants, or the grandchildren, trying to get into the State Department so they can shape the US policy toward China. That would be the equivalent, but that has never happened in US policy toward any other part of the world, and it’s the piece of the story that I don’t think has been told, and I hope it’s one of the pieces of Boiling Point that turns out to be a major revelation and point of discussion.
JPR: With much of Ukraine’s industrial base, energy infrastructure, and population severely diminished by the war and emigration, what realistic prospects does the country have for rebuilding?
SK: Rebuilding prospects are very difficult to imagine. First of all, you have to have an end to active fighting. Now, in the Russian-speaking regions, there’s been a tremendous amount of destruction. But if you look at what Russia did in Chechnya, where the capital city essentially was completely destroyed, you get the idea that they do know how to rebuild things, because Grozny is now a thriving city. What about the rest of Ukraine, the western part? I think Ukrainians would be very justified in turning to the Europeans and saying, “You’re the ones who pushed us into this war; how about helping us resolve some of the damage?”
JPR: Finally, is this the end of NATO expansion, or is there room in the Balkans for more?
SK: I don’t believe there’s gonna be any expansion of NATO anytime soon. But what I would really like is that since everybody in Washington realizes this, they would say it. Instead, they try to keep it vague to pressure Russia. Announcing that would be a way to lower global tensions, but in some circles that is seen as a concession to Russia, and maintaining tensions is actually thought to be in our interest. I don’t believe that’s true, and until that mindset fades, it’s difficult to see a prosperous future for Ukraine.
John P. Ruehl is an Australian-American journalist living in Washington, DC, and a world affairs correspondent for the Independent Media Institute. He is a contributor to several foreign affairs publications, and his book, Budget Superpower: How Russia Challenges the West With an Economy Smaller Than Texas’, was published in December 2022. Follow him on X @john_ruehl.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Battles Early Flu Surge as Thanksgiving Approaches
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City is seeing a sharp early-season surge in flu cases with infections more than doubling from the same time last year as officials urge residents to get vaccinated ahead of Thanksgiving gatherings.
There were 6,467 reported flu cases last week, up from 2,489 at the same time last year, according to Health Commissioner Dr. Alister Martin. Nearly 12% of emergency room visits last week were related to respiratory viral illnesses, he added.
“Flu season in New York City started earlier than it has in the past few years,” Martin told reporters. “And now, while we don’t have enough information yet to make judgments about why that might be, we are tracking these developments closely.”
The warning comes after a particularly severe flu season last winter, when New York recorded more than 146,000 laboratory-confirmed cases and hospitalizations across the state hit record levels.
More than half of the city’s reported cases during last year’s flu season involved children under 18. City officials have said the surge contributed to major delays in emergency room treatment, including an average 27-hour wait for a hospital bed at Kings County Hospital, as The City Reporter previously detailed.
The hardest-hit area so far is Jamaica, Queens, where 15% of ER visits were tied to respiratory illnesses, according to the city’s Respiratory Illness Data Portal. Pelham and Fordham in The Bronx were a close second at 14%, the data shows.
Health officials aren’t sure why there has been an early spike in flu cases.
More than 360,000 children between six months and 18 years have received their flu shots in New York City this season, according to Dr. Andrea Howard, the deputy commissioner for disease control.
“That number is very similar to this time last year,” Howard said, noting the city doesn’t have complete data on adult vaccination because healthcare providers are not required to report those jabs.
The last time the city saw a surge in flu cases in late October-early November was in the 2022-2023 season.
MORE: A 27-Hour Wait for a Hospital Bed? Why Delays Are Growing at New York Hospitals
Health officials are particularly concerned because the flu, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) typically spread during indoor family gatherings and plane travel, especially when people are bunched together.
They are urging everyone six months and older to get the annual flu vaccine. Additionally, most New Yorkers six months and older should receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine and eligible New Yorkers should receive RSV immunization.
“We’re asking everyone to do their best,” Martin said.

This is an entry from: Live: Senate resolution to curb Trump's war on Iran fails again
Israel’s ambassador to US says the decision to strike Iran lies with Trump
19 November 2026 23:40 GMT
Israel’s Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter said on Thursday that the decision to renew strikes against Iran “will be taken by President Trump”.
Speaking to US media outlet Newsmax, Leiter said Israel will support the US if Trump decides to attack Iran.
“If he decides to go back kinetically, we’ll be there with the United States once again”, he said.
In reference to Trump’s claims that Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons during the interview, Leiter said that the threat to Israel is “existential” and immediate.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: ‘País que emite dívida na própria moeda não quebra’, diz economista sobre mito do colapso fiscal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: BdF Entrevista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
A aprovação do Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) 299/2026, o texto do ajuste fiscal, no Senado e a votação prevista para acontecer na Câmara dos Deputados na próxima segunda-feira (23) colocaram no centro do debate político as pressões exercidas pelo mercado financeiro sobre o governo federal.
Ao BdF Entrevista, o economista André Campedelli, professor da Universidade Federal de São Paulo (Unifesp), avalia que o chamado Plano Moretti (em referência ao ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti) surgiu como uma tentativa do governo Lula de conter a especulação sobre o dólar e a bolsa de valores. Segundo o docente, a forte reação do setor financeiro reflete uma disputa política ampla. “A Faria Lima não aceitou a derrota do Flávio [Bolsonaro] e está querendo impor a sua visão e também o seu plano de governo para dentro do governo Lula”, pontua, ao mencionar o nível especulativo que vem acontecendo, com oscilações no Ibovespa e a alta do dólar.
Apesar do tom alarmista difundido por setores da imprensa comercial, Campedelli desmistifica a tese de que o país estaria à beira do colapso fiscal. “Falar que o Brasil vai quebrar é uma falácia. País que emite dívida na própria moeda não quebra. Esse é o primeiro ponto. A gente emite dívida na moeda que a gente imprime. Não tem como quebrar. O que a gente tem hoje é uma dívida que é alta, mas não é por culpa do gasto do governo”, argumenta. O professor reforça que “a dívida está alta por causa dos juros que estão altos”.
Ele explica que o déficit primário, que está em torno de 0,5% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB), é moderado em termos históricos e que os gastos rotineiros do governo estão bem comportados, sendo o crescimento da dívida pública impulsionado essencialmente pelos juros altos definidos pelo Banco Central. “O mercado financeiro vai querer exigir o corte em quê? Nos juros com os quais ganha trilhões ao ano ou no posto de saúde da dona Maria?”, questiona. “O único governo que conseguiu entregar superávit primário na história foi o governo Lula 1 e 2. Eu acho que a gente deixou muito mal acostumado o mercado financeiro”, ironiza. “Na verdade, o problema é no rentismo, no financismo.”
Entre as fragilidades do projeto de ajuste fiscal, o professor aponta a trava que limita o crescimento real das despesas a 2% em anos de contingenciamento, o que pode paralisar obras públicas e enfraquecer o ritmo econômico, além de abrir brecha para chantagens no Congresso. “Se você tem que os relatórios fiscais começarem a mostrar que existe um mínimo, mas mínimo risco de não chegar lá, a gente pode ter esse contingenciamento de só poder elevar até 2% o crescimento do gasto real. E aí vai impactar, sim, mas vai impactar porque a gente vai continuar respeitando os mínimos constitucionais de saúde e educação”, explica.
Outro ponto sensível é a exclusão das receitas extraordinárias do petróleo no cálculo dos investimentos mínimos da saúde. “Se a gente eliminasse esse gatilho [do contingenciamento], já melhoraria muito a questão do ajuste, porque esse gatilho é o meu grande medo: ele pode fazer com que o crescimento econômico perca força justamente porque o governo perde capacidade de investimento”, alerta Campedelli.
Por outro lado, o professor destaca como aspecto positivo o fato de cerca de dois terços do ajuste incidirem sobre grandes empresas, via redução de isenções fiscais e limitação no uso de créditos tributários, sem mexer no Bolsa Família ou na Previdência. Para ele, embora não seja o cenário ideal, o pacote preserva programas essenciais à população. “Esse ajuste não foi um ajuste tão contra o povo; ele bate muito mais forte nos empresários e na Faria Lima do que no povo”, conclui.

https://gothamist.com/news/hudson-valley.title: Hudson Valley duck farm suing over NYC foie gras ban destroyed in fire
https://gothamist.com/news/hudson-valley.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/hudson-valley.text:
A Hudson Valley duck farm at the center of a high-profile lawsuit challenging New York City’s foie gras ban was destroyed in a fire early Thursday morning, according to Sullivan County fire officials.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras is one of only two remaining foie gras farms in the entire country, alongside La Belle Farms, which is also in Sullivan County. The two farms are asking the New York Court of Appeals to overturn the city’s ban on the fatty delicacy made from the livers of force-fed ducks and geese.
County officials said they received a 911 call from Hudson Valley Foie Gras’ facility in Bethel at 1:10 a.m. Thursday. By the time firefighters from the Smallwood-Mongaup Valley Fire Department arrived on scene the largest building was already fully engulfed, with the fire spreading rapidly through other wood-framed structures.
“The fire took off so fast, there was no way to get inside,” said Smallwood-Mongaup Valley Fire Chief Charlie Kalinowski. More than two dozen nearby fire departments responded to the blaze.
Kalinowski said most of the buildings at the Hudson Valley Foie Gras property were completely destroyed. Fire officials said “some” of the ducks and geese were rescued, including hundreds of hatchlings, but others were killed by the flames.
It’s not clear how many ducks and geese were on site. Hudson Valley Foie Gras Manager Marcus Henley told a Gothamist reporter at a previous visit to the farm’s nearby Ferndale facility that they process about 6,000 ducks a week. Reached by phone Thursday, Henley declined an interview but said no employees or first responders were injured.
Henley told Radio Catskill Thursday that the fire is suspected to have started due to an electrical malfunction. The Sullivan County Fire Investigation Team said its investigation is ongoing and no cause has been determined.
Henley’s farm is at the center of an ongoing legal battle pitting the New York City Council, which banned the sale of foie gras in 2019, against the farms and the New York Department of Agriculture, which argue the local measure violates state agricultural policy. Animal rights activists say the process of making foie gras amounts to animal cruelty.
Radio Catskill’s Kimberly Izar contributed to this report.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi Debuts to Brisk Sales and Confident Dealers
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
On the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.
“It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects.
The dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.
“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews.
The fair is under the umbrella of Frieze and has rebranded from Abu Dhabi Art fair, and attendees are noticing a difference. The exhibitor list has been streamlined to 89, down from 142 last year. Dealer Asmaa Al-Shabibi told ARTnews that when she walked through the fair’s new entrance, it felt “a little bit like going into Frieze London, and it feels like a different fair.”
Samy Ghiyati, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, agreed. “The quality is definitely higher, and galleries made an effort to bring very good inventory. Usually fairs in the region are slower and sales happen over the course of several days,” he told ARTnews.
One of Ghiyati’s clients placed three orders on pieces ranging from $10,000 to $400,000. Within an hour of opening, dealer Sundaram Tagore had already placed two works on hold, one by Hiroshi Senju and another by Chun Kwang Young, ranging from $40,000 to $400,000. By late afternoon, Timothy Taylor had sold its entire solo presentation of paintings by Hilary Pecis to institutional and private collections in the region and internationally, to the price of $65,000-$205,000. The London-based antiquities gallery David Aaron sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele for a seven-figure sum to a private collector, while Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects also sold out its booth of mosaic works depicting 70s-era architecture in Abu Dhabi.
Regional collectors reportedly spent big at Frieze Abu Dhabi. Iris Projects sold two works by Shamsa Al Omaira, a sculpture acquired by a new foundation in the UAE for $32,000 and an acrylic on canvas by Juma Al Haj for $20,400. UAE-based collectors also bought two ceramics by Eman Al Hashemi, priced at $17,000 and $15,000, an oil pastel on linen by Dhabia Al Qubaisi for $10,500, and a photograph by Ammar Al Attar for $12,500.
By then, Lawrie Shabibi had sold seven pieces by artists Hamra Abbas and Shaikha Al Mazrou, priced from $10,000 to $120,000. “People are recognizing the work when they’re coming here,” said the gallery’s cofounder Asmaa Al-Shabibi, referring to a new client who bought a work by Al Mazrou, who has a solo exhibition at the Cultural Foundation.
Rayan Ben El Mlih, sales and marketing manager at Waddington Custot, told ARTnews that a large contingent of collectors with reserves hailed from Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Qatar and Bahrain. The gallery brought works by Etel Adnan, Sophia Vari and Fabienne Verdier.
Dealers noted that local collectors, some of whom began their collections by acquiring Western artists, are now deepening their collections with more historical pieces by regional artists.
“We’ve been seeing European collectors diversifying their collections, too,” said Ghiyati. Dubai’s Carbon 12 sold a painting and a sculpture by 28-year-old artist Sarah Al Mehairi, as well as two works by Mexican artist Edgar Orlaineta, priced between $17,570 and $35,000 (€16,000-€32,000).
“We’ve engaged mostly with collectors that we’ve cultivated relationships with for a while, and this is our home fair,” Judy Karkour, associate director of Carbon 12, told ARTnews.
Collectors are branching out beyond SWANA this year, with notable interest in art from the African continent and its diaspora and Latin America. Meanwhile this year’s Frieze Masters section is dedicated to trade across the Indian Ocean, taking its cues from the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s current exhibition “Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean.” An hour into the fair, Efie Gallery had placed two works by Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté on reserve, both priced between $45,000 to $65,000, in addition to two works by Cuban artist Maria Magdalena Campos Pons ($27,500-$55,000).
“Frieze Abu Dhabi has got off to a strong start for us with a high volume of enquiries in the first few hours from both institutions and private collections,” Kwame Mintah, cofounder of Efie Gallery, told ARTnews, which specializing in artists of African descent. “One of the more encouraging developments across the Gulf has been the gradual maturation of its collecting community, accompanied by a growing appreciation for artistic practices beyond established geographical and institutional frameworks,” he added.
At Daniel Crouch Rare Books, a private collector bought the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832. While dealer Daniel Crouch declined to say how much the map sold for, he priced the booth’s total value between $10,073 and $1.19 million (AED 37,000 to AED 4.4 million).
“Abu Dhabi is becoming a cultural hub in the region with a lot of development,” Crouch said. “It’s the logical place to come to for dealing in the larger Indian Ocean region and the Louvre Abu Dhabi exhibition has attracted quite a lot of attention—we’ve obviously jumped into it with alacrity.” London-based antiquities gallery ArtAncient, carrying pieces ranging from $5,000 to $5 million, sold a collection of shipwreck jewels for an undisclosed sum—the gallery also had a visit from Venus Williams, who was admiring the Graeco-Roman mummy portrait Portrait L, which had recently been dubbed the “Mona Lisa of the Middle East.”
Throughout the opening, the blue-chip-leaning powerhouses, including Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddaeus Ropac, and Victoria Miro, boasted crowded booths. Gagosian’s dedicated Roy Lichtenstein booth became the step and repeat for many visitors—the gallery said it “placed many” orders without revealing specifics.
Judging by its debut, Abu Dhabi has become a no-brainer stop on the art fair calendar. The emirate is slowly integrating into the art circuit. Earlier this month, Christie’s hosted its first fine art auction there, with Sotheby’s own version due next month, joining a colorful lineup of events that includes the Formula 1 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Finance Week and Culture Summit Abu Dhabi.
Several dealers cited the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi’s upcoming December opening with the strong pull to participate in Frieze Abu Dhabi, characterizing the museum as a bridge between West and East.
“The Guggenheim is going to open now in the next few weeks, it’s literally where contemporary art gets space to breathe and to grow,” said Milo Gatti, fair coordinator at Galleria Continua.
