Art Basel Miami Beach is set to open on December 4, but the collective Artists 4 Artists Miami has launched a campaign to boycott the fair, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors, and residents to abstain from participating and to consider long-term alternatives to the commercial juggernaut.
According to the Art Newspaper, Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for a boycott at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition. Of primary concern is the extent to which the economic activity at the fair actually concerns the city’s artists and residents (as opposed to visitors), particularly as it becomes increasingly expensive to live and work in Miami. Organizers also question the associations between some of the fair’s partners and investors and various political and corporate influences.
Signatories to the boycott must pledge not to attend Art Basel Miami Beach, not to exhibit work at the fair, not to exhibit during Miami Art Week, or to withhold their labor from the fair. They can also choose alternatives to these options, which allows participants to assess what is realistic for their situation.
As economically significant as the fair is for the city—generating nearly $60m for the city of Miami Beach and $570m for Miami-Dade County in 2025, according to local officials—some desire more robust local support year-round. Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years and who signed the pledge, told The Art Newspaper, “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach.”
Artists 4 Artists Miami organizers are contacting local cultural and political organizations for endorsements and partnerships. misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami, said, “We realize that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative.”

Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M
The 1920 painting smashed its original sale estimate and the previous benchmark for a work by the Swedish forebearer of abstraction.
Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.
The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-its-time-.title: Opinion: It’s Time for Stricter Enforcement of Unpaid Building Fines
https://citylimits.org/opinion-its-time-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-its-time-.text:
Share This Article
“When he was running for mayor, Mr. Mamdani said he’d work on collecting fines the city was owed as part of finding funding for policy proposals like universal childcare. The time is here.”
Many times over many years, I have pointed out—to mayors, the City Council, state elected officials, at Charter Commission and city agency hearings, community board and Civic Association meetings, even in letters to editors—that there are hundreds of millions in unpaid Department of Buildings and Environmental Control Board (DOB/ECB) fines. I found this out via freedom of information requests to the City’s Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) several years ago. Nothing has been done.
With the recent, tragic building collapse on Brooklyn’s major Flatbush Avenue attracting so much attention, perhaps it’s finally time to wake up.
In fact, there is this clause in NYC’s Charter chapter 45A, re. “Environmental Control Board” section 1049-a(d) (1)(i): “A judgment entered pursuant to this paragraph shall remain in full force and effect for eight years.” I have argued for its repeal—finding that many officials are unaware of it.
I have not been able to find out exactly when, how and why this sentence came to be in the City Charter. Keep in mind that real estate developers are prime donors to campaigns for candidates running for city and state office. Indeed, imagine a candidate for, say City Council, asking developers for campaign contributions one day and the next introducing a bill to collect on their long-overdue violations?
If you check the city’s Buildings Information Systems site and enter the address of a building with a history of violations, you are bound to come across the phase “written off” for fines levied more than eight years ago, even where a dangerous condition existed.
While recognizing that real estate development is an important sector, and does contribute to the economy in many ways, I submit that it should not hold so much influence that it is able to control elected officials in order to get whatever it wants—or ignore “Stop Work Orders” at construction sites.
While more affordable housing clearly is needed, I have seen Brooklyn neighborhoods become unaffordable with the creation of high-end condos and “starter castles” (a term borrowed from former City Councilman Tony Avella when he visited us).
Whether it’s former Mayors Bill de Blasio’s Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH) and Zoning for Quality and Affordability (ZQA) or Eric Adams’ “City of Yes” initiatives, they actually are developer dreams. Ask homeowners and you’d learn that the initiatives do nothing for preserving the character and safety of neighborhoods.
So, now my question: will the attention to and investigation of this Flatbush building collapse force Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the City Council, along with NY State Assembly and Senate oversight committees, to finally push the City’s Department of Finance to stop making excuses and aggressively pursue owed fines, and the Department of Buildings to assure that accompanying violations are fully addressed?
Furthermore, besides—very importantly—trying to prevent more avoidable tragedies like this building collapse, imagine adding nearly hundreds of millions to the city’s budget?
After all, when he was running for mayor, Mr. Mamdani said he’d work on collecting fines the city was owed as part of finding funding for policy proposals like universal childcare. The time is here.
Ed Jaworski is president of the Madison-Marine-Homecrest Civic Association and co-founder of the Brooklyn Neighborhood Congress.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.title: Just Rinse It Off, Army Says Before Blowing Up Five Tons of Lead Compound
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.author: Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.text:
When the U.S. Army blows up nearly five tons of unstable lead azide in southeastern Iowa on Friday, blanketing communities in lead-containing particles up to 100 miles away, it has a simple solution for concerned Iowans: Just rinse it off.
“The good thing is, if people have concerns about it being on their property, all they have to do is hose that off, and it’s gone,” Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa earlier this week.
This won’t be sufficient to mitigate the harm of the toxic plume the Army plans to release, environmental health experts based in Iowa told The Intercept. And, while the Army’s publicly released dispersion modeling shows that airborne lead particles could travel northeast from the detonation site near Burlington, Iowa, as far as Maquoketa, the experts found the Army’s modeling incomplete.
Burlington is in southeastern Iowa, just west of the Mississippi River and the Illinois border. Because the Army’s plume modeling is a prediction based on anticipated weather conditions, changes in wind speed or direction could carry lead-containing particles into neighboring Illinois, even if the published projection does not show that path.
“They put out this plume model, which is basically a colored blob, so to speak, on a map,” said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa. “What they didn’t show was the projected or estimated concentration of settled dust within that plume.”
That settled dust will come from lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive commonly used in detonators. The Army has been storing the material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in a water-and-ethanol solution intended to keep it stable, but dangerous crystals formed during storage, according to an Army environmental assessment The Intercept found using the military’s Digital Visual Information Distribution System. Army officials determined that the resulting instability made the material too hazardous to move or transport, leaving an in-place detonation as their best option for disposal.
Now, the Army is warning residents and workers within the areas identified on its projected airborne exposure map to remain indoors, close windows and doors, and adjust air conditioning systems to prevent outside air from entering their homes “until the plume passes.” Children and pregnant individuals are among those specifically warned to avoid outdoor exposure.
O’Shaughnessy said the airborne plume could dissipate within hours, potentially ending the immediate inhalation hazard by Friday evening. But residents may not know how long they need to take precautions.
“Should I stay indoors all weekend? You know, the public doesn’t know, and no fault of theirs,” he said.
The Army environmental assessment shows that military officials considered several alternatives to Friday’s detonation, including chemically neutralizing the explosives or transporting them to an existing demolition facility, both of which were rejected as too dangerous. The Army also warned that leaving the explosives in storage could leave them to blow up by accident — and indefinitely disrupt the installation’s ability to make new ammunition.
The assessment does not establish how long the explosives had been stored, whether their deterioration was detected before March, or whether earlier intervention could have prevented them from becoming too dangerous to handle.
The Environmental Protection Agency, which issued an emergency permit authorizing the detonation, said the risk of an accidental explosion presented an “imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”
“The Army, which has unparalleled expertise in matters concerning explosives safety, concluded that this material cannot safely be handled or moved and therefore, cannot be treated by any method other than in-place detonation,” an EPA spokesperson told The Intercept.
The permit requires the Army to notify potentially affected communities, conduct environmental sampling before and after the detonation, clean up contaminated areas, and report its findings to the EPA. At the University of Iowa, which is 60 miles away and not in the predicted pathway, researchers hadn’t gotten details about how that monitoring would be conducted, O’Shaughnessy said.
“We don’t know where it’s going to be conducted. We don’t know what instrumentation they’re going to use or how they’re going to report the information,” he said. Researchers there are preparing to assess the consequences independently, including by measuring potential lead contamination and conducting their own plume modeling.
The Army’s environmental assessment also acknowledges that contaminants from the detonation could enter waterways through stormwater runoff or seep into groundwater.
It’s clear, said Peter S. Thorne, professor emeritus of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, that washing away lead dust would not eliminate the contamination.
“Hosing lead dust off of cars and other surfaces will indeed move it to the soil or into surface water,” he told The Intercept. “This could lead to human and animal exposure beyond inhalation of the generated lead dust plume.”
Asked what scientific evidence supported the advice to hose lead dust off residential property, the Army did not provide any studies or technical analysis. Instead, it said the EPA had provided cleanup guidelines as a condition of the emergency permit.
In an environmental handout prepared for an Oct. 15 community open house, the Army acknowledged that the detonation could damage nearby homes and contaminate surrounding property. The military said it would conduct environmental sampling on private property with homeowners’ permission and clean up lead contamination exceeding regulatory thresholds. It also acknowledged that cleanup operations could temporarily disrupt agricultural leases.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has found that no safe blood lead level in children has been identified. Even low levels of exposure can harm children’s brain development and ability to learn.
Asked what concentrations of airborne lead it expected in surrounding communities, the Army did not provide specific projections. Instead, it pointed to naturally occurring lead in soil and contamination associated with leaded gasoline, lead-based paint, and hazardous waste sites. Asked about plans to monitor potential long-term health effects, Barati, the Army spokesperson, said only: “We do not anticipate long-term health impacts.”
O’Shaughnessy recommended testing surfaces in communities affected by the plume, including playground equipment, every three or four days for approximately a month to determine whether lead contamination persists after airborne particles have settled. “You can’t just sugarcoat this,” he said.
The Army’s assurances come against a documented history of lead contamination at military installations, including cases in which officials failed to address known hazards.
A 2018 Reuters investigation found that children living in Army housing had been exposed to hazardous lead paint, with military medical records documenting more than 1,000 elevated blood lead tests among young children processed by one Army medical center between 2011 and 2016. The investigation also found failures to report some test results to state health authorities.
Additionally, a 2024 investigation by The Intercept found that the Army National Guard had failed to adequately remediate lead contamination at armories used by soldiers and civilians, including children. A 2020 Army audit obtained by The Intercept found that 73 of 83 indoor firing ranges examined in New Jersey, North Carolina, and Ohio had not undergone thorough remediation or the required evaluations of lead hazards.
At New Jersey armories, officials had used high-pressure washing to remove lead contamination, despite a 2020 Army audit warning that the method was prohibited because it could embed lead throughout facilities and generate hazardous waste.
Asked whether earlier intervention could have prevented the explosives from deteriorating to the point that detonation became the safest available option, the Army did not answer directly. Instead, it referred The Intercept to previously published information about the operation.
“It strikes me that this is a case of neglect leading to only bad choices available to avoid a catastrophe,” Thorne said.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anthropic-ai.title: Anthropic Is Already Part of the Security Establishment
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anthropic-ai.author: Jacob Davis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anthropic-ai.text:
Anthropic Is Already Part of the Security Establishment
Four trustees elect most of Anthropic’s board, and one of them runs a leading national security think tank. The establishment didn’t have to buy Anthropic to get a seat at the table.
Anthropic, which priced its initial public offering (IPO) last night and began trading on the Nasdaq today, published an S-1, the corporate prospectus for the offering. The document, which extends over five hundred pages, is intended to provide potential investors with an outline of its corporate structure, business model, and financial situation. Much of the document is, accordingly, dedicated to mundane legal minutiae: long lists of hypothetical events that might adversely affect investments, specific provisions for investment to comply with foreign nations’ securities law, etc.
Some points, however, are quite instructive. As the filing explains, large-scale corporate decisions are overseen by a “long-term benefit trust” (LTBT): a five-person body responsible for appointing a majority of Anthropic’s board and entitled to a special class of corporate stock. Unlike most benefit trusts, the LTBT is a “‘purpose trust’ that is managed for the achievement of a purpose rather than for the benefit of a particular set of beneficiaries.”
While the LTBT itself has received mainstream attention, less notice has been given to the identity of the trustees. Of the four currently appointed, one is Ben Bernanke — infamous as the architect of the Obama-era Wall St bailouts. And one is Richard Fontaine, chief executive officer of the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) and North American executive director of the Trilateral Commission. The latter appointment is especially noteworthy, for it speaks to an increasing coalescence of Anthropic, effective altruism, and the US national security establishment.
Company Purpose
The LTBT is something of a novelty in corporate structure. It is a fine-tuning of the usual public benefit corporation (PBC) — a form of corporate governance that allows the company to balance other stated interests against the pecuniary interests of its shareholders. Anthropic’s innovation is to hand over much of the responsibility of enforcing these competing interests to the LTBT, which will eventually appoint a majority of the board of directors. The company is also unusual in the sweeping humanitarian nature of its “company purpose,” against which shareholder returns are to be balanced: “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
The LTBT is an important indicator of Anthropic’s ethical self-understanding. According to the S-1, it “is intended to operate as an independent body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” These experts are selected for their perceived competence in promoting the humanitarian company purpose and “the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct” — a class which, given Anthropic’s stated beliefs about its potential impact, includes all living humans. In addition to vesting them with material power, therefore, Anthropic’s choice of LTBT members says something about what the company understands those humanitarian interests to be.
A Greater Degree of Moderation in Democracy
Both CNAS and the Trilateral Commission enjoy a dark reputation among critics of the US-aligned international security community. The commission is especially notorious, and has long starred as the villain in a number of conspiracy theories of varying levels of plausibility. CNAS, however, may yet be the more influential of the two, and is to all appearances more bound up with the emerging hybrid of corporate AI, effective altruism, and the security establishment.
The Trilateral Commission is a private, international membership organization intended “to discuss and propose solutions to some of the world’s toughest problems.” Members include various senior government officials, business executives, and academics. They are drawn primarily from the commission’s eponymous three regional groups: Europe (mainly Western), East Asia (mainly Japan), and North America (mainly the United States). Their official 2025 leadership list, which names Fontaine as executive director of the North American group, mourns the passing of two founders: David Rockefeller and Dr Henry Kissinger. The commission’s operations are famously clandestine, which together with the elite status of many of its members has contributed to its perennial mystique.
Among leftists, it may be best known for its 1975 report (one of only a handful available to the public), “The Crisis of Democracy” — which was prominently criticized at the time by Noam Chomsky. The report’s section on the United States, authored by conservative intellectual Samuel P. Huntington, ascribes the preceding decade’s social turmoil to an “excess of democracy” — to be counteracted by “a greater degree of moderation in democracy.” Included in this excess were protest movements opposed to the Vietnam War and in support of racial justice. These movements helped dangerously integrate hitherto marginal populations, like black Americans, into the political process. “This marginality on the part of some groups [ . . . has] been one of the factors which has enabled democracy to function effectively.”
Half a century later, a similar attitude toward protest survives in Anthropic’s commercial and political activities. As Daniel Boguslaw details in The American Prospect, the company has been explicit about its plans to deploy AI to surveil, predict, and stifle protest activism. These plans include collaboration with law enforcement, and fit well with historical calls for digital surveillance from AI safety lobbyists at organizations with ties to Anthropic. Fontaine, who has served as the commission’s North American executive director since 2019, was appointed to Anthropic’s LTBT in 2025.
The Revolving Door
CNAS, on the other hand, is a Washington-based national security think tank with extensive ties to both Republican and Democratic White House administrations. Joe Biden and Donald Trump staffers with CNAS ties include senior figures like Avery Alpha, who occupied high-level roles at the Central Intelligence Agency and Department of Homeland Security from 2017 to 2025 before turning to consultancy work. The organization has traditionally pursued a broadly neoconservative line on foreign policy. Fontaine was elevated as president in 2012, only to be promoted again to CEO in 2019 — five months before his Trilateral Commission executive appointment.
CNAS also has an exceptional history of conflicts of interest and likely illicit influence. Several of these came to light in a 2021 bombshell report by the Revolving Door Project, which also helped expose CNAS members’ deep presence in the Biden and Trump administrations. The center has repeatedly championed private sector industries, international organizations, and foreign governments from whom it has received funding — often without explicit acknowledgement in the course of their advocacy.
Fontaine himself has taken direct part in these ethically suspect lobbying campaigns. In 2009, for example, he coauthored a policy paper defending the use of private military contractors in the war on terror — without any explicit acknowledgement of CNAS’s funding from several military contractor firms. He also did not acknowledge the $25,000–$50,000 funding the think tank had received from the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, during an event to promote NATO in 2019 at the Truman Library.
Anthropic is now itself among the beneficiaries of this conflict-ridden advocacy. On November 3, CNAS published a report advocating a suite of policy recommendations to protect against autonomous AI agents. The proposed policies align largely with Anthropic’s own stated regulatory agenda. And, conspicuously, certain of the policies clearly serve Anthropic’s commercial interests — especially against Chinese competitors. These include crackdowns on potential avenues of model distillation by foreign entities as well as diplomacy to erect barriers to powerful open-weights models. Model distillation by Chinese competitors has long been a sore point for Anthropic, and these competitors overwhelmingly favor open-weights licensing. At no point does the report mention Fontaine’s ties to Anthropic.
This hidden connection is just one part of a broader integration of CNAS, Anthropic, and affiliated organizations. CNAS affiliates now include major figures at Anthropic, like the center’s adjunct senior fellow, Michael Sellitto. Sellitto, who served on the National Security Council during the Obama and first Trump administrations and currently serves on the Council for Foreign Relations, is head of Anthropic’s Global Affairs team. The team is associated with Anthropic’s known surveillance activities and advocacy.
Effective Altruists and New Cold Warriors
CNAS has also maintained a partnership with the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) — an Anthropic-linked AI safety lobbying organization with deep ties in Washington. In 2025, for example, CSET announced its new advisory board, including CNAS member Michael Brown. It has also collaborated on several policy documents and research projects, particularly on combating Chinese AI development.
CSET enjoys extensive connections with Anthropic. These include personal overlaps, like Anthropic adviser and CSET Senior Fellow Ben Buchanan, or Anthropic policy executive and CSET advisory board member Joel Meyer. The two organizations have collaborated on the CHIPS Act and export controls against China, and are generally united under the ideological banner of effective altruism and AI safety.
In addition to personnel, CSET, CNAS, and Anthropic are linked financially through Coefficient Giving, the premier effective altruist donor body. Since its founding in 2019, CSET has received over $100 million from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), most of it in advance of its collaboration with CNAS. CNAS, too, has received funding directly from Coefficient Giving, albeit in smaller quantities. The bulk of this transfer was conducted in 2022 and 2025, when it received grants of a bit over $5 million and $8 million, respectively, for work in AI governance and security. These larger grants built on a series of smaller ones (from around $24,000 to $260,000) starting in 2017.
Anthropic enjoys deep ideological and personal ties with Coefficient Giving. Both emerged from the effective altruist and AI safety movements, which continue to shape their rhetoric and policy directions. Holden Karnofsky, cofounder of Coefficient Giving’s precursor GiveWell, is married to Anthropic board member Daniela Amodei, herself the sister of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Neil Shah, another LTBT member, served as managing director of Givewell until 2022. And Joe Carlsmith formerly led the AI-focussed “Worldview Investigations” team at Coefficient Giving (then Open Philanthropy). Now, he heads the “character” team at Anthropic, which is devoted to tailoring the values and personality of the company’s “Claude” assistants.
In the coming years and months, we are likely to witness a new influx of Anthropic money into Coefficient Giving and similar funding organizations — and thereby to more distant beneficiaries like CSET and CNAS. Many employees and executives have announced their intention to donate large portions of their wealth to charity, sometimes up to 80 percent. Coefficient Giving, itself a tax-deductible 501(c)3 nonprofit, has been recognized as a “favorite” of Anthropic executives, whose personal net worths extend into the tens of billions. In addition to laundering the donors’ reputations, these wealth transfers thus promise to further entrench the financial and organizational ties between Anthropic on the one hand and the Washington security establishment on the other.
Entanglement
The foregoing connections only scratch the surface of Anthropic’s ever-deepening entanglement with the security state. Beyond Fontaine, for example, the LTBT includes Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs — who in addition to his academic appointments serves as a member of the independent scientific advisory group JASON. JASON’s work (much of it classified) largely concentrates on defense and nuclear strategy, including “studies under contract to the Department of Defense, the Department of Energy, the National Nuclear Security Administration, the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the FBI.” Most notoriously, it collaborated with military leadership during the Vietnam War, as revealed by Freedom of Information Act disclosures in 2002.
These connections do not merely speak to the increasing influence of the security establishment over Anthropic (and vice versa). They are also a clue as to the meaning of the company’s professed concern for human welfare and survival. Together with statements from company leadership, they paint a picture of long-term human interests deeply inflected by interventionist, antidemocratic, and anti-privacy strains in modern American foreign policy. Those who distrust such strains would do well to regard Anthropic, or any company with similar entanglements, with serious apprehension.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/minurso.title: Sahara occidental : le départ de la Minurso n’efface pas le droit d’un peuple
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/minurso.author: Latifa Madani
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/minurso.text:
La Mission de l’ONU achève son mandat, après trente-six années de présence, alors qu’un référendum d’autodétermination n’a toujours pas été organisé. Il faut agir pour maintenir une responsabilité internationale effective envers le peuple sahraoui et éviter une escalade du conflit. Par Najem Sidi, président du Comité Action et Réflexion pour l’Avenir du Sahara occidental (Caraso)
La Mission des Nations unies pour l’organisation d’un référendum au Sahara occidental (Minurso) se retire du Sahara occidental sans avoir organisé le référendum qui justifiait sa création. Pour le peuple sahraoui, cette issue pose une question fondamentale : que devient une promesse internationale lorsque la mission chargée de contribuer à sa réalisation disparaît ?
La fermeture d’une opération de paix ne peut tenir lieu de règlement politique. Elle oblige, au contraire, les Nations unies et leurs États membres à répondre de ce qui demeure inaccompli.
Le mandat de la Mission des Nations unies pour l’organisation d’un référendum au Sahara occidental a expiré le 31 octobre 2026, faute d’accord au Conseil de sécurité. Sa liquidation a commencé le lendemain. Après trente-cinq années de présence, les Sahraouis n’ont toujours pas pu exercer le choix auquel cette mission devait contribuer. C’est à partir de cette promesse non tenue qu’il faut comprendre la gravité du moment.
Car le désaccord au Conseil de sécurité portait aussi sur le sens même de la présence onusienne. Le projet américain prévoyait de rebaptiser la Minurso en Minuso, en supprimant la référence au référendum. Cette modification aurait effacé de son intitulé l’objectif qui avait fondé sa création, alors que celui-ci n’avait jamais été réalisé.
À mes yeux, retirer le « R » revenait à faire de l’échec du référendum un argument pour en abandonner la perspective. Une mission ainsi transformée risquait de servir la consolidation de l’occupation marocaine.
C’est pourquoi je considère que le veto russe a préservé une part de la crédibilité qui reste à l’ONU : il a empêché que celle-ci avalise cette transformation. Mais il n’a pas préservé sa présence sur le terrain, puisque le projet russe de prolongation de la mission n’a pas non plus été adopté.
L’autodétermination est un droit inaliénable
Cette distinction est essentielle. On peut refuser la dénaturation de la Minurso tout en mesurant les dangers de son retrait. Préserver un principe dans les textes ne suffit pas lorsque les moyens de le défendre s’affaiblissent. La question est désormais de savoir comment maintenir une responsabilité internationale effective envers le peuple sahraoui.
Antonio Guterres a apporté une réponse de principe. Dans son communiqué du 1er novembre, il rappelle que le départ de la mission n’abolit pas le droit inaliénable des Sahraouis à l’autodétermination. Il réaffirme l’engagement de l’ONU en faveur d’une solution politique juste, durable et mutuellement acceptable permettant l’exercice de ce droit, ainsi que la poursuite des efforts de son envoyé personnel, Staffan de Mistura.
Le dossier demeure donc ouvert. Encore faut-il que cette continuité diplomatique produise une perspective réelle ?
L’histoire invite à prendre au sérieux l’écart entre les paroles et les actes. En mars 2016, dans la dernière année de son mandat, Ban Ki-moon avait employé le mot « occupation » à propos du Sahara occidental. Son entourage avait ensuite présenté ce terme comme une réaction personnelle aux conditions de vie des réfugiés sahraouis.
Faut-il attendre la fin d’un mandat, ou la fermeture d’une mission, pour rappeler avec force les droits que l’on devait faire respecter ? La crédibilité des Nations unies se mesure aussi à leur capacité à donner effet à leurs propres principes, tant qu’elles disposent encore des moyens d’agir.
Prévenir l’aggravation du conflit et faire respecter le droit
Or, sur le terrain, le temps presse. Le 10 novembre, le secrétariat national du Front Polisario a proclamé la mobilisation générale. Dans son communiqué, relayé par l’agence sahraouie SPS, il dénonce des concentrations de troupes et d’armements marocains le long du mur de séparation, qu’il qualifie de dangereuse escalade. Ces déclarations constituent un signal d’alarme et rendent plus urgente la prévention d’une aggravation du conflit.
Pour nous, Sahraouis, cette inquiétude concerne la sécurité de nos proches, la séparation de nos familles et l’avenir de nos enfants. Une attente sans horizon nourrit le sentiment d’abandon. Prévenir l’escalade exige donc à la fois de protéger les populations et de rendre crédible une issue politique fondée sur leur libre choix.
La France doit prendre sa part de cette responsabilité. Le communiqué publié le 12 novembre par le Parti communiste français offre un point d’appui : il réaffirme le droit à l’autodétermination, exprime sa solidarité avec le Front Polisario et demande une politique française conforme au droit international. Il rappelle surtout qu’une solution durable ne peut être décidée à la place des Sahraouis. Cette exigence doit devenir un sujet de débat public et d’interpellation des responsables politiques.
C’est aussi le sens du travail mené par la diaspora sahraouie et les associations de solidarité. La conférence organisée à Paris par le Comité action et réflexion pour l’avenir du Sahara occidental (Caraso) et le PCF Paris 18e a permis de réunir informations, témoignages et échanges.
Ces rencontres contribuent à faire comprendre ce qui se joue derrière les décisions diplomatiques. Elles doivent se prolonger par le soutien aux défenseurs des droits humains et aux familles de prisonniers, par l’exigence d’un accès des journalistes et des observateurs au territoire, et par des initiatives auprès des élus.
Comme militant sahraoui, je défends l’indépendance de mon peuple et son droit de choisir librement son avenir. Les valeurs que nous défendons au Sahara occidental sont aussi les vôtres : la liberté, la justice, la paix et la dignité humaine. Notre combat rejoint celui de tous ceux qui refusent l’injustice et défendent le droit des peuples à disposer d’eux-mêmes. Soutenir le peuple sahraoui, c’est faire vivre ces principes universels.
Le départ de la Minurso ne dispense personne de cette exigence. Il rend plus pressante la recherche de garanties internationales, d’échéances crédibles et d’actes qui protègent les populations. Le « R » du référendum désigne une promesse faite à un peuple. La fermeture d’une mission ne doit pas devenir le moyen de l’effacer.
Être le journal de la paix, notre défi quotidien
Depuis Jaurès, la défense de la paix est dans notre ADN.
- Qui informe encore aujourd’hui sur les actions des pacifistes pour le désarmement ?
- Combien de médias rappellent que les combats de décolonisation ont encore cours, et qu’ils doivent être soutenus ?
- Combien valorisent les solidarités internationales, et s’engagent sans ambiguïté aux côtés des exilés ?
Nos valeurs n’ont pas de frontières.
Aidez-nous à soutenir le droit à l’autodétermination et l’option de la paix.
Je veux en savoir plus !
