https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in New York
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Judd Tully
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.
Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.
Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.
Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.
Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.
Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a new home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).
A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.
The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.
Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.
Gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.
Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in New York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.
A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).
A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.
Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.
The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime New York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.)
Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.
Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.
The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.
Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.
Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and important champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.
The evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.)
Apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca said. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”
The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

https://apache.be/2026/11/20/open-brief-.title: Open brief: “Kinderrechten hoef je niet te verdienen”
https://apache.be/2026/11/20/open-brief-.author: Netwerk Kinderrechten
https://apache.be/2026/11/20/open-brief-.text:
Op 20 november 1989 maakten wereldleiders samen een belofte aan alle kinderen: kinderen hebben rechten. Vandaag, 37 jaar later, zien de ondertekenaars van deze open brief dat die belofte steeds meer onder druk komt te staan. Kinderrechten kunnen niet gegarandeerd worden als overheden sociale rechten afbreken en besparen op dienstverlening.
Dagelijks zien onze organisaties honderden kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen. We zien wat het betekent wanneer rechten gewaarborgd en gerealiseerd worden. Maar we zien ook wat er gebeurt wanneer ondersteuning afhankelijk wordt gemaakt van steeds meer voorwaarden.
Kinderen die opgroeien in een onzekere woonsituatie. Kinderen voor wie geen plaats is in de kinderopvang. Kinderen die maanden wachten op een plek in de jeugdhulp. Kinderen met een ouder in detentie. Kinderen met een handicap die soms jaren moeten wachten op gepaste ondersteuning. Kinderen die niet welkom zijn op school, of die niet op kamp kunnen omdat het te duur is. En dit is slechts een greep uit heel veel voorbeelden.
Het is aan overheden om inspanningen te leveren voor kinderen die, vanwege hun omstandigheden, bijkomende noden hebben
Deze kinderen betalen de prijs voor omstandigheden waar ze geen controle over hebben. Dat mogen we als samenleving niet normaliseren. 
Niet elk kind en elk gezin beschikt over gelijkwaardige mogelijkheden, middelen of kansen. Minderjarigen hebben bovendien minder controle over hun eigen leven en zijn, meer dan anderen, afhankelijk van de acties en beslissingen van volwassenen. 
Het Kinderrechtenverdrag, dat ontstond vanuit de internationale politieke wil om kinderen te beschermen, schrijft voor dat de kansen van kinderen niet mogen afhangen van omstandigheden waar zij zelf geen vat op hebben. Daarom zijn overheden verplicht om de rechten van alle kinderen te waarborgen, zonder discriminatie. Dat betekent dat de realisatie van rechten niet afhankelijk mag zijn van inkomen, handicap, afkomst of andere omstandigheden van het kind of de ouders. Integendeel: het is net aan overheden om inspanningen te leveren voor kinderen die, vanwege hun omstandigheden, bijkomende noden hebben. 
Wanneer toegang tot rechten afhankelijk wordt van steeds meer voorwaarden, dreigen rechten in de praktijk gunsten te worden. Extra voorwaarden voor sociaal wonen, zoals lokale binding, werkbereidheid en voldoende taalkennis, zetten een rem op het recht op wonen. De besparingen bij De Lijn dreigen vervoersarmoede te vergroten, waardoor ook meer kinderen en jongeren moeilijk op school, bij de dokter of op vrijetijdsactiviteiten raken. Daarnaast maken de snellere sancties binnen het Groeipakket bij problematische schoolafwezigheden gezinnen en kinderen in een kwetsbare situatie nog kwetsbaarder. 
Die evolutie is niet onschuldig. Als voorwaarden de toegang tot rechten onmogelijk maken voor wie die het meest nodig heeft, versterken we onrecht. De verantwoordelijkheid voor structurele 
ongelijkheid verschuift dan van de samenleving naar individuele gezinnen en kinderen. Zo duwen we wie al kwetsbaar is nog dieper in de put. De gevolgen voor kinderen zijn voelbaar thuis, op school en in hun gezondheid. Kinderrechten waarmaken is een collectieve verantwoordelijkheid. 
Individuele inzet kan niet opvangen wat structurele beleidskeuzes onmogelijk maken
Heel wat mensen zeten zich in voor kinderrechten: middenveldorganisaties, leerkrachten, jeugdwerkers, leefgroepbegeleiders, jeugdadvocaten, vrijwilligers, onderzoekers en ambtenaren. Hun engagement maakt dagelijks het verschil voor kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen. Maar wat zij kunnen betekenen, wordt begrensd door de beleidskeuzes van politici. Individuele inzet kan immers niet opvangen wat structurele beleidskeuzes onmogelijk maken.
Op Internationale Kinderrechtendag roepen wij beleidsmakers op om de belofte na te komen die in 1989 werd gemaakt: kinderrechten zijn geen gunsten, maar fundamentele rechten voor elk kind. We vragen hen om maatregelen systematisch af te toetsen aan hun impact op kinderen en jongeren. Om voldoende te investeren in collectieve voorzieningen die rechten daadwerkelijk waarmaken. En om actief te luisteren naar de ervaringen van kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen.
Beleid dat kinderen armer, onzekerder of minder kansrijk maakt, is geen goed beleid. De vraag is niet of kinderen hun rechten verdienen. De vraag is of wij als samenleving bereid zijn ze te garanderen.
De dertig lidorganisaties van Netwerk Kinderrechten namen het initiatief voor deze open brief. Nog eens 60 andere organisaties, 21 personen verbonden aan hogescholen en universiteiten en 26 andere 
individuele ondertekenaars schaarden zich achter de oproep. Hieronder ziet u de volledige lijst.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Christie’s Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
Christie’s finished out New York’s fall auction week on Thursday evening at its Rockefeller Center salesroom, bringing in $145.9 million in a 56-lot sale of 21st-century art (after works by Jeff Koons and Ed Ruscha, estimated to sell for as much as $11 million between them, were withdrawn). Leading the sale was a $32.9 million Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that fell just shy of its low estimate.
The sale included 20 works from the collection of Antonio Homem, longtime director of the storied Sonnabend Gallery, which was founded by his adoptive mother, Ileana Sonnabend. Sold to benefit their foundation, the works totaled $41.9 million. Also on offer were 10 works from the estate of beloved New York philanthropist Agnes Gund, who died last year, totaling $25.7 million.
After the withdrawals, the sale was estimated to bring between $126 million and $192 million; the hammer total on the night fell considerably shy at $117.7 million. Over the two-hour sale, the house found buyers for 51 lots, for a sell-through rate of 91 percent. Works by John Currin, William Eggleston, Wade Guyton, Gerhard Richter, and Yayoi Kusama failed to sell.
Many prominent advisors were in the room, including Erica Barrish, Amy Cappellazzo, Ralph DeLuca, and Gabriela Palmieri, as well as well-known dealers like Marianne Boesky, Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn, and Christophe Van de Weghe. But there were a notable number of empty seats, and the atmosphere was unmistakably enervated after a long week of sales.
The sale started inauspiciously, with the first 19 lots, all from the Sonnabend collection, failing to hammer above their estimates. Bidding picked up only on the final lot of that trove, Jean Prouvé’s Table “Centrale” (“Trapèze”), petit modèle. The piece sold after five minutes of bidding between several specialists and a bidder in the room, before Sara Friedlander, Christie’s chairman of postwar and contemporary art in the Americas, nabbed it with a winning bid of $1.3 million. With fees, the total came to $1.7 million on a $700,000–$1 million estimate. But, all told, 10 of the 20 Sonnabend lots hammered below estimate. The collection hammered for $33.4 million, or $41.9 million with fees, against a pre-sale estimate of $35.25 million to $53.15 million (minus the withdrawn Koons, Wild Boy and Puppy). Not great any way you slice it.
The most notable of the Sonnabend works was Andy Warhol’s 1962 painting Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), tagged at $6–$8 million. The soup cans show one of Warhol’s most iconic images and are practically synonymous with Pop art. Adrien Meyer, global head of private sales and the auctioneer at Tuesday evening’s 20th-century sale, traded bids with a bidder in the room, who nailed it down with a $7.3 million bid, translating to $9 million all in.
Also from the trove was Roy Lichtenstein’s Large Spool (1963). Standing nearly six feet high, the work had been off the market since the Sonnabends bought it from Leo Castelli Gallery four years after it was painted. It has hung in museums all over the world, and its sale comes amid a major Lichtenstein retrospective at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art. Auctioneer Yu-Ge Wang tossed out a handful of absentee bids from the rostrum before Friedlander got it for her client with a $7 million bid, for a total of $8.6 million with fees. The work’s pre-sale estimate was $10 million to $15 million.
Jeff Koons’s six-foot-high sculpture Hulk (Friends), 2004–12, also from the Sonnabend collection, shows the comic-book hero with small creatures perched on his shoulders and was estimated at $3.5–$5.5 million. It hammered after only a few bids at $3.3 million, or $4.15 million with fees, to the house’s Michael Baptist. (Koons was also a seller this week, bringing seven artworks to auction at Christie’s on Tuesday night, totaling $104 million.)
Bidding improved marginally from there, but for the most part, this was a sleepy sale. Even the biggest attraction of the night, Basquiat’s much-touted painting Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), which dates to 1983 and measures seven feet square, failed to generate much excitement. Wang opened the bidding at $23 million, and for a few long moments it seemed there would be no bids. Then Ana Maria Celis, head of postwar and contemporary art, rescued the painting, beating out Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president and global chairman of 20th- and 21st-century art. It hammered at $28 million and sold for $32.9 million with the house’s fees.
The hammer price was just shy of the $30–$50 million estimate. But the work, inspired by a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci, had been off the market for two decades, so the seller no doubt made a tidy profit. The painter’s auction market has famously exploded in the intervening years: every one of his paintings to sell for more than $10 million, all 83 of them, has done so since then.
The large canvas, featuring the artist’s trademark scratchy messages and the titular sketchy heads against an orange background, had appreciated enormously since its previous trips to the block. It appeared at Sotheby’s London in 2000, when it fetched just above $400,000, within estimate, and again at the same house five years later, when it tripled in value to bring an above-estimate $1.3 million.
Vija Celmins’s 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean) was one of the few lots of the evening to generate a genuine bidding war. The painting came from the Gund estate; Gund bought it the year after it was painted. It drew bids from Joanna Szymkowiak, head of private sales; Arco Yu, a Christie’s Hong Kong specialist; and a woman bidding in the room. For four minutes, the three traded incremental bids until the room bidder won out. Still, that brought the hammer to only $5.75 million, just under the $6 million low estimate. With fees, the total came to $7.1 million.
The 10 Gund works fared better than those from the Sonnabend collection, hammering for $20.4 million on a $16.95 million to $24.65 million pre-sale estimate. With fees, the total squeaked past the high estimate to reach $25.7 million.
There wasn’t much rhythm to the proceedings. A 1990 Gerhard Richter Abstraktes Bild painting from the estate of legendary art dealer Marian Goodman, who long represented the artist and bought the work from him that year, carried a $6 million to $8 million estimate. It failed to sell after garnering no bids. Three lots later, another Abstraktes Bild, from 1991, measuring three feet square and dominated by red, blue, and green, sparked a short contest between Friedlander and Rotter. Rotter eventually won it with a $7.6 million bid. With fees, the total came to $9.4 million. The painting’s pre-sale estimate was $7 million to $10 million.
“The estimates were too high for this market,” Greenberg Rohatyn told ARTnews on her way out of the salesroom partway through the night. “We need to readjust, and the houses need to be at the forefront of managing expectations.”
Boesky agreed that the estimates were too high. “And the energy was low,” she said on her way out. “The lots that were estimated too high were punished, and those estimated low were rewarded.”
On a brighter note, a few records were notched: Jim Nutt ($1.1 million), Antonio Santín ($486,400), and Julia Jo ($409,600).
The Jo, a swirling, gestural abstraction of fiery oranges and yellows breaking against cool blues and teals, was the night’s final lot, estimated at $30,000–$50,000. Sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, the abstraction generated arguably the most spirited bidding of the evening. Wang opened bidding at $20,000, and it quickly climbed into the hundreds of thousands as a cacophony of specialists and a bidder in the room called out bids. It eventually went to the room bidder at a hammer price of $320,000, or $403,200 with fees. That set off a hearty round of applause, at least for one lot.
The sale finished out an auction week that started Monday with a two-part $378.7 million Sotheby’s auction including works from cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum as well as a various-owner The Now and Contemporary sale. Christie’s staged a nearly three-hour 20th-century sale on Tuesday that totaled $626.6 million, led by a record-breaking $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The same night, Phillips sold $104.4 million in modern and contemporary art on Tuesday, led by a $44.6 million Amedeo Modigliani sculpture. On Wednesday, Sotheby’s staged a $777.8 million Impressionist and modern art sale, led by a record-breaking $190.4 million Vincent van Gogh.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-shuts.title: Mamdani shuts Bronx migrant shelter at center of ICE fight over residents’ data
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-shuts.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-shuts.text:
The Mamdani administration closed the last remaining migrant shelter, a Mott Haven facility that was the target of an ICE subpoena seeking the names and birthdays of men residing there.
Lawyers for the city filed a letter in court late Thursday night arguing the South Bronx shelter’s closure rendered the subpoena moot since there are no current residents to identify, a copy of the filing shared with Gothamist shows.
“There will be no more residents living inside of Bruckner, and the site is officially closed,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Our administration believes that every homeless New Yorker should not only have access to shelter but to spaces that are safe, humane and truly livable. We cannot accept a system that treats people without dignity or stability.”
The megashelter on Bruckner Boulevard, that once housed as many as 2,000 migrant men, was slated to shut down by the end of the year under an executive order signed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The order directed city agencies to phase out its remaining emergency migrant shelter and bring other facilities into compliance with city rules, such as capping the number of residents at 200.
A federal judge earlier this month ordered the Mamdani administration to hand over the personal information of certain residents staying in the shelter. U.S. Customs and Border Protection argued the information was needed to investigate whether anyone inside the facility was subject to deportation.
Under the judge’s November ruling, the city and ICE agreed to the appointment of a special master who would identify shelter residents with serious criminal histories, and arrange for their information to be turned over.
Under the Trump administration, ICE had tried at least four times to obtain information about shelter residents. But the city fended off those requests.
It’s not clear how many residents were living in the facility in the weeks before it closed. But as recently as this summer, the shelter was still home to 1,500 residents, many of whom were migrants from Latin America or West Africa.
City officials said some of the residents had left and found housing or were staying with friends. Others were relocated within the city’s municipal shelter system.
The Bruckner location was operated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing Recovery Operations and first opened in February 2025. It was one of about 250 sites propped up under the former Adams administration to accommodate the influx of asylum seekers in 2024.
Many of those sites skirted stringent rules imposed on traditional homeless shelters. For example they did not provide kitchens for homeless families with children, and they ignored rules about how far apart the beds should be. The migrant population has declined in recent years, allowing the city to close these sites,
Several residents inside Bruckner had previously complained about poor conditions, like bad food and bug infestations.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: IZA destaca a força política do reggae ao lançar “ZAZA” no Dia da Consciência Negra
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Wallace Leray
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Antes de cantar para o país inteiro, IZA já cantava reggae em bailes, casamentos e batizados. Foi com “Pesadão” que sua voz ganhou projeção nacional, e é àquela época que ela volta para explicar o que buscava em “ZAZA”, seu terceiro álbum de estúdio, que chega às plataformas nesta sexta-feira (20), Dia da Consciência Negra. Com dez anos de carreira, a cantora queria recuperar um pouco da liberdade de escolher o que cantar sem antecipar o que o público esperava ouvir. “Eu sempre enxergo o reggae como a minha primeira porta”, disse.
A escolha do 20 de novembro veio quando o álbum já estava quase pronto. Ao olhar o calendário, IZA encontrou na data uma ligação com o que ouvia no reggae desde os primeiros palcos. “Acho que o reggae é um estilo musical social, político, de resgate, de denúncia às vezes, de elevação da autoestima, pertencimento e ancestralidade”, afirmou em coletiva na quarta-feira (18), após a exibição do filme musical “IZA apresenta Rádio ZAZA”, no Cine Marquise, em São Paulo. “Dia 20 tava gritando ali, né, porque fazia muito sentido”, completa.
O caminho de volta ao reggae passou por São Luís. Para gravar “Reggae Maranhão”, uma das 13 faixas do disco, IZA procurava alguém que trouxesse para a música a experiência de quem canta reggae na capital maranhense. “Não faria sentido eu fazer essa música sozinha, e encontrei a Núbia, e foi amor à primeira vista”, conta.
Na voz de Núbia, IZA ouve uma continuidade com a geração que abriu caminho para as mulheres no reggae do Maranhão. “A Núbia, para mim, é a sucessora da dona Célia Sampaio”, afirmou. A busca teve um paralelo no dancehall. Embora já tivesse cantado o gênero, IZA queria gravar com alguém que fizesse parte daquela cena. Foi o que a aproximou de Mya Akoma, que divide com ela e King Saints os vocais da faixa “Dancehall”.
Pedir licença
Ao falar dessas parcerias, IZA fez uma distinção entre o alcance da música negra e o espaço que seus criadores encontram para cantá-la. “O mundo tá muito acostumado a consumir música preta, mas não quer consumir os artistas pretos”, disse.
Mesmo com o reggae presente em sua trajetória desde os primeiros palcos, ela sentiu que gravar um disco inteiro dedicado ao gênero exigia escutar quem o mantém vivo. “Eu sinto que ele sempre foi nosso, sempre foi meu, mas eu também senti a necessidade de pedir licença”, ressalta.
ZAZA é também o nome do alter ego que IZA assume no projeto. A pesquisa que começou com o reggae do Maranhão passou pela música da Jamaica e chegou ao Egito antigo. “Eu comecei com essa pira de Kemet, por querer descender e acreditar que existe alguma fração em mim dessa nobreza, né?”, contou. Outra referência africana aparece em “Sankofa”, faixa que leva o nome de um conceito da tradição akan sobre buscar no passado aquilo que pode orientar o futuro.
De mãe para filha
IZA já queria contar essa história antes do nascimento de Nala. A maternidade, no entanto, deu outra dimensão ao que significa para ela se reconhecer como mulher negra. “Eu acho que eu acolho minha criança quando eu olho para a Nala”, disse. Para a cantora, os privilégios com que a filha cresce não vão poupá-la de viver situações de racismo que ela própria conheceu na infância.
Em casa, essa preocupação se traduz em gestos cotidianos. Nala vê a mãe acordar, chorar e se frustrar. IZA quer que a filha também a veja falar sobre o que sente. “Eu tenho que falar sobre os meus medos, eu tenho que dizer para ela quando eu tô frustrada, para que ela entenda também que ela também pode”, afirma.
Se Nala a faz olhar para a menina que foi, é na história das mulheres mais velhas da família que IZA procura entender a própria fé. Catequizada e crismada, ela começou a cantar na Igreja Católica. Na família, há também praticantes do candomblé, da umbanda e do espiritismo.
Ao recordar a tataravó indígena, que vivia em uma aldeia, a cantora chamou de “inteligência ancestral” a intuição que reconhece nas mulheres de casa. “Eu sinto que eu tô ampliando minha visão, ampliando meu olhar, me entendendo como bruxa também, no melhor sentido da palavra. Me entendendo como guardiã da sabedoria das mulheres que vieram antes de mim”, destaca.
Uma rádio jamaicana
Pensado desde o início para ganhar o palco, “ZAZA” chega também em um filme de uma hora. Dirigido por Felipe Sassi, “IZA apresenta Rádio ZAZA” reúne a cantora, sua banda e os convidados do álbum no cenário de uma rádio jamaicana. Núbia também participa do filme.
Para gravar as 13 faixas, IZA reuniu a banda inteira na mesma sala. As sessões registraram também o resultado de um trabalho que ela vinha fazendo todos os dias com a própria voz. Depois de um período em que sentiu o timbre mais grave, a cantora começou a recuperar os agudos. “ZAZA já faz parte de uma cura, sabe? De meus agudos voltando, eu botando voz de cabeça de novo, uma coisa que eu tinha feito lá em ‘Dona de Mim’”, conta.
Antes que o público pudesse ouvir o disco, a capa já circulava fora do Brasil. IZA, que está há mais de sete meses sem aplicativos de redes sociais no celular, soube da repercussão por telefone. Sassi foi um dos que ligaram.
“A gente sabia que a gente estava fazendo a capa na hora em que a gente tava fotografando, mas em nenhum momento imaginei que as pessoas fossem se conectar tanto com aquilo”, disse.
Na imagem, a cantora aparece entre caixas de som azuis. A ideia era que a foto parecesse uma página de revista de moda dos anos 1990 que passou por uma fotocopiadora, com “essa estética meio lavada, mas ao mesmo tempo super contrastada”. Entre as referências, ela citou editoriais com Erykah Badu, Lauryn Hill, D’Angelo e TLC.
A cantora também confirmou que “ZAZA” será o primeiro disco de sua carreira a ganhar edição em vinil. A turnê está prevista para 2027, com datas a serem anunciadas após o Carnaval.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/the-sup.title: The Superintelligence Racket
https://inthesetimes.com/article/the-sup.author: Alberto Toscano
https://inthesetimes.com/article/the-sup.text:
The Superintelligence Racket
In the face of rising opposition to data centers, the AI industry is holding us for ransom.
Alberto Toscano
In the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, opened on the Nasdaq on Nov. 19 at a valuation of about $2 trillion.
Its 335-page prospectus, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Oct. 26, devotes 93 pages to risk factors and declares that AI systems could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” especially if “misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
Sociologist Charles Tilly once defined a racketeer as someone who “produces a danger and, at a price, the shield against it.” By that definition, the AI industry is operating like a racket. And we are being asked to accept U.S. imperialism as the shield against its dangers.
On the face of it, the AI industry’s warnings of possible human extinction seem a bizarre departure from how companies should do marketing. And yet it makes sense.
The industry holds populations, governments and even markets hostage, while warning that failure to risk everything for the “superintelligence” project — even geopolitical stability — could spell “p(doom)” for us all.
After former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and made the media rounds, Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger personally put the odds of AI triggering human extinction within a decade at greater than 10%. The company’s public filing does not refute that. On the contrary, estimating the odds of an irreversible, AI-driven cataclysm — “p(doom)” in industry shorthand — is so routine that the depiction of Coxon as a whistleblower is hard to sell.
Scratch under the surface of the apocalyptic tone frequently used when discussing AI, and you will find eminently economic and political concerns, such as speculation on tech stocks and big spending on data centers and semiconductor chips. These have been the primary drivers of U.S. economic growth and a buoyant stock market.
Advanced AI models, like those built by Anthropic and OpenAI, require colossal cloud-computing infrastructure, and that buildout has put the companies driving it at the core of today’s capitalist economy. They include both “hyperscalers,” such as Amazon, Alphabet (Google), Meta (Facebook) and Microsoft and chip designers and producers, like Nvidia, TSMC and Broadcom. Speculation about AI’s impact on the future of humanity is now inextricable from their bottom lines. Their warnings of catastrophe and their pursuit of profit have become one and the same enterprise. This is the superintelligence racket. 
In the wake of Coxon’s revelations of the end, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry to “pace the frontier.” Critics quickly labeled this a ploy to promote “regulatory capture” — rules shaped to favor the firms already on top — using the specter of catastrophic risk to dig a “moat” against competitors.
As the journalist Steve Howell put it, Amodei’s strategy was “to form a cartel with the other major players so that they work at the same pace, while disadvantaging emerging rivals through regulation.”
Big Tech companies, while competitors in some respects (the hyperscalers have rival AI arms), are profoundly interlocked — from their financial structures to their supply chains to the political strategies they pursue in Washington. Anthropic’s IPO makes this plain.
Amazon, Google and Microsoft are at once Anthropic’s investors, customers, cloud providers, distributors and competitors, according to its filing. Anthropic has committed to pay Google at least $121.3 billion, Amazon $110 billion and Microsoft $44.9 billion for computing power through the mid-2030s. It carries about $161.2 billion in equipment leases tied to the chip designer Broadcom.
The IPO, meanwhile, is a windfall for the same giants: Google’s $33 billion investment is now worth more than $140 billion, and Amazon’s $18 billion in early financing has ballooned to more than $250 billion, the New York Times reported. The company has also turned to special purpose vehicles (financial devices that played a key role in the 2008 financial crisis) to keep “massive hardware deployments entirely off its corporate balance sheet,” as Yahoo Finance previously reported.
In the frenzy to build the data centers required to run ever more demanding AI models, the companies that control the hardware — that design and fabricate the chips, build and manage the data centers — hold an important advantage. Industry commentators have called them “compute landlords,” stressing their outsize power over the sector.
Chip designer Nvidia sits high on the list of global companies ranked by market capitalization and has accordingly been described as the AI boom’s “bank.” (Nvidia’s stock fell sharply after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid a scandal over his affair with an executive of a Singapore-based company, who U.S. officials reportedly believe was passing information to China. But it remains the second most highly valued company after Apple.)
Those who discern the lineaments of a bubble point to Nvidia’s “circular financing.” Typically, Nvidia has invested billions in data infrastructure built by companies like OpenAI, and, in turn, these companies have populated their servers with Nvidia chips. But this tells us little or nothing about the customer demand or productivity gains that would justify the trillion-dollar valuations of AI companies.
Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI has demonstrated an ability to reliably turn a profit. Yet the perceived centrality of AI to U.S. economic dominance and military primacy has been touted by the White House. As President Donald Trump wrote in September:
In the wake of Coxon’s apocalyptic declarations, Trump dismissed demands to regulate AI — a product subject to fewer rules than milk or washing machines, according to the president of Microsoft. Instead, he summoned Big Tech executives, including Amodei, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Huang and OpenAI president Greg Brockman, to a White House lunch to sign a “constitution” aimed at coordinating federal policy and corporate strategy, and a few days later announced the creation of a “Superintelligence Task Force” to help ensure U.S. leadership in AI development. Trump then proceeded to promote AI’s new designation of superintelligence, or “SI”: From now on, use of the term artificial intelligence would be treasonous, as he implied on Truth Social: 
Trump’s semantic preference likely owes less to the philosopher Nick Bostrom, whose book Superintelligence helped shape the industry’s doom talk, than to the idea that saying AI “makes it sound fake.”
For Trump and his entourage, AI is crucial to U.S. dominance. (“WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” Trump declared on Truth Social.)
This dream of unchecked primacy is shared even by Big Tech companies outside of MAGA’s far-right inner circle. As the diplomat and historian Julian Gewirtz noted, Amodei believes that, in Gewirtz’s words, “getting ahead now could allow the U.S. to prevent anyone from ever catching up.”
Amodei calls this an “eternal 1991”: the West’s moment of triumph after the Cold War prolonged indefinitely by AI. This is the Faustian bargain tech oligarchs champion. The possibility of human extinction must be countenanced. After all, eternal domination is at hand.
The AI oligopoly is animated by its pact with unending U.S. global dominance. This pact has even led some oligarchs, like Palantir CEO Alex Karp, to envisage a “nationalization” of the industry, in which the federal state assumes the technology’s “unlimited risks.”
The industry’s turn to the state, even to fantasies of state capitalism, is entirely unsurprising. How could this industry — which feeds on gargantuan investments in fixed capital infrastructure and skyrocketing quantities of energy and water — not turn to the concentrated power of the state as its ultimate guarantor?
As tech analyst Paris Marx has observed, the AI industry is “incentivized to make most clients’ business more computationally intensive to guarantee revenue.” It is this imperative that makes it such a threat to local communities and collective survival. As OpenAI CEO Sam Altman fantasized: “I do guess that a lot of the world gets covered in data centers over time.”
As Anthropic’s SEC prospectus makes clear, it is not the obliteration of mankind that keeps AI moguls up at night. That would be the questionable viability of their business model, which is predicated on lack of regulation and suppression of dissent. In other words, it is not human, but corporate extinction that they fear.
More so than firms with more diverse revenue streams, Anthropic is vulnerable to regulatory changes — especially when it comes to its infrastructure. As the prospectus notes, the company’s “collective data center infrastructure is currently concentrated primarily in the United States, which exposes us to risks associated with regional regulatory changes, power grid constraints or failures, disruptions to network connectivity between facilities, natural disasters, physical attacks — including those motivated by geopolitical events, opposition to AI and opposition to data center development.” 
Popular discontent with data center buildout and its disastrous effects on the planet is a critical risk AI firms are strategizing against. Their alliance with an administration that is ratcheting up its repression of dissidence is no mystery.
Already, federal security agencies have identified “anti-tech violent extremism” as a counterterrorism threat. The warning signs of what may lie ahead are flashing. As protests of AI’s social, economic and ecological effects, and its signal contribution to war and genocide, continue, opposition is being framed as a threat to U.S. national security and the viability of a leading sector of U.S. capital.
The Anthropic prospectus can be understood as, among other things, a planning document for a preemptive struggle against social opposition to AI primacy. This opposition was incontrovertibly felt in the “blue wave” of the November midterms. A Democrat won a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, arguably the nucleus of the data center boom, for the first time since 1988. Democrats also took over the Texas House of Representatives. This was after public pressure had caused outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott to institute a moratorium on new data centers. And across the country, ballot measures curtailing or forbidding data center buildout prevailed in 46 out of 47 cases, mostly with ample margins.
While we can’t quite say that data factories are sites of class struggle, the intimate link between AI capital and the growing movement against it shows that the industry has a class consciousness of its own.
Wall Street clearly isn’t flinching yet, but Anthropic’s own prospectus lists opposition to data center development among the risks to its business. AI capitalists know that movement could collapse their model, and they’re using warnings of extinction to postpone their own demise. The superintelligence racket is one we all need to protect ourselves from.
ALBERTO TOSCANO is the author of Late Fascism: Race, Capitalism and the Politics of Crisis (Verso) and Terms of Disorder: Keywords for an Interregnum (Seagull). He lives in Vancouver.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/dubai/.title: Photos d’exécutions, tonnes de cocaïne, millions en liasses : comment la police a infiltré Sky ECC, la messagerie du crime organisé
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/dubai/.author: Bruno Rieth
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/dubai/.text:
Pendant des semaines, des enquêteurs ont été « assis à la table des trafiquants les plus importants du monde », après avoir réussi à pirater Sky ECC, une des messageries préférées du narcobanditisme. Retour sur ce coup de force technologique que raconte la série documentaire la Messagerie du diable.
La lutte contre le crime organisé est un sport hybride, au carrefour du marathon et du sprint. Pour les connaisseurs, cela revient à se lancer dans une course fractionnée qui alterne les phases d’accélération et de relâche, mais sur des centaines de milliers de kilomètres. Avec parfois des sections sacrément pentues, dignes d’un « véritable Everest technologique », selon un enquêteur chevronné.
« Les acteurs du crime organisé sont très tech-friendly ! Le capitalisme criminel a besoin de prestataires de services pour développer ses affaires. Nous sommes dans une course effrénée à la technologie avec nos concurrents. Tout l’enjeu est de ne pas se faire distancer », nous confiait, il y a un peu plus d’un an et demi, le colonel de gendarmerie Florian Manet, à la tête de la division des enquêtes spécialisées, de la donnée et des investigations techniques (DEDT). Cette unité du commandement du ministère de l’Intérieur pour le cyberespace (COMCYBER-MI), aussi discrète qu’efficace, a accroché au fil des ans de nombreux trophées à son tableau de chasse : EncroChat, Sky ECC ou encore Ghost.
Des noms peu connus du grand public, mais très populaires au sein des organisations criminelles internationales. Du moins, tant que ces technologies de cryptographie des communications sont restées imperméables aux oreilles policières. Comme celle de Sky ECC, développée par la société canadienne Sky Global, et dont le procès devait s’ouvrir le 26 octobre 2026 devant la cour d’assises spéciale de Paris – il a finalement été reporté.
Elle a en revanche été au cœur...

https://taz.de/Serbiens-neuer-Parlaments.title: Serbiens neuer Parlamentspräsident: Der ruhige Mann mit dem wilden Bart
https://taz.de/Serbiens-neuer-Parlaments.author: Andrej Ivanji
https://taz.de/Serbiens-neuer-Parlaments.text:
Serbiens neuer Parlamentspräsident: Der ruhige Mann mit dem wilden Bart
Aleksandar Čupić ist neuer Parlamentspräsident in Serbien. Es ist das erste öffentliche Amt, das ein Vertreter der Studentenliste bekleidet.
Der derzeit mächtigste Mann Serbiens trägt einen langen, wilden, grauen Bart. Er ist Vater von sechs Kindern, Professor an der Verkehrswissenschaftlichen Fakultät und betreibt einen ökologischen Landwirtschaftsbetrieb am Stadtrand von Belgrad. In jeder Hinsicht widerspricht er dem Bild, das sich die Serben bislang von Politikern gemacht haben.
Aleksandar Čupić (48) wurde am Donnerstag zum Präsidenten des serbischen Parlaments gewählt. Bis zur Präsidentschaftswahl, die spätestens Ende des Jahres stattfinden muss, übernimmt er zugleich die Amtsgeschäfte des Staatspräsidenten und des Oberbefehlshabers der serbischen Streitkräfte. Es ist das erste öffentliche Amt, das ein Vertreter der Studentenliste bekleidet, die bei den vorgezogenen Parlamentswahlen das autokratische Regime des ehemaligen serbischen Präsidenten Aleksandar Vučić deutlich besiegt hatte.
Als Abgeordnete der früheren Regierungspartei versuchten, die parlamentarische Arbeit mit endlosen Redebeiträgen, Beleidigungen, Zwischenrufen und Provokationen zu sabotieren, wies sie Čupić mit der Ruhe eines Professors und Geduld eines Biobauers in ihre Schranken.
Vučić, bis vor Kurzem noch unangefochtener Herrscher Serbiens und inzwischen Fraktionschef der Opposition, brachte diese Gelassenheit derart auf die Palme, dass er wütend ausrief, er könne Čupić nicht mehr ansehen, so widerwärtig sei ihm dessen Anblick, und drohte, sein Abgeordnetenmandat zurückzugeben. Vučić hatte Serbien in eine persönliche Beutezone verwandelt und ein System parteipolitischer Willkür errichtet.
Erster Kontakt zur Studentenbewegung vor zwei Jahren
Seinen ersten Kontakt mit der Studentenbewegung hatte Čupić im Dezember 2024. Damals besetzten die Studierenden ihre Fakultäten und begannen mit Protesten, die sich zu einem landesweiten gesellschaftlichen Aufstand ausweiten sollten. Die Studenten luden ihn gemeinsam mit drei weiteren Professoren zu einer Diskussionsveranstaltung ein.
Trotz Bedenken ging er hin, denn er war überzeugt, dass Professoren an der Seite ihrer Studenten stehen müssten, um sie zu schützen. Selbst dann, wenn sie für Ziele demonstrierten, die er persönlich nicht teilte. Die Teilnahme an diesem studentischen Plenum veränderte ihn.
In einem Interview mit dem politischen Magazin Vreme schilderte er, wie sehr ihn die Konzentration beeindruckt habe, die eine mehrstündige Debatte erfordere. Noch stärker habe ihn die Art und Weise überrascht, wie die Studierenden miteinander kommunizierten. Statt des erwarteten Wettstreits habe er erlebt, wie unterschiedliche Argumente tatsächlich angehört wurden und eine Entscheidung erst fiel, nachdem auch die Einwände der Minderheit berücksichtigt worden waren.
Eine Kultur des Dialogs und ein Neustart
„Ich war positiv verblüfft. Mir wurde klar, dass sie besser miteinander kommunizieren als irgendjemand sonst in unserem gesellschaftlichen System. Diese Kultur des Dialogs scheint außerhalb dieser Gesellschaft und dieser Zeit zu existieren“, sagte Čupić.
Er ist überzeugt, dass das serbische politische System einen Neustart braucht. Erst danach könne ein breiter gesellschaftlicher Dialog beginnen, an dessen Ende eine Verständigung darüber stehen müsse, wie es mit dem Land weitergeht.
Bescheiden, der Antipode eines Politikers, fast wie ein Demokratiepilger im Parlament, setzt Čupić auf drei zentrale Prinzipien: Dialog, die Erneuerung der Institutionen und Verantwortlichkeit. In der Studentenbewegung erkannte er ein Modell, das auf die staatlichen Institutionen übertragen werden sollte.
Nun hat er die Gelegenheit, das zu verwirklichen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Cop31 live: crunch time as deeply divided climate talks enter final day
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Matthew Pearce
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Cop31 heads towards another late finish amid bitter divisions
Graham Readfearn
Welcome to the final day of Cop31 in Antalya where the hosts Turkey and the president of negotiations, Australia, will bring the UN climate summit to a gentle and uneventful close and everyone will go home on time.
Only joking.
Turkey and Australia face an uphill struggle today to bridge the practically permanent divides between rich developed countries and fossil fuel producers, and everyone else, on progressing climate action across a whole suite of areas.
An on-time finish isn’t impossible, but feels unlikely (the last time a Cop finished on time was Italy in 2003, according to Carbon Brief). We will probably still be here on Saturday (and possibly Sunday).
Turkey and Australia have pushed for a “cover decision” – an overarching agreement that sets the direction of travel for climate action, energy investment, science, climate finance and adaptation around the world.
The latest draft text came out yesterday afternoon, cutting the areas under discussion from more than 140 in Monday’s text to 79.
But it was derided for expunging the words “fossil fuels” while including “carbon capture and storage” – the technology mentioned so fulsomely by the fossil fuel industry for decades while delivering almost nothing.
The hoped for term to “transition away from fossil fuels” was replaced by a weaker pledge of an “irreversible global transition” to lower emissions and climate resilience.
This Cop is the first to admit that the 2015 Paris goal to work to limit global heating to 1.5C would be breached. Pacific countries want language to keep that goal alive.
And then what to do about Panama?
The UN climate convention works on consensus – meaning everyone has to agree. This protocol has been used in the past by high-emitting fossil fuel producers (looking at you, Saudi Arabia and Russia) to slow and block progress.
But Panama put a stake in the ground yesterday, writing to the Cop presidents to say it would formally object to any agreement that didn’t satisfy eight issues that run across plans to protect biodiversity, capping oil production at current levels, forcing big emitting countries to part with finance and changing the convention’s voting laws to allow majority voting instead of consensus.
Every day for the past two weeks, Turkish artist Ersut Biçkin has posted up in the breezy thoroughfare at the centre of the Blue Zone to beautifully transcribe names. Some have chosen to have their own names done. Others asked for causes or organisations. He’s done them all (along with some drawing or caricatures that were not publicly displayed).
On Friday morning a couple dozen people were waiting – perhaps the last chance to take a bit of personalised Turkish art home as the summit nears its end.
In a conversation through a interpreter, he estimated that he’s done thousands since COP31 began. It’s been a pleasure, he said, to meet so many people from around the world.
“I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.”
Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia.
As the Cop31 summit nears its close, with a scheduled finish of Friday but which is likely to push into the weekend, Pacific islanders are becoming increasingly frustrated with the UN’s decades-old system of annual climate summits.
The region has its own cash fund – the Pacific Resilience Facility – to pay for damages from climate-driven extremes and to prepare for the future.
The Australian government pledged US$67m (A$101m) three years ago, but the fund has otherwise struggled for support. It is still about US$300m (A$451m) short of a US$500m (A$751m) goal, and a “showcase” event at the summit with the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, garnered only one new offer – US$5m (A$7.5m) from Andrew Forrest, an Australian miner and philanthropist.
It is a far cry from what has been promised.
“Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word,” Ishoda says. “We have money for wars but not to save communities.”
The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).
But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.
Good morning. I’m Matthew Pearce, bringing you the Cop31 liveblog from London. Today is (supposedly) the final day of negotiations, and my colleagues on the ground will be guiding you through the conclusion of these contentious climate crisis talks.

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

- Over 115 strikes claimed by Iran or groups aligned with Tehran have damaged 26 military bases and other infrastructure belonging to the US across the Middle East, The Associated Press reported. The analysis, using satellite imagery, indicated that Iranian attacks on US sites in the region have mostly targeted early-warning systems, aircraft and buildings, resulting in billions of dollars’ worth of damage to US equipment.
- A Pentagon official told lawmakers that the US war on Iran has cost an estimated $48.3 billion. "That number includes munitions, equipment replacement costs, and operational cost," Arthur Miller said. However, the figure does not include the price of repairing US military installations in the region damaged since February.
- Israel’s Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter said on Thursday that the decision to renew strikes against Iran “will be taken by President Trump”. Speaking to US media outlet Newsmax, Leiter said Israel will support the US if Trump decides to attack Iran.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.title: Ukraine-Krieg | Willig auch bei wirtschaftlicher Unterstützung
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120401.text:
- Politik
- Ukraine-Krieg
Willig auch bei wirtschaftlicher Unterstützung
Am zweiten Tag des Ukraine-Gipfels in Berlin geht es um die Wirtschaft. Tags zuvor war der Krieg auch Thema bei einem historischen Treffen in China.
Berlin. Nach politischen Beratungen über einen Ausweg aus Russlands Angriffskrieg sprechen Vertreter der Ukraine und Deutschlands in Berlin heute über vertiefte wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit. Angesichts des bald fünf Jahre dauernden Kriegs soll die Kooperation im Rüstungs- und Energiesektor großen Raum einnehmen. Als Teilnehmer beim jährlichen Deutsch-Ukrainischen Wirtschaftsforum in Berlin werden auch Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (beide CDU) erwartet. Die Delegation aus Kiew führt Ministerpräsident Serhij Korezkyj an.
»Entscheidend ist, dass aus politischer Solidarität wirtschaftliche Perspektiven werden. Dafür brauchen Unternehmen Rahmenbedingungen, unter denen sie trotz erheblicher Risiken Aufträge übernehmen, investieren und Arbeitsplätze schaffen können«, sagte Peter Adrian, Präsident der Deutschen Industrie- und Handelskammer.
Zwei höchst verschiedene Gipfel am Donnerstag
Dem Wirtschaftsforum gingen zwei sehr unterschiedliche Gipfeltreffen am Donnerstag voraus. In der chinesischen Wirtschaftsmetropole Shenzhen kam es zum ersten Dreiertreffen des chinesischen Staatschefs Xi Jinping mit US-Präsident Donald Trump und Kreml-Chef Wladimir Putin. Neben der Gefährdung durch Atomwaffen ging es laut US-Angaben auch um den Ukraine-Krieg.
In Berlin kam unterdessen die »Koalition der Willigen« aus fast 40 Staaten, die die Ukraine politisch und militärisch unterstützen, zu ihrem bisher größten Treffen zusammen. Dort Merz appellierte an Putin: »Beenden Sie den Krieg in der Ukraine und lassen Sie uns gemeinsam nach diplomatischen Lösungen suchen. Wir wollen nie wieder in einem geteilten Europa leben. Wir wollen in Freiheit und wir wollen in Frieden leben – zusammen mit der Ukraine.« Die »Koalition der Willigen« werde der Ukraine beistehen, solange es nötig sei.
Europa drängt an den Verhandlungstisch
Fortschritte brachten die Treffen bei einem wichtigen Punkt: Mittlerweile sind sich die europäischen Staaten und die Ukrainer mit den USA einig, dass die Europäer in die Gespräche mit Russland über ein Kriegsende einbezogen werden müssen. Jedes Abkommen, das man schließe, werde in enger Abstimmung mit der Ukraine und Europa zustande kommen, versicherte der Schwiegersohn des US-Präsidenten, Jared Kushner. Über Trump, der sich aus seiner Air Force One zum Berliner Ukraine-Gipfel zuschalten ließ, sagte Kushner: »Er hat nicht die Absicht, irgendetwas einseitig durchzusetzen. Er möchte dies gemeinsam mit Europa und der Ukraine tun.«
Auch Putin räumte in Shenzhen ein, über die Sicherheit Russlands, der Ukraine und Europas könne nicht ohne europäische Vertreter gesprochen werden. Seiner Vorstellung nach sollen die Europäer aber zunächst Moskau besuchen, um dort ihre Vorstellungen vorzutragen. Die europäische Seite hat beschlossen, mit Vertretern Deutschlands, Frankreichs, Italiens, Polens und Großbritanniens sowie der EU und Nato in die Gespräche mit Moskau zu gehen.
Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj pocht darauf, die Europäer direkt zur nächsten Gesprächsrunde mit Russland und den USA dazuzuholen. Die Amerikaner und Russen sollten dafür rasch einen Ort und Termin ausmachen, schlug er vor.
Kushner berichtete in Berlin, Russland sperre sich mittlerweile nicht mehr gegen Sicherheitsgarantien für die Ukraine nach dem Vorbild von Artikel 5 des Nato-Vertrages. Dieser besagt, dass Bündnispartner im Fall eines Angriffs auf Unterstützung zählen können und eine Attacke auf ein Nato-Mitglied als Angriff auf alle gewertet wird. Die USA hätten die Russen damit vertraut gemacht, dass jedes Schutzversprechen auf diesem Grundsatz fußen werde, sagte Kushner. Eine Bestätigung dafür aus Moskau steht aus.
Währenddessen geht das Kampfgeschehen weiter. Auch in der Nacht griff Russland die Hauptstadt Kiew und andere Ziele in der Ukraine wieder mit Raketen an. dpa/nd
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://gothamist.com/news/federal-gover.title: Federal government claims control of Newark Housing Authority
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-gover.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-gover.text:
The Trump administration has taken over the Newark Housing Authority, according to a letter posted to the homepage of the authority’s website and later confirmed by its executive director.
The letter posted by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said the largest public housing authority in the state had failed to “attain specific occupancy targets” and to “improve financial performance,” but provided no further specifics as to how the authority fell short.
There was no public announcement of the move outside of the letter and federal officials did not respond to questions Thursday night.
The Newark Housing Authority operates 44 housing developments around the city.
According to the letter dated Thursday from HUD Assistant Secretary Benjamin Hobbs to the leaders of the Newark Housing Authority, federal authorities had issued a final determination of substantial default for breaching the terms of a 2024 agreement between HUD and the authority.
HUD wrote that it warned the authority of its findings in two separate letters, dated Sept. 22 and Nov 5. While the local authority responded, the federal agency said the responses were insufficient.
“NHA has not taken good faith efforts to substantially improve,” Hobbs wrote in Thursday’s letter. “HUD considered NHA's reported progress and claimed corrective efforts before determining whether further action is warranted. Those efforts do not outweigh the continued failure to meet benchmarks that NHA itself agreed to over two years ago.”
Neither HUD nor Mayor Ras Baraka’s office immediately responded to requests for comment.
As part of the takeover, HUD dismissed the authority's entire board of commissioners. The Newark Housing Authority’s website had been updated on Thursday night to show that responsibilities of the board had been transferred to two officials in HUD’s Office of Public and Indian Housing: Deputy Assistant Secretary Shylon Ferry and Associate Deputy Assistant Secretary Daniel Sherrod.
A Newark Housing Authority board meeting scheduled for Friday has been cancelled, according to a notice posted on the authority’s website.
“NHA's day-to-day operations and resident services will continue as usual under HUD oversight,” the notice read.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Fachin envia à PGR relatórios sobre relações de Moraes, Nunes Marques, Toffoli e Mendonça com Daniel Vorcaro
