https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Sarah Marsh
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning.
Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays.
“It was something quite different. Most people reacted really well to it,” said Steve Anderson, 57. “The only negative reaction I heard was to the ginger shot, which some found too strong … but that’s a preference thing. The pods themselves were very palatable.”
Global packaging waste is on course to hit a projected 434.5m tonnes in 2025, rising to 525m tonnes by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 3.9%, according to research from Smithers. Plastic is at the heart of this: between 2000 and 2019, the volume of plastic waste doubled, with packaging responsible for about 40% of it. Yet plastic is among the least recycled materials, with a worldwide recycling rate of just 27.9% in 2024. The UK’s overall plastic packaging recycling reached 52.5% in 2023, up from 51.4% in 2022.
Edible packaging could be part of the answer to this problem, with the market size valued at $1.04bn (£790m) in 2024 and poised to grow to $1.84bn by 2033, driven by consumers’ environmental concerns.
But market research says challenges exist. One report said this was “due to the sensitivity of edible packaging to fluctuating environmental conditions, necessitating special handling during shipping and storage”. It also said customers were reluctant to use edible utensils and the challenges hindered “widespread adoption”.
However, beyond the science of packaging, a wider debate remains about our consumption habits. Environmental campaigners argue that the ultimate solution to the plastic waste crisis is not finding better ways to wrap single-use items, but moving away from a throwaway culture altogether.
Even for those who do want to create better packaging, money remains a hurdle. Prof James Elliott at the University of Cambridge, who is working on plastic packaging alternatives, said manufacturers were not keen to pay more for biodegradable alternatives. “They are very cost driven,” he said, adding that the non-biodegradable plastic market was $265bn “so the $1bn proportion being edible is small”.
Andrew Wallis, packaging lead at Innocent Drinks, said 78% of consumers would consider buying ginger shots encased in seaweed, according to a survey. He said it could also be used in Innocent’s kids’ range, which currently uses paper straws in plastic packaging. “Could that wrap be exchanged for a seaweed wrapper?” he said.
Notpla created similar pods for the London Marathon. Other examples of innovation in this area include Xampla, which created a stock cube wrapped in edible film, and Cupffee, which made the world’s first edible cup.
At Notpla’s headquarters, in east London, seaweed is used to encase small amounts of olive oil as well as for sandwich packaging and to replace plastic film in cardboard packaging. The team has also made spoons out of seaweed, which are used in ice-cream parlours including Ice Cream Union in London.
Rodrigo García González, co-founder of Notpla, said seaweed was a good sustainable solution because it grew rapidly. “Some seaweed can grow up to 60cm a day,” he said. “It’s one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth, much faster than bamboo, and it doesn’t compete with anything on land.” He also said it biodegraded more quickly than a leaf.
At Notpla, a machine pushes out ginger shots into seaweed casing, like sausages on a factory conveyor belt. The company is still working out how a product such as this could work in a supermarket: it lasts only three days, but in an unopened bottle could be kept for weeks.
Elliott said one of the big problems with edible packaging was about scale: “About 30-40% of all plastics used worldwide are used in packaging … the scale is phenomenal. We use 2m tonnes of plastic in the UK per year.” He said it would be hard to “harvest that much seaweed without making huge changes”.
But González said seaweed “already operates at a scale most people don’t realise”. He added: “Around 40m tonnes are harvested every year, almost all of it farmed, and it’s already in everyday products from toothpaste to ice-cream. It’s also one of the fastest-growing organisms on the planet.”
Elliott has been working on developing a non-edible packaging made from cellulose. “It’s designed to be composted. Cellulose is abundant in every plant, so we take waste plant material and turn it into films.”
He pointed to Xampla, another company developing plastic alternatives, which makes film from pea protein. A big advantage, he said, is that the material was not just farmable but could be made in vats, like a biochemical process.
Lubomila Jordanova from Cupffee and a Berlin-based expert in sustainability solutions, said the hardest part “was that there was nowhere to turn for answers”. She said an edible cup “isn’t bread and it isn’t a wafer. It has to behave like a real cup: hold coffee at 85C, not leak, and not go soft in your hand while you drink.”
Cupffee is now producing millions of edible cups, and its recipe is patented in 14 European countries, she said. But it was very difficult to scale. “Because customers expect every cup to be identical, exactly like a plastic or paper cup. But we’re making food. Getting that consistency took heavy investment in automation, quality control and our own machines.”
Elliott said cost was also an issue. “The manufacturers’ question is whether they pass the cost on to consumers, or whether consumers are prepared to pay extra for things in edible packaging. There may be niche applications. A ginger shot is a premium product, but if you have a cabbage wrapped in film, will you pay double to wrap it in something edible?
“But the more you scale up, the lower the cost will be. We could get there with edible films, but it will take time and investment.”
Sian Sutherland, co-founder of the campaign group A Plastic Planet, said: “Edible packaging is fun, it’s eye-catching and it’s brilliantly marketable. It’s the ultimate proof point for the safety of plastic alternatives. If you can safely eat the packaging, nobody can tell you that plastic-free materials aren’t safe enough, or that they can’t break down harmlessly.
“But I’m sceptical about its long-term feasibility. The whole job of packaging is to shield what’s inside from the outside world. Anything that’s been handled, stacked, shipped and left on a shelf will have picked things up along the way. People will always worry about eating it, and that’s understandable. So, I don’t think wrapping our food in more food is a solution for the long run.”
She said she wanted to “keep the broader picture front of mind”.
“Any innovation that takes us away from plastic is a good innovation,” she said. “Government must lead and support the pioneers making this shift.”
Make your own ginger shot
- 60g ginger, skin on
- 400ml apple juice
- juice of half a lemon
Chop the ginger and blitz in a blender with the apple and lemon juice. Strain over a very fine sieve, pressing the pulp with the back of a spoon. The drink will keep in the fridge for up to four days.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Lionel Messi of Inter Miami tops Major League Soccer salaries
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Lionel Messi of Inter Miami tops Major League Soccer salaries
Argentinian football legend Messi, who joined Miami in 2023, signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.
Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer, with $28.3m in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release on Thursday by the players’ union, with Chicago’s Robert Lewandowski second.
Argentinian legend Messi topped the league list revealed by the MLS Players Association with compensation almost $8m higher than last year, although his figures include only playing compensation, not income from other sources.
Messi signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.
Poland’s Lewandowski, who joined the Chicago Fire earlier this year, was second overall with $19.51m, followed by Orlando’s Antoine Griezmann of France at $13.94m, South Korean star Son Heung-min of Los Angeles FC at $11.15m and Swiss international Breel Embolo of Atlanta United at $10.81m.
Among MLS clubs, Miami topped all teams in total guaranteed compensation at $59.37m, with Chicago second at $41.29m, Atlanta third at $38.35m, the Los Angeles Galaxy fourth at $34.91m and LAFC fifth at $32.91m.
The league’s lowest total team compensation was Philadelphia Union at $12.64m, with Sporting Kansas City second-lowest at $13.30m and DC United third-lowest at $14.55m.
The figures are through October 9 and are annualised for players who arrived in the summer transfer period.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.title: US-Demokraten | Doch kein »Bluenami«?
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.author: Raul Zelik
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.text:
- Kommentare
- US-Demokraten
Doch kein »Bluenami«?
Mit der Nominierung von Hakeem Jeffries zum Sprecher des US-Repräsentantenhauses behält das Establishment die Zügel in der Hand. Ein Kommentar.
Die Nominierung des Demokraten Hakeem Jeffries zum künftigen Sprecher des US-Repräsentantenhauses verheißt nichts Gutes. Als Führer der Mehrheitsfraktion wäre Jeffries formal der dritte Mann im Staat; vor allem jedoch würde er darüber entscheiden, welche Gesetzesvorhaben wann im Parlament erörtert werden und zur Abstimmung kommen.
Die Wahlen Anfang November wurden als stärkste Linksverschiebung in der US-Geschichte wahrgenommen. Zwar ist der Kreis der Linken im US-Kongress weiterhin sehr überschaubar – zu den »Demokratischen Sozialisten« bekennen sich nur acht Kongressabgeordnete, selbst Senator Bernie Sanders ist kein DSA-Mitglied. Doch unter den Neugewählten sind viele Abgeordnete, die wie der Texaner James Talarico Wahlkampf gegen Krieg und Milliardäre geführt haben. Dementsprechend groß war die Hoffnung, dass die Einführung einer öffentlichen Gesundheitsversorgung und ein Ende der US-Unterstützung für Israel nun auf der Tagesordnung stehen könnten.
Hakeem Jeffries steht bislang gegen solche Vorhaben. Überraschen darf das nicht: Die mit Abstand größte Einzelspende im Wahlkampf 2024 erhielt er vom pro-israelischen Lobbyverband Aipac. Danach folgten Spenden von Blackrock, der Vermögensverwaltung Apollo und dem Rüstungskonzern Lockheed Martin.
Zwar hat auch die Linke Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez die Nominierung Jeffries’ unterstützt. Deshalb wird spekuliert, ob dieser inhaltliche Zugeständnisse gemacht hat. Doch die Macht des Kapitals ist auch bei den Demokraten gewaltig. Sollte sich nun auch noch Chuck Schumer als Mehrheitssprecher im Senat durchsetzen, wären die Weichen dafür gestellt, dass der »blaue Tsunami« ohne größeren Politikwechsel bleibt.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-looks-to-.title: NYC looks to close a 'loophole' in sanctuary protection for immigrants
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-looks-to-.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-looks-to-.text:
The New York City Council's immigration committee is considering a set of bills that meant to close a “loophole” in the city’s sanctuary laws, which limit local officials' cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
A bill introduced by Councilmember Elsie Encarnación, the immigration committee chair, would explicitly prohibit city jail officials from notifying federal immigration agents of a detainee’s release unless provided with a judicial warrant.
A similar bill, also introduced by Encarnación and set for review during a Council hearing on Friday, would establish similar restrictions for the NYPD.
Under the city’s sanctuary protections, an immigrant detainee must have been convicted of a serious or violent crime, or come up as a possible match on a terrorist screening database, to warrant being turned over to federal immigration officials. The law also requires that federal officials provide a warrant from a judge.
But city jails have transferred dozens of people to federal immigration authorities in recent years, without receipt of a judicial warrant, jail officials have repeatedly testified in the City Council. From July 1, 2025, to June 30 this year, the city's Department of Correction transferred 24 people to federal immigration authorities, and 19 people during the year prior, according to agency data.
James Conroy, the Department of Correction’s chief lawyer, justified these transfers in a March Council hearing, citing another section of the city’s sanctuary laws. Those provisions under certain circumstances allow jail officials to share information with federal authorities even without a judicial warrant, he said.
The proposed revisions in Encarnación’s bills would remove any ambiguity and make plain that a judicial warrant was required under almost all circumstances.
Rosa Cohen-Cruz, director of immigration policy at the Bronx Defenders, who helped draft and lobby for the bills, said they are important measures for ensuring due process for immigrant detainees and preventing individuals from ending up in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which she called a “rogue, violent, dangerous organization.”
“ We should be protecting all New Yorkers,” Cohen-Cruz said in an interview. “We should not be funneling any New Yorkers into that system, regardless of their criminal legal system contact.”
The Department of Correction did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the NYPD said the Council’s bill is already the law, and that the NYPD can’t transfer a detainee into ICE custody without a judicial warrant, and hasn’t transferred someone into ICE custody in about a decade.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not respond to requests for comment.
New York City agreed in December 2024 to pay up to $92.5 million to settle claims it unlawfully detained more than 20,000 undocumented immigrants beyond their scheduled release from city jails, to allow for their transfer into federal immigration custody.
The hearing at 10 a.m. on Friday will also include an update on the current state of immigration enforcement in the city.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Festival Recife do Teatro Nacional chega à 25ª edição com 32 espetáculos e programação gratuita
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Fátima Pereira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Recife recebe, entre os dias 19 e 29 de novembro, a 25ª edição do Festival Recife do Teatro Nacional, que ocupará teatros, parques, praças e outros espaços culturais da cidade com 32 espetáculos, sendo 17 produções nacionais inéditas na capital pernambucana e 15 montagens locais.
Com programação gratuita e solidária, mediante arrecadação de alimentos não perecíveis, o evento reúne diferentes linguagens das artes cênicas, incluindo musicais, comédias, dramas, performances e experiências imersivas.
A abertura acontece nesta quinta-feira (19), às 19h, no Teatro de Santa Isabel, com o espetáculo “(Um) Ensaio sobre a Cegueira”, do Grupo Galpão, de Minas Gerais.
Com o tema “Teatro e Música: A Cena que se Escuta”, a edição deste ano propõe um diálogo entre as artes cênicas e a musicalidade, destacando o papel dos sons, ritmos e canções na construção de narrativas e na preservação das tradições culturais. A curadoria é assinada por André Brasileiro.
O festival também presta homenagens a três nomes de destaque da cultura: o músico armorial Antonio (Zoca) Madureira, o ator Jeison Wallace e o artista e pensador Jomard Muniz de Brito, em memória. A programação contempla ainda atividades formativas, rodas de diálogo, leituras dramatizadas e lançamentos de livros.
Entre os destaques da programação está a participação do Grupo Galpão, que retorna ao Recife com “(Um) Ensaio sobre a Cegueira”, adaptação do romance de José Saramago. Com dramaturgia e direção de Rodrigo Portella, a montagem convida parte do público a subir ao palco com os olhos vendados, propondo uma experiência sensorial que questiona os limites da percepção e da capacidade humana de enxergar o outro. Além da estreia nesta quinta-feira (19), às 19h, no Teatro de Santa Isabel, haverá apresentações nos dias 20 e 21, no mesmo horário.
Outra companhia de destaque é a Cia do Latão, de São Paulo, que volta à capital pernambucana depois de dez anos. O grupo apresenta “Experimento H”, com dramaturgia da atriz Helena Albergaria a partir de contos do escritor Truman Capote. A peça aproxima duas mulheres de realidades sociais distintas: uma trabalhadora doméstica de Nova York e a atriz Marilyn Monroe. As sessões acontecem nos dias 20 e 21, às 20h, no Teatro Hermilo Borba Filho.
A dramaturgia pernambucana também ganha projeção nacional com duas obras recentes de Newton Moreno. “A Última Cova”, musical protagonizado por Marco França, acompanha a trajetória de um coveiro nordestino que procura a mãe em São Paulo.
Já “As Centenárias” retoma a história das personagens Socorro e Zaninha, duas carpideiras do Sertão do Cariri, agora interpretadas por Laila Garin e Juliana Linhares. As montagens serão apresentadas no Teatro Barreto Júnior, nos dias 21 e 22, e no Teatro do Parque, nos dias 24 e 25, respectivamente.
A presença dos musicais é um dos pontos centrais desta edição. Entre as produções nacionais está “Minha Estrela Dalva”, com dramaturgia de Renato Borghi, que homenageia a cantora Dalva de Oliveira, conhecida como a Rainha do Rádio. A montagem reúne Borghi e Soraya Resende em uma narrativa que revisita a trajetória e o legado da artista. As apresentações acontecem nos dias 28 e 29, às 20h e 17h, respectivamente, no Teatro do Parque.
Também integram a programação “Abre Alas: Concerto à Doidivana”, musical cômico do Distrito Federal que homenageia Chiquinha Gonzaga, com apresentações nos dias 21, às 17h, no Parque da Tamarineira, e 22, no mesmo horário, no Parque Eduardo Campos.
A mineira Maria Cutia traz “Ópera de Sabão”, espetáculo que mistura humor e música para contar a história de uma rádio em decadência que tenta sobreviver à chegada da televisão. A peça será apresentada nos dias 28 e 29, às 20h e 19h, no Teatro de Santa Isabel.
Outra atração é “O Pequenino Grão de Areia”, fábula musical escrita e dirigida pelo pernambucano João Falcão. Depois de mais de cem apresentações em São Paulo, a montagem chega à cidade natal do artista nos dias 28 e 29, às 17h, no Teatro Luiz Mendonça.
A programação também inclui “Medeia Depois do Sol”, da atriz pernambucana Luciana Lyra, radicada em São Paulo. A montagem transporta a personagem da tragédia grega para os canaviais pernambucanos do período colonial e estabelece conexões com a história das guerreiras de Tejucupapo. O espetáculo aborda temas como maternidade, violência de gênero e resistência feminina, com música instrumental executada ao vivo. As sessões serão no dia 22, às 16h e às 19h, no Teatro Hermilo Borba Filho.
Entre as produções locais, a Orquestra Malassombro apresenta “Rádio Malassombro”, no dia 21, às 20h, no Teatro do Parque. Inspirado nas histórias reunidas por Gilberto Freyre em “Assombrações do Recife Velho”, o espetáculo combina lendas urbanas, esquetes e arranjos musicais que passeiam por ritmos populares, incluindo o frevo.
No dia 22, também às 18h, no Teatro do Parque, a orquestra participa da homenagem a Antonio Madureira. Sob direção de Ronaldo Correia de Brito, a apresentação percorre mais de cinco décadas da produção do músico, da música armorial a gêneros populares e composições infantis. O espetáculo contará com um coro de cinco vozes, incluindo Isadora Melo e Carlos Filho, além da participação especial de Spok.
O ator Jeison Wallace também integra a programação em homenagem à sua trajetória. Nos dias 26 e 27, às 20h, no Teatro de Santa Isabel, ele apresenta “Cinderela, a História que sua Mãe Não Contou”, comédia que há 35 anos mistura contos de fadas e humor popular pernambucano. A montagem reúne integrantes do elenco original, como Roberto Costa, intérprete da Bicha Madrinha, e Paulo de Pontes, que vive a Madrasta, além de convidados.
A programação pernambucana reúne produções de diferentes gerações e propostas estéticas. Entre elas está uma nova montagem de “O Auto da Compadecida”, clássico de Ariano Suassuna, que será apresentado no dia 22, às 18h, no Teatro Luiz Mendonça.
Também estão na grade “Não se Conta o Tempo na Paixão”, de Auriceia Fraga, no dia 27, às 20h, no Teatro Apolo; “Que Muito Amou”, que reúne personagens da obra de Caio Fernando Abreu, no dia 29, às 19h, no Teatro Hermilo Borba Filho; e “Ilha”, do grupo Bote de Teatro, com sessões nos dias 27 e 28, às 21h, na Praça do Sebo.
Outro destaque é “A Casa: Uma Experiência Imersiva”, que propõe uma vivência intimista em homenagem à atriz Socorro Raposo. Com capacidade para pouco mais de 20 espectadores por sessão, a montagem será apresentada nos dias 28 e 29, às 18h, no Espaço A Casa, em Santo Amaro.
A mostra OffREC integra o festival com dez montagens, entre espetáculos e leituras dramatizadas, além de encontros, palestras e lançamentos editoriais. A proposta é ampliar o espaço para experiências cênicas e discussões sobre os caminhos do teatro contemporâneo.
A programação começa no dia 23, com “Cordéis Minimalistas”, do grupo Teodora Lins e Silva, às 17h, no Teatro Apolo, e o monólogo “Edson”, do carioca Matheus Macena, às 19h, no Teatro Hermilo Borba Filho. A peça aborda a história de um estudante secundarista assassinado durante a Ditadura Militar.
No dia 25, às 20h, o grupo mineiro Quatroloscinco apresenta “Velocidade”, no Teatro Hermilo. Inspirada na obra da escritora mexicana Vivian Abenshushan, a montagem investiga as diferentes percepções sobre a passagem do tempo.
Outro destaque é “Veias Abertas”, do Rio de Janeiro, que será apresentado no dia 28, às 19h, no Teatro Hermilo Borba Filho. A obra tem como referência o livro “As Veias Abertas da América Latina”, de Eduardo Galeano, e aborda as memórias políticas do continente.
A mostra também promove os Atentados Teatrais, três encontros dedicados ao pensamento e à produção artística de Jomard Muniz de Brito. As rodas de diálogo abordam os eixos poesia, política e pedagogia, sempre acompanhadas de intervenções do performer Edjalma Freitas. Os encontros acontecem nos dias 24, 26 e 28, em espaços culturais da cidade.
Além dos espetáculos, o festival oferece cinco oficinas gratuitas que começaram no dia 17 e vão até 25 de novembro, voltadas à formação e ao intercâmbio entre artistas.
Entre os dias 22 e 25, Marcelo Bosschar conduz o workshop “O Corpo Instrumento: Pulsação e Vibração na Cena”, no Paço do Frevo, das 9h às 13h30.
As duas últimas atividades acontecem nos dias 23 e 24. Marco França ministra “Música da Cena: O Corpo Musical”, das 10h às 13h, no Teatro de Santa Isabel. Já Vanessa Garcia conduz “Corpo Cena: Dramaturgia do Movimento em ‘As Centenárias’”, das 14h às 17h, no Paço do Frevo.
As inscrições para as oficinas devem ser realizadas pelos canais indicados pela organização: O Corpo Instrumento: [email protected]; Música da Cena: [email protected]; Corpo Cena: [email protected].
A programação completa, com horários e locais das apresentações, pode ser conferida nos canais oficiais do Festival Recife do Teatro Nacional.

https://taz.de/Krieg-in-der-Ukraine/!623.text:
Krieg in der Ukraine: Tote bei russischen Angriffen auf Kyjiwer Brücken
Nach den ukrainischen Attacken auf die Krim-Brücke hat Russland nun zurückgeschlagen. Kyjiws Bürgermeister fordert die Einwohner der Stadt auf, möglichst von zu Hause aus zu arbeiten.
dpa | Russland hat bei Angriffen mit ballistischen Raketen in der ukrainischen Hauptstadt Kyjiw nach Angaben von Bürgermeister Vitali Klitschko erneut Menschen getötet und insgesamt drei Brücken beschädigt. Es gebe 3 Tote und 15 Verletzte, teilte Klitschko bei Telegram mit. Unter anderem sei die bereits zuvor getroffene Südbrücke erneut Ziel der feindlichen Attacken gewesen.
„Das Ausmaß der Schäden an den Bauwerken können Experten erst nach Ende des Luftalarms untersuchen“, sagte der Bürgermeister. Er forderte die Bewohner der Hauptstadt auf, möglichst von zu Hause aus zu arbeiten. Die Brücken über den Dnipro sind strategisch wichtig für die Stadt.
„Angesichts der erschwerten Verkehrsbedingungen zwischen dem linken und dem rechten Ufer der Hauptstadt bitte ich die Einwohner, die Hauptstadt nicht mit dem Privatfahrzeug zu verlassen, sofern dies nicht unbedingt notwendig ist“, teilte Klitschko weiter mit. Der Raketenangriff des Feindes auf Kyjiw dauere an. Die Einsatzkräfte seien dabei, die Folgen der Attacke so schnell wie möglich zu beseitigen.
Putin drohte mit Vergeltung nach Attacken auf Krim-Brücke
Russland hatte die Brücken in Kyjiw bereits in der Vergangenheit angegriffen. Danach attackierte die Ukraine erneut die umstrittene Brücke vom russischen Festland zur annektierten Schwarzmeer-Halbinsel Krim. Kyjiw hatte die für die Versorgung der Menschen auf der Krim wichtige Brücke in dieser Woche dreimal getroffen und dabei auch ein Stück der Autotrasse weggesprengt. Nur für den Zugverkehr kann die Brücke derzeit noch genutzt werden.
Kremlchef Wladimir Putin drohte am Donnerstag angesichts der schweren Schäden an der Brücke eine harte Reaktion an. Er gehe davon aus, dass die russischen Gegenmaßnahmen „weitaus schmerzhafter“ sein werden als das, was Kyjiw mit der Krim-Brücke getan habe, sagte er bei einer Pressekonferenz nach einem historischen Dreiergipfel mit US-Präsident Donald Trump und Chinas Staatschef Xi Jinping im südchinesischen Shenzhen.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Xan Brooks
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Andrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.”
Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma. He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.”
Zvyagintsev’s new film, Minotaur, is a mighty, mesmerising drama of personal and political corruption that has Ukraine as its touchstone, or perhaps its dark fork in the road. He makes no bones about his opposition to the war. Taking the stage at this year’s Cannes film festival, where Minotaur won the grand jury prize, he called on Vladimir Putin to “stop this butchery”, adding that “the whole world is waiting”. In September Russia named him as a “foreign agent” spreading disinformation. He now risks arrest and imprisonment if he dares to go home.
Today he is living out of a suitcase in a central London hotel; sipping bottled water and buffing the lenses of his specs. At 62, Zvyagintsev has the air of a college professor hosting a one-on-one tutorial. He’s erudite and charismatic, peppering his answers with quotes from Borges, Nietzsche and Savonarola. Who’s Savonarola? “A medieval friar,” he says. “A Catholic preacher. Very fierce.”
Zvyagintsev looks well but explains that his health is precarious. “My illness in 2021, 2022 has been following me ever since. It caused irreversible damage and presents serious challenges to the peripheral nervous system. So I’m not confident in my steps. I spend a lot of energy just to keep my balance. In Cannes, if you remember, I stumbled going up the steps to collect the award.” He shrugs. “Maybe you didn’t notice. My friends all noticed. Zoe Saldaña noticed. She had to reach out and catch me.”
There are no stumbles in Minotaur: it barely puts a foot wrong. Zvyagintsev’s film tells the tale of Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), a businessman caught between the proverbial rock and hard place. Gleb suspects that his wife may be having an affair, but he has also been asked to sacrifice 14 employees to fight on the frontline. Ukraine, one comes to realise, is the film’s peripheral horror and malign guiding spirit. The war is at once a faint, distant rumble and a monster so present that it might be breathing down Gleb’s neck.
Minotaur, Zvyagintsev’s first film since 2017’s acclaimed Loveless, is a loose remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller La Femme Infidèle. The director explains that he initially tried to make it back in 2018 but wasn’t able to obtain the rights. “Looking back now, this was a good resolution. It would have been a completely different film, without any historical context.” Ukraine provided the project with the spark that it needed. Tangentially perhaps, his illness did too.
In the summer of 2021, he was given the Sputnik V Covid vaccine and came down with a fever. He was transferred from Moscow to a hospital in Germany where his condition became critical. Insofar as he knew what was happening, Zvyagintsev feared the worst. “August 2021. I associate it with death. Because the reality is that I should have died. Every day, that’s what my wife heard from the doctors. ‘Be ready, be prepared. It could be today.’ They were signing me off to the afterlife.”
Was the vaccine to blame? He shrugs. “No one knows. Symptom-less Covid – it seems that’s what it was. Then on top of that I had the vaccine, which set off a big storm. The bacteria entered my body and beat my immune system. My body started consuming itself. It’s a terrible thing. It is called Klebsiella [a bacteria that can cause pneumonia]. I had 92% lung damage and spent 40 days in an artificial coma. Full disconnection. A millimetre from death. And so afterwards you have to build everything from the ground.”
The director was in hospital for 11 months – first in Wiesbaden, then in Hanover. For much of that time he was at least partly paralysed by polyneuropathy and had to relearn how to use a knife and fork. He was on the ward when he heard Russia had invaded Ukraine. “My first thought was that it was no longer my country. That I must now live in a different country.”
Zvyagintsev seems to have broken with Russia in the way that Hemingway heroes go bankrupt: gradually, then suddenly. The government loved him when his 2003 debut, The Return, won the Golden Lion at Venice, and international critics were hailing him as the successor to Eisenstein and Tarkovsky. But it disliked 2011’s Elena, with its bleak portrait of life on Moscow’s dilapidated housing estates, and outright hated his 2014 masterpiece Leviathan, which painted the country as a hotbed of corruption and Christian nationalism. Leviathan, said Vladimir Medinsky, the then-minister of culture, was “opportunistic”, unrepresentative of “real Russians” and part of a new breed of films that “defiled” the motherland. Medinsky, incidentally, now serves as Moscow’s chief negotiator in peace talks regarding the war in Ukraine.
As for Zvyagintsev, he was simultaneously tracking Russia’s shift and drift under Putin. “There have been so many changes in these past 26 years,” he says. “They’re hard to trace. I’m not a specialist, I only know that around 2011, 2012, there was a crack in society. And in 2022 the crack became a collapse. The war is a catastrophe.”
The authorities claim he is a paid agent of the west. And in one sense they are right. Minotaur was shot in Latvia with French funding and has since been selected as France’s official submission for the Oscars. But it is a Russian film at heart, he says. “I know how the Russian press works. Not just the press. Instagram. Social media. Of course they will say that I’m working under orders, doing someone else’s will. I know the rhetoric. I get it. But this film isn’t [anti-Russian] propaganda. It’s a scream for help.”
Zvyagintsev now lives in Paris with his wife, Anna, and teenage son, Pyotr. He chose France over Germany because he regards it as a natural haven for film-makers; also Anna and Pyotr speak the language. But the adjustment has been hard and he doubts they’ll ever truly fit in. “So it’s a constant stress. Everything is new. The boy in particular has had a difficult time. In Russia he had friends. Here it is zero. Everything’s gone.” He smiles. “We’re like a family of astronauts in zero gravity.”
The knight in the forest has a hard choice to make. So does Gleb, the businessman in Minotaur, who has been tasked with delivering names to the draft board. Zvyagintsev says that no one in the world is intrinsically good or evil. Instead, they’re a complex series of arrows and vectors. Some turn left, some turn right and some remain in one place and leave it for others to decide.
The director insists he has no regrets. He stands by his decision to make his films and speak out. “If you don’t do anything you become a pawn on the board. You can be pulled around, compromised. You’re a marionette on a string.”
Zvyagintsev knows he should have died and feels it’s a miracle that he didn’t. I tell him that his post-Covid existence amounts to an unlikely third act. It might not be the one he’d have chosen, I say, but it beats the alternative. The director nods. “Better than laying in the ground,” he agrees.
The director was so sick before he began shooting Minotaur, but the production was a breeze, it felt as if he was flying. This makes him think that film-making itself was his real rehabilitation and that he only needs to keep going in order to fully build up his strength. He plans to make another feature next year, possibly in English or French, and then another one after that, who knows?
Zvyagintsev peers at me through his specs, like a kindly professor gently correcting a student. He says, “I’m not sure that you’re right about this being a third act. That makes it sound like I’m finishing my life. I think it’s the third act of a four-act play. With an epilogue. And a sequel.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: The Gambia stood up for the Rohingya, now the world must act
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
The Gambia stood up for the Rohingya, now the world must act
The ICJ has delivered a historic judgement, but justice will depend on what happens next.
There are moments in history when a nation is defined not by its size, wealth, military strength or political influence, but by the courage of its conscience.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, in breach of its obligations under the Genocide Convention. For the Rohingya, it is a long-overdue recognition. For The Gambia, it concludes a case our country brought to the Court seven years ago.
The Rohingya have lived in Myanmar’s Rakhine State for generations. Their basic human rights have been systematically denied over time, leaving them stateless and subject to dehumanising rhetoric, hate speech and legal persecution. Following the Myanmar military’s “clearance operations” in 2016 and 2017, over 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. The military killed an estimated 10,000 civilians, raped and sexually assaulted women and girls, and burned villages to the ground. There are currently 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, the majority in the camps of Cox’s Bazar, and 520,000 remain in Myanmar.
When confronted with reports of unimaginable suffering, persecution, displacement and the destruction of communities, The Gambia chose to act. In 2018, our then Minister of Justice, Abubacarr Tambadou, visited the camps in Bangladesh as part of an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation delegation. As a former prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, he recognised the signs of genocide in the accounts of the survivors.
With the support of the OIC’s 57 member States, The Gambia brought the case to the International Court of Justice in November 2019. It was the first time in the court’s history that a state with no direct connection to the alleged crimes had filed a case under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which obliges all state parties to prevent and punish genocide wherever it may occur.
Yet, The Gambia’s action before the Court was never only about legal obligations or diplomatic considerations. We asked ourselves one fundamental question: if we remain silent in the face of such suffering, what does our silence make us?
As Gambians, we know the value of dignity. We understand what it means to yearn for justice. We know the pain that comes when our rights are denied, and voices are silenced. Our own history of political struggle taught us that freedom, accountability and human rights are lived realities that shape the lives of us all.
Perhaps that is why this case has resonated deeply with many Gambians: it speaks to our common humanity. In January, Rohingya survivors of the violence testified before the court about what they had lived through. We recognise that the fear of being driven from one’s home knows no nationality, and compassion does not stop at national boundaries.
The years since the case was filed have required patience and perseverance. International justice can often move frustratingly slowly. However, the court’s order in January 2020, the rejection of Myanmar’s objections in 2022, and the interventions from 11 states (Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, the Maldives, Slovenia, the DRC, Belgium, and Ireland) on how the Convention should be interpreted have reaffirmed our shared commitment.
The judgement by the world’s highest court today is a reminder that the obligation to prevent genocide applies to every state, large or small, near or far. This is the first time in the history of the court that a state has been found responsible for committing genocide. The court concluded that the widespread rape and sexual violence committed by Myanmar’s security forces were part of the genocide, and that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.
Myanmar is now under a clear obligation to comply fully with the judgement. It is required to investigate and prosecute those responsible, to facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya and to protect them from discrimination and persecution. Justice for the Rohingya will also require the restoration of their citizenship and the recognition of their right to be called Rohingya.
Parliamentarians also have a role to play. As the court made clear today, punishing genocide requires laws that explicitly criminalise it. The court has held Myanmar to that standard, and we must hold ourselves to it, too. We must ensure that genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes are fully incorporated into our domestic laws, and that our courts can try them wherever they are committed.
In our National Assembly, we will ask our government about the next steps, monitor Myanmar’s compliance, and ensure that The Gambia continues to press for that compliance at the United Nations and within the OIC. Other states must now step in by ensuring that Myanmar complies, supporting Rohingya refugees and ensuring they will not be sent back into danger.
As Gambians, we have chosen empathy over indifference, principle over convenience, and action over silence. The Rohingya have shown extraordinary courage and determination in their search for justice, and today international law has finally answered them. Our collective responsibility now is to call for compliance and prevent any future acts of genocide.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Over 115 strikes claimed by Iran or groups aligned with Tehran have damaged 26 military bases and other infrastructure belonging to the US across the Middle East, The Associated Press reported.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120402.title: Sport und Gesellschaft | Wie der Fußball den Friedensprozess in Kolumbien stärkt
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120402.author: Ronny Blaschke, Bogotá
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120402.text:
- Sport
- Sport und Gesellschaft
Wie der Fußball den Friedensprozess in Kolumbien stärkt
Auch zehn Jahre nach dem Friedensvertrag mit der Farc ist der Fußball weiter ein wichtiger Kitt für das politisch und sozial fragmentierte Land.
Mauro Alfonso hat sich die Freude am Fußball bewahrt. Er trägt eine knallrote Trainingsjacke, auf der das Logo des kolumbianischen Fußballverbandes abgebildet ist. Er lacht viel, erzählt Anekdoten mit lebhafter Körpersprache. Mauro Alfonso spricht über die Freude und die gesellschaftliche Bedeutung des Fußballs in seinem Heimatland Kolumbien. Aber er kommt immer wieder auf diesen einen Tag im Mai 2002 zurück, der sein Leben verändert hat.
Alfonso lebt in der kolumbianischen Hauptstadt Bogotá, aber er ist seit seiner Jugend in den 90er Jahren Fan des Vereins América de Cali. Mit Freunden baute er eine Ultra-Gruppe auf: Disturbio Rojo, roter Aufruhr. Sie begleitete América de Cali zu zahlreichen Spielen. Viel Geld hatten ihre Mitglieder nicht, daher mussten sie stundenlang in Bussen sitzen, so auch im Mai 2002 nach ihrer Partie bei Atlético Nacional in Medellín.
Es war eine Zeit, in der der bewaffnete Konflikt in Kolumbien, der seit den 60er Jahren stetig schwelte, wieder stärker in den Vordergrund trat. Kein konventioneller Krieg zwischen zwei Parteien, sondern ein komplexes Geflecht aus Kämpfen zwischen mehreren Akteuren. Daran beteiligt: der kolumbianische Staat, linksextreme Guerillas und rechtsextreme Paramilitärs. Ihre Konfliktthemen: Landrechte, politische Teilhabe, wirtschaftliche Interessen. Insgesamt hat dieser Konflikt wohl mehr als 400.000 Menschen das Leben gekostet.
Guerillas in der Kurve
»Die bewaffneten Gruppen haben in den Fankurven nicht offen nach neuen Mitgliedern gesucht, aber der Fußball war für sie durchaus von Interesse«, sagt Alfonso. Häufig gab es in Städten wie Cali, Medellín und Bogotá Überschneidungen zwischen Guerillas, Kartellmitgliedern und Fußballfans. Es war ein soziales Milieu, in dem Gewalt eine große Rolle spielte. »Aber in unserer Gruppe wollten wir Gewalt heraushalten«, sagt Alfonso.
In dieser Phase des Konfliktes, Anfang des Jahrtausends, errichteten bewaffnete Gruppen oft illegale Straßensperren, um Reisende zu kontrollieren, auszurauben oder zu verschleppen. Auf ihrem Heimweg von Medellín im Mai 2002 durchquerten die Fans von América de Cali das Departamento de Caldas, zu jener Zeit unter der Kontrolle rechtsextremer Paramilitärs. Gegen 23 Uhr wurden die Fans gestoppt. Sie mussten ihren Bus verlassen und sich auf den Boden legen. Von zwei Fans mit langen Haaren fühlten sich die rechten Paramilitärs offenbar provoziert. Aus kurzer Distanz wurden Alex Julián Gómez Ramírez und Juan Manuel Bermúdez Nieto erschossen, im Alter von 21 Jahren.
Trauernde Ultras
Mauro Alfonso musste mitansehen, wie zwei seiner Freunde einer willkürlichen Machtdemonstration der Paramilitärs zum Opfer fielen. Für eine Weile geriet er aus der Bahn, er hatte Schuldgefühle. Doch dann fassten Alfonso und Luis Bermúdez, der Vater seines ermordeten Freundes, einen Entschluss. »Wir wollten unsere Trauer in etwas Konstruktives umwandeln«, sagt Alfonso. »Mithilfe des Fußballs möchten wir die Prävention stärken.« Sie gründeten eine Stiftung für die Aufklärung gegen Gewalt, Drogen und Waffenbesitz.
Der Aufbau der Stiftung fiel in eine Übergangsphase des Konfliktes. Nach Jahrzehnten der Eskalationen setzte sich bei den Paramilitärs die Erkenntnis durch, dass sie ihre Interessen gegen den Staat langfristig nicht durchsetzen konnten. Insbesondere Juan Manuel Santos, zwischen 2010 und 2018 Präsident von Kolumbien, bemühte sich um eine diplomatische Lösung. Und er nutzte den Fußball.
Im Sommer 2011 fand die U-20-Weltmeisterschaft in Kolumbien statt. Santos besuchte die Stadien. In seinen Reden verknüpfte er Begriffe des Fußballs wie Teamwork, Einigkeit und Disziplin mit der kolumbianischen Gesellschaft. Santos trug mehrfach das gelbe Nationaltrikot und traf sich mit verdienten Spielern. Auf seinem Twitter-Account habe er mehr als 500 Verweise auf die Nationalmannschaft gegeben, sagt der britische Lateinamerika-Forscher Peter Watson. »Santos machte den Fußball zu einem Kernelement für die nationale Einheit.«
Und damit meinte Santos auch Menschen, die zuvor noch als Staatsfeinde galten, zum Beispiel Farc, die größte linksextreme Guerillabewegung in Kolumbien. Im Sommer 2014, während in Havanna Friedensverhandlungen liefen, freute man sich in Kolumbien auf die erste Teilnahme der kolumbianischen Nationalmannschaft bei der WM seit 1998. Wenige Wochen vor dem Turnier rief das kolumbianische Verteidigungsministerium in einem Spot die Farc zur Demobilisierung und zum gemeinsamen Fußballschauen auf. Zudem warf das Militär Fußbälle über dem Dschungel ab, wo sich Tausende Kämpfer versteckt hielten.
Brüchiger Frieden
»Während der Friedensverhandlungen tauschten Farc-Unterhändler ihre militärische Kleidung gegen das Nationaltrikot«, erklärt Watson, der zum Thema promoviert hat und an der Universität von Leeds lehrt. Womöglich trug der Fußball einen kleinen Teil zum Friedensvertrag bei, der vor genau zehn Jahren am 24. November 2016 unterzeichnet wurde und Santos den Friedensnobelpreis einbrachte.
Aber auch ein Jahrzehnt später ist Kolumbien von einem tatsächlichen Frieden ein gutes Stück entfernt. In Regionen, die einst von der Farc kontrolliert wurden, entstand ein Vakuum, in das kleinere Guerillagruppen vorgestoßen sind. Außerdem gehen die Reformen, mit denen die extrem ungleiche Landverteilung rückgängig gemacht werden soll, nur schleppend voran. Es gebe allerdings auch Regionen, in denen der Friedensprozess erfolgreicher verlaufen sei, zum Beispiel im Südosten des Landes, sagt die Politikwissenschaftlerin Maria Paula Leon, die für die Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung in Bogotá tätig ist. »Dort haben auch soziale Fußballprojekte einen kleinen Beitrag geleistet. Einige Profispieler haben sogar Stiftungen für Versöhnung gegründet.«
Eine schmerzhafte Einigkeit
Kolumbien ist ein geografisch, politisch und sozial fragmentiertes Land. Der Fußball bietet eines der wenigen Themen, auf das sich alle gesellschaftlichen Gruppen einigen können, in den Städten und auf dem Land, ob arm oder reich. Aber der Fußball ruft auch die schmerzhafte Vergangenheit in Erinnerung. Zum Beispiel an Andrés Escobar, der 1994, nach einem Eigentor bei der WM, in Medellín erschossen wurde. Oder an den derzeitigen Bayern-Spieler Luis Díaz, dessen Eltern 2023 von einer Rebellengruppe entführt und später wieder freigelassen wurden.
Die Krisen werden den Fußball weiterhin prägen. Von den 26 Spielern, die Kolumbien bei der WM 2026 bis ins Achtelfinale führten, stammen neun aus den Regionen, die am stärksten vom bewaffneten Konflikt betroffen waren, insbesondere aus dem Departamento del Chocó an der Pazifikküste. Das zeigen Recherchen des Onlineportals Rutas del Conflicto.
»Der Fußball hat für den Friedensprozess großes Potenzial«, sagt Mauro Alfonso. Am Anfang wurden er und seine Mitstreiter auch skeptisch beäugt, denn die Verbindung von Fußball und Politik war in Kolumbien lange kein großes Thema gewesen. »Aber wir haben einfach weitergemacht.« Ihre Stiftung organisiert Gedenkabende, Workshops und Spendenaktionen, fördert Graffitis und Kultur. Und zwischendurch gibt es Fußball, trotz allem.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://gothamist.com/news/black-and-his.title: Black and Hispanic Staten Islanders get nearly half of obscure pedestrian law tickets
https://gothamist.com/news/black-and-his.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/black-and-his.text:
NYPD officers don’t issue many “pedestrians on roadways” criminal tickets. Most New Yorkers probably don’t even know that offense exists.
It criminalizes walking in the street when a sidewalk is available – an offense that sounds similar to jaywalking, which was legalized in the city in 2024 in part because lawmakers said its enforcement disproportionately targeted Black and Hispanic residents.
So far this year, officers have issued 68 criminal summonses for pedestrians on roadways, according to researchers at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. Of those, officers wrote 30 in the 120th precinct on Staten Island, all but one to Black and Hispanic people, the researchers found. The disparity has caused residents, researchers and attorneys to question if those groups are being unfairly targeted.
Gothamist has previously reported that police have disproportionately targeted residents of some city neighborhoods as part of a quality of life crackdown. Some residents and police reform advocates have criticized the NYPD and Mayor Zohran Mamdani for prioritizing such enforcement, saying it’s a waste of resources and disproportionately affects low-income people of color. Prior to his election, Mamdani campaigned on moving police away from low-level enforcement so officers are more able to focus on solving larger crimes. Earlier this month, the department issued guidance to officers instructing them not to enforce offenses including spitting and engine idling in certain circumstances.
“ That reminds me of stop and frisks,” said Asar Glenn, 45, a Staten Island resident of the sprawling Park Hill Apartments, near where officers have issued six pedestrian tickets so far this year. “ I think they just want to get IDs off of people that they stop, see if they got a record or whatever. It's like fishing.”
NYPD spokesperson Brad Weekes defended the ticketing in a statement and said the offense being enforced is not the same as jaywalking.
"These summonses were not connected to jaywalking and were the result of legitimate law enforcement activity," Weekes said.
Officers from the 120th precinct, which covers Staten Island neighborhoods including Tompkinsville, New Brighton and Stapleton, have written more than 44% of the pedestrians on roadways tickets citywide, according to the analysis by researchers at John Jay College. Of those ticketed for the offense in the precinct, 26 were Black, three were Hispanic and one person was white, the researchers said.
Officers in the precinct with the second highest number of such tickets — the 33rd precinct in Washington Heights — have issued a total of five tickets for the offense so far this year. In all of 2025, officers from the 120th precinct issued 11 of the summonses.
‘Hot Spots’
Matthew Weiss, a New York attorney who has specialized in traffic infractions for decades, said in the 30 years he has practiced law, he’s never defended a client against a pedestrians on roadways ticket.
Under the law, if a sidewalk is available, pedestrians are required to walk on it and not walk in the roadway, Weiss said. If there is no sidewalk, pedestrians are required to walk as far left as possible on the road or on the shoulder facing oncoming traffic.
“Pedestrians that receive such a ticket should argue for dismissal … if in fact they're just crossing the street, not walking along on the street,” Weiss said. “If they go to court and make that legal argument it has strong potential for being successful in my opinion.”
Michael Rempel, a researcher who worked to compile the summons analysis at John Jay College, said the infraction is strikingly similar to jaywalking.
Rempel noted that he and the other researchers identified “hot spots” within the 120th precinct where police officers wrote a disproportionate number of tickets for the offense. They include intersections near large housing complexes, including the Stapleton Houses, a NYCHA development, the Park Hill Apartments, and intersections near single-level attached homes along Jersey Street on the border of the St. George and New Brighton neighborhoods.
“They are all in urban places,” Rempel said. “It confirms that we're not dealing with really fast roads where someone walking in the road is creating a public safety danger to themselves.”
‘Tension’
The North Shore of Staten Island, a large slice of which is patrolled by officers from the 120th precinct, is a racially diverse set of neighborhoods that feature a mix of large apartment buildings, bustling urban blocks, as well as streets dotted with large Victorian homes in what can feel like a suburban setting.
Criticism of how police respond to low-level offenses in this section of Staten Island is not new. The issue exploded more than a decade ago when an NYPD officer killed 43-year-old Eric Garner with a chokehold after stopping him for apparently selling loose cigarettes.
White residents make up the largest racial group on Staten Island’s North Shore, and nearly a quarter of residents identify as Black. Asian residents and residents of other races make up another 27% of the population, according to numbers released by the State Comptroller’s Office in 2024.
The New York Civil Liberties Union, a legal nonprofit that has previously challenged NYPD officers disproportionately stopping Black and Hispanic residents, said in a statement the fact that officers are writing a disproportionate amount of the pedestrian tickets in this area is disconcerting.
“Time and time again, we’ve seen the NYPD disproportionately target Black, brown, and low-income people with low level enforcement under the guise of quality-of-life policing,” said Daniel Lambright, director of Criminal Justice Litigation at the NYCLU. “Mayor Mamdani must act now to bring an end to these racist broken windows policing tactics.”
Residents who spoke to Gothamist near the streets where the tickets were issued had a mix of opinions about the cluster of pedestrians in roadways tickets that were issued in their neighborhood.
On a recent afternoon, Mildred Cosme was walking down Jersey Street near where police officers have issued six of the pedestrian tickets so far this year.
She said seeing police makes her feel safer when she is running errands at a nearby Family Dollar or when she’s heading to the laundromat.
“I don't like to walk here around certain hours,” she said. “It concerns safety.”
Across the street from the Stapleton Houses, Steven Velez, 36, said he wished police would focus on larger crimes in the neighborhood, noting the number of walls around the NYCHA development that are covered in memorial murals in honor of residents killed in the neighborhood.
Velez recalled that police officers stopped one of his coworkers and accused him of trespassing as the man was leaving Velez’s building recently.
“You over here stopping a guy from trespassing when he wasn't trespassing,” he said. “ It's kind of stupid to be honest with you.”
Outside of the Park Hill Apartments, Glenn added that he’s concerned for young people in the neighborhood who may be stopped by police for low-level offenses.
“ There's always going to be tension between the community and the police,” he said. “The older residents might feel a little comfortable 'cause they don't come outside, they don't get hassled as much, but the younger people, they always going to feel it.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Cinco creches parceiras do governo do DF mantêm paralisação por atraso nos salários
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Cruz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Professores de cinco creches parceiras do Governo do Distrito Federal (GDF) continuam sem receber salários e mantêm a paralisação nesta quinta-feira (19). Segundo atualização divulgada pelo Sindicato dos Professores em Estabelecimentos Particulares de Ensino do Distrito Federal (Sinproep-DF), duas das sete instituições que apresentavam pendências na terça-feira (17) regularizaram os pagamentos.
A creche Pequeno Príncipe e o Cepi Cajuzinho efetuaram os pagamentos. Permanecem com salários atrasados profissionais do Cepi Baru, Cepi Perdizes, Cepi Tamanduá Mirim, Fazer Valer e Centro de Convivência Divino Espírito Santo.
A situação é marcada por informações divergentes sobre os repasses públicos. Segundo o sindicato, a Secretaria de Educação afirma que os recursos já foram transferidos às instituições, mas as organizações responsáveis pelas unidades negam ter recebido os valores.
Em nota divulgada nesta quinta , o Sinproep-DF cobrou providências para resolver o impasse e permitir a retomada das atividades. “É inadmissível que os profissionais da educação sejam prejudicados pela falta de pagamento e pela ausência de uma solução definitiva. Cobramos esclarecimentos imediatos do GDF e das instituições responsáveis, além da regularização urgente dos salários, para que os professores possam retomar suas atividades”, afirma o sindicato.
O Brasil de Fato DF procurou anteriormente a Secretaria de Educação do DF para esclarecer a divergência sobre os repasses, informar quais valores foram transferidos e questionar quando os salários dos trabalhadores serão regularizados. Até a publicação desta matéria, não houve resposta. O espaço segue aberto para manifestação.

https://www.humanite.fr/vie-quotidienne/.title: Découverts bancaires en dessous de 200 euros : ce qui  change ce 20 novembre
https://www.humanite.fr/vie-quotidienne/.author: Mélanie Mermoz
https://www.humanite.fr/vie-quotidienne/.text:
À partir du 20 novembre, les découverts seront davantage encadrés et les banques tenues d’étudier la solvabilité de leurs clients avant de leur accorder une autorisation de découvert, même en dessous de 200 euros. Cette obligation, issue d’une directive européenne, impose également aux prêteurs une meilleure information sur les frais de crédit. Que Choisir salue une « avancée de la protection » des usagers.
Le 20 du mois, votre compte bascule dans le rouge et vous êtes à découvert. Vous êtes loin d’être le seul. Selon une étude de YouGov France pour MoneyVox réalisée en août, un tiers des personnes interrogées déclarent avoir été à découvert au moins une fois au cours des douze derniers mois et, pour 45 % d’entre elles, il s’agit de sommes inférieures à 200 euros.
À partir du 20 novembre, fini les découverts automatiques, y compris pour les petites sommes. Les banques auront désormais l’obligation de vérifier votre solvabilité avant d’autoriser votre compte à être débiteur.
Jusqu’à cette date, cette obligation ne concerne que les découverts de plus de 200 euros, elle s’appliquera aussi désormais pour les « petits » découverts, ceux de moins de 200 euros et d’une durée inférieure à un mois. Ils sont, en effet, intégrés à la réglementation qui régit le crédit à la consommation.

https://taz.de/Immer-groesserer-Finanzbe.title: Immer größerer Finanzbedarf: Ukrainische Wirtschaft steht „mit dem Rücken zur Wand“
https://taz.de/Immer-groesserer-Finanzbe.author: Mathias Brüggmann
https://taz.de/Immer-groesserer-Finanzbe.text:
Immer größerer Finanzbedarf: Ukrainische Wirtschaft steht „mit dem Rücken zur Wand“
Die Lage der ukrainischen Ökonomie ist schlimmer, als bisher wahrgenommen wurde. Am Freitag findet in Berlin ein Wirtschaftsforum mit Merz und Premier Serhij Korezkij statt.
Die russischen Luftangriffe setzen ukrainischen Unternehmen so stark zu, dass im Parlament gerade beraten wird, bis zu welchem Grad von Luftalarm Beschäftigte noch arbeiten und Läden, Restaurants und Tankstellen noch offen bleiben dürfen. Bei Alarmstufe Rot – anfliegenden russischen Raketen – geht gar nichts mehr. Bei Gelb – erwarteter Drohnenangriff – machen bisher Schnellrestaurants wie McDonald’s zu.
Das wird jetzt in der Werchowna Rada überprüft, da viele Supermärkte und Imbisse keine eigenen Schutzbunker haben und das ständige Schließen angesichts inzwischen immer häufigerer russischer Angriffe auf Stadtzentren zu enormen Umsatzausfällen führt, bis dahin, dass Läden und Restaurants ihre Mieten nicht mehr erwirtschaften.
Noch schlimmer steht es um die bisherigen Top-Exporteure: Die drei Stahlwerke sind so heftig von russischen Raketen und Drohnen attackiert worden, dass sie nicht mehr produzieren. Vor der russischen Vollinvasion im Februar 2022 lag die Ukraine mit 15,7 Millionen Tonnen exportierten Stahls noch in den globalen Top-10. 2025 wurden immerhin noch 4,1 Millionen exportiert. Jetzt muss Stahl für den Wiederaufbau importiert werden.
Ein Fünftel der großen Firmen fährt Verluste ein
Auf dem Agrarsektor ist die Lage inzwischen so dramatisch, dass das Land nach Angaben von Agrarminister Taras Wysozkyj in diesem Jahr die Hälfte der Getreide-, Ölsaaten- und Speiseöl-Exporte einbüßen könnte. Schon jetzt seien Export-Erlöse im Wert von 3 Milliarden Dollar verloren. Mehr als 1.100 Hafen-, Lager-, Verlade- und sonstige Infrastrukturanlagen sind durch russische Angriffe zerstört worden.
Von gut 9.500 Unternehmen, die mehr als 100 Millionen Hrywnja (gut 2 Millionen Euro) Umsatz machen, erwirtschaftet jedes fünfte Verluste. „Die in den letzten Monaten verstärkten russischen Angriffe auf die kritische Infrastruktur und die Produktionskapazitäten der Ukraine haben die wirtschaftlichen Aussichten erheblich verschlechtert und die erheblichen Risiken für die makroökonomische Stabilität verstärkt“, heißt es in der jüngsten Analyse der Kyiv School of Economics (KSE).
Infolgedessen erwartet die KSE nun für 2026 ein Rückgang des realen BIP um 0,3 Prozent und für 2027 um 0,6 Prozent. Im Sommer wurde noch ein Wachstum von 1,9 bzw. 2,1 Prozent prognostiziert. Die Wirtschaft des Landes stehe „mit dem Rücken zur Wand“, heißt es auch in der jüngsten Analyse des Wiener Instituts für Internationale Wirtschaftsvergleiche (wiiw). „Der fünfte Kriegswinter dürfte die Ukraine vor eine harte Bewährungsprobe stellen“, meinte Olga Pindyuk, die wiiw-Ukraineexpertin.
Leitzins auf 16,5 Prozent angehoben
Während in Berlin am Donnerstag 37 Staats- und Regierungschefs der „Koalition der Willigen“ über weitere Ukraine-Hilfen berieten und Kanzler Friedrich Merz und der ukrainische Premier Serhij Korezkij am Freitag auf einem Deutsch-Ukrainischen Wirtschaftsforum auftreten wollten, wachsen die Haushaltslücken in der Ukraine immer weiter. Eigentlich hätte auch Präsident Selenskyj dabei sein sollen, wird aber aus Sicherheitsgründen voraussichtlich nicht teilnehmen. Die KSE sieht trotz des gerade verhandelten 45-Milliarden-Euro-Kredits der EU bis 2029 eine Finanzierungslücke von 90,5 Milliarden Euro.
Denn ukrainische Firmen müssen in Betonmauern und andere Sicherheitsanlagen investieren, statt in Innovation und Expansion. In der Folge gehen Steuerzahlungen zurück. Die immer häufigeren russischen Luftattacken tun ein Weiteres. Und der auf 16,5 Prozent erhöhte Leitzins bei zuletzt 10 Prozent Inflation erschwert Investitionen weiter.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Guardian readers
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
Antwerp is a winter jewellery box
In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh. The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap.
 
Emily
Cable cars and an Alpine zoo in Innsbruck, Austria
When I got off the train in Innsbruck last December, its setting took my breath away immediately - dramatic mountain peaks soaring over the majestic imperial roofs of the city. The stunning golden dome of the town hall, glowing in the crisp morning sunshine, was another wonderful sight as I began exploring the cobbled streets of the old town. I stayed at the youth hostel right next to the River Inn, enjoying a lovely breakfast as the city woke up and the water rushed by, energising me to go out and enjoy the city. The Alpine Zoo is best explored in winter, with its native mountain creatures such as brown bears and ibex. The Nordkette cable car takes you up 2,000 metres in 30 minutes for great views and access to walks or skiing pistes. I used the Innsbruck Card (€79 for 48 hours) for free public transport and lots of discounts.
 
Helen
Bamberg in Germany casts a magical spell
I first went to Bamberg in the summer – but a local pub owner told me it was much better in winter. How right he was. Last December, Bamberg greeted me in the guise of a gorgeous fairytale. Light snow dusted the medieval and baroque rooftops of the Unesco-listed old town, while soft mist rose like as if by magic from the Regnitz River around the pretty Little Venice area. The Altes Rathaus (town hall) looked as if was floating like a painting on ancient bridge, free from the weight of summer crowds. The central Maximiliansplatz lured me towards it in the evening as darkness descended, with the welcome warm glow of wooden stalls at the Bamberger Weihnachtsmarkt, filling the cold air with the scents of roasted almonds, gingerbread, and hot mulled wine. A trip up to Bamberg Cathedral was well worth it, offering wonderful views of the houses and forests around the city, making a perfect winter canvas day and night.
 
Joe
Medieval streets, waterways and soaring peaks in Annecy,France
Annecy in Haute-Savoie, France, comes into its own in winter, with medieval streets hosting an array of beautiful cafes and shops, all surrounded by soaring mountains topped with snow. The winter sun reflects on the aquamarine lake while you dine on tartiflette or raclette. The area was controlled by Sardinia for centuries, giving it a unique atmosphere; the Savoyard flag is seen as often as the tricolor. For a longer stay, an early season day of skiing is easily accessible by bus. Cycle around the lake to the Chateau Menthon. It’s easy to get there from the UK by train.
 
Brian Lowry
Baltic beauty in abundance in Tallinn, Estonia
Tallinn is a Baltic beauty that embraces winter with charm and panache. The cobbled streets of the old town, with its huge Christmas tree, horse-drawn taxis trotting along, candlelit cafes and snow-covered squares give the city a cool – in every sense – Christmas card quality. The city’s medieval walls are home to twisty lanes that are lined with spice-scented bakeries, medieval spires and secret cellars serving mulled wine with warming spicy salami. My breath frosted over as I walked up the Hellemann Tower, but it was worth it for the chance to walk along the 15th-century city walls for views over snow-dusted terracotta rooftops. I made good use of the Tallinn Card for €63 (for 48 hours) giving free entry to more than 50 museums and free public transport.
 
Peter
The Hanseatic glory of Norway’s Bergen
In Bergen, take the Fløibanen funicular from Bergen city centre up Mount Fløyen for spectacular views over the snow-dusted city, fjords and surrounding mountains. In winter it’s great to get there in the afternoon twilight in time for sunset to see Bergen’s lights come alive below. Afterwards, wander down toHanseatic Unesco site Bryggen for a warming coffee or hot chocolate.
 
Daniel
Defy the winter winds of Leiden, the Netherlands
While Amsterdam is the big cheese in these parts, Leiden, 30 minutes away, more than holds its own as far as charming cities of Holland are concerned. What’s more, it has a young, student vibe with not a whiff of dope anywhere. If you want canals, windmills, culture, good bars and restaurants, a great market with lots of vintage shops too, then Leiden oozes enough good hormones to envelope even the most jaded of travellers. In a lovely curved 1930s building, you can find Anne and Max for a gratifying and warming breakfast to get you going for the day. Strolling the streets of Leiden is like stepping into history when you consider that Rembrandt strutted his teenage genius around the place probably past the former Caecilia Hospital, now the excellent Rijksmuseum Boerhaave Museum. The vintage shops on Breestraat are perfect for very blissful and rewarding rummaging. The wind whips round those canals in winter like a razor blade, so remember to take the thermals!
 
Liz
Berlin will blow your cobwebs away
Berlin in winter can be cold, wet and rather brutal looking. However, it also offers amazing museums, ample opportunities for hot drinks and cake to re-warm one’s heart and stomach, and attractive Christmas markets. Even better, a short train ride can take you out to one of the beautiful lakes that surround the city. A brisk stroll will blow any cobwebs away and then sausages and beer will provide the energy for the trip back into town. Berlin: scruffy, grey and probably bloody freezing, but always brilliant.
 
Rachel
Prague’s joyful squares and carnival
From our hotel in Prague, I followed the smell of roast chestnuts and baked gingerbread last December to the snow dusted streets of the old town. I quickly sensed that Prague embraces and enhances winter rather than fights against it. The Christmas market stalls were everywhere in its medieval streets and a towering tree in the Old Town Square was a joyful gathering place for families and friends. The Letná Masopust Carnival (held in late winter) was in full flow, featuring parades, theatre performances and stalls serving warming local treats such as smoked ham and spiced trdelník cake. I chanced on Golden Lane, a cool historic street of independent and vintage clothes shops. The Castle and Charles bridge are magically lit up and you can ice skate among the spires of Wenceslas Square.
 
William
Winning tip: pastel shades in the crisp air of Wrocław, Poland
Wrocław is perfect for those looking for a winter city break beyond the main tourist trail. The city positively twinkles in the crisp air. Head over to Cathedral Island with its cobbled streets to watch the lighting of the gas street lights at dusk. Take a walk around the illuminated Market Square with its pastel-coloured buildings. Stay at the wonderfully restored art nouveau Hotel Monopol, the setting for Andrzej Wajda’s 1958 Ashes and Diamonds – a masterwork of Polish cinema.
 
Donia Slyzuk

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: EU and Britain to agree steps towards relations reset
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
EU and Britain to agree steps towards relations reset
A decade after Brexit, London is signalling a willingness to align more closely with the EU on various policies.
British and European Union leaders are set to meet at a summit billed as a chance to reset relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa, who heads the European Council, on Friday in Brussels. In the second such meeting since Britain formally left the bloc in 2020, deals on food, emissions and youth mobility are expected to be sealed.
The previous summit in 2025 was billed as a “stable foundation” upon which to rebuild the relationship between London and Brussels. Friday’s meeting is being sold as a chance to start on a reset of relations.
Burnham said earlier in the week that it was an “obvious truth” that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit, which followed a non-binding referendum in 2016 in which 52 percent of the British public voted to leave the EU. He has signalled that a reformed relationship with Brussels is on his agenda.
The most valuable agreement on the table concerns the cross-border exchange of animals, plants and related products. Britain has estimated that the removal of the current controls could be worth 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) annually.
A potential deal on emissions trading systems could see London and Brussels mutually exempt each other from carbon border levies on goods like steel.
An agreement on youth mobility, which would allow 100,000 people from the EU to live and work for up to three years in the UK, and vice versa, is also reportedly set to be signed. The UK had originally wanted half that number.
The EU is also pushing for students to qualify for “home fees” at British universities – often one third of the international price. London, however, has only agreed to apply “significantly reduced” fees.
The UK also wants to be part of the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules. Brussels has said it may be open to this, but it would require the UK to accept its policies. That could prove tricky for Burnham, given that the UK still hosts a significant Eurosceptic population.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist radical right-wing Reform UK party, accused Burnham of a Brexit “betrayal”.
“We don’t need to be in political union of any kind at all to do business and have good relations with our neighbours,” he told the BBC. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again.”

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.title: Halbleiterindustrie | Tensordyne verspricht energiesparende KI-Chips
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.author: Anjana Shrivastava
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120400.text:
- Wissen
- Halbleiterindustrie
Tensordyne verspricht energiesparende KI-Chips
Ein deutsch-kalifornisches Unternehmen will Rechenzentren mit einer neuen Technik effizienter und schneller machen.
Chiphersteller und die KI-Branche schauen in den nächsten Monaten auf eine spektakuläre neue Technologie, die eine neue Geschwindigkeit und immense Energie- und Platzersparnisse für Betreiber von KI-Sprachmodellen wie ChatGPT und Claude in Rechenzentren weltweit verspricht. Gilles Backhus, Mitbegründer der Firma Tensordyne mit Sitz in München und in Kalifornien, wartet auf die letzten Phasen der Feinmontage seines Halbleiterbausteins »Napier«, die derzeit in Taiwan erfolgt.
Auf der Basis von internen Simulationen erwartet Tensordyne einen Energieverbrauch von lediglich 20 Prozent im Vergleich zu herkömmlichen Chips wie von Nvidia, eine viermal so hohe Geschwindigkeit und einen Platzverbrauch von lediglich 25 Prozent im Vergleich zu dem Chip-System GB300 von Nvidia. Nach der Feinmontage und der Produktion der ersten Chips wird man großangelegte Tests in Betriebssystemen durchführen; in der zweiten Hälfte nächsten Jahres soll der kommerzielle Vertrieb anfangen.
Das Grundprinzip der neuen Halbleiter-Bausteine basiert auf mathematischen Erkenntnissen des schottischen Mathematikers John Napier und des Schweizer Mathematikers Jost Bürgi von vor 400 Jahren: Der Logarithmus von A multipliziert mit B ist gleich dem Logarithmus von A plus des Logarithmus von B. Nach diesem Lehrsatz ersetzt Tensordyne Multiplikation durch Addition und kann so die künstlichen neuronalen Netze entlasten. Denn Addierer sind kleinere und energieeffizientere logische Schaltungen als Multiplizierer. Schließlich ist es auch für ein menschliches Hirn erheblich leichter, Zahlen zu addieren, als zu multiplizieren.
Die Technologie von Tensordyne ist nicht der erste Versuch, einen anderen mathematischen Ansatz beim Halbleiterdesign zu verwenden. Bisherige Versuche erwiesen sich aber als zu fehleranfällig.
Backhus und anderen Ingenieuren von Tensordyne ist es nun gelungen, eine Anwendung zu finden, die nahezu so präzise wie die herkömmlichen KI-Chips arbeitet. Tensordyne erwartet Ergebnisse, die sogar zu 99,9 Prozent so präzise wie die von Nvidia sind. »Bis jetzt hat es niemand hingekriegt, wie man von linearen zu logarithmischen Zahlen wechselt und zurück von logarithmischen zu linearen«, sagte Backhus der Zeitschrift »IEEE Spectrum«.
Platzsparend ist das Tensordyne-System auch deswegen, weil man die Phasen des Verfahrens von KI-Sprachmodellen zusammengeführt hat. Zu leisten sind zwei sehr verschiedene Phasen: das Einspeisen der Information als Input und die technische Verarbeitungsphase oder Decode, bei der aus komprimierten Informationen eine strukturierte Ausgabe wie ein fertiger Text oder eine Übersetzung entsteht. In der ersten Phase nimmt das Modell den Input-Text und stellt sogenannte Tokens her. Tokens sind die kleinsten Einheiten, die von einem Sprachmodell mathematisch verarbeitet werden können. Die erste Phase ist rechentechnisch extrem aufwändig; die zweite dagegen wird eher langsam formuliert, weil die Antwort in vielen, nacheinander folgenden Schritten entstehen muss.
Daher bieten herkömmliche Chiphersteller zwei Systeme für KI-Rechner an. Nvidia bietet zum Beispiel einen Netzwerkschrank mit Grafikprozessoren für den Input und mehrere Schränke mit Groq-3-Prozessoren für das Dekodieren an. Tensordyne kombiniert beide Phasen in einem Schranksystem. Daher wird laut R. K. Anand, dem kalifornischen Mitbegründer der Firma, nur ein Viertel des Platzes in Rechenzentren gebraucht. Die logarithmische Mathematik sorgt für eine schnelle und effiziente Vorphase; die schnelle Abwicklung des Decodes kommt von einer sehr minimalen Verzögerung zwischen dem Absenden einer Anfrage und dem Erhalt der Antwort.
R. K. Anand und Backhus gründeten zusammen im Jahr 2017 die Firma Recogni, die Chips für die Autoherstellung entwarf. Erst im Jahr 2024 wurde die Firma in der Ära von ChatGPT umbenannt und umgewidmet. Backhus redet bereits von einer Eroberung von 20 Prozent des Halbleiterbaustein-Weltmarkts innerhalb von fünf Jahren. Er glaubt, dass die Tensordyne-Technik sehr schwer zu kopieren sei. In diesem Jahr verzeichnet die Firma Bestellungen im Wert von 200 Millionen US-Dollar, im nächsten Jahr erwartet Backhus einen Umsatz von einer Milliarde.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
