Debatte um Transidentität : Wir sind trotzdem da
Trans Menschen gelten als kleine, aber bedrohliche Minderheit. Doch das System zu hinterfragen, eröffnet neue Chancen für alle.
J etzt bitte nicht in Panik geraten: Es gibt mehr trans Menschen unter uns, als Sie vielleicht vermuten. Und: Sie sind überall. Ein empathischer Nachbar, die Freundin aus dem Sportverein oder die ehemalige Redaktionsvolontärin, die man auf dem Flur gegrüßt hat – sie alle könnten trans sein, ohne diese Information mit Ihnen geteilt zu haben. Doch das muss Ihnen keine Angst machen.
Denn was ist Transidentität eigentlich? Menschen, die sich nicht mit dem bei der Geburt zugewiesenen Geschlecht identifizieren. Nicht mehr und nicht weniger.
Die Zweiteilung von Menschen in Geschlechter sagt vor allem etwas darüber aus, wie unsere Welt geordnet ist. Sie ist das Fundament für bestehende Herrschaftsverhältnisse. Würde man Menschen nicht in zwei Gruppen einander gegenüber stellen, eine herrschende und eine beherrschte, um einem Geschlecht unbezahlte Arbeit aufzuzwingen, würde der Kapitalismus kollabieren. Dem Patriarchat ohne vermeintlich männliche Überlegenheit fehlte die Existenzgrundlage.
trans taz
Zum Trans Day of Remembrance am 20. November wird die taz zur trans taz. Der Gedenktag erinnert an die Opfer transfeindlicher Gewalt. Während trans Menschen weiterhin Diskriminierung, Anfeindungen und Gewalt erleben, wird auch politisch über ihre Rechte und ihre Existenz gestritten. Auf 22 Seiten widmet sich die trans taz den Lebensrealitäten von trans Menschen. Autor:innen und Fotograf:innen aus der Community und ihre Verbündeten erzählen von Transfeindlichkeit, räumen mit Klischees auf und zeigen, wie vielfältig trans Leben ist. Im Mittelpunkt stehen die Menschen selbst, ihre Geschichten und Perspektiven. Mehr über die Sonderausgabe erfahren Sie hier.
Machtvolle Systeme bleiben erhalten, wenn sie niemand hinterfragt. Wer dies aber wagt, wird bestraft – mit sozialem Ausschluss bis hin zu Gewalt. Deshalb schließen Menschen lieber einen Vertrag mit der binären Ordnung. Sie opfern die Chance auf authentische Entfaltung oder Selbstexploration und verbleiben in der zugewiesenen Kategorie. Im Gegenzug garantiert das System eine normative Existenz.
Trans Menschen können keine verlässlichen Vertragspartner:innen sein, egal wie sehr sie es versuchen mögen. Sie sind, wer sie sind, und stören damit das System.
Bespuckt, geschlagen, vergewaltigt
Allerdings weiß das System sich zu wehren. Die meisten trans Menschen bemerken von frühester Kindheit an die Diskrepanz zwischen der inneren Wahrheit über sich selbst und dem, was die Außenwelt behauptet. Dies fördert langfristig ihr Misstrauen gegen die eigene Person und die Welt da draußen. Sie fragen sich: Wieso akzeptieren Menschen nicht einfach, wenn man sagt, wer man ist? Wenn man, wie alle anderen, seinen Interessen nachgehen und selbst entscheiden möchte, was man anzieht?
Irgendwann wird das Misstrauen von Scham und Schuld abgelöst. Scham ist ein soziales Gefühl, es entsteht nur, wenn das Umfeld einem erfolgreich einredet, dass die eigene Existenz beschämend sei. Manche, die ihr wahres Selbst nicht mehr verleugnen können, erfahren Gewalt. Sie werden in der Schule isoliert, am Arbeitsplatz gemobbt oder anderswo beleidigt, bespuckt, geschlagen, vergewaltigt. Die Kontrolle über den Körper und damit die Bestimmung über ihn wird gewaltsam genommen, sobald man sich traut, dem Diktat der Gesellschaft zuwiderzuhandeln.
Schockiert von der Gewalt redet eine innere Stimme einem ein: „Du bist ja selbst schuld.“ Diese Stimme ist das System, das man verinnerlicht hat. Aus Selbstschutz fängt man an, Erklärungen zu finden. „Meine Umwelt kann nicht anders, als mich zu misgendern, zu verleugnen, auszugrenzen. Ich entspreche ja nicht der Norm.“ Einsamkeit und Selbstisolation ist dann eine logische Konsequenz.
Bis zur Selbstvernichtung
Weil man nicht immer kämpfen kann, fügt man sich. Entweder unbewusst, indem der Gedanke an eine andere als die vorgeschriebene Identität bereits abgetötet wird, bevor er gedeihen kann. Oder mit Maskierung. Schon im Kindesalter erschöpft, entwickeln viele die Überlebensfähigkeit, soziale Situationen nach der eigenen Sicherheit einzuschätzen. Man teilt nur bestimmte Dinge mit bestimmten Leuten oder eben gar nicht, isoliert sich und fängt an, sich selbst zu verleugnen, um zu überleben.
Nicht selten wird Selbstverleugnung zur Selbstvernichtung. Die Suizidrate von trans Menschen ist, je nach Studie, vier- bis siebenfach höher als bei cis Menschen. Dies ist kein Versagen des Systems, sondern dessen Ergebnis. Unsere Gesellschaft hat nicht versagt, diese Personen zu „retten“, sie hat dabei versagt, ein System abzuschaffen, das Trans-Sein nur als schamvolle und gefährliche Existenz erlaubt.
Denn allein die bloße Existenz von trans Personen gefährdet das System. Ein extrem fragiles System, das sich von einer Minderheit von nur einem Prozent dermaßen bedroht fühlt – sofern sich die Zahl überhaupt richtig schätzen lässt. Angesichts der massiven Drohkulisse ist es denkbar, dass deutlich mehr Menschen trans sind, als bekannt ist. Einen Hinweis darauf gibt auch die Geschichte. Vorstellungen von Geschlecht waren schon immer und überall verschieden. Und schon immer gab es auch eine Bandbreite von Geschlechterkonzepten. Das ist historisch und global eindeutig dokumentiert und kein Trend, der durch Social Media aufkam, wie viele behaupten.
Befasst man sich mit der aktuellen Art von Transgeschlechtlichkeit im Globalen Norden, fällt auf, dass es mehrere Arten von Transition gibt. Die prominenteste ist die medizinische. Bei dieser werden primäre und/oder sekundäre Geschlechtsmerkmale verändert. Für viele cis Menschen ist das die einzig vorstellbare Art, weil sie glauben, dass Geschlecht im Körper verankert sei und er somit bestimmt, wer wir sind. Doch viele trans Menschen können ihre geschlechtliche Identität auch anders leben. Etwa durch eine innerliche Transition (verstehen, dass man trans ist), durch eine soziale (Vornamens- und Pronomenwechsel, neue Kleidung etc.) oder durch eine legale (Ändern des Personenstandes und Namens in Dokumenten).
Diese Transitionen können unter Umständen wichtiger sein, weil Geschlecht vor allem eine soziale Kategorie ist. Mit Namen, Pronomen und Kleidung kommunizieren wir unserem Gegenüber oft mehr als über unseren Hormonspiegel.
Kaum Mitspracherecht
Medizinische Transition ist in Deutschland ein langer, aufwendiger und bürokratischer Prozess. Die Krankenkasse übernimmt die Kosten unter strengen Bedingungen und nur dann, wenn die offizielle Diagnose Geschlechtsinkongruenz vorliegt. Diese Diagnose beinhaltet auch die Geschlechtsdysphorie, also den Leidensdruck, nicht selbstbestimmt leben zu können. Wird dieser von anonymen Gutachter:innen als groß genug eingeschätzt, bewilligen sie Maßnahmen. Trans Personen selbst haben kaum Mitspracherecht.
Mehr noch: Weder Begriffe oder Diagnosen noch der staatlich regulierte Prozess wurden von der trans Community in die Welt gebracht. Cis Psychiater:innen erklären der cis Öffentlichkeit das Schicksal der „armen“ trans Menschen und geben das pathologisierende Narrativ für ihr Leben vor.
Damit wird Transgeschlechtlichkeit zum krankhaften Antagonisten von Cisgeschlechtlichkeit. Trans ist krank und pervers, cis ist gesund und normal. Das hält einerseits die Hierarchie aufrecht – und offenbart das Bedrohungspotenzial, das trans Menschen für die bestehende Ordnung und das System der Cis-Normativität haben.
Wie so oft fungiert der Staat dabei als ausführende Gewalt für das herrschende System. Er garantiert, dass es nicht zu viele Menschen gibt, die selbstbestimmt leben und die rigiden, disziplinierenden Grenzen der Zweigeschlechtlichkeit unterlaufen. Bis ein Urteil vom Bundesverfassungsgericht es als menschenunwürdig einstufte, wurden in Deutschland bei Änderungen des Personenstandes Zwangsscheidungen und bis 2011 sogar Zwangssterilisationen vorgenommen. Garantiert war damit: Solche Leute dürfen sich nicht fortpflanzen.
Natürlich vererbt sich Trans-Sein nicht – das wissen auch die Rechten, die seit Langem vor allem gegen trans Personen agitieren. Deshalb verbieten sie in den USA Bücher über trans Themen und sogar Wörter, die damit zu tun haben. Eigentlich wollen sie die Menschen selbst verbieten. Ihr Kreuzzug gegen den:die vermeintliche:n Staatsfeind:in Nummer eins hat nach Meinung von Beobachter:innen längst genozidale Ausmaße angenommen.
Die entscheidende Frage ist also nicht: Warum sind Menschen trans?, sondern: Wieso fühlt sich das Cis-tem so sehr von ihnen getriggert?
Regeln lassen sich ändern
Die Existenz von trans Menschen macht ihnen etwas klar: Der Vertrag, den sie mal vor langer Zeit abgeschlossen haben, hat ihnen etwas weggenommen; nämlich die Möglichkeit, zu ergründen, wer sie sind und wer sie sein könnten. Stattdessen haben sie sich mit einer Ideologie von Geschlecht als „natürlicher“, unveränderbarer Kategorie abgefunden.
Transexistenz konfrontiert cis Menschen so auch mit der Idee, dass ihre Identität nicht selbstgewählt sein könnte, sondern das Produkt eines Systems ist. Sie zeigt aber auch eine Gefahr. Es ist möglich, Grenzen zu überschreiten und Regeln zu ändern, wenn sie nicht für einen passen. Und sogar ein glückliches Leben zu führen, wenn man in Ruhe gelassen wird. Damit leisten trans Menschen allein durch ihre Existenz jeden Tag Widerstand gegen ein System, das alle Menschen in jeglicher Hinsicht gefügig machen will.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Trans Menschen sind der Mittelfinger ans System. Sie hören nicht auf zu existieren, wenn man Gewalt androht oder ausübt, Bücher verbietet, sie ihrer Rechte beraubt, sie ermordet oder sie in den Suizid treibt. Auch unter den widrigsten Bedingungen bleiben Menschen trans und werden es auch immer sein. Ihr Drang nach Selbstbestimmung wird sich immer einen Weg bahnen.
Die vermeintliche Gefahr, die von ihnen ausgeht, ist in Wirklichkeit eine Hoffnung: Indem sie existieren, trotzen sie dem System, kämpfen, hoffen, träumen und lieben weiter. Nicht nur für sich selbst, sondern für die Möglichkeit aller Menschen, selbstbestimmt zu leben.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: ‘We will become cyborgs!’ Peter Gabriel on bonobo ape duets, building a Jurassic Park for plants – and why AI will make great music
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Alexis Petridis
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”
It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles.
I had mentioned the two versions, a routine enough inquiry, but it quickly turns into a discussion about the potential replacement of car stereos with immersive sound systems, which then unexpectedly shifts into an explanation of the work of Michael Levin, an American professor of bioengineering who specialises in morphogenesis. “He’s found some bio-electric instructions that can make an eye grow on the leg of a frog, for example,” says Gabriel, and has apparently “created life forms that never existed before, which really challenges evolution.” Gabriel is interested in “sonifying” some of his data and using it in a subsequent mix of the album.
From there, we move on to software engineer Blaise Agüera y Arcas, whose experiments with an esoteric 90s programming language called Brainfuck have led him to “the radical idea that some constants in maths might actually have some form of life”. This leads us, via the “re-evaluation of what consciousness is and what intelligence is”, to the belief of internet pioneer Vint Cerf that attempting to communicate with other intelligent species might prepare us for the possibility of encountering aliens, and thus to Savage-Rumbaugh and Kanzi the bonobo.
“She used to allow the bonobos to watch videos, and to choose the videos they watched,” Gabriel says, laughing, “and their favourite, perhaps obviously, was Planet of the Apes, then Harry and the Hendersons, which is a film about a sasquatch who came to live with a family. The whole thing blew me away. I think we’re the most arrogant of all apes, and there’s just so much intelligence we’ve chosen to ignore and instead see the world as something that’s entirely available for our exploitation, and I think that’s cost us, as we are now learning.”
Morphogenisis, inter-species communication, the re-evaluation of consciousness: it should go without saying that you don’t usually end up discussing these things when you ask an august rock legend about his latest album. But, as it turns out, that’s what inevitably happens when you ask Gabriel a question. We meet in a pub not far from his home in Notting Hill. He says he’s here “to sell the new album”, but almost every query about it seems to lead him somewhere completely different: science, activism, the nature of consciousness, how language is “a fairly crude tool” for communication, the controversial 1970s self-improvement courses of Werner Erhard.
You can’t fault his diversity of interests, even if that diversity of interests is why it takes so long for him to make albums. o\i is essentially the second part of a project that began with 2023’s i/o, which was his first album of new material in 21 years. Like its predecessor, it contains songs that Gabriel has spent decades tinkering with: he started work on A Hard Lesson in 1989, when he was still a huge mainstream pop star thanks to 1986’s So, an album that shifted more than 5m copies in the US alone.
Yes, he concedes, it is a bit weird to find yourself, at the age of 76, still working on songs you started writing in your 30s: “I recognise that guy, but you’re bound to make different decisions having lived a little longer.” But that’s just the way it is. His friend Laurie Anderson once suggested that Gabriel’s problem was that he was more interested in the process of making something than in finishing it. He thinks the real issue is that he’s easily distracted.
“If you have some measure of success, you end up meeting all sorts of people and having fascinating conversations, which lead to detours, and you think, ‘Well, life is for living,’” he says. “If you get on that conveyor belt of album-tour-album, there’s not time to breathe or have any kind of life, and that always seems somewhat sad to me. I think the diversions feed the music. You know, if you want a better class of shit, you’ve got to eat a more varied diet.”
Hence the digressive nature of our interview. Gabriel seems to have developed a genuinely intriguing theory about virtually everything, from theme parks to funerals: he thinks people should “plant a tree over their dead body, or the dead body of their loved ones, so you’d get woods where there wouldn’t be any signage, but if you go and sit under your dad’s tree, your phone would have the GPS position and you would start seeing his videos, hearing his voice, all the digital data would be locked into that GPS point”.
Moreover, he has an incredibly engaging way of talking about all this stuff, evincing such enthusiasm and curiosity that you’re carried along with him: on the off-chance that you wanted to pitch the idea of growing eyeballs on the legs of frogs, you could do substantially worse than get Gabriel to act as your salesman. It probably helps his cause that Gabriel has a hugely impressive track record of thinking ahead of the curve.
At the height of his fame as the frontman of Genesis, he was sharp enough to realise that the genre of progressive rock they had helped invent was becoming too grandiloquent and remote for its own good – “prancing around in fairyland” as he once put it – and that the band he had formed might be more successful without him. The latter opinion wasn’t very popular with the rest of Genesis, but nevertheless proved to be spot on.
A few years later, he was the first British artist to realise that the future of pop lay in sampling: for some time in the early 80s, if you wanted to use a sampler on your new track you had to borrow Gabriel’s, because he was the first person in the country to own one; he then set up a company to import and distribute the new technology. Twenty years later, he cottoned on very quickly to the idea that music was going to primarily exist online, co-founding a streaming platform that might have become the industry standard had it not launched at exactly the same time as a competitor called Spotify.
If he was right about everything from sampling to streaming to the latter-day career of Genesis, perhaps he’s also right about AI. In a musical world filled with people decrying its malign influence, Gabriel is one of its few high-profile boosters: he recently suggested that ultimately “everything will be done better” by AI than by humans.
He says it again today, albeit with caveats. “The application of AI and robots in warfare is really scary. There’s the sense that we’re creating a species that is way, way more intelligent than we are. If we look around, there are not many good examples of intelligent species looking after less-intelligent species, except as pets.
“You can see the worry on [computer scientist and ‘Godfather of AI’] Geoffrey Hinton’s face,” he continues. “I think we need to slow it down a bit, we need some international agreement, for which there are precedents, like in air safety or the Start treaty for nuclear weapons. We need guard rails, like a seed of wisdom in every algorithm before it’s allowed to be released that could allow for monitoring and a measure of control and an ‘off’ button. But it interests me in the moment as a whole new set of tools that could encourage people to consider themselves film-makers, painters, musicians, to explore themselves in that way.”
With or without AI, Gabriel says he thinks that’s true anyway: “Being those things is just a matter of walking around and saying, ‘This is what I am’, then committing to learning about it. You can get accelerated learning through AI – even though you haven’t learned all the skills to get there, you can quickly access some of the joy of making really nice-sounding things or have the AI eliminate some of your worst moments. So in the long run, as a creative tool: absolutely extraordinary. It’s like you’ve been painting in black and white and someone suddenly throws a colour palette at you, saying: ‘What can you do with this?’”
Contrary to most, Gabriel genuinely seems to believe that AI is capable of creating great art. “It’s just down to better algorithms. So how do we deal with this as a species? I think long-term, if you can’t defeat it, you have to join it. I think we will become cyborgs, because we’ll have these brain-computer interfaces, where you insert something in your brain that allows you then to communicate to the computer … I don’t think there’s any reason why we shouldn’t use our brains to become more AI.”
He’s keen to point out that “any of these things can be used positively or negatively”. He recently had a conversation with American technologist Mary Lou Jepsen, who was concerned about the human rights implications of the whole brain-computer-interface idea and its capacity for being used as a form of torture. But nevertheless, Gabriel seems fascinated by the idea: he has a concept for something so vague, I don’t really understand it, called “the brain show”, that will “allow you to see how the brain affects us and how it might be manipulated” and which would feature some of the songs from o\i as part of its soundtrack. “It could be a virtual thing or a stage thing or both, but how it all works, and the story, I’ve got no idea,” he shrugs. “I’m at that stage where you can feel a sort of lump in the mist and you’re trying to imagine it becoming something, which I think is the way most people approach creativity.”
In the meantime, he has umpteen other ideas floating around. He’s intrigued by the concept of a virtual performance, somewhere between Abba Voyage and U2’s “wonderful and inspiring” shows at the Sphere in Las Vegas. There’s a plan to make a film based on The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, the 1974 concept album that preceded his exit from Genesis: you might have thought it was pretty much unfilmable, given that it features a scene in which the lead character has sex with three snake-like creatures, and another in which his recently amputated penis is snatched away by a passing raven, but Gabriel seems optimistic: he’s been working on the script with Argentinan writer Nicolás Giacobone of Digger fame.
And he wants to “dig into” another of Levin’s ideas, “that you might be able to communicate with cells and get them to behave in a certain way and sound might be a medium for it. I’m fascinated by explorations of consciousness,” he says, then goes on to tell me about experiments in the sentience of plants. “There was a cool guy at MIT who took a plant and put it in a sort of box with a computer on wheels, then moved the plant’s light source around the room and the plant was saying ‘OK’ and moving the box to follow the light around the room. I was wondering if you could do that with an oak tree. Like a sort of Jurassic Park, but with plants instead of dinosaurs. I mean, all these ideas are such great fun to explore.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Tashima says Balogun red card row at World Cup prompted FIFA presidency bid
Tashima is one of three names on the ballot for the March election, along with current President Infantino and Diallo.
Japanese football official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that the handling of Folarin Balogun’s red card at the 2026 World Cup was what prompted him to run for FIFA president against Gianni Infantino.
FIFA suspended forward Balogun’s automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after United States President Donald Trump said he had personally asked President Infantino to review the sanction.
The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, led to opposition to Infantino’s re-election as president.
Tashima said he wanted to restore trust in FIFA, drawing parallels with 2016, when Infantino took charge after a corruption scandal.
“Ten years ago something similar happened, and Mr Infantino became president to reform and improve things,” the Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president told a news conference.
“He has certainly done wonderful things. But in this year, 2026, 10 years later, events have occurred that ignored governance.
“I have worked in football, especially as a player and coach. As such, I cannot accept Balogun’s red card in any way. On top of that, no explanation has been given even now. I felt very indignant about this, and that is why I decided to stand here.”
Following the Balogun incident, FIFA’s disciplinary committee said it had the authority to suspend the one-match ban, and that it operated independently.
FIFA last month said it would amend the rule in its disciplinary code, which had allowed for the reversal of the ban.
Working with Diallo
The election, set to be held in March next year, will be the first time since he won the post in 2016 that Infantino will face a challenge after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.
French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo also announced a challenge on Monday with the backing of European governing body UEFA. Infantino has the support of Asia and Africa’s confederations.
“I have not actually received a nomination from any continental confederation. So I’m well aware that I’m at a considerable disadvantage in this race,” Tashima said.
“It’s a fact that Gianni’s support has been gradually declining. I will keep appealing to voters.”
Diallo said at a news conference on Tuesday that he would reach out to Tashima to “unite forces”. Tashima said he was open to the idea of coordinating with the Frenchman’s team to avoid splitting the anti-Infantino vote.
“I don’t think the French candidate’s entry puts me at a disadvantage. In fact, France has ties to Africa and other regions, so Mr Diallo’s entry may bring those votes,” he added.
“Watching his press conference, I saw that he pointed out FIFA’s accounting and other figures in great detail. I find it reassuring that such a professional has joined.”
‘Least conspicuous’ FIFA president
Tashima is a former Japan international and youth coach and the first Japanese candidate to stand for FIFA president. He has served on the FIFA Council since 2015.
The 68-year-old said that if elected, he would shun the spotlight.
“A foreign media person described me very accurately. They said that if I’m elected, I might become the least conspicuous president ever,” he said.
“That may have been a bit of irony, but I’m fine with it. It’s not the president who should stand out, but the players.”
He added that he would need to be modest in his campaigning, much of which would be funded by his own money.
“The JFA’s budget for this year is already set, so of course, I would like support from the JFA, but we’ll also have to gather funds, for example by creating a fund or running crowdfunding,” he said.
“I won’t spend wastefully. I also have no intention of flying by private jet or anything like that.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: Conversa Bem Viver
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
Estreia nesta quinta-feira (19) nos cinemas por todo o Brasil, o filme “Camisas Negras”, dirigido por Jefferson Mello. A obra chega ao público em meio ao mês da Consciência Negra e resgata a campanha histórica da equipe do Vasco da Gama no Campeonato Carioca de 1923, abordando a luta contra o racismo no futebol desde seu primórdio.
Em entrevista ao programa Conversa Bem Viver, o diretor do longa explica que o Vasco, ao passar para a primeira divisão do estado, rompeu com o elitismo do futebol na época. O time foi buscar novos jogadores na classe trabalhadora do subúrbio carioca, selecionando alguns homens negros, o que não era habitual para o período nessa divisão.
“Dirigentes do Vasco entenderam essa realidade, que os grandes craques vinham do subúrbio, porque existiam as divisões de base e o campeonato comia solto. Então, os olheiros foram lá selecionar esse jogador e fizeram essa mescla, porque alguns jogadores já faziam parte de outros clubes que não eram da elite. Essa mescla foi muito interessante e revolucionária, mas eles pagaram o preço alto, sofrendo todo tipo de perseguição por parte da Liga Metropolitana e até dos torcedores de elite. Eles nunca abaixaram a cabeça, e eu mostro isso no filme.”
A produção une duas linguagens, documentário e ficção, e conta com nomes de peso da dramaturgia e do audiovisual brasileiro, como Juan Paiva, Sérgio Malheiros, Bruno Mazzeo, entre outros.
O cineasta Jefferson Mello explica que gravou em seis países diferentes e que o racismo no futebol é uma questão generalizada. “Era importante mostrar para a sociedade que o crime de racismo é um problema social grave global, e só mostrando isso nesse formato híbrido, de ficção e documentário, para criar o choque com a realidade. Mostrar o que é passado há mais de 100 anos. E o mecanismo do racismo persiste.”
Segundo Mello, um dos objetivos do longa é promover um diálogo e uma revisão de atitude por parte da sociedade brasileira. “O primeiro objetivo do filme é transformar essa obra cinematográfica em mais uma ferramenta de luta contra o racismo, impactar a sociedade civil, um indivíduo para que ele saia do cinema refletindo sobre suas e nossas atitudes. No Brasil, a gente tem avanços. Aqui, já é crime. Nos outros países, não.”
O diretor avalia que há muito a se fazer. “Por exemplo, banir esses torcedores dos estádios. Eu não consigo entender: com o nível de tecnologia que nós temos nos estádios, como não ter criado um cadastro de racistas?”
Ele recorda que o racismo pode ainda acontecer de forma velada, como na exigência da Associação Metropolitana de Esportes Atléticos, em 1924, de que os atletas fossem alfabetizados para disputar o campeonato. A ação foi vista como uma reação dos clubes da elite contra o time do Vasco. Em resposta, a agremiação disponibilizou aulas para os jogadores.
“Eu optei por ressignificar. Sei do meu direito de licença poética como diretor roteirista. Quem deu aula para eles foi um homem, e eu falei: ‘Não, eu vou colocar uma mulher negra, porque naquela época existiam mulheres negras professoras, mas era raro.’ Então, na cena que eu escrevi, era uma torcedora negra que se formou no Instituto de Educação, o que não era algo simples”, relatou o diretor.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/ces/on-a-t.title: « On a trop demandé aux travailleurs européens » : Esther Lynch, de la Confédération européenne des syndicats, appelle à la mobilisation
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/ces/on-a-t.author: Lina Sankari
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/ces/on-a-t.text:
Les organisations syndicales françaises, espagnoles, italiennes, britanniques, portugaises, grecques et belges appellent à une mobilisation européenne contre la vie chère les 20, 21 et 22 novembre. La secrétaire générale de la Confédération européenne des syndicats (CES), Esther Lynch, présente un plan pour les investissements d’avenir et pour l’emploi.
Assistons-nous à l’émergence d’un mouvement social paneuropéen capable de transcender les frontières nationales et de constituer un levier face aux gouvernements et aux institutions européennes ?
Esther Lynch
Secrétaire général de la Conférence européenne des syndicats (CES)
Les travailleurs et leurs syndicats descendent dans la rue, se mettent en grève, recourent à d’autres formes d’action collective, comme le travail au ralenti, autour d’un ensemble commun de revendications. L’expérience partagée par les travailleurs concerne les salaires. Ces derniers ne suivent pas la hausse des prix et des loyers, au point que, dans certaines villes, avec deux emplois au salaire minimum, on ne peut pas toujours se payer un studio.
Ressentez-vous un tournant lors de vos rencontres avec les travailleurs ?
Pendant longtemps, on a fait croire...
